en: The *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, composed by Ācārya Anantavīrya, who lived under the guidance of the venerable Ravibhadra, on the *Siddhiviniścaya* authored by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Akalaṅkadeva.
The Establishment of Direct Perception (*Pratyakṣasiddhi*), accompanied by the commentary titled *Āloka*.
Oṃ, homage to the Arhat.
Having bowed with devotion to the Jina Akalaṅka, to my Guru, and to the Goddess Sarasvatī,
I shall proclaim this pure commentary for the sake of certain attainment in this Kali age, [an age] in which the word of Akalaṅka is not perceived even in its smallest fraction.
Even if it is obtained only in some small measure among men, may my mind remain fixed right there;
for even though the state of the Lord Anantavīrya is everywhere manifest, [it is difficult to attain].
Even though he is endowed with infinite power— or, in another sense, the author of the work—
the statement is clear.
No one on earth knows this supreme marvel of Akalaṅka’s [work].
Although the jewels of well-spoken verses are taken up by many from the ocean of Akalaṅka’s speech, he alone is a true mine of gems.
Even while proclaiming the selflessness of all phenomena in every respect,
how indeed could the Buddhist master Dharmakīrti not attain a stainless status?

At the beginning of the treatise, having in view such fruits as the accomplishment of its completion without obstacles and its wide dissemination, Akalaṅkadeva uttered this auspicious invocation: "The Omniscient One,
who teaches the logic of non-dualism regarding the meaning of all principles."
Having worshipped Śrī Vardhamāna, I shall proclaim the *Siddhiviniscaya*.
The meaning of this is as follows: having worshipped—that is, having honored—the Omniscient One, the All-Knowing One.

Now, one might object: since there is no existence of anything other than the non-duality of manifestation (*pratibhāsādvaita*), that alone is everything; thus, he who knows that is "Omniscient" (the Knower of His Own Nature). If it is argued that [the text] would therefore mean "having worshipped him," the author replies: "Śrī Vardhamāna."

"Śrī" here is understood as the perfection consisting of the knowledge of the meaning of all principles and so forth; that [perfection], increasing through the adoption of successive states while not abandoning preceding ones (*ajahadvṛtti*), proceeding without cessation, belongs to him—having paid homage to that Akalaṅka, I, a wise man, shall speak this commentary named *Āloka*, which provides an understanding of the meaning for comparison, titled *Mahendra-ṭippaṇa*.

Thus addressed, he said: "The relationship of qualifier and qualified is according to one's preference; therefore, the word *śrī* functions as the qualifier while the other [word] functions as the qualificand, just as in the case of *vardhamānākṣara-nityā* and similar compounds. Otherwise, the word *vardhamāna* would have been placed first and the word *śrī* placed last, since a compound with a qualifier is normally placed first."

[Objection: "Even with such a qualification, the aforementioned defect is not removed. For a rival position is not refuted merely by a qualification of one's own position, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Rather, it is refuted by logic (*nyāya*); therefore, let that very logic be stated. To this, he replies: "One who teaches the logic of *syādvāda*, which [encompasses] all the principles of reality" (*sarvatattvārthasyādvādanyāyadeśinam*). All principles of reality (*tattvārtha*) are the soul (*jīva*) and so forth. *Syādvāda* is their non-absolutism (*anekānta*). This is because the word denoting the subject (*viṣayi-śabda*) is used metaphorically for the object (*viṣaya*). The "logic" (*nyāya*) of that [non-absolutism] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which apprehends it. One whose nature is to teach—that is, to explain—that [logic] is "one who teaches it" (*tad-deśinam*).

This is what is meant: when it comes to his instruction, who else could there be for one with the eye of flesh? Thus the Blessed One has become the instructor of this; and through his instruction, we alone—having shaken off the darkness of ignorance—are capable of conducting ourselves and others upon that path.

For instance: through analysis, just as in the case of the perceived and the attainable, even in the mere perceived—which is of the nature of representation (*vijñapti*)—the parts such as the pillars and so forth lack unity. Consequently, only atoms (*paramāṇu*) remain. And since, upon perceiving a single atom, the others are not apprehended and thus—as with another continuum (*santānāntara*)—are non-existent, that [atom] exists only as its own self; of what, then, would there be the perception of momentariness? By what [reasoning], therefore, could it be said: "In whatever manner something appears," and so forth; or "That which appears is cognition," and so forth?

Or for whom is there the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaitatā*), by virtue of which this is also said: "If you are satisfied with non-duality, you are liberated in every respect" (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 2.37), and so forth?

Prajñākara, the proponent of the non-duality of appearances, stated that non-dual appearance alone is the ultimate reality; it is precisely through the realization of that non-duality that the Blessed One is a valid authority, and not through the complete cognition of all objects.
However, the thorough knowledge of all objects is merely conventional according to worldly usage;
and so it has been said: "The non-dual vehicle is supreme" (*Pravacanavārtikālaṅkāra* 2).

Comparison: Because the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) is perceived in that which is the object of a cognition characterized by the continuity of a subsequent form while not abandoning the previous form—a cognition that functions without relinquishing [the prior state]—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 65.
The subject matter [of this work] is characterized by the exclusion of one nature and the acquisition of another, as well as their respective persistence—[as stated in] *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p.
123. Having paid homage to Akalaṅka, who brings about the understanding of the meaning through comparison, I, a wise man, shall speak this commentary named Āloka on the *Mahendra* [work]. (1)
The term *vardhamāna* has *syādvāda* as its object because it denotes it, and *anekānta* is its object because it is what is denoted by it; thus,
[the term] resides in *anekānta*.
With eyes of compassion,
[they perceive] by means of the intellect that which has become the object of non-conceptual vision.
The comparison of their parts—such as the ocean and its pillars—is as follows:

if there were a plurality of cognitions such that for every atom there were as many cognitions [as there are atoms], it would follow that there is a grasping of individual atoms and an impossibility of multiple simultaneous apprehensions; furthermore, because there is no mutual cognition [of these atoms], there can certainly be no cognition of plurality regarding those [atoms] which are self-cognized, since it would follow that even another person's mental continuum would appear [to oneself]. — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.136–137.
But if this is so, since even the cognition of blue is distinct for every atom, there ought to be cognitions of the blue atoms that are mutually distinct...—*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 77.
For instance, a cognition directed toward blue does not operate upon yellow and so forth; therefore, yellow and the like would be non-existent, just like the mental continuum of another person.
Just as that [cognition] which has engaged with yellow and so forth does not engage with blue, there is likewise an absence [of the object];

similarly, a cognition that engages with the subtle part of a blue lotus is not capable of perceiving other parts, and thus those [other] parts are also absent. Since the remaining cognized part, being itself partless, does not manifest [as such], there is a total absence [of the object]. — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 97.
Because there is no manifestation of a single partless atom among atoms, the atom itself does not exist.
In whatever manner cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way. — Pramāṇavārttika 3.222.

Comparison—Likewise, it must be admitted that whatever appears in a certain way exists exactly in that way; just as a blue water-lily, appearing as blue, exists in that very form, so too all entities appear in a form delimited by the moment. This is established even through inference (*nyāyakumuda*, p.
378). Comparison—For instance: whatever appears is indeed cognition, just like pleasure and so forth, and entities do appear.
— Nyāyakumuda, p. 117;
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
83; Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā, p. 45.

There is no other world, nor this world, nor any obstruction of the other world, nor doubt, nor the transformation of the great elements, and so forth; all is indeed representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Nevertheless, this [conventional reality] exists through worldly usage (*vyavahāra*); likewise, if you find satisfaction in non-duality even regarding the other world, then you are liberated in every respect.
If worldly convention proceeds, then the next world should also be considered. (398) — *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 57.
If, on the other hand, that [consciousness] is held to be devoid of the conceptual constructs of being one or many, then it must be admitted that it is not devoid of appearances.

For that non-dual variegated [consciousness] does not appear as empty of the forms of atoms, nor as a single self through past and future states, just as there is an absence of a grasper in both cases. If it is held that [the consciousness] consists of the forms of blue and so forth; then, at the time of seeing a multi-colored gem, since the forms of blue and so forth are not seen in relation to one another, they would be non-existent, like the mental streams of other persons.

If there were unity in perception, it would be the doctrine of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*); otherwise, even if they are not perceived in that way, their existence does not entail the absolute negation of the next world and so forth. How then [could this be]? Because other things exist as having their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), that alone is everything; thus, one who knows that is omniscient.
That form by which entities are determined does not exist in reality, because neither a single nor a manifold form is found in them— *Prajñāpradīpa* 3.

Whatever does not possess a nature that is either one or many is not ultimately real, just like a sky-lotus; and consciousness does not possess a nature that is either one or many—*Tarkabhāṣā*, Chapter on Negation, p. 38.
That [consciousness] is held to be empty of the forms of blue and so forth by way of conventional usage.

It might be thought that there could also be another world and so forth, because the perception of those forms is neither [simply] seeing nor not seeing; but that too is not sound, because the same consequence would apply even to their own nature (*svarūpa*).
If it is argued that this is not so because of the perception of that [nature], then the fault already stated applies to the perception of [the object] as distinct from others.

Now, if there is no perception of another [entity] by that [perceiver], how does it understand its own distinctness from that other? How, in the absence of perceiving primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), and so forth, can there be the cognition of blue and other objects as being distinct from them? Or how can there be the knowledge of pleasure and so forth as being devoid of a self (*ātman*), such that there is the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*)? If they were perceived, non-duality (*advaita*) would be firmly established! If you say that their non-existence follows precisely from their non-perception, then what is this "non-perception"? If you say it is the cessation of perception, how can that cessation exist unperceived, like primordial nature and the rest? If you say that the perception of blue and so forth is itself the non-perception of that [other], then how can the perception of one thing be the non-perception of another, given the contradiction? If you say it is because of having a form distinct from the other, then in the absence of perceiving primordial nature and the rest, what is this "distinctness" of this [object]? Otherwise, even in the absence of perceiving the "not-blue" and so forth, there would still be the cognition of blue as distinct from them—so how is the aforementioned fault avoided? If you say, "But surely blue is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the not-blue; and in the absence of the not-blue, how could there be its exclusion?"—then the same must be said for yellow and so forth. In that case, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the exclusion of non-self-cognition; therefore, in the absence of that non-self-cognition, let that [self-cognition] also not exist.
If it is argued that this is its very nature (*svarūpa*), then let blue and so forth also be exactly like that;
thus, it would not be variegated (*citram*) by virtue of the forms of blue and so on.
Or, even if it were so, when one considers the distinction of those [colors] even within mere blue—just as there is a distinction among various shades of blue—the same fault remains.

If it is argued: "Since even a mere blue [atom] is not tenable—just like a variegated single cognition—then let that too not exist in ultimate reality. There is no fault in its being non-existent, like the water in a mirage or like the appearance of a magical mirage," according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* (3.211); then let this matter rest for now.

However, if you maintain that a mere blue [atom] is a single entity by virtue of its own parts, then likewise, a variegated [cognition] should also be accepted as a single entity by virtue of its blue and other [colors].

If it is argued that a single cognition, though possessing variegated appearances, is indeed accepted [as one] because it is distinct from external variegation—on the basis of such statements as *Pravārtikālaṅkāra* 3.220 and so forth; then, in that case, it is established that there is some form of identity (*tādātmya*) through non-interruption not only between the perceived and the attained, but even between the states of saṃsāra and its opposite. Thus, it was rightly said: "Salutation to the venerable Vardhamāna. In this same manner, other extremist views (*ekāntas*) are also to be refuted.
And this will be explained in its proper place according to the nature of the essential character by means of the essential character itself.
The non-existence of those [entities] such as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), which are asserted by the Sāṃkhyas and others.
If [it is argued that it is not perceived];
then the cessation of perception is simply its being distinct from primordial matter (prakṛti) and the other [categories].
The distinctness of blue and so forth from yellow and so forth is also self-cognized.
Prajñākaragupta stated that there would be the consequence of non-existence even for the mere blue.

"A painting can be analyzed [into its parts], but the blue and other [colors] of cognition cannot be analyzed..."—this means that a single Self, which persists through the states of both saṃsāra and liberation, is established.
This is another explanation: having worshipped Vardhamāna, the last of the Tīrthaṅkaras, who is characterized by prosperity (śrī).

Of what nature is he? He is omniscient (*sarvajña*), having directly realized all words and sentences. But how is he established as being such an omniscient one? If it is argued that this is because the establishment of a property (*dharma*) is inseparable from the cognition of its substratum (*dharmin*), as stated in the *Tattvasaṅgraha* (verse 3230): "He is omniscient," [we reply: here it is said, "the teacher of the non-dual logic of the meaning of all reality" (*sarvatattvārthasyādvādanyāyadeśinam*). From the expression "teacher of the meaning of all reality," his existence is understood to have been stated, because a statement is not deviant with respect to the existence of its speaker.
There is no deviation [of the reason] by means of the Veda; this will be demonstrated because it is stated that "it belongs to the teacher of the logic of Syādvāda" and "his omniscience."
Having worshipped him, what [is said]? To this he says: "I shall declare the certainty of attainment (siddhi-viniścaya)"; here, *siddhi* means valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The Mīmāṃsaka says:
"There exists some person who is omniscient; yet even that proof which is employed to establish that he is omniscient is merely a thesis."
This verse appears with some variation in reading in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (p. 841) under the name of Kumārila;
see also *Nyāyāvatāra-vārttika-vṛtti*, p. 55: "Dharma is omniscience."
The existence of the self, which is the substratum of omniscience, has been established by that which is not of human origin.

[Objection: But surely accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it will be stated [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*] that "the fruit of the means of valid cognition is directly accomplishment" (Siddhivi. 1.3). Therefore, how can it [accomplishment] itself be the means of valid cognition? [Response: This will be explained later.
The word *vi-* is understood as occurring in the senses of excellence, intensity, duality, and multiplicity.

Regarding that excellence (*atiśaya*), I shall first state the certainty of other principles as well, such as the *jīva*; however, I shall state the excellence of *siddhi* (accomplishment). What is its excellence? It is the status of being the cause for the establishment of all objects of knowledge (*prameya*). As it will be said: "That which is established does not depend on another" (*Siddhiviniścaya* 1.24), and so forth.
Likewise, regarding excellence (*prakarṣa*): I shall state its excellent determination (*viniścaya*).
What is this excellence? It is the superiority over the determinations postulated by the Buddhists and others.

Likewise, regarding twofoldness (*dvaividhya*): I shall state its twofold determination by way of the distinction between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*parokṣa*), or by the distinction that some means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and some is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), or by the twofoldness of objects as being one's own or another's, or by the twofoldness of results as being immediate or mediated.

Likewise, regarding their diversity: I shall state the various determinations; for accomplishment is indeed distinct due to the diversity arising from the removal of disagreements concerning its essential nature, number, object, and result.
The comparison regarding certainty: validity is established intrinsically through practice, otherwise it is extrinsic—*Pramāṇapaddhati*, p. 63.
Examination 1.13:
A comparison— here, misconception is fourfold, concerning number, definition, object, and result.
—Nyāyabindu 1.2;
Pramāṇasamuccayaṭīkā, p. 4.

If it is objected: "But since the determination (*viniścaya*) of the *nayas* and so forth will also be presented here, how can it be said that [this work concerns] 'the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)'? [Response]: No; for they are included within that very [treatise] by way of being subdivisions of *śruta* (scriptural knowledge).
As it has been said: "There are two types of application (*upayoga*) of *śruta*: by way of the distinction between *pramāṇa* and *naya*" (Laghīyastraya, Śloka 62).

And the application of *pramāṇa* is not non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because that would be a contradiction. [Furthermore: "Comprehension is attained through *pramāṇas* and *nayas*" (Tattvārthasūtra 1.6).

If it is argued that this [definition] is contradicted by the fact that [the means of knowledge] must be described as "attaining" (adhigama) like other instruments of cognition, we reply: no. There is no fault, because such a description is made for the purpose of demonstrating that even the partial statement (*vikalādeśa*) is a variety of that [means of knowledge].

Therefore, although the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the viewpoints (*naya*) are equal in being causes for the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the word "means of knowledge" is excluded from the viewpoints and applies only to the complete statement (*sakalādeśa*), just as the word "cow" applies only to those specific individuals from which the male characteristic has been abstracted.
As will be stated in the text regarding the very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
There are two types of cognitive application (*upayoga*) known as *syādvāda* and *naya*.
*Syādvāda* is the comprehensive description (*sakalādeśa*), while *naya* is the partial discourse.
The statement of an object consisting of multiple aspects (*anekāntātmaka*) is *syādvāda*; indeed, *syādvāda* is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
— Laghīyastrayā-svavṛtti, verse 62:
The nature of *naya* as a division of *pramāṇa*.

It should be understood that while *sakalādeśa* (the comprehensive mode of predication) alone constitutes the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), *naya* (the partial perspective), which arises from valid cognition,
is an investigation— a means for reaching a definitive conclusion— that must be subjected to critical examination.

Thus, according to the authority of the *Siddhiviniścaya-prastāvanā* (10), regarding the distinction of the *naya* within the absolute [view], [the author] states in the *Pramāṇasaṃgraha* and other works on valid cognition: "In the *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, verse 2," having thus declared this, the subsequent formulation of the *nayas* and so forth would be improper because they are not included therein.
Therefore, just as elsewhere the inclusion of the *nayas* and so forth occurs within valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so it is here as well; thus, everything is well-established.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), the *Laghīyastraya* and the *Nyāyaviniścaya* are to be understood;

for thus it is summarized: "Direct perception is clear cognition, while indirect perception is all other cognitions—this is the nature of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) according to primary and conventional usage."
—Laghīyastrayā 3; Nyāyaviniścaya 469:
by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

If it is asked: "In the *Pramāṇasaṃgraha* and other works, isn't it established that the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is apprehension (*adhigati*)? What is the fault in explaining [the verse] as 'I shall state its determination (*viniścaya*), which consists of the nature of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*)'? Why has this [explanation] not been adopted? [The answer is: It would result in the non-inclusion of all objects.

For in such a case, only the removal of disagreement regarding the fruit would be included, but not the removal of disagreements regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth for all opponents. Therefore, the previous explanation [is the correct one].
Some have offered the following explanation:

"Is this not already established? Why then is it said, 'I shall explain the *Siddhiviniścaya*'? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of setting forth the connection (*sambandha*), the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*)."

To explain: by the word *siddhi* (accomplishment), the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of the treatise—is stated, in order to dispel the doubt that [the treatise] might be devoid of a subject matter or impossible to practice.
By the word *viniścaya* (ascertainment), the purpose (*prayojana*) is stated, in order to prevent the suspicion that it might be purposeless.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by this [word], the relationship (*sambandha*) between the treatise and its subject matter—characterized as that of the signifier and the signified—and between the treatise and its purpose—characterized as that of the means and the end—is also effectively stated.
In this way, the objection regarding the similarity to the initial statement beginning with "asat" (non-existent) has been refuted.

Now, one might argue: "Just as in the case of a treatise (*śāstra*), the purpose (*prayojana*) of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) must also be stated separately, in order to preclude the suspicion that it is useless like a crow's teeth. If it is further argued: "Since the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this [treatise] is stated for the sake of explaining those [means]; therefore, the purpose is already implied," we say: no; for that too has already been stated by the word "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).

Since this [word] applies the term "accomplishment"—which primarily denotes the fruit of the means of valid cognition—metaphorically [to the treatise], the fruit is indeed already mentioned. This is because there can be no metaphorical usage in the absence of a primary sense.

A listener proceeds to listen to a treatise only when its purpose is established and the connection [between them] is understood; therefore, at the beginning of the work, the connection must be stated along with the purpose,
for as long as the connection of this [treatise] with its purpose is not declared.
Because it would result in incoherence due to being mere senseless chatter,
those who desire the components of an exposition must state the introduction to the treatise along with its reason and its purpose; no other [introduction] exists that is fruitless.
A discussion of the fourfold connection (anubandhacatuṣṭaya), both individually and collectively, is to be found in the following works: *Mādhyamakavṛtti*, p.
3; *Hetubinduṭīkā*, p. 1; *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Pratijñāsūtra, verses 17, 20, and 25.
*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, folio 5;
*Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā*, folio 5;
*Vādanyāya-ṭīkā*, folio 1.
*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, page 2;
*Sambandhaparīkṣāvṛtti*, page 7;
*Māṇḍūkya-kārikās* with Gauḍapāda’s *Śāstra-bhāṣya*, page 4.
Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, page 4;
Nyāyamañjarī, page 6.
Ta.
Śloka-vārttika, page 3; Nyāya-kumuda-candra, page 20; Prameya-kamala-mārtaṇḍa, page 2.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 269; Śāstradīpikā, p. 4;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 14.
Jainatarkavārttika, p. 11;
Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 5:
"But regarding those [topics] not mentioned, the listeners might suspect that the subject matter of this treatise is purposeless, like an examination of a crow's teeth."

Or [a teaching] may be impossible to carry out, like the instruction to adorn oneself with the crest-jewel of the serpent Takṣaka as a means to cure fever; or its purpose may be undesirable, like the instruction on the sequence of a mother’s marriage (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p.
14). Therefore, a sentence devoid of purpose, or its meaning, is neither undertaken to be performed nor expounded by a discerning person, just like the sentence "ten pomegranates" and so forth.
—Hetubinduṭīkā, p. 2. Compare: "The establishment of the object of cognition (prameya) is indeed from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)" — Sāṃkhyakārikā 4;
and "For the comprehension of the object of cognition is dependent upon the means of valid cognition" — Pramāṇavārtikālaṅkāra, p. 340.

If it is asked, "For what purpose are the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth stated at the beginning? [the answer is: for the sake of engaging the listener. Just like farmers and others, even those who act with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*) proceed to act upon such a statement because of doubt regarding its purpose; thus say some. Regarding this, Prajñākaragupta says: "If one proceeds out of doubt, what is the need for seeking further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) elsewhere?"
Some of our own school [of thought] maintain that from his statement there arises faith and curiosity regarding the subject matter and so forth, and from that, activity [toward it].

To them, others say: if that speech is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could there be activity on the part of discerning persons even when faith and the like have arisen from it? Otherwise, it might arise from just anything.
And if it were a valid means of knowledge, it would not be perception, because it is a verbal statement.
Nor is there inference, because speech lacks an invariable connection with its object;

for this very reason, there is also no scripture [as a source], since activity would not proceed from it. To this we reply: there is no fault, because, as will be explained later, the validity of verbal testimony (śabda) as a means of knowledge is established just like perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, it is established that the presentation of the statement concerning the purpose and so forth is for the sake of engaging the audience—*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 6;
and some say that this is for the sake of engaging the audience—*Hetubinduṭīkā*, p. 1.

And that [purpose] is for the sake of engaging the listener; for some, such as Dharmottara and others, hold this because engagement is observed even through doubt, as in the case of farmers and the like (Nyāyāvatāra-vivṛti-vṛtti, p. 1; Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 6).

Even if things are mentioned in a context that has not been heard, they are not ascertained; however, when the subject matter and so forth have been stated— even if they lack a formal means of valid cognition— doubt arises,
and from doubt, people engage in action.

—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 6:

"...therefore,
once the means [of knowledge] have been determined, let the authoritative persons proceed [to act], just like farmers and others"—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 26.

The purpose of the opening statement has been described without ambiguity;
yet, if that [purpose] were already established by the words of a trustworthy person (āpta), this present statement would be redundant,
because faith and so forth arise from the very command of a trustworthy person, just as they do from an opening statement.

Otherwise, even in the initial statement, one would have to await another statement as the cause for the arising of faith and so forth, resulting in the misery of infinite regress; moreover, if this were the word of an unreliable person, it would be like the speech of a child or a madman.
"How is the arising of faith and curiosity to be expected from this? (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇapramāṇaprakaraṇa*, p. 55).
Alternatively, this is a summary statement of the meaning of the treatise; [the topics] are explained by being taken up and extracted from this location within the work.
Comparison— this summary of the meaning of the treatise is restated [as an *anuvāda*] and is not prescribed as something new (*apūrva*)—
Nyāyabhāṣya 4.2.1.

For this very reason, the objection that "the introduction of the opening statement is intended solely to set forth the thesis regarding the subject matter of the treatise" and so forth is also refuted—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 172;
*Syādvāda-ratnākara*, p. 19.
Indeed, taking up this very point again and again, [the author] provides an explanation—*Hetubindu-ṭīkāloka*, p.
243. In that regard, demonstrating first the determination of the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "If there is establishment," and so forth.
If validity were merely apprehension, even in the absence of the sole cause of non-contradiction,

then the proof of momentariness and so forth would not be established through inference; for if there were no determination whatsoever by itself, then no cognition at all— being free from conceptual construction— would be a self-validating means of knowledge.
If its validity arises from that [result], then let the determination be intrinsic for that very reason.

Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established there through a metaphorical designation of the result; the metaphorical application of the means of valid cognition and its own result is based on their being somehow identical.

If, then, because of their being somehow connected, sometimes the result is designated by the means of valid cognition and sometimes the means of valid cognition is designated by the result—just as in the case of clay and a pot, where one says "this is a pot" when it is clay, or "this is clay" when it is a pot—then [the same applies here].

If it is asked, "For what purpose is this [statement]?"—it is for the purpose of refuting the views of others. For the view of others is that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is something other than the result characterized by the apprehension of self and other; namely, that contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth, being insentient, are the means of valid cognition. It is for the purpose of refuting that:
"Contact and so forth are not the means of valid cognition, because they are insentient, like a jar and the like."
There is no deviation [of the definition] due to lamps and the like, because those too are included within the subject (*pakṣa*).

If it is argued that lamps and the like are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they are causes of determinate cognitions—such as those of jars—which are non-verbalizable, non-erroneous, and of the nature of ascertainment (*vyavasāyātmaka*), that is not tenable; for, just like their validity, the fact that lamps and the like are causes of such cognitions is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the opponent.

A lamp or similar object is not the cause of the cognition of a jar and so forth, because it is an object of that cognition; for whatever is an object of a cognition is not its producer, just as the category of existent and non-existent things, which is the object of the cognition of Īśvara, is not its producer; and a lamp or similar object is an object of the cognition of a jar, since it appears in the same single cognition along with the jar.

Now, if the knowledge of the Lord is not produced by its object—since otherwise it would be impossible for that [knowledge] to determine that [object]—then there can be no apprehension by it of those things coexisting with it, because they are not its causes. And thus, the argument that "the entire class of existent and non-existent things is the object of a single person's direct perception, because it is manifold, like a cluster of fingers," is contradicted. Furthermore, what determines this distinction: that those [coexistent things] which are not causes are apprehended by it, while others are not? If it is argued that the knowledge of a jar arises from a lamp and the like even when they are not its cause, and that such knowledge would occur even in their absence; we reply that there is no fault here, because it is actually observed.

Indeed, it is observed that for certain people who have been treated with collyrium and other remedies, visual cognition of form occurs even in the absence of [the normal functioning of] those [remedies];
yet that which occurs even in the absence of something else cannot be the effect of that thing, because such an over-extension would lead to absurdity.
Furthermore, the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of the eye will be refuted later.

And if there is no cognition of form in the absence of a lamp and so forth, how then is there the perception of a mass of darkness? If it is argued that darkness is nothing other than the non-arising of cognition, let this be;
[nevertheless] there is a figurative usage based on some kind of identity.
For the Naiyāyikas and others,
perception (pratyakṣa) is the functioning (vṛtti) of each sense organ (akṣa) toward its respective object;
this functioning, moreover, is either contact (sannikarṣa) or cognition (jñāna).
When there is contact, then cognition is the valid means of knowledge (*pramiti*); when there is cognition, then the cognitions of avoidance and acquisition are the result—
*Nyāyabhāṣya* 1.1.4.
Because the contact of the sense-faculty with its object functions as the instrument, the production of valid cognition does not occur without an instrument.
— *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 6.
The validity of non-cognition, such as sense-object contact and the like, is untenable, just like other extraneous things— *Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti* 1.3.
Cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not non-cognition such as sense-object contact and the like.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā-manorathanandinī*, p.

3. Therefore, that factor (*kāraka*) which, being distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), produces the cognition of an object characterized by non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and other such qualities, is called the instrument (*karaṇa*). And it is precisely this that is designated by the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*): "I see with a lamp," "I look with my eyes," "I understand through a logical mark (*liṅga*)," "I know through a word (*śabda*)," "I ascertain with the mind (*manas*)" — *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 14.
For the Jaina, even illumination is not the cause [of cognition], because it is an object to be determined, just like the object itself—
Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti, verse 55.
Examination of Perception 2.6; Source of Valid Cognition 1.1
In the cognition having the form "this jar is set on fire," [there is no contradiction].
If it is argued that [the example] of a lamp is not [applicable], then the word "not" (na) here is redundant in the case of God's knowledge.
Because it is impossible to delimit objects,
and because there is no causal relationship between things existing at the same time as God’s cognition.

The comparison: "The collection of existent and non-existent things has a single cognition as its objective support because it possesses multiplicity, like the five fingers"—this is found in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
142, and the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 477.
Even for things that coexist, such as a donkey's horn and the like, [there would be cognition] through the knowledge of Īśvara.
Even in the absence of a lamp,
for cats and other such creatures, even in the absence of lamps and the like.
Darkness is not a negator of visual cognition, because that would entail the non-existence of consciousness of darkness;
for there is no postulation of the production of darkness. — *Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti*, verse 56.
For darkness would be a substance by virtue of possessing color; and being composed of multiple substances, it would be perceptible to the eye.

However, there are no such constituent substances. Even if they did exist, they would have to be combined even during the day; thus, the notion of "blueness" in the case of the blind is said to belong to the sky itself—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 143.
The Prabhākaras consider darkness to be the absence of the cognition of light; see Tantrarahasya, p.
21, and Pramāṇasamuccaya-setu, p. 42.
Nyāyakumudacandra, page 663.

The following view might be held: "When there is cognition of form even in the absence of a lamp and so forth, let there be another cause for it; but when a lamp and so forth are present, let that [lamp] itself be the cause. Otherwise, since such cognition is observed even in the absence of the eye during a true dream, the eye would not be its cause at all times, and thus it would follow that the sense organ and the mind are supersensible causes" (Laghīyastraya, Sva-sambodha, verse 54); and this contradicts the statement that perception is supersensible (Laghīyastraya, Sva-sambodha, verse 61). This too is not sound. For if a lamp and so forth, though being perceived together with a jar and so forth, were the cause of the cognition of that [jar], then the jar and so forth would also be the cause of the cognition of the lamp and so forth; consequently, like the eye, it would have to be composed of light (*taijasa*) because of its illuminating form.

If there were sublation by perception and so forth even in other cases, then since a lamp or the like is perceived alone, the jar or the like would not be the cause of its cognition; for it has been stated that the lamp and so forth would likewise not be the cause of the cognition of the jar, since they too are perceived alone.

Furthermore, just as for some people there is no cognition of the form of a jar or similar objects without the light of a lamp or other sources, so too for certain nocturnal creatures (naktañcara) there is no such cognition even without darkness; therefore, that [darkness] must also be a cause of that [cognition]. Consequently, the argument—"the eye is composed of fire (taijasa), because among color-forms (*rūpa*) and the rest, it illuminates only color-form, like a lamp" (Pramāṇavārttikavyākhyā, p. 256)—is subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

If, on the other hand, darkness is not the cause of that [cognition], then light would not be either; thus, the illustrative example "like a lamp" would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhanaśūnyatā*).
Therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule] in the case of lamps and the like.

Now, if it is argued: "Validity is not pervaded by the state of being a cognition (vedanatva), such that it would necessarily cease in its absence; rather, it is pervaded by the state of being a producer of a cognition that accords with reality (yathārthajñānajanakatva).

And since this quality exists in sensory contact (sannikarṣa) and so forth—excluding lamps and the like—let that [contact] be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," we reply: No; for the status of sensory contact as a cause of cognition will be refuted later.

Only the sense faculty remains, yet even that is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for although it is the cause of that [cognition], it lacks consciousness, just like a jar or similar objects—as discussed in the *Pramāṇasaṃgrahabhāṣya*. Therefore, the term "means of valid cognition" is applied metaphorically to the result; hence, it is well said that there is no distinct means of valid cognition.
The knowledge of form is the eye;
therefore it is well said: the sense organ and the mind are the cause of consciousness, while the object is its domain.
Furthermore,

supersensuous perception (atīndriya-pratyakṣa) is of the nature of determinate cognition (vyavasāyātmaka), vivid, non-erroneous, supersensuous, unobstructed, supramundane, and has the self and its objects as its domain. —
Laghīyastraya, Svavṛtti, verse 61.
Even darkness is a cause for the cognition of a jar, just as a lamp and other such things are.
And that [eye] is composed of fire (*taijasa*), because among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], it invariably manifests color-form.

Whatever among color-form and the others invariably manifests color-form is composed of fire, such as a lamp; and likewise, the eye invariably manifests color-form among color-form and the others; therefore, it is composed of fire. — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 256.

Its luminous nature (*taijasatva*), however, is established because, among its qualities such as color and so forth, it invariably manifests only color, just like a lamp—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p.
40; *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī*, p. 73.
In the Vaiśeṣika Upaskāra, page 128:
although those sense organs are causes of knowledge by virtue of being knowledge itself...
Because it is devoid of consciousness; that is to say, because it is insentient.
If, therefore, "establishment" means a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then...

What is that? He says: "mere apprehension" (*upalabdhi-mātra*). Apprehension (*upalabdhi*) is that by which the reality of an object is apprehended; it is the cognition (*buddhi*) produced from an object and bearing its form.
How is that alone the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he replies: "because it is the sole cause of non-discrepancy," and so forth.

Non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is the state of an object being as it is (*arthatathābhāva*). Its single, primary cause—or its cause characterized by the number one—is the determination (*nirṇīti*), which is a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) that accords with reality (*yathārtha*). Without that [determination], this is what is meant: there are four positions, namely, that [the means of knowledge] is ineffective, produces doubt, produces error, or produces a determination that accords with reality.
Among these, regarding the latter position, the refutation beginning with "if it were produced from that" will be stated.
Regarding the objection that there is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the other three positions, he states the refutation: "The establishment of momentariness and so forth," etc.
Here, the term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent.

Then, that whose beginning is momentariness—referring to the proof of [properties] such as being cognition which are non-different from it—is thus described; the establishment of that [momentariness], its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), would not be inference (*anumāna*), it would not be that which establishes it, but rather only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it too is cognized from that very [object] alone due to complete similarity in every respect.
To the question "Of what [is this]? he says: "Of oneself," meaning of the Buddhist himself.

If it is argued that [the inference] exists because it performs the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*), to this he replies: "In every way"—meaning by all methods of proving momentariness and so forth, or even by any other method of excluding superimposition—it would not exist. Why? Because there is no connection [between the inference and the exclusion]. That is to say, inference does not effect the exclusion of superimposition because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), just like perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, since it is stated [in the *Nyāyabindu*] that "the non-conceptual nature of all minds and mental factors is a perception consisting of self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) which is non-conceptual" (NB 1.10),
if this were not accepted, then like that [self-awareness], the self-awareness of all cognitions would necessarily be conceptual.
In this regard, the refutation will be stated: "If [there were] determination," and so forth;
for even momentariness is established through perception alone.

Because it does not exclude superimposition regarding blue and so forth, the mind (*citta*) grasps the mere object; the mental factors (*caitta*), such as pleasure and so forth, grasp specific states.
"...there is no state of consciousness in which the self's own cognition would not be directly perceived" (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p.

64). If it is argued that even non-conceptual perception, when acting toward a future object during the stage of practice (*abhyāsa*), excludes superimposition (*samāropa*), and therefore the reason [adduced] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); we say: no, because at that time, such [superimposition] is absent in the case of blue and other objects by its very nature.

But [the conceptual cognition] certainly exists regarding momentary destruction and so forth; otherwise, how could that perception be non-erroneous? Thus, this [objection] is trivial, because there is no exclusion of superimposition at the stage of cultivation.

If it is argued: "Let it be that [cognition] is non-conceptual with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), but conceptual with respect to the object (*artha*); therefore, the reason is unestablished in its existence (*bhāvāsiddha*)," then does it possess two real forms? If so, since it is possible for a single entity to have two forms even sequentially—as in the case of a cognition of blue and so forth—it would not be a superimposition (*samāropa*). How then could it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by way of excluding that [superimposition]? Alternatively, if its conceptual form therein is merely imagined (*kalpita*), then the charge of partial unestablishment (*bhāgāsiddhatva*) remains firmly established; for in that case, the same consequence of partial unestablishment would apply even to the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), because in the Veda there exists non-producedness through imagination when proving the impermanence of sound in general.
Or how could that [cognition] exclude a conceptual superimposition (*samāropa*)? For the imagined "fire-ness" in a boy does not exclude coldness;

if it is argued that its exclusion is likewise of such a nature, then it follows that its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is also of such a nature—so how could there be an establishment of reality for the opponent? If it is argued that the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) is established from that very [source], let this matter rest for now.

Therefore, since there is an exclusion of that [superimposition] from the nature of conceptualization as apprehended by inference, that [exclusion] must be accepted as real; thus, the same fault characterized as the absence of superimposition remains, and it will be stated: "When there is a restriction to a single appearance... (Siddhiviniścaya 1.11), and so forth.
Inference is the superimposition of permanence and other such qualities upon the self and so forth.
For the Buddhist, inference [operates] with respect to the form of the object.

Whether it be some kind of inference that effects the exclusion of superimposition, even so, there is no destruction of superimposition by means of it; for it is admitted that [superimposition] is causeless.

Now, because of the proximity of inference, the preceding moment of superimposition—being incapable of producing the subsequent moment of superimposition—perishes by itself at that very moment. Consequently, since the subsequent [moment] does not arise due to the absence of its cause, it is said that "superimposition has been destroyed by inference," just as darkness is dispelled by a lamp. If that were so, then why would a cognition such as the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a real pearl-oyster and so forth—which arises from the proximity of some object in space and consists of a succession of preceding moments of superimposition (such as silver) that are each incapable of producing their respective subsequent moments—not also be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? For if it were, there would be only two types of valid means of knowledge. As it has been said:
Because the causelessness of destruction is accepted, [there is the consequence] of the moment of superimposition— that is,
of the superimposition itself.

"Since the conceptual construction of [an object] such as mother-of-pearl occurs through the exclusion of superimposition, it is logical that the conceptualization following upon that direct perception should also possess the status of a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa). Thus [it is said].

If it is argued that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it excludes superimposition (*samāropa*), since it determines an object not determined by perception (*darśana*); to this he says: "If the determination... and so forth.

This is its meaning: since inference is the determination of momentariness and so forth not determined by perception, therefore—if indeed—the establishment of momentariness and so forth [occurs], such is the connection.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Nirvikalpa," and so forth.
The entire fourfold perception (*darśana*), being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), would not exist—that is, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—according to the Buddhist himself.

The intention here is as follows: just as, according to the Datta [school], because the determination of momentariness and so forth is not achieved by perception (*darśana*), inference (*anumāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there and not perception; likewise, because the determination of blue and so forth—which was not determined by that [perception]—is achieved by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurring immediately after it, that conceptual construction alone would be the means of valid cognition there and not perception. Thus, for the Buddhists, if mere apprehension (*upalabdhi-mātra*) were the means of valid cognition, there would be no inference of momentariness and so forth, and no determination of objects at all; everything would be non-conceptual. Therefore, this is a "noose" (a trap) from the Buddhist position, and it follows that the definition of perception—whether sensory, mental, self-cognizing, or yogic—is established by means of *darśana*.

"Indeed, wherever [the cognition] produces this [conceptualization], there alone lies its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, because it generates conceptualizations and inferences regarding blue and so forth—such as their momentariness—the non-conceptual [cognition] is a means of valid cognition; this is the view of Dharmottara and Prajñākaragupta. To that, he replies with "If of that... and so on.
The connection is: if [it is argued that] the non-conceptual is a means of valid cognition because it generates that [determination] consisting of conceptualization and inference.

For this very reason—namely, because even non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka*) is not intrinsically a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to its failure to produce a definitive determination (*nirṇīti*)—let it be for this same cause that the conceptual determination (*vikalpa*), called inference (*anumāna*), is itself intrinsically the means of valid cognition. The sense is: "Rather than the validity of the [non-conceptual] vision belonging to something else, let that validity belong to this [conceptual determination] itself," in which [determination] there arises the conceptual cognition regarding the aspect of blue and so forth.
This [verse] has been extracted from the *Nirvikalpa*—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 35;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 512.
*Nyāyabindu-vivaraṇa-prakaraṇa*, p.
523; *Śāstravārtā-ṭīkā*, p. 151:
"Therefore, perception becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when it performs a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*)."

"Perception grasps only the proximate form and so forth; it becomes a motivator for action when there is a conceptual determination of identity through another conceptualization"—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 216. *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* 1.21.
Comparison: Even non-conceptual knowledge possesses the power to give rise to conceptualization; by means of that [power], it becomes a constituent part of all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*).
(Tattvasaṃgraha, verse 1306)

Is conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it that in the case of non-habituation, inference—which is capable of taking the visible form as its logical mark—is the means of valid cognition regarding the object to be attained, such as color and so forth; whereas in the case of habituation, non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-adhyakṣa*) is the means? There is no other state in which conceptual cognition could be the means of valid cognition, and that [non-conceptual state] alone is accepted by the Jains. Therefore, how can it be said: "I shall explain the *Siddhiviniścaya*"? (Siddhiviniścaya 1)
Regarding this doubt, he says: "If [there were] proof," and so forth.

This is its meaning: if "proof" (*siddhi*) means valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and if that [proof] is merely perception—merely the perception of the middle [moment] devoid of preceding and succeeding forms, being nothing more than mere perception—then he states the refutation here: "The proof of momentariness and so forth," and so on.

The inclusion of the term "momentary" (kṣaṇika) serves as a definition of the probandum (sādhya) that is non-different from the means of proof (sādhana); by the word "etc. (ādi), fire and other such things are included. The establishment of these [would require] inference as a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa)—[otherwise] it would not arise, because it would be grasping what has already been grasped by itself. This is what is meant: just as there is a difference between the object seen and the object attained, so too, because there is a difference between the visible object and the act of seeing at every moment, there would be no perception of anything at all; thus it was stated in the *Pramāṇasaṃgrahālaṃkāra*.

Likewise, since there is an absence of the [required] factors such as the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth, there is no inference; therefore, it is not something to be practiced. If it is argued that perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that case because inference alone is admitted through practice (*abhyāsa*), and thus it may exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), [the author] says here: It would not exist in any way—not even by way of convention—just as it does not exist by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because in the absence of any existing entity (*bhava*), there is an absence of conventional conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Since this [inference] is preceded by that [conceptualization], how could it ever be a means of knowledge? To this he says: Without a definitive determination (*nirṇīti*), there is the perception of a coarse, singular similarity; without that, [there can be no inference].

Of what kind [is this cognition]? To this he says: "of that which has non-contradiction as its sole cause. Non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is the comprehension of the thesis, the reason, and the example according to their true nature; the sense is that this [cognition] has that alone as its cause, because the comprehension of the thesis and so forth consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Suppose it is argued: "Let it be that, because there is the apprehension of the object of perception (*dṛśya*) along with its distinctions, determinate perception (*savikalpaka-darśana*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) therein, but not at the prior or subsequent limits [of the continuum]. To this, he says: "If the determination... and so forth. If the determination—the determinate perception—is the valid means of knowledge because of the apprehension of the middle moment along with its distinctions; here is the refutation: all non-conceptual [perception], even that born of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), would not be valid by itself, whereas other [non-conceptual perception] would indeed be invalid. The sense is that for the Buddhist, [perception] would be invalid whether occurring successively or simultaneously, because the existence of things with their distinctions arises [only through conceptualization].

[Objection: "But surely, whether in its own form (*svarūpa*) or another's form (*pararūpa*), the perception of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—whether non-sequential or sequential—is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*). However, the conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) arising in its wake initiates the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of inference and so forth; therefore, by virtue of that [conceptual cognition], the former [perception] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this, he replies: "If [it is argued] 'of that' and so forth. The meaning of this has already been explained:
where there is a movement toward a future [object], inference is accepted as the means of valid cognition.
In the present [context], when the activity is excessive, there is non-perception by the senses;
this is the authority (*pramāṇa*)—*Pravārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 218.

Convention (*saṃvṛti*) is a mere conceit of cognition through conceptual construction during repeated practice, even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.
For conventional reality has as its objective support entities that lack real form, because it conceals the ultimate truth—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 203.
Because conventional conceptualization is preceded by experience,
it is non-conceptual.

Now, if it is thought that this [text] should be brought down [into the commentary] and explained as follows: "The definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is stated to be the exclusion of what is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*);

yet, there is no such thing as an object to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*), namely, a non-valid cognition, because the perception of a double moon and so forth does exist"—if one asks, "Why is that [perception] not a valid cognition? Because it is sublated (*bādhyamānatvāt*)," [the reply is]: "No, because that [sublation] is impossible in every respect. If it is argued that, "Just like waking perception, the perception of a double moon and so forth is either a valid cognition or nothing at all; thus, due to the absence of an object to be excluded, the statement 'I shall explain the *Siddhiviniścaya*' would be meaningless," to this he says: "If [there were] a valid cognition... and so forth.

If accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how can that which is mere apprehension—the general nature of cognition—be a means of valid cognition? To this he says: "Because it has non-contradiction as its sole cause," and so forth; the meaning of this has already been explained.

The intended meaning here is this: if [the opponent claims] that "only that [cognition] which is non-contradictory is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not any other," without regard for the distinction [between direct perception and inference]; to this he states the refutation: "the establishment of momentariness and so forth," etc.

That is to say, "momentariness" is the first of those realities accepted by the opponent, and thus it is so described; the "establishment" (*siddhi*) of that would require a means of valid cognition related to it, namely, inference (*anumāna*).

The intended meaning is as follows: if mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) were the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then, just as in the case of blue and so forth, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and the like would also be valid knowledge regarding gross objects (*sthūla*) and so forth. Consequently, because its object would be sublated by that [recognition], the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) regarding sound and other phenomena would not be a valid means of knowledge.
Furthermore, multiple means of knowledge for one and the same thing are not purposeful for an opponent, as such a position is not accepted.

If it is argued that the cognition of gross objects and the like is not a valid means of knowledge because it is being sublated, then only un-sublated cognition should be regarded as a valid means of knowledge, not every cognition whatsoever.
If that were so, [the opponent] says here: "If ascertainment," and so forth.

If uncontradicted cognition—whose sole cause is non-discrepancy—is ascertainment, and if that ascertainment is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then for the Buddhist, all cognition without exception—that is, entirely—would not be a means of valid knowledge by itself, because it would be free from conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and distinct from the ascertainment [of conceptual thought]. However, [if one holds that only] a specific kind of cognition is [the means of valid knowledge], there is a loss of the original thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), because it is impossible for that [specific cognition] to be subject to sublation.
The meaning is that for the Buddhist, inference— being merely a mental construction— would not be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

Since it is not accepted that multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operate upon a single object of cognition (*prameya*), the Vaiśeṣika and others here state: "It is not the ascertainment (*nirṇīti*) itself [that is the means], but rather contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth are the means of valid cognition because they are the cause of that [ascertainment]. To this, the following reply is given: If there is a means of valid cognition other than the production of that ascertainment, let it be so; for in this very case, the ascertainment is self-evident (*svataḥ*). For that whose existence brings about establishment independently of anything else is rightly considered the means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, its establishment occurs through the state of ascertainment (*nirṇīti*); for in the absence of that [ascertainment], even when other [conditions] are present, it is not established. Otherwise, the eye would also establish taste and so forth, since there is no difference in the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamaveta*).
Thus, [the opponent] considers [perception] to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it generates ascertainment.
And the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the cause of apprehension— Nyāyabhāṣya 2.1.11.
In the absence of definitive determination, [cognition] is independent of external factors such as sense-contact and so forth.
The connection is that [the cognition] would [arise], because it is not established even when there is the existence of sense-object contact and so forth.

If, because taste also inheres in a jar that is in contact with the eye, [taste were perceived], then as for the one who speaks thus—the proponent of the collapse of valid cognition (pramā-bhaṅga-vādī) Prajñākaragupta—who says: "There is no reality beyond the non-duality of manifestation (pratibhāsa-advaita); therefore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding that, since this non-duality is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana-adhyakṣa), and thus there can be neither disagreement nor lack of comprehension regarding it; hence, the formulation of the definition of valid cognition for the purpose of refuting that is useless, like [proving] the existence of an elephant," to that he replies: "If [its] establishment... [The opponent asks: If its establishment... [is claimed, then... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly after "siddhiścet". The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument presented.)

This is what is considered here: would the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this case be an appearance that transcends all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or rather an appearance such as "I know the jar" and so forth? Refuting the first position, he says: if the establishment [of the object] is the means of valid cognition, then if there is a mere appearance devoid of distinctions such as unity or plurality—mere apprehension, the act of apprehending, or the apprehension itself—that alone is the "mere-ness" (*tanmātra*).

As it has been said: "Since a manifestation is merely a manifestation, how can it be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he replies: The cognition "I know the jar," and so forth, is a definitive ascertainment (*nirṇīti*). Without that [ascertainment], its absence would follow.
Of what kind [is this cognition]? It is the sole cause of non-contradiction, being the single cause of non-discrepancy (*avipratipatti*).

If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", he says in response: the "establishment of momentariness and so forth"—where "momentary" is the first of a series including similarity, other continua, and so on—the establishment of these would not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the Buddhist himself, because that [inference] accepted by others is an inference that is sublated by the very perception of the person (*puruṣa*), which cannot be denied. If it is further argued that such [perception] is a valid means of knowledge from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), he says in response: it would not be valid even from the perspective of conventional reality, just as it is not valid from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). He will demonstrate that, in that same way, even the inference of a permanent God (*īśvara*) and so forth would have to be considered a valid means of knowledge.

If it is argued that determination (*nirṇīti*) alone is then the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), to this he replies: If determination—defined as a cognition consisting of the ascertainment of both self and other—is the means of valid cognition, then non-conceptual [awareness] would not be a means of valid cognition by its own nature. For [in such a case], there would be duality (*vikalpa*)—the distinction (*bheda*) consisting of "I" as the cognition, the jar and so forth as the object, and the ascertainment of that [object] as the result—which would exclude non-dual awareness (*advayavedana*). Thus, it could not be a means of valid cognition in its own right.

Therefore, what was stated—that "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge" and so forth is the definition of valid cognition in terms of conventional usage, while "the illumination of an unknown object" is [the definition] in terms of ultimate reality—because self-awareness, which is the appearance of non-duality as an unknown object by means of another means of cognition, is designated in this way;
that is refuted. The remainder is to be explained as before.

Now, if blue and so forth are objects, then since they are not perceived apart from that [consciousness], there is no grasper of them [other than it]; and as for the body, pleasure, and so on, since they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), how can it be determined that consciousness is not their grasper? If this is asked, we say: no; because an answer has already been given and will be stated immediately thereafter. Furthermore, the ultimate reality is non-duality (*advaita*); the very manifestation of that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus, the nature of cognition and so forth is understood by itself—*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* 2.
When everything is investigated, it falls apart; there is no reality other than non-duality (advaita).
— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, 2.6,
In the non-duality of manifestation, there would be no inference— no inferential cognition— within the non-duality of manifestation.
The establishment of momentariness and so forth occurs through the perception of a person whose nature is the eternally one Brahman;

or else, it is the illumination of an unknown object—alternatively, this is the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "illumination" (*prakāśa*) is that by which something is illuminated, and thus a means of valid cognition is knowledge that illuminates an object not yet known.
Alternatively, by the word "object" (artha), the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is meant;
thus, "the illumination of an unknown object" means the illumination of the ultimate reality.
And since the ultimate reality consists in non-duality (advaita), the very manifestation of that is what constitutes valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And thus, the nature of the conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth is understood through itself; and it has been stated that "validity [is established] by means of worldly transaction" (*vyavahāra*).

In that regard, this is the definition of ultimate validity (*pāramārthika-pramāṇa*), whereas the former [definition] pertains to conventional validity (*sāṃvyavahārika*)—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 30.

If it is asked: "What kind of establishment is this—occurring through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*)—that belongs to the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which was already answered [in the case] of the grasper of blue and so forth? To this he says: "Of the means of valid cognition," and so on.

The direct fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accomplishment, which is the ascertainment of its own object. Therefore, it has been said: "The direct fruit of the means of valid cognition is accomplishment, which is the ascertainment of its own object" (*Pramāṇanirṇaya*, p. 2).
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which depends upon the cognizer, and not the former [the object]. [Commentary on the verse]:

Since the determination of its respective object of cognition occurs through itself, that very cognition is a means of valid cognition by virtue of being self-established; for if it were to proceed from something else, there would be no possibility of a rule regarding non-contradiction.
Furthermore, its status as a cause for perception is not like that of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth;

rather, since validity is established through the power of definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) even when there is no error, one must admit that the cognition of reality (*tattva-buddhi*) is in some way identical with that [determination].
Otherwise, being fruitless and lacking a means of proof, it would not be distinguished from what is non-existent.
The nature of a definitive cognition (*nirṇaya*) consists in its exclusion of doubt and error that are ineffective [for establishing truth], and not otherwise.

Furthermore, the statement that "valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a consciousness that apprehends an object not previously apprehended" merely denotes the determination of an object not yet determined; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For it is untenable for that which has already been apprehended, that which is non-concordant, or that which falls within the scope of dependence on other means of proof to be the most effective instrument of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*).

Even when there is the apprehension of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) not previously apprehended, it would follow that no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could function regarding what has already been seen; thus, in the exclusion of a superimposition (*samāropa*) based on a common nature, there is no difference between conventional perception and inference.
To claim that [inference] arises directly from experience is a great error.

The subsequent [cognition] is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the cognizer because it serves as its instrument, but not the preceding one, since such a consequence would apply even to inference.

Regarding what is the result of a valid means of knowledge—which is a specific instrument—that is directly and immediately produced, rather than being mediated by the cognition characterized by rejection and so forth? To this he says: "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).

Since there is observed disagreement among the teachers regarding what is denoted by the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), as if asked what that fruit is, he shows it, saying: "the ascertainment of the object for oneself" (*svārthaviniścaya*).

Here, "self" (*sva*) is the nature of consciousness and "object" (*artha*) is the jar and so forth; or alternatively, the "object for oneself" (*svārtha*) is an entity capable of being apprehended by itself. The "ascertainment" (*viniścaya*) of those two, or of that [consciousness], is their apprehension through the exclusion of such qualities as "inefficacy" (*akiñcitkaratva*).

By the second explanation, it should be understood that even cognitions of pleasure and so forth—which do not grasp objects such as a jar—possess the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because they determine their own nature as their object.

[Objection: But there is nothing other than blue and so forth for which the determination of its own object could be the result; if you say that blue and so forth themselves are that [result], [we reply: no, because even in the case of the determination of itself, there is no determination of an [external] object, since there is no object other than that [blue]. Therefore, the claim that "the determination of its own object" is the result is untenable.

If it is argued that this is correct by relying on the second interpretation, we say: no; for in that case, the doctrine of representation-only (vijñaptimātra) would be undermined, since blue and other objects would incur the status of being cognition itself by virtue of being their own perceivers.

If it is argued that bodily pleasure and so forth follow from that [consciousness], and thus there is no fault because its activity toward blue and other objects is like its activity toward its own nature; we say no. This is because the body, like blue and other objects, is an object of cognition (*prameya*), and it is not admitted that pleasure and so forth are the apprehenders of blue and the rest. If you then argue that the principle "it does not have itself as its object" and so on is logical; we say no. When consciousness is perceived through the "I-am-I" (*ahamahamikā*) mode, what confidence can there be in anything else—whether in blue and the like, or in pleasure and the like—that it is not of the nature of that [consciousness]? For from this [certainty] it would follow: "Blue and the like are cognitions, because they appear [in consciousness], just like pleasure and the like."

[Objection: Let it be granted that there is the notion of "I" (*ahampratyaya*). However, since it is perceived as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the body—as in "I am fat," "I am thin"—it does not differ from the body, but is rather that very same thing; and it has already been stated that this [notion of "I"] does not grasp blue and so forth. [Reply: No; this will be chewed along with the chewing of the Cārvāka doctrine, so why be so eager about this alone? [Objection: Let it be that this [self] is different from that [body]; even so, how is it the grasper of blue and so forth? [Reply: How is it the grasper of its own nature (*svarūpa*)? If you say it is because that [nature] appears to it, then let it be the grasper of blue and so forth for this very same reason. And thus is the common worldly perception: "I know blue," "I know yellow."

Therefore, as for what was said—"If it is the grasper of blue and so forth which exist at the same time, then blue and so forth would belong to that [grasper] because there is no distinction"—that is refuted.

For if, due to being simultaneous, the property of one were to belong to all, then in a variegated [cognition], just as there is the form of blue, there would have to be blueness even in the yellow and other forms, or else the form of yellow and so forth would have to be in the blue. Consequently, how could there be something called "variegated," since variegation would simply be variegation? Furthermore, there is sublation by perception;
for elsewhere too, it is certainly not the case that the status of being a grasper is perceived in that way through perception as it is perceived in the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*).

Or, just as blue and other objects possess the status of being apprehended, so too does the cognition of them possess that [status] with respect to them; otherwise, since there would be no dispute, the entire Buddhist position would be established and the composition of this treatise would be purposeless.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), doubt and error are to be understood as included within the result.
The grasper of blue and so forth [is] of blue and so forth.
The determination of one's own purpose regarding bodily pleasure and so forth [is made] by means of that which is distinct from blue and so forth.
And just as there is no consciousness other than pleasure and so forth, so too there is nothing other than blue and so forth— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 3.387: "Other than blue, etc."
The very nature of the body, and [the nature] of the body and so forth.
Because the intrinsic nature [of the self] appears precisely within the cognition "I."
