The comparison regarding the grasper of the notion of "I": "If [the cognition and the self] were simultaneous, then just as cognition is the grasper of the object, so too the object would be the grasper of the cognition,
because there is no distinction in their being produced at the same time."
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 162; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 85, regarding blue and so forth.
The state of being the object of apprehension for the notion of "I" is recognized.

It might be thought: "Neither 'objectivity' (*grāhyatā*) nor 'subjectivity' (*grāhakatā*) is perceived as something other than the blue [object] and its cognition. But in that case, even the apprehension of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) would be difficult to obtain; for here too, there is no objectivity or subjectivity other than that essential nature, and in the absence of those, there can be no apprehension of them. If, however, it is argued that they are apprehended by themselves because they are self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), then let the "I-cognition" (*ahampratyaya*) be the apprehension of another because it consists in the illumination of another, and let the blue and so forth be apprehended by another because they consist in being illuminated by another.
Indeed, according to the Jaina, no apprehendedness or apprehendingness other than the inherent capacity (yogyatā) is admitted;
as it has been said regarding the blue object and its cognition: [nīlāditatpratyayayoḥ].
In the absence of the grasped and the grasper, there would be the grasping of another; consequently, let there be the state of being a grasper of another,
just as an object produced by its own cause is held to be self-grasped.

"Likewise, knowledge arising from its own causes is itself considered to be the grasper of that [object]. (Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra, Śloka 59) By this, the following objection raised by the opponent is also refuted: "If cognition is the grasper because it performs the grasping that constitutes the very nature of blue and so forth, then that [nature] must be produced by it; thus, its status as knowledge would follow from being an effect of knowledge, like a subsequent cognition. Alternatively, if it performs the grasping of something other than the object, then nothing has been done for the object, and thus there is no grasping of it by that [cognition]."

How is it that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*) in the act of grasping after what has already been grasped? Because this [process] is the same even in the case of grasping its own nature (*svarūpa*).

For instance: if consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the apprehender because it performs the act of grasping its own nature (*svarūpa*), then it would be its producer and not its apprehender; and this is not logical, because an action upon itself is a contradiction (*svātmani kriyāvirodha*). If it is argued that there is no fault because it performs that [act] as something distinct from itself, then since nothing has been produced in its own nature, how can it be grasped by it? Furthermore, if it were to perform the act of grasping by means of another [act], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*);
and if it grasps its own nature directly, it would likewise grasp the object.
If it is argued that there is identity between the two [the cognition and the object] when the object is grasped through the power of grasping itself, but otherwise they are distinct;

and if it is further argued that a single entity possesses two powers, and even those two powers are known by another pair of powers, leading to an infinite regress— this too is easily resolved by the "single variegated cognition" (citraikajñāna) which will be explained later, so let this matter rest for now.
Only the blue object and so forth are produced; for it is its own inherent nature, the apprehension, that is produced by that [blue object],
and in the production of an apprehension distinct from the blue object and so forth...

Comparison by means of conviction: Now, if the cognition of an object arises from the act of grasping it, is that [cognition] produced by it as something distinct from the object or as non-distinct? If it were distinct, nothing would have been done to the object; how then could it be its apprehension? Furthermore, the relationship "this belongs to that" would be unestablished.
And if that [cognition] were to produce another act of grasping for this [object], there would be an infinite regress.

But if there is no difference in meaning [between the object and its cognition], then when that [cognition] is produced, the object itself is produced by it; thus, its status as knowledge follows from its being an effect of knowledge, just like a subsequent cognition—[as stated in] *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
85: "Cognition [is the cause] of its own form."
In the view that apprehension consists of a cognition whose nature is the grasping of its own object, [it applies] to the two own-objects.

Now, as for what was said—that while the *ahaṃpratyaya* (the notion of "I") possesses the capacity to grasp blue and so forth, it does not possess that same capacity to grasp the cognition of those [objects]—this must be considered: from the observation of the effect, which is the grasping of the object, it is understood that the capacity exists therein; yet there is no grasping of that [capacity] itself, because it is to be inferred from its effect.

If it is thought that it is understood from that very [cognition] itself, then there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): namely, that the establishment of its capacity [to know itself] depends on it, and its establishment depends on that capacity. To this it is replied: Just as even a very sharp sword does not cut itself, so cognition does not determine itself, because of the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) within itself. As for what was said—that cognition determines itself, whereas a sword does not cut itself due to the opposite being the case—that argument applies equally here as well.

For example, the establishment of that [cognition's] power is due to its grasping itself, because that power is to be inferred from its effect; however, the establishment of its grasping itself does not arise from that [power]. If it is argued that the establishment of its grasping itself results from the establishment of that [power], there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the establishment of its grasping depends on the establishment of the power, and the establishment of that power depends on the establishment of its grasping. If, on the other hand, the grasping of itself is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then to the objection "from what [is it established]? the answer "from its own power" is given; yet, in that case, the establishment of that [power] does not result from its grasping itself. One should consider whether this same logic applies elsewhere or not.

If it is argued: "Let there be the apprehension of blue and so forth by that [cognition] just as there is of its own nature; what is the fault?"—this is the response: In the inference—"That which appears is cognition, just as pleasure and so forth appear, and blue and so forth appear"—the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddha*), because the manifestation of itself by itself, which is observed in the case of pleasure and so forth as being pervaded by the nature of cognition, is not observed in the case of blue and so forth. Otherwise, since it would be a distinct cognition by virtue of having self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as its essence, it would—like the cognition of an omniscient being—not be made an object for the proponent and the opponent; consequently, for them, there would be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

If it is held that even though cognition is a distinct entity, its apprehension by those two [the eye and the mind] occurs while the object itself remains unapprehended, on what basis is this distinction made? Now, if—relying on the view that a single cognition is variegated—it is maintained that the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) possesses identity with the forms of blue and so forth, then the "I-notion," though distinct from blue and the rest in terms of its own nature and other attributes, would at times attain identity with blue and the rest through its capacity (*yogyatā*); and by that very capacity, it would become the grasper of them.
If this is not accepted, then this would follow: "I, a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), do not desire to see a Caṇḍālī woman, yet I desire to touch her."
In the cognition of blue and so forth, there is fitness.
By that very apprehension of the object, there is an apprehension;

indeed, from the apprehension of the object itself comes the comparison: "But how does the blue manifest its own form? For objects such as jars, which are to be illuminated, do not become self-illuminating through a lamp or similar means; an action upon oneself is a contradiction."

For indeed, that very edge of a sword cannot be cut by that same edge; here is the resolution: just as light is held to be the illuminator of its own nature because it manifests through identity with it, so too is the intellect (dhī) the knower of itself.

From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it understood that there is a contradiction in an action directed toward itself (*svātmani kriyāvirodha*), [namely] that [consciousness] has neither the form of the object known (*vedya*) nor the form of the knower (*vedaka*)? For the establishment of a desired point is not achieved by a mere example (*dṛṣṭānta*), since an example such as a lamp is possible even in the opposite case.

If a jar is illuminated by a lamp through its external nature, and the lamp likewise [is illuminated] by another of the same kind, there is no objection to this... since this is simply the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of things, what loss is there here? Now, if it is argued that there is a contradiction in an action operating upon itself, it is said in reply: when that very essence is its own [object], how can there be any contradiction? For if there were a contradiction with one's own essence, everything would perish;
indeed, nothing is in contradiction with its own form.
If that were so, nothing would exist in its own form, and thus everything would have vanished;
moreover, "cutting" is the production of something distinct, and it cannot be produced by that very same thing—
this is precisely what is meant by the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
"But its nature, which is self-luminous, is not contradicted by that very [nature]... (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 353–54).
On this point, some say: "Self-awareness of the mind and mental factors is not possible, because there is a contradiction in something acting upon itself;
for even a well-trained boy cannot climb onto his own shoulders."

For even a sharp sword-blade does not cut itself, nor does a fiercely blazing mass of fire burn itself; likewise, how could the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta) perceive themselves? To this it is replied: the relationship between the knower and the known in cognition is not described by way of the relationship between agent and object, as in the case of cutting and being cut; rather, it is by way of the relationship between the determiner and the determined.

Just as a lamp illuminates itself by itself, so too knowledge—being distinct from insentient objects and arising from its own cause with the very nature of luminosity—is established as self-cognizing (svasaṃvedana), because it possesses the power to apprehend itself. (Tarkabhāṣā, p. 9–10).
This is due to its capacity for self-apprehension.
By means of the notion of "I," [the self perceives] blue and so forth according to its own capacity.
It appears pointless [to argue] that the blue and so forth attain the status of being the grasper of themselves by that very same [cognition], as asserted by both the proponent and the opponent.

If it is argued that when one thinks "I am [perceiving]," then even though there is a grasping of what is non-different from blue, how is its status as an object understood? If you say it is "because of the manifestation," then [objects] seen in dreams and the like would also exist; thus, that cognition would also be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And if that were so, what would be the point of formulating a definition of a valid means of knowledge, since there would be nothing to be excluded?

If it is argued that [the world] does not exist because it is the object of a perception produced by a defective cause (*duṣṭakāraṇa*), then from what source is it known that the perception is such? If it is said "because its object is unreal," there is a circularity (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): for only when the perception as such is established is its object unreal, and only then can it be said that the perception is such. Furthermore, the claim that it is non-existent because it is the domain of a sublated cognition (*bādhitapratyaya*) is also untenable. For a sublation does not, at the time of the cognition's arising, strip away its own nature; since that cognition is perceived at that time, and only at another time is it gone due to its perishability, by what could it be sublated? Indeed, *kiṃśuka* flowers are naturally red; we have no effort to alter that.

Nor is there a removal of the object (*viṣayāpahāra*); for that too is observed. Furthermore, the removal of the object is not a property of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇadharma*), but rather of the sovereign. Now, if "removal of the object" does not mean its sublation (*bādhana*), but rather the making known of its appearance while it exists, that too is not tenable. For if it were non-existent, how could there be an appearance, like a donkey's horn? If there is an appearance, how can it be non-existent? In that case, even a jar or the like seen during the waking state would be just the same.

If it is argued that this [cognition] is false because the cognition "this is not a jar or the like, but something else" does not arise—[we reply: surely, when one mistakes a mirage for water, or when there is sudden death or travel to another land, such a cognition does arise; would that water then be real? Furthermore, even when a specific object exists, such a cognition is observed in some cases.
If this cognition were to have a non-existent object, how could it make known the non-existence of another [object]? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If [the later cognition] has the same object [as the former], then the same consequence as before follows, as well as infinite regress.

Furthermore, if this cognition has the same object as the preceding cognition, it cannot be a sublater of that [former cognition] in any way; otherwise, there would be a mutual relationship of the sublated and the sublater among all cognitions of a single object.
If, on the other hand, it has a different object, then even more so it cannot be its sublater; otherwise, let the cognition of a jar be the sublater of the cognition of a cloth!

If it is argued that [the silver] is not real because the cognition "it is not" does not arise, then why does that very cognition not arise? Because there is no single locus [for both cognitions]. How can there be a single locus for the cognitions of silver and mother-of-pearl? Because there is no evidence for it; this is because such a locus is not perceived by the preceding and succeeding cognitions—this has already been discussed in the section on *kṣaṇabhaṅga* (momentary destruction). If it is argued that the unreality of the blue objects seen in dreams is due to their being the objects of sublated knowledge and being the objects of non-corresponding perceptions, we say no: non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is the attainment of the object as it was seen, and that is observed even in dreams.

Now, that [object] is not an object at all, because it does not perform a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). If it is argued that purposeful action is indeed seen there, since effects such as water are observed for purposes like bathing, then [we reply]: if that purposeful action is not real because it is not perceived by one who is awake, then other [actions] would also not be real, since they are not perceived by one who is asleep.

Furthermore, if purposeful action were non-existent, how could the existence of anything else be established? If it exists intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then an entity (*bhāva*) is likewise existent in that same way; so what is the need for dependence upon it? If it exists through something else, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is argued that "this is merely something insignificant," we reply as follows:
For the occurrence of mere cognition is indeed the same in all cases, whether it arises from cognitions other than dreams or from dreams themselves—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.
4—even the knowledge of an object seen in a dream [is such].
Cognition of an object seen in a dream is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For the non-existence of the cognition of a dream-object is not brought about by another cognition— whether that be the dream-cognition itself or any other— because at that time, it perishes of its own accord.
Nor is sublation perceived when knowledge has perished due to the closing of the eyes—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 4;
for how indeed could *kiṃśuka* flowers, which are naturally red, be dyed by anyone?—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 75.
"For the *kiṃśuka* trees are naturally red; who could dye them now?
(*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 374).
"For the clusters of *kiṃśuka* flowers, used as ear-ornaments, are naturally red."
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 584:

"For there is no sublation (*bādha*) by another cognition consisting in the removal of its object, characterized by the making known of its non-existence; nor is a cognition that has functioned with respect to its own object capable of effecting the removal of another object. For it is the nature of cognitions that their own object is the means of establishing their own object."
The seizure of another's domain, however, is the duty of a ruler of men—
*Pravacanavārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 359—
as in the case of what is seen in a dream.
The communication that "this is a mere appearance" would be non-existent if the jar and so forth were non-existent; rather, they are real.
The meaning is that, because the latter is not known through the former and the former is not known through the latter, there is no perception of them as having a common substratum;
this is illustrated by the example of what is seen in a dream.
That causal efficiency is not performed by one who is awake; therefore, it is not causal efficiency at all.
Even the causal efficiency perceived while awake would not be causal efficiency.

Is this objection regarding the lack of distinction between the waking and dreaming states raised so that there may be external objects even in dreams—just as in the waking state—or so that even at other times it might be like the dreaming state, such that both [waking and dreaming] are equally doubtful, or perhaps so that there may be a state beyond all conceptual constructions? In that regard, if the first position is held—that because external objects are established even in the dreaming state, that cognition is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—then the formulation of its definition would be improper due to the absence of anything to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*).
What fault is there in this view? None other, for it does not negate the categories of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
What is the fault in the opponent’s position? It is the total destruction of one's own system, because [tenets] such as "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) would remain unestablished.

Furthermore, just like cognitions in dreams and the like, the inference of a Lord (*īśvara*) and so forth is also meaningful by virtue of the object appearing to one's own [consciousness]; thus, Prajñākaragupta’s statement denying that [inference] is merely a secret concealment. Alternatively, if it is argued that [the inference] is devoid of an object because it is produced by faulty causes such as fallacious logical marks (*liṅga*), then look at this: he himself, having rejected the idea that his own dream-cognitions and the like are produced by faulty causes, now accepts it here! This is truly laughable.
Even dream-cognition possesses the characteristics of valid cognition;
this is stated in the refutation of the inference of Īśvara and other such entities.
It should be observed—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 32: "Inference regarding Īśvara and so forth" [is discussed] in the section on the inference regarding Īśvara and so forth.

By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: "Cognition is not purposeful for inference and so forth, because it does not lead to anything other than what is already determined by itself"; for otherwise, such a consequence would apply even to dreams and the like.
Thus, there is no cognition of the non-existent for Prajñākaragupta, as it has been said:

If there were an absolute adherence to the external object as the sole reality, then because fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) would be denied, the establishment of all objects would follow even for those who propound contradictory meanings—
this is stated in Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 81.
Furthermore, this would constitute the point of defeat known as *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenet).

If [the opponent] were to argue that there is no fault because "this is my own tenet," we say: no. For according to the Mīmāṃsaka tenet, it is held that all cognition possesses an objective basis (*sālambana*);
however, the distinction here is that some maintain that the object of cognition is sometimes worldly (*laukika*) and sometimes non-worldly (*alaukika*).

If it is asked why everything is not mundane, [we reply: then why does another person's water in a mirage not serve for bathing and so forth, just like ordinary water? If you say it is because it arises in that way from its own specific causes, then what is its cause? If you say it is an unstable latent impression (*vāsanā*), then why is there not a single uniform latent impression everywhere, or some other kind? If you say it is because it is not perceived as such, then for that very reason, not every object—whether mundane or non-mundane—is real.

Now, if it is thought that because dream-activity is equal to waking activity, dream-activity is worldly, and therefore its effect is also of that same nature; then, since everything that exists is momentary—just as a jar—and sound exists (Hetubindu, p. 55), the cognition of a permanent God and so forth would also be an "activity" (arthakriyā) due to the equality of activity in establishing momentariness, and thus the collection of causes for that [cognition] would also be a real object.
If, however, this were not an activity, then it would not exist even in a dream.

If it is argued that [the same] would not occur even in the waking state, then the Buddhist's objection— that there would be no proof for momentariness and so forth— is based on a universalization of this lack of distinction.
The perception of an eternal Lord and so forth is merely worldly, [referring to] an entity such as Īśvara.
Others maintain that in dreams there is *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension), because that which is situated in one place appears as being in another place.
If it is asked why this [misapprehension] does not occur everywhere, the answer is: no, because it is not so perceived.

For just as in the world it is understood that the sun, though in another place, appears as if joined to the mountain at dawn, it is not likewise understood that the mountain, though in another place, appears as being in that [sun's] place.

If, however, this insistence is that "the same [nature] must exist everywhere," then just as in inference an indistinct universal form appears through the superimposition of the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), otherwise there would be no activity toward that object based on it—so too, in every cognition, the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) appears as something else superimposed upon it, and in another case, something else appears superimposed elsewhere; thus, others argue, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the exclusion of non-existence (*asattvavyāpti*). This will be examined immediately thereafter;
therefore, that is not the first position.
Comparison: "Let it be, then, that there is erroneous cognition (viparītakhyāti); for what is seen at a previous time is perceived as belonging to that [present] time... (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra*, p.
195). Therefore, the Jains and others hold that erroneous cognition should be accepted by the wise.
—Nyāyamañjarī, p.
173; Nyāyakumudacandra, p. 66:
"By virtue of being in the location of the sun."
This statement is meaningless, for [the particular] does not appear elsewhere as something superimposed upon the particular through inference.

Even in the second case, having perceived the absence of external objects in a dream, one would have to rely on this inference when establishing their absence elsewhere: "All cognitions are without an objective basis (nirālambana), because they are cognitions, like a dream-cognition" (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra* 3.331).

In this regard, the following is considered: if being a condition (*pratyayatva*) is not pervaded by its own probandum (*sādhya*) in its entirety, how can the probandum be established from it? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, on the other hand, it is pervaded, how can it be so when it is not cognized? If its cognition is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), that is the very same fault; otherwise, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason by this very [cognition]. By this, inference (*anumāna*) has also been examined.

Now, inference is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because its object is the exclusion of all cognitive objects; rather, it is so because it excludes superimposition (*samāropa*). This would indeed be the case if that [exclusion] were established by some other means of valid cognition, but this is not so, as will be demonstrated.

Furthermore, just as the Buddhist does not establish the non-existence of external objects everywhere by means of the example of dreams, so too, if another [proponent] were to establish the non-existence of consciousness by means of the example of the form of the apprehended (*grāhyākāra*), how could there be the establishment of mere consciousness (*saṃvedanamātra*)—that upon which the Buddhist’s reliance rests?
The meaning is that even in the waking state, just as in the dream state, there is no external object; the point is that in this conceptualization,
one has fully realized during the waking condition that [the cognition] is pervaded by its own probandum.
The inference for [the existence of] an objective support is established by means of the example of a dream.
The Jaina and others claim that [the term] "not" (na) is meaningless;

let it be so, for it is as follows: that which is determined by a state of erroneous perception is not ultimately real, just like the two moons perceived by one with jaundice; and cognition and so forth are determined by a state of erroneous perception.

In this case as well, would something other than ultimate existence be established, or would its mere absence be established? Regarding that, the discussion concerning the second alternative will occur under the first and fourth sub-alternatives;

however, in the first alternative, the same fault as before applies, for there can be no establishment of error within a state of universal delusion, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
In every instance of error, their error itself is not established, since it would have as its object a perception that is non-concordant with reality—
*Nyāyaviniścaya* 1.

54. [Objection: But surely, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of anything by anything is admitted, nor is anything established from anything whatsoever. Rather, just as in worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), for one who maintains the existence of external objects, because smoke is seen in one place due to fire, that [fire] is [inferred] everywhere and at all times from that alone and not from anything else, and because smoke is seen, fire is inferred—so too, the subject at hand is practiced by another. If this is argued, it has been said here: "The establishment of the goal for all would be through the authority of a reliable person" (Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 81).

For they too could say: "We do not establish the pervasion (vyāpti) of anything by anything; rather, because we observe the coexistence of 'being an effect' and so forth with 'having an intelligent cause' and so forth in the case of jars and the like, and because that [coexistence] is observed elsewhere, the probandum is inferred. Thus, the definition of a logical mark (liṅga)—such as 'the reason is a property of the subject' (Hetubindu, verse 1)—need not be stated, since there is nothing to be excluded. If you think that in this way there would be no ultimate establishment of the probandum, that [objection] is equally applicable elsewhere as well.

If that [duality] is not ultimately real there, then what is ultimately real? If it is the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvedanādvaita*), no; because the appearance of duality has been established, this position too is not tenable, as in the case of a kitchen hearth and so forth.

Just like smoke from fire, even by the Naiyāyikas and others, [the self] is the subject of dispute as the cause that supports cognition because it is an effect; whatever is an effect is supported by a cause of cognition, just like a jar and so forth—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 382.
In regard to the body, the instruments [of perception], the world, and so forth,

the reason (hetu) is that which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds because of the rule of inseparable connection (avinābhāva), and others are therefore fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
— Hetubindu, verse 1; Pramāṇavārttika, chapter 3, verse 1.

In the third alternative, there is no absolute negation of the object, because its occasional existence is not negated; for when there is doubt as to whether "this is a post or a person," there is no certainty that "it is not a person," due to contradiction. [The opponent objects: "Let it be so; nevertheless, what is the use of that which is a cause for non-activity? For the external object is desired precisely for the sake of activity. [The author replies: How can there be activity for you in mere consciousness alone? Because, given the doubt regarding the external object, there is doubt even with respect to that [consciousness].

Or how could there be doubt regarding the object? If it is argued that this is because its appearance is observed even in the absence of the object, as in dreams and the like; [we reply: in that case, its non-existence alone is logical, not doubt. Otherwise, how could everything be exactly so after one has perceived something through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which are themselves non-conceptual? Even here, doubt would be more appropriate.

Furthermore, on what basis is the non-existence of external objects established in a dream? If you say it is because [the Yogācāra] himself does not accept [external objects], because it contradicts the negation of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, or because of the acceptance by others;
[we reply: no, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For just as the non-existence of that [object] in that [place] has been admitted by the opponent, so too has it been admitted regarding the mode of momentariness and the like; thus, there would be doubt everywhere, even concerning momentariness and so forth.

If you say, "There is doubt even regarding a dream," from what does that arise? If you say, "From not seeing it," how is there non-seeing? For if there were seeing, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If you say, "Because it deviates (*vyabhicāra*) from that," then what is this that is seen in both cases, such that this is so? If that is the case, then the absence of the object is not absolute; therefore, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is also not tenable.
Even in the case of mere cognition accompanied by an external object,
even though the object is non-existent.
At the time of dreaming,
there is an absence of external objects in the dream.

If the non-existence of external objects is accepted even in the fourth alternative, then just as there is a transcendence of the alternatives of existence and non-existence regarding the external, so too there would be a transcendence of the alternatives of self-cognition and cognition of another regarding consciousness; thus, nothing at all would remain.

Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because there is the cognition of a feeling through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) independent of anything else—how is it free from fault? Because even in the case of self-awareness, since it transcends the conceptual alternatives of existence and non-existence, its establishment is not achieved in the same way as an object; otherwise, there would be no negation of the object. Furthermore, in the other [opponent’s] position, the conventional definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—such as "non-discrepant cognition" and so forth—or the ultimate definition—"the illumination of an unknown object"—is undermined by the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, because there is no distinction between the two cases.

Therefore, how can this person remain composed while asserting non-duality through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) even as he speaks of no distinction between the internal and the external? If you maintain that what is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) is intended to exist within self-awareness to the exclusion of external objects, then by the same logic, what was seen at another time [by someone else] should also be accepted as real to the exclusion of what was seen in a dream by another. Thus it is established: "The fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the ascertainment of the object" (*arthaviniścayaḥ pramāṇasya phalam*).

Furthermore, "one's own ascertainment (*svaniścayaḥ*), however, is established for one who has accepted self-awareness," as stated in *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.19 and elsewhere: "that which is established without dependence on another" (*na parāpekṣam*). *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.1.1.9.
And the establishment of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) will be demonstrated in such passages as this;
see page 12, note 7.
Even for a proponent of the non-duality of consciousness, such as a Jaina and others, during the waking state...
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what follows from that?"—to this he says: "of the cognizer," and so forth.

One who cognizes—that is, one who makes an object his own by taking it as a content—is a "cognizer" (*pratipattṛ*), namely the person. That which is required by him, the cognition (*jñāna*) which is relied upon for the cognition of both self and other, is alone the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Indeed, it is not the preceding [cause], such as indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*) or sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and the like, because the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) denotes a cause.

Indeed, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the production of that result [of cognition] than [the cognition itself], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is asked: "But surely there is no cognizer (*pratipattṛ*) other than the specific instances of the cognition of blue and so forth, such as pleasure and the like; how then can it be said 'of the cognizer'?"—[we reply: No; the refutation of this will be explained in the section on the proof of the soul (*jīva*). Why such eagerness? Thus spoke Prajñākara, the proponent of the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*):

Comparison: Therefore, since there is no other cognition in this world apart from pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth, it is logical to conclude that blue and so forth are self-cognizing just like pleasure and so forth— *Pravartikālaṅkāra* 3.508.
Since the first half of the verse is easy to understand, he states the meaning of the second half along with its reasoning, beginning with "yathāsvam" (according to their respective [objects]).

Its meaning is as follows: the *vyavasāya* (ascertainment) of an object of cognition (*prameya*) such as a jar is a definitive determination, not merely a bare apprehension; for if it were mere apprehension, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) operating upon what has already been seen.

The words "that which" and "from which" are to be supplied [to the text], meaning: that alone—and nothing else—is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), depending upon or arising from which [ascertainment occurs].

Regarding the statement that "the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) occurs in some cases through direct perception," Dharmottara has said: "Its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) exists only where it produces this [ascertainment]. This is refuted; they demonstrate this by means of the particle *eva* (only), for the determination of the object of knowledge does not arise either by depending upon that [perception] or from it. As will be stated right here: "Because there is no difference, [there would be] a memory of the similar" (*Siddhiviniscaya* 1.7), and so forth.

Or, let it be granted that there is a conceptual determination (*vyavasāya*) arising from non-conceptual perception; nevertheless, showing that even so it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he says: "from itself" (*svataḥ*).

This means from its own self, not through a succession [of cognitions], because it does not generate a conceptualization, due to the aforementioned fault (as stated in *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.2) and the fault that will be mentioned later, and because such a consequence would apply to inference as well. For this reason:
By this, the [notion of] sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth has also been considered.

If, then, that from which the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya-vyavasāya*) arises by itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then—given that indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) is not independent of the primary transformation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pradhāna-pariṇāma*)—indirect knowledge would never be a means of valid cognition by itself. To this he says: "according to its own nature" (*yathāsvam*).

This word "own" (*sva*) denotes the nature of the cognition itself; the meaning is that "according to its own nature" (*yathāsvam*) refers to that from which the determination of that [object] occurs together with the determination of itself.

The comparison of proximity and so forth—the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) being ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛtti*, p.
18. In that context, the establishment of the property of the subject upon the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) occurs either through perception or through inference—*Hetubindu*, p. 53.
In whichever part, such as blue and so forth,
there is conceptual cognition for one who is non-conceptual.
From non-conceptual vision, there is the ascertainment of the objects of knowledge in the treatise.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that knowledge is indirect (*parokṣa*); the Naiyāyikas maintain that knowledge is perceived by another cognition (*jñānāntara-pratyakṣa*); and the Sāṃkhyas maintain that knowledge is a transformation of primordial matter (*pradhāna-pariṇāma*).

Others, however, having introduced a different [objection], explain this as follows: "If that which produces the determination is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then only the knowledge of an omniscient being would be a means of valid cognition. To this, he replies: "According to their respective [capacities]" (*yathāsvam*);
that is, without overstepping that which is suitable for each specific cognition to apprehend itself.
In this regard, because it is capable of being measured—that is, fit to be its own object of cognition—it is understood [as the means].

Now, one might argue: "Let that cognition not be the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); rather, since the object of cognition appears within the Person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is consciousness, like a cluster of stars, he alone is the instrument of knowledge. To this, he says: "Cognition" (*jñāna*)—meaning Mati, Śruta, Avadhi, Manaḥparyaya, and Kevala are cognition (Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.9).
9. That [cognition] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not the person, because the person is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and because [the person's] permanence has been refuted.

If it is argued: "The fruit of that [cognition] is the ascertainment (*vyavasāya*); it is not the cognition itself that is the *pramāṇa*, but rather [the cognition] which possesses the form of its object as its own cause," [we reply]: No. For then even the perception of a mirage, which is the cause for the superimposition of water and so forth, would result in being a *pramāṇa*. Consequently, from that [perception] too, the accomplishment of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) preceded by correct knowledge would occur; thus, the pursuit of a mirage by one seeking water and the like would not be improper. Yet such a pursuit is observed to be improper. Therefore, [the cognition] is indeed the *pramāṇa*.

Now, if you claim that there is no cognition other than that of water and so forth, whether occurring at the same time as or prior to the perception of a mirage and the like; then what is this careless statement? For [it contradicts] such passages as *pra.vā. 3.43*: "not by means of a cause of error," and likewise: "nor is there a simultaneous perception of partless atoms" from the conceptualization of blue and so forth. This too is a careless statement, for [it contradicts] *pra.vā. 2*: "because of the simultaneous functioning of the two minds."

133. "Let it be that there is the observation of the cause of that [object]; however, that [observation] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is not the cause for [purposeful] activity, whereas another [cognition] is a *pramāṇa* by virtue of being the opposite. To this, he says: "From another," etc.

Since that which is other than the result consisting of the ascertainment of its own object is "another" (*para*), when activity occurs with respect to that which has become the object, there is no non-contradiction—that is, no absence of disagreement—with it, because such a necessity (inevitability) is impossible.

For ordinary people do not understand—nor have they ever understood, nor will they ever understand—that "we have acted, we are acting, or we shall act" based on the perception of partless atoms that are distinct from one another.
This is because even in the state of habitual practice (*abhyāsa*), there is the perception of a single gross object, such as water, which pervades its constituent parts.

If it is argued: "But surely activity does not proceed even toward an object that has already produced its fruit, because that [fruit] is already being experienced; nor does it proceed toward a future object, because it has not yet appeared," we say: No, for we observe activity even in animals toward grass and other such things.
This will be demonstrated in the *Siddhiviniścaya* (1.5) and elsewhere, where it is stated that perception consists of a determinative nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*).

Granted that activity proceeds from such a vision, nevertheless, that [vision] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, even the cognition of water in a mirage would be a valid cognition.
If it is argued that "valid cognition is that which is non-contradictory," to this he replies with the words "from another," and so forth:

when there is activity based on a non-conceptual perception from another [source], the non-contradiction—which is the attainment of the perceived object—is necessarily impossible, because from the perception of partless, momentary atoms, there can be no attainment of something gross, unitary, and stable. If it is objected: "But even when activity proceeds from the fruit of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), there is no attainment of what was seen, because at that time [the seeing] has already passed away"; [we reply: No, for just as in the case of a single variegated cognition, there is no contradiction in some kind of identity between the perceived and the attained.
The commentators [state] in passages such as *siddhivi.* 1.10: "One will perform a bath here, seeing the single specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."

That which has as its fruit the determination of the object of cognition— the person himself, who is the ascertainment of self and other, and whose ascertainment thereof is the certainty regarding the object of knowledge.
The meaning is that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that knowledge which bears the form of the object that constitutes its own cause. This is comparable even to the perception of a mirage.
As stated in *Nyāyabindu* 1: "The accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by correct knowledge."
Nor would it be improper to follow that [interpretation], so writing it here again would be redundant;
unless, however, another quality were superimposed by means of a cause of error.
Or rather, the form of silver appears in mother-of-pearl because of the perception of a similarity in appearance— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.43.
"Because conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions arise simultaneously in the mind, or because their occurrence is so rapid, the deluded person determines them to be one"— *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.138.
Even from the result of the determination of one's own purpose, at the time of engagement...

If it is argued: "Surely there may be no non-contradiction regarding momentariness, partlessness, and so forth, because those perish; however, there would be non-contradiction regarding blue and the like, where identity is superimposed between the perceived and the attained," [the author] says here: "From another," and so forth.

The phrase "from another" has its meaning explained previously, as does the word "in activity. Because it is impossible for that rule of non-contradiction—which consists in the existence [of the object] everywhere within the range of perception—to apply to blue and the like, there is no connection [between the two] when there is a distinction between preceding and succeeding moments.

With respect to a person engaged in worldly practice (*vyavahārin*), even in that case, through non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) upon repeated practice, perception would become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding what is to come; otherwise, for one who has recognized deviation—as in the case of the cognition of yellow in a conch shell—this so-called inference would be useless, since the cognition of yellow in a conch shell would not be a valid means of knowledge regarding its actual form (*saṃsthāna*). Thus, let it be as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* (p. 5):

"The appearance [of an object] is a valid means of knowledge only with respect to that [object], and its connection [with that object] is a valid means of knowledge only there, not elsewhere"; in this way, the status of being a valid means of knowledge or its opposite belongs to a single [cognition].

If it is argued that "let that [conceptual nature] also exist from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)," then what is this "conventional usage" other than the very consideration [of the definition]? For [the definition] begins with: "Perception is free from conceptual construction" (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍhaṃ*, *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.123).
If that were the case, the statement regarding its fourfold division would be improper, because such a division is impossible from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Therefore, this is incorrect: [the claim] that "one who acts after having determined the object by means of these two is not deceived regarding purposeful action," and [the claim] that "perception is a valid means of cognition because it prompts activity toward a future [object] through habituation.

Now, if it is argued: "Granted that perception is not directly the prompter of activity or the non-deceptive factor, nevertheless, because it generates such a conceptual construction (vikalpa), it too is of that nature"; to this he says: "Its being the cause thereof," and so forth.

[Objection: But has this point not already been stated by the passage beginning with "If [cognition] were established through the production of that [subsequent cognition]" (Siddhiviniścaya 1.2) and ending with "that very cognition" (Siddhiviniścaya 1.4), which explains that the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*); so what is the purpose of this [present argument]? [Reply: No; we offer it for the purpose of demonstrating another solution (*samādhi*).

For instance: the cause (*hetu*) of that aforementioned conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is its state of being (*bhāva*), which is its essence (*tattva*); this is just like [the cause] of perception (*darśana*), which consists of the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) with the object and so forth, beginning with the sense faculties (*indriya*). It is "like that" (*tadvat*).

This is what is meant: just as, because the eye, ear, and mind function without reaching their objects (*aprāpyakāritva*), contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is not the cause for their respective cognitions—just as the sense organ is not the cause for the cognition of a true dream—and thus in those cases neither contact nor the sense organ possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather the cognition itself; likewise, with respect to the cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever exists is momentary," perception (*darśana*) is not the cause, because it is absent therein. Therefore, perception is not the means of valid cognition in that case, but rather conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone.

Now, if there is perception [of all], then because of that perception of everything, the state of being an all-seeing one (sarvadarśitva) for everyone would be established without any means; otherwise, how could there be the comprehension of pervasion (vyāpti)—that is, the comprehension of a relation residing in two loci—given such statements as "pervasion is not limited" (*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vārttika* 2.1)?
For pervasion is never merely partial.

Now, if this [future object] is not accepted [as a valid object], how could there be inference, such that there would be two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If it is argued that it is accepted because it is so in worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), and if "all" is meant [to include that], then just as a means of valid cognition is accepted regarding a future object to be attained through worldly convention, so too must it be accepted in that case. Consequently, the cultivation of the path for that purpose would be useless, because that cultivation—which is of the nature of inference—would already exist even prior to [the attainment].

If it is argued that it is a conventional conceptual construction (*saṃvṛti-vikalpa*), then it is established that, like sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth, it serves as a non-pervasive cause (*avyāpi-hetu*) with respect to that [attainment].

Therefore, just as perception alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) everywhere because it occurs even when proximity and other conditions are excluded, so too, for this very reason, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) alone is the means of valid cognition because it excludes non-conceptual perception;
the non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) of non-conceptual perception has already been explained.
However, the cognition of a yellow conch and the like is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all, because there is no attainment of such purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

If the accomplishment of purposeful action consists merely in the [perceived] configuration, then another cognition—namely inference—is the valid means of knowledge; for instance, a manifestation of such a kind is never devoid of configuration.
Since this has been observed elsewhere, it is an inference, and thus it is so.

One who has at some time perceived an instance of deviation is indeed deceived because of the discrepancy regarding what was intended; however, one who is aware of the possibility of deviation proceeds after deliberation. First, the mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is obtained, while regarding the other [the internal object], there is either doubt or error. Therefore, there is inference with respect to the configuration, and doubt with respect to the other. These two cognitions—one valid and one invalid—constitute this pair.
The existence of non-contradiction is established by perception alone. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p. 5)
The remainder [of the statement] is: "Conceptual construction, which relies upon names, is to be personally realized by all";
and that [construction] is fourfold—Nyāyabindu 1.
Through perception and inference, due to the distinctions between sensory perception, mental perception, self-reflexive awareness, and yogic perception.
This has been extracted from: Tattvopaplava, p. 29;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 468; Nyāyaviniścaya-vivaraṇa-prakaraṇa, pp. 256, 532.

Comparison: Where there is engagement even without conceptualization due to extreme habituation, there perception is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it generates a non-contradictory conceptualization that prompts action—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 218.
From "even perception" up to "thus."
Because they produce cognition even without contact, the eye, mind, and ear do not reach their objects— Abhidharmakośa 1.43.
Validity [belongs] to the perception free from conceptual construction regarding the object of pervasion, because pervasion has everything as its object.
Non-conceptual perception [occurs] regarding the object of pervasion which encompasses everything.
The remainder [of the argument] is that because there is no cognition of multiple forms, when the two natures are grasped, there is a cognition of their relation.

Regarding the path of selflessness (nairātmya) such as momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), or as it was stated by Prajñākaragupta—"Because it prompts one toward what is yet to come, perception (*darśana*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when there is direct practice; when there is no such practice, inference arises therein"—to that he says: "Furthermore, its being the cause of that," and so forth.

The existence—that is, the reality—of that cause, which is the conceptualization of inference, is "again" (punah); this term serves to include another alternative in both cases. Just as with sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth, the same applies to "that-like" (*tadvat*):
for just as sensory contact with an object and so forth is not the cause of inference, so too is [mere] perception (*darśana*).

If, on the other hand, the sense organs and so forth are not the cause of that [cognition] because they are insentient, how can vision be sentient? If it is argued that it is so because it manifests by itself (*svataḥ pratibhāsanāt*), no; for you do not admit the manifestation of that [vision] as something distinct from the body, pleasure, and so forth, or from blue and so forth. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the manifestation of the body and so forth is conceptual (*vikalpaka*). Thus, these are the snares of the opponent. Now, if it is argued that sentience belongs to another [entity], then pleasure and so forth would likewise be insentient, since the Sāṃkhya admits that very thing [of them being distinct from consciousness].
Thus it is established that perception, unlike sensory contact and the like, is not the cause of inferential conceptualization.
Regarding the comparison: where there is a movement toward the future, inference is accepted as the means of knowledge;
whereas when [the object] is present and exceeds [the limits of the senses], perception is the means of knowledge.
—the Buddhist should look at *Pra-vārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 218—p. 19, note 14.
[The phrase] "of the Jaina system" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

If it is argued that, because it is non-erroneous, perception alone is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in all cases, whereas conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not, because it is erroneous—here he says: "Even though it is non-erroneous," and so forth.

This is its meaning: if that perception [of a pillar, etc. were non-erroneous (*abhrānta*) in the form of a gross pillar and so forth, then—since there is a deviation due to the appearance of grossness in the case of distant, sparse hairs—the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*) could not be established on the basis of such an appearance. Furthermore, this would contradict the statements in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (3.196): "In this regard, the meaning is as follows... and "Everything is erroneous with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*)," as well as the fact that [the perception] would lack freedom from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*), because it would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
Now, it might be argued that it is "non-erroneous" because there is no other state that is non-erroneous, and thus the term is meaningless.

Or, if it is said to be so designated by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then its object must be stated. If you say it is the waking state and so forth, it has already been stated here that "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) is difficult to find; thus, one enters into a dilemma before the opponent. Therefore, he does not obtain [the truth], for that [waking state] is not what is called "non-erroneousness" in that [ultimate] sense.

Having granted [the opponent's position], it is said: even if there is non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*), because of the connection with the term "from another" (*anyataḥ*) which has acquired the sense of transformation (*pariṇāma*), it is understood as "of another.
To the question "In what way is that so?", he says: "in every respect" (*sarvathā*);
that is, not only in the manner of blue and so forth, but also in the manner of the distinction between preceding and succeeding moments, and so on—in every respect.

If one asks what follows from that being the case, he says: because validity is established through ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), and because the status of another [cognition] as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) depends upon this, the nature of reality—which is to say, the nature of ascertainment—must be accepted for a means of valid knowledge that possesses non-erroneous cognition, since it is through the establishment of reality [that validity is known]. If one asks how the establishment of validity occurs, he says: "in some way" (*kathañcit*).

This means in a manner such as [the perception of] blue and so forth, and not in a manner such as momentary transformation (*pratikṣaṇapariṇāma*) and the like; for in that regard, there is no practical activity (*vyavahāra*) based on perception for those engaged in worldly conduct.

If one thinks, "I do not see this [object], such as its moment-to-moment transformation," that is because an insufficiency of inference would result; for there is a contradiction between the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) and the superimposition (*samāropa*), since the former does not effect the exclusion of the latter. Therefore, it is not purposeful [to claim otherwise].

Now, if—transcending conventional usage—one desires the establishment of that [object] even by that mode [of perception], then the principle is already established: "Validity is by way of conventional usage" (*prāmāṇyaṃ vyavahāreṇa*, *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.7). Etc.

Furthermore, in the non-duality that appears as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the occurrence of momentary destruction and so forth is impossible, because that [non-dual reality] is accepted as being beyond all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, just as momentary destruction is accepted through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), so too must perception therein be validated by that very same [convention]; thus it was well said: "in some way" (*kathañcit*).

[Objection: But surely this meaning has already been shown by the third explanation of the passage beginning with "from another" (*anyataḥ*); so what is the purpose of this? [Response: No; for previously it was stated: "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory... (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.7).
With reference to this [definition], and now with reference to *Nyāyabindu* 1.4, which states "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," there is no fault;
for he considers that both of these [definitions] apply to definitive cognition (*nirṇaya*) and not elsewhere.

Just as hairs appear to a Buddhist to be in a dense mass even though they are not actually in contact when at a distance, so too are atoms; thus, there is no contradiction—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 296, 287.
The initial manifestation of atoms as mutually distinct occurs through conceptual cognition, whereas their appearance as a dense mass arises from that same conceptual consciousness—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 336.
In the definition of perception as "cognition having an object," the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) is included for the sake of the object of perception.
The term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is stated because, if its object were something like a pillar perceived while awake, it would be conceptual (*vikalpaka*); this is the intended meaning.
The word "if" (*yadi*), however, appears to be redundant.
The term "tā" is the technical designation for the sixth case ending (genitive),
[referring here to] the exclusion of superimposition through the inference of momentariness.
"Since one accepts the non-duality of appearances, surely this [state] proceeds as the dissolution of all cognitions; here there is no arising of cognition"—*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 293.

If it is argued: "If the establishment of reality (*tattvasiddhi*) occurs through conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) alone, then there would be no identity with that [reality]; what fault is there in this? To this he says: "In practice," and so forth. Otherwise—that is, by means other than the mode of determination (*nirṇaya*) which constitutes the establishment of reality, namely by way of non-conceptuality (*avikalpakatva*)—that [establishment] would be fruitless; thus the previously mentioned statement is here brought to completion.

That which is other than that is fruitless, meaning it lacks a purpose because it is of no use anywhere; for this very reason, it is "non-establishing," i.e., not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because [it] would not be distinguished from, nor differ from, a non-existent thing such as a donkey's horn"—this is to be connected with the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
Or else, "having the nature of a definitive conclusion" (*nirṇayātmakatva*) is the technical name for that which ends in the nominative case;
the meaning is that it is something ending in the nominative case.
The meaning is that the word *anyataḥ*, ending in the ablative case, is connected here with the form *anyat*, which ends in the nominative case.

Now, if it is argued that "the nature of being a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) consists in the apprehension of its own object," and if it is further asked whether that is impossible, [the author] says here: "akiñcitkara" and so forth.
That which does nothing is "akiñcitkara. It is established that the perception during sleep and so forth is independent of anything else (Siddhiviniścaya 1).

24. This and so forth will be explained in the commentary on the *kārikā*: doubt (*saṃśaya*) is the cognition "Is it a post or a person?"; error (*viparyaya*) is the perception of a person in what is a post, or a post in what is a person. That which produces these two is "that-producer" (*tatkara*). Furthermore, there is a *dvandva* compound; [the nature of] being of the essence of ascertainment (*nirṇaya-ātmakatva*) occurs through the exclusion—that is, the rejection—of those two, and not otherwise.
The word "puruṣe" (in a person) is written twice here.
If it is argued that "the exclusion of that [doubt] exists even in non-conceptual perception when there is a dependence on blue and so forth," to this he says: "Otherwise," etc. The sense is:

by whatever manner the exclusion of that occurs in relation to blue and so forth, therefore its being of the nature of that must be accepted as established in reality; thus it is settled that there is the exclusion of doubt and the like.

[Objection: But surely, since there is the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.5), "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the illumination of an object not yet known," perception alone is the means of valid cognition because it apprehends what has not been previously grasped, whereas conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not, due to its being erroneous (*viparyaya*). To this, [the author] says: "In regard to that which is not yet cognized," and so forth.

"Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that consciousness which, not being manifested by another means of knowledge and being unapprehended, apprehends—that is, determines—an object; this is also [the definition]. Thus, it is not only in the manner previously stated that the determination of an object independent of anything else is expressed. He states the fault in not accepting this [definition] with the words "otherwise," etc. "Otherwise" means in a manner different from the mode already described; he considers that if one were to say that only a perception which apprehends an unapprehended object is valid cognition, and not a determinative cognition (*nirṇaya-jñāna*), [it would be incorrect].

Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): since perception itself would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even regarding momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth—just as it is for blue and so forth—inference of that [momentary destruction] would be purposeless. Therefore, because it would lead to such an over-extension, the formulation of the words is "the determination of an object not yet determined.
For this very reason, a means of valid cognition has an unapprehended object (*anadhigata-viṣaya*), because it apprehends what has already been grasped (*gṛhīta-grāhitva*). (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p. 19)

As for the inference that "everything is momentary," this point—that because [if it were otherwise] there would be the consequence of the non-operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding what is perceived—will be established by this [very argument]. So what is the purpose of this [present discussion]? Therefore, it is explained differently: it is the very determination (*nirṇīti*) of objects such as jars—which consist of stable, gross, inherent qualities and parts—that is recognized as the apprehension of an object not previously apprehended.

If, on the contrary, another means of valid cognition distinct from that were postulated as the apprehender of an unapprehended object, then yet another of the same kind would have to be postulated after that, and yet another after that; thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), which is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, it is stated that [valid cognition] is the determination of an object not yet determined.

As for what was further stated—"that is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*)—in that context, "it is a means of valid cognition because by means of it something is correctly measured (*pramīyate*)," which refers to the instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*). And it is logical that this [instrumental factor] is indeed the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) with respect to the action of determining its own object;
showing this, he says: "of that which has merely been apprehended," and so forth.

Of what kind of [cognition] is there the mere perception of the form of its own cause? To this he says: "of that which is non-discrepant" (*visaṃvādakasya*). Because the establishment of the most effective means of proof (*sādhakatamatva*) is untenable for a cognition that perceives partless, multiple, momentary atoms while leading one to obtain a gross, unitary, and stable jar or the like—which is thus deceptive—the determination of that [non-discrepant cognition] is being stated.
Furthermore, this qualifier "of that which is non-discrepant" should also be understood as a reason (*hetu*).

From this, the following meaning follows: mere apprehension (*adhigati-mātra*) is not the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the realization of its own object, because it is subject to contradiction (*visaṃvādakatva*), like the vision of two moons; therefore, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Consequently, that [subsequent cognition] alone is designated as such.
To state yet another reason, he says: "by another means of proof," and so forth.

Apart from the mere accomplishment of apprehension (*adhigati*), conceptual cognition regarding blue and so forth, or inference regarding momentariness and so forth, requires something else subsequent to it—namely, that object (*gocara*) or domain (*viṣaya*) which, in some cases, has as its domain a dependence upon another means of proof (*sādhana*). Even according to the reading of the sūtra, "another means of proof is required," for that which has such an object dependent [on another means], the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) is untenable; therefore, its determination (*nirṇīti*) is here stated. In this case as well, as before, the qualification beginning with "means of proof" (*sādhana*) should be understood as the logical reason (*hetu*).

For example, mere apprehension (*adhigata-mātra*) is not the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the realization of reality (*tattva-pratipatti*), because it falls within the domain of dependence upon other means of accomplishment, just like sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth. Therefore, it is well said: "Non-determination (*anirṇīti*) is what is expressed," referring to the conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) that takes the form "this is blue."

If it is argued that [in the inference] "everything is momentary because it exists," and so forth, although there is indeed the apprehension of a general object (*sāmānya-artha*) not previously apprehended, there is nevertheless no apprehension of a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) not previously apprehended; therefore, since there is no apprehension [of the latter], that [inference] is designated by the definition "a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which apprehends an object not previously apprehended," because in that case the word "object" (*artha*) denotes the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and thus it is perception (*darśana*) alone that is being designated—[the author] says here: "That," and so forth.

By that mere apprehension— even though there is an apprehension (pariccheda) of a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which consists of an object capable of causal efficiency and has not been apprehended by another cognition nor made an object of it—

the particle "api" indicates an admission that perception is certainly not observed to apprehend a unique particular that was either previously apprehended by another [cognition] or is otherwise [unapprehended].

What is established in that regard? To this he says: because there would be the consequence of non-occurrence for another means of knowledge—inference—regarding momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) once it has been made an object by perception, just as in the case of blue and so forth, due to the fear of grasping what has already been grasped; therefore, its determination is indeed stated.

For in this way, by the ascertainment of the previously unascertained states of being blue and being momentary, the quality of having a novel object (*apūrvārthatā*) is obtained for both conceptual construction and inference; such is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "Granted that there may be no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operating there because of the certainty of momentary destruction which has not yet been ascertained; however, [it must be another means of cognition] because it performs the exclusion of the superimposition (*samāropa*) of non-momentariness upon what is momentary. To this, he says: "In the case of the similar," and so forth. When a thing that is similar—that is, like—has been seen through perception, there is a superimposition, which is a specific kind of erroneous cognition. In the exclusion or removal of that [superimposition], there is no distinction or difference between conventional [cognition] and inference—that is, between the conceptualization following perception and the inference. If [you claim] it is inference, then the meaning is that conventional cognition would also be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because there is no absence of what has not been apprehended, that determination appears to be meaningless by the term "apprehender of an unapprehended object."
In the case of momentary phenomena,
conventional conceptualization is the means of valid cognition.

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that, whereas there is no superimposition of non-momentariness upon what is momentary, there is such a superimposition of non-blueness upon the blue—such that [the inference] is said to be 'equal' for the purpose of excluding that [superimposition]? The intention here is as follows: Just as inference is purposeful because it excludes the superimposition of identity between preceding and succeeding moments—which are distinct from one another—so too, by the statement "the five groups of consciousness have a composite object (*sañcitālambana*) in the middle moment, which has a gross and unitary form," conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) would also be purposeful through the exclusion of the superimposition of perceiving atoms.
The opponent, demonstrating the distinction between those two by way of excluding the superimposition of water upon a mirage, says "directly," etc. [He means:

its arising is from direct experience—that is, from perception—without mediation, and not from the object, which is a mere conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). He thinks that because it imitates the object that is the domain of activity produced by experience, its operation is not distinct from that [experience].
To this, he states the reply: "A great offense! (i.e., a grave error).
This is a ground for ridicule, because it is expressed even in the absence of the slightest fault;

furthermore, since that [cognition] arises from that [object], its status as having an object is thoroughly established. Moreover, its having the same object—due to the necessary connection with the object, as in the case of inference—is not contradictory, just as in the case of the cognitions of an omniscient being and others. And here too, there is a distinction of mental continua (*santāna*) between the omniscient and non-omniscient, and there is conventional usage [based on this].
Concluding with the words "of the cognizer" (*pratipattuḥ*) and so forth, he says:

"The subsequent conceptual cognition (*uttaraṃ vikalpajñānaṃ*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that subsequent [cognition] has the nature of a means (*sādhanabhāvāt*), that is, because it is the cause; but it is certainly not the case that the preceding [factors], such as sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) or perception (*darśana*), are the means of valid cognition.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Even in the case of inference," and so forth.

This is not only the case with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), but by the same reasoning stated above, it follows that even in inference (*anumāna*), the cognition that has the appearance of the means of proof (*sādhana*) would be the cause [of the result] and thus the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the object to be reached; inference itself would not be the valid cognition because it does not take the object of comprehension (*prameya*) as its direct object, a principle that applies elsewhere as well.
This refers to the superimposition (*samāropa*) characterized by the attribution of oneness (*ekatva*) which pervades that [inference].
The established tenet is that the five groups of consciousness have accumulated [atoms] as their object— *Pramāṇavārttikamanorathaṇī*, 2.194.

It appears that [the statement] "like the subsequent cognition of an omniscient being which contradicts the continuum of conventional and inferential [cognitions]" is stated twice; and what was said by Prajñākara is also pointless: "In the state of cultivation, perception is non-conceptual; at other times, inference is the means of valid cognition because it is that which prompts action."
Furthermore, since a definitive conclusion (nirṇīti) is of no use anywhere and since no other alternative is possible, it lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (apramāṇatā);
for a means of valid cognition is said to be that which impels one toward what is to be avoided or what is to be adopted.
And in that regard, regarding the initiation of action, cognition alone is primary;

even though the object to be realized has not been apprehended, it is nonetheless a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it initiates action therein. Just as it will be demonstrated that in inference there is no acceptance of the actual nature of the thing (*vastu-svarūpa*) despite its non-perception, so too, one does not initiate action from the eyes and other sense organs without cognition; rather, even without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one initiates action through the intellect (*buddhi*) by virtue of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

Therefore, regarding the objects of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, only the preceding cognition (*dhī*) is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it initiates action, not conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the like;

however, where there is no repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), only inference (*anumāna*) is [the means], not recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and so forth. Thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 22, 218.
In that context, showing the utility of determining what constitutes "non-repetition" when repetition is [otherwise] assumed, he says: "of one whose nature is resolute," and so forth.
