This has been extracted from the *Pramāṇapaddhati*, page 54: "the impression (*saṃskāra*) or indeed the memory (*smṛti*) of the perception of one whose nature is resolute."
"The impression (*saṃskāra*) [arises] from the perception of one whose nature is resolute determination" (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, Prastāvanā, p.
493; p. 521). [This occurs] when there is a perceived object that is of the same class as what was previously seen, and not otherwise, as in the case of momentariness and so forth.

Due to the proficiency gained through repeated practice of seeing, the context, and other factors, when the awakening of the memory of an impression of a similar perceived object occurs, the pursuit of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—even regarding momentary destruction and the like—is untenable without an inherent resolute determination, because there is no distinction [between such objects] and [ordinary objects] like blue and so forth.

This is its meaning: the *adhyāhāra* (supplementation) is that from the prior perception (*dṛṣṭi*) of both the means of pleasure and the pleasure itself, there arises a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is the seed of memory (*smṛtibīja*) and a transformation of the self (*ātmapariṇāma*).
Or rather, memory (*smṛti*)—that is, recollection—is produced from perception.

If it is objected: "But perception is the latent impression, and from that [impression] memory arises, not perception," we reply: no; there is no fault, because the subsequent perception arises from that [impression] acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*).

[Objection: But surely this single word "dṛṣṭi" (perception) cannot convey this meaning [of both perception and recollection]. [Response: Through repetition and connection, there is an understanding of a distinction because a single perception operates in both cases.

If it is asked, "Where then do recollection and its cause, perception, occur?"—to this he says: "The object perceived" (*dṛṣṭa*) refers to that which has been made an object by the perception that is the cause of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

In that regard, the subsequent perception gives rise to a memory which is its effect; otherwise, how could there be the cognition "this was seen by me"? By this, he demonstrates that the impressions (*saṃskāra*), the perceptions (*darśana*) preceding and following, and the memory have a single object. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in what is similar to what was seen"—that is, something which is both "seen" and "similar" (to the previous) with respect to the subsequent individual—[the question arises] "whence does that impression come? To this, he says: "from the perception."

To the question, "Where there is a mental impression (saṃskāra), memory arises from the perception of that very thing; but from where does that [impression] itself come? he says: "From perception" (dṛṣṭeḥ).

Where does that [recognition] occur? To this he says: "In a similar one"—that is, in a subsequent particular individual that is similar to the object of a previous perception seen among its own kind. What is meant is this: for one who has once perceived an individual instance of water as a cause for bathing and so forth, and in whom a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has been deposited, there arises a memory upon seeing another instance similar to it when a similar thing is perceived. By this, he explains that the previous and subsequent perceptions, the impressions, and the memory all have a common, similar object.
From direct perception, memory arises;
this is the meaning of the word "dṛṣṭi."
Others, however, explain it as: "a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) [arises] from what is seen, and memory [occurs] regarding that which belongs to the same class as what was seen.
Whether this meaning is thereby obtained or not must be considered by the commentators.

Furthermore, if the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) were produced by what is seen, then the memory must also occur with respect to that very same object, according to the principle that "memory [occurs] regarding what has been experienced.
For it is not logical that there should be a memory in the western ocean—similar to which the impression was deposited by the sight of the eastern ocean.
To the question, "Of what kind of seeing? he says: "Of that which consists of ascertainment (*vyavasāya*), that is, of that which is of the nature of a definitive judgment (*nirṇaya*)."

Why is this so? To this he says: "Not otherwise"—that is, there is no latent impression (*saṃskāra*) or memory of that perception which occurs through another mode, namely the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Where is this like? To this he says: "Like momentariness and so forth";
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities such as partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) are included; it is just like that case.

But surely it should be stated that its mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is nothing other than memory; what then is the purpose of the word "or" (*vā*), since the conjunction [of other factors] is understood even without it? No; there is no fault, because it serves to include those things not explicitly mentioned.
For by this word, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), inference through elimination (*ūha*), inference (*anumāna*), and so forth, which were not previously mentioned, are included.

From this, the following sequence of meanings is obtained: first, there is memory upon seeing an object that was previously seen as a means to pleasure, provided one possesses the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that prior experience; from that, there arises recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), such as "this is that very same thing" or "this is similar to that"; from that, there arises inference (*tarka*), namely, "this is capable of being a means to pleasure, just like the previous one"; from that, there arises inference (*anumāna*), namely, "by acting toward this object of inference, the attainment of pleasure will occur"; and from that, there follows purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and the attainment of the object.
And this will be stated later:
"only with respect to an object already perceived."
For memory is [based] on what has been experienced—*Hetubindu-ṭīkāloka*, p. 269;
memory is a recollection of an experienced object characterized by the form "that"—*Pramāṇapaddhati*, p.
69; memory is the non-forgetting of an experienced object—*Yogasūtra* 1.11.
Or [it is] of the vision or of the word.
Immediately after the man's memory,
having recollected through sensory cognitions and recognized, he reflects.
"One proceeds after having ascertained its specific varieties through direct confrontation" (Siddhiviniścaya 1.28).

Now, as for what was stated—that there is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) from the perception of pleasure and its means—this must be considered here: how is it cognized that "this is the means of pleasure" and "from this [means], this pleasure [arises]"? It cannot be from the perception of the means itself, because at that time the pleasure has not yet arisen, and what has not arisen cannot be grasped by the senses.
Nor can it be from the perception of the pleasure, because at the time of that [perception], the means has already passed away.
Nor can it be by means of their collection, because such a collection does not exist for two things that occur sequentially;
for it is a contradiction to have a single perception of what occurs at a prior time and what occurs at a subsequent time, since all things are momentary.

If, on the other hand, one maintains that the self understands "from this, that arises," even then, if [the self] were to do so by its mere existence, it would follow as an absurd consequence that [understanding] would also occur during states such as sleep or fainting.
Now, from the perspective of perception (*darśana*): as before, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows.

Therefore, the existence of that [pleasure] is not established by the perception of pleasure and its cause, nor by inference (*anumāna*); for since inference is preceded by that [perception], it would be absent in the absence of the latter.
By this, the claim that the production of successive mental impressions arises from prior perceptions and so forth is refuted;
[this follows] from the valid means of knowledge that pleasure and its means are subject to destruction.
Because a composite whole is impossible,
[inference]— being preceded by perception— is [sublated] by the means of valid cognition that is perception.

To this, the following reply is given: since the transformation into the apprehension of pleasure occurs precisely while the perception of the means to pleasure does not abandon its orientation toward grasping that [pleasure], there is no refutation;

and this will be stated right here in the second section: "Because each preceding [cognition] is the most effective instrument for the succeeding one, without abandoning its connection with the apprehension of its own object, just like a memory-cognition" (Siddhiviniścaya 2).
Thus, this is not non-evident, because there is the cognition: "From this entity, my state of pleasure arises.
It will be demonstrated that if one denies this, even the perception of pillars and the like would result in being impossible to observe.

That it simultaneously pervades or knows a single [object] in its manifold aspects, and not sequentially—this is supremely profound! Therefore, the perception of the causal relationship between pleasure and its means is established;
by this, the same has been considered for the self regarding the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of seeing and so forth.
This prohibition is illogical;
to state that a single self, being sequential, neither pervades nor knows various successive states is truly most astonishing.

Regarding the understanding of the relationship between cause and effect, as for what was further stated—that from what is the single objectivity of the impressions and memories resulting from the perceptions of preceding and succeeding moments known? That too has not been discarded by this [argument], because the understanding of that is possible through a self (*ātman*) that pervades the preceding and succeeding states; such is the meaning.

Now, let it be so; nevertheless, since pleasure is not apprehended at the time of activity, how could the causality of that which is being perceived there be understood, such that you would engage in activity? Or, if it were apprehended, there would be no activity, because the pleasure would have been attained at that very moment.

If the realization of pleasure occurs only after the activity has taken place, then activity would occur toward the realization of its means; and for that [realization], there would likewise have to be an activity as there is for the pleasure, or else no activity at all, because the pleasure would have been attained at that very moment. Alternatively, if the realization of pleasure occurs after the activity, then there is activity toward the realization of its means; and from that realization of pleasure, there follows the realization of its means—thus, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).

Now, upon the mere sight again of a previous means of pleasure or something similar to it, the thought occurs: "This is a means of pleasure because it is that very thing or because it is similar to it, just like the previous one. From this, activity ensues. But is this not inference? And if that [pleasure] is not being perceived, how can one understand its causality with respect to that [present object]? If it is argued that one understands it because the understanding of causality is inseparable from the understanding of the effect; to this it has been replied: "In that case, there would be no activity."

If, on the other hand, one cognizes that [object] not as something already established (*siddhatayā*), but rather as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatayā*); then, since it is non-existent insofar as it is to be accomplished, the cognition of it would be an act of extreme audacity. Thus, if it is argued that there is no engagement with it because no means of happiness is cognized, we say:
no; for the same dilemma as before applies regarding the two alternatives of either perceiving it or not.

If it is argued that "therefore, since there is no activity [of the self] from anything whatsoever, what is the use of postulating a self?"—to this it is replied: If the preceding and succeeding moments are not perceived through the perception of the object, how could there be a cognition of its continuity by means of those two, such that momentariness would be established through direct perception? Thus, this is not well-said: "Whatever appears in a certain way, that exists as such in ultimate reality and enters into conventional usage; for example, blue, appearing as blue, enters into usage exactly as it appears; and entities appear as momentary."

Now, if their perception occurs through the perception of the object and the perceiver, and their simultaneity with the object is likewise accepted by the opponent, then for those two as well, when their activity is established by two other preceding and succeeding moments, there must be a perception of those two by that [third moment], and again, when the activity of those two is established by others, there is a perception of them by that [fourth moment]. Thus, there would be a simultaneous perception of all moments in the entire continuum, and consequently, just as there is the apprehension of permanence, so too in the apprehension of momentariness, there would be the apprehension of the states of birth and death occurring simultaneously; therefore, one would be both born and dead at that very same time.

Now, just as there is a perception of those two [the object and its means] at their respective times through the perception of the visible object, so too is there a perception of pleasure; thus, there is no contradiction in engaging with the means to that visible object for the sake of pleasure,
such as water and the like.
The reading contained within these brackets appears to be a repetition,
as there is already an engagement with water and so forth.
Cognition with respect to water and other objects for the sake of pleasure.
At that very moment, because happiness is to be accomplished through its attainment,
[one should apply oneself] to the means of happiness.

The realization that the middle moment is devoid of the preceding and succeeding moments is derived from the root *ut-tṛd*, meaning "to injure," belonging to the *raudhādi* class; this form is produced because the grammatical operation (*gaṇakārya*) is not invariably obligatory.
It should be observed— page 2, note 10— that through the direct perception of the middle moment,
there is direct perception of the preceding and succeeding moments.
In that case, for the preceding and succeeding [moments], there would be the occurrence of a present moment;
yet even for those preceding and succeeding moments, there is either the state of being in flux or the state of being momentary, or rather, their absence [of such a state].

By means of perceiving the middle moment, there will be [the cognition] of the preceding [moment] as having been produced in the preceding moment, and of the succeeding [moment] as being in the process of production in the succeeding moment.

It might be thought: "The state of being presently manifest (*kadyattā*) belonging to the middle moment is its very nature [in relation] to the preceding and succeeding moments; therefore, even when those two are not seen, it is cognized simply from the perception of that [middle moment]. If that is so, why is its status as a cause of pleasure (*sukhahetutā*) not likewise cognized even when pleasure itself is not perceived? For that [status as a cause] is not different from that [manifestation]. If it is argued: "In that case, since everything would be cognized merely through the perception of the entity, the engagement of one seeking pleasure in the means to suffering, or the withdrawal from the means to pleasure, would not occur due to error," we reply: No; for this is equally true even regarding the apprehension of the state of being manifest, and thus the inference of it is useless.

If it is argued that since such conceptual superimposition (*samāropa-kalpanā*) occurs elsewhere as well, how can there be activity toward the means of pleasure? [The response is: How [can there be activity] regarding what is currently being experienced (*kradyattā*)? It is through the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavacchedāt*). The solution is the same in the present case: just as, because one observes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of existence (*sattva*) and so forth by momentariness in things like a jar, one infers momentariness in another thing from that [existence], so too, let the status of being a cause of pleasure be inferred from seeing again in some place a particular form (*ākāra-viśeṣa*) which has been observed to be pervaded by being a cause of previous pleasure.

Now, it may be argued: "If pleasure is not apprehended through inference, how can its causality be apprehended? And if it is apprehended, there would be no [subsequent] activity. To this it has been replied: "In that case, if the preceding and succeeding moments are not made objects of cognition, how could the 'presentness' belonging to the middle moment be perceived—by virtue of which superimposition might be removed?
And if they are made objects of cognition, then the continuum (santāna) exists only for a single moment, as do the preceding and succeeding ones."
Since it is of the very nature of the means [of proof] for water and so forth simply by being seen in the middle,
let it therefore be understood from the knowledge of the means itself.
From the realization that [the world] is a means to pleasure through its being produced, there follows the inference of momentariness.
The momentariness of sound and other phenomena is established when,
through the perception of the middle moment, both the preceding and succeeding moments are apprehended.

By this, the following objection raised by the opponent is also refuted: "Even if the causality of the visible object (such as pleasure) is perceived despite its not being seen, it cannot be determined by you either. Why? Because the same [lack of certainty] applies even in the case of what is currently present (*kadyattā*). Or, let there be that lack of determination; even so, what is the fault? [The opponent might say: "In that case, the perception of that [object] would not be the cause for purposeful action (*pravṛtti*)."

How can the observation of a perceived object (*kradyattādarśana*)—being itself indeterminate—be the cause of inference, such that the statement "whatever appears in whatever manner" and so forth is well-said? This [observation], being indeterminate, cannot be the cause of inference prior to the activity [of the subject], for that would imply a great degree of "prudence" (*prekṣākāritā*)! Furthermore, if its status as a cause is not determined at the moment when the effect is not yet determined, then how could there be a determination of the distinction between the perceived and the attainable when the attainable itself is not determined—by virtue of which this threefold alternative is raised: that for one who identifies the perceived and the attainable as one, perception is the means of valid cognition regarding the attainable; for another, it is a semblance thereof; and for one who has determined their distinction, it is inference? If you argue that this [threefold distinction] is raised by worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), then by that very convention, even if the effect is not determined, the cause is determined, and thus activity toward the cause becomes possible. Therefore, enough with activity directed toward a future result, or with the description of causality for the sake of absolute certainty (*ekānta*), since that would contradict worldly convention.

Even in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), which consists of the non-duality of a single variegated cognition, just as the blue form—whether not assimilating or not seeing the yellow and other forms—assimilates or sees their common nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatā*), so too, even when the effect is not determined, there is a determination of its causality; and by the perception of that cause, this very point must be stated regarding that [reality] which transcends all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). For instance, in the apprehension of conceptual constructions such as "causality," there is no awareness of anything distinct from them;
indeed, for one who has not apprehended [the distinction], there can be no certainty that "there are no mosquitoes here."

If that is so, then non-duality is well-established! If, however, there is no such apprehension, then the relevant [argument] follows by implication: just as the conventional usage of the existence of something is established from the perception of something distinct from it, so too the conventional usage of its being a cause is established from the perception of a specific form. Thus, it is well said that "the state of being a cause of pleasure" [belongs] to that which is of the nature of a determinate cognition, and so forth.
The perception of the means is the perception of the means such as water, which reveals the state of being interrupted.
If it is argued that the apprehension of conceptual constructs such as causality occurs within non-duality solely by way of conventional usage;

Just as there is an apprehension of the exclusion of those [factors] such as being a cause even when the conceptual constructions of "being a cause" and so forth are not apprehended, so too there would be an ascertainment of causality even when the effect is not determined.

Now, as for what was said—"Not otherwise, like the momentary and so forth"—if indeed no mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises from the perception of the momentary and so forth through non-conceptual vision, nevertheless it does arise with respect to blue and the like, because it is observed;
and what is observed cannot be made otherwise.

Nor is it the case that perception alone is everywhere the cause of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth with respect to its own object; otherwise, even if [perception] were of a determinative nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*), there would be no forgetting of grasped objects such as water-jars and the like.

If you argue that [the impression] depends on the clarity of the perception and so forth, then the case at hand [of momentariness, etc. would depend on exactly the same thing; thus, due to the absence of that [clarity], there would be no impression regarding momentariness and so forth, whereas it exists elsewhere because the opposite is true. To this, he gives the answer beginning with "darśana":
"The heaviness of comprehension is the clarity of perception."

And that capacity for effects such as mental formations (*saṃskāra*) consists of *abhyāsa* (repeated cultivation), which is the constant churning within the mind; that which has these two as its primary factors is what is so described [as "beginning with those"]. From that—namely, from the awakening of the memory of a mental formation belonging to the same class as what was previously perceived—the term "belonging to the same class" (*sajātīya*) refers to something similar to the object of prior perception by way of a subsequent particularity; this is an elliptical expression, meaning that even if only one instance was seen, it is called "seen. In that context, when the awakening—that is, the production—of both the mental formation and the memory is accepted:

"Without what? To this he says: "Without the determination of intrinsic nature"—that is, without the ascertainment that constitutes the very essence of perception. The mention of "impressions and memory" is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), intended to include recognition and so forth. Regarding the question, "What would happen in that case?", he says: "Even in the case of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and the like"—by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the capacity to lead one to heaven and so on is included; the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that this applies not only to [objects] such as blue, etc. "Following a mark" (*liṅgānusaraṇa*) means relying upon a logical reason (*hetu*). He considers that what was previously stated is untenable, because that [momentary destruction] is established through perception itself.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction in that"—that is, because there is no distinction in that [perception], such as its clarity or lack thereof, even in cases like momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
He provides an illustration for that very point: "just as in the case of blue and so forth.
For perception does not possess the nature of being either clear or otherwise with respect to its own object, since that would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*).

The Buddhists also possess the practice of repeated occurrence of either momentary perception or its conceptualization; likewise, they possess desire and so forth, yet there is no awakening to that [object] therein, and therefore that [desire, etc.
is not the effect of that [perception].

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: that which does not arise even when another thing is intact is not its effect; for example, a cloth is not the effect of a wheel and so forth because it does not arise even when the wheel and so forth are intact. Likewise, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the like do not arise regarding momentary entities and so forth, even when proficiency in perception and repeated practice are intact. This is the argument by way of contrapositive (*viparyaya-prayoga*). That which arises when another thing is intact is its effect; for example, a jar is the effect of a wheel and so forth because it arises when the wheel and so forth are intact. And mental impressions and the like do indeed arise when certainty (*nirṇaya*) is intact.

If it is asked, "Let it be that [the cause is] 'due to the clarity of perception' and so forth; what is the purpose of including the term 'practice' (abhyāsa)?"—it is for the sake of connecting the word "etc. (ādi) with both [terms]: namely, "due to the clarity of perception etc., and due to practice etc.

Thus, by the word "etc. in one instance, the deficiency of the superimposition of another quality—which acts as an obstacle to perception—is included, as established in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.43) and elsewhere by the passage beginning, "or by the cause of error... and so on.

As will be stated right here: "Even when there is no difference in the clarity of vision and so forth," and so on; elsewhere, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of "desire for the object" (arthitva) and other factors is intended.
Alternatively, the mention of "practice" (abhyāsa) is for the purpose of demonstrating the primacy of practice in all cases.

As for what was stated by the opponent—that in the case of repeated practice perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas in the absence of repeated practice inference (*anumāna*) is the means—it must be asked:

in cases such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, just as in the case of blue and other objects, how can there be a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and so on in the absence of repeated practice, from which inference would arise? If it is argued that one should instead say "upon the awakening of a latent impression and so forth belonging to a class similar to what was seen," and that the term "recollection" (*smṛti*) is unnecessary; [we reply: that is done for the sake of what follows, for in that context recollection alone will be considered as the primary factor, because of its non-difference [from the original experience] in the case of a recollection of a similar object (*sādṛśya-smṛti*). (Siddhiviniścaya 1)
In this and other such passages, the meaning of the verse is explained by way of negation (*vyatireka*): "knowledge."
The cause of formative factors and so forth would be the section;
the section is knowledge characterized by ascertainment.
Non-conceptual perception depends upon factors such as proficiency with respect to blue and other objects.

"Comparison [occurs] due to the presence of proficiency, practice, and so forth—those, however, for whom practice, proficiency, and the like exist as causes of certainty possess great intellectual power... (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p.
240). Just as the form of what is seen is a particularity dependent on other conditions such as practice and proficiency, because of the apprehension of that [particularity].

For it is not the case that whatever is seen is grasped by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) simply because it was seen; for if there were no distinction in the act of seeing, it would follow that conceptual constructions would arise regarding all possible aspects (*ākāra*). Rather, only a certain [aspect] is grasped depending on conditions such as repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). Thus he explains through the mention of "grasping the aspect" (*ākāragrahaṇa*):
"Because conceptual constructions arise from experience when they are assisted by other conditions such as proficiency in practice" (Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 26).

"Now, it might be thought: 'From perception, even though it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*) arise regarding blue and so forth due to [the factors of] repetition, context, sharpness of intellect, and interest; but they do not [arise] regarding momentariness and so forth, because those [factors] are absent. — *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p.
22; *Pramāṇapaddhati*, p. 54.
And proficiency [is found] in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 33, and in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 84.

"Acuity" (*pāṭava*) means sharpness of the intellect; by virtue of the context and the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of proximity, degrees of intensity, and so on—see *Hetubindu-ṭīkāloka*, p.
271. Just as there is acuity regarding blue and so forth, there is likewise a lack of acuity regarding momentariness and so forth.
In the case of momentary phenomena and so forth, the awakening of latent impressions and memory is the effect of repeated practice, proficiency, and other such factors.
For what purpose is there a superimposition of permanence and so forth upon momentariness and the like, which are clearly perceived?
Or rather, another quality would be superimposed upon the mother-of-pearl, in the form of silver, because of the perception of a similarity in appearance; this is the remainder of the argument.
This should be understood from the commentary on the practice (abhyāsa), page 22, note 17.
Supporting this very point, he says: "Let [the mind] place," and so forth.
Let it be granted that a highly acute cognition of its own object, being momentary and exclusive,

always produces memory through constant practice; yet it is illogical to claim that such [memory] does not determine the synthesis of what was previously seen due to the deception caused by the arising of a similar subsequent [moment], because similarity in every respect is impossible.
If there were no determination of distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
even the claim that there is an exclusion of the causes of its conceptualization (*tadvikalpakāraṇavyatireka*) is exactly the same.

Since there is an absence of the determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in both the perception of an object and its recollection, how could there be a synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*) from which the recollection of conventions and so forth arise? If it is argued that even in non-conceptual perception there is a determination of what belongs to the same class, as in the case of one who has awakened from sleep, we say no; for such a consequence would follow even when there is no actual perception of the object.

Now, one might object: "Has this matter not already been stated in the commentary on the immediately preceding verse? And by stating it again, is that very point not merely being reaffirmed? This would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Rather, it must be for some other reason, yet that reason has not been stated here; therefore, this subsequent verse does not state a new meaning. To this Anantavīrya replies: "The meaning of this [verse] is as follows: 'O Unmanifest One, bestow upon me that momentary, singular self-awareness of my own true nature.'"

The term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) is an expression emphasizing the state [of being]; therefore, the cognition—that is, the vision—of those two objects which have as their single, unaccompanied limit the property of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), being of what nature? To this he says: "more acute" (*paṭīyasī*), meaning more sharp.
When? To this he says: "always," at all times.
Why? From practice.
To the question "What [does it do]?", he says: memory.

To the question "What would memory do?", he says: "That memory also" (*sāpi smṛtirapi*) may effect "the synthesis of what has been seen" (*dṛṣṭasaṃkalanādikam*). "Synthesis" (*saṃkalana*) refers to the correct unification or determination (*nirṇayana*) of that which was made an object by a previous perception with its subsequent occurrence, either as identity or similarity; this is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), inference (*tarka*) and so forth are included; [memory] may effect that.
It must be maintained that this "Anantavīrya" who is the author of the *Hetu* is indeed distinct from Anantavīrya, the author of the *Prakṛta-ṭīkā*, who lived under the patronage of Ravibhadra-pāda.

As for what was stated—that even regarding momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, following a logical mark (*liṅga*) is improper because there is no distinction between them—the author replies with the words "in the absence of another perception" (*parādarśane*), etc. This has its meaning explained as follows: the arising of another subsequent moment which is similar to the preceding one—that is, of the same kind—and the perception whose object is that arising (where the term for the object is applied metaphorically to the subject).
Indeed, the mere arising of that [cognition] is not the cause of deception, for that would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) at all times.

Deception consists in the superimposition of other qualities; therefore, one does not ascertain—that is, one does not determine—momentary destruction and so forth. This is to be connected by changing the case-ending (from *tasmāt* to *tena*).
The meaning is that, in that case, a person possesses latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the like.
He states the rebuttal to that: "This is inconsistent," and so forth.
Thus, the opponent's position is inconsistent and irrational.

Why is this? To this he says: because similarity is impossible in every way—that is, in all respects—and because even the possibility of a correspondence between the preceding and succeeding moments is absent.

To explain: if each subsequent moment of superimposition arises entirely similar to each preceding moment of superimposition, then, just like that preceding moment, the subsequent one would also possess the capacity to produce its own succeeding moment, and so on for each following one. Thus, there would be no cessation of moments as long as *saṃsāra* lasts.

For when the preceding [moment] is capable, it is not possible for the subsequent [moment] to prevent the effect; since that [preceding moment] exists, the [effect] necessarily follows, and its capacity cannot be obstructed, because it is impossible to obstruct what already exists.
In the view concerning origination,
there is origination.
However, the view concerning origination is either the delusion of something stable, gross, and so forth,
or it is deceived by the production of a similar [moment] immediately following; for the cognition "this is that very same thing" arises with respect to what is similar.
"Even here, one is deceived by the production of another similar [moment], as in the case of hair or nails that have been cut and grown back again... (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 2.209).

Therefore, this erroneous determination of reality—occurring among those whose hearts are captivated merely by the similarity of form, as in the case of hair or plantain trunks—must be understood as being based solely on the occurrence of another similar state.

Furthermore, why is it not accepted that for those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*), there is an illusion of oneness produced by the perception of successive similar states, as in the case of nails and hair that have been cut and grown back again? (pṛ॰ 86).

And regarding the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of identity based on the connection with a subsequent similar state—just as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again—there is no contradiction here.
(Hetubindu-ṭīkā, pṛ॰ 136).

With the words beginning with "tulya," he anticipates the rebuttal of Bhadanta Śubhagupta: "Just as there is the delusion of permanence due to the arising of similar subsequent moments, so too, if there is the apprehension of an uninterrupted [stream] of homogeneous [moments], there is the delusion of grossness" (*Tattvasaṃgraha* v. 1972).
Just as in the case of a moment of superimposition, there is another moment of superimposition in the causal moment of superimposition.
Whether his power or lack of power, which exists by its very nature, can be restrained—
since it is partless, who is capable of diminishing it?
In this same way, it should be stated regarding all entities.

If it is argued that this being the case, there would be an absence of a final moment, let this be another fault of his [position]. For in reality, there is no similarity even in terms of the capacity to produce a subsequent effect between the preceding and succeeding moments of such superimpositions;
and just as the preceding [moment] is the cause for the succeeding one, so too must the succeeding one be the cause for that [preceding one], which would entail a similarity in every respect.

But this is not the case, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory to a self-identical entity. Now, if it is argued that from the preceding moment of superimposition—which is aided by the inference of momentary destruction—there arises a subsequent [moment] that is incapable, more incapable, and most incapable of producing [an effect]; then there is no similarity by way of being a superimposition in the manner described, otherwise [if there were], the doctrine of partlessness (*niraṃśavāda*) would be lost.
This should be applied everywhere accordingly.
Therefore, it is well said: "in every way," and so forth.

What is meant is this: in the extreme view of partlessness (*niraṃśaikānta*), because there is no production of a subsequent [moment] similar to the preceding one, there would be no deception; thus, there would be the ascertainment of that [object].
In the absence of an obstruction to its capacity,
the Buddhist [position] results in the momentary entity possessing distinct intrinsic natures consisting of existing at the preceding moment and existing at the succeeding moment.
If the north were also prior to the east, then...

The meaning is that there is no similarity even in terms of having an identical superimposition between those two— the preceding and the succeeding moments— when the second moment of superimposition arises from the third moment of superimposition.
The determination of momentariness would indeed arise from perception itself.

[Objection: "Granted that there may be no continuity of common properties (*samānadharmānvaya*) between the preceding and succeeding moments, yet there might still be similarity (*sādṛśya*), which is the non-determination of difference (*vailakṣaṇyānavadhāraṇa*). To this, he says: "In the case of difference," and so forth.
Difference is the dissimilarity (*vaisadṛśya*) between the preceding and succeeding moments; if there were a non-determination of that, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

To explain: would that non-determination (*anavadhāraṇa*) be of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or of the nature of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? In the first case, how could mere absence of determination constitute similarity or a cause for deception? Otherwise, even things like a donkey’s horn would qualify. In the second case as well, what else could be denoted by the term "non-determination" other than the determination of its difference [from the object]? If you say it is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it applies to potsherds and the like; and thus, due to such deception, there would be no awakening of latent impressions or memory regarding them.

Now, if the ascertainment of identity is itself that non-ascertainment, then what would be meant by "deception due to similarity"? It would mean that the ascertainment of identity [arising] from the ascertainment of identity is deception;
yet one thing cannot be the cause of itself, because that is contradictory.

Furthermore, from where does that ascertainment of identity arise? If you say it arises from the perception of another similar object, no; for since similarity is impossible in every respect, there would be an over-extension of the principle and an infinite regress.
Furthermore, [your argument] amounts merely to the non-apprehension of a difference between the preceding and succeeding moments.

Moreover, by asserting that following a logical mark (*liṅga*) is improper even in cases such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), you have yourself pointed out that very non-apprehension of it. In that case, since that non-apprehension is equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*), this [argument of yours] based on similarity is also not tenable.
The opponent further states [the point] regarding the non-apprehension of difference: "That," etc.;

that is, the conceptualization (vikalpa) of that difference is its determination (niścaya); the cause of that [determination] is its absence (vyatireka), which is non-existence; [and] similarity (sādṛśya).
To this he states the following reply: "‘Even this’ and so forth;

not only the previous [case], but even this is exactly like that, being identical to the former, because its causes—such as the proficiency and practice of perception—are present, and because it is impossible for there to be an absence of the causes of such conceptualization in every respect. This is what is intended: since one does not discern [the difference] due to similarity, even this is exactly like that."

The Buddhist [responds]: Just as for non-conceptual perception—even when it is free from defects such as obstructing conditions—there is no causality toward [the formation of] mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding momentary destruction and so forth, so too is there none regarding blue and the like; having stated this, now wishing to state it by another method as well, he says: "In the absence of the determination of the nature of its own object and its perception and recollection," etc. That is, in the absence of the determination of the very nature or essential form of both its own object (*svārtha*) and its perception (*dṛṣṭi*) and recollection (*smṛti*).

If it is argued: "Granted that there may be an absence of determination (*vyavasāya*) in perception, but not in memory, because its nature is determinative," we say: no. If there is an absence of determination in its very nature, then it would be impossible for it to exist even with respect to the object. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) at the beginning of this passage is for this reason; otherwise, one would have said "determination" (*vyavasāya*) and so forth. In that case, determination is intended for memory with respect to the object; it would follow that the same applies to perception as well. Moreover, the mention of them together—as in "perception and memory"—is for the purpose of demonstrating that they possess identical characteristics.
Furthermore, for the opponent, memory is non-conceptual because it is the effect of such an experience, just like the subsequent moment of experience.

If it is asked, "When that [non-conceptual experience] exists, what happens?"—to this he says: "From where," and so forth. From nowhere does the synthetic cognition, or the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same thing" or "it is similar to that," arise; for here too, the aforementioned reasoning applies.
"What is that [nature] like? To this he says: "From which," and so forth.

From which—that is, from which synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*)—arise the recollection of conventions and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the joining with verbal expression and other such factors are included. He considers that in the absence of that [synthetic cognition], those [recollections and so forth] would be absent due to the absence of their cause.

This is what is meant: first, there is the perception of the object that was the subject of the convention; then, from the perception of that same object or something of its kind, there arises the memory of it; from that, there follows the synthesis [of recognition] such as "this is that very thing" or "this is similar to that"; from that, the memory of the convention; from that, the application of the word to the object present before one; and from that, the conceptual cognition (vikalpa-jñāna) such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth. All of this would not be possible.

But surely, just as water comes from a cloud and soot from a lamp—both arising from something of a different nature—so too, from every non-conceptual perception (*darśana*), there would arise through conventional usage a non-conceptual [cognition] regarding its own form, while elsewhere there would be its opposite, such as memory and so forth.

This very point he states with the words beginning "nirvikalpa": that which has emerged from conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is this very "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*); even when that exists, there arises a determination (*avyavasāya*) of what is of the same class, and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of synthesis (*saṃkalana*) and other such functions is intended.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "like one who has slept and then awakened.
This refers to a continuum that was previously asleep and subsequently awakened; it is just like that.
What is meant is this: just as there is a state of being awakened following sleep, so too is the case here at hand.

In this regard, the following is investigated: who is this so-called "one who has slept"? If it is argued that he is the dreamer overcome by sleep, [we reply] no, because he is not relevant to the subject under discussion. If it is argued that he is the "seer," [we reply] no, because he is equal to the subject under discussion. If his seeing is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), then even for him, one who possesses such a vision is "awakened"; it does not belong to the subject under discussion, who possesses memory and so forth. Thus, there is equality with the probandum (*sādhyasamatā*).
Nor is it accepted that another perceives him, because [the Buddha] is admitted to be insentient.
If it is argued that "asleep" refers to being devoid of sentience, then one does not awaken from that state, since you admit that this is distinct from the waking state;

how then can this be shown as an illustration involving another? [Reply: No, for it is explained otherwise: "asleep like one who is asleep" means he is like one asleep because he does not directly perceive specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); this is the distinction of the Sugata’s vision through inference. "Awakened like one who is awakened" refers to the various states of one who perceives all things. Therefore, there is no fault, since even the opponent admits that the Sugata possesses [knowledge] through inference.
The word "ce" (if) indicates the opponent's intention;
he states the answer to this as "nārtha" and so forth,
where "na" (not) serves to negate the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Even when there is the perception of an object, it is not merely in its absence that [the error occurs], because of its persistence—namely, the persistence of a determinative cognition (adhyavasāya) of a similar kind.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of non-difference," etc., [referring to] the deficiency of other causes.
Having stated that [the self] is not the cause of formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth,
there is likewise an absence of determination of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) even in the case of memory.
According to their established doctrine that all cognition regarding intrinsic nature is non-conceptual,
there is the determination [of the object] from memory.
The non-conceptual experience of a Buddhist regarding that which was previously perceived.
It has the nature of ascertainment regarding the form of an object for one who is asleep.
Because it is accepted that for one who is asleep, there arises a consciousness of the waking state from the consciousness of sleep.

It is certain that the consciousness of one who has been in deep sleep arises at awakening through the mediation of time, due to the recollection of prior experience— *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 68.
The example well-known in the Buddhist tradition is as follows:

the cultivation consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*), which occurs prior to the attainment of the state of a Sugata, should here be understood respectively as inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) and inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).

A yogi does not become such merely through cultivation alone; rather, it is when one has grasped objects through knowledge derived from hearing, established them through reasoning derived from reflection, and cultivated them until their perfection—that [knowledge] whose object is non-erroneous is indeed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the yogis endowed with that are [the authorities].

"The manner of cultivation (bhāvanākrama) for yogins, as it was determined and set forth [by Dharmakīrti] in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (3.285) beginning with the words 'consisting of hearing' (*śrutamaya*) and so forth... — *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* (Dharmottara), p. 68.
Established in moral conduct and possessing [the wisdoms of] hearing and reflection, one applies oneself to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The cognitions arising from hearing and so forth have as their objects names, both [names and things], and the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

For wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) is the certainty produced by the authority of a reliable person (*āpta*); wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) is the certainty produced by rational investigation (*yukti-nidhyāna*). — *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 6.75–76.

"Because there is no difference [between them], why is this not extracted by means of a cognition that does not conceptualize the object through a similar recollection?"—*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Prathama-prakaraṇa, p. 520.
The mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) would be regulated by their respective proximate causes.
This is the nature of things: that a mental impression deposits a seed of memory; from that, through the power of auxiliary causes, the awakening of the seed of memory occurs.

In that regard, for one who depends upon the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, the perception [of similarity] prior to and after the awakening of that [consciousness] toward a non-conceptual construction is purposeless, whether occurring sequentially or simultaneously. The conceptual cognition of similarity and identity is called "recollection of similarity" from the perspective of another's view; for the other's position is as follows: atoms which perform a single causal function, being excluded from what does not belong to that continuum and being similar to themselves, are the causes of that [cognition] through a series, because there is no distinction [among them] when that [cognition] is to be produced.
Of what things? To this he says: "of those whose cognitions are not conceptual" (*arthākalpadhiyām*), meaning both objects (*arthāḥ*) and non-conceptual cognitions (*akalpadhiyaḥ*).
What is meant by this is: just as from a partless experience the occurrence of a similar memory arises, so too let that [memory] arise from such an object itself.

Nor should this objection be raised here: "Recollection is preceded by the perception of an object; how could it occur in the absence of that [perception]? Otherwise, why would there not be a universal consequence [of recollection] everywhere? For if recollection were produced regarding a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) within the range of perception, then it would be preceded by that; but it is not so, because its object is a universal (*sāmānya*). It has already been stated that it is for this very purpose that [recollection] occurs in the case of a similar recollection.
Even so, if it were preceded by that [perception], then the recollection of blue would be preceded by the perception of yellow.
"Let the arising of a similar recollection from that which is partless be granted;
for recollection follows the positive and negative concomitance with the practice of a previous experience"—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 610.

Regarding the absence of perception, the opponent here objects: "It is not from the mere perception of an object that a memory of a similar thing arises—such that this fault would follow—but rather, the subsequent memory of that [object] is born from a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by a previous memory of something similar. Perception, however, is called its cause because it is the cause for awakening that latent impression; therefore, the fact that it possesses a similar form is not contradictory. To him, he replies: "Not at all," and so forth.

The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by successive prior conceptualizations would be restricted—that is, they would be made determinate in producing memories similar to the specific objects determined in each subsequent instance. Why would this not be the case? Indeed, they would certainly be so restricted, because the double negation leads to the understanding of the intended meaning.
By what means? To this he says: "according to their respective [conditions]" and so forth.

*Sannikarṣa* (proximity) is the presence in a suitable location, not conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like, since that will be refuted later. Those objects and sense-faculties in which such proximity exists are called *sannikarṣiṇaḥ* (those possessing proximity); [the restriction occurs] by means of these.

The Buddhist maintains that perception has no utility regarding any object whatsoever, because it occurs according to its own nature, without overstepping the proximity of whichever formative impression (*saṃskāra*) is capable of awakening it.
From the non-conceptual [state], it is the cause of memory;
it resides in memory.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the contacts of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in what is inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) are to be understood as the means of contact for indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpa*).

Having provided the commentary on the preceding two verses because they are easy to understand, he speaks while providing the commentary on the subsequent verse, which contains two additional syllables, beginning with "This is the nature of the object" (*vastusvabhāvo'yam*), and so forth.

This is the nature—that is, the essential form—of the object (*vastu*, i.e., the *padārtha*). Because of this, from that state of being, a determination (*vyavasāya*)—which is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the seed of memory (*smṛtibīja*) and the cause of recollection. This has been considered in such passages as *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.4: "Of perception whose nature is determination," and so on.

This is not tenable. If it is asked, "What would follow from this—that the nature of things is such that a vivid experience deposits a seed for memory?"—to this he replies: "From that," meaning from that [deposition], there would arise a "resemblant memory," which is an awakening of the seed of memory, a distinct cognition free from doubt and other such defects.
Does this arise from that [seed] alone, or even from something else? To this he says: "by the power of auxiliary causes" (*sahakārikāraṇavaśāt*).

That which acts together with that seed of memory is the "auxiliary" (*sahakāri*); and that which is its cause is the "cause," such as the sense organ, the object, and so forth. By the phrase "by the power of that," he demonstrates—according to what is established by others—that the cause for the perceptibility of a similar memory is [this set of conditions].
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "In that case," and so forth.
In that case, when such a possibility exists, for what [recollection] would there be that awakening of a similar recollection?

Of what nature? That which depends upon the contact between the sense organ and the object—that is, having the character of depending on the contact of the sense organ and the object. Why? Because, in the case of non-conceptual construction, perception before and after [the recollection] would be purposeless.

Now, one might object: "Even if this were so, there is still no clarity in a memory that resembles [its original object]. As it has been said: "For that which is permeated by conceptual construction (vikalpa), there is no manifestation of a clear object, even in a dream. And what is remembered is not a memory; nor is that perception of an object such as that [perception of a clear object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.285)
If it is argued that "thus, clear cognition is your direct perception," to this he replies: "Clarity," and so forth—
there is no appearance of a distinct object for that which is permeated by conceptual construction.
"Even in a dream, that which is conceptualized is remembered as something remembered; yet such memory is not a perception of an object of that [same] kind. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.283).
Therefore, clarity belongs only to memory whose nature is determinative.
For indeed, there is no lack of cognition even for those who do not perceive [the object] due to a failure of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

What contradiction is there in a cognition whose nature is determinate (*vyavasāya*), which experiences clarity (*vaiśadya*) by itself through the totality of causes that awaken the mental impression? Clarity means distinctness; it occurs precisely because of the dependence upon the contact between the sense organ and the object.

Of what? Of one whose nature is resolute, [this arises] from memory. Now, if it is argued that since memory can arise from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—which has another name, "latent tendency" (*vāsanā*)—that memory would be objectless even when vivid, like a cognition overwhelmed by desire and so forth; to this he says: "non-obliteration of the impression," and so on. "Non-obliteration of the impression" (*asaṃskārapramoṣa*) means the non-disappearance of the impression, i.e., the existence of the impression. For in that case, [the cognition is] clearly [vivid]. Therefore, the phrase "for this very reason" should be connected here as well. That cognition is "correct" (*sam*), meaning a valid cognition free from doubt and the like.

This is what is meant: [the opponent claims that] memory arises solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and is devoid of an object; however, this is not so, because external objects and other causes are also established as its basis.
For indeed, such a vivid and correct [recollection] is observed regarding water and the like when they have been well-practiced, just as in the case of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

[The opponent replies: "Surely, clarity does not belong to memory, which is by nature a conceptual determination (*vyavasāya*), but rather to the original perception; it is designated as belonging to memory only because that perception is superimposed upon it. [The author answers: Not so.
As it has been said: "From a memory of similarity, [arises] memory."
In this context, it is meaningless [to argue] that recollection and so forth do not exist within memory.

Due to the simultaneous occurrence of memory and mental cognition— whether conceptual or non-conceptual— an ignorant person, because of their rapid succession, determines them to be one and the same. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.133)
If this is argued, [the author] says here: "Nor even for those who see," and the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) must be supplied here as well.

Consequently, the meaning becomes this: since that awakening depends upon the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, what is the use of the conceptualization of non-conceptuality? For this very reason, there is no such lack of clarity (*avaishadya*) even for those perceptions which take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object.

The intended meaning here is as follows: if clarity were established as an inherent property in philosophical systems (darśana) just as redness is in hibiscus flowers, then one could say that it appears there through superimposition from elsewhere; otherwise, this cannot be maintained, as it would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Thus, in conceptual construction (vikalpa), there is the awakening of latent impressions (saṃskāra).
Explaining the meaning of the verse by way of removing misconceptions, he says: "Of that which is of the nature of determination," and so forth.

For one who possesses the nature of determination—that is, whose essence is ascertainment—and for whom there is a preeminent, correct awakening (bodha), which is a transformation of consciousness (*cetana*) consisting of the arousal of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), the latter being synonymous with *vāsanā*—for such a person, what contradiction is there in accepting that the clarity (*vaiśadya*) belonging to the various perceptions arises from itself, independent of the contact between the sense organs and their objects? There is none whatsoever; this is not like the logic of borrowing ornaments.
Why is this so? To this he says: "By the totality of causes," and so forth;
this is easy to understand and was stated from the perspective of the Supreme (Parā).
Furthermore, from the perspective of the Buddhist, clarity arises from the attainment of non-obstruction;
however, from the ultimate standpoint (paramārthataḥ), it is as follows:
Clarity in knowledge arises only through the destruction or the subsidence-and-destruction of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*).

Now, if direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) were conceptual (*savikalpaka*) regarding its own object, it would necessarily grasp [the object] only as conjoined with its own designation; and since those designations themselves would likewise be grasped as conjoined with their own designations, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the simultaneous cognition of multiple designations, which contradicts experience.

And here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): whatever is conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) grasps an object associated with a verbal designation, just like the cognition "this is blue"; and perception is conceptual. To this [the opponent] says: this is incorrect, because the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Demonstrating this, the Buddhist says:

"In the case of 'similar' (*sadṛśa*), etc."—there is a recollection of one's own object and its verbal designation arising from similarity, yet that [recollection] is not itself expressive (*abhilāpinī*).
If non-conceptuality were established by that alone, then conceptual cognition would be void.
For an object perceived as qualified by something cannot exist without the apprehension of the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and so forth;

therefore, it is established that the recollection of an object similar to what was perceived—which is the basis for verbal expression—is itself free from verbalization, even though its objects are verbal expressions and the like.

If it is argued that there is no fault because of the qualification that "conceptualization is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression"— since otherwise, in dependence on verbal expressions other than that [first one], an infinite regress would follow— then we do not perceive any purpose for that qualification other than the absence of a specific manifestation resulting from the contact of the object with its own sense-faculty.
What follows from this?

"Similar" (*sadṛśa*) means identical with what is proximate; "its own object" (*svārtha*) refers to that which exists at the time of the convention; the "expression" (*abhilāpa*) or designation of that [object] is the beginning of [the complex of factors] such as the relation between qualifier and qualified and worldly convention—this is what is meant by that term. Furthermore, it is not "expressive," i.e., possessed of words, because the same logical fault projected against the opponent's position would apply here as well, since the reasoning is identical. For this very reason, the inclusion of the term "object-expression" (*arthābhilāpa*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that the expression and the appearance of the object occur simultaneously.

Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) because even in the case of the expression of what is being remembered, that which has been remembered must be joined [to a word], and for that too, "that which has been remembered" [would apply].
Therefore, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
It is not inconclusive, because that [memory] is non-conceptual; conceptual construction (kalpanā) is a cognition accompanied by verbal expression (abhilāpavatī pratītiḥ).
Others say that the others are non-conceptual;
he states the reply to that: "By that much alone," and so forth.

If non-conceptuality is accepted merely on the basis of that very fact of being inexpressible, then—by changing the case ending—the connection is with "the memory of that" (*tatsmṛteḥ*); the resulting cognition (*dhī*) would be equal [to it], i.e., void, formless, and would not be conceptual (*vikalpikā*), meaning it would be mere imagination (*kalpanā*) itself.

This is what is meant: when the memory of its expression is non-conceptual, then, because it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatvāt*), it would be nothing other than perception (*pratyakṣa*), according to the statement: "Perception is free from conceptual construction" (*Kalpanāpoḍhaṃ pratyakṣam*, Pramāṇasamuccaya, p. 8).

Furthermore, because its object is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), perception has the specific characteristic as its domain; therefore, there can be no application of a designation to that which is its object, such as "this is blue," and thus the absence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Consequently, the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) in the definition of perception would be meaningless, as there is nothing to be excluded. To avoid this fault, one must admit that even the memory of that [perception], though non-expressive, is conceptual; thus, the same fault remains.

Because verbal expression and the memory of verbal expression are devoid of conceptualization (*avikalpaka*) due to being empty of words, a cognition that manifests as an object associated with qualifiers and so forth does not depend on another word; this is *kalpanā*—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 245.

Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition characterized by the association of the forms of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*). — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, Manorathanandin 1.125.
"Conceptual construction (kalpanā) is a cognition associated with verbal expression"— *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 1214;
"This perception is useless [if it were] free from conceptual construction"— *Nyāyapraveśa*, page 7.
The particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) would be its object of direct perception— Nyāyabindu 1.12.
Because of the absence of the conceptual construction that is to be excluded,
the recollection of verbal expression is also devoid of words.
By this, the following argument advanced by the proponent of the non-duality of word (śabdādvaitavādin)— namely, "There is no such cognition... (Vākyapadīya 1.124), and so forth— is also refuted.
...in the world,
everything appears as if permeated by the pursuit of words; the ellipsis is that "everything is established in speech."

Explaining the verse, he says: "Something," etc. Something such as Devadatta, being perceived as qualified by something else such as a staff; the qualifier is the staff and so forth, the qualified is Devadatta and so forth, their relation is conjunction and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes worldly conventions and the like. The apprehension of these, which is the comprehension [of them] at the time of linguistic convention, cannot occur without that [relation]; rather, it occurs when that [relation] exists.
This has been stated by the opponent:
"Having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and conventional reality, and having synthesized these, one cognizes [the object] in that way and not otherwise. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.145).
What follows from this? To this he says: "From that," and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore: the object present before one's eyes which is similar [to the object seen] at the time of the convention; the recollection of that denoting expression, which is non-verbal—meaning devoid of association with verbal expression and having as its object the absence of verbal expression—is established. He states the fault in not accepting this: "That," etc. If another verbal expression were required for that verbal expression being recollected, an infinite regress would result; thus, it is established as being non-verbal.

The following is what is being said: if conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is a cognition accompanied by verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), then its opposite would be non-conceptualization (*akalpanā*); thus, even a slight degree of cognition would be conceptual. Anticipating this objection, the opponent says: "Verbal expression," and so forth.

That by which something is expressed, or that which is expressed—namely, the universal of the word (*śabdasāmānya*) and the universal of the object (*arthasāmānya*)—is "expression" (*abhilāpa*). The connection or conjunction of the object with that word is "association" (*yojana*); the cognition or awareness whose manifestation is suitable for that [association] is thus described as "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*). Because of this qualification, there is no fault; namely, the fault that "limited cognition would be conceptual. This is because even the recollection of an expression similar to what was perceived possesses the nature of conceptualization.
If this is the case, the word [in the original text] indicates the intention of the opponent.
Regarding this, the Teacher says: "svārtha" and so forth.

"Sva" (self) and "artha" (object), or "svasya arthaḥ" (the object of the self); its "sannikarṣa" (contact) is the connection with the sense faculty. That which is produced by that [contact] is both that [cognition] and a specific manifestation (*nirbhāsaviśeṣa*), namely the manifestation of partless atoms. Its "vaikalya" (deficiency) is its non-existence. From the perspective of *paryudāsa* (relative negation), the very appearance of a single gross [object] is that deficiency. Apart from that—that is, setting that aside—we do not conceive of any qualifier, whether expressed or denoted, for the purpose of qualifying it; rather, we perceive only that [gross appearance].
"Then what? What [fault] follows from that definition of it? asks another Buddhist:
"Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression."
— Nyāyabindu 1.5: by means of the generality of sound.
Regarding the commonality of objects here, the Teacher says— starting with "perceiving," and so forth—
"perceiving the individual characteristics as a single, gross, non-momentary, and manifest [entity]."
This has been cited—*Nyāyabindu-vivaraṇa-prakaraṇa*, p.
98: "Know that whatever clarity one determines [in perception] arises from a similar recollection.

(v. 9) Even for one who perceives particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves—characterized by momentary destruction and atomicity—there appears only a single, gross form residing within cognition, manifesting with extreme vividness.
If it pleases you,
then just as in the case of a memory resembling its original object, because [the object] does not appear to the unengaged sensory cognition,
one indeed remembers the wordless [object] through words as having a similar form.
And its validity is logical;
for, having determined an object by means of that [cognition], one is not deceived regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
It is argued that [its validity] is illogical because it lacks the quality of apprehending an object not previously apprehended; to this, it has been said:
Since it is impossible for either [of the two] to possess validity within a means of cognition characterized by their conjunction,
there exists a non-verbal, non-contradictory recollection resembling [the object] during the state in which all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn, because it appears in that very manner.
Since this perception of the object, having occurred, generates its own recollection, it is logical that it should present an aspect inseparable from its own nature, just like the object itself.
That perception does not have a unique and exclusive object, because for one whose senses are active, such [an object] is never perceived at any time or place;
for we never perceive an aspect—either external or internal—that is solitary, since it is not determined in the manner that has been described.

This is because externally, objects such as a jar are perceived as consisting of various parts, forms, and so forth, and as being unitary and subject to transformation; whereas internally, the mind is perceived as having a single form, like a variegated painting.

Nor is there any cognition that reveals a contrary object which could render the subject under discussion erroneous; for it is not possible for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to occur absolutely at a time when [the entity] is both existent and non-existent. If that were the case, how could existence—by virtue of the contradiction of causal efficiency with respect to both succession and simultaneity in the state of non-momentariness—be excluded from non-momentariness (like the maxim of the bird not seeing the shore) and thereby abide in momentariness? Thus, the momentary destruction of all that exists is established. This is because those two [succession and simultaneity] are contradictory to it [non-momentariness] in that very context.
Therefore, whatever exists is multiform in nature;
for absolute oneness is non-existent, because it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception,
otherwise it would be unprovable.

The Buddhist or any other Victor (Jina), perceiving particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as mutually distinct and partless moments, has thereby demonstrated the opponent's tenet that "the five groups of consciousness have a collection as their object. If one asks for what purpose this was shown:
that object whose difference in the appearance of cognition depends upon its proximity or non-proximity is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That alone is ultimately real— Nyāyabindu 1.13, 14.
Form, sensation, consciousness, and so forth [are established] by means of the fivefold collection— *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, verse 17:
"Perception, which is free from conceptual construction, is established by perception itself."

This is for the purpose of demonstrating the sublation [of the opponent's position] by the perception that is about to be described, beginning with "one" (*ekam*), namely: "The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of all [beings] is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*) and relies upon names" (*Pravṛttiviniścaya* 2.123).
For indeed, [the opponent claims] perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), yet [that very claim] is refuted by perception itself.
Comparison— perception is free from conceptual construction and is not sublated by perception and the other [means of valid cognition]— Nyāyabindu 1.4.
Here, for all people, another distinct category is clearly perceived as being in some sense both eternal and non-eternal;

namely, the Buddhist person determines and ascertains a gross object such as a jar, which possesses magnitude, but not a subtle atom that is unitary and simultaneously shared by multiple parts and qualities.
By this, the non-exclusive nature of the [argument] regarding succession is shown;
for in the case of non-momentary things such as lumps of clay, whose bodies are composed of a conjunction of prior and posterior limits, there is somehow seen a unity of the clay— by this,
the non-exclusive nature of [the argument regarding] succession is shown.

If it is argued that "it indeed determines [the object] as being such, but because it is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), it is not vivid due to its being imagined," to this he replies: "Vivid" means clear;
therefore, what was stated by Prajñākaragupta—that "in relation to many non-material things, that [single material thing] is material"—is refuted, for it is not ultimately real.
For the intrinsic natures of things do not exist in dependence upon others, because that would lead to an over-extension;
how so? Because it would follow that they lack clarity.

It is exactly so; this is not dependent on another. The conventional usage of "grossness" regarding a gross object itself, such as a wood-apple (*bilva*) or a *kapittha* fruit, is in relation to a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*).
For it does not become that [gross] by depending on another without having undergone such a transformation, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, know—that is, understand—that clarity belongs to perception (*dṛṣṭi*) which is of the nature of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) accompanied by a recollection of a similar thing.
The perception that grasps grossness has been shown to have as its object a cluster (skandha) that simultaneously pervades multiple substances;
whereas the perception that grasps stability has as its object a single substance that is pervaded by a succession of prior and subsequent modes (paryāya).
"The parts are ultimately real, while the whole is conventionally real"—thus they accept existence [in this manner]. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p. 555, l. 187)
