In that same way, it exists as transformed precisely by itself and not in dependence upon another; likewise, it cannot exist as untransformed [by itself]. For conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) alone occurs in dependence upon another, but not its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

If it is argued: "If [the definition] 'perception is free from conceptual construction' (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham*, *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.123) is for the purpose of negation, then the statement 'one' (*ekam*) and so forth is intended to exclude [the opposite]; in that case, since that [opposite] would be refuted either by the term 'one' or by the term 'gross' (*sthūla*), both statements would be redundant. [Response: No; for that statement is intended to demonstrate the equal strength of the two opposing views—namely, the non-exclusive [alternatives] of succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*akrama*).

For instance—just as Prajñākaragupta’s perception of the middle moment is incapable of seeing the preceding and succeeding moments, and thus cannot, by that [perception], realize their identity, the relation of cause and effect, or any other connection, because of the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (2.1) and elsewhere that "the cognition of a relation residing in two [terms]... nor can it realize their existence, since non-duality is accepted;

likewise, the middle moment, being submerged in the grasping of its own prior, subtle, partless, single part, is not able to indicate the existence of other states, and thus the same situation would apply to those as well.

And since that cognition of a part is not itself possessed of a universal, there would follow the undesirable consequence of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*); lest this occur, one must admit a single cognition of the pillar. And that [cognition], while operating upon the middle portion, without abandoning its connection with the apprehension of that [middle], operates likewise upon the upper, lower, and lateral portions; similarly, while operating upon the lump of clay, without abandoning its connection with the apprehension of that, it gradually determines the palanquin and so forth. Thus it is established: "it clearly determines [the object] as non-momentary"—this is the remainder [of the argument]. In this manner, the opponent's ill-conceived position is to be refuted.
Because the preceding and succeeding moments are not perceived as having a single identical form by the intermediate moment.
The implication is that when the essential natures of both [relata] are perceived, the cognition of their relation follows.
When everything is investigated, it falls apart; there is no reality other than non-duality—*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 31, *Darśana*.
The meaning is that [the object] would lack existence as "east," "north," and so forth;
that is to say, it does not obtain its own nature independently of anything else, which is the sense of being "devoid of existence."
Alternatively, it possesses a universal (*sāmānyavat*); the meaning is that it possesses existence (*astitva*), being endowed with existence.
Thus, the cognition of a gross aggregate (*sthūlaskandha*) is a single cognition of a pillar (*stambhajñāna*).

In the preceding verse, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the opponent's reason was demonstrated by the words "similar" (*sadṛśa*) and so forth; by the words "just by that much" (*tāvataiva*) and so forth, the absence of anything to be excluded (*vyavacchedyābhāva*) from the definition "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*, Pramāṇavārttika 2.123) was shown; and by this [present] verse, its impossibility (*tadasaṃbhava*) is shown—this is the distinction regarding the reason "because it possesses conceptualization" (*savikalpakatvāt*) when proving the thesis that [perception] grasps an object associated with verbal expression (*abhidhānasaṃsṛṣṭārthagrāhakatve*).

While explaining the verse regarding the impossibility of a non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*) that grasps momentary particularities (*kṣaṇika-svalakṣaṇa*), he says: "The particularities," and so forth.

Of what nature are these particularities? They are those atoms whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, their essential nature—is characterized by a destruction occurring at every moment, which destruction is accepted (*abhimata*) by the Buddhist himself (*ātmanā saugatena*)—not by the Jaina, nor by the Naiyāyika and others—and which is neither a total cessation without continuity (*niranvaya*), nor characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*), nor characterized by the six-fold spatial position (*ṣaṭkoṇasthāna*). Those [atoms] are thus described.

What are they? To this he says: even for the Buddhist (*saugata*) who is looking—that is, for one who is actually perceiving—it is not only for one who is not seeing that a single, massive configuration of cognition (*jñāna-sanniveśa*), namely a gross form (*ākāra*), appears quite clearly.

Now, if it is argued that it is contradictory to say that such a form appears to one who is seeing such particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), because the statement that "to one seeing blue, yellow appears in that way" is not non-contradictory; [we reply: no, because of a failure to understand the meaning.

This is its meaning: the established tenet of the opponent is that the five groups of consciousness have accumulated [atoms] as their objective support (*ālambana*). In that case, there are not as many cognitions as there are atoms that conform to their respective forms; for, like [the case of] different mental continua (*santāna*), if there were a distinction [for each atom], the cognition of a collection and so forth would be lost. Therefore, one must admit that their cognition is a single apprehender (*grāhaka*).

And that [single cognition] is said to be released [from contradiction] precisely because it conforms to the forms imparted by multiple atoms that are distinct from one another—it is a single [cognition] common to the diverse forms imparted by the multiple atoms.
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*); its connection is with the phrase, "because such non-contradictory recollection of similarity exists.
Here too, the word *tat* (that) should be understood as meaning "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

To the question, "Of what nature is this? he says: it is the "arrangement of cognitions" (*jñāna-sanniveśa*). By the intention to express distinction, it refers to the forms (*ākāra*) imparted to cognition by atoms; it is "arranging" (*sanniveśin*) because it has the nature of being properly arranged (*samyak-niveṣṭum śīlaḥ*) with the cognitions through some form of identity (*tādātmya*).
Furthermore, of what nature is it? To this he says: "sthavīyān," meaning more gross (*sthūlatara*).

Now, one might object: since the *kārikā* states "it determines the gross" (*sthūlaṃ vyavasyati*), the term "exceedingly" (*ati-*) is not heard there; yet it is present in the commentary (*vṛtti*). How, then, is there consistency between the *vṛtti* and the *kārikā*? The intention is as follows: compared to the Buddhists, the middle moment is "gross" because a single [moment] pervades multiple entities. That very same [middle moment], when compared to the Jains, is "exceedingly gross" (*atiśayena sthūlaḥ*) because it possesses parts (*sāvayava*) and pervades both preceding and succeeding moments. Therefore, it was explained at the beginning that [the object] is "gross by nature."
Therefore, the explanation is "it is non-momentary" (*akṣaṇika*).
To the question "What is this that is non-momentary?", he says here: "the nature of the entity" (*vastusvabhāvaḥ*).
How does it appear? To this he says: "perfectly clear" (*parisphuṭam*), which is an adverbial modifier of the action.

[The opponent objects: "But if, while I am perceiving my own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which consist of momentary atoms (*kṣaṇika-paramāṇu*)—such a form appears [to me], why do I not know it as such? Otherwise, how could the inference to be stated later—that 'whatever exists is all of a non-absolute nature' (*anekāntātmaka*)—be meaningful? For that inference would not be purposeless even on the alternative view of momentary destruction. To this, he replies: This is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of his knowledge; if it pleases you, the Buddhist, then cast aside your bias (*diṇḍika-rāga*) and take pleasure in it yourself.
But this is not the case; therefore, it is considered that inference is for the purpose of producing conviction (*rucikaraṇa*).

Now, [an objection may be raised]: "A gross form appears as inherent in cognition; however, because that cognition is not produced by the senses (*anakṣaja*), sense-produced cognition is perfectly clear regarding its own object. Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the appearance of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as words, generality (*jāti*), heaven (*svarga*), and so forth, it does not appear clearly. To this, he says: "In the present case," and so on.

The connection is with the phrase "of a single, gross, and distinct form residing within cognition," by means of that transformation [of the mind]. This is because that conceptual cognition—which belongs to one whose eyes are not engaged in grasping an object and who is not occupied with looking [at it], and which is the very same as the similar memory under discussion regarding the production of valid cognition—does not manifest [that external object].

This is what is meant: just as the appearance of its form occurs in the memory of something similar to the object at hand, so too it would be logical if this were to occur in a conceptual cognition whose senses are not engaged; however, this is not the case, because while it appears clearly in one instance, it appears in the opposite manner in the other, and furthermore, because the word—which serves as the cause—does not appear in the cognition.
Thus, the word follows a different course [from the cognition].
What happened after that? To this he says: "having a similar form," and so forth.

One who possesses a similar—that is, a common—own-form within the parts occurring simultaneously or successively, remembers and indeed determines the non-verbal object, which consists of momentary destruction and atoms.
The Buddhist's position is to be examined: it is like the cognitions of different persons (pṛ॰ 39, note 2).

In the case of "sthavīyān" (thicker), where there is a suffix expressing a degree of excellence that distinguishes one thing from another— as in "sthūlaḥ" (thick) with the addition of the comparative suffix— the direct expression (*śruti*) of that sense of excellence exists within the compound formation (*vṛtti*).
Therefore, the opponent [writes] "non-momentary" twice for the sake of the Buddhist.
The Jain does not grant permission; therefore, how could it be otherwise for the other, the Buddhist? This same logic should also be applied here.

The inference of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣayānumāna*) is the "passion of the *Ḍiṇḍika*"—that is, an misplaced insistence (*asthānābhiniveśa*) characterized by the thought: "When another has stated [a position], I must necessarily declare it to be untenable and fruitless. (Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p.
71, regarding conceptual cognition).
Non-conceptual knowledge arising from the sense faculties is so called because it is equivalent to the appearance of conceptualization produced by words.

The term *tā* is the designation for the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhakti*) in the Jainendra-vyākaraṇa, referring to a person who is solitary, whose gross form is absent, and who is devoid of sensory activity, as perceived in conceptual knowledge produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

If it is argued: "Granted that such an appearance of that form occurs in a conceptual cognition produced by the senses—that is, in a mental construction—and likewise in the recollection of something similar to the object under consideration; nevertheless, let that [recollection] not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because we observe the manifestation of such a form even in the case of distant or sparse hairs and the like, despite the absence of such a form [in reality]. To this, he says: "And of that," etc.

It is logical and appropriate that validity belongs only to this very recollection resembling the object under consideration; for, because one who proceeds after having determined the object—the thing possessing a similar form—by means of that recollection resembling the object under consideration, does not fail in regard to the activity or attainment of the object, just as one does not suffer deception when perceiving a single coarse form in distant, sparse hairs and the like. Let it be that this [recollection] is non-contradictory; nevertheless, it possesses no validity, because its object is merely what was previously seen in perception.

He states this very point: "It is untenable because of the absence of the capacity to apprehend an object not previously apprehended. This means that since perception lacks the capacity to apprehend an object that is unapprehended—that is, undetermined—its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is untenable. To this, he provides the reply:

"In this regard, it has been said," referring to the response given to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with the words "the establishment of the unapprehended" (*anadhigata-siddhi*), etc., by the Buddhist.
Memory is the clear manifestation [of an object]. Memory is memory.

Because memory has as its object that which has already been experienced, memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since a means of valid cognition is defined as non-discrepant knowledge (*avisaṃvādijñāna*). (Pramāṇavārttika 1)

3. Because, as stated in *Siddhiviniścaya-vṛtti* 1.3, "In the case of [cognition] proceeding from another [source], there is no possibility of a rule of non-contradiction," and because of the statement in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.7, "That which makes known an unknown object," etc., it is established in *Siddhiviniścaya-vṛtti* 1 that "a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which apprehends an object not yet apprehended."

Having thus refuted each individual position with the words beginning "anadhigata" (not previously known) and so forth, [the author], while refuting the collective position—since a rule of non-contradiction is untenable if [the means of knowledge] were to function based on something else—says: "The collection of those two," and so forth.
These two are defined as: "A means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory cognition" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.3), or "the illumination of an object not yet known" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.7).

7. Thus, when that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which has as its characteristic the collection or aggregate of these two—is accepted, then between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), because the validity of either one—perception or inference—or even of both (as indicated by the word "api") is impossible, the connection is that the validity of that [other] is not tenable.

For instance, in the case of another’s perception, there is the illumination of an unknown object, but there is no non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*), because in that case, the two objects are subjects of dispute.
In inference, there is non-discrepancy, but not the illumination of an unknown object, because its scope is already grasped by the cognition that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*);
and this will be stated [later] in the passage beginning with "Pervasion is established from the outset in its entirety" (Siddhiviniścaya 3.3).
Or, as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "The illumination of an unknown object.

Since this reading is written twice within these brackets, it follows that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has for its object an object not yet apprehended; therefore, this must be further qualified by the phrase "when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not yet apprehended."
—Because even there, non-contradiction is apprehended — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.
30; cf. *Hetubindu*, p. 53.
Therefore, both characteristics must be understood as being mutually dependent— *Pramāṇavārttikamanoratha* 1.8.
Concluding the discussion on the non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*) of the Buddhist, he says: "That," and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore [the cognition] is "non-verbal" (*aśābdam*); that is to say, it is not produced by words—meaning it is not born of the senses (*akṣaja*)—but is non-contradictory and brings about the attainment of the object as it has been determined by itself. It is a "recollection of similarity," a cognition of a common form belonging to both parts occurring either simultaneously or successively. By way of what is established for others, it is called a "recollection of similarity. [Objection: "Surely this exists, but it is not born of the senses; rather, it is mental, because the sense-born [cognition] is seen otherwise in the state where all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn. To this, he says: "When withdrawn," and so forth.

"In that state in which all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have been withdrawn—not only in any other [state], but precisely in that one as well—there is manifestation in the manner already described, namely, of both the self and the object. [Objection: "If that is indeed the state, how can there be manifestation in that very same way? If there is such manifestation, then it is not that state, because manifestation in that manner consists of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpātmaka*). [Response: "True. Nevertheless, because no other conceptual construction exists apart from that [state], there is the expression 'withdrawn' and so forth.
Alternatively, this statement is made from the perspective of another [subject]; thus, there is no fault."
For even that state which was described by another [author] with the words "having withdrawn all thought from every side" (*pra.vā.
2.124*) and so forth— in that state as well, because there is a manifestation in exactly that same way—
it is stated by this [text] that that very [state] does not exist.

Therefore, that which was stated by the opponent is refuted: namely, that "whatever meets the conditions for perception and is not perceived in a certain place does not exist there, as in the case of a jar in a particular location; and since conceptual constructions meeting the conditions for perception are not perceived in the visual field during the state in which all mental constructs have been withdrawn, how [can they exist]?"—because this thesis is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatvāt*).

In the same way, the very appearance [of cognition], being conceptual in nature, refutes at every step the erroneous conceptualization regarding itself; thus, when all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn, perception is established as being free from conceptualization. Regarding this, the proof stated by the opponent is as follows: "Whatever conceptual construction exists at a particular time is remembered as being connected to that specific time, just as the conceptualization of a horse [is remembered] as being connected to the time of seeing a cow; however, that [conceptualization] which occurs during the state where all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn is not remembered. This has been said: [The opponent's argument: Whatever conceptual construction exists at a given time is subsequently remembered as being related to that time, just as the conceptualization of a horse [is remembered] as being related to the time of seeing a cow; yet, that [conceptualization] occurring in the state where all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn is not remembered.
This has been stated:
It exists in a clearly manifest form, as stable, gross, and so forth.
Even while remaining with an inner self that is tranquil, one perceives form with the eye; that is cognition born of the senses.
Thus [it is] the remainder;
by the Buddhist [it is understood as being] of the nature of non-conceptualization.

Furthermore, when one subsequently conceptualizes, "I had such a conceptualization," this does not occur through the senses during the previously mentioned state, as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.125.
To that, he provides the following reply: "The perception of that object," and so forth.

Perception (*darśana*), the agent which consists in the seeing of the object without conceptualization, having approached—that is, having presented itself—becomes immediate in the production of its own effect; it does not do so by generating the recollection of a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).
Otherwise, this objection would apply:
[perception] ought to be otherwise.
"That which was previously not a producer of cognition, because there is no difference in its utility"—this has been extracted from *Tattvopaplava*, p.
40, and *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 86.
Nyāyaviniścayaṭīkā, p. 136;
Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 122;
Sanmatitarkaṭīkā, p. 525.
That [cognition] would not, for him, be the cause even later, even when the object has disappeared;

the meaning of this is as follows: that non-conceptual cognition which previously, at the time of its own existence, was not the producer of a conceptual thought or a similar memory—because there is no difference in its application (upayoga), that is, no difference in its operation—it would not be the producer for that Buddhist even later, i.e., after the time of the memory of the convention. What would follow from that? To this he says: "even upon the disappearance (apāya), that is, the absence, of the object characterized by non-conceptual cognition, the visual cognition—that is, the conceptual cognition born of the sense-organ—[would still arise]."
Therefore, this [previous argument]—namely, "wherever one should produce this," and so forth—is not tenable.

Consequently, it is well said: "having approached" (*upanipatya*) means by oneself, by one's own self, and not by way of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus the residual traces (*saṃskāra*) would be restrained. (Siddhiviniścaya 1)

Thus, because it would produce memory—that is, recollection—memory cannot properly or appropriately place before itself, or display at its forefront, a form that is not inherent to its own nature; namely, a universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) which does not exist within the self, whose nature is the perception of that object.
To illustrate this point, he says: "like the object of that [perception]";
the object of that perception is the partless particular (*niraṃśasvalakṣaṇa*), and "like that" means similar to that.
Just as that object, having presented itself, is logically fit to manifest its own form which is inseparable from its manifold nature, so too is the cognition;
otherwise, since the cognition appearing as a universal would arise from the object alone, this [position] would be untenable— for the phrase "the capacity of that object" and so forth,
by the word "object," refers to the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) whose domain is the object.
In this very context, it should be understood that "its validity" is the ellipsis to be supplied— see p. 10, note 3—
if it were to display a form that does not exist.

Regarding that, it has been said concerning conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): "For that [conceptual construction], arising through the power of the object, would necessarily conform to the very form of that [object]. (Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p.

195). To explain: because it arises through the power of the object, he says—that [conceptual construction], arising through the power of the object, would necessarily conform to the very form of that [object].

—*Prajñākaragupta’s Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 278: Furthermore, what has been stated here by Prajñākaragupta—that this is not an independent proof (*svatantrasādhana*), but rather a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*)—is as follows:

If perception is held by the opponent to be the grasper of external objects, then it must be admitted that [perception] arises from them and conforms to their form; otherwise, such [grasping] would be impossible. Thus, because it conforms to partless objects, it is established as being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

Thus, by this [statement], that [objection] is refuted; for a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) is that case where the acceptance of the pervaded is shown to be inseparable from the acceptance of the pervader, and such is not the case here, because there is no contradiction even with the conformity to another aspect (*ākārāntara*).
If it is argued that "the establishment of the object would not occur," [we reply: in that very same way, the establishment of non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*) would also not occur.

And thus, the conceptualization of blue and so forth does not possess the character of apprehending what has already been apprehended; therefore, [the objection] beginning with "it is not logical that there be a cognition of an object not previously known" (*Ajñātārthaprakāśa* 1.7) is incorrect.

Furthermore, when a person engaged in worldly discourse says: "Just as an object that is not produced from my cognition, or which does not conform to its form, is the cause of that [cognition], so too a cognition that is not produced from the object, or which does not take its form, is the apprehender of that [object]," even then, how can this constitute a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum)? Therefore, it remains established: "that [cognition] is like that object."

And thus, just as that [cognition] which arises from an object is non-conceptual according to its mode of perception, so too is the memory arising from that perception; therefore, even the talk of conceptualization has vanished. Hence, this is not tenable: "Again conceptualizing something, one knows: 'Such was my conceptual construction'. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.225).

Furthermore, there is no state in which all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have been withdrawn while one is not recollecting [them]; for even conceptualization would exist at that time in exactly the same way [as it does now], otherwise it would be different.

If you maintain that memory manifests as a universal (*sāmānya*), then perception (*darśana*) should also be accepted as such. Thus, the point is: how is it that the conceptual construction occurring in that state is not recollected?
"Not occurring in between" (*nāntarā bhavati*) means "not occurring in the interval," that is to say, "inseparable" (*avinābhāvī*).
The *prasaṅgasādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) consists in establishing what is undesirable for the opponent by means of what is accepted by him...

Its purpose is to demonstrate that once the relationship of pervader (*vyāpaka*) and pervaded (*vyāpya*) between the probandum and the probans is established, the acceptance of the pervaded is inseparable from the acceptance of the pervader, or that the absence of the pervader is invariably concomitant with the absence of the pervaded—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 544.
The Praśastapādabhāṣya, page 43:
[An object] does not conform to the form of the cognition.
The state in which all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn would be non-conceptual with respect to the object.
Introducing [the following], he says: "That perception," and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore perception (*darśana*) is not that which has for its object a unique, exclusive, and singular [particular] (*asādhāraṇaikāntagocara*). That which has for its object (*gocara*) a unique (*asādhāraṇa*), single (*eka*), unaccompanied (*asahāya*), and ultimate (*anta*) property (*dharma*) is described as such.
Why is this so? He says: "For one whose senses are engaged," and so forth.

For one whose sense-faculties (*akṣāṇi*) are engaged and directed toward the production of cognition, there is at no time—whether in a state where all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn, or in any other state, whether externally or internally—any perception (*darśana*) in that very same manner, namely, in the form of a unique object (*asādhāraṇa-gocara*). This is the syntactical construction of the words. Elaborating on this very point, he says: "For not," and so forth.

For we never, at any time, perceive the form—the essential nature of a thing—either outside or inside [the object], such that it is devoid of a companion and free from the properties of its opposite; [this is] understood by supplying the words "as it is described" or "as it is told" by others.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no determination in that very way," that is, because there is no determination or certainty in the manner described.
And it is held that what is "determined" is what is apprehended.
Why is this so? To this he says: "consisting of various parts, forms, and so forth," etc. Of what is it [the object]?
Of that which has a jar or the like as its beginning—namely, the body and so forth—and not of cognition.
Of what kind is that? It is an object (*artha*), not a cognition (*jñāna*).

Whence is this? The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because there is a determination (*saṃpratīti*)—that is, a certain cognition—of something other than external knowledge, in another location, we do not perceive the form of a single [object] consisting of an accumulation of atoms as being without a companion.

If it is argued that even so, the position of the Naiyāyikas and others is established because that [object] is cognized as distinct from its parts and qualities, he says in response: "Because it consists of various parts, forms, and so forth."

That which has various parts (*avayava*)—such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth—as its constituent selves (*ātman*) is described as such. These parts are mobile and immobile, covered and uncovered, colored and the opposite thereof, and destroyed and undestroyed; these are the "various parts. Because of the statement "having that as its self," it is meant that it is mobile through mobile parts such as the hands and so forth, and immobile through those [parts] that are the opposite. If one asks, "How can it be one in such a way? we reply: "Because it is perceived as such. For there is no other recourse for the fact that even when a part such as the hand moves, it is not the case that it (the whole) does not move, since it is perceived as being so.

If it is argued that this alone is the [defining] cognition and not others, we say no; for even when only a single part moves, one observes the worldly convention that "the body moves. To illustrate: when there is some doubt as to whether a person is dead or alive, one observes the conventional usage: "He is alive, because he moves his hand, which implies he moves his body."

If it is argued that such conventional usage [of motion] occurs because the action of the parts is metaphorically attributed (*upacāra*) to the whole—just as there is the conventional usage "the man goes" because the action of the horse is metaphorically attributed to the man—then, in that case, there would be no action in the part either in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), since the usage there too would arise from the metaphorical attribution of another's action. If you then argue that the non-slippery cognition (*askhalat-pratyaya*) is the same in both cases, and that it is illogical for a single entity to possess both moving and non-moving natures due to contradiction, we say: no; for contradiction is not established with respect to its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*).
For that which is the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of something is not contradicted by itself, because otherwise it would follow that this is the case for all entities;
and its intrinsic nature is indeed perceived as such,
whether it be the whole (avayavin) or the substance (dravya).
Even when a part moves, the whole does not move; such is the [cognition] regarding the part as well.

If it is argued that the uncontradicted cognition regarding the action of a part is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then as for what another says: "When a limb of the hand moves, the body does not move;
why? Because a specific action is established through a specific cause."

Indeed, that effort which is the cause of action for a small part such as a finger is not the cause of action for the large body. Nor is it the case that whatever conjunction moves a blade of grass is the same [conjunction] that moves a mountain; nor is there a cognition that "the body moves" when a part of the finger moves. This [objection] too is refuted by the following: we certainly do not perceive another motionless nature inherent in the moving part of the finger, because there is an absence of any perception of a dancing form therein.
Even so, if that were to be postulated, one would have to postulate a mobile form for the whole (avayavin) within its immobile parts;
this would contradict perception, and the Vaiśeṣika would not be deterred from such a position even in other cases.
Objection: But there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the existence of a whole (*avayavin*). To explain:

when the hand is trembling, the body resting upon it does not tremble; or when the foot is trembling, the body situated upon it does not tremble. Thus, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a single entity possesses contradictory properties. Reply: That is incorrect. For there is no rule of necessity that the body must tremble whenever the hand trembles.
When the cause exists only to move the hand alone, then only that much moves, and not the body, due to the absence of a cause for its movement.

But when [the power] becomes the cause of movement even for the body, then the body certainly moves; since there is no state of non-movement for it, how can there be a contradiction?—*Praśastakandali*, p.
41–42, because it would follow that there could be no such perception as "the body dances within the body."

Furthermore, that which was stated by that same [author]—namely, "If the motion of the whole were to occur at the same time as the motion of its parts, then when a part of the finger moves, there would arise the cognition 'the body moves.

What is the reason? Because, in the absence of spatial separation, the motion inherent in the perceptible substratum would be directly perceived; yet, when a part of the finger moves, such a cognition as 'the body moves' does not occur"—that too is not tenable, because it has already been answered, and because we observe the conventional usage "he moves the body" even when only the hand is moving.

Furthermore, if the whole were identical with its parts, then when a part such as the hand is separated from space and so forth, the separation [of the whole] from them would necessarily be established; likewise, when there is conjunction with them, conjunction [of the whole] would be established. This is not the case if there is a difference [between the whole and the parts].
For it is not logical that when the hand is separated from something or conjoined with something, that [separation or conjunction] should belong to the moving [hand] and the non-moving [body].
Now, if the production of separation from separation is admitted, then the production of conjunction from conjunction is also admitted, and thus this fault does not arise.

Why is this so? If it is argued that an effect must necessarily be separated from or conjoined with its cause—just as a cloth and the like are separated from or conjoined with the shuttle and other tools that are conjoined with the threads and so forth—it might be so only if there were some kind of identity between cause and effect. Otherwise, every effect such as a jar would be separated from or conjoined with any other thing, whether separate or conjoined, that serves as a cause for the potter himself.

This fault does not apply because of the qualification "by the inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇena*). [Objection: How so? For if there were an absolute distinction between effect and cause, there would be no cause for the distinction between the inherent cause and other causes, and thus inherence itself would be its own cause. [Response: No; because that [notion of inherence] is about to be refuted by such passages as *Siddhiviniscaya* 2.26, beginning with "perception is conceptual," and so forth.
Even though it is not explicitly denied, just as there is inherence (samavāya) between the intended cause and effect, so too is there [inherence] between the pot and its maker, the potter.

Now, even if there is no difference in their relational status, if it is argued that due to some proximity (*pratyāsatti*), one thing is inherent (*samavāyin*) to another, or that something is conjoined with or disjoined from something else by means of that which is being conjoined or disjoined—then, since the identity (*tādātmya*) of one thing with another is established through that very [proximity], what is the use of inherence, of disjunction produced by disjunction, or of conjunction produced by conjunction? Furthermore, we do not observe a disjunction or conjunction of the body resulting from the disjunction or conjunction of the hand and so forth with something else;
yet, if one were to postulate such [a primary relation], nothing at all would remain as a single entity.

Now, there is also a distinction between the hand and the body. Why? Because of the distinction in their disjunction (*vibhāga*). There is a mutual dependence: from the establishment of the distinction between the hand and the body, the establishment of the distinction in their disjunction follows; and from this, the matter at hand is established. Furthermore, apart from a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*), there is no other disjunction between the hand and space that could serve as the cause for the disjunction between the body and space. Otherwise, [if such a cause were required], there would be a disjunction of the effect from a disjunction of the cause, and immediately after the disjunction of the effect, there would be a fear of their becoming one; and if there were yet another [disjunction] even in that case, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is argued that its very own nature (svarūpa) is what is divided from that [space], then let this be the case elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, if the perception of the division of the hand and so forth from space were to occur only when the body is perceived as being in conjunction with space, then this would be logical: namely, that from the division of the hand from space follows the division of the body from space, and from that follows the cessation of the conjunction of the body with space.
But this is not the case, because no such sequence is perceived; for at the very moment of the disjunction between the hand and space, the disjunction between the body and space is observed.
Indeed, no one who is conjoined with space thinks, "My hand and so forth have been disjoined from that [space] within my body.

If it is argued that this sequence is not perceived due to its rapid occurrence—like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals—we reply: this would be so only if the difference in the nature and time of those disjunctions were established in some way, as is the case with the difference in nature and location of the petals themselves. But this is not so, because such a claim is contradicted by experience.
According to the Vaiśeṣika,
[it belongs] to the body which is characterized by activity.
Conjunction and disjunction are each of two kinds; however, disjunction produced by disjunction is of two types: from the disjunction of causes and from the disjunction of cause and non-cause.

Regarding the first, concerning disjunction from a cause: when an action has arisen in a cause that is occupied by its effect, it produces a disjunction from another constituent part at that time, but not yet from a location such as space; whereas when it produces a disjunction from a location such as space, it does not [simultaneously] produce a disjunction from another constituent part—such is the established rule.
Therefore, the action of a part initiates disjunction from another part;

from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance. When that [conjunction] has perished, due to the absence of its cause, there is an absence of its effect—namely, the destruction of the whole. At that time, the disjunction residing in the two causes, depending on either the time characterized by the destruction of the effect or the independent part, initiates a disjunction of that very active part from a location such as space (ākāśa) which was previously conjoined with the effect; it does not belong to the inactive part, because in the absence of a cause, there would be no production of subsequent conjunction, resulting in the undesirable consequence of its being unenjoyable.
However, the action of that part does not produce disjunction from a location such as space, because the time for its origination has already passed;
yet it certainly produces conjunction with another location, since there is no lapse of time for an action that has not yet produced conjunction.

How [is it] even from the disjunction between the cause and the non-cause? When an action produced in the hand, without effecting a disjunction from another part, initiates disjunctions from points of space such as ether and initiates conjunctions with other points of space, then those disjunctions between the cause and the non-cause—taking into account the direction toward which the action is oriented for the commencement of the effect—initiate disjunctions between the effect and the non-effect. Immediately after that, from the conjunction between the cause and the non-cause, there arise conjunctions between the effect and the non-effect. —Praśastapādabhāṣya, pp. 67–68.
For it is a logical principle that an effect must necessarily be conjoined with that which is conjoined with its cause—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.
485; "The effect is conjoined with that which is conjoined with its cause"—*Praśastapādakārikā*, p. 149; "Like the shuttle conjoined with the cloth"—*Praśastapādakārikā*, p. 149.
Because there is a proximity between the thread and the cloth, even though [the thread] serves as the cause (nimitta).

The refutation by means of comparison: If [the disjunction] resides in a single location, that which produces a disjunction from one thing is the very same as that which produces it from another; thus, there is no such thing as a "disjunction produced by disjunction."
— if [it is argued that] it is a particular state (avasthāviśeṣa), Nyāyamañjarī, p. 123.
One disjunction [is produced] by another disjunction,
as in the case of space and so forth.

Regarding what has been stated by the opponent—that the destruction of the conjunction between the hand and space results from their disjunction—that is not correct; for as long as the conjunction exists, disjunction cannot arise. Just as when a disjunction, which is the opposite of conjunction, has arisen, the conjunction is destroyed, so too, while a conjunction that is the opposite of disjunction persists, disjunction does not arise.

If it is argued that while fire, which is opposed to cold, remains present, there can be no production of cold, and that such production occurs only when the conjunction [of the fire] has perished; then from what does that destruction [of the conjunction] arise? If it is said to be from disjunction (*vibhāga*), there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): disjunction arises when the destruction of conjunction has occurred, and from that [disjunction], its [the conjunction's] destruction follows.

If it is argued that disjunction is indeed observed to arise even while conjunction still exists—since there is no such thing as the "untenable" regarding what is actually perceived—we say no, because such a perception is absent.

Since there is the cognition of disjunction as having the nature of the destruction of conjunction, [one might argue] that "destruction of conjunction" and "disjunction" differ only in name and not in substance. If it is asked: "In the absence of disjunction, how can there be its destruction? [we reply: "In the absence of its destruction, how can there be disjunction? If it is argued that [disjunction arises] from its own cause, namely action (*karman*), we say that action also [arises] from its own cause, such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth—as will be stated later: "the destruction of conjunction."
And from disjunction arises the destruction of conjunction, [which itself arises] from action.

"The substance, which is without beginning or end, desiring to arise, remaining stable, and subject to destruction, transforms by itself or through another, sequentially, in the form of cause and effect" (Siddhiviniścaya 3.21). Furthermore, there is no action (*karman*) other than the mutual displacement of entities that could serve as the cause of disjunction or anything else; otherwise, even when [actions such as] throwing upwards arise and perish, if the substance does not move by its own nature, then there can be no disjunction or conjunction for it with another location or the like, because [if it did,] it would follow [absurdly] that this would apply to everything without distinction.

Now, as for the notion that "it belongs to that very [entity]," to which [entity] does it belong? Since the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) exists in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth as well—there being no distinction in that regard—it would follow that this [space] is what is perceived as "that which moves. This is not so; for since that [space] does not move by itself, such a perception is impossible, and it would result in the fallacy of error.

If it is argued that [the substance] moves by itself, then action (*kriyā*) would be nothing other than a particular state of the substance's own nature and not something distinct; this is not tenable, for the definition of action is: "that which resides in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15).
Thus [it is said]: "An action that is contrary to its purpose is fruitless" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.14).
And:
By this, the destruction of the conjunction between space and the body is explained,
as is that of a conjunction involving something possessing the nature of motion.
Because inherence is all-pervasive,
[it exists] even in that which is devoid of the action of motion.
"The independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions"—*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*;
"the independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions"—*Nayacakravṛtti*, p.
30; "fruitless" means purposeless.

The term *kāryavirodhin* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has an effect as its opposite"—see Vaiśeṣika Upaniṣad, p. 21. Furthermore, regarding this [point]: from the conjunction of the hand with the subsequent space (*uttarākāśa*), there arises the conjunction of the body with space (*śarīrākāśasaṃyoga*).

This too is not perceived as such; for there is no perception that first there is a conjunction of the hand—devoid of the body—with space, and afterwards that of the body. Any illusion of simultaneity due to rapid succession has already been refuted. Furthermore, if the body were to separate from those [parts] such as space when the hand separates from them, or if it were to join with them when the hand joins with them, then while the feet and other parts remain unseparated from them at that very time, the body would neither separate nor join; thus it would be simultaneously joined and otherwise.

It might be thought that the body must be [considered] as a whole— that it is entirely devoid of [contact with other things]— yet, when the feet and other limbs come into contact with space and so forth, there is an immediate contact [of the body] with them, and thus there is no interruption in the cognition of it as being in contact. That is not a well-defined statement, because there is no contradiction even otherwise.

For it is not the case that one and the same thing is mobile in relation to its moving parts and immobile otherwise; likewise, being conjoined and being disjoined in relation to its conjoined and disjoined parts would be contradictory, just as [the properties of] being mobile and having a single form [are contradictory].
If this too is not accepted, then how [do you explain] the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.14): "And qualities [produce] another quality"?

In this sūtra, the purpose stated for the word *antara* (distinct) is as follows: there is no fault because it serves to indicate that in certain cases, the qualities of cause and effect belong to different classes (*jātyantara*).
How so? For example, the color of a cloth produced from threads that are both white and non-white is a different class from the colors of the constituent causes.
What, then, is the class-characteristic (*jāti*) of that color? We say it is variegation (*citra*).
Because its specific qualities are not determined— that is, because its specific qualities such as whiteness and the like are not apprehended from it—
this substance is not formless; for if it were, it would follow that it could be perceived [without those qualities], like wind,
whereas in fact it is perceived like a thread, and thus it is the substratum of form.
Thus,
there is a conjunction with the body,
because the inherence of color is the cause of visual perception.
By this, that which was stated—

"If it is argued that the variegated is one, then this is a great marvel indeed" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.200)— is also refuted; for we do not admit that the word "variegated" (citra) has multiple objects as its referent.

If it is asked, "Where then does it reside? [the answer is: It resides in a single variegated form (*śabala-rūpa*), and thus there is such an appearance—namely, "the cow is variegated" and "the horse is indeed variegated.

How so? For even if many distinct colors such as blue and so forth reside in a cloth produced by white and non-white threads, nevertheless, multiple actions do not reside simultaneously in a single substance. This is because, while they share the properties of being of the same genus, being perceivable by the same sense organ, and residing in a single substance, they reside in a non-omnipresent substance, just like color (*rūpa*).
In this case, the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).
Furthermore, where do blue and other qualities reside? If you say they reside in a substance (*dravya*), then the same fault [previously mentioned] applies.

If you say they are of the nature of that [substance], by what relation? If you say by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then blue and the rest would possess substantiality (*dravyatva*) just like that [substance].

If it is argued that [color] exists [in substance] by way of inherence (*samavāya*), then its nature as a substance would follow from its being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of blue and so forth.

If it is argued that it exists by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāvena*), then color and the other qualities would also exist in the substance by that very same relation, and thus there would be no inherence.
Since blue and the others are not included among [the categories of] substance and so forth, they must be distinct categories (*padārthāntaratva*).

If [it is argued that the two] exist through identity (*tādātmya*), then it is established that [the object] possesses a single variegated form (*śabalaikarūpa*); therefore, the statement "of one [entity] consisting of multiple parts" is intended to demonstrate its state of being both conjoined with and disjoined from moving and non-moving [parts]. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the visible [parts] consist of the visible while the invisible [parts] consist of the non-visible, since the admission of [the object as having] multiple forms has not been accepted.
The term *citra* signifies comparison: at one time, only one action occurs in a single substance; and one action occurs in only one substance. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 290.

"In an all-pervading substance, there is no inherence of specific qualities that are perceptible by the same sense organs"—this [reason] is contradicted; for in the aforementioned inference, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). (Pramāṇavārttika-vyākhyā, p. 220)
In the case of variegated color, it arises from the conjunction of two substances alone.
Since only a substance can be an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa),
let them exist merely as qualifiers, like a variegated single form; this is the illustrative example.

If it is argued that, in this case, even upon the perception of a single thread-part, the cloth would be perceived—yet this is not so because the perception of the whole is produced by the contact of the sense organ with the whole, which is assisted by the contact of the sense organ with multiple parts—this might indeed be so if there were an absolute difference between the part and the whole; however, that is not the case, as has already been established.

And thus, the contact between the sense organ and the parts is not one thing, while the contact between the sense organ and the whole is another, such that it could be said: "Because the contact with the whole is the perceiver of the whole when aided by the contact with many parts"; for assistance is based on a distinction [between the two contacts].

Furthermore, if there is sensory contact with the whole (*avayavin*), why does cognition not arise in that regard? Otherwise, how could there be cognition of the whole in darkness and similar conditions, for in those cases there is no sensory contact with many parts, as there is in a well-lit area? Otherwise, there would be no conventional usage regarding the lack of clarity in that cognition, [which] the opponent holds to be caused by the non-perception of the parts. Moreover, if sensory contact with it is not admitted, then it would not belong even to a single part; thus, there would be no perception of that either.
Therefore, this is incorrect: that from the conjunction of a single thread and a *vīraṇa* grass there arises the conjunction of a cloth and a mat. This is because there is no means of perceiving it.

If you say that their conjunction remains [unperceived] due to the proximity of those [other factors], then the same would apply to the cloth as well; for according to the statement in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p. 64), "the effect must necessarily be conjoined with that which is conjoined with its cause," otherwise, there would be no conjunction even with the *vīraṇa* grass.

Furthermore, if even the sensory contact with a single thread-part is a perceiver of the thread only when assisted by sensory contacts with many of its parts, then the sensory contact with those parts must also be a perceiver of those parts only when assisted by sensory contacts with many of their own parts, and so on down to the atoms; yet there is no sensory contact with those atoms. Consequently, there would be a non-perception of everything.

Furthermore, if cognition were not to arise there from the sensory contact with even a single part, then one would not have the recognition "an elephant stands here" upon seeing only the trunk of an elephant submerged in water; yet this is accepted by the opponent.

Therefore, it was rightly stated that the phrase "consisting of multiple parts" is intended to demonstrate the principle that "by visible parts, [the whole] which is of a visible nature [is perceived], and by those contrary [to being visible], that which is of a contrary nature. Likewise, this applies to the acceptance of a whole composed of parts regarding the principle that "by covered parts, [the whole] which is of a covered nature [is perceived], and by those contrary [to being covered], that which is of a contrary nature."
Because it is apprehended through contact with the whole (*avayavin*) aided by repeated contacts with the sense organ and its parts—
*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 46—

it is perceived together with those parts whose contact with the sense organ allows for their apprehension, but it is not perceived together with those parts whose apprehension is prevented by obstruction.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 2.1.32
In the case of a whole (*avayavin*) such as darkness and so forth, there is the conventional usage of "indistinctness" with respect to that whole.
The sensory contact with even a single part [of an object] is the apprehender of that single part.
As many atomic-form parts as there are, that many conjunctions are necessary for the whole (avayavin). This is the trunk [of the argument].
A form that is moving is seen as moving by those who are moving, not by others; one that is lost is seen as lost by those who are lost, and not by others;
one that is covered is seen as covered by those who are covered; and one that is red is seen as red by those who are red.
— *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 102.
Nyāyaviniścaya 2.271:
But surely this is untenable, because it is impossible for a single thing to be both covered and uncovered.
Indeed, even when there is an obstruction of a single part, such as the hand, there is no obstruction of the body because of its magnitude (*mahattva*).

For it is not the case that the entire conjunction with the obstructing substance which covers a part also covers the whole; rather, due to its magnitude, another specific conjunction with an obstructing substance covers the whole, just as a specific conjunction with a screen or the like covers a wall.

However, a substance that covers a part does not conceal the whole (the *avayavin*) when it is conjoined with it, because of its lack of magnitude (*amahattva*) and the absence of a specific type of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*), just as a small cloth covering the private parts or a lower garment [does not conceal the person]. If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the whole in its entirety; we reply: no, because the terms "entire" (*samagra*) and "not entire" (*asamagra*) refer to the domain of difference (*bheda*), whereas the whole is non-different (*abhinnatva*). Indeed, the whole is neither "entire" nor "not entire," because it is a single unity (*ekatva*).

Furthermore, what do you consider to be unperceived of the whole (*avayavin*) that is being perceived, such that you say it is perceived incompletely? If you say that the covered part is not perceived, [we reply: let it indeed not be perceived; however, the whole is still perceived, because it is distinct from those parts. If you argue that there is this distinction—that it is perceived together with those parts whose sense-organ contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) occurs, but it is not perceived together with those parts whose sense-organ contact does not occur due to being covered—[we reply: it is said in response that this is not unreasonable, since a single whole can be both covered and uncovered, just like a variegated color (*śabala-rūpa*).

First of all, there is no such thing as the perception and non-perception of a single whole (*avayavin*) [simultaneously]. Even when its parts are covered, it is not correct to say that the whole is unperceived because of the non-appearance of such "grossness" (*sthaulya*), since some of its parts remain in their position and are indeed perceived—just as it is when many parts are perceived. For grossness is a difference in dimension (*parimāṇabheda*), which is a property of the whole; and even if such [grossness] does not appear, the whole itself does not fail to appear, because the two are distinct. Therefore, the perception of the whole arises from mere contact with the sense faculty.

The perception of differences in magnitude occurs due to the contact of the sense organ with the object, of the parts of the sense organ with the object, of the sense organ with the parts of the object, and of the parts of the sense organ with the parts of the object. Thus, because of the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the perception or non-perception of the whole and its respective differences in magnitude are logically established—since there is no concealment of the whole when only one of its parts is concealed (Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 384).
For that [whole] is indeed perceived as one among many [parts] through the apprehension of some parts—whether unobstructed or otherwise—because it is non-different in all respects;
[see *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kanda* p. 42 on the whole (*avayavin*)].
Since there exists a specific conjunction that covers both the small and the large,
and since there is no division within a single entity— rendering the application of the term "division" untenable— the question is invalid.

"11. 'Whole' (kṛtsna) is the designation of the entirety of many [parts]; 'part' (ekadeśa) is the designation of some [part] when there is plurality. These two terms, 'whole' and 'part,' have difference as their object and are not applicable to a single composite whole because of the absence of difference. — Nyāyabhāṣya 4.1.34.
2.11 From the constituent parts.

As for the fact that a cognition of grossness does not occur even when many parts are perceived, that is because there is an absence of the perception of a greater accumulation of parts, which is the cause for the cognition of the excellence of magnitude (*parimāṇa*).

However, where there is an obscuration of many parts and only a few parts are perceived, there is no perception of the whole (*avayavin*), as in the case of seeing only the head of one submerged in water—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 42.

As for the argument that was repeated—that the extent of the conjunction with the obscuring agent which covers the parts does not cover the whole (the avayavin)—that too is not well-said; for according to the statement in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p. 64), "the effect must necessarily be conjoined with that which is conjoined with its cause," there exists a conjunction with the obscuring agent for the whole (avayavin) just as there is for the parts (avayava).

And if, upon its production, the whole (*avayavin*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and it is the cause of that [conjunction] in its entirety; then there would be a perception of that conjunction everywhere. How then could that very same conjunction not be the concealer? For it is said: "But it is a specific kind of conjunction with another concealing substance that conceals the whole.
If, on the other hand, it is not in its entirety but only by way of one part, then the whole must possess parts (*sāṃśatva*).

But was it not said—that because the words "complete" and "incomplete" refer to distinct objects, while the whole (*avayavin*) is non-different [from its parts], that [distinction] is untenable? True, it was so said; however, by one who asserts its non-difference, a single nature (*svarūpa*) for it is admitted. If that very [nature] is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the conjunction, then since the conjunction appears as inherent (*samaveta*) therein, its form cannot exist devoid of it; thus, there is no avoidance of the aforementioned fault regarding the conjunction.
The impossibility of a composite whole possessing parts [is established] because of the [logical] inconsistency of a composite whole.
In its own nature,
the whole is of a single nature and is devoid of conjunction.

And as for what else was said—"Furthermore, you [must admit that] the whole (avayavin) being grasped," and so forth—to that also we reply: neither the nature of the whole nor the nature of the parts is grasped;

this is because, in some way, there is identity (tādātmya) between the parts and the whole. Otherwise, if this were not the case, there would be no doubt regarding the visible portion of a whole such as a pillar while it is in the midst of obscuring water and the like—namely, "Does it exist or does it not? or "How much of it exists?"

And as for the other [objections], such as "but there is this distinction," etc.—that too is refuted by this very argument. For just as parts that are covered are not perceived by the senses because they are not in contact with them, and likewise the whole (avayavin) together with them is not perceived, so too the [whole] alone, even when conjoined with the coverer, is not perceived.

Therefore, it is established: the statement "consisting of various parts" (*nānāvayavātmanaḥ*) is intended to demonstrate that, in relation to the covered parts, the self of the whole is one way, while in relation to other [parts], it is otherwise;

and likewise, it is intended to demonstrate that, in relation to the destroyed [parts], it is the self of the destroyed, while in relation to the undestroyed [parts], it is the self of the undestroyed.
And the whole is perceived as qualified by its veiled parts.

Regarding the statement "of that which consists of various parts": surely those parts have perished—those very parts which, being distinct from the inactive parts, are separated and joined with other locations, just as hands and so forth are distinct from feet and so forth. Furthermore, the prior whole-body (śarīra) does not exist within them, such as the feet and so forth, by virtue of which it could be said—"it is unperished in relation to its unperished parts. Otherwise, there would be no separation of the variegated hands and so forth from the inactive parts, just as there is none from space and the like.

As it has been stated: "That which resides in substance, possesses qualities, and is not a cause [of action] with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent [of other causes]"—this is the definition of a quality (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.16).

Regarding this sūtra, some maintain that the disjunction of the two bamboo halves, which are the causes, in order to bring about [the subsequent] disjunction, depends upon the destruction of the bamboo.
Why? Because as long as the lineage has not perished, there is a lack of independence.

Disjunction, which resides in its own constituent parts independently, initiates another disjunction, but not that which resides in parts bound to an effect; we shall explain how this is well-established later on. To this it is said: if it is argued that from the disjunction of the two bamboo halves (the causes), there occurs a disjunction of a certain part—the bamboo half—from space and so forth; it might be thought that the disjunction of the active part—the bamboo half—from space and so forth is produced by action, [but] such is not the case for an action that initiates a disjunction which is opposed to the conjunction that originates the substance.

Actions that initiate a disjunction which opposes the conjunction initiating a substance do not initiate a disjunction that opposes the conjunction initiating a substance, just as the actions of the parts of a dancer [do not produce such a disjunction]. Likewise, in this case as well, if the actions of cutting, splitting, and carving were to produce disjunctions from space and so forth, they would not be initiators of disjunctions that oppose the conjunctions initiating a substance.

And this being so, the following is stated: the actions of cutting, splitting, and carving do not initiate a disjunction of their own substratum from space and the like, because they produce a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction initiating the substance; whereas those actions which do initiate a disjunction of their own substratum from space and the like do not initiate a disjunction opposed to the conjunction initiating the substance, as for example, the actions of the parts of a dancing person.

If it is argued that because it is conjoined with both, it must be disjoined from both—meaning, one might think that just as this active part is conjoined with another part, so too is it conjoined with space (*ākāśa*) and other [substances]; therefore, just as it is disjoined from the other part due to having been conjoined with it, so too it must be disjoined from space and the others due to having been conjoined with them—[we reply: no, because this is not universally true (*anekāntāt*). This is not an absolute rule: action produced in a part of the hand does not initiate disjunction from all things conjoined with its own substratum; rather, it initiates it from only some. This is because such is observed.

It is indeed observed that the action of a finger initiates a disjunction from space and other such entities, but it does not initiate a disjunction from another part [of the body] that is opposed to the conjunction producing the substance; likewise, this action of a part, such as tearing, initiates a disjunction from another part that is opposed to the conjunction producing the substance, but not from space and other such entities. Therefore, the claim that "it is separated from both" is incorrect.
If it is asked, "From what cause does this distinction arise?"—it is due to a specific cause, namely, that which produces the substance.
From [the whole] there arises a spatial division, such as that of space and so forth,
which is a division of parts.

The weighing of substance: when an action produced [in a part] creates a disjunction from another part that destroys the conjunction initiating the substance, it does not at that time create a disjunction from a location such as space which is incompatible with the substance; and when it creates a disjunction from a location such as space, it does not at that time [create one] from another part—this is the rule of established order.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kanda, p. 155:
Because the hand is conjoined with both [the space] such as the location of the ether and another part [of the body].

It might be thought: although there is no difference in their residing in parts such as the hand, why is it that some actions initiate a disjunction of their own substratum from space and so forth, while others initiate a disjunction from another part that is opposed to the conjunction that produces a substance? What causes this distinction in disjunction? It is due to a specific cause; this distinction arises from a specific cause of action.
As it has been said: "From a specific impulsion (nodana) comes a specific throwing upward (udāsana)" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.6).

Thus, when the cause is occupied by the effect, the action produced therein initiates a disjunction from another part; from that disjunction follows the cessation of the conjunction that originates the substance; thereupon the effect-substance ceases to exist; once that has ceased, the disjunction residing in the two causes initiates a disjunction of the active part from [substances] such as space (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 68).

If it is asked, "What is the reason?"—it might be thought: when the effect-substance has ceased to exist, a disjunction from space and so forth arises for the active part from the disjunction existing between the two causes, but not previously; what is the reason for this? The reason is its concomitance with the destruction of the effect-substance. If the disjunction of the active part from space and so forth were to arise while the effect-substance still exists, then it would not be concomitant with the destruction of that effect-substance, like the disjunction of a finger from space. To this, the following reply is given:
Forms such as moving and shaking,
forms such as uprooting, and throwing far upward.
It should be observed— see page 45, note 10— that "na" here is meaningless.

As for what was stated—that the disjunction of the two bamboo halves, which is to bring about [their] further disjunction, depends upon the destruction of the bamboo, and so forth—if, upon the destruction of the conjunction resulting from the disjunction of one part from another due to the act of cutting a finger-joint, the whole (the body) were to be destroyed, then, since the body would be destroyed by the mere action of cutting its parts and so on, its qualities would also be destroyed. Consequently, there would be the perception only of those constituent parts, such as the feet, that are devoid of the perception of that whole.
But this is not the case, because there is the recognition that "this very same body" exists prior to, after, and even at the same time as its cutting;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the collapse of worldly conventions such as, "This is indeed my son, even though his finger has been cut off.

If it is argued that when the conjunction of one part is destroyed and the previous substance ceases to exist, another substance arises from the remaining parts through their continued conjunctions—and thus this fault does not apply—then this point must be understood by drinking from the vessel alone (i.e., by mere assertion), for it is not supported by cognition, since we always perceive the identity of the whole.
If it is argued that this cognition of oneness is an error, we say no, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

If it is further argued that the very production of another substance upon the destruction of the previous substance constitutes the subverting evidence, then from what is that [production] established? If it is said to be from the error of that very cognition, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the production of another substance is established once the error of that cognition is proven, and the error of that cognition is proven once the production of another substance is established.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that—while the body is always perceived as a single entity—the destruction of the conjunction of one part results in the cessation of the previous substance, and then another substance arises from the remaining parts with their conjunctions intact; then it would be better to simply accept atoms themselves, both simultaneously and successively. In this way, you would be liberated from the laborious effort of proving the existence of composite wholes (*avayavin*) and so forth, for the refutation by means of the perception of a single gross object applies equally to the qualities of the body, which is itself a composite whole.
If the destruction of the body were to occur from the cutting off of its parts,
then this person would be worthy of trust immediately after drinking wine, because another body has arisen there.
If one were to argue that "this very thing is the body," then the cognition of the body and so forth would occur only with respect to the atoms;

furthermore, when a finger-part moves or is covered, the body neither moves nor is it covered, because such is our experience. Thus, how can one who asserts the destruction of the whole (the composite) upon the destruction of the conjunction of even a single part be considered sound? For the experience [of the body remaining] is identical in both cases.

Furthermore, even if there were the destruction of the conjunction with one part, what would follow from that such that the whole (*avayavin*), which is distinct from it, would be destroyed? For this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It is not necessarily the case that an effect produced from the destruction of its cause must itself be destroyed; for here, the conjunction is not the material cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) according to the opponent's own admission. If it is argued that its destruction follows from the destruction of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) because it is perceived as such, we say no; for even when the conjunction with one part is destroyed, the effect-substance is perceived to persist in some manner.
Because the Vaiśeṣika accepts that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) residing in a part (*avayava*) is an non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

By this, the destruction of the effect [the whole] resulting from disjunctions and so forth has been refuted; for when one part is separated from another part through disjunction, the destruction of the prior whole is denied. Indeed, when a single part of the ear is pierced, the body is not perceived to be destroyed; nor when a single thread is torn, the cloth; nor when a single node of a bamboo is cut by a sharp axe, the bamboo itself is destroyed. [Objection: But surely, the disjunction of a part from space and so forth occurs through an action belonging to the bamboo that does not destroy the effect-substance, because [the action] lacks independence.

If it is asked: why is it that disjunction (*vibhāga*), which functions as an independent constituent [of action], is admitted to exist for a moving part in relation to space and so forth? If you say: because such disjunction from space and so forth is observed in that part as being concomitant with the destruction of the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*); then, when the effect-substance has not yet been destroyed, what is perceived regarding its disjunction from another part? If it is not perceived, how can there be a distinction such that "one exists and the other does not"? What would constitute that disjunction?

It might be thought: "The disjunction from that [whole] belonging to a part, being inferred from the impossibility of explaining the destruction of the effect otherwise, exists previously [with respect to its own parts], but not with respect to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. This is not so. For if there were no disjunction from space and so forth—just as there is none from its other parts—then the destruction of the effect would follow, because disjunction is the opposite of the conjunction that initiates the substance. [Objection: But if there is no prior disjunction from its other parts, how can there be one from space and so forth? [For] an effect does not arise in the absence of a cause. [Reply: This would indeed be so, if the action of the part did not produce disjunction from space and so forth, just as it produces disjunction from its other parts.

If it is asked how multiple disjunctions can arise from a single action, [the response is: How is it that from space, time, direction, the self, and so forth, there simultaneously arise many disjunctions of that [action], or conjunctions with them— by virtue of which the purpose of the plural number in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.20), "Action is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions," would be rendered meaningful?

From an action residing in a single part, two disjunctions arise from that part [with respect to its other parts], and many disjunctions arise from the parts [themselves]; yet they do not arise from space and so forth— this [assertion] is merely fabricated according to one's own whim regarding the disjunction of a part from another part.
Action is the common cause of conjunction, disjunction, and velocity; the word "is" is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].

In whatever substance an action has arisen, having produced as many disjunctions as there were substances with which that [substance] was conjoined, it likewise produces that same number of conjunctions again elsewhere— Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-upaskāra 1.1.20.

It might be thought: "The action of cutting does not initiate a disjunction of its own constituent part from space and so forth, because it generates a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction that originates the substance;
