whereas that which initiates a disjunction of that constituent part from space and so forth does not initiate a disjunction opposed to the conjunction that originates the substance, as in the case of the action of a limb belonging to one who is dancing. This is not a valid reason, because it is unproven (*asiddha*); for it has already been considered that disjunction is nothing other than the destruction of conjunction.

Furthermore, it is not established in every respect that cutting and so forth produce a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance with respect to another [object], because that would entail the destruction of the whole (avayavin).

And if the action of a limb belonging to a dancing person is the cause of its disjunction from space and so forth, yet it is not observed to be the cause of disjunction from another limb, then even cutting and the like should be postulated as not being the cause for that [disjunction] in the same way; for if that were so, then the disjunction existing between the two halves of a bamboo-stick—which are the causes—would not be observed to be the cause of the disjunction of the inactive part from space and so forth, and thus it should be postulated to be likewise for the active part as well, since there is no distinction; and thus, in the present case too, there would be a subversion of the means of valid cognition.

"Occupied by an effect" means pervaded by it, that is to say, having begun its activity; in such a cause, action arises, not in a mere cause. When [the action] produces a disjunction from another part—which is opposed to the conjunction that initiates the substance—it does not [then produce a disjunction] from a location such as space; but when it [produces a disjunction] from a location such as space, it does not [then produce] a distinct disjunction from another part. This is the established rule regarding the consideration of disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī*, p.
499; *Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 250.

The property of being the agent of a disjunction from space is pervaded by the property of not originating a disjunction that opposes the conjunction which initiates a substance; and the property of originating a disjunction that opposes the conjunction which initiates a substance is contradictory to the former. Therefore, wherever this [latter property] is perceived, since the non-origination of a disjunction opposing the conjunction initiating a substance is absent, the property of being the agent of a disjunction from space—which is pervaded by it—is also absent, just as smoke is excluded when fire is excluded.
— Praśastikāṇḍa, p. 156,
considered with reference to the Jaina.
Furthermore, action is not the cause of the disjunction of its own constituent parts; rather, according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.16), action is the general cause of conjunctions and disjunctions.

If it is argued that, according to this statement, why do the actions of the parts of one dancing not initiate mutual disjunctions among the parts such as the hands? If this were the case, then from the destruction of those conjunctions, there would follow the destruction of the dancing whole—[we reply: no; for it is stated that when the conjunction with one part is destroyed and the previous substance ceases, another substance arises from the parts whose conjunctions remain intact. Furthermore, due to specific subsequent actions, another substance would arise through specific conjunctions; and the perception of continuity occurs because of the rapidity of the process.

If it is asked, "What is gained by this? [the answer is as follows]: An action belonging to a part that possesses activity does not initiate a disjunction from space and so forth, because it generates a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction initiating the substance;

whereas that which initiates a disjunction of that part from something else is not the generator of that [substance-initiating conjunction], just like the action of a limb of a dancer—as this [argument] floats away due to the destruction of the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Therefore, just as there is a disjunction from another part due to the action of a part possessing action, so too [there is a disjunction] from reality, such as space and the like;

nor is this reason inconclusive. For if it is argued that the reason is inconclusive because—just as from the disjunction of a finger from space there arises the disjunction of the hand from space, yet this is not born of action—the following has been stated in response: when the finger moves, the hand also moves in some way; thus, when there is a disjunction from space and the like, the hand also undergoes disjunction at that very moment. Otherwise, there would be a separate establishment [of the hand].

Now, if this disjunction of the active part from space and so forth were produced by action, then it too would arise immediately after the action, just like the initial disjunction of the parts; yet it has not arisen. As it was said: "Are you a child? For [the effect] does not follow from that [action], due to the falling away of the essence."

If it is argued that the opportunity for this [action] to produce disjunction has been lost because the moment for its performance has passed, this is not true; for the same applies to disjunction as well.

Indeed, one could say: if this were produced from disjunction, it would arise immediately thereafter; but it is not so. Since it is accepted that the destruction of conjunction follows from the disjunction of parts, and from that, the destruction of the substance, and then again disjunction, there is disjunction from another part and from space and so forth immediately after the action; otherwise, nothing at all would occur immediately after it.
Therefore, it is not logical that the previously perceived [object] should be destroyed in its entirety due to the severing of a single part, such as the ear;
rather, [a new object] would arise upon the mutual separation [of parts].
And the cognition of identity, "this is that very same [thing]," occurs in the case of space and the like, which possess active parts.

That which produces a disjunction that opposes the conjunction initiating a substance—for example, from the disjunction of the finger and space arises the disjunction of the hand and space...—Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p.
509; [this refers to] the finger and the hand.
Immediately after the disjunction, there is the destruction of the previously perceived body.

As for what was stated—“Actions arise in the parts, from which follows disjunction; from those, the destruction of conjunction; from that, the destruction of the substance” (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 46)—that too is not capable of withstanding scrutiny; for even if actions were produced as distinct from the parts, since there would be no movement of their own nature [as a whole], it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
There is no separation of those [atoms] even from that [action]; even if there were, for that very reason, there would be no destruction of their conjunction by it.

Even if this [destruction] were to occur, since it is distinct from the conjunction, while the conjunction remains in its original state, actions do not arise in the effect-substance; from those [actions] come separations, from the separations comes the destruction of the conjunction, and from the destruction of the conjunction, the effect-substance perishes.
— Praśastapādabhāṣya 46:
Regarding the nature of the parts,
if one were to accept motion elsewhere than from the action of a distinct substance...
Because the actions of the constituent parts are also distinct.
By this [argument regarding destruction], the opposition between action and conjunction has been refuted;
for that which is destroyed by something is opposed to it, and action is not destroyed by conjunction.

Therefore, even if there were destruction [of the whole] upon the action, nothing at all would arise; nor is this sequence within the range of another's perception—namely, first the action in these [parts], then the disjunction, from that the destruction of the conjunction, from that the destruction of the substance, and from this the destruction of the color and other qualities dependent upon it. Rather, what is within the range of perception immediately after the falling of the staff and so forth is simply the destruction of the jar and so forth.

Thus it is established: the statement "consisting of various parts" is intended to make known that the whole is destroyed by those parts whose destruction has occurred, while it remains undestroyed by others.
Through conjunction,
it indeed comes within the range of perception for the Vaiśeṣika.
By this, the following [Vaiśeṣika] position is also refuted: "Substances originate another substance" (VS 1.1.10);
namely, that the effect-substance is both a substance and something other than the causal substances. How so? Because its absolute difference from them is denied.
In some way, because inherence would be redundant and because it is denied that the causal substances are distinct from the resultant substance,

as for this further point— that substances and [other] substances begin another substance after them— it is not the case that there is a conjunction of one with those two, because this [conjunction] subsists in many things.
If it is argued that [the cloth] is the conjunction of its parts, we say no. For by that [conjunction], the substance of the thread is not produced.

And if it is further argued that at the very moment one substance inheres in the parts, another [substance] inheres in them as well, we say no; because the arising of an aggregate from another aggregate is not thereby prohibited, and because we observe the production of a small lump (śivaka) and so forth from a mass of clay, wherein the parts that constitute the small lump are not perceived prior to its production as being possessed of the actions and conjunctions [required for the production of a new substance].

Regarding this conjunction, one might argue as follows: "The *śivaka* (the small lump of clay) and so forth are composed of parts that have been conjoined, because they are effect-substances (*kāryadravya*), like a cloth and the like. This is not so; for if, upon seeing such a state in one instance, one were to postulate that state to exist everywhere, then it would follow that "diamond is scratchable by iron because it is earthy, like wood," and so on.

If you say that this [latter inference] is not valid because it is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣabādhana*), then what are the constituent parts (*ārambhakāvayava*) of the *śivaka* and so forth that are established by perception prior to [the production of the object], such that there would be no contradiction [of your inference]?

Furthermore, how are the threads the producers (*janaka*) of the cloth? If you say it is because [the cloth] exists when they exist and does not exist when they do not, then for that very reason, a lump of clay should also be the cause of the *śivaka* (the first stage of a pot). If you argue: "Indeed, the *śivaka* exists only upon the destruction of the lump of clay; otherwise, it would have been seen even at that time, just as the threads are seen at the time of the cloth," we say no. This is because the lump of clay is not the cause of the *śivaka*.

Moreover, the threads are not perceived in the cloth while still encased in their previous nature; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a continuous production of ever-new cloths.
As it has been stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*: "In the case of cloth and such,
there is no restriction [of cause and effect] observed anywhere, just as with earthy objects that can be scratched by iron."

—Even though the property of being scratchable by iron is observed in many earthen objects such as wood and stone, [it is still] only earthen; and even though the property of not being scratchable by iron is observed in the diamond (vajra), it is still only earthen... —*Pramāṇavārttikamanoratha* 4.240, even at the stage of the *śivaka*.
The observation of the lump of clay [is the example].
Since the cause is not exhausted when distinguished by its prior state, how can there be a cessation of those effects? (Nyāyaviniścaya 1)

103. Thus, it is not the case that [the threads] have not ceased [to exist]. Threads obstructed by a cloth do not initiate another cloth; this is what was stated by the opponent: "The threads, having initiated a cloth, do not initiate another cloth because of the obstruction by that cloth. In this regard, the following must be considered: would the obstruction to the production of another [cloth] consist in the removal of the cause's own nature (*svarūpa*), the removal of its capacity (*śakti*), the removal of its operation (*vyāpāra*), or the negation of the arising of the substance that is the effect? Among these, it is not the first alternative, because the existence of the cause is admitted even at the time of the effect.
Nor is the second [alternative] possible; for that is incompatible with what is eternal, as it has been said by some:
"But rather, it is only when [the cause] has ceased..."
Because it is accepted that the threads exist even at the time of the cloth, when another cloth is being produced.
Because there is no removal of its capacity; otherwise, it would follow that [the entity] is impermanent.
For that which, whether capable or incapable, exists by its own nature, who is able to destroy it, since it is eternal and incurable? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.22).
For this very reason, the third [alternative] is also not tenable; since that which possesses a single efficacious nature must necessarily operate toward the production of the effect.
Furthermore, the fourth is absolutely impossible; for it is illogical to deny the arising of an effect produced by a cause that is individually capable.

Consequently, even at the time of one cloth, another cloth would arise because the inherent (samavāyin), non-inherent (asamavāyin), and instrumental (nimitta) causes—the threads, their conjunctions, the Lord (Īśvara), and so forth—continue to exist.
Otherwise, this would be illogical: that when one cloth has ceased [to exist], they begin another cloth from the conjunctions residing therein;
yet, nothing that is ineffective should be depended upon.
Because conjunction is eternal, the word "prati" appears to be meaningless.

By this, the following argument advanced by the opponent is also refuted: "In the same way, a cloth, having originated from color and so forth, does not originate another color because it already possesses color;
likewise, an action, being the cause of further action, does not originate a subsequent action due to the obstruction of the mace and so forth.
How can this be? For when a capable cause exists, it is impossible for there to be any obstruction.
Therefore, the threads, possessing their prior nature, must be admitted to exist within the cloth; thus, the proof of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is established.
Furthermore, it is proven that even a single substance can be the initiator of another substance.

Consequently, one must state that "substances initiate other substances," by which it is understood that one substance initiates another substance, or multiple substances initiate [another] substance, as the case may be.

For just as multiple substances are seen to originate a single substance, so too a single substance is observed to originate one, two, or many substances; for example, a single jar [originates] two or many potsherd-substances. Now, it might be argued that in those cases only their disjunction (*vibhāga*) arises and not the substances themselves, because they already existed previously;
in that case, let the jar also be conceived as existing in the state of the lump of clay.
There is an absence of metaphorical designation, causal efficiency, and so forth, even in other cases;

therefore it has been rightly said: "because a jar and the like, which consist of multiple parts, are perceived externally," as well as [the absence of such] in the case of another action belonging to that which has the nature of multiple forms and so forth.
That which initiates another substance is called an agent with respect to something else.
The skulls of the skulls, of the skulls.
The point is that even when the shards are accepted as being present in the state of the jar, there is no purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), designation, or the like.
Now, if it is argued that this is logical because form and so forth are distinct from that [jar], and thus how could they be of its nature? That is not so, because it contradicts perception.

Furthermore, if there were an absolute distinction between quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*), then when the jar and so forth reach another location, the form and other qualities would necessarily not reach that location.

Furthermore, there is no disjunction produced by disjunction nor any conjunction produced by conjunction here; for it is stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.16): "A quality resides in a substance and is itself devoid of qualities."
This position has already been refuted;

furthermore, form and the other [qualities] do not themselves possess an action that serves as the cause for reaching another location, because they have attained the status of being substances. For the definition of substance is: "that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause" (VS 1.1.15).
If it is argued that, because of this statement, one must therefore accept that the jar and so forth have color and other qualities as their very nature;

then, in that case, the commencement of another causal substance occurs only through those things whose nature is color and so forth, not by means of those independent of color and so forth, nor does that commencement occur devoid of color and so forth.

Therefore, it is not correct to say that "the very same [process] by which substances originate other substances is also the process by which qualities originate other qualities"— as stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.10): "And qualities [originate] another quality."
The reaching of another location by a jar or the like, which consists of [qualities] such as color.
That which exists in color and the rest,
which resides in substance, which possesses qualities, and which is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent— this is the definition of a quality (guṇa)— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra.
If there were absolute difference characterized by the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality,
then, given the mutual identity of the pot and its color and so forth, the production of the pot and such would [not occur].
Because there is no separate commencement [of a new substance], substances commence another substance and qualities commence another quality—*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the opponent: "In the production of the color and other qualities of a jar, the jar is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), while the color and other qualities residing in the potsherds are the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*)."

Thus, that too has been refuted by this [argument]: for prior to the production of color and so forth, a jar devoid of color and so forth is not established by any means of knowledge such that it could serve as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); and in the absence of such a thing, it is untenable for the color of the potsherds and so forth to be the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
Therefore, this remains established: [it belongs] to that which consists of various colors and so forth.

But of what kind [of thing]? To that which is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*); "transformations" (*pariṇāmāḥ*) are manifestations (*vivartāḥ*) such as newness, oldness, and so forth, and [the object] possesses those.
And this will be considered:

indeed, apart from its various parts, no other entity such as a jar is perceived as having that nature; nor is it perceived apart from its color and other qualities, because there is no means for apprehending it [independently].

For instance: form is perceived by the eye, sound by the ear, smell by the nose, taste by the tongue, and touch by the body, because they are perceived in that way. Furthermore, no other form of a substratum (*guṇin*) is observed to appear therein, nor is there any other sense organ to grasp it. If it is asked, "Then how is it that the jar and so forth, which possess such a nature, are perceived?"—to this he replies: "Of the internal mind (*citta*), which has a single variegated form," and so on; [this refers to] a single, unique cognition (*jñāna*) having the form of blue and so forth.

For this very reason, he says: "of the variegated"—that is, of the variegated cognition consisting of doubt and so forth, which has as its object both the beneficial (*artha*) and the non-beneficial (*anartha*). The word *iva* (as if) is used in the sense of "just as" (*yathārtha*); that is, just as there is an end to such a mind, so too is there the perception of objects like jars in the manner previously described.

Others read the text as *citrasyaiva* ("of the variegated itself"); for them, it must be considered whether this meaning is actually contained within the verse. For us, however, there is no fault because of the inclusion of the particle *eva*.

The example that will be established by the passage beginning with *pratibhāsaika-niyama-siddhi* (Siddhiviniścaya 1.10) is praised here [in this context] according to the maxim: "There is no entry or exit for a vessel that has not been indicated. Indeed, such an appearance exists, whether external or internal; however, it is erroneous (*bhrānta*).

Regarding this, it has been said by Prajñākara: "If it is argued that there is no fault even if [the object] is non-existent, because it is like an appearance such as a magical illusion or a mirage" (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra* 3.211); to this, he replies with the words beginning "And not," and so forth.

Furthermore, there exists no cognition—whether perceptual or inferential—that reveals a meaning contrary to the aforementioned meaning, by virtue of which the reality of the subject matter under discussion would be considered erroneous. For it is only when a [cognition] is sublated by another cognition that reveals a contrary appearing object that it is conventionally designated as "erroneous," just as the cognition of two moons is considered erroneous when sublated by the cognition of a single moon.

"Surely, since there is no cognition whatsoever that reveals an object contrary to that [reality], for that very reason the reality of the matter under discussion is not erroneous"—so says another. By one who speaks thus, the very distinction between error and its opposite would be discarded, but not the non-absolutism (*anekānta*) of succession and non-succession. Consequently, perception would have no occasion in the proof of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and the like. If that [perception] were admitted, the reality of the matter under discussion would have to be accepted as erroneous; and that [error] occurs only when there exists a cognition revealing an object contrary to it—so how could there not be a state of sublation? Yet, such [a contrary cognition] does not exist.

If one asks "How so?", he says here: "For indeed," and so forth. The word "hi" means "because. "In that absolute [position]" (*tadekānte*) refers to that which is both "it" (*tat*) and "absolute" (*ekānta*), namely, the absolute position characterized by partless, momentary atoms (*niraṃśakṣaṇikaparamāṇu-lakṣaṇa-svalakṣaṇa-ekānta*). In this context, "one's own time of existence and non-existence" (*svasadasatsamaye*) means: "one's own" (*sva*) refers to the Buddhist's (*saugata*) own; "time of existence" (*satsamaya*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-samaya*), while "time of non-existence" (*asatsamaya*) is the non-ultimate reality (*aparamārtha-samaya*), which is to say, the conventional reality (*vyavahāra-samaya*). As it has been said:
Upon what basis is the nature of the possessor of qualities perceived through direct perception?

The commentators have employed this [example] in the following sense: "In the state of being a lump of clay, the pot's comparison (upamā)—that is, its similarity [to other pots]—its causal efficiency (arthakriyā), such as carrying water, its designation (vyapadeśa)—that is, the name 'pot'—and by the word 'etcetera,' its defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa), qualities (guṇa), and so forth, are not perceived; therefore, at that time, the existence of the pot is absent. Thus they explain.
The Buddhist [asserts] that the jar and so forth have the characteristic of momentary destruction and so on.
The distinction between "this is erroneous" and "this is non-erroneous" is the differentiation [of objects];
and if one accepts that perception is of no utility in proving momentary destruction and so forth,
then [perception] would also be erroneous.
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:

the conventional truth of the world and the truth that is ultimate. (Mādhyamakakārikā 24.8) Thus, in this regard, for this non-dual cognition imagined by the Sugata, there is no possibility of the occurrence of an action—that is, an experience—of that [object].

For instance—just as for him the moment of existence is the absolute distinction of the middle moment from the preceding and succeeding moments, so too within the middle moment, all parts such as pillars and the like are distinct from one another; thus, the ultimate reality is merely a collection [of atoms]. In that case, a perception restricted to a single atom is not capable of perceiving other atoms, because it is impossible for a single [act of] cognition to have multiple objects, just as the perception of the middle moment cannot have the preceding and succeeding moments as its objects, since the defect is equal in both cases. And thus, there is no manifestation of a future world.

It will be demonstrated that a perception terminating in a single atom entails the non-duality of the Person (puruṣādvaita). Therefore, the occurrence of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is not possible when [the object] exists, nor when it does not exist; for in that case, if the perceived and the attained were one and the same, the validity of direct perception would be accepted.

If it is argued that "let there be the possibility [of causal efficiency] at that time," to this he replies: "In that case," and so forth. In that manner—by that way, namely, during its own time of existence and non-existence—if causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) were perfectly possible in that absolute state, then how could there not be the performance, or experience, of the function characterized by momentariness through succession or simultaneity, given that the entity persists through the three times? This is because of the contradiction involved: for instance, if something perceived once is perceived again and again, that constitutes causal efficiency through succession.

Nor is it perceived that there is a repeated apprehension of that very same object by means of a prior apprehension, because at that [subsequent] time, due to the absence of later perceptions and the absence of the object to be seen, there is no perception [of the prior one];

nor is it perceived that what was previously apprehended is cognized by means of the absence of later perceptions, because at that time as well, both the prior perception and the form of the object to be seen by it are absent,
and thus it cannot be [cognized] through their combination, since they do not exist simultaneously.

It is not tenable that a single cognition exists across both times; for, due to the aforementioned fault, if the subsequent perception were to grasp the preceding one, or the preceding one the subsequent one, there would be a grasping of everything without distinction. This contradicts [the claim], as well as the direct, simultaneous experience of the entire nature of the preceding and succeeding moments, and [the resulting] causal efficiency.

And in that case, because that which has a beginningless and endless nature appears in a single moment, that very thing is momentariness; thus, there is no contradiction for her [the Yoginī]. To the question, "How is the momentary destruction of an existing, perceived object established in its entirety? he says: "In that very [case]," and so forth. The meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is: "in that very [case], in that very extreme [of perception], and not in the case of non-momentariness," since the lack of contradiction in that regard will be demonstrated in the third chapter.
Because of the contradiction with those two—succession and simultaneity—there is a contradiction regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

To explain: first of all, there can be no successive activity or experience of an object characterized as a partless, momentary, ultimate atom (*paramāṇu-svalakṣaṇa*); for that would entail the consequence of it being non-momentary, since succession is the defining characteristic of such a thing. Nor can there be simultaneous [activity]; for the effects of experiencing that [atom], beginning with the vision of a yogi and so forth, would be unestablished due to the confusion of the form, location, time, and nature of a single atom. Otherwise, even if one were to see all locations simultaneously, there would be no confusion of time.

[Objection: "Surely, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not accepted as having the nature of an atom as previously described, nor does it produce multiple simultaneous cognitions such that this fault would arise. Rather, it is [the characteristic] according to its appearance; for there is the statement: 'Whatever appears in a certain way, that exists in that very way in ultimate reality,' and so forth. To this, he says: "Therefore, that which exists... and so on. This acceptance by the opponent—that the reality is not of the form of the aforementioned atom, but rather according to its manifestation—implies that whatever exists and moves within the range of apprehension (*upalambha*), where apprehension is existence (*sattā*)... [Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra 3].
Because of this statement, all that is of a non-absolute (anekānta) nature, since there is no other alternative;

its isolation and absoluteness (vivekaikānta)— that is to say, its differentiation— is merely the collection of ultimate realities, which are the atoms of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇaparamāṇu).

The meaning is this: for the world beyond is understood through the realization of the identity between the final moment of consciousness in this life and the initial moment of consciousness in the next life; yet that very [realization] is impossible, and thus the denial of the afterlife has effectively occurred.
For an object that has become a domain of perception, having produced the perception, perishes due to its momentariness.

Therefore, in response to the objection that "what is seen by perception is not what is obtained; thus, one thing is seen and another is obtained, making perception inconsistent," the following is resolved: by superimposing identity upon the moments of the perceived and the obtained, one thinks, "that which was seen is precisely what was obtained. Thus, there is non-inconsistency (avisaṃvāda) therein due to this determination of identity.

Consequently, the meaning is that for the sake of establishing the validity of perception, the Buddhist has in some way accepted causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) belonging to a time other than its own—at the time of the prior apprehension.
Even at the time of perceiving the subsequent [moment], there is the causal efficiency of both the preceding and the subsequent.
In the case of simultaneity,
because that which is capable of performing an action is absent in the subsequent moment, there is indeed an absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
In the case of the absolute momentariness or the eternalist position,
there is no contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
The meaning is that non-momentariness consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) through a sequence characterized by a single entity pervading multiple moments.

In the view of the Yogins, all those atoms existing in prior and subsequent times appear [simultaneously]; therefore, for all those who maintain that the object is the cause [of cognition], there would be co-location (*ekadeśatā*) and simultaneity (*ekakālatā*) between the effect—which is the experience consisting of the perception of them—and the experience which is the effect of the present atom. And this confusion (*sāṅkarya*) is unestablished.

If that were not the case, then even on the position of permanence (*nityapakṣa*), how could one avoid the consequence of a confusion of times (*kālasāṅkarya*) when causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is established simultaneously?
The proponent of the non-duality of manifestation (*pratibhāsādvaitavādī*) says:

"Or rather, as for what was stated—that [the cognition] does not manifest an object contrary to that [appearance], and so forth—even if direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not exist there according to the aforementioned reasoning, there might still be an inference (*anumāna*) such as: 'Whatever exists is momentary, like a jar, and the subject of dispute is likewise'; if this is argued, he replies: 'Not so,' and so forth."

For it is not the case that in the absolute extreme of momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*), there is "existence and non-existence" at the time of its own existence and non-existence; this is an expression where the state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: the performance (*kriyā*), that is, the production (*karaṇa*), of an object or effect—its possibility consists in one case in the termination of a beginningless and endless continuum within a single moment, and in the other case, in the non-arising of the effect due to the absence of a cause. This is what is intended.

Comparison: If the effect exists only when the cause exists, then the three worlds would exist in a single moment, because the entire subsequent series of moments would have to exist at the very time of the causal moment; consequently, there would be no continuity (santāna), as no other alternative is possible.

On the other hand, if the effect were to exist even when the cause does not exist, then the time prior to and after the causal moment—being beginningless and endless—would be accompanied by the effect, since the absence of a cause is indistinguishable [in both cases].
— *Aṣṭaśatī*, p. 187.

In the position that [an entity] exists at its own time (satsamayapakṣa), the second moment produces the third precisely at its own time—that is, in the second moment itself; therefore, the third would have to exist in the second moment, and likewise, the second would have to exist at the time of its own cause, the first moment. Thus, it follows that all subsequent effects would have to exist at the very first moment.

If it is argued that in the case of "non-existence at the time [of the effect]," waking consciousness and the like produce effects such as awakening even at a time when they themselves lack existence; how then can it be said that "the performance of causal efficiency is impossible for what is non-existent at its own time"? [Reply: No; if it was previously capable [of producing the effect] but had not yet arisen, how could it—arising later in the absence of that [prior capacity]—be the cause of that effect by itself? If it is argued that it is the cause because it is produced by that [prior state], how can something non-existent be its producer, like a donkey’s horn? If it is argued that it is existent at the very moment of its own production, then let the effect exist at that same time, since the power to produce it exists only then.

Now, if it is argued that such is its power—that because the effect is seen exactly as it is at a later time, it must be exactly as it is seen—[we reply: no; for even from a permanent cause that was previously capable, the production of the effect again would not be contradictory. If it is argued that an effect arising thus from a permanent cause is not observed, [we reply: since it is not observed from a permanent cause, and likewise not observed from a momentary cause, it is therefore not observed from either.
For the momentariness of waking consciousness, or of anything else, is not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, it is well said: "Not indeed," and so forth.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—to this he replies: "That being the case," and so forth.

If that were the case, and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) being impossible therein, how could the proof of momentariness for all that exists—which is efficient—be established through the principle that "since causal efficiency is incompatible with non-momentariness due to the impossibility of [producing effects] either successively or simultaneously, existence, by the logic of the bird not seeing the shore, must turn away from non-momentariness and abide in momentariness"? If you ask, "Why is this not so?", he says here: "In that very [case]," and so forth.
In that very [state], in that absolute solitude, by those two—succession and simultaneity—there is a contradiction because of the contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Now, one might object: "But even a momentary waking consciousness produces specific effects such as exhalation and so forth, as well as the form of the body, and produces exhalation, awakening, and so on in succession; how then can it be said, 'in that very [state],' and so forth? [Response: No; for it has been stated here that its momentariness is not certain. Furthermore, if a non-successive effect could arise from a momentary [cause], then successive entities would not arise from a non-successive [cause] (*Pravāḍavāda* 1).
If this were so, it would contradict [the aforementioned] statements; therefore, this is trivial.
Prajñākara, who maintains the theory of a remote cause, asks:
"What is the meaning of 'the production of that which does not exist'? It means its existence immediately following that [cause]."
This immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is the same with respect to both [the preceding cognition and the object];
yet immediate succession alone is not the basis for [establishing] reality, because even a mediated cause can be a cause.
For instance, the consciousness of one who has been in deep sleep arises from a prior experience at the time of awakening.
"It is certain that [the effect] arises after an interval of time...

Therefore, the basis for the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekānuvidhāyitva*), which exists even in the case of that which arises later."
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 68:
[This occurs] in waking cognition, in the absence of waking cognition.
Awakened cognition must be admitted to exist only at the time of awakened cognition itself.
Subsequently, at the appropriate time, because its capacity arises in that very same way,

whatever exists is necessarily momentary; for if it were non-momentary, there would be a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whereby its status as a real entity— defined by that very efficiency— would be lost.

If everything that is existent or produced were not subject to momentary destruction, then because a non-momentary entity cannot perform causal efficiency (arthakriyā) either successively or simultaneously, it would be excluded from the definition of existence as the capacity for causal efficiency; thus, it would be non-existent. (*Hetubindu*, p.
54; *Vādanyāya*, pp. 6–8).

Just as it is said that when merchants aboard a ship release a bird with the hope that it might see the shore, and when, after wandering everywhere, it fails to find the shore and returns instead to the very ship, so too should this be understood: [from the *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p.
193, regarding the eternal].

The meaning is that just as the simultaneous production of effects from a non-successive, eternal cause is contradictory, so too is the non-successive production of effects from a successive cause equally contradictory.

He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*) and so forth: since, even for one who perceives particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which are themselves characterized by momentary destruction and atomicity—a single, gross form residing within cognition appears quite clearly, and since there is an impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in that absolute [view] regarding the time of its own existence or non-existence; therefore, he states another thesis to be proven (*sādhyāntara*) with the words "of that absolute" (*tadekāntasya*) and so forth: "whatever exists, all that is of a manifold nature" (*anekāntātmaka*).

The word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is understood here; that is, from the aforementioned reasoning. When is there the non-existence—that is, the non-presence—of that absolute [position], namely the absolute momentariness? To this he says: "When the conditions for perception are met. The definition of perception consists in the completeness of all other causal factors and a specific nature [of the object]; when these are met, he thinks as follows: that absolute [position] is non-existent because, while meeting the conditions for perception, it is not perceived.

[Objection: "But if that absolute [non-existence] were at some place or time within the range of perception, how could its absolute non-existence be established? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And since its absolute non-existence is what is intended, it is not accepted that it exists in such a way at any place or time; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the qualification is unestablished. [Reply: No; this is not so, because the intention is otherwise. This proof is not employed with the intention of an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*), but rather with the intention of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*).
For instance: if that absolute [absence] is held to be perceptible, then because it is not perceived despite being perceptible, it would be non-existent;
if it is imperceptible, then it would be unprovable, since it would be useless for practical discourse due to not being an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By this, it has also been stated that the objection regarding the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is likewise untenable.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Otherwise, there would be the consequence of being immeasurable.

For the formulation of two opposing positions (*pakṣa*) is appropriate only in a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) and not elsewhere. Furthermore, it is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* because of the statement "provided the conditions for perception are met" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptau*), since even the non-perception of something invisible is accepted as being itself a means of cognition (*gamaka*).
"The conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) consist of the completeness of all other causal factors for perception and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).

"The completeness of the other conditions for apprehension" means that for a cognition, the jar is also a producer, as are others such as the eye and so forth; "other conditions" refers to causes other than the visible jar, and their "completeness" is their presence.
That specific nature which, when the other conditions for apprehension are present, becomes directly perceived—that is the specific nature [of the object]—*Nyāyabindu* 2.
The absolute doctrine of momentariness; the absolute doctrine of momentariness.
The one-sided doctrine of momentariness is unestablished because the object of apprehension is not necessarily characterized by the conditions for being perceived.

As for what was said regarding "the existent and the non-existent"— namely, that it is like the single mind of a painter within— this is incorrect, because even he does not admit [the existence] in that way.
Thus it has been said:
Even in the case of variegated cognition,
how could that which is one exist in the form of multiple aspects? That variegation would not exist even in that single cognition.

If it is argued: "If this [consciousness] itself finds pleasure in objects, then who are we in that matter? (*Pravāraṇā-vākya* 2.210), then this must be considered: Is this stated with reference to the view of the Sautrāntika, the Yogācāra, or the Mādhyamika? Regarding the first position, he states the refutation: "The restriction of the unity of appearance," and so forth.

Now, if that variegation were to exist in a single cognition, and by means of it a single variegated substance were established, what would be the fault? He replies: It would not exist even in that cognition—not only in the substance, but even in that single cognition, how could there be variegation? It would be like the perception of many persons [in a single object].

How, then, is there cognition? He says: "If this [appearance] itself pleases [the mind] regarding objects, who are we in that matter?"—that is, if this manifestation of identity (*tādrūpya*) in things that are not actually identical, namely the appearing blue and so forth, "pleases" [the mind] of its own accord—without being prompted by another—then who are we, even if unwilling, to prevent such a manifestation? Furthermore, if a non-entity (*avastu*) appears, it is clearly false. [As stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikamanoratha*: "If there were a restriction to a single manifestation, the cognition would not be expressed by a single term."]
Or else, they indeed produce a cognition of their own appearance in another way. || 10 ||

If this were an absolute rule—that there could be no unity when contradictory properties (viruddhadharma) are superimposed either internally or externally—then how could there be self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) for those whose minds are deluded regarding external objects? Furthermore, if there were a confusion between the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*), how could the unity of the mind be refuted on the grounds of a difference in appearance and so forth? If conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognitions were somehow one, why would it not be the same for pleasure and pain? Therefore, one who adheres to such an absolute position while professing to understand that the nature of the mind—which consists of internal and external appearances, error and its opposite, and conceptualization and its opposite—is inseparable from non-absolutism (*anekānta*), is both a hater and a practitioner of that very [non-absolutism] and thus deserves to be disregarded.

In this context, there are two uses of the word *pratibhāsa*: the first denotes cognition (*saṃvedana*), while the other denotes the form of the object (*viṣayākāra*). From this, the following meaning results: if the necessity of the unity of appearance—that is, the necessity of its partlessness—is accepted, then the intellect (*dhī*) would not be one, but rather manifold;
what would it be doing? It would be "bearing" [multiple forms].
What? The cognition of the appearance, which is the grasping of the form of the object; of what nature? Expressive, that is, possessing a verbal designation;
in what way? Otherwise, by means of a different mode.
How else could this be? [The phrase] "other than from the cognition of the self's own nature" means as follows:

since the cognition of the self is the self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors—which is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), according to *Nyāyabindu* 1.10—it is non-verbal. Therefore, a cognition that maintains a verbalized appearance-cognition—[an appearance-cognition] which is subject to error induced by cataracts, rapid spinning, traveling in a boat, physical agitation, and so forth—could not be one and the same; rather, it would necessarily be many.

For instance: for those whose minds are deluded regarding external objects, the perception of a mass of hair and the like is entirely distinct from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because it is impossible for a single cognition to possess two forms—one erroneous and the other otherwise—and because that [perceived object] does not exist as a form of cognition, which would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, if that mind were known through self-awareness, there would be no error in that cognition, since it would be imitating its own form, just as blueness is present when imitating the form of blue.
If its form were different from that [object], the same fault would apply and there would be an infinite regress.
If it does not imitate the form of that object, then cognition of it would not occur by means of that [form]. Otherwise, there would be a perception of a formless [cognition];
yet, if one accepts its self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), then—fearing a duality of forms in a single entity—one must further accept another cognition for the awareness of that [self-cognition].
And since that [object] does not exist in an unknown form, if this objection is raised, the same fault remains in that very answer, and there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Thus, because things such as a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*) are non-existent due to their non-perception, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for the purpose of excluding them is useless.

If it is argued that there is no fault because that [non-erroneous nature] is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); then, by that very [conventional usage], all cognitions [would be valid]. (Nyāyabindu 1)

If it is argued that, because of such statements as "therefore," a single entity may possess two forms; likewise, even through succession, a single entity may have them—then the proof for momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) would be irrelevant. However, this is not accepted by the opponent; thus it was rightly said: "the restriction to a single appearance," and so forth.
And this explanation is intended by the author of the treatise as well, not merely by me, because it will be stated later in the commentary: "If this were an absolute [rule], etc.";
"timira" is a disorder of the eyes; this cause of error resides in the sense organ, such as the rapid whirling of a firebrand and the like.

For when a firebrand or similar object is rotated slowly, the illusion of a wheel does not arise; therefore, the rotation is qualified by the term "rapid. Furthermore, this is a cause of delusion residing in the object itself, as is the movement of a boat, which is "navigation" (*nauyāna*).

For one standing on a moving boat, the illusion of moving trees and so forth arises; thus, the mention of "motion" is included. Furthermore, this cause of delusion is situated in external supports, as is the agitation of wind, bile, and phlegm.
For when the wind and other [humors] become disturbed, an illusion such as [the appearance of] flaming pillars arises;
In the supportless sky, there is a cognition appearing in the form of hair and in the form of a cataract;
this cognition has two aspects: it is erroneous with respect to the object-form and non-erroneous with respect to its own form.

Regarding the statement in the *Nyāyabindu* (1.4), "Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," this refers to cognitions such as that of a mass of hair [seen by one with an eye disease].
The attainment of two forms by the Buddhist commentator.

This is another explanation: regarding the rule that appearances are one, "intellect" (*dhī*) refers to conceptual cognition. If it is asked, "How is this [conceptual nature] obtained from the general term 'intellect'?"—because it is impossible for anything other than what will be explained immediately hereafter to be so, that [intellect] would not be singular; or rather, because of its connection with the word "would be" (*syāt*), which is yet to come, what is it doing?
It is "bearing" (*dadhatī*).

What? The cognition of appearance, that is, the awareness of the form of the object; of what nature? Expressive, meaning capable of being associated with verbal expression. "Conceptual construction is the cognition of an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression" (Nyāyabindu 1).
According to this statement, what else does it convey? Of what nature is the self? Otherwise, [it would be] a cognition that cannot be expressed.
And so it has been said:
"The nature of pleasure and the like is indeed conceptual, for its essence cannot be conventionally designated, as it is not shared by anything else."
"Therefore, their self-awareness is not associated with verbal expression" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.249). ...
Thus, because [the mind] does not partake in anything other than passion and so forth, their self-awareness is not associated with verbal expression.
"...[the cognition] does not partake of anything other than blue and so forth; therefore, their consciousness... — *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p.
378; the reading in the present context is from the *Vidhiviveka-ṭīkā*, p. 190.
Śāṅkara Bhāṣya on the Bhāmatī, 2.2.24.
...because names and so forth are non-different from [the object],
therefore their difference in any way whatsoever is not logically tenable—
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 185.
...thus, for one who holds such a view, expressibility is not possible in any way—*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 290.

This is what is meant: just as the unobstructed is entirely different from the obstructed, the immovable from the moving, the non-red from the red, and the unconditioned from the conditioned, so too the conceptual cognition (*pratibhāsa-pratīti*) which is expressible is different from the non-expressible self-cognition (*svapratīti*).
Nor is that [cognition] unperceived, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
if it were perceived by itself, its self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) would be non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), otherwise even the subject under discussion would not exist.
If this is the case, that same fault follows—therefore, it is distinct.
Furthermore, if that [cognition] is apprehended by itself, the aforementioned defect recurs;
if it is not apprehended, there is an infinite regress;
and if it is apprehended by the primary cognition, then if that [primary cognition] is of the same nature as it, it would be conceptual, or else that [subsequent cognition] would be non-conceptual.

If [the object] does not have that [cognition] as its essence, then how could that cognition—whether it has arisen from that [object] or merely imitates its form—be a perception of it? Furthermore, since conceptualization is self-aware by nature, its priority [over the object] would depend on the self-awareness of that [cognition]; yet if one accepts the self-awareness of that [cognition], the same inquiry applies, leading to an infinite regress.
If, on the other hand, one does not accept that [self-awareness], then because there is no distinction in the object itself, that [form] would not be the form of the cognition.

Thus, since such a cognition does not exist because it is not perceived, there is no so-called "conceptual construction" (kalpanā)— that is, a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression— because the definition [of conceptual construction], namely "conceptual construction is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression" (Nyāyabindu 1.5), is absent. Therefore, the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is also useless and redundant.

By this [it is shown that] these conceptual constructions do not arise and pass away without being cognized through verbalizable cognition; for if they were, even though they exist, they would remain unperceived.
Thus, because all things, by virtue of their own intrinsic nature,
are established in their respective natures and therefore participate in exclusions from both intrinsic and extrinsic natures, [concepts] are based on whichever exclusions of objects there may be.
Distinctions among universals are conceptualized based on their penetration into specific particulars;
therefore, whatever particularity is perceived through one property cannot be apprehended by another, and thus the establishment of difference is determined by that [specific property].
And the section beginning with *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.39–41 has been refuted.

How so? Since there is an absence of conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*), the claim that "their arising and passing away are their defining characteristics" and that "different types of universals (*jāti*) are postulated as the basis for exclusion" is merely a matter of faith and is difficult to establish; thus, there is no relationship of probandum and probans between impermanence and existence, because they are non-different.

If it is argued that "this [distinction] exists from the perspective of conventional reality (saṃvṛti)," then we reply: surely conventional reality is nothing but conceptual cognition (vikalpabuddhi), and that does not exist; therefore, this is utterly contradictory.

If it is further argued that "it is like a dream, due to error," we say: no; for even in that case, if this [cognition] were non-conceptual (nirvikalpikā), then it would not be logical [to speak of such distinctions].

Otherwise, if it were [conceptual], then because of that very reason, it would follow [the same conclusion] at other times as well; thus, this statement—"All this is by Ācārya Dignāga," and so forth—is contradicted.

If [the cognition] is conceptual (*vikalpika*), that same fault remains: that very [external object] does not exist, and therefore this [cognition] is [conceptual]; thus, these two are contradictory. Consequently, in order to avoid this fault, even the Sautrāntika must admit a single cognition that is both variegated and non-variegated, or both conceptual and non-conceptual, regarding both the external object and its opposite. Therefore, how can there be an establishment of the absolute partlessness (*niraṃśaikānta*) for him? This is the intended meaning. [For] all entities, by their own nature, are established in their respective natures.
Since things possess exclusion from both their own-nature and other-natures, therefore,
based on each respective exclusion of objects, distinct universals are conceptually constructed which penetrate those specific differences.

Therefore, that specific property by which a distinction is perceived cannot be [perceived] by anything other than itself; thus, the established distinction between them is separate. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.39–41) This is the relationship between the probandum and the probans.
Conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is a mere conceit of cognition in the absence of valid means of knowledge (p.

183). Conventional reality is conceptual consciousness; it expresses a mental inclination arising from beginningless predispositions (p. 185). It exists conventionally—that is, it "exists" from the perspective of deluded people (pp. 377–378, *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*).
This is conventional reality.
The relationship between the probandum and the probans is an error;
[it arises] from error.
Even in the waking state, it is due to error alone;

thus, this entire conventional usage of inference and the object of inference is indeed constructed by the intellect through the distinction between property and property-bearer as mounted upon the intellect—as was stated [by Dharmakīrti]. He says "and likewise," etc., indicating that this was also stated by the teacher Dignāga (*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*, *Ṭīkā*, p. 24).
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "If this," and so forth.

If this—namely, the "extreme" (*ekānta*), which means necessity (*avaśyaṃbhāva*)—is internal in the mind or external in [objects] such as a jar (the word "or" [*vā*] being a conjunction), then, when there is the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), there would be no unity; the word "it would be" (*syāt*) marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "How," and so forth.

For those cognitions—meaning those consciousnesses characterized by the erroneous perception of yellow and so on regarding external objects such as a white conch—how could their self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? It was intended that it could not be so at all.

By this, it should be understood that for those cognitions characterized by the error of [perceiving] the mountain, the sun, and so on as being joined together, how could the apprehension of the mountain and so forth be direct perception?

With the words "of someone" (*kasyacit*) and so forth, he raises the objection of another's view: "Of someone"—that is, of one whose delusion has been induced by cataracts, rapid spinning, traveling in a boat, or agitation; when there is a confusion between the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*), and if a certain identity is accepted between the nature of the cognition characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and the nature of its semblance consisting in the apprehension of two moons and so forth—then he states the refutation: "How? and so on;
[the answer is] "not at all."

By what [is unity refuted]? He says: "That which has the difference of appearance as its beginning"—that is, that which begins with the difference of appearance, such as the difference of place, time, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and so forth, caused by the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*); by that [difference], how could unity be refuted? The word "of the mind" (*cittasya*) should also be supplied here, because it occurs in the middle [of the sentence]; the meaning is "of the mind, [which is] the self" (*ātman*), as in the case of "the sun rises on the mountain peak," and so forth.

By this, the following argument of the Vaiśeṣikas and others is also refuted: "The ascertainment of a subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by the generality of verticality—'this is it'—is *nirṇaya* (certainty); whereas the non-ascertainment of a specific [alternative], such as 'it is either a post or a person,' is *saṃśaya* (doubt). It is not a single cognition that can consist of both ascertainment and non-ascertainment, as this is logically impossible. If this is argued, we reply: there is no prohibition because it is observed. This single cognition is observed to consist of the ascertainment of an object qualified by its generality while simultaneously consisting of the non-ascertainment of its specific [features].
By this, error (*viparyaya*) is also explained.

For that [cognition] as well, being of the nature of a determination regarding an object qualified by a universal, would be an error with respect to the particular—just as the cognition "this is a person" in regard to a post.

How so? If a single cognition is held to possess the natures of doubt, error, and [correct] knowledge, then everything would likewise consist of both universal and particular aspects. Otherwise, cognitions such as "this," "post," and "person," which exist with their forms mutually exclusive of one another, could not be established as distinct categories such as doubt and so forth.
In that case, doubt is first of all a cognition whose nature is the non-determination of the true form of an object.

And [the claim] that "cognition is non-determinative" is contradictory; it is not a contradiction because its own nature is determined, for its own nature is determined as "I have a cognition of doubt," yet the actual nature of the object is not delimited by this [cognition].
— *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 12.

For this [cognition] is produced by the perception of a substratum qualified by a general property, acting in conjunction with the non-perception of specific properties and the recollection of two contradictory specific properties; thus, while ascertaining the substratum as qualified by the general property, it does not ascertain the specific [nature], such as "Is it a post or a person? and is therefore a cognition whose nature is non-ascertainment.
Indeed, it is observed that where the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct, the effect is likewise distinct, as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 176.

The reversal [of the previous argument] is also explained by way of its independent nature through one meaning in the verse; now it is explained by means of the second: "of the two natures of consciousness, the conceptual and the non-conceptual," so it is considered.

Of what? It follows that [the question refers to] the mind (*citta*). If their identity in some way is accepted, he states the refutation therein: "Why would it not be the same for pleasure and pain?"—that is, by that very same manner, there would indeed be some kind of identity.

Why is this so? This has already been discussed in the passage beginning with "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*), as stated by Dharmottara and others: "Perception is that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (*Nyāyabindu* 1).

In this context, "worldly error" refers to cognitions such as [the appearance of] a mass of hair, and "conceptual construction" consists in the apprehension of things as qualified by universals and so forth; this is what has been examined here. This is because of the statement "of a certain mind," for that [perception] belongs to a particular mind and not to a previous one; otherwise, since a conceptual construction-free or erroneous [cognition] might occur, the definition of direct perception would be impossible.

And as it was stated by that very same [author]: "Since the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that all cognition of an objective support (*ālambana*) is erroneous regarding its support, and that all cognition perceived in the form of grasped and grasper is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), how is this understood? Because it is stated without distinction; for that [conceptualization] is common to all cognitions, and if it were included [in the definition], no cognition whatsoever would be found to be free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) or non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
Refuting that, he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.
The particle *tat* functions in the sense of *saḥ* (that);

therefore, the meaning is as follows: having relied exclusively upon this very dharma—the ultimate reality of momentary, partless atoms—is that [possible]? To this, he says: "externally," and so forth.

That whose manifestation is both external and internal is described as such, being the nature of the mind that is distinct from delusion and distinct from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This is what is meant: according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* (3.196), "Delusion is outward-turned; the entire mind is deluded regarding its objective support," delusion is outward-turned. The other, non-delusive mind-nature is inward-turned. Likewise, conceptual construction is outward-turned and has that [delusion] as its nature, as stated in the *Prakaraṇavārtika* (3).
Because of such statements as [Nyāyaviniścaya 1.10], "The other is inward-turned and free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*)," and so forth—one might ask:

in what manner is he [described]? To this, he says: "He who perceives that which is inseparable from non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is thereby censured; for the reason that he is both a hater of non-absolutism and a practitioner of it, he deserves indifference and contempt."
This was composed for the purpose of eliminating misconceptions such as [the perception of] a tuft of hair;
for, as in the case of those with ophthalmia, there is the appearance of a tuft of hair and so forth even in the absence of an external object— Tattvasaṃgraha, verse 1312.

"Just as a mass of hair is falsely perceived by people suffering from ophthalmia"—Madhyāntavibhāga, p. 15; "Just as a mass of hair is falsely perceived by people suffering from ophthalmia"—Laṅkāvatārasūtra, p. 274.
There are birds called *keśoṇḍuka* which pull out the roots of hair—*Śikṣāsamuccaya*, p. 70.

Just as for one who is exhausted by long-term study and the like and is not standing still, something called a *keśoṇḍuka*, characterized by qualities such as blue or red, appears clearly before the eyes.
Alternatively, that which appears as a mass of hair within the rays of light from eyes rubbed by the hand is a *keśoṇḍraka* (a hair-net illusion)—Śāstradīpikā-Yuktibhāṣya, p.
99. Now, what kind of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is it? He says: it is the association with name, genus, and so forth.

In the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), an object qualified by a name is expressed, such as "Ḍittha"; by a genus-word (*jātiśabda*), [an object] by its genus, such as "this is a cow" (*gaur ayam*);
and by a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*), [an object] by its quality, such as "white" (*śukla*).
In the case of action-words, [the relation is] by means of the action, as in "cook";
in the case of substance-words, it is by means of the substance, as in "staff-bearer" or "horned one"—*Pramāṇasamuccayaṭīkā*, p. 12.
"But others say that mental cognition associated with genus and so forth is conceptual construction"—so state [the authors of] the *Nyāyapravēśavṛtti*, p.
35; and the *Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī*, p. 21.
Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition that, having connected the preceding and the succeeding, takes the form of being associated with words or the form of internal discourse;
all [such cognitions] are erroneous with respect to their objective support (*ālambana*). — *Tarkabhāṣā*, p. 7.

...but from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthatas*), everything is indeed erroneous with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*)—this is cited from *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 280, in *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 512.

And according to the Yogācāra view, apart from the non-dual gnosis of the Tathāgata, all cognition is conceptualized as consisting of the grasped and the grasper; this is "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*). (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī, p.
21). Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p. 320, 467.

Therefore, since the conceptualization of the apprehended and the apprehender proceeds from the postulation of external objects based on inference—a process that functions through a beginningless succession of such inferences—it is established that, in ultimate reality, there is only undivided consciousness; this is the conceptualization [of duality]. —*Pravṛttivārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 398.
Conceptualization.

Thus, for those of impure intellect, there is this reflection on the characteristic of the apprehended object regarding form and so forth, as well as the mind; however, the realization of yogins is inconceivable. — *Pravṛtti-vinīścaya* 3.117.23–24.

Although the nature of cognition is indivisible, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the grasped object, the grasping subject, and self-awareness to those whose vision is distorted by error.
"The self-cognition of all minds and mental factors is perception"— *Nyāyabindu* 1; "The self-cognition of all minds and mental factors is perception"— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.354.

But surely he is neither a hater of that [system] nor a practitioner of it, because the Buddhas always accept that the single *citrā* (the variegated) possesses an identical *yogakṣema* (security and well-being); whereas regarding the "exclusive" (*ekānta*), it was stated by Dharmakīrti outside [of this context]:
Yoga is the following after dharmas not yet attained; kṣema is the following after dharmas already attained.
— *Pravacanāvatāra-svopajña-ṭīkā* 1.24.
At every moment, yoga is characterized by the discernment of objects, while security (kṣema) is characterized by the performance of purposeful action and consists of preservation—Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p.
37. Blue and so forth, in variegated cognition, are attributes of cognition that do not exist apart from it.
For it is impossible to perceive that [object] while discriminating it;
for if cognition appears in whatever way, it is experienced exactly in that way—thus there would be a single nature in the mind even for a variegated form. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.220–21)
Even by Prajñākaragupta it has been stated: "The intellect (*buddhi*) is indeed one and the same, because it is distinct from external variegation (*citratva*).
For an external variegation can be distinguished [into its parts], whereas the forms such as blue and so forth belonging to the intellect cannot be distinguished" (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 3.220).
To this, he replies: "Because of the appearance of being oriented inwardly or outwardly," and so forth.
If the internal and external manifestation of appearance does not divide the cognizer— which is not sequential— then it must certainly divide pleasure and the like, which are dependent upon sequence.

If [consciousness] does not divide cognition—which is mutually distinct in terms of being directed outward or inward, being erroneous or otherwise, conceptual or non-conceptual, valid or otherwise, and so forth—then how could it imply a whole (*avayavin*)? Or how could joy and the like [imply] a self (*ātman*), from which the proof of selflessness (*nairātmya*) follows? Furthermore, why would one not accept the coexistence (*saṃplava*) of appearances that are capable and incapable of association with verbal expression, even when they refer to a single, undivided object? For a difference in the nature of a thing does not constitute a difference in the thing itself.

That which has its manifestation (*mukha*) both internally and externally—that is, that which has as its primary feature the appearance of the grasped and the grasper, such as the nature of valid cognition and its opposite—is so described; it does not divide consciousness (*saṃvit*). That is to say, even when that [manifestation] exists, consciousness remains one alone.
If this is so, of what nature is it? It is "without succession" (*akrama*), meaning it is like the non-experience of arising and destruction in relation to consciousness itself.
By this, the identity of purpose and security (*abhinnayogakṣematva*) is demonstrated;
here, the refutation [of that objection] deserves to be disregarded.

This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here: if the appearance of internal and external aspects does not divide consciousness because it is non-sequential (*akrama*), then it likewise does not divide the entire collection of cognitions occurring in a single moment. Thus, the entire world at once would be a single cognition; and again, being thus, and yet again, being just so, it would be nothing more than a single continuum (*ekasantāna*). This is the inference for the sake of another (*parārthānumāna*) according to the *Nyāyabindu* (3).
This is incorrect; because there is no "other," cognition does not differentiate from one another.
Furthermore, even the collection of cognitions arising in the second and subsequent moments does not differentiate from one another; thus, the implication is that only a single continuum results.

By this [argument], the Yogācāra who maintains the doctrine of multiple streams of consciousness (*nānāvijñānasantānavādin*)— referring to another stream of being (*santānāntara*) as the object to be established— should also be considered as having been refuted.

It might be thought: "Consciousness does not experience unity through the appearance of being inward- or outward-facing due to its lack of succession—whereby this fault would arise—but rather because it appears in some way as identical [to its objects]. To this, he gives the reply: "That which is dependent on succession would certainly divide [consciousness]; pleasure and so forth" means that pleasure, which is the beginning of suffering and the rest, is dependent on succession; that [pleasure] would certainly divide consciousness. It is thought that there would be a single consciousness whose nature consists of pleasure and so forth appearing in succession, because of such an appearance. And thus, the opponent's proof for the refutation of the recognition of moments (*kṣaṇapratyabhijñā*) is rendered irrelevant.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Externally and internally," and so forth.

Those things which have both an external and an internal face are such; and those which consist of the categories of error and non-error, conceptualization and non-conceptualization, and valid cognition and its opposite, are likewise described. That which has these as its beginning—namely, the entire collection of forms such as the blue object and so forth—is what is thus described.
How is that [collection] characterized? He says: "Mutually," and so forth.

What, then, should one do? He says: "If one does not divide consciousness from the intellect"—by which it is meant that, according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* (3.196), "Outward-turned delusion is entirely erroneous with respect to its objective support," whereas inward-turned [consciousness] is the other, non-delusive state, as stated in the *Nyāyabindu* (1).

Because of such statements as these, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*) are explained [as the basis for] being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or otherwise. Furthermore, regarding the state of being directed outward, this depends on [the object's] momentariness and so forth in the case of sound, and on [the appearance of] two moons and so forth; whereas regarding the state of being directed inward, it depends on [the object's] capacity to bring about existence, consciousness, the attainment of heaven, and so forth.
Now, this [world] consisting of error and so forth, as well as the apprehended object and so forth, is of the nature of a single consciousness.
[Objection: But surely, validity and invalidity consist simply in being erroneous or non-erroneous; so for what purpose [is this distinction made]? This is not a fault.
To this, the reply is: "Joy," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
In this regard, the intended meaning is: "it pierces"; this [objection] is refuted by the fact that there is equality [of the process] in the case of the joy of the single Self and so forth.

Let it be so; yet, if it is asked, "What is the fault in that?", there is none at all. However, whatever appears in a certain way must enter into conventional usage as being ultimately real in that very way—just as blue, appearing as blue, enters into usage precisely as such. And since all entities appear as momentary, in this case the thesis is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), and the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
