Thus, what was intended as the establishment of selflessness (*nairātmyasiddhi*) is not actually the establishment of selflessness, but rather the establishment of a self (*sātmasiddhi*); therefore, [your] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is actually non-valid (*apramāṇa*).

It should be understood and observed that [the scripture] possesses validity with respect to such things as the sentience of sentient beings, while it lacks validity with respect to such things as the power to attain heaven (pṛ॰ 2,
note 10). By this [reasoning], the living body is possessed of a self because it possesses breath and so forth (Nyāyabindu 3).

Regarding what was stated by the opponent in this context—that because the existence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is observed in some conscious entity (*sātman*), the doubt that they might exist even in its absence is not removed, and thus there is the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*); and furthermore, that there is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddhatva*) because [the breath] exists only within the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*)—he shows that this has been refuted.

How? If, according to the logic already stated, even what is seen there is considered as "not seen," or what is seen elsewhere is what is being spoken of; then let it be assumed that the presence of smoke in a place possessing fire is either "not seen there" or "seen elsewhere."

This living body is not soulless, because [if it were], it would follow that it lacks breath and other vital functions—Nyāyavārttika, p. 123—for thus there is no certainty regarding either the probandum or its opposite. (108)

"And since no other category is possible besides those possessing a self and those lacking a self, there is doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of a self in the subject—the living body—on account of its possession of breath and so forth; thus, breath and the like are inconclusive"—*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, p. 222.
The possession of vital breaths and so forth exists in the continuum of consciousness that possesses a self.
Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Agnimatī*:
"For one who perceives the Self, that [Self] becomes eternal within his own self."

"Out of affection (*sneha*), one thirsts for pleasures; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) conceals the fault (*doṣa*). (*Pravāraṇa-vākya* 1.219), and so forth. That too has been refuted by this [argument]: if indeed affection and the like, which constitute *saṃsāra*, necessarily exist within a mental self that is characterized by the non-exclusive nature of both succession and simultaneity (*kramākrama-anekānta-citta-ātman*), then liberation would never occur for the Buddhist, since he would always perceive that very [self]. If it is argued: "Let the mind be a single, variegated entity (*eka-citra*) through succession as well as through non-succession, but not so the external object"; to this he replies: "The whole (*avayavin*)... and so forth.

How could one refute [this]? For surely, when a sense faculty is engaged with one part or one quality, it is not capable of perceiving another part or another quality; how, then, can there be a perception of a form common to them? If it is argued that it is perceived neither as being of that nature nor otherwise, to this he says: "In one," and so forth.

Even in the case of a single, non-different object—that is, even regarding the object of apprehension, and not merely regarding the mind as the subject—how could one, such as a follower of the Sugata (Buddhist), not accept the simultaneous engagement (*saṃplava*) [of multiple cognitions]? One must certainly accept it.

Of which two? He says: the universal (*sāmānya*), which is capable of association with verbal expression and common to many particulars, and the particular (*viśeṣa*), which is incapable of that; [the phrase] "of those two" refers to the appearances (*pratibhāsa*) of those two. Thus, the intention is that just as in the case of the mind, there is an appearance of both the universal and the particular even in the object.

Likewise, there is worldly cognition in the form of: "I touch that very thing which I see," and "I touch that very thing which I saw"—[this occurs] within the self, which consists of a continuum of mind (*cittasantāna*) that is in some sense both eternal and non-eternal.
In that case, the cause would be the Sugata himself, because he is the omniscient one whose very nature is mind.
The category of the whole (avayavin), which consists of various parts and possesses multiple qualities, as if appearing simultaneously.
Alternatively, it should be explained as "of two appearances, one capable of association with verbal expression and the other incapable";
as it has been stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*: "By itself, [it appears] in manifold forms" (*Nyāyaviniścaya* 1.9), and so forth.
...the apprehension of the external object as such is manifold; it is clear that [this apprehension] possesses the relationship of qualifier and qualified— this is the remainder [of the sense].

If it is argued: "In that case, one thing would be characterized by a nature capable of being associated with verbal expression, while another thing would be characterized by a nature contrary to that; otherwise, there could be no distinction between them anywhere," [the author] says here: "Of the thing," and so forth.

In this regard, the following is considered: there are two types of divisions belonging to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, such as the state of being erroneous or non-erroneous in the case of cognition, and another type, such as that of a different cognition. That alone is the intrinsic nature of the entity; since the distinction between its own forms (*svarūpa*) is not a divider of that entity, how could it [the distinction] imply [a difference in the entity]? Therefore, in the Sautrāntika system, the statement beginning with *pra॰ vā॰ 2.210*—"How could that which is distinct..."—is logical.

Even when there is the superimposition of contradictory properties, if there is no difference [in essence], there is no real distinction between things; for even that which is of the nature of an error externally is, in its own nature, non-erroneous.
What would be the point of that variety even in a single cognition, if this [variety] were pleasing by itself from the objects? In that case, what role do we have?
— *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.205.
Furthermore, as for this view of the Yogācāra: "The nature of consciousness, though undivided, is perceived by those whose vision is distorted..."
"It appears as if possessing the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.354).

Showing that even in this case [the opponent's position] is not tenable, he says: "If it appears as if possessing parts," and so forth; "if it appears as if possessing parts, why is it not non-existent? Why is it not as if possessing succession? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.355ab).
"The nature of consciousness (*buddhyātman*), though devoid of parts, appears as if possessed of parts through [distinctions such as] being directed outward or inward.

(12) Regarding this, one view is that although the nature of consciousness is itself partless, it shines as if it were possessed of parts. Another view is that the subsequent conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpikā buddhiḥ*) determines it to be possessed of parts, even though it appears otherwise.
Having first presented the former view, he now refutes it: "That which has no parts is the nature of consciousness; and that very thing is consciousness itself."
What is that? He says: What is it like that shines?
By what [means] does it shine? He says: by those directed outward, inward, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), consciousness (saṃvitti) is included.

If it is argued—as stated by the opponent in *Prakaraṇavārttika* 2.354—that [consciousness] possesses a distinction between the apprehended, the apprehender, and self-awareness (*grāhya-grāhaka-saṃvitti-bhedavān*), then the refutation is as follows: why does the undivided nature of cognition (*avibhāgo buddhyātmā*), which is non-sequential (*akrama*)—meaning devoid of a sequence of pleasure and so forth—not appear as if it were sequential, as if it possessed a sequence of pleasure and so forth? Thus, since even the distinction of pleasure and so forth is not real within the awakened consciousness (*saṃbuddhau*) in the same way that the distinction between the apprehended, the apprehender, and self-awareness is not, the description of the perception of that [distinction of pleasure, etc. as being direct (*pratyakṣatva*) is useless.
Now, if this [consciousness] appears as possessing a sequence, what kind of object could it be? For it is not logical that blue, while appearing as blue, should be like [something other than] blue.

And if it does not appear in that way, even so, what kind of object could it be? If you argue that blue, even while appearing as non-yellow, cannot possibly be like yellow; then, if it appears as if there were a distinction between the apprehended, the apprehender, and the cognition, what kind of object could it be? Otherwise, too, the question "what kind of object could it be? remains the same for the experience of pleasure and so forth.
Furthermore, as for the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) being undifferentiated:

if that undifferentiated state were ever established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the conventional usage "it is as if differentiated" would be justified upon seeing it as differentiated at other times—just as one might say "there is water there" because of having seen water in a mirage at some point. However, this is not the case, as will be demonstrated immediately hereafter by the statement: "because the non-dual [reality] is perceived as appearing as duality."
And thus this has been refuted: [the notion] that there is water in a mirage-circle where no water exists.
Even though [the object] is undifferentiated— as stated in *Pravāha* 2.354 and elsewhere—

just as for those whose senses are afflicted by mantras and the like, objects such as fragments of clay appear in a manner entirely different [from their true nature], even though they are devoid of that [apparent] form.
For those whose vision is unimpaired, gold and other such objects are not perceived in that same way [as they appear to others];
or rather, it is like how a great garland or similar object is seen from a distance in desert lands.

"As this establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result is made according to appearance—even though [the distinction between] the grasped, the grasper, and consciousness does not exist" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.355–57);
how so? Because there is no similarity between the example and the thing illustrated.
For the perception of the nature of the intellect is not like the perception of a fragment of clay and so forth by those with unimpaired eyes;
nor does a desired conclusion follow from a mere example alone, otherwise everything would be established for everyone without distinction.
By this, the following [objection] is also refuted:
The sense is that [the clay] never exists in an undivided form as merely a fragment of clay, distinct from forms such as gold;
otherwise, a single entity would appear in manifold forms.

"How could the forms be real? Because that would entail the loss of their oneness" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.358). Since that which is perceived lacks reality due to its appearance in manifold forms, and since the ultimate reality is beyond perception, nothing at all would exist. Thus, how is one to determine whether this establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result is according to appearance, or according to reality?
[This concerns] the cognition that has become the object of perception.

Because non-duality is unreal and undivided, the following might be thought: "The nature of the intellect (*buddhy-ātman*) is not experienced as something distinct from the pleasure and other states that arise sequentially; rather, it is merely the experience of pleasure and so forth arising in succession. How then can it be said to appear as if it were sequential? Otherwise, one would have to say that a donkey’s horn appears in that way. [To this we reply: This is the same [as our position], for even though it is distinct from the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*), the blue and so forth are never perceived [apart from the subject], as the cognition always occurs in the form "I know [this] blue. Thus, the two cases are identical.
If one were to postulate that it possesses those forms, there would be the same undesirable consequence as in the case of another mental continuum;
furthermore, this consequence is that [consciousness] would be of the nature of an undivided cognition.

If one imagines that there is a form of the apprehended object, then the form of the apprehended object, the form of the apprehending subject, and the form of consciousness would belong to different continua.
Furthermore, regarding this which has been written twice as "the consequence" (*prasaṅga*), namely the objection raised by Prajñākaragupta in his work *Dvayasiddhiprakaraṇa*:

"If it is said that although this [consciousness] appears sequentially, it appears as if it were sequential, then why is it not said that what is non-existent appears as if existent, and the insentient appears as if sentient? This too must be considered whether or not it applies to the present case;
thus, that is not the first view.

Conceptual construction (vikalpa) refutes the second [position] by demonstrating: "The nature of the intellect (buddhyātmā) appears as if it were possessed of parts through its outward- and inward-facing aspects; it is perceived, and if it is held that it is determined by a conceptual construction following upon that perception of partless [reality], then what is the fault here? Why does that which is non-successive not appear as if it were successive, and why is it not determined by that very same conceptual construction? For this logic applies equally to everything.

Furthermore, consider this: even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), when determining an object in that manner, does or does not possess the distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*). Close your eyes or open them and reflect for a moment: if it possesses such a distinction from some source, then let the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) itself be so; what is the use of postulating a conceptual construction? Moreover, if one were to postulate such a distinction there as well, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And it has already been stated that, according to the opponent, there is no such thing as conceptual construction.
Therefore, even the second view is not superior,
as it involves conceptual construction characterized by the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.

Since the *kārikā* is easy to understand, I shall not provide a word-by-word commentary. Nevertheless, one might raise this objection: "Even if the self—which is partless and devoid of cognition—appears or is perceived as if it possessed parts or as if it were sequential, the doctrine of either the Buddhist or the Advaitin (Vedāntin) would be established, but not that of the Jaina;

for it does not become 'just so' merely because it appears as such. Indeed, a circle of sunbeams [mirage] is not water simply because it appears like water. Keeping this objection in mind, he refutes it by saying: "In that regard, by the wise... and so forth, ending with "...as if possessing parts or as if sequential."

If, for some [object], there were unity between that which possesses parts or possesses succession and that which appears therein, whether by those who hold it to be real or those who hold it to be unreal;
"In that very way, why is there not an inconclusiveness [of the reason] by means of successive [parts], given that [the object] has a non-successive nature?

(13) The intended meaning here is this: because of the statement "as if having parts," the parts such as the apprehended object (*grāhya*) which appear there in the nature of cognition (*buddhyātman*) are not ultimately real. Yet, even though they are unreal, they are not distinct from the nature of cognition, because—as will be stated later in the *Siddhiviniścaya* and other works—there would otherwise be the fault of the appearance of an object [without a basis] in consciousness.
Therefore, those [atoms] must be accepted as somehow non-different from one another.

[Objection: Even so, one ought to say "by those that are non-existent" (*asadbhiḥ*), because that is logical; what is the point of saying "by those that are existent" (*sadbhiḥ*)? [Reply: True. Nevertheless, whatever appears in a certain way, that very thing enters into conventional usage as being ultimately real in that same way—just as blue, appearing as blue, enters into usage precisely as such. And since all entities appear as momentary, if the nature of cognition (*buddhyātman*), though appearing as possessing the parts of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness, were not ultimately real in that same way, then there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason for that very reason. Therefore, the statement "by those that are existent" has been explained as being intended to demonstrate that it is ultimately real in that very manner; this is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
It should be understood— see page 2, note 10—
that [this occurs] precisely through the intellect (buddhi),
by virtue of its possessing distinctions such as the grasped and the grasper.

The meaning of the word is explained: by the "existent" (*sat*), such as those possessing consciousness, and by the "non-existent" (*asat*), such as the water in a mirage; the word *ca* (and) indicates a conjunction.
By what [means]? He says: "externally," etc.; the word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to include "consciousness" (*saṃvitti*).
What follows from this? He says "yadi" (if), etc.

The general term "kasyacit" (of something) is used for the purpose of including the previous alternative, namely that which consists of the nature of cognition (*buddhyātman*). In this case, the refutation is as follows: "ekatvaṃ sidhyet" (unity would be established), and so forth.

In that very same manner, by means of pleasure, pain, and so forth—which occur sequentially and exist either as real or unreal—how could there not be the establishment of a non-sequential self characterized by unity? This is what is being considered. What, then, is established thereby? He says: "non-absolutism" (*anekānta*), and so on.

In both cases—whether by those [attributes] existing in the mode of unity or even by those existing in the absence of unity—the establishment of both error and its opposite for a single entity results; thus, there is an absence of the establishment of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

Having thus demonstrated the establishment of what is undesirable for the opponent, he now says— beginning with "perception" (pratyakṣam)— stating the absence of what is desired within this very prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The perception of the Buddhist is free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍham*), as stated in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.

If the mind is indeed partless (*avibhāga*) and directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), why does it appear as if it has parts externally? That very same [mind] is not directly perceived internally; it is truly free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). If there is the possibility of conceptual and erroneous confusion even regarding that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous, then on what basis could one distinguish between a true perception and its semblance? Thus, another definition of perception can be stated: [it is that which is] like the mental illusion of seeing two moons in one who perceives only a single moon, or like the experience of a distinction between subject and object constructed by conceptualization within a cognition that is itself partless.
Even externally, determinate knowledge such as inference appears to arise from some cause as if it were conceptual;

therefore, there is no fixed distinction between direct and indirect objects. Since there would be no distinction between valid and invalid cognition, a distinction between reality and its opposite would be impossible.
If the mind is consciousness, then even that which is undivided appears as if divided, like a rope appearing as a snake.

Here he states the refutation: "The mind itself, when within its own nature, is perception free from conceptual construction; because it is free from conceptual construction, and because it is non-erroneous, that which was stated by the opponent—that it is not perceived—is connected with the verb from the previous verse. The meaning is that it is perceived not merely by will, but directly in the ultimate sense (*paramārthena*).

Furthermore, since partless things appear as having parts, and since conceptual construction shares the same form as error, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished due to the very nature of conceptual construction. This is the intended meaning.
"Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous"— this [definition] from the *Nyāyabindu* (1.4) repeats what has already been stated regarding "conceptual construction."

If it is argued that the first perception indeed perceives the self as undivided, while the conceptualization arising immediately thereafter determines it as if it were divided—and therefore this fault does not apply—then [the author] says here: "Is it external? This phrase "no" must also be connected to this point because it is placed in the middle. Thus, the meaning is: why is it that the mind, when directed toward external objects such as the moon, is not observed by everyone to be free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), as is the case with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); rather, it is indeed observed to be free from conceptual construction.
Explaining the nature of the *kārikā*, he says: "Perception" (*pratyakṣa*), and so forth;
[it refers to] that which is perception and that which is its semblance (*tadābhāsa*); of these two...
"Could it be that one does not perceive difference by relying on some cause or condition? The meaning is that one would perceive it as accidental.
To the question "When? he says: "free from conceptual construction," and so forth.

Here, the term "of the mind" (*cittasya*) connects with the previously recurring phrase "of the mind which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," and refers to its transformation into the state of having become [the object].
The word "api" (even/also) indicates the opponent's admission;

for when conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and error (*bhrānti*) are possible—given that there exists a single entity common to both the aspects of existence and non-existence, and given that conceptual construction, though partless, appears as having parts, and error likewise occurs.

This is what is meant: since being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) and being non-erroneous (*abhrāntatva*) are the two pervaders (*vyāpaka*) of perceptuality (*pratyakṣatva*), and since these two—being pervaded by their own opposites, namely conceptualization and error—are excluded from all cognitions [that are not perception], they cease to exist along with their pervaded property, perceptuality. Thus, there would be no such thing as "perception" at all; and in its absence, there could be no "semblance of perception" (*tadābhāsa*), because the latter depends upon the former. If this is so, one might ask: even in the absence of being free from conceptual construction and non-erroneousness, can another definition of perception be stated and established? To this he says: "The moon," and so forth.

The mention of a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative illustration); by this, the perception of white objects such as conch shells, elephants, and horses, as well as their locations and so forth, is included. Even for one who sees—that is, directly perceives these through visual cognition—it is not only for one who does not see them that [the following occurs].
To this he says: "the delusion of two moons.

Here too, the mention of the perception of two moons is an *upalakṣaṇa*; thus, during sleep and so forth, there is the perception of location and so forth, and its "delusion" is its apprehension otherwise. And that [delusion] should be understood as mental (*mānasī*).
Since there is no possibility of anyone else seeing that [consciousness], for whom [is it seen]? To this he says: "By itself," and so forth.

Just as there is the perception of the distinctions between the perceived, the perceiver, and the consciousness—which are constructed by conceptualization within one’s own intellect (buddhi) that is itself undivided and partless—so too [is the case here].

This is what is meant: just as for one who perceives non-dual cognition (*avimāgabuddhi*), the mental experience of the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakasaṃvitti*) is an error, so too is the case here.
Therefore, the position that "it is perception" and so forth is established.

Previously, it was stated that because there is no [true] perception, one should not characterize it as a variety of its semblance (*tadābhāsabheda*); now, it is stated that because there is no semblance of it, one should not characterize this as perception.
Therefore, this is refuted:
that the genitive case (*tāsām*) is used [to denote possession] in the absence of direct perception.
For one who apprehends a pseudo-perception through sensory perception,
it is a sensory error.
Conceptual cognition is threefold, arising from a disturbance of the basis;

conceptual cognition that resembles perception is threefold: erroneous cognition that determines water in a mirage; conventional cognition that is deceptive because it involves a determination that contradicts reality; and cognition of signs, the objects to be inferred, and so forth, which proceeds by conceptualizing identity with what was previously perceived.
And one [type], non-conceptual cognition, also resembles perception.

Of what kind? It is that which arises from an impairment (*upaplava*) of the basis, namely the sense faculty (*indriya*), such as an affliction by cataracts (*timira*) and so forth; thus it is "of that nature.
And in this way, there are four types of fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*)—*Pramāṇavārttika-manoratha*.
"And non-conceptual, it is one; thus perception-like [cognition] is fourfold" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.288).
How so? Because there is no such thing as a conceptual cognition that is perception-like.

But surely, if the illusion of a double moon is mental, then what now is sensory cognition? If you say: "That which possesses existence or non-existence according to the existence or non-existence of the sense organ belongs to that [organ]," then let the cognition of a double moon and so forth belong to that very [organ] for that reason.
If it is argued that "that which undergoes modification belongs to that [cause] because it possesses modification," this too has not been relinquished by him;
as it was said—compare: "If, first of all, this cognition of two moons and so forth were mental, it would not conform to the presence or absence of the sense organ."
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 336: "If [it is argued that] a certain sense-faculty conforms to the presence or absence of the moments [of the object],"
What indeed is sensory [cognition]—that which [arises] from the sense-faculties (*akṣa*)? Is that very thing being denied here?

Even for one who does not accept [the cognition of] an optical illusion (*timira*) as an error, what kind of sensory cognition is intended? If it is argued that "sensory [cognition] is that which conforms to the presence or absence of the sense-faculties by following their existence or non-existence," then this conformity to the presence or absence of the sense-faculties is equally true for the cognition of one with an optical disorder (*taimirika*).
For the cognition of one with an optical disorder does not arise without the operation of the sense-faculties.

If sensory cognition is defined as that which possesses modification due to a modification of the sense organ, then why do you object to our statement that the cognitions of a double moon and so forth—which possess modification due to a modification of the sense organ caused by cataracts and the like—are characterized by error because they consist in the presentation of unreal objects?
[Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī, 2.296] "If it is argued that this is similar [to other cognitions], then why is this modification not accepted [as the cause of error]? [Pramāṇavārttika 2.296]

Furthermore, if the illusion of two moons and so forth were purely mental, then it would cease even when there is a defect in the sense organ—just as the illusion of a snake and the like does—or else it would not cease even when the impairment of the sense organ has been removed.
This too has been stated:
just as the illusion of a snake in a rope, though being mental, ceases through mental reflection even while the defect of the sense organ persists.

Furthermore, like the error regarding a snake and so forth, this [error] would cease even when there is no defect in the sense organs; it would not be averted even when the impairment of the sense organs has ceased. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.297) Moreover, like the error regarding a snake and so forth, this [error] would involve the communication of it to another mental continuum by means of words that denote it, the dependence upon the recollection of a previously seen double moon and so forth, and an indistinct appearance.
And so it has been said:
because the sense organ is not the cause of errors such as the appearance of two moons, there would be no clear manifestation.

If it is argued: "Sometimes [the object] might be projected in the same way onto another mental continuum by means of expressive words; it would depend upon what was previously seen and remembered, and thus it would not appear with complete clarity" (*Pravāṇavārttika* 2.298); that is not so, because this [objection] applies equally to the case at hand as well.

For instance: if the perception of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and their cognition is an error, then is it mental? What, then, is sensory cognition? If [it is argued that sensory cognition] conforms to the presence or absence of the sense organs, then that is equally true in the other case as well.
The same should be said for the rest.
Nevertheless, one considers that this [perception of duality] is mental; likewise, one thinks that the illusion of two moons and so forth would also be so.
Error consists in the perception of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and their cognition.

By this, the following argument of the opponent is also refuted: "All cognitions are without an objective basis (nirālambana), because they are cognitions, like a dream-cognition" (*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* 3.331).
How so? Because, with respect to the proponent, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because the opponent does not lack that [cognition], then, by following the opponent's view, the proof of self-cognition as an indivisible cognition would not be established. Therefore, the purity of the means of valid cognition is as follows: "All cognitions are without an object of contact, because they are cognitions, like dream-cognitions" (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.
359). Thus, perception is both non-conceptual and unitary (*Pramāṇavārttika* 2.1).
Having thus refuted these three types of conceptual cognition that appear as perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), [the author], while rejecting them, says "outside" (*bahiḥ*) and so forth.
The term "outside" is used because the opponent maintains that inference and the like are non-conceptual; even in those cases, [perception] is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
What is that? He says: "the determinative cognition (*nirṇaya-jñāna*) of inference and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of erroneous cognition (*bhrānti*), conventional cognition (*saṃvṛti-saṃjñāna*), and the like.

If inference and the rest were non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) like perception, then even regarding what is grasped by them, there would be superimposition (*samāropa*); therefore, in order to exclude that, [it is stated] that determinative cognition appears as if conceptual—like a mental construction (*mānasavikalpa*)—due to some influence of conceptualization. This has been refuted: "Erroneous cognition, conventional cognition... (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1).
8. Thus,
the absence of such conventional usage is the same elsewhere as well, in the case of intrinsic nature (svarūpa).
Even by a Buddhist, even when [an object] is apprehended externally through inference.
Error, conventional knowledge, inference and its result,
recollection, and desire— these, along with that which is accompanied by visual impairment, are pseudo-sensory cognitions.
The erroneous cognition arising from the conceptualization of water and so forth in a mirage and the like is a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
For conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is indeed a semblance of perception because it superimposes another object upon itself and thereby conceptualizes its own nature;
likewise, inference and its result are not perception, because they involve the conceptualization of a prior experience.
—*Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1.8.

For an object (*artha*) is indeed of two kinds: perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and imperceptible (*parokṣa*). Among these, that which reproduces its own positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) within the manifestation of cognition (*jñāna-pratibhāsa*) is the perceptible object; the other is the imperceptible. Now, refuting this, [the author] says: "That is not so," and so forth.

Therefore, for that reason, according to the logic already stated, there is no establishment of perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), because when conceptual error is possible, there is no object of perception due to the absence of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); this is what is intended.

Nor is there an establishment of an object as "remote" (*parokṣa*), because a single moon and so forth—which is considered remote by one suffering from ophthalmia—is actually perceived directly by oneself, and fire and so forth—which is considered remote by an inferential cognizer—is likewise directly perceived by oneself; such is the sense.
Consequently, this [position] is refuted: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold because the objects of cognition (*meyadvaividhya*) are twofold" (Pramāṇavārttika 2).

Thus [it is said]; because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says the following—beginning with "pramāṇa"—in order to demonstrate the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmin*) in this very context:

"In the determination of those two, namely, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as non-discrepant knowledge and the other as invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), from what [source] does this [distinction] arise? To this, he replies: "Tattva-itara... and so forth.

Reality is non-dual knowledge in the ultimate sense; anything else is not ultimate, such as a double moon and so forth, because the establishment of those two is impossible and is negated by the reasoning already stated. There is no possibility of another object of cognition other than the direct and the indirect—*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.1.2.
That object for which there is a difference in the appearance of cognition due to its presence or absence is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
anything else is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
— Nyāyabindu 1.13, 17: Because that which is to be known is one alone, having the nature of both the universal and the particular.
Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge— Pramāṇavārttika 2.1.
Therefore, even in the Yogācāra view, [the objection] beginning with "What would [be the case]? (*Pravārttika* 2.210) and so forth is not tenable;
for there is no fault, as [objects] are like appearances such as illusions or mirages, despite being non-existent (*Pravārttikālaṃkāra* 3).
This very point has indeed been established by the passage beginning with *Pra.vā.

2.209* and so forth; thus, the Madhyamaka view remains as the final position. Demonstrating that even there it is not tenable, he says: "Self-cognition," and so on—"this is what comes by the force of the nature of things, as the wise declare."
In whatever way objects are conceptualized, they fall apart in that very same way— according to the *Pravāha-vāda*, self-awareness, though non-erroneous, appears as if divided due to delusion.
Is not the visual perception of a moon seen by one with ophthalmia [taimira] an instance for those who hate the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekānta)?

For it is not logical that the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of an error be itself erroneous; because if it were not perceived, there would follow the consequence that its own nature—just like the object—is unestablished.
Nor is it entirely non-erroneous, since even though it is itself non-dual, there is the cognition of the appearance of duality.

If, however, this were indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), why would it not belong to those whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts? Therefore, he considers that in the absence of the cognition—that is, the grasping—of the nature of the error itself, namely the internal and external delusion, [the object] would be like something non-existent because it is unestablished; thus, "that which is non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) means "non-false" (*avitatha*). This should be explained with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*).

Alternatively, the word "yadi" (if) should be supplied; otherwise, the error [of the opponent's position] would remain unestablished. Here he states the refutation: "It appears as if possessing differentiation;
it appears—that is, it shines—its cognition is similar to that which possesses differentiation, such as a variegated butterfly and so forth. This means it is like that [object].

This is what is meant: just as a variegated butterfly or the like appears in both a single and a manifold form, so too its cognition appears in both a delusive and a non-delusive, single and manifold form.
To the question "To whom does it appear thus?", he says: "To those who hate non-absolutism (anekānta)," that is, to those who maintain the doctrine of absolute delusion.
In this very context, he states another fault [in their view]: "Perception," and so forth.
"Belonging to the moon" means pertaining to the domain of the moon (*cāndram*).

Is this all? No; "timira" refers to the apprehension of darkness, which is an indicative mark for the cause of error. Therefore, the meaning is that the cognition of two moons and so forth arises from that [cause].
What is that? He says: "It appears as something differentiated, even though it is somehow direct perception"—that is to say, it is direct perception.
Of whom? Of those who are enemies of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) alone.

And thus, that which was stated by them—namely, "That which appears is not real, such as a double moon and the like; and knowledge, a jar, and so forth, do appear"—is refuted. The sense is that even in the illustrative example, an error (vibhrama) is not established in every respect.
[The word] *kāku* refers to the mode of posing a question.

Another Mādhyamika holds that the reality is established as mere self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), devoid of all conceptual constructions such as oneness and multiplicity, as in the case of a double moon, which arises from causes such as rapid spinning or travel by boat. This [term] is an illustration that includes other such causes.
Regarding that, he says: "Self-cognition," and so forth.

Because it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* (p. 365) that "the cognitions of blue and so forth, which are erroneous, are without an external object and have their own form as their object," self-cognition is the grasping of one's own nature, which is non-erroneous and devoid of the form of delusion; otherwise, the emptiness of all conceptual constructions would not be established—this is what [the opponent] thinks.
Herein lies the refutation: that self-cognition of the error appears as something distinct, just like a variegated butterfly and the like.

This is what is meant: since that which is partless—by virtue of transcending all conceptual constructions—appears as if it were possessed of parts through the forms of the objects of perception, how could it not be erroneous? For if it were erroneous, how could the actual reality of the object under discussion be established? Nevertheless, he states the refutation regarding its being a case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "Is that self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) not direct perception, and the cognition of two moons and so forth—which is caused by ophthalmia (*taimira*) regarding the moon—is not direct perception? On the contrary, it is indeed direct perception for whom? To this he replies: "For those who hate the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness), namely, for those who maintain the doctrine of absolute exclusivity (*ekāntavāda*) that transcends all conceptual construction."

Furthermore, the intention [of the opponent] is this: that which appears in clear perception is not ultimately real, just as a double moon and the like; and waking objects such as pillars appear in that manner.
Thus, in the example cited by the proponent, there is a lack of the property to be proven (*sādhyahīnatā*).
That form by which entities are defined does not exist in reality.
Because neither a single nor a multiple form exists for them— *Pravāraṇāvastu* 3.460.

Therefore, what is the meaning of the statement that all conditions whatsoever are without an objective support (*nirālambana*), like the conditions of a dream? [The answer is: they have their own nature as their objective support (*svarūpālambana*). The word *nirālambana* signifies having one's own part (*svāṃśa*) as its objective support—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 372. (See also *Pramāṇavārttika*, p. 365, n.).
Explaining the *Mādhyamika-kārikā*, he says: "Indeed not," and so forth.

It is not possible—that is, it is neither logical nor tenable—that there should be a perception or apprehension of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) as being exclusively characterized by the delusion of internal and external [objects] due to error; rather, it is only non-erroneous that is logical. Thus, the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is proven.
He states the refutation [that follows] from not accepting this: "That," and so forth.

The meaning is that if that self-awareness of error were not perceptual—that is, if it were erroneous—then, like its object, such as a jar or the like, there would follow the consequence of the non-establishment of its own nature; that is, there would follow the consequence of the non-establishment of the very essence of error. As it was stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*:
"In their case, even the error [of error] is not established" (Nyāyaviniścaya 1.54).
Stating this second point, he says "nāpi" and so forth; the word "api" indicates an alternative position: in every way and in its entirety, that self-cognition of error is indeed non-erroneous.
Nor is it the case that it is not at all non-erroneous;
why is this so? To this he says: "By itself," and so forth.

This means that, according to the Buddhist position, even though cognition is non-dual and transcends all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is nevertheless the perception of a dual appearance. This is because cognition is perceived through the forms grasped by consciousness as having both unitary and manifold aspects.

Now, if it is argued: "If blue and so forth, as well as the body, pleasure, and so forth, are the apprehended object (*grāhya*), then no other [entity]—neither an apprehender (*grāhaka*) nor an act of apprehension (*grahaṇa*)—is perceived;

and if that [object] is the apprehender, then there is no other apprehended object or act of apprehension," then this is incorrect, because of the statement beginning with "by itself" (*svayam*). This is not so, because if one were to deny the perception "I know blue and so forth," it would lead to the undesirable consequence of denying everything.
For everything is non-erroneous with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), whereas there is error with respect to the nature of another (*pararūpa*).
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 372.
[Regarding] blue and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth:
compare— "Therefore, it is determined that there is no cognition (*bodha*) called 'intellect' (*buddhi*) apart from blue and so forth."
One does not perceive the cognizing consciousness as distinct from the blue;
rather, the difference [perceived] subsequent to the cognition is constructed by the artisan of conceptual construction—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 406.
Indeed, apart from white, black, and so forth, no state of being a subject (*grāhaka*) or the like is perceived as appearing [independently]. — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 372.

By this, the following argument advanced by the opponent is also refuted: "Whatever cause exists for the determination that 'this is the form of the object (*grāhya*),' 'this is the form of the subject (*grāhaka*),' and 'this is the form of consciousness (*saṃvedana*),' if there is a difference in that [cause], then there must also be a difference among those [forms]; thus, it is not logical that they constitute a single [entity]. Otherwise, such a determination would not be possible."

Thus [it is asked]: how so? If one investigates each individual part in this manner, then since everything would dissolve into atoms, neither the establishment of a distinct mental continuum (*santānāntara*) nor even mere universal emptiness (*sakalaśūnyatāmātra*)—which is a state of total defenselessness—would be possible.
For this very reason, even a mere appearance devoid of the conceptual constructs of unity or plurality is not tenable.
Therefore, by one who accepts that there is merely an appearance, it must be admitted that there is a single cognition in the form "I know blue. Thus, it is well said: "by oneself," and so forth.
Nevertheless, he states the refutation for one who accepts that [cognition] as non-erroneous: "If, however," and so forth.

This non-dual cognition, which possesses the appearance of duality—if it were indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), meaning that consciousness itself is not non-perceptual—then why would it not belong to those whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts? It would certainly be a direct perception having the moon and so forth as its object.
Whence is this? To this he says: "That," and so forth;
this is easy to understand, and the same should be applied even to the previous explanation.

However, this is the distinction: since it is said there that "in some way" (*kathañcit*), how could that [not apply] even in the Madhyamaka system? Thus, the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (2.210), "How could that not be established? and so forth, is justified.

That which consists of the grasped object and so forth— this variety would not exist even in that single cognition if it were to manifest itself from its own accord rather than from objects; in that case, what are we [to say]?
—Pravāhaṇa:
Concluding the point already stated, he says: "The particular characteristic of its own object," and so forth;
[it means that] cognition should be characterized as having its own object as its particular characteristic and as being transformative (pariṇāmin).
"In what sense, then, is this [object] characterized as being both internal and external through direct perception?

Since, in ultimate reality, there is the cognition of a dual appearance within the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since externally a single, gross [form] appears, the intellect—which displays that one, gross, transforming form as something unerring and witnessed by all the world—establishes non-unity (*anekānta*) and thereby refutes unity (*ekānta*) of its own accord; so why worry about this?"

The cognition (*jñāna*), acting as the agent (*kartṛ*) and undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmin*), should—according to the aforementioned logic—characterize and ascertain both its own specific characteristic (*svasvalakṣaṇa*) and the object's specific characteristic (*arthasvalakṣaṇa*). "Its own" means that which is suitable for grasping itself; "the object's specific characteristic" is that which has become the objective (*karmatāpanna*). It has been stated that [it ascertains] the transformation accepted by others.
Where? To this he says: "Internally and externally.
"Internally" refers to its own specific characteristic (*svasvalakṣaṇa*); "externally" refers to the object's specific characteristic (*arthasvalakṣaṇa*).
What happened after that? To this he says: "Then where is this," and so forth.

Since it is thus, therefore, where—anywhere at all, whether externally or internally—is this [perception] spoken of by the Buddhist? What kind of perception? One whose definition has been formulated as "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (Nyāyabindu 1).

That which has its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) thus established is described as such. Regarding the phrase "in any case whatsoever" (*kvacid api*), it may be explained as follows: where is that object perceivable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), grasped by sight, whose characteristic is established—that is, whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is determined?
Explaining the verse, he says: "Internally," and so forth.

What follows from the perception of the internal particular characteristic—that is, the particular characteristic of cognition—as appearing as a duality, or from its perception as having both unitary and manifold forms? [The answer is:
From the perspective of ultimate reality, this is not due to error; rather, it is because that which exists otherwise is apprehended otherwise.
By the phrase "of one external [object]," he demonstrates that the opponent's position—that the five groups of consciousness have a composite (*sañcita*) as their objective support—is untenable.

By the word "sthevīyasaḥ" (of that which is more massive), he refutes the view that reality consists of partless atoms alone; [he does so] because of its appearing [as such]. From this, it follows that it is an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpaviṣayatva*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That one," and so forth.

The cognition that demonstrates—without error and as witnessed by the entire world—the aspect or characteristic of that [object], which possesses both internal and external specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is common to a single entity despite its manifold forms, which is for that very reason gross (*sthavīyas*) and consequently subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), and which possesses both the intended and other modes (*paryāya*); this cognition is the "establishment of non-absolutism" (*anekāntasiddhi*). That [cognition] in which such a proof exists is so described; or rather, what does its own establishment (*siddhi*) itself accomplish? To this, he says: "Itself," and so forth.
[The opponent] thinks that he refutes the absolute [position] by himself alone and not by another, because the establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta) consists in the negation of absolutism;
for this reason, what is the use of our concern— the investigation into the purpose of negating absolutism?— for the Buddhist.
It should be observed— page 25, note 10— that the connection is: "he refutes" means "he explains away."
If it is asked, "How does she [the scripture] refute absolutism? Is it not because it is sublated by inference whose object is absolute? To this he says: "Knowledge," etc.
Cognition is the establishment of non-absolutism;
knowledge arises from the power of its own object and is distinct from the particular (svalakṣaṇa).
The universal characteristic is established because of its non-exclusivity and because it is observed in that way.

Just as the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) postulated by others— whether internal or external— does not sustain the definition of direct perception, so too the universal (*sāmānya*) [does not exist] anywhere in substance...
Knowledge that has arisen—not produced by the force of a logical mark (*liṅga*) or the like—of its own apprehended object, is what is meant by "perception" (*adhyakṣa*).

Just as [perception] is distinct from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and is turned away from the apprehension of partless, momentary atoms, so too is inferential knowledge (*anumāna*); it is called such because it is that by which or that in which a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—that which is characterized as a universal or that by which a universal is characterized—is apprehended. The connection is that [inferential knowledge] is distinct from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

And thus, from where [could there be] that [cognition], or rather, the cognition of that? This is the sense. Even without the words *yathā* and *tathā*, this meaning is obtained by resorting to the *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) ornament.

[Objection: "In that case, how is the establishment of reality (*tattva*) achieved? To this he says: the establishment (*siddhi*) of reality—meaning its attainment of its own nature (*ātmalābha*) or its definitive determination (*nirṇīti*)—is [achieved] by means of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), that is, by resorting to non-absolutism or by that very reason.
Why? Because of seeing in that way; that is, because everything is seen through manifold modes. Explaining this verse, he says: "Just as," and so forth.

Just as—in whatever manner—the internal or external specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), having become the object, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) characterized as immediate cognition (*adhyakṣapramāṇa*), acting as the agent, does not nourish—that is, does not grasp.

Of what nature is that? He says: "imagined by others"—that is, imagined by the Buddhists—and likewise, the universal (*sāmānya*), through the metaphorical application of the term 'object' to the subject, nourishes that inference;
thus, the phrase "imagined by others" should also be applied here.
Why is this so? To this he says: "in substance," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
In an inference whose object is a universal, [the reason] does not sustain the reality [of that universal]. Thus,
regarding the universal...
Alternatively, this verse may be introduced in a different manner: if there is no non-conceptual perception anywhere as imagined by the Buddhists, then let this be so— namely,
that there exists the initial non-conceptual "perceptual awareness" (ālocanājñāna) as maintained by the Mīmāṃsakas.

If it is argued that [this cognition] is like the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth, arising from a pure object (*śuddhavastuja*)— as stated in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Pratyakṣa, verse 112— the author replies with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*), etc.

Here too, by resorting to the poetic figure of *prativastūpamā* (parallelism), it is shown that just as knowledge arises by the power of its own object— which consists of partless, momentary atoms— as a non-conceptual perception (*darśana*) distinct from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and turned away from its own graspable [part], so too the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), having the universal as its object, is distinct from the specific characteristic and turned away from grasping its own [specific] object.

The meaning of the term *lakṣaṇa* (definition/characteristic) is derived from the etymology "that which is observed in both [cases]. From where does this [meaning] come? He says: "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) means determination. Because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) are non-exclusive (*anekānta*), they are observed or seen in such a way by relying upon non-exclusivity—this is what he expresses through the verse beginning with "yathā" (just as). "Just as," whether internal or external, a particular characteristic imagined by others—that is, imagined by the Buddhists—is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The agent [of perception] is the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*) [Nyāyabindu 1].

[Objection: "In that case, [the cognition] does not sustain the nature of the perceiver as having become the object, because it does not present that nature; likewise, why does it not sustain the universal (sāmānya) imagined by others? To this, he says: "In some cases," etc.
[Objection: "Why is even this so? To this, he says: "In a substance," etc.

Furthermore, demonstrating that inference and the like possess a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) distinct from the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of another [the object], he says: "Accepted," and so forth. "The description of non-conceptual [cognition] as being accepted as self-awareness [is untenable], because the nature of inference and the like is conceptual, since they do not conceptualize the object through non-conceptuality. (18)
Without its own self-experience (*svānubhava*), there can be no experience of an object by cognition.

Just as it is impossible for everyone to be all-seeing if the experience of an object occurred merely through the existence of knowledge, likewise, if the determination of an object occurred merely through the existence of an undetermined self-experience, then everyone would have the determination of everything. How could that which is not determined by a determination be its object, like an external object, such that perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*)? Or, if [cognition] were cognized by another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and other faults.

The Buddhist accepts—that is, acknowledges by refuting the Naiyāyikas and others—the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvitti*) of all minds and mental factors, which is the grasping of their own nature. Its description as "non-conceptual" refers to its being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatva*). As for inference and so forth, their "self" is their essential nature; they are non-conceptual insofar as they lack conceptual construction. Because [inference] does not conceptually construct, determine, or take as its object things such as momentary destruction, how could that nature which is not determined by determinative cognitions (*niścaya*) be an object for them?
The meaning is: since this has been stated, how can there be a sublation of cognition by those [reasons], given that the non-contradictory nature [of the reason] is established?
Explaining the tenth verse, he says: "One's own experience," and so forth.

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: just as the experience or apprehension of an external object such as a jar is not possible through the mere existence of cognition—by way of depending on the mere existence of the cognition in another continuum for the experience of that object, whereby everyone would become an all-seer—so too, by that same principle, if the determination of an object occurred through the mere existence of an undetermined self-experience, then the determination of that [object] would also occur through the mere existence of the cognition in another continuum; thus, by the principle that "everyone would determine everything," the determination of one's own object is not possible without the determination of one's own [cognition].

And thus there is the following inference: Wherever someone has a cognition whose nature is not ascertained, in that case, for that person, with respect to that [object], there is no ultimate conventional usage based on ascertainment; just as, for example, Devadatta does not have such usage regarding a jar and so forth with respect to Yajñadatta’s cognition [of it]; and for the Buddhist, every conceptual cognition (vikalpajñāna) everywhere has an unascertained nature. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because one's own conceptualization takes something as its object while another's is the opposite, the author says in response: "That which is the intrinsic nature," and so forth.

That intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) which, being of such a character (*svarūpa*), is not ascertained by determinations (*niścaya*), how could that intrinsic nature not be the object (*viṣaya*) of those very determinations?
Regarding this, he provides an example: "just like an external object" (*bahirartha iva tadvat*).
And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*): the intrinsic nature is not the object of determinations, because it is not ascertained by them, just like an external object.
If that [conceptual cognition] had that [particular] as its object, then for them, the state of having the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its domain would be undesirable.

It might be argued: "The perception of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is what distinguishes it from the external object. No; for how can there be a perception of something that is not ascertained, such as momentariness? Demonstrating the established result, he says: "Since," and so forth.

Since that [conceptual cognition] has that as its object, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), and there would be self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Or, if "yataḥ" (from which) is used in the sense of an objection—namely, that the nature of determinations (*niścaya*) could not exist at all [if they were self-established]—then there would be no fault, as determinations would be determined by other determinations. To this, he replies with the words "from another," and so forth:

if the cognition or determination of determinations occurs from another experience or from another determination, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he includes the lack of distinction between the qualifier and the qualified, as [would follow] for the Buddhists and the Vaiśeṣikas.

Therefore, just as it is incorrect for a Vaiśeṣika to claim that a reason (hetu) adduced immediately after stating a thesis (karmanirdeśa) that is sublated by perception, inference, or scripture is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) due to the absence of perception and so forth resulting from a lack of experience, so too is it incorrect for a Buddhist to claim [a reason] is "unrefuted" (anirākṛta), according to Nyāyabindu 3.40; the point is that there is no refutation by anyone else.
This refers to another self (ātmāntara).
The determination of meaning is [effected] by determinations;
[it is the determination] of determination.

If [the cognition] has its own nature as its object, it is contradicted by perception and scripture; this is what is intended by the term "kālātyayāpadiṣṭa" (mistimed). — *Nyāyakalikā*, p. 15; *Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 320, note 7.
It is not tenable that a thesis (pakṣa) is [defined as] "that which is intended by oneself and not refuted" in its own nature alone—[as stated in the] *Nyāyabindu*.

For indeed, for a Buddhist or any other proponent of an extremist view (*ekāntavādin*), perception never possesses a defined characteristic; nor does it support either the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

If it is asked, "In what state is that [perception], or what kind of specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) does it nourish?", he says here: "Perception," and so forth;
that is, perception.
Direct perception is clear cognition regarding those with clear eyes and so forth;
in whatever case there is non-discrepancy, in that case there is validity. (19) For comparison: "In whatever way a means of knowledge is non-discrepant, it is considered valid in that way."
— This is quoted from *Laghīyastraya*, verse 22; see *Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 170,
and *Aṣṭasāhasrī*, page 163.
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 595:

"If [non-validity] could occur even when there is a cognition common to contradictory properties (*pratyanīka-dharma*) due to its own non-completeness, why would it not also occur regarding the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object? On what basis, then, is invalidity attributed to that [cognition of the *svalakṣaṇa*]? Furthermore, since it is impossible for a clear sensory cognition to be restricted to correspondence in every respect, why is it not also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that another means of knowledge does not operate upon what has already been seen?"

Even for those whose eyes are impaired, it is observed that there is no lack of non-contradiction when they act after determining an object—even without the comprehension of the relationship between the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin);

and since validity is established by that much alone, the point here is this: when someone accepts perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is not affected by defects in the causal complex of the eye and so forth, then, by the force of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*), the status of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) is attributed to it, because such perceptual valid knowledge is pervaded by the nature of cognition.

If it is asked, "For what purpose? [it is replied: because for one who does not accept that, there is a reversal of the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum). [The purpose is] so that this knowledge may be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) as perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, when someone maintains that even an indistinct cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is perception, then it is established that "perception is a distinct cognition," because otherwise the existence of other means of cognition to be mentioned later would be untenable.
The use of the singular number in "cognition" (*jñānam*) is with respect to the genus (*jāti*), for the purpose of including all distinct cognitions.

Why is this so? To this he says: "In the case of those with clear eyes and others"—here, "those with clear eyes" refers to persons with clear vision, while "others" refers to those with unclear vision; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), persons who are near, nearer, and so forth are included. Thus, the connection is as follows: in whatever manner and regarding whatever object [the cognition] is clear, in that same manner and regarding that same object, it is perception (*pratyakṣa*); the intention is that in other cases, that very same [cognition] is indirect (*parokṣa*).

Not only perception, but furthermore, in whatever way and by whatever manner—in which cognition among those such as clear-sighted or otherwise—there is non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*), that is, description, by that very manner and in that very cognition there is the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatā*).

By this he says the following: all worldly cognition is a means of valid knowledge regarding its own object, whether it be clear or unclear; thus there is non-absolutism (*anekānta*). Likewise, that very [non-absolutism] nourishes what is to be established by it.

Now, what is this so-called "non-contradiction" (*avisamvāda*)? If it is argued that it is the determination of its own object (*svārthavyavasāya*), because of the statement that "there is no non-contradiction other than this," [we reply: this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding dreams and the like, for even there, since non-contradiction characterized by the determination of its own object exists, cognition would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, there would be an unqualified destruction of the distinction between what is a valid means of knowledge and what is not.

It might be argued that even in cases such as dreams, there is neither [the object] nor its own meaning [i.e., the objective referent], because they are sublated; therefore, there is no non-discrepancy characterized by the determination of that [object].

But what is this "being sublated"? If it means the removal of its own nature or the communication of its non-existence by another subverting cognition at the time of its appearance, then that is not credible.

Neither can the intrinsic nature of cognition or anything else be removed, for that which is appearing would then entail the consequence of not appearing at all; nor can there be a communication of its non-existence, because this would lead to the same consequence regarding pillars and so forth during the waking state.

If you think that this fault does not apply because there is no subsequent cognition [of error] such as "this was falsely conceptualized," that too is not tenable, since such a cognition may sometimes occur even in the case of the unreal, and may sometimes be absent even in the case of the real.
If the object of cognition (*pratyaya*) also exists [at the time of the cognition], the same fault applies; furthermore, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If [the object] exists at a later time, then how can that which is entirely non-existent be negated?
Or rather, that [later existence] is not "non-contradiction" (*avisaṃvāda*), which is the determination of its own object.

If it is argued that [non-contradiction] is the repeated apprehension of what has already been apprehended, or its connection with a result— no; because that [object] is momentary, such [repeated apprehension or connection] is impossible due to its destruction, and because [such apprehension occurs] even in dreams,
there is therefore no non-contradiction anywhere,
as in the case of dreams and the like.

In reality, regarding the comparison between one's own purpose and the determination of that purpose: what is this so-called "sublation" (bādha)? If it is held to be the communication by another of the non-existence of the object;
How could a cognition that functions toward its own object make known a non-existence?
For non-existence is not produced by another cognition—whether it be dream-cognition or any other—at that time, because [the cognition] perishes of its own accord at that very moment.
Furthermore, sublation is not perceived when a cognition has perished due to the closing of the eyes.
For its sublation—defined as the cognition of non-existence which deprives it of its object—is not effected by any other cognition.

If the arising of a cognition of a different class were called "sublation," then why would the cognition of a cloth not logically be a sublation of the cognition of a jar? Therefore, this is the established principle: just as a waking cognition sublates a dream cognition, so too does a contrary cognition [sublate] due to the apprehension of the mere [object].
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 4–7:
Non-contradiction regarding pillars and other objects perceived while awake.

Since there is no connection with a result for the repeated apprehension of the first cognition, this is answered as follows: For if all appearances were thus without distinction, there would be no differentiation between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its opposite; consequently, how could there be the establishment of mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-mātra*), from which either the non-duality of appearance or something else might follow? If it is established through appearance, then the external object is established.

For this very reason, since that [object] is established even in a dream, there is a separation from both error and its opposite; otherwise, because external objects would be established elsewhere, the world would be non-Buddhist (asau-gata).

A specific appearance (*pratibhāsa-viśeṣa*) is not precluded in other cases either. If it is argued: "Let there be self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of cognition because of its appearing; there is no internal or external object because of the contrary [nature of objects], since even jars and the like consist of the nature of self-awareness"; [we reply: then that which appears within the body of cognition as an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is unreal, like the hairs seen by one with ophthalmia. And since waking jars and so forth appear in that same way, the reason [adduced by you] is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the proponent.

If it is argued that [the reason] is established for the opponent; no, for if it were established by means of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be established for both parties, since a valid means of cognition cannot possibly exhibit partiality toward one side over the other.

If that [unconsciousness] were established merely through such an admission, then the probandum would not be proven for anyone from that [admission] alone, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Otherwise, why was the Sāṃkhya—who, by means of what is well-known to the Buddhists, attempts to prove the unconsciousness of pleasure and so forth on the grounds that they possess the nature of arising and perishing like a jar—refuted by Dharmakīrti? If you argue: "There is no fault, because this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum). For instance, if the proponent of external objects (*bahirarthavādin*) accepts that waking jars and the like appear as objects of cognition, then they must admit their non-existence, just like the hairs perceived by one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*); otherwise, the absolute rule that 'nothing appears to anyone' would follow. [Response: No, because this lacks the defining characteristics of a *prasaṅga-sādhana*.
For a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) is that in which the admission of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is shown to be inseparable from the admission of the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

But this is not the case here, because even in dreams and the like, the appearance of pillars and so forth as objects of cognition (*grāhya*) is not established for either the proponent or the opponent in the view of absolute self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana-ekānta*). Of what, then, would there be non-existence such that a pervasion could be shown, wherein the admission of one thing is inseparable from the admission of another? If it is argued that all this is established for the opponent, we reply: it has already been stated that if it were established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be established for both; otherwise, it is not established even for the opponent.

And when someone, having accepted that molasses is poison—specifically a lethal poison—and then, out of delusion, further understands even sugar and the like to be poison, should he be addressed by a wise person in this way: "If you accept that it is poison, then do not eat it so that you do not die; or, having been told [not to eat it], do you die after eating it? Therefore, it is established that for one who accepts the reason, the appearance of external objects must necessarily be accepted; thus, [the opponent's claim] is incorrect because it is the reverse [of the logical consequence].

"This so-called distinction between dream and non-dream is merely conventional usage; likewise, the distinction between valid and invalid cognition will be stated [later]—*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra*, p.
5—in the context of establishing that [all is] established solely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)."
In the waking state, there is no distinction between error and its opposite based on mere appearance alone.

Regarding the comparison with the Jains and others concerning knowledge: if [the self] were established by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would not be called "unestablished," because it is as well-established for the opponent as it is for the proponent, since that which is established by a valid cognition is a subject of non-disagreement for everyone. That which is established without a valid cognition is not established even for the opponent.
— Aṣṭaśa°, Aṣṭasa° pṛ 36–37:
because the reason is established through the opponent's own admission.

Someone might say that pleasure and so forth are insentient because they possess the quality of being produced, like a jar and other such things; thus, they claim that pleasure and so forth are external objects of perception that lack sentience.
For such a person as well, the simultaneous apprehension of both [the object and its cognition] is not logically possible.
By such statements as *Praśastapādabhāṣya* 2.268,

"pleasure and so forth are insentient," when this is to be proven, the property of having an origin (*utpattimattva*) or impermanence (*anityatva*) is unestablished for the Sāṃkhya himself, the proponent.
—Nyāyabindu 3.60; Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 470.

That which exists without [the absence of] jars and so forth is "antarīyaka," meaning "occurring without" (vinābhāvī); that which is not antarīyaka is "nāntarīyaka," meaning "not occurring without" (avinābhāvī),
according to the opponent.
In the absence of establishment through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for both the proponent and the opponent, it applies to the opponent as well.
Thus it has been stated that sugar and so forth are either [mental] representations or not external objects, because of the contrary [nature of the latter].

Furthermore, from what source does the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) belong to jars and the like? If it is argued that this follows from inference—namely, "whatever appears is cognition, just as pleasure and so forth; and jars and the like do appear; for it is impossible for an insentient thing (*jaḍa*) to manifest"—we reply: the impossibility of an insentient thing manifesting means simply the absence of manifestation in it.

In that case, if this [cognizer] does not apprehend some insentient counter-instance (*vipakṣa*), how can he understand the absence of the means of proof (*sādhanābhāva*) therein? For one who has not apprehended the ground cannot have the certainty that "there is no jar on this ground"; otherwise, the statement that [the absence] is perceived by the observer's direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in a particular location would not be tenable.

Just as the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) under discussion is ascertained regarding an insentient object even when that object is not perceived, why is the absence of probans such as "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*) not likewise ascertained regarding an omniscient being, even though he is not perceived? For this inference [is made]: "The Sugata is not omniscient, nor is he free from passion, because he is a speaker, like a man on the street.
Or else, although some insentient thing may not be perceived, there is still an ascertainment of the absence of the probans therein due to its non-existence.
