Why is this? If you say it is because of non-perception (*anupalambha*), then does the perception of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) actually exist? Thus, one who—while not desiring the non-existence of an omniscient being based on mere non-perception—desires the non-existence of insentient matter (*jaḍa*) for that very same reason, acts according to his own whims; for there is no contradiction in the perception of insentient matter by someone, just as there is none for an omniscient being. Therefore, what was stated by Dharmakīrti is incorrect: "Whatever is perceived, that alone is accepted."

For instance, it is only the blue [object] residing within that manifestation which appears, and nothing else; therefore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apart from the manifestation, and thus there is no acceptance [of an external object]. — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 389, on the insentient (*jaḍa*).
The proponent of the non-duality of appearances [states]:

"Just as there is non-apprehension of an insentient object there— such as 'there is no jar in a particular place'— this occurs in the perceiver's direct perception regarding a specific location," as stated in the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (2).
The Mīmāṃsaka claim that [the object exists] "because it appears" would not hold true.
Because of the absence of insentient matter,
no omniscient Buddhist speaker is perceived; since non-perception of this kind has as its object that which is invisible by nature, it serves as a cause for doubt.
— Nyāyabindu 3.70:
[This follows] from non-perception in general, but not from the non-perception of what is perceptible.
"That which has its negative concomitance (vyatireka) established merely by non-perception is illustrated as 'the remainder' (śeṣavat), because it is a cause for doubt" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.13). Thus,
"having a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class" (sandigdha-vipakṣa-vyāvṛttikatva) is called "the remainder," meaning that there is an absence of a necessary connection (pratibandha).
—[Praśastapāda: By one who accepts that [argument], it must not be accepted that there is an absence of proof regarding the unperceived insentient [object].

The venerable Prajñākaragupta says: "If the effect or the cause is not apprehended, there can be no ascertainment of the relation of cause and effect; or, if another's consciousness is not made an object [of knowledge], its occurrence in one's own [experience] cannot be ascertained. By saying this, he understands that even when an insentient thing (*jaḍa*) is not perceived, the absence of a logical reason (*hetvabhāva*) applies to it. How, then, is he not insane? If you argue: "Even though that [insentient thing] is not apprehended, its manifestation may occur either through itself or through another; thus, from such an investigation, the absence of a means of proof (*sādhana*) is understood," we reply: If this [investigation] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could there be the establishment of any affirmation or negation regarding anything anywhere? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even if it were a valid means of knowledge, it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*); because investigation consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), whereas perception is the opposite of that.

Or, even if that were the case, [the cognition] does not itself comprehend the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāva*) in a counter-instance (*vipakṣa*) that has not been made its own object; otherwise, as Dharmakīrti stated in the *Viniścaya*, one would comprehend the absence of that [probans] in [matters such as] the next world. Thus, the claim that "that very thing is absent there, and from that alone the non-existence of that [probans] is established" is untenable. Furthermore, inference is not applicable either, because it is not produced by a logical mark (*aliṅgaja*).

Furthermore, since it is stated that "whatever negation there may be, all of it arises from non-apprehension, because the existence of something un-negated cannot be established through apprehension," the absence of that [object] in that [place] is to be understood from its non-apprehension.

If this is so, then if this modification (*vikāra*) is accepted as being of the nature of inference, produced from the non-perception of self-nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), it is logical that there should be a proof of the absence [of the probans] in some insentient counter-example (*vipakṣa*), given that the appearance of the two sides—the jar and so forth, or pleasure and so forth—is perceived. However, the cognition of the insentient object as distinct from the thing to be negated must be admitted, because that very cognition consists in the non-perception of that [thing]; just as the cognition of the ground as distinct from a jar consists in the non-perception of the jar. Yet, this is not accepted by the opponent.

Moreover, if a reason contradictory to intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhahetu*) has been produced, then what is that contradictory reason? If you say it is "insentience" (*jaḍatva*), then in the absence of the cognition of that [insentience], with respect to what could its contradiction be perceived? Otherwise, for those things whose nature is invisible, as well as for their contradictories, either establishment or non-establishment must be understood [to apply], because for others, the contradiction, the causal relation, or the absence thereof cannot be established (Nyāyabindu 2.47). Thus, there is a contradiction regarding insentience.
Because it is non-conceptual, investigation does not take as its object that which is not an object of discursive thought.
Whatever negation there may be, it all arises from non-apprehension— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 520, 638—
for the object of negation is a manifestation, [negated] precisely through the cognition of an insentient thing that is devoid of that manifestation.

The intended meaning is that [the absence of cognition] consists in the non-perception of appearances. Now, one might argue: "Is it not the case that in the case of pleasure and so forth, appearance is recognized as being pervaded by cognitivity? And insentience is contradictory to cognitivity; therefore, cognitivity, when it ceases from this [insentience], must cease taking its own pervaded—appearance—with it. Thus, this [non-existence] is produced by the non-perception of the pervader. This argument is also worthless; for in this way, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For it could indeed be argued that in some street person, non-omniscience—which pervades the state of being a speaker—is apprehended as being contradictory to omniscience; therefore, when that [omniscience] is excluded, it excludes its own pervaded [property], such as the state of being a speaker, thereby establishing the speaker’s non-omniscience.
Consequently, just as there is no pervasion of the state of being a speaker by non-omniscience, so too there is no [pervasion] of appearance by the state of being cognition.

If it is argued that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this [consciousness] by that [insentience] due to their contradiction, then there is a circularity (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): for only when the contradiction of this with insentience is established is there pervasion by it, and only when this [pervasion] is established is the contradiction with it established.
Therefore, it remains the case that this reason is "residual" (*śeṣavat*), like the [reason] "being a speaker" and so forth.
Furthermore, if one admits some [instance of] the insentient, then the reason "because of appearing as such" is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Or, let us grant that this fault does not arise; nevertheless, if the inference produced from this reason does not take as its object a probandum (*sādhya*) that is distinct from itself, how can it be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard? For otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that even an erroneous cognition is a valid cognition by virtue of its connection [to reality], then surely, in this case, the connection between the reason and the probandum is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), while the connection between the reason and the inference is characterized by cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇa*), since no other [connection] is possible.

What follows from this? Just as a cause produces an inference—either simultaneous with itself or otherwise existing—by virtue of its causal capacity (*yogyatā*), so too, if cognition apprehends an object in such a manner, what contradiction is there, since everything is equal in this respect? If, however, no relation—whether characterized by the nature of cause and effect or otherwise—is admitted here, then it would follow that the manifestation [of the object] does not belong to an omniscient being.

The meaning is that [the reason] has a doubtful exclusion from the heterologous instances (*vipakṣa*) by virtue of being a cognition; furthermore, even an error is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) through its connection with a real entity— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.
Regarding this, the proponent of Nyāya says: "Even error is valid cognition (pramā) by virtue of its connection [to reality]"—Nyāyabindu-dharmottara, p. 78.
This has been cited: "Even error is valid cognition (*pramā*) by virtue of its connection with the object" (Tattvopaplava, p.

"Even error, which is the apprehension of something as what it is not, is valid cognition by virtue of synthesis" (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā, p. 481); and "Even error is valid cognition by virtue of synthesis" (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā, p. 41).

"Or, even when the cognitions of the sign (liṅga) and the bearer of the sign (liṅgin) belong to different times, there is no deception because they are indirectly connected to the real entity, despite being devoid of its appearance. Thus it is stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.82. This [objection] floats [unanswered].

If it is argued that there is no fault because that [word] is used in common usage (*vyavahāra*); what, then, is this so-called "common usage"? If it is argued that it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding that [object] even in the absence of a real relation; how then can discerning persons perform an inference based on a relation shown by such [a concept]? Or, having performed it, how could they infer the probandum from a [conceptual] entity? For otherwise, since the conceptualization of such [a relation] would be indistinguishable everywhere, it would follow that everyone’s own purpose would be established through the inference of God and other [entities] from everything.

Just as the Buddhist accepts inference regarding fire and so forth for the sake of conventional usage and to establish his own position—much like a forest-clan [accepts] its own customs—so too does the proponent of God and other such entities accept the Buddhist inference.
That inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of the connection with the probandum; it is merely a conceptualization of a relationship.
From the perspective of ultimate reality,
there is no conceptualization of a relationship apart from conventional usage as it is observed in worldly practice.

By this, the claim that "it is a valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to that [object] because it effects the exclusion of superimposition" is refuted; for the apprehension of an object by a cognition—which effects the exclusion of superimpositions occurring at its own time as well as at other times—would not be contradictory, since it wards off superimpositions arising immediately after perception.
However, inferential knowledge is accepted as a valid cognition... — *Tattvasaṃgraha* verse 1302.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the opponent—that inference is a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) which produces its own effect, namely the preceding moment of superimposition, at a moment incapable of generating the subsequent moment—this too is refuted by the same [argument]. If it is argued that, just like the relation of cause and effect, the relation of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva*) is established conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), and therefore that [superimposition] is so [incapable] in that respect; then why would there not be a sublation of the position (*pakṣabādha*) by perception itself, since even for an insentient thing there is no appearance [of such incapacity]? Even from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the exclusion of that [insentient thing] is difficult to establish.

If it is argued that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its instrument being established conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), whereas there is no sublation of the subject (*pakṣabādha*) by a perception that apprehends things like jars which are established by that [conventional] means—on what basis is this distinction made? Alternatively, if you say that because this [perception] is sublated by inference, there is no sublation of the subject by it; and because inference is also sublated by this [perception], it does not exclude that [inference]—then the situation is equal.
Therefore, one who accepts inference regarding the cognition of jars and so forth must admit that inference has those very objects as its domain.

The claim that another cognition does not experience an object as distinct from itself by its own nature because it is insentient is merely a presentation of a doctrine fabricated by one's own fancy; this is the moment of superimposition,
the third moment of superimposition.
By means of what is established conventionally, through the performance of superimposition and negation on the level of conventional reality alone.

This is refuted by the fact that [the object] is experienced from its own [time]; for if an object existing at a different time were apprehended by cognition, then, due to the lack of distinction, it would follow that a single cognition would apprehend all such objects of that kind.

Now, if they are simultaneous, since there is no relationship [between them], what is apprehended by what? If it is argued that cognition is apprehended by the blue object and so forth because the act of grasping (*gṛhīti*) is its instrument—such that cognition is the grasper of that [object]—this is not so. If this [grasping] is non-different from that [cognition], then cognition is the blue object and so forth, because it is produced by that, like a subsequent cognition. If there is difference, then cognition, the blue object, and the grasping are three things mutually unrelated; thus, what is apprehended by what? Furthermore, if another [act of grasping] were to be produced by that [first grasping], there would be an infinite regress.
How is this so? Because the same logic applies to the case at hand as well.

Furthermore, if that inference is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can the reality of the subject under discussion be established? Nor is "from perception" a satisfactory answer, because the dispute would remain unresolved on that basis.

If it is argued that just as pleasure and the like—though non-existent [externally]—are called self-cognizing when they appear and are established by perception, so too are jars and the like; if this were possible, it would be well enough, but it is not possible. This is because they are always tasted in their own essence (*ekarasa*) through being known by cognitions that manifest with a sense of "I" (e.g., "I know the jar," "I know the cloth"), and there is no refuge other than such an appearance even in self-cognition. As for the fallacious arguments of others, they have already been considered previously.

Thus, since the form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*) appears just like self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), let there be an equal ontological status for both in every respect, as in the case of the forms of the apprehended objects in dreams and their opposites. Nevertheless, if self-awareness alone were the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then the waking state’s apprehended form itself would have to be the ultimate reality; thus, "non-contradiction" (*avisaṃvāda*) is the determination of one's own object, and it is not over-extensive. Furthermore, non-contradiction is the attainment of what was previously perceived.

Regarding what was stated here— that because [the object] perishes due to its momentariness, there can be no attainment of it— this has been refuted by the passage beginning with *siddhivi° 1.10*, "because of the necessity of the identity of appearance," since there is no distinction in their being at different times.
Thus, there is the over-extension [of the argument] regarding the apprehension of blue and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of grasping another [object]":
those for whom there is no cognizer distinct from direct perception— meaning, those for whom [cognition] is self-cognized (svasaṃvidita).
The "bad reasoning" (*durṇaya*) or ill-intentioned argument of others regarding jars and so forth—

namely, that what is seen is attained even in a dream, and therefore the seeing itself would have to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) there as well— that [objection] applies equally to the appearance of the object (*grāhyapratibhāsa*).
Therefore, the well-said principle— that wherever there is non-contradiction, there is validity—
is clearly applicable even to objects seen in a dream; thus, the qualification "perceptual" (pratyakṣa) is inappropriate [in this context], because there is nothing to be excluded.

Some maintain that in the case of universals, inference, and so forth, as well as the cognition of a composite whole (*avayavin*) such as a distant tree, the cognition is indeed clear because its defining characteristic is the grasping of its own object; however, the conventional designation of "clarity" is merely due to the non-apprehension of specific details. Others argue that since a blurred form—like the forms of blue and so forth—is a real entity by virtue of being a mental form (*buddhyākāra*), no cognition is unclear in relation to that [mental form]; rather, the external object is not its [the cognition's] object, and thus the cognition is not unclear with respect to that [external object], or else it is [unclear].

By this, its having the form of the object has been examined; if it did not have the form of the object, cognition would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding it because of its lack of correspondence (*visaṃvādakatva*). Therefore, others maintain that "non-contradiction" alone should suffice, in view of clarity being relative to a blurred form.

To this it is replied: It is incorrect to claim that because the specific parts are not apprehended, there is a conventional usage of "indistinctness" even when [the object] is apprehended. Indeed, the application of a property to one thing cannot occur based on the non-apprehension of something else; otherwise, upon the non-apprehension of a jar, the application of that [property] would occur regarding a cloth that has been apprehended.
Furthermore, since there is an absolute difference between a genus and its possessor, or between parts and the whole, there can be no relation between them.
Therefore, it should be inferred that the cognition is inherently indistinct, like a thread obscured by a gem or similar object.
When a specific part is perceived, there is the conventional usage of "indistinctness."

Furthermore, as for that statement beginning with "of that which has a darkened form" and so forth—it contains no substance. This is because there is a lack of similarity (sārūpya) [between the cognition and the object], and because the proposition [that cognition possesses such a form] is sublated by direct perception (pratyakṣa).

For a formless cognition that grasps an object through a competitive impulse (*ahamahamikā*) is established by the direct evidence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Moreover, this form is not external to that [cognition] because it appears therein; for that very reason, even a universal form (*anugatākāra*) would exist—thus, the entire Buddhist position is refuted.

If it is argued that even so, just as there is a clear cognition despite the absence of duality and so forth in the case of the moon and other objects, so too it is with respect to its [the object's] form—such that nothing at all can be called "unclear"—that is not correct. For while in the case of the moon and so forth, duality and the like are absent, the substratum (dharmin) itself is clearly perceived; however, in this case, the substratum is not clearly perceived.

Nor does this mean that nothing at all is apprehended; for if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of establishing reality (*tattva*) through inference (*anumāna*). And if that were so, how could the non-existence of the relation between cause and effect and so forth be established, from which [non-existence] the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) would follow? If you say it is because of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), is this [non-apprehension] ever perceived as being invariably concomitant (*pratibaddha*) with that [reality], such that this [establishment] could occur? If it is so, then why should inference not be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? To claim that one accepts it when it concerns conventional reality but not when it concerns ultimate reality (*tattva*) is contradictory. Therefore, the term "clear" (*viśada*) is included in order to exclude indistinct inference.

Likewise, for the purpose of precluding such cognitions of pervasion as "whatever place possesses smoke, all of that possesses fire," [the cognition] is not indeed clear, because its manifestation is no different from the manifestation of inferential cognition;
nevertheless, if one were to accept it as such, nothing would remain unclear.
Non-perception when [an object] is not present is invariably concomitant with non-existence.

By this [verse], the cognition of fire here from the sudden perception of smoke— though indistinct— is considered by Prajñākaragupta to be perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, this inferential cognition is sometimes [indirect] perception and sometimes indeed direct perception, as in the case of the realization of fire from smoke occurring suddenly.
For there is no conceptualization of what was previously experienced— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.288.

Some maintain that because it arises from the contact of the mind with the sense-objects, even though the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indistinct, it is nonetheless perception (*pratyakṣa*) for every instance of knowledge.

If it is asked, "Why so?"—and if one argues: "Because that knowledge is knowledge produced by the contact of the sense-organs with their objects, since it possesses the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*), like the knowledge of color and so forth produced by the eye and other organs"—we say: No, because this is contradicted by inferential and other types of knowledge. Furthermore, if these too are made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), how can there be a distinction between them and direct perception? [The Sūtra states: "Perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.3).

3 Thus, since the number [of means of knowledge] would be fixed, and because [inference] exists without a direct connection between the sense organ and its object, it would therefore be distinct [from perception]; the same would apply to the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti) as well.

For even that [cognition] does not arise from its connection with objects past, future, and present in that manner, because of the contradiction; nor is the connection of a connection prevented elsewhere, since it serves as a cause such as a logical mark (*liṅga*). If there were a difference, then analogy (*upamāna*), which establishes the probandum through observed similarity, would have to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); furthermore, it will be demonstrated that cognition of distant objects and so forth arises from everything as direct perception (*adhyakṣa*).
Therefore, it is well said that its distinction [from other means of knowledge] arises precisely from clarity— that is, "clear cognition alone is perception"—
as the Naiyāyikas have recorded in two places.

Since it is possible to know all instances of smoke as "smoke-ness" and all instances of fire as "fire-ness" through the cognitive proximity of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇāpratyāsatti*), by means of a non-sensory contact with the object (*alaukikārthasannikarṣa*),
that [knowledge] as well is produced by sense-object contact through a mediated sequence; thus,
it is included within the enumeration of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃkhyā*).
Inference [is more remote] than perception.
The sense is that if there were a relationship of succession (*paramparāsambandha*), then inference (*anumāna*) would also have to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Or, even if that [definition] were not to be refuted by him, nevertheless, the qualification "clear" (*viśada*) is added to *pratyakṣa* for the purpose of negating the definition of others, such as [that found in] the Nyāya-sūtra: "Perception is that which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object" (NS 1.1.4).

If [it is argued that] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is defined by the characteristic of being the experience of pleasure and so forth, then [the cognition of pleasure] would not be direct perception because it lacks that characteristic;

yet, if it is said that this too is produced from the contact of a sense faculty with its object because it possesses that nature, like the cognition of color and so forth produced by the eye and other faculties—that is not correct. Why? Because it contradicts actual experience.

Indeed, there is no such experience as "the experience of pleasure arises through the contact of the sense faculty with pleasures that have already arisen. For when a young man meets his beloved, the experience has the form of joy, as is felt through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Thus, the opposing position is sublated by the direct perception of self-awareness.

Furthermore, the reason [adduced] is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) because of the experience of pleasure and so forth; if that too were made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkaraṇe*), it would lead to the undesirable consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). How will this be demonstrated? [It is shown by the verse: "That which is established does not depend on another" (Siddhiviniścaya 1).
By this [argument] beginning with "23," the knowledge of a true dream is explained.

[The opponent argues: "The collection of existent and non-existent things is the objective support of a single cognition for someone, because it is manifold, like the five fingers"—this inference has already been refuted by the definition of perception. How, then, is that [inference] supported by the definition of another [type of knowledge, namely perception]? If you say, "Because it arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object," then how does it take the entire collection of existent and non-existent things as its object simultaneously? Indeed, there is no simultaneous contact of the mind or any other sense organ with all objects, due to contradiction [with the nature of the senses].
The relation [of inherence] belongs to all living beings; therefore, even for such a person, that cognition would arise.

Furthermore, the postulation of a restrictive rule regarding specific auxiliary causes is even more flawed. Since in the doctrine of absolute difference (*bhedaikānta*), there is no distinction in inherence (*samavāya*), a restrictive rule for the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is likewise unestablished. Thus, how is it not the case that the aforementioned defect remains—that this cognition is not produced from the contact of sense-organ and object? Moreover, it will be demonstrated that visual cognition of form occurs even without the contact of sense-organ and object, for as stated in the *Siddhiviniścaya*: "Indeed, one sees even at a distance" (4).

By such statements as "perception is that which is inexpressible, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature," the remainder [of the definition]— namely, that perception consists in sense-object contact— is indicated within the definition of perception.
Even the experience of pleasure and so forth is the experience of pleasure and so forth as that which is self-cognized.
Therefore,
the six positive categories— substance, quality, and action— are included by the term "the class of non-existents" because they possess a connection with existence (*sattā*).
Generalities, particularities, and inherence are what is intended here.

Regarding the definition of perception as produced by sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) as stated by the Naiyāyikas, the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with all objects; the mind (*manas*) and the sense organs are likewise conjoined with the self; therefore, there would be an indirect (*paramparā*) connection with all objects. Thus, there would be perception of everything through the direct perception of the omniscient one.

The meaning is that since there is an absolute difference between the two unseen [entities] and since inherence (*samavāya*) is all-pervasive, it would follow that the cause for its connection with all selves would be the knowledge of the omniscient one.
Furthermore, as for that [statement] beginning with "contact" (Mīmāṃsā-darśana 1.1.4) and so forth— that too has not been abandoned by this [argument].

When there is contact of a person's sense organs with existing objects, the resulting birth of cognition is perception; it is not a means [for knowing dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is already present— *Mīmāṃsā-darśana* 1.1.4.

The Sāṃkhya maintains that the functioning of the sense-faculties (*indriyavṛtti*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*); this too should be understood as having been answered by the preceding [argument], because such functioning is impossible in the case of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) and the like.
Furthermore, if the functioning of the faculties in one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) were perception, then there would be the disappearance of its appearance (*tadābhāsa*).
If it is argued that [perception] is the cause of knowledge of an object as it truly is, we say no; for there is no such qualification.
It has already been discussed that perception, or any other means of valid cognition, is not insentient.
Therefore, it was rightly stated: "Perception is clear cognition."

But is it not the case that—perception is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which, through the channel of the sense organs and by means of the coloring of external objects, primarily determines the specific aspect of an object that consists of both the universal and the particular? (Yoga-bhāṣya on Yoga-sūtra 1.7, p.
27). [This occurs] due to the contact of the mind with the objects, via the channel of the sense organs and the intellect.
Direct perception is the present cognition that determines the specific [object]. — Yogakārikā 23.
Comparison: "The functioning of the auditory organ and so forth does not indeed not exist even in one who is deluded;
nor is the functioning of the auditory organ and so forth possible without cognition. — *Prakaraṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 340.

If perception is the functioning of the auditory and other senses, then there is the undesirable consequence [of perception] in those suffering from ophthalmia and similar conditions; for how could that which is not such a functioning conform to their defects? — *Nyāyaviniścaya* 1.1.20.
*Prasannapadā*, page 64;
*Tattvopadeśa*, page 61.
Nyāyavārttika, page 43;
Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, page 155,
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 100; Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 187; Nayacakra-vṛtti, p. 107.
*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, page 41; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 19;
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, page 24.

"According to the principle stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.42: 'Since the object's nature is unitary and directly perceived by itself, what other part could there be that has not been seen which would need to be examined by means of further instruments of knowledge?'—because that which has already been cognized cannot be a portion yet uncognized, how can it be said: 'In whatever case there is non-discrepancy, in that case there is validity'? To this, he replies: "The adversary," and so forth.

Those factors which are mutually opposed and contradictory—such as error and its opposite, conceptualization and its opposite, doubt and its opposite, and the cognitions of the grasped and the grasper—are the "opponents. What is that common consciousness? It is the self-cognition (*svapramiti*), the self-determination (*svaparicitti*). If it were admitted that this [consciousness] could exist incompletely—that is, if it were admitted that it could exist in fragments—then the following would be the case: for fear of the imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), one does not accept two forms (one being cognition and the other its opposite) for a single entity; yet, since that imposition occurs otherwise [than through such duality], one must necessarily admit the possibility of that self-cognition existing incompletely, or else [the contradiction remains].

What does he say?—He says that even regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object, the object is of two kinds: the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, since the universal is conceptualized, there is no fault for the Buddhist even in its absence; hence the inclusion of the term "particular" (*svalakṣaṇa*) therein as well. Furthermore, why would this not apply to the aforementioned cognition alone? On what basis is it claimed that there is a diversity of contradictions regarding its validity? Why is the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*timira*) not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that it is somehow in accord with reality in terms of the moon's nature and so forth? It is not merely invalid.

And if, due to some lack of correspondence, that [cognition] were indeed invalid, then nothing at all would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for another person. Demonstrating this, he says: "Clear," and so forth.

For even that cognition whose instruments—the sense faculties (*akṣa*)—are clear and faultless, not only in the case of a cognition of cataracts (*timira*), but in every respect and in every way, there is an impossibility of a rule of correspondence regarding aspects such as momentary destruction, just as there is with blue and so forth. Because of this reason, why would it not also be a valid means of knowledge through some degree of correspondence?
If it is asked, "Why is there an impossibility of that rule?"—to this he replies: "Because when [an object] is perceived, there is no operation of another means of knowledge."

When an object such as sound (*śabdādi*) has been perceived—that is, when the subject (*dharmin*) has been made an object of perception—the operation of another means of knowledge, such as the inference of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*), occurs "completely" (*ā samantāt*); thus, there is no lack of restriction regarding that [inference]. From the construction of the words "therefore, that" (*tataḥ tad*), the intended meaning here is as follows: if perception were to be consistent (*saṃvādaka*) with respect to destruction and so forth, just as it is with respect to "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) and the like, then that inference would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), like conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

Alternatively, if it were inconsistent (*visaṃvādaka*); in that case, let it be non-authoritative just as in the primary instance. Since the property (*dharma*) and so forth would not be established, how could there be the operation of another means of knowledge? Yet, it does exist; therefore, the primary point stands.
The superimposition of contradictory properties;
as it has been said: "There is no object of cognition other than the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa);
perception has the particular as its object, and inference has the universal as its object."

"There is no other object of cognition (prameya) with a characteristic distinct from the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)" — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 169; "There is no other object of cognition with a characteristic distinct from the particular and the universal" — *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti*, p. 4.
Even in the absence of non-contradiction,
a cognition of two moons produced by ophthalmia and the like would be invalid, because— like conceptual cognition— it apprehends what has already been apprehended.

On this point, Prajñākaragupta says: "Precisely because there is the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding what has been perceived, for that very reason there is also the perception of momentary destruction and so forth, just as there is [the perception] of sound and other objects. Otherwise, there would be a sublation either of the perception by the inference of momentariness, or of that [inference] by the perception.

[He continues: When one whose eyes are impaired sees a white conch as yellow, and having thus experienced a deviation [between appearance and reality], he performs an inference such as "this [conch] is white because it is a conch, like a previously seen conch," then at that time his perception should perceive whiteness just as it perceives the nature of being a conch.

For it could indeed be argued that, precisely because another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) directed toward whiteness operates when a perception by one with impaired eyes is seen, it is for that very reason that it cognizes that whiteness; otherwise, there would be a sublation (*bādhana*) of that other means of valid cognition by this [impaired] perception, or of this by that.
But such is not the case, for a snow lion is not devoured by a *ḍākinī*.

If it is claimed that this [scripture] sublates that [perception] merely by its being yellow, we say no; for that would entail the non-establishment of all properties (dharma) and so forth in their entirety. Therefore, it was rightly said: "In the case at hand as well, let it be accepted in the same way"—namely, that it is "clear" and so on.

Furthermore, he [the author] himself has said: "One who has not recognized the possibility of error, such as a person with cataracts, is deceived when acting on the basis of that cognition; therefore, that is not perception in any way whatsoever. However, one who has recognized the possibility of error proceeds after reflecting that 'this appearance possesses the intended configuration, just like the appearance of what was previously seen'; thus, in that case, it is inference alone that is non-deceptive.
As it has been said:
"He by whom no error has ever been perceived is indeed deceived because of the deception regarding his intended object."

But he who perceives the possibility of error proceeds after deliberation; first, the mere configuration is obtained, while regarding the object itself there may be doubt or error; therefore, the inference [is made] with respect to the configuration...—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 2.1.
"The appearance that I have is not devoid of configuration, because it is seen to be so elsewhere; such being the case, there is an inference [to that effect]. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p.
5). To this, the reply is: "Even for those whose senses are impaired," and so forth.

For those whose eyes are impaired, not only do they perceive erroneously, but even without the comprehension of the relationship between the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*), there is the appearance of a specific sign—namely, the particularity of the manifestation—and the signified—the possession of a [certain] configuration; their relationship is identity (*tādātmya*). Without the comprehension of these, when one acts after determining an object, a lack of discrepancy is observed. Indeed, those with impaired vision are never found to be acting at all times on the basis of such thoughts as "it is for me thus," and so forth.

Nevertheless, even if that [distinction] were accepted, since there is no difference between the cognition of an optical illusion (*timira*) and inference regarding their status as error, then even in the case of an inferential appearance, one would face the consequence of infinite regress by imagining, "To me, such an appearance has occurred," and so forth. Thus, while one desires inference to be non-contradictory for the sake of conforming to the linguistic conventions of ordinary people, yet does not desire an optical illusion to be so in any way, this is merely acting according to one's own whims.

If it is argued that "let it be non-contradictory, but let it not be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," [the author] says here: "And by that much, because validity is established simply from the observation of non-contradiction, it follows that it must be a means of valid cognition in some sense. This is the established position. The remainder, beginning with "just as in which," has not been explained because it is easy for those with clear faculties to understand.
It would be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) solely by virtue of conforming to the conventions of worldly people, provided it is non-contradictory.

Thus, first of all, even a cognition that appears as variegated is indeed one, because it is distinct from external variegation, according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* (3.220): "Cognition is a single variegated [entity]. For one who accepts that knowledge is variegated and unitary, it has been stated that the possibility of consciousness being incomplete with respect to its own measurement arises. Now, [it is said]: "The nature of cognition is also undivided" (*Prakaraṇavārtika* 2).
Based on such statements as these, [the author], showing what follows for one who does not accept that [cognition], says: "From cognition," and so forth.
For one who does not admit variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), there is no perception of the distinction between the cognition itself and the appearance of the object.
The occurrence of contradictory forms is established in some cases regarding that which has been cognized.

When one accepts contradictory properties such as having an outward-facing or inward-facing manifestation, then even if there is a realization of the ultimate truth consisting in the distinction between the object and its manifestation, the proof of non-absolutism (anekānta) is established in some way. Furthermore, for those whose eyes are directed toward objects at varying distances, since there is no contradiction regarding the mere existence of the thing, and since its specific differences are not perceived, the means of cognizing it remains consistent.
For as long as there is no apprehension [of an object], other means of valid cognition cannot function, which would result in the impossibility of worldly transaction;
furthermore, as for that other [teaching]: "They see his grove, yet no one sees him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14).
14. Thus it is; even there, this same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) applies, being merely an entry into another system of tenets regarding the cognition of consciousness (vitteḥ).

Of what nature [is it]? It is of that which is "cognized," meaning apprehended by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), for otherwise its existence could not be established. "Relation" refers to the object (*viṣaya*) to be grasped, such as a jar; or it may refer to its very manifestation, its form (*ākāra*). "Distinction" (*viveka*) is its difference from the cognition itself. The "non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*) of that [distinction]—from that [non-apprehension], and in some cases, such as the moon perceived by one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*), there is established—that is, certain—the possibility of a "contrary" (*viruddha*) form, such as oneness (*ekatva*), which is the opposite (*pratyanīka*) in relation to a visible form like the multiplicity of moons. This is because the latter is invisible.

The intention here is as follows: if this gross form of a jar or the like were non-different from consciousness—that is, if it were of the very nature of consciousness—then that consciousness would be variegated (*citra*), and the fault already mentioned would apply there. On the other hand, if it were not of the nature of consciousness, then since it does not perceive its own difference from consciousness, how could there be an illusion of its form? For that which appears is cognition, just like pleasure and so forth; and since pillars, blue objects, and the like appear, there would be no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) in the argument. Indeed, when a white conch-shell appears devoid of yellowness, an illusion of yellowness is not tenable.
Now, if one does not know that [cognition], then it is established that there is the possibility of incompleteness in one's own cognition; thus,
in the absence of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), there would be no consciousness.
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "Whether directed outward or inward," and so forth.

Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of perception, conceptualization, and their opposites. That very manifestation is the form (*ākāra*), and that itself is the contradictory property (*viruddho dharmaḥ*). Even if its [the cognition's] non-acceptance were considered—not only its acceptance—the distinction belonging to that consciousness regarding the manifestation of the object, such as the form of a jar and so on, is itself the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Even when that [distinction] is perceived, because it is experienced in some way through forms such as existence or sentience, the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is achieved.

Thus far, by means of the example of the cognition of the perceptible and the imperceptible, which is well-known among the Buddhists, it has been stated that the impossibility of complete [cognition] exists regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object.

Now, with regard to that same point, it is stated by means of the example of external things—perceptible and imperceptible—which is well-known in the world, beginning with the words "dūre" (at a distance), etc.

Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of "further distant" (*dūratara*) and "most distant" (*dūratama*) is intended. In that case, for persons whose eyes are directed toward an object such as a tree, its mere existence (*sattāmātra*) is the cause of non-contradiction; therefore, it is appropriate and logical that this constitutes a proof for the incomplete nature of that cognition.

"Even when what exists? To this he says: "Even when there is no cognition (*apratipatti*)—not only when there is cognition—of those particular distinctions (*viśeṣa*), such as trees and so forth, which belong to that mere existence of the thing (*vastu-sattā-mātra*);
the word 'api' (even) has this meaning.

What is meant is this: just as in cases such as at a distance or further away, although the particulars are not grasped by perception, there is still a grasping of their mere existence, so too in the present case, there would be the state of being visible or otherwise."

With the words "Since" (*yataḥ*) and so forth, he elaborates on this very point: since (*yataḥ*), for whatever extent (*yāvad api*) and of whatever measure (*yat-parimāṇasya*) the prior perception was stated by me, and just as that [perception] occurs for that specific measure and not for anything more, so too when it is stated by another, then for that same extent and in that same manner, there is perception; because, in the absence of that [perception], another means of knowledge—namely inference (*anumāna*)—does not function or operate, and for the reason that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the impossibility of worldly transaction (*asaṃvyavahāra*), the means of establishing that cognition (*tat-pramiti-sādhana*) is logically consistent (*samañjasa*). This is the connection [of the sentence].

This is what is meant: just as there is no perception of its distinctions at various degrees of distance and so forth, if there were likewise no perception of the mere existence of the object itself, then those whose eyes are directed toward it would be as if blind;
for indeed, there is no reality (*tattva*) apart from the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) that could appear therein.

And thus, this [object] is merely a particular, because it possesses a certain particularity, like the mere element (*tanmātra*) previously perceived; therefore, there would be no application [of cognition] to it, and there would be no application of that [cognition] to it. But this is not the case, since we observe the application [of cognition].

If it is argued: "Surely, just as with difference, there is no cognition of that [universal] alone there either; since the cognition arises from non-difference, it is erroneous, and for that very reason, another means of knowledge must operate"—as stated in *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 2.1 and so forth; to this it has been replied: "In that case, for those whose eyes are directed toward it, because one observes non-contradiction regarding the mere existence of the object, even if there were such an error, nothing would be non-erroneous."
Because it possesses specific distinctions at varying degrees of distance and so forth, whether by way of existence (*sattva*) or sentience (*cetanatva*), and so on.

If it is argued that, "Alternatively, since for the Buddhist there exists the example of the cognition of what is visible and what is invisible, let there be the possibility of non-completeness regarding the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) which is the object of one's own valid cognition; whereas for the Naiyāyika, the opposite is the case," to this he replies with the words beginning "dūre... and so on.

By the phrase "for those whose eyes are directed toward that," he shows that perception has as its object the mere existence of the thing. A "thing" (vastu) refers to substance (dravya) and so forth; because it is non-contradictory regarding mere existence, it is the means of cognizing that [existence]. It is "proper" (samañjasa)—that is, logical—that it be the means of a non-complete cognition.

"Even when what is present? To this he says: "And when there is no cognition of its distinction"—that is, even when there is no cognition of the distinction of that *tanmātra* (the subtle element), which consists in its specific nature as being the locus (*ādhāra*) in relation to the substance (*dravya*) and so forth that are the located (*ādheya*).
For indeed, if the locus is not apprehended, its being the located—which depends upon that locus—cannot be cognized, even though it is its very essence.
If it is objected: "But surely, just like its distinction, there is also no cognition of the *tanmātra* itself," to this he says: "Since... and so forth.

When there is perception of the generality (*sāmānya*), doubt and the like arise upon the recollection of either its specific particulars (*viśeṣa*) or those particulars contrary to it; and for the purpose of excluding those [alternatives], another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) operates.

However, this is difficult to achieve if that generality itself is not perceived, because that would lead to the impossibility of practical discourse (*asaṃvyavahāra*). Therefore, the means for accomplishing that valid cognition is properly established as being possessed of particulars (*viśeṣavat*).
Doubt arises from the perception of a common property, the non-perception of specific properties, and the recollection of specific properties— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.17.

Furthermore, when one accepts that a cognition such as doubt—"Is this a post or a person? or "It is certainly a person"—which has a single substratum (*ekadharmī*) and refers to an object, is otherwise [than certainty] in other cases, how is it not one's own doing to claim that the form of the seen and the unseen coexist in a single [cognition]?

Now, the Naiyāyika and others demonstrate that very same fault found in the Sautrāntika and other schools, showing that it is equally applicable even to the Advaita doctrine of the Self (*puruṣa-advaita-mata*), by means of the passage beginning with "yat punaḥ."
Furthermore, as for that opinion which is other than the Buddhist (saugata) and other views—is it based on scripture?

[The answer is: "Do the seers see this [reality] as distinct from consciousness and so forth, or do they not see that Puruṣa and so forth as being of a non-dual nature?"—the word "any" (kaścana) among those seers means "none at all."
By that— meaning "in this manner"— the supreme form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision.
This is the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas;
this verse of Kārikā is cited in the following texts: "And likewise is the instruction of the Śāstra: 'Of the guṇas...'"—Yogabhāṣya 4.13.
The instruction of the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* teaching: "Of the guṇas... — *Yogabhāṣya-tattvavaiśāradī* 4.13;
the venerable Vārṣagaṇya: "Of the guṇas... — *Śāṅkarabhāṣya-bhāmatī*, p. 352.
The very great form of the qualities...—*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 4; *Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 63; *Tattvopaplava*, p. 80.
12 Laghīyastraya, Sva-bhāṣya, p. 14; Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, p. 144.
The supreme form of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas is Pradhāna;
that which has come within the range of vision is utterly hollow, like an illusion.

The Advaitavādin maintains that the single ontological category here is substance (dravya), which consists of the modifications such as Mahat and so forth, while its essence is eternal pure Being (sanmātra) and its form is manifold manifestation.
That which has entered his womb— water, earth, air, and living beings—

constitutes one part of him, which possesses the nature of worldly existence (saṃsāra) among animals, gods, humans, and denizens of hell; another part of him is eternal, from which flows incomparable, auspicious bliss, and which is of a twofold nature.
The phrase "and so forth" includes that [system] as well; therein, what was indicated by the word "that" (yat) is referred to by the word "therein" (tatra).

Not only in the systems of the Buddhists and others, but even in that [system], every aforementioned fault appears clearly in the mind as if it were a direct perception (pratyakṣa); therefore, he points to it with the word "this" (ayam).
The common or shared consequence (*prasaṅga*) is as follows:

for it has been stated regarding the Buddhist— that we never perceive an aspect (*ākāra*), whether external or internal, that is without a companion (*asāhāya*), because it is not determined in the manner in which it is described (Siddhi-viniścaya 1).
And so forth; this is the same here as well.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the non-existence of an absolute [entity] occurs when it meets the conditions for perception, otherwise it would be unmeasurable" (*Siddhiviniścaya* 1.9), that too [is the same], as is the rule regarding the unity of appearance (*pratibhāsaikya*) in *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.1.

If this is so, then because of the statement in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (4.3.14), "His garden [is that]," since there is some kind of identity between him and his garden, there necessarily follows the admission of identity with that [garden] regarding forms such as error, non-error, conceptualization, and non-conceptualization.

Now, if it is argued that— on the basis of such scriptural passages as "Indeed, the self of beings is one alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.12) and "Just as the pure ether... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārttika 3.5.43)— Brahman, though indivisible, appears as if possessed of parts, then [the same logic applies] to the real or the unreal according to the *Siddhiviniścaya*.
The same [argument] applies to this and so forth.

For it can be said: if the oneness of some Brahman with [entities] that are either existent or non-existent, or with forms such as conscious or unconscious, is established in that very way through external, internal, and other [modes], then why would that not be established for some whose nature is the intellect (*buddhyātman*)?

If, however, because of the contradiction between knowledge and its opposite, oneness is not accepted and therefore scripture is held to be distinct [from the object], then the following is equal: if that [scripture] is not perceptible, then—just like the object—it follows that its own nature is unestablished (*svabhāvāsiddhi*), because of the consequence stated in the *Siddhiviniścaya* (1).
15. And thus,
because neither that [object] nor its cognition appears [to consciousness], the refutation is that everything is empty.
Indeed, the single Self of all beings, which is both Brahman and its manifestation, is established in every being;
it is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.
— Tri-tantra 5.12 ...
people who are overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance.
Just as one perceives something as being mixed with various diverse elements,
so too does this stainless Brahman, though changeless, appear through ignorance as if it had attained impurity and is seen in the form of differentiation— Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārttika 3.
5 43, 44 Oneness
It might be thought: "The garden is perceived by itself; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of its being] like a form grasped through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
But when he perceives himself as distinct from the garden, then there is no error.
If this is argued, then the following applies equally: "of cognition," and so forth.
Thus, since the consequence is the same for both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the Brahman-Self—there being no difference in the acceptance of their abandonment—it is so considered.

[The opponent objects: "But how can they be the same? For while there is great effort required in establishing the momentariness of the intellect when it is accepted, there is none in the case of accepting the Brahman, because the absence of such [momentariness] is accepted therein. To this, he says: "Merely," and so forth, which is easy to understand.

This is the intended meaning here: even for one who does not accept a single cognition as having that appearance, there is an entry into another system [of thought] for the opponent; this is the sense of the synonym favored by the Sugatas.
Momentary destruction and the existence of other continua: when these two are being established...

Having thus established, by means of the passage beginning with "What follows from that?", that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consisting of genus, quality, and action exists within perception, [the author] now addresses what was stated by the opponent: "Verily, words do not exist in the object, nor are they of the same nature as it, such that when the object appears, they too would appear. To this, he says "sthūlam" and so forth, demonstrating the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) of the opponent's reason according to the Buddhist's own admission. In that regard, the argument is: "Whatever does not exist in something does not appear when that thing appears, just as taste does not appear when color appears; and words do not exist in the object. To show the deviation of this reason, [the author] states: "sthūlam," etc., from the perspective of the Buddhist.
This has been extracted from: *Nyāyapraveśavṛtti*, p. 35;
*Aṣṭasāhasrī*, p. 118;
and *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa*, p. 132.
For those who perceive a gross, single, and constant form within atoms—which are [in fact] particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—why does the word (*śabda*) not likewise appear therein?

If the particular characteristics being perceived are not identical with that [gross form], how can a gross, recurring form appear there, as it does in the case of taste and so forth? For this reason, one would see the object devoid of any association with words.

How can a gross form—endowed with magnitude, unitary, common to multiple parts and qualities, and [according to the opponent] non-existent and unmanifest within the particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*)—be perceived by the Buddhists who [assert that things exist only] in atoms? The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates an alternative position; for them, why would a word not manifest in those [atoms]? It certainly does manifest, since there is no difference in their lack of existence.
And thus, for one who perceives in this way, it is indeed difficult to maintain that he perceives the object without its verbal form.

But surely, in cases such as a mirage, it is the very form of water and so forth that appears, not the form of a verbal designation; likewise, in those [objects], it is only the gross form that appears, not the form of a word, because errors are restricted to their specific objects.

If it is argued that this is because [the object] is seen in that way, this is not so. For, simply because a gross form (*sthūlākāra*)—which is never non-existent in those [atoms] at any time or place—is observed to appear, it does not follow that it must appear as such everywhere and at all times. Likewise, there is no certainty that because the form of a word (*śabdākāra*) is observed to appear in that way, it therefore cannot appear [otherwise]. Even when the form of silver, which is non-existent in a particular fragment of stone, is observed to appear at some time, one still observes the appearance of the form of gold—which is also non-existent therein—at another turn of events. Thus, the doubt that "the form of the word appeared in them, appears here, and will appear there" is not dispelled. Indeed, that [cognition], arising through the power of the object (*arthasāmarthya*), imitates the form of the object itself, not that of the word and so forth; this is a fundamental principle.
In the atoms characterized by their own specific marks, there is for a person a gradual [process].
Regarding someone seeking gold among various individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
it has been said: for that [cognition], arising through the power of the object, would indeed conform to the form of that [object].
—Hetubinduṭīkā, p. 195;
Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 278: "This is incoherent; it is Prakrit, used in a vulgar sense, meaning it is unrefined (asaṃskṛta)."

Others, however, think: "By means of the eye and so forth, there is no apprehension of the atoms of color and so on that belong to the objects of other senses, even though they exist [there], because such is not observed. For indeed, even in a state of delusion, odor does not appear to the eye; otherwise, there would be the futility of other senses and the non-existence of the deaf. This is not tenable; for it is impossible to reach such a certainty based merely on the non-observation of one who is not all-seeing. Otherwise, precisely for that reason, since the apprehension of all tastes and so forth by a single perceiver would be unestablished, the world would be non-omniscient.

Since the opponent admits that a single form of a universal—which is coarse, consisting of the mind’s object, and common to many parts and qualities—appears even in other sense organs such as the eye, the charge of "inconclusiveness" (anaikāntika) is refuted; otherwise, if the universal were grasped by the eye and other senses, inference would become redundant because its object is the universal, according to the statement in *Nyāyabindu* 1.16–17: "The other [object] is the universal, which is the object of inference," as is the case with odor and so forth.
Merely from non-perception by means of that which is beyond the senses, [one concludes] that the omniscient is non-existent.

Furthermore, as for what was said regarding inference—that there would be deafness—that too does not constitute a fault, because it is admitted that such an appearance occurs for someone; even if that person is not deaf, it does not occur for everyone, or let him indeed be deaf, since he does not perceive sounds through hearing. If it is argued: "Surely sound also appears to them [the senses], but this does not imply the conceptualization (kalpanā) of sound within perception (adhyakṣa), because that which is non-existent cannot be associated with it"; then, conceptualization would not occur in any cognition at all, because there is no appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression (abhilāpa). Moreover, that [appearance] is not ultimately real (paramārthasat), whether it exists therein [in the cognition] or elsewhere.

Alternatively, just as the gross form is non-existent within the state of atomicity yet is not contradicted in its own nature because there is no sublation, so too is the case with sound; thus, there is no fault,
even for one who is omniscient regarding everything.
Even for a child who has not yet mastered linguistic conventions, there occurs through a word a mental appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression.
Furthermore, as for what was stated by the opponent:
"Even when the object is present, if sensory perception were to depend upon the application of a word based on memory, that object would become mediated."

Non-conceptual perception [would be affected] by the mental application of words through recollection; and thus, sensory cognition would not arise from the object in its direct form as a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This has been extracted from the *Tattvopaplava* (p. 40).
Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 122;
Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 136;
Nyāyamañjarī, Part 1, p. 86.

That too has been refuted by this [author]: because there is no contradiction in the appearance of the form of a word within those [particulars], even if it is not remembered, just like the form of a gross object; or rather, [it appears] in the sensory perceptions that grasp those particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*). *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 525.

He explains the verse with the words "like sound" (*śabdavat*) and so forth: if it is admitted that the perceived particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which consist of atoms, are not of that nature—that is, they do not possess that [gross] intrinsic nature—then how can that gross form appear there as a persistent (*anvayin*) form? He provides an illustration for this: "just like taste and so forth."

Just as taste and the other [sensory objects] do not appear within one another because they are mutually non-self (anātmatā), so too is the case with the subject at hand. If that form (*ākāra*) were possible to manifest, why would the word (*śabda*) not also manifest within the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? For, due to its non-manifestation, this Buddhist world—or "this world"—would perceive an object devoid of the application of words; or rather, the word *yataḥ* implies a rhetorical objection: it would not perceive it at all. Thus, since valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in a determinative cognition (*vyavasāyātmaka*), this is well-established: "the fruit of the means of knowledge is direct," and so forth.
In the absence of grossness, there is no proof of that which is more gross.
(Siddhiviniścaya 1)

Here another says: "Since there is an absence of both [the object] itself and its purpose, or because of delusion, for whom is there the establishment of anything, such that—on account of the existence of some means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—that [establishment] might be well-stated? To him he replies with the words beginning "bruvan" (speaking), etc., [addressing] either the proponent of non-existence or the proponent of delusion.
If the Tathāgata, being ignorant of the self, asserts through the power of inference that direct perception— which is non-erroneous and devoid of external or internal objects—

exists, how can he, while characterizing the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nairātmya*) of all things as being directly perceived and non-erroneous, not be insane? Furthermore, why would he either understand for himself or teach others that the establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result exists only according to how it appears (*yathādarśana*), and not according to reality (*yathātattva*), given the absence of any means of valid cognition and so forth?

"In whatever manner objects are conceptualized, they fall apart in that very same manner. Thus, one ought not to rely upon false knowledge; for, like other systems, it is impossible to attain any realization of reality without some degree of such attainment.

Therefore, this is a failure of wisdom on the part of Śauddhodana—who, while asserting that there is only a momentary, illusory, and exclusively singular stream of consciousness, or that there is intrinsic selflessness (*svabhāva-nairātmya*), and so forth—speaking exactly according to his own [erroneous] vision. How is it that even he has followers who repeat his words? What else can this be but a lack of self-knowledge?

If one accepts that the mind, appearing according to its perception, has an outward-turned form while simultaneously being the singular cognition of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), why would the establishment of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) not occur? Since the reality (*tattva*), which is non-sequential and transcends all conceptual constructions, descends into a false state of arrangement according to its perception, one must accept the identity between the nature of reality and the nature of falsehood. And if that is so, why is it not observed that [reality] consists of both the universal and the particular, and is transformative both externally and internally? For in every respect, the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) remains unavoidable.
(Pramāṇavārttika 2)
Comparison—In that regard, how could we not be filled with great wonder as to why it was only Śauddhodani who became so negligent in wisdom?
Even now, the dull-witted remain attached to that [delusion], for there is nothing higher than darkness (ignorance).
—Nyāyaviniścaya 1.52, 53; Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 116.
"How has such a lapse in wisdom occurred even for this very teacher?"—thus our minds are filled with both wonder and compassion;
and since others also repeat this, fie upon that all-pervading darkness which mercilessly overcomes the world!
(Vādanyāya-ṭīkā, p. 51)

Of what nature is that which arises neither externally nor internally? It is "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*), meaning it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because, in the case of its own realization, for the Tathāgata, direct perception alone constitutes the means of valid cognition, as there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition; so he thinks. If one asks, "Why is this so? he says here: it is "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), being free from delusion, because only such a thing is truly direct perception. Otherwise, like water in a mirage, how could it be direct perception? What is he doing? He says: "speaking," that is, explaining it to those beings who are to be trained.

Why? Because [the cognition] arises from the power of inference—that is, from the efficacy of the three-fold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*)—since it is impossible for them to be understood through mere words; the implication is that it would otherwise have to be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Here too, the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) should be connected as an adverbial modifier of the action, meaning "acting in such a way as to be non-erroneous."
Who is he? He says: the Tathāgata, the Sugata.

Of what nature is he? He says: one who does not know the self (*anātmajña*). How so? Because like a madman, he does not know the self, which is his own true nature; thus he is "one who does not know the self.
How [is this known]? It is evident and clear (*adhyakṣam*).

For instance: if there were the non-existence of everything, then even perception would not exist; how, then, could there be the apprehension of that [non-existence] by which one might speak of it to another?
Or, if perception does exist, then there is no total non-existence.
For if this [perception] were distinct from that [non-existence], its nature would be excluded from it, and since no relation would be established, there could be no apprehension of it.
If one posits that [the cognition] arises from that [object] and possesses its similarity, then there is no universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*).
Likewise, the undesirable consequence remains unavoidable regarding the existence or non-existence of the signs and words that serve as the means for communicating to another.
Furthermore, if cognition is erroneous, how can it be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Therefore, its establishment would be like that of its object.
In the same way, it should also be stated regarding speech and so forth:
there is the realization of the absence of external and internal objects when there is a distinction.
If the existence of gender and number is their actual presence (*sadbhāva*), then there is no universal emptiness;
if it is their absence (*abhāva*), how can there be a cognition of another [object] by means of them? This is the point regarding direct perception.

With the words "the nature of the non-existence of all things," etc., he states the meaning of the verse: [The Buddha] is one who speaks to those beings to be trained (*vineyasattva*), declaring that the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanairātmya*)—which is the absence of form—belongs to all entities, whether conscious or otherwise, in every respect, just as they lack the form of others, so too they lack their own form. How could he not be insane? Whether it be the Sugata or anyone else, he would be truly insane if he were to characterize as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—that is, as a clear, non-erroneous, and delusion-free cognition within oneself—a knowledge whose object is such [non-existence]. As for what was further stated by the opponent:
Defining [perception] by means of such [definitions] as "Perception is that which, with respect to its own nature, is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (Nyāyabindu 1.4).
"Just as it appears, so is this establishment of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge— the establishment of the means, the object, and the result—
performed, even though they do not exist [ultimately], in the case of the apprehended, the apprehender, and consciousness. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.357).
Regarding this, he says: "And from what? and so forth.
"From what" means from nothing whatsoever;
the word "ca" (and) has the sense of a cumulative conjunction with what precedes.

"The establishment of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the result (*phala*) occurs precisely according to how they appear—that is, exactly as they manifest—and not according to their true nature (*yathātattvam*), nor by way of not transgressing ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). One should understand this for oneself, or one should cause another to understand it. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the absence of the means of knowledge and so forth"—for in the case of self-awareness, there is no direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), and in the case of making another aware, there is no means of knowledge such as inference (*anumāna*) or, by the word "and so forth," verbal testimony (*vacana*).
Or, if they were present, it would result in a contradiction with one's own words; this is what is intended.

But surely, no one either understands or explains that the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanairātmya*) is exactly as it appears through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that this fault would arise; rather, it is through investigation (*vicāra*).
As it has been said:
"This which the wise declare has certainly come to pass."

If it is argued that this follows from the force of the facts— as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "In whatever way objects are conceptualized, in that very way they fall apart" (PV 2.209)— to this he replies with the words beginning "in whatever way," and so forth.

In whatever manner and by whatever means—whether as part or whole, external or internal, real or unreal, and so forth—objects (arthas) or entities (bhāvas) are conceptualized and investigated, in that very manner they fall apart and become void. Thus, one ought not to accept [this view] because it arises from false cognition (mithyājñāna); the point is that this investigation lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) because it consists of perception and inference, both of which are false cognitions.

If it is argued: "But surely, in establishing the reality of all things, this very investigation is the ultimate refuge, since in the ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ) there is no such thing as a valid means of knowledge and so forth," [the author] replies here: "Like another [doctrinal] system" (samayāntaravat).

The meaning of the example is as follows: just as this Sugata or anyone else is unable to understand anything from other systems of tenets—such as the doctrines of eternalism and so forth—due to their being false cognitions, so it is with one's own system as well;
for if there is an absence of validity, whether by way of perception or inference, the result is necessarily nothing but false cognition.

Having stated, "In other systems, [it is] just as it appears," and so forth, he says "in some way" (*kathañcit*) etc., demonstrating the intellectual error of the Sugata who, through the various tenets of the Sautrāntikas and others, asserts momentary destruction and so on:

"In some way" means by any manner of perception or by a manner of inference; "without that"—meaning without the realization of the true nature of things—"speaking" or "asserting" such statements as "just as it appears," and so forth.

Which ones? Momentary, exclusively erroneous, and distinct mental continua (*cittasantānāntara*). The inclusion of the term "momentary" is for the purpose of indicating the essential nature of the Sautrāntika school; by this, the cognition of all paths belonging to both saṃsāra and its opposite is grasped. The expression "exclusively erroneous" is for the purpose of including the doctrine of the specific Mādhyamika school, according to which whatever does not enter the path of clear perception is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), such as the hair-threads perceived by one with ophthalmia. The statement "the mind and its distinct mental continua" belongs to the Yogācāra school. These [terms] form a copulative compound (*dvandva*): "those."

It is not only those [faults], but rather, when one speaks of the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanairātmya*) or the emptiness of all things (*sakalaśūnyatva*), what has happened to whom? To this he says: "Of Śauddhodani," and so forth.

This intellectual error belongs only to Śauddhodani, the Sugata, and not to anyone else; how and in what manner did it arise?—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
