For this reason, our mind is filled with wonder (*savismaya*), with astonishment (*sāścarya*), and with compassion (*sakaruṇa*) and pity (*sadaya*).

The intention behind the qualification beginning with *vidhūtakalpanājāla* (Vṛtti on Pramāṇavārttika 1.1)— that he was born even without a cause— is now shown to be the fault of those who follow that [view], as he says: "There exist," and so forth.

Even for him who has committed an error of wisdom (*prajñāparādha*), there are followers who speak after him and support what he has said; what else could this be but ignorance of the Self? It is precisely that [ignorance].
For the sake of summarizing the doctrine:
*Śauddhodani* means the offspring of Śuddhodana; it refers to that Buddha.
"Homage to Samantabhadra, whose form is profound and vast, who has shaken off the web of conceptual construction, and whose radiance shines forth everywhere.
Thus [it is said] here.

But surely, with reference to the aspect of the apprehended object—which is common to both dreams and other states, and which is charming so long as it is not investigated—it has been stated [in the *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.357] that "it is exactly as it appears," and so forth.

Thus says Prajñākaragupta: "Valid cognition is non-discrepant knowledge," and so on; this definition of valid cognition is established by way of conventional practice (*vyavahāreṇa*) [as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 2].
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "according to perception" (*yathādarśanam*).
According to perception—in the form of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—it is "delightful when not investigated.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "the mind, which is knowledge" (*cittaṃ jñānam*).

Of what nature is it? It has an outward-turned form; by that form, one thinks "it is so," whereas with respect to the self-awareness [of consciousness], it is in the ultimate sense alone of the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.

And thus he himself said: "Or, the illumination of an unknown object"—this definition [applies] because, in the ultimate sense, there is the illumination of non-dual awareness (*saṃvedanādvaita*) which is unknown by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). (*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* 2).
He also says this with the words beginning "paramārtha":
the connection is that the mind (*citta*) is described as such because its ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is a single, indivisible, real consciousness whose form is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
The sense of the opponent's argument is that [the means of knowledge and so forth] are unestablished (*asiddha*), because of the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the rest.

To this, he states the following reply: "By [the words] 'himself' and so forth... For the Buddhist who accepts—that is, who acknowledges—such a mind, the very establishment of the supreme self (paramātman)—that is, the establishment of the supreme self, the soul (jīva) characterized by manifoldness (anekānta), according to the aforementioned reasoning—would surely occur; there can be no doubt.
Or rather, the reading should be understood as "the establishment of the ultimate reality" (paramārthasiddhi) itself.

The meaning here is as follows: just as there is, in ultimate reality, a distinction between what is real and what is otherwise regarding the two forms—the cognition itself and that which is directed toward the external—even though they are indistinguishable in their appearance; so too, despite their lack of difference, there is a distinction between the form directed toward the external in a dream and that in other [waking] states.

This has been largely established by Prajñākaragupta. In that regard, this is the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the ultimate sense, whereas the previous one was that of the conventional. (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*)

It might be thought: "The distinctions between philosophical systems such as the Sautrāntika and others, as well as the distinction between the reality and unreality of the cognition and its apprehended aspect, were taught by the Tathāgata according to conventional usage and not from the perspective of ultimate truth; therefore, this is not a fault.
And so it has been said:
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths."

Or alternatively, it may be that those [two truths] were stated by him for the sake of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), since he subsequently established a refutation of them— namely, "the conventional truth of the world and the truth from the perspective of ultimate reality" (Mādhyamakakārikā, Chapter 24,
Verse 8).

"One who seeks the truth must first say that 'everything exists'; later, for one who has understood the object, the grasping at existence ceases. Thus, the grasping that "external objects exist" is an adherence (*abhiniveśa*).
This has been extracted— *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, second part, page 17.
Regarding the statement that "reality transcends words and conceptual constructions," he says the same thing with the words beginning with "tattva" (reality).
The reality (*tattva*) is the ultimate nature of consciousness, which is non-sequential—that is, devoid of temporal sequence and the like.
Furthermore, what is it like? To this he says: it is "beyond all conceptual constructions" (*sakalavikalpātīta*).

All conceptual constructions—such as eternal and non-eternal, real and unreal, self and other, the grasped and the grasper, cognition, one and many, and so forth—are "all conceptual constructions"; it is beyond them.
If it is asked, "How is that so? he says here: "Just as" (*yathā*), etc.
Demonstrating the refutation here in accordance with the appearance—that is, without overstepping the manifestation—he says: "False" (*mithyā*), etc.

If it is asked, "How does one enter into a false arrangement—that is, an unreal state?"—it is said in reply: If its being beyond all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and its lack of succession (*akramatva*) exist in reality (*bhāvataḥ*), then how can it be beyond all conceptual constructions? For those two [properties] themselves are conceptual constructions.

On the other hand, if they do not exist, even so, how can it be beyond them? Because if the state of being beyond them is negated, there follows the consequence of all conceptual constructions, since the negation of a non-existence is of the nature of an affirmation (*vidhi*).

Alternatively, as for what was said—that it is not eternal because of the absence of such perception—eternal means that which persists through the three periods of time; therefore, the non-perception of such a thing from any source is indeed a flaw in your position.

For just as in the middle moment, perception—having its scope exhausted—cannot perceive the preceding and succeeding moments, so too, from the observation of blue, it perceives blue and not white and so forth; likewise, this should be considered even regarding the parts consisting of mere blue, until the proof of cognitions restricted to each individual atom is established like that of the middle moment. And in that case, through the cognition of one atom, there is equality with other [simultaneous] streams of consciousness because of the non-perception of others; since even that cognition is within the range of dispute, what indeed could be that reality which is non-sequential and transcends all conceptual construction?
In this regard, it must also be considered how that [object] cannot be impermanent:

for just as the existence of the middle moment, nor its distinction from the preceding and succeeding moments, cannot be apprehended when those two moments are not perceived—such that its momentariness could be realized—in the same way, how can the existence or the distinction of blue and its parts be apprehended, such that reality (tattva) would be beyond all conceptual construction?

Comparison: Those specific distinctions—such as self and other-nature, truth and falsity, permanence and annihilation, eternity and non-eternity, pleasure and pain, purity and impurity, self and non-self, emptiness and non-emptiness, the characterized and the characteristic, unity and difference, arising and cessation, and so forth—are not possible for that [Reality], because it is non-successive and transcends all conceptual constructions. (*Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā*, p. 366)
The meaning is that, because it transcends all conceptual construction, it is non-existent like another mental continuum; this is shown by the preceding and following [passages].

By this, the emptiness of the conceptual constructs of unity and plurality has been examined, since the logic is the same; nevertheless, because even when postulating reality, that [construct] falls into a false arrangement, one must therefore accept the identity between the nature of reality characterized by consciousness and the false nature characterized by the forms of the apprehended object such as permanence and grossness. And when that identity between the natures of reality and falsity is accepted, [the object] consists of both the universal and the particular.
Where? Both externally and internally.
How? In accordance with what is perceived, without overstepping that perception.
Of what nature is it? It is subject to transformation. Why is that not perceived? It is indeed perceived as the reality (tattva).

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is precisely the form of the jar and so forth, and nothing other than that—neither a separate [consciousness] nor a form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*)? How then can there be a single nature consisting of both reality and falsity? To this he replies: "In every way," and so forth.

Because the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) cannot be precluded by any means—namely, by the oneness of the nature of reality and falsity in the case of the consciousness of the jar-form and others, or by the manner already stated—the definition beginning with "the cause in its generality" and so forth is observed;
thus, these entities, whether propounded by ourselves or by others, are in reality devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
"Because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a reflection"—

thus, having first established that "attainment" (siddhi), which is the determination of the object, is the direct fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he now says "it is established," etc., while supporting that attainment as the self-determination [of the cognition] and its corresponding fruit.

That which is directly established, being independent of anything else for the establishment of its own and other forms, is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, nothing else is [valid], such as that which is non-conceptual or insentient. (23)
This has been extracted from the *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, page 98:

"The state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) in its entirety is the common form (*sadṛśaṃ rūpam*) of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the act of knowing (*pramiti*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, however, there is this much distinction: the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is self-established; establishment (*siddhi*) is non-disagreement (*avipratipatti*); and the cessation of ignorance characterized by lack of proficiency, doubt, and error is the act of knowing (*pramiti*)."
That from which [an object] is established is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, that [means] consists in the establishment of both the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*) independently of anything else, because it has the nature of a valid cognition (*pramātmatva*). It is not, however, mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvinmātra*) devoid of determination (*nirṇaya*), for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For those who maintain that the self-awareness of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*) and capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, what distinction could possibly exist between sleep and waking? Since, [if this were so], the accomplishment of all human goals preceded by correct knowledge would not occur during sleep and similar states.
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for those who maintain that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) are non-existent during sleep and so forth;

nor is there, for those [factors] existing at that time, any other characteristic apart from self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) by which their definition could be excluded from the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

We do not perceive any distinction whatsoever between the self-cognition of sleep and so forth, and the self-cognition of the moments of arising and ceasing of the mind and mental factors during the waking state, such that [the former] would remain unperceived.

Because there is no difference in the nature of direct apprehension, and since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object its own referent, if even that which is of the nature of direct perception—namely, the awareness of the momentary destruction of waking consciousness and so forth—were not a valid cognition, then awareness would not possess the character of direct perception.

Conversely, if awareness were indeed direct perception, it would still not be a valid cognition; therefore, the definition of a valid cognition must be established in a different way, so that it does not become over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
And thus, everything is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in some respect, whether with regard to its own nature (*svabhāva*) or the nature of another (*parabhāva*), but not in every respect.

If even the cognition of the eye and so forth were established as valid only through something else (*parataḥ*) in every respect, how could there be non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) for one who acts after having determined an object by means of that [cognition]? Even if there is contradiction regarding momentary destruction and the like, it is reasonable to establish through investigation that a cognition of blue and so forth possesses validity in some respect, despite contradicting [the reality] regarding water and so forth in the case of a mirage-cognition; otherwise, it would follow that the person seeing that [mirage] is no different from being asleep.

For just as there is non-apprehension due to infinite regress when validity is held to be exclusively extrinsic (*parataḥ*), so too, when there is the exclusive position that the nature of all cognitions is not determined intrinsically (*svataḥ*), this [position] necessarily negates the fact that all cognitions consist in the determination of their own form— which is the definition of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*)— for mind and mental factors.

This is because, just as the apprehension of an object is impossible without self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it has been stated that the determination of an object is impossible without the determination of its own form.

Therefore, this is not an absolute rule: that every cognition, even though it has the nature of consciousness, necessarily cognizes its own form. For if it did, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of error; or else, because cognition is determinative by nature, it must determine its own form in every respect.

Thus, a cognition possessing a nature other than the experience of its own object—whether characterized by the determination of its own and other forms, or by a nature other than the determination of self and other—could not be established in any way without that [determination].

Therefore, non-conceptual perception (*avikalpa-darśana*) is not itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because even though its own nature is self-experienced, it is in every respect like something never experienced; and although it is conscious, like deep sleep and so forth, it depends on something else for the object that has become its own domain.

Thus, only that upon which it depends possesses validity. Even if it were the cause of that [valid cognition], primary status as a means of valid cognition would be untenable—just as with sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and the like—since the designation of sensory contact and so forth as a means of valid cognition is only figurative.

From the moment that human activity becomes preceded by critical investigation (*prekṣāpūrvikā*), it is established as primarily valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is essentially non-contradictory, independent of anything else regarding what is perceived by itself, and consists of conceptual objects (*vikalpaviṣaya*). Since this [cognition] functions without faltering in the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful— acting without confusion or error— one should disregard those who hate it and those who act upon it.

That which is established (*siddha*) and certain (*niścita*) is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is not, however, as the Mīmāṃsakas and Sāṃkhyas imagine, an indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*). Wherein lies its validity? To this he says: "When the establishment—that is, the ascertainment—is to be performed, and not upon mere apprehension (*adhigati-mātra*), because otherwise there would follow the absurdity of the futility of inferences such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*). [Objection: But surely that which is ascertained by another ascertainment—whether it be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), conceptual (*savikalpaka*), or self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—is valid cognition; therefore, you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). To this he says: "Not dependent on another" (*na parāpekṣam*).
Since that [consciousness] is established as being independent of anything else and self-established, there is no means of valid cognition other than what has been described.
What is it? To this he says: "That cognition which is non-conceptual, insentient, devoid of self-awareness, and like a jar or similar object."

The realization of momentary destruction arises solely from non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*); therefore, that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard, and there is no necessity for inference (*anumāna*). Explaining the verse, he says: "The cognizer, the cognition," and so forth.

The knower (*pramātā*) is the conscious, transforming soul (*jīva*), which will be described later; valid cognition (*pramiti*) is the ascertainment of one’s own object, which is the direct removal of ignorance—the immediate fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the entity such as a jar. Their state of being objects of knowledge—that is, their being the domain of the means of knowledge—is "similar" in form, meaning they share a common nature. The sense is that otherwise, the existence of both the means of knowledge and the determinative cognition (*nirṇayajñāna*) could not be established.

If it is argued: "In that case, since everything is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), and because they are already included by the term 'object of knowledge' itself, for what purpose are the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the others mentioned separately? The answer is: so that the word *prameya* may apply specifically to things such as jars and the like. From this, the following meaning is obtained: the status of being an object of knowledge belongs to the knower and the rest as well, just as their status as a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth does; however, for the object of knowledge (*prameya*), that [status] alone exists. Thus, the objection raised by the opponent—that lamps and the like, though objects of knowledge, are also means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they cause cognition—is refuted. A *pramāṇa* is that by which the reality of an entity is measured—that is, determined—through the exclusion of doubt and other cognitive errors.

Furthermore, nothing is measured by a lamp or the like in that manner, because it would follow that the postulation of [such] cognition is futile. If it were argued that they are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they are the causes of that [cognition], then even a jar or similar object would become its own means of knowledge, as there is no difference between them. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because of the statement that "a means of knowledge is that which, when accompanied by an object, produces a cognition that is determinative, non-verbal, and non-erroneous," and because of the statement that "the means of knowledge is an entity distinct from the object of knowledge (*prameya*"); then, for that very reason, the status of being a knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth for the knower and others would be impossible.
Nevertheless, regarding their true nature, the status of being an object of cognition (*prameya*) necessarily entails the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For this reason, it was stated that their status as objects of cognition consists in having a similar form.

Therefore, just as jars and the like do not possess the status of a means of valid cognition despite being causes of knowledge, so too lamps and the like do not; rather, they possess only the status of being objects of cognition. Thus, they are included [in the category of objects].

The very fact of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is an auxiliary factor for the apprehension of jars and so forth, just like the light of a lamp— *Nyāyabhāṣya* 2.1.15.
Because there is no distinction in their being causes of that [knowledge], by virtue of being causes of knowledge.

If it be argued: "Let this be granted—that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is established as independent of anything else; but why, in the present context, is the irrelevant status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) introduced for them? We reply: Because it has been stated that the means of knowledge is a distinct entity from the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), it would follow that, like the means of knowledge, the knower and the act of knowing (*pramiti*) must also be distinct from it.

But this is not so, because [the object] does not exist due to its non-apprehension; therefore, that which was stated is not well-said: "In these four—namely, the knower (*pramātṛ*), the act of knowing (*pramiti*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—reality is fully encompassed" (Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 1). Now, if it is maintained that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is also included within that same tetrad, there is a contradiction with the principle that "the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is an entity distinct from both the knower and the object of knowledge. To demonstrate this, the following is introduced:

Alternatively, as for what was stated—that "knowledge is known by another knowledge distinct from itself because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*), like a jar and so forth"—in that regard, just as a jar or the like, being an object of cognition, is observed to be known only by a distinct knowledge, so too is the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the rest.

Then, just as by the example of a jar or the like it is established that because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatvāt*), its cognition is itself made an object without [the mediation of] that [cognition], so too for that very reason, let it be established that the cognizer (*pramātā*) is also made an object without [the mediation of] that [cognition], since there is no difference [in the logic]. Furthermore, if that which stands between them is also made an object without [the mediation of] that [cognition], then due to infinite regress (*anavasthā*), there would be no comprehension for any cognizer; thus, [the cognizer] would be non-existent.

Now, if the cognizer himself cognizes himself when there is no distinction [between the instrument and the agent], then the argument that "knowledge is known by another knowledge because it is an object of cognition" is contradicted by that very same case; this is why [the definition] is elaborated:
"The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*), but not the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) or the object of cognition (*prameya*). (Nyāyavārttika, p. 6).
The term "instrument" (*sādhana*) is employed in order to exclude the cognizer and the object of cognition, and to indicate its distinction from the result (*phala*).
And because it is derived from the sense of "instrument" (karaṇa), this [pramāṇa] should be understood as distinct from both the agent (kartṛ) and the object (karman). — Nyāyasāra, p.
2; Nyāyakalikā, p. 1.
"Cognitions under dispute are cognizable by another cognition alone, because they are cognitions;

likewise, being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*), being qualities (*guṇatva*), existence (*sattva*), and so forth, are also to be employed as reasons for being cognizable by another cognition" — *Vidhiviveka*, *Nyāyakaṇikā*, p. 267.
Cognition is cognizable by another cognition because it is an object of cognition, like a jar and so forth—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p.
529; [it is cognized] by another cognition indeed, and by another subject indeed.

If it is asked: "Even so, since it must be stated that the cognizer, the cognition, the object of cognition, and the means of cognition are all equally of the nature of being objects of cognition (*prameyatva*), for what purpose is the means of cognition mentioned separately with the words 'and of the means of cognition'? [The author] says the following—beginning with "In this regard, to such an extent"—in order to demonstrate that this [means of cognition] possesses primacy over the object of cognition by virtue of its self-established nature (*svataḥ-siddhatva*).

Among those [factors] such as the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, the specific distinction or difference of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is this much greater: that it is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*). If it is objected that "the knower too is self-established," [the reply is: True; for that very reason, one must not restrict it by saying "only the means of knowledge [is self-established]," but rather [one should say] "it is indeed self-established. Thus it is established, determined, and understood.

Therefore, this is refuted: "For our cognition is imperceptible, while the object is perceptible; for that [object], being connected with an external location, is experienced through direct perception, whereas once it is known, one understands it through inference" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5).

How so? For that by which the object of cognition (*prameya*) is directly determined is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and nothing is determined in such a way by a cognition that is indirect (*parokṣa*). Otherwise, one might as well be determined by the cognition of another person’s mental continuum (*santānāntara*), and thus the claim that "all things are seen through the cognition of the Self" would not be a valid answer. Indeed, because there is an absence of such certainty regarding what is indirect, a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) certainly does not possess the certainty that "knowledge exists in the Self but not in another."
Whether directly, indirectly, or in the form of something imperceptible, [it pertains] to the means of valid cognition.

The Mīmāṃsaka might hold the view that "this is the cognition of the self"—that is, the certainty "in me" arises from the production of the direct manifestation of the object. But even that is not sound; for by what is that direct manifestation of the object, though produced by it, itself cognized? Not by the object itself, because, being insentient, it is like any other object.
Nor can it be by means of cognition, because that [cognition] is itself beyond direct perception and because it would lead to an over-extension;
for this very reason, it cannot even be apprehended by the self, since the direct manifestation of the object has not arisen.

Furthermore, how is it that "this [cognition] belongs to me"? If you say it is because it is produced by my intellect (*buddhi*), then there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for only when it is established that it is produced by my intellect is it determined that "this belongs to me"; and only when that is determined is its production by my intellect established.

Thus, even in the determination "this belongs to me," there is no determination of its being produced by my intellect, since we observe the use of the term "mine" (*mama*) even for things produced by causes belonging to others—just as one says "my removal of poison" (*mama viṣāpahāra*) when it was actually performed by another.
Therefore, this object is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5)
Such statements as these are well-said by the Mīmāṃsaka.
Because it generates a direct perception whose object is the thing itself,
the immediacy of the object is produced by the cognition as well.

The meaning is that when another person employs a mantra for the sake of removing poison from one's sons and so forth who are devoted to wealth, although the removal of the poison occurs for the other person, the conviction "it is mine" arises even in that case.

By this, the statement from the *Śābarabhāṣya* (1.1.5), "When [the object] is known, one understands it through inference," is refuted; for the reason (*hetu*)— namely, the "knownness of the object"— is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, in what respect is that "cognizedness" established as being dependent upon cognition, such that the inference of it [cognition] could proceed from it? Or, if it is argued that the perceptibility of the object is the effect of something because it is occasional, and therefore the name "cognition" is applied to that cause—let it be so, provided that cause can be established as distinct from the eye and other [senses]. However, this is the correct view: since the object exists immediately after the operation of the eye and other [senses], those alone are its cause, just as the wheel and other [implements] are the cause of a jar because the jar exists immediately after their operation.

If it is argued that the name [pratyakṣa] applies only to the eye and so forth, then what is this childish talk—"That which arises when there is contact with an existing object is perception" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.4)? That is not so; for the cognition of an object is an inference, according to the logic already stated, because even the cognition of another person has those [senses] as its cause, and [the same applies to] one's own cognition.

Furthermore, what is that inference? It is simply the cognition of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); if that [presumption] is itself beyond one's perception, then the same objection applies and there is an infinite regress.
Therefore, that view of the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) is not well-stated.
Because it is already known,
the cause for the direct perception of the object is indeed the eye and so forth.
By this it has been considered that the sense organs perceive the object, the ego-sense conceives, the mind resolves, the intellect determines, and the person (puruṣa) cognizes;
for if the person were imperceptible, neither his intellect nor anything else could function, since the same logic applies equally to both cases.

The Sāṃkhya doctrine is as follows: the sequential functioning of the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), mind (manas), and the eye is observed—[namely], the eye sees the form, the mind conceives it, the ego identifies with it, and the intellect determines it. (Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti, Kārikā 30).
If it is argued that it is established because it is apprehended by another cognition, he says in response: "by itself" (svataḥ).

The intention here is as follows: Just as for the Mīmāṃsaka, since an object graspable by a non-perceptual cognition is not established, another cognition is postulated; likewise, since a cognition graspable by a non-perceptual cognition is also not established, yet another [cognition] must be postulated for that as well. Otherwise, even the second cognition would not need to be postulated. Thus, because of infinite regress, the claim that "one's own cognition is grasped by that very [second] cognition because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), like a jar," fails due to the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Now, if that knowledge is held to be self-established (*svataḥsiddha*), then the reason (*hetu*) would be "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth; it cannot be established—
see page 98, note 1.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the opponent—"In the case of one cognition being known by another cognition, I have the example of a jar and so forth, but the Jaina has no such example for self-cognition"—that is not correct. For him (the opponent), there is no example at all; moreover, for you, there is an absence of the entire apparatus required for inference.

Furthermore, even for you, in the case of "blue is blue," there is no example whatsoever because it is established through perception; the question of what is the use of that [example] is equally applicable to both sides.
Just as there is indeed no dispute among people regarding the blueness of what is blue, so too there is none regarding self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), which is perceived through the sense of "I, I."

If, however, you maintain this insistence—that its establishment cannot occur without inference, and that even inference cannot occur without an example—this too is not the case. For [the purpose] is fully accomplished merely by such [inferences] as: "The living body possesses a self because it has breath and so forth," or "Cognition of an object consists in the grasping of itself because it consists in the grasping of an object; whereas that which does not consist in the grasping of itself does not consist in the grasping of an object either, just like another object. Therefore, it is well said that [cognition] is "self-established" (*svataḥ-siddha*) for the Jaina alone.
For the Mīmāṃsaka, [the object] is indeed blue by nature,
as shown by the example.

If it is argued that since cognition is self-cognized, even inference [is so], and that even so, the word *dṛṣṭa* (seen) in the verse and the commentary should be used for clarity rather than the word *siddha* (established), we say: no. For if the word *dṛṣṭa* were used, the suspicion that even what is seen by non-conceptual self-awareness might be included would not be dispelled, nor is that [non-conceptual awareness] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intended to be that which makes known; yet it is not so [in the case of the opponent's view]. Otherwise, the capacity of the minds intent on generosity, non-violence, and abstention from harm to bring about heaven would itself be the indicator of the attainment of fruits such as heaven, but this will be demonstrated to be not the case by the proponent of the perception of objects (*viṣayadarśanavādin*). Furthermore, when a statement regarding an established fact (*siddhavacana*) is made, it is understood that "the established has been determined," because we observe the common usage that "the established position (*pakṣa*) is determined.
Therefore, it was rightly said: "The means of valid cognition is established by itself (*svataḥ siddham*)."
The non-conceptual state (nirvikalpaka) favored by the Buddhists possesses the capacity to lead to the attainment of heaven in both the mind of generosity and the mind of non-violence.
Furthermore, in the Buddhist view, a real entity (*vastu*) exists without parts;

therefore, according to the principle that "of a perceived object, every quality is indeed perceived," the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) apprehending the mind of giving and so forth would also necessarily apprehend its causal capacity (*sāmarthya*). Consequently, the fault arises that the knowledge of results such as rebirth in heaven would occur solely from the mind apprehending the act of giving and so on.
If one asks, "Why is this so? he says here: "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*), etc.
Accomplishment is the ascertainment of reality (*tattva-nirṇīti*).
He states a synonym for this: "non-disagreement" (*avipratipatti*), which is the cessation of ignorance characterized by lack of understanding, doubt, and error.
By the statement, "The attainment [of the object] by means of this [cognition] is its fruit," he dispels such doubts as whether there is the establishment of that [object] alone, and so forth;

for in that way, [the object] is not established [as something separate]. To the question, "What is that? he says: "Valid cognition (*pramiti*) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By all of this, the phrase "in the establishment" has been explained.

Others claim that the object from which that certainty arises—that is, from which it reaches its completion—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
To those, he provides the following reply: "But that [certainty], moreover," and so forth.

Then, from that [definition], regarding the phrase "again" (*punaḥ*) in the context of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is stated that the knowledge of one who is not yet perfected (*chadmastha-jñāna*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only partially with respect to whatever two things—whether intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*)—and whatever their extent may be.

What is the case for those two? It is the "means" (*sādhana*) or the "prover" (*sādhaka*). From the statement "of whatever extent," it is understood that it is a means of valid cognition for that much, according to the logical rule that there is a constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.
What is that? He says: "independent of anything else" (*anyānapekṣam*).
This has been explained.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvāt*);
that is, because of the state of being that which has valid cognition (*pramā*) as its essence (*ātman*), meaning its very nature (*svabhāva*).

This is what is meant: the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and that is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*); furthermore, it is not logical for it to depend on anything else with respect to the fruit of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Therefore, what is the fruit of this means of valid cognition? It is the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameyādhigati*)—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 3.
Merely the attainment [of knowledge] itself is the accomplishment;
for if it were dependent on anything else, its status as the most excellent means of realization would be untenable.

If it is argued: "Granted that cognition dependent on another, as conceived by the Naiyāyikas and others, may not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); however, could that which is the opposite of this, as conceived by the Sugatas (Buddhists), not be so? To this he says: "But not... and so forth. This mere self-awareness, which is devoid of determination, is self-cognition; but it is certainly not a means of knowledge regarding either its own nature or the nature of another. Why is this? To this he says: "Because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."

Even the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of one who is asleep, intoxicated, within a womb, or unconscious would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because there is no distinction [between these states and those that are clearly conscious].
Now, if it is asked: "What is meant by 'because there is no distinction,' since there actually is a distinction?"—to this he replies: "Of all minds and mental factors" (*sarvacittacaittānām*), etc.

All minds (*citta*) associated with waking, sleeping, fainting, and so forth—namely, cognitions of blue and other objects—and all mental factors (*caitta*)—namely, the conceptual experiences of pleasure and so on—their awareness of their own nature (*ātman*) is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and it is a valid means of knowledge by virtue of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
Of what nature is it? He says: "beneficial," and so forth.

According to the statement in the *Nyāyabindu* (1.1), "The accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge," that which is beneficial consists of garlands and the like, while that which is harmful consists of poison and the like. It is capable of both the attainment and the avoidance of these two respectively. For the Buddhists who desire this, there is sleep—the state of seeing pleasant dreams—and awakening—the state of consciousness having arisen from that; regarding these two states, what difference is there? No distinction whatsoever is conceivable, because there is no difference in the absence of direct apprehension (*sākṣātsampratipatti*). This is his thought.

Because—*yataḥ*, *yasmāt*—due to that specific [absence], in states such as sleep (the word "etc. including intoxication and so forth), the accomplishment of all human goals would not occur preceded by right knowledge;
or, *yataḥ* may be used as an objection, meaning "it would surely be so.
By this, he demonstrates the opponent's lack of the fourfold states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death.
Independent and free from conceptual construction, it is the accomplishment of all human goals—[as stated in] the *Nyāyabindu*:

"Everyone seeks the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful" (p. 28), and it has been stated that the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful are preceded by correct knowledge.

—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 40. It might be thought: "Since they are not perceived during sleep and so forth, they are non-existent; how then can this fault apply? To this he says: "For indeed," and so on. For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that demonstrates the absence of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) for those who maintain [their existence] during sleep and so forth. Whatever negation there may be, all of it is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), and that exists even upon waking.
Therefore it has been said: "What distinction could possibly be conceived between sleep and awakening?

And it is held that the probandum cannot be established by an inconclusive reason, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), with respect to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*).

Furthermore, would that non-perception be related to itself or related to another? If it is related to itself, then if it consists in the cessation of perception, how can there be the establishment of its absence [from that very fact]? Even otherwise, that cessation would have to be known in order to indicate the absence;
and if that which indicates it must itself be known—just like smoke—then if its cognition were to depend on something else, there would be an infinite regress.

If [the mind] has the nature of another perception; then, while that other [perception] exists, how could there be an absence of the mind and mental factors? Furthermore, if that absence were a mere void, it would involve moving to another state, such as the nature of the body during sleep and so forth. If that [other perception] is not apprehended, there is no certainty regarding its absence;
for indeed, when the ground is not perceived, there is no perception of the absence of a jar upon it.

If, on the other hand, the cognition of being awake is the non-perception of that [dream], even so, its absence is not established therein; otherwise, the absence of the next world would be established from the perception of this world. Furthermore, whether that [non-perception] belongs to oneself or to another, how can it ascertain the absence of those things which are invisible at that time? For that would entail the undesirable consequence of the non-establishment of other mental continua (*santānāntara*).

Now, the non-existence of that [the self] is established because the four states are otherwise inexplicable. In this regard, it is considered as follows: just as when the self imagined by others is unestablished, the body of a living person cannot be proven to possess a self by means of that [imagined self], so too, when the absence of non-conceptual mind and mental factors is unestablished, the waking and sleeping states—which depend upon them—cannot be established; likewise, the states of death and deep sleep, which depend upon their cessation, are also not established.

If consciousness is not established in trees and the like, then—just as death, characterized by the cessation of consciousness, the sense faculties, and life-force, is unestablished—the fourfold [set] is likewise unestablished.

If you argue that it is established for the worldly person (*vyavahārin*), then if it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇataḥ*), the same fault applies to the original case. This too is merely a triviality; let death also be established in the same way for trees and the like.
Since the accomplishment consisting of the cessation of cognition is a property of cognition,
it is the cessation of apprehension.
If other minds and mental factors exist during sleep and so forth, one enters the position of the Naiyāyikas.
If it is argued that the non-existence of the mind and mental factors during the time of sleep and so forth is determined by the non-perception of what is invisible, then [the following applies]:
In the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, death, and so forth, there exists the presence of the mind and mental factors.

In the same way, whatever this may be— that upon such investigation, non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) remains— even there, according to statements such as *Prakaraṇavārtika* 3.220, "the variegated appearance is also a single cognition," if you are satisfied by [the view that] it consists of a single cognition of variegation, then let satisfaction also be found in [the view that it] consists of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which arise in succession.

Now, [the opponent suggests: "Let it be done by that which is devoid of the conceptual constructions of one and many, and even there, by that which is devoid of all appearances. Having thus deliberated, [the author] concludes: "Not so," and so forth.
If it is argued, "In that case, let those [appearances] exist even there," he says here: "And not," and so forth.

And it is not the case that for those minds and mental factors during the state of sleep and so forth, there exists any other characteristic apart from self-awareness while they are present and existing; for it is held that knowledge has self-awareness as its characteristic. [The opponent argues:
"If the definition of perception were some other characteristic, then it would indeed be excluded from them.
But surely, even for you, their non-existence does not occur at that time, because it would follow that the self itself must also cease to exist."

If it is argued that for those [cognitions] of the wise, there is no characteristic other than their being illuminators of both self and other, and therefore the fault is equal; to this he replies: "In sleep, etc. and so forth.

Self-awareness of sleep and so forth is "self-cognition of sleep etc."; its nature is the momentary destruction and so on of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) during the waking state—the word "etc. including partlessness, the capacity to attain heaven, and so forth. Regarding that self-cognition or apprehension, we do not perceive any distinction whatsoever, such that while this cognition of the nature of momentary destruction and so on remains unperceived, the self-cognition of sleep and so forth is likewise [unperceived].
If one asks, "Why is this so? he says here: "Directly," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since there is no distinction between the two cases regarding the nature of that direct, perceptual determination (*saṃpratipatti*) or ascertainment (*nirṇīti*), otherwise the inference of states such as momentary destruction would be purposeless.

The intention is that the determination from a logical mark (*liṅga*) occurs in both cases: in one case from "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth, and in the other from activity and speech, as in the state of sleep and the like.
The existence of the mind and mental factors during sleep and so forth: if there were no cognition during sleep and so forth, then there would be an absence of the self.

If it is further argued that—just as smoke, though seen from fire, is subsequently seen only from smoke, so too activity and the like, though seen from the mind (citta), are subsequently seen only from activity and the like—how then can self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) be established for that [mind] on that basis? To this it is replied: [the phrase] "because of the cognition of another's thought" (*anyadhiyo gateḥ*) would be meaningless, because there is a lack of any means for cognizing that [other's thought].

For it could be argued: "Just as in the case of fire, even when the consciousness of a previous birth has ceased, activity and so forth in this life arise from activity and so forth in all other bodies; therefore, the composition of a treatise for that purpose is unnecessary.

Furthermore, how could those who speak thus explain the fact that, upon seeing a specific form such as water, a person desiring its practical utility invariably engages in action toward it? For even if that specific form is seen at some time, the doubt remains that "this might be the same thing again" because of that very [previous] experience.

Likewise, even if the taste of a form and so forth is perceived, how can this be an inference— such as "the activity and so forth [of the cause] depend on the same causal complex" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.18)— if that [taste] arises from the taste itself?
Because of the existence of the general categories of valid cognition and its opposite during sleep and so forth, because of the apprehension of another cognition,
and because of the negation of something [else], there exists another means of valid cognition.
"This verse was stated by Dharmakīrti," having thus [concluded], it appears on page 64 of the *Pramāṇaparīkṣā* and on page 4 of the *Tarkabhāṣā-muktāvalī*,
for the purpose of rescuing the mental continuum of others.
The aspect [of the cognition] arises precisely from the aspect itself,
by virtue of its being a cooperative cause.
From the taste alone, which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*),
there is the cognition of [the other qualities] such as color from the taste;
this is by means of inferring the property of the cause (*hetudharma*), just like [inferring] the transformation of fuel from smoke— this is the remainder [of the sense].
By this, the perception of what is contradictory to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth is also considered, since the underlying logic is the same.
In the same way, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) must also be considered;

for that too, from the first moment of the object blue, takes on its form, and from that very [moment] onwards until the end of saṃsāra. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is redundant.

The practitioner does not think [consciousness is absent] even then; how much less would he think there is an absence of consciousness during sleep and so forth? If he were to do so, then, as with a corpse, he would perform such violent acts as cremation even then.
This is because, according to the definition of perception, it consists precisely of the appearance of blue and other such forms.
By this [argument], the Naiyāyika and others who postulate the non-existence [of cognition] therein during sleep and so forth are also refuted;
for how could [cognition arise] upon awakening from the conjunction of the self and the mind? Let this matter rest for now.

[This is] from the cognition of waking; let this too be set aside. Whatever that single [object] might be, in the absence of perceiving its specific qualities, self-awareness in sleep and so forth is established as unperceived. However, showing another refutation, he says: "And thus," etc.
"In that way" means by that manner of not perceiving its specific qualities; the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis, meaning "in exactly that way."

Or rather, their own object and [the cognition] itself are the two objects and domains regarding which validity is intended for the Buddhist in the waking state. As for the cognition that has as its nature the momentary destruction and so forth of that [object], its awareness is not a means of valid cognition because it functions dependently, like Devadatta’s [awareness of] his teacher’s wife.

Alternatively, if it is held that the apprehension which grasps its [the object's] momentary destruction and so forth is its very nature (*svabhāva*), then— despite its being of the nature of perception— one must supply the words "if its invalidity is desired" out of fear that inference regarding momentary destruction and so forth would lack validity; in that case, the validity of cognition— that is, of the nature of consciousness itself— as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*) is not established, [just as there is no knowledge] in states such as deep sleep due to the absence of cognition.
If it is argued that there is no compound because of a lack of capacity [to form one], we say no; for the sense is that a compound is observed even in the case of that which is dependent on another.
Now, if it is asked: "But since that [inference] lacks perceptibility, how can it be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)?"—to this he says: "If," and so forth.

If, however— this being a conjecture (*vitarka*)— consciousness (*saṃvitti*), even while existing in that very manner through the mode of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), were not to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), meaning it would not possess the nature of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), or if it were not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-discrepant (*saṃvādin*), then the definition of valid cognition as "therefore, the self-awareness of all minds and mental factors is direct perception and a valid means of cognition" (Nyāyabindu 1.14) would have to be established in a completely different way.

Of what nature is it? To this he says: that which possesses the characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must not be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), meaning it does not exist in the experience of sleep and so forth; for consciousness [is defined by its capacity to cognize]. But has it not already been stated: "Only where it produces this [cognition] is there its status as a means of valid cognition"?

If it is argued that the statement from the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, page 151, line 22—"The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which sets [the object] in motion"—applies to sleep and so forth, or to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) and so forth; to this he replies with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*), etc.

And thus, even in the manner imagined by others, every means of valid cognition—perception and the rest—is a means of valid cognition only in some respect (*kathaṃcid eva*) regarding its own nature (*svabhāva*), its own form (*svasvarūpa*), or regarding the nature of another (*parabhāva*), the form of another (*pararūpa*), specifically in the form of being existent, conscious, blue, and so on, but not in the form of momentary destruction and the like.
Therefore, he says: "It is established that [it is] not in every respect (*na sarvathā*)."

For one who maintains that perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it functions as an instigator toward a future object during the stage of repeated practice (*abhyāsadaśā*), even for him, perception is a valid means of knowledge only with respect to that [object's] form (*tadrūpa*) and so forth, and not with respect to the distinction between the perceived and the attainable (*dṛśyaprāpyaviveka*), even though that distinction is itself made an object [of cognition]. Otherwise, the determination of identity between those two would not occur due to contradiction.

Furthermore, if the existent were not made an object [of cognition], it would contradict such statements as Prajñākaragupta’s *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (PVĀ) 3.42: "Of a single nature of the object... and so on.
The conceptual cognition [is the means] for the non-conceptual perception which exists by itself.
"What other part [of reality] would not have been seen that is examined by the means of valid cognition?"—this is the remainder [of the argument].
Here, he states another refutation: "the eye and so forth," etc.

Not only for the self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors, but even for visual cognition and the rest—the word "etc. including auditory cognition and so forth—if validity is accepted as being extrinsic (*parataḥ*) in the case of blue and other objects just as it is in the case of momentary destruction and the like, then how could there be non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) later on for one who acts after having determined the object through that visual cognition? It follows from this that [non-contradiction] comes from nothing at all; the connection with the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) implies that action itself would be impossible, because [according to your view] action is possible only extrinsically. Thus he thinks.
Furthermore, he states another refutation in this very context: "In the case of momentary destruction, etc.
The word "etc. refers to circularity and so forth; the connection is that even when there is a discrepancy regarding such things, visual and other cognitions [are considered valid].
If validity were admitted for [cognitions] regarding blue and so forth, then it would follow for the cognition of a mirage and the like as well—not only for others.

Of what nature is it? It is that which does not contradict [the perception of] water and so forth, because there is no contradiction regarding its intrinsic nature, such as whiteness; thus, it is in some respect, and not in every way, appropriate to establish the validity of the investigation through reasoning.

One might think: "The cognition of a mirage and the like is non-conceptual and non-erroneous; it does not have water and the like as its object, so how could there be a contradiction of it with respect to that? Otherwise, the cognition of blue would be contradictory with respect to yellow."

And as for the claim that the cognition of water and so forth is equivalent to the cognition of a mirage, because the delusion regarding water and such is admitted to be mental; this is not so, because two distinct cognitions are not perceived there.
Even if one were to postulate them, it could be said: "Even for one seeing a single moon, there is the delusion of two moons," and so forth.

If it is argued: "Since the cognition of a mirage does not grasp the nature of whiteness and so forth, how can there be non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāda*) with respect to that [object], such that it might be established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in some respect? To this, he says: "Otherwise," and so forth.

Otherwise—in the manner of non-existence already described—there would follow the consequence that a person who perceives such things, namely one who sees water in a mirage and the like, would be no different from one who is asleep; therefore, it is proper to establish its validity in some respect.

If one imagines that even a manifest nature such as white and so forth is not perceived, then what confidence can there be in the appearance of water and the like? If it is asked, "What is the purpose of these two examples? it is said: when another person maintains that within a single cognition there is an appearance of water and so forth, but no appearance of white and so forth, then—according to the logic already stated—since even the appearance of water and so forth would be denied, it follows that there would be no distinction between one who is asleep and one who does not see dreams; thus it is said.

Furthermore, when one accepts that there is a clear non-conceptual vision (*darśana*) whose object is the nature of white and so forth, and that there is also a clear conceptual mental cognition (*mānasa-jñāna*) whose domain is water and so forth, then it is argued that [the former] would result in no distinction from the other, because even though a non-conceptual [cognition] exists, it is not perceived, whereas [conceptual cognition] exists even in the absence of a clear cognition of water and so forth.

Now, in the context of investigating the determination of self-aware direct perception (*svasaṃvedanādhyakṣa*), there is no utility for visual and other sensory cognitions such that they would be investigated here. Rather, this is for the purpose of providing an illustration that self-aware direct perception applies to one's own nature (*svarūpa*) only in some respect (*kathaṃcit*) and not in every respect (*sarvathā*).
For this very reason it was said: "Whether in its own nature or in another nature"—this refers to the cognition of a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇikājñāna*).

Having demonstrated that very refutation of the Buddhist— which is well known for being leveled against the position that knowledge is exclusively cognizable by another cognition, as when [the opponent] says, "Its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatā) exists only where it produces this [subsequent cognition]"— and thereby establishing that all knowledge is intrinsically (svataḥ) of the nature of the determination of its own form, he says: "For just as," and so forth.

For just as the validity of the first cognition—its determination of its own object—is derived from another subsequent cognition in some manner, according to the statement that "the validity of cognitions is their determination of their own objects," so too, in this absolute position imagined by the Naiyāyika, there is no apprehension of either the object or its validity due to infinite regress, since even that subsequent cognition would require yet another. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.

In that very same manner, if one accepts the absolute non-determination of the intrinsic nature—that is, the essential form—of all cognitions, whether conceptual or non-conceptual, by means of themselves, then due to the resulting infinite regress (*anavasthā*), a failure to apprehend their own objects must necessarily be admitted.

This is what is meant: just as it was stated that the initial perception, though arisen, is as if unarisen because it lacks the capacity for determination regarding its own nature—expressed in the passage beginning "wherein one would produce this"—likewise, even when a conceptual cognition has arisen with respect to that nature, it is inherently devoid of the capacity for self-determination; thus, though arisen, it is as if unarisen. Consequently, there would be a search for another [cognition] to determine its nature, and a further search for yet another in that case as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Then, because of that immediately preceding fault, [the author] states—by connecting it with the phrase "the nature of all cognitions must be understood as being determinate" (which has undergone a change in gender from neuter)—what does that [fault] effect? To this he says: "nirvikalpam... and so forth. That which is both non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa*), thus becoming the object [of negation], is indeed refuted. Whose [is it]? To this he says: "of the mind and mental factors" (*citta-caitasikānām*).
In the case of a non-conceptual form, there would be another conceptual cognition, which is termed an infinite regress.

It might be thought: "In the absence of the nature of determining its own form (*svarūpa*), what is untenable that it must be established? To this he gives the answer: "Self-cognition" (*svasaṃvedana*), and so forth.

Just as the apprehension of an object is untenable without the apprehension of oneself—that is, self-cognition—so too has it been stated that the determination of an object characterized by its own purpose is untenable without the determination of one's own form, which is the ascertainment of the self.
By this, the self-cognition of one who accepts [the existence of] the self is established. (Siddhiviniścaya 1)
By the words beginning with "ityādinā," he shows that the objection raised by the opponent has been addressed;
then, summarizing the point already stated, he says: "Therefore, this [is not so]," and so forth.

Since it has been established—starting from "because of the cognition considered to be a means of valid knowledge regarding oneself and others" and ending with "lest there be the undesirable consequence of being indistinguishable from deep sleep"—it follows that this absolute position of yours is not tenable: namely, that every single consciousness (*saṃvitti*), or intellect (*buddhi*), without exception—even that of one who is not omniscient—must necessarily cognize its own nature, its own self; the meaning of the particle *eva* (only/necessarily) is that it does not fail to cognize anything of itself.
In response to the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "even though its essential nature is consciousness.

This is because, as stated by Dharmottara, there are two kinds of error: the worldly, consisting of the perception of two moons and so forth, and the scriptural, characterized by the differentiation of the cognizing consciousness; [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the latter.

For instance: if that [consciousness] perceives in the self the distinction from its own error—just as it perceives its own nature as being real, conscious, and so forth—then how could there be that delusion? Otherwise, the cognition of blue would be a delusion regarding yellow.
By this, worldly delusion is refuted; for such delusion cannot exist in the absence of the form of the object to be grasped, since it is dependent upon that.
Thus begins [the argument].
Up to this point,
there has been delusion, because it is based on the form of the apprehended object.

On this point, another says: "The absence of error is not a fault for the Buddhist, because he accepts that [very thing]. That is not so; for if one accepts reality exactly as it appears, there would be the consequence of the Jaina view, and if that were the case, what would be established for you? To this, he says: "Determination," and so forth; here too, the phrase "this is not an absolute [position]" follows.

The meaning of this is as follows: since consciousness belonging to another is of such a nature, therefore—either for that reason, or for the very reason that it consists of a determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*)—consciousness determines its own form in every respect because it takes the form of the object; however, this is not an absolute certainty, because it would follow that error (*bhrānti*) could not exist. This is the connection [of the argument].

For just as the cognition of a Vaiśeṣika is of a determinative nature (*vyavasāyātmikā*) and determines the subject (*dharmin*) being thus apprehended as "this," so too, if its discrimination between either "pillar-ness" or "person-ness" were inherent to its very nature—otherwise there would follow the consequence of the non-establishment of its own nature—then it must determine it. From where, then, could there be the establishment of doubt and so forth? [It would lead] to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, concluding the established consistency of the entire one-sided doctrine (*ekāntavāda*) with the self, he says: "And in that manner," meaning in that way, when there is the state of all being a single sentence, [the cognition] bears—that is, possesses—the characteristic, the definition, or the essential nature (*svarūpa*), which consists of both the experience and the other, the non-experience, of its own object (*svārtha*) or of itself and its object (*sva-artha*).

What is that? This [definition of] cognition (*vijñāna*) was stated with reference to the Buddhist (*saugata*); or else, it was spoken with reference to the Vaiśeṣika, bearing the nature of either the determination of its own and others' forms or the opposite thereof—where "determination" (*vyavasāya*) means ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), and "the other" (*itara*) means non-ascertainment, and these two constitute the nature or essential form (*svabhāva/svarūpa*). Thus, it is this [cognition] that possesses such a nature.
If it is asked how this could not be established in any way without the principle of manifoldness (anekānta), he states the conclusion with the words beginning "that" (tat).

Since this is so, therefore there exists no "non-conceptual perception" (*avikalpada-darśana*). That is to say, that perception—such as that imagined by the Sautrāntikas and others—in which conceptualization (*vikalpa*), defined as the determination (*vyavasāya*) of one's own or another's nature, is absent, has been described thus. It is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it is direct (*pratyakṣa*) regarding both self-nature and other-nature.
Why is this? To this he says: "By itself," and so forth.

Whatever nature (*svabhāva*), or essential form (*svarūpa*), or own-being (*svo bhāvaḥ*)—that is, the object (*padārtha*) as such—is experienced and grasped by itself, by its own [nature], even that is not [grasped] merely in some other way; rather, it is [not grasped] in every respect, just as in the case of momentariness and so forth, so too in the case of blue and so forth.

Alternatively, since [the cognition] is of the nature of a non-experience even with respect to that mode of dependence—just as it is with respect to the mode of dependence on the absence of another experience of conceptual construction—it follows that it is like something unexperienced.

Now, if it is argued: "Let it be that the Nyāya and other systems do not have perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because, being insentient like a jar and so forth, they lack the capacity for self-apprehension; but the Buddhist system does, because it possesses that capacity and is therefore sentient"; to this he says: "Even if there were sentience," and so forth.
The word "even" (*api*) is used in the sense of possibility, because in reality sentience is not established therein, even in that case.
The connection [of the words] is: "because even that which has been personally experienced is, in every respect, as if never experienced";
regarding this, he states an illustration—*as in deep sleep and so forth*—which has already been considered.

If it is asked: "Since consciousness exists there by its very nature, for what reason is it said that 'even though there is consciousness'?"—to this he replies: "In regard to an object made its own [object] (*svaviṣayīkṛta*), etc.

That is to say, regarding an object experienced by itself (*svenātmanā*) in the form of a momentary blue thing and so forth, after that, inference and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arise because they depend upon that [direct perception], which is why it is said "even though there is consciousness," [referring to the authority of] the "vision" (*darśana*) as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) imagined by others.

If it is argued: "Surely a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which establishes valid knowledge (*pramiti*). Since that [knowledge] has already arisen from direct perception (*darśana*) alone with respect to blue and so forth, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not at all a means of valid cognition there; why then is it said to be 'subsequent to that'? To this he replies: "That," and so forth.

Because only inference—[which is] dependent upon that [perception]—is the means of valid cognition regarding momentariness and the like, and because only conceptual construction is established as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for valid knowledge regarding blue and the like, it is held that validity belongs to that [conceptual construction] alone.

Now, since a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for valid cognition (*pramiti*), perception (*darśana*) is also said to be the most effective means for that [cognition].

As Arcata stated: "The ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā-niścaya*) arises from perception; therefore, it is said that the ascertainment of the property of the subject is 'through perception'.
To this, he provides the following reply: "Even though it is its cause," and so forth.

Because there is no difference [between the object and its cognition], as stated in *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.6, "In the case of a similar recollection," perception (*darśana*) lacks the status of being a cause for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For this very reason, even if it were a cause thereof, the word "even" (*api*) implies a possibility;
however, just like sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth, it does not possess primary validity (*pramāṇatā*). Therefore, non-conceptual perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that its establishment occurs by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), [the author] replies here with the words "by way of metaphorical designation" and so forth.

This means that because there is no obstruction to the linguistic designation in the manner of saying "it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to metaphorical designation," such as proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and so on, [the cognition] is not self-cognized (*asvasaṃvedita*).
In the case of non-conceptual [cognition], there is valid cognition by way of self-awareness.
The meaning is that because it apprehends what has already been apprehended,
the conceptual construction "this is blue," which arises subsequent to direct perception, is itself the cognition.

"The establishment or ascertainment of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) in the locus of the probandum (sādhyadharmin), whether through perception or inference"—this is [the definition of a reason] (*Hetubindu*, *Ṭīkā*, p.

39). Now, one might object: "In conventional practice, there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) than perception; for it is only non-conceptual vision that can be established as the primary means of valid cognition. To this, he says: "Since," and so forth.
This word "since" (*yataḥ*) has the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*), and it is a term used to denote the origin.

The meaning of this is as follows: from the very beginning—that is, from that primary cognition (*vijñāna*) by which the activity of the person (*puruṣa*) proceeds—it is established that such cognition, being of the nature of determination (*vyavasāya*), is primarily a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By the word "from" (*prabhṛti*), he shows this: previously, when there is a sudden perception of a cause of pleasure or a cause of pain, and subsequently the experience of pleasure and so forth, the person does not yet understand in this way: "This is the means for my pleasure," or "This is the means for my pain."

Furthermore, as for this objection raised here—that at the time of perceiving the means to pleasure and so forth, there is no experience of the pleasure itself, and at the time of experiencing that pleasure, there is no perception of its means; therefore, how can the relationship of cause and effect between the means to pleasure and the pleasure be known?—this has been refuted by the passage beginning with *siddhivi. 1.10*, "because of the rule of the unity of appearance" (*pratibhāsaikyaniyame*).

From that, there arises an impression (*saṃskāra*) due to the comprehension of it; then, at another time, through the perception of that same object or something of its kind, that impression is awakened, resulting in memory (*smṛti*) of it; from that, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) arises in the form "this is that very thing" or "this is similar to that"; from this also, there arises reflection (*tarka*) in the form "whatever is thus, by such a duration of time or by a specific collection of causes, produces such an effect"; from that also, there follows inference (*anumāna*) in the form "this being thus, therefore—as before—it will produce the intended effect"; and from this, the person's activity (*pravṛtti*) ensues.

And this will be stated right here [in the same work], starting from the verse *siddhivi° 1.27*: "Having recollected by means of sensory cognitions (*akṣajñānaiḥ*)... and so forth, at the time of experiencing pleasure and the like.

Regarding this further point—that because activity lacks a resultant fruit, no one would ever engage in any activity whatsoever—this is contradicted by perception, since a single variegated cognition can occur both simultaneously and sequentially.

If it is argued that even from the cognition of water in a mirage and the like there is human activity, and therefore that too should be established as primarily a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [the author] says here: "Those preceded by deliberation" (*prekṣāpūrvikā*).

That which has as its preceding cause—its antecedent condition—a preeminent vision (*kṣā*) free from doubt and other defects is thus described; that is to say, it is preceded by right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). This is because [wrong knowledge] is excluded through the negation of extremes such as being beyond all error and conceptual construction. Now, one might object: "Since human activity proceeds precisely from non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*), therefore that alone is established as the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To this it is said:

When those [objects] are seen with foresight, practical activity proceeds through desire arising from the memory produced by the power of cognition regarding what has been seen. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p. 24)

If this is argued, here he says: "In that which is seen by oneself," and so forth. This means that regarding an object perceived by oneself—that is, experienced through one's own [consciousness]—there arises a cognition consisting of a determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*) that is independent of anything else. For this very reason, it is held that recollection and the like do not arise from anything other than this; and this has been stated in this very same work: "From perception consisting of a determinative judgment... (Siddhiviniścaya 1).
