From such statements as these, it might be thought: "Let it be granted that human activity preceded by deliberation arises from cognition consisting of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka-jñāna*); nevertheless, its status as a primary means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not established, because it is non-concordant (*visaṃvādaka*) due to having a universal (*sāmānya*)—which is not a real entity—as its object."
As it has been said: "Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a manifestation of a non-entity; because it is deceptive, it is a corruption.
To this, he replies: "Non-deceptiveness," and so forth.
The sense is that since there is a single existence of non-deceptiveness independent of anything else, and because the object of conceptual construction is, in reality, an entity.
It is for this very purpose that [the author] has extracted this [verse], beginning with "svekṣite" and so forth, regarding the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*); see *Praśastakandali*, p. 190.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 31; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 500; Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa, p. 314.

In the *Ratnāvalī*, page 32, and the *Dharmasaṃgraha*, page 134, it is here objected: "The activity of a person toward the past does not arise from a determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*), because that [past] has already been experienced; nor [does it arise] toward the present, because that is currently being experienced."
For no one acts when pleasure and the like are being experienced, because that would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress of activity;
nor does one act toward what is yet to come, because it is not apprehended through perception, which would mean there is no human activity anywhere.
To this, the reply begins with "Because this... and so forth.
Whether this objector Prajñākaragupta or someone else were to proceed, even while conducting such an investigation, he would not remain [in his position].
Of what nature? "Of unswerving activity.

This is what is meant: if this discerning person were to see with certainty that there is no object of engagement, he would not proceed toward it with constant, unswerving activity; yet, such is not the case for one who investigates thoroughly, for even while investigating, he does not fail to remain [in his course], being of unswerving activity.

This is what is meant: since even a person who has thoroughly investigated [the situation] is seen to engage with water and so forth, one who acts thus toward that [object] and one who feels aversion toward it deserve to be treated with indifference.
If it is asked, "Where, then, would he act?"—to this he says: "In what is beneficial," and so on.

This is a dual number referring to two causes; therefore, it refers to the cause for the attainment of what is beneficial, such as rice and the like, and the cause for the avoidance of what is harmful, such as poison and the like.

Nor is this objection valid—that if pleasure and pain are not apprehended, it is impossible to know whether something is beneficial or harmful and thus act accordingly; nor that if inference is not apprehended, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) cannot be recognized as its cause, so that one seeking that [result] would not engage in it, because [inference] does not arise; and therefore, due to the non-arising of inference, how could one understand reality for oneself or enlighten another? This is because self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedanādhyakṣa*), which is partless, has become the subject of dispute.

If it is asked: "In that case, while this person does not perceive the future inference, he nevertheless understands that the mark (liṅga) is its cause; yet, one who has not perceived such pleasure and so forth does not desire that food and so forth are its cause—how then can his activity proceed according to his own will? To this, he says: "Confusion," and so on.

The attainment of that which is abandoned, and the abandonment of that which is attained—this is confusion (*saṅkara*). Where there is attainment, there is abandonment; and where there is abandonment, there is indeed attainment—this is intermixture (*vyatikara*). Because of the absence of distinction (*vyatireka*) between these two, from whatever point [it begins], the activity (*pravṛtti*) being experienced is thus established. Therefore, since activity would also occur therein, there is an infinite regress of activity (*pravṛtty-anavasthā*).
The reading contained within this has been written twice.
One who desires happiness seeks the inferential object through the logical mark.

Regarding this, another Buddhist proponent of inference states: "Its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) exists only where it produces that [cognition]. This is the view of Dharmottara.

And by the very same reasoning by which we have refuted it, the Jains have likewise refuted it; thus, their position is merely a case of standing on already established ground. However, perception (*darśana*) is a means of valid cognition independent of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

If conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), how can it depend upon direct perception (*darśana*)? If it were a means of valid cognition, there would be a contradiction regarding the number of such means.
To this, the specific Buddhist [teachers] provide the answer: "Like the sight of poison," and so forth.
For the Jains,
the perception of the ignorant person, though free from conceptual construction, is like the sight of poison.

Then nothing would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it would lack non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*). Having observed this discrepancy, the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Fools), like an ignorant person, treats it as a valid means of knowledge; yet he does not define valid cognition as being of a determinate nature and non-contradictory. Thus, with a perverted understanding of definitions, how can he claim that every perception (*darśana*)—being non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*)—is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that is nonetheless contradictory, like an ignorant man’s vision of poison?
For it is only that which is determinate in nature that can be established as non-contradictory, whereas its opposite, being indeterminate in nature, is contradictory.

[Objection: But surely cognition that manifests pleasure, blue, and so forth, even if non-conceptual, is non-contradictory; and it is not that this [non-conceptual cognition] is non-contradictory, but rather that it is precisely conceptual because it is determinate in nature.

Since non-conceptual perception, though non-erroneous and consistent with reality, requires another means of proof—just as [the existence of] momentary destruction and so forth does—because it lacks certainty, even such a vision that is "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) fails to provide a reliable cognition. This is because a definitive determination cannot be made in accordance with the vision itself; for objects do not appear in their specific forms, and no ascertainment occurs through a universal form.

It is argued that defining a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*) according to the intention of each individual practitioner is untenable, because its object would be sublated by other means of valid cognition, which would contradict one's own position.

Therefore, this non-conceptual experience, which grasps the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is not capable of determining the appearance as it truly is; thus, it cannot be called "non-contradictory.

Furthermore, it is not logical to establish the particular characteristic through a non-conceptual nature, because—like [the doctrine of] non-duality (*advaita*)—there would be an absence of differentiation (*bhedābhāva*).

Even if there were an absolute distinction between conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established; therefore, just like the perception of poison belonging to one who is ignorant—possessed of non-understanding, doubt, and error—which, regarding an object experienced by oneself, produces doubt or error and is thus ineffective, so too is [the case here]. Consequently, all four types [of perception] would not be valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or rather, if it were so, even perception born of repeated practice (*abhyāsaja*) would not be valid cognition, just like that which is not born of repeated practice. Of what nature would it be? It would be non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*); for "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) is defined as a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃsargayogya-pratibhāsā pratītiḥ*), according to Nyāyabindu 1.1.1.
"It does not have that as its essence" means that it has as its object an entity devoid of parts (*niraṃśārtha*).

Here the intention is this: if perception independent of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then alas, the perception of poison by one ignorant of poison would likewise be unimpeded and thus would also be a valid means of knowledge.
And if that were the case, no one would ever act toward poison due to doubt and the like.

Furthermore, as for the explanation that "that which is free from conceptual construction (kalpanā) is valid only where it produces inferential cognition"—that too is refuted by this [very argument]. For even here, since there may occasionally occur the perception of a specific sign (liṅga) in the form of poison associated with a future death, as well as the recollection of similar instances—which are causes of inference—inferential cognition would be produced, and thus [the indeterminate perception] would be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
But this is not the case; therefore, like the perception of poison, every non-conceptual perception of one who is ignorant is invalid.

If it is argued: "But surely, even in the state of habitual practice (*abhyāsadaśā*), the perception of poison or other things, though conceptual in nature, is seen to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, for one who says that all perception is invalid, there is a contradiction with what is observed (*dṛṣṭabādha*)," [the author] replies here: "Because of the loss of non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādahānitaḥ*). This means: because of the loss of that non-contradiction—that is, the absence of disagreement—regarding the claim that "in the state of habitual practice, perception restricted to each individual atom is a valid means of knowledge"; or alternatively, it should be explained as being "because of the loss of that which is observed," namely, the fact that only atoms are not actually attained.
Because even for an ignorant person there is no loss of non-contradiction regarding the sight of poison,
he says "poison," etc., explaining by way of contrast (vyatireka) the sight of poison with derision.
Having observed poison—that is, having made it an object of perception—he establishes it there; he declares it to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "What [does he declare]? he says: "Like an ignorant person.
An "ignorant person" has already been explained; like him, the Buddhist is unrefined, characterized by lack of proficiency, doubt, and error—this is the intended meaning.
And regarding that, the objection has been stated: "Why does it not [itself] function as a means of valid cognition? To this he says: "But not," and so forth;
[the sense is that] a means of valid cognition, which is of the nature of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*), functions as a means of valid cognition, but it does not [function as such] again.

In what sense is that [means of valid cognition]? To this, [the author] characterizes and determines it as such by stating, "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory knowledge" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.3). For this reason, the "Beloved of the Gods" (*devānāmpriya*), whose intellect is characterized by a contrary definition, [is refuted].

If one thinks that whatever is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not non-contradictory (*avisamvādaka*), and that whatever is non-contradictory is not known to be a means of valid cognition, then [it follows that] the perception of poison would not be a means of valid cognition, nor would a determinative cognition (*vyavasāyātmaka-jñāna*) be non-contradictory; for even water is merely a perception (*darśana*). To this, he says: "All indeed," and so forth.
By this, he explains the remainder by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "all indeed" means without exception, every perception.
Of what nature is it? It is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). In what manner does it belong to the ignorant? How is it not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

In what way, then, is it [non-conceptual]? To this he says: "It is non-concordant (*visaṃvādaka*); because it is non-concordant," as is understood when it is said, "It is existent and impermanent," [whereby it is implied] "because of its existence" (*sattvāt*).

To the question, "Whose [perception] is it, and what is it like? he says: "It is like a poison-vision for one who is ignorant. And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): "Every non-conceptual perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is non-concordant (*visaṃvādaka*), like a poison-vision for one who is ignorant. Regarding that which was stated by the opponent—"The non-conceptual perception under discussion is a direct valid means of knowledge because it is non-concordant"—he says, demonstrating the contradictory nature of that reason: "Only of that which consists of determinate cognition (*vyavasāyātmaka*)," and so forth. The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is: "of that alone, and not of any other."

If it is argued that what was stated [previously] is redundant because its non-contradictoriness is already established even without it, and that the phrase "even the water" is likewise written twice and thus useless—referring to the statement beginning with "all this indeed," and so forth—and that in that case the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) because non-contradiction exists only for such a perception (*darśana*); to this, he says: "That," and so forth.

Regarding that cognition which is of a determinate nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*), what is its other [corresponding factor] by whose non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) [it is so characterized]? To this he says: "By being of a non-determinate nature" (*avyavasāyātmakatvena*), that is, by having as its object a non-substantial, partless, and absolute [entity].

If it is argued: "But surely, when it is said that perception (*darśana*) is non-correspondent because it is of a non-determinate nature, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) as being a part of the very thesis (*pratijñātārthaikadeśa*), just like [the argument] 'Sound is impermanent because it is sound'"; let this be for now, since this will be examined later.

It might be thought: "Although non-conceptual perception is non-correspondent regarding momentary destruction and the like, it is nevertheless correspondent regarding blue, pleasure, and so forth; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished with respect to a portion [of the subject].
Demonstrating this very point, the opponent says: "But surely," and so on;
"but surely" (*nanu*) is used here in the sense of a deliberation (*vitarka*).
And regarding the claim that non-conceptual cognition appearing as pleasure, blue, and so forth is non-erroneous, he states the following reply: "And not," and so on;
for that cognition appearing as pleasure, blue, and so forth is certainly not non-conceptual and non-erroneous.

What then is it? To this he says: "But rather, it is indeed conceptual. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because it consists of ascertainment (vyavasāya)," that is, because its nature is the determination of an object that possesses both real universality and particularity.

Nor can it be maintained that the property of non-contradiction belonging to one thing belongs to another, for if such a conceptualization were possible, then one could likewise conceptually attribute "non-existence" and so forth—well-established in some cases like sound as being a universal (sāmānya)—and thus that too would have to be pointed out as a "partially unestablished" (bhāgāsiddha) reason.
If it is asked, "How is it known that this [reason] is conceptual?"—to this he says: "That... (tad).

If it is accepted that this non-conceptual perception—which has the appearance of pleasure, blue, and so forth, and which is non-erroneous—requires another means of proof (sādhana) for [the establishment of] the appearance of momentary destruction and so on, then [the sentence] "perception requires another means of proof" is to be connected by changing the case ending [to the genitive].
Why is this so? To this he says: because, like non-ascertainment and so forth, the nature of pleasure and so forth is not ascertained by perception;
therefore, it does not depend upon that [other means], and thus it is indeed conceptual.
Because there is no exclusion of superimposition regarding the momentary aspect, it is a conceptual construction of the Buddhist.

If it is argued that non-conceptual perception indeed depends upon another means of cognition, this does not render it non-authoritative; for by being assisted by another means of cognition, its non-contradictory nature is all the more established, just like scripture. To this, he says: "Free from conceptual construction," and so forth.
"Free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous"—the word "also" (api), meaning possibility, should be connected with both [terms];
and this being so, even in the case of perception, its own object is established. (Svārthasiddhi-vṛtti 1)

Since conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) has been established by [the passage] beginning with "23" as the internal perception of the two-fold appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since error (*vibhrama*) has been established by [the passage] beginning with "Siddhi-vi°," how is it that perception (*darśana*) indeed contradicts [reality]? To this he says: "In accordance with perception" (*yathā-darśanam*). Because a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) cannot occur without conforming to perception—namely, if the determination were in accordance with perception, then by virtue of following that [perception], it would necessarily be non-contradictory to it; however, this is not the case—so he considers.
And this [cognition] is not non-conceptual and non-erroneous;
regarding this very point, he states another argument beginning with "viśeṣa" (the particular):

because objects—such as pleasure and so forth, or blue and so forth—are not manifested by the cognitions of the eye and other senses in their particular form, that is, in a form distinct from those of its own and other classes, the connection is that "this is not non-conceptual and non-erroneous," but rather it is indeed conceptual. He says the same regarding this as well, beginning with "sāmānya" (the universal).

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction, meaning "both in a general form and in a specific form. Because there is no determination following from the initial apprehension (*vyavasāya*), the construction of the phrase "but even for objects in the cognition of the eye and so forth, it is indeed conceptual" indicates that [the cognition] is a perception merely by virtue of its dependence on another means of proof.

Having demonstrated the opponent's reasoning—which holds that non-conceptual cognition appearing as pleasure, blue, and so forth, is indeed non-erroneous (*avisaṃvādaka*)—he refutes it, saying: "According to the intention of the cognizer," and so on.
Non-erroneousness is the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); a means of valid cognition is non-erroneous cognition (*pramāṇam avisaṃvādi jñānam*). (Pramāṇavārttika 1.7)

Based on this statement, one might ask: "In what manner is that [identity]? To this he says: "According to the intention of the perceiver (*yathāpratipatrabhiprāyam*). There is no identity between the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the attained (*prāpya*); otherwise, there would be either only the perceived or only the attained.

Nevertheless, because of the determination of their identity, the intention of perceivers is that "whatever was seen, that very thing was attained. It is "according to the intention of the perceiver" in the sense of not transgressing that [intention]; the intended meaning is that it is not ultimately real (*na pāramārthikam*).

Alternatively, just as the water in a mirage is not ultimately real despite being regarded as real, nevertheless, due to the firmness of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the persistence of its appearance for a long time, it is their intention that "this water is real because it performs a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*), whereas the other [water] is not because of the opposite. Without overstepping that [intention], [the statement is made] according to the perspective of those who perceive it thus.

Alternatively, since there is non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*)—that is, the attainment of what was seen—even in dream-states as in the waking state, it would follow that such cognition is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nevertheless, living beings do not become satisfied by that [dream-cognition], and thus that attainment of the object is not [true attainment]; however, in the waking state, the opposite is the case. This is their intention. [The phrase] "in accordance with the intention of the perceiver" (*yathāpratipatrabhiprāyam*) means without transgressing that [intention]. If it is argued that even so, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) would result in being non-contradictory because its existence occurs precisely therein, he says in response: "having an object uncontradicted by another means of knowledge."

That whose object is not sublated by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is described as having the characteristic of valid cognition; furthermore, this is possible only in non-conceptual [perception] and not in conceptual [cognition], because universals and the like are sublated by other means of valid cognition. Regarding this, he states the refutation: "This is improper";
that is, even this definition of perception is improper.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the contradiction of one's own doctrine.
For the Buddhist, his own (sva) or personal (ātmiya) doctrine is that everything internal and external is momentary and partless; [the objection is] because of the contradiction of that.
For there is no intention on the part of cognizers that momentary, partless atoms have been seen or attained, such that their definition would be tenable by not transgressing that [intention].

Furthermore, if that characteristic is not ultimate (pāramārthika) because it conforms to the intentions of those who hold specific views, then how could there be an ultimate establishment of such [doctrines] as "all conditioned phenomena are momentary" or "there is nothing other than the cognition itself to be experienced," as in the case of other systems? Since the non-duality of appearance has already been refuted and will be refuted immediately hereafter, and since it has been considered that valid cognition consists solely in non-conceptual perception whose object is not sublated by other means of knowledge, this [notion of momentariness and so forth] is merely a conventional usage based on the simple unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object.
—*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 398;
"Where there is firmness of latent impression (*vāsanā*), that is a waking cognition," p.
72; "That which is seen in a dream perishes instantly."

This is due to the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and not because the object itself can be established as real—even in the case of dream-cognition (*svapnajñāna*). — *Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 360.
The definition of direct perception is the attainment of what was seen in a dream, according to one's intention.

In this regard, it was said by the Blessed One: "All conditioned phenomena are momentary; how could there be activity in things that are stable? That which is their arising is itself the agent, and it is that very thing which is called the doer. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 11)

"All conditioned phenomena are momentary; this triple world, O sons of the Conqueror, is indeed consciousness alone"—*Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā*, p. 376; *Tantravārttika*, p. 120; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 731.
There is nothing else to be experienced by it, nor is there any other experience of it;
since the same objection applies to that as well, it shines forth by itself—
*Pravāḍavāda*, 2.
This [verse] is cited with the variant reading "buddhyāsti... svayaṃ... grāhyagrāhakavaidhuryāt" at *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā* (Vyomavatī), p. 525.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 540;
*Ślokavārttika*, p. 121;
*Āptaparīkṣā*, p. 47.
Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 110; Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika-ṭīkā, p. 275; Śāstradīpikā, p. 195.
Prameyakaṇṭhābharaṇa, p.
90; Nyāyakumudacandra, p. 133;
Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p. 251.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 483;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 150;
Syādvāda-mañjarī, p. 139.
As in other doctrines, [this is stated] on page 31 of the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* and on page 174 of the *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-ṭīkā*.

If it is argued that there is no proof [of duality] because one accepts the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaita*), he replies by stating the conclusion: "Therefore, this non-conceptual experience—of what nature?—is a grasper of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇagrāhī*) which manifests according to the object (*yathārthanirbhāsa*). Yet, because it is incapable of making a determination (*vyavasāya*) without overstepping the manifestation of the object, it is not what is called 'non-contradictory' (*avisaṃvādaka*); rather, it is indeed contradictory."

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that [cognition] is non-contradictory not because it produces a conceptual determination (*vyavasāya*), but rather because it grasps the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

For even the conceptual determination is nothing other than the grasping of that [particular], since the appearance of universals (*jāti*) and so forth has been refuted in sensory cognition"; to this he replies: "And not... and so forth.

That is to say, it is neither at all logical nor tenable to establish the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) by means of an unconceptualized—that is, undetermined—intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or essential form (*svarūpa*).
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "like non-duality" (*advaitavat*).

Here, "non-duality" is understood as the non-duality of the Person (*puruṣādvaita*), and not the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaita*), because there is no dispute with the Buddhist regarding the latter. [The opponent objects: "Is it not the case that there is a distinction between non-duality and a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) based on whether they appear or not? Therefore, 'like non-duality' is incorrect. To this, he replies: "because of the absence of difference" (*bhedābhāvāt*).

Because there is an absence of differentiation—that is, of particularity—and because even the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) does not appear, he considers this to be so; therefore, it is well said: "like non-duality" (*advaitavat*).

Now, if it is thought: "If that non-duality consists of the manifestations of pleasure and so forth, or blue and so forth, then the name 'Person' (*puruṣa*) would have been applied within the Buddhist (*saugata*) system of 'with-aspect' (*sākāra*); otherwise, it is incorrect to say that the insentient does not manifest. Furthermore, if pleasure, blue, and so forth exist, there is no such non-duality; and if they do not exist, let it be the same for the subject under discussion as well,"—to that he gives the reply beginning with "of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpānām*), etc.

The point is this: even if there were an absolute distinction among conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as pleasure and so forth, or blue and so forth—and even if there were an absolute [monism of] partless particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—it is not only in the case of non-duality (*advaita*) that the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) or the consequence of non-existence (*asattva*) would follow; for in those cases as well, there occurs an appearance otherwise [than the thing-in-itself]. Otherwise, the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) [would be impossible], as was stated [previously];
and because of the apprehension of particular characteristics, the non-duality of the Person (*puruṣādvaita*) [is refuted].

This is another explanation: just as the objects of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising immediately after the perception of partless particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) are distinctions such as "gross" and "distant," so too the objects of those [constructions] arising immediately after the perception of the partless person (*niṣkala-puruṣa*) are distinctions such as "pleasure" and "blue. And since it is established that even in the absolute difference (*bhedai-kānta*) of those conceptual constructions, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the term "own" (*svaḥ*) refers to the entity (*bhāva*) or category (*padārtha*) imagined by the Buddhist; the state of being "excluded from that" (*tasmānniṣkrāntānām*) is the meaning. The connection is that because of the establishment of that [absence of nature], there is an absence of difference (*bhedābhāva*).

To this, the following is said: "Non-contradictory cognition is necessarily conceptual"—let it be so; nevertheless, that [cognition] is not perception, because, being mental in nature, it lacks clarity (*vaiśadya*). And thus it has been said: "For one who is permeated by conceptualization, there is no manifestation of a clear object even in a dream; nor is that [dream-cognition] remembered as such, for it is a memory-cognition, and a memory-cognition does not possess the vision of such an object."
If it is argued as in Prajñāpradīpa 2.283, he says in response: "And this is not [the case]," and so forth,
which is a conceptual construction (*vikalpaka*).

It is not remembered even in a dream that for a cognition permeated by conceptual construction there is a manifestation of a clear object; nor is that [dream-cognition] a memory, for it is a perception of such an object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.283) And this [perception of a clear object] is not considered to be a mental perception whose nature is determinative.

Because it is not subject to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and because it depends on the presence of an object, mental conceptualization in the form of passion and so forth is averted by analytical discernment—that is, by the knowledge of reality which serves as its antidote. For this [conceptual cognition] is not a mental perception whose nature consists in the determination of its own object; for even when a cow is present, once the mental cognition of a cow has been averted, if one then forms a conceptualization of a horse, there is still the certain determination of the cow itself.
Furthermore, that ascertainment would not depend on the presence of an object, just like other conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, it is logical that this clear, determinate cognition—which conforms to the positive and negative concomitance with the presence of its own object, which is suppressed by analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and which is non-contradictory—is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
this applies to cognitions manifesting as pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth.
Of what nature is it? It is of the nature of determination (*vyavasāya*), consisting of ascertainment, and mental—that is, caused by the mind. And it is certainly not [perception] in this sense.

Why is that? To this he says: "Perception" (*pratyakṣa*) means clear—either dependent on the senses (*indriyāśrita*) or otherwise—and since this [determination] is not so, it is not mental perception.
And that [cognition] which depends upon them [the senses], because it follows the presence and absence of the sense organs and because it does not exist when they are absent, is likewise [sensory].
However, if this were purely mental, then even the cognition of two moons and so forth would have to be mental; thus, this [position] regarding conceptual construction is contradicted.

Furthermore, if that which conforms to the presence or absence of the sense organs (*akṣa*) is [the cognition], then it is the same [as the argument previously stated]. According to *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.296, if it possesses transformation (*vikriyāvat*), then the question remains: why is this very [transformation] not denied? This is the implied meaning (*śeṣa*).
Right here he states another argument, beginning with "by means of *pratisaṃkhyā*," and so forth.
Because it is not subject to cessation—that is, because it is not being negated—by means of *pratisaṃkhyā*, which is to say, by means of individual conceptualization (*prativikalpa*).

And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: this knowledge, which has entered the sphere of dispute, is not mental (*mānasa*), because it is not subject to cessation by means of *pratisaṃkhyā*; for whatever is mental is not subject to cessation by means of *pratisaṃkhyā*, just like the mental conceptualization "this is a cow" when a cow is present.
Again, he states the subsequent [point], beginning with "the object" (*artha*), and so forth:

the proximity (*sannidhi*) of an object such as a jar, which is its presence in a suitable location and so on; because of the dependence upon that, the wisdom (*prajñā*) that takes impure things and the like as its focal point (*ālambana*) and serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to passion and the rest is "discrimination" (*pratisaṃkhyāna*). (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 547)
"Cessation is that which is to be attained by means of that specific wisdom; thus it is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Commenting on the verse [from the *Sphuṭārthā*] on page 16, he says: "For this is not... and so forth.
What is the nature of this knowledge that has become the subject of dispute? It is of the nature of a determinate cognition of its own object; what is that? It is rightly argued that it is mental.
"Is it not so? Certainly not.
Why is this? Because [perception] is clearly dependent on the senses (*akṣa*), and for this reason it is not mental (*mānasa*). Thus he says: "In the case of a cow," and so forth.

In what state is the cow, that specific animal? It is present before one. Having formed a mental ascertainment (*viniścaya*) consisting of a conceptual reflection (*parāmarśa*) such as "this is a cow," "it is large," "it is white," "it is long," or otherwise; for at that time, during the process of that [reflection], there is an ascertainment of the cow itself.
"Under what condition? he asks, and replies: "Even when there is the conceptualization of a horse—not only when there is no such conceptualization.

This is what is meant: if this determination of a cow regarding its stable, gross, and common form were mental, like the cognition of a cow under discussion, then it would cease upon the conceptualization of a horse, just as that [previous] cognition did; but it does not so cease. Therefore, it is not mental."
By the phrase "due to ascertainment" (viniścayāt), he demonstrates this:

if, at the time of that conceptual construction, the perception of the cow were non-conceptual, then—just like the perception of momentary destruction—there would be no conventional usage of it, because no conceptualization of it arises, and because two simultaneous conceptualizations are not admitted.
Therefore, it must consist of ascertainment.

Furthermore, by the word "only" (*eva*), this is stated: if the conventional usage of "cow" occurred from mere perception, then the conventional usage of "momentary destruction" and so forth would also occur [simultaneously], because there is no distinction;
yet this is not the case at the time of the conceptualization of a horse.

If it is argued that the cognition of a cow does not arise from the conceptualization of a cow because, at the time there is a certain determination (*niścaya*) of a cow, there is no conceptualization of a horse—since for a Jaina two simultaneous cognitive applications (*upayoga*) do not arise—[we reply: two simultaneous mental cognitive applications are not denied, but neither are two sensory and mental ones. Otherwise, how could [the Jaina] explain the principle of "simultaneous qualities" (*sahabhuvo guṇāḥ*) as stated in the *Nyāya-viniścaya*?

One [cognition] is produced by a sense organ and the other is mental; thus, substance (dravya), which possesses qualities (guṇa) and modifications (paryāya), has simultaneous and successive functions—

"111. Pleasure has the form of exhilaration; consciousness is that which cognizes the object of knowledge. Power (śakti) would be inferable from action, as in the case of a young man during union with his beloved. Would this be an illustration?
As it has been stated in the *Syādvādamahārṇava*: "Pleasure has the form of exhilaration... (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa*, p. 428;
*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 78; *Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 129).
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 478;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 178;
Pramāṇa-ratnamālā, 4.

By this, the claim that "the inference of momentariness is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it excludes the superimposition (*samāropa*) characterized by non-momentary cognition" is refuted; for the superimpositional nature of non-momentary cognition is unestablished, and even when there is the conceptualization of a horse, the exclusion of that [non-momentary nature] remains unestablished.
Thus, he states another argument, beginning with "sa punaḥ," etc.

The word "again" (*punar*) in the phrase "that aforementioned [cognition] again" indicates another logical argument. If the ascertainment (*niścaya*)—the determination that "this is a cow"—were mental, like other conceptual constructions such as those involving God (*īśvara*) and so forth, it would not require the proximity of the object, that is, its presence in a suitable location and so on;
yet it does require it. Therefore, it is not mental.
By this, the point that "it requires the proximity of the object" has been explained by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For the purpose of conclusion, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Since this is the case, therefore this aforementioned cognition—which is clear (*spaṣṭa*), distinct (*viśada*), and of a determinate nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*)—is rightly established as the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Of what nature is it? It conforms to the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of its own object; it is not suppressed by deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodhyā*) and is non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādaka*). It is logical that this is the means of valid perception.

Now, if it is argued that [the cognition] conforms to the presence and absence of its own object—that is, it is an effect of the object—then the refutation of that [object-causality] in the *Laghunyāyasūtra* would be contradicted. This is not so; for conformity to the presence and absence of the object does not pertain to its production, but rather to its operation: it operates toward the correct apprehension of the object, and not otherwise. If it is asked how this is understood to be the intention of the Teacher, [we reply]: from the mention of "its own" (*sva*).
For nothing whatsoever conforms to its own presence and absence during its own production, as that would involve a contradiction.
Therefore, everything is well-established;
the denial that perceptual cognition has an object as its causal efficacy is refuted.
"If the object is the cause of cognition through positive and negative concomitance,
then let it be examined from where the arising of doubt and other such states comes about" (verse 54), and so forth, as is being argued.

It might be argued that there is a conformity with the presence and absence of the object; however, let it not be that [the cognition] is mental, but rather that the sense organ itself is thus erroneous.

Furthermore, errors of the sense organs are not removed by analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), because even for one who contemplates the moon as being one, the appearance of two moons does not cease.
To this, he states the reply: "If that," and so forth;
for if, by means of the knowledge of reality, that [cognition] were invalid because its object is non-existent, then [the objection would hold]. From another [source], however...
Because establishment consists in the nature of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), and because the establishment of an object is impossible [otherwise],—

in the case of a proposition asserting the establishment through perception, since the establishment of that which is the subject of dispute and which awaits another means of proof would be untenable,
even "comprehension" (*adhigati*) is nothing other than a definitive conclusion (*nirṇiti*).

And thus, a cognition that is non-contradictory by way of ascertaining an unascertained object—whether it be of clear appearance or otherwise—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and nothing else.

Therefore, it must be understood that the restriction of non-contradiction and the attainment [of the object] reside only in determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), because they exist only therein and are established solely on its basis. If that which was just mentioned were not a means of valid cognition...
Why is this so? Because its object is a non-entity;
that is to say, it is described as such because its object is a reality consisting of both universal and particular, which is a non-entity.
What, then, is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? The meaning is: none at all.

If it is argued that perception is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), to this he replies with the words "from another," and so forth: the establishment of an object from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) imagined by those who maintain the extreme view of falsity is absolutely impossible.

If it is objected that "establishment" (*siddhi*) is merely apprehension (*adhigati-mātra*), and thus it is possible even from that [non-conceptual perception], to this he replies: because establishment consists of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*).
He states the refutation even if this [cognition] is not admitted due to its being non-conceptual: "In perception," and so forth.

"Perception" means the direct realization of an object; that is to say, the acquisition of its own nature through the form of a partless object. Regarding that very thesis of the Buddhist that "this itself is proof," since proof—that is, cognition—is untenable for perception, it follows that proof consists in the nature of a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*).
Of what nature [is it]? Of that which is the object of conflicting views. Furthermore, of what nature? Of that which awaits another means of proof (*sādhana*).
By this, it is stated that because there is no perception [of it], its establishment does not occur.

As for the claim that "attainment (*adhigati*) is its fruit," that has already been refuted in meaning; now, refuting it in terms of its verbal expression, he says: "Even 'attainment'—not only other things, but even the word 'attainment'—is considered to be nothing but a determination (*nirṇīti*), a synonym for determination. What follows from this? He says: "And thus," and so forth.

And thus, in that manner, the ascertainment of an object not previously ascertained is not mere perception; by that [ascertainment], a cognition that is non-discrepant—whether it be one with a clear manifestation or otherwise one with an unclear manifestation—is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and nothing else. This we consider logical.
And here, self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the result (*phala*). — *Pramāṇasamuccaya* 1.8.
The fruit is one's own cognition; and here, the apprehension of the object is accepted as the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.336)
Or his own experience...— [this is] from *Tattvasaṃgraha*,
verse 1244. He says "therefore," and so forth, for the purpose of concluding the Buddhist [position].

Since this is so, therefore, it must be determined that only in ascertainment (*vyavasāya*)—that is, in determination (*nirṇaya*)—lies the rule of non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādaniyama*), as well as apprehension (*adhigama*) and the grasping of its own object (*svārthagrahaṇa*). Why is this? To this he says: "Because only in that very [ascertainment]—namely, in ascertainment alone—do these two, the rule of non-contradiction and apprehension, exist. Why is this also so? To this he says: "Precisely because of that—namely, because of ascertainment alone—is their establishment (*pratiṣṭhāna*). That is, because those two are established upon it.

Having thus established that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists of determinate, non-contradictory knowledge, he now demonstrates the sequence of activity resulting from it and outlines the future course of action with the words "by means of sensory cognitions," and so forth:
"Having recollected by means of sensory cognitions, having recognized, and reflecting, one proceeds after having ascertained its specific varieties through direct confrontation. (27)
This has been extracted—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 189; *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, second part, page 41:
"The sense organs are touch, taste, smell, sight, hearing, and mind."

Through these [senses], there occurs the apprehension of their respective objects, which constitutes cognition (*mati*) consisting of perception (*avagraha*) and the rest; this pertains to things that are manifold, manifold-in-kind, rapid, explicit, unspoken, and constant, along with their opposites.
Precisely for this reason, non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is established:

for the forms such as "manifold" and "manifold-in-kind" do not arise or perish while remaining entirely unconscious of themselves—such that they might exist yet remain unperceived like conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*)—in the same way that their opposite forms [do not].

Furthermore, we do not perceive forms of cognition as being exclusively characterized by either specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Not perceiving them in such a way, how can we deceive ourselves? Thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), "attainment" (*siddhi*) is considered to be "thinking" (*manana*) because of its manifold nature; or rather, *mati* is [defined as] recollection (*smaraṇa*), which is *smṛti*; recognition (*saṃjñāna*), which is *saṃjñā*; reflection (*cintana*), which is *cintā*; and direct discernment (*abhinibodhana*), which is *abhinibodha*. Thus the authors of the *Tattvārthasūtra* maintain: "Mati, smṛti, saṃjñā, cintā, and abhinibodha are synonymous. (TS 1.13)
13. Thus,
since it is not an absolute rule that cognition, memory, and so forth do not occur without the association of words— such that they would have to be included therein— then,
on the contrary, if that were the case, they would never occur at all, because the recollection of their names would be impossible due to infinite regress and other such faults.

From this foundational passage, other sentences emerge: "Having ascertained its particulars through sensory cognitions (*akṣajñāna*), one acts"—this is the first sentence; "Having recollected its particulars, one acts"—this is the second; "Having recognized its particulars, one acts"—this is the third; "Reflecting and deliberating upon its particulars, one acts"—this is the fourth; "Having ascertained its particulars with direct presence (*ābhimukhyena*), one acts"—this is the fifth; and "Reflecting and having ascertained its particulars with direct presence, one acts"—this is the sixth, taken together.

In this context, the "senses" (*akṣāṇi*) are the faculties such as the eye and so forth; by means of the cognitions that constitute their effects, a person proceeds after having determined their specific distinctions—namely, the particularities of objects that are beneficial or harmful. And this sequence of engagement is to be understood as occurring in the state of habitual practice (*abhyāsadaśā*);

for in that state, a person engaging [in an action] does not necessarily depend upon the recollection of similar previous experiences, since it is not perceived to be so. It is with reference to this very point that it is said: "Perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it functions as an instigator toward what is to be practiced."

All that is correct, but this which was stated by Prajñākaragupta is improper: namely, [the claim that the cause is] "future" (*bhāvini*). If it is asked, "Since people are seen to engage with fire and the like—which are causes of burning and so forth—how can that [fire] be understood as their cause when the burning and such are not yet perceived? [The answer is: Why should it not arise from habituation (*abhyāsa*)? Furthermore, one who, relying on worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), desires to perceive the future through direct perception even though it is not yet apprehended, cannot tolerate another who, relying on that very same convention, maintains that the present [cause] is what is directly perceived. Such a person is of a primitive intellect (*prākṛtabuddhi*).
When an activity occurs with extreme intensity, there is a state of non-cognition by the senses;
where, due to extreme habituation, one acts even without conceptualization, there perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 218.

Therefore, relying on inference established merely through worldly convention, and depending on a well-known relationship, one proceeds toward the apprehension of the means for touching and so forth by seeing [it] as "this is the means for accomplishing purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*).
Subsequently, even without inference based on repeated practice, activity occurs from mere intuition alone; thus, perception is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it prompts action.
Therefore it is said: "Validity [is established] by means of practical efficacy" (*prāmāṇyaṃ vyavahāreṇa*). — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 25.

Or rather, it concerns conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), as it has been said: "When a cow is present, even if one were to set aside the cognition of 'cow' and instead conceptualize it as a horse, one would still determine it to be a cow. In that context, this statement refers to practical activity (*pravṛtti*); for there, because of the contradiction with recollection and so forth, one acts toward the specific instances [of the object] by means of recollection, for the sake of engaging with deposits and other things previously established.
Regarding the statement "having recognized [the object], one acts toward its particulars," this refers to acting upon the mere synthesis of "this is that very same thing" or "this is similar to that.

When one acts while reflecting on these particulars, one acts after having ascertained those particulars with directness (*ābhimukhyena*) regarding their occurrence in a different location and so forth—through the definitive discernment of distinctions such as Mount Meru or the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*), which are otherwise invisible. This is the case when, from the sudden sight of smoke, one acts with the thought, "There is fire here."

Reflecting upon [the reason] and ascertaining its specific varieties, one proceeds; this refers to proceeding from an inference such as "sound is impermanent because it is audible. However, a complete sentence proceeds from an inference such as "there is fire here, because there is smoke; wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen and so forth; and there is smoke here."

In this regard, once the relationship between these two has been previously apprehended by sensory cognitions (*akṣajñāna*), and smoke is subsequently made an object by those very same [sensory cognitions], there occurs the awakening of the prior mental impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*). From that, memory arises; from that, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); then, reasoning (*tarka*); from that, inference (*anumāna*); and from that, purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
Thus, the statement that "one acts after having ascertained the distinction between them through sensory cognitions" is indeed [correct].
Explaining the verse, he says: "Touching," and so forth.
What are touching, tasting, smelling, seeing, hearing, and the mind? They are the sense organs (*indriya*).
The mind will be examined in the proof of the omniscient one.

Regarding those [senses] such as touch and the rest, which serve as causes for the apprehension of their own respective objects—touch and so forth—it is asked: what is that cognition which is produced and acts as the grasper of them? To this, he says: "Cognition" (mitiḥ).
"What is its nature? To this he says: "Avagraha," and so forth;
that is, it consists of avagraha and the others which are to be described later. To the question "Of what is it [the nature]? he says: "Bahu," and so forth.

And there is the simultaneous apprehension of many things of the same class, and of many kinds of things of different classes; it is swift, that is, instantaneous; it is not dependent on light and the like; it is unexpressed, such as the specific taste of molasses and so forth in a drink; it is unspoken;
it is certain, being a cause for firm recollection at a later time.
Of what nature are these? They are "possessing their opposites," meaning they exist together with their opposite modes, such as non-multiplicity and so forth.
And this being so, what is established? To this he says: "For this very reason," and so forth;

because their apprehension of their own objects is of such a nature, for this very reason there is the establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta) through the stages of apprehension (avagraha), speculation (īhā), perceptual judgment (avāya), and retention (dhāraṇā).
Tattvasaṃgraha Sūtra 1.15:
Of the many, the manifold, the quick, the drawn-out, the unspoken, and the constant, along with their opposites.
—Tattvasūtra 1.16.

Now, if it is argued: "Indeed, all this is established from scripture alone and not from anything else, because [otherwise] there would be no perception of it; therefore, for you, this is merely scriptural," he says here: "Not so," and so forth.

For the forms such as "many" and "of many kinds," which belong to consciousness—that is, to cognition produced by the senses—do not arise or perish while remaining unperceived or unknown by themselves; because their arising and perishing are unperceived, they would remain unobserved even if they were real.
Regarding this, he provides an example well-known to the opponent: "like conceptual constructions" (*kalpanāvat*).

Just as these conceptual constructions—such as those of Īśvara and so forth—do not arise or perish unobserved (as stated in the passage beginning with "for these conceptual constructions..."), so too are the entities under discussion.
If you argue that, in the same manner, other forms—such as those of the *abahu* (non-many) and so forth—which are not real, nevertheless arise and perish while remaining unperceived;

and if you further contend that, likewise, the forms of the cognition of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) or the forms of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) themselves arise and perish while being self-cognized; to this we reply: "The particular and the universal," etc.
We do not, moreover, perceive the forms of the cognition of either the particular or the universal in their absolute isolation.
If it is argued that although this has been refuted, those [entities] must nevertheless be considered real, to this he replies with the words "in that very same way" and so forth.

In that very same way—namely, by the manner imagined by others—since one does not perceive them, how can we, through the conceptualization of the forms of cognition within the absolute dichotomy of particular and universal characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), deceive ourselves? That is, we delude ourselves.
That these [cognitions] follow scripture is well-known among the followers of the Sugata;
thus he says: "And these conceptual constructions do not arise and perish entirely without being cognized."
In the *Pravacanaprameya-svopajña-ṭīkā*, page 127,

he states the conclusion with the words "tadevam" and so forth: "Thus, in this manner, the ultimate establishment (*siddhi*)— meaning the production (*niṣpatti*) or cognition (*pratipatti*)— of all things occurs through non-absolutism (*anekānta*), that is, by relying upon non-absolutism."
Showing the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of *mati* and the others, he says: "It is thought" (*manyate*), etc., which is easy to understand.
Demonstrating the consistency between himself and the author of the *Tattvārthasūtra*, he says: "In that way," etc.
In that manner, the authors of the *Tattvārthasūtra* declare [this] in the following way.
How so? He says: "Intellection (*mati*), memory (*smṛti*), recognition (*saṃjñā*), deliberation (*cintā*), and discernment (*abhinibodha*) are synonymous" (TS 1.13). Thus [it is stated].
Since all sūtras possess supplementary explanatory material (*sopaskāra*), the word "is the initiator" (*pravartaka*) must be supplied here.
The word "iti" at the end of its own sūtra serves to mark the conclusion of another sentence;

from this, the following meanings arise: "cognition (*mati*) is the initiator," "recollection (*smṛti*) is the initiator," "perception (*saṃjñā*) is the initiator," "reflection (*cintā*) is the initiator," "determinate cognition (*abhinibodha*) is the initiator," "reflection and determinate cognition are the initiators," and "cognition, recollection, perception, reflection, and determinate cognition are the initiators."
"Manana is mati; smaraṇa is smṛti; saṃjñāna is saṃjñā; cintana is cintā; and abhimukhyena niyataṃ bodhanaṃ is abhinibodha"—thus [it is stated in] Tattvārthavārttika 1.13.5.

If it is argued: "But are these [cognitions] such as cognition (mati) and so forth mutually different or non-different? In either case, [your position] contradicts [the principle that] the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) [is unique]," to this he says: "Not a different object" (*anarthāntara*). Here, the prefix *na* functions in the sense of "slight" (*īṣad-artha*); thus, "not a different object" means "slightly, or in some way, a different object."

And it is stated in the *Laghīyastraya*: "Even though there is a sequential occurrence between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), their identity (*tādātmya*) is to be understood" (*Laghusvopajñavṛtti*, verse 6). Alternatively, when that which has been made the object of apprehension (*avagraha*) is cognized by inquiry (*īhā*), and what has been inquired into is ascertained by determination (*avāya*), and what has been experienced through determination is retained by retention (*dhāraṇā*); this should be applied similarly to the subsequent stages as well. Thus he says, "not a different thing" (*anarthāntara*); the meaning is that cognition (*mati*) and the others have, in some sense, non-different objects. Or, with reference to the final statement, it may be explained as "not having a different purpose for its activity" (*abhinnapravṛttiprayojana*).

[Objection: "But surely, since all [cognitions] such as sensory perception (*mati*) understand their own objects only by means of a preceding verbal designation, they are included within the category of 'hearing words' (*śabda-śruta*) alone; and thus, the investigation of these would occur precisely during the investigation of that [category]. Therefore, a separate investigation here is useless. To this, he replies: "The joining with words," and so forth.

The meaning is that there is no absolute rule (*ekānta*) that sensory perception, memory, and the rest do not exist without the joining of words, but rather that they exist when that joining occurs; for if there were such an absolute rule, they would have to be included therein.
Alternatively, the word "since" (*yataḥ*) may be used in a sense of denial (*ākṣepa*): they certainly would not be conflated [with verbal cognition].
He states the refutation regarding the opposing view: "In that case, [if] absolute [unity]," and so forth.
If that very absolute unity is accepted, then cognition, memory, and the rest would not exist anywhere, whether externally or internally.
Why is this? To this he says: "That which is named," and so forth.
That by whose association memory, recollection, and so forth arise is called its "name"; however, since such [automatic] recollection is impossible, this is what is meant:

it is not the case that wherever there is its own referent, there it must be its name, because memory, recollection, and so forth would necessarily occur from the mere association with that [referent]; rather, they occur from the association with a convention (saṅketa), and precisely because such recollection [of the convention] is impossible, the present topic [remains unestablished].

To the question "How is this so?", he says: "Because of infinite regress and so forth"—that which has infinite regress as its beginning, namely mutual dependence (anyonyasaṃśraya), is described as such; therefore.

To explain: first, there would be the recollection of the name based on the recollection of the designation for its object; that [designation] too would depend on the recollection of the name for its object, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, when an object is present and determined by perception (*mati*) and so forth, there would be a recollection of its specific name, and from that [recollection], perception and so forth would arise—thus resulting in mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
For this very reason, there would be non-comprehension (*apratipatti*), an absence of comprehension, and one must consider that the world would become blind and mute.

And this has been explained [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*] by means of the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*) in the passage beginning with: "The recollection of a similar object, expression, and so forth" (Siddhivi. 1.8).

Thus, by way of supporting the statement that "the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is directly the attainment [of the object], namely the ascertainment of its own referent" (Siddhiviṣaraṇa 1.3), the claim that "comprehension is its result" has been refuted; now,
[we shall refute] the view that "similarity (*sārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition" (Nyāyabindu 1.20).

20. Refuting this by means of another method, he says: "Perceptible," and so forth. By the proponent of Syādvāda-hatred who prattles that "these external atoms are perceptible and are the objects of a single, gross, variegated form of consciousness," [the following follows].
Enough, enough with the Buddha, whether he be external or internal; he is indeed vulgar and confused.
That selflessness (*nairātmya*) is not consistent with the other [the Self], for it is not of the nature of discernment. (28) The object of the Buddhist is twofold: the perceptible and the inferable.
In that regard, he asks: "What are the objects that exist as perceptible domains? He replies: "Where are the atoms? Outside."

Who, then, are they? He says: "These [are] those which possess the designations of the perceived jar and so forth. To the question "Of what [consciousness]? he says: "Of what kind of consciousness? He says: "Of that which has a gross, single, variegated form"—that is, she whose form (ākṛti) or appearance is gross, single, and variegated (śabala); of her [is this]. This is because of the established tenet: "The five groups of consciousness have a collection [of atoms] as their objective support" (*sañcitālambanāḥ pañca vijñānakāyāḥ*).
What is the use of prattling with anyone else, let alone with the Buddha? How can one who prattles such things— being vulgar, incoherent, and confused— be considered wise?
The word "api" (also/even) should be understood here as breaking the sequence of the sentence, and its meaning is "ca" (and).
To the question "By what kind [of person]? he says: "by one who hates the *syādvāda*.

This is what is meant: just as for a cognition having a blue form, the blue is the object of perception and not the yellow and so forth—out of fear that the postulation of similarity (*sārūpya*) would be futile—likewise, for that [cognition] having a single gross variegated form, its perceived object must also be postulated as being of that very same nature, and not atoms.
There is no other object of cognition possible apart from the perceptible and the imperceptible— *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.63.
Because consciousness has the five aggregates as its object— *Prakaraṇasamuccaya* 1.17.

Furthermore, as for what was stated here by Prajñākaragupta—that the establishment of such a [cognition] regarding such an object occurs because that [cognition] is seen even with respect to distant, sparse hairs which do not possess that nature—[we reply:

in that case, atoms are not its objects while being perceptible, but rather they are inferable. Otherwise, even distant, sparse hairs would likewise be objects of a manifold cognition, and thus there would be nothing at all called "error" for the purpose of whose exclusion the inclusion of the term *abhrānta* (non-erroneous) would be meaningful.

If it is argued that those atoms are perceptible because—even though they do not imitate the separation from one another—they imitate mere blueness, just as [a mass of hair] may imitate mere blackness even when it does not imitate the thinning out of the individual hairs; then, since a single thing would possess both a perceived and an unperceived nature, the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekānta) would be established. Therefore, enough with this hostility toward the Syādvāda!

If you say that this is not so in reality—that those atoms are not perceptible in truth, but only by way of conventional usage (vyavahāra)—we reply: it has already been stated that, just like the blue object, the cognition of the blue form would also entail the consequence of being a direct perception of a single, gross, and variegated object.
Just as hairs, even when not in contact with one another at a distance, appear to be arranged in a dense mass, so too are atoms; thus there is no contradiction—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.
296, p. 94, in the section on the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, atoms are indeed atoms;

moreover, just as in the case of consciousness (*saṃvitti*), even a single gross and variegated form is not contradictory. It is for this purpose that the expression "having the form of a single gross variegation" is used.
In that case, since there is a distinction for every atom, consciousness too would be of such a nature;
as it has been said:
"What would be the variety [of objects] in a single [consciousness]? It would not exist even in that cognition."
If it is argued that [this is so] because of such passages as Prajñāpāramitā 2.210 and so forth, he says in response: "Not even that," and so on.

Not only is the external object [untenable], but that consciousness as well—being of the nature of discernment—is not impossible; indeed, it is quite possible, since through a double negation the intended meaning is understood. Otherwise, by the logic already stated, there would be a total void (sakalaśūnyatā);
if one thinks, "Let that [consciousness] be so," he says here: "That selflessness," and so forth.
Because it is thus, therefore the connection is with the phrase beginning "by those who prattle such things as 'selflessness,' which is a total void, whether external or internal."
The meaning is that without the doctrine of manifold aspects (*syādvāda*), that [object] cannot be apprehended.
Thus ends the first chapter, "Establishment of Direct Perception," in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by Anantavīrya, who lived under the guidance of the venerable Ravigupta.
The Second Chapter:
The Establishment of the Conceptual [Cognition] (Savikalpasiddhi)

Desiring to support the meaning stated in the passage beginning with *akṣajñānaiḥ siddhi-vi° 1.27* by means of the subsequent text, he first states three summary verses beginning with *svārthe*, starting as follows:
"This cognition (*mati*) consists of the desire for the specific objects of the distinctions led forward by the sensory apprehension (*avagraha*) of its own object."

Having accepted this distinction, this [cognition] becomes a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) through the process of determination, just like memory or recognition; because it does not have the word as its object, it is non-verbal inference (*aśābdānumā*).

Therefore, that which is associated with a word should be considered "derived from scripture" (*śrutamata*), while that which is produced by the intellect (*ābhinibodhika*) is to be postulated as distinct.

This is its meaning: "Sva" (self) and "artha" (object); the apprehender of these two is "avagraha" (perception). Thus, "svārthāvagraha" is formed from the root *i* with the prefix *ni* and the suffix *ktin*, because no other [root] is under discussion and due to proximity [to the term *avagraha*]. It is understood that [the object] has been brought to or comprehended by means of *avagraha*. In that context, because of the presence of a word denoting a distinction, it is said that "generality is twofold. That desire or inquiry (*īhā*) for which this distinction—namely, the particular—is the object is described as such. This cognition (*mati*) possesses those two as its own nature or essence; therefore, it is called "tadātmikeyaṃ matiḥ" (this cognition having that as its essence).
What does it do? To this he says: "It attains the state of *saṃskāra* (latent impression); it becomes of the nature of *dhāraṇā* (retention).

Having done what? To this he says: "Having approached—that is, having presented—the differentiation (*bheda*), it becomes essentially composed of that [differentiation], meaning it consists of a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*).
Therefore, according to this view, there is no other cognition more indistinct than this; for it is said in the *Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā*, page 237: "The 'heard' (*śruta*) is an indistinct reasoning."
How does that arise? To this he says: "When remembered," and so forth.

The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is also connected with this—therefore, from the mental cognition (*mati*), memory arises; and by means of that memory acting as the cause, the state of recognition (*pratyabhijñānatā*)—in the form "this is that very same thing" or "this is similar to that"—is to be postulated through inference (*anumā*) by a person possessing recognition, based on a logical mark (*liṅga*) which is the object of deliberation (*ūha*).
Of what nature is it? It is "non-verbal," meaning it is an inference for one's own sake (*svārthānumāna*).
He states another name for this: *ābhinibodhikī*.

"Abhinibodha" means a certain cognition (*bodha*) or grasping (*grahaṇa*) of an object (*artha*) from all sides (*abhi*), both in its general form (*sāmānya-rūpa*) and its specific form (*viśeṣa-rūpa*). That which is applied (*niyuktā*) to that [cognition] is so called; it is not considered to be merely the grasping of a general exclusion (*sāmānyāpoha*).

Alternatively, with respect to prior knowledge, the grasping of a somewhat new or unprecedented object (*apūrva-artha*) is *abhinibodha*; that which is applied to that is *matipūrva-śruta* (scriptural knowledge preceded by sensory perception), according to Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.2.3.

From this statement, it follows that from *mati* comes *smṛti*, from that, *pratyabhijñā* (recognition), from that, *ūha* (inductive reasoning), and from this, non-verbal inference (*aśābdānumā*). Thus it is said that [the result] is "heard" (*śruta*).
Furthermore, the word *api* (also) is used with a shifted scope; it should be understood as following immediately after the phrase "heard from *mati*" (*śrutamataḥ*).

Therefore, even beyond this, the meaning is that when the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the past tense (*bhūtakāla*), forming the word *śruta* as "knowledge joined with words" (*śabda-yojita-jñāna*),
there is an analysis (*vigraha*) using the genitive case.
This has been extracted from: *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Vol. II, pp. 187, 360;
"Scriptural knowledge is an indistinct reasoning" (*śrutam avispaṣṭatarkaṇam*)—*Nyāyakumudacandra*, p.
404: "Just as inference for the Buddhists has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, it is not so [for us]."

"Scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) is preceded by intellect (*mati*), and it is divided into two, many, and twelve types"—this might be the thought: "Since perception (*darśana*) [is the basis] and from that comes the determination of distinctions (*bhedaniścaya*), what need is there for an intermediate stage? To this, he provides the answer, beginning with "clarity" (*vaiśadya*); thus says the Buddhist.
If non-conceptual [cognition] were indeed conceptual, and if clarity were absolutely and in reality the cause for determining distinctions;

May [the Lord] effect the severance of the superimposition of the contrary, which is superior to everything; may he effect the striking down everywhere of the variegated manifestation resulting from the transformation of latent impressions deposited by volitional constructions.
For those whose intellects lack continuity with that [Reality], there is no direct perception; so what talk can there be of latent impressions? 2.

If it is argued that clarity (*vaiśadya*), which is the direct perception of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), produces a determination of difference (*bhedaniścaya*) by effecting "ascertainment" (*avāya*); [we reply: why should that clarity, which belongs to the seeing of what has been seen, necessarily and invariably produce it from everything—whether from another object of the same class (*sajātīya*), a different class (*vijātīya*), or from any other entity whatsoever? [It would have to do so] because there is no distinction in its capacity to effect the cutting off of the superimposition of the contrary—that is, the destruction of the erroneous cognition (*samāropa-jñāna*) which superimposes some other contrary quality.

And thus, thinking that all inference—which, like [perception], possesses expectancy and is intended to function by way of excluding superimposition—is useless, he considers this not to be a fault, because in all cases there is an absence of clarity of vision and so forth; having considered that the opponent’s underlying intention has already been answered, he anticipates another position of his, beginning with the words "saṃkalpa" (conceptual construction), etc.

*Kalpanā* is conceptualization (*kalpa*), which is determination (*vyavasāya*). A "correct conceptualization" (*samīcīna-kalpa*) is the ascertainment of distinctions as they truly exist (*yathāvasthita-bheda-niścaya*). That which is produced or established by this is *vāsanā*; its "transformation" (*pariṇati*) is the ripening of its capacity to produce its own effect. This [transformation] is variegated (*citrā*) and manifold; even though there is no difference in the clarity of the perceived object, it is the cause for the ascertainment of distinction in only certain parts, not everywhere. As it has been said regarding oneness and so forth: [the verse continues...]

Inferences such as "everything is momentary because it exists" do not produce conceptual constructions; therefore, inference is fruitful for the purpose of excluding superimpositions regarding things like blue, but not regarding [properties] like momentariness.
This has been extracted—*Sarvadaraśana-saṃgraha*, page 30: "The ascetic's mark [is placed] upon a single female body; the notion that 'the woman is to be devoured' is a conceptual construction."
If this is argued, he says here:
"Effort" (*īhana*) means striving (*īhā*). Therefore, let perception be of the nature of effort, arising from the diversity of that transformation [of consciousness].

What is meant by this is: there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) other than the cognition of the material cause (*upādāna*); since that transformation is diverse, it is said that the transformation of cognition itself is diverse.

And nothing other than the cognition of apprehension (*avagraha*) is perceived prior to the cognition of judgment (*avāya*); therefore, let that [cognition] have the nature of a transformation characterized by a desire for the specific details of what has been apprehended. Thus, showing that this is not the case for the opponent, he says: "In the absence of continuity," and so forth. For those Buddhists whose intellects have departed from continuity (*anvaya*), what talk can there be of latent dispositions (*vāsanā*)? This will be established: "There is no relation of cause and effect" (Siddhiviniscaya 4).
[Objection: By such statements as these, [it is shown that] the ripening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) occurs.

Now, surely perception (*pratyakṣa*) operating upon a preceding moment (*paryāya*) does not function with respect to a succeeding moment, nor is perception directed toward a succeeding moment capable of perceiving what has passed away in the preceding moment. For this very reason, inference (*anumāna*) is also impossible. Therefore, how can anyone perceive the nature of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth? Furthermore, a single entity cannot possess a manifold nature due to contradiction. To this, he replies: "Perception," and so forth.
One's own perception, which apprehends preceding and succeeding mental states, is momentary and consists of a single cognition of various object-appearances.
If reality consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion as a single common substrate for various forms,
and if the individual soul (jīva) bears the distinction between acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema), then from what source would there be a distinction in the mental continuum?
For [if that were so], there would be a simultaneous perception of the co-arising moments of consciousness, which are subject to momentary destruction.

"Variegated" (*vicitra*) means manifold, such as the objects blue and so forth; that single, undivided cognition which has an appearance (*ākāra*) as if it were the form of those [objects] is described as such. Even for the Yogācāra, who maintains that [cognition] is formless, the phrase "a single cognition regarding the forms of variegated objects" should be explained [in this way]. Of what nature is it? It is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*) of the Yogācāra: "Cognition is momentary, because, while being perceptible to persons like us, it is a specific quality of an all-pervading substance, like sound."
