Furthermore, of what nature is it? To this he says: "perceptible" (*pratyakṣam*), meaning that which has been made an object of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) or of another cognition (*jñānāntara*).
What of it? To this he says: "if it were the reality" (*tattvaṃ cet*).

Thinking that if reality (*tattva*) were ultimately existent (*paramārthasat*), then nothing would be established for the Buddhist who accepts it otherwise, he asks this very question. Furthermore, he states the refutation of one who says "it is so" regarding the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (*yogācāra*) position—which accepts a distinction between cognitions for each respective object—on the grounds that the category of the existent and non-existent cannot be the objective support (*ālambana*) of a single cognition because of its multiplicity, like five fingers; thus, there is a contradiction between the probandum and the example (*sādhyadṛṣṭāntavirodha*). He says: "In pleasure," and so forth.

The mention of pleasure, pain, and delusion is illustrative; by it, all past, future, and present modes (*paryāya*) are included. These are manifold in form, and among them there is one common [element]. That one is the *jīva*.
Alternatively, he is so called because his inherent qualities (*dharma*)—pleasure, pain, and delusion—are manifold in form. Is he not a reality? Indeed, he is precisely a reality.

The point is that just as a variegated cognition simultaneously perceives its own manifold nature and is not contradicted by that perception, so too the individual soul (jīva) perceives it sequentially and is not contradicted by that either; such is the view of the Naiyāyika regarding knowledge.
Comparison: Sound is impermanent because, while being a quality, it is an object of the sense organs of persons such as ourselves, like cognition—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 299.
Here, "all-pervading substance" refers to the self (*ātman*).

Indeed, [the argument] regarding that which is not reality, presented in various and manifold forms with many aspects, is undesirable for the Buddhist who maintains the theory of cognition with form (*sākārajñānavādin*), but it is not [undesirable] for the Yogācāra who maintains the theory of formless cognition (*nirākārajñānavādin*).

If it is argued that he indeed makes multiple objects the domain of a single formless cognition, we say no; if they are made the domain by means of a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can there be a distinction between the objects? Otherwise, there would be a distinction in effects arising from a cause that possesses only a single intrinsic nature, and this will be demonstrated in the refutation of Īśvara by the Yaugas.
If it is argued that even when [pleasure and so forth] are apprehended as having a single nature, there is still a difference in their objects—[the Buddhist replies]:

"Indeed, when pleasure arises or is being experienced within a single continuum (*santāna*), suffering, delusion, and the like do not arise or are not experienced. Since they perish [simultaneously], and because their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are distinct, they must be different entities, just like Rāma and Arjuna," so says the Buddhist. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Yoga... and so on. Yoga is arising (*utpāda*); *kṣema* is perishing (*vināśa*) or being cognized (*saṃvedana*). If it is claimed that these two [arising and perishing/cognizing] follow [the object] through both difference and non-difference in the case of pleasure and the rest under discussion; to this he gives the answer: "In the continuum... and so on.

The intended meaning here is as follows: when the difference between things designated as belonging to a single continuum is to be proven, pleasure and the like constitute the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) because they possess different fates (*bhinnayogakṣema*). Since that [counter-example] is pervaded without exception by the opposite of the reason—namely, by having a non-different fate—the reason characterized by having a different fate, when it is excluded from that [counter-example], would prove their difference, and not otherwise. Furthermore, if the opposite of the reason were also pervaded by the opposite of the probandum, then a single, variegated, and momentary cognition would be established by virtue of having a non-different fate.

And that being the case, from what source could there be a distinction—that is, a plurality—among mental continua? From no source of knowledge whatsoever. Of what things? Of minds. Of what nature? Of those that are subject to momentary destruction.
Furthermore, what is their nature? By the two words "co-existent" (*sahabhuvām*), their simultaneous arising and perishing are stated.
He further provides a qualification for them: "Because there is no perception of their existence, but there is perception of their co-existence."

The meaning here is as follows: because they arise simultaneously—that is, because they are experienced together—this also explains their simultaneous production and experience; therefore, since they share an identical status regarding existence and non-existence (*abhinnayogakṣema*), they are one, just like the intended single variegated cognition.
By this, the fact that they are inseparable (*aśakyavivecana*) has also been considered.
When pleasure perishes, suffering, delusion, and so forth do not perish,
because pleasure, suffering, delusion, and the rest are present in their entirety [within the cause].
From the variegated cognition which constitutes the opposing side,

it follows that even though cognitions of pleasure and so forth possess variegated appearances, they are nonetheless a single cognition, because they are distinct in character from external variegation.
A painting can be analyzed as consisting of many [parts], whereas blue and other such qualities cannot be analyzed apart from the cognition [of them]—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.220.

Here, another proponent of the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*) says: "If it is asked, 'Since there is no continuum (*saṃtāna*), of what and by what is non-difference being asserted?'—if you reply, 'Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that negates it, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the means of valid cognition'; [we say] no. Because pleasure and pain do not mutually experience one another, they are non-existent; otherwise, the reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as all non-apprehension is unestablished (*asiddha*)."

Some maintain that this will be examined in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*, where it is argued that because even the mental continua (*santāna*) of the wise share an identical state of acquisition and preservation (*abhinna-yogakṣema*), they are non-different; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) [of the reason] by them, since they are included within the subject (*pakṣīkaraṇa*). That too is not tenable; for if there were no deviation simply because the object of deviation is included in the subject, then no reason whatsoever would be deviant. Furthermore, one who points out the deviation of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth by means of the very [entities like] the axe and the like which have themselves been made the subject, speaks in such a manner as to be saying something quite trivial.

Therefore, just as a single variegated cognition arises simultaneously from a variegated [object], so too does it arise sequentially; thus, the Buddhist who negates the continuity [of the self] establishes his own position with the words "it is established" and so forth.

In the inference for God—namely, "the earth, mountains, trees, bodies, and so forth have an intelligent cause because they are effects"—a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is raised by means of the trees and other things that constitute the subject (*pakṣa*): it should be observed that these are effects, yet they do not have an intelligent cause. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.14–17)
The meaning is that a single soul pervades both its preceding and succeeding modes;
extracting this point from the *Saṃgraha-vṛtti* and explaining it, he says:
"At first, the sensory cognition grasps its own object non-differentially."
One understands [the object] specifically through *īhā* (investigation) and retains it; otherwise, there would be no memory.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*), having grasped its own object in a general way, understands it again specifically according to that form (*tadākāra*) in order to take it up—just as *avāya* (determination) does—thereby producing a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
This is because, although intended particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) are in some sense unique, they appear to the mind as having a similar nature.

In sensory cognition, we perceive a single, gross, and continuous form appearing with its own constituent parts, which follows [the object] from beginning to end, is perfectly clear, and functions without faltering;
otherwise, it would not appear so clearly.

Furthermore, because it cannot be rejected by analytical investigation (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), if there were no single nature consisting of a clear appearance following [through] mutually distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), then sense-perception would be established as conceptual (*savikalpa*). Otherwise, how could that very [cognition] conceal the form of another with its own form, such that it appears clearly as a similar entity externally?

Now, how could this ultimately real [atom] possibly exist exclusively in its unshared state? For that would contradict perception. If it were argued that, due to some proximity, internal atoms appear as if accumulated externally, then—because they do not interpenetrate one another, just like [atoms in] different continua—a cognition of a gross, unitary, and continuous form would not occur.

In that error, one establishes a certain reality—neither as "this" nor as "not this"—which is unestablished externally or internally from any source; thus, the reality is well-established! Nor should it be thought that the desire for a particular by one who has grasped a universal is purely mental; for that is indeed accepted, because in its absence, the sensory cognition would necessarily lack the recollection of a similar form already grasped.

Indeed, it is not logical that [cognition]—which arises from the power of a present object, is restricted to its own form and nature, and has as its object a unique and exclusive essence—should necessarily be the cause of the recollection of a desired similar thing, just as one ignorant of linguistic convention lacks the capacity for the recollection of effects. If, however, there is a diversity arising from the awakening of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then why is it not admitted that there is a perfectly clear perception characterized by a desire for a specific object of a similar form previously grasped by itself, due to the engagement with the present object? For this reason, the absolute establishment of the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) is not proven.

It is therefore logical that even sensory cognitions, such as those of the eye, apprehend generalities and particulars—such as substantiality, configuration, and color—which possess the nature of pervader and pervaded, and thus generally determine their own intended object preceded by the grasping of the pervader.

If it is argued that the cognition of the eye and so forth is not itself *īhā* (investigative effort), but rather that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by the mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) arising immediately after it—which grasps the object immediately following that [sensory] object—is what constitutes *īhā*, and from that comes memory; then, what exactly has been gained by this recourse to the conceptualization of mental perception?

The sensory cognition (*akṣadhīḥ*), that is, the sense-perception, first—at the very beginning—apprehends its own object (*svārtham*) non-differently, that is, in the form of a universal; it then cognizes (*avaiti*), meaning it ascertains, the object specifically, that is, in its particular form. This is the connection [of the words].
By what means does it do so? To this he says: "by specific inquiry" (*viśeṣeṇehayā*). Inquiry (*īhā*) is the desire to know;
what, then, does that do? It sustains [the object], that is, it deposits a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the object.
Why is this so? Otherwise—that is, in the absence of apprehension (*dhāraṇā*)—there would be no recollection (*smṛti*), because recollection is the absence [of non-recollection];

or rather, in the absence of the general perception (*sāmānyāvagraha*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of recollection due to its lack of distinction from non-recollection.

Indeed, it is not logical for you to claim that recollection of a universal arises from a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); otherwise, recollection of yellow would arise from the experience of blue.

Now, it might be argued: "If the particular (viśeṣa) is not apprehended, how can there be an apprehension of the universal (sāmānya)? For when the pervaded (vyāpya) is not perceived, the pervader (vyāpaka) cannot be cognized. This is not so; for just as in a single variegated cognition, even though the form of yellow and other colors is not replicated by the form of blue, there is no fault because it replicates the mere cognition that pervades them, so too memory is non-different [from perception] insofar as the memory corresponds exactly to the experience.
Regarding the non-apprehension of a specific quality that is capable of pervading [the object],
he explains the verse with the words "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth: let perception grasp its own object.
In what manner? What does it do further while acting in a general way? To this he says: "further," and so forth.
Later, in a specific manner—that is, by assuming its own particular form—it cognizes, meaning it determines, by means of that very specific form alone.
Furthermore, what does it do? To this he says: "In whatever manner," and so forth.
In whatever manner (*yathā*)—by which mode—the ascertainment (*avāya*) [occurs] regarding its own two objects, in that same manner it deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Why is this so? If it is asked, "Because it has grasped [the object] through a universal (*sāmānyena*)," he says here: "The desired," and so forth.

The intended *svalakṣaṇas* accepted by the Buddhists are characterized as partless atoms; although they are in some way—by any manner of distinction such as spatial location and so forth—unique (*asādhāraṇa*) and distinct (*vilakṣaṇa*), [they appear] only with a similar nature (*sadṛśātmanā*), that is, with a common nature such as blue and so forth, and not with a unique nature. This is the meaning of the particle *eva*. [This is] because they manifest [in this way]; otherwise, if it were due to the isolation of individual atoms, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of manifold cognition (*anekapratīti*).

This has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position], but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Thus he says: "having its own parts as its intrinsic nature" (*svāvayavasvabhāvam*), and so forth.
Its own parts are the parts of other substances; therefore, this [objection] is refuted by the passage beginning with *pra.vā. 3.181*: "If everything were of both natures," etc.
That which has such a nature—that is, such an essential form (*svarūpa*)—is described in that way.
By this [sūtra], the absolute [position] that "substances originate another substance" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.10) is refuted; we perceive that very form [of the argument].
Of what nature is it? "The grossest" (*sthavīyāṃsam*).
This qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also to be understood as a means of proof (*sādhana*): because it is the grossest, therefore it has the nature of its own parts (*svāvayavasvabhāva*).

Indeed, if there were the absolute exclusion of partless wholes (*niravayava-avayavikalpanaikānta*), then—just like atoms (*paramāṇu*)—there would be no mutual distinction of magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth among wholes; consequently, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "gross," "grosser," and so forth, would not be possible therein.

If it is argued that all this conventional usage depends upon the multiplicity of the constituent parts that initiate it, to this he replies: "One. This means that this massive form is perceived as one. However, when the conventional usage [of "one"] depends upon the multiplicity of parts, then what is perceived there is "that" (the collection), and not the "massive," because the quality of massiveness cannot ultimately exist even in the parts themselves.
Doing what? He says: "appearing.
Where? "In sensory cognition," that is, in the knowledge of the eye and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates that for the Yogācāra, the absolute thesis regarding the distinction between parts and the whole is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhitā*).

By means of this specific formulation, Dharmakīrti has offered the refutation: "Having imagined that all substances possess the nature of everything, why does one who is told 'eat curd' not run toward a camel? This objection is rejected with respect to the whole (*avayavin*).

Regarding the conventional usage of "gross," "grosser," and so forth, the opponent says: "It is true that you perceive such a form, but that is momentary, for otherwise perception would be impossible. To this, [the author] replies with the words "prior and posterior," etc.: we perceive in sensory cognition the appearance of prior and posterior transformations which have the nature of being connected [as a continuum].
The remainder will be examined here.

By this [argument], he demonstrates the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason in such formulations as: "Whatever appears in a certain way, that exists as such in ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sat*) and enters into conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

If it is objected: "But surely you perceive that single form—which is non-existent—just as one perceives distant, sparse hairs and the like," he replies: "We perceive it in such a way that its occurrence is unerring (*askhaladvṛtti*), because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*). This is his thought.
To one who asserts, "We perceive [the object] as appearing not in sensory cognition, but in conceptual cognition," he replies with the words "perfectly clear" (*parisphuṭam*) and so forth.
Otherwise, in the manner of its non-appearance in sensory cognition, it would not manifest in such a way as to be perfectly clear.
He states another refutation with the words "by means of deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyānena*) and so forth.
This has already been explained [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*] starting with the verse "nacaitad vyavasāyātma" (1.25).

Thus, although the appearance of its own object in the form of a universal (*sāmānyākāra*) within sensory cognition has been established by the force of its manifestation, [the author] states another refutation for one who, like one stretching out his legs in indifference, does not accept this: "of the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)" and so forth.

Regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) external [to cognition], which are partless and momentary atoms—of what nature are they? They are mutually distinct. If one accepts the absence of a single nature of continuity characterized by a clear manifestation—that is, if one accepts the absence of that which possesses both a clear manifestation and a single nature of continuity—the refutation begins with the word "the sense-organ" (*akṣa*), and so forth.

The intention here is this: even though it appears as having that nature, if it were the object of sensory perception—like the hairs seen by one with ophthalmia, and so forth; to this, the reply is: if it exists but not externally, then, since there is no other possibility, it must belong to cognition. Thus, sensory cognition is established as being conceptual (*savikalpa*) and differentiated (*sabheda*). Otherwise, in the manner of lacking conceptuality, how could that very same sensory cognition conceal the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is of a different nature, by means of its own nature—which is a single essence consisting of a clear manifestation and continuity? It certainly could not.
Because of that concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*), [the object] appears clearly and distinctly as if it were outside, by means of a similar self—that is, by means of a homogeneous nature (*samānasvabhāva*).
Others, however, read the text as *spaṣṭanirbhāsānvayaikasvabhāve*; for them, how could there be a contradiction such as "otherwise" and so forth?
For by that [concealment], that very thing is not concealed; otherwise, a cloth would be concealed by its own self.

If it is argued: "Let it be then that its nature exists externally as well, just like sensory cognition, because it is impossible to reject what is established by the force of logic," [the author] says here: "Now, this... and so forth.

The meaning is: "Now, this form (ākāra) just mentioned, existing in the ultimate sense (paramārthena), exists externally just as it does internally"—this refers back to "unique, mutually distinct particular characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
How is there an occurrence that is exclusively and necessarily so?
From what [source] is this known? To this, he says: "Because of the contradiction with perception regarding those," and so forth.

In that case, it is atoms themselves that appear, both externally and internally, as accumulated through an inseparable mode of existence and production; as it has been said— this is the Buddhist view to be examined— page 2, note 10.

In this regard, the following is the most substantial prima facie argument: by means of a cognition that presents a single object and relies upon distinct entities, their extrinsic form is concealed by their own intrinsic form.
With the words "others, however," the commentator indicates another interpretation of this [verse]:
"This has surely come about, as the wise say;
this has come about by the force of reality, as the wise say."
Just as objects are analyzed, they fall apart— *Pravāraṇāvākya*; just as objects are analyzed and discriminated, so do they [fall apart]— *Pravāraṇāvākya* 2.209.

If this is argued, then having raised this very doubt, [the author] refutes it by saying "from something" and so forth. This is the opponent's objection: "If, on the other hand, the internal atoms were accumulated—that is, gathered into a mass—and thus appeared in such a way that they possessed a single nature characterized by a clear manifestation and continuity, due to some proximity defined by an inseparable mode of existence and arising, just like external atoms. This is the suspicion of the opponent's view.
Regarding the refutation there, beginning with "mutually," etc.:

"mutually" means *anyonya*, because of the lack of commingling (*asaṃplava*). Since there is no commingling—meaning no meeting or penetration—of the nature or the activity of a single cognition-atom (*jñāna-paramāṇu*) into those [other atoms] adjacent to it, or of theirs into that [central atom], he provides an example well-known to the opponent: "like other continua" (*santānāntaravat*).

"Like other mental continua, so too [is this]"—this is what is meant: just as for those [continua] there is neither a confusion of their own nature with another nor a commingling through being made objects of cognition, so it is for internal atoms.
What follows from this? He says: "A single gross [object]," and so forth.

The cognition of a single gross form characterized by non-duality—that is the "cognition of the form of a single gross continuity"—would not exist, just as in the case of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*); this illustration placed in the middle should also be connected with the present context.
Therefore, just as there is no such cognition in relation to objects grasped within other continua of the three worlds, so too the cognition in question (the *dārṣṭāntika*) would not occur.

As for one who thinks that because [external objects] are not perceived and because there is no other mental continuum (*santānāntara*), the example is unestablished— how could such a person accept another [object] being cognized by a single atom of cognition, on the basis of which the Buddhist doctrine of non-dual variety (*citrādvaita*) might exist?
For [in that view], there would be no other mental continua.

Having established the non-existence of another continuum (*santānāntara*) on the grounds of its non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), he has thereby contemplated reality as being beyond all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). [The opponent objects: "This is merely some triviality, for one who accepts that the appearance of blue—which is being perceived—and the appearance of pleasure and so forth exist, yet asserts the negation of another continuum. To this, the other says: "This cognition exists, though it is erroneous. As it was stated by Prajñākaragupta: "There is no fault even if [the object] is non-existent, just like the appearances in a magical illusion, a mirage, and so forth" (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 3).
211 Thus [it is said]; to this he states the reply: "That error," and so forth.
If an error in that cognition of it is admitted, where [would it occur]? Both externally and internally.

What has been produced? To this he says: "Something"—such as pleasure and so forth, or blue and so forth—which is unestablished and undetermined through some means of perception or inference; in what manner [is it established]? As "this-ness" (*idantā*), because it is not knowable by momentary cognitions other than itself and is beyond all delusions and conceptual constructions; nor as "not-this-ness" (*nedantā*), because it does not possess a form contrary to that. Thus the Buddhist establishes such a reality (*tattva*). This statement—"the reality is thus well-established"—is a mockery, for he believes that due to delusion, nothing at all would be established, leading to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the argument.
Therefore, the statement beginning with "direct perception" (*pratyakṣam*) and so forth is well-established.

Now, the proponent of the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavādī*), refuting the dispute regarding the cognition of effort (*īhājñāna*), says: "But surely, when that [cognition] exists, the investigation proceeds as to whether it is mental (*mānasa*) or something else, because the investigation of a property (*dharma*) is dependent upon the existence of its substratum (*dharmī*)."

If it is argued that, therefore, its very existence (*sattā*) is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), this is not so; for the existence of that [object] is established by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

This is because, once the general property (*sāmānya*) in the subject (*dharmin*) is established, there is a cognition in one who desires to grasp its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), since the employment of appropriate means occurs for one who is thus disposed, whereas for one devoid of such disposition, it is impossible.
It is with this meaning in mind that it was stated right here: "Indeed, the forms (*ākṛti*) such as 'many' and 'of many kinds' do not belong to consciousness" (Siddhiviniścaya 1).

27. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it should not be thought that this—namely, the desire for particulars (*viśeṣākāṅkṣaṇa*) concerning a generality (*sāmānya*) that has been grasped and made an object by apprehension (*avagraha*)—is mental, being caused by the mind (*manonimitta*), and not caused by the sense organ; for while it is indeed accepted as being mental, the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is that it is *not* exclusively that [mental state].

When it is said that "the desire for that [generality] is mental," it is implied that the cognition of apprehension (*avagrahajñāna*) itself is also a transformation (*pariṇāmi*) of that [desire]; just as when it is said "a clay pot" (*mārdo ghaṭaḥ*), the lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍa*) which is its material cause is also called "clay" (*mārda*).

Although this has already been refuted by the passage beginning with *na caitad vyavasāya-siddhi-viṣayaḥ* (PVin 1.25), there is no fault [in repeating it], as it is for the purpose of refuting it by another method. Why? To this he says: *tad-abhāva* and so forth.

In the absence of that [cognition] which is the transformation of apprehension (*avagraha*), in whose absence would there be [recollection]? This means: when sense-cognition (*akṣajñāna*) is admitted as having the partless particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, recollection is impossible because there can be no recollection of a similar form that was previously apprehended by *avagraha*—that is, made an object of *avagraha*—or of what was seen previously as being similar to what is now being apprehended. Nor should it be thought that this is so; why? To this he says: "For not... and so forth.

The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because. Because [it is] not present—that is, because of the power of that object which is not proximate—the connection is made by changing the case ending to "even though sensory cognition has arisen" (*udbhūtam utpannam api*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? To this he says: *tad-ityādi*.

Its nature (*svabhāva*), which is its own form (*svarūpa*) characterized by imitating the form (*ākāra*) of that proximate object, is restricted (*niyata*) to that; the meaning is that even in a dream, it does not perceive anything other than its own form.
Showing its qualification once again, he says: "Asādhāraṇa" (uncommon), etc.

That which has as its object an internal property (*dharma*) of the self or its own nature that is uncommon—meaning distinct from everything else and unique, being without a companion—is logically the cause of the recollection of a desired similar [moment]. A prior moment is similar to a subsequent one, or a subsequent moment is similar to a prior one; thus, the recollection [of this] is the "recollection of a desired similar," and it is logical that such a thing is its cause.

Indeed, it is not logical for there to be such an external recollection arising from an experience whose object is a unique and exclusive [particular], just as there is no recollection of yellow from an experience of blue; and thus, the opponent considers that the conventional usage of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth would be difficult to establish. With the words beginning "samaya" (convention), he supports that very point through an illustration: "convention" (*samaya*) refers to a linguistic agreement (*saṅketa*) such as "this is high-pitched" or "this is another"; for one who is ignorant of that, just like a cowherd and the like, the differentiation of accents and so forth in the composition of scriptural commentaries and the like is said to be the "effect" (*kārya*); in that case, the capacity for recollection is untenable.

This is what is meant: just as there is no recollection of [the word] by cowherds and others when the convention regarding the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth is not grasped, likewise there is no recollection of it when the similar form is not grasped.

By this, the statement "because of non-recollection otherwise due to non-difference"—that is, because of the absence of recollection—is explained, provided that the cognition of inquiry (*īhājñāna*) is indeed present.
The external object, distinct from the mind, is the transformative cause (pariṇāmikāraṇa) of the knowledge of purposeful activity (īhājñāna).
Now, the connection is this: sensory cognition does not have a unique, exclusive object as its domain such that it would be the cause of its own recollection.

What is meant is this: just as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) arising from the experience of blue is the cause of the recollection of blue and not of yellow, so too the impression of that sensory cognition is the cause of the recollection of its unique object, and not the cause of the recollection of that [other] object; thus, sensory cognition [is established].

This is another explanation: since sensory cognition (*akṣajñāna*) is of the aforementioned kind, for that very reason, not only would its memory (*smṛti*) not exist, but even its latent impression (*vāsanā*) would not arise—that is, it would not be produced. Therefore, the latent impression of sensory cognition does not have a common, uniform object as its cause; rather, it is the latent impression of a previous memory of a similar nature [that is its cause].

If it is argued that "the distinction here is this: once awakened by that sensory cognition, [the impression] becomes its cause, and that awakening occurs only with respect to blue and so forth, not with respect to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) and so forth"; to this he says: "If, however," and so on.

The internal latent impression (*antarvāsanā*) is the predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by the conceptualization of a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression. Its "awakening" (*prabodha*) is the transformation consisting in the production of a subsequent memory of the same kind [as the original perception] following that perception. Its "variety" (*vicitratā*)—meaning that this awakening occurs only with respect to blue and so forth, and not with respect to momentary destruction and so forth—is what is intended when one says, "if it is accepted"; [the word "if" is supplied]. If that is so, then why is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of that variety not admitted on that basis? It is indeed admitted.

Of what nature is it? To this he says: that which has as its characteristic (lakṣaṇa) or essential nature (svarūpa) the desire for, and the orientation toward grasping, those specific qualities (viśeṣa) belonging to an object of similar form (samānākāra-artha) which has been itself grasped—that is, made an object—by the self (ātman).

Again, of what nature is it? To this he says: it is "perfectly clear" (parisphuṭa), that is, distinct; why? because of its application to a proximate object (sannihita-artha-upayoga), i.e., because of its operation upon a proximate object.

This is what is meant: by the statement beginning with "What would follow from that conceptualization? it has been stated that perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by that [perception] is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of another similar kind; its diverse awakening consists in the desire for the determination of some particular feature.
Since there is no inference, there is the establishment of the absolute non-conceptual [nature of perception].
Or, if "since" (*yataḥ*) is taken as an objection, [the answer is] that such establishment does not occur at all.
And by the words "nor should this be thought," etc., the commentary beginning with "clarity" and so forth has also been explained.
He states the second verse for the purpose of conclusion: "That," etc.
Since this is so, therefore it is logical and appropriate.
What is that? He says: even visual and other forms of cognition—not only mental cognition—discerns and knows [objects] in succession.
Of what things? He says: of the generalities and particularities such as existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), configuration (*saṃsthāna*), color (*varṇa*), and so forth.
When each preceding [factor] is the universal (*sāmānya*), then the subsequent ones are the particulars (*viśeṣa*); thus it is said, "those particulars.
How does it delimit them? To this he says: "The pervader," and so forth.
That particular whose nature is pervaded by the pervader is described as such; [the cognition] apprehends—that is, determines—that [particular].
Of what nature is it? It is "willed by itself," that is, by its own self.
How is it willed? To this he says: preceded by the apprehension of the pervasive [universal].

Regarding what has been stated here with these and other words: "If the cognition of the eye and so forth is itself non-sequential in nature, how can it determine [its object] sequentially? This would involve a contradiction. Alternatively, if it is sequential in nature, then it must be determined by another [cognition], and that too by another through its own sequence; thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*).

This [objection] is not tenable, because each preceding [cognition] serves as the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) for the succeeding one precisely while not abandoning its own inherent grasping [of the object]. (Siddhiviniścaya 2)
This will be investigated here in this very context in due order.
Regarding this, the opponent says: "Certainly not the cognition of the eyes and so forth," and so on.

The cognition of the eye and so forth is by no means the effect of the eye and so forth; rather, that which is cognition is *īhā*. However, what is it? It is that which has its birth immediately following that cognition of the eye and so forth as its immediate material cause (*samanantara-upādāna*). By what [is it apprehended]? By mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).

Of what nature is it? It is that which apprehends the object immediately subsequent to that [first] cognition of the eye and so forth—namely, the momentary object that acts as a cooperative condition for that cognition.

As it has been said: "Mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is that which is produced by sensory cognition (*indriya-jñāna*) acting as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), with the assistance of the object immediately following its own [sensory] object" (Nyāyabindu 1.9).
The construction of words here [in this context] gives rise to conceptual construction.

"Therefore," for that reason, "recollection is not perception" [and] "desire (īhā) is not [perception]," because there is no other possible way to account for the cognition whose object is that [past experience], which is the effect of the original experience—this is the sense. If this is so, the Teacher asks here: "What, then, is gained by the conceptualization of mental perception? What is obtained by the Buddhist through the conceptualization of that distinction, namely, mental perception itself? Does that perception appear at the time of the operation of the eyes and other senses, or at another time? It does not appear; it is merely constructed by the artifice of conceptualization. This is what is meant by "by conceptualization."

Regarding this, the Buddhist Śāntabhadra says: "By that conceptualization, mental recollection of an external object is obtained; for that [recollection] is not connected with visual or other sensory cognitions because they belong to different mental continua (*santāna*). Otherwise, Yajñadatta would have recollection of what was experienced by Devadatta. Since that recollection arises from mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), there is no contradiction.
Anticipating this objection, [the author] refutes it, saying: "From perception," and so forth.
Śāntabhadra, however, says: "Even if a difference from that [external object] is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is certainly perceived through its effect (*kārya*).

For the effect—consisting of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as 'blue' and designated by another term, namely 'recollection' (*smaraṇa*)—cannot exist occasionally (*kādācitkatva*) without a cause.
Nor is sense-perception itself the cause of that [recollection], because there is a difference in the continuum (*santāna-bheda*), just like the cognition of another well-known continuum."
"That cause is indeed something other than sensory cognition, and that very thing is mental perception"—Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, Prastāvanā, p. 526.

Here, Śāntabhadra, presenting the view of the Sautrāntikas, explained that first the eye [perceives] form, then visual consciousness arises; subsequently, by means of that sensory consciousness acting as a simultaneous auxiliary cause, mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) is produced in the third moment... Here, having raised the objection that "there would be no absence of conceptualization because [the object] has been experienced by the preceding visual consciousness and so forth," he stated: "If it were so, there would follow the consequence that Yajñadatta could also have a conceptualization regarding what was seen by Devadatta" (Nyāyabinduṭīkā, p. 61–62). [And:
"Apart from mental perception, there is no memory of external objects for the sensory cognition."
If it is argued that this [mental consciousness] is like [the mental consciousness] of another being, then what is its immediate antecedent?

For, even though the continua of mental and sensory cognitions are distinct, there is nonetheless the establishment of them as non-different beings and their mutual status as immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*); therefore, the recollection of the sense-object by the mind would occur from that very [source].
Thus, enough with this internal goiter of an external mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).
From what kind of perception? From mental [perception], for without that, there is no external memory. From what source? From sensory cognition, i.e., from the knowledge of the eyes and so forth.
He provides an illustration: "like another sentient being" (*sattvāntaravat*);
"another sentient being" means another continuum (*santānāntara*), from that [continuum].

If it is argued that the refutation here is: "Just as there is no memory in Yajñadatta of what was experienced by Devadatta, so it would be for the present cognition"—then what follows immediately after that? This is the intended meaning here: would the continuum (*santāna*) of sensory perception and mental perception be non-different or different? If it were non-different, then what would that immediately preceding mental perception be for this effect, which is memory? It would be nothing at all.

This is what is meant: just as mental recollection does not arise from sensory cognition belonging to another continuum, so too it does not arise even from mental perception belonging to a continuum non-different from that [sensory one].

For indeed, a horse of noble breed does not [arise] from a donkey, nor would it be different from its own son if it were distinct [from him]; so then, is that sensory cognition the immediately preceding substantial cause (*upādāna*) of this mental perception? By no means; like memory, that [mental perception] also does not arise from it.

Regarding that which was stated by Prajñākara—that there is no establishment of sensory perception based on the mark of memory—[we reply]: why is it not established through direct cognition? For the cognition of blue and so forth is of a determinate nature, and because it is of the very essence of sensory perception.

Thus, that [objection] too is refuted by this: if sense-perception, which is its material cause (*upādāna*), were of the nature of a determinate judgment (*nirṇaya*) like that [mental perception], then all objects would be established from that very [sense-perception] alone, since that [object] itself would be perceived. What, then, would be the point of this immediate [mental perception] following that sense-perception? If, on the other hand, it were not of the nature of a determinate judgment, then what would that non-determinate sense-perception have to do with this immediately preceding mental direct perception (*mānasādhyakṣa*), which is of the nature of a determinate judgment? For that [mental perception] arises precisely from the contact of the sense-organ with the object; since it arises from that, there is no difference [between them].
This has been discussed in such passages as *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.6, regarding "similar recollection" (*sadṛśasmṛti*).
That cognition such as "this" and so forth, which arises from repeated practice through direct perception of what stands before one, is considered mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 305.

Furthermore, like the cognition of blue and so forth, if that [cognition] has as its object momentary, partless atoms (*paramāṇu*), then no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates therein, because there is no possibility of superimposition (*samāropa*) regarding what has been definitively determined.

As it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.50): "Because of the relationship of the sublated and the sublator between the cognitions of certainty and superimposition," if that middle moment does not ascertain its own nature as the causality relative to the preceding and succeeding moments, there would be no apprehension of anything at all; otherwise, a single entity would possess both an apprehended and a non-apprehended form.

If it is argued that [the mind] determines [the relationship] even when the prior and posterior [terms] are not grasped, then this is a confused statement: "The cognition of a relation residing in two [terms] does not arise from the perception of a single form;
rather, the cognition of a relation occurs when there is the grasping of the essential natures of both.
(Pravārtikālaṅkāra 1).

Thus, even when determining the prior and posterior states, there would be non-comprehension either because [the self] does not itself abide or because it does not determine [them]. And if, on the other hand, those two are apprehended, then the determination of the causal relation between them must likewise depend on the apprehension of another; thus, the grasping of the prior and posterior limits—the beginning and the end—is inevitable. Likewise, if its distinction from everything else is to be ascertained through something external, then everything must be explained.
Sensory cognition consists of its own intrinsic nature;
it is not a perception of a relation residing in two things, because there is no cognition of a single form [belonging to both].
"When there is the apprehension of the two natures, there is the cognition of the relation" (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra 1.2). Thus,
because the persisting subject is not determined when the prior and posterior [states] are apprehended...

Therefore, that which was stated by the opponent—that through the perception of the middle moment, there is likewise the perception of all past and future moments because of its being of that nature—is refuted; for the same [objection] applies elsewhere as well.

Now, if it is claimed that the causal relationship itself is not accepted in some cases, this is not so; because in the absence of sensory cognition, the mental perception arising from it would not exist.
If its existence is established through conventional usage, then the very same defect remains in that case.

The remainder here should be understood from the *Pramāṇasaṃgrahabhāṣya*. The comparison is as follows: if the perception of an object pervading a fraction of time were unimpaired, there would be a perception supported by all those temporal fractions until the limit of death.
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p.
592: Because it exists like a middle moment, sensory cognition does not arise from the sense organs.
Explaining the verse by way of exclusion (*vyatirekamukhena*)—that which is produced from sensory cognition—he says: "The mind and the senses," and so forth.

Even though there is a plurality of continua (*santāna*) for mental and sensory cognitions—that is, for mental and sensory perceptions—not only is there no [plurality] of that [continuum], because through a certain proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there is the establishment of a single sentient being (*ananyasattvavyavasthā*), meaning the establishment of a single living organism, and furthermore, there is the state of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyayatā*) and an appropriating cause (*upādānakāraṇatā*) among the mutual cognitions of the mind and the senses.

[Objection: Is it not the case that only sensory cognitions (*akṣasaṃvit*) are the immediately preceding causes (*samanantarakāraṇa*) for mental cognitions (*manasaṃvit*), and not these [mental cognitions] for those [sensory ones]? How then can it be said, "mutually," and so forth? [Reply: It is not possible to say this. For just as smoke arises from fire alone, and fire is not perceived as arising from that [smoke], it is certain that fire alone is the cause of smoke, and smoke is not the cause of fire; in exactly the same way, if mental perception arises from sensory cognition alone, and sensory cognition is not perceived as arising from that [mental perception], then it would be logical to conclude: sensory cognition alone is its cause, and that [mental perception] is not the cause of it.

To the extent that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is the cause of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*), let it also be the cause of some other sensory cognition by that very same [process], since it is unrestrained in all cases. Therefore, the intention is this: just as the cognition produced from sensory cognition is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), so too would there be another perception produced from that [same conceptualization]. For this very reason—due to that same proximity (*pratyāsatti*)—there would arise from the mind (*manas*) a recollection (*smṛti*) or an inquiry (*īhā*) regarding the sense-objects, such as the domain of the eye and so forth, through mental perception; it would not arise from any other cause. This is the underlying meaning.
Then, what has been gained by the Jaina? He says: "That," and so forth.
"That" means for that reason, according to the logic stated; "enough" (alaṃ) means sufficient. What is the use of an imagined external mental perception (*bahir-mānasa-pratyakṣa*)?

Of what nature is it? It is like a "goitre" (*antargaḍu*); that is, existing like a goitre between the two—smṛti and sensory cognition—just as a goitre exists between the temples or the forehead, and thus it is ineffective. The sense is that the object at hand is established through sensory cognition alone.
The mental [perception] is the cause of mental cognition, which is the consciousness of the mind.
Even the mental [cognition] is [produced] by conceptualization alone, from conceptualization.
A "goitre" (*gaḍu*) is so called because it is like a lump of flesh situated between the neck and the head; it is [called this] due to its fruitlessness—*Hetutattvopadeśa-ṭīkā*, fol.
295a; *Pravāha-svopajña-ṭīkā*, fol. 217b.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Conceptual construction," and so forth.
Conceptual construction is the clear awakening [of cognition] from the latent impressions of conceptualization due to the proximity of the sense-organ and its object;
it has as its domain the self-nature of objects consisting of the universal and the particular, which are the pervader and the pervaded. || 6 ||

The cognition that apprehends a specific pervaded (vyāpya-viśeṣa) preceded by the grasping of a pervasive generality (sāmānya) following upon a conceptualization (vitarka) is common to both mental and sensory conceptualizations.

In this regard, the contact between the sense organ and its object, through the restriction of convention, clarifies the awakening of internal latent impressions (vāsanā) according to what is appropriate; thus, this [process] is common to them.

Consequently, even if the [specific] manifestation of the object is not perceived, it would still differ [from non-conceptual perception], yet the effort (īhā) [to discern it] would not be negated—just as in the case of a conceptualization based on the recollection of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin)—because otherwise, such a manifestation would be impossible. Furthermore, without conceptualization and recollection, the pervasion (vyāpti) would not be established, due to the lack of comprehension.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the successive cognition of [perceptions] such as *avagraha* (initial apprehension) and so forth; the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by that is "its impression" (*tadvāsanā*). From what does its clear awakening—that is, its manifestation—arise? To this he says: "From the proximity of the sense-organ and the object," meaning from the contact of the sense-faculty with the object, and not from mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) and the like.
How is it [the awakening]? To this he says: "Pervasive," and so forth.

The pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*), these two, are respectively the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*); the pervasive is the universal and the pervaded is the particular. That which has as its objects those two natures, which are the essence of the referent (*arthātman*), is described as such. Explaining the verse, he says: "Investigation" (*vitarka*), and so forth. Investigation (*vitarka*) is the act of investigating; it follows after the transformation of investigation that consists in the desire for particulars. That [investigation] is both that and the apprehension of the pervasive universal; that which has this as its prior cause through a succession is described as such. What is that? He says: "the knowledge of the apprehension of the particular which is the pervaded."
What is its nature? To this he says: "Common to mental and sensory conceptualizations.
This means it is common—that is, similar—to both mental conceptualizations and sensory conceptualizations, which are cognitions derived from the sense organs.

If one asks, "In the context of a discussion on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for what purpose are mental conceptualizations, which are not the subject at hand, being introduced?"—it is for the sake of providing an illustration.

Just as for mental conceptualizations there is first a cognition that grasps a pervasive generality followed by a cognition that apprehends a specific pervaded [particular], so it is for sensory conceptualizations;

thus, the example is not unestablished. First, there is a determination of the generality by the mind, immediately after which there is a desire for its particularity, and from this arises the cognition that apprehends a specific [object] such as "it is a person" or "it is a post. This is well-known even to the Buddhist.

Now, one might object: "Even if it is true that for mental conceptualizations (*manovikalpa*) there is first the apprehension of a pervasive generality (*sāmānya*) accompanied by discursive thought (*vitarka*), followed by the cognition of the specific particular (*viśeṣa*) which is pervaded [by it], what does this have to do with sensory conceptualizations (*akṣavikalpa*) such that they would possess that [same process]? For the property of one thing does not necessarily belong to another; otherwise, why would the bitterness of the *arka* plant not also belong to molasses (*guḍa*)? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

In that regard, the simultaneous mention of those mental constructs (vikalpa) along with the nature of the example and its counterpart is as follows: because the contact of the sense organ and the object (*indriyārtha-sannikarṣa*), the proximity of a suitable place and so forth, and the restriction of time—meaning the period of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so on—unerringly and invariably clarify, that is, make distinct, the awakening of internal latent impressions (*antarvāsanā*); "internal latent impression" refers to the latent impression of mental constructs, and its "awakening" is its manifestation. For this reason, they are said to be "similar to that.

What is meant is this: it is not the case that mental constructs alone become distinct from that sensory contact; therefore, the distinction between the example and its counterpart is not contradicted.

If it is asked: "Surely mental conceptualizations produced from the mind of a *dhattūra* [poisonous plant] are devoid of clear form; so how do they become clear?"—to this he says: "According to what is appropriate," and so forth.
Concluding by stating that [the cognition] becomes clear upon encountering a specific collection of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) as is appropriate and fitting, he says:

"Therefore, for that reason, the appearance of the object (*arthapratibhāsa*) would differ among those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) by way of being clear or otherwise; however, the effort (*īhā*) [to discern it] would not be negated. He provides an illustration, both for the case where there is no perception and for the case where there is perception, beginning with the words "the mark" (*liṅga*).

Some explain the matter as follows: the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*) is *avinābhāva* (inseparable concomitance). The "non-perception" (*anupalakṣaṇa*) of that [relationship] refers to a type of discursive thought (*vitarka*) consisting of the recollection of such a relationship. Just as for a person who has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), at the moment of cognizing smoke after seeing smoke, there is a non-perception of the discursive thought regarding the relationship even though it exists in the interim; so too it is with *īhā*. Thus, because this probans—"because it is not perceived even in the case of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)"—is present, *īhā* is not thereby refuted; this is their intention.

When those [people] recognize fire immediately after seeing smoke, even if there is the presence of a memory of a relationship that was not previously perceived, the cognition "there is fire here" arising suddenly from the sight of smoke—even if it is in an embryo—is said by you (the Buddhist) not to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) from perception (*bauddha*). How then would this not be contradictory? If you say: "When one does not admit a memory of that [relationship] when it is unperceived, then what was stated [by us] is not otherwise," even then, since the object of the deviation of the reason under discussion—which is established for the opponent—is absent, that [cognition] would be a separate means of valid cognition for the opponent; furthermore, the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) remains the same, namely that "investigation (*īhā*) is lost."

Therefore, it is explained otherwise: the recollection of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), which is well-known to others, is itself called "reflection" (*ūha*). "Reasoning" (*vitarka*) is the desire for specific detail; that which operates similarly to this is "like that" (*tadvat*). What is meant by this is as follows: just as the Mīmāṃsaka—who desires the recollection of the general relationship between the mark and the bearer of the mark—is not refuted by the Buddhist even when such a recollection is not perceived, but rather is indeed accepted [by the Buddhist], so too is this present "investigation" (*īhā*).
If one asks why this is so, he says here: "That," and so forth.

Since that recollection of the relationship cannot otherwise be established—namely, by way of the absence of such conceptualization (vitarka)—one might ask: "Why is this so? To this, he says: "Atarkita," and so forth. That recollection (*smṛti*) is one in which *tarkita*—the desire for further particulars—is not present; from the standpoint of such a recollection, the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) in its entirety, would not be established.
If it is asked, "Why?"—to this he replies: because of non-comprehension;
that is, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not grasped by one who lacks reasoning and memory.
For when the pervasion of the generality of smoke with the generality of fire is being grasped, that [pervasion] is not said to be grasped.

Because there is only the cognition of the generalities of the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), it would follow that no activity could occur toward the particular; this will be demonstrated later.
Furthermore, this illustration should be seen as applying to the passage beginning with "accompanied by deliberation" (*vitarkānugata*) and so forth, as well as to the case of fire.
The commentators [state] that even while Bhaṭṭākalaṅkadeva was still in the womb...

[Objection: Is it not the case that if the pervaded (vyāpya) is not apprehended, there can be no apprehension of the pervader (vyāpaka)? How then can it be said that [perception] "is accompanied by vitarka," and so forth? Or, if the apprehension of the pervader occurs upon the apprehension of the pervaded, then—just as with the generality of the pervader—the particularity of the pervaded would also be grasped by the initial apprehension (avagraha); what, then, would be the use of īhā and the subsequent stages? If you argue that this is because doubt and the like do not arise [in that case], the author replies here with the words beginning "varṇa" (color/syllable), etc., regarding īhā and the rest.

The commonality of color, shape, and so forth is apprehended by one standing at a distance; its specific details are grasped through investigation, though sometimes even in the absence of that [investigation].

For just as it is improper for one who perceives a universal distinct from the individual to fail to notice it—since the arising of a non-differentiated cognition regarding diverse substances and so forth occurs by the power of perceiving that [universal]—in the same way, it is improper for one who perceives the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) to fail to notice it, since the arising of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that excludes what is other than it occurs by the power of perceiving that [particular].

How can that which assimilates to itself the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) induced by the experience of that [particular] be called "non-indicative" (*anupalakṣaka*)? For one who perceives the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), even without a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that indicates the particular, why would a cognition regarding things that are distinct from others—though arising from some cause—be contradictory, even if there is no conceptual construction indicating them, just as in the case of one who perceives a universal (*jāti*)? Because the power of causes is inconceivable, this very answer applies elsewhere as well, since there is no difference in the underlying principle.

Color (*varṇa*) refers to white and so forth, and shape (*saṃsthāna*) refers to upwardness and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), action (*karman*) and other such qualities are included. The commonality (*sāmānya*)—that is, a similar transformation (*pariṇāma*)—of these is apprehended, meaning it is made an object of cognition through *avagraha*. For instance, even when the specific white color that qualifies a crane and the like situated at a distance is not grasped, there is still the apprehension of the general form (*rūpa-sāmānya*) of that color. Similarly, in the case of a person or the like situated at a distance, their specific upwardness and so forth are not seen; the same should be applied to action as well.
Therefore, [your claim] is not tenable: that there can be no apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in the absence of the apprehension of the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
How is that [determination] apprehended? He says: "By the inquiry into its particulars" (*tadviśeṣehayā*).
The particulars of that generality—by the inquiry, that is, by the desire for them, together with that [inquiry].

If it is argued that, in that case, because there is necessarily no attainment of the particular from that inquiry, there would be an absence of doubt and so forth; to this he replies: "Determination" (*avāya*), etc.
Or rather, determination (*avāya*) itself is the causal capacity for that [cognition]; even in its absence—and not only in its presence—it is never, at any time, and not always [the cause].

Now, an opponent might argue: "Surely, for one who is at a distance, that universal (*sāmānya*) is not apprehended, but only the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); however, because of the arising of a certainty regarding a universal consisting in the exclusion (*vyapoha*) of what is neither its cause nor its effect, the worldly person (*vyavahārī*) considers that universal to be apprehended. Refuting this, the author supports the meaning of the verse, saying: "For just as... and so forth.

For indeed, in whatever manner there is a distinction—that is, a difference—of that universal (*sāmānya*) from the individuals, it is illogical and untenable for one who perceives it, such as a Vaiśeṣika or similar proponent whose nature is to observe that [universal], that such a universal should not be perceived or determined; rather, its perception alone is logical. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the power of seeing that," etc.; because of the power—the efficacy—of seeing that universal, even among those things that are distinct by way of differences in location and so forth.
"In what [things]? To this he says: "In those beginning with substance" (*dravyādiṣu*).

Those things for which substance (*dravya*) is the first among qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are thus described. In them, the mention of "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is an illustration; by that, the "production of denotation" (*abhidhānotpatti*) is also included.

This is what is meant: particulars such as substance and the like are the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), while the universal (*sāmānya*) such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth is the qualifier. And that [universal], if unperceived, cannot be the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*) regarding them; otherwise, even when a staff is not perceived, there would sometimes be the cognition "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍī*).

But this is not so, because of the statement: "There is no cognition of a qualified object without the qualifier having been apprehended. In that very same way, for the follower of the Sugata (the Buddhist) who perceives the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—that is, one whose nature is to see the particular—it is illogical that there should be a non-perception of that, namely, a non-perception of the particular.
From what [source] is this known? To this, he says: "In the perception of that," and so forth.

Because the perception of that particular (svalakṣaṇa) gives rise to a conceptual construction (vikalpa) that excludes everything else—since there arises a conceptual determination (niścaya) regarding the exclusion or differentiation of other dissimilar things, such as white horses (*karka*) and the like, from that intended particular such as a fragment of clay (*khaṇḍa*)—[the particular is indeed indicated].

[Objection: Even if that conceptual construction arises by the power of that [perception], nevertheless, the particular is not indicated [by it], because there is no necessary connection (*niyamābhāvāt*). To this, he says: "That," and so forth.

The experience of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is its perception; by means of that, the "exclusion" (*vyapoha*)—the differentiation from what is dissimilar—which is sought or desired, is attained. Alternatively, because it has exclusion as its object, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is itself called "exclusion. How then can the Buddhist be said to be one who does not perceive, or one who does not ascertain? On the contrary, he is indeed a perceiver. For certainly, if Devadatta were not perceived, his exclusion from Yajñadatta could not be established or cognized; and if that [exclusion] were not cognized, there would be no perception of him.

The intention here is as follows: when this Buddhist [cognizer] becomes a perceiver of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that has been experienced, then—since there is no apprehension even conceptually (*vikalpataḥ*) of the universal (*sāmānya*) such as color or shape belonging to something situated at a distance—the doubt or error based on the apprehension of that [universal], such as "Is this a crane or a banner? or "Among cranes, is it a banner?", or likewise "Is it a post or a person? or "Among persons, is it specifically a post?", would not occur; yet it does occur. Therefore, that universal of the distant object is first apprehended.
The conceptual determination of a universal— which consists in the exclusion of that which is neither its cause nor its effect— arises;
this universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) serves as the qualifier.

Now, having raised another objection from the opposing side regarding the commonality of color, shape, and so forth based on the power of perception, he says "svalakṣaṇe" and so on, while refuting it.

For the Tathāgata who perceives the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by which or in which there is the discernment (*upalakṣaṇa*) or determination (*niścayana*) of that specific characteristic is so described. Even in the absence of that [discernment], there is the exclusion (*apoha*) or differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*) of another—that is, of something of a different class—from that intended specific characteristic; the conceptual construction having that as its object is likewise so called. When such a conceptualization is being performed, even for one like the Vaiśeṣika who perceives universals (*jāti*), how could it be contradictory for there to be a cognition regarding certain distinct things—such as those possessing the universal "cowness" and so forth—which are inherent (*samavāyin*) in certain capacities, and not in others, even without the conceptual construction of discerning that [specific characteristic] or without the determination of discerning a universal?

If it is asked, "How can a universal (*sāmānya*) that is not perceived be the cause of its cognition?"—to this he replies: "Because it is the cause," and so forth. The universal is the cause of that cognition because its causal power (*śakti*) is inconceivable. [Objection: But when a question is raised regarding a perceived object, the answer "because its causal power is inconceivable" is not applicable elsewhere, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As it has been said:
"That which has exclusion as its object is called 'exclusion' (apoha)."

If it is argued that whatever is considered by oneself as the self [is the object], as stated in the *Prakaraṇavārtika* on page 35 and elsewhere, and that a universal (*sāmānya*) is never observed anywhere; to this he replies: "In the other case as well.

This means that not only in the position of the proponent of the universal (*jāti*), but also in the other case—the position of the proponent of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—the answer is precisely this: "because the power of the cause is inconceivable. This is what he considers to be the response.

Now, if it is thought: "Since there exists a distinction between the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) based on their being perceived or not perceived, how can there be a claim that they are indistinguishable? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction. Since, like the universal, there is likewise no perception of the particular, you must consider that for both of them, there is either existence or non-existence [equally]. Therefore, it is not tenable to say that the universal is grasped by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) born of perception; thus the opponent has been rendered speechless.

"In this case, what is to be expressed by means of the intrinsic natures of things would likewise be so in the subsequent [case], and thus everyone would be victorious"—this is the remainder [of the argument].
Or, let it be so; nevertheless, demonstrating the establishment of his own position, he says "of the non-existent," and so forth.
Just as a cognition devoid of sensory particulars excludes the non-existent, so too let it be admitted that clear sensory cognition, due to the presence of its own object, excludes the non-existent.

(8) If the perception of an object situated at a distance were to produce a conceptual cognition— such as "something exists"— which excludes its own object from among non-existent things, then likewise, even when the nature of all other entities is not perceived, the vision of what is distant could be considered to grasp mere existence.

Indeed, it is not only that one who perceives an object in close proximity fails to notice the specific differences in its even or uneven forms; rather, because one is incapable of perceiving the sequence of specific conceptual distinctions such as "existence" (sattā) and so forth,
this person— having asserted that he sees only the unique [particular]— must undergo the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (kośapāna),
for those with impaired senses do not perceive the specific qualities of the moon and other objects even when they are seen.

In that regard, one who postulates the non-perception of the moon and so forth does not merely fail to perceive the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so on because their appearance is absent in what is seen; rather, by entering into the conceptual construction of the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nairātmya*), he degrades himself— since the probandum is unestablished— by failing to perceive his own internal specific characteristic as it was heard [in scripture].

Therefore, [the distinction] has been made both externally and internally! Consequently, one might perceive something as distinguished by a certain similar transformation; perceiving it as thus distinguished, one does not necessarily cognize the specific difference, just as when one recollects what is non-existent—this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which "from everything undesirable" is understood; and "existent" (*sat*) is also an elliptical expression, referring to everything desirable.

The connection is as follows: just as by whatever mode of fitness (*yogyatā*) a cognition that is non-sensory and conceptual (*anakṣavikalpadhīḥ*)—that is, a mental conceptual cognition (*mānasī vikalpabuddhiḥ*)—might take as its object [the six categories] delimited by [the category of] "existence" (*sadvidyā*), so too, by that same mode, a clear sensory cognition (*spaṣṭākṣadhīḥ*), i.e., a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣabuddhiḥ*), would exclude the non-existent from the existent. Regarding the qualification "non-sensory" (*anakṣa*): this is stated with respect to our own system (*svamatāpekṣayā*), not with respect to the Buddhists (*saugatāpekṣayā*). For according to them, every conceptual cognition is indeed non-sensory; thus, for them, that qualification would be redundant. Therefore, the sense is that in this manner, the clear sensory cognition excludes the non-existent from the existent.
Why? To this he says: "Because of the proximity of its own object.

Here, the word "śabda" (sound) is to be understood as meaning that an object capable of being perceived is the "own object" (svārtha), and its "proximity" (sannidhi) is its presence in a suitable location and so forth;
thus, let this be accepted or admitted.

For the Buddhist, [the cognition] is not produced by the sense faculties, but rather is mental or produced by non-conceptual [perception]; explaining the verse, he says: "At a distance," and so forth.
If the perception of an object by a person standing at a distance were to produce a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), what would it be doing? What would it be excluding (*apohantī*)?
To this he says: "its own object" (*svaviṣayam*).

Why? [Because] in what manner could it exclude the non-existent, such as a donkey’s horn, neither from anything else nor from the existent? To this he says: “In some way” (*kim api asti*)—that is, by that manner; even one whose vision is directed at a distant object would not be conceived as a cognition devoid of sensory conceptualization. Of what nature would it be? One that apprehends pure existence (*sanmātra-grāhinī*).

Again, regarding the word "punaḥ" (furthermore) used in the sense of inquiry—"under what condition [is this]?"—to this he says: even when there is the non-perception of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all things, not only when there is their perception.

Now, if it is thought: "The cognition consisting of non-sensory conceptualization (*anakṣavikalpadhīḥ*) is thus appropriate because its object is a non-entity (*anartha*); but sensory cognition (*indriyabuddhi*) is not so, because the opposite is the case"; [we reply: no, for it will be demonstrated that even that [sensory cognition] has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object.
And he will say: "The conceptual constructions of statements, when correctly investigated, have reality as their object" (Siddhiviniścaya 5.4).
Therefore, it remains that [the cognition] such as "the commonality of color, shape,
and so forth" is indeed produced by the object, because it arises from the capacity of the object;
this is true even for conceptual cognition.
Page 133, Line 1:

Now, one might argue: "Let there be no absence of *avagraha* and the other stages in the perception of distant objects because they serve as its indicators; however, in the perception of nearby objects, those stages would occur because the opposite is the case. To this, he says: "Certainly not merely," and so forth.

The word *vai* indicates a shaking of the head (in negation). It is not merely that [the sense-organ] perceives an object that is close; rather, it does not even discern those specific distinctions such as apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth, which consist in the perception—that is, the grasping—of the two forms, namely the similar and the dissimilar, i.e., the forms of transformation that are alike and otherwise. What then? It does not discern even the specific conceptualizations of existence (*sattā*) and so on; for "existence" is the first among those [qualities] such as "soundness" (*śabdatva*), and their conceptualizations are the determinations (*vyavasāya*). It does not discern even those specificities.

This is what is meant: just as one who perceives objects nearby—having previously observed in some case that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "existence" or "knowability," which arise sequentially, nevertheless establishes that their activity occurs in a sequence even when there is simultaneous determination (*vyavasāya*), because multiple simultaneous conceptual exclusions (*vyāvṛtti-vikalpa*) are impossible—likewise, having observed the specific perceptions of even and uneven forms arising sequentially at a distance, one establishes them in the same way when nearby; for the proof of the unperceived by means of the perceived cannot be denied.

Now, if it is thought: "If one who perceives an object nearby perceives its specific manifestations (*darśanaviśeṣa*), why does he not determine them in that very same way?"—to this he replies: "Because the sequence is impossible to perceive.

This means that for those specific manifestations perceived by one who sees an object nearby, the sequence cannot be perceived, just as in the case of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth; [this applies] precisely because of the sequence.
