It might be thought that, in due order, one who perceives a proximate object sees only the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a momentary, partless atom; because of the specific nature of that perception, one does not perceive [other things], nor indeed those that exist. How then can it be said that "it is equal"? To this he says: "Perceiving this," and so forth. The meaning is: having asserted that this Buddhist or the world perceives only the unique [particular] and nothing else, one must undergo the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (*kośapāna*), because there is no other way to establish that claim.
Therefore, the hymn beginning with "sama" (equal) and so forth is [appropriate],
because of the specific perception of even and uneven forms [of the body] without the drinking of intoxicants.
Now, establishing the apprehension of a universal by means of the power of sensory cognition that is admitted to be erroneous by others, he says: "by those with impaired senses," and so forth.

Those whose senses (*indriya*) are impaired (*upahata*), meaning corrupted by jaundice (*kāmalā*) and other such conditions—even when there is the perception of the moon and so forth (the word "and so forth" [ādi] referring to its circularity and the like), not only in the absence of such perception—likewise, regarding those with impaired senses, the Buddhist and others postulate the initial absence of the perception of the moon and so forth. From what do they postulate this? To this he replies: "that," and so forth.

The distinction of that moon and so forth is its oneness and so on; the non-perception of that [distinction] means the non-observation of the moon and so forth when such [oneness] is not perceived, because it is considered impossible for a single entity to possess two forms—one grasped and the other not.
What does it do? To this he says: "Not only... and so forth.

Not only does one not perceive the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth—namely, partless, momentary atoms of form and so forth—for what reason? Because of perception (*dṛṣṭi*).

Because the perception of form and so forth lacks that appearance—due to the absence of the appearance of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) imagined by others—it is considered that there is no perception of external objects even by those whose faculties are unimpaired, just as there is none for those with impaired faculties.
If it is argued that even if such perception does not occur, the Vijñānavādin has nothing [to lose] thereby; to this he replies: "But rather," and so on.
That is to say, however, one does not perceive even the internal specific characteristic—the specific characteristic of cognition itself—by oneself, through one's own self.
From where is this [known]? To this he says: "Just as," and so forth.
The connection is: "because the internal particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear, just as it is heard and just as it is accepted.
If it is argued, "In that case, let there be a total voidness elsewhere as well, since the analysis is the same as for the external," he says here: "The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)," and so forth.
The Buddhist, entering into the conceptualization of the selflessness (*nairātmya*)—the formless nature (*svarūpa*) of both cognition and the cognizable—shamelessly exposes himself.

Why is this? To this he says: "To be proven," and so forth; [it is] thus established both externally and internally! Just as there is the appearance of a universal (*sāmānya*) even when there is no manifestation [of its particulars], so too is there the perception of the moon and other objects by those with impaired senses even when their specific qualities are not perceived. Thus, he thinks: "How could perception not be considered as grasping only the existent (*sanmātra-grāhin*)?"
For the purpose of the conclusion, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Since this is the case, therefore this worldly person (*vyavahārī*), seeing some object such as a man (*puruṣa*) as qualified by a certain similarity of transformation with something else such as a post (*sthāṇu*), and even while striving toward that specific difference of transformation qualified by that [similarity], does not necessarily perceive the distinction; nor does the distinction become manifest. He provides an illustration: "even while remembering," and so forth.

Just as someone, while recollecting something by means of some kind of similar transformation, may perceive its particularity yet not necessarily remember that particularity, so it is with the subject at hand; thus,
when the particulars such as unity and so forth are not perceived, this is the position favored by the Buddhists.
An external object also becomes the object of an internal, non-erroneous, and determinate cognition.
If one does not necessarily perceive the distinction, what then would that be? To this he says: "For one of equal vision," and so forth:

"For one of equal vision, the desire for a distinction and the doubt regarding the determination of its own object constitute an error (*bhrānti*)—the apprehension of that [object] as being something else—which appears clearly even though it is an error. (9)

Observing a pervasive nature and yet seeking another [nature] regarding its specific qualities, the practitioner does not necessarily understand it, because of the possibility of a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Thus, the non-apprehension of either the true or other-nature is doubt, which is indeed instability;
furthermore, apprehending it otherwise is contradiction (*visaṃvāda*).
The ascertainment of the true nature [of an object] is the conclusion;
and all this is invariably concomitant with purposeful activity,
because doubt arises from the perception of a general property, the non-perception of a specific property, and the recollection of a specific property.

From *avagraha* (perception), which consists of a general vision, there arises a desire for particulars, which is *viśeṣehā* (inquiry into particulars). To the question "What is that [desire]? he says: "*Ārekā*"—that is, *viśeṣehā*.

Here, the case-ending of the word "arisen" (*jātā*) is to be understood as having been transformed; thus, it connects with the phrase "of that," meaning "of that inquiry into particulars, there is *ārekā*, i.e., doubt (*saṃśītiḥ*)."
Is it always the case that [doubt] arises from that?

He says: no. By the word "own" (*sva*), "endeavor" (*īhā*) is understood. When there is non-ascertainment of its object—the specific feature desired by it—there is doubt, not ascertainment; the intention is that sometimes ascertainment of it also arises from that.
Showing that from that [doubt] not only uncertainty (*āreka*) arises, but also error (*viparyaya*), he says: "Error is the apprehension of something as what it is not.

Thus, he states its nature to show that from that [doubt] not only uncertainty and misconception (*avāya*) arise, but also error and misconception: "Apprehension of something as what it is not" means, for example, the apprehension of a post as a person, or like the apprehension of the external where there is no external object.
Nor is the apprehension of that [multiplicity] unestablished, because it appears.
Just as the pervasion of mutually distinct forms such as blue and so forth occurs through a single cognition, so too is there the apprehension of things distinct from themselves;

this has been explained and will be explained further by the passage beginning with "the world is non-delusory for the Buddhist" (*avibhrame saugataṃ jagat*). And this is accepted in the case of non-delusion.

If [it is argued that] it transcends all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that same fault remains, because there would be no apprehension of it in any way whatsoever. Therefore, one must admit that there is an external error; thus, everything is well-established.
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "appearing clearly," meaning "distinct."

By this, the view that all mental error arises from the perception of similarity is refuted; for such [an error] cannot logically possess a clear manifestation, yet it is perceived—as in the case of a mirage—that even the error of water and so forth arising from that [perception of similarity] appears in such a manner. This is the designation of the fifth case ending (*pañcamīvibhakti*).
Comparison: "Some say that even that [erroneous cognition] is mental; for them, the following text is contradicted:
'The sense organs are also the cause of cognitions such as blue or a double moon'—" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 3).
Even that which arises from similarity is clear.
He explains the verse, beginning with "the pervasive" (*vyāpaka*):

The connection is as follows—that the practitioner, perceiving an object whose nature is pervasive rather than non-pervasive, and whose nature consists of similarity, unity, and transformation, yet further seeking its internal differentiation toward its specific particulars (*viśeṣa*), does not necessarily—that is, not by rule—cognize or ascertain that particular.
Why is this so? To this he says: "The causal complex" (*sāmagrī*), and so forth.

Having demonstrated the nature of doubt and other such states— which arise from the conceptualization of that causal complex characterized by proximity in space and so forth, which pertains to a specific [object]— he says "tattve" etc., showing their production from *īhā*: "cognition is doubt."

Of what nature is it? It is "of an unstable nature" (*anavasthaiva*), because of the statement that "the pervading nature is [the cause]. Since the pervaded nature is also implied by that—due to its being inseparable from it—and since that [pervaded nature] is manifold, it follows that when the pervading nature is observed, there is a "nature of reality" (*tattvasvabhāva*) consisting of the intended pervaded nature, and an "other nature" (*itarasvabhāva*) consisting of the unintended pervaded nature. That which has no stable state or fixed position (*avasthiti*) regarding these two is so described; the meaning is that it is wavering between both.

Some maintain that even the cognition of reality as consisting of both the universal and the particular is a state of doubt, because the pervaded does not exist without the pervader; however, the word "only" (eva) is used for the purpose of refuting that [view], since such cognition consists of the states of being either the nature of reality or its opposite.

Otherwise—that is, by means of one mode of the nature of reality as another mode of nature, or by means of another mode of nature as the mode of the nature of reality—there is again non-correspondence, which is error. *Avāya* is the determination of the intended pervading nature; it is the realization of reality. And all of this, beginning with doubt (*saṃśīti*), is invariably concomitant with *īhā* (investigation).
The Buddhists and others [hold this] because of their realization of reality as consisting of both the universal and the particular.
Now, even if there were indeed such an impartial vision (*samadṛṣṭi*), what follows from that by which there could be an inquiry (*īhā*) regarding particulars and consequently doubt (*ārekā*)?
Indeed, it is not logical for that [cognition] to occur elsewhere than where the perception occurred; otherwise, the perception of a jar might occur with respect to a cloth.

Furthermore, regarding the perception of a universal, if a particular is present and meets the conditions for perceptibility yet is not perceived, then there is simply its absence, and thus neither inquiry (*īhā*) nor doubt (*ārekā*) can arise with respect to it.

On the other hand, if it is otherwise—that is, if there is doubt precisely because of the non-perception of something imperceptible—then what is the point of saying "from the perception of the common"? For there is no doubt regarding heaven and such things due to their perception. To this, he says: "Regarding the universal," and so forth.

Because of the continuation of the phrase "seeing the pervading nature," that universal which is the pervading nature of those particulars for which there is desire and apprehension is what is understood here; from the perception of that through direct perception arises the "perception of the universal" (*sāmānyadarśana*) for one who possesses equal vision.
The very absence of a specific distinction does not fail to meet the conditions for perception for one who possesses equal vision.

By this [argument], it is not logical that the [cognition] of one thing should occur upon the perception of another; otherwise, the cognition of a jar would occur upon the perception of a cloth. That [objection] is refuted:

for indeed, just as that universal possesses the nature of the intended particular, so too the cloth possesses the nature of a cloth—this is stated for one who is striving to grasp the particulars pervaded by that [universal].
By this, that which was stated— namely, that "if the universal is not perceived, there would be an absence of the particulars because they are by nature perceptible"—
is refuted; for at that time, the Teacher did not admit that they possess that nature of being perceptible, otherwise he would not have said "of one who is striving," since who indeed,
while seeing what is perceptible, would strive to grasp it?

As for what was stated regarding the pervasive universal—that this being so, doubt arises from the non-perception of the unobservable rather than from the perception of the universal—this too is refuted by the following: since doubt is necessarily appropriate there because of the observation of a reason that is inconclusive due to the non-observation of the nature of that [universal] and its opposite, it cannot arise merely from the non-observation of something unobservable.

Otherwise, because the consciousness of another, which is unobservable, would not be perceived, its non-existence could not be established, and the conventional usage of "dead" and so forth would be abolished.
Comparison: Otherwise, non-existence results from the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, and not from mere non-perception;
yet, even so, doubt arises from non-perception alone. Thus, [the claim] that "this [doubt] is due to the perception of the universal" is futile—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 18.

As for what was said—that in some cases doubt arises even without the perception of a universal—that too is not well-stated; for even in that case, if there is no cognition of the universal through verbal testimony or other means, such doubt would not occur. Furthermore, the doubt regarding the meaning of a treatise for one who does not perceive inherence (*samavāya*) arises from this very fact, since the statement "due to the perception of the universal" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), and for this purpose, the *Siddhiviniścaya* (2) states that it is accompanied by deliberation (*vitarka*).
Thus it has been stated;
by this [statement], the convention (*samaya*) is considered due to the teacher's disagreement and so forth.
Because its particulars are not perceived—that is, because those particulars of that universal are not perceived or seen—this too is an indication of the non-grasping of them.

The connection is as follows: because of the recollection of specific qualities (*viśeṣasmṛti*), that is, from the memory of two specific features, doubt arises; therefore, "all this" [doubt] is invariably concomitant with *īhā* (investigation).
This [mention of *īhā*] is merely an illustration; by it, one should understand other cases such as the arising of error from the recollection of contrary specific qualities, and so forth.
As for the comparison: in places like Kānyakubja, doubt is observed to arise from memory at the very first moment, even without the prior perception of a commonality (*sāmānyapratyakṣatā*).
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 18: Because doubt is absent, there is no uncertainty regarding the meaning of a treatise for one who has not grasped the linguistic convention.
Rather, the connection is that there would be a mere non-apprehension of it, namely,
the non-apprehension of the specific difference.
Indeed, there is no doubt other than the recollection of specific features, because this [doubt] consists in a recollection that grasps both aspects—*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p.

18. Now, if this is an error, it must be preceded by memory; in that case, it cannot have a clear manifestation like inference. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that "even an error has a clear manifestation," if one objects thus; we reply: No, for this is contradicted by errors regarding water and the like.

For the Naiyāyika, [the probans is] by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*); otherwise, how could it be "perceptual" (*adhyakṣa*)? Thus there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), for recognition—which is preceded by memory—is nonetheless perceptual and possesses a vivid manifestation (*spaṣṭāvabhāsi*).

Now, one might object: "Doubt and the like are specific types of memory, and since that [memory] arises from non-conceptual experience by virtue of the very nature of the object, what need is there for effort (*īhā*) in that regard? To this he says: "In non-conceptual [perception]," and so forth.
Is it not the case that, through the very nature of the object, a memory of a similar kind arises in memory by means of a formless cognition precisely from non-conceptual vision? (10)

Since linguistic and practical activity proceeds precisely upon those things already seen when they are perceived—by the force of consciousness itself through the recollection and desire for what is of the same class—what is the use of postulating the form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*)? Merely pure awareness (*avabodhamātra*), by its very nature as an entity, would be understood as the cause of the relevant recollection.

Even if one were to postulate the form of the object, that specific distinction must still be sought by which [awareness] would differ from object to object; otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of confusion].
By that [specificity] alone, cognition would be the perception of a restricted object.

If it is argued: "Since the cognition that has arisen functions as the cause for a memory of a specific type, it belongs to that [cognition] alone and not to another; thus, how can there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? For a real object-form that is not itself perceived does not exist in memory, and since there is no distinction [between cognitions], and because one perceives a form in the case of error (*viplava*), while in the case of anything else it would be mere conceptualization (*kalpanā*)—which would lead to over-extension—it is precisely by this much that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is established, so let it be so," [we reply: this is merely incoherent prattle, as it fails to establish even the mere error intended by oneself. This is because the establishment of knowledge (*vidyā*) from ignorance (*avidyā*) alone cannot be prevented, which leads to an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭānuṣaṅga*).

Since [the object] is merely an illusion and its nature is not established in the ultimate sense, the Buddhist—who wishes to establish entities as "this" or "not this" through the reversal of conventional perception—is strictly non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) alone. Enough of this digression.

The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that [non-conceptuality arises] from the perception of the non-conceptual, from the experience of the non-conceptual, and from the very nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*) and the inherent nature of entities (*bhāva-svābhāvya*), and not from anything else.

Showing that this is a refutation if one were to admit a conceptual cognition with a universal as its object (*sāmānya-viṣaya-vikalpa-buddhi*) within the memory of a similar class (*sajātīya-smṛti*), he says: "formless," and so forth.

By means of a formless cognition—that is, by a perception devoid of conformity to the object—why would not every conceptualization of a universal (*sāmānyavikalpa*) arise as a memory of its own kind? This must be supplied [to the argument].

Why does it indeed arise? Because of the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*), that is, due to the power of existence (*bhāvaśakti*). For this reason, the postulation of a grasped form—the form of the object—within this cognition is not tenable.

If memory is such a kind of cognition, and its arising occurs from experience—which is devoid of the form of the object—then how can it [memory] possess that [object]? *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.374. For just as it is asked how that [memory] can possess the form—that is, be endowed with the form—from an experience that is itself formless, so too it is the same [question]: how can it possess that form [of the universal] from that [experience] which is devoid of the form of a universal? Thus, the logic is identical.
And thus, the claim that "recollection of a similar thing" is for this purpose has been stated;

furthermore, the argument based on the intrinsic nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*) is also no answer. Otherwise, since there is a cognition devoid of form (*nirākāra-avabodha*), the objection is raised that "it [the cognition] possesses that [form] for that very reason," which is quite trivial.
Thus the refutation is offered.
From the very nature of the object, through perception, it would possess a form.

Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "In the very perception of that," and so forth. "Perception of that" (*taddṛṣṭi*) refers to non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpikā dṛṣṭi*). When that exists, if one were to accept that conventional linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) does not proceed with respect to those things perceived [by it], from what [source would that usage arise]? To this, he says: "Cognition" (*saṃvitti*), and so forth.

The "power" (*bala*) of cognition is its capacity; from that arises a memory of a similar kind, and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), aversion is included. What, then, is gained by postulating a grasped form for perception—that is, by postulating a similarity [between cognition and the object]? One might as well understand that mere awareness, devoid of a grasped form, is—by the very nature of things (*bhāvasvabhāvataḥ*) and due to the causal power of the entity—the cause of memory arising from its own kind, meaning it is the cause of recollecting what is similar.
The rest has been discussed there:
in that context, it is held that because memory possesses a form, perception must also be established as possessing a form.

Regarding comparison (*tulanā*): "If linguistic usage arises from a memory produced by the power of consciousness regarding things already seen, precisely upon seeing that [comparison], then it is inference. — *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 24.

For which reason the author of the *Vārttika* stated thus: "When those very [objects] are seen, because there is no recollection of the cause that consists in their own operation arising from the power of consciousness," and so forth (*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī*, p.
31). And he said: "When those very [objects] are seen... through recollection, practical activity proceeds by means of desire" (*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 498).
Furthermore, it has been said: "From the memory [of what] arises through the power of consciousness regarding things seen," and so forth (*Pravāhaṇavāda-svopajña-ṭīkā*, p.

6). Now, even if the establishment of the objectivity of the perception is not proven by means of a memory possessing a form, its establishment may still occur through another way; that is, through the determination of each respective object—so it was stated.
The perception of the possession of form connects this [cognition] with the object by means of that form; for it does not do so apart from the nature of the object.

If it is argued: "Therefore, because the object is cognized from that [cognition], the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the conformity to the form of the object (*meyarūpatā*), which is a non-conceptual awareness of the object" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 2.305); [we reply:
the proof [of this] is the conformity to the form of the object.
—*Pravāha*:
"Therefore, the conformity to the form of the object of cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it brings about the apprehension of the object"—*Tattvopaplava*, p. 53.
The relevant passage is found at Nyāyakumuda 167,
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa 107,
and Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī 123.
Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, page 240;
Sanmatitarkaṭīkā, page 312;
Syādvādaratnākara, page 136.
Prameyaratnamālā 2.9;
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 137.
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 33;
*Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p.
36. Here he says: "Even having postulated," and so forth.

Not only without conceptualizing, but even by conceptualizing the form of the object, one must seek that specific excellence (*viśeṣa*) or distinction (*atiśaya*) of the vision which consists in its similarity to the object—that excellence by which it would be differentiated with respect to each respective object. Otherwise, in the absence of such a search for that distinction, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If the determination of [the cognition] according to each object were based merely on that [external] form, then some cognition of blue would belong to all blue things, or a cognition having the form of existence would belong to all existent things; thus there would be over-extension. Therefore, since a specific distinction must be sought, the determination of [the cognition] according to each object is established otherwise [than through mere similarity]. This is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that for you as well, since cognition is formless and thus indistinguishable everywhere, the same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) applies; to this he replies with the words "by that very [capacity]," and so forth.

The connection is to be understood as follows: by that very specific capacity (*yogyatāviśeṣa*), there would be a correct perception—a grasping that consists in the cognition of a specifically determined object—so how can there be an over-extension?
And by that very [capacity], it would serve as the cause for a specific memory, so how can there be an over-extension?
The sense is that it should conform to the form of every existing thing;
thus, being currently a Naiyāyika, the learned teacher, warding off an over-extension of the argument, says "since," and so forth.

Because cognition arises from an object endowed with properties such as grossness, that [cognition] belongs to that object and not to another object which is not its producer; for this reason, how could there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? Otherwise, smoke might arise even from what is not fire. It might be thought that if "that which is produced belongs to that [from which it arose]" were stated, it would apply to the sense organs and so forth as well. To this he says: "Of whatever kind... and so on.

That which is similar—that is, of the same class—is treated as the cause of memory for that [object]; it causes a person engaged in practical activity (*vyavahāra*) to act toward that [object] and not toward another. So how can there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? Nor does the sense organ and so forth treat [an object] as the cause of memory for its own kind. [Objection: But surely, when cognition—which is a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*)—is itself of the nature of experience (*anubhava*), then by that [cognition] the object becomes known; and in that case, it is the cause of memory for that [object], and not otherwise. This is not the view of the Naiyāyika. To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

When there exists a specific object such as blue and so forth, that cognition which has an "aspect" (*ākāra*)—meaning an aspect similar to that object—is described as such. Since that [cognition] is unperceived and undetermined, it does not differ from non-existence, such as a hare's horn and the like;

for what [difference could there be]? When memory is being produced, there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) because [the cognition] has already arisen, and so forth—this is the connection [of the argument].

This is what is meant: if non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*) were devoid of that excellence [of form], it could not be the cause of memory as conceived by the Naiyāyikas; for then, even in the case of an error (*viplava*) where the object is absent, since there is the perception of its form, the cognition being manifested must possess a form, as there is no other possible explanation.
Thus it has been said:
"the form of the object..."

If it is argued that "there might be a suspicion of the form of a non-object even when the mind possesses an object" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.371), [the author] replies here with the words beginning "in the case of confusion" (*viplave*).

"In confusion," that is, in a state of error, there is a perception of an image (*sākāradarśana*) which is non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpaka-jñāna*); and the use of the term "perception" (*darśana*) is for this purpose—otherwise, the use of the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) would have been appropriate. Therefore, by that reason, relying upon that [perception]; the particle *tat* should be understood as having the meaning of *tasya* (of that).

If one were to construct a conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of that objective form (*grāhyākāra*) elsewhere—in the cognition of the waking state—it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because it would follow that any object whatsoever could be established from any unestablished example. This connects with the phrase "it is not thus perceived" (*naivaṃ saṃvedanam*).

Even in the case of a cognitive distortion (*viplava*), the perception of an objective form is unestablished; for by means of a formless perception, due to some error, there is the grasping of something non-existent, such as a jar, as if it were external. This is the intended meaning.
This has been stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*: "And this is not merely external; rather, it appears as if it were external.
Why is this so? Because of error (*bhrānti*); for that [error] is the same elsewhere," as shown by the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Here the opponent says: "By that much alone," etc. By that much alone—by the mere appearance of the non-existent—let everything, including all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) consisting of valid cognition and its opposite, which are constructed by false conceptualization, be established. This is because of the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.7), "Validity [is established] through worldly convention," and so forth. Let everything be in that very way; let it be entirely so that the non-existent pot and such are apprehended by that very formless cognition. If this is the case, the Teacher replies with the words beginning "by itself" (*svayam*).
Since that which was intended and accepted by the Buddhist himself—that it is mere delusion—is unestablished for him due to his failure to comprehend it, [the opponent] asks:
"What [follows]? He replies with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*) and so forth:
"In every way, by every manner, it is merely a disconnected or incoherent prattle. This has been determined in the first section.
The Buddhist states the refutation regarding the establishment of that which he intends— the passage beginning with "Brahman," etc.—

and the intended meaning here is as follows: just as delusion is established from delusion alone, so too, since the establishment of Brahman from knowledge characterized as perception and so forth cannot be prevented, [the opponent's position] is merely incoherent prattle.

[The opponent objects: "Granted that its establishment [as consciousness] occurs, nevertheless, since it appears like a jar or other objects, its status as an error is established; thus our desired conclusion is proven. To this, he replies: "Because of the undesirable consequence for the Buddhist. His "desired" [position] is that cognition is manifold, momentary, and entirely erroneous. His "undesirable" [consequence] is the reality of Brahman—unitary, non-momentary, all-pervasive, and non-erroneous. The connection is that because of the consequence of this [latter], [the world] would be *tanmātra* (mere-consciousness). For just as an error, even when perceived within an error, is not itself an error, so too, he thinks, is the reality of Brahman.
If it is argued that, according to the proponents of error (*vibhramavādins*), even error itself is not perceived from anything at all, [the author] says here: "From mere error," and so forth.
Therefore, it is indeed an error.

From what kind [of source]? From that which, in the ultimate sense—that is, in reality—is of an unestablished nature and an undetermined form. By means of the reversal of common perception—the worldly consensus that "in states such as dreaming there is erroneous cognition, but not in the waking state"—the Buddhist, desiring to establish entities (bhāvas) as being either this or that (i.e., as having their own intended nature or the nature intended by others), through the inversion that "at other times it is otherwise erroneous, or even in dreams and so forth it is non-erroneous," [does so] with words that are strictly non-conceptual and devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). The particle *eva* has the sense of "exclusively" or "necessarily. The word *na* has the sense of "not this" (*nedantayā*), meaning neither as having their own intended nature nor as having the nature intended by others. The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with what precedes. Thus, the Buddhist intends to establish things as being of one or another form.
Or if this [memory] is only slightly unestablished—enough, let there be no further prolixity.
Therefore, by means of the cognition devoid of form (*nirākārāvabodha*), and so forth, it is established.

Showing that not only is the object-aspect (*grāhyākāra*) lacking in the experience (*anubhava*) when there is a recollection of a similar kind (*sajātīyasmṛti*) due to non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpadarśana*), but that this is also the case for that [recollection] as well, he says: "From all sides," and so forth.

If the nature of consciousness itself, perceiving everything in every way as entirely distinct from [external] characteristics, is the cause of memory, then why is sensory contact not likewise [the cause]?

By the very nature of things, the immediately preceding cognition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), characterized by apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth, is itself distinguished by the contact of the sense organ with its object and serves as the cause for conventional activities such as memory; this is because, through a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the awakening and clarity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) become possible, as in the case of dreams and the like.

Thus, this [cognition], which consists in the awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) arising from the appearance of a continuous succession of its own clearly perceived and non-erroneous specific objects, being directly caused by perception, establishes the reality of manifoldness (*anekāntatattva*).

This occurs because it does not perceive—nor ascertain—all things intended as its own objects as being entirely distinct and excluded in form, even in terms of their existence and other such modes, just as it does in terms of all modes such as blue and so forth, from everything both similar and dissimilar.

Who is this? [It is] consciousness (*bodha*), whose nature is awareness (*bodhātman*) and which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). If it is the cause of memory—that is, if it is contact (*sannikarṣa*), the conjunction of the sense organ with its object—then why is it not likewise the cause of memory in that same manner, by way of the very nature of the thing? It would certainly be so;

and thus there would be a deficiency in experience and a failure to perceive that [object]. Therefore, he considers that there is no distinction [between the two cases] based on its being conscious, as compared to mere contact.

Since the *kārikā* is easy to understand, he does not provide an explanation, but concludes the subject at hand by stating: "By the very nature of the object itself, and not from similarity (*sārūpya*) and so forth"—this is the meaning of the particle *eva*. The "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) is as follows: it is "equal" (*sama*) in terms of being cognition (*jñānatva*), "immediate" (*anantara*) in terms of being the material cause (*upādāna*), and a "condition" (*pratyaya*) consisting of the awareness of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "By itself," and so on.

That is, it is [cognition] by itself (*ātmanā*), and not—as the Sāṃkhya maintains—indirectly (*pāramparyeṇa*) through the contact of the sense organ with the object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*), nor is it distinguished by its own activity in its production; this is what has been considered.

Therefore, the abandonment of that [perception] which is not distinct from mental perception, which is the cause of conventional usage such as memory and so forth—where "and so forth" refers to recognition and the like—that itself, or its very nature, is the cause of conventional usage.

It might be argued: since the cognition of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so on has as its object a reality consisting of both the general and the particular, it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*); therefore, due to the absence of clarity (*vaiśadya*), how can it be non-distinct from that [mental perception]? To this he says: "The causal complex," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: because of the excellence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), characterized by the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects and so forth, there arises the clarity of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus it is "distinguished by that.
Here he provides an illustration: "like dreams and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of disturbances such as desire, grief, and the like is intended.

It might be argued: "Because it is caused by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), this cognition must be erroneous, like those in dreams and so forth. To this he replies with the words "Therefore, this... and so on. "Therefore" (*tat*) means for that reason; because of a specific causal complex consisting of the contact of the sense organ with its object and other factors, "this"—namely, that which is designated as the cognitions of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth—is "not false," meaning non-erroneous, "clear," meaning distinct, and possesses the manifestation of its own "particulars and their continuity," that is, difference and non-difference. Furthermore, this [cognition] is characterized by the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā-prabodha*). Again, by the phrase "not false" and so forth, its validity is established.

This is what is meant: although the cognition of an object arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is nevertheless not erroneous because it originates from a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), as is impossible in cases such as dreams.

If it is argued that the awakening of the latent impression deposited by a previous perception occurs due to the sight of another [similar] object and not from the contact of the sense organ with the object, the author replies: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*), etc.

Let that awakening be caused by a direct, unmediated perception; it establishes the reality of non-absolutism (*anekānta-tattva*), because there is no other perception—distinct from the perception of non-absolutism—that could serve as its cause. This is the intended meaning.
The term *indriyārthasannikarṣa* is a *karmadhāraya* compound characterized by the proximity [of the sense organ] to its object.
He says "we do not see," etc., demonstrating this very point: that which has perception as its sign is the cause for the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

We do not perceive anywhere either a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); rather, we perceive something belonging to a different class (*jātyantara*). Therefore, the reasons [adduced] are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

As has been stated, we never at any time perceive either a particular characteristic or a universal characteristic; in perception, we observe a variety of colors, shapes, and so forth, which possess a common continuity (*anvayin*).

If one does not somehow accept direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which consists of the self-awareness of both oneself and others—as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could one maintain another means of valid cognition? For inference (*anumāna*) is the comprehension of an imperceptible object based on the consideration that something established by itself cannot otherwise be accounted for;

it is not, however, non-occurrent when direct perception is established in some way, whether in relation to oneself or another, as being ultimately real (*paramārtha*). How then could this [inference] establish the absolute falsity of that [perception] independently of anything else, such that one might say: "The status of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result is established exactly according to appearance, and not according to reality"?

Even for another person who describes the reality of the supreme self (*paramātmatattva*)—whether according to their own desire or beyond the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or otherwise—their mouth does not become distorted; for it is only the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves that are established according to their actual nature.

We do not perceive anywhere, whether externally or internally, anything superior or inferior, distinct from individuals, or a universal (*sāmānya*) devoid of them. The word "or" (*vā*) shifts its position and is to be understood immediately after "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*);
thus, we do not perceive either the specific characteristic [as distinct] or [the universal].

We do not perceive anything that is imagined, nor anything having the nature of the ultimate reality, nor the sense of "as if," nor a universal as if it were a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
whether according to its formal arrangement or with a different sequence.

"What then do you see? To this he says: "We see, moreover, another class [of things] which is non-exclusive (anekānta). By this, he demonstrates the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) in proving the absence of absolute exclusivity (*ekāntābhāva*). Showing that not only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) fails to satisfy regarding the nature of being non-exclusive, but rather all logical marks (*liṅga*) as well, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Therefore, following that logic, the remainder of the sentence—"all reasons for non-absolutism (anekānta) are indeed related"—is stated while clarifying the meaning of the verse, beginning with "as has been said" (*yathoktam*), and so forth.

In what manner (*yathā*)—by what method—is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as asserted by the Buddhist, or the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as asserted by the Naiyāyika and others, not seen at any time, whether in the state of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) or in the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)? To the question "Why is this so? he replies with "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), and so forth.
Whence is this? To this he says: "color," and so forth.

"Color" (*varṇa*) refers to blue and the like; "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to circularity and the like; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is connected to each term. By this, in one case there is the inclusion of taste and other qualities, while in another case there is the inclusion of distinctions such as newness or oldness. Thus, how is it? It is manifold (*vicitra*) and variegated (*śabala*). Of what nature is it? We perceive it as something that persists (*anvayin*), since...
If it is argued that, like a forest and so forth, that [perception] is an erroneous indication because it possesses conditions (*pratyaya*); to this he replies: "Of self and other," and so forth.
That by which or in which there is the awakening—that is, the grasping—of both self and other is thus described.
What is that? He says: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If, by some means—whether through a mode of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or a mode of inference (*anumāna*)—one does not regard [the other] as a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇayan*), or if one speaks of another means of knowledge distinct from this valid perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇāt*), how could that Buddhist not establish or maintain that "other" [means], namely non-conceptual vision (*avikalpada-darśana*) and inference (*anumāna*)? This is the rule for establishing [the system].

Now, if it is argued: "Even if, according to the logic already stated, non-conceptual vision is not established, one may nevertheless rely upon conceptual inference (*sāvikalpakam-anumānam*)," to this he replies with the words beginning "by itself" (*svataḥ*).

Inference (*anumāna*) is the comprehension of an imperceptible object (*parokṣārtha*) based on a reflection (*vitarka*) of the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of some established and ascertained mark (*liṅga*), whether it be an effect or something else, which is established not by itself nor by another means of proof. However, that inference is untenable if perception (*pratyakṣa*)—whether with respect to its own nature (*ātman* or *svasvarūpa*) or with respect to another thing such as *dharma*, in its form as existence (*sat*) and so forth, and not in the manner of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)—is being established in an ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) without depending on anything else. This has been discussed [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*] beginning with the verse: "That which is established does not depend on another" (Siddhivi.

How could that [argument] not establish the absolute falsity of perception and the absolute delusive nature of perception? For that which is itself untenable cannot establish another, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, this Buddhist’s proof appears meaningless: just as the cognition of a "forest" is erroneous because it is merely a mental apprehension of a collection (*samūhālambana*) and there is no independent forest existing apart from the trees, so too the establishment of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the result (*phala*) occurs exactly according to how they appear.

"It is performed" (PV 2.357); the ellipsis is "even though the cognitions of the grasped and the grasper do not exist," and one should not say, "on the contrary, it is performed according to reality. Thus he says.

[The opponent objects: "Surely, even for a conventionalist (*vyavahārin*), there is no inference in reality. However, if he resorts to that which is agreeable only so long as it is not investigated (*avicāritaramaṇīya*) for the sake of establishing worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), then I too shall do exactly the same; thus, there is no fault. To this, [the author] replies: "In accordance with what is intended" (*yathehitam*), and so forth. "In accordance with what is intended" means without transgressing that which has been made the object of one's own will. Regarding one who—whether it be the supreme self-reality (*paramātmatattva*), the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*), or otherwise in the manner of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so on—merely speaks or propounds through words alone something that transcends the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātīta*) and is thus non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*); [this applies] even to another person, such as a proponent of the non-duality of the Person (*puruṣa-advaitavādin*).
It is not only the mouth of the Buddhist that becomes distorted;

this is what is meant: just as for the Buddhist, an error that lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is established through inference—which, though lacking validity, is renowned among others—so too for the opponent, non-duality of the Person (*puruṣādvaita*) and so forth are established by means of speech and other factors renowned in worldly convention (*vyavahāra*).
Indeed, it will be demonstrated that a person engaged in worldly convention cannot survive even for a moment without speech.
Because, due to the curvature of the speaker's mouth, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves—and nothing else—would be established according to their actual nature;
or, the word "since" (*yataḥ*) may be used in the sense of an objection, implying that they would not be established at all; and "nanu" is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*).
From the perspective of ultimate truth,
inference is accepted by either the proponent of Brahman or the Sāṃkhya.

If it is argued that by this [argument] one can establish the absolute distinction between error and its opposite through the fact of "being perceived," the author replies here with the words "just as intended" (*yathehitam*), etc.

The intention here is as follows: just as self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone—which is devoid of the forms of both error and its opposite—is established through appearance (*pratibhāsa*), so too is the reality of the Person (*puruṣa*) and other principles established, whether they transcend the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or otherwise, or are accompanied by such means.
The remainder is as before.
Immediately following that, the aforementioned direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists of the awakening of oneself and others, should be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Having first established it as a single [cognition] consisting of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth through the grace of the unique knowledge of conduct (*caritraika-jñāna*), he now says "to be inferred from its fruit" (*phalānumeya*) and so on, establishing it in another way.

Is that which has as its essence a power inferable from its result, and which exists in a differentiated form within itself, a single perception of its own object—either simultaneously or successively?

If the perception characterized by its own object, whose nature consists of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and whose capacity is inferable from its own result, were one, why would it not also be one in its grasping of the general and particular aspects of a proximate object, consisting of *avagraha* (initial apprehension) and *īhā* (investigation)? For it is precisely from the perception of the particular that the recollection which excludes the superimposition of a reality contrary to it must be postulated.

Since the establishment of a single nature for things whose essential characters are mutually contradictory is not precluded by the realization of an entity that has a single ultimate nature despite its diverse manifestations occurring either simultaneously or successively, this [argument] is as follows: because there is some degree of identity (*tādātmya*), a relation cannot be established between the capacity and the possessor of capacity if they were distinct; furthermore, in the extreme view of non-difference (*abhedaikānta*), it would follow that a manifestation, like its capacity, would necessarily be imperceptible.

This is not a fault of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), for it is conventional reality that conceals this [momentariness], just as it conceals circularity and so forth. Thus, this conventional reality, by not concealing the capacity [of the object], establishes its non-exclusive nature (*anekāntatva*).

Therefore, this superimposition (*samāropa*)—occurring with respect to momentary circularity and so forth in perception—leads to the disappearance of the conception of exclusivity (*ekānta-kalpanā*), because perception itself consists in the ascertainment (*vyavasāya*) of the very exclusion of superimpositions such as "blue" and so forth.
When [the term] *dṛṣṭe*... *svalakṣaṇa*...

is used in its own words (*svaśabdena*), an extremist (*ekāntavādī*) is understood; for the sake of that [extremist], regarding that self-cognition (*svasaṃvit*) which has an object, [the author asks] what kind of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is related to them—that which is to be determined by perception? To this he says: "The result" (*phala*), etc.

Power (*śakti*) is to be inferred from its fruit (verse 123). That whose nature (*svabhāva*) is such [power] is described as "that which is so. Or, simultaneously—as if at once—that perception (*pratyakṣa*), being single, why should it not occur sequentially? To this he says: because of the "seeking" (*īhā*) for distinction (*bheda*), that is, for a specific difference (*viśeṣa*), there is the object-mode (*arthaparyāya*) to be grasped by it; likewise, there is the specific mode of cognition (*jñānaparyāyaviśeṣa*). By that very thing—its nature (*ātman* or *svabhāva*)—and by the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning to be established is: why should it not exist with the nature of apprehension (*avagraha*), assimilation (*avāya*), and so forth?
Explaining the verse [beginning with] "īhā," he says: "svārthe" and so forth;
the word *sva* (self/own) is to be explained as before.

Its definition is simply the object (*artha*); that is, the nature of the object which is directly perceived. That which is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the specific nature (*svasvarūpa*) which is directly perceived and cognized by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), consists of a capacity (*sāmarthya*) that is to be inferred from its own result (*svaphala*).

By the word "own" (*sva*), [the author] rejects the absolute difference between the capacity and that which possesses it (the possessor of the capacity), because such a distinction is untenable in this context.

Indeed, it is not logical for causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) to be distinct from that [entity], because the entity is dependent upon it; otherwise, everything would possess that capacity for everything. Furthermore, since *inherence* (*samavāya*) has been refuted and because there is no distinction [in its relation] to all things, how could it be that even if there is no such distinction, a certain thing possesses the capacity for a certain other? If you say, "Because the powers of entities are diverse," then does that possessor of power have other powers distinct from itself by which this is so? If that were the case, the same fault would apply, or else there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If they are not distinct; then it is well said that "the initial capacity is of that nature"— for if there were an absolute difference between the substance possessing the capacity and the capacity itself, the relationship between the capacity and the possessor of the capacity would be impossible.

The point is that because its nature consists in functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), even though it is distinct [from its substrates], if one accepts that "it belongs to this," then since it is eternal, all-pervading, and unitary, inherence (*samavāya*) is equally present with respect to everything.
Granted that there is no distinction between [the two cases],

let it simply be that [the capacity] consists in a power to be inferred from its result; what is the use of the word "intrinsic" (*sva*), since that meaning is understood even through common worldly usage?

If it is argued that people in the world, when perceiving fire from smoke, do not say, "There is fire here because of its own smoke"; it is replied: there is no fault, because [the statement] is intended to refute the views of others. For the view of others is that since an entity consists of multiple potencies, it has multiple effects; therefore, they infer the existence of an entity consisting of a single potency [from a single effect]. To refute that, [the author] uses his own words:
"If it were one, it would be so."
To this, the following reply is given: "The proximate object," and so forth.

A proximate object is a jar or the like; its universal and particular aspects—since those two are the very means of apprehension for that object—why should they not be one and of the same nature as that object? Indeed, they would be so.
This is merely an illustration; it would likewise be of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the rest.
Since that [perception] does not exist, why should one assume that perception itself depends solely upon the observation of a specific feature? To this he says: "That," and so forth.

The meaning is that if there were an imposition (*āropa*) of a contrary reality onto those specific features, and if there were no recollection of its exclusion (*vyavacchedasmṛti*), then the inference of momentariness could not be established at all; for the word "since" (*yataḥ*) has the sense of an objection, and thus the status of that contrary cognition as a superimposition (*samāropa*) would remain unproven.

Why is this so? To this he says: "mutually," and so forth. Because there is no contradiction between the two natures—perception and inference—as regards their mutual identity (*tādātmya*), the realization of an entity whose ultimate nature is a single, manifold manifestation through both simultaneous and successive [modes] is not precluded; therefore, the following [objection] is refuted: [The objection: "If perception and inference were identical in nature, then since perception is non-conceptual and inference is conceptual, they would be mutually contradictory. Furthermore, if they were identical, the distinction between the object of perception and the object of inference would vanish, and the very existence of inference would be undermined. This is refuted because the establishment of the identity of the two natures—perception and inference—is not contradicted by their mutual opposition, given that the cognition of an entity as a single ultimate nature consisting of diverse manifestations occurs through both simultaneous and successive means. Thus, the aforementioned [objection] is discarded.
The view of the Naiyāyikas is that there is inference of Śiva even without his own word (svaśabda) regarding existence.

If, however, it were not [so], then another quality would be superimposed by means of a cause of error— as in the case of "a shell" [being perceived as silver] (Pra.vā. 3.43)— due to the observation of a similarity in form, such as the appearance of silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell.
Thus, the remainder [of the commentary] says "this very [is... and so forth for the purpose of the conclusion;
this is easy to understand.
Why is this so? To this he says: because of their identity in some sense, due to the oneness of the stages beginning with *avagraha*.

If it is argued that "it is not logical [to say] 'the power and the possessor of power are inferred from their effects,' etc., because if the absolute difference between power and the possessor of power is denied, then there is no possibility of any other alternative, and thus they must be identical," to this he replies: Regarding the absolute identity (*abhedaikānta*) accepted by the Buddhist based on the impossibility of a relation (*sambandhāsiddhi*)—as admitted by the Naiyāyika when there is a difference between power and the possessor of power—if that were the case, then when the nature of either the conscious or the non-conscious entity is made an object of cognition through a manifesting act (*vyakti*), that manifestation would result in being entirely imperceptible (*parokṣa*) and invisible, just like the power itself.
And thus, it is thought that there would be the annihilation of all conventional usage regarding entities;
likewise, power (*śakti*) would result in being perceived just like the individual manifestation (*vyakti*).
Therefore, by means of a complete cause... [Pravāha 3]
Thus,
[the passage] beginning with "the cognition of a relation residing in two" (*pra.vārtikālaṃkāra* 1.1) and so forth floats [as a citation].
The material cause of the effect is inferred through the doctrine of identity-in-difference;
because it does not depend on any other entity, it is described as its own inherent nature (svabhāva).
This is the remainder [of the argument]:
because there is no entry into multiple forms, when the essential natures of both are apprehended, the cognition of their relation occurs.
This is the remainder [of the sentence].

Here, he anticipates the opponent's view: "Even though power (*śakti*) is perceptible, this fault—the error consisting in a contrary conceptualization—occurs because one conceals this power, just as one might conceal circularity (*pārimaṇḍalya*) and so forth;
by the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*), momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and other such qualities are included. If this is the case, he says in response: "Of power," and so on.

What does this "power" (*śakti*), which is called "concealment" (*saṃvṛti*) or "covering" (*saṃvaraṇa*) by others, do? He says: it establishes the non-absolutism (*anekāntatva*) of that immediately preceding [moment]. Doing what? He says: not concealing power (*śakti*).
The meaning is that, in this way, the form would be apprehended as either determined or otherwise; thus,
while refuting the example, he says "in the case of sphericity," etc.,
which is intended primarily as a mockery of others.

For the purpose of conclusion, he says: "Therefore" (*tat*), etc. Since this is so, therefore this superimposition (*samāropa*)—that is, a contrary attribution (*viparītāropa*)—occurring with respect to what is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) within the range of vision, such as momentariness or sphericity, causes the disappearance of the conceptualization of permanence (*nityatva-kalpanā*) regarding that which is blue. This is because non-contradiction (*anekānta*) is established; so he thinks. [Objection: "Indeed, this fault would arise if one were seeing something apprehended as certain, like the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropaviveka*); otherwise, there is no fault. If [this] is said, he replies here: "Of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*), etc.

123kha2. Perception (*pratyakṣa*) possesses the nature of determination (*vyavasāyātmaka*); therefore, it causes the cessation of the "snake" [of doubt] regarding that very object, and not regarding anything else, because perception belongs only to that which has been determined. This is the connection [of the words].

[Objection: But surely determination arises from perception. In that case, how can perception itself possess that nature [of determination]? [Reply: To this he says: "Of perception" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*), etc. This has already been considered in the first section.
And showing that conceptualization is not [identical to] perception, which is non-conceptual, he says: "Regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), etc.
This too has been explained in that very same [work]:
"Determination (*vyavasāya*) arises as conceptualization; however, it is not itself of the nature of a certainty regarding that [object]."
Having thus established *avagraha* (perception) and *īhā* (investigation), he speaks while establishing *avāya* (comprehension): "That [cognition] regarding its own object," and so forth.

This very *avāya* regarding its own object is, in some way, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because it arises from a non-conceptual perception, since the conceptualizing mind does not [directly] perceive it. (14)

For perception does not determine its own object without excluding it from others; nor does it exclude [others] while failing to determine [the object] in any way, because that would entail the impossibility of establishing the nature of the object altogether. Furthermore, since what is grasped by non-conceptual [perception] is like what is ungrasped, conceptual cognition would be without an object, and thus no conceptualization could arise from it. Consequently, even conceptualizations of color, shape, and so forth would not occur.

How could one not act like a sleeping person in this way? And how could one, being utterly dissimilar in nature, devoid of any reflection on what precedes or follows, and unperceivable, join together a conceptualization of similarity—like the sight of the son of a barren woman—since there is no non-contradiction among conceptualizations due to the failure to establish a relationship? Therefore, the systematic arrangement of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and results (*phala*) does not exist in the case of an absolute particular (*asādhāraṇa-ekānta*), just as it does not in the case of an absolute universal (*sādhāraṇa-ekānta*).
The particle *tat* should be understood in the sense of "that" (*sa*).

When this very [term] is examined, the particle *eva* (only/itself) is to be understood as having a shifted scope (*bhinnaprakrama*), following the word "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). Thus, that determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) by which something different—that is, of a dissimilar class—is excluded from its own object and established as distinct, is precisely the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), which is the apprehension of its own object as intended by the Jains.
Alternatively, let the particle *eva* remain in its original position; the meaning would then be that the apprehension of that [object] itself is the exclusion of others, and nothing else.
Why is this so? To this he says: "In any way," and so forth.

In any way—either by some mode of being its own material cause (*upādāna*) or by some mode of awakening the latent impressions of conceptualization (*vikalpa-vāsanā*)—it could not arise from non-conceptual perception (*avikalpa-dṛṣṭi*), that is, from non-conceptual vision, because the conceptual mind (*vikalpamana*) does not [originate] therefrom.

This is what is meant: if the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) were simply the non-apprehension of that [object], or if this [non-apprehension] were not the non-apprehension of that but rather something else—a mental conceptual construction (*mānaso vikalpaḥ*) produced by perception—then there would be only the absence of that [object]. To explain: if the perception of that [object] were at some time within the range of apprehension, then it would be logical to say "because it is a mental conceptualization," but not otherwise, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And yet, such is not the case; thus it has been considered.
The attainment of one's own goal is non-conceptual vision (*nirvikalpadṛṣṭi*).
To explain the verse by way of negation (*vyatirekamukhena*), he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
The word "hi" has the sense of "because":

because perception determines its own object (*svārtha*) by not excluding it from anything else—that is, by not making as its object that which is different from it—[but rather] it determines its object precisely by excluding [others]. By this, it is explained that the very apprehension of one's own object is *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others).

Nor does it exclude [an object] while failing to delimit its own referent in some manner, such as through the mode of a real cognition of blue and so forth; by this, it is shown that exclusion of others (anyāpoha) alone constitutes its determination. Why is this so? To this he says: "In every way," etc. For if it were to exclude from everything else while not delimiting its own referent in any way whatsoever, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the object is not established. By the phrase "it excludes," it is meant that it does so in this manner: by excluding from everything else while delimiting its own referent in some way. Otherwise, the nature of the object would remain unestablished.
Regarding "not so," and so forth—why is this? He says: "because it is free from conceptual construction," and so on.

This is because the conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) has as its cause the conceptualization of what is not apprehended regarding that which is apprehended by means of a conceptual exclusion of others (*anyavyavacchedavikalpa*); and furthermore, because such a conceptual exclusion of others is devoid of an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*).

If it is argued that non-conceptual [cognition] alone grasps the intrinsic nature of the object because it generates a determination of its own object, to this he says: "And not," etc.; and from that [non-conceptual cognition], the occurrence of conceptualization—the apprehension of its own object—does not arise by means of the non-conceptual.

If it is argued that because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has as its object a universal (*sāmānya*) which is not a real entity, it might follow—unlike non-conceptual [perception]—that it does not have momentariness and so forth as its object, but rather has blue and so forth as its object; to this he says: "Therefore, color," and so on.

The point is this: from that non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpakadarśana*), let there not arise only conceptualizations such as momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and so forth, but also conceptualizations of color, shape (*saṃsthāna*), and the like; for it is impossible for a single [perception] to produce both its own object and something else within its own domain.

This is another interpretation: "From that, through the connection with a mental cognition of it, let there not be a conceptualization of shape and so forth by means of color as a logical mark (*liṅga*), nor even the inference thereof; because a logical mark that has been made the object of mere perception cannot be the cause of that [inference].
In this case as well, the previous example applies by way of the relationship.
That is not correct— for conceptualization arises from the non-conceptual.

The point is that it is impossible for a non-conceptual [cognition] to possess two such forms— namely, the production of a conceptualization regarding the blue aspect and the non-production of one regarding the momentary aspect— because it is itself non-conceptual.
"Because there is an absence of a logical reason for inference, that appearance which I have is not devoid of configuration. (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 2.1), and so forth;
since this has been observed elsewhere, such being the case, there is inference.
This is the remainder [of the sentence].
What then occurred? To this he says: "How," and so forth.
When a fault exists in the manner just described, how is it that one does not act as if asleep? Right here he states another objection, beginning with "How," and so forth.

And how is it that conceptual perception—which is absolutely and in every respect dissimilar and distinct from its cause, object, intrinsic nature, and so forth—could, by a shift in grammatical case, necessarily and inevitably be joined with a similar conceptualization? Otherwise, it might join the cognition of blue with a conceptualization of yellow, since there would be no distinction. Of what nature is that [conceptual perception]? He says: "devoid of the reflection upon the prior and the posterior. The prior is the moment of the cause; the posterior is the moment of the effect. Reflection upon these two means making them objects of awareness; [the perception is] devoid of that.

This is what is meant: when that perception does not operate with respect to the prior and posterior [moments], then it does not take their similarity as its object; how, then, could it be the cause of memory regarding them? For it is impossible for memory to arise regarding what has not been experienced;

otherwise, the sense organ, while functioning in the present, would be the cause of perception regarding those [past and future moments], which is not tenable—since there is no difference in their being distinct entities.
It does not extend to the past or the future because of the absence of memory regarding them.
The activity of the sense-faculties occurs only with respect to what is present, not with respect to what is past or future;
the activity of the sense-faculties occurs only toward an object situated in a suitable location, not toward what is past or future;
and the consciousness dependent upon them does not pertain to what exists at another time.

—Cited in the *Prakaraṇavārttikālaṅkāra*— "How could cognition, which depends upon that [object], function with respect to what is past or future? (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Vol. 1, p. 142; *Prakaraṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 3.126).

Now, if one were to claim that the perception of the later object, aided by the recollection of the former, joins it with its conceptual construction— even so, there would be only a memory of the former, because the similarity in the object similar to the later one has not been experienced;
nevertheless, if one still maintains that construction, then the eye, aided by the recollection of fragrance, would produce a cognition of smell,
for the lack of being an object is equal in both cases.

If it is argued that, although similarity established through non-difference from the two [respective] perceptions of the prior and posterior [moments] has indeed been apprehended, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding it arises solely from the subsequent perception aided by the recollection of the prior one—then, in that case, oneness established through non-difference from those two perceptions would have indeed been apprehended, and a cognition of oneness regarding it would arise from the subsequent perception aided by the recollection of the prior one.
Yet this is not what the opponent accepts;
therefore, it remains established that for the opponent, that [subsequent perception] cannot produce a conceptual construction of similarity.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "unperceivable" (*alakṣya*).

Because it exists in the form of partless atoms, it is either non-existent—like another continuum—or indeterminate due to doubt; thus he shows that one cannot apply [conceptual constructions] to it, just as one cannot apply them to the sight of a barren woman’s son. For it is from the application of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—which are otherwise determinate cognitions—that there arises, through some indirect succession, a non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) originating from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If it is asked, "Why?"—to this he says: "Because the relationship is not established.

This means as follows: if the arising of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) were to occur for another [cognizer] from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or from the perception of that [particular], then, because the relationship would be established therein, there would be non-discrepancy;
but this is not the case.
He states [the conclusion] for the sake of summary: "Therefore, etc.
Since it is so, therefore, in the case of an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) absolute [position], the systematic arrangement of means of valid cognition, objects of cognition, and results is not seen;
he provides an example: "like a common (sādhāraṇa) absolute."
Memory would arise through a conceptualization of similarity between the prior and the posterior,
by way of an identity between the prior and the posterior.
The conceptual construction "this is similar" [arises] through the mental [cognition] by way of the identity between the preceding and the succeeding moments.
Or, it arises from the perception of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of each and every Buddhist phenomenon.

Having established that the result of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is its direct accomplishment, which is the ascertainment of its own object— as stated in *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.3— he now says "the pervasive," etc., demonstrating the sequential form of the result according to his own position.

"Apprehension (avagraha), inquiry (īhā), judgment (avāya), and retention (dhāraṇā)—which, occurring in succession, constitute the characteristics of the fruits of valid cognition—this person, seeing [the object], sees only the unique [particular] because of [its] perception. This is utterly inconsistent, for a gross form appears therein; who would believe such a fabrication as "floating stones," which claims that individual particulars appear there quite clearly apart from that [gross form]? For accumulated atoms do not abandon their spherical shape or momentariness, such that they would otherwise appear [as a gross object].

Thus, having grasped this universal which is pervasive and apprehending the particular, it determines and maintains [the object] accordingly; therefore, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) is logical.

In this very context, the connection for that establishment exists because each preceding [cognition], without abandoning its own continuous engagement in grasping its object, serves as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for each subsequent one, just like the case of recollective cognition (*smārtajñāna*).

The determination of validity and so forth is everywhere according to mere appearance and not according to reality; how then could there be the realization of reality in such a one-sided view? Since other means of knowledge are also unestablished—because they would themselves be of the nature of perception and thus entirely unestablished—the universal, which is the pervader, and its apprehension (*avagraha*), as well as the particular, which is the pervaded, and its subsequent stages of *samīhā*, *avāya*, and *dhāraṇā* [would likewise remain unestablished].
What are they like? To this he says: "attained," and so forth.
Those by which the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) has been attained are described as such.
How? To this he says: "by way of sequence" (*paurvāparyeṇa*).

If it is argued that this is incorrect—namely, the claim that [the universal] is pervasive and so forth—because only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is perceived everywhere, the author replies here: "This person," and so on.
This Buddhist person, or any other individual, perceives only the non-common (*asādhāraṇa*), not the common (*sādhāraṇa*).
Why is this? Because of the perception—that is, because of the observation—of the non-common. Thus, [the opponent's position] is utterly inconsistent.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Of the gross form," and so forth.
If it is argued that "there is no appearance of that [gross form] there at all, because only the particular (svalakṣaṇa) appears"; to this he replies: "Apart from that," and so forth.

Who would believe this fabricated "floating stone"—that apart from that [object], namely apart from the aforementioned gross form (*sthūlākāra*), the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) appear in that sensory cognition (*akṣabuddhi*) in such a way as to be perfectly distinct? Even if the aforementioned form appears there, one considers that to postulate the appearance of these [specific characteristics] would be like postulating a "floating stone" upon a "floating log. Now, if it is argued that those very [atoms], when aggregated, appear in that manner, to that he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
