For indeed, since atoms—whether conscious or otherwise—are existent, they do not abandon their spherical nature (*pārimaṇḍalya*), their non-pervasiveness, or their partlessness (*niraṃśatva*), nor do they abandon their momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), because that would entail the consequence of their having parts or being non-momentary; this is what [the author] intends. For if they were to abandon those [qualities], they would otherwise appear in a different manner—that is, in a mode characterized by having parts and being non-momentary, rather than in the mode characterized by sphericity and momentariness. Or, the word "since" (*yataḥ*) may be used in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepe*): they would simply not appear at all.
Nevertheless, the point is that if there were such an appearance, no cognition whatsoever would be non-erroneous;
thus, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has as its object only that which is primary and unique—*Hetubindu*, *Ṭīkā*, p. 25.
In the perception of a gross form, in the perception.
In order to bring together the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of atoms, he says: "This very [is... and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore, having grasped this perceived direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), what [is established]? To this he says: the universal (*sāmānya*), which is of two kinds, being of what nature? It is pervasive (*vyāpaka*), having as its own nature all its particularities (*viśeṣa*), because nothing else possesses pervasiveness. What does it do, and how? To this he says: "striving toward the particular, which is its pervaded differentiation," and thus, "ascertaining" (*avayat*)—that is, determining—in the manner of the particular sought, it "maintains" (*dhārayati*), meaning it becomes the sustaining support (*dhāraṇī*). In this way, the establishment of the result of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*) is logically consistent.

Regarding this, the Naiyāyika and others state the distinction between the horizontal (tiryak) and the vertical (ūrdhva): "When the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), which is the universal (*sāmānya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), which is the particular (*viśeṣa*), is the result (*phala*); and since it is stated that when this [cognition of the qualified] is the means of knowledge, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the result, this systematic arrangement is established only in my own doctrine. To this, he replies:

"In this very [system]"—the connection is that when this very non-absolutist (*anekānta*) reality is being examined, that systematic arrangement is established therein; the sense is that such an arrangement of the universal and so forth does not exist elsewhere.
When there is contact, then knowledge is the valid cognition; when there is knowledge, then the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference are the result...— Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.3.

In that regard, with respect to universals and particulars, perception as a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) is the mere observation of the essential nature (*svarūpālocana-mātra*). The resulting valid cognition (*pramiti*) is the knowledge whose objects are substances and so forth. Alternatively, when among all categories (*padārtha*) a non-erroneous, non-verbalized knowledge arises from the fourfold contact (*catuṣṭaya-sannikarṣa*), that is perception as a means of valid cognition; the resulting valid cognition is the observation of qualities, defects, or neutrality.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 187).

When indeterminate knowledge of universals and particulars is the means of valid cognition, then the meaning is that determinate knowledge whose objects are substances and so forth is the resulting valid cognition.

When even non-conceptual knowledge of the universal and the particular is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*) because it consists in the apprehension of an object, then, at its arising, perception is merely an undifferentiated observation (*ālocanamātra*). In that case, the knowledge of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñāna*) is the result of the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), while the knowledge of the qualifier is not the result of another distinct cognition. When non-conceptual knowledge of the universal and the particular is the result, then the contact between the sense organ and the object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); when the knowledge of the qualified is the result, then the observation of the universal and the particular is the means of valid cognition—this much has been stated. Now, he says that when cognitions such as rejection (*hāna*) and so forth are the results, then the knowledge of the qualified is the means of valid cognition. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 199)
When the two cognitions [of the qualifier and the qualified] constitute the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and its result (phala),
then too the previously mentioned refutation of their having different objects applies.
However, when only a mere indeterminate perception (ālocana-mātra) occurs regarding the qualifier to be known...
Only after producing a certainty is there the postulation of its validity;
for in that case, certainty is the result. When that [certainty] has not yet been perceived, there can be no validity at all, because the object has not been ascertained.
If it is argued that the cognition of the qualified object is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because its fruit is the cognition of exclusion and so forth, [we reply:
if this [cognition of the qualified] is separated by the recollection of assistance and so on, then this [recollection] is the fruit. — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Pratyakṣa, verses 70–73.

[Objection: Surely, perception, which is exhausted by perceiving only the middle moment of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), is not capable of perceiving the preceding and succeeding moments; nor does the observation of the preceding and succeeding stages perceive the middle moment. Since that [perception] which exists in a fragment does not exist in the shaven head and so forth, how then can there be a universal (*sāmānya*) residing in them, which is its pervader? To this, he says: "Of each preceding... [and so on].

The meaning is as follows: for each preceding cognition, there is a subsequent cognition which is its apprehension; because that [subsequent] cognition is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the realization of the former, and because it produces [the result] without intervention (*avyavadhānena*), it arises through the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the preceding cognition into the succeeding one.

Of what nature is this [preceding cognition]? It does not abandon its connection with the grasping of its own object; that is, while still grasping its own object, it transforms into the form of grasping another object.
This is how it connects with the phrase "then, this very... and so forth.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "like conventional (smārta) knowledge.
Smārta-jñāna means knowledge that is merely based on memory; "like that" means similar to that.
And this is well-established for the opponent [the Mīmāṃsaka]; otherwise, how could he even construct a conceptual linguistic usage such as "universals" and so forth?
It culminates merely in the observation of the middle moment,
[pertaining] to the individuality residing in a particular cow.

If it is argued that for the Buddhist, indeed, in all cases that determination exists only according to appearance and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), [the author] says here: "Just as," and so forth.

Just as in other systems, in the Jaina system as well—both internally and externally—the determination of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth exists only according to appearance and not according to reality (*yathātattvam*). If this [view] is accepted as an absolute position (*ekānta*), then how could there be [a determination] of reality at all? [From] nothing at all. (Pramāṇavārttika 2)

"Is there a cognition of such a nature, or of a nature characterized by momentary destruction and so forth? What is meant by this? If its establishment therein is exactly as it appears, like an external object, then it is not established [as you claim].
Or, if it is according to reality; then there is the abandonment of your absolute thesis.
If it is argued: "Let it be that there is no cognition of it through perception; it may arise from investigation," to this he says: "Of another means of knowledge as well," and so forth.

The intended meaning here is as follows: if every kind of inquiry whatsoever is invalid (*apramāṇa*), then the establishment of the fundamental reality under discussion cannot occur, just as [the existence of] external objects [cannot be established].

If, on the other hand, it is valid (*pramāṇa*), it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*), because perception is by nature free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), whereas this inquiry consists of conceptual thought.

If it is inference (*anumāna*), then since even another means of knowledge—namely, inference—is unestablished, how can there be an understanding of reality? And why would that [inference] be unestablished? To this he says: "Because its nature is that of perception."

Because its nature consists in being of the same character as non-conceptual perception—whose nature is that of momentary, partless atoms—the following is meant: just as non-conceptual vision is not an object of definition, so too is inference;
this has already been considered [in the passage]: "For one who accepts self-awareness" (Siddhiviniścaya 1).

By such statements as these, it is shown that it (the self) does not possess two forms by which it might somehow be characterized, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of abandoning its absolute unity;
this too has been stated in the *Prasiddhibhāṣya* (Siddhi-viniścaya-ṭīkā), verse 1.
By such statements as these,

or alternatively: because of the nature of that which has a nature like that of perception— namely, its nature being either error regarding self and other or the state of transcending all conceptual construction—
therefore, just as there is no establishment of self and other through perception, so too there is none through inference.
The sense is that just as there is no established distinction for error and so forth, so too there is no established distinction for perception and inference.

If it is argued that their establishment occurs through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), he replies here: "In every way" (*sarvathā*). This means that just as there is no establishment in any ultimate sense, there is likewise no establishment in any conventional manner. For if there were no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), conventional usage would be utterly abolished; and because [the object] is not apprehended in the extreme view of falsity (*mithyaikānta*).
From the perspective of conventional practice,

this establishment of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results is formulated according to how things appear, even though the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the consciousness itself do not [ultimately] exist.
[As stated in] the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (*Nyāyabindu* 1.4), because this is the definition of perception.

Thus, the non-establishment of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated by way of the absence of an object for another; now, in order to show that it is being stated by way of the absence of a cause, he says: "Understand," and so forth.
The non-establishment of other means of valid cognition consists in understanding [the nature of one's own cognition] while not perceiving anything else as distinct from it.
The absence of effort [is established] through the recollection of similarity; thus, there is no conceptual construction.

It is contradictory to say that perception—which manifests as a specific object within its own domain—does not in any way characterize itself, because it is apprehended according to its conventional designation;
otherwise, it would follow that another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would be required for that apprehension.

Since one who perceives a specific distinction is free from further expectancy, how could there be a recollection for one who does not exert any effort, from which a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that excludes superimposition (*samāropa*) might arise? For if it were so, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the superimposition characterized by that [recollection]. [This would be] like the perception of something that is ineffective and so forth.

If, however, one were not to perceive in any way what has been experienced, how could there be an effort to exclude superimposition? For one who perceives or discerns a particularity—as in deep sleep—a memory of a similar form is entirely illogical, because there would be no connection between those two;
for in that case, there would be an over-extension of the principle.

If it is argued that this perception of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) capable of causal efficiency is not purposeless—since it is the apprehender [of the object] because conceptual cognition does not have that as its object, because for one who sees reality it is impossible to exert effort toward producing a memory contrary to that, because [the memory] arises through the power of seeing that [reality], and because it leads one to engage with reality just like inference—then its validity is indeed logical, since without it there could be no correspondence (*saṃvāda*). [The sentence ends with:
*pramāṇa...*
Therefore, this cognition—which, through the perception of a particularity, initiates the conventional usage based on the recollection of a universal—is indeed non-conceptual;
it is the cause, the instrument, for another means of valid cognition. Thus, the absence of conceptualization is the conceptualization of both.

Doing what? Not perceiving—that is, not determining—a thing imagined by others as distinct and differentiated from everything else, whether of the same class or of a different nature, because [such a thing] is established only through properties (*dharma*) and so forth. It has already been stated that if this undetermined thing were the cause of inference, it would lead to the absurdity [of inference occurring] even during sleep and similar states. If it is argued that "it is the cause [of inference] insofar as it depends on a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising at a later time," to this he replies: "by means of a recollection of similarity"—that is, by means of a conceptualization of similarity as its cause, it is its cause. Even this is non-conceptual, because if it were a conceptualization, it would result in the fallacy of there being another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As he will state in this very commentary, beginning with "In that case, then... and so forth:

"If it is argued that 'he, perceiving that [object], is the cause of that [cognition],' to this he replies with 'Anīhaḥ' (devoid of effort), etc. Even when an object is perceived in its form as momentary and so on—just like [the qualities] existence and the rest—that [perception] can occur even without being [explicitly] characterized [by those features]; thus, the conceptualization that 'one who possesses expectancy is the cause of that [cognition]' is rejected, because once [the object] is determined, other means of valid cognition would be redundant. This is what is intended.

Since there is no recollection of similarity when the dissimilar is being characterized, the cause [of inference] is not that; thus, understand that "non-conceptualization" refers to the cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth.
In the commentary,
*nibodhaḥ* means effort (*īhā*).
"Surely this fault would apply to Nibodha if it did not perceive everything in every way.
If it is argued that it does indeed perceive [everything], the author replies here: "In its own object," and so forth.

One's own nature of consciousness (*bodha*) is the object (*viṣaya*). If its two specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), namely its differences (*bheda*), exist because they are excluded from everything else, then that cognition in which their manifestation—that is, the assumption of those forms—exists is so described. Of what nature is it? It is perception (*pratyakṣa*), a non-conceptual vision. This is an elliptical expression; by it, one's own self-nature (*svarūpa*) and the nature of the object are implied. [The opponent argues: "It does not destroy [the object] in some way, such as through the form of existence (*sattva*) and so forth"—thus [he thinks], for it is contradictory for a single thing to be characterized by both its own nature and a different nature, since that would entail the consequence of manifoldness (*anekānta*).
If it is argued that [the definition] characterizes [reality] in every respect, the author says: "In accordance with convention," and so forth.
Because reality is apprehended without transgressing the convention imagined by the Buddhists, it is contradictory to say that it "characterizes" [itself].

He states the refutation regarding the acceptance of such an apprehension: "Or, if there were such an apprehension, it would be contradictory because it would entail the consequence of the non-operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
From what [source] is this known? To this he says: "Because one who perceives a particularity is free from further expectancy.
If it is argued that even so, there might still be a mental state directed toward that [particularity], he replies: "In some way," and so forth.

For one who does not exert effort—that is, one who has no desire to establish the reality of the object through such modes as momentariness just as they do through modes such as blue and so on—from what cause would there be recollection, namely the recollection of an example, by means of which recollection there arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that excludes superimposition (*samāropa*), and which is the inference (*anumāna*) that effects that exclusion?
Whence is this? He says: "Having come together," and so forth.

Nevertheless, he states the refutation regarding the possibility of that [superimposition]: "That," and so forth. If superimposition were admitted upon what is characterized by perception, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), such that it would also apply to what is characterized by inference.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—to this he replies: "What is it that is ineffective," and so forth.
He considers that [the definition] is useless for practical discourse (*vyavahāra*), just like the perception of something that is ineffective and so on.
If it is then argued, "In that case, it does not characterize [the object] in any way whatsoever"—to this he replies: "But if, moreover," and so forth.

If that which has been experienced—that is, made an object of experience—in every respect, such as through its momentariness and so forth, were not also characterized by its blueness and so forth, then how could it be connected with the term "perception"? Why would there be an effort to exclude superimposition? For the exclusion of superimposition is inference; why, then, would there be an effort toward that [inference]? It would be like that of one who is fast asleep; thus, [perception] is that which excludes superimposition.

It might be thought: "Perception is said to characterize [the object] because it generates a subsequent conceptualization (*vikalpa*); therefore, this fault does not apply. To this, he says: "Of one who perceives the qualifier," and so forth.
For a person in the world whose vision perceives a qualifier, a memory of a similar form is indeed illogical.

Of what kind [of person]? Of one who "characterizes" (*lakṣayataḥ*) the qualifier—that is, of one for whom the qualifier has been made the object of characterization (*lakṣaṇīkṛta*). Even in such a case, the repeated use of the word "characterizing" (*lakṣayataḥ*) is intended to demonstrate another fault.

Why is that [recognition] not tenable? He says: because there is no connection between those two—the perception of the particular and the memory of an identical form—due to the absence of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
Although the investigation proceeds only by taking the perceived object as its specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇīkṛta*), [the two are unrelated].

Regarding "recollection of a similar [object]," suppose it is thought: "Let there not be a relationship characterized by identity between two dissimilar things; rather, let there be a relationship characterized by 'arising from that' (tadutpatti), as in the case of fire and smoke. To this, he says: "For in this way, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); the recollection of yellow could arise from the experience of blue, because there is no difference in their being dissimilar, [if the relationship were merely] one consisting of the nature of cause and effect."
Having accepted that [the cognition] arises from that for a person who possesses the experience of blue, he states another refutation: "And this is purposeless," and so forth;
"purposeless" means lacking a utility.

The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the previous refutation. To the question, "From where does this memory of a similar form arise? he says: "Because of the perception [of the object]," and so forth; that is, because the perception—the act of seeing—is the apprehender of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

If it is argued that, in the same way, the memory of that [object] is also a grasper of that [object], to this he says: because conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-buddhi*) does not have that as its object—since its object is not that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*)—let it be that it is "without an object" (*anarthikā*), i.e., it does not have that as its object. Even so, if it is argued that we still have a purpose for its very existence, to this he says: "In reality," and so forth. For a Buddhist who perceives reality (*tattvadarśin*) or for anyone else seeking causal efficiency, the effort directed toward producing a memory that has a similar form but is contrary to that reality is untenable; therefore, [the memory] is useless (*anarthikā*).

For one who perceives blue and seeks its corresponding action, an effort toward the recollection of yellow is not appropriate, just as it is not appropriate for the perception itself; thus, the recollection of a specific object is likewise [not required].
Because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which performs purposeful action is not its object,
[the person] desiring the purposeful action of the blue object [acts] solely through the presence of conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*).
Here, the opponent's view is raised—beginning with the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth—in order to refute it. [The opponent argues:

"Because the perception of that reality possesses its power, that is, its capacity, and because it functions toward the production of [the cognition] therein, it is not purposeless, just like inference. To this, he replies: "In that case, validity would be appropriate for that memory which has a similar form, but validity is not appropriate for the perception.
Why is this? He says: "That," and so forth.

In the absence of that [the object], there is an absence of its recollection; because of this, correspondence is impossible, and consequently, the non-disagreement regarding dharma and so forth is impossible.
Why? He says: "In the case of a means of valid cognition," etc.;
this has already been explained in the first section.
Concluding with the words "viśeṣam" and so forth, he says: "tad" and so on.

Since this is so, therefore this Buddhist, while initiating the conventional usage of the recollection of a universal based on the perception of a particular, is indeed non-conceptual and devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
Thus, there is no establishment of this as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); how, then, can there be an understanding of reality? This is the established conclusion.

"In that case, let the Buddhist's memory have a uniform form, and let the determination of means of knowledge and so forth be exactly according to reality; and since that [determination] belongs only to the Buddhist system," to this he says:

If conceptual cognition manifests an unreal object and is non-concordant with reality, is perception then merely an appearance of that [conceptual content], or is it indeed a separate means of valid cognition?
Conceptual cognition does not only manifest what is non-existent; it is also non-concordant because it apprehends a universal while [the object] is actually a particular.
One who acts after determining an object by means of this [conceptual cognition] is nevertheless deceived regarding purposeful action;

thus, due to the intention of the agent, when validity and invalidity are established based on inference regarding such things as momentary destruction, it follows that the distinction between valid and non-valid cognition applies equally to conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions.
In reality, however, there is just as much deception for a non-conceptual cognition as there is for a conceptual cognition.
If it is asked, "In what way does there appear an object? [the answer is: because a single gross thing appears, whereas a real entity (vastu) possesses characteristics contrary to that [appearance];
for this very reason, there is also a lack of correspondence (visaṃvāda), just as in the case of conceptual construction (vikalpa).

If perception (*pratyakṣa*) were [defined as] conceptualization (*vikalpa*), inference (*anumāna*), or any other appearance of a non-object (*anartha-nirbhāsa*)—that is, an aspect of a real universal (*vastu-sāmānyākāra*) which is deceptive and free from the proliferation of disagreement (*vigatāvipratipatti-prapañca*), or rather, if it were a non-deviating, true, non-conceptual vision (*darśana*) grounded in a single, partless, momentary atom (*kṣaṇika-niraṃśa-eka-paramāṇu*)—then what would be perception? Would it be no conceptual cognition whatsoever, or something else; or would it be self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), or something else? If that were so, then this well-stated definition—"Perception is cognition free from conceptual construction" (*Kalpanāpoḍhaṃ jñānaṃ pratyakṣam*, Pramāṇasamuccaya, p. 8)—would be applicable. But what would be its "appearance" (*tadābhāsa*)? Nothing at all, because this [conceptual cognition] exists in dependence upon perception, and in the absence of the latter, it does not exist. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) for the purpose of excluding that [conceptual cognition] is improper.

For behold: just as externally, so too internally, there is not even an atom-sized reality; therefore, even the perception of things such as a double moon cannot be established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).

As for inference (*anumāna*), that is either internal [to consciousness] or is that very same [consciousness]; how then could this [external object] be beautiful? [As stated in the *Nyāyabindu* 2.3: "Inference arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing three characteristics," and so forth.
The phrase "having that appearance" (*tadābhāsam*) is connected here as well because it occurs in the middle [of the verse].

Or rather, is it "having the appearance of another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarābhāsam*)? That is well said: "The fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those," and so forth [Hetubindu, verse 1], for it is considered that there is no establishment of the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhyajñāna*) from either the thesis (*pakṣa*) and its fallacies, or from the reason and its fallacies.
Regarding pseudo-perception,
in the absence of true perception,
[the definition of] perception is given as "perception is that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous."

Regarding that, he says "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate the meaning of the *Nyāyabindu* verse: "The Buddhist [definition] therein is the cognition of the inferable (*anumeya*) which arises from a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*)."

The nature of the conceptualizing intellect, which has the logical mark (*liṅga*) as its object, is not only an appearance of a non-entity; what then? It is also [characterized by] non-correspondence and verbal expression. Therefore, this [position] is refuted: [The opponent says: "But how can there be non-correspondence for that which is devoid of an external object? [The author replies: This is not so. Even in the case of a dream, there is non-correspondence because of the lack of correspondence with the waking state. Furthermore, since the cognition of a dream is not produced by an external object, it is established that the cognition of the waking state is also not produced by an external object. "Thus, because the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are indirectly connected to the real entity, there is no deception even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.82)— this is the connection.

Regarding the question, "How is there non-deception—that is, non-contradiction—between the correct sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*), which are free from the fallacies of the sign and the signified? he says: "Because of the perception of particulars," and so forth. This refers to a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) in which there is the apprehension of a universal; because of the subsequent perception of particulars by that [cognition], just as by the subsequent perception of white in a conch shell following the apprehension of yellow.

If it is argued that "even if there is a discrepancy regarding the particulars, there is no such discrepancy regarding that which is to be accomplished by them," the author replies here with the words "the object" and so forth: "Having determined the object, such as fire, a person who acts on the basis of this conceptual cognition is deceived in regard to purposeful action (arthakriyā) characterized by burning and the like. This [consequence]—namely, that [the cognition] results from the apprehension of a universal rather than the perception of a particular—is to be understood as applying here as well.

This is what is meant: when a person acts after having determined an object in a certain way, there is non-discrepancy (avisaṃvāda) regarding that [object] only upon the attainment of the purposeful action (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by such an object, and not otherwise. Otherwise, if one were to act based on the cognition of a yellow [conch shell] and then attain the purposeful action of a white conch shell, the cognition would have to be considered non-discrepant with respect to that [white conch].

If it is argued that one is not deceived by inferential conceptual cognition (*anumāna-vikalpa-buddhi*), the author replies with the words "again" (*punaḥ*) and so forth: "Again," meaning after the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*), one who acts having determined the object through inference is indeed deceived. Where? Regarding [theories such as] momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and the like, because there is a comprehension of a universal (*sāmānya*) despite the perception of particulars.
Surely, it is the commentators (*vyākhyātāraḥ*) who analyze in this manner, not the practical users (*vyavahartāraḥ*).

If it is argued that "those [people] indeed proceed at will by unifying the two objects—the perceived and the conceptualized—and thus, by virtue of their intention, they are said not to be deceived" (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1.72), to this he replies: "The intention of the conventional user," and so forth.

For those engaged in practical discourse (*vyavahartṛ*), whatever is apprehended by us through the cognition of the sign (*liṅga*) or the cognition of that which possesses the sign (*liṅgin*) is precisely what is attained; it is on account of this intention that, when the validity of momentary conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is established, or when the invalidity of conceptual constructions such as "permanent" and so forth is established, the distinction between validity and invalidity would result from being applied to conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions alike.

The determination of blue and so forth that arises subsequent to perception is here called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and not inference (*anumāna*), because there is no dispute among opponents regarding this point. As for the establishment of its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "Whatever is determined by it is precisely what is attained. If, on account of such an intention, the non-conceptual [perception] were to be established as not being a means of valid cognition, then the following would follow: "Having determined the object by means of this [perception], we act and thereby attain it"—such an intention [would be undermined]. Otherwise, statements such as *pra-vā-ṣū 2.123*, "because of the simultaneous operation of the two minds," and so forth, would be rendered meaningless.
For the Buddhist,
[the distinction] between conceptual and non-conceptual [cognition] is due to the intention of the conventional user.
The ellipsis is that one who is deluded, or due to the rapidity of its activity, determines the identity of those two;
by this, the claim that conceptual construction has as its object what has been seen through perception is also refuted, because such an intention is absent in that [conceptual construction].

If it is argued that the non-existence [of the object] belongs to the conceptualization of the thing itself, the author replies here: "In reality," meaning "from the perspective of the ultimate truth" (*paramārthataḥ*), which indicates an alternative position. Since even another conceptual cognition—that is, inferential conceptual cognition—is accepted by others as being itself a reality, there is also a contradiction; it is not merely a manifestation of a non-existent thing that constitutes deception.
Thus, he considers that like other conceptualizations, inferential conceptualization would likewise not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[Opponent: "Let it be then that all conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) is invalid because it is non-concordant (*visaṃvāda*) and because it manifests as a non-entity (*avastunirbhāsa*); however, non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpabuddhi*) is valid because the opposite is the case. To this, [the author] replies with the words "In the same way" (*tathaiva*), etc. Since the Buddhist accepts that non-conceptual cognition has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, the opponent, thinking "for what purpose would that [cognition] have a non-entity as its object?", asks: "How is there a manifestation of a non-object (*anartha*)? To this, he gives the answer: "Because a single gross [object] appears," etc.
[The opponent might say: "This alone is the definition of a real entity (*vastulakṣaṇa*). To this, he says: "Of a real entity," etc.

Observe that the characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*), which is a thing capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*), is otherwise—that is, of a different nature—than the aforementioned characteristic; it is of a non-dual form. This is stated on the basis of what is established for others (*paraprasiddhyā*). Therefore, precisely because of the appearance of a non-entity (*avastunirbhāsa*), there is also non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*); the connection is that this is not merely the appearance of a non-entity for non-conceptual cognition.
And thus, "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge" (*pramāṇam avisaṃvādi jñānam*, *Pramāṇavārttika* 1).
Thus, it follows that the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as formulated by the opponent is untenable,
because he accepts that its status as non-contradictory is restricted to objects perceived through direct observation (*darśana*).
Because it is non-contradictory and because its object is a thing possessing its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
[it is a valid cognition] according to the Buddhist intention.
Now, it has been stated that, relying on conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge" (Pramāṇavārttika 1).

Because of such statements [in the scriptures], people are not perceived as being in accord with reality even when there is the appearance of that non-entity (*avastu*). This is because satisfaction is observed upon engaging in activity through the superimposition of a real entity onto that very appearance of a non-entity; and this satisfaction is what constitutes "non-contradiction" (*avisaṃvāda*), according to the Buddhist view. If one asks, "To whom, then, would there be contradiction for that [cognition]?"—to this he replies: "Like conceptual construction" (*vikalpavat*);
that is, just like a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which arises subsequent to perception, so too [is the case here].

This is what is meant: just as there is a discrepancy in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*)—which manifests a non-real universal (*sāmānya*)—even when a person engaged in worldly activity (*vyavahārin*) feels satisfied after acting upon it, so too is it with non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpabuddhi*). Otherwise, the establishment of the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of conceptual cognition, the restriction on the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the absolute uniqueness of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) would have no place;
for validity [is established] by way of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

[From] the *Pramāṇavārttika*: the enumeration of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) for one whose intellect is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpabuddhi*).

By this, the following argument stated by Arcaṭa is also refuted: "The validity of conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) is said to be based on its grasping what has already been grasped due to the intention of the user, not from the perspective of reality (*bhāva*), because that [grasping of the ungrasped] is absent therein; furthermore, from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthatas*), it is a manifestation of a non-entity. How so? Because this same [charge of grasping what has already been grasped] applies equally even to non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpabuddhi*).

Comparison: Although it is described that by means of that [inference] a universal (*sāmānya*) not previously apprehended is apprehended, nevertheless, because it does not accomplish any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the conceptual construction (*vidhivikalpa*) that apprehends it—resembling the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) and the like—is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since a genus (*jāti*), however, lacks the capacity to accomplish purposeful action, even when it is apprehended as something not previously apprehended, it possesses no validity, just like the cognition of [illusory] hairs and the like. — *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 27. Now, he shows the refutation of the Yogācāra position with the words "Just as," etc.
"How could the forms (ākāra) and appearances (nirbhāsa), which manifest apart from the object-form of that [consciousness] in whatever way it may be, be real, since they appear as if external?"—
all of this is equally applicable even to the doctrine of representation-only (vijñaptimātra).

Because it appears otherwise than its own true nature (svatattva). Having set aside [its own nature], how? In whatever way and by whatever means—be it through the mode of a universal (sāmānya) or otherwise—for that which appears, whether conceptual (vikalpa) or non-conceptual (avikalpa).
What having done? Having set aside.
What? The form of the object.
Of what nature is it? Real—that is, non-false—because it alone is real;
and what of that? To this he says: "How," and so forth.
The word "true" (satyam) should also be applied here, with its case-ending modified to agree with the gender of the noun;
thus, the meaning is as follows: how could the forms—the appearances—possibly be true, that is, non-erroneous? [This is so] because [they appear] outside of those true forms.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
To this, he provides the following reply: "Cognition" (*vijñapti*), and so forth.

Cognition alone, which is empty of external objects, is "that-only" (*tanmātra*). Furthermore, not only regarding the external object, but everything without exception—the refutation of the external object immediately preceding—applies equally here. Therefore, it is thought that even this [cognition] must be abandoned by those who are authoritative (*prāmāṇika*) and committed to neutrality, just like the external object.
Why is this so? To this, he says: "Its own nature" (*svatattva*), and so forth.

The intended meaning here is as follows: by stating, "It is more wonderful that a single thing is variegated" (*Pra.vārtikālaṃkāra* 3.200), it is shown that even a mere *tanmātra* (subtle element) should not be accepted as a single variegated entity, but rather as a single partless [unit]; and thus, even a cognition appearing as variegated is indeed one (*Pra.vārtikālaṃkāra* 3).
Statements such as these are self-contradictory;

furthermore, that [consciousness] is not distinct from blue, pleasure, and the body, because the opponent does not accept it as such. Otherwise, Prajñākaragupta’s statement—that there exists no grasper of insentient objects distinct from blue, pleasure, and the body—would not be well-spoken.

Moreover, because it does not appear [as something separate], how else could even the appearance of Brahman be refuted? Therefore, one must accept that it has the nature of blue, pleasure, the body, and so forth.

And apart from its own true nature (*svatattva*), which is its essential self (*ātmasvabhāva*) consisting of momentary, partless, atomic dimensions, it appears in a completely different manner—as stable, gross, and common to all;
as it has been said in this very context: "Seeing the unique particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) as one [gross thing]," *Siddhiviniścaya* 1.10, and so forth.

Otherwise, the following objection raised by Prajñākara would be misplaced: "In the passage beginning with *prativāraṇam* (PV 2.210), having established the appearance of atoms, [Dharmakīrti] states that even for one who investigates with extreme subtlety, the appearance of a single gross object does not cease; yet, fearing this, he says in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* (3.211) that there is no fault even if [the object] is non-existent, just like the appearances of a magical illusion or a mirage.
This would be irrelevant, because such an objection cannot apply when there is the manifestation of its own true nature (*svatattva*).
If it is argued that even mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*) is manifold yet one, this is even more manifold than that...

If it is argued that this manifold thing consisting of blue, yellow, and so forth is a single butterfly or the like; then that which is called "this manifold one" is even more manifold, even more wondrous, than that variegated butterfly.
"It is variegated" means that those very same manifold forms are again said to be one; thus he mocks [the opponent],
even regarding "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*)— *Pravāha-manoratha*.
As stated by Prajñākaragupta:

since no other form of cognition is perceived apart from blue and so forth, or pleasure and so forth (p. 345), and just as there is no consciousness other than pleasure and so forth, so too there is none other than blue and so forth (pp.

Cognizing consciousness is not perceived as distinct from the blue [object] (p. 406); for no state of being a "grasper" or the like is apprehended appearing apart from white, black, and so forth—(Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p.
378). This is what the wise declare, which follows from the force of reality itself.
To whatever extent objects are analyzed, they fall apart to that same extent; thus,
the answer provided in the *Pravāraṇāvastu* would be out of place.

Furthermore, that which was stated by that same [opponent]—namely, "whatever manifests is cognition, such as pleasure and so forth, and blue and so forth manifest"—is refuted by this [argument]: if blue and so forth, whose nature is partless atoms (*niraṃśaparamāṇu*), are taken as the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and pleasure and so forth as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then everything beginning with the subject of the thesis is unestablished (*asiddha*) because they do not manifest. However, if the reality is a single variegated form (*citraikarūpa*), then everything is established because the opposite is the case. But this [point], namely "that is cognition," is unestablished, because it is impossible for that [atom] to be cognition there and because it is not admitted; for the opponent has not established a single variegated cognition.

Therefore, since the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*)— namely, "being cognition"— subsists in a partless entity, and since the subject of the thesis (*sādhya-dharmin*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-dharmin*) are distinct (the latter being that in which the property to be proven subsists), this [objection] amounts to nothing,
because both the status of being the subject of the thesis and the status of being the example are established through appearance.
The intention of Prajñākaragupta is that because there is no such conventional usage regarding that which consists of partless cognition, [the object] does not exist as its own nature.

Now, one might object: "Even if blue and so forth appear in a form that is gross and so on, setting aside their own true essence, they do not do so by way of being self-cognizing; therefore, whether real or unreal, they do not exist in their primary form through that [self-cognition]. To this, he says: "In whatever way," and so forth.
In whatever way it may be, apart from its own nature as that which manifests, would there not be a real form within the cognition, even if not externally?
[This refers to] that [cognition] which consists merely of blue, pleasure, and so forth.
Of what nature [is it]? Manifesting, that is, possessing appearance, or having that as its habit.
Having done what? Having abandoned its own form, that is, having discarded its non-dual nature.

How does it manifest? In some way or another, by whatever manner such as the gross and so forth, or the grasped and so forth. Its aspect would be real by virtue of being the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), and not by virtue of being a gross form and so forth.
Of what? Of cognition (*jñāna*).
[The opponent] thinks: "In their own nature, they exist as such; thus, cognition may be a single manifold [entity] by way of having both delusive and non-delusive forms.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—to this he replies: "What external object would there be, [since] even in delusion, there would be a single [cognition] with a true form?"

Alternatively, the objective aspect (*satyākāra*) of that cognition—whether in the form of blue and so forth, or in the form of something gross and so forth—would not be anything at all; where could it be? It would be outside [the cognition].
And in that case, the Sautrāntika triumphs, not the Yogācāra, because [that aspect] is somehow connected with the waking state, and not connected with states such as dreaming.

Therefore, this [position] has been refuted by what has already been refuted: "All cognitions are without objective support (nirālambana), because they are cognitions, like a dream-cognition" (*Pravārttika* 3.331). "The form of the apprehended object, which has entered the scope of dispute, is unreal, just like the form of that same object seen in a dream."

How so? Because cognition appears as having forms such as grossness and the like, it would follow that even the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) lacks reality; thus, like external objects, the establishment of that [self-aware] form would not occur.
Therefore, the word "rejected" (*nirākṛta*) is redundant, for there is no other state of being apprehended apart from blue and the rest.
Furthermore, since blue and other colors appear even in a deluded consciousness as clearly manifesting before one, why is the clarity of manifestation not seen as belonging to the delusion itself?
Therefore, there is no such thing as "grasped-ness" that exceeds what is found in delusion.
For blue and other [objects] are unreal, like appearances in a dream (pṛ. 177); objectivity does not exist apart from appearance (pṛ.

Therefore, by relying on inference—which proceeds through a beginningless succession of such inferences—and in the context of postulating external objects, since the postulation of the apprehended and the apprehender proceeds [from that basis], it is established that the postulation of the apprehended and so forth is, in ultimate reality, nothing but undivided cognition itself (pṛ. 398). For the state of apprehended and apprehender does not exist at all in ultimate reality; rather, the nature [of cognition] is independent of another and is thus [defined] by the exclusion of what is not that.
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 427.
Since the verse is easy to understand, the author provides no commentary; instead, concluding what was previously stated in order to introduce the system of Karṇaka, he says "Just as," etc.
This refers to the Buddhist master named Karṇakagomin, the author of the *Svavṛttiṭīkā* on the *Pramāṇavārttika*.

Because the cognition appears falsely despite having the form of the object as it truly is, its own nature (svarūpa) is not established as distinct [from that appearance]; therefore, it is not so [as you claim].
Since a delusive appearance is impossible without an intrinsic nature, [the two cases] are not equal; for even in the absence of an external object, such appearances are frequently observed.

Just as, by whatever manner or cause the appearance in cognition is false, the external object-form—the form of an insentient thing such as a jar, characterized by multiple momentary and partless atoms—cannot be established on that basis for the Sautrāntika; likewise, the intrinsic nature [of the atom] is not established from that cognition for the Yogācāra either.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction," that is, because there is an absence of difference, since the appearance is equal in both cases insofar as it excludes the actual nature of the thing.
Or, just as he (the Naiyāyika) does not accept a gross, single form existing externally, so too the Yogācāra does not accept such a thing internally.

Alternatively, just as for the Naiyāyika and others, the form of an object is not established because cognition appears falsely during states such as dreaming—this being true without distinction—so too, for the Yogācāra, neither the [object's] own nature (*svarūpa*) nor self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of cognition is established without distinction. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction," meaning because there is no difference between the two positions regarding the object and the cognition; for in one case (dreaming), the dream state is the example, and in the other case, the apprehended aspect (*grāhyākāra*) is the example. Thus he considers them to be equivalent.

Just as in the case of those whose minds are overwhelmed by ignorance, cognition arises with false aspects in dependence upon their respective conditions, like [the appearance of] floaters and so forth— *Prajñāpradīpa-vṛtti* 3.
According to the Sautrāntika,
in the position that [the object] is an external thing.
Kallaṭa says: "Apart from its own nature," and so forth.

He considers that since it is impossible for there to be an appearance of an error—that is, of a mistaken form—apart from that which is characterized by the direct realization of the mere nature of cognition itself, and because an error would be untenable if that [nature] were to appear by itself, he maintains that the lack of distinction between his own position and the opponent's position is unproven (*asiddha*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of cognition exists, because otherwise the appearance of error would be inexplicable.
And it has been said: "For one who does not perceive the apprehension itself, the perception of the object is not established.

If it is asked: "In that case, since the appearance of that [cognition] is impossible even without an objective form (*artharūpa*), why is its existence not thereby established? To this he replies: "The object," and so forth.

If it is argued that "it is not the same" because cognition is perceived everywhere and at all times as the grasper of an object—even when the object, such as a jar, is absent, and not only when it is present—then the refutation here is stated as follows: "Otherwise," etc.;
the meaning is that this perception would be imperceptible for one whose cognition is not self-cognized (*asvasaṃvidita*).
Comparison: "The cognition of an object is not established for one whose perception is unestablished"—
this is cited from *Tattvasaṃgraha* verse 2074— see *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa*, page 82.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 29;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, page 81: the manifestation of cognition.
The establishment of the logical object (*arthasiddhi*)—namely, the impossibility of its existence otherwise (*anyathānupapannatva*)—is not established for that which is unproven (*asiddha*).
This is the comparison: the impossibility of its existence otherwise is not established for that which is unproven.
—Nyāyaviniścaya 1.12; Pramāṇanirṇaya, p. 12.
One who knows the universal of consciousness is capable of perceiving the universal of its own object. (Prameyaratnamālā 3.15) || 22 ||
How can the unique nature of cognition, whose self is somehow unestablished, be inferred? For that [inference] could only be possible if its own nature as consciousness were established;

and once its unique nature is established, how could the perception of external objects—even those that are substantially real—be denied, given that the pervasion (vyāpti) is established by the principle that "whatever exists is entirely composed of general and particular aspects"? Indeed, a mere form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) that has not grasped the generality of an object does not penetrate into perception, such that through it the absolute certainty of pure sentience alone would be distinguished.

The intended meaning here is this: since the objection beginning with "in some way" (*yathākathañcit*) was stated regarding the possibility of cognition being perceived in some manner or other, its non-perceptibility must be accepted in every respect. And that being the case, the occurrence of an illusory appearance is impossible, because even the opponent accepts it as such.

Furthermore, in no other way—that is, by any other mode than the absence of the nature of cognition—is the impossibility of an illusory appearance established, given that it remains unproven and undetermined.
For it cannot be said that the non-existence of an unestablished entity, such as the son of a barren woman, is "otherwise inexplicable" (anupapanna) by way of its absence;
by this [statement], he demonstrates that the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is "being otherwise inexplicable," and that this is established when [the reason] possesses that quality.
If it is argued that cognition is perceived in the form of existence, consciousness, and so forth, and not by another [means], he says here: "In the universal of consciousness," and so on.

If it is asked: "Has this not already been refuted by the statement 'Is this not external?'; why then is it stated again?"—the answer is: No; for that [previous statement] was made on the assumption of some kind of non-difference between the cognition and the form of error (*vibhrama*), whereas this [present statement] is made on the basis of their absolute difference.

The meaning is as follows: either consciousness itself, or its universal (*sāmānya*), is perceived through the perception of that [form]; that is, by perceiving pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) while turning away from grasping the distinction of the form of error which constitutes the nature of the cognition.
It is logical and appropriate to observe the universal of that object which is capable of being perceived by oneself.

By this, the contradiction between earlier and later statements has been shown for one who asserts that cognition is somehow directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to a single nature of an object, as in *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.42 and so forth,
while [simultaneously] asserting that cognition is not directly perceived.
Since perception itself exists in a specific form, what other part of it could there be that is not already seen, which would then need to be examined by other means of valid cognition?
Thus [is] the remainder;
explaining the verse of the Buddhist, he says: "In some way," and so forth.

In no way whatsoever—neither through the exclusion of the form of error (*vibhrama*) nor by any other means—is it possible for cognition (*buddhi*), whose nature is unestablished and whose form is entirely ungrasped, to have an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) nature that is excluded from both insentient things and errors; how then could that non-dual self-cognizing nature be inferred on the grounds that the appearance of error would otherwise be inexplicable? It is thought that this cannot be so, because the reason itself is unestablished. The connection is that, since it is being inferred, its uncommon nature might be presumed to exist.
It might be thought: "Its nature as being, consciousness, and so forth is established by itself. To this he says: "By itself," and so on.

The connection is as follows: "by itself" means not from anything else; its very form is consciousness (*cit*). When the establishment of that [consciousness] is accepted, what kind of [consciousness] is it? To this he says: "Possibly," and so on.

Regarding that which has been described as having a "probable" (*saṃbhāvita*), "inferable" (*anumeya*), and "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) nature—what [follows] therein? To this he says: "In its entirety," and so forth.

Once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established—that everything which exists, both externally and internally, consists of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*)—how could the perception of what is perceptible (*pratyakṣapratipatti*) be denied by means of perception itself? To whom would it not be denied? He says: even for the external object (*bahirartha*), and not merely for cognition (*jñāna*).
Of what kind [is it]? He says: "conceived" (*saṃbhāvita*), and so forth.
Again, of what kind? He says: "substance" (*dravya*), and so forth, up to the end of the word "of the ultimate reality" (*paramārthasya*).

Now, if indeed cognition does not have a nature conceived through perception, what follows for the external object, such that it too would be like that? To this he says: "For [it is] not unapprehended," and so forth.
For perception does not penetrate [the object] to make it its own object;

what then? He says: "That which consists of nothing but the nature of consciousness"—that is, that entity whose form is characterized by self-awareness of consciousness (citsvasaṃvedana); that alone is the "mere" object, meaning the generality of cognition (jñānasāmānya).
Of what nature is it? He says: "not grasping the external generality"—that by which no external generality is grasped is so described.
The meaning is that it penetrates precisely that universal which has been grasped as the object;
by this, he demonstrates that the universal is established by perception in both cases.
For, since it penetrates only that [universal], the establishment of the absolute nature of consciousness would be distinguished—that is, differentiated—from the establishment of the object.

The word *yataḥ* is used here in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepa*). By the passage beginning with *saṃbhāvitā*, the following is intended: just as when the pervader (*vyāpaka*), which is pure consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is not perceived, there is a non-perception of its pervaded (*vyāpya*)—which possesses a probable, uncommon form characterized by the discernment of the nature of delusion—so too is the case with the subject at hand. As Prajñākara has stated: "Even when the past and future states are not grasped, that which exists in those states is grasped. To this, [the objection is]: how can there be a cognition of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) when the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is not apprehended? (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra 1).

Thus [it was argued], but this has been refuted by the following: even when there is no cognition of the distinction from the form of error, just as there is a cognition of the mere nature of consciousness—which pervades that [error]—so too, even when the particularities are not grasped, it is possible to have a cognition of the universal which pervades them.

[Objection: But even if the pervader is perceived externally, if the particulars are not seen, how can there be a cognition of "this belongs to that"? [Reply: If you say, "Because they are seen again later," then from what is that subsequent perception established? It cannot be from the previous perception, because that [previous perception] occurred earlier and did not function with respect to that [later state].
Nor can it be established through subsequent perception, because that [subsequent perception] did not exist previously and thus cannot operate upon the pervader;
nor can it be established from the collection of those two, because such a collection is impossible for two things occurring sequentially;
and that single entity existing at both times, being attended by the successive operations of the eye and other senses, does not withstand close scrutiny.

Furthermore, because there is no possible means of apprehending that [external object], and because the mere existence of the self (ātman) is indistinguishable [from its non-existence], it is not established by that; for the case of perception has already been answered,
and thus the external object of cognition is also [unestablished].
Perception, which has become an object,
is merely the nature of consciousness.

Furthermore, if the states are not apprehended, there can be no cognition of their pervasion by the preceding and succeeding [moments]; and if the states are not apprehended, how could there be a cognition of the substratum?
For as long as the pervaded is not cognized, the other cannot be cognized as the pervader—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*.
In response to the doubt as to what constitutes the self, it was stated that [it is] the pervasive elements.
Those are the particulars of the pervasive universal; thus, [they exist] in each respective pervaded instance.

The sense is this: since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend a single entity that exists at both times, if a single entity were established as pervading both [moments] occurring in succession, then the self (*ātman*) existing in such a manner would also be established.
By this, inference (*anumāna*) has also been considered. If it is argued that "in its absence, this [inference] is absent," he says here: "the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*), and so forth.
Because inference is absent in the absence of direct perception,
for one who perceives the nature of consciousness as ultimately non-different from all things.
Its specific nature should be accepted as external in the same way that it is experienced.
Seeing the universal—which is not itself excluded from anything—while striving to grasp the self, one would gradually apprehend consciousness as a substance distinguished from the insentient;
therefore, the self is directly perceived and is not itself contradicted. It should be understood that just as it grasps internally according to its capacity, so too does it grasp externally.

Since it is impossible to negate an object of cognition that is of a single nature consisting of both the perceptible and the imperceptible, how could one conceive of an entity if it were in some way imperceptible? For, in such a case, there would be no established mark (*liṅga*) or other means of proof; thus, the nature (*rūpa*), that is, the essential character (*svabhāva*), of consciousness (*cit*)—or of the intellect (*buddhi*)—is like that of one overcome by deep sleep.

Of what nature is it? It is undivided (*abhinnam*), meaning non-excluded (*avyāvṛttam*). From what? From everything—both from the similar (*sajātīya*) and the dissimilar (*vijātīya*). This is because the universal of existence (*satsāmānya*) is of such a nature; so thinks the Buddhist who perceives it, making it an object through conceptual perception (*vikalpadarśana*). Its particularity (*tadviśeṣaḥ*)—the particularity of that universal belonging to consciousness, characterized by sentience (*caitanya*) and so forth, which will be described in the commentary—is a distinction (*bhedaḥ*). In whatever manner (*yathā*) it is to be known or grasped in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), [that manner] is to be connected to both [the universal and its particularity] by placing "in the middle" (*tanmadhyekaraṇāt*).

In that same manner, for one who perceives the existent universal (*satsāmānya*) as an external object, the particular (*viśeṣa*) is likewise to be known. The illustration has been established by the immediately preceding reasoning and is not established again here, because [the universal] is not excluded from anything at all. He states the meaning of the verse with the words "from anything" (*kutaścit*) and so forth: "not excluded from anything whatsoever"—not merely from one thing alone—by itself, through its own nature. What is this? It is the universal, which one perceives while seeing.
What should one do? He says: what should one grasp? Consciousness (*caitanya*). What kind of action is that?
Of what nature is it? And so forth—it is that which is distinguished from the insentient (*acetana*).
Who is it that would grasp? To this he says: the self, the living soul (jīva).
Again, doing what? To this he says: striving.
What to do? To this he says: "to grasp consciousness"—this is the connection.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "Substance," and so forth.
How [is it]? Gradually, after that, from above that, of what nature is it? He says: "Perceptible," and so forth.
The meaning is "having the nature of the perceptible.
If it is asked, "But how can this be so, given that the self (ātman) has been negated?", he says here: "by itself," etc.
By itself—that is, by its own nature—it is uncontradicted and not refuted; this has been considered both in the initial introduction and here.

If it is argued that, because there is no distinction in that [capacity], one should perceive everything at all times and in all places, he says here: "Just as," etc., [meaning] it perceives without overstepping its capacity;
applying this to the present subject, he says: "Just as," etc.

It should be understood that just as one apprehends internally by means of a process—either by first apprehending the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and then the pervaded (*vyāpya*), or else by the process of apprehending the capacity (*śakti*)—one likewise apprehends externally by that very same process.

Thus, what was stated by Prajñākara—"That which appears is cognition, such as pleasure and so forth; and blue and so forth appear, because it is impossible for an insentient thing (*jaḍa*) to manifest"—is refuted by this [argument], since there is no obstruction to the manifestation of the insentient just as there is for cognition.

However, this is the distinction: that knowledge [is known] intrinsically (*svataḥ*), while other things [are known] extrinsically (*parataḥ*). Nor is the denial of this [distinction] logical, because that [knowledge] is perceived through the cognition "I know this pillar and so forth. Otherwise, what confidence could there be regarding blue and other objects? Nor is the objection "How can it be the apprehender of itself? tenable; for since the objection would then equally apply as to how it can be the apprehender of its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is no distinction, as it is perceived to be the apprehender of the nature of others (*pararūpa*) just as it is of its own.

Furthermore, the remainder here is the statement of another [opponent]: that even within the doctrine of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one refutes the causal relationship, the relationship between the object of exclusion and the excluder in inferential superimposition, the non-duality of variegated cognition, or whatever else [is asserted]. This will be demonstrated by means of the eternal self from the perspective of another.
The appearance of that which is insentient and mental.
By means of inference, the superimposition [of the object] is excluded; thus, there exists between those two the relationship of the excluded and the excluder.

As for this argument—"Cognition of blue and so forth is [the apprehension of an external object], because it is perceived immediately after the operation of the eye and other [senses], like the cognition intended to be its grasper"—in that case, the undesirable consequence would also follow that "Blue is not [an external object], because it is perceived immediately after the operation of those [senses], like a conch shell.
In both instances, there is subversion by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Comparison: "No cognition as a subject is observed apart from the blue; the distinction [between them] following upon the cognition is constructed by the artisan of conceptualization" (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 406).
Furthermore, he raises the following objection: if blue were not [itself] blue, then even the inference [of its existence] would be impossible.

Moreover, if the eye and other [senses] were external objects, then because there would be no perception [of them], their apprehension would not occur immediately after their operation; thus, the reason (hetu) would be unestablished (asiddha), and the example (dṛṣṭānta) would lack the probans (sādhanavikala). Alternatively, if the apprehension of that [object] did occur immediately after the operation of some other sense-organ or inferential mark (liṅga), then the original reason would be inconclusive (vyabhicāra). Furthermore, even if blue and so forth are apprehended immediately after the operation of cognition (jñānatva), the cognition of that [cognition] itself is not apprehended by another; thus, the example remains unestablished.

Now, if the proponent of the *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) claims that this is established [by scripture], there is no fault; for if that is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is established for the Buddhist as well, since valid cognition has no partiality toward any particular side. Thus, there is no contradiction in the statement that "there is no further grasper of blue and so forth. However, if it is established by what is not a valid cognition, then it cannot serve as an illustration, because that which is established by non-valid cognition is unfit for such a purpose—just like a logical reason (*hetu*). Otherwise, even "being visible to the eye" and the like would constitute a valid reason, which is absurd. Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
The perception of blue and so forth by the eye and other [faculties] occurs in a distinct form.
If the eye and so forth were themselves cognitions,
then there would be a second cognition intended to grasp that [first] one.
If the cognition considered to be the apprehender is cited as an example for that which is not established by a means of valid cognition, [the argument would be]:
"Sound is impermanent because it is visible."

As for this further argument—that the cognition of a waking pillar and so forth is the effect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like the perception of a beloved woman by one whose vision is afflicted by desire, grief, and the like—that too is not sound; because its being an effect of that [latent impression] is unestablished with respect to another person.
Therefore, it is well said: "Just as internally," and so forth.

If it is argued that even so, there is neither the manifestation nor the possibility of an external object consisting of both the universal and the particular, because such an object has been refuted; to this he replies: "In perception," and so forth.

That specific nature which is perceptible, consisting of a general form, being an essential part of the entity’s own self, is a particularity that can be conceived; and that specific nature which is imperceptible, characterized by its uniqueness—of these two, he is called "that which has a single common essence" (*sādhāraṇa-ātmā-svabhāva*).

Of what? Of the object of cognition (*prameya*), which is external and graspable, because it is impossible to negate or refute it; otherwise, one would have to negate the cognition itself as well—this is what is intended.

If it is argued that, just as there is non-perceptibility through an uncommon form, both externally and internally, let there likewise be non-perceptibility through a common form as well; to this he replies: "In some way" (*kathañcit*).

If there were non-perceptibility of the object—that is, an absence of perceptuality—how could one conceive of the object through a mark (*liṅga*) or other means? One would not be able to apprehend the object through inference at all, because the mark and so forth would be unestablished. [The phrase] "in some way, like the uncommon" is a comparison to one who is overcome by deep sleep. [The opponent objects: If [the object] exists only through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then it follows that it is merely a cognition.
Latent impression (*vāsanā*) is defined as the cause of memory and recognition— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 319— [stated] with respect to the Jaina.
Since it has not been established that [the world] is an effect of latent impressions (vāsanā),
he states the concluding verse regarding the subject under discussion, beginning with "of the nature of existence" (sadrūpam):
"One should discern that which is distinct from it, because it is known as being of the nature of existence in every respect."
Furthermore, the conscious self (cidātman) is subject to transformation and is differentiated by time and other factors.
Perceiving the existence of all things through their commonality as either sentient or insentient, a person first delimits the insentient by distinguishing it from the sentient.

Then, distinguishing that very same [insentient object] from other insentient things, one gradually delimits its specific qualities—such as color and shape—through the differentiation of time and other factors; it cannot be otherwise.

This is precisely the sequence for the internal practice of realization: having distinguished the commonality of one's own and others' consciousness as distinct from the insentient, and having further differentiated it from the "other," one gradually discerns the specific particulars, because the partless nature has not yet been definitively ascertained.
The meaning here is this: the conscious self, whose nature is perception, should discriminate and grasp.
To the question "What [should it grasp]? he says: "Being" (sat), which is the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*).

Since it is stated in the *Gommaṭasāra-jīvakāṇḍa* (verse 481) that "perception (*darśana*) is the grasping of the universal (*sāmānya*)," one might [wrongly] assume this refers to the universal as conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas and others. To this, he replies: "Of what is 'form' (*rūpa*) the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
He then says: "Of cognition (*vitti*), that is, of the intellect (*buddhi*), meaning of the self (*ātman*)."

Furthermore, later on, from what would that [object] be distinguished and differentiated? Being in the form of *avagraha* (perceptual apprehension), one should distinguish it from another—that is, from something heterogeneous and insentient. Then, being in the nature of the transformations of *ākāṅkṣā* (desire to know) and so forth, one should distinguish it from everything—both from the homogeneous and the heterogeneous. And again, by means of distinctions such as time (*kāla*) and so forth, the form of that which is to be divided is described as "that which is produced by time and other factors"; the connection is that one should distinguish that [object] as qualified by time and so forth. [The verse states: "One should not, having grasped the general perception (*sāmaṇṇa-gahaṇa*) of entities, make it one's conduct. [This means: One should not take that initial, general apprehension of things to be the final mode of behavior.
"In the *Samaya* (Jain doctrine), it is stated that 'vision' (*darśana*) is so called because it does not differentiate among objects."—
This verse has been extracted from the *Satprarūpaṇā* section of the *Dhavalā-Ṭīkā*.
That which is the general apprehension is vision (darśana); this same [apprehension], when specified, is knowledge (jñāna).
— *Sanmatitarka* 2.1.

One should discern that commonality which is this recurring, non-distinct genus—the form "existent, existent" (sat-sat) which is shared by all entities—and furthermore, one should discern that nature of the person (pudgala). Of what kind? From every [instance of] cognition that is devoid [of it], from another cognition, that is to say, from another person; [one should discern it] from everything without exception.

Furthermore, the explanation that "one should discern by making distinctions through time and so forth" means that "that reality (sat) is twofold: consisting of the person (pudgala) and consisting of the soul (jīva) and so forth, which are distinct from the person," and so on.
In order to explain the *kārikā*, he says: "All," and so forth.
Perceiving the existence of an entity as common to all—that is, as shared with others—a person or the self (*ātman*) delimits the insentient *pudgala*.
Doing what? He says: "while excluding the *pudgala*."

Why? Because of consciousness (*cetanā*). Furthermore, distinguishing that very [object] from another—namely, from what is non-conscious (*acetana*) and from other things (*arthāntara*), such as other persons (*pudgalāntara*)—it sequentially determines the specific qualities of that person, such as color and shape.

How? By means of distinctions of time (*kāla*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of place (*kṣetra*) and other factors is intended. It is not otherwise, nor by any other mode.
