If it is asked: "But if time is not apprehended through perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), how can one determine [the object] by its distinction? This is not correct; for conventional time (*vyavahārakāla*) is [apprehended through perception], while ultimate time (*paramārthakāla*) is the domain of reasoning (*tarka*).
Of time, which exists in the form of moments, hours, and so forth through divisions such as [the passing of] kalās,
and which consists of atoms of time.
Demonstrating the application of the second verse regarding inference, he says: "In the internal," and so forth;
this alone, and no other, is the sequence for the realization of the internal consciousness.
Showing this very point, he says: "One's own and others," and so forth.
The phrase "perceiving the existence of all things in their commonality as sentient or otherwise" is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: perceiving them through that commonality, one first delimits the commonality of one's own and others' consciousness as distinct from the insentient; then, having delimited oneself from another self (the other), one gradually delimits the specific natures, such as apprehension (*avagraha*) and the rest.
Whence is this? To this he says: "partless," and so forth;
this is easy to understand by way of the commonality between the conscious and the non-conscious.

Showing that the reality of an object is impossible when there is an absolute delusion regarding it—just as the cognition of an external object [is impossible]—the cognition of another mental continuum is likewise difficult for the Buddhist to obtain; thus he states the verse beginning with "buddhipūrvām":
"Having observed an action preceded by cognition in one's own body, one perceives it elsewhere [in another]; [therefore, another mind exists]."
Intelligence is perceived by unerring persons in some other instance.

And it has been said: "That which is preceded by intelligence is considered to be the presence of intelligence; where that [preceding cause] does not exist, there is no intellect" (Tattvavaiśāradī, p.
In Dharmakīrti’s *Santānāntarasiddhi*, the first verse also has such a first half:

"Since there is no evidence for the assumption that a cognition appearing as an activity or speech could be directly subject to a rule of being produced by the desire to act or the desire to speak," (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa, p. 303).

It has been stated only briefly that an action preceded by cognition, consisting of activity and speech, is the cause of an imperceptible cognition; however, since there is no prohibition against a specific form [of cognition] also being a cause, how could one—despite the absence of those two in states such as deep sleep—recognize the cessation of the senses and life-force in those whose nature is remote from perception? For this reason, one might claim that death, characterized by the cessation of those [senses and life-force], is impossible in the case of stationary beings (plants).

But if death were merely the cessation of life-force, what would it be that distinguishes it from that [mere cessation], given that it is distinguished by the cessation of consciousness and so forth? I do not even know such a thing myself.

Therefore, this person—failing to perceive his own non-dual self-cognition as being delimited by spatial or temporal intervals—claims to determine or exclude another's mind, which is absolutely beyond the senses; thus, his mental activity is entirely devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What kind of action has that [cognition] for its prior cause? [The answer is: none whatsoever.

What? Having seen [it] where? In one's own body or elsewhere in another's body; because of the apprehension of that—namely, the apprehension of intentional action—it is known that the intellect exists elsewhere. This is the construction of the words.

By whom? By non-deluded persons. It is not known by delusions—that is, by various delusions—regarding that mere generality of cognition (*buddhisāmānya*) in some instances, because even the appearance of activity, speech, and so forth, which serves as the mark (*liṅga*) for that [cognition], is without a real objective basis (*nirālambana*), just like the appearance of objects such as food and drink. This is what is intended.

It might be argued: "In the waking state, the manifestation of activity and so forth arises directly from the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the like, whereas elsewhere it arises through a causal chain; therefore, this is not a fault. To this, he provides the answer beginning with "by itself" (*svayam*).

"Self" (*svayam*) means by oneself; "activity" (*vyāpāraḥ*) is the movement of the body, and "utterance" (*vyāhāraḥ*) is speech. That consciousness in which these two appear is described as such. How could a restriction arising from the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) or the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) be possible for that very [consciousness]? To this he says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*), because there is a lack of evidence for such a conceptualization in the state of awakening immediately following deep sleep.

However, for one who maintains that the body exists even in the state of dream— who accepts that even in the dream state, the knowledge appearing as speech and so forth is necessarily produced directly by volition and the like— for such a person, the doctrine of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) would be without foundation, because it would be established that even the knowledge appearing as external objects is necessarily produced directly from the reality of external objects,
given the observation of the movement of the body within dreams. —
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 2.154–155.
Just as the body in a dream, through fear, leaping, and running,
causes transformations in the waking body, so it is also in other births.

As for what was stated by that same author [in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 2.37]—namely, that "because another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) is not admitted, its non-establishment is not a fault"—that too is not true. For this fault is leveled against the Yogācāra, whereas the opposite is the case for the Proponent of Non-dual Appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*). For him, since even his own appearance, when analyzed, cannot be established as being like a permanent entity, the fault is simply the non-existence of everything; so what is the point of stating that particular refutation?

Now, demonstrating the unestablished nature (*bhāgāsiddhatā*) of the reason "another continuum" as employed by the opponent— against one who asserts a plurality of consciousness-streams— in the form of the undesirable consequence that another continuum would be unestablished, he says: "preceded by cognition," and so forth.

An intellect preceded by [another] intellect is itself an effect and is nothing other than an action. Of what nature is it? It consists of activity and verbal expression, and is the cause—the logical mark (*liṅga*)—of a remote intellect, that is, an intellect residing in another body. Thus, very little has been said; the point is that this [reason] is impossible in every case where [the subject] has been made the locus of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛte*). Now, as for the argument that the *maṇḍa* (curdled milk) and so forth are the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) because they are insentient and not the locus of the thesis (*pakṣa*), he states the reply: "Even of a particular form," and so on.

It is not only because of that [specific] action; for there is no contradiction regarding the logical mark (*liṅga*), namely the cause which is consciousness—a property belonging to another property (such as the intellect) that is well-known in the world and accompanies the inferable cognition.
What is meant is this: in that case, if consciousness were absent, it would constitute a counter-example (*vipakṣa*);
but it is not so, because there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its presence.
Action, consisting of activity and speech,
belongs only to that action which is preceded by cognition, as in the case of a tree and so forth.
Furthermore, showing that there is no means for him to apprehend the absence of consciousness in another's body—which is the opposite of his own activity—he says: "In deep sleep, etc.

Although one should have said "of that which is remote by nature, other than the subject and the similar instance," he uses the term "senses" (indriya) with the intention of providing a subsequent refutation. How, in what manner, could this Buddhist not cognize cessation—that is, non-existence—such that some contrary instance (vipakṣa) might exist?
Why would he not cognize it? To this he says: "Non-apprehension," and so forth.
If it is argued that one should recognize cessation because its effects, such as speech and so forth, are not observed, [the author] says here: "In deep sleep and so forth"—
by the word "and so forth," states such as fainting are included— despite the absence of those two, namely activity and speech,
[this is known] from intentional action.

Now, one might ask: when it could have been said simply as "in the absence of that activity" (*tasyāḥ kriyāyā abhāve*) or "even in its absence" (*tadabhāve*), for what purpose is the expression "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) used? It is for the sake of removing ambiguity; otherwise, because [the word *tad*] exists even in the absence of a specific form (*ākāraviśeṣa*), the thought might arise that it refers to that as well. How then would one know that [consciousness] belongs to them? Such is the connection [of the argument].
Thus he thinks: the understanding of non-existence arises from the absence of an effect whose causal capacity is restricted; however, consciousness is not like this.

Praśākarastvāha: "Even there, in the absence of consciousness, the four states would otherwise not exist. He does not act with reason, because it would follow that awakening is impossible, since an effect cannot arise from a cause that has been destroyed—this will be demonstrated right here in the immediately following section. Showing what else follows for one who does not understand their cessation, he says "yataḥ" and so forth:
"Since," that is, because of that cognition of cessation, one would declare death—which is characterized by that cessation—to be non-existent even in stationary things such as trees.
Or, the word "since" (*yataḥ*) may be used in a sense of objection: one should not say [this],
because he accepts that death for a Buddhist consists in the cessation of consciousness, the sense faculties, and vitality, and because that [cessation] is impossible in trees.
— Nyāyabindu 3.59:
For according to the Buddhist awakening, death is indeed the cessation of consciousness and the other [mental factors].
"The cognition of which is unestablished regarding trees, his mind is likewise"—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.
46. Here, a certain bystander says: "If, however," and so forth.

If, however, death were merely the cessation of life-force (*āyus*), what would be the case? What fault (*dūṣaṇa*) would there be, such that—on account of that fault—that death is distinguished from the cessation of consciousness and so forth (the word "and so forth" [ādi] referring to the cessation of the sense-faculties)? Not seeing a fault here, the Master says: "No," and so on. "I too do not know"—meaning not only does another not know—such a conclusion as has been stated by the opponent. He states the summary with the words beginning with "that" (*tat*).

Since this is so, therefore this follower of the Sugata (Buddhist), not perceiving self-cognition as non-dual—of what nature? He says: "delimited," and so forth; the meaning is that it is established as being identical with itself.

Alternatively, it should be explained as follows: "delimited" means not apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and "obstruction" refers to karma, which is the cause of obscuration because it acts as an obstacle to the grasping of both self and other. This is because he maintains the absolute position of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Thus he thinks.
What does he do? To this he says: "The other," and so forth.

Of what nature is the mind of another? It is absolutely imperceptible. How does one discern it—that is, make it an object of cognition for oneself and distinguish it from something else, such as a tree—either through some intentional activity or by the absence of its effects, such as speech and the like? Thus, the activity of this Buddhist is entirely without any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇikā*). He thinks that [the inference] "the living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth" is not different from this [absurd] logic.

Now, if it is argued that what was stated—"since the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is somehow unestablished," and so forth—is incorrect because that [intellect] is indeed perceived through its own form as being existent, conscious, and so on; to this he replies with the verse beginning "And by itself" (*svataśca*):
"If the intellect were established in every respect by itself, what would be the use of a reason for it?
If the intellect were not established in every respect by itself, what would be the use of a reason for it? (26)

For just as the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) is not possible for one who does not conceptualize without conceptual perception (*savikalpapratyakṣa*), so too, once conceptual perception has occurred, the memory that excludes superimposition does not establish any object by itself, because superimposition does not arise spontaneously [at that point] and because there is no performing again what has already been done. Otherwise, if what has already been accomplished were established by itself, one must understand that further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be both purposeless and impossible; and this has already been thoroughly examined.

If cognition (*jñapti*) is established independently by itself without depending on anything else, then why is it not established in every way and at all times—even in its other forms—just as it is in its form as "existent" and so forth? The point is that there would be nothing [unestablished] in that cognition, because it would be directly perceived (*pratyakṣa-siddha*) through every aspect by means of a cause (*hetu*), an inferential mark (*liṅga*), or even the form of blue and so on.
And thus, whatever appears is cognition, just like pleasure and the like.

Whatever appears in a certain way is real in that very way from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as it enters into conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*); for example, blue, appearing as blue, enters into discourse exactly as it appears. And since all entities appear as momentary, [this argument] does not support any point for Prajñākaragupta, the proponent of the absolute monism of consciousness (*vijñānaikāntavādin*), because the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) will be refuted immediately hereafter. [The opponent objects: "If [the cognition] is established by itself, then there is no proof whatsoever; what is the use of a reason (*hetu*) in that case? For when dharma and so forth are unestablished, a reason cannot function. This is the sense [of the objection].
(Page 2, Note 10)

In response to the objection that inference excludes superimposition because the mind of certainty (*niścayacitta*) and the mind of superimposition (*āropacitta*) stand in a relationship of mutual sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*), he says:

Thinking that the refutation established against the Sautrāntika applies equally to the Yogācāra as well, the Master takes that very point as an illustration and explains the verse with the words "tathaiva" and so forth.

For in exactly what manner and by precisely what means [the inference] is not possible for the Sautrāntika? He says: [it is not possible] because of the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*). Since inference is the cause for the exclusion of superimposition, it is called "that exclusion."

In the absence of what? The intention is that [it occurs] in the absence of conceptual perception (*savikalpapratyakṣa*), [that is,] in the absence of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpapratyakṣa*).

Of what one doing so? Of one who does not reflect (*avitarkayataḥ*), that is, one who does not ascertain [objects such as] *dharma* and so forth; and that which is not ascertained is not capable of serving as the basis for inference. The rest has been considered here, as will be stated: "And this has been cleared away."
If it is argued that conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) then becomes [the means of knowledge], he says: "In perception," and so forth.

Whether in the conceptualization or the differentiation of perception, the cognition regarding perception is merely a determination (*vyavasāya*). Furthermore, the recollection that excludes superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda-smṛti*) and the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇika-anumāna*) do not establish any object at all, because the nature of momentariness and so forth is already ascertained through perception—this is the sense.
If it is argued that [inference] performs the exclusion of superimposition, he says here: "By itself," and so forth.

Because there is no self-imposed superimposition (*samāropa*), because such [superimposition] is impossible in the case of certainty (*niścaya*), and because of the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.50): "There is a relationship of the sublated and the sublator between the mind of certainty and the mind of superimposition," it is thought that [the opponent's position] does not establish any object whatsoever; nevertheless, he states the refutation of its production: "because there is no production of what has already been produced."

Otherwise, if the cognition produced by this [means] were established and determined through itself, there would be the futility of another means of knowledge, namely inference; and if it were not established, its occurrence would be impossible. Thus, both its futility and impossibility are to be understood, and since this has been thoroughly examined, it is called the "exclusion of superimposition" (samāropavyavaccheda), by metaphorically applying the term for the cause to the effect.
The sense is that if the subject (*dharmin*) and so forth are not established in themselves, inference is impossible.

Having thus refuted the non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-adhyakṣa*) of the Buddhist, he says "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), etc., in order to refute the conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*) of the Vaiśeṣika.

If perception were conceptual, there would be no cognitions of continuity regarding universals and inherence, because in that case, there would be the ascertainment of only a single [particular] therein.
For a recurring cognition or a perception of similarity is not logical with respect to distinct substances and so forth.
Why would it not be logical that this is simply the cognition of a single relation? Because there is no error [in such a cognition].

Nor is it the case that a uniform cognition does not arise among distinct substances and so forth without a relation to a single entity; for if that were so, it would follow that universals could not be perceived as existing in themselves or as being objects of knowledge.

The activity [of asserting] that some things possess intrinsic existence while others do not is likewise without any basis in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, it would entail the infinite regress of universals and inherence. It is logical that there is identity (*tādātmya*) between a universal and its possessor;
for if inherence functions even in the absence of another inherence, why should other things not function in the same way?
Furthermore, there would not be such cognitions as "the cow is in the horns" or "the tree is in the branches."

Even though universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are all-pervasive, the possibility of such a diversity—that they cause the intended cognition only in certain instances and not elsewhere—implies that it must be substance (*dravya*) itself that is variegated. How could one who is sound-minded establish that a universal or an inherence, being partless and inactive by nature, pervades its own particulars? For, due to the difference in their substrates such as substances, they would lose their own essential nature. Therefore, it is logical that this [reality] is directly perceived as consisting of both substance and mode (*paryāya*).
If [it is asked], "Of what is this determinate (*vyavasāyātmaka*) perceptual cognition? he says: "In the universal," and so forth.

This refers to substances, qualities, and actions which possess inherence by virtue of being inherent in a universal; or alternatively, it refers to universals, substances, qualities, actions, and ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*), all of which possess the relation of inherence. By implication, it is stated that this [cognition] applies to inherence as well—according to the principle that "there is no cognition of a substratum (*viśeṣya*) without its qualifiers (*viśeṣa*) having been apprehended."

Regarding the objection that if inherence (*samavāya*) were imperceptible, one would be unable to say "this belongs to the inherent things," he states the refutation here: [the verse begins with] "anusyūti" and so forth. The "pervasions" (*vyāptayaḥ*)—which consist of the threading together (*anusyūti*) by way of some form of identity (*tādātmya*)—are as follows: the pervasion of substances, qualities, and actions by the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), and of that [existence] by them; the pervasion of each of the substances and so on by the generalities of substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*), and of those [generalities] by them; the pervasion of qualities and actions by substance, and of that [substance] by them; and the pervasion of composite wholes by their parts, or of those [parts] by the whole. If these [pervasions] were not grasped by cognition, then, while this determinate perception (*savikalpa-pratyakṣa*) is being admitted or occurs, such perceptions would not be possible.
From where is this [known]? To this he says: "Because of the determination of each one.
Here, a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is to be understood for the word "each" (*ekasya*).
Therefore, the meaning is: because of the determination of each and every one—whether it be a universal, a substance, a quality, an action, or anything else—that is independent or solitary.
Thinking that because those [entities] are as if non-existent, there would be a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the opponent upon their non-existence,
the commentary beginning with "for not" (*na hi*) will address this very point.

Alternatively, why would there not be those cognitions which are the continuous perceptions of generalities such as existence (*sattva*)—namely, the cognitions "this is a generality," "this is a generality"—and, because of their plurality, the corresponding verbal designations? To this he says: "Of one [generality]," and so forth;
that is, because of the determination of each individual generality, such as existence, when it is devoid of the assistance of any other generality.

Here too, the passage beginning with "nor is there a relation to a single entity" has already been explained. Furthermore, those cognitions of continuity which belong to the inherent causes (*samavāyin*) would not exist; the plural number is to be explained as before.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Of one," and so forth.

Regarding the determination of a single entity—whether it be a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*karman*), or inherence (*samavāya*)—as well as anything else, the explanation here is as follows: "of inherence," and so forth;
that is, because of the determination of inherence itself as something independent, being devoid of any further relation of inherence.
Regarding this, the explanation beginning with "not here" and so forth [refers to] perception by way of substanceness, qualityness, actionness, and so on.
Comparison—[is] a qualified cognition; and here, it is not [possible] for that which has an unknown qualifier [to be] perception.
(Pramāṇavārttika, Apohapariccheda, verse 88). Perception.
Of the generality of existence [in relation] to substances and so forth;
[and] of the generalities of substantiality, quality-ness, and action-ness.
By means of the qualities and actions of a substance, or by its parts.
The cognitions that are permeated by either the particular whole or the whole itself.

He states the meaning of the verse with the words "substantiality, quality-ness, and so forth are not lower universals," etc., asking: "In which distinct things? and answering with "in substance," etc.

Regarding those [categories], what [is the case]? To this he says: "The knowledge of recurrence," such as the inclusive cognition that "substance exists," "quality exists," or "action exists," is logical (*yukta*) or appropriate (*upapanna*), or else there is a "similar perception" (*sadṛśapratīti*), meaning the cognition "this is similar to that. It is not, however, logical—this is the connection [of the argument]. He states what is logical for the opponent: "What then? [He asks] why the connection—that is, the inherence (*samavāya*)—of those [categories] such as substance and the rest with a single, unique [universal] such as "existence" (*sattā*) is not perceived; rather, only its perception is logical, just like the perception of the connection of a thread [with a cloth] when other [objects] have been experienced.

Alternatively, the cognition of those [particulars], as well as the universal and so forth, and the relation—which is inherence—is indeed possible as mutually distinct. If it is argued that because inherence is extremely subtle, it is not perceived, and thus the cognition of its persistence is an error; to this he replies: because there is no error, a delusion regarding the cognition of persistence is impossible. For when the distinction between the genus and its possessors, parts and wholes, qualities and their possessors, actions and their possessors, and the relation itself is determined, there is an absence of delusion.

Indeed, it is not the case that when two distinct things, such as a jar and a cloth, are determined, one perceives the persistence of the other; this is what the Vaiśeṣika maintains regarding substance and the rest.

As for what was stated regarding the pot or the cloth—that the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttijñāna*) among distinct substances and so forth is not based on a universal (*sāmānya*); that is incorrect, because the proposition is sublated by inference (*anumānabādhanāt*).

And that inference is as follows: "The non-differentiated cognition among distinct substances and so forth is based on a distinct qualifier (*bhinnaviśeṣaṇanibandhana*), because it is a cognition characterized by that [distinct] cognition, just like the cognition 'the man with a staff' (*daṇḍī*) in relation to a person. To this, he says: "And not one," and so forth.

Nor is it the case that a uniform cognition regarding distinct substances and so forth does not occur at all without a connection through a single entity such as a universal; rather, it certainly does occur, since the intended meaning is understood through the use of two negations.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Of universals," etc.

For universals—such as the genus *sattva* (existence) and so forth—which are by their very nature devoid of connection with anything else, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that there is no cognition of their own existence, knowability, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the category of being a "category" (*padārthatva*) is included. This is because [otherwise] there would be an absence of the cognition of that [existence].
The connection with what has preceded is by the words "And yet," etc.:

"And yet, there is the cognition of that [existence]; therefore, the reason is inconclusive. He considers this as follows: the cognition "existent, existent" regarding substances, qualities, and actions is based on a pervasive cause distinct from the qualified objects, because it is a pervasive cognition among diverse things, like the cognition "blue, blue" arising from the connection with the substance blue in the case of blankets and other such items.
...thus, in the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), the staff is the cause (*nimitta*)—Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p.
687; Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p.
313—because it is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*) distinct from the cognition of substance (*dravya*) and so forth.
By this, the cognition "the universal is a universal" has been examined.

Now, why is it said—"because that [universal] would result in non-existence"—given that their capacity for that [cognition] exists inherently (*svata eva*), and that [cognition] arises from that very [capacity]? To this, he says: "Inherently," and so forth.

For some—namely, universals (*sāmānya*), inherence (*samavāya*), and ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*)—there must be existence (*sattva*), that is, actuality; otherwise, like *pradhāna* and other [unproven categories], how could their status be established? For, without a connection to another "existence," they cannot be the cause of the cognition of continuity (*anusyūti-pratyaya*), unlike the other categories such as substances (*dravya*) and so forth. Thus, for this Vaiśeṣika as well—not only for the Buddhist—his activity is devoid of valid means of knowledge (*niṣpramāṇikā*), because it would entail the non-existence of the cognitions of existence, knowability, and so on, regarding universals and the rest.

Regarding this, someone who follows the Sāṃkhya school says: "Since existence (*sattva*), knowability (*jñeyatva*), and so forth will be established even for universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, how can there be a proof of universals and so on through the inversion of *pradhāna* and the rest even for yogis? And how could that [existence] be metaphorically applied (*upacarita*) there? For it arises without a connection to a distinct entity such as existence; it might be so in the case of substances (*dravya*) and the like, but here too, because that [connection] is absent, it is not perceived.
As it has been said: "We do not perceive any universal whatsoever anywhere" (Siddhiviniścaya 2).
12. And so forth;
the inference regarding that [cognition] has been considered here because of the perception of it there.

If, however, the thought is that "because of the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of that [term] there, this [cognition] here is caused by a different qualifier, since otherwise it would be impossible," that too is not tenable; for it would follow that what is metaphorical here must be primary (*mukhya*) there.
Nor can reality be established through a distinction between primary and metaphorical [meanings] as conceived by oneself, because that would lead to over-extension; thus,
[the qualities of] existence and so forth are perceived even in universals and the like.
If it is argued that "the primary [usage] has a distinct qualifier, like 'one who is to be punished' (daṇḍya) and so forth" (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 195), [then the usage] is metaphorical.
Because there is no relation between distinct entities such as existence (sattā) and so forth,
a distinct universal is not perceived in substances and the like.
For this very reason, [the term "existent"] is primary in the case of universals and so forth,
whereas it is secondary in the case of substances and so forth.

Another, however, says: "Because the notion of continuity—such as 'the universal is a universal'—is caused by inherence (*samavāya*), it is incorrect [to say] that [the universal exists] 'by itself' and so forth. This is not correct; for the notion "this is here" has that [inherence] as its cause, otherwise, since the notions "this is a jar," "this is a jar," and so forth would also be established as having that [inherence] as their cause, what would be the use of a universal? Furthermore, when asked "What is this so-called universal?", what answer should be given? If you say, "It is one and subsists in many," then there is the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to composite substances, conjunction, duality and other numbers, and so forth.

If it is argued that [the universal] is the cause of the cognition of recurrence (*anuvṛttivijñāna*), then it follows that the universal must be *inherence* (*samavāya*). Thus, it was rightly stated that the cognition "this is a universal" does not have that [universal] as its cause.

Now, suppose it is argued: "Let it be then that universals and so forth also possess their existence through something else and are the cause of the notion of persistence. To this, he says: "Otherwise," and so on.

This means that if, by another way—that is, by a mode other than their being the cause of that notion through themselves, but rather by a mode of having that existence through something else—universals and inherence were to exist, there would follow an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, the subsistence (*vṛtti*) of even this [inherence] would be without proof (*niṣpramāṇikā*). This is the connection [of the argument].

To explain: if, like substances and so forth, universals also possess existence or serve as the cause of the cognition of "existence" due to their connection with another universal, then because that [first] one would have a connection with another "existence," and that [second] one would have a connection with yet another "existence," there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

This is because even *samavāya* (inherence) would require another for its own reality; and if another *samavāya* were required for that *samavāya*, there would be an infinite regress of *samavāyas*, since they are caused by *samavāya*.
[Pervading all its own objects, undifferentiated in nature, and subsisting in many...]—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 311.
[There would be the consequence of it being a universal (*sāmānya*) because it subsists in many;
for even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), there certainly exists the basis for the recurring cognition "inherence, inherence" due to its subsistence in many.]
For the Vaiśeṣika as well,
existence is the cause of inherence, and it is the cause of the cognition thereof.

Now, suppose it is thought: "There is an infinite regress regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*); for if these too were related to existence (*sattā*), they would have to be related to another universal, just like substances and so forth, and this is not the case. Let this fault belong only to the opponent, not to the Jaina, because he does not admit the reality of anything else in such cases. To the question, "How is this so?", he says: "Regarding the universal," and so forth.

The identity (*tādātmya*) of the universal and its possessor— that is, of the genus and that which possesses it— is somehow logical and established as a form of unity; this reading, contained within these brackets, has been rewritten by the Vaiśeṣika himself.

Having thus refuted the universal (*sāmānya*) as distinct from substance and the other categories, he now speaks—beginning with "of inherence" (*samavāyasya*)—in order to refute its relation. [Objection: But has that not already been rejected by the statement, "because it would entail an infinite regress of inherences" (*samavāyānavasthānuṣaṅgāt*)? [Reply: True; nevertheless, there is a distinction: while the reality of universals and so forth was previously refuted from the perspective of their being [inherently] established, they are now refuted in another way. In this regard, the opponent holds several views: one is that inherence exists in the inherent things (*samavāyiṣu*) by its own nature alone.
"Because of the relation of being a qualifier"—this is another [view]; "it does not subsist"—this is yet another.

Having fixed these three views in the mind, he first applies the refutation to the first: even in the absence of another inherence (*samavāya*), [inherence] exists by its own nature—meaning that if it is accepted that inherence subsists in the inherent things (*samavāyin*), then why should other things such as substances (*dravya*) and so forth not likewise subsist in the very same manner in which inherence subsists? Indeed, they would.
And thus, the sense is: "What is the use of postulating *samavāya* (inherence)?
In this very context, he states another refutation, beginning with "na ca" and so on:

"Nor would there arise—would there not be—such a cognition or understanding here [in the case] of horns and the like as 'this is a cow,' or of branches and the like as 'this is a tree'; for [the cognition] would be related to *samavāya* by virtue of its being an effect. This is the connection [of the words].

He thinks as follows: here, in the case of horns and so forth, the inherence (*samavāya*) is established by the cognition "this is a cow" or in the case of branches and so forth, "this is a tree," because that cognition is its effect; however, when inherence exists in something by itself, then the cognition "inherence exists" is not caused by inherence. Just as that is the case, so it is with the subject under discussion; by this, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of that reason is stated.

In the second case, even though inherence (*samavāya*) lacks another inherence, and because of the word "also" (*api*), there exists another relation of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*) in its occurrence; why then would the other categories, such as substance (*dravya*) and so on, not likewise have an occurrence through inherence? [The opponent replies: They certainly would. Thus, he states another refutation, thinking that for inherence and those substances and so forth, there must also be a relation of being a qualifier in their occurrence in some instances—beginning with the words "And here... and so on, the explanation is as before.

However, this is the distinction: just as the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*) is the cause for the cognition "inherence exists here" in this case, so too is it the cause for another [cognition].

Alternatively, if the state of being a qualifier—which is itself a relation—subsists in its own relata by means of another relation, then there is the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and so forth.
If, on the other hand, it subsists intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then inherence also subsists in that very same way; thus, the argument beginning with "of inherence" remains in force.

If, on the other hand, that same consequence does not apply to inherence (*samavāya*), then from what source does the cognition "this is here" arise? Regarding the third [alternative] as well, since there is no further inherence within that [inherence], the word "also" (*api*) shifts its position; it should be understood as following immediately after the word "inherence" (*vṛttau*) in the commentary.

Thus, the meaning is this: even in the case of inherence—by changing the grammatical case of the word "also," the connection is made as "how much more so by inherence?"—from what [source] would this [cognition] arise? To this, he says: for the others, such as substance and so forth, there could be no such inherence in that very manner.

Indeed, it is not tenable that this [universal] follows that [particular], because there is no connection between them. If it is argued that it might follow from some connection or association with something else, then from what would that connection—namely inherence (samavāya)—arise? For it would lack connection, like the sky and so forth. He states another refutation: "And not here," etc.

The meaning here is this: for precisely the reason that substances and the rest do not subsist anywhere, for that very reason their cognition would also not occur; otherwise, it would belong only to God and the like.

Or how could inherence (*samavāya*) be perceptible to anyone, given the absence of sense-object contact? If it were perceptible in every respect, what would be the use of establishing sense-object contact for the eye?
For the Vaiśeṣika, since inherence—which is partless and consists of the nature of subsistence—has no other mode of subsistence, its subsistence is within itself.
"— because of the relation of qualifier and qualified in both inherence and non-existence" — Nyāyavārttika 1.1.4.
Therefore, it is established that the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) must be accepted even without another relation—[as stated in] Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p.
111: "In this case, the cognition 'the tree is here [in these branches, etc. also [arises] from itself alone."
For here, even from the cognition "the tree" with respect to its branches and so forth,
[the relation] is simply inherent by its own nature.
"Weight-measurement [arises] from inherence which is unconnected with that which possesses inherence"—this is incorrect; that relation is not tenable with the possessors of inherence.
(Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 64)
Indeed, no relation whatsoever can exist that is not connected by its own relations;
for if there were no such occurrence [of a relation], then even when that [relation] is perceived, the fault would be that such perception could simply arise from God, time, and so forth,
despite the absence of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*).

Regarding this, he offers a rebuttal to the objection raised by the opponent—that if every universal were omnipresent, there would be a confusion of cognitions such as "cowness" and so forth due to inherence (samavāya)—as expressed in the verse: "One who is told, 'Eat curd,' might run after a camel" (*Prakaraṇavārttika* 3.183). He refutes that [objection] by stating "In the universal," etc., [meaning]: Even though the relation [of inherence] is present in the particular, it does not belong to the relatum itself; for the conjunction between a bowl and a jujube fruit does not exist in the bowl in the same way that it exists in the jujube fruit. Thus he says: "In the universal," and so on.

The intended meaning here is this: regarding the universal (*sāmānya*), is this response directed toward one that is omnipresent in all things, or one that is omnipresent only in its individual manifestations? In the first case, even though both the universal and inherence (*samavāya*) are all-pervasive, the fact that the cognition of "substance-ness" occurs only in earth and so forth, the cognition of "quality-ness" only in color and so forth, and the cognition of "action-ness" only in movement and so forth—such that these serve as the causes for the respective perceptions of substance and the rest, and not elsewhere—is possible only if a variegated nature (*śabalatva*) is admitted in those two through a distinction between their capacities and incapacities. If this is accepted, then substance itself must be variegated, consisting of both the universal and the particular.

He thinks as follows: this is not a valid rebuttal under the view that those two [the universal and the particular] are all-pervasive—that is, that even though the relation is non-distinct, it belongs to that specific related entity; for, just like the relation, the universal as the related entity is itself non-distinct. However, this is more reasonable: that there is a specific capacity to produce its own inherent effect despite that non-distinction.
And in that case, the proof of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is established everywhere.

In the second case, how and by what means could one who is sound-minded and unafflicted by spirits such as Piśācas establish the pervasion of its own particulars—that is, the pervasion of multiple forms of itself differentiated by space and so forth—by a universal that is partless and inactive, or by inherence?
If it is argued that even for such [a universal], because it exists in its own forms in its entirety, it would indeed establish that [pervasion]; to this he says: "In a substance," and so forth.

Since that [perception] would undergo a loss of its own nature due to its differentiation with respect to each individual substratum such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, how could one establish it? Therefore, for this very reason, this perception—which is being established in the context of the present discussion—is itself composed of both substance and mode (*paryāya*);
or rather, it is logical that this very object under investigation, which is perceived and determined by it, must likewise be composed of both substance and mode. Thus [says] the Vaiśeṣika.

When asked by the Buddhist, "If one is urged, 'Eat curd,' why does he not run toward a camel? there is no distinction [in the response], since that which is related and called "curd" would otherwise take the form of a camel.
Because conjunction resides in both [relata],
the substance called the jujube fruit cannot possibly reside in both [the pot and the ground] in the same way that universals and inherence do.

Although universals (*sāmānya*) are undivided in space because they possess the capacity to serve as the cause for the cognition of their intended objects in some instances while lacking that capacity in others—due to a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—nevertheless, by virtue of the restriction of their manifesting conditions (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the restriction of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), they are omnipresent within their own respective domains. Just as there is a restriction regarding the relationship between container and contained (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) despite the oneness of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between a bowl and its curd, so too, although inherence (*samavāya*) is one, there is a restriction regarding the locus and the located (*ādhārādheya*) among universals such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) due to the difference in their powers of manifestation and being manifested.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 327)
In the case of generality (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*), there is a distinction between their inherent powers;
and if one accepts such a distinction in their inherent powers, [the following applies].
Regarding the position that [the universal] is omnipresent within its own manifestations,

[the author] states "perception," etc., demonstrating that even for that which is partless and inactive, there is the impossibility of [its existence] otherwise, as well as other points such as the non-perception of the particular (svalakṣaṇa), and the refutation of the subsistence of a [universal] possessing parts even according to the Vaiśeṣika.
Since a substance consists of qualities and modes, perception [establishes] the negation of the activity of a partless Buddhist [atom].
"Even though [the substance] is beyond the senses, because it is established through inference by itself...
(28). The word "even" (*api*), which has been displaced, is to be understood immediately after "perceptible" (*pratyakṣam*);

thus, even a substance such as a jar, which is perceptible, may also be seen as beyond the senses in its nature as invisible [in certain respects], and therefore it consists of qualities and modes (*guṇaparyāya*).

From where is this [known]? To this he says: because a substance that is established and ascertained by its own nature (*svarūpa*) is the object of inference (*anumeya*); otherwise, every logical reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), and this is not accepted by the opponent.
If it is asked, "If it is already established, how can it be an object of inference?", he replies: "In the form of the capacity for producing a result (*phala-upajanana-śakti*) and so forth."
For its power (*śakti*) is not perceived directly like the individual entity itself; otherwise, the inference of that [power] would result in futility, and because there is no such linguistic usage.

If, however, the Naiyāyika—like the Sautrāntika—possesses a non-conceptual perception (*avikalpa-darśana*), then this fault does not apply. That too is no answer, for it would mean surrendering the very position of the Sautrāntika, and it has already been stated that when something is ascertained, there can be no state of error (*vibhrama*).

Therefore, power (*śakti*) is not perceptible, nor is the manifest entity (*vyakti*) non-perceptible like power; for otherwise, everything would fall into blindness, which contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Even so, if there were no difference between the manifest entity and its power, then it could not be said that "it consists of qualities and modes" (*guṇaparyāyātmaka*); [otherwise] there would be no absolute distinction between what is perceptible and what is otherwise.

If it is argued that [the power] is distinct [from the substance], how can there be the designation "the power of the substance"? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is said that [the designation occurs] because of inherence (*samavāya*), we say no; for that has been refuted. If the power of inherence—which is the cause of the cognition "it is here"—is distinct from the substance, how could it be designated as "its" (the substance's), given that there is no other inherence? This has already been examined; therefore, this [objection] is trivial. As for the substance:
The inference of the power of a substance [is possible] because it consists of the power of its manifestation.

The sense is that if there were no distinction [between the universal and the individual], the individual would be perceptible while the power [of the universal] would be imperceptible; thus, the dual nature [of the object] would not exist.
Furthermore, due to the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), even a jar would become a cloth.

Because of inherence, he states another refutation regarding that: "The absolute [distinction] from the universal [is untenable], because the universal and so forth are inseparable from the object due to inherence; for [otherwise] it would be non-existent."
In each case, whether there be two or many [individuals], the operation [of the universal] occurs through its own parts; it does not occur by means of its entire self.

Is the universal and so forth entirely distinct and separate? Why? Because of "inherence in the object" and so on—that is, because of inherence in the substance (the object) and so forth; the inclusion of "and so forth" refers to ultimate particularity (antyaviśeṣa).
The mention of inherence and the rest is for the purpose of providing an illustrative example.

"Just as its [the universal's] generality and so forth are non-existent because they are perceived as distinct from it and are thus invisible, so too is this [the inherence]. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is not cognized in a certain form throughout the three times is not existent in that form; for example, the self (*ātman*) and so forth, which are not cognized in the form of a person (*pudgala*) throughout the three times, are cognized as being non-existent in that form. And since the universal and so forth are invariably perceived as distinct from the object, the inherence (*samavāya*), and so on—here he states another refutation, beginning with the words 'pratyekam' (each individually)."
The universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth—each one individually—subsist among their respective inherent substrates (*samavāyin*).

Among what kind of substrates? "In two or many": this mention of "two" refers to the fact that a causal substance (*kāryadravya*) and so forth subsists in two [substances], such as two atoms (*paramāṇu*). The supplement is that it does not subsist "by its own parts," meaning by its own portions (*svaikadeśaiḥ*), nor "with its entire self," meaning by its whole nature (*sarvasvabhāvena*). This has been discussed previously.
The six [categories],
beginning with inherence,
as well as substance and the others.
Thus ends the second chapter, "The Establishment of Conceptual Cognition," in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by Anantavīrya, who subsisted at the feet of the venerable Vibhadra.
Chapter Three.
3. Establishment of Other Means of Valid Cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having thus established conceptual perception as a valid cognition through two introductory sections, [the author], now desiring to establish the validity of recollection, recognition, inference, and so forth—which are non-discrepant—recalling the meaning of the two preceding sections as being based on non-discrepancy with respect to their own nature, says at the beginning of the section: "Correctly," and so forth in the verse:
"The correct cognition of the universal does not indeed deviate from its real nature due to another."

The mind, being incapable of determining its own nature— which is devoid [of objects] and consists of the single form of the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished— is itself devoid of the forms of conceivable objects; yet, if it were to enter into that which is a single variegated entity appearing as a manifold, it would, by those very internal transformations, lead one to perceive a single substance externally as having a variegated appearance.

The meaning is as follows: according to the Buddhists, it has been stated that the consciousness of recollection and so forth is "universal consciousness" (*sāmānyasaṃvit*); regarding that, since it is precisely that [consciousness] which constitutes universal consciousness, he asks:
"What is it? and answers: "Correctly" (*samyak*), meaning it is some [consciousness] that is non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādinī*). This is what is required.

Regarding this, he states the following argument concerning the deviation [of cognition]: "Cognition (*jñāna*) does not deviate from, nor does it ever abandon, the mind (*citta*); for by its very nature, it is the existing essential form (*svarūpa*) of both the object and the self. If, in some instance of a worldly or scriptural delusion (*vibhrama*), there were a single cognition consisting of both the delusory and its opposite forms—meaning, if such were the case—then that very [cognition] would be incapable (*anala*) of determining (*nirṇetuṃ*) or ascertaining (*niścetuṃ*) itself; this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which the other [the object] is also included.
How is it [incapable]? It is because it has become devoid of, or excluded from, [its own definitive nature]."

Why? Because of the statement that it is "devoid of another," meaning different from both its own kind (*sajātīya*) and other kinds (*vijātīya*); otherwise, it would be understood as incapable of determining [its object]. The meaning is that if it were like something else whose nature is not to produce a determination regarding its own object. And if that very thing is considered to have a single form consisting of both the established (*siddha*) and the to-be-established (*sādhya*)—that is, if one considers it to have a single form where the established is the certain [nature] and the to-be-established is the result to be inferred, such as the attainment of heaven and so forth—then this is stated with reference to conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
Regarding the meaning of the *kārikā* in the Buddhist (Saugata) system, Dharmottara further maintains:

"The gross, singular form of the apprehended object is false, because it cannot withstand analysis; therefore, that which is distinct from it—partless pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) alone—is ultimately real."

Thus [it is said]. To this he replies with the words "saṃbhāvya" and so forth: "If one thinks that the mind is a single entity, whose absence of objective form is conceivable and whose distinctions such as light and so on are observable"—this is what Prajñākaragupta maintains. [He argues: "There is no cognition distinct from blue and so forth, or pleasure and so forth, or the body, because it is not perceived" (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*); "that very same cognition is manifold and yet one, even though it has a variegated appearance" (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra* 3).
In response to such statements as these, he says: "Variegated," and so forth.

That whose manifestation (*bhā*) is variegated (*citrā*)—meaning diverse—due to the forms of the perceived objects (*grāhya*), such as blue and so on, which are visible, is described as such. If that [manifestation] were one, it would not be devoid of [diversity], but rather possessed of it.

By what means? By "modes" (*paryāyaiḥ*), that is, by successive transformations (*kramapariṇāmaiḥ*). The Buddhists (*saugatāḥ*) would understand—that is, they would realize—that [the entity] is one and undivided according to the logic already stated.
By the phrase "if," he shows this: that if this were not understood, there would be a total void (*sakalaśūnyatā*); therefore, it must be understood.

Consequently, the following objection raised by the opponent is refuted: "The recollection of what was experienced is not known through that experience itself, because the experience is not made an object of that recollection; for by this [recollection], the experience is not determined."

Regarding such [objections] as "this is that," there is no recognition other than memory and perception; in the absence of those, even inference (*tarka*) does not exist. How then can it be said that [recognition] is sublated by cognition? If one asks, "What causes it to be so? he says: "Externally" and so forth—let it follow or make known [the object] externally and independently elsewhere.
What [is it]? He says: "In substance," and so forth.
For just as that single [cognition] bears within itself a manifold nature, in that very same way it projects such a [nature] externally.

And thus, what was stated by the opponent—that because the object of memory perishes due to its momentariness, there is an absence of anything within the scope of recognition, and therefore no attainment upon purposeful activity, and consequently no non-contradiction—this is refuted by this [argument].
Then it is established: if the mind were of such a nature, then there would be a perfectly pure universal consciousness;
for no other form of cognition is perceived apart from [objects] such as blue or [feelings] such as pleasure—*Pravārtikālaṅkāra* 3.313.
Even though it possesses variegated appearances, cognition is indeed one, because it is distinct from external variegation;
for variegation is divisible and manifold, whereas the blue and other [colors] within cognition are indivisible— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*.
The meaning is that it is impossible for recollection to determine the fact of having been experienced through experience itself.

Comparison: [Objection] But by what means is this—that [the cognition] arises regarding what has been experienced—cognized? It cannot be by the experience itself, because at that time memory does not yet exist;
nor can that which is non-existent be made an object [of cognition];
nor is there a comprehension that "it arises therein" without being made an object.
Furthermore, at the time of experience, there is no "having been experienced" (*anubhūtatā*) of the object, because at that time it is currently being experienced (*anubhūyamānatvāt*).
Thus, if memory were of what is currently being experienced, it would follow that memory occurs regarding something presently perceived;

however, memory is understood to occur regarding what has been experienced. [Objection: No, for if this [memory] does not take as its object both the past experience and the object, such a cognition would be impossible.
"—this is that very [object]"—these two cognitions [are distinct]. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 336; Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p.
22). That which is past is not the object of apprehension; and when it is the object of apprehension, it is not [past] in that way.
That which has passed away does not exist as a real entity in the form in which it is being remembered;
furthermore, because its determination is firm, the validity [of memory] is established.
Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is likewise [valid], whereas the connection with the senses (*akṣayoga*) is purposeless.
—*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 593;
*Prakaraṇavārtikasvavṛttiṭīkā*, p. 78:
in the absence of recognition.
For the Buddhist,

cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of the existence of non-contradiction; however, this non-contradiction pertains to the present, not to that which has already perished.
If that unity did not exist, then why would there be no causal efficiency? ...

[from *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 593]. Thus, when the non-contradiction of memory and so forth has been established, the author says "it is a means of valid cognition," etc., showing what else is thereby established.
"Valid cognition [is so called] because of its non-contradiction; it is false because of the opposite of that."—[This is] the comparison.
"Valid cognition [arises] from the connection with the object; memory is associated with direct perception"—*Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, verse 10.
If it is argued that [memory] is not a means of valid cognition because it grasps what has already been grasped, we say no, because its purpose is different.
Even for perception, validity arises from non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*), and not from the mere imitation of the form of the object, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, if memory were to possess validity, it would define it as being based on what was previously experienced.

If it is argued that [conceptual cognition] is untenable because it lacks the determination of an unapprehended object in the case of conceptual [cognition], we say no; for there is a specific purpose. In some cases, when there is a desire for a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished through successive particular states (*paryāya*) characterized by differences in similar forms, there is no contradiction in its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely in that way.

Otherwise, even the apprehension of an object not previously apprehended through differences in time and so forth would not be accepted as a valid means of knowledge. Therefore, memory is a valid means of knowledge.
Why? Because it is non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādāt*).
The connection is: "Recollection (*smṛti*) is false and not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Why? Because it is the opposite of that [non-contradiction].
"Because of non-conformity, like perception and its semblance"—this illustration must be stated here.

[Objection: But surely non-conformity alone is not the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that this would be the case; rather, it is also "the illumination of an object not already known."

Because that [object] is absent in memory, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus he says: "Because it grasps what has already been grasped"—that is, because memory grasps what has already been made an object by perception (*darśana*), for that reason, if memory were not a means of valid cognition, he states the answer here:
"No," and so forth.
As for what was stated by the opponent, why is that not so? Because of the difference in purpose (*prayojana*);

for the purpose of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is its fruit—namely, the cessation of ignorance and [subsequent] activity—and because of the distinction between them, there is a difference between the purpose of perception and the purpose of memory.

Therefore, just as direct perception (adhyakṣa) first removes one's own prior ignorance regarding its object and then causes a person to engage with that object, so too does memory— since there is no difference [in this regard]—
either reveal an unknown object (*ajñātārthaprakāśa*)— *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.7.
Because it lacks the illumination of an unknown object, conventional [cognition] is not accepted [as valid], since it apprehends what has already been apprehended— *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.5.

Now, as for what was said—that "recollection is a valid means of knowledge because it is non-contradictory, like perception"—that is not sound. If it is argued that the establishment of validity in the case of the example [perception] arises from its conformity with the object, whereas such conformity is absent in recollection, to this he replies: "Of perception also," and so forth.

It is not only for other [means of knowledge] but for perception as well that validity arises from non-contradiction, and not from the imitation of the form of the object. Why is this? He says: "Because of the over-extension [of the consequence]."
If it is argued that "let it be so, because that [cognition] is non-contradictory," the author replies with the words "But that... and so forth.

That non-contradiction would indeed constitute validity if it were due to the recollection of an experienced object; thus, by the words "conceptual" (*savikalpa*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's view in order to refute it.
In the view that conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is a form of perception, memory lacks the determination of an unapprehended object, and thus its validity is untenable.

By this, [the author] shows the following: the opponent [argues], "Just as my inference regarding the impermanence and other qualities of an experienced object is valid because it determines an uncertain object or excludes a superimposition (*samāropa*), memory is not so, because it is the reverse [of such an apprehension] and is therefore impossible in regard to what has already been determined. If this is the case, [the author] says here: "No," etc.; that which was stated by the opponent is not [correct].
Why? Because of a specific purpose, and that has already been stated.
Here, demonstrating his own unity of discourse with the opponent, he says: "In some cases," and so forth.

In some cases, such as with a beautiful face and so forth, regarding those distinctions—which are specific variations within a continuous stream—of perceptual objects that possess similar forms, there is no contradiction in their validity when there is a desire for purposeful action to be accomplished through successive specific stages; thus, it is logical that memory possesses validity by virtue of its specific purpose.

Why is this so? To this he says: "By the distinction of time, etc."—the word "etc. includes the field (*kṣetra*) and so forth. Otherwise—that is, by another way in which there is no specific purpose—not only from other [causes], but even from the apprehension of an object not previously apprehended (*anadhigatārthādhigati*), i.e., from the grasping of an object not yet grasped, there would be no acceptance by the Buddhist (*saugata*) of the status of those specific [cognitions] as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is just as, when there is a desire for the single causal efficiency of obtaining water, the specific intermediate perceptions [of the mirage] are not accepted as such. Otherwise, the perception of a mirage, being the cause of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of water, would likewise be a valid means of knowledge; however, this is not the case because the cognition lacks conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*).
The Buddhist [view] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because there is an absence of anything that determines an object not yet determined.
The sense is: since there is no application of superimposition (*samāropa*), how can there be its exclusion?

If, however, this insistence is maintained—that memory is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it grasps what has already been grasped—then for that very reason, inference (*anumāna*) in its entirety would likewise not be a valid means of knowledge. Demonstrating this, he says: "The pervasion (*vyāpti*) from the beginning in its totality," and so forth, just like memory.
If the pervasion between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) were previously established in its entirety from the outset,

then the recollection of the object to be inferred would already be established and would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as it would be like [the memory of] a particular [already known].
For as long as the pervasion— that whatever place possesses smoke, all such places possess fire— is not established, the comprehension of the object to be inferred is impossible.

If inference were established in this manner, it would not be distinguished from other forms of memory; consequently, the distinction between what is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and what is not, regarding the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), would become confused.
Furthermore, if there were a difference from what has been personally experienced, it would be impossible to establish a universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) without exception.

If it is argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, because the inference is qualified by that [universal]; [we reply: even in the case of the recollection of what was previously experienced, such a specific [particular] is not excluded, so this is trivial.

If pervasion—that is, inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)—is established and certain in its entirety, in its totality, from the very beginning, prior to the initial operation of all inference, then of what two things? Of the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*).
"Inference would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in its entirety because it is a recollection of the object to be inferred"—this [objection] should also be connected here.
To this, he states an example: "like a particular" (*viśeṣavat*), meaning "like a recollection that is not an inference."

With the words "yāvān" and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse: whatever region possesses smoke—this being an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication) that includes time as well—that entire region and so forth, and not merely some one [region], must possess fire; since such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished, the cognition of the object of inference—which is otherwise unestablished—is untenable. Therefore, it would not be distinguished from, nor differ from, a mere recollection arising from something other than a mark (*aliṅga*).

This is what is meant: just as there can be no further recollection (*smṛti*) of something never previously experienced because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), so too it is not logical for there to be a cognition of an object of inference—which is not determined as the pervader—from a mark (*liṅga*) which is not determined as the pervaded. Otherwise, one who has grown up in an underground cellar might suddenly perceive fire upon seeing smoke; for you, there would be the possibility of such a cognition from that [mark] even though it has not been grasped as a pervader. Since inference is a specific kind of recollection, it is for this reason that it was said: "from another recollection" (*smṛtyantarāt*). Therefore, he thinks that [the object] should not be qualified by its non-existence.

If it is asked: "Even if that [universal concomitance] is unestablished—namely, that whatever entity exists, all of it is necessarily momentary—what fault is there if it were established? To this he says: "In its establishment" (*siddhau*).

This connects with "of such pervasion" (*vyāpteḥ*) by changing the case-ending; thus, the meaning is: "in the certainty of its establishment. [Otherwise,] inference would not be distinguished from other forms of memory.
Why is this so? He says: "The object of inference," and so forth.

That which is to be proven (*sādhya*), which is possible, intended, and not yet established, is the "object of inference" (*anumeya*). Since its comprehension is untenable—because it is impossible for it to be ascertained by the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) [prior to the inference]—it follows that inference is the cognition regarding the object of inference arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics. (Nyāyabindu 2)
This is merely a statement; it is considered a fallacy of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) because its subject matter consists of what is already established and what is yet to be proven.

The mention of "inference" (*anumāna*) is also an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); by this, even the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a location and so forth would not be distinguished from it, because the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) also grasps the location and other such factors. Otherwise, the cognition that "all of this [location] possesses fire" would be impossible, just as there is no cognition of the pervader when the pervaded is not cognized, so too there is no cognition of the contained (*ādheya*) when the container (*ādhāra*) is not cognized. It is for this purpose that the term "location" (*pradeśa*) is used; otherwise, one might simply say "whatever smoke there is."
Furthermore, there is nothing other than the momentariness of an entity that is not apprehended by one cognition but is apprehended by a subsequent perception;
therefore, the pervasion [of momentariness] is not established by that [perception], nor is inference accepted [as a means of proof]. Thus says Prajñākaragupta (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3).

If it is argued that this was stated "in terms of conventional usage" (*vyavahāreṇa*), then by that very same logic, just as inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped through a cognition [of it], so too would memory be a valid means of knowledge regarding what has been directly perceived. Thus, the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* that there are only two means of knowledge is false.
Furthermore, if pervasion is established without a means of knowledge within conventional usage, why seek one elsewhere? That same fault remains, and thus that statement is false.
Moreover, since the doctrine of the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) has been refuted, he must remain right here.
For a person who has not grasped the pervasion (vyāpti) by way of what is to be proven (sādhya).
In the context of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the probandum (*sādhya*) is that which is possible, intended, and not yet established— *Nyāyabindu* 2.3.
The locus of the recollection of that which is to be proven.
In the formal argument that "whatever entity exists, all of it is momentary," validity must be accepted through conventional usage alone.

Prajñākaragupta maintains that by accepting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one should simply state that there are only two means of valid cognition; however, because of the admission of non-duality (*advaita*), even the means of valid cognition itself must be abolished. To this, he replies:
What happens if there is no distinction between that [inferential cognition] and that [perceptual cognition]? To this he says: "From that," and so forth.

From that—that is, from the lack of distinction between them—the demarcation between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its opposite would be confounded. Of what two? He says: "Of the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*). In the case of the cognition of the mark—which is the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—there would be the demarcation of valid cognition; in the case of the cognition of the possessor of the mark—which is inferential cognition—there would be the demarcation of its opposite.

If the opponent maintains that there is a reversal—that is, if he maintains that the operation of the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) occurs elsewhere than in the object of that cognition of the mark—then this fault does not arise. To this, [the author] replies with the words beginning "by itself" (*svayam*): if a distinction (*vyatireka*) is admitted between the object of the cognition of the mark and the object of the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), then, because a pervasion (*vyāpti*) established in its entirety—that is, in its totality—is impossible, the pervasion would become confused (*vyatikīryeta*). This is the connection [of the sentence].
It is considered that inference [is unnecessary] because it would be futile regarding what has already been experienced, and because it does not operate toward anything else,
based on another recollection.
The sense is that [the cognition] would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge because it apprehends what has already been apprehended;
such is the established distinction between inference and that which is other than a valid means of knowledge.

He raises an objection in order to refute the view of Arcaṭa—that [the pervasion] pertains to the universal (sāmānya) as the object of the cognition of pervasion—by stating: "If it is argued that the establishment of the pervasion of smoke in such a state by means of fire devoid of specifications such as place is called a 'pervasion whose object is the universal,' because through the force of the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā), there is an inference of that [fire] as qualified by those specific distinctions such as place and so forth by means of its particularity (viśeṣa); to this he provides the answer: "That which was previously experienced," and so forth.

The memory of what was previously experienced is not [invalidated] merely by inference; for there is no refutation of such a specific feature postulated in that inference. The meaning is that this is trivial—it is nothing at all.
To explain: we see no contradiction in the recollection of something previously experienced either devoid of qualifiers such as place and so forth, or accompanied by them.

If it is asked: "How can there be such a recollection of that which was not experienced in such a way, since that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? [The reply is: "How then can there be an inference of that which is of such a kind and was not made an object of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāptijñāna*), since that too would lead to an over-extension? Thus, the power of the subsidence of karmic obstructions (*kṣayopaśama*)—which consists in the grasping of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) within the same cognitive continuum—is what accounts for this; no distinction is observed here. For it is seen that even when a certain section of a commentary is grasped by an expounder devoid of some particular feature, there is nevertheless a recollection of it as qualified by that very feature due to the specific nature of the rememberer;
it is for this reason that it was stated: "because that [particularity] is not excluded."

Comparison— when a general positive concomitance has been established, its restriction to a specific [subject] occurs through the connection with the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva), by way of grasping the relation— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.106.
40. In the case of inference, [it occurs] in memory.
Because the specific distinction has not been refuted,
by this [the following] which was stated by the Mīmāṃsaka is addressed: "In that case, the cognition of a previously unknown object is certain and free from sublation."
