"A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is produced by non-defective causes and is accepted by the world";
this verse from the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, page 21, is found in the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, page 318, as being stated by the Mīmāṃsakas.
That [position] is refuted in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p.
61) and the *Hetubindu-ṭīkā* (p. 280);

for even in the case of recollecting what was previously experienced, this [recollection] exists just like inference, which would result in the undesirable consequence of a seventh means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, having become a Naiyāyika regarding the nature of validity (*prāmāṇya*), the Master (*sūri*) says "tadevam" and so forth, in order to show that Arcata— who asserts that pervasion (*vyāpti*) has a universal as its object while inference (*anumiti*) concerns a particular— thereby implies another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

Thus, for one who perceives [the object] through the refinement of the sentence of comparison, there arises a cognition of the qualifier regarding the relationship between the name and the named, just as in the case of inference.

For one who has understood the relationship between the name and the named from the sentence "A gavaya is similar to a cow," the subsequent apprehension of the qualifier—"this is its name"—does not exceed the scope of inference; since inference is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no other.
If...
the particle *tat* should be understood in the sense of *tasmin* (in that);

when that [object] is remote (*parokṣa*) and the principle has been stated in the manner described, the sentence "the *gavaya* is like a cow" is a sentence of comparison (*upamānavākya*). From the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that—because of the statement: "a latent impression is born from knowledge and is the cause of knowledge"—[the cognition arises].
If it is asked, "How can it be said that 'it [the cognition] arises from that [sentence]'?"—there is no fault, because it arises from that through a traditional succession (*pāramparyeṇa*).

To explain: from that sentence there is comprehension, which is a cognition having that as its object; then, by means of the mind acting in conjunction with that [cognition], there is produced a mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) whose object is the general relationship between the signifier and the signified, namely: "whatever object is similar to a cow, all that is denotable by the word *gavaya*. From that, an impression (*saṃskāra*) arises; [the ellipsis to be supplied is: "recollection (*smṛti*), that is, memory, is produced.
Where? To this he says: "That," and so forth.
And those two—the name and the named, and the word "gavaya" and the specific object that is a gavaya—[are related] in their relationship characterized as signifier and signified;
of whom? Of one who sees what? A gavaya.
What is that [distinction]? He says: "It would be distinguished"—that is, it would differ from other recollections. To the question "In what way?", he says: "Like inference; like that, so this.

The intended meaning here is as follows: Just as an inference arising through a particular instance regarding a pervasion whose object is a universal (*sāmānya*) apprehends a previously unknown object, so too, when the relationship between a name and the named has been understood through mental perception by means of a universal, the subsequent apprehension of that same relationship through a particular instance—such as seeing a *gavaya* in the forest due to the recollection of all that [previously perceived]—is indeed an apprehension of a previously unknown object.

Formative impression (*saṃskāra*) is that which is born of knowledge and is the cause of knowledge— the realization of the relationship between a name and the named object— [as stated in] *Prakaraṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.527.

Furthermore, as for what was stated here—that because the universal resides in the particular, the cognition of the particular follows from the cognition of that [universal]—that is without substance, since the same applies elsewhere.
Explaining the verse, he says: "The gavaya is similar to a cow," and so forth.

From the sentence "The gavaya is like a cow," one who has understood that [similarity] through that cognition—which acts as a cooperative cause—and who has grasped the relationship between the name and the named, subsequently perceives at another time the sight of a gavaya. For one who has seen the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there arises a specific realization regarding this perceived object: "This is the name 'gavaya'. This [realization] in its particularity does not exceed inference; for if it were to exceed it, then inference would not be the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, comparison would not be a valid means of knowledge.

The word *yataḥ* may be used in the sense of an objection: "How could there be nothing else? Indeed, there would be; for the Buddhist, based on the cognition of the sentence, might accept comparison (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or, [the author] anticipates the opponent's view in order to demonstrate another means of valid cognition for the other [school], beginning with the words "If... and so forth.
He states the refutation here, which is easy to understand: "Another means of valid cognition" and so forth;
"another means of valid cognition" refers elsewhere to memory, because that designation cannot possibly apply [to perception]. 1/2

For one who has acquired a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from that statement, the fact that the name is not connected to non-cows is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); just as the apprehension of the relationship between a mark and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgaliṅgisambandha*) in general is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), so too this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is a distinct means of knowledge. [Otherwise,] what kind of means of knowledge would the recognition be for those who have previously acquired impressions from statements such as "the *khaṅga* has one horn" or "the *saptaparṇa* has seven leaves" when they subsequently perceive them directly? For they do not think, "This is a *khaṅga*," or "This is a *saptaparṇa*," because [the specific animal] was perceived in that manner [previously]. Alternatively, [if recognition were not a distinct means of knowledge], what means of knowledge would there be for the recognition of those who have acquired impressions from such statements, upon seeing those things again?

A means of knowledge other than comparison would be a separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). Apart from the *gavaya*, in the case of others such as the buffalo and so forth, there is the designation "gavaya"; that is its name. [The author] explains the fragment of the verse beginning with "the recollection of the impossibility of that name" by means of the passage beginning with "in that sentence": for one who possesses understanding—that is, one in whom an impression (*saṃskāra*) has been deposited by that sentence, namely the statement "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow," according to the aforementioned method.
What is that? It is the absence of a connection with that name—that is, the absence of a connection with the designation "gavaya.
Where? To this he says: "among non-cows, i.e., among dissimilar things," by himself, that is, by his own [intellect].

If it is asked: "Granted that the mind, aided by the comprehension of the sentence 'the gavaya is like a cow,' may achieve the cognition of the relationship between the name and the named in general with respect to things similar to a cow; but by what means is the cognition of the non-connection with that name achieved with respect to things dissimilar to it? To this, he replies: "By presumptive implication (arthāpatti)."

Since a *gavaya* is similar to a cow, by implication (*arthāt*), that which is dissimilar to it is not a *gavaya*; this comprehension of the sentence is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). He demonstrates that [it] is established by that very [presumption]: "Just as the comprehension of the relationship between the sign and the signified, or between the name and the named, through a general rule is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) from inference and the rest, so too is this [presumption]. What follows from this? He says: it is a distinct means of knowledge, a means of knowledge other than comparison (*upamāna*).
What is it? He says: recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Of what nature is it? He says: "This is not a gavaya"—meaning that this visible object, which resembles a cow, is not a gavaya, i.e., it is not denotable by the word 'gavaya'.
By the use of the word "this," he shows its distinction from inference, as it is an arthāpatti (presumption) based on a general sense.
From what does that arise? He says: "from such a perception," meaning from the perception of similarity to a cow. By the term *pratyabhijñāna* (recognition), he conveys this:

if another were to claim that this [recognition] is included within *vaidharmyopamāna* (analogy based on dissimilarity), then the Jaina would also say that this [recognition] is included within *asādṛśyetara-pratyabhijñāna* (recognition other than non-similarity). Therefore, these two are not distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) from one another, just as they are not distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, because the same state [of being a cognition] exists in both.
The Naiyāyika [establishes] that which is called inference by means of valid cognition.

Now, another meaning of this section of the *Kārikā* is explained: "In another case" means in a different subject matter; "the recollection of the possibility of its name" refers to the name (*saṃjñā*) of that other thing, and the recollection of its possibility is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For if this were not explained, the subsequent meaning would not constitute the meaning of the *Kārikā*. Elucidating this very point, he says: "And in the object," and so forth.

Alternatively, this indicates another explanation: when persons who have previously formed mental impressions through such statements as "the rhinoceros has a single horn" or "the saptaparṇa tree has uneven leaves," subsequently perceive those very rhinoceroses and so forth, they possess a recognition—namely, the re-cognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "this is the object denoted by the word 'rhinoceros' and so on. What kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would this be? Since it is not included within either similarity-based analogy (*sādharmyopamāna*) or dissimilarity-based analogy (*vaidharmyopamāna*), it is considered that because its characteristics differ from those, it must be given a distinct name.
Right here, he provides another example with the words "tathā" and so forth:

furthermore, for one who perceives [the object] in that way after hearing the characteristics of a woman and so on, there is the apprehension of number and other qualities through the observation of what precedes and follows. || 5 ||
When stairs and the like are perceived either together or separately, the recollection of their sequence and so forth depends precisely upon that [perception].

"Woman" and so on form a *dvandva* compound; then, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is a *bahuvrīhi*; and for that too, by the word "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), there is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound; and for that, by the act of hearing. Therefore, the connection is as follows: what indeed is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the recognition of one who perceives in that manner of hearing—namely, one who desires to see a woman and so forth? Showing yet another distinct means of valid cognition for this, he says: "Number and so forth," etc.

The grammatical connection is as follows: those things characterized by number, unity, and so forth—which are the first among [the group] beginning with the relation of cause and effect, and including terms such as "distant" and "near"—are referred to as such; and the apprehension of them is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

This knowledge, such as "this is that woman denoted by the word," is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) because it arises from the contact of the self with its object, just like the apprehension of pleasure and so forth. Some maintain that this [apprehension] is indeed [mental perception].
To this, he says: "The former," and so forth.
From the observation of the former and the latter, there is the comprehension [of the middle].

Here, the intended meaning is as follows: just as knowledge arising from the contact of the self, the mind, the eye, and other [senses] with their objects is called visual perception (*cakṣurpratyakṣa*) and nothing else, so too let that which arises from the contact of the self, the mind, and the object be called mental perception (*mānasa*); it is not the subject under discussion [here].

If, on the other hand, that [knowledge] too, being a form of cognition, were produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object—just like the cognition of color and so forth produced by the eye and other organs—then there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to inference and the like.

If it is argued that there is no fault because even this [inference] is made a subject (pakṣa) and thus possesses the nature of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) since it depends upon its causes, such as the logical mark (*liṅga*), then [we reply]: that is not the same, because in other cases [such as visual perception], there is no dependence on the prior observation of a preceding and succeeding moment. Thus, the two cases are not equal.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) indeed consists of a third perception, preceded by memory, which occurs upon the cessation of the initial perception and the sight of a second [object], when the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) previously deposited has been manifested—*Nyāyavārttika*, p.
400. Thus, recognition is a mental cognition in which the qualification of the pillar or other object is specified by a prior cognition, having as its object a past moment.
—the *Nyāyamañjarī*, *Prameya* section, p. 33:
that which is being produced, called recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
The cognition of number and so forth must also belong to that [perception],
because it is a cognition, for the very same reason as mental cognition.
Explaining this, he says: "On the staircase," etc.

Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the cause and so forth is intended. When those staircases are perceived either together or separately, or when the cause and so forth are perceived separately, the cognition of number and so on that arises would, according to the aforementioned reasoning, exceed the scope of perception and other [means of knowledge]; therefore, it would become a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To the question, "Of what nature is it? he says: "Preceding," etc. (*paurvā* etc.).

The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is this: the cognition that "this is one" and "that is the second," and so forth, occurs only in dependence upon the recollection of that [prior object]—whose beginning is the state of being prior and posterior, such as grossness and subtlety—and not otherwise.

For instance, when there is a subsequent perception for one who possesses the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by a prior perception, and when there is a recollection of that prior [perception], from that [recollection] arises the understanding: "This is one; therefore, that is the second," and so on. This should be applied similarly to the relation of cause and effect and other such cases.
Showing yet another point, he says: "Name," and so forth.

Another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)— namely, that called recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which is the knowledge consisting in the association of names and so forth— is seen by those who perceive it to be like analogy (*upamāna*).

Every knowledge consisting in the association of words and so forth, which is invariably concomitant with the individual instances of prior and subsequent means of valid cognition, is another means of valid cognition.

"Name" (nāman) refers to the designation; those things such as genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), and so forth, which have that [name] as their beginning, are described as such. The "knowledge of their connection" (yojanājñāna)—of whom? To this he says: "of those who see," meaning those perceiving the denoted object, the designating term, and so forth. The word "and" (ca) is used in a different syntactical order and is to be understood after the word "knowledge" (jñāna). What is that [knowledge]? To this he says: "like analogy" (upamānavat).
The meaning is that, in the same way, there would be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
He explains this with the words beginning "pūrva" (the former):

the individual instances of prior and subsequent means of valid cognition belonging to the designator (*abhidhāna*), the designated (*abhidheya*), the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), and so forth; and whatever knowledge of the connection of words and so on is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with those—all of that, without exception, would be another means of valid cognition, just like comparison (*upamāna*).
But someone might ask: "Are these alone the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or are there others? To show that there are others, he says: "Presumption (*arthāpatti*)," and so forth.
This reflection—namely, the exclusion of other objects of knowledge—is presumption.

For one who sees or hears something restricted by place, time, and so on, there arises a pair of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) characterized by affirmation and negation, such as "this is exactly thus and not otherwise. Would this pair of conceptual constructions, which is somehow purely mnemonic (*smārta*), be mixed with [other cognitions] or not? It is purely mnemonic, being essentially a conviction of possibility and intent upon ascertainment.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is that which, when an object known through the six means of valid cognition is necessarily absent in the absence of another [fact], leads one to postulate an unseen object.
As it has been said:
"When an object known through the six means of valid cognition cannot be otherwise..."

"That which, being invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*), leads to the postulation of an unperceived object, is cited as presumption (*arthāpatti*). (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Arthāpatti, v. 1). By this [definition], the recollection of a cow in the city arising from the sight of a *gavaya* in the forest is what is intended, because any other [type of recollection] has been established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) without distinction.
The cognition that "whatever place possesses smoke, all of it possesses fire," and so forth, is *cintā* (reflection).

Now, as if asked what the nature of this [cognition] is—which has never before been seen or heard—he says "the object of measurement" (*meyo*) and so forth to demonstrate its nature: the "object of measurement" (*meya*) is the inferable [object], such as fire; the "counter-example" (*vipakṣa*) is that which is other than it, namely the non-fire and so forth; from that [counter-example], there is "exclusion" (*apohana*), which is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); the "reasoning" (*ūhana*) regarding that is the act of deliberation (*vitarkaṇa*).

Some maintain that "cintā" (reflection) means the exclusion (*apohana*) of the object of measurement—the probans such as smoke—from other things such as non-fire; however, this is incorrect, or rather, it should be considered otherwise. For there would be no purpose in explaining its components within the *sūtra* itself, it would lead to a lack of distinction from the *vṛtti*, and it would result in an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, it is explained otherwise: the "object of cognition" (*meyah*) is that which is delimited by means of valid cognition such as perception, consisting of existence and non-existence in its own and other forms, such as a jar and so forth. The "investigation" (*ūhanam*) of that [object] is the mental deliberation (*cintanam*) following direct observation by means of mental conceptualization (*mānasavikalpa*), in the form of "this is long" or "otherwise," and so on. Within that very [deliberation], the "exclusion" (*apohanam*) of another thing, such as a cloth, is its differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*), [thinking] "that [other thing] does not exist here"; this investigation is "reasoning" (*vitarkaṇam*).

The meaning is this: just as the means of knowledge called "non-existence" (abhāva) is accepted because one observes the inference that "this is not here," so too another means of knowledge called "existence" (bhāva) should be accepted because one observes the inference that "this is thus. Since the aspect of non-existence, like the aspect of existence, is apprehended through perception and other means, that [separate category] called non-existence should not be admitted; all of this is "like comparison" (upamāna)—such is the connection.
The commentators' intention is that there would otherwise be no distinction between the Sūtra and the commentary (ṭīkā).
Because it is possible to apprehend [the object] in the form of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
the two middle terms will be explained respectively by the following two verses.
Having established that the first and last words [of the verse] carry a further meaning, he says the following in order to explain them: "Of one who sees," and so forth;
what [happens] for one who sees—that is, perceives directly—by means of the eyes and other [senses]?
Thus he says "place," and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of substance and intrinsic nature is intended.

By these [factors], the following intention is fixed here: just as the existence of an entity is perceived through direct perception by means of its own place and so forth, so too is its non-existence perceived by means of another's place and so forth.
Therefore, this [objection] is refuted:
"First of all, the cognition that 'this is not' is not produced by the sense organ;
for the sense organ has a connection only with the positive aspect [of an object], due to its functional capacity" (Pramāṇavārttika, Abhāva-pariccheda, verse 18).

For just as that [cognition] is capable of apprehending the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) therein because it is perceived from that [object], so too is it capable of apprehending the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*); let it be capable of that here as well, since there is no distinction regarding the perception of the positive aspect through direct perception and the like.

As for this [argument] beginning with "perception and so forth"— namely, that "non-existence is known by a means of valid cognition of its own kind, because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), like existence"— that too is refuted by this [preceding argument], because the thesis is contradicted by perception.

Thus, by means of hearing the word or understanding its meaning, he demonstrates the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the previous reason through the restriction of place, time, and so forth. For from the sentence, "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (*Kṛṣṇayajurveda-Kāṭhaka* 6.7), there is the cognition not only of the existence of what is intended [by the speaker] due to its own nature, but also of the non-existence of what is not intended. Otherwise, what would be the purpose of uttering it? To this he says: "Furthermore," and so forth.
Furthermore, after seeing and hearing, two types of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arise; this is the supplementary explanation.

Of what nature are they? He says: "characterized by affirmation and negation" (*vidhipratiṣedhalakṣaṇam*). That which has, or in which there is, the characterization—that is, the ascertainment—of affirmation and negation, i.e., existence and non-existence, is described as such. In what manner? He says: "in this way," and so forth.
And this which is being perceived is thus, in this very manner of its own location and so forth, and not otherwise— that is, not in the manner of another location and so forth;
the particle *eva* (only/just) is connected here as well,
and the word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction.
The word *iti* is used here in the sense of "in this manner.
Furthermore, being of what nature [is it]? It is said to be primarily for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
If one asks, "What is that? he says: "In some way" (*kathañcana*), and so forth.

In some way or by some method of reasoning, does the word "smṛti" (tradition) follow after the preceding [word] "smārta" (that which is based on tradition), such that they become conflated as "it exists"? Or do they not? If they were conflated, then, like an option characterized by a positive injunction (*vidhi*), an option characterized by a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) would likewise not be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from tradition. On the other hand, if they are not conflated, then, like an option characterized by a prohibition, an option characterized by a positive injunction would also be a distinct means of valid cognition—this is what is being considered.

Therefore, O Kumārilā, just as non-existence (abhāva) is not an object of knowledge for one who maintains that there are only six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), so too let it be accepted that [non-existence] is not a means of valid cognition either;
for just as non-existence lacks the status of a means of valid cognition when the object of knowledge is of a positive nature (bhāvātman).
Likewise, even when the object of cognition is a non-existence, there is no means of valid cognition for a positive entity—
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Abhāva section, verses 45–46—
because the non-existence of a jar or the like is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Just as [the text] teaches sacrifices such as the Agnihotra, etc., [so too does it teach] loving-kindness, etc. (maitrā°). 6.36.
The sense is that from that [scripture], the cessation of undesirable matters imagined by Buddhists and others— such as "one should eat dog meat"— is also understood;
thus the phrase "it exists in this very way" is written twice because of the incidental mention of the seventh means of valid cognition called recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

As for Prabhākara, who maintains that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a separate means of valid cognition because it is a residual category of the five means of cognition beginning with perception—to him he replies with the words "Possibility" (*sambhava*), etc.

The meaning of this is as follows: it is designated by the terms "inference" (*anumāna*) and "presumption" (*arthāpatti*); the word "and" (*ca*) here should be understood as having the sense of a cumulative conjunction; and the connection is with the phrase "the two alternatives" (*vikalpadvayam*).

Of what nature is it? He says: "Possibility" (*sambhava*) is existence when the probandum exists, and necessarily non-existence when that is absent; it is the cognition or apprehension of that which is perceived or heard as restricted by place, time, and so forth—meaning, the grasping of its impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).
That very thing is its own inherent state (*bhāva*) as its cause; thus it is so described.

By this, he demonstrates that just as for inference the cause is the determination characterized by the restriction of the impossibility of the probandum's absence, so too it is for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "It is primarily characterized by restriction"—meaning that the soul (*jīva*) and so forth are subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) from [the qualities] such as *sattva* and the rest, and not otherwise;
this states that there is no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of those two.

What is that? He says: "Would it be merged or would it not be merged? How so? He says: "In any way whatsoever"—would it become one with [the object] through the mode of inference (*anumāna*) or through the mode of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or would it not? If it were to merge; then, just as Kumārila’s talk of six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely a hollow report, so too would the talk of five means of valid cognition for this [proponent] be rendered utterly useless.

Now, if it were not confused [with inference], then just as there is a distinction between inference produced by a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) and presumption (*arthāpatti*) which lacks an example based on similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*), so too would there be a distinction from that [inference] which is devoid of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*); thus, one considers that the same fault remains: a contradiction regarding the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃkhyāvyāghāta*).

If it is argued: "Inference is born of memory, because it exists when there is the recollection of an example, whereas presumption is not so because the opposite is the case; therefore, there is a distinction between the two," to this he replies: "It is merely mnemonic" (*smārttam eva*).
That which is born of memory is "mnemonic" (*smārtta*).

By the word "only" (eva), he says this: if the object that gives rise to inference is not capable of producing an inference without the recollection of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then let it be the same for the object that gives rise to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Or, if you argue that the object produces presumptive testimony solely through the force of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that excludes its existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), then we shall demonstrate that inference functions in exactly the same way.

Furthermore, if there is no recollection of an example because it is non-existent in presumptive testimony, yet it exists in inference, what is the use of recollecting something that is ineffective? Thus, the absence [of the example] is equal in both cases.

Now, if this insistence is that a logical mark (*liṅga*) cannot be known as inseparable from the probandum (*sādhya*) without an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then it is well said that the object which gives rise to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is likewise [dependent]. Thus, "it is merely a matter of memory" means that non-existence is simply the state of not being cognized, and nothing else; nor is the state of not being cognized itself an object of cognition (*prameya*). For the non-cognition of that object consists precisely in the self's possession of an experience unconnected with that object, and that state of the self is indeed self-evident (*svasaṃvidita*). Therefore, no further object of cognition remains.
—*Bṛhatī*, Paṭala 1, pp. 119–20.

Therefore, it is precisely the non-occurrence of the means of valid cognition that apprehends a positive entity (*bhāva*) which gives rise to the comprehension of non-existence (*abhāva*). Since there is no comprehension of a distinct intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) for non-existence, the absence of an object of cognition (*prameyābhāva*) is not something other than the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*).

Furthermore, the absence of a means of valid cognition is not distinguished from the non-apprehension of another intrinsic nature; and since the apprehension of another positive entity is itself of the nature of self-luminosity, it does not undergo the status of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*). Thus, the status of being an "object of cognition" for the means of valid cognition called "non-existence" is untenable.
And since there is no object of cognition [to be known], it is established that no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) can be conceived (pṛ.
124). Furthermore, the non-existence of the means of valid cognition is understood through their very non-arising;
for the apprehension of non-existence does not occur anywhere without that [non-arising].

Because the non-arising of a valid cognition [of its absence] is accepted as the cause [for determining non-existence], even the fault of over-extension finds no opportunity— *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 129.
*Nayaviniścaya*, p. 162;
*Tantrarahasya*, p. 17;
*Prabhākaraviniścaya*, p. 57.
In the case of inference and presumptive testimony,
the grasping of pervasion in a similar instance is not necessary for presumptive testimony;
rather, the state of inseparable concomitance is apprehended right at that moment.
Even though it is not previously apprehended, this [non-apprehension] is not the cause of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—
*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Arthāpatti* section, verse 30.
"Even if there were a difference [between the two],
the presumption (arthāpatti) devoid of that [difference] would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)" — *Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 519.
Because Kumārila and Prabhākara do not accept inference and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) [as independent means of valid cognition].
If it is argued that there is an absence of an example such that [the relationship] could not be known as being inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvitā*),

and that what was stated— that memory is like comparison (*upamāna*)— is not a fault because it is accepted [as such], then the author replies here with the words beginning "the memory of a cow," and so forth.

How could the memory of a cow be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for one who is seeing a *gavaya*? Why, for the sake of some purpose, would it not be so even in another case that is dissimilar to it? 7. For comparison: "Analogy (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing what is to be established through similarity with a well-known object."
Because it is dissimilar to that, how could the communication of a named object be a means of valid cognition?
*Laghīyastraya*
From the *Nyāyāvatāravārttika*, verse 14:

Just as there is the apprehension of similarity from a sentence of comparison (*upamāna*), so too there is the apprehension of dissimilarity between something and something else. Let the recollection of a prior [perception] following from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) without distinction, due to its utility. Since comparison (*upamāna*) is the establishment of what is to be proven through well-known commonality, and the apprehension of the relationship between a name and the named is the purpose of comparison—what is the use of this exhaustive enumeration? For everyone who observes what has not been previously done, comparison occurs.

"Surely, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-difference between analogy (*upamāna*) and inference (*anumāna*). Let it be so; let that very [inference] be the means of proof there [in the case of analogy] as well, either together with or apart from the similarity and dissimilarity of the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya-vaidharmyābhyām*), because no distinction is perceived. Thus speaks the dull-witted one, whose intellect is skilled in defining things in a contrary manner.
Therefore, it is inference alone [that is the means of knowledge], because validity is impossible without the apprehension of the relation of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) in every respect;
for this same consequence applies equally to perception as it does to inference.

Comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing what is to be proven through a well-known similarity, because the subsequent [cognition] does not occur for anyone in any way without the self-establishment [of the object], like the cognition of a comparison (*upamiti*). — *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.6.

Having heard that "when a *go* (cow) is to be obtained, the function of that [cow] should be performed by means of a *gavaya*," someone asks a forest-dweller: "What is a *gavaya* like? He replies to him: "A *gavaya* is like a cow.

Having thus asked and heard this, and subsequently either finding a cow in the city while wandering the forest again, or else finding a *gavaya* there and remembering the cow, the memory of that cow as qualified by its similarity to the *gavaya* would be the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the Mīmāṃsaka known as *upamāna* (analogy), for a person who is seeing the *gavaya*.
The word "ca" (and) should be understood here, or its meaning should be explained as "kā" (having done).
Here he states the refutation: "How," etc.;
in what manner? It is not that it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather it is indeed a means of valid cognition.

The connection is that "recollection occurs elsewhere, in some [animal] such as a buffalo. To the question "In what kind of [animal]? he says: "tad" and so forth. Because it is perceived as having a form dissimilar to that gavaya, it is "tadvilakṣya" (dissimilar to that); [recollection occurs] in that [animal] as well, and not only in a cow that is similar to it.

This is what is meant: just as memory—which is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—occurs with respect to a cow qualified by similarity, or with respect to similarity qualified by that [cow] (where the mention of the "cow" is illustrative), so too does it occur with respect to a buffalo or the like qualified by dissimilarity, or with respect to dissimilarity qualified by that.

If it is objected: "But while the sacrificial slaughter of something similar to a cow and so forth serves as a purpose for the memory of similarity, such is not the case for the memory of dissimilarity," the author replies: "By virtue of its purpose.
The sense is that, as in the Vedic case, there is no other purpose [for this memory].
Let there be another means of valid cognition for one dwelling in the forest within the wilderness.

The sense is that since the touching (*ālambhana*) [of an animal] in sacrifices and the like is performed upon something resembling a cow, there exists a Vedic purpose for the recollection of similarity; furthermore, the sense is that there certainly exists a worldly purpose consisting of the knowledge of buffaloes and other animals as distinct from cows. He explains the verse with the words beginning "Comparison" (*upamā*).

Just as from the sentence "The gavaya is like a cow" there arises an understanding of similarity in some cow, so too, from what source does the understanding of dissimilarity of a certain buffalo or other animal arise in relation to a cow or other animal? [It arises] from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because such is the case; therefore, let the recollection of the previously perceived cow or other object, following the subsequent perception of the gavaya, be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) without distinction. Just as the recollection of the similar is a means of valid cognition, let the recollection of the dissimilar also be a means of valid cognition. Why is this so? To this he says: "For the sake of a purpose," and so forth.

Now, as for what was said—"like inference based on reflection" (*cintopamāna*): if the cognition of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) is reflected upon in its entirety, then because it arises either directly or through a succession [of cognitions] from the contact of the mind with the object, it would be a form of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) and thus its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Or, as for what was said—"it is another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntara*) and so forth—that too is exactly the same; for this [comparison] is a comparison by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyopamāna*), while the rest is mental perception, according to the Naiyāyikas and others.
To them, he says: "well-known," etc. (*prasiddha*, etc.).

Based on a well-known object such as a cow, or based on a well-known similarity, there arises the means of establishing the knowledge of the relationship between a name and the thing named—the probandum. This collection of causes, which is distinct from both the knower and the object of knowledge, is the means of valid cognition (*upamāna*).
Its result is the [knowledge] "this is the name," and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the meaning of comparison is the result of comparison" serves to include the preceding [points]. What is the point of this exhaustive enumeration? Nothing at all.
What, then, should be the case? To this he says: "By what is done," and so forth.

By means of what is done—that is, what is certain—there arises for every single instance of the knowledge that perceives (*vīkṣaṇa*) the unmade (*akṛta*), i.e., the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), an analogy (*upamāna*) without exception. He thinks that there should be no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the imperceptible than analogy.

This is what is meant: just as that which is produced directly or indirectly from the contact with sense-objects—whether clear or unclear—is called perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it shares the same nature as knowledge born from the contact of clear senses and objects, so too let analogy (*upamāna*) be the cognition of the unperformed through the performed, based on the similarity between the thing to be established and the means of establishment, due to its well-known commonality; for since a certain internal distinction exists everywhere, its apprehension occurs through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) aided by direct perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).

Having perceived smoke as accompanied by fire through the sense organ, and having known it to be excluded from non-fire such as water and so forth through non-perception, one determines with the mind that "smoke does not deviate from fire"—this is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). (Nyāyakandalī, p. 3)
The status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) belongs to something other than the knower (pramātṛ) and the object of knowledge (prameya);
for no distinctness arises merely through some internal difference.
The opponent says: "But indeed," and so forth.
The word "but indeed" (*nanu*) is used here in the sense of censure.

[He thinks: "If this were the case, it would follow that comparison (*upamāna*) and inference (*anumāna*) are non-different; yet their difference is well-established in the world. This is what he considers.
To the Teacher who replied, "So be it," he said: "That very [means] therein," and so forth.
Among those two—comparison and inference—the means of proof is inference.
By what [two]? He says: "By the example," and so forth.

An example (*udāharaṇa*) is an illustration (*nidarśana*). By means of that, there is similarity (*sādharmya*), such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, which is a likeness through a common property (*samānadharmeṇa*); and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), which is a difference through the absence of those properties. By the word "together" (*saha*) in the phrase "by means of those two," he demonstrates inference (*anumāna*) as having both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), namely: "the previous" (*pūrvavat*), "the remainder" (*śeṣavat*), and "that which is generally unperceived" (*sāmānyato'dṛṣṭa*). Alternatively, by the word "separately" (*pṛthak vā*), he states that the purely positive inference (*kevalānvayi*) is "the previous," the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki*) is "the remainder," and the definition of analogy (*upamāna*) is "that which is generally unperceived. Thus, [inference] is not mentioned [here as a separate category].
Inference, which is preceded by that [perception], is of three kinds—namely, *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (NS 1.1.5).
"Of three kinds" means: positive (*anvayin*), negative (*vyatirekin*), and both-positive-and-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*).
—Nyāyavārttika, p. 46.
Regarding this, the Teacher states the refutation with the words "In this case also," and so forth:

not only in the previous case when one assumes that the cognition of pervasion is a mental perception, but furthermore, in this case as well, there would be no distinction between analogy (*upamāna*) and inference based on similarity (*sādharmya-anumāna*), because [the latter] establishes the probandum through similarity to what is already known (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.6).
1.6. The establishment of the probandum through similarity with the example [is inference]; Nyāyasūtra 1.1.5.
And because no distinction is perceived between these two, [the opponent] thinks thus;

and so, while stating that they are different in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he describes their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) as identical. Thus, he is one whose understanding of characteristics is perverted and is of a dull nature.

This is indeed a true illustration. By this, it should also be understood that there would be no difference between the inference based on similarity (*sādharmya-anumāna*) and the inference based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-anumāna*).
When the Naiyāyika and others have thus been refuted by the Teacher himself, the Sugatas (Buddhists) say: "Therefore, [the world] is indeed inference," and so forth.
The meaning of this is as follows: because everything consists of the perception of the uncreated through the created; here, the connection is made by changing the case-ending of the word *sarvam*.

Here the opponent says: "Let inference be the means of proving the probandum (*sādhya*)—whether through a well-known similarity (*prasiddhasādharmya*) or otherwise—provided it is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with that probandum; however, there must also be means such as comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth. To this, the Buddhist replies: "In every way," etc.

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: since the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-sambandha*) is understood in every way—either through the aforementioned mode of well-known similarity or by any other means—and since validity (*prāmāṇya*) is untenable without that [concomitance], let there be only inference.

This is what is meant: if there were a cognition of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) for something else that possesses a well-known similarity, then our desired conclusion would be established.
Otherwise, nothing arising from such [a cognition] would be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is objected: "Just as perception (*pratyakṣa*) possesses validity even without a cognition of the relation of invariable concomitance, so too might it be for analogy (*upamāna*) and the rest," the author replies here with the words: "Even in the case of perception," and so forth.

Not only elsewhere, but even in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), the same consequence— namely, the application of [the requirement of] inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) and so forth— is equally applicable;
for that too is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there because of its necessary connection with the real object (*vastu*), and not otherwise, according to the Naiyāyika.
The intention is that whatever cognition arises from similarity without the apprehension of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) should be considered analogy (upamāna); thus,
even perception is included within analogy and the like.

Here the Cārvāka says: "In that case, since there is no apprehension of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) in inference, it would lack validity. To this he replies: "In the same way," and so forth.
The construction of the words is as follows: "In the same way" means by that same mode as perception; thus, the same consequence applies not only elsewhere but also to inference.
He considers that "that [apprehension] exists there too."
As it has been said:
"Even in the case of perception, there is the apprehension of the invariable concomitance with the object."
"Because [the cognition] would be absent when the object is absent, even in the case of perception there is validity;
since that which has a nature necessarily connected [to the object] is the cause of it, both are equal. Thus [are defined] perception and inference.
For this very reason, he says: "In the absence of the object... (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra* 3.117;
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 775).
Āptapa° pṛ° 173;
Nyāyavi° vi° pra° pṛ° 20; Sanmati° ṭī° pṛ° 555.

Dharmakīrti also said this in the *Nyāyāvatāra-vṛtti*, page 86, and in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*, page 8. Having thus established his own position, the Buddhists might at some point say: "How is it for us that [the object] is like a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?"
Regarding this, the Teacher says: "Of something," and so forth.

For some thing, such as smoke, there is an establishment—that is, a determination—by some means whatsoever, either through itself or by another means of knowledge, without depending on [further] cognition. Without that, the subsequent [cognition], whether perception or inference, does not occur, just as in the case of reflection or comparison.
Herein the intention is this: if this establishment exists, then to reject the very possibility of inference based upon it is improper.

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the object of inference] is included within one of the two—perception or inference—the author replies here: "All existing things, past and future, are momentary," because [inference] is included within reasoning (*tarka*). All entities (*bhāva*) that exist, whether past or future, perish in each moment.
Thus, for you, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*), whether it be perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inferential (*laiṅgika*). [For it is argued:

"The establishment of something imperceptible through its connection with another thing that is invariably concomitant with it is nothing but inference. In this regard, the connection itself cannot be perceived such that an inference could be established;
for no one's knowledge of pervasion in its entirety is ever perceptual at any time, because perception arises from the power of a present object and is non-discursive (*avicāraka*).
If the conceptual cognition produced by that [perception] did not exist, there would be no inference;

and even if there were a determination of the specific characteristics of the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) previously unapprehended, if it were not another means of valid cognition, then even perception would not exist.
Thus, through those two—perception and inference—which are non-conceptual and conventional, there would be no such thing as the apprehension of an object.
Since even the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) is absent,
when it is established by direct perception that "whatever exists is entirely momentary," why should the momentariness of sound itself be an object of inference?
All existing things, all entities without exception, are real.
Who are they? He says: "beings," and so forth.
Regarding the pervasion—that is, regarding the object of pervasion—the proof for you, the Buddhist, is neither perceptual nor inferential (laiṅgika).
Some say that this is not a fault because [for you] the absence of such [proof] is accepted.

If it is argued that "inference does not exist for those who do not grasp pervasion (*vyāpti*)," this is incorrect. If it is replied that there is no fault because those two—perception and inference—are designated as such by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then how is it to be determined that this is so by way of convention and not in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*)? It is not tenable to say "from investigation" (*vicārāt*); for if that [investigation] were not itself a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatve*), it could not determine that [convention], as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Validity, moreover, cannot be established through perception, because that is not admitted and because it would involve a contradiction;
nor can it be established through inference, because that is not admitted. Therefore, it is to be determined through investigation.

"From perception"—no; for one who speaks thus, since nothing other than self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) is possible, and that [perception] does not have its operation directed toward anything other than its own nature, how could there be the understanding of another perception or inference through conventional usage? Indeed, the cognition of blue is not capable of establishing yellow and so forth as being "this" or "not this," because it would follow that the postulation of another cognition is futile.

Now, if it is argued that other means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) are non-existent, and that the conceptualization of the non-existent as existent or otherwise does not arise from anything other than linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), then from what is the proof of that non-existence established? It is not a valid answer to say "from non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*); for by this very [convention], another person establishes inference (*anumāna*) and speaks of the negation of something. If its validity rests upon such linguistic convention, how can there be a final establishment of the non-existence of others in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), from which it would follow that non-duality (*advaita*) alone is proven through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? Thus, [the position that] non-duality is proven is logical.

Nor is its non-existence established by this alone, because [the reason] has no operation with respect to that; otherwise, since pleasure and so forth are not perceived one another, there would be a total non-existence of everything.
The knowledge of pervasion is of two kinds; it is correct cognition.
Perception and inference— Nyāyabindu 1.2; Pramāṇavārttika 2.1.
Valid cognition (pramāṇa) is to be understood as being of only two kinds, distinguished as perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna)— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 2.1.
The meaning is that the status of non-conceptual perception is accepted precisely because of the investigation of that investigation, since investigation itself is of a conceptual nature.
Or by the Buddhist [position] through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) as non-existent.

Dharmakīrti also said this: "The existence of another means of valid cognition [besides perception] is established because the generalities of both valid cognition and its opposite are understood through another cognition, and because of the negation of something. (Pramāṇaviniścaya, p. 8)
And so it was said by the Tathāgatas: "When the generality of another means of valid cognition is established... (*Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p. 19). *Prameyaratnamālā* 2.1.

By this, what was stated by Prajñākara—namely, that since there is nothing other than the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsa*), how can it be said that [the senses] are "real" (*bhūta*) and so forth—is refuted.

The mention of this [perception] is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it applies to others as well. Consequently, the claim that "it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [other]" results in the destruction of inference (*anumāna*).
Thus, it is established that consciousness alone is non-dual, because of the absence of anything else.
"There is no reality other than non-duality"—this is stated in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 30.
To demonstrate the meaning of the verse, he says "of the imperceptible," and so forth.

Because of the connection with the imperceptible object of the senses—that is, from something else which is invariably concomitant with it—its establishment occurs through inference alone, not through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the opponent's position; the Sage says: "In this regard," and so forth.

Here, in the opponent's position, the connection between the mark (*liṅga*) and that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*), namely their inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), cannot possibly be perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). This is because, since that [connection] must be capable of being perceived for inference to be established, [it would follow that inference is redundant].
Or, if "yataḥ" is used in the sense of a challenge (*ākṣepa*), it means that [the object] would simply not exist;

for according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇavārtika* (3.54), "perception is existence," since there is an absence of the fitness for perceptual manifestation, everything is absent. And in the absence of that [cause], there can be no inference, because an effect does not arise in the absence of its cause.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For indeed," and so forth.

For (*hi*) because, for no one—neither for any Buddhist (*saugata*) nor for a Naiyāyika or others—there can exist a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāptijñāna*), that is, the grasping of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), either in its entirety (*sākalyena*) or in its totality (*sāmastyena*), in any practical activity (*vyavahāra*) or ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), in any place, or at any time—whether in the state of an ordinary transmigrating being (*saṃsāridaśā*) or in the state of a yogin (*yogidaśā*).
Therefore, this [position] is refuted: "For whomsoever there is [knowledge] according to the measure of a single location... (*Pramāṇavārttika-alaṃkāra* 3).
Thus, it is not clear by virtue of any particular property, because that [clarity] is absent therein and because no such linguistic convention exists there;
nevertheless, if one were to admit it in that case, there would be no cognition whatsoever that is unclear.

Nor does it arise from the sense organs such as the eye, because those [organs] do not operate therein; otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the fixed number of types of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is argued that it arises from habituation (*abhyāsa*), then this must be considered: would that [cognition] be a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) brought within range by the preparation of habituation, or would it be inference (*anumāna*)? In the first alternative, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), like a vision corrupted by passion and the like.

In the second [case], the cause is that which possesses a correspondence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) derived from the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*); for it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that "that which is not a cause is not an object," since a means of knowledge is purposeful because it leads to successful activity through the comprehension of an object (*Nyāyabhāṣya*, p. 1). Furthermore, according to the statement that "the means of knowledge is distinct from the knower and the known, being a cognition characterized by the cooperation of the object and by ascertainment (*vyavasāya*) and so forth," it must exist as an effect of its own object; thus, there is no apprehension of something existing at the same time as itself, because such a thing is not its cause.

And as for that cause, it too must be situated in that very place and so forth; not everything is intended [as the cause]. Otherwise, it will be demonstrated immediately hereafter that it would have to produce its effects in the location of its own effects and elsewhere. Therefore, it is well said: "because of being proximate," and so on. Because perception arises by the power of an object that is proximate—that is, an object belonging to the time immediately following that [moment]—that cognition cannot be considered perception.
He states another reason: "because of its non-investigative nature" (*avicārakatvāt*).

If it is argued that, because it does not determine even a proximate object due to its being non-conceptual and its consisting of the non-apprehension of itself, that [perception] cannot be that [perception], and therefore the cognition of its pervasion must be inference—here he says: "By the force of that," etc.;
not only is that cognition unable to be perception, but it would also not be inference.

If conceptual cognition were not a form of knowledge, what kind of thing would it be? It exists because of the statement: "Inference (ūha) is based on intelligence and arises from the power of that [perception]," meaning it arises from the capacity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, it is merely [a form of] cognition and not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that even as a means of knowledge, it is only inferential (*liṅgika*); to this, he says: "Regarding the unapprehended," and so forth.

If there were no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) even for the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)—and not merely for its non-determination—of that specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) which has not been previously attained or made an object by perception and the like;
then, for instance, if it were not a means of valid cognition, even perception would not be one, because it too lacks a distinct definition from that [conceptual determination].
If it is not a separate means of knowledge but is indeed inference (*anumāna*), then inference itself would be impossible due to infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is what is intended.
"Apprehension is existence"—this is the established rule;
this was cited in the *Vyāptijñāna* [section] of the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*—see *Anekāntajayapatākā*, p. 207.
Dharmasaṃgraha, p. 176;
Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā, p. 398;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 219.
Āptapa° pṛ° 168; Prameyaka° pṛ° 355, 502;
Nyāyakumu° pṛ° 640.
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 769;
Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa, p. 290;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 206.
And how can an object be without a cause? *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.406;
"An object is not without a cause"—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.1.298.
For that which is not a cause is not an object of cognition—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p.
80; "A cause is not one whose positive and negative concomitance are not replicated, nor is that which is not a cause an object"—*Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 640.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, folio 510; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, folio 34; Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhadvṛtti, folio 37.
Since there can be no relation of cause and effect between two things that exist at the same time,
the knowledge of pervasion is perceptual.
[Objection: "Granted that there may be no knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and thus no inference (*anumāna*); nevertheless, there is no loss for the Buddhist, since he himself accepts its absence.

For he maintains that the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaita*), which is accepted as the ultimate reality, is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To this, [the author] replies with the words beginning "In that direct perception," and so forth.

And those two—direct perception and inference—as conceived by the followers of the Sugata, exist in the forms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). By which two? He says: "non-conceptual" and so forth, which is easy to understand. There is no such thing as the "comprehension of an object" in conventional practice; for in the ultimate sense, there is no comprehension of an object characterized by differentiation, nor of that characterized by non-duality. This is because direct perception, being devoid of all conceptualization, is unestablished for the opponent, and because inference, being merely conventional, cannot prove the ultimate reality (*tattva*). This is what he intends.
The Jains and others [hold this view] regarding that which has the nature of non-dual appearance,
while it has the form of conceptual construction.

Now, as for what was said—"Let there be no inference"—meaning that there is indeed no comprehension of an object by means of inference; [we reply] that this is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we do not admit that comprehension occurs through it, since it is held to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only because it effects the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa*). To this, he says: "Superimposition," etc.—[it is invalid] not only because of the absence of the comprehension of an object, but also because of the absence of its exclusion.

The meaning is: "Let inference not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)," because, as in the case of sleep and so forth, the exclusion of that [inference] is impossible without the apprehension of an object; this is what is intended.
By means of inference...
Furthermore, when the exclusion of superimposition has not been accomplished by means of inference, another [inference] proceeds for that purpose— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*, p. 125.
It is understood that its activity occurs in the isolation from superimposition— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.48.

To one who thinks that the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) constitutes yogic knowledge or the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāptijñāna*), Prajñākaragupta replies with the words "that which exists," and so forth.

Whatever exists and performs a causal function is all necessarily momentary and not eternal; since this is established by perception, why should the momentariness of sound alone be subject to inference? Rather, everything would become inferable, and thus nothing at all would remain an object of the means of knowledge that is perception.

If, on the other hand, pleasure and so forth, or blue and so forth, are accepted as objects of perception, then let momentariness also be perceived, as there is no difference between them; therefore, nothing would remain inferable.

Furthermore, that which has been made an object of yogic cognition cannot be an inferable [object] by means of excluding superimpositions (samāropa) arising from the state of repeated practice; nor, if there were a superimposition, would its pervasion (vyāpti) be established through perception, nor could it serve as the instrument of inference like a certain sign (liṅga). This is the comparison. Others, however, assert that at the time of grasping the pervasion, the cognizer possesses a complete knowledge of all objects, just like a yogin.
"The establishment of pervasion through yogic perception is also difficult to maintain"—Tattvasaṃgrahaślokavārttika, p.
179; Nyāyakumudacandra, p. 432.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 351:
The object of cognition through direct perception is pervasion (vyāpti).
By this, mental perception arising from the connection of connections has been considered;
for all objects are connected with the self through its conjunction with the mind.

Thus, having first demonstrated in general that it is impossible for another [opponent] to grasp pervasion in its entirety, we address what was stated by Arcaṭa: "The grasping of pervasion in its entirety through the momentariness of everything does not occur via perception; rather, existence, while being excluded from all non-momentary things, establishes itself in the momentary because there is no other alternative—according to the maxim of the bird watching for the shore—and is thereby determined to be pervaded by it. Furthermore, that exclusion [from the non-momentary] follows from the exclusion of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), which is the pervader [of existence], and this [exclusion of causal efficiency] follows from the exclusion of succession and simultaneity, which are the two pervaders [of causal efficiency]."
To this he replies: "Existence," and so forth.

It is not on the basis of perception or the absence of an effect that the absence of all causal capacity is asserted in the case of non-momentariness; rather, it is because of the absence of its pervader.
For instance, the performance of an action is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity, since no other mode is possible.

Therefore, since there is a contradiction between non-momentariness and those two [existence and causal efficiency] which pervade causal efficiency, the [non-momentariness] being excluded, there is also the exclusion of causal efficiency which is pervaded by it; thus, non-existence—characterized by the absence of all powers—is drawn toward non-momentariness by the non-perception of the pervader, because two contradictory things cannot coexist in one place.

Consequently, existence, being excluded from that [non-momentariness], remains only in momentary things and experiences identity with them; thus, the establishment—that is, the ascertainment—of the pervasion in the form of positive and negative concomitance, "whatever exists is necessarily momentary," occurs.
—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 146.

It is said that when merchants aboard a ship release a bird in the hope that it might perhaps see the shore, and when it wanders everywhere but does not find the shore, it returns to the very ship; this case should be viewed in the same way.
Since this position must necessarily be accepted, there is no purpose served by this direction of yours, which lacks any established foundation.

—Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 193: "If [the opponent argues that] existence (sattā), by its own exclusion from all non-momentary things, would exclude causal efficiency (arthakriyā) which is pervaded [by existence], then by what means is that [causal efficiency] established in the momentary? (9)

Since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in a momentary entity must occur either successively or simultaneously—both of which are pervading [alternatives]—the very occurrence of perception regarding that [efficiency] in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) constitutes the operation of the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).

But how can that [perception] be perceptual, given that the destruction of moments is not perceived? And even if it were perceptual, how could it be related to that [momentary entity]? How indeed is it perceptual?

If existence, being excluded from that which is non-momentary, were to somehow establish existence in the momentary without the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), then—since there would be no distinction [of the reason] from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*)—this [reason] ought to establish causal efficiency itself in the momentary through some means; otherwise, the exclusion from the heterologue is not established.

If it is argued that for the momentary cause, existence itself is causal efficiency and is thus perceived, then by parity of reasoning, for the non-momentary as well, there is no distinction [between existence and causal efficiency], since there is no difference in their being objects of cognition.

The production of an effect is the same in other cases as well, if it is due to a cause. What is pervaded by what? Therefore, the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) alone is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Furthermore, that perception of momentariness is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*) because of disagreement; otherwise, the means of proof would be redundant.

If [existence] were to exclude existence from that which is non-momentary—whether from everything, from that which persists over time, or from something other than what is intended to be perceived—of what nature would that [excluded] existence be?

It should be understood as being "pervaded" (*vyāpyā*) and "its own pervader" (*svavyāpyā*). Just as in the expression "one must behave toward one's mother," the word "toward" (*mātari*) implies "toward one's own" (*svasyām*);
to the question "What is that? he replies: "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*).

Under what condition? He says: "upon its own cessation. Regarding that, the refutation is as follows: by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or by what manner is that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) established in a momentary entity? By none whatsoever.

This is what is meant: the non-perception of succession and simultaneity—the two pervaders—is found not only in the non-momentary, but also in the momentary; thus, their absence there as well means that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is absent everywhere. Explaining this verse, he says: "Succession," and so forth.

In what manner are "succession" and "simultaneity" [to be understood]? They are pervasive; this is the connection with "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*). That is to say, regarding a momentary, non-persistent entity, the engagement of perception—the arising of direct apprehension—of that causal efficiency which occurs through either succession or simultaneity, is absent in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), namely, the non-momentary.

For when sound is established as momentary because of its existence, then everything else that is momentary becomes the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the non-momentary becomes the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). This is the operation of the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), namely, [the proof] regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); this is the connection with what has been stated previously. The comprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself is the comprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Otherwise, how could the statement of that [concomitance] be considered a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), since the understanding of negative concomitance occurs by implication from the very statement of the certain positive concomitance? Furthermore, it is thought that even if breath and so forth are not observed in some living things, there might still be their exclusion from that which is soulless (*nirātmaka*) based on some [other evidence].
He states the fault for one who accepts [the opponent's position] as follows: "That," and so forth.
"That" refers to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a deliberation (*vitarka*). Since it is not perceived as perishing moment by moment (*kṣaṇakṣaya*), in what manner (*katham*)—by what means—is it directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*)? He considers that this too is because it is not perceived as being momentary (*kṣaṇikatva*) within the absolute doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*).
Even if [the universal] were perceived, how could it be established as related to that [momentary entity], namely related to its momentary destruction?
He states an example—beginning with "of the genus"—asking:
in what manner, by what means, would it be perceived?
"It is easily understood that [existence] would not establish that which is related to it. If one asks, "What is the fault?", he says here: "Of the momentary," and so forth.

Without the establishment—that is, the determination—of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for the momentary, how could existence (*sattā*), by being excluded from causal efficiency, somehow establish existence or causal efficiency in the momentary?
Whence is this? To this he says: "Because of the non-exclusion from the counter-example" (*vipakṣānatiśāyanāt*). He states the conclusion: "Therefore," and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore this Buddhist ought to establish causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the momentary [entity] through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, by way of the absence of proof for that [efficiency] therein, there would be a failure to establish the exclusion from the counter-example—that is, the failure to establish the exclusion of causal efficiency from the counter-example, which is the non-momentary.

Regarding the term *kā*, through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), it is understood as *kā-saḥ* (the letter *ka* followed by *sa*). As in the rule *taparaḥ*, another says: "Of what kind of cause?

Of that which is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Existence itself (*sattaiva*)—that is, the very nature of its being—is causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). As it has been said: "For those [things] whose arising (*bhūti*) is itself their action (*kriyā*)."
"What is its nature? he asks. [The opponent replies: "It is directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*).

If this word *cet* indicates the intention of the other [the opponent], the Teacher gives the answer: "In that manner (*tathā*), by that way, the very existence (*sattā*) of a non-momentary cause is the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is directly perceived; therefore, [the probandum] does not deviate from that," so he thinks.

A lamp and so forth, or the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or the statement of either positive or negative concomitance— since in the formulation of a proof characterized by similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the goal is established by the expression of only one of these, the second is incapable [of contributing further]. Therefore, the statement of that which is not a constituent part of the proof is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), precisely because it is a useless statement.
—*Vādanyāya*, p. 65: Because it is beyond the senses, [the relation] belongs to momentary destruction.
"Arthakriyā-kā" is a name for the fifth case ending (pañcamīvibhakti);
it is a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound.
"All conditioned phenomena are momentary; how can there be activity for those that are unstable? That which is their arising is itself the activity, and that very thing is called the agent.
— *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, p. 376;
*Madhyamakavṛtti*, p. 116, note 1.
*Brahmavidyābharaṇa*, p.
531; *Ratnākara-avatārikā*, p. 29;
*Syādvādamañjarī*, verse 16.

If it is asked: "How can it be said that [momentariness] exists, given that its absence is not established? For non-momentariness is the state of existing across the three times, and that cannot be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because perception lacks the capacity for that; whereas momentary existence is the state of being delimited by the prior and posterior limits [of time], and that can be apprehended through it [perception] because the former is absent"—to this he replies: "Because there is no distinction," meaning because there is an absence of any such distinction.
For just as the existence of a single entity persisting across the three times is impossible to perceive, so too is the existence of an atom—whether external or otherwise—for only a single moment.
However, it is considered that through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), both of these— namely, persistence throughout the three times and momentariness— are possible.
The connection is that even though it is eternal, it cannot be perceived through direct perception.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that momentariness is not predicated of the atom (*paramāṇu*)—which has no [spatial] extent in terms of front or back—but rather of the gross (*sthūla*) object of perception? Therefore, this is a distinction. To this, he says: "In perception," and so forth.

Here the intention is as follows: according to this position, just as a single gross object possesses a nature that is both one and many simultaneously, so too does it possess it sequentially. Thus, in the position of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*), the distinction characterized by perception—the difference from the non-momentary position—is the acceptance of perception (*pratītyanugraha*).
