Otherwise, in the position of momentariness, there would be some other [distinction] characterized by the acceptance of perception; otherwise, one thing would be conceived in one way, while the activity of another would proceed in a different way.

The other says: "Non-existence" [is the case]; here the refutation begins with "the production of an effect," and so forth—[the objection] applies equally even otherwise, that is, even in the case of the non-momentary.

He raises the objection of the opponent's view, stating "that would be its origination from that," with the word "if" (*cet*) indicating the intention of the other: "But surely this has already been raised and refuted by the passage beginning 'of a momentary cause' (*kāraṇasya kṣaṇikasya*) and so forth. True; nevertheless, it is raised again for the purpose of demonstrating another fault, and he says exactly that: "What is the use of that? (*kiṃ tena*) and so forth.

Is existence pervaded by the pervading characteristic of manifold causal efficiency? One thinks: "No, by nothing at all"—for when existence itself is causal efficiency, then because there is no difference between them, there is not even an imagined relationship of the pervaded and the pervader between the two;
for that very thing cannot be both of those.
This being the case, he states the refutation: "From that," and so forth.

From the aforementioned reasoning, it follows that only the non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is the very essence of existence, has been stated, and not the non-apprehension of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). This is the meaning of the particle *eva*. By this, he demonstrates Arcata’s failure to recognize the specific type of non-apprehension [required].
If it is argued, "Let that very thing be so; what is the fault?"—to this he says: "That, moreover," and so forth.

"That" refers to what is being stated by the opponent. The word "moreover" (*punaḥ*) indicates a deliberation (*vitarke*). "Momentary apprehension" (*kṣaṇikopalabdhiḥ*) is momentary existence (*kṣaṇikasattā*); it is expressed in this way by applying the term for the subject (*viṣayin*) to the object (*viṣaya*).
Alternatively, it is derived from the etymology: that which is apprehended (*upalabhyate*) is "apprehension" (*upalabdhiḥ*).

"Why is it that [the non-momentary] is unestablished, that is, unknown? To this he says: "Because of contradiction" (*vipratipatteḥ*). A "contradiction" (*vipratipatti*) is a contradictory cognition regarding the non-momentary;
by means of this [reason], he demonstrates the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) in proving its absence.

Alternatively, due to the absence of practice or because of misconception, he states the refutation regarding the non-acceptance of this non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*): otherwise—that is, by another way in which misconception is absent—the proof consisting of the inference of momentariness would be futile; therefore, that [proof] remains unestablished (*asiddha*).
The exclusion of superimposition has also been considered first.

This is the intended meaning here: for an existence that meets the conditions of perceptibility, there is first of all no non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) as a proof of its absence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because such a thing is not admitted by [the opponent] himself;

nor is there [non-perception] of that which meets the conditions of perceptibility; for even in the case of a momentary entity, just as in the case of a permanent one, since no other means of access exists when it is not perceived, its meeting the conditions of perceptibility remains unestablished.
Therefore, the establishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in a momentary entity is not achieved through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
for this very reason, it is also not achieved through inference (*anumāna*), because the latter is preceded by the former— this is what [the opponent] considers to be existence itself (*sattva*).
The pervaded and the pervader are indeed apprehension, which is of the nature of cognition; a metaphorical designation is applied to existence, which is its object,
[in the form of] "the non-existence of the non-momentary."

Regarding the observation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), since inference is preceded by perception, it might be argued that what was previously stated—"the same applies elsewhere"—is not correct; for there is a contradiction in the production of an effect from a non-momentary entity, whether successively or simultaneously. Dispelling that objection, he says: "Previously," and so forth.
Why is the effect not produced from a non-perishing [cause] that is capable, rather than from a perishing one?
Indeed, there is no contradiction in the production of an effect by means of the existence of the cause.
(10) This has been cited in *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, page 475.

When the existence of B occurs only when A exists, B is the effect and A is the cause; this [definition] is simply not possible under the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), because it would entail simultaneous production. How, then, could there be a continuity of a stream (*santānavṛtti*)? Therefore, one must admit—even if it involves death—that while the capacity to produce B exists previously, B remains unproduced, and its non-existence itself is what will become the effect.
On the other hand, in the opponent’s position, the only difference is that of the cause...
nor would the production of the effect be contradicted by the absence of the cause.

This cause, whether it persists at the time of the production of the effect or not, must have been capable of producing it previously; yet it does not produce it later. It is certainly not the case that it produces it later because of its non-existence [at that time]; rather, it comes into being itself later. Even in this regard, a specific time must be expected, because the effect occurs in its own respective sequence—namely, first at the time of its own existence—from that which is potent and capable.
Why? [The ellipsis] "an effect is produced from that which is perishable and momentary" is to be supplied.
When? Later, at another time.
Here he states the refutation, beginning with "why not," and so forth.

Why is it that the effect, though [the cause] is indestructible, non-momentary, and previously capable, is not produced later? Since there is no difference in its nature as that which has the property of producing [the effect], one might object:

"In that case, since the cause would still exist even at the time of the effect, how can the effect come into being? To this he says: "The production of the effect would indeed be contradicted—not by the existence of the cause, but rather by its absence," because the coexistence of cause and effect is a contradiction.

Regarding what was stated by the opponent—that the relationship of cause and effect is based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), wherein *anvaya* is the presence [of the effect] when the cause is present, and *vyatireka* is its absence when that [cause] is absent—the author, desiring to refute that and demonstrate the meaning of the verse, says: "In which," and so forth.

"When one thing exists only when another exists, and not when it does not exist, the latter is the effect and the former is the cause. This [definition] is simply not possible if the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of entities is accepted.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of simultaneous origination," and so forth.
Because of the consequence that cause and effect would arise simultaneously, how could there be the operation of a continuum (*saṃtāna*)?
This is what is meant: if an existent cause produces an effect, then it must produce it at the very time of its own origination, since it is only then that it exists.

Likewise, at the time of its own production, the entire causal process (*viśvakārya*) occurs; thus, there is simultaneity for the whole continuum. Therefore, because of the aforementioned fault, one must accept—even though it is like [something] crushed by a pestle—that at the very moment prior to its own production, while the capacity to produce that intended effect exists, the production (i.e., the accomplishment) of that specific effect is impossible; and since that effect has not yet arisen, its non-existence implies that it will only come into being when the cause is absent, and thus it would be the effect of that which has already perished. This is how it must be admitted.

The intention here is as follows: Just as an effect produced later from a preceding efficient [cause], even though that cause is perishable, is designated as "belonging to that," so too is it designated from a non-perishable [cause]. Therefore, Dharmakīrti did not state this objection [against such a designation]; rather, by stating it, he brings honor to his own reputation.
If it is argued, "In this way, you have shown there to be no distinction between the two," he replies with the words "In the opposing position" (*parapakṣe*), etc.:

in the opposing position—that is, in the position of the proponent of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇika*)—there is this much additional distinction which differentiates it from the position of momentariness.
Who is this? He says: "Of the cause," and so forth.
If it is objected that in this way the production of an effect would not occur because of the contradiction with the existence of the cause; to this he replies: "And not," and so forth.
What then? It is thought that the production of that [effect] would be contradicted by the absence of the cause; otherwise, there would be the consequence of being without a cause (*nirhetukatva*).

He states the conclusion of the present topic: "Since it is so, therefore—let this perceived cause, such as the father and so forth, remain as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) when the effect is being produced, or let it maintain its existence at that time, or let it not exist; or even if it were to attain a formless state beforehand—it does not fail to produce [the effect] later, having been capable of producing it previously. Rather, it produces it precisely beforehand.

For the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established by perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha-sādhana*): 'when this exists, that exists; when this is absent, that is absent. (Hetubindu, p. 54)

For the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect is based upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "When the [effect] exists, that [cause] exists; and the very existence [of the cause] is the state of being the producer. Thus, the status of cause and fruit is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). (Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 170)
—*Sambandhaparīkṣā*, verse 16; *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra-bhūṣaṇa*, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 510.

The establishment of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is accomplished by means of the two proofs that establish presence and absence (*bhāvābhāvaprasādhana*), as follows: "This occurs when this [cause] is present, even though other capable causes for it are also present; yet, in the absence of that [cause], it does not occur."

"The Blessed One has stated that the definition of a cause is precisely this: 'When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. (*Vādanyāya*, p. 14; *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, pp.
67–68). "Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) means the presence of the reason wherever the probandum exists, by way of pervasion. (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 27).

And when the probandum is absent, the absence of the reason is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 224— if the effect were present at the time of the cause in the case of cause and effect.

The entire causal operation occurring in successive moments does not belong to a non-momentary entity at any time or place, because such an entity lacks the capacity for causal activity through either succession or simultaneity.
— *Hetubindu*, p. 63.

If there is no contradiction in the arising of an effect due to the absence of a cause, then surely, according to the Buddhist, entities do not remain after a moment; so for what purpose is this said—"let them remain"? Just as it is said, "Let that which remains perform its entire prior function right now," so too let the opposite be said, since there is no distinction between the two cases.

Another says: "By no means does it perform [the action] later, because of its own non-existence at that time. What then? It should be understood here as well that "its effect occurs later by itself"; for this reason, this is an adverbial qualification of the action, specifying a particular time.

The phrase "by itself" (*svayam*) continues [from the previous context] in its respective order; thus, the statement that "the effect comes into being" has been refuted by this, as in *Pravāha-vāda* 1.45: "Entities characterized by sequence do not arise from that which is non-sequential," and so forth.

If it is argued: "Just as from a non-eternal cause that lacks sequential order, its effect—though arising later—is not produced all at once, so too it is not logical [to claim] that it arises from an eternal cause either, because [the effect] occurs at specific times," etc., then the author replies:
"Whatever [effect], whenever it is about to arise, at that very time [the cause] consists of the production of that [effect]."
This has been cited—*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p.
475: "The cause is not divided by the difference of its effects, just as [the cause] is momentary (kṣaṇika).

(11) Just as a momentary cause, such as a lamp, produces multiple successive effects—such as the burning of oil, wick, and flame—which are distinct in terms of their own-nature (*svabhāva*), location, and so forth, without any diversity in its own-nature; likewise, a non-momentary [cause] produces effects that are distinct through the difference of time..."

It is incorrect to say that "what has not arisen immediately after something else cannot be its effect, because the cause acts without delay," for such a consequence would apply even when there is a spatial separation, as it applies to time alone. Rather, when an effect— whether of the same or a different class— is about to arise, the production of that effect consists in the causal operation which is essentially the connection with existence (*sattā*).
What is that? He says: "the cause.

[Objection: But in this way, its distinction would arise from the distinction of its effects; as it has been said: "If this cognition arises sequentially, it also implies a sequence in that [cause]. (Pravā. 1)

If this is argued, here he says: "The cause is not differentiated by the differentiation of its effects"— this construction of words provides an example, stating "just as [the cause] is momentary," referring to the cause.

He explains the illustration: a momentary cause, such as a lamp-flame, is differentiated by its own nature, location, and so forth, even without a diversity of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), in relation to the ancient Buddhists, "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is included; in relation to contemporary [Buddhists], "time" (*kāla*) is included. For, from a single instance of burning a creeper, a sequential effect arises—such as its ripening—and it likewise produces multiple effects, such as the burning of the oil, the wick, and the vessel.

Having explained the example, he applies it to the subject of the illustration: "In the same way, [an entity] produces multiple effects differentiated by temporal succession; thus, even here, the phrase 'without a plurality of intrinsic natures'—meaning that it is non-momentary—must be supplied.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Regarding the effect," and so forth.
The opponent replies: "That which immediately follows," and so forth.

That object which has not arisen immediately after it, but only later at a different time, is not its effect; why is this so? Because the cause acts without delay. He provides the following answer to this objection raised by the opponent—thus, the opponent's position is untenable.

Why? He says: "Even when there is a spatial separation—not only when there is a temporal separation—because that [undesirable] consequence would follow. To explain: whatever has not arisen in the immediately adjacent location of something is not its effect, because a cause acts only with reference to [its immediate] object. Therefore, the cognition of a yogin would not be the effect of the three worlds, and thus the existence of an omniscient being would be impossible. Otherwise, it would follow that he must exist in the very location of all objects;
this intervening passage is redundant.
"The burning of the wick" (*daśāvartikā*) means the burning of its face (*ānana*), that is, the burning of the mouth.

By means of the knowledge of a yogin, that which has arisen even when there is a spatial separation is said to belong to him, but not when there is a temporal separation; thus he says, "of time alone," and so forth,
and therein provides the answer, beginning with "not having reached," and so forth.

Because the time for its effect has not yet arrived, just as that which is separated [in time] is not a cause, nor is its subsequent [moment] its effect; and this is not the case for the universal (*jāti*) when that [time] has passed. If an effect were to arise from something separated [in time], then because there is no distinction in the exclusion [of other causes], the utility [of the specific cause] would not be distinguished; for cessation (*nivṛtti*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).

Since a distinction can somehow arise even within an entity itself—just as in the case of a momentary cognition appearing as variegated—it follows that this [subsequent state] must exist even if you do not desire it when the preceding one has ceased; for non-existence is everywhere undifferentiated.
Otherwise, it would transcend its own characteristic of having an effect at a restricted time, since no differentiation is possible for non-existence.

For "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) does not qualify non-existence (*abhāva*), because that would entail [non-existence] possessing the nature and continuity of an object. To illustrate: for something that exists after another by necessity, its being the effect of that [prior thing] is contradictory if it were non-existent; why would it not exist even at a later time, since there is no difference in its non-existence compared to the moment immediately following?
(Aṣṭaśahasrī, Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 90)

The intention here is as follows: for Dharmottara and others, the preceding [moment] is the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the subsequent [moment] is the effect (*kārya*); the reverse is the non-effect and non-cause (*akāryakāraṇa*). In that regard, whatever is immediately preceding them must be accepted as the cause, yet that does not become a cause;
why? Because its time of producing the effect has not arrived, since it exists when the time for the effect has not yet been reached.
He provides an example: "just as that which is separated."
Just as a husband is, with respect to the fetus of a widow, a non-cause because he is separated by time, so too is the subject at hand;
thus he states the second formal argument (prayoga): "And that [effect] is neither simultaneous with nor immediately following its cause;
why is this? To this he says: because of the production from birth, and upon its cessation, when that which is considered the cause has ceased."
Here too, the illustration "just as that which is separated" should be applied:
just as the effect of a widow’s pregnancy does not belong to the deceased husband because it is separated by a future time, so it is with the subject at hand.

Since this verse is easy to understand, no commentary has been provided; however, regarding what was stated by the opponent—that even though there is no difference in the state of the [effect's] time not having arrived, only the immediately preceding cause is the cause and not the separated one, due to the variety of the power of entities—[this is now addressed].
"For not every cause, even when its time has arrived, [necessarily produces its effect]; thus, the reason [you have offered] has an exclusion from the counter-example that is doubtful.
By this, the second reason as well has been examined.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of that which is obstructed," and so forth.

When the production of an effect occurs from that which is separated [by other factors], that which has long since perished, and that which has just perished, there is no distinction in their exclusion (*vyāvṟtti*) or cessation (*nivṛtti*); thus, their utility—that is, their operation (*vyāpāra*)—would not be differentiated. Consequently, even a remote cause would be [as effective] as an immediate one, because the power of entities (*bhāva-śakti*) is diverse; and in this regard too, [the principle] "it is not held by the staff" applies. This is considered to be the view of Prajñākaragupta alone, and not that of Dharmottara and others. Why is it not differentiated? He says: because cessation (*nivṛtti*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatvāt*).

Now, if there is no distinction because cessation (*nivṛtti*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), then of what could there be a distinction? To this he says: "It is only of an entity (*bhāva*), and not of a non-entity (*abhāva*), that a distinction—that is, a difference—is possible in some way or by any means, such as through being capable or incapable; thus, the utility [of the cause] is not indistinct.
For Prajñākara, indeed, is a proponent of the theory of remote causes (*vyavahitakāraṇavādin*).

Here someone objects: "Even something separated [in time] can be a cause of waking consciousness and so forth; and since that exists at its own time, a specific result arises. Thus, the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). To this, he replies with the words beginning "citra":

"That which has a variegated appearance is so described; and that is the momentary cognition. 'Like that' (*tadvat*) means like that which is similar to a single momentary variegated cognition; the meaning is: of an entity that undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*)."

This is what is meant: that waking cognition, which was cited as an example for the status of being a cause even when separated [in time], has a nature that ultimately consists of partless, single atoms (*paramāṇu*); therefore, it is not established through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for either the proponent or the opponent. How, then, can it serve as an illustration, like the case of the person? Or, if one were to argue that even a cognition appearing as variegated is indeed a single unity—as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (3)—[the response follows].

Because of such statements as these, the manifold is one; this does not follow the Buddhist view, but rather that of the Jaina, since they establish the manifoldness of the self through both its non-sequential and sequential aspects, as well as through its nature as both perceptible and imperceptible.
Therefore, this waking consciousness is nothing at all [in the Buddhist sense].
He states the conclusion regarding Prajñākaragupta, the Jaina, and others who maintain the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (vijñānādvaitavāda): "Since it is thus, therefore by this..."

By what? By a subsequent effect. Of what nature? He asks: "What is to be accomplished by that which arises only in the absence of a prior cause, and not in its presence? He replies: "It must exist at the immediately following time even when [the cause] is undesirable, and not merely when it is desirable," because the prior non-existence—that is, the cause—is indistinguishable at all times.
And he considers that it is not logical for an effect not to arise when its cause is complete.
[Objection: But surely, even though that [cause] remains unchanged at all times, the effect arises only at a specific time? To this, he says: "Otherwise," etc.

Otherwise—that is, by way of the absence of arising at an undesired time—it would follow, by its own nature (*svata eva*), that there is a sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting in being causeless (*nirhetukatva*) which indicates a specific time; thus, the characteristic of an effect—namely, dependence on another (*parāyattatva*)—would be transcended, because existence and non-existence would not be dependent [on anything].
Because it is independent,
it is the maker of wisdom;
for the consciousness of one in deep sleep [is so] because of the recollection of prior experience upon awakening.
"It is certain that [the effect] arises after an interval of time"—this is stated in the *Prakaraṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p.

67. It might be argued: "Even though the non-existence of the prior [cause] exists at an undesired time just as it does at the intended time, nevertheless, the effect occurs only at the time of the intended non-existence"; to this, he says: "And of non-existence," etc.
The intention is that if an absence were differentiated from another absence, it would somehow be a presence, because it is impossible for it to be distinct from that [other absence].

Why is this so? To this he says: "In that case, immediate succession," and so forth. For immediate succession—the existence of the absence immediately prior to the arising of the effect—qualifies the absence and distinguishes it from other absences; this is because a void absence (tuccha-abhāva) is incapable of being qualified.
Why is this so? He says: "Because of the object," and so forth.
This means that because the nature (*svabhāva*) of an object, such as a living being (*jīva*), would result in continuity (*anvaya*).

What is meant is this: when the transition of a preceding state into a subsequent form occurs in some way, then that [negation] could be delimited by the non-existence of something like the son of a barren woman; but it cannot be delimited otherwise.

Alternatively, "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is the existence of the immediate cause prior to the production of the effect; this qualifies its absence. For it is not the case that the absence of the immediately preceding [cause] belongs to everything.
Why? He says: "The object," and so forth.

This should be applied as before, as stated by Sāntabhadra: "The cause being in the process of ceasing is [already] ceased. That is without substance; for if that which is in the process of ceasing exists at the very time of its own arising, then there would be simultaneity of cause and effect. But if it does not exist at any other time, what indeed can be called "in the process of ceasing"? Otherwise, there would be the fault [of the argument] beginning with "the object," and so forth.

From this it follows: just as an unproduced effect, which arises spontaneously at a fixed time later from a cause that was previously capable and eternal, cannot be the effect of that [cause], so too, even in the case of a momentary thing, an effect that has not arisen during the time of its own existence but arises again later cannot belong to it—
whether that [cause] be eternal or momentary.

But surely, when whatever effect is about to arise, its cause must possess the nature of producing it. If that eternal [cause] requires successive auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*), then that itself constitutes impermanence; for there is no other way for it to appropriate the assistance (*upakāra*) provided by them. Otherwise, what would be the point of depending on them? It would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As it has been said: "The other [auxiliary] might be required for the sake of the effect... (*Pravacanasāra* 3).

If it is argued that [the cause is momentary] because of such statements as these, the author replies here: "Because of the cause," and so forth, with reference to the auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*).
If there were anything whatsoever that was a non-productive entity, then what would it depend upon? This is the implied meaning.
The essence of a cause would not differ due to its auxiliaries, whether for a permanent entity or for a momentary one that produces effects of diverse natures.

Just as there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of non-delayed momentary things despite a diversity of effects due to the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)— because they possess no excellence that can be added or removed— likewise, let there be no difference in the intrinsic nature of things persisting over time, even when there is no distinction in the effects intended to arise sequentially.

At the time of the effect, of what kind of cause—that is, of the material cause (upādāna)—is it intended? Of one that is stable and eternal; its self-nature (ātman), its essential form, would not undergo change.
By what [means]? He says: by "auxiliaries" (sahakāribhiḥ), meaning instrumental and non-inherent causes.
Under what condition? To this he says: "when there is production.
Of what things? He says: "of effects" (phalānām) that possess a manifold nature, having essences differentiated by place and so forth.
The phrase "by means of auxiliaries" (*sahakāribhiḥ*) should also be connected here;

from this, the following meaning arises: by means of auxiliaries, when the various kinds of effects are produced, the nature of the cause does not undergo differentiation, even during the production of the assistance to the material cause (*upādāna*).
However, if one maintains this insistence that the auxiliaries produce the intended effects only while performing an assistance upon the material cause, [then the following applies].

In this regard, the following is considered: Do the auxiliary causes (sahakāris) produce the primary effect by producing another assistance for the material cause (upādāna), or do they do so without producing such another assistance? If it is the first position—that they produce the primary effect by producing another assistance for the material cause—then even while performing that further assistance, they must again produce an assistance for the material cause, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, the auxiliary causes, whose capacities have been exhausted solely in the production of successive further assistances, would never have the capacity to operate toward the production of the primary effect.

Regarding the second position: [you might argue that] the auxiliary causes (sahakārin) produce the assistance even while not performing the assistance for the material cause of the assistance; whereas the auxiliary causes do not produce the effect for the material cause of the effect while not performing it—what is the basis for this distinction? To support this very point, he states an example well-known among the Buddhists: "And of the momentary," where the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "as if" (iva), since particles have multiple meanings.

Thus, the meaning expressed is as follows: just as the nature of a momentary material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is not differentiated by its auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*), even though various kinds of effects are produced by them, so it is with the subject under discussion as well.
For even that [cause], being partless and produced from its own cause, has nothing done to it by external objects, since no differentiation could occur; thus, there is no assistance (*upakāra*).
The intrinsic nature [of] even that which is momentary [is established] by means of auxiliary causes alone.
Explaining the verse because [otherwise] there would be a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he says: "By virtue of the causal complex" (*sāmagrīvaśāt*).

This means that even though there is a difference in the effect—that is, a plurality of results—there is no difference in the intrinsic nature, which is to say the essential form (*svarūpa*), of those things that are momentary.
In what state are they? To this he says: "of those that act without delay," meaning those that act without hesitation.
Why is this so? To this he says: "because nothing can be added," and so forth;
for, due to their partless nature (*niraṃśatva*), there is no addition or removal of any excellence (*atiśaya*) within them—this is what is intended.

In the same way, by that very same principle, one should also connect this here: "Let there be no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) of eternal things that persist over time, even when a specific effect is about to arise in succession, due to the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
He thinks that by virtue of that [complex], only a distinct effect is produced, and there is neither the addition of excellence (*atiśaya*) nor the removal [of it] in those [eternal causes].
If it is asked, "From what then does the effect arise in succession? he says: "At the time of the effect," and so forth.

This has been examined—by the passage beginning with "whatever effect is about to arise when," etc.—that being the case, there would be the futility of successive auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), because the successive effects would be produced from the material cause (*upādāna*) alone. Why, then, is that material cause taken up for the production of those effects, given that the auxiliary causes lack capacity in that regard? Otherwise, why would there be this distinction: that the auxiliaries produce the effect even before [the final moment] while the material cause does not?
When eternal things accomplish their effects through the presence of auxiliary causes (sahakārin), [the following occurs].

If it is argued that the material cause (*upādāna*) is capable [of producing the effect] even before [the auxiliary causes], or that it is indeed capable because it follows their presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and not because of the proximity of eternal and pervasive [entities], since that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); to this he says: "And by eternal [entities]," etc.
Only the auxiliary factors possess causality with respect to that [effect],
since among eternal things, other mutually auxiliary factors produce their respective objects.
Among those [causes], when one is capable of producing the effect, the others would not cease [from acting] due to their non-temporal nature.

Just as at the time of the effect, by their very nature, [the causes] arise from their own causes as agents capable of that production; likewise, when those adventitious [auxiliaries] have arisen—each mutually assisting and each individually capable of producing that effect—then, provided even one among them is capable of producing it, the others certainly would not cease, because each possesses the inherent nature (svabhāva) to produce that effect, just like a momentary entity.
Thus, the two positions—the absolute momentariness and its opposite—do not surpass one another.

If it is argued that when cause and effect coexist—as in the case of curd and milk—the consequence of their non-difference follows from their simultaneous perception; [we reply: even though consciousness and its nature as either erroneous or non-erroneous coexist, there is an absence of simultaneous perception and so forth. Who can prevent one from postulating this elsewhere as well? ...transformation...
variegated...
The word "ca" (and) is used out of its usual sequence and has the sense of "iva" (as if); it should be understood immediately after the word "akālikaiḥ" (not of the same time).
Thus, the meaning is as follows: in what things? In objects—that is, in tasks—to be produced once they have arisen.
By what [means]? He says: "by the eternal.
Of what nature are they? He says: "mutually cooperative," meaning those that assist one another toward a single effect;

or alternatively, in a certain effect, when one [cause] serves as the material cause (*upādāna*), the others included within that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) serve as its auxiliaries (*sahakārin*), and when those [others] serve as the material cause, that [first one] serves as their auxiliary—thus they are "mutually cooperative," and by them [is the effect produced].
What [is this]? He says: "Others," and so forth.

Among those objects, when one single material cause (*upādāna*) or auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*)—which is capable—is active, other auxiliaries or material entities that are causes would not cease [from acting]; rather, all of them perform those [effects], because their very nature consists solely in producing them. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "by those that are non-temporal" (*akālikaiḥ*).

Just as in the case of produced objects, where multiple causes that are non-temporal, momentary, and mutually cooperative do not exclude one another from operating upon a single effect, so it is in the present case as well;
thus, with the words "just as... even in the eternal," he explains the verse.

Without exceeding the time for the effect—that is, according to the time required for each respective effect—when there is some producer as the agent, from what [does it arise]? To this he says: "By its own nature," meaning by its own inherent character.
When which [conditions] are present? To this he says: "That," and so forth.
In this case as well, the phrase "by way of their own nature" (svabhāvataḥ) must be understood.
Regarding those things capable of producing that [effect]—that is, those possessing the power to generate the effect intended to arise at its respective time—he asks:
"Of what kind? and answers with the words beginning "from their own causes" (svakāraṇa), etc.
Furthermore, in what kind of circumstances? To this he says: "Again," and so forth.
Even though that [cause] was previously capable, subsequently, when adventitious factors arise, he further qualifies those very same factors with the words beginning "mutually" (*paraspara*).
When that exists, what has occurred? To this he says: "That," and so forth. By the word "that" (tat), the intended effect is referred to.
When any one of its material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) or auxiliary conditions (*sahakārī*), which are capable of producing it, exists, surely—meaning certainly—not others would cease [to exist].
Regarding the question "How so?", he says: "Each one," and so forth.
The meaning is that each individual possesses the inherent nature of being the cause of that [cognition].
He provides an illustration for this: "like momentary [entities]."

"Just as in the case of the momentary," that is to say, just as in the case of something momentary capable of producing an effect, others [auxiliaries] would not cease [to assist], so it is with the eternal as well. Furthermore, as for what was stated here by the opponent—that the nature of the momentary, which depends on auxiliary causes to produce an effect, does not belong to the eternal because of the absence of such [causes], and that if [the effect] were accidental, there would be the consequence of lack of restriction—that is without substance; for it has not been ruled out that effects could be eternal.
The meaning is thus stated as "not so for those that persist through other times," and so forth; otherwise, he would have said "for those that are immutable" (*kūṭasthānām*) and the like.

Even in the case of the immutable position, this fault does not apply because their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is eternal; for it is logical that an impermanent nature, being produced by itself, would be non-deterministic.
For this very reason it was said: "according to the time of the effect," and so forth.
Concluding the subject at hand, the Buddhist says: "Therefore, in this way," and so forth.

For that reason, in the manner thus described, the two exclusivist positions—the momentary and the non-momentary—do not surpass one another; they do not attain distinction from each other. Just as in the case of the momentary, since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible even in the non-momentary, there is a non-perception of the pervader [of existence], and thus the pervasion by existence is established.

Alternatively, it is thought that even in the case of the momentary, if there is no connection [between cause and effect], the pervasion of the one by the other is not established—just as in the case of the non-momentary.

Where something that meets the conditions for perception is not perceived, it does not exist there, just as a jar does not exist in a particular location; and likewise, such a cause is not perceived in the effect. This is the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, if that [cause] were perceived, it would follow that everything would be perceived everywhere.

But this is not the case; therefore, since there would be no perception of the effect in its cause—just as there is none of a jar in a particular location—and likewise no perception of the cause in that [effect], the non-existence of a perceptible object would follow, and thus the proof of momentariness would be untenable. Anticipating the view of one who thinks "it is thus," etc., [the author] addresses the objection beginning with "the effect," etc., [stating]:
if the coexistence of cause and effect were admitted, what would be meant is this: just as an existing cause abides in its effect, so too the effect abides in its cause.

What would follow from that? He says: "In the case of curd, milk, and so forth, there is the consequence of non-difference [between cause and effect] because they are perceived together"—this is the connection. This refers to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their being non-distinct.

This is its meaning: if an effect, such as curd and so forth, is perceived together with its prior cause, such as milk and so forth, and the cause, such as milk and so forth, is again perceived together with the effect, such as curd and so forth, then there is an absence of that distinction—namely, "this is the cause of this" and "this is the effect of this"—which constitutes non-difference (*abheda*). Alternatively, when the Jaina and Sāṃkhya schools maintain that the effect exists within the cause through identity (*tādātmya*), then, given their co-existence—that is, their existence as one—at times, in the case of milk and so forth...

By what [means] and what [is established]? He says: "By simultaneous perception"—that is, by the perception of identity—there would be non-difference; [it might be argued that] the effect itself, or the cause itself, would be [the object], and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of designations such as "presentness" and so forth is intended; if such a [consequence] were to follow, he states the answer to this: "Consciousness," etc. [The meaning is:

regarding consciousness—that is, cognition such as that produced by cataracts—which has the nature of an error with respect to the double moon and so forth, due to cataracts, rapid motion, or [mental] confusion... (Nyāyabindu 1).

From such statements as these, that which is the nature of the other [the object] is, in relation to its own form (*svarūpa*), of a non-erroneous nature for all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
according to the declaration in *Nyāyabindu* 1.10 and elsewhere;
or else, it is the erroneous nature of consciousness— that is, of all conceptual cognition— which consists in the association with verbal expression, according to *Nyāyabindu* 1.1.
Because of such statements, that which is of a different nature has also been described. Even when those two coexist, [the distinction remains];

not only when they do not coexist—what [is the reason]? He says: "Because of simultaneous apprehension and so forth," meaning because of the absence of that [distinction] such as non-difference, of which simultaneous apprehension—that is, simultaneous perception—is the first.

Indeed, at the very time of the appearance of a cognition such as that of two moons, there is no apprehension of its true nature (*svabhāva*), because if there were, there would be no disagreement [regarding it], and consequently, there would follow the absurdity that no one would ever engage in any activity whatsoever, at any time, or in any place; yet this is not the case, since activity is observed despite this. Furthermore, it would follow that there would be no distinction between the various doctrines, such as those asserting non-existence (*asattva*) or misapprehension (*khyāti*).
This is an explanation intended to demonstrate the aforementioned fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) against the Sautrāntika.

This objection—that even if there is coexistence between the two [existence and momentariness], they might somehow be one, or that even if they exist, there is no apprehension of their being entirely identical—is to be explained as follows: existence is pervaded by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and that [efficiency] occurs either successively or simultaneously. Since these two [successive and simultaneous modes] are absent in a permanent entity, they are excluded along with their own pervaded [concomitant], causal efficiency; and since that [efficiency] is pervaded by existence, the pervasion of existence by momentariness is established through the force of the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). The point is that if causal efficiency were established in a non-momentary entity, then the pervasion between existence and momentariness would not be established.
It should be observed— page 190, note 4—
that in the absence of causal efficiency (arthakriyā), there is no existence.
Through the proof of pervasion by momentariness— namely,
that all minds and mental factors in an effect [are momentary] and so forth— the self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) of even conceptual cognition is indeed non-erroneous in its essential nature.

If there were no further engagement from that point, then an explanation regarding the practice of yoga would now be given: namely, that which is the nature of the delusion of consciousness—consisting of the triad of the nature of the perceived, the perceiver, and the act of perception—and that which is its other nature, the nature of non-dual consciousness;
and so it has been said:

Although the nature of consciousness is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the grasped object, the grasping subject, and their cognition to those whose vision is distorted—
just as pieces of clay appear so to those whose senses are impaired by spells and the like.
"They appear in one way, even though they are devoid of that nature," as stated in *Pravāha* 2.354,
55, and so forth.
Even if there is coexistence of these two, or simultaneous existence, or even some kind of oneness—what of it? He says: "simultaneous," etc.;
the explanation is as before.
For instance: its error consists in the non-perception of its own nature when there is the perception of another nature;
for when a yellow color is perceived in a white conch-shell, the white nature is not perceived.
Therefore, it is not tenable [to say] that "the nature of cognition is undivided" (*Pravāraṇavāda*, 2).
354. Thus, there is nothing other than consciousness that can be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of that [intellect] itself.

"Because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, that very consciousness manifests by itself" (Pravā. 2.327). Thus, since consciousness does not perceive itself even in a dream—just as a person [does not see himself]—it would therefore be established as being merely an illusion.

Even when other natures are not perceived, the claim that "this talk of delusion has been transcended" is devoid of meaning— given such statements as "it possesses the forms of the non-cognized and the cognizer" (Pravāhaṇa-vāda 2.330) and so forth,
as well as "though undivided" (Pravāhaṇa-vāda 2).
And so forth;
for indeed, when the moon appears without division, the conceptualization of an appearance of two moons is not accepted because it is contradicted by common worldly experience.

The statement that "the light of cognition first [appears] as the perception of the self through a non-discriminative intellect, and then it is characterized by a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as if possessing the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness," is made by him [Dharmakīrti] without having understood Dharmakīrti’s intention, for nothing at all is actually characterized by a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). This is because such an intention is absent; otherwise, the illustration beginning with *mantrādyupaplutākṣāṇām* (Pramāṇavārttika 2.355) would indicate his lack of foresight.

Indeed, the confusion regarding the sense-faculties (*akṣavibhrama*) is not the sole illustration of confusion, because there exists confusion regarding Īśvara and so forth that belongs to the same class;

nor is it established that even the illusion of two moons is born of the sense-faculties, for one could argue as follows: first there is the perception of a single moon, and subsequently, through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its duality.
And thus, the infamy of Dharmakīrti—who sought to prove that [cognition] is born of the senses—has arrived;
the remainder of this matter, which was stated in the first chapter, should also be understood here. Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Just as they are perceived by those who are deluded— with the remainder being that they appear as a distortion of the forms of the grasped and the grasper, characterized by distinct features.
It is established through conventional usage by means of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from experience;
"subsequent observation" (*anudarśana*) is a conceptual construction corresponding to the [initial] perception— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.1.20.
Prajñākara was the [disciple] of Dharmakīrti.
The delusion of two moons and so forth—
wherein even the sense faculties are the cause of cognitions such as the blue double-moon— is this [delusion] sensory in nature, since it conforms to the presence and absence of the sense faculties?
If it is argued that [the cognition] is similar to that [object] and possesses modification, then why is this very [modification] being denied?—
this is stated by one who establishes that error is born of the senses, beginning with *Pra.vā.* 2.290–96.
By this, the Naiyāyika and others should also be understood as refuted when they speak to the Jaina regarding "the cause and effect," and so forth.

To explain: there is that which is of the nature of doubt and error—such as the cognition "Is this a post or a person? or the delusive states "It is a post" with respect to a person, or "It is a person" with respect to a post—and there is that which is of the nature of non-delusion, consisting merely of the substratum (dharmin) such as "this. Regarding these two, the rest is as previously stated.

If it is argued that "let there be one cognition that is non-contradictory," to this he says: "of consciousness" (*vijñapteḥ*), and so forth. Who can prevent one from imagining that what was just mentioned applies equally to other objects as well?
From where does this [certainty] come? To this he says: "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), and so forth.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason— beginning with the words "variegated" (*citra*) and so forth—
along with an illustrative example, [showing that it] has the nature of being non-erroneous (*avibhrama-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, regarding what was stated by the opponent concerning the proof of non-existence (*abhāva*) through both existence and destruction:
"Because destruction is causeless, it is inherent to the nature [of things];
for that which is perishable does not depend on a cause for its existence, since perishable things arise from their own causes alone."
—*Pravāha-svabhāva*, p. 360: "Because all things exist without dependence regarding their destruction...
and all produced things are everywhere independent with respect to their destruction."
In every respect, because the causes of destruction have no efficacy therein—
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 353, 357—
a thing whose destruction is certain does not depend on anything else for that [destruction].
The meaning is that there is no dependence upon other causes for destruction,
because those [other] causes lack the capacity [to produce it];
showing that this is the same in other cases as well, he says "of arising, duration, and destruction," and so forth, in order to establish that [point].
Arising, abiding, and destruction are inseparable from the intrinsic nature [of things] because their causes lack efficacy; therefore, reality consists of these three aspects.
For just as a cause of destruction does not produce the destruction of an entity that is already part of its own intrinsic nature, since there is no production of what has already been produced.

Nor does it produce something other [than itself], because even if such production occurred, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving it exactly as it was before, since its state remains unchanged;
furthermore, no relation can be established, so that even the designation "of this" would not be possible.
Moreover, there is no destruction called "destruction" that is distinct from the jar or other objects.

Even while existing, [the cause of destruction] conceals that very state without destroying its identity, such that it is no longer perceived; therefore, this is the cause of destruction. How could it be dependent on something devoid of activity other than that [destruction], since destruction occurs only occasionally? Origination (*utpāda*) is the acquisition of self-nature by what was previously non-existent; destruction (*bhaṅga*) is the non-existence of what exists again; and stability (*sthiti*) is the persistence of the former in the second and subsequent moments. These are necessarily connected—that is, invariably concomitant—with their own nature, which serves as their essential cause.

From where is this [known]? To this he says: "Because of the incapacity of the causes," and so forth. The connection is made by changing the case-ending [of the word *hetūnām*] to "because of the incapacity of those causes which belong to those [three], namely arising, persistence, and destruction.
Therefore, by this logic, reality—the essential nature of the soul (*jīva*) and so forth—is threefold, consisting of arising, persistence, and destruction.
Showing the meaning of the verse along with an illustration, he says: "Just as indeed" (*yathaiva hi*), and so forth.

"Just as" (*yathaiva*) means in whatever manner; "indeed" (*hi*) is used for emphasis (*vitarke*). "The cause of destruction of an entity," such as a jar, "would be its own nature" (*svabhāvabhūtaḥ*); here too, the phrase "belonging to the entity" (*bhāvasya*) should be connected. [The question is: "Why does it not produce destruction, which is non-existence? To this, he says: "Of that which is already produced," and so forth.

Since there is no further production of an entity that has already been produced by its own causes, what would be accomplished by [an alleged cause of] destruction? It would amount to nothing more than the non-production of a destruction that is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity, for that [destruction] arises from its own cause.
If, on the other hand, one thinks that [the cause of destruction] produces something that is not its own nature, [the author] says: "Nor... and so forth.

It does not produce something else, that is, something distinct (*arthāntara*). For even if such a distinct destruction were produced, the entity would remain as it was before—unmoved from its prior state—because it would follow that the entity would be perceived exactly as it was previously.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the consequence of [the object's] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth is included.
Showing another refutation, he says: "Because the relation," and so forth.

Because the dependence (*pāratantrya*) of the relation is unestablished, there is even this designation—that the destruction of this jar and so forth [occurs through that cause]—as well as its verbal expression; the word "even" (*api*) indicates that this is not merely the immediately preceding fault. Let it not be [that the fault does not apply].

Because a cause of destruction is untenable, entities are perishable by their very nature; for these things, once produced from their own causes, there is no arising of destruction from anything else, since that [other cause] lacks efficacy.
Indeed, a cause of destruction does not produce the very nature of an entity, because that [nature] has already been established by its own causes.
Nor is it simply another entity; for since the entity remains in that same state, it would follow that it would be perceived as such [as before].
Nor is there an obscuration by another entity; for while that [entity] remains in its state, obscuration is impossible.

Nor is non-existence produced by a cause of destruction; for if non-existence were accepted as something distinct through a positive affirmation, one would have to transcend the dilemma of whether it is different or non-different [from the entity].

In the act of negating an entity, nothing at all happens to it; it simply ceases to exist. Thus, there is no agent, and since there is no agent, there is no cause; therefore, there is no cause for destruction, as any such cause would be purposeless.
If it is perishable by its very nature, there is no need for causes of destruction, because it perishes of its own accord through that very nature.
For whatever has a certain nature becomes such precisely while arising from its own cause; it does not depend on another cause for that state—*Hetubindu*, p. 56.
Pra.vā.sva. 1.272:
As before, it is characterized by the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perception and so forth.

Now, if it is asked: "Why is it said that the relation is unestablished, when the relation between existence and non-existence as qualifiers is indeed established?"—we reply: No, because an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has been demonstrated here.

Some say: "Let there be no relation or even a designation for those two; nevertheless, there is no fault, because we admit [the cognition] to be devoid of a relation. That too is not correct; for whether directly or indirectly, it cannot be unrelated to the sense faculty, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its non-perception.
Even if it were perceived despite this, the postulation of a relation with it [the object] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth would be useless.

It might be thought that existence and non-existence [are perceived] together with the sense organ; however, because it is obscured by non-existence, there is no such apprehension, and thus it is incorrect— this applies even to the case of its being produced, and so forth.
To this, he states the reply: "And not," and so forth.

And indeed, there is no such thing as destruction—which is distinct from the jar and other objects and exists as a separate entity—the word "nāma" (indeed) being used in the sense of "clearly"; for [such destruction] does not exist, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could apprehend it.
He states another refutation: "tadātmānam" and so forth.

This is its meaning: even though existing, it conceals that very nature—that is, the nature or essence (*svabhāva*)—of that visible object such as a jar, without impairing or destroying it; it remains in that same state while concealing it. And he thinks that because of this concealment it would not be seen, for [he maintains] that an existing thing, being capable of producing a cognition of itself, must necessarily perform that [function].
In that case, the same fault applies to the refutation of the self (*ātman*), as well as the problem of infinite regress;
and whether the refutation of the self is performed as being different from or non-different from [the self], etc.—concluding the present topic, he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore, how could this well-known cause of destruction in the world, such as a mallet and the like—which is devoid of performing that [specific] action or its opposite, and which is devoid of producing the destruction of either the nature or the non-nature of the jar—not be required for the effect of destruction? For one who employs such a figurative expression (*upacāra*), the destruction of an entity would be merely occasional (*kādācitka*) because of its dependence;
or, if "since" (*yataḥ*) is used in the sense of a challenge (*ākṣepa*), it would not be so at all—it would mean that [the entity] would be eternal.
Devoid of the causes of destruction that are either distinct or non-distinct, he states another refutation right here with the words "If destruction were non-existence," etc.:
"If destruction were non-existence, [it would follow] because of the negation of action; if not..."
Since it does not produce an entity, by what means could it ever be expected [to act] anywhere?

Consequently, an object that perishes by its own nature is established; likewise, a cause for the arising of an entity is ineffective, because there is no purpose in producing what has already been produced.
For this very reason, non-existence is also established by itself.

If it is argued that the cause of arising is that which makes prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) into existence, why is it not accepted that the cause of destruction is that which makes prior existence into non-existence? Furthermore, if the subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of an entity is also—just like other absences—inherently an absence by virtue of its own cause alone, then the persistence (*sthiti*) of the entity must likewise be so.

And just as it is established that for an entity which does not itself desire to arise, there is no dependence on causes of arising or causes of duration—since it is its own nature that determines whether it arises, persists, or ceases—it would be logical for arising or destruction to depend on and have as their cause certain specific factors of substance, place, time, and nature, provided these are excluded from others, because this is not contradicted by our experience.

If destruction is non-existence—that is, the cessation of existence in the form of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—then if a hammer or similar instrument produces that non-existence, it follows that it does not produce existence. Because it is a negation of action, it entails the refutation of the production of the jar or other objects; thus, the cause of destruction is ineffective (*akiñcitkaratva*), since a simple negation consists in the negation of action. Therefore, by what could it be required? By nothing at all, in any effect; this is the meaning. Furthermore, if this negation of action does not produce existence at all, even so, the lack of causality is established, because the agent loses its status as a cause.
Concluding [the argument], he says: "Therefore," and so forth;
since this is so, it is established that an object is by its very nature perishable.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is independent with respect to something is necessarily restricted to that nature; for example, the final causal complex (*antya-kāraṇa-sāmagrī*), being independent with respect to the production of its own effect, is restricted to that nature. And an entity (*bhāva*) is independent with respect to its destruction.
Having thus explained the example, he speaks—beginning with "in the same way"—to elucidate the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*):
"In the very same way," by that same manner, the cause of the arising of an entity such as a jar is non-productive (*akiñcitkara*).
If it is asked, "Why is this so? he says here: "Because it would be the production of what is already produced," and so forth.

The intended meaning here is as follows: just as destruction, being a non-entity (*abhāva*), is subject to an analysis of its difference from that which possesses existence (*bhāva*), so too is production, since there is no distinction between them.

To explain: if production, which is the very nature of an existent thing, were to be produced, then that [existent thing] itself would be produced; consequently, because there is no purpose in producing what is already produced, it would be like the nature of a cause.
By this, it has also been considered that even if [the production] were of the same nature [as the pot],
it would not serve any purpose; for indeed, even if it were something distinct from the existing pot, being produced,
it would not further any objective toward which it does not already depend upon other causes.

In that regard, it should be known as certain because it arises from its own causes; for a causal complex is independent in producing its own effect, just as all things that are born are independent with respect to their own destruction.
— Tattvasaṃgraha, verses 354–55:
Arising is the production of its own effect, determined by its own nature.
It might be thought: "Since these two alternatives lack a basis (*nirālambanatva*), the point at issue is not established by them. To this he says: "Precisely for that reason," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: "Precisely for that reason"—that is, from the very distinction of the immediately preceding alternative, and not from anything else—because even non-existence, let alone arising, is established by its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), the cause of arising is ineffective (*akiñcitkara*).
He considers that if these two alternatives were without a basis, the Buddhist’s desired conclusion would remain unestablished.
He anticipates the opponent's view with the words "prāgabhāvam" and so forth:

Now, what is this so-called prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)? If it is argued that it is the non-existence prior to production, then would it be something other than the lump of clay, or would it be that very same thing? In the first case, since that is the position of the Naiyāyikas and others, it is not the Buddhist's own view; thus, because he is unfamiliar with their doctrine, [the argument fails]. Furthermore, no one can turn a void non-existence into a future entity, for if they could, it would follow that even the son of a barren woman could be produced, and it would also follow that the conceptualization of a material cause (*upādāna*) for an entity is useless.
Therefore, the first position is not tenable.

As for the second position, it was stated that the clay lump itself is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and that [the agent] makes that [lump] into a future entity; however, this is untenable because it is impossible for something already existing to become what it already is.

If, on the other hand, the intended meaning is that [the agent] makes that [clay] into the nature of the absence of a jar, that too is not logical, because the jar would then exist as something distinct from it, resulting in a difference in designation and so forth.
Therefore, the second [alternative] is also not tenable.

As for the response given here—beginning with "prior existence" (*prāgbhāva*) and so forth—that too is examined: what is this "prior existence"? If you mean that the pot existing at a time prior to its destruction is the "prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*), then, since for the Buddhist there is no such thing as a void (tuccha) destruction, of what could there be existence either prior to that or at any other time? Indeed, nothing whatsoever exists prior to the son of a barren woman.

Therefore, it is incorrect to say that "it makes that [pot] non-existent," because non-existence cannot be either distinct from or non-distinct from that [pot], as the aforementioned faults would ensue.

If, on the other hand, it is said that "making it non-existent" means "making it into shards," that is untenable; for that very [pot] would possess the state of being shards, whereas the state of being shards is impossible when the pot has not yet perished. Consequently, this argument amounts to nothing, as it would lead to the absurd conclusion that it is actually producing existence.
Because all effects arise precisely from non-existence,
[the cause] of a lump of clay is the lump of clay itself.
Prior to the state of the lump of clay,
[the effect] exists in relation to the two positions of being either different or non-different [from it].

To this, the following response is provided: Just as for the Buddhist (Saugata), prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) are non-entities (*tuccha*) and do not exist because of their being [mere absences], so too the effect does not exist as something absolutely distinct from its cause; rather, it has been established by [the passage] beginning with *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* 3.14 that the material cause itself becomes the product (*upādeya*).

If it is argued that the cause of arising (*utpādahetu*) is the material cause (*upādāna*), which is the collection of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa-kāraṇakalāpa*), because it brings about the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—the substance in the form of a lump of clay distinct from the jar—making it exist as a jar, producing it as endowed with the modification (*paryāya*) of a jar; then why is the cause of destruction (*vināśahetu*) not likewise accepted? For this very [cause] makes the prior existence of the jar non-existent, rendering it distinct from its own modifications such as the potsherds. This indeed is the Master’s intention.
Furthermore, by the words "yadi punaḥ" and so forth, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*); however, by the words "yadi punaḥ" and so forth, he shows the opposing position (*aparapakṣa*).

The word *yadi* indicates the opponent's intention, while *punaḥ* expresses a deliberation (*vitarka*). Even the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of an entity such as a jar—not only its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—is due to its own inherent nature of perishability, and not from something else such as a mallet. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "like other types of non-existence," that is, like mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Why is that nature [so]? He says: "from its own cause alone. Destruction is an entity in the form of potsherds; it arises from itself because it is a non-existence, just like mutual non-existence. Here, he states the refutation: "in that very same way," and so forth.
In exactly that same manner, the persistence of an entity—its remaining in subsequent moments—is also possible by its own nature, not merely its destruction.

Indeed, it can be argued that the persistence of an entity occurs by its own nature because it is a property of the entity, just like its destruction. Nor is the substratum (dharmin) unestablished here; for the non-distinction [of the preceding moment] from the succeeding moment is well-known, just as there is distinction [between them]. Thus it has been stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*:

Another collection of causes is likewise independent regarding stability; it is stationary because its cause is incapable of acting upon it, since [the cause] cannot produce anything that is either distinct from or non-distinct from it—thus, all [the arguments] are the same.
—Aṣṭaśa° Aṣṭasa° pṛ. 185–86:
The subject (*dharmin*) whose nature is stability is unestablished, just like that which possesses difference.
If both manifestation and disappearance were perceived through the cognition of difference even when there is non-difference,
then [these two] would not be established by the cognition of non-difference in that which is partless; [as stated in] *Nyāyaviniścaya* verse 114.
Therefore, the reason is not unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), nor is the subject (*pakṣa*) sublated by perception and other means of knowledge.

By this, he states that the previous reason is contradictory (*viruddha*): as for what was previously stated, beginning with "prior non-existence" (*prāgbhāvam*), that is incorrect; because if the cause of destruction makes that [entity] non-existent while it is already perishable, what is the use of it? [The entity perishes] by itself.
If, on the contrary, it is the opposite [i.e., it is not perishable], then [making it non-existent] is impossible.
If it is argued that no one is capable of rendering that which is imperishable non-existent, to this he says: "And just as," and so forth.
By the use of the word "just as" (*yathā*), it is understood—even though not explicitly stated—that "in the same way" (*tathā*).
Thus, the connection is as follows: for one's own self, which is unarisen and does not desire to arise, a cause of arising would likewise be ineffective (*akiñcitkara*).
The sense is that the first [moment] arises by itself, whereas the other does not arise even when the causes are present, like the horn of a hare.
He demonstrates this regarding duration as well with the words "of that which endures," and so forth;
thus, everything is the same, in that the cause of duration is ineffective.

He demonstrates this very point: "The independence of an entity with respect to arising, persistence, and destruction is established because it depends on its own nature. If it is argued that even regarding its destruction, [the entity] does not depend on anything else because its own nature is always present—since such is our experience—that is equally true in the other case as well.
And thus:
An entity that, by virtue of a cause of destruction, possesses a non-perishing intrinsic nature.

Every reason (hetu) propounded by another would be a "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī), because it is equal [in force] even with respect to the opponent's position; or else, one might as well construct such a reason oneself.
Now, if arising were without cause, there would necessarily be either eternal existence or eternal non-existence.
As it has been said:
"Existence or non-existence must be eternal, because they do not depend on any other cause;
for it is through dependence [on other factors] that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.34)
If this is argued, [the author] says here: "Certain substances," and so forth.

The word *viśeṣa* (particularity) should be connected individually with each of the terms *dravya* (substance), etc., referring to certain intended particularities of substance, space, time, and intrinsic nature. Having excluded what? Elsewhere, the particle *vā* (or), which occurs in the context of the intended time and so forth, has the sense of "as if" (*iva*) and should be understood immediately after the word *utpāda* (arising).

Therefore, just as arising [is dependent], so too would destruction—being dependent on that [arising] and dependent on other substances—be logically consistent as having those [substances] as its cause; why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no contradiction with our experience," or else, the word should be explained according to its literal placement [in the compound].

Just as destruction, so too arising occurs from itself alone; this is stated against the proponent of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādin) by means of the introduction of the words "certain [things]" and so forth.
And here, the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction;
the remainder is as before.

Even though this is so, because there is no apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) even when an example exists, [the author] has established the probative capacity of all reasons regarding momentary destruction and so forth. Now, establishing that same point due to the absence of an example, he says: "In the living body," etc.; or alternatively, as Arcaṭa stated: "Even in the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for [the reason] 'existence' and so forth, there is probative capacity through exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Having thus performed the refutation, he concludes by saying: "In the living body," etc.

And this subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), which consists in the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), will be explained by [the author] himself later when the occasion arises; thus, through the operation of this subverting proof, the fact that the real entity (*vastu*) which is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has the nature of the proving property (*sādhanadharmasvabhāvatā*) is established—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 44.

Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are non-reasons (*ahetu*) in a living body due to the absence of anvaya (positive concomitance), so too every property such as existence (*sattva*) is a non-reason with respect to anything momentary.

Since everything is included within the categories of the subject (*pakṣa*) and the counter-subject (*vipakṣa*), just as the vital breath and so forth lack anvaya in a living body, so too do properties such as existence and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) lack anvaya even in the case of momentariness.

Indeed, there is no third category apart from momentariness and its opposite wherein a cause could reside, since such [a cause] is not ascertained even in the case of sound. Furthermore, because the successive operations of the palate and other [articulators], the eyes, and oil and so forth are productive of results, the successive nature of sounds and other phenomena is established; thus, their momentariness is determined. Consequently, the mere property of impermanence is established in some cases, precisely because the operation [of the cause] is effective only therein. Therefore, when there is doubt regarding these two very forms [of existence], the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For example: "The living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth.

Indeed, there is no third category other than those with a self and those without a self in which this breath and so forth could reside, since everything is subsumed under the presence or absence of the self's activity.
...it does not follow there, because [the reason] is unestablished even in the case of a single self— *Nyāyabindu* 3.

When the possession of a self (*sātmakatva*) is to be proven in a living body, the reason (*hetu*), such as breath and so forth, is not a valid reason; why? He says: because of the lack of continuity (*niranvaya*), that is, due to the absence of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Likewise, every [reason] such as "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth, which has a nature that is both pure and impure, is a non-reason (*ahetu*) due to the absence of positive concomitance (*niranvayatvāt*).
