This applies when proving momentariness in some particular case, such as sound; or when proving momentariness in some other case; or else, when proving the possession of a self (*sātmakatva*) in a living body, the reason such as "breathing" (*prāṇādi*) is a non-reason because it lacks positive concomitance (*anvayābhāvam prāpya*), just as that which was previously mentioned. It is a non-reason in the same manner—that is, by way of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatirekābhāva*)—as the aforementioned "existence" and so forth;
the rest is as before.
"Purity is the reason [for existence],
qualified by non-distinct attributes because of having an origin," and "it is qualified by distinct attributes because of being produced"—
these two are impure.
It should be observed— while explaining the verse from *Nyāyabindu* 3.9–11, he says: "The thesis," and so forth.

The entire living body is the *pakṣa* (the subject), and the jar and so forth are the *vipakṣa* (the counter-example); since all categories of sentient and insentient things are subsumed within these two, just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth in a living body lack positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) and are devoid of a similar instance (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*), so it is when momentariness is to be proven. The word "api" (also/even) is displaced; it should be understood immediately after "existence, being produced, and so forth," or rather, let the word "api" remain in its original place.
In that case, the meaning is as follows: "even in the case of momentariness"—by the word "api," [it implies] "even in the case of non-momentariness."

"Even there, there is no similar instance (sapakṣa); how then can there be the requirement for positive concomitance (ananvaya)? To this he says: "For indeed," and so forth. Because, when establishing pervasion through existence and the like by means of proving the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with momentariness and its opposite, there is no third category called a "similar instance" (sapakṣa) in which that reason—existence and the like—could reside.
If it is argued that there exists a third category consisting of sound and so forth, the author replies here: "Sound," etc.

By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that this applies not only to the object under dispute, but likewise because existence (*sattva*) and other such properties are not ascertained in the manner of momentariness.
Furthermore, an object whose existence is not thus ascertained cannot serve as an example (*nidarśana*); otherwise, the probandum (*sādhya*) would also [qualify as an example] without distinction.
Furthermore, when sound itself is the probandum as being momentary, then the inclusion of sound together with cognition and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating their similarity;
[that is,] by means of sound, [the momentariness of] cognition and the rest [is established].

Regarding this, another says: "The establishment of the successive natures of sound and so forth—and the determination of their momentariness—follows from the efficacy of successive operations such as those of the palate and other [articulators], the eyes and other [senses], and oil and other [substances]. Showing that this is insubstantial, he says: "Precisely for that reason," and so on.

Since that subsequent operation would be untenable without a successive nature in sound and the rest, because it would be fruitless, for that very reason, mere impermanence—or rather, transformational permanence—is what is to be proven in some cases for the Buddhist, since the operation in question is efficacious therein according to the method already stated.

This is what is meant: by that reasoning, the impermanence of sound and so forth through transformation is established; that illustration is stated because it is not a case of proving what is already proven elsewhere. And since there is thus an absence of a corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta), it was said that this is not to be proven.
If one asks, "What is the point of saying 'this has been stated'?"—it is not so, because the intention is otherwise.

As it was stated by Prajñākara: "When momentariness is to be proven, there is no lack of an example for everything, such as blue and so forth. Whatever appears therein does so as being ultimately real and entering into conventional usage; just as blue appears as blueness and thus enters [into usage], so too does everything appear as momentary. By this, the sublation of the thesis (*pakṣa*) by perception and the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of the reason (*hetu*) are expressed.

Alternatively, since blue and so forth are momentary, there is no distinction [between them and the cognition]; thus, like them, that [cognition] would also possess a spatial remoteness of its own nature (*svabhāvaviprakarṣa*). Consequently, the example lacks both the probandum and the probans.
If that [remoteness] is not admitted in that case, where could the application of the reason (*hetu*) take place? This is demonstrated by the activity of the palate and other [articulatory organs].

It might be argued that, just like momentariness, even [the existence of] blue and so forth [is unproven for us], because for the Buddhist, it is only the mental states of giving and so on that bear the designation of "merit" and "demerit," and since these are objects of the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), they do not possess a spatial remoteness of nature; thus, the example lacks the probans (*sādhanavikalatā*). This is an unlearned statement, because since the fruit is not established at a later time from those [mental states alone], the necessity of admitting something other than them [i.e., a persisting entity] follows.

Now, if it is thought that because merit and demerit are established by all disputants even when their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is remote, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*); that is untenable, because of a failure to understand the context.
For, since [the proof] establishes what is not yet established from that [remote nature], the property to be proven has indeed already been stated.
Now, because the reason is contradictory, that [thesis] cannot be proven; thus he says: "Because of the proof of the undesired.
Just as [the reason] would prove what is undesired—namely, that there is purposefulness for another (pārārthya)—just as one might argue:
"The eyes and other [senses] exist for the sake of another, because they are composite, like the parts of a bed, a seat, or the like."
It is a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of what is intended: namely, that [the subject] is not a composite whole for the sake of another (*asaṃhatapārārthya*).
— *Nyāyabindu* 3.87, 88.
Likewise, the state of being a composite and existence are concomitant with the momentariness of sound.

"The eyes and other [senses] are for the sake of another... [is stated]. This is the objection raised by the opponent: that it is not the case that [the reason] is determined only in the absence of the opposite (vipakṣa), as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).

For whatever depends on various other factors for its existence is restricted to that very state of being, just as the final causal complex is restricted to the production of its own effect. This is the challenge posed to the opponent.

If that were so, then an entity, because it is independent of anything else for its arising at a later time, would be established as necessarily existing at that time; otherwise, what further requirement could there be for an existent thing to remain at a subsequent time, such that its persistence would be merely occasional? Likewise, it is the same in the case of the arising of something about to arise: nothing further needs to be required. Furthermore, if an entity were neither persistent nor about to arise, it would never persist or arise, like a sky-flower.
It is not correct to say that this alone proves its perishability, for there is no distinction in other cases either;
thus, these objects, arising spontaneously as they do, appropriate to themselves, as the case may be, mutual assistance and the conferring of excellence,
such that when something perishes due to some cause, another entirely different thing is born.
Now, if there were a cessation without any continuity (*niranvaya-nivṛtti*), for what would there be the arising of an effect produced by a cause?

Since this would establish the undesired impermanence of transformation (*pariṇāmānityatva*), and because all causes are observed in that very [process], it is not something to be proven; furthermore, the proof is futile—this is the remainder [of the argument]—because that for whose sake the proof was employed is not established, and thus the undesired consequence is proven. By the words "for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*) and so forth, he establishes the agency of the eyes and other organs through their state of being composite (*saṃhatatva*); for by that same mode of observation, [the conclusion follows].

What is it? He says: "Being-for-another" (pārārthya). Of what nature is it? It is undesirable [to the opponent]. That which is intended by the Sāṃkhya to prove as a composite entity would indeed establish a composite entity; having thus established an example well-known to the opponent, he establishes the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika): "In the same way, sattva, in its pure and other forms, would establish what is undesirable"—this is the connection.
What kind of being is it? To this he says: "Sound," etc.
He clarifies the meaning of the verse [beginning with] "The eyes and so forth are for the sake of another" by means of the passage beginning with "The eyes and so forth."
"Why is this so? To this he says: "For indeed," and so forth.
Because the determination of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) occurs only in the case of transformation (*pariṇāma*), which is the very counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

Now, the opponent objects: "Even if the determination of 'being produced' occurs only there [in the case of transformation], nevertheless, it does not follow that it is pervaded by that [transformation], because inference establishes a pervasion with its opposite."
Demonstrating that very point, he says: "Whatever state... and so forth.

If it is asked, "But was not all of this already stated previously in the passage beginning with 'of arising, duration, and destruction' (utpādasthitibhaṅgānām)? For what purpose is it stated again?"—the answer is: True, it was stated; however, there is a distinction: previously, this [destruction] was presented as an independent cause of destruction, whereas now, its necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, by virtue of its being perishable (*nāśitva*), is being established. This is the division.

Alternatively, by pointing out that the reason "because of the determination [of the property] only in the counter-example" (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the opponent himself, he refutes that very point. This is the intended meaning of the phrase "this objection has been raised by the opponent. Regarding the expression *yadbhāva*: the state of a thing is its "being that" (*yadbhāva*). That thing which is independent with respect to that state is necessarily determined to have that state. The second occurrence of the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to what was previously mentioned. He provides an illustration for this, beginning with the words "just as," and so forth.

And this is both "final" and a "causal totality"; thus, that totality, being independent with respect to the production of its own effect, is necessarily restricted to its existence—that is, necessarily restricted to the production of its own effect.
He states the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) with the words "In the same way," etc., which is easy to understand.
The word "cecc" (if) indicates the opponent's intention;
here he states the reply: "existence," and so forth.
This term "existence" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which "being produced" (*kṛtaka*) is also included.

Because it is independent with respect to both duration at another time and arising, its existence would be established as necessarily determined by that—namely, as necessarily determined by duration at another time and by arising.
He states the refutation should this not be accepted: "Otherwise, the non-existence of perishability would not be established from this reason, because the reason would be inconclusive.

By this he shows the following: just as existence and so forth are contradictory to momentariness because they are ascertained only in the counter-example (vipakṣa), so too the reason "because of independence"—which establishes the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of that [perishability] with something else—is ascertained in that very same [counter-example], without distinction.
The adversary itself is the position itself.
Because it does not depend on anything else for its existence, [the reason] resides only in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) in some respect regarding permanence.

It might be thought: "The claim that [the entity] is independent with respect to its duration at another time and its production is unproven; for since the entity is necessarily bound to exist, it must be dependent with respect to those two.
To this he provides the reply: "Of an existing object," and so forth.

The meaning is: for an existing (*sat*) object—that is, one currently present and capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*)—what could possibly be required again (*punah*), in the sense of a deliberation (*vitarka*), for its production or its duration at a subsequent time? Nothing whatsoever.

Because there would be a fault in either the production or the destruction of an existing entity—whether that [production] be its own inherent nature or something else—and for this reason it was stated, "of an existing entity. For, if there were a dependence on something else such that its persistence were occasional, then likewise, in the case of the arising of an entity about to arise in that very same manner, there would be nothing at all to depend upon, from which a dependence could result in an occasional arising.
This follows from the recurrence of the phrase "from which" (*yataḥ*) and so forth;
thus he considers that this [argument] applies equally to destruction as well.

If it is argued that "the reason is unestablished because, even in the absence of this [external] thing to be depended upon, there is a dependence on the nature of being stationary (*sthāsnu*) or about to arise (*utpitsu*), and since this [nature] is never present, the reason fails," to this he says: "If, however," and so forth.

If an entity (*bhāva*), such as a living being (*jīva*) and the like, were to be either stationary or about to arise, it would never remain stationary nor would it ever arise, just like a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*).

If it is argued: "Since it both persists and arises, its nature is such that non-dependence regarding its existence actually proves its perishability alone—because there is no sublation by perception and so forth—and not a nature of persistence and arising, as that would be the opposite," to this he says: "Not indeed," and so on.
For (*hi*) because non-dependence regarding its existence proves only perishability and nothing else, [the claim] is not *samajjasa*, i.e., not logically tenable.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction"—that is, because there is an absence of difference even in other cases where the probandum is yet to be established; for in those cases as well, he considers that there is an absence of sublation by perception and the other means of knowledge, [the nature of which is] arising and persistence.
Because of the existence of a sublation,

with respect to that which is to be proven— the produced thing whose nature consists of arising and abiding, and which has the form of arising and abiding as its essential character— [there is a contradiction].
By way of a summary, demonstrating the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the opponent’s reason, he says "that" and so forth:

Since this is so, therefore it is logical that these objects perceived through direct perception—such as living beings (*jīva*) and the rest—while arising by their own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*), that is, by their very essence, and while proceeding toward a subsequent form without abandoning the previous form (through a process of non-abandonment), appropriate them to themselves; is this not so?
He asks: "What is it? [The answer is: "The imparting of excellence (*atiśayādhāna*), which is the establishment of capacity (*yogyatāsthāpana*)."

How so? He says: "according to their respective application" (*yathāyogam*). "Application" (*yoga*) refers to the connection with the auxiliary causes of production and destruction; [the process occurs] without overstepping that.
How so? He says: "mutual assistance" (*parasparopakāram*).

The analysis of the compound is either: "that in which there is assistance to the material cause (*upādāna*) by means of the mutual auxiliary," or "that by which there is assistance to the auxiliary by means of this [material cause]."

Thus, by this [argument], it has been stated that since a produced entity (bhāva) or a conditioned thing (kṛtaka) is dependent both upon its arising and upon its destruction, the lack of dependence on its existence for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of that entity is unproven. Now, as for what was said—"those objects arise spontaneously of their own accord"—that is incorrect. If it is argued that when some preceding thing is destroyed by something, another entirely different thing arises, to this he replies: "Now... and so forth.

Now, one might object: "If there were a cessation without any continuity (*niranvaya-nivṛtti*), that is, an absolute non-existence, how could the production of an effect—brought about by causes and non-causes—occur for any cause at all? For that would lead to the contingency of a lack of causal regularity (*aniyama*). To this, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: the abandonment of the previous form and the assumption of the subsequent form occur in a manner that does not exclude each other; rather, it arises precisely while maintaining its state of permanence (*dhrauvyatva*). (Page 1, Note 9)
The meaning is that the reason— namely, "because the destruction of the cause does not depend on anything else by means of grasping"— is unestablished (*asiddha*).

How, then, does the production of an effect occur from a modification? To this he says: "beginningless and endless," and so forth—"the substance is beginningless and endless, [yet] it is about to arise, it is stable, and it is perishable."
"It would evolve from itself or from another, sequentially, in the nature of cause and effect. (The latter half of the verse is extracted from *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Vol.

2, p. 414). If everything that exists were not characterized by origination and persistence at all times, it might as well never exist even momentarily, like the horn of a donkey. Therefore, it is logical that this [reality], constantly evolving through the nature of prior and subsequent transformations, manifests every moment with three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*). By conceptualizing within itself the arrangement of cause and effect, it becomes the recipient of the designation "cause" and "effect" in relation to others, because its opposing natures are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*).

Being non-existent, it is without beginning or end—that is, without beginning and without end. If it were to have a beginning, then in the absence of a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) for the effect, even an auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) would be ineffective.

Nor can it be asserted that at one time the production of an effect occurs without a material cause, while at another time it is otherwise; for such a thing is never observed, and the determination of reality follows what is actually observed.

And how, for those who speak thus, can there be an inference of a material cause from the observation of an effect? Because doubt would never cease regarding anything, the practical activity [of the world] would be destroyed.
On the other hand, if there were finitude [to existence], there would be the cessation of the entire continuum;
this will be examined in the *Jīvasiddhi*.
But what is it that is thus constituted? To this he says: "Substance" (*dravya*).

Nor should this objection be raised: "What is that [substance] apart from form (*rūpa*) and the rest? For this has been established by such statements as *Pratibhāsaikyaniyama* (Siddhiviniścaya 1.10) and so forth.
Furthermore, as to what that [universe] is like, he says "that" (tat) and asks: "Is it about to arise, stable, or perishable? and so forth.
What should it do? He says: "How would it evolve?"—in what manner? "In the nature of cause and effect," such as the essence of a lump of clay and a jar, and so on.
The meaning is that, in every respect, there is an absence of a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) for the production of something new;
[this is] from the material cause.

In the fourth section, it is stated that if one accepts total destruction without any continuity (*niranvayavināśa*), there would be an absence of the conventional discourse regarding cause and effect.
The intention of the doubt is that there is no substance distinct from its qualities (*guṇa*).

[Objection: But surely the *pradhāna* evolves (*vivartate*) into the form of effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), and not into the form of its own cause, because of the statement in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*: "Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is unevolved" (SK 3). [Reply: No; for if the nature of producing transformations such as the Great Principle were not occasional, there would be no cessation of that [evolution]. Consequently, neither Kapila nor anyone else could be liberated. If, on the other hand, it is thought that the cessation occurs due to the absence of contact with Kapila and others, that too is not tenable; for when the cause is complete, the effect necessarily follows.

Now, if that very nature [of the effect] arises only through contact with that [cause] and did not exist previously, then alas, how can it be the *mūlaprakṛti* (primordial nature)? To this, the Sāṃkhya replies: "It is appropriate [to call it primordial] because it consists of cause and effect"; for the *pradhāna* has not arisen from any other cause, since it is eternal.
If it were eternal and not an effect, there would be the constant production of effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth; [thus,
it is the individual self].
There is an absence of the production of effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) with respect to Kapila and others,
even when there is contact with the eternal cause called Pradhāna.
If its nature is the production of effects and it is unchanging, how can it be said to be eternal?
By this, the doctrine of the Vaiśeṣikas and others is also considered.
At the very moment that a substance possesses the nature of a cause, it simultaneously possesses the nature of an effect.

However, there is this distinction: some maintain that while everything exists everywhere at all times, there is sometimes the manifestation of one thing and the non-manifestation of another; to such a person, he replies: "By way of succession" (*kramāt*), meaning by relying upon a sequence. Otherwise, as in the case of the left and right horns of a cow, there could be no designation of cause and effect.
Since this objection remains unresolved even if one accepts the relationship between the manifested and the manifester,
does the Sāṃkhya, relying on the Sāṃkhya doctrine, maintain that everything exists everywhere?
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p.

180. Because there can be no relationship of cause and effect between two things that exist simultaneously, [the world] manifests in that form, but [in fact] it is by its own nature alone; thus say the proponents of the non-duality of Puruṣa and so forth: "This is indeed Puruṣa" (*Ṛgveda* 10.90.2).
2 From such statements as these,

that which arises is dependent on another (*parataḥ*) and is perishable, because of the contradiction of an action [acting] upon itself and because of the absence of its own nature at the time of its arising.

Some [opponents] claim that [an entity] perishes only from another cause and not from itself, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its destruction at all times. To them, he says: the connection is "it might transform from itself or from another.

If, due to a lack of the inherent nature (svabhāva) to transform in such a way, it does not transform even from another cause—just like a donkey's horn—then this very point has already been stated [in the verse]: "And this object, desiring to arise," and so forth.
If one were to deny that transformation occurs from another [cause], there would be a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge;
for [the scripture states]: "The Person alone is this, whatever has been and whatever is to be, existing in the form of cause and effect."
And he is the lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food—
Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.15.
The Buddhists hold that the connection is "it does not arise from itself," and the connection is "it perishes by its very own nature."
The Naiyāyikas and others—
this was stated from the perspective of the Naiyāyika school—
support the claim that "substance is about to arise," and so forth, by means of the passage beginning with "yadi" (if).

If that [entity] were not at all times characterized by origination as long as it exists—even for a single moment—it would not exist in such a manner of being characterized by origination; yet it does so exist. Therefore, we consider it to be characterized by origination at all times.
By this, he shows that the discussion regarding the final moment is exhausted.

[Objection: Suppose indeed that an entity is characterized by origination only occasionally; what does that matter to it, such that it would have to be characterized by that [nature] at all times? [Reply: In that case, one could no longer infer that because it is perceived as momentary at some time, it is always thus.
The remainder has been discussed here:
if that which consists of persistence did not exist at all times, it would not exist even once;
yet it does exist as such, since its existence is established through cognition.

Consequently, the claim that "it is always of that nature" is refuted. As for what was stated by Prajñākaragupta—"In the case of [objects] such as a jar or a gift, their persistence over time exists during the state of perception, but not at other times because of the contrary"—how so? Because it would follow that unperceived things such as knowledge and the like could not establish their intended nature;
furthermore, the establishment of reality in accordance with what is perceived is the same elsewhere, as in the case of a donkey’s horn—this is the illustration for both cases.
Pointing out that this [rule] does not apply elsewhere, he says "tathā" and so forth.

Its separate mention is for the sake of illustration, because it is already established for the opponent; the distinction is that for the Naiyāyikas and others, this is for the purpose of proving the thesis (*sādhya*), whereas previously it was for the purpose of illustration.

Since this is so, therefore, everything that exists—which is constantly evolving through the nature of prior and subsequent transformations, moment by moment, at every instant—possesses three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), namely arising, persistence, and cessation; thus, the connection is that "everything is characterized by these three."
What does it do while doing what? To this he says: "The determination of cause and effect," and so forth.

The worldly convention regarding cause and effect is that the preceding is the cause and the succeeding is the effect. By this [statement], whatever was asserted by someone—that the effect comes first and the cause comes later—is refuted; for it would be subverted by common consensus, just as in the case of the argument: "A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being" (*Nyāyapraveśa*, p. 2).
Alternatively, [the opponent might argue that] the very nature of cause and effect is those various distinct states or conditions;
thus, the produced (*janya*) and the producer (*janaka*) are simply the essential nature itself. This is refuted by the following:

how so? By conceptualizing [the relationship], one perceives the state of being produced and producer within oneself, in one's own essential nature. By thereby imagining that such an arrangement is merely conceptual (*kālpinikatva*), it is said to be "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*).
Since even specific qualities such as blue or pleasure appear as conceptual constructions, non-duality (*advaita*) would likewise be so;
thus, the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) is the same in both cases.
For it has been stated that nothing devoid of prior and subsequent transformations ever appears in a perceptual cognition.
Since there is no such moment from which the arising of the subsequent moment does not occur, the very absence of a final moment would constitute the inference that existence,
being of the nature of arising,
is indeed momentary.
When Devadatta, who is stable and characterized by persistence, is not seen, at that time—

The sense is that if the nature of a thing is established only for what has been perceived, then the nature intended to be the form of the appearance— which is unperceived and unseen— would remain unestablished,
as in the case of Devadatta and others.

Just as for the horn of a donkey—which is empty of an intrinsic nature such as arising—the proponent of real causes (bhāvikāraṇavādin) [holds] that through wisdom there is no effect without the prior existence of a cause; likewise, it is necessarily the case that there is no cause without the other-nature (parabhāva) of the effect. Thus, the basis for the relationship of cause and effect is the same for both, and therefore, between the two, there exists a mutual relationship of cause and effect.
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 28.
An example of that which contradicts worldly consensus (*lokaviruddha*) is: "A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell or mother-of-pearl"—*Nyāyapraveśaka*, p.
2; *Parīkṣāmukha*, 6.
That which is the view of the proponents of non-duality regarding the systematic arrangement of cause and effect.
Speaking thus, he is indeed devoid of discernment and merely consisting of conceptual construction.
Alternatively, it has been stated that the view—that the states of a persisting entity are absolutely distinct—is untenable.

It is logical that when there exists another continuum (*santānāntara*) acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), the [entity] becomes designated as the "effect," while the beneficiary [of that cooperation] becomes designated as the "cause.
But why is everything that exists of such a nature? To this, he says: "The adversary," and so forth.

Stasis (*sthiti*) has the nature of being the opposite of arising (*utpāda*); because it is inseparable from that [arising], for the Naiyāyikas and others, it is not a separate category of entity from the arising that constitutes the nature of a thing.
Regarding an object capable of being assisted, there exist both the beneficiary (*upakārya*) and the benefactor (*upakāraka*); for this very reason, they consist of cause and effect.
If one asks, "Why is this so? he says here: "From substance," and so forth.
And it has been stated: "Being non-different from their own substance and yet mutually distinct,
they emerge and submerge like waves in water."
This was also stated by Deva himself elsewhere, as follows:
"From its own substance... (*Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 370; *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa*, p. 432).
Qualities and modes are perceived as being either conceptual or non-conceptual by the intellect;
they are in some sense non-different from the possessor of qualities, whether they be color-form and so forth, or pleasure and so forth, whether perceived simultaneously or sequentially.
Thus it is established.

Furthermore, regarding this [objection]: "If the conjunction of atoms is admitted to involve a division of spatial directions (*digvibhāga*), then they would necessarily have six parts; if they were partless, there would be no differentiation of accumulation (*pracaya*) because of their mutual interpenetration"; to this, the answer is given:

by the word *dravyāt* (from substance), he negates the absolute [view] that qualities and modes (*guṇaparyāya*) are [identical to] the substance; by the phrase *abhinnāśca* (and non-different), he negates the absolute difference between those [qualities/modes] and their possessor (*tadvat*); by the phrase *vyāvṛttāśca* (and distinct), he negates the Sāṃkhya doctrine; and by the phrase *parasparaṃ vā bhinnā vyāvṛttāśca* (or mutually different and distinct), as well as *svasmāt* (from themselves), he [negates the view] that everything possesses both forms. (Pramāṇavārttika 3)

181. Thus, qualities such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth are co-existent with the soul (*jīva*); form (*rūpa*) and so forth belong to matter (*pudgala*); and modifications (*paryāya*), such as pleasure and pain, as well as [the stages of a clay object] like the *śivaka* and so forth, are perceived and determined by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).
Since these are established through cognition, their status as mere mental constructs (*kālpānika*) is refuted.
This refutes the Sāṃkhya doctrine, which asserts the non-difference [of qualities] from substance.
He refutes the objection raised by Dharmakīrti regarding the living being, the clay, and the person (pudgala).
The connection is that [the author] refutes [this].

To one who says, "I do not believe it even after seeing it, because it does not stand to reason," he provides an illustration: "like conceptualization and non-conceptualization of the intellect" (dhīvikalpāvikalpavat);
this means that it is like the conceptualization and non-conceptualization of the intellect (dhiyaḥ).

Just as two conceptual forms (*vikalpa-ākārau*) are perceived as both distinct and non-distinct from the cognition (*dhiyaḥ sakāśāt*), so too are the [subjective] entities (*prakṛtāḥ*) [non-distinct] from their own substance (*svadravyāt*). By this, he demonstrates his abandonment of his own position to one who is clever at harsh scrutiny—namely, the Naiyāyika and others—for whom no such illustrative example has been stated, since they accept the establishment of substance and so forth by the force of direct perception (*pratīti-bala*). Alternatively, the two conceptual forms belonging to the cognition exist in a manner similar to those [two types of forms] through their own distinctions and non-distinctions, namely: [distinction/non-distinction] with respect to their own delusive and non-delusive aspects, their doubt-free and doubt-filled aspects, their visible and non-visible aspects, their graspable and non-graspable aspects, and their blue and non-blue aspects. Thus it is "like that" (*tadvat*).
This has been extracted from the *Aṣṭaśatī* and the *Aṣṭasāhasrī*, page 234:
"The qualities and modes belong to those who maintain the doctrine of absolute [identity]."
Explaining the verse from the perspective of the Naiyāyikas and others, he says: "From the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*),

those qualities such as color-form (*rūpa*) or pleasure (*sukha*)— which are in some way not entirely distinct from it— are perceived simultaneously at one time, as established by examined means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
What do they do? He says: "In succession," and so forth.
The intended meaning is that because it conforms to what is observed, the reality [of the sequence] is established at all times.
Showing that [the result] comes even from one who does not accept that [sequence], he says: "In that way," and so forth.
Here too, the explanation should be provided by connecting the words "in this sequence" and so forth.
Concluding the present topic, he says: "That is established," and so on.

Now, one might object: there is indeed the appearance in the intellect of a single gross entity consisting of various parts, qualities, and modes; yet it is not logical for that to be a single whole (*avayavin*) or a single possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), because it cannot withstand critical analysis.
Demonstrating that very point, he says: "As for this," and so forth—the remainder being that which was stated by the opponent as a refutation of the aforementioned object of knowledge (*prameya*).
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates another argument; this is being presented because, since the gross is invariably concomitant with the subtle, it has been said [to refer to] atoms (*paramāṇu*).

And those [atoms] produce that [conjunction] only by depending upon conjunction, not otherwise, because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Keeping in mind that this conjunction must occur either "by one part" or "in its entirety," since there is no other possibility, he states the refutation of the first position: "By the division of directions," and so forth. If conjunction is accepted as occurring through the division of directions—that is, the East and so on—then the consequence of having six parts (*ṣaḍaṃśatā*) follows; for, because they would possess parts, they would not even be atoms, just like a jar or similar objects. This is what he intends.

Regarding the second position, he says this: if the partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) of atoms is accepted, then because they would interpenetrate one another, there could be no differentiation through aggregation (*pracaya*), nor any differentiation of aggregates (*skandha*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). As it has been said therein: "In that case, by virtue of the distinction of spatial directions, atoms would have six parts;
otherwise, the mass would be the size of a single atom, and they would not be objects of cognition."
Refuting this [view] stated in *Nyāyaviniścaya* 1.86, he says: "In this regard," and so forth.
In this regard, the response to the prima facie argument is stated—the ellipsis being "is said":
because of simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts;
and because the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be no larger than a single atom.
—Vijñānaviṃśikā, verse 12;
Catuḥśataka, p. 48;
Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 203.
"Without [something] in between, it does not exist," thus it is "invariably concomitant" (nāntarīyaka), meaning "not existing without [the other]" (avinābhāvī);
[this refers to] atoms [being invariably concomitant with] a composite whole.
The conjunction of atoms through spatial division.

Since all [atoms] are conjoined with atoms situated in the six directions, they must have six parts according to the distinction of spatial divisions; otherwise, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom, and they would not be objects of cognition. (Nyāyaviniścaya 1.86)
Even without the words *yathā* and *tathā*, by superimposing them [onto the verse], the *kārikā* is explained by relying on the poetic figure *prativastūpamā* (simile based on a parallel):
"A moment situated in the midst of moments does not abandon its partlessness;
likewise, an atom situated in the midst [of others] likewise increases through accumulation. (21)

Even in the case of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), if cognition—which exists between its own cause and effect—possessed parts, it would follow that there are infinite moments, because [the process] would be completed by that much alone, rendering the postulation of anything else beyond it useless. Furthermore, if [parts] were to enter [one another], the world would, without exception, exist as a single moment.
On the other hand, if atoms were somehow partless, there could still be a distinction in their accumulation due to the absence of mutual penetration.
Regarding the sequence: that being so,

just as [consciousness] stands within a moment of consciousness— that is, it stands in the interval, the space between those two moments which consist of the nature of consciousness and stand in the relation of cause and effect— it is therefore "standing therein" (tatstha).

Who is this? He says: the *kṣaṇa* (moment) is a part that is the effect of what precedes it and the cause of what follows it; yet even that is of the very nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), because nothing else exists apart from it. What does it do? He says: it does not abandon, it does not relinquish—what? He says: "partlessness" (*niraṃśatām*). For a partless entity, the conceptual alternatives of [abandoning] "in its entirety" or "by a single part" are impossible, according to the principle that it simply remains there. Likewise, even the atom (*aṇu*), even the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*)—not only the moment of consciousness—standing in the middle, does not abandon partlessness; such is the connection [of the words].

What is established from this? He says: "From that, there would be an increase in accumulation. From that principle, there would be an increase in spatial accumulation as well, just like the increase in temporal accumulation; the word "would be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied.
This is because there is no causal relationship between the accumulated [atoms] themselves.

What is meant is this: is the moment situated in the middle of the consciousness-moment separated from the preceding and succeeding moments, or is it contiguous? First, it cannot be the former alternative; for the ancient Buddhists do not accept such a thing, since they maintain that only moments characterized by contiguity can stand in the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*).

Even for those such as Prajñākaragupta and others who accept [the existence of atoms], what is the basis for the distinction that it is only the unmixed moments (*asaṃsṛṣṭa-kṣaṇa*) that perform their own function, and not the atoms? Here too, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is difficult to avoid.
Therefore, it is not logical to imagine conjunction (*saṃyoga*) in the production of effects by atoms and then contemplate the faults based upon it.

Since the causal relationship between the mind of waking and the mind of awakening—which stand in the relation of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*)—is denied when there is an interval, as if they were eternal, that doctrine is not well-established.
Furthermore, there can be no intervention between those two [moments] by way of non-existence (*abhāva*) nor by way of time (*kāla*), because neither is admitted.
For this very reason, there is no intervention by cognitions of the same class (*sajātīya-vijñāna*), because such is not admitted during states such as deep sleep.
If there were intervention by cognitions of a different class (*vijātīya*), it would not be "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

Or, let there be an interval between them; even so, if they are again separated from one another and from those two minds, that same objection and that same answer apply, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that must be applied individually like spreading across the expanse of the sky.
When the second alternative—that they are without interval (*nirantara*)—is reached, it was stated in general terms that "the moment (*kṣaṇa*) stands between the preceding and succeeding moments."
That too is not tenable because of the same fault as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
We perceive that "proximity" (*nairantarya*) is merely a difference in terminology for "conjunction," not a difference in meaning.

Others, however, think: "There is neither proximity nor its opposite between all cognitions; so how can there be such faults as 'this is a moment' or 'this is a non-moment'? Therefore, those whose intellectual forms have been crushed by the broad-headed mallet of that [objection]—what indeed are they establishing by way of "this-ness" or "not-this-ness"? This is merely something trivial.
That a single cognition should appear as variegated all at once, rather than through a perception of succession and so forth— this is an extremely profound point [of the system].
According to the ancient Buddhists,
other atoms arise from the connection with different objects.
"You have stated that those [atoms] when accumulated are indeed the cause for the arising of cognition;
and that specific quality (viśeṣa) of atoms does not exist without other atoms. — *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.125.
Are atoms uncombined?
Conjunction is based on whether it occurs with its entire essence or by way of a single part. This is the basis for [the inquiry into] conjunction.

The waking consciousness that exists prior to sleep and the awakened consciousness of one who has risen after sleep— between these two, there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect according to the view of Prajñākaragupta, who maintains that there is an absence of cognition during the state of sleep;
just as there is no relationship of cause and effect between eternal entities, so it is here with respect to the waking and awakened consciousnesses.
To claim that objects distinct from consciousness are in immediate proximity is a source of ridicule.

But another says: "Cognition is perceived only as it is; it is neither prior nor subsequent. Therefore, how can it be said that 'the moment stands between two moments'? This person, too, does not act with reason, because such a claim cannot withstand scrutiny. For instance, since there is no existence of cognition apart from blue and other objects—just as there is none apart from Brahman—and since blue and the rest are variegated (*citratvāt*), one does not simultaneously perceive a single variegation consisting of blue and the rest.
The proponent of Brahman, possessing ordinary intellect, does not hold that the diversity of pleasure and so forth occurs sequentially;
for him, there is neither a prior cause nor a subsequent effect.

Regarding the reading "due to the absence of moments" (*kṣaṇānāmabhāvāt*) or "the moment situated between two moments" (*kṣaṇamadhyasthaḥ*), the meaning here is as follows: the insentient [object] such as blue and its form, and the sentient [subject] whose nature is the cognition thereof—being indeed sentient—the "moment" (*kṣaṇaḥ*) or that which is "like a moment" (*kṣaṇa iva*) stands between those two, whether they be insentient or sentient, or even between those very two existing as cause and effect; it does not abandon its partlessness (*niraṃśatām*) even in the slightest degree (*aṇurapi*).
The remainder is as before.
To clarify the verse, he says "vijñapti" and so forth;

the meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is that this applies not only to the Sautrāntika school, but also to the doctrine of "cognition-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), which maintains that the object of knowledge is internal.
Regarding the word "jñānasya" (of knowledge), the particle *api* (also) should be understood as elided here; thus, it refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*) as well.

Of what nature is that [ignorance]? It is "that which abides between its own cause and its fruit" (*svahetuphalamadhyavarttin*). This means that its nature is to abide in the interval between whatever is its own cause and whatever is its own fruit. Furthermore, if one were to admit that even an atom abiding between six other atoms possesses parts (*sāṃśatva*), then because of the consequence that it would occupy multiple moments (*tatkṣaṇaprasaṅga*), it would follow that it is completed by that much alone—merely by the consequence of infinite moments—since there would be no purpose for a beginningless and endless continuum. This is what is intended.

The futility of postulating other moments: the postulation of those moments other than those infinite moments [already considered] is useless. For instance—even if a moment situated in the middle of them resides within its own part, there is still the postulation of another part; and while that [first part] exists, there is again the postulation of something else. Furthermore, when considering the presence of an interval, one must consider that very same consequence. Let those whose intellects are adept at investigation examine whether this [process] is possible or not in the case of co-existent moments belonging to other continua (*svasantāna*).

If [this] were possible, for what reason would only atoms (*paramāṇu*) be the object of cognition? Showing the refutation regarding their partlessness (*niraṃśatva*), he says: "penetration" (*anupraveśa*), etc.;
the word "of cognition" (*jñānasya*) is understood from the previous context.

If penetration is admitted—either of that [cognition] into those [atoms], or of those [atoms] into it, or of both into each other—then [the consequence is] "again," which indicates an alternative position.
The world would exist for only a single moment; what kind [of world]? "Without succession" (*niṣparyāya*), meaning devoid of sequential variation (*paryāya*).
By this, he demonstrates the refutation of all the tenets of both the Sautrāntika and Yogācāra schools.

Even for one who accepts the position of Prajñākaragupta, it has been stated: "Since there is no denial that cognition occurs sequentially—just as there is simultaneous apprehension of a variegated object—there is no contradiction with perception regarding the [cognition] of an atom. Thus, [the objection against] the cognition of an atom [is refuted].
Because there is a cognition of variegation between the preceding and succeeding moments that exist within a single instant.

With the words "If, however," etc., he raises the objection of another's view: "If, however, in some way or by some means, [it] is desired [to exist], even though it is partless"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the absence of penetration.
To that, he gives the reply: "In that case, of atoms," and so forth.

"In that way," meaning by that manner, "there would be a difference in the accumulation"—that is, a specific arrangement—of atoms, which are the insentient subtle parts that initiate the jar; this is the connection with what has preceded.
Here, the illustration is "sequence" and so forth.
Showing what is established when this is the case, he says: "When that is so," and so on.
That being the case—
those atoms, which have not abandoned their spherical nature and possess multiplicity and visibility, directly assume a self that is the opposite of those [qualities] through conjunctions. (22)

The atoms, having broken through their spherical dimension (*pārimaṇḍalya*), are observed to have themselves attained a single gross nature due to such a transformation; for it is not so when they have not thus transformed, as that would involve a contradiction. This being the case, those which have not abandoned their spherical dimension, partlessness, plurality, and invisibility are described as such; and these are the atoms (*aṇavaḥ*).
What do they do? To this he says: "That," and so forth.

They "bear"—that is, they accept—as their own nature (ātman) or essence that which is the opposite of those [qualities], namely, that which is contrary to sphericity, manifoldness, and invisibility; in other words, that which is composed of parts and is visible.
By what means? He says: by conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), that is, by uninterrupted successions (*nairantarya*), directly (*añjasā*), meaning from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).

By the phrase "not abandoning sphericity" (*atyaktapārimaṇḍalya*), he refutes the notion that, like a jar, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because the constituent parts (*parāvayava*) of that [sphericity] would themselves possess parts. By the expression "not abandoning multiplicity" (*atyaktanānātva*), he indicates that the whole (*avayavin*) is partless (*niraṃśa*). By the statement "not abandoning invisibility," he shows that no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies to what is perceived. By the term "atoms" (*aṇavaḥ*), he refers to the views that "primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the cause" and "the person (*puruṣa*) is the cause," as these are the opposites of his position. Thus, from atoms, atoms themselves arise in immediate proximity as visible objects. By the word "self" (*ātmānam*), he refers to the system of the Vaiśeṣikas and others; by the word "directly" (*añjasā*), he indicates that [those systems] are merely conceptual constructs (*kalpitatva*).
The atomic dimension is eternal in atoms and the internal organ;
its name is "spherical" (pārimaṇḍalya).
For instance: "The atoms are spherical; their state is sphericity (*pārimaṇḍalya*), which is precisely that dimension" (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 473). Sphericity is the most minimal of all dimensions.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, *Kanda* section— page 133;
"Sphericity is the dimension of the atom"
— *Saptapadārthī-ṭīkā*, page 49.
Muktā-śloka 15:
Even for the Sāṃkhya, [this applies] to the skull, the female skull-bearer, and so forth.
The connection with the preceding [verb] is "he refutes the proponents of Brahman.

Now, from what source are atoms established, such that this could be the case? Certainly not from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is no appearance of them therein, and because [the opponent] himself does not admit it.
That is not tenable—for here, as stated in the *Hetubindu* (p. 54), the causal relation is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*);
therefore, it cannot be established even by inference, since that [inference] does not apply when its basis, perception, is absent.

Nor can it be established through the absence of the effect, as in the case of the sense organs; for even when other causes are present, there is no absence of any particular effect that would necessarily fail to arise in their absence, since we observe the production of such a jar from a gross lump of clay itself.
The comprehension of positive and negative concomitance is achieved through perception and non-perception...—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p.
183; [this refers to] inference preceded by perception.

Just as one might argue that if the sense faculty did not exist, then the cognition of form and so forth would not occur, so too: if atoms did not exist, from what would effects such as jars arise? Thus, in the absence of atoms, the gross [object] [could not exist].

Furthermore, as for this argument: "Whatever is gross is produced from causes of small dimension, just like a cloth; and since effects such as the *aṣṭāṇuka* (eight-atom aggregate) are gross, they must have causes of small dimension"—this establishes the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*). This is without substance, because something is called "gross" only in relation to something "subtle," and no form exists beyond the *aṣṭāṇuka* that could serve as a point of reference by which the *aṣṭāṇuka* might be considered gross.

If it is argued that its establishment [is proven] from this very [fact], then from what is this established? If you say "from that," there is a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): for only when that other [substance] of such a nature is established can the grossness of this [effect] be established from it, and from this [grossness] the establishment of that [other substance follows].

Likewise, since the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) must be smaller in dimension than its effect, and its [cause] must be smaller still, it is understood that the first effect is composed of atoms whose dimensions are unsurpassed. — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 224.
A subtle entity is subtler than that which is gross, namely the octad (aṣṭāṇuka).

And as for the other [argument]: "Whatever is gross, when divided, is seen to have parts, such as a jar; and since the eightfold atom (*aṣṭāṇuka*) is gross, it too must be divided until one reaches the indivisible limit"—this is how its existence is established. This too is a flawed statement. If you say: "Because beyond the division of the eightfold atom nothing further exists, due to a lack of evidence, therefore the atom is not established," we reply: regarding the *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom)...

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Just as the ultimate limit of the magnitude of consciousness is established through the excellence of the increase of magnitude, so too is the ultimate limit of the smallness of the person (*pudgala*) established through the scope of its decrease.
The formulation is: The decrease of magnitude reaches its ultimate limit in some instance, because it possesses gradation (*atiśaya*), like the excellence of that [consciousness].

Furthermore, the example is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); otherwise, the non-existence of an omniscient being and so forth would be contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇabādhita*).

Just as the attainment of the ultimate limit of consciousness is established through the observation of its progressive excellence, or just as the nature of "measure" is proven to exist in the form of an immensely great measure,

so too, the state of being increasingly smaller among the causes of causes of jars and other objects must rest somewhere, because it is expressed by comparative terms such as "more" and "most. That in which it rests are the atoms (*paramāṇu*).
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī*, pūrvapakṣa 224;
*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, pṛṣṭha 31;
*Nyāyakumudacandra*, pṛṣṭha 217.
In the *Ratnākara* (p.

870), it would follow that there is an absence of both omniscience and magnitude; and whatever is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated by the opponent: "There is no certainty as to whether [the entity] exists at the limit of its diminution, or whether it perishes entirely. That is insubstantial, because its total destruction does not occur, as this is refuted by reasoning.
Furthermore, because there is no destruction of the substance even when its dimension reaches a state of excellence,
this faulty conceptualization would persist even at the highest degree of magnitude.

He explains the *kārikā* with the words beginning "atoms" (*paramāṇavaḥ*), the connection being that atoms are "perceived" (*samupalakṣyante*). This is for the purpose of demonstrating that they are perceived in a clear, uncontradicted, and correct manner. The word "equally" (*samaḥ*) is used to state that their designation is such that they have approached proximity to the cognition that apprehends them by itself, and not through the imparting of a form. The word "perceived" (*lakṣyante*) is used for the purpose of stating that they are "ascertained" (*niścīyante*), and not seen by means of non-conceptual perception (*avikalpadarśana*).
"What is he doing? What? To this he says: "The gross, single, perceptible self"—this phrase continues [from the previous context].
In some places, "its own nature" (*svabhāva*) is heard instead.
Again, "What is he doing? To this he says: "Sphericality," and so forth.
How is this easily understood? To this he says: "In that way," and so forth; "in that way" means by the manner just described, because of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "For not," and so forth.
For (hi) because, in that manner—that is, by the immediately preceding mode—it does not become an object that has not undergone transformation;
why? Because of contradiction (vipratiṣedhāt).
The mention of the prefix is for the sake of illustration.

By way of concluding the present topic, he states—beginning with "This very [is]..."—that [the means of knowledge such as] comparison (*upamāna*) and the rest are included within the cognition admitted by himself.

This aforementioned [category], beginning with comparison, is characterized as a division of sensory-cognition (*mati-jñāna*). It consists of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth, as well as memory (*smṛti*), recognition (*saṃjñā*), reflection (*cintā*), and discernment (*abhinibodha*). Its objects are both substances and modes (*paryāya*), as well as generalities and particulars. Prior to its association with verbal expression, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory; even that which is the opposite of this is likewise characterized as a division thereof.

False knowledge is invalid (*apramāṇa*), such as inference based on the perception of an absolute object, or any other such section of the *Cūrṇi*; since this is so, therefore the connection is that the knowledge beginning with comparison (*upamāna*) which is being defined immediately following this is [the subject].

"What is that? he asks, and says: "The variety of sensory cognition (*mati-jñāna*), etc. That which has the variety—the detailed expansion—of sensory cognition as its characteristic or essential nature is thus described; that is to say, it is a specific type of sensory cognition.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Apprehension (*avagraha*), etc. It is a compound meaning that cognition (*mati*) of which apprehension is the beginning; and that [cognition], along with recollection (*smṛti*), recognition (*saṃjñā*), deliberation (*cintā*), and retention (*abhinibodha*), are its constituent parts—it is thus described.

And this means of knowledge (*sādhana*) should also be seen as a qualification of its specific divisions; therefore, because it consists of that [perception], the cognition of comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth is characterized by the specific divisions of *mati*,
since it consists of *avagraha* and the other stages.

If it is asked: "Since the inclusion of comparison (*upamāna*) and the other [means of knowledge] therein has already begun to be examined, for what purpose is the mention of apprehension (*avagraha*), etc., as well as memory (*mati*) and recollection (*smṛti*)?"—True; nevertheless, there is no fault, for that mention is intended to demonstrate the sequence of the arising of cognitions such as those with well-known names within comparison and the rest.

To explain: just as for one who possesses mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the apprehension (*avagraha*) and subsequent stages regarding a previous mode (*paryāya*), there arise from the apprehension of a subsequent mode the well-known stages of recollection (*smṛti*), recognition (*saṃjñā*), reflection (*cintā*), and discernment (*abhinibodha*); in exactly the same way, for one who possesses mental impressions deposited by the apprehension and subsequent stages regarding a cow that is similar to a *gavaya*, when the recollection of the cow occurs upon the apprehension of the *gavaya*, the knowledge arises that "this is similar to that. Thus, it does not differ from recognition (*saṃjñā*).
By this, the knowledge of distinctions such as number and so forth within sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) has been discussed.
Analogies arise for a person.

Now, an objection is raised: if knowledge arising from the recollection of a previous apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth were of the nature of *saṃjñā* (recognition), then after the apprehension of a jar—which is distinct from everything else—leaves a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and subsequently, upon the apprehension of a similar object such as a patch of ground, there would arise through the recollection of the previously apprehended jar the cognition "this jar is not here," which would be *saṃjñā*. But this is not the case; for it is admitted that [the true nature of] recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consists precisely in the reflective judgment of similarity and identity, as stated in the Nyāyabindu: "Recognition is twofold" (NB 2.50) and so forth. Therefore, the Mīmāṃsaka maintains that this is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called non-existence (*abhāva*).
As it has been said:
"Because recognition is admitted to belong to that which is excluded from everything else."
Based on similarity and having as its object unity,
[the cognition] apprehends the existence of the thing, recollects the counter-correlate,
and [perceives] the thing as the bare ground.

If it is argued that the object whose absence is being established is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and that the mental cognition of non-existence arises with respect to that [counter-correlate] without depending on the sense organs (as stated in *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 27);
That is not the core point; for even that [recognition] is admitted to be a reality (*tattva*), since recognition consists in the reflective discernment of what has been perceived.

As for the statement in the *Nyāyaviniścaya* (2.50), "Recognition is twofold," and so forth, this is intended to demonstrate that recognition applies to similarity just as it does to identity, and is not meant to be an exhaustive enumeration; otherwise, there would be [the inclusion of] "cognition" and "memory" [as separate categories], according to the *Tattvasūtra* (1).
One might think that the aforementioned sūtra would be contradicted because [the opponent] accepts [this as] a case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

For instance, when the mutual distinction between a jar and the ground is perceived through those two direct perceptions—just as the similarity between a cow and a gavaya is perceived—there would then be a subsequent reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) which constitutes recognition. However, this is not so, because that perception occurs solely through a mental cognition of non-existence (*mānasa-asattājñāna*).
And so it has been said:
"The cognition of non-existence [arises] from the two perceptions that apprehend the jar and the ground."
If it is argued: "The cognition that 'this is not' is not first produced by the sense faculty,
because the sense faculty has a connection only with the positive aspect [of an object], due to its capacity" (Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika,
Abhāvapariccheda, verse 18);

That is not tenable; for just as in the case of the positive aspect, if the counter-positive—which is distinct from everything else—were perceived, there could be no negation whatsoever upon its recollection, because that would contradict your own admission.
Furthermore, the recollection of that which is unassociated [with others] must have occurred in that same way during the prior experience; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that even in that case, such a cognition occurs through the recollection of another counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—just as [the cognition of] a ground devoid of a jar arises from the recollection of the jar—then this is a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, this is trivial.

Likewise, knowledge arising from the stages of sensory apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth, through memory (*smṛti*) and recognition (*saṃjñā*), is of the nature of reflection (*cintā*); thus, being characterized by that specific variety [of conceptual thought], it is not yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*), because the latter is incompatible with that.
Because even non-existence is perceived, when there is the cognition of non-connection...

The claim that "the cognition of the jar's non-contact with the ground arises from the recollection of the ground as distinct from the jar, and the recollection of the ground as distinct from the jar occurs when there is the cognition of the jar's non-contact with the ground"—
that is to say, that this [cognition] consists of a differentiation of mental states and is therefore a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*)— is thereby refuted.
Furthermore, because it arises from a causal complex distinct from the causal complex of sensory perception such as the eye,
there would be the over-extension [of the definition] to the cognition of non-existence (abhāva-jñāna), even though it is likewise [a form of knowledge].
That [cognition] is not of the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it arises from reflection (*cintā*);

likewise, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is well known to be like inference (*anumāna*). Since its characteristic consists of the differentiation of that [inference], it possesses the characteristic of the differentiation of sensory cognition (*matijñāna*), which is of the nature of determinate comprehension (*abhinibodha*).

It might be thought: "Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of identity; it is not the case that the reflective awareness of similarity and so forth is included within its specific definition. To this, he says: "In substance," and so forth.

This is the meaning: because this cognition—which is being described by the opponent—has both substance and mode (*paryāya*) as its object, as well as generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*) as its object;

therefore, since the aforementioned generality is indeed nothing but similarity, and the cognition having that as its object is also accepted by the opponent as recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), [the opponent] is so considered.
Is all of that not its definition? He says: "prior to association with verbal expression.

The sense is that the cognition arising from comparison and other means prior to the application of words such as "gavaya" is not yet the cognition [in the form] "this is what is denoted by the word 'gavaya'," and so forth.
Showing that this is not only its definition but is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he says: "it is a valid means of knowledge."
The word "and" (*ca*) is to be understood here;
why? Because of non-contradiction.
Showing that there is yet another type of cognition characterized as a division thereof, he says: "That," and so forth.

Therefore, the knowledge of comparison and so forth—such as that of a Naiyāyika who possesses mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by traditional authority (*āgama*) in the form "the *gavaya* is like a cow," or one who possesses mental impressions produced by traditional authority in the form "a tree has branches and so on," or "a *haṃsa* has a beak for separating milk from water"—is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by the differentiation of substances and other categories, because it exists as such; this is the connection [of the argument].
Even according to the Mīmāṃsaka and others, this is considered sensory-cognition (*matijñāna*).
This very definition of the subdivisions of sensory knowledge (mati-jñāna) has indeed been heard by the person.
Now, demonstrating what is non-authoritative (apramāṇa), he says: "False ignorance" (mithyājñāna).

This means that false [cognition]—consisting of sensory apprehension (avagraha) and so forth, as well as memory (mati), recognition (smṛti), conceptualization (saṃjñā), reflection (cintā), and discernment (abhinibodha)—is "ignorance" (ajñāna), which is non-authoritative; it is not authoritative because it is false sensory cognition (matyajñāna). This should be understood.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration, saying "Just as," and so forth.
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes scripture (*āgama*) as that which pertains to the perception of an exclusive object, such as inference and the like; by this,
he demonstrates two examples, one worldly and one scriptural, namely other cognitions such as those occurring in dreams.

Alternatively, this should be understood by setting forth another prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), as follows: regarding the knowledge that was considered in the first two sections—beginning with sensory perception (*avagraha*) and ending with retention (*dhāraṇā*)—and the memory (*smaraṇa*) discussed here through such statements as "valid cognition is non-contradictory recollection" (*pramāṇam avisaṃvādismṛtiḥ*); and regarding recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) which will be defined in the fourth section; and the inferential knowledge (*tarka-jñāna*) previously considered in that same [fourth] section under the heading "those who were [formerly] existent but are no longer" (*bhūtābhavyāḥ*) according to the sequence of the topics; and the inference (*anumāna*) which will be considered in the sixth section—in which of these five types of knowledge should these be included? To this, he says: "This very... and so forth.
What is this that has been described and what is yet to be described?
What is that knowledge? To this he says: it is characterized by the divisions of sensory cognition (mati-jñāna); the meaning is that it is included within sensory cognition.
Of what nature is it? He says: "beginning with avagraha," and so forth.
Again, of what nature is it? He says: "substance," and so forth.
Is it all [of these]? No; he says: "previously," and so forth.
Due to association with that, one considers it as "heard" subsequent to that;
at the third recitation, at the third recitation.
Page 187:

[This occurs] in the case of sensory cognition (mati), scriptural cognition (śruta), clairvoyance (avadhi), mental perception (manaḥparyaya), and omniscience (kevalajñāna) due to the association with words.

If it is asked: "But was it not previously stated here and elsewhere that all [cognitions] such as memory and so forth are 'heard' (śruta)? How then is there no contradiction? There is no contradiction, because it is designated as such metaphorically due to its similarity to the primary sense of "heard.
And why is that a valid means of knowledge? Because it is non-contradictory.
"In that case, it follows that all knowledge would have that [substance] as its essence and possess its characteristics. To this, he says: "Its opposite," and so forth.

This means that knowledge which is the opposite—that is, distinct—from that knowledge which has substance and so on as its object and consists of that [substance] is understood to be *matyajñāna* (sensory non-knowledge), not *matijñāna* (sensory knowledge).
Why? Because it is not a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*), since it does not have substance and so on as its object; such is the intended meaning.

The remainder is as before, since it is stated [in the source]. In some manuscripts, there exists the entire *Cūrṇiprakaraṇa*, beginning with: "Others know that perception alone is the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," and so forth; however, this has not been commented upon by some, because of the presence therein of tautology and the mention of irrelevant matters.

The commentators [object]: "Now, as for what was stated—that knowledge characterized by the divisions of sensory cognition (*mati-jñāna*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory—that is incorrect; because there is an absence of non-contradiction in some cases.
For instance, there is no re-attainment of what has already been seen; or even if such re-attainment were to occur, it exists even in dreams."

If, however, this [non-delusion] is not the attainment of that [object], how can it be anything else? Since there is no distinction [between them], suppose it is the non-contradictory perception of the object and not its attainment; even this is the same, because it exists even when there is a cognitive distortion (*viplava*). Suppose then that the determination of the object is like [the determination of] the opposite side; and the cognition of that [determination] is either through perception or through inference, since there is no other possible way? Furthermore, a challenge from another party is not appropriate here, as it would lead to the consequence of mere incoherent prattle.
If it is argued that "let it be so from that very [cause]," it is replied:
the attainment of the object occurs even in the case of false cognition.
That by which the knower surpasses the other worldly being is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in every respect;
however, for the establishment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, mere experience—which is like an unreality and free from conceptual construction—would not suffice.
Intellect (*mati*) consists of perception, memory, recognition, and inference through reasoning concerning self and others as its objects.
This thought, whose nature is inconceivable, brings about [the realization] of that which is other than the object, elsewhere, upon its accomplishment.

(24) The "knower" (*jñānī*) is one who possesses direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other forms of knowledge; by means of such direct perception and other knowledge, he excels—that is, he triumphs—since it is impossible for him to excel by any other means. From the word "by knowledge" (*jñānena*), this is understood. Of what does he excel? To this, he says: "the bearer of worldly existence" (*bhavabhṛtam*), [that is,] one for whom there is the manifold expansion of delusions, such as various births, shown by the playful manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Of what nature is it? He says: "the other," namely the ignorant one, who is possessed of delusion, error, misconception, and indecision regarding the true reality of the beloved [object], such as the Naiyāyika and others.
What is that? He says: "that" and so forth.

That by which he is surpassed is referred to by the phrase "that, that"; it is that valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, how could his own desired goal be established from that, just as [it is not established] in the case of an external object? Thus he thinks.
For what purpose? To this he says: "On all sides," and so forth.

That reality which is to be abandoned (*heya*) in every respect—characterized by the distinction between the real and the unreal—and that which is to be accepted (*upādeya*), having the nature of being free from error and the like: for the establishment of these two, and as the cause for their establishment, this has been stated.

The meaning is this: if there were no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever, how could the desired establishment [of anything] occur? If it does exist, then there is a contradiction with the total refutation of the validity of cognition (*pramābhanga*).

Another, however, says: "No cognition whatsoever is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nor is it a non-means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because reality (*tattva*) transcends all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and because that [reality] is established through the direct perception (*adhyakṣa-pramāṇa*) of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); furthermore, there is no contradiction with the refutation of the categories of valid knowledge, since such a refutation applies only to external objects. To this, he replies: "But not... and so forth.
Furthermore, the connection is that experience (*anubhava*) is not at all a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Where [is this stated]? He says: "In the establishment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. What is to be abandoned is the reality of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); what is to be accepted is pure awareness (*saṃvedana*) devoid of those [constructions]. Regarding the phrase "in their establishment," he asks: "What kind of experience? and answers: "Non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*).
