That in which no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "real" or "unreal," nor any differentiation, exists, is described as such.
Why is this so? To this he says: "it is an unreal construction" (*abhūtakalpa*).
It is "unreal" (*abhūta*) because it is unproduced (*ajāta*) from any cause; it is "construction" (*kalpa*) because it is similar to that eternal reality, such as Brahman and the other *tattvas*.
And this qualification should also be understood as a reason—namely, "because it is a construction of the unreal" (*abhūtakalpa*).

If one asks, "In what sense is it a construction of the unreal? it is said: Just as some [Brahmanists], fearing that a single entity could possess multiple natures, postulate a certain *brahman*-reality whose body is distinct from blue, pleasure, and so forth, and which transcends all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); in the same way, for that very reason, the Buddhist must accept a consciousness-reality (*saṃvedanatattva*) of that same kind—partless and momentary. And just like that [Brahman-reality], it cannot be the cause for establishing itself or others; therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, let it be granted that nothing exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha) in whatever way it may be; nevertheless, even by this much, there is no impairment whatsoever to the established distinction between valid and invalid cognition according to conventional reality (saṃvṛti). Your position is indeed intended by us as well, for it is impossible to proceed by overstepping the actual nature of things (*vastutattva*)—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 186.
Because it negates the means of valid cognition and so forth within the non-duality of consciousness,
it transcends all conceptual constructions.

If the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin) should object, saying: "Surely neither I nor another accepts that [the one] possesses a manifold nature out of fear of such a consequence; rather, we accept it exactly as it appears," to this he replies with the words beginning "perception" (pratyakṣa).

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists of [cognitions] beginning with apprehension (*avagraha*) and ending with retention (*dhāraṇā*), since these alone are the subject under discussion. "Recollection" (*smṛti*) and "recognition" (*abhijñā*), as well as that which has both self and others as its objects (*svapara-viṣaya*), and that which has inference (*anumā*) as its essence—such cognition (*mati*) would be, or indeed is, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the syntactical connection.

By this, he says the following: if cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in accordance with its appearance, then the aforementioned consciousness (*mati*) must be established as a valid means of knowledge, because it appears as being useful for worldly transactions ranging from perception to the attainment [of results] within a single [object];

otherwise, if it were established through extremely subtle investigation, that Brahman would not be anything at all, since there would be no other alternative for the opponent—thus says the proponent of non-duality (*advaitavādin*).
That which is unseen by the Buddhist is, in his view, unauthoritative.

[Objection: Why is it that only *tarka* (logical reasoning) is qualified by the terms "one's own" and "another's," and not other means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*)? For the Jaina, even those [other means] are of the same nature. [Reply: True. However, for the sake of one who does not accept it as such, *tarka* is qualified in that way in order to establish its nature as an example.

Just as *tarka* has both oneself and others as its object, so too must perception and the other means of knowledge be accepted as having both oneself and others as their objects—by an opponent who desires to establish the universal pervasion (*sākalyavyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans. Thus, this is refuted: "There is no other object of experience for the intellect" (*Pra.vā. 3*).
"How can reasoning (*tarka*) have that as its object? To this he says: "Cintā," etc.
"Cintā" is a designation for reasoning, according to the established usage of former teachers.

"Thought (*cintā*) is reasoning whose nature is inconceivable; it is 'inconceivable' because its essence (*ātmā*), that is, its own-nature (*svabhāva*), is such that it cannot be deliberated upon as to how it might be analyzed in this way. Why is this [thought], which is determined by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) for each individual cognizer, of an inconceivable nature? To this he says: 'It conceives,' and so forth;
for it conceives, that is, it determines."
What? Another object;
from what is it another? To this he says: "from the object," meaning from that which is within the range of perception and so forth; it is another, i.e., imperceptible (parokṣa).
Where? To this he says: "elsewhere than its own location," meaning in another place. This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), by which "at another time" is also understood.
For what purpose does he employ this [inference]? He says: "In order to establish another [property] elsewhere"—that is, for the sake of establishing something else in a different locus.

If this were not accepted, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) by the probandum (*sādhya*) would not be established in its entirety; consequently, an inference such as "whatever appears is cognition, like pleasure and so forth" would have its range obstructed.

Nor can that [cognition] be established through an investigation such as "because an insentient object cannot appear unless it relies upon its own constituent part," for otherwise, yellow and other colors would be established from the cognition of blue. Enough of this digression.
Its experience is nothing other than that which has itself and its own object as its domain, due to reasoning.
Because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] shines forth by itself;
this is the remainder [of the argument], which has both self and others as its object.
The proof of the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvedanādvaitasiddhi*) has been demonstrated by Umāsvāti and others in works such as the *Tattvārthasūtra*.

Alternatively, having established the validity [of memory] under the view that perception is conceptual (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*)— on the grounds that "even though memory apprehends what has already been apprehended, it possesses a specific purpose" and so forth— he now states "the knower," etc., while refuting the charge of its being a mere apprehension of what was already apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*) as asserted by the opposing school.

By what nature does the knower, being conscious, excel? To this he says: [he excels] the other, which is unconscious, such as a jar, by that nature through which he is distinguished from it—this is the meaning.

Now, if it is argued that he excels it by means of a property consisting in the apprehension of an object, while being averse to the apprehension of himself, then that property too would have to be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); to this he replies: "the sustainer of existence" (bhavabhṛtam).

The word "ca" (and) is to be understood here; [it refers to] those who uphold existence, namely the Naiyāyikas and others who nourish Maheśvara. That means their "pramāṇa"—that is, knowledge which is a definitive determination of both itself and the other—is "pramāṇa.
For what purpose? He says: "Samantāt" (completely), etc.;
this has already been explained.
"Therefore, that which is considered [to be] non-conceptual experience (avikalpānubhava) is the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). To this, he says: "But not," and so forth.

"Non-existent conceptualization" (*abhūtakalpa*) refers to something unreal, unarisen, such as a donkey's horn, which is slightly unestablished. Non-conceptual experience (*avikalpo'nubhavaḥ*) is not a valid means of knowledge, nor is it a cognition that determines an object.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: non-conceptual experience is not the apprehender of anything because of its non-existence, like a flower in the sky.

Therefore, how can a certain consciousness that has grasped that [object] grasp it, and not otherwise? For if it were otherwise, it would follow that it too grasps what has been grasped by another, just like any other [consciousness]. Consequently, even the non-conceptual experience would lack experience [of itself]; and if that experience were not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be no means of valid cognition at all, because nothing else is perceived and thus lacks existence—so says another [opponent].

He replies to that: "It has been explained" starting with the words "perception," etc.; he considers that memory is not a means of valid cognition because its object is one previously experienced through non-conceptual [perception], since it arises from the manifestation of that [object].
Page 175: Memory is insentient.
An insentient object apprehended by non-conceptual [cognition].
Showing another refutation on this very point, he says: "Cintā," and so forth.

This "cintā" (reflection) consists of the apprehension of what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhi-jñāna*), in the form "all valid cognition is such [as previously established]"; it is of an inconceivable nature (*acintyātmikā*)—that is, its essence is beyond thought—because, like a woman of good family who lacks a protector and is deprived of a husband, it is devoid of the protection of a means of valid cognition (*māna*).
From where does this [conclusion] arise? To this, he says: "Kalayati," and so forth.

When two [objects] are apprehended as established in one place while [another] is excluded by the word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*), it is understood that some intended establishment exists in the mind of the sage, because the word "elsewhere" is a relative term;

therefore, it exclusively determines (*kalayati*) and ascertains (*adhyavasyati*) another object distinct from the object of the intended establishment. However, he considers that this is not the case, because multiple establishments can occur for a single object due to differences in location and so forth, and because such [exclusive determination] would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as it would lead to the consequence of non-engagement [with reality].

If it is argued that this is not so because an object is momentary, we say no; for there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for this. If it is argued that the non-perception of that [object] between the preceding and succeeding moments is the valid evidence, we say no; because this [non-perception] is entirely unestablished in the absolute view of momentary, partless atoms (*paramāṇu*). Even at the time when the reality of a jar or similar objects consists of their own constituent parts occurring simultaneously, the cognition consisting of perception and so forth is all the more established as valid evidence in the system of Akalaṅkadeva.
Even in the Jaina doctrine, there is [the relation] of the middle moment with its preceding and succeeding moments.
Alternatively, having formulated the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) otherwise, this passage should be explained as follows:

If it is asked, "Is not perception alone the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for what purpose, then, are the three subsequent means of cognition—recollection and so forth—investigated here?", he says in response: "The knower," and so on.
A knower is one who possesses critical inquiry (*parīkṣāvān*), specifically the Cārvāka himself, by means of which inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*) he excels [over others].

Whom? He says: "the sustainer of existence" (*bhavabhṛtam*). Existence (*bhava*) is *saṃsāra*; that which sustains—that is, nourishes or supports—it is the "sustainer of existence," such as the Jaina and others. [The inference] excels him, like the other [proponent], who is a negator of his own disciples and so forth; thus it attains superiority over him.
For what purpose is that inferential knowledge a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? He says: "completely," and so on.

"Completely" means in its entirety, for the sake of establishing—through definitive determination—the objects to be abandoned (*heya*), such as the next world, specific deities, merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and other means of valid cognition; and the objects to be accepted (*upādeya*), such as the four elements, supreme consciousness, and the primary means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If the Cārvāka were to say: "As for that supreme consciousness which consists of the four elements, its establishment is indeed through direct perception alone; therefore, that [perception] itself is the means of valid cognition," to this he replies: "But not again," and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not the case that direct experience—perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*)—is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; this is understood from the context.
Of what nature is it? It is conceptual (*vikalpa*), consisting of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*). This was stated in relation to others.
Again, of what nature is it? He says: "it is like a past event" (*bhūtakalpa*).
The elements, such as earth and so forth, are "of that nature," meaning similar to that [intellect].

This is what is meant: just as the elements like earth are themselves insentient and thus not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing what is to be avoided or acquired—otherwise, the postulation of consciousness would be purposeless—likewise, experience (*anubhava*), being their material cause (*upādāna*), is itself insentient and is not a means of valid cognition in that regard. Indeed, it is not logical for that which has an insentient material cause to be sentient; otherwise, a sentient jar would arise from an insentient lump of clay.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which has non-conscious matter as its material cause (*upādāna*) is not conscious, just like a jar or similar objects; and the cognition of the opponent has non-conscious matter as its material cause.

If it is argued: "But surely the thesis is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhita*), because even while having that [non-conscious matter] as its material cause, it is perceived as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)," we reply: this is merely a delusion arising from the cognition of its suchness [as conscious] due to ignorance (*mṛta*); for we shall establish this in the fourth chapter.

Alternatively, it should be explained as: that by which the elements (*bhūta*) are conceptualized (*kalpyante*), established (*vyavasthāpyante*), and made objects (*viṣayīkriyante*) is "that which conceptualizes the elements" (*bhūtakalpa*).
Nor does that [perception] have the capacity to establish that [other world and so forth], because it does not have those as its objects;
nor is that which does not have something as its object capable of negating or establishing it, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It is experience alone [that is the basis].
And because the knowledge of the Cārvāka is derived from the primary elements.
If it is asked, "Granted that inference may be a valid means of knowledge regarding the condition (*pratyaya*), what is its utility in the present context?"—to this he replies: "In perception," etc.;
this has already been explained.

The intention here is as follows: by one who accepts inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it must be admitted that there is first the perception of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*); then, at some time, the observation of the mark for the most part; then the recollection of the relationship; then recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*); then deliberation (*tarka*); and finally, inference itself.
Furthermore, just like inference, its own objects such as memory and so forth must also be accepted as valid means of knowledge.

Now, if one were to object: "If the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) is apprehended in its entirety through perception, then the cognizer would be omniscient. If it is apprehended by that very inference, there is mutual dependence; if it is without that [inference], there is an infinite regress. Therefore, how can there be an apprehension of the relationship from which inference arises? To this, he says: "Cintā," and so forth.

By using the term "cintā" (reflection), which is a designation based on its etymological meaning, he demonstrates that *tarka* (reasoning) is described as a mental conceptualization (*mānasavikalpa*). He shows that this does not lead to an undesirable consequence for the Jaina who, while denying [the existence of] perception, attains universal concomitance (*sākalyavyāpti*) through it; for such a position is accepted [by the Jaina].
This has been stated by him:
"The arising of inference occurs once the relationship is established, and the establishment of that relationship occurs when [inference] exists."

If the apprehension of pervasion occurs through another inference, then the cognition of all things— both existent and non-existent, as well as their commonalities— is undermined by mental conceptualization.

"O Jina, if even an ordinary human being becomes omniscient by knowing the entire range of entities through his commonality with other beings, then what wonder is there if one who possesses all-encompassing knowledge (*akhilajñāna*) is omniscient? (Pātrakeśaristotra, verse 19).

By the phrase "having an inconceivable nature" (*acintyātmikā*), even though there is an absence of the [usual] grounds for cognition—namely, the arising of an object, its similarity [to the cognition], and its dependence on a logical mark (*liṅga*)—there is no fault inherent in that position, because [the cognition] determines its own object through its inherent capacity (*yogyatā*).

Furthermore, by the word "this" (*iyam*), since it is directly perceived through individual self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), any attempt to negate it would be contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhana*).
To the question, "What does she (the Goddess) do?", he says: "She fashions" (*kalayati*), meaning she determines [all things] in their totality.
What? Another means of proof [is required] because it is distinct from the probandum; what [is gained by this]? It would be the cause of establishing the object;
where? Elsewhere.
What is the reason for saying that the probandum (sādhya), which is distinct from the means of proof (sādhana), is the basis for inference? He says: "From the object" (viṣayāt).

Just as when it is said, "One must behave properly toward one's mother," or "One must serve one's father," it is understood to mean "toward one's own [mother]" or "one's own [father]," so too, when it is said "from the object," it is understood to mean "from its own object," characterized by the impossibility of being otherwise (anyathānupapannatva).
If a negation were made, then [it would follow that...].

Thus ends the third chapter, "The Establishment of Other Means of Valid Cognition," in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by the bee at the lotus-feet of Śrīmad Anantavīrya. ||| Obeisance ||| cha ||| The Fourth Section: 4. Proof of the Soul.

Thus far, having considered that the direct proof of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the ascertainment of its own object, memory has been examined in detail as another means of valid cognition.

Now, having observed that "the preceding [cognition] would be the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the succeeding one would be the result (*phala*)" (Laghīyastraya 7), and considering that very [perception] produces the result of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as well as recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) which generates reasoning (*tarka*) preceded by the establishment of the self (*ātman*), he stated in his own *Laghīyastraya*: "The wise and the eloquent have understood... and so forth (p.
Having recollected through the supernormal power of the mind all objects previously cognized by the various sense organs,

and having brought reasoning to its conclusion regarding what is within its scope and what is not, one understands everything; for the eye does not indeed take as its object that which is already endowed with the ear and other senses.

For one perceives [objects] as having intervals and as being more distant; how then could there be an emergence of rays?—Compare: "If [the sense organ] reached [the object], there would be no perception of intervals, nor of that which is larger than the cognition;
the sense organ does not exist outside its physical locus, nor does it have the power to perceive the object."

But when there is contact with all objects, there is the perception of both the distant and the near; that which is seen by means of sound and form is obstructed [by the intervening object] when it is without interval.
Prajñāpāramitā-samuccaya 1.20, 41

The mind (*manas*) is so called because it "thinks" (*manyate*) or "cognizes" (*budhyate*) objects. What does this self (*ātman*) do? To this he says: it cognizes, that is, it knows. It is not a cognition-series devoid of continuity (*niranvaya-jñāna-santāna*), nor is it a transformation of primordial matter (*prakṛti-pariṇāma*), nor is it volition (*vyavasāya*), nor is it earth and so forth—such is what it thinks. If it is argued: "There is no self apart from pleasure and the like; how then can it cognize? And if it is asked: "Why is there no contradiction [in accepting] pleasure and the like as being the self? [The answer is: Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is momentary, a single consciousness possessing the forms of various objects (*vicitra-viṣayākāra-eka-saṃvedana*). (Siddhiviniścaya 2)
Because this is established by such passages as these, and he will state its proof immediately thereafter, [the author] asks:
"What is cognized? and answers: "Objects."

Regarding objects consisting of substance, mode, generality, and particularity, which present their own forms [to consciousness], that which was stated by someone—namely, "whatever is known by something is not different from that thing, just as the nature of that very knower is [not different from it]; and blue and so forth are known by the self"—is refuted by this [argument]. This is because the thesis is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhanāt*), since the knower is perceived through its own distinct identity (*ahamahamikayā*) in various instances such as a jar and so forth. Otherwise, one could even say: "The flock of cuckoos is white, because they are birds, like cranes."

Now, how does the self, being distinct from that [object], know it as not dependent upon it? Because it is observed to be so; otherwise, how could an object of such a nature be its producer? Capability is not precluded even in other cases;
the rest has been considered here according to the Sāṃkhya school.
According to the Cārvākas,
*nirbādhatā*,
*paścāttāpa*, *anutāpa*, and *vipratīsāra* are synonyms— thus says the Amarakośa.
In that regard, the practice of remorse consists in this: when one commits an unwholesome deed, one becomes filled with intense regret right there and then—[Śikṣāsamuccaya, p.
160]. "Without regret" (*avipratisāra*) means being free from regret; that is, being devoid of fault.
Even if [an object] is sublated by perception internally or externally, it would still be a probandum.
From knowledge [arises] that which generates knowledge.

By this, the following claim of the Sāṃkhya is refuted: "The sense organs perceive the object, the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) conceives, the mind (manas) forms intentions, the intellect (buddhi) determines, and the person (puruṣa) cognizes"; for there exists a direct perception of the object itself, just as there is of the form of the intellect.
And what is this restriction—that the intellect is perceived without that [object], but the object is not, nor is there a perception of its reflection in it as in a mirror when it is unknown?

If it is argued: "If it perceives those objects by its mere existence, then, because there is no distinction [in that existence], everyone would be an all-seeing one," to this he says: "By recognition" (*abhijñayā*), meaning by means of *pratyabhijñāna*.

Thus, the sequential functioning of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the eye is observed: the eye sees form, the mind conceptualizes, the ego conceives pride, and the intellect determines— Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti 30, regarding the intellect.
The self [perceives] objects like a mirror.

It might be thought: "Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the cognition that 'this is that very same thing. In this, 'that' is the reference of memory, and 'this' is the reference to the present; there is no other cognition that could be designated as recognition. This is without substance, because since the existence of a cognition restricted to each individual atom has already been refuted, the reference of either perception or memory is like the reference to a donkey's horn. Furthermore, it is by accepting a single, variegated, simultaneous consciousness that one establishes a single recognition which delineates both references—the reference to the prior state and the reference to the subsequent state.
That [cognition] is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): that cognition by which the self perceives objects is a means of valid knowledge, just like the cognition of a jar and so forth; and he perceives objects through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Now, if it is thought: "If he is perceived by that [recognition] as having gone [to another state], then even for an object never seen before, its identity between prior and subsequent states would be perceived by it at the very first sight"; that too is not tenable. Thus he says: "of those already known" (*vijñātān*).

By what means? To this he says: "by all the instruments (*aśeṣakaraṇaiḥ*). When a citron fruit or the like is present, there are all the instruments—the eyes and so forth—which have as their objects form, taste, smell, and touch; or alternatively, the cognitions themselves, since the cause is metaphorically designated by the effect; or else, those which previously occurred and those which subsequently proceed—these are the "all-inclusive instruments," and [the cognition arises] by means of them.

If it is objected that, in this way, higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it consists of the cognition of what has already been known, he replies: "Is it not so? and so forth.

Is it not inferred that "avagraha" and so forth are its range or object (*gocara*), while the other is the positive (*vidhi*) nature? For the term *vidhi* is derived from the etymology "that which is established by its own causes" (*svakāraṇair vidhīyate iti vidhiḥ*). Having taken that [meaning], the word "objects" (*viṣayān*) is understood to follow.

To explain: when the eye perceives a single gross object such as a citron (*bījapūra*), which consists of color-form (*rūpa*), there is no perception of its other qualities; likewise, even when one experiences its taste, which consists of flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, there is no experience of its color-form. Similarly, although a prior cognition determines an object as qualified by its previous state (*pūrvaparyāya*), it does not determine it as qualified by its subsequent state (*uttaraparyāya*); nor does the apprehension (*avagraha*) of a later state apprehend the object as qualified by its prior condition. However, through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the object is understood as qualified by both states; thus, the point is that [recognition] does not exclusively grasp what has already been grasped.

[Objection: "But surely, if the oneness of something were apprehended by either a prior or a subsequent perception, it would be appropriate for that [oneness] to be grasped by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), since this [recognition] follows upon those perceptions. And yet, a perception of the oneness of the prior and the subsequent is not possible; otherwise, recognition would have as its object that which does not exist. [Reply: It has been stated in this regard—that [recognition] would occur even in the absence of a prior perception.

If it is argued that [recognition occurs] when there is a perception of that [object]; or if it is argued that it occurs when there is a rapid recollection of a forgotten perception of that [object]; or if it is argued that from the perception and recollection of a cloth, there would be a recognition of identity in a jar, but not because of a perception of identity in that [jar];
or if it is argued that for this very reason, let there be no [recognition] elsewhere either, as there is no distinction—here he says: "It is non-different."
"They go toward another [object] by abandoning the previous sequence" means "toward" (*abhi*); this meaning is stated because it is a particle (*nipāta*).
"Previous-ness" (*pūrvatva*) consists in having existed at another time. The connection is: "having cognized the objects through all the instruments of perception.
As it has been said: "Perceiving the individual characteristics as one... (*Siddhibindu* 1).

9. And this is not an absolute rule—that the triad [of moments] is perceived whenever successive states are observed. Otherwise, how could there be a cognition of their distinction through the perception of the middle moment while the preceding and succeeding moments are not perceived? The rest of this matter has been considered previously;
therefore, these two cognitions are "this is that very same thing."
The self is distinct from perception and memory. (Pra.vārtikālaṃkāra, p. 22)
The self [perceives] the states through supernormal knowledge.
The characteristics of the object have arisen within the cognition that is the effect of the sense faculties.
Even if it were granted that the possibility of perceiving the identity between the prior and the subsequent is precluded for the recognition of oneness, nevertheless...

If it is argued that this unity residing in the jar might belong to the person— namely, that when the self perceives objects known through all the sense organs by means of higher cognition (*abhijñā*), it then perceives everything from birth onwards as a totality— here he says: "by remembering" (*smṛtvā*).

By means of subsequent cognitions of objects, one perceives previously known objects through recollection as being identical; one does not perceive them all [simultaneously]. By this, he demonstrates that recollection possesses validity because its fruit is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
[This applies to] the states.
The meaning is that recognition through higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) is the fruit of memory;
now, describing recognition as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of its being the fruit of reasoning (*tarka*), he says: "Reasoning," and so forth.

This is the meaning: by means of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) acting as the instrument, having brought about reasoning (*tarka*), that is, having led [the objects] to the state of being inferred; the sense is "having made those objects such that they are graspable by reasoning.
Having led those objects [to that state], he has caused them to become apprehended by that [reasoning].
What kind [of object]? To this he says: "reasoned out" (*tarkita*), and so forth.

The object (*gocara*) is that which is deliberated upon (*tarkita*) and determined by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*). "Other than that" (*itaro 'nyaḥ*) refers to an entity (*bhāva*) existing in a different place and so forth. "In that regard, its affirmation" (*vidhis tatra*) means that for which there is an affirmation (*vidhāna*), i.e., an origination (*utpatti*); he is described as such.
By the word "that" (*tam*), he absolutely refutes [the claim] that this [cognition] is the result of direct perception.

What does it do? He says: "It cognizes" (*budhyate*). "On all sides" (*abhitaḥ*) means everywhere (*samantāt*). "Objects" (*viṣayān*)—this is the connection [of the word], with the case-ending changed accordingly (*vibhaktipariṇāmena*), [meaning] "by means of deliberation" (*tarkeṇa*).

If it is argued: "Since an object of recollection and so forth does not exist at the time [of its cognition], how can it be apprehended by that [cognition]? For it is logical that an object is apprehended by a cognition that is simultaneous with it; otherwise, even visual and other sensory cognitions would become apprehenders of all things, past and so forth," [the author] replies here: "The ear and so forth... This sentence, even without the words *yathā* and *tathā*, is to be explained as containing the words *yathā* and *tathā* by virtue of the poetic figure *prativastūpamā*.

That [sense] of which the ear is the first—referring to the nose and so forth—is described as such; the connection is made by changing the wording to: "just as [the other senses] would apprehend an object only when it is in contact (*samupeta*) with them, and not when it is not in contact. However, the eye certainly does not apprehend an object only when it is in contact; rather, it is perceived as apprehending an object even when that object is not in contact.
And since this is well-known to the Buddhist (*saugata*), it does not require further proof.

Just as visual and other sensory cognitions take as their object a thing qualified by its own time, whereas recollection and the like take an object qualified by a different time— since there is no distinction in the fact that such a cognition occurs in all cases—
the eye, accompanied by the words "just as" and "so," [perceives] an object even though it is unconnected [to the present moment].

By this, the following argument advanced by Prajñākara is also refuted: "Recollection and the like, when operating upon the past and so forth, are without an object because the object does not exist at that time. That is refuted; for in that case, visual perception would likewise be without an object, since its object is absent in that place. Furthermore, there is no recollection at the very moment the object is being perceived, for recollection occurs only after the perception has ceased.
If that [object] was grasped in the past and lacks form [now], it is not that memory;
for how could a memory arisen now know its former state?
How can that which is non-existent and formless be the form of the memory?
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 602:

Now, for the Buddhist, the ear, like the eye, does not apprehend its object by coming into contact with it, because of the established tenet that the eye, ear, and mind function without reaching their objects (*aprāpyakāritva*). Why, then, is it said "the ear and so forth," rather than saying "the nose and so forth"?
Therefore, it should be stated in this way: "the nose and so forth."

If it is argued that the cognitions "the sound is far" and "the sound is near" prove that the ear, like the eye, functions without reaching its object (aprāpyakārin); let this matter rest for now, as it will be examined in the section on scripture (āgama), where it is stated:
"The eye, the mind, and the ear do not reach [their objects]" (Abhidharmakośa 1.43).

Here the Vaiśeṣika says: "Since the eye, like the ear and other external senses, possesses the nature of an external organ, it must necessarily apprehend its object; so for what purpose was it said that 'the eye does not [see]'? To him he replies: "For it indeed sees," and so forth. The particle *hi* has the sense of "because. The meaning of the restrictive particle *eva* is that it "indeed sees" or "perceives," and not that it "does not see"; the word "eye" (*cakṣus*) is understood to follow from the context.

If it is argued that "the mind sees, not the eye; otherwise, its postulation would be useless," we say no. There is no fault, for it is said that "it sees" because the eye acts together with the self as it perceives the object.

What does it see? He says: "with an interval"—that is, existing at a distance from a location such as a river, or separated by a substance such as a pane of glass or a film—[it sees] an object such as a jar; this is the connection [of the sentence], with the word "object" understood through grammatical transformation (*vacanapariṇāma*).

This is what is meant: if the term "eye" (*cakṣus*) is taken to refer to the physical eyeball (*golaka*) according to common worldly usage, then the reason [proposed] to establish contact with a jar or similar object—which is spatially separated from it and perceived as entirely distinct—would be *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), because it is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitakarmanirdeśa*) due to being employed immediately after such a sublation, and because [the eyeball] is an external sense organ (*bāhyendriyatvāt*). This is just as in the argument: "Sound is not audible, because it exists," or "The eye reaches its object, because it is a sense organ, like the nose and other organs" (*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 36).

The eye reveals objects that are within its reach, because it does not reveal obstructed objects, like a lamp; and because it is an external sense organ, like the sense of touch. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p.
23. *Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 122.
The eye and the ear determine their objects by reaching them, because they are external sense organs, like the organ of touch;
thus, the postulation of the mind [as a separate sense organ] is redundant. (Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 73)
Regarding that very point, he states another argument for what is to be proven: "pṛthutaram" (more extensive).

The connection is as follows: the eye is more extensive than subtle objects such as mustard seeds; therefore, it perceives mountains and the like, which are even more extensively large, as being "pṛthutaraṃ" (more extensive).

The intended meaning here is as follows: according to the previously stated method, because it is obstructed by distance and so forth—such as mountains and the like—which are themselves separated by distance and so forth, there is no contact between the eye and that object due to the sublation of its existence by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nevertheless, if one were to insist on [contact] merely for the sake of argument (*pādaprasārikatayā*), then only that portion of the mountainous region with which the eye has a connection—being as broad as a water bubble—would be perceived by it, and not the much larger extent measured in *yojanas* and so forth.
Indeed, when a blind man’s hand is in contact only with the trunk of an elephant, he does not have a complete cognition of the entire elephant.
And since there is the perception of a larger object by means of the eye,
we therefore conclude that the eye sees what is not in immediate contact with it,
even when [the object] is small.
Indeed,

the eye is not a specific physical globe (*golaka*), such that this fault would arise; rather, it is the rays, for it is they, when in contact with the object, that serve as the means for its illumination.

And if it is argued that in this view, the statement "it sees that [object] more extensively" is not contradicted because subtle rays exist at the base and become gross at the tip—just like the rays of a lamp or similar light—then the author replies with the words beginning "of the ray" (*raśmeḥ*).

Here, the singular number in "ray" (*raśmiḥ*) is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*); however, if reference were made to individual instances (*vyakti*), how could there be a connection between "the rays" and "the eye" by changing the case-ending? It is from no source of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because the root *sar*, meaning "to go," is understood here in the sense of "cognition" (*jñāna*).
It cannot be established through perception, because that [object] does not appear therein,
because it would lead to an infinite regress, and because those [senses] too would have to be apprehended through their connection with the rays [of consciousness];
nor can it be established through inference, because such [an inferential mark] is absent.

Now, if it is argued: "The eye possesses rays; being connected with its own rays, it illuminates its object everywhere because it is composed of light (*taijasa*), like a lamp"—then from what source does its luminous nature derive? If you say "from its possession of hot touch," we say no; for that specific quality [of heat] is absent there, and mere warmth exists even in the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) and other organs. If you say "from its possession of radiant form (*bhāsura-rūpa*)," then what is this radiance of form? If you say "it is brilliance (*ujjvalatva*)," we say no; for the cause of this [brilliance] exists in things such as a sword-blade.

If it is argued that [the color] exists in the state of being brown (*kapiśatva*), we say no; for that [brownness] is absent from the eyes of beautiful women which are white as milk, yet it is present in the petals of the *kanaka-ketakī* flower which are like gold.
By this, the eyes of cats and other animals are also explained;
their perception [of objects] occurs due to a specific contact between the rays [of light] and the object.
— Nyāyasūtra 3.1.32
The perception of those two large objects occurs due to a specific kind of contact between the visual ray and the object, just as it does for the light of a lamp and its object—*Nyāyabhāṣya*.
"The eye, having gone outside, attains the dimension of the object through its connection with external light"—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 159.
The inclusion of the term "separate" (*pṛthu*) is also justified by its having a separate tip (*pṛthvagratā*), for it is established in that very same manner—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī*, p.
74; *Cakṣu*.

The comparison for the root *sṛ* (in the sense of "going") is as follows: the black antelope [skin] is like a ray of light, because, while being a substance, it serves as the instrumental cause for the perception of form in a restricted manner;
or alternatively, the eye is like a ray of light, because, while being a substance and being restricted [to its function], it illuminates objects obstructed by glass and the like, just like a lamp.
—Nyāyavārttika, p. 381;
Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 525 [concerning] the eye.
Because of the specific quality of heat found in items such as whetted sharp weapons made of śāṇī cloth,
and because of the observation of the rays from the eyes of nocturnal creatures.
For the rays of the eyes are indeed seen at night in nocturnal animals such as cats and the like; by this, there is an inference regarding the remainder—
Nyāyabhāṣya 3.1.1.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 480:

The view of others is as follows: "The eye is composed of fire (*taijasa*), because among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], it illuminates only color-form, like a lamp. To them [we reply]: why then would all well-known things such as jars not also be composed of fire, since they exist like fire? If you say: "This is not so, because the thesis is sublated by perception (*adhyakṣa*), which apprehends jars and the like as distinct from the hot, radiant touch and color-form [of fire]," then this is equally applicable to the case at hand.
See page 8, note 4.

Furthermore, the eye is not composed of fire (*taijasa*), because it does not illuminate what is extremely close to it. Whatever is composed of fire illuminates even that which is extremely close, as in the case of a lamp and so forth. Why does this negative inference (*vyatirekī hetu*) not manifest here? Nor is this [reason] inconclusive for the opponent; otherwise, the statement "the living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth" would not be well-said.
Comparison: The eye does not function by reaching its object, because it does not perceive what has been touched;
for if it were to function by reaching its object, like the sense of touch, it would perceive collyrium that has been touched, yet it does not perceive it.
—Tattvavārttika, p. 67: For the Naiyāyika, this living body is not soulless, because [if it were], it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth.
—Nyāyavārttika, p. 46.
Or else, because it illuminates darkness; for that which is fiery does not illuminate darkness, such as a lamp and so forth—this is what should be understood.
As it has been said:
The eye is not composed of fire; [this is] the comparison—the eye is not composed of fire because it illuminates darkness—*Nyāyakumuda*, p. 80.
In the *Ratnāvalī*, page 324, it is said:
"When darkness is extinguished, the supreme [object] is perceived; it is not obscured by darkness, nor is it hidden by walls and the like."
As stated in *Laghīyastraya*, verse 56:

"Since the cognition of form is observed to arise in some cases even in the absence of light from lamps and the like, how can it be said that such light invariably illuminates form—lest the example be deficient in its probans? Thus, because the ocular rays are unestablished, if they were taken as the subject (*dharmin*) under the designation 'eye,' the reason ['because it is an external sense organ'] would be unestablished in its very substratum (*āśrayasvarūpāsiddha*); therefore, this [argument] is trivial, especially in the case of nocturnal animals and the like."

This is another explanation: from what cause does the emission—the emergence—of the ray, that is, of the visual rays, occur from its own substrate? For that which is uncaused and unseen cannot be postulated as existing, due to the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Some maintain that the illumination of the object is its cause.
For instance: it is observed that a sense organ reveals an object connected to itself;

in that case, if the rays [of the eye] were not connected to the object—just as the physical orb [is not]—how could there be its revelation? Since there is [revelation], we conclude that there is an emergence of rays.
There is no fault [in our position], because, like the mind (*manas*), it would result in the manifestation of that object through a connection with a connected thing (*sambandha-sambandha*).

To explain: just as the mind is conjoined with the self (*ātman*), and the self is [conjoined] with space (*ākāśa*), and that [space] is [conjoined] with all entities—thus, through a connection with a connected thing, it manifests those objects;
for indeed, its conjunction with its own object, or the conjunction of its rays with the object, is not admitted by others.

Likewise, the eye is connected with the mind, that [mind] is also connected with the self (*ātman*), and that [self] is also connected with space; and that [space] is also connected with all entities. Thus, through this chain of connections (*sambandha-sambandha*), the eye illuminates its object. Indeed, it is not accepted by others that there is a direct contact of the eye with its rays and the object. In the same way, the eye is connected with the mind, that [mind] with the self, and that [self] with the objects; thus, through such connection, the eye itself is the illuminator of that [object]. Therefore, enough with the conceptualization of the emission of rays.

Nor do we perceive any distinction such that, despite there being no difference in their status as sense organs (*indriya*), the mind (*manas*) is thus [all-pervading] while the eye is not; in this way, the simultaneous perception of the branch and the moon becomes logically consistent. Otherwise, since the rays travel in succession, there would first be contact with the branch and thus its perception, followed by contact with the moon and thus its perception; consequently, there would be a perception of them in sequence, which is not the case.
In the case of a real object,

instruments such as an axe used for cutting or weighing are observed to function by reaching their objects; and since the sense organs are likewise [instruments], they must therefore function by reaching their objects.
—Because the sense organs, by virtue of being causal agents, function by reaching [their objects] (prāpyakāritva). —Nyāyavārttika, p. 36;
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 37.
Comparison: In the same way, causality is subject to deviation by the mind, or by a mantra that effects the expulsion of serpents and the like.
—Tattvasaṃgrahaślokavārttika, p. 234; Nyāyakumudacandra, p. 82;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 330.
Even space is conjoined with the eye.
The reading "the self (ātman) also is included herein" is written twice;
for comparison: "If the eye, after a long time, were to see that which has gone far away..."
Furthermore, why is it that form is not clearly perceived when it is too close or too far away?

(13) If the eye were to travel to the location of the object because its operation requires contact (*prāpyakāritva*), then one would not perceive objects such as the moon or stars merely by opening one's eyes.
"The eye perceives the branch and the moon at the same time... — Tattvavaiśāradī, p. 68; Catuḥśataka, p. 186.
Of the branch...

Others maintain that the connection of the moon with [the branches] is an illusion of simultaneity due to the rapidity of perceiving the moon and the branches—like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals through with a needle. This is not correct; for when a material object that is not omnipresent, such as a needle, comes into contact with petals situated in different locations, a simultaneous perception is logically possible because of the sequential contact. But this is not the case elsewhere, where the conditions are the opposite. Otherwise, the wretched report of a single cognition would be utterly groundless.

As for the claim that "the branch and the moon are perceived at the same time," that too is not the case, because we do not accept it. For what person of sound mind would maintain that the branch and the moon are perceived simultaneously?
Since there is no perception of a difference in time, this is a false cognition, like the [illusory] impression of piercing a hundred lotus petals one after another—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 35.
Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 120; Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 23; Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p. 159.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
74; Muktāvalī, p. 178:

If it is thought that even in other cases, there is a sequential conjunction of such a ray with the branch and the moon located in different places, this might be so if there were some perception of the movement of the ray—as there is in the case of a needle—but it has already been stated that such [perception] does not exist.
If that delusion is not established, there is a mutual dependence;

for instance, the establishment of the delusion depends on the establishment of the rays' gradual movement, and the establishment of the rays' gradual movement depends on the establishment of the delusion.
Therefore, it remains settled: from where does the emergence of the ray come?
Regarding the establishment of the illusion of simultaneity for that which possesses form:

if indeed one holds that cognition has the nature of grasping all objects of knowledge, and the self likewise possesses that same nature, how could it be the grasper of any object whatsoever by itself— such that there would be a sequential apprehension of objects depending on the senses, as in the case of an omniscient being?

If it is argued that [the omniscient being] does not perceive by himself because of the existence of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), from what source is this established? Not from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that [obstruction] does not appear therein.
If space and so forth were the obstructions, there would be no omniscience, since they exist at all times.
Furthermore, even when passion and other afflictions (*rāga-ādi*) are present, they cannot be considered obstructions, because the perception of objects still occurs.

There is no cognition of another [self] through inference, because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*) that could establish its existence. If it is argued that its existence is established because that which has the nature of illuminating all objects does not illuminate them [when in a state of bondage], then from what is its possession of that nature established? If it is said: "Because it has the nature of illuminating everything once its obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) has been removed," then there is a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): for the obscuration is established only when the nature of illuminating everything is established, and the nature of illuminating everything is established only upon the removal of that obscuration. To this, he replies: "False knowledge," and so forth, regarding the self (*ātman*).
The establishment of the obscurations [arises] from the impossibility of the removal of passion and so forth, due to the non-existence of [suitable] places and so on.
The existence of an obscuration of the self is established because there is no probative reason for its inference.
One's own false cognition is invalid due to its non-correspondence with reality, like [the cognition of] poison and the like;
it arises from the manifestation of an obscuration in the knower, originating from the cause of a defect, even though it exists inherently. || 2 ||

The varieties of sensory ignorance, such as *avagraha* (perception) and so forth, are fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) because they consist of false apprehension; for while the self, which is inherently a means of knowledge characterized by non-remorse, may undergo error through external influence— just like one who is intoxicated or unconscious— if the knower were not inherently [aware], how could there be error through another, being as insentient as a stone?

For why should a transformation in that manner not be postulated for the self (ātman) itself, rather than postulating a further excellence in another, when it is devoid of such a transformation? There is no contradiction whatsoever in the case of one whose nature is knowing, who does not act by reaching [the object], and who knows all substances throughout the three periods of time in some respect, provided there is no obstruction; for the self experiences clarity regarding its own object, like the distinction between indirect and direct perception, due to the power of its own cause through the subsidence and destruction of veils.

If it is argued that conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)—whose nature consists in the latent impressions of conceptualization established by the perception of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—constructs linguistic usage through the determination of mere entities (*vastumātra*), [we reply: no; because it is certain that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is incompatible with the absolute view of momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*).

Therefore, this is the meaning: in that regard, false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is established in the world as non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*) due to its lack of correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) and its deceptive nature; for that [cognition] has as its subject (*dharmin*) things such as "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
Regarding that, he states the thesis (*sādhya*): "From the manifestation of the veil" (*āvaraṇodbhūteḥ*).

Karma such as *jñānāvaraṇīya* (obscuration of knowledge) is the "veil" (*āvaraṇa*) because it prohibits the soul (*jīva*) from engaging with its own objects; its "manifestation" (*udbhūtiḥ*) is its orientation toward performing its own function. From that [manifestation], [the result] arises—this is the remainder of the sentence, which constitutes the thesis.
He states the reason: "from the cause of a defect" (*doṣahetoḥ*).

A "defect" (*doṣa*) is the apprehension of something otherwise; that itself is the "cause" (*hetu*), meaning the mark (*liṅga*). For that reason, he provides an example: "like poison and so forth" (*viṣādivat*).
That of which poison and the like are the beginning—such as wine and so forth—is described as "that [beginning with poison]. "Like that" means just as that.

What is meant is this: just as the perception of objects such as the spinning of the earth, which arises from poison and the like, occurs due to the manifestation of an obscuration caused by the poison and so forth, so too does the perception of objects such as primordial nature (prakṛti) occur, due to the manifestation of an obscuration caused by one's unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), which has entered the scope of dispute, arises from the manifestation of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), because it is false cognition; and since "false cognition" is used as an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*), it includes [the reasons] "because it is ignorance" (*ajñānatva*) and "because it is indistinct" (*aspaṣṭatva*). This is like the kind of cognition produced by poison and so forth; and the mention of "poison etc. is for this very purpose, because when that [poison] is consumed, its specific action does not cease.

Thus, according to the Sāṃkhya school, the first [category] consists of the eight karmas: knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*), perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇa*), feeling-producing (*vedanīya*), deluding (*mohanīya*), life-span-determining (*āyus*), name-determining (*nāma*), status-determining (*gotra*), and obstructive (*antarāya*).
— Tattvasūtra 8.4: False Knowledge (mithyājñāna)
Due to the arising of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), there is falsity, ignorance, and lack of clarity.

Here, the Sautrāntika and others object: "Since the substratum of that [falsity] exists prior to false cognition as something whose nature is to illuminate its own object, it is better to postulate a veil for it [the substratum]; moreover, such a [veil] does not exist, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*)."
Even false cognition arises without a substratum, according to the statement that "cognitions are like paintings on the wall";

therefore, what kind of obscuration could be postulated for that? In this regard, the position that "it is due to the non-perception of another state" is contradicted by perception, and the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavaikalya). To that, he replies: "of the knower"—he who previously knew the conch as white, now knows it as yellow, and will know it again as white, is called the "knower."

And that [perception] is shown briefly through such passages as Siddhiviniścaya 2.3: "Direct perception is momentary, consisting of a single cognition of various object-aspects," and so forth; however, it will be demonstrated in detail right here.
As it was said in the Nyāyaviniścaya:
The knower even of the self of the self.

In the *Nyāyaviniścaya*, [it is stated]: "He who, through the delusion of ignorance, perceives the true object as an untrue one—or the untrue object as a true one—due to the force of his own [faulty] vision.
(Nyāyaviniścaya 1)

38. Thus the Vaiśeṣika says: "The self exists prior to the arising of knowledge; however, at that time, due to the absence of knowledge, it does not take an object as its object even though the object exists, and this is not because of an obscuration. Since it is said that "the *kiṃśuka* flowers are naturally red," we have no effort to expend there regarding the proof of an obscuration; rather, in that case, the distinction is simply that from the causal complex of merit (*dharma*) and so forth, valid knowledge arises, while from another [complex], erroneous knowledge arises.

To this, he states the reply: "By itself" (svataḥ) means by way of its own nature, not through a connection with the cognition of another object; this will be demonstrated in the commentary [vṛtti] at the point where it is argued that there is no apprehension because of the absence of cognition.

In the *Ṭīkā*, the proponent of the doctrine of absolute error says: "Let there be some self-knowing subject; yet he perceives objects erroneously by his very nature, not due to an obscuration. To this, they read the reply: "Of that which exists"—meaning of that which is non-erroneous and whose nature is to grasp its own object as it actually exists.

The term "from itself" (*svataḥ*) should also be connected here; otherwise, how could even the cognition of absolute error be established? For it is not logical that its cognition arises from error alone, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As it has been said by someone:
The realization of delusion is known;
this mind is radiant by nature, and its impurities are adventitious.

Regarding *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.210, the opponent further thinks as follows: "Its nature as false perception arises from itself, while its nature as correct perception arises from something else. This view is refuted by the phrase "as [the case with] poison and so forth"; for if one were to postulate that false perception—which is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the consumption of poison and the like—arises from something else, then even smoke would not originate from fire.

And if all cognitions were false by their own nature, how could the ultimate reality of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) be established? For in that case, there would be no operation of anything other than the prior cognition itself—such as the restriction of objects to the eyes and so forth, the conformity to the object’s form arising from the object, clarity arising from light, or the cognitive nature of consciousness arising from consciousness—as stated [by the Buddhists]. Furthermore, if the ultimate reality of self-awareness were not established, the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) would not be able to remain at ease for even a fraction of a moment, because for them, neither affirmation nor negation of anything would be possible.
Then it was stated: "Because it exists by itself" [means] its nature is knowledge.

Now, if this is so, then let this inference simply be a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) and thus invalid (*apramāṇa*); what is the use of the phrase "due to non-correspondence" (*visaṃvādāt*)? To this it is replied: When someone says to a person who is proving that a false cognition under dispute is obscured by unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭāvaraṇa*)—namely, that because no such false cognition exists, both the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of the probandum are unestablished—then, for the sake of establishing that subject for him, the phrase "due to non-correspondence" is stated.

For even by Prajñākara himself, who accepts this non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*), he must admit that there is a lack of correspondence—otherwise known as being devoid of an object—for conceptual cognitions such as "this arises from that," "this is distant," or "this is near. Otherwise, how could there be a non-duality of appearances? And if that is so, how can the subject (*dharmin*) be unestablished? If it is argued: "Let it be that false cognition results from a lack of correspondence; what is the use of the term 'invalid cognition' (*apramāṇa*)? We say: No. You establish the existence of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) through inference, yet that [inference] is false. How, then, can its establishment occur in reality? This is stated in response to one who argues thus.
Because false cognition regarding the subject of the thesis and the subject of the example is established through inference.

Regarding the obscuration from the perspective of ultimate truth, this is the intended meaning: if inference is considered to be false, then it would be invalid due to its lack of correspondence with reality; yet it is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and therefore it is not false.

[Objection: This might be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) if it were non-discrepant (*avisamvādaka*); however, even though it is false, it is non-discrepant because there is a connection with the object to be established (*sādhya*), just like the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel. [Response: But if that cognition of the jewel is not a valid means of knowledge despite being non-discrepant, then how can inference be [valid], since its defining characteristic would be subject to deviation? If it is a valid means of knowledge, is it perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be perception, because there is a determination of the jewel in one place while the jewel is obtained in another; otherwise, the determination of water in a mass of mirage rays would be perception when water is obtained in a well or similar location.

One might object: "This occurs for one who has already attained satisfaction. [We reply: If the illusion of the jewel were sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*), it would not be so; for it depends upon the observation of a similarity in form, it arises even without a modification of the sense organ, it is communicated by others through a different mental continuum, and it is sublated by analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*). However, a mental [illusion] is logical, just like the illusion of silver in a conch-shell.
But if this [cognition] were born of the senses—such as the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel—[it would possess the aforementioned characteristics].
The means of valid cognition [is directed] toward the luster of a gem situated in the keyhole within the interior of the room.

The means of valid cognition is comparison (*tulanā*): sometimes it would be presented in exactly that same way by verbal expressions within another mental continuum; it would depend upon the recollection of what was previously perceived, and it would not appear with complete clarity.
— Prajñāpāramitopadeśa 2.298:
by means of the knowledge of reality.
If it were not for error, another quality would be joined [to the object] by means of a cause of error,
such as similarity and so forth.
The form of silver [appears] in mother-of-pearl because of the perception of similarity in appearance, due to its characteristics such as permanence; *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.219.
Thus, it is contradicted because it is untenable for a sensory illusion (*akṣavibhrama*) to serve as an illustration for a mental illusion (*manovibhrama*).

If it is argued that "let the non-existence of the object be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the mind," [we reply: since it is other than perception, it would follow from its conformity with that [perception] that it is itself perception; therefore, it is incorrect to describe a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising subsequent to a direct observation as being a memory (*smṛti*) for a person engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*).

Indeed, the practitioner of conventional discourse does not desire a conceptualization other than [the immediate] perception, because of the description [in the *Pravāhaṇa*] that "there is no simultaneous functioning of two minds" (PV 2.133) regarding the conceptual and non-conceptual [cognitions].
The ellipsis is: "the deluded person, due to the rapidity of the mental process, determines the identity of those two.

Let it be granted that there is darkness [in the gem], as fire is [perceived] in smoke when one has reached the jewel; and let it be granted that there was previously a determination of its luster, as in the case of determining a *śiṃśapā* tree within the determination of a tree. But this is not so, because its invalidity is described for the sake of the practical agent who, lacking inquiry, finds no satisfaction in such [determinations].

By this, their status as having an effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*) is refuted; for prior to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [jewel], there ought to be a determination of the light, just as there is a determination of fire [prior to the determination of smoke]. How, then, could there be a determination of the jewel in that case? Indeed, one who ascertains smoke is never observed to have a determination of fire or anything else;

therefore, if the determination of the jewel were inferential, the passage from the *Pramāṇavārttika* beginning with "between the jewel and the lamp-light" (PV 2.57) and so forth would be easily established.

What then of one who, having ascertained the specific characteristics, performs an inference in this way: "This particular room is possessed of a jewel, because it has a specific luster associated with a jewel, like another such place observed elsewhere," or "This specific light from the keyhole possesses the shape of a jewel, because it has that specific quality, like the previously observed specific instance"? What is the status of such cases? We say: that too is indeed inference.

However, this is the distinction: if this false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) were invalid (*apramāṇa*), how could it serve as an example for the validity of another such inference? Indeed, that which is itself the probandum (*sādhya*) cannot become the example, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, it is established: if inference were a false cognition, it would be invalid; the term "invalid" is employed to demonstrate the point that [inference] arises from an object [only when valid], just like the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika-jñāna*).
This is illustrated by the case of two people running toward a [shining] gem with the thought that it is a jewel.
The meaning is that even though there is no difference in erroneous cognition, there is a distinction with respect to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*);
or else, this should be explained after having first formulated an objection (*pūrvapakṣa*).

To explain: as was stated in the immediately preceding section, beginning with "This very [cognition] has for its object substance, mode, universal, and particular" and ending with "it is a means of valid cognition because of its non-contradiction"; regarding that, the Naiyāyikas and others hold that because that cognition inheres in the self (*ātman*) which is its own nature, the self alone perceives those [objects] in such a way;
the Cārvākas hold that because it inheres in the body, the body is the mind (*manaḥ*);
and the Sāṃkhyas hold that it is the primal matter (*pradhāna*).
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that such knowledge is self-validating (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*) and not dependent on another;
as it has been said:
[Siddhiviniścaya 2].
The self is awakened.
It should be understood that the validity of all means of valid cognition is known through itself;
for a capacity that does not exist inherently cannot be produced by anything else.
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, chapter 2, verse 47.
Regarding this, he says: "False knowledge," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: for the knower, that which consists of *avagraha* (perception), *mati* (sensory cognition), *smṛti* (memory), *saṃjñā* (recognition), *cintā* (reflection), and *abhinibodha* (comprehension)—prior to its association with verbal expression—is knowledge characterized by the various divisions of *matijñāna*.
It is neither [the cognition] of the body nor of *pradhāna*; for it will be demonstrated that the latter lacks the capacity to be a knower, as it is insentient like a jar or similar objects.
From what, then, does the knower [derive his status]? He says: "From itself," that is, from its own inherent nature (*svasvābhāvya*), and not from a connection with an external object of knowledge.
And that cognition has been described as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Why? Because it is non-contradictory (*avisaṃvāda*). This is stated now: from the knower who exists by his own nature, this object arises—that is, that cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory, due to its non-deviation from its own object as it has been made its own objective domain.

Because this [cognition], characterized by its engagement in its own function, requires the apprehension of itself, it is said to be "from another" (*parataḥ*). By changing the case-ending, the connection is with "from the knower himself" (*svataḥ*); the word "of arising" (*utpatteḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder, and it is connected with "valid cognition" (*pramāṇam*) through the construction.
From what kind [of source]? He says: "from that which exists by itself" (*svataḥ sataḥ*).
This has been explained by him [the author] as well: "Because it arises from the qualities of its cause, that [invalidity] is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

Here he states an illustration: "Invalid cognition is extrinsic because of its non-correspondence and because of its emergence from an obscuration (*āvaraṇa-udbhūti*)," the remainder being "just as [validity is]. "Emergence from an obscuration" (*āvaraṇa-udbhūti*) means arising from an obscuration; [this is derived] from the root *iṇ*.
Of what nature [is it]? It is "from a cause of defects"—this is to be understood from the refutation of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) by Anantakīrti, as stated above;
page 217.

The word *kā* refers to the ablative case (*pañcamī-vibhakti*), whether it denotes validity or the cause of defects, and so forth; having introduced the matter differently, it is now explained as follows: From what indeed does the manifestation of obscuration arise? If it were from itself, then false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) would likewise have to arise from that very same source.
If it is argued that [the obscuration] arises from something else, he should be told: that does not exist, because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatvāt*).
For no one perceives or infers any such thing that produces an obscuration—just as a seed produces a sprout—due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
It is true that passion and the like are perceived; however, immediately following that, the arising obscuration is neither perceived nor inferred.

Or, let it be granted that the obscuration has a cause; nevertheless, because it is material (*mūrta*), there can be no connection between it and the immaterial (*amūrta*) self, just as there is none between a heap of dust and space. To this, he replies: "Because of the cause of the defect," and so forth.

The "defect" (*doṣa*) is passion and the like; that itself is the "cause" (*hetu*), the reason, from which the arising of the obscuration occurs. Alternatively, [it means] "that of which the cause is this. He provides an illustration: "like poison and so forth."

"Just as with poison consumed by a living being, so it is with that"—to explain: the manifestation of an obscuration inferred from false cognition is preceded by the passion and other defilements of the knower, because it is the cause of their impairment, just like poison consumed by a living being;
thus, "it is like that, as with poison consumed by a living being."

And he will state: "By means of mental, sensory, and karmic [influences], as well as by pure and impure [actions] according to their respective natures, there is the bondage of merit and demerit for living beings" (*Siddhiviniścaya-prastāva* 4), and so forth.

As for what was asked—namely, "How can there be a connection between that which is formless and that which is formed?"—that too is refuted by this, because the defect that causes such a connection exists even in the formless.
This also will be stated: "By nature, one is bound by impurities" (*Siddhiviniścaya-prastāva* 4), and so forth.
Or it may be explained as "just like that," meaning like the objects and so forth which are the causes of the defect;

thus, while commenting on the *kārikā* regarding the soul (*jīva*), he says: "Mati-ādi" means the varieties of sensory ignorance (*matyajñāna*), that is, the specific types of sensory ignorance. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which the varieties of scriptural ignorance (*śrutājñāna*) and others are included.
"What are they? he asks; [the author] says: "Avagraha and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of īhā and the others is intended;
this too is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the various distinctions such as anusmaraṇa and the rest.

What are they? He says: "They are fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*)," meaning they do not constitute valid cognition. Why? He says: "Because they are false" (*mithyā*); that is, because they consist in the apprehension of things otherwise than they are.

If it is argued: "But surely inferential cognition, although grasping a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as something other than how it actually exists, is still a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, this definition of invalidity does not apply because of such deviation (*vyabhicāra*)," [the author] replies here: "Of the means of knowledge," and so forth. This is because the very nature (*tattva*) of a means of knowledge consists in its being characterized by a determination of the object exactly as it exists.

This is what is meant: validity (*prāmāṇya*) is pervaded by being a determination that accords with reality (*yathārtha-nirṇaya*), as is established for all living beings. Even by opponents, when describing the validity of knowledge regarding a particular object within doctrines such as absolute falsity (*mithyā-ekānta*), it is only that [knowledge] which has that object as its referent that is described as valid. Therefore, when [the quality of] corresponding to reality ceases, validity also ceases, just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* ceases when the property of being a tree ceases. Otherwise, if everything were valid, no one would be devoid of the establishment of their own position; thus, if inference (*anumāna*) is false, it is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
The remainder here has been considered, and will also be considered: of what kind [of soul] and from what do [the faculties] arise? To this he says: "From itself," and so forth.
"From itself" means from the self, the individual soul (*jīva*); it is neither without support, nor does it belong to the body, nor to primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
Of what kind [of soul]? He says: "of that which is the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇabhūtasya*).

"How can there be [error] for that which has the nature of grasping an object as it truly is, since it does not inherently possess the cognition of another object? To this he says: "Because of the occurrence of error from something else. Here too, the word "of the self" (ātmanaḥ) is to be supplied; that is, the occurrence of error from something else—namely, from external material karma—which consists in the induction of a different nature [into the self].

Regarding this, he states an illustration: "Like one intoxicated," and so forth. "Like that" means just as, for one who is intoxicated or unconscious, false perceptions such as misapprehension arise due to external factors like poison because of the occurrence of cognitive distortion, so it is for another person as well; such is the meaning of the illustration.
And in a general sense,
[the refutation] of that which is asserted by the Cārvākas and that which is asserted by the Sāṃkhyas.
