By this, the following objection raised by the opponent is also refuted: "If action does not impair the essential nature of the self, then for the Jaina, everyone would remain omniscient; if it does impair it, the self would be non-eternal. Furthermore, an obscuration existing between the object and the illuminator—like a covering between a jar and a lamp—obstructs the manifestation of the object alone, but not that of the illuminator. For an internal curtain does not prevent a lamp from illuminating itself; thus, even when that obscuration exists, the self should manifest its own nature in every respect."

Thus [he says], because the refutation of the essential nature of the self (*ātman*) is somehow intended, and because the occurrence of error regarding the self through another [cause] is described; otherwise, what would be the meaning of this? Furthermore, because impermanence exists in some way, since it is impossible for it to exist in every respect even elsewhere;

for indeed, in the case of others whose bodies are defiled by rust, scales, and so forth, a variegated manifestation is seen even in their own essential nature—[this occurs] with respect to the obscuration (*āvaraṇe*).

Just as in the example of a gem and the like, the manifestation of a gem pierced by impurities occurs in various ways, so too does the manifestation of the Self, pierced by karma, occur in various ways.
*Laghīyastraya*, verse 57.
Thus, he states the refutation regarding the non-acceptance of the principle that [the self] is "intrinsically authoritative" (*svataḥ-pramāṇabhūta*)—beginning with the words "If," and so forth.

"If" (*yadi*) indicates a condition; "again" (*punaḥ*) expresses a deliberation or suggests an alternative position. If the knower—the one who apprehends objects as they truly are—were not "by itself alone" (*svata eva*), meaning not by its own nature or from its own cause, then [it would follow that] the "self" (*ātman*) would not exist; this is the connection, with the case ending being modified accordingly.

What is the fault in that? He says: "From another," and so forth. The connection is as follows: from that [cognition] which is other than its own nature or its own cause, how could there not be a knower?
Regarding this, he provides an example: "like an insentient thing."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "A jar and so forth are insentient (*acetana*); it behaves like that [insentient thing], therefore it is 'like that' (*tadvat*). Furthermore: "That which is devoid of the nature of consciousness (*jñāna-svabhāva*) is not a knower (*jñātṛ*), just like a jar and so forth; and the self (*ātman*) of the opponent is devoid of the nature of consciousness. Now, what is this "insentience" (*acetana*)? It is that which lacks the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of consciousness. In that case, it follows that its inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) must be sentient (*cetana*). Thus, since the self is also sentient, how could it be a non-knower? This contradicts your own accepted doctrine (*abhyupagama-virodha*), for you maintain that the designation "knower" applies only to that which is sentient.

Nor is it the case that [the pot] does not have consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*cetana-svabhāva*) nor as its inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*); for it is logically possible for a pot and the like, even though they do not have consciousness as their intrinsic nature, to possess color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth as their inherent causes. Alternatively, if there were something non-conscious other than consciousness, that would not exist, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the entire example is deficient; there is no possibility of a subject (*dharmin*) for the property to be proven (*sādhya*). Or, if such a subject did exist, since it would be unestablished by that very fact, what is the use of this inference? For this very reason, if it were established, there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): namely, when the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is established, other things like pots serve as the examples, and from that, its establishment follows.

If it is argued that, despite the lack of distinction in their insentience, the fact that the self is the substratum while the jar and so forth are not is obtained through the general statement "that [jar] is insentient," we say no; for there is no fault in either case.

To explain: let it be granted that the jar and so forth are insentient and that consciousness has them as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and that the self is sentient and its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); even so, this does not entail the abandonment of our position, because only that which is the cause of the transformation into consciousness is the inherent cause, and nothing else. Otherwise, it would follow that the eyes and other sense organs would also be its causes.

If it is argued that [the effect does not arise] because of its non-inherence (*asamavāya*) therein, then what is this "inherence" (*samavāya*)? If it is defined as the acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*) when that [substratum] exists, then the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before would follow.
We do not understand how that very thing could be "contained" (*utkalita*) therein.
If it is argued that its emergence as that very nature occurs when that [substratum] exists, nothing has been resolved.
The claim that "it is the state of being located therein" [is the definition of inherence] is also untenable; for it would entail that a pot and the like inhere in the ground.

If you say, "because [inherence applies only to] what is inseparable (ayutasiddha)," then what is this "inseparability"? If you say it means "established non-separately," then if this non-separate establishment means being established as absolutely non-different from the cause, that is the Sāṃkhya system; if it means [non-difference] in some sense, that is the Jaina teaching.

It might be thought: [let] the state of having its origin in the same space and time as the cause [be the definition]; why then should space (*ākāśa*) and so forth not be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) [of consciousness]? For consciousness is not possible apart from those [space and time], since that would entail the consequence of it being non-omnipresent (*asarvagata*).

Whether or not this occurs for consciousness itself when the spatial location of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the self (*ātman*) is non-different from that of the eyes and other [senses] must be considered. Therefore, it is established that consciousness alone is the inherent cause of consciousness, while that which is not its cause is non-conscious (*acetana*).
The meaning is that whatever does not serve as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of consciousness is insentient (*acetana*);
[consciousness] exists because there is the designation of a knower (*jñātṛ*).
Alternatively, if volition exists,
it possesses both the status of the subject and the status of the example.
The meaning is that whatever does not serve as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of consciousness is insentient;
for it would follow that only that which transforms itself into the form of consciousness could be the inherent cause of consciousness.
Because volition does not exist as an inherent property (samavāya) in the eye and other [senses].
Since it is observed that consciousness acquires its own existence when the eye and other [faculties] are present,
and because the Sāṃkhya accepts the non-difference between cause and effect, the [internal organ] is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of consciousness.
Because it would follow that space is not omnipresent.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that jars and the like, though having a nature devoid of color and so forth, are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of color and the like—that too is refuted by this [very argument]. If it is argued: "But then, since the self, like a jar, does not have consciousness as its intrinsic nature, if it were the inherent cause of consciousness, there would be no distinction between the probandum and the example"; let this matter rest for now, as it will be examined immediately hereafter.

Or, let there be something else that is insentient (acetana) distinct from volition (cetanā); even so, there is no lack of distinction regarding the example for everything. For, although [the self] is insentient, it is taken as the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), whereas another insentient thing serves as the example. Just as when it is said, "This object possessing a dewlap and so forth is a cow," another cow serves as the example, yet there is no injunction to establish the properties of one thing upon another; because once that [subject] is established by logic, there is merely the negation of properties attributed to it by others.

This is another explanation: Furthermore, if the Self were not by its own nature and through its own form a knower subject to transformation for the apprehension of objects, how could it [become so] from something else, namely from a non-inherent instrumental cause? It could not at all; for there is no other such transformation for anything that lacks the inherent nature of such transformation, just as in the case of insentient things like earth and so forth, or, from the perspective of the Lokāyata, like a jar and so forth.

Now, as for what was said—"If there were no difference from the conscious self, then the eye and other organs would also be its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), since there is no distinction between difference or inherence"—that is not correct. If it is argued that even though difference is non-distinct, the status of being a cause toward a particular effect is established for only some [organ] due to a specific proximity (*pratyāsatti*) to that effect, because the potencies (*śakti*) of entities are diverse; to this, he says: "Of another," and so forth.

In the postulation of another knower, or of some other cause, excellence, or capacity, the phrase "from itself alone" (svata eva) is understood to carry over; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress—this is what is intended.

Why then would the Naiyāyika not postulate for the self an excellence in its own apprehension from itself alone? He would certainly postulate it, since the logic is the same—as he considers the case to be like that of the self.
Because its status as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is established;

or else, having raised an objection from another perspective, this should be explained as follows: "The self is not a knower either intrinsically or extrinsically, because it lacks a connection with cognition; rather, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is the knower, for the opposite is the case. Therefore, its false cognitions, grasping, and so forth arise extrinsically due to the occurrence of error, since it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), whereas the self is not subject to error. To that Sāṃkhya, he replies: "Of the other," and so forth.

If one postulates an excellence (*atiśaya*) in another—that is, in the *pradhāna* distinct from the self—namely, the capacity for knowledge that is either true or otherwise, why is that same excellence not postulated in the self, the person? For it is thought that, just as with the *pradhāna* of the Sāṃkhya, there is no contradiction in the self undergoing transformation (*pariṇāma*). [The opponent objects: "Let it be that the self is inherently a knower and yet possesses an obscuration; nevertheless, in the absence of that obscuration, let it grasp the object in its actual state at the very same time as the operation of the sense organs, since its capacity is restricted to that alone."

For example, a lamp illuminates only that which is suitable for it, even in the absence of an obstruction, and not everything; thus says Prajñākara. To this he replies: "Of that whose nature is knowing," and so forth. What contradiction is there in the fact that the Self, whose nature is knowing—that is, whose nature is to know—is a knower? He asks: "What? and then replies: "Substance, not quality or modification."

He thinks that because a single, gross entity consisting of parts such as form is grasped by that [cognition], there is no contradiction for one who knows it as qualified by the present time. To this, he says: "having the three times as its object" (*trikālagocara*)—that which has the three times as its range is so described; the meaning is that it is a composite form belonging to the three times.
Even so, he says that one knows [it] in fragments; in what manner is it "entirely" (*aśeṣa*)? He says: "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*), by whatever means whatsoever.

For instance: first, there is the perception of a jar qualified by the attribute of newness through the eye and other senses; then, there is the perception of that very same jar as qualified by oldness; and immediately after that, there is the recollection of it as qualified by its previous mode. Through this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), one perceives the continuity between the preceding and succeeding modes. When, by means of reasoning (*tarka*)—which arises from the observation, recollection, and recognition of modes that are invariably concomitant with unity from birth until death—one has grasped their general inseparable connection with the probandum (unity) in its entirety, the infinite nature of the substance (*dravya*) is then cognized through inference.
Substance belongs to the jar alone, as do its modifications.
Some [ask]: "How can that which is born of inference be mental perception? This should be considered;
for since it is produced by the senses (*akṣaja*), nothing would fail to be perception.
When was this considered? He says: "In the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*)."

If it is argued: "When there is an absence of that karma which acts as an obstacle to a cognition functioning toward its own object, then surely for the soul—which is of the nature of cognition and free from obstacles—there would be the grasping of objects even when they are not distinct in space and time; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)," [the author] replies here: For one whose nature is to act without reaching [the object] (*aprāpyakārin*), it is impossible to make something reached—that is, to make it co-spatial and co-temporal with the grasper—such that what is not thus made remains unreached. It is held that for one whose nature is to act without reaching, there is no contradiction in grasping even that which is different in time, just as in the case of [objects] different in space.

But as for one who thinks that cognition has no activity toward anything other than its own nature, how can it be said that it "acts without reaching [its object]"? He ought to be asked: "How does it have activity toward its own nature? If he says, "Because we observe it functioning there," then that is the same in the other case as well. Prajñākaragupta intends this to be demonstrated.
Here the Mīmāṃsaka says: "There is no contradiction whatsoever for one who knows all that [reality] through the six means of valid cognition.
To him, he replies with the words beginning with "sva" (one's own):

for the self as previously described, everything that exists within its own domain is [known]; otherwise, there would be no comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). In that case, for one experiencing clarity, there is no contradiction—provided, as is understood from the context, that there is an absence of any impediment (*pratibandha*).
He states an illustration: "In the case of the imperceptible," and so forth.
If it is argued that one ought to say "like the perceptible and the imperceptible" because that is more logical, we reply: no; for this formulation is made with reference to the views of others.

For instance, regarding what was stated by Prajñākaragupta—"How can successive cognitions be understood in one [object], since the entire substance would then be known? How could there be no contradiction?"—with reference to that, it should be explained as follows: indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*) has as its object conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) characterized by a common, clear form, and that [conceptual cognition] is similar to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in terms of its own nature; thus, "like that" (*tadvat*) is to be interpreted.
Just as one [object] is apprehended simultaneously as possessing two common forms, so too is it considered to possess multiple successive cognitions in common.
Addressing the Mīmāṃsaka: An indistinct cognition of trees and so forth, which arises from a distance or due to other causes, is called "indirect" (parokṣa);
likewise, even in the absence of the word "ca," it is said to be "direct" (pratyakṣa) when it is present [as a cognition]. This should be explained as "like that" (tasyeva), meaning "similar to that.
If an omniscient being could exist through the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), by whom could he be prevented?

But by whichever single means of valid cognition an omniscient being is postulated, he must surely perceive all [objects], such as tastes and so forth, by means of that very eye— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra, verses 111–12.
Because pervasion pertains to the three times,
there are successive cognitions regarding the self.

The Buddhist, demonstrating that his knowledge is indirect (*parokṣa*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), uncontradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇābādha*), and showing the probandum (*sādhya*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), says: "Not for us," and so forth. For us Buddhists, "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to karma such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya*); and since another [type of obscuration] is not under discussion and has not been mentioned, "destruction" (*kṣaya*) and "subsidence" (*upaśama*) are understood to refer only to the destruction and subsidence of one's own obscuration. And their cognition (*buddhi*) is not a false cognition (*mithyābuddhi*) due to the influence of obscuration, whereby [the opponent's objection] such as "because of the division of sensory ignorance" (*matyajñāna*) and so forth would be appropriate.

Nor does the cognition correspond to reality by virtue of the subsidence of that [karmic obscuration], because [the soul] is of the nature of a knower, and so forth. From what, then, does it arise? To this he says: "But rather," however, from the power of its own cause; for the cause of false cognition is sometimes defiled, such as the eyes and so forth, due to cataracts, rapid motion, and the like—according to the statement in *Nyāyabindu* 1.6—and for correct cognition, that very same [cause] is the opposite. The connection is: "from the power" (śakti)—meaning the capacity to produce the aforementioned knowledge—"of that," [namely] of the cognition.
"...due to darkness, rapid whirling, the agitation of a boat, and so forth..."—darkness (*timira*) is a disorder of the eyes; this is a cause of error residing in the sense organ.
"Rapid whirling" refers to the swift rotation of a firebrand (*alāta*) and the like.
For if a firebrand is rotated slowly, the illusion of a wheel does not arise; therefore, the whirling is qualified by the term "rapid."
And this cause of error resides in the object;
the term "going" (yāna) is used because for one standing on a moving boat— where "boat-going" means the movement of the boat— an illusion of moving trees and so forth arises.
And this cause of delusion resides in the external basis;
it is the disturbance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
For when the wind and the other humors have become disturbed, the illusion of a blazing pillar and so forth arises.

And this internal cause of error must affect the sense organ itself by means of all causes of error— whether external or internal, pertaining to the senses, their objects, or their substrates— [as stated in] Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā 1.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that just as sensory error arises from the eyes and other faculties when they are defiled by jaundice and so forth, so too does this mental error of conceptual construction arise for the self when it is defiled by the veil of karma? To this, he says: "In the continuum established... and so on. This refers to the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for conceptual construction—which serves as the cause of such constructions—that has been instilled or established within the continuum through the perception of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by previous successive conceptualizations—which is directed toward the production of its own effect through the influence of seeing that [object]—is itself the "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). This conventional arises from its own nature as the manifestation of obscuration; because it conceals reality (*tattva*), it is the conceptual cognition of universals and so forth.
What does it do? He says: it constructs conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) in both false and non-false forms.

Why? He says: "from the determination of the mere thing" (*vastumātravyavasāyāt*)—that is, from the determination of one's own form as if it were a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), even though it is not a particular.
If it is argued that this word indicates its falsity by illuminating the opponent's position, [we reply: no.

Now, one might object: even though the sensory or mental error of one who is intoxicated or unconscious is seen to arise from a prior mind defiled by poison or the like, it is nevertheless postulated as being preceded by a mind that has come into contact with an unseen state of that same kind; if so, why is the sprout—which is seen to arise from earth and other factors when assisted by a seed—not likewise postulated to arise from earth and other factors alone, even when the seed is hidden in a granary or similar place? Furthermore, if the removal of falsity in cognitions were to occur in some manner other than the way the removal of intoxication and the like is observed, then the cessation of an effect would not be invariably caused by the cessation of its cause, and thus no certainty could be established anywhere. Although this objection was already addressed by the author when he said "false cognition" and so forth, he says "no," etc., in order to provide a different line of refutation. "No," etc. [The full verse is: "No, because of the observation of the production of effects from those very causes, and because of the non-observation of their production from others; for otherwise, there would be no restriction regarding the cessation of the effect upon the cessation of the cause. [This means: It is not the case that the sprout arises solely from earth and other factors. Why? Because we observe the production of effects from those very causes (earth, water, etc., when accompanied by the seed), and because we do not observe their production from others (earth, etc., when the seed is absent). For if it were otherwise, the cessation of the effect would not be contingent upon the cessation of the cause, and thus there would be no fixed rule anywhere. This is what is intended. Thus, although the point was already settled, he speaks again to refute it by another method.

To the question, "Why is there the word 'no' (na) in the negation of what was stated by others? he says: "In the absolute view of momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*), the performance (*kriyā*)—that is, the production (*karaṇa*)—of an object or effect is impossible; this [negation] is purposeless, because of the determination of its contradiction in the immediately preceding discussion. This is the remainder of the sense.
What happened then? He says: "In the effect," and so forth. There is no causal relationship at all among minds; why?
Because, like other [distinct] continuums, they are separate. How, then, can there be the relationship of the perfumed and the perfume? (3)

And if the relation of cause and effect were real, how could there be a restriction of the mental continuum to specific instances? Since there would be no distinction in the immediate succession of all things everywhere, even if there were a relationship of the "perfumed" and the "perfumer," it would not occur at all due to the absence of proximity;
consequently, conceptual construction itself would not arise.

Because that contradiction is resolved, for whom could there not be the relation of cause and effect, or causality itself? To this he says: "Of cognitions, in the case of the absolute [view of] momentariness"—the sense being that this [causality] consists in the nature of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
"Let that not be so; even then, what [of it]? To this he says: "From where would there be a *santati*—that is, a *santāna* (continuum) of cognitions?
The connection is that this is because a continuum is characterized by a specific relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*). He thinks:

"Or, let there be causality among them in that regard; nevertheless, there is still a fault. To this he says: "How could there be the state of being the perfumer (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*)? The preceding cognition is the perfumer, and the subsequent cognition is the perfumed—from where [could this arise]? It could not be at all."
Why? Because of their difference, that is, because of their plurality; this is the connection [of the argument] regarding those minds considered to belong to a single continuum.
He provides an illustration with the phrase "like other continua," meaning "as in the case of other continua," in order to demonstrate the absence of a causal relationship.
Explaining the *kārikā* on the mental states (*cittānām*), he says: "And when [the cause] exists," and so forth;
the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also" (*api*) and expresses possibility.

Even if a causal relationship exists, why is there no restriction of the continuum—namely, the distinction that "this is one continuum" and "these are various continua"—in the case of a certain absolute [monistic] view? The phrase "in that absolute view" is to be connected here.

If it is argued: "Surely, those moments which exist in a sequence of prior and posterior states constitute a single continuum, while others are the opposite," [the author] replies: "In all cases, of all [moments]," and so forth.
Because there is no difference in the immediate succession of all moments—whether they fall within distinct or identical continua—in every instance, whether external or internal...

Alternatively, since there is no distinction [in the causal capacity] among all those things considered as causes and effects in every case—this is how it should be understood—another person here objects regarding cognitions: "The restriction of the mental continuum does not arise from immediate succession, because that [succession] exists even otherwise, as in the case of the waking mind and the dreaming mind. To this, he replies: Why do the waking minds of someone at the same time not belong to a single continuum? For the difference in location and so forth is indistinguishable everywhere.

If it is argued that [the five cognitions do not arise from one] because a single [cause] lacks multiple material causes (*upādāna*), then how is it that from a single waking-consciousness of Devadatta, the five cognitions of awakening sometimes arise? If they arise from that very same [consciousness], then the others would lack a material cause. If those [five cognitions] have a prior cognition as their material cause, then the coexistence of entities dependent on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*) would not be possible; thus, this argument is hollow. (Pramāṇavārttika 3)
18. Thus, and so forth;

for since there is no necessity of dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*) regarding the coexistence of tastes and other qualities, it has been stated that there is no designation of a "single causal complex" due to the absence of time.

If it is argued that even when those [subsequent cognitions] exist, it is not known which one is the material cause (*upādāna*) of which—just as a cognition of color is the cause of a cognition of color, and this may be applied similarly elsewhere—it follows that the first Buddhist cognition would be without a material cause, because prior to it there was no such material cause of that kind. Otherwise, how could there be the state of being a Sugata (a Buddha) along with its means? Furthermore, if inference were of a different continuum from conceptualization (*vikalpa*), then conceptualization would be the material cause of perception; otherwise, due to their non-difference, there would be the refutation stated in the *Siddhiviniścaya* (1.7) beginning with "in the case of a similar memory... and so forth. Thus, the objection remains unshaken.

Therefore, just as one [cause] is the material basis (*upādāna*) for many, so too are many [causes] the basis for one. Otherwise, since no single [effect] would ever arise from the five-fold waking consciousness, other [causes] would be useless.

If it is argued that this is not the case because they function as co-operative causes (*sahakāritva*), then the meditation on Garuḍa and the like would be useless for the awakening of those who have fainted from poison and so forth, since they occur at different times.

Furthermore, if things occurring at different times were to act as co-operatives toward a single effect, then a taste simultaneous with the inferred form would be a co-operative cause in the production of a preceding form and so on; thus, it would follow that a single part of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the complex itself.
Prajñākara, who maintains the theory of an intervening cause,
[asserts that] even when separated by an interval, [the causes] are simultaneous.
This is useless for one whose mind is awakened,
whose consciousness is awake.
If the omniscient Buddha possesses the knowledge of an omniscient one even prior to his waking consciousness, then from what means (*upāya*) would his omniscience arise? Such would be the question.
Furthermore, [the term] *kālya* refers to that which exists at a time, such as the meditation on Garuḍa and so forth.

Moreover, if it were possible for multiple cognitions—possessing distinct times, substrata, and cooperative causes—to operate upon a single object, then the restriction of the continuum (*santati-niyama*) would not be known within the extreme of difference (*bhedaikānta*); thus, the fault remains as it was.

Nor have we understood [the following]: that when those [causes] are employed for a homogeneous effect, they are not employed elsewhere; or that their employment occurs at a time distinct from awakening; or that there is such an operation of a single [cause] toward an effect that arises sequentially. Thus, we do not accept the claim that "sequential entities do not arise from a non-sequential cause" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.45).
Or [if one holds] the extreme view that sound is momentary, it would be like the case of an object.

But others say: "The material cause (*upādāna*) is neither immediately preceding nor simultaneous, but rather similar; therefore, this restriction exists. For those of tranquil mind, when a state of awakened consciousness arises from some cause, let it be explained how that [restriction] could exist? It might occur in the case of a son following the mental qualities of his father, but there is no such restriction elsewhere as well.
Thus it is established that there is no restriction regarding the mental continuum;
for the restriction of the continuum exists only when anger and other such states are present.
Regarding the restriction to a single continuum—
that is, the state of being a single continuum—
it was said that by virtue of this restriction, a son does not follow the mind of the father; to this, he replied:
Or, let that restriction be granted; nevertheless, there remains a fault, as he says: "Even though... and so forth.

Why is it that the preceding consciousness has the capacity to perfume (*vāsakatā*) and the subsequent one has the capacity to be perfumed (*vāsyatā*), yet this does not occur? He says: "Because of the absence of proximity (*pratyāsatti*)."

Now, what is this "proximity" (*pratyāsatti*) of which you assert the absence here? If you say it is the "relation of cause and effect" (*hetuphalabhāva*), then that indeed exists, and thus the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because of the statement "even when [it] exists," etc.; or else, if another [type of] proximity is accepted, such as spatial nearness (*deśādinaikaṭya*), then even in its absence, the relation of "infuser and infused" (*vāsyavāsakabhāva*)—just like the relation of "material cause and its product" (*upādānopādeyabhāva*)—is not contradictory. Thus, the reason has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika*).

If, moreover, in the absence of that [object], the existence of both the non-appropriated and the other is also not admitted, then there is a contradiction with the accepted position that [it exists] "even when [the object] is present"—this is the fault already stated. If, however, [you argue it is due to] capacity (*yogyatā*), how can there be an absence of that [capacity] in the case of absolute difference? [It would be absent] because of the spatial and other differences between those two things intended to be the impressed (*vāsya*) and the impressioner (*vāsaka*). To this it has been said: because the capacity for the relation of producer and produced is absent. Furthermore, this capacity is not contradictory, as it is observed; for indeed, it is observed that the waking mind, possessing the equipment of thorough knowledge of the scriptures and so forth, deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*)—whether manifest or subtle—in the awakening consciousness that is separated by space and time.
For indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is directly perceived;

nor is the state of deep sleep not experienced, even by those whose minds are attentive to its surroundings, since they experience that state for fear of its non-existence, and it is on that basis that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is postulated. Thus, it is like a flower from the *kalpa* tree or a fruit from the *kustha* tree, which, though separated by time and other factors, eventually bears fruit.
Since the stalks and other parts of the *bījapūra* (citron) and similar plants become red from the stalk onwards,
this would occur even in the absence of proximity in space and so forth, were one to accept the existence or non-existence of the causal relationship (*hetu-phala-bhāva*).

The comparison with the state of sleep and so forth [is made] because one observes the presence of a substrate such as lac-dye even when it is separated [from the seed]; thus [it is said in] the *Prakaraṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.
433: "Like seeds sprinkled with the juice of lac and so forth... (*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 182).

Furthermore, as for this illustration—"like another continuum"—that too is not well-stated, because of the disparity [between the cases], since the relation of cause and effect is necessarily restricted, and because this objection applies equally elsewhere as well. That is not so, because the intention is otherwise. For instance: just as in the case of a king and his sons, let there be some sort of worldly restriction of a continuum despite their difference; however, the state of being the "infuser" (*vāsaka*) and the "infused" (*vāsya*)—which is the relation of an effect conforming to its cause—is not tenable once the cause has previously perished.

For it is not the case that, as when a father has died, his sons and others take up his lineage at a later time, so too [the child] takes on his form; for even today, one born to a king while he is still established in his kingdom is again settled in his own kingdom and partakes in the designation of being his lineage. Otherwise, even if the husband had died long ago, a widow’s offspring would have to bear the form of her husband, or in the case of a maiden whose marriage is yet to come, [her child] would likewise bear his form; yet they do not take on the father's form as his lineage, nor is there a relationship of perfumer and perfumed, nor a relationship of effect conforming to its cause.

Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the husband— that even when he has died, there arises in the waking mind an awakening-knowledge corresponding to him— that too is not substantial, because it has already been examined in the investigation of the verse beginning with *siddhaṃ yanna parāpekṣyam* (Siddhiviniścaya 1.24).

Furthermore, if the non-existence of the self were established merely by its non-perception during sleep and so forth, then it would follow that it is likewise absent in jars and other objects; thus, this [argument] is not free from confusion. If you argue that because the self is imperceptible, its absence in jars and the like is not established through non-perception, and therefore the "selflessness" (nairātmya) of jars and such is not proven—since vital breaths and so forth do not necessarily cease in things that lack a self—it follows that non-existence is not established by the mere non-perception of the imperceptible, but rather by the four states of the subject’s intention. If that is so, then why is the selflessness of jars and other objects not refuted on the basis of the distinction between states with and without a self? Just as there is a difference in conventional usage, such as saying "Devadatta is asleep," "he is in deep sleep," "he is dead," or "he is alive," so too there exists a difference in the conventional usage of establishing a probandum based on cause, effect, essential nature, or something else. Why is this not accepted? Since we observe the application of causes even when there is no living being present, if one loses confidence in all cases due to observing the deviation of non-perception of the perceptible—as in the case of sleep and so forth—how could there be any suspicion of existence, such that awakening could be determined to belong only to a waking consciousness? Moreover, conventional usage does not regard the state of sleep and so forth as being devoid of consciousness, for the convention of being "alive" continues even in such a state.
Furthermore, because they do not perceive the absence of that [consciousness] there, the observation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) would not be established by them regarding non-existence.
If consciousness during sleep and so forth is not perceived by them, how is this distinction made—that it exists [in one case] but not [in the other]?
For comparison: "This living body is not devoid of a self (*anātmaka*), because otherwise it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth."
Since breath and so forth are not observed in soulless things such as jars—whether visible or invisible—their absence [in a living body] leads to the inference of a soul;

however, since non-existence cannot be established through the non-perception of the imperceptible, the soullessness of jars and the like remains unproven, and thus there is no exclusion of breath and so forth [from the soul]. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti, p. 62)
In this context, the four states— waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death— are to be understood;
for even when a person possesses sleep and the other states,
they are [perceived] by those engaged in worldly discourse.
Because those engaged in worldly affairs do not contemplate momentary flux, they treat consciousness as being absent during states such as sleep.
Furthermore, as for what was stated by the proponents of worldly convention—

that there is a perception of momentary destruction, such that from the dyeing of flowers like cotton with lac and so forth, there arises a latent impression (vāsanā) of that dye in the fruit— that too is an extreme rashness; for if a dyed flower were the cause of a distant fruit, then intermediate factors such as seeds and sprouts would be rendered useless.

And how is there such a rule—that cognition produces its own form—by which those who desire that [object] act toward a restricted place and so forth? Therefore, it is established: in the absolute doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*), there is no relationship of the impressed and the impressioner (*vāsyavāsakatā*).
What is the fault in the absence of that? To this he says: "Therefore," and so on;
since this is the case, consequently, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself would not exist due to the absence of its cause; thus he thinks.

If it is argued: "Since the production of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is admitted, the non-existence of all this does not invalidate the Buddhists who maintain the doctrine of the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitavāda*), because it is their very desired position; nor can the subject (*pakṣa*) itself be the counter-subject (*vipakṣa*), as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," [the author] replies here: "Also from another [source]," and so forth.
This is pointless:
the cognition, having turned away from other things, conforms to its own nature;
thus, perception and the other means of knowledge [establish] the self as one, yet distinct at every moment.

It is illogical to claim that one rejects the very self—which is distinguished from everything else, which follows the nature of being both directed outward and inward, and both deluded and non-deluded, and whose characteristic is to exist for a single moment—by instead postulating it to consist merely of its own qualities and modes (paryāyas), when that self is established through its own self-awareness.

The intention here is as follows: Is it that the variegated (*citra*) is a single cognition—that non-duality (*advaita*), which is merely a partless manifold cognition, beyond all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or a mere illusion (*vibhrama*)—regarding which it has been said: "There is no fault even in its non-existence, like the appearance of a magical illusion (*māyā*), a mirage (*marīci*), and so forth" (*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 286)? Regarding that, in the first position: the intellect (*dhī*), the cognition (*buddhi*), which is withdrawn (*nivṛtta*) or turned away from other things—both of the same class (*sajātīya*) and of a different class (*vijātīya*)—follows after, or pervades (*anuvartate*), its own inherent forms (*ākāra*), which are its very nature (*svabhāva*).
Which ones? He says: "Perception and so forth"—those things such as erroneous blue and so on, for which perception is the first [member] and is non-erroneous, are thus described.

By this, he shows that the objection—that if the superimposition of contradictory properties were possible in one thing, then nothing could be manifold, and there would follow the absurdity of everything being useful for everything—has been refuted;
for the Buddhists accept that even when there is a superimposition of contradictory properties, a single variegated cognition (*citraikacitta*) can still function.

Just as the word "thus" (*tathā*) is inferred here from the hearing of the word "just as" (*yathā*), though it is elided, so too—by that same manner of appearing as the identity of a single [subject] with multiple forms that constitute its own nature, and by the manner of perceiving simultaneous arising and destruction—the consequence follows that all co-existent moments would be one, resulting in a single continuum; thus, the connection is that the Self (*ātman*), the Person (*puruṣa*), persists as a single nature.
To the question "Of what kind? he says: "At every moment," and so forth.
By this, it is shown that even that which is impossible to distinguish is capable of being refuted;
for even that [error] does not arise from anything other than the appearance of identity with its own form, since otherwise the aforementioned fault would follow.
Furthermore, the appropriation of the essential natures of others is not—as difficult to accomplish as seizing the wealth of a fierce king—something impossible to achieve.
By this, their perception as the Supreme Self has been defined.

The comparison [is as follows]: two contradictory natures cannot coexist in a single entity, because the consequence would be the loss of its unity due to the superimposition of contradictory attributes—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 220.

Granted that it is impossible to distinguish [the object] as having distinct modes because of its appearance as non-dual— since there is no existence of anything apart from the intended cognition— how can it be said that "cognition is excluded from others"?

For nothing whatsoever is excluded from that which is non-existent, and even regarding that which is existent, if it is not perceived, how and by whom can its cessation be cognized? If it is argued that among cognitions that are not known by another, there is no cognition of one by another, it has already been stated here that there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the existence of another.

Furthermore, just as the absence of suffering follows from the non-perception of pleasure, so too, because that [pleasure] does not perceive the existence of pleasure, pleasure would be non-existent; thus, nothing at all would exist.
Observe the wicked conduct of the opponent, who— while regarding suffering as existing yet not being made an object by pleasure, and other cognitions as non-existent—
speaks thus regarding things known to himself (*svavedyeṣu*).

As for what was further stated— that there is no realization of the cessation of anything that exists if it is not made an object— that too is merely the opponent’s own self-inflicted pain, since even his own appearance (*svapratibhāsa*) is unestablished, and because cognition does not negate properties contrary to its own [object], but rather accepts the non-perception of such [an object].

If, on the other hand, the mere experience of pleasure and so forth independent [of an object] constitutes the negation of its opposite properties, then it follows that cessation is understood even from that which has not been made an object of cognition.

Furthermore, this person, while himself engaging in all conceptual constructions, claims to realize the reality that transcends them and says that cessation is not established from what has not been made an object; thus, being both a practitioner of that [reality] and a hater of it, he deserves sharp punishment with indifference.
Because one does not perceive phenomena that are contrary [to reality],
consciousness is, in the ultimate sense, entirely free from conceptual construction and transcends all mental constructs.
—*Pra-vārtikāla*, p. 308, 398.

Thus, it is a great wonder that another point has been stated: "In cognitions that are not cognizable by anything else, there is no cognition by another. That too is not correct, because it would entail the non-establishment of the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaita*) and the non-establishment of all cognitions being without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
Then, in order to explain the verse [from the *Sūtra*], "the cognition is turned away from others," he says: "from everything else," and so forth.

Having conceptualized the mind—that is, cognition—as being excluded and withdrawn from everything else, namely from that which is of a different class (vijātīya), from what is considered the material cause (upādāna) and its effect (upādeya), and from anything other than itself (svato bhinnāt).

In what manner is it? He says: "from that which has the nature of both external and internal delusion. Those two are so described because they possess an outward-facing manifestation (mukha) both externally and internally; and those two possess the nature of being both deluded and non-deluded. That which has the habit of following them, or that which possesses such a following, is "that-which-follows" (*tadanvayi*). Alternatively, it should be understood as that which has the habit of following the external and internal natures, as well as the deluded natures.

For instance: according to the statement, "All conceptual cognitions (*vikalpajñāna*) of another [school] are non-erroneous with respect to their own nature, because all minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) [are direct perceptions]," and according to the statement, "They are erroneous with respect to the form of an external object; yet even error is a valid cognition (*pramā*) by virtue of its connection [to reality]," this is merely an illustration. By this, both the non-conceptual and other [conceptual] cognitions that apprehend a nature following upon blue and its opposite are included.

Furthermore, what is its nature? To this he says: "it has the property of existing for only a moment" (*kṣaṇasthitidharmaka*). One might object: "Since this was already stated by the phrase 'excluded from everything else,' why is it said again? For that which is excluded from everything else must necessarily have the property of existing for only a moment; otherwise, it would not be excluded from everything. This is true; nevertheless, this statement—"that moment," etc.—is intended to establish that [property] for one who does not accept its exclusion from preceding and succeeding moments.

For instance: because that which has the property of existing for only a moment possesses a perishable nature, it is independent with respect to destruction; therefore, it is necessarily subject to destruction at every moment.

Alternatively, while it was stated previously that [the entity] is excluded from everything coexisting with it, what does this [statement], "from both the preceding and the succeeding," specifically do? He says: it rejects—that is, it refutes.
What? He says: "The self alone," meaning the living being (*jīva*) alone and not merely that mind; such is the sense of the particle *eva* (alone).
Of what nature is it? He says: "By its own qualities," and so forth.
Again, of what nature is it? He says: "Inherently," and so forth.

Because it is established by self-awareness through itself alone, this statement of the opponent— that "everything is [unreal]"— is improper and untenable; moreover, to the Buddhist, it appears as if redundant.
Even an error is indeed a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) by virtue of its connection with a real entity— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.175.
Having just stated that [the object] is excluded from the two moments,
he now says "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) and so forth, desiring to refute the three subsequent alternatives:
"And not abandoning non-erroneousness, it does not abandon its own consciousness."

Having perceived and experienced itself at every moment, observing "this is the conscious one," and having turned away from everything else, it does not abandon its self at all times; for that entity is characterized by the continuity of its own qualities and modes (*guṇaparyāya*), and thus a state of separation from it is logically untenable. How then could it be with cause or without cause?

The intellect (*buddhi*)—which, in the waking state, is non-erroneous regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*), while in the dreaming state, is erroneous regarding both the object-form (*grāhyākāra*) and itself (*ātman*); and which, at every moment (*pratikṣaṇam*), never relinquishes but rather maintains its own essence (*svabhāva*)—what does that intellect, which is the specific cognition of everything, do? To this he says: "Having tasted" (*sītvā*), etc.
The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also/even) and is displaced [in the sentence structure]; it is to be understood after the phrase "it relinquishes its own consciousness" (*muñcatyātmacetanām*).

"No" (*na*) is used here because particles have multiple meanings; in this context, it signifies negation (*ākṣepa*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: "Does the intellect not indeed abandon the self-consciousness alone, but rather the possessor of qualities—that is, the subject who undergoes transformation? [If so,] would there not be a total void? Having raised this question, he asks: "By doing what? He replies: "Having perceived it as real" (*saditvā*). Even though [an object] has a single nature such as grossness and so forth, through subtle investigation it is found to be, like a fruit, composed of many partless atoms in its state of infinitesimal particles, [devoid of] smell and the rest.
Furthermore, having done what? Having drunk [the world] with such bliss, the meaning is that they have become like atoms outside [of it].

And thus, when the entire world has arisen as suchness (sarvadātve), since even mere appearance has utterly subsided, one considers: "What basis could there be for one to state the negation of causes and so forth?
By this, the two middle alternatives are refuted.
The connection is "is to be seen," meaning like a fruit that has been boiled or like a fruit that has withered;

this is another explanation based on the final alternative: [the view] that does not release the deluded self; otherwise, there would be no fault even if [the world] were non-existent, like the appearances of a magical illusion, a mirage, and so forth (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra* 3).
Because there is an absence of any authoritative means of proof (*pramāṇa*) to establish this [position], it would result in being a mere assertion (*pratijñāmātra*);
for indeed, an error is not established by means of an error, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

This is because even a nature that is incapable of withstanding analysis—one which, while never relinquishing its status as an erroneous self, is superposed with contradictory attributes both externally and internally—is also manifested therein. Thus, the phrase "cognition at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇaṃ buddhiḥ*) is connected to both [cases].

What does it do? To this he says: "It does not release its own consciousness"—that is to say, it carries the consciousness, which has another name, "Self," through its preceding and succeeding states; it does not abandon it.
Having done what? To this he says: "having sat and having gone. This is a common worldly way of speaking.

Alternatively, the connection with the preceding verse is that the intellect (*buddhi*), not releasing that Self at every moment, follows it by virtue of its own nature, even though it is distinct at every moment.

If it is argued that cognition does not maintain itself as either erroneous or non-erroneous, because reality transcends all conceptual constructions due to its being beyond such states, [the author] replies here with the words beginning "sīrtta":

[cognition] does not abandon its own self-luminous consciousness (*ātmacetanā*). Otherwise, just like the form of gross objects and so forth which are grasped, if that were abandoned, then—just as the existence of external objects would not be established—the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous would also fail to be established. Thus, this [consciousness] has the sense of being "unknown" (*ajñāna*); this is the ultimate definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and therein this ultimate definition of valid cognition prevails.

But first, regarding the conventional [subject], while demonstrating the meaning of the verse intended to show his own position, he says: "This is a conscious being," and so forth. (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 2.6)

If one considers that the self (*ātman*)—which is conscious, has the nature of grasping itself and others, and is unitary—is this very thing postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others because of its connection with what has been explained [above], then it is perceived by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanādhyakṣa*). However, it is not the self postulated by the Sāṃkhyas who maintain the non-duality of the *puruṣa*, because in that case there is no mental application of the term "this" (*ayam*), since it is eternally accessible only through scripture (*āgama*). If it is argued: "But just as with scripture, the direct perception of self-awareness also operates in that regard; therefore, this is not a fault"; to this he replies: "turned away from," etc. It is "turned away" (*parāvṛtta*) or withdrawn from another self and from objects such as a jar, because it is perceived as such.

The Sāṃkhya says: "The Self is not thus [as Brahman]; because that non-duality has ceased, my Self is such. To that, he replies: "It is turned away from everything—by every means, as if by its own nature, and even by place and so forth—from 'everything' up to the end of the recitation beginning with 'ādi'."
Alternatively, since it is not the case that the Sāṃkhya self exists as everything, in every way, everywhere, and from everything— due to the contradiction with this [position]—
the proof of the all-pervasiveness of this self is shown by the opponent to be entirely sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, he excludes the views of others.
If there were acceptance of otherness, it would contradict the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda).
The Buddhist [maintains] that the self is a continuum of moments perishing at every instant, being of such a nature; regarding this, he says: "at every moment," etc.

Although it abandons its own nature (svarūpa) at each and every moment, it does not abandon it "absolutely" (*atyantāya*); in this sense, the particle *ava* functions as a synonym for *ati*, meaning that it abandons [its nature] only in some respect (*kathañcit*).
Whence is this [known]? To this he says: "In its own qualities," and so forth.

Those qualities (*guṇas*) which belong to itself—that is, its own—and those modes (*paryāyas*) which do not belong to another substance; the "concomitance" (*anvaya*) among them is their following along, and that is the "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning the apprehension or indeed the very nature (*svarūpa*) of which. Because of the existence of such a thing—whether it be a conscious entity or another state of being—within its own self, as is the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, the term "of an entity" (*vastunaḥ*) is used as a general expression for the purpose of demonstrating that, in the example, there is no perception admitted by the opponent.
Why is this so? He says: "By its exclusion," and so forth.

By its exclusion—that is, by the exclusion of the entity just described—existence (*bhāva*), like Brahman, would be partless consciousness; [the opponent] considers that even a continuum (*santāna*) is untenable because of the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

What happened after that? To this he says: "How could there not be anything [that is] with a cause (*sahetu*)—meaning having a cause—or without a cause (*ahetu*)—meaning lacking a cause? Furthermore, whatever is independent of other factors with respect to its being [a certain state], that is restricted to that very nature (*tatsvabhāvaniyata*); just as the final causal complex (*antya-kāraṇa-sāmagrī*), being independent in producing its respective effect, is restricted to that state of existence; and an entity (*bhāva*) is likewise independent with respect to its destruction. This is poorly stated, because the final property (*dharmya*) to be proven is unestablished; the particle *api* is a fourth kind of pseudo-particle (*pratirūpaka*).

The formal argument (*tulanā*) is as follows: "Whatever things are independent with respect to a certain state are necessarily restricted to that state; for example, a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) whose fruit is immediately subsequent is restricted to the production of its own effect. And all produced (*kṛtaka*) entities that possess birth are independent with respect to their destruction. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
See *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 132; see also p. ... [note].
Furthermore, demonstrating the fault in the opponent's position regarding destruction having a cause, he says: "If [destruction] has a cause," and so forth.
If destruction were to have a cause, then because that [destruction] would itself be subject to destruction, the entity would arise once again;
otherwise, all causes of destruction that lack a [further] cause would not be absolute.

If destruction were not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, what could a cause possibly do to it? It certainly cannot produce it, because production is characterized by a connection with the existence of a thing delimited by a prior limit. Furthermore, if it were to be produced in any way whatsoever by anything, it would not transcend the intrinsic nature of an entity; thus, it would be an entity, since a real thing is defined by that very characteristic. To claim that an occasional existent is unproduced is merely a verbal description, as it is contradictory.

Likewise, that which has the nature of non-arising (anutpattidharma) possesses an essence to which no excellence can be added nor any deficiency removed; furthermore, it does not perish because it lacks the causal conditions for its own destruction. Alternatively, if there were destruction, it would imply either the existence of what is already destroyed or the non-arising of what already exists, due to the absence of a cause for arising.

If this were the case, it would follow that even things such as jars [would be eternal], because there is no necessary rule that a cause for their destruction must necessarily arise from their own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*). Consequently, no cause whatsoever would be non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*) regarding destruction.

If you argue that the cause of destruction produces the very nature (*svabhāva*) of destruction—which previously did not exist—and not its connection with existence (*sattāsambandha*), then who is the producer of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) and prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of entities? For it is from that [producer] that the stability of their respective natures is maintained.
Is there some distinction such that we understand non-existence as a transformation resulting from the mutual exclusion of intrinsic nature, place, and time?
Likewise, the state of having a cause for that which is momentary is sublated by contradictory means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For the present cannot possess the quality of the past, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Herein lies the intended meaning: since an entity postulated by those who maintain extreme views (*ekāntavādin*) does not exist due to the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there can be no statement regarding its cause or destruction. Regarding the worldly object, the opponent must conceive of its destruction; yet even there, since the designation of "destruction" and "origination" refers to a modification characterized by the relinquishing of a prior form and the acquisition of a subsequent one, the Jaina doctrine is established in both cases. This was stated in the immediately preceding section concerning the proof of origination, persistence, and dissolution under the position that destruction is causeless (*ahetuvināśapakṣa*). (Siddhiviniscaya 3)

By such statements as these, even in the position that destruction has a cause, [it is shown that] substance is without beginning or end (*anādinidhana*), yet it is subject to arising, transformation, and destruction,
as stated in *Siddhiviniścaya* 3.21 and elsewhere.
Therefore, out of fear of that [consequence], he must necessarily admit that arising is entirely distinct from destruction and origination.

And thus, if it is admitted that destruction—which is entirely distinct from existence—is caused, meaning it possesses a cause, then the entity, such as a jar, would come into being again after its destruction; that is to say, even later on, it would exist just as it did before, performing its own perception and causal functions.

This is what is meant: destruction, or any other produced entity, arises from the operation of another; for it is stated in the *Nyāyabindu* (3.14) that "an entity is called 'produced' when it depends upon the operation of another. Since this [destruction] also arises from something, there is no contradiction in designating it as an "entity" (*bhāva*). And being produced, like a jar or similar objects, it necessarily perishes.

Now, one might object: "Let this fault apply to him for whom a produced thing arises from its own causes as perishable; it does not apply to us. For even a produced thing that is non-perishable by nature perishes upon the encounter with a cause of destruction, not by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*);

moreover, there is no cause that can destroy destruction itself"—so say some. To this, he replies: "Otherwise they would not be certain," and so forth. The meaning is: otherwise—that is, in the manner of the absence of destruction of destruction—it would follow that they are not "certain" (*ekāntika*), i.e., not unerring; rather, all [produced things] without exception would be "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*).

What [are these]? He says: "Causes of destruction having a cause" means the causes of a destruction that has a cause, namely the logical marks (*liṅga*) such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), or else their causes, which are the instruments such as a mallet. For just as, even though destruction is something produced, those [marks] are not necessarily its causes of destruction, so too are the causes of the destruction of jars and the like.
Or else, out of fear of contradicting the tenets of the Jaina school,
there would be the arising of even destruction.

In this regard, there is another view: even when the destruction [of a thing] is destroyed, the entity does not reappear, for it is not the case that when the killer of Devadatta is killed, Devadatta reappears. That is not sound, because of the disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration; for the annihilative state of an entity is not the same as the killer of Devadatta, since the latter brings about the absence of another—the self—within Devadatta.

Upon its destruction, that [other] necessarily arises; otherwise, the non-existence of the former would be purposeless. If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence that Devadatta, though still living, would be invisible, as he would have undergone transformation into the form of destruction (pradhvaṃsa). Likewise, the killer undergoes transformation into the form of the destruction of Devadatta by means of the act of killing.

Others, however, say that concealment—which consists of the absence [of perception]—is like the destruction of a jar; even its own destruction obstructs perception, and thus it is "non-perception. That too is not well-said, because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For instance: if the absence of one thing were to cause the obstruction of the perception of another, then the absence of a cloth would obstruct the perception of everything, because there is no proximity or remoteness [to distinguish them].

Furthermore, for an opponent, this relation of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*)—or whatever relation it may be—between an absence and a presence is unestablished, due to infinite regress and the lack of any further relation.

If, on the other hand, you claim that being a qualifier can be predicated of something even without another relation, then qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth could also be predicated of something even in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*) and the like, since there is no distinction between the two cases.

And if that [destruction] were perceived while being unconnected with a sense faculty, what would be the point here— or anywhere else— of postulating a connection between the sense faculty and its object? Furthermore, even in the case of the "destruction of destruction," when the potsherd— which is of the nature of destruction— is itself destroyed, the pot is not seen.
The contact of a substance with a non-existence.

Furthermore, just like the destruction of a thing already perished (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), the destruction of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would also obstruct the perception of the jar, and thus the jar could not arise again. If it is argued that because the intention for that [jar] is set aside by the existence of the jar, this [prior non-existence] does not obstruct its perception—[we reply: does this existence of the jar not exist at the time of its destruction, such that it would not be the cause of that [non-perception]?
For it is contradictory for a single entity to both act and not act with respect to the same object at the same time.

Some maintain that because prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is beginningless, like space and so forth, it is not subject to destruction. For them, just as before, the jar would be perceived as a visible object at the time of its production; thus, there would still be the cognition, "the jar has not yet been produced," just as previously. If it is argued that although it exists, it is not perceived due to being obscured by the presence of the jar—just as a cluster of stars is not seen by the sun—that is not tenable, because it is impossible for an eternal entity, which is capable of producing a cognition of itself and possesses all other necessary causes, to be obscured. Furthermore, for an eternal and all-pervading entity, there can be no physical obstruction, unlike the case of sound.

Thus, even if the causes of non-perception— such as distance and so forth— are absent, if prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were to exist at the time of the jar, and likewise if sound were to exist before and after the operation of the palate and other organs, then it would be improper to postulate that it is a quality produced by space (*ākāśa*),
because there is no distinction in its status as non-existence, just as in the case of the production of a jar.
If the prior absence (prāgabhāva) were the perception of a jar,
then that prior absence would exist even at the time of the jar's production.

If it is argued that, just as for a word whose prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is eternal and pervasive, there might be an obscuration by something— even though [the word] exists and is perceptible— just as in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like; we say no, because the fault is equal in that case as well.

If, however, this view is held—that its concealment consists in the negation of its visibility due to the absence of that [other thing]—then the destruction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would also have to be admitted.
Furthermore, let the absence of that [other thing] also be the concealer of posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa*), since it conceals an entity just as prior non-existence does;
for if this were not admitted, there would be no established system of inference.
Then the following verse is appropriate: "Because of having a cause," and so forth,
[referring] to the prior non-existence of prior non-existence.
Regarding the non-existence of the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāvābhāva*),

some raise this objection: "If this refutation is stated by the Master with reference to a destruction that is distinct from the entity (*bhāva*), then since the entity remains in that very same state even at that time, for what purpose is it said that 'the entity would come into being again through the destruction of the destruction'?"
For it is not logical that there should be a further arising of that which already exists, such as space and so forth.

If it were to arise again, it would—just as before—become an object of perception and so on; yet even this interpretation is not sound, because even then its status as an object is negated by that [word], since this very fault is pointed out right here by the particle *iti*.

To explain: if the destruction [of an entity] were admitted to possess a cause, then from that destruction, the entity—such as a jar—would [arise] again; the word "again" (*punaḥ*) has the sense of restriction and is to be understood immediately after the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*). "Otherwise" means "in a completely different way," that is, by another [cause] exclusively, in an absolute sense, it would be distinct; the phrase "at the beginning" (*sādhadi*) is the ellipsis here. Regarding this position, the refutation begins with "the ones who hold to exclusivity" (*aikāntikā*);
the particle *iti* should be seen as having a displaced construction (*bhinnaprakrama*), and is to be understood as preceding the word *aikāntika*.

The meaning of this is as follows: those reasons or causes for the destruction of that which possesses a cause which have been propounded by the opponent are not absolute, nor are they such that they must necessarily be accepted; for it is considered that even when destruction has been produced by them, the jar and so forth are perceived in exactly the same way both at the time of destruction and previously.

If it is argued that by the word "or" (*itiśabdena*), the [reasons] are non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*) because they necessarily produce that [effect], and thus the previous refutation—"if this were so, it is sufficient"—is redundant; we say no. For there would be no distinction between the commentary passage beginning with "if destruction [belongs to the cause]" (*vināśo yadi*) and the passage stating that "an occasional effect is not produced" (*kādācitkam akāryam*), for those who accept that the cause undergoes destruction and that through this [destruction] the entity is concealed.
Explaining the verse by means of another point, he says: "If destruction," and so forth.

The meaning is that if destruction (*vināśa*), which is utter annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*), were not an entity (*bhāva*)—that is, if it did not consist of a subsequent transformation—it would instead be distinct from the entity.
What could a cause do for such a destruction? Doing nothing at all, the hammer or other instruments would not be its cause.
Alternatively, it should be applied as follows: what would destruction do to that entity, and what would a cause do to destruction?

For instance, when destruction is indeed distinct from the entity, then it is said that "it does nothing to it," because a real relationship between two distinct things depends upon some benefit conferred; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle.
Even in the case of a relationship based on capacity, as in the case of color and taste, there is merely an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), but not the cessation of the entity itself.

If it is argued that "it is precisely that [destruction] which is produced by that [cause]," then if it were of the same nature [as the thing itself], let the first destruction also be exactly like that; thus, enough with the assumption of an absolute distinction.

If, on the other hand, it is a different entity, then the same fault remains and there is an infinite regress, because one destruction would have to be produced by another destruction; therefore, let that [destruction] belong to that very [thing], just as smoke belongs to fire.

Likewise, by means of destruction, those very [entities] would be destroyed due to their connection with it, and not the entity itself. If it is argued that there is no fault because the cause belongs to the entity; it has been stated in this regard that since it does not provide any assistance to the entity, the connection with it is untenable. If it is argued that the entity also produces this [destruction], and therefore it is connected to it; then both would be the case: for you, the entity would be the cause of its own destruction, which leads to the undesirable consequence of its being eternal, since an eternal thing cannot have a dependence [on causes].

Since the relation of being a qualifier exists only in that [particular], the claim that "it belongs to that" is also untenable; for in the case of absolute difference (*bhedakānta*), that relation cannot be established as inseparable.

If it is argued that the destruction of the entity follows from the removal of that [relation]—either through the cessation of its existence or through the obstruction of its perception—it has already been stated in this regard that such is impossible for an entity remaining in that same state.
Furthermore, [the following applies]:
Because if every entity were distinct from everything else, it would follow that everything could be designated as anything.
It may be that the very cessation of existence is itself existence.
May [he] be non-different from destruction;
may he be non-different.
Because of its connection with destruction,
there is the destruction of destruction.
Since even the state of being a qualifier cannot obstruct perception,
those [non-existents] which are concealed are not accepted by the yogis themselves as existing.
Furthermore, how could yogins not be capable of knowing all objects?
Thus, one should also consider where those who, out of their own devotion, describe omniscience in such a manner fall short of being among the knowers of all things.
When these [objects] are perceived by those [senses], then for the yogi, this report regarding the perished and the unarisen is exhausted and utterly destroyed;
for the Sāṃkhya yogi, all [objects] have long since lived and now exist only in the present.

Since entities never exist in any way whatsoever, from which they might be established— just as a yogi [perceives] the world as empty like the sky— where indeed can those beings go for refuge? To whom can they resort?
For indeed, how could pieces of wood, which are constantly being perceived, not be subject to destruction?
Otherwise, everything—including the sky and so forth—would have to be perishable.
Thus, while the path praised by the venerable sage Kapila was being extolled, [the opponent spoke].

"But since it does not depend on any impermanent states, tell me, how could it perish? For that which is real has no connection with anything else here; therefore, its cessation is not even a matter of discussion. Thus.
That remains established: if destruction were not the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, what would it be doing for which there would be destruction?

Now, as for what was said—"What would the cause of that destruction be doing?"—if it is argued that it would be "doing" the production [of the entity], to this he replies with the words beginning "previously" (*pūrva*), etc.: it does not, first of all, produce it.

The word "tāvat" (so long) refers to deliberation (*vitarka*) and does not signify sequence, as no other purpose has been stated. [The phrase] "the cause, such as a hammer, does not produce or generate destruction"—this is to be connected by changing the case ending.

Why? He says: because of the existence (*bhāva*), that is, the state (*tattva*) of that which has as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) the inherence (*samavāya*)—which is a relation (*sambandha*) with the being (*sattā*) of an entity such as a jar, which is distinguished and delimited by its prior limit (*pūrvāvadhi*), i.e., prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Of what? He says: "of arising."
