Furthermore, there can be no connection between non-existence and existence prior to destruction, because the opponent does not accept that "existence" (sattā) is that which causes the three categories [substance, quality, and action] to exist, as stated in their own doctrine;
nor does the Vaiśeṣika maintain that destruction is admitted by the opponent to reside within substances and the other categories. This is what is intended.
"That which, because of its presence in substances, qualities, and actions, causes them to be called 'existent'— that is *sattā* (Being)" — Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.7.

An objector from the Vaiśeṣika school might say: "This which you have stated is far too little; namely, that the cause does not produce destruction. For even the cause of a jar or the like does not produce that [destruction].

To explain: the cause of a jar or the like does not first bring about its production, characterized by the acquisition of self-existence, since that [jar] is previously non-existent; for otherwise, it would follow that the postulation of any other kind of production would be useless."
Nor is it characterized by a relation with existence (*sattā*) for that which was previously non-existent, because the inherence (*samavāya*) with existence is eternal.

Furthermore, there can be no relation with existence or anything else for that which is unknown from any source—like the son of a barren woman—by virtue of which something might be produced by someone. If you say, "It is for that which has already attained its own self-nature," then the aforementioned fault applies: what is the use of another production? If you ask how there could otherwise be a distinction between things such as a hare’s horn and others, let this be another fault of the opponent.
Indeed, even those possessing the fault of impermanence do not adhere to a flawless object, just as the cause of a jar does not adhere to the jar itself.
The connection is that it produces origination,
either through inherence (samavāya) according to the Vaiśeṣika.

If it is argued: "Surely, in the case of the stainless *Akalaṅka* logic, there is no production—characterized by the relation to existence (*sattā*)—of that which was previously non-existent, whether it be destruction or the first [moment]; rather, let its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone be produced," to this he replies with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*).

If that destruction were an effect—by some manner characterized either by the production of a relation with existence (*sattā*) or by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and thus being a causal factor—it would not produce [anything] because it does not transcend the nature of an entity, that is, it does not deviate from the form of an existent. [The opponent] thinks that in such a case, the entity would be a "relation" (*sambandha*).

Even so, if one asks, "How could that be an entity?"—to this he replies: "Because an object has that as its characteristic. This should be explained as follows: with respect to the view of the opponent, because an object—that is, the category of existents (*sad-varga*)—has that relation with existence as its characteristic, it possesses that nature.

However, from the perspective of our own system (*svamata*), [the definition of an entity is as follows]: because of the existence—that is, the reality—of that which has the characteristic of obtaining its own nature (*ātmalābha*) from a cause that previously did not exist. Otherwise, destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) would not be distinguished from its own prior non-existence (*svaprāgabhāva*), due to the absence of a connection with a distinct intermediate genus (*avāntarajāti*). If it were otherwise, there would be a connection with "existence" (*sattā*) just as there is for substances (*dravya*) and so forth.

If, on the other hand, one does not admit such a connection even in some cases despite the absence of that [prior non-existence], then how could there be the distinction that substances and so forth alone possess the connection with an intermediate genus, while universals (*jāti*) and so forth do not, even though they lack that [connection with *sattā*]?
By this, the commentator considers that the possibility of any other distinguishing property is also refuted; thus,
by means of a single object, the verse [applies] to a jar and so forth.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "If one accepts a relation with a universal (jāti), then properties such as antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāvatva) and destruction (pradhvaṃsatva) would [necessarily] exist."

Although there is an absence of intermediate universals (avāntarajāti) in universals and the like, their connection with existence (sattā) is currently possible; thus, explaining the negative concomitance (vyatireka) first, he says: "occasional," and so forth.

The intention here is as follows: according to the immediately preceding reasoning, destruction—which was previously non-existent and subsequently arises from some cause—is an effect; for this very reason, it is established as a real entity. That entity characterized by destruction is occasional, restricted by place, time, substance, and so forth, and being existent, it is not an effect. This [position] is merely a description of a theoretical system, a mere enumeration of the manifold categories of the sixty-eight-fold *kṛtānta* (the established doctrine).
By the word "mere" (*mātra*), he indicates that the reality [thus presented] is unstable.
Why? He says: because of the contradiction between the preceding and succeeding assertions, due to their mutual sublation.

To explain: if destruction is a real entity that was previously non-existent and arises from something, how can it be non-produced (*akārya*), like a jar or other such things? Or, if it is non-produced, like space and so forth, how can it be occasional? That it is both occasional and non-produced is mutually contradictory.
Therefore, because it occurs only occasionally, it is considered an effect;
this is the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
Likewise, the description that what is occasional possesses the property of non-arising is merely an exposition of the underlying process (*prakriyā*).
Why? He says: "Because of contradiction.

For example, how can that which is occasional—being previously non-existent and subsequently attaining its own existence like a wall or similar object—be of a nature not subject to arising (*anutpattidharmaka*), i.e., one for whom the property of arising is absent? Furthermore, since the very attainment of self-existence is of the nature of arising, and because any connection with a separate entity called "existence" is denied, [it must be so].

Alternatively, if it were of a nature not subject to arising, like space or the son of a barren woman, how could it be occasional? This is the contradiction. Therefore, the point is that because it is occasional, it is of a nature subject to arising.
The meaning is that origination is simply the acquisition of self-existence by what was non-existent.

Likewise, the description of the process—that [the effect] is occasional, consists of a nature to which no excellence can be added nor any deficiency removed, and possesses the inherent capacity for being unproduced and indestructible—is merely a verbal elaboration.
Why? Because it is contradictory.

And thus, its nature as being incapable of having any excellence added to it or subtracted from it is difficult to establish—like that of a sky-flower—because obtaining its selfhood from something else necessarily entails that its nature consists of excellences that can be added or subtracted.

If, on the other hand, it were of a nature that cannot be augmented or diminished, like space and so forth, how could it be occasional? If it is argued that it is called "of such a nature" because it is impossible to either add or remove any excellence (*atiśaya*) once it has arisen; that is incorrect. For when its occasional nature or its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is established, who can prevent one from inferring—just as in the case of a jar—that it possesses a nature consisting of augmentable or diminishable excellences?

Likewise, the description of something as "occasional" (*kādācitka*) yet "imperishable" is merely a formal exposition, because it is contradictory; for everything that is occasional is perceived to be perishable, like a jar or similar objects. Furthermore, the claim that "the occasional does not perish due to the absence of the cause of its own destruction"—whereby the word "own" (*sva*) refers to the entity of destruction itself, or where "its destruction" means its own destruction or its inherent destruction—and thus it does not perish due to the non-existence of such a cause—is likewise merely a formal exposition, because it is contradictory and because it contradicts one's own tenets.

For one who accepts that even the world has a cause for its destruction due to its occasional nature, what hesitation can there be regarding the present case? The phrase "in destruction" (*vināśe*) or "in annihilation" (*pradhvaṃse*) is connected with "of the destructible object" (*vināśavastunaḥ*).

The word *vā* indicates either an alternative acceptance or a different position. [The view is that] for the Buddhist, there is a connection with existence (*sattā*) of a jar or the like that has been destroyed—that is, characterized by annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*).

Alternatively, if one accepts a cause for destruction, why would there be no further arising—that is, no reappearance—of that which is existent, distinct from destruction, and already existing by its own nature? To this he says: "Because of the absence of a cause for production."
In the production of an entity, there are three kinds of causes— namely, the inherent (samavāyin), the non-inherent (asamavāyin), and the instrumental (nimitta)—

yet destruction is not any one of these. Furthermore, in the case of darkness characterized by the absence of sunlight, even when that [absence] is dispelled by the presence of a lamp or similar object, the light returns once more.
Nor is there a rule that another cause for that [destruction] must exist; this is merely a description of the process.
Why? Because of contradiction:

if there were an emergence even when destruction is destroyed, then the destruction of destruction would not be its [the original thing's] existence, since that is the very definition of it. Otherwise, how could the existence of a self be established by the negation of selflessness?
Therefore, if there is the destruction of destruction, why is there not the manifestation of an entity? If not, how can there be its destruction?

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that it is because of the existence of a cause for origination—that is insubstantial; for in the origination of a jar, the conjunction of parts is the cause, and for that [conjunction], action is the cause. Thus, when the destruction of the destruction of action occurs, there is the manifestation of that [conjunction]; from that, conjunction [arises], and from that, the jar.

Alternatively, if the destruction of conjunction is brought about by disjunction, then it too has a cause; and upon the destruction of that [disjunction] by some means, there is the resurgence of conjunction.

Alternatively, since destruction is distinct from the jar, when that [destruction] exists, there is "nothing [remaining]" of it; thus, upon the destruction of destruction, there is the perception of the absolute alone, free from all opposition, like the destruction of darkness—so what is the need for a cause?
[This applies] even to the destruction of conjunction, which is the manifestation of an action.

Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the jar— that even when darkness is destroyed by the absence of light, there is no manifestation of the sun's light— that too is not a well-examined statement; for the objection applies equally there as well,
since darkness is not merely the absence of light, because darkness is perceived by one who has entered a room filled with light from a region of intense illumination.
And since that [darkness] is absent everywhere in the absence of consciousness here, let it be so; let darkness not be the absence of sunlight,
but rather let darkness be the very absence of consciousness.

The nature of knowledge is darkness (*tamas*); in its absence, there is no manifestation of knowledge. Indeed, it is not considered to be merely the non-existence (*abhāva*) of that [knowledge]. Otherwise, even light would be the non-existence of darkness, because [darkness] is cognizable through a positive cognition (*bhāvapratyaya*), and thus darkness is not a mere non-existence like a jar or similar objects.
Then the following verses are appropriate: "Occasional," and so forth;
and "The darkness that is the absence of knowledge," and so forth.
Regarding that very point, he states another refutation: "Of cloth and so forth," and so on.

Not only in the case of destruction, but because even for things such as a jar, when there is occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) while possessing a cause, there follows the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as in the case of destruction; therefore, the description of the process is merely a formal elaboration—this is the connection.
Furthermore, he states yet another fault: "Arising from its own causal complex," and so on.

The meaning is as follows: for any entity or non-entity that arises from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*), that which is accepted by the opponent as its cause of destruction is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*); and because there is no necessary rule regarding the occurrence of that cause of destruction, no probans such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would be non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*) as a reason for proving impermanence.

As it has been said: "The production (*utpatti*) of destruction—which does not exist previously—is not brought about by anyone as characterized by a relation to existence (*sattā*); rather, it is its very own nature. To this, the Buddhist replies with the words "the cause of destruction" (*vināśahetu*), etc. [He means: If it is argued that the cause or reason of destruction, as accepted by the opponent, produces the nature or essence of destruction—which was previously non-existent, i.e., not existing prior to its own arising—and not a relation to existence; if that is so, then he states the refutation therein with the words "who, moreover," etc.

"Who? means "no one at all. Furthermore, regarding the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of entities such as pots and the like—since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is a specific variety of this, it is not mentioned separately—and regarding that which is prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), who is its maker? For how could the nature of a maker persist [in relation to non-existence]? Or, if "from whom" (*yataḥ*) is used in the sense of an objection, then there is no such persistence of that [nature].
And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*): whatever is a non-existence is causeless, just like prior non-existence and so forth; and destruction is indeed a non-existence.

[Objection: "Granted that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest may lack a cause, yet that does not mean the same applies to destruction (*vināśa*). Otherwise, since space (*ākāśa*) and so forth lack a cause, jars and other things would likewise [be causeless].
If you argue that the contradiction with perception is equal in both cases, we reply: 'Is there, indeed,' etc.
Is there some distinction or difference between antecedent non-existence and destruction caused by place and so forth? The meaning is: no."

This is what is meant: just as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others do not conform to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of causes and are thus uncreated (*akṛtaka*), so too is destruction (*vināśa*). For when a large collection of causes such as a staff and so forth occurs, the destruction is not of a different kind [than the object]; since mere cessation (*vinivṛtti-mātra*) is indistinguishable everywhere, antecedent non-existence and the others do not exist as real entities (*bhāva*). Thus he says: "mutually," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: we understand that for entities (*bhāvānām*), there is a mutual [relation] of each other, as well as their own nature (*svabhāva*), place (*deśa*), and time (*kāla*); by the exclusion of these, we know their transformation, which is the attainment of selfhood and then non-existence.
This is a comparison with the cause: for the cause of destruction does not produce the very nature of the entity, since that [nature] has already been established by its own causes.
—Hetubindu, p. 56: There would be causelessness in the case of the small.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), having thus turned the Naiyāyika away [from his position], the Buddhist himself now leads him toward his own [position] and says: "And likewise," and so forth.

That is to say, by that aforementioned mode of perceiving the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the state of possessing a cause (*hetumattva*)—that is, the state of having a causal basis—is sublated by a contradictory means of valid cognition (*viruddhapramāṇabādhita*).

Of what? He says: "of a momentary entity"—this is to be connected by changing the grammatical case of the word. The intended meaning here is as follows: for the Naiyāyika, who does not accept the destruction of even a caused destruction, the reasons for impermanence are inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*); for one who accepts antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth as being causeless, destruction is without a cause, or rather, its absence [is without a cause];

but for the Buddhist, who accepts momentariness, [reasons such as] being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth are simply unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus, he (the Naiyāyika) does not surpass the other (the Buddhist).
"Why does that [past entity] not have the status of a cause? To this he says: "For not by the past," and so forth.

For (*hi*) because by means of a past entity—one that has already perished prior to the arising of the effect—the present [entity] cannot possess "that-ness" (i.e., the state of having that as its cause), lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), which would entail that everything would possess that-ness in relation to every past thing. And this has been established: "The causal relation is not established at all" (Siddhiviniścaya 4).
3. Thus,
the Buddhist [refutes] "aversion"— that is, the state of being devoid of logical reasoning.
The Naiyāyika [position] is that it possesses a logical reason (hetumat),
page 239.

If it is argued that, in this way, just as for the Naiyāyika, for the Buddhist as well there would be only total emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in the absence of a doctrine, [the author] says here: "Directly perceived," and so forth.
"Directly perceived is the proof of substance (*dravya*) whose nature consists of qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*);
it is excluded from the opposite side because of the impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and from that which is of the nature of error. (Verse 7)

Thus, it is established that all this... [is] "in the presence of qualities" (*guṇasamakṣam*), meaning directly perceived (*pratyakṣam*). The meaning is: the proof of that substance (*dravya*) which has qualities (*guṇa*), modifications (*paryāya*), natures (*svabhāva*), and essences (*ātmānaḥ*)—both externally and internally—is due to the direct perception of the substance consisting of qualities and modifications.
By this, he demonstrates the contradiction with direct perception for one who postulates the emptiness of everything.

It might be thought: "That which appears in perceptual cognition is indeed erroneous because it is sublated, like the appearance of two moons. To this, he says: "In the case of the counter-example," and so forth. Because causal efficiency—characterized by perception and the like—is impossible in the absolute existence [of a thing] within the counter-example, how could it have been excluded or removed? The connection is: "[excluded] from that which is of the nature of a delusion," meaning from that which has an erroneous nature, "before one's eyes" (*samakṣam*).

This is what is meant: just as the perception of two moons is an error due to the absence of the perception of a single moon, so too, if there were the absence of the perception of oneness and so forth, the immediately preceding [perception] would be erroneous;
but this is not the case.
Since the meaning of the verse has been established in many ways like a royal highway, he says "Thus it stands" and so forth, concluding the present topic.
This is established and certain;
what is it? To this he says: "all," and so forth.
Likewise, he says that the Supreme is established: "the qualities," and so forth.
However, its existence must be acknowledged here, because it serves the purpose of negating any other characteristic of a substance.

For surely, due to the lack of a relationship between the conscious and the unconscious, or the embodied and the formless— namely, between the soul (*jīva*) and karma— when one moves or remains stationary, the other does not necessarily move or remain stationary, as is the case with a cow and a horse.
Even if the relationship were characterized by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), that same fault would remain, as in the case of a jar and its potter.

However, if the relationship is characterized by "identity" (*tādātmya*), this fault does not apply, as in the case of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "sound" (*śabda*). If it is argued that even here, one of the two must be [the primary entity] or the difference must be imagined, he says in response: "consciousness," etc., regarding the relationship of identity.

Either the soul alone or karma alone would be [the cause]; these two, being conscious and unconscious respectively, must depend upon one another for bondage, as they are entirely distinct by definition, like gold and its black impurity. (8)
Although the sentient and the insentient are mutually distinct, they attain oneness with respect to bondage, just as gold and its dark tarnish do;

nor is the conjunction of the corporeal and the incorporeal contradictory, for that would entail the non-existence of the aggregate of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), as well as [the invalidation] of the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-sannikarṣa*).

The conscious self (*cetana*) and the unconscious category of karma (*acetanaḥ karmapadārthaḥ*): these two, the conscious and the unconscious—this is an illustration; by extension, these two, the formless and the formal, which are perceived through direct perception and inference, do not reach a state of identity with respect to bondage, which is a specific kind of conjunction. Why? Because of the contradiction between two distinct substances (*bhinnadravyayoḥ*). How could there be identity? To this he says: "Because they are distinct, being composed of different substances. By what means? He says: "By their characteristics (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), that is, by their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇena*)," ending with the reading "beginning with 'ādi'. Relying precisely upon those characteristics, [they remain distinct].

To explain: since the utilization of knowledge and perception is the defining characteristic of the soul alone, while the nature of form and so forth belongs to matter (pudgala) alone, how could they be distinct? To this he says: by this [statement], he demonstrates the absolute absence of any mutual transfer of characteristics throughout the three periods of time;
he provides an illustration for both cases, such as gold and its blackness, and so forth.

By the first word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of rubies and the like; by the other, there is the inclusion of dross and the like. "Like those two" means in that same manner; thus, utility is the defining characteristic—Tattvārtha Sūtra 2.8.
Pudgalas possess touch, taste, smell, and color—
Tattvārthasūtra 5.23.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Mutually," and so forth.

Although mutually—that is, reciprocally—distinct in character (*vilakṣaṇa*), meaning dissimilar in their defining marks, the conscious and unconscious—the soul (*jīva*) and the matter of karma (*karma-pudgala*)—attain oneness with respect to bondage, like gold and its black impurity; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is connected to each term respectively.

If it is asked: "But how can there be a bondage characterized by a specific kind of conjunction between these two, one of which is corporeal and the other incorporeal, such that this would be possible? To this, he replies: "And not," and so forth.

And it is not the case that there is no contradictory conjunction between the embodied and the unembodied, which are of the nature of karma; why is this? To this he says: "consisting of the five aggregates," etc., [referring to] the soul and karma.
Is this not already refuted by the statement "like poison and so forth"? Therefore, there is no fault;

for [otherwise] there would follow the non-existence of the aggregate—that is, the collection—of the five aggregates, form and the rest. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the conjunction of the corporeal and the incorporeal; such is the construction of the words.

To explain: in a certain body, the aggregate of form is corporeal, while sensation and the others are incorporeal; for the designation "saṃsāra" applies to that which arises as a composite of those aggregates, appearing in various forms.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the corporeal and the incorporeal; since form is in one place and sensation and the other aggregates are in another—like the Sahya and Vindhya mountains—it follows that there would be no experience of pleasure and so forth within the body.
[Page 231] Form, sensation, consciousness, perception, and mental formations.

If it is argued that "if that cluster [of atoms] is conjunction, then its absence does not constitute a fault for the Buddhist, because he accepts it," [we reply: since even he accepts contiguity (*nairantarya*),
and there is no conjunction other than contiguity even for the Jaina,
just as there is a conjunction characterized by contiguity between the five aggregates— whether they be material or immaterial— so too is there such a conjunction between the soul (*jīva*) and karma.

The "contact of the self" is the conjunction of the self and the mind, based on the statement in the *Nyāya-sūtra* (1.1.16): "The self is conjoined with the mind. That which has this as its beginning is so described; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of its non-existence. Nor is the conjunction of those two contradictory, for by the word "beginning," the contact between the mind and space, as well as the contact between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), are included, [just as] the aggregate of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The absence of conjunction is, by its very nature, the state of contiguity resulting from the attainment of a relationship characterized by the absence of any intervening space.
Those two things which one perceives and brings [together] are of such a nature;
those two things which arise in immediate succession are precisely what is denoted by the term "conjoined."
—Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 221.
Even conjunction (saṃyoga) is not perceived as something other than objects situated in immediate proximity—Nyāyakumudacandra, p.
In the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, page 677,
[it is stated that] the Sāṃkhya position regarding the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) [is as follows].

Granted that bondage is inferred for the soul—which is by nature the apprehension of reality—from false knowledge; but by what cause does that [bondage] occur? To this, he says: "By the auspicious and inauspicious," and so forth.

The conscious living being (jīva) is bound by its own insentient [influences], namely its respective inflows (āsravas), which consist of its own mental, vocal, and bodily actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (9)

Regarding the fact that living beings (jīvas) incur bonds of merit and demerit through their own respective pure and impure outflows (āsravas) consisting of mental, vocal, and physical actions, no one can reasonably disagree; rather, this is universally accepted by all.

What, then, is the nature of this living being, the self (ātman)? It is consciousness (cetana), characterized by the capacity to perceive both itself and others; it is not as conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas, for according to them, there would be an absence of the fruit of bondage.
For its fruit—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—is neither false cognition nor anything else; moreover, it is not always appropriate for that which is insentient, because of the contradiction.
Even if it were produced as something distinct, it would have no effect on it, due to the over-extension of such a principle and the refutation of inherence (*samavāya*).
What is that? He says: "He is bound," meaning he is conjoined.

With what? He says: "With insentient *karma-pudgalas* (karmic matter), not with actions (*karman*) of a sentient nature as imagined by the Buddhists, because of the Tathāgata’s statement: 'Action is consciousness' (*Abhidharmakośa* 4.1)."

How could it [be karma]? Because that would contradict its nature as action (*karman*), and because volition (*cetanā*) has the self as its intrinsic nature. If you argue that "contrary volition is karma," from what does its existence arise? If you say "from latent impressions (*vāsanā*"), no; for that has just been refuted. Furthermore, at the very moment of knowing the reality of that [volition], one perceives its capacity to lead to hell and other such states. Consequently, everyone would desist from actions such as violence and contrary volitions without needing the instruction of another, just like yogis who know reality. Indeed, no conscious person who knows a precipice and fears suffering would ever intentionally step onto it.

Furthermore, it has been well-considered that even if there is a determination of consciousness upon seeing the partless [agent], one cannot postulate a determination of its capacity; and since its capacity is not apprehended, the possessor of that capacity is likewise not apprehended. Thus, there is no distinction whatsoever from the position of non-conscious karma, for [the agent] is in every respect eternal, partless, and itself unconscious.
Pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as volition, are mental action— Abhidharmakośa, Chapter on Volition.
And of the contrary latent impression,
in the non-conceptual vision.
Because it would entail the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by certainty and uncertainty.

[Objection: Surely they are bound by those [fetters], but he (the Self) is not, for he is impelled by Maheśvara. To explain: whatever is bound by a conscious being is bound by one who is impelled by an intelligent agent, just as a thief is bound by shackles and the like; and the Self is likewise bound by such [a being]. Therefore, that which impels him is Maheśvara. To this, [the author] replies: "By himself."

Indeed, that conscious being who is bound by those [elements]—neither by himself, nor by Īśvara, nor by another—is himself the impeller of them for the sake of his own bondage; what need is there for another, such as Īśvara, in this regard?

Nor should this objection be raised here: "How can he be their impeller if, being one of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*), he does not perceive them? For it is observed that even in dreams and the like, one acts as the impeller of one's own hands, feet, and so forth, even though they are not perceived.
Furthermore, for one who holds that God’s knowledge is singular, eternal, and non-cognizant of itself, the claim that "God perceives those [dharma-s]" is highly incredible.

If, on the other hand, it is impermanent, then it must have been previously unperceived by Him; otherwise, according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.1), "Dharma is that from which the attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good results."
Thus [the argument] is refuted, because of this deviation (*vyabhicāra*);
for if its connection with the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) was made by another intelligent being, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*),
and if it were made by itself, let it be the same for the other as well.
Thus it has been well said:
"This ignorant creature is itself not the master of its own pleasure and pain through its actions."
"Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to a chasm or even to heaven.
— Mahābhārata, Vanaparvan 30.28.
The actions of actions belong specifically to the Vaiśeṣika.
Actions [are the cause] of the Lord's knowledge; [this is] the Lord's [view].
Let there be a direct connection [between the soul and bondage] itself.

Now, if it is thought: "If the conscious being were to bind himself by his own accord, then even liberated souls would be bound, as there would be no distinction [between them and those still in bondage]," to this he replies: "By the *āsravas*.

Those by which or from which the karmas of transmigrating living beings flow in (*āsravanti*) or come together are the *āsravas*, namely passion (*rāga*) and so forth; it is by means of these, acting as instruments, that [bondage occurs].

It is not only by these [names], but also by the actions of mind, speech, and body—that is, by the activities of the mind, voice, and physical form—if the word *eva* (only) applies to these as well as to passion (*rāga*) and so forth due to the similarity of their causal basis, then why are passion and the rest denoted by the word *tat* (that)? True; because the mind and the others are not designated by their own specific names, they are denoted by the word *tat*. This is just as in the verse from the *Āptamīmāṃsā* (1.4), "The destruction of faults and obscurations," where although the word *doṣa* (fault) also denotes the two obscurations, because the obscurations are mentioned separately, the term *doṣa* refers specifically to passion and the rest.
Action of body, speech, and mind involving desire is *yoga*;
1, 2 By the word "āsrava," by the word "āsrava."

By the very force of the statement regarding passion (*rāga*) and so forth, it is understood that the defect of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the like is the cause of the transformation of oneself and others; furthermore,

because it is an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), this defect of ignorance and so forth is inferred to be of a nature distinct from the karmic matter of the *jñānāvaraṇa* (knowledge-obscuring) and other *paudgalika* (material) karmas.
Alternatively, the connection should be made through grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇya*), namely: "by means of the *āsravas*, which are the actions of mind, speech, and body.

And in that context, according to worldly convention, by the phrase "by means of mental actions," mental activities such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth are also included. Therefore, he considers that [the liberated ones] are not bound by them, because they lack a substratum (*anāśrayatva*). —*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 51.

By all of this, he says the following: "The object under dispute is caused by an intelligent agent because it is an effect, like a jar. In this case, if it is argued that the bondage of the self—which is insentient—is produced by itself through a sentient, impure self, and thus that very self is established as the intelligent cause, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
However, if [the cause] is something other [than the self], then the proof of that [intelligent cause] is established even in the example; thus, there are liberated persons.
Because it is devoid of passion and the like, and because it is an effect,
the four great elements are preceded by one who possesses cognition, since they are effects...— Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 55.
Nyāyakusumāñjali 5.1:
It is produced by itself from itself.

Now, one might object: "Even though he is bound by *āsravas* that are themselves insentient, he is nevertheless bound by those belonging to others just as if they were his own. For the Mīmāṃsaka indeed accepts that even for ancestors who have long since passed away, there is bondage through such relatives as sons and so forth; or the Buddhist accepts that one person is bound by the karma of another. To him, [the author] says: "By his own"—that is, by his own, personal *āsravas*, not by those belonging to others, because that would lead to the fallacy of a lack of fixed order (*avyavasthā*).

Indeed, a son's desire to see liquor and so forth does not cause a father who is an extremely learned *śrotriya* to partake of liquor even while he is alive, much less when he is dead. Otherwise, a father who has performed many religious observances might go to hell due to his son’s fault; thus, no discerning person would ever consistently perform virtuous deeds out of fear that his son might become a wrongdoer. Or else, a son should not even be born;
for a man fearing the death of an enemy does not bring that very enemy into his own presence.

If, however, someone were to engage in the act of procreating a son because they have seen another person’s son who is obedient to his father—thinking, "Another such [son] might be born," for uncertainty regarding the result is indeed a factor in engaging in action, like that of a farmer and others—that is incorrect. For, since one might think, "Someone might even turn out to be harmful [to me]," the cessation of the perception of benefit would not occur.
Therefore, it is well said: "by their own";
or else, "by their own" means he is bound by insentient things; otherwise, everyone would be bound by the sins of others.
If he gives that [merit] to another, then he too is bound;

for instance, every Buddhist says, "By this merit acquired through my birth, may all sentient beings be happy. If it were otherwise, then when a wicked person says, "By my great sin, may all yogins be miserable," while he himself becomes free from all the sufferings of saṃsāra, the yogins would instead become possessed of them. Thus, by means of his merit, others are indeed made happy.

If it is argued that "whatever is desired by the one to whom it is given, all that the yogin desires," this is not tenable; because when one desires long life for someone who is dying, and bestows his own lifespan so that the other has a hundred-year life, at that very moment death would occur for the giver and long life for the other, which is not the case. Furthermore, [this is untenable].
The self [is not affected] by the influxes because of its momentariness; the implication is that one [moment] is acted upon while another is bound.
Thus should one who follows the Vedas reflect from their proximity.
The term *ṭhaka* refers to one who seizes property through the occupation of a thief; thus,
since it follows that all such persons are also "seizers of property," it appears redundant here for this to be written twice.

By that stainless merit in skillful means which I have attained, may there be for this world at all times a perfection that accomplishes the welfare of the entire universe. — *Pravacanavārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 648.
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, page 936,
and the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā*, page 605, it says:
"A certain person of evil intent..."
A certain sinful person is beloved; yet,
for that beloved one who is devoid of fortune, she speaks crookedly, though she herself possesses merit.
One who gives may be devoid of merit, yet through the sacrifice, one goes to the station of Cakrin.
Then, he asks: "By what kind of things [is this achieved]? and says: "By auspicious and inauspicious [deeds]."

By means of the causes of merit, which are wholesome, and the causes of non-merit, which are unwholesome— namely, the outflows consisting of the actions of mind, speech, and body— it will be explained in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) that these serve as the causes for that [result] in the *vṛtti*.

But surely, one might object: "Are not those very things which are causes of merit also causes of demerit, since we observe the occurrence of miserable rebirths even for those who practice virtuous conduct? Likewise, are not those very things which are causes of demerit also causes of merit, since we observe prosperity even for one devoted to the performance of violence and the like? Thus, when there is such a confusion of causes, how can a discerning person undertake the practice of the means to dharma and so forth? To this, he says: "According to their own [nature]" (*yathāsvam*). This means:
those which are their own, or in whatever way they are their own—thus, "according to their own."

This is what is meant: for whatever volitional action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—the mental, vocal, and physical activities that are its own immediate causes, or whatever the *āsravas* (influxes) may be, it is by not transcending these that the conscious being is bound by the unconscious factors.
Indeed, the causes of an unconscious auspicious [action] cannot possibly become the causes of an inauspicious one; otherwise, the causes of a rice sprout would be the causes of a barley sprout.

As for the misfortune that is observed even in one who possesses virtuous conduct, that does not arise from that conduct or the karma produced by it; rather, it arises from previously committed evil karma. Otherwise, since the fruit of that conduct would have been realized at that very moment, no one would ever possess the fruit of future practices such as the propitiation of specific mantra-deities.

And if, at some time, because an evil state (*apāya*) is seen immediately after a virtuous one, that [virtue] alone—or its cause—is considered the cause of that [evil state]; then alas, for one who eats divine food mixed with poison, death would have to be considered caused by that food! If, however, it is generally not observed from that food, but is observed from the poison, then that [poison] alone is postulated as the cause and not the food; so, in the case of the present [argument], what contradiction would there be such that it should not be accepted? For the occurrence of an evil state is seen only from contrary conduct (*viruddhācaraṇa*).

If it is argued: "This might indeed be so, provided that merit (*puṇya*) were established from some source through auspicious conduct (*śubhācāra*)," [we reply: let this matter rest for now; the commentary (*vṛtti*) will state later that those things which cause the influx (*āsrava*) arise from auspicious conduct.
It is auspicious indeed,
for even in a state of woe there is divine food.
Death is like poison;

for, since the performance of violence and other such acts sometimes results in the acquisition of gold and other wealth, the claim that their performance is a means to dharma is refuted, because that acquisition arises solely from previously performed meritorious deeds.

Even when that [action] is performed, since its reality is not perceived, this might be the case: "In this way, that action was performed by him such that, accompanied by its performance, it yields a fruit;
and for that very reason, in the absence of that [performance], there would be no fruit from such acts as approaching the teacher's wife."
For, in the case of sacrificial fees and the like, the acceptance of the means of happiness such as gold results precisely from the performance of acts such as violence.

The attainment of the means to happiness is established by this as well: "A desire born from the conceit of favorability toward things favorable to another produces in the desirer an action directed toward that object, just like the desire produced for those things favorable to oneself. How so? Because it would follow that even a son’s desire for what is favorable to his teacher’s wife—such as approaching her while she is with another man—would be a cause of merit (*dharma*).

If it is argued that [merit] does not arise because of hostility toward the guru; or if it were the case that even when the guru has died or is hostile, a desire for what is favorable to asceticism would not be a cause of merit—[we reply with the following] comparison:

A desire born from the conceit of being favorable toward things that are favorable to another fulfills a specific quality of the self (*ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*) which is the cause of an action directed toward the object of the desirer, because it is a desire born from the conceit of being favorable toward things that are favorable, just like a desire born from the conceit of being favorable toward things that are favorable to oneself. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 555)

The Mīmāṃsaka says that the word "yadi" (if) is meaningless. He argues: "For how could the performance of acts such as violence, when accompanied by mantras, lead to [undesirable results], whereas poison alone leads to death? It is because [the mantra-aided act] results in prosperity and the alleviation of disease. This is incorrect; for a meaning is not established by mere whim, and because of the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, since the authority of the Veda will be refuted later, this distinction cannot be understood from it; moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that [distinction] being understood even from the scriptures of wandering mendicants (*khārpaṭika*).
Therefore, whatever this may be,
it is a cause of sin according to the Veda.

If it is argued that "this violence is a cause of merit and this is a cause of sin," or alternatively, that "one is bound by non-conscious merit and demerit, whether auspicious or inauspicious," and consequently that "the conscious being is bound by them without distinction," then the author replies: "according to their respective natures" (yathāsvam).

To explain the verse—namely, that [the vow] is "without transgressing" the specific nature of a particular conscious being's own anger and so forth, whether mild, intense, or otherwise—he says: "By means of mind, speech, and body," and so on;
that is, by means of the outflows (*āsrava*) consisting of the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Alternatively, the word "and" (ca) should be understood in the phrase "by the outflows" (āsravaiḥ). [The question is: "Of what kind? To this he says: "By the auspicious and the inauspicious.

Now, if it is asked: "In the verse, the designation 'by the auspicious and inauspicious' was made as a compound; why is it here made as a separate expression? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of avoiding confusion and the like.
The purpose of such an instruction is to demonstrate that "those [actions] which are pure are indeed pure, and those which belong to oneself belong only to oneself and not to another.
How is this explained? He says: "according to their respective [nature]" (yathāsvam).
What does this mean? He says: "the bondage of merit and demerit" (puṇyapāpabandhaḥ).
Of whom? He says: "of the *jīvas* (souls), not of *prakṛti*, nor even of the moment of cognition.

In the *Kārikā*, it was stated generally as "the *jīva*"; here, the expression "of the *jīvas*" (*jīvānām*) is used with reference to individual instances in order to demonstrate the plurality of souls. Otherwise, even here, by using the singular form "of the *jīva*," a doubt might arise in one of dull intellect—namely, that according to the Teacher’s view there is only one single soul.

Nor is there bondage for that [Self], because of the absence of its cause; rather, the term "jīva" (living being) is employed for the purpose of establishing the Self—which is of the size of the body, a transformation of consciousness, beginningless and endless, the agent and the enjoyer—because it is this very [Self] that is commonly known by that designation. This is so because words such as "ātman" and others, while referring to this, may also apply elsewhere in relation to something else.
The separate enumeration [is] of that which is accepted by the Sāṃkhyas and of that which is accepted by the Buddhists.
It has been stated repeatedly that this very [soul] is grasped as the eternal and unitary *jīva*,
particularly in comparison with the Vaiśeṣikas and others.

If it is argued that, since [the Self] is eternal, all-pervading, and inactive, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated here in order to refute the misconceptions of others; to this he replies: "In this matter," and so forth—no one ought to hold a misconception regarding this point.
It might be thought: "No one can disagree regarding an object of knowledge (*prameya*) that has been made an object by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
yet this [self] has not been made an object by such a means.
For instance, it is not [known] by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it does not appear therein."

Indeed, the bondage of merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*) for living beings through the influxes (*āsrava*) of pure and impure mental, vocal, and physical actions is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as is the case with the contact of a jar and the like with a heap of dust; for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no disagreement [regarding its existence].
Nor is it established by inference (*anumāna*), because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor can those karmic influxes themselves serve as the logical mark, since one can only infer an effect from its cause. This being the case:
But this is not the case, because of deviation; causes do not necessarily possess their effects (*Praśastapādabhāṣya* 1.66).

Nor are those [causes] perceived elsewhere or at another time as having that [bond] as their cause—like *atasī* seeds and oil—such that bondage could be inferred from them, as the binding of the belly is inferred from the contact of *mālavaka* with *atasī* seeds and oil.

If it is argued that another reason (*liṅga*) here is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*) because it is made an object of cognition by scripture (*āgama*), then how could anyone possibly disagree with it? For it is precisely because they are made objects of cognition by scripture that disagreements arise—just as we see in cases such as "Nature (*prakṛti*) is the cause" or "The Person (*puruṣa*) is the cause. Otherwise, if they were not made objects of cognition even by scripture, disagreements would not proceed at all, being without a basis. Furthermore, since the very cause of disagreement is itself the means for its cessation, there is no fixed relationship of cause and effect.
Even a specific scripture is difficult to comprehend regarding supersensuous matters, because it is impossible to ascertain that it was composed by a distinguished person and so forth.

If it is argued: "The statement 'the binding of merit occurs for living beings due to the influx of those karmas,' etc., is authoritative because it is the word of the Arhat, just like his words that establish transformable objects such as jars," that too is not sound, because the reason "being his word" is unestablished in this case.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that even this statement [of yours] has as its object a reality characterized by manifoldness (*anekāntātmaka*), just like any other well-known statement whose object is not that [reality]; then that too is exactly the same. For there is no contradiction in its having such an object, since it is not the case that the mouth of one who says, "There is a seventh substance beyond the senses named 'this,' which undergoes transformation at every moment," becomes distorted. Therefore, it is not made an object of knowledge even by scripture (*āgama*).
The [list] beginning with *atīsīta* (excessive cold) and *taila* (oil) is to be understood from *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p.
210, and *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, p. 2.
From Mālavaka oil or from Atīsī oil for the Sāṃkhya practitioner.
For the Vedāntins, since the status of being the word of the Arhat is unestablished,
there is no contradiction even with the contrary cognition held by the opponent, the adversary.

Others think as follows: "This matter is not something to be accomplished through mere effort; rather, it is undisputed by all, for it is free from contradiction among all disputants. Who can restrain those who, like elephants intoxicated by the pride of supporting their own views while lacking the goad of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), proceed in disagreement? Indeed, we see the Cārvākas and others disputing on this very point. And they should not be ignored regarding the realization of truth by the impartial Akalaṅkas, who are consecrated in their dedication to the welfare of others."

Nor do their misconceptions cease in this very manner; rather, they cease through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, that alone must be stated to them: "What is the use of this [objection], for there is nothing here," and so forth.

Even the Mīmāṃsaka accepts that substances and the like constitute merit (*puṇya*) based on the scriptural injunction, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice a white goat," and he accepts that the killing of a Brahmin and the like constitute demerit (*pāpa*) based on the injunction, "A Brahmin is not to be killed. Beyond these two, there is no further bondage of merit or demerit.
Prabhākara said:

"For the welfare of man is human pleasure; that is to be accomplished through substances, qualities, and actions characterized by Vedic injunctions (codanā). Therefore, dharma-ness resides in those alone."
"One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa" — Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2; "One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa" — Manu-smṛti 8.
This has been extracted from the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, page 731:
"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse."
"For activity alone belongs to living beings, while cessation is the fruit;
this activity of beings leads to further birth, whereas cessation yields great fruit.
— Manu Smṛti.

The followers of the Sugata (Buddhists), however, further declare that merit and so forth consist solely of the mental states and the like involved in giving, non-violence, and so on, as stated in *Manu* 5.56.

Because the minds characterized by generosity, non-violence, and abstention possess the capacity to attain heaven, it is determined from the words of the Master that "this is so," even though these [minds] are not themselves perceptible;
for in the ultimate sense, due to the absence of cause and effect, no one is bound by them— thus says another who maintains the doctrine of the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*).
By insentient karmas,
they are neither bound nor liberated; conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras), which are subject to arising and passing away, are as before— the sentient being is neither bound nor liberated.
—Mādhyaṃdina Kāṇva 16.5.

However, the view of the Sāṃkhya is as follows: from those [evolutes], a specific transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) arises; therefore, that bondage belongs to that very [nature] and not to the *puruṣas*, who are pure by nature.
In that very context:
[it arises] from nature alone through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
The supreme form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision; that which has reached the range of vision should be regarded as utterly insubstantial, like an illusion— page 89, note 5.
Because of this statement, one [opponent] claims that the existence of bondage and its fruit is not ultimately real;
in the same way, other fallacious arguments (kunaya) should also be stated.
Since such conflicting views are observed, how can it be said: "But this [view] is undisputed by all"?

To this, the following reply is given: regarding the statement that "there can be no one who would disagree with the fact that living beings (jīvas) are bound by merit and demerit," the intended meaning is as follows—since the non-existence of universal non-duality is negated and the plurality of living beings is thereby established, there can be no one who would disagree with the phrase "of the living beings."

If it is asked, "How is that [non-duality] refuted?", it has already been stated on this point; nevertheless, something further is said: If one postulates a non-dual reality characterized by consciousness or otherwise that has not been perceived, then since such a postulation of other streams of existence—whether they be subject to transformation or otherwise—is inevitably dependent upon a person (puruṣa), how can there be non-duality? If, on the other hand, one postulates what has been perceived: if its perception comes from another, then its lack of an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is established in the ultimate sense; thus, how can there be non-duality? Otherwise, just like the difference between objects of apprehension, the establishment of that [non-duality] does not follow from it for other selves.
Of the postulation of the unseen [principle] for the sake of non-duality.
By this, the establishment of that [self-awareness] through scripture is refuted;
for let it be understood that this self-perception occurs within cognition itself.
Indeed, neither self-perception nor any other perception can establish a state of affairs without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The Advaitasiddhi is its own philosophical system.

Now, it might be thought: that non-duality consists precisely of blue and so forth, because anything else does not appear and is therefore non-existent; and because blue and so forth consist of their own appearance—just like pleasure and the like—since while they exist as appearing, no grasper other than themselves is observed. That is not tenable; for if the determination of reality is based on appearance, then since one perceives blue and yellow as distinct from the nature of cognition itself through the competitive assertion "I know blue," "I know yellow," it must be so. Otherwise, if it were not so, it would not be the knower of anything at all, and thus the claim that it grasps itself would be utterly discarded.

There is sublation by perception in both cases, and this objection does not apply here: that [the object] is identical to itself and other things through a single nature, or distinct through multiple natures; for if it were the latter, there would be an infinite regress, since that [multiple nature] too would have to be apprehended again through yet another distinct nature.
Furthermore, for cognition whose very nature is grasping, its own nature cannot remain ungrasped, because that would be a contradiction.
How so? Because even a single nature is perceived as both self and other when it is cognized;

therefore, while it perceives those two, there is no identity between them, since such identity is not perceived. Otherwise, if the very same nature by which the cognition of blue is distinguished from yellow were also the nature by which it is distinguished from red, then those two would be identical—what a great and wondrous monism of diversity! If one were to postulate yet another nature [to account for this], the same problem would persist, leading to an infinite regress.
The remaining point here might be considered as follows:

even if that [object] which possesses it were to have a manifold nature, there would still be no infinite regress; for even when grasping that which possesses [the capacity], there is no necessity of grasping the capacity itself, since it is of the very nature [of the object].

Rather, that capacity—which is identical with its essence—is inferred solely from the observation of the effect, and practical activity is not undertaken at this present moment [on the basis of such an inference].

When that which possesses [the property] is apprehended, there is no infinite regress even in the apprehension of that [property], because it manifests in that very way as being of the nature of that [property],
just like a cognition having the form of blue, which consists of [the properties of] middle, beginning, and so forth.

If this [distinction] is not admitted, how can that non-duality (advaita) exist? Thus, how could it be logical to claim that the refutation of the plurality of souls is without foundation? Or, if it does exist, then if its prior absence (prāgabhāva) and its subsequent destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) are not admitted, there is no difference from the non-duality of the Self (puruṣādvaita); thus, the non-duality of the manifold (citrādvaita) would be firmly established! Alternatively, if those two absences are admitted, how is the removal of the two aforementioned alternatives achieved? For instance: by what nature is it non-existent before and after, yet existent at its own time—is it by that very same nature, or by another nature? In the first case, it would follow that it exists before and after because it exists even at its own time; or else, the relation of cause and effect would be negated, since the designation of "existence" applies only to the specific preceding and succeeding moments.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the absence of that [external object] is admitted even in the case of mere-cognition (*vijñaptimātra*); how is there no fault? For as long as the middle moment is produced from something by means of a certain intrinsic nature, and if by that very same [nature] it is the cause of another, then there is identity between the prior and the posterior.
If one conceives of an interval between them, then the creeper of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) will persist, entwining the tree of the Sugata’s doctrine until the end of the aeon (*ākalpa*).

Furthermore, if one does not admit preceding and succeeding moments, then just as for a non-momentary entity that produces its own effects without succession—having ceased after simultaneously producing the entire cognition of its own object—the result would be emptiness (*śūnyatā*) due to the absence of perception in the second and subsequent moments; so too, let the wise consider whether or not emptiness would likewise follow for a cognition that relies upon only a single moment? And if, even in the case of such emptiness, nothing undesirable happens to the opponent, then let that very emptiness always remain;
for the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge is the same elsewhere as well, should one refuse to accept the manifestation of blue and other objects.
In feeling, one regards both oneself and others as both self and other.
From the cognition of yellow, there is the capacity for both the cognition of yellow and the cognition of red.
The sense is that [the entity] would result in being eternal;
for if one accepts prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva), there is the consequence of its existence [at all times].
Let the causal relationship itself be emptiness;
moreover, that very [emptiness] manifests by itself (Pravā. 2).
Even this [position] would be untenable under such circumstances; for, like an insentient object, it would be impossible [for consciousness] to exist without the capacity to apprehend itself.

That capacity to be apprehended by itself, in turn, depends upon a further capacity; and in that case, the recurrence of the two aforementioned alternatives is inevitable due to the previously stated fault.

Therefore, it is not logical to refute the self- and other-illuminating nature of cognitions—which is established by perception—on the grounds of its being non-conceptual, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
"There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there another experience of it,
because of the absence of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper"— this refers to the former part [of the argument], as self-luminosity is untenable.

Now, it may be argued that cognition does not illuminate another object that exists simultaneously with it, because there is no causal obstruction [between them] and because both appear as independent entities; or else, the object itself—such as blue—would be its own illuminator.

Or, if it is held that the status of being an object (*karmatā*) is perceived in the blue and so forth, and therefore the object is illuminated by this cognition and not the cognition by the object due to the reverse being the case; in that regard, if it is argued that since the perception of the status of being an object occurs without any distinction from the blue, the very nature of the blue itself is the status of being an object; we say no, because that [status of being an object] exists in the cognition as well.

If, however, it is argued that cognition itself is the grasper of that [object] through the act of grasping (*gṛhīti*), then if that grasping is made distinct from [the object], the triad—grasping, cognition, and "blue"—would appear as independent entities, and nothing would be the grasper of anything else.

Furthermore, if another internal entity were produced by that grasping, the same fault would apply and there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because yet another internal entity would have to be produced by that one too.
Consequently, even the grasping would not be grasped as having an external object.

Furthermore, if those two [the cognition and the object] are grasped, there follows an endless succession and an infinite regress, because even in that case one would require the grasping of yet further [cognitions].

If, on the other hand, they are non-different; it follows that blue and so forth are produced by that [cognition] alone. But that is not tenable, because that [blue] exists from something else, and it is impossible to produce what has already been produced.
Moreover, blue and so forth being produced by that [cognition] would result in its being merely a subsequent cognition, and not an external object.

If it is argued that [the objection does not apply] because [cognition] takes the object as its material cause (*upādāna*), we say no; for since the object is not apprehended [by itself], its status as a material cause is unestablished.

Alternatively, if it were apprehended, how would the aforementioned fault not arise? There would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) or a circularity (*cakraka*), because even in that case, since the apprehension is non-different [from the object], that very same [apprehension] would have to function again and again once it has been apprehended.
Therefore, there is no simultaneous apprehension of that [object] and another by means of the intellect,
for the intellect is what makes [the object] manifest.
The apprehension of its own nature, such as blue and so forth.

The same undesirable consequence that can be asserted regarding the internal [cognition]— namely, that it exists— would also apply here, as it is invariably connected with the position that [the cognition] has an object.
Having grasped the previously perceived blue and so forth, having grasped.

By this, the apprehension of even that which is at a different time by that [consciousness] is established; for there is no distinction [between them], and because it would follow that all past and future things would be apprehended.

If it is argued that "there is no apprehension of one distinct thing by another, just as a wall is not like a living being," we say: no. For it has already been stated that it is impossible to refute the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer between cognition and blue (or other objects), which is perceived by non-conceptual direct perception (*avikalpa-pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, the manifestation of blue and so forth is not, like [the manifestation of] cognition, independently established for another; otherwise, even in a dream, the thought "I perceive blue" would not occur, because that [cognition] does not function with respect to an object that is not present.
Indeed, one who perceives blue never, by means of cognition, engages in the linguistic convention "I perceive yellow."
The meaning is that there is no establishment of a conscious living being (*jīva*), nor of an unconscious wall;
thus, [the capacity for cognition] is self-dependent (*svādhīna*), not dependent on another (*parādhīna*), according to the etymological derivation *apara-adhīna*.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—"Why does sound, which is blue, not become a grasper?"—that too has been refuted by the aforementioned well-established understanding.

If it is argued that a cognition having a blue form would likewise either grasp another cognition having a yellow form—just as it grasps itself—or else fail to grasp even itself, because it is perceived as being a grasper of itself while not being a grasper of another; then the resolution is the same for the proponent of the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*): cognition, which is perceived through the "I-am-I" impulse (*ahamahamikā*), is perceived as the grasper of both self and other, and blue and so forth are perceived as its objects of grasping.
Like its own nature,
or like the cognition having a yellow form,
[it belongs] to the cognition having a yellow form.

Furthermore, as for this argument—that "the state of being an object of cognition does not appear apart from the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of blue and so forth, and just as the intrinsic nature of blue is relative to the cognition, so too is the cognition relative to that [blue]"—this too is not sound. For all entities possess mutually distinct intrinsic natures;
the intrinsic nature of one is not that of another, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of everything being one.
Thus, the intrinsic nature of the cognition consists of both the apprehended and the apprehender, whereas that of blue and so forth consists only of the apprehended, since it is perceived as such.
Otherwise, by whatever capacity the cognition of blue assimilates its own form as blue, by that same capacity it would have to assimilate the cognition of yellow;
for this very reason, no grasping of that [object] is performed by the intellect, but rather its own nature alone is grasped—just as the nature of an effect is produced by a cause.
And how, for those who speak thus, could the intellect be the grasper of the self? Because it performs grasping; the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) is as before.

Now, if it is argued that [cognition] does not grasp that [object], but rather shines forth by itself—no; for this is merely a difference in terminology, as it would still mean "it grasps itself. Furthermore, one might as well say that it does not grasp blue, but rather manifests it, in relation to the blue object.

As for what was said regarding the self—that [consciousness] is not the apprehender of another [object] whether at the same time or otherwise—that applies to all cases. For indeed, it must be stated that cognition bears within itself the form of blue and so forth, whether simultaneously with the act of knowing or otherwise, in accordance with how it is observed. This has been stated elsewhere as well.

[Objection: But surely the cognition "I know blue" occurs even in a dream; what follows from that? [If you say: "In that case, just as there, even in the waking state the appearance of blue and so forth is established as having no real object," [we reply: No; because the fact that something is so in one instance does not establish a rule that it must be so in all instances. Otherwise, since such a status would be established for self-cognition (svavedana) as well, that too would have to be abandoned just like external objects, and consequently, the purpose of means of knowledge (*sādhana*) and so forth would fail to be established, just as with external objects. Otherwise, if one accepts that [self-cognition] despite its lack of difference from an unreal appearance, one would be practicing the logic of partiality (*ardhavaiśasanyāya*).

Therefore, just as the Buddhist maintains that although there is no difference in the nature of appearances, the appearance of external objects is held to be of an unreal object while the appearance of self-cognition is not, so too the opponent maintains that the appearance of dream-objects is of an unreal object while the appearance of the waking state is not.

Now, one might object: "If, just as pillars and other objects appearing during the waking state possess ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), then that same reality would belong to them in the dream state as well; what fault is there in this for the proponent of external objects (*bahirarthavādin*)? If you say that the formulation of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and their fallacies (*tadābhāsa*) would be useless [in that case], then why would it not likewise be useless for the Buddhist (*saugata*) as well, given his principle: 'Everything is erroneous with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*), but not with respect to its own nature' (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 280)? Moreover, if ultimate reality were established for both the dream and its opposite [the waking state] based on that [same reasoning], then the formulation of valid means of knowledge and their fallacies would belong solely to me [the opponent]; whereas for the Buddhist, his entire philosophical system would fail because consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is not established. Oh, how clever he is at refuting others!"
Because it is self-cognized, like the state of dreaming,
due to the acceptance of self-cognition.
The principle of the "half-entrance" (ardhaveśanyāya) [256]:

Just as it is impossible for a certain Yavana, desiring to eat the flesh of a hen and also desiring its offspring, to cut off its neck and so forth to eat it while leaving the belly for the sake of obtaining offspring— so too is it in the present case.
"...And a partial mutilation (ardhavaiśasa) is not appropriate when the knowledge of reality is intended to be expressed...

[it would be like saying] that one part of a hen, for instance, is fit for laying eggs while another part is cooked; this is what is meant by 'partial mutilation'... — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Vārttika-Ṭīkā 1.1.23.104.
4 1276 Worldly Maxim No.
On the Two [Types of Causes]
The existence of pillars and so forth should be observed by means of the Jains and others— page 64, note 5.

The view of others is that [reality] possesses parts and is not partless; they hold that even at other times, as in a dream, there is an absence of the distinction between the real and the unreal. For them also, "representation-only" (vijñaptimātra) is not established, because it follows from their position that something which transcends all conceptual construction (vikalpa)—just like consciousness itself—is established. If you ask, "What is the use of establishing such a thing?", we reply: what is the use of consciousness? Moreover, in this extreme monism (ekānta), neither the state of transcending all conceptual construction nor the monism of momentariness (kṣaṇikaikānta) is established; this has already been stated extensively.
Since non-difference is perceived both externally and internally just as difference is, it is like a snake in a bracelet and the like;

nor is this perception of a constructed nature, because even for one who conceptualizes "this" as being present, the recollection of the perception as "that" does not cease— just as the cognition of a cow does not cease for one conceptualizing a horse—
and thus, even while conceptualizing in such a way, the emptiness of all things has been taught.

It is not maintained that there is an absolute sublation by another [cognition], because that would result in the absence of an object even in the case of dream-cognition, since the same consequence would apply there as well, thereby destroying that absolutism.
If it is asked, "From what does this cognition arise? the sequence is: from the eye and so forth, just like the cognition of difference;
and a further distinction has been described arising from successive operations of those [senses].

It is solely through the recollection of the preceding state and the perception of the succeeding state that another reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*) is produced, namely, "this is that very same thing. For, while abiding in subsequent transformations, the state established in the preceding transformation is determined [as persisting]; and it is not the sensory cognition itself that possesses an object, since everything possesses an object by virtue of its own appearing object (*svapratibhāsin*). This is especially so in the case of [the doctrine of] absolute momentariness (*tadekānta*).

By this, the cognition of the relation between cause and effect is also explained; since there is a cognition, free from contradiction, that "this has arisen from that," the postulation of distinctions among all cognitions is not more beneficial for the opponent than the cognition of non-difference.
From the operation of the eye and other [senses].

Furthermore, as for this argument: "That which appears on the path of clear perception is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), like an elephant or similar object perceived in a dream; and that which is seen during the waking state, such as a pillar, appears on the path of clear perception"—in that case too, from what source is the absence of ultimate reality established in the example, such that through it the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason—whether it be "appearing on the path of clear perception" or some other—is established? For, just as the presence of a soul (*sātmakatva*) is not established by means of breath and so forth, or as the quality of being withdrawn [into the heart] and so forth is not established by means of the soul, the pervasion of any [reason] remains unproven.

If it is argued that [the object] is apprehended [by perception]; if it is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) because of being clearly perceived, how can the reason (*hetu*) be non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*), given that this [reason] is deviant? If it is not ultimately real, then its establishment is like that of an external object (*bahirartha*); thus, the same fault remains—that there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) by it—and by this, the apprehension of that [object] through inference (*anumāna*) is also refuted; for in that case as well, if one seeks another illustration (*nidarśana*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that the pillar and so forth perceived while awake serve as the illustration, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): for the non-existence of ultimate reality in the elephants and such seen in dreams is established only when the existence of the pillars and so forth perceived in the waking state is established from them, and the establishment of those [dream objects] depends on the establishment of the latter.
