If, however, because the proponent accepts that a jar or the like seen in a dream lacks ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason is thereby established, and thus the reason is not subject to the fault of being "without a substratum" (*niranvaya*), nor is the example deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*) or of doubtful nature (*sandigdhadharmatā*); then why was the Sāṃkhya—who asserts that pleasure and so forth are insentient because they arise impermanently, like a jar—refuted by Dharmakīrti as being "without cause" (*akāraṇa*) while he was explaining the term "itself" (*sva*)? For the Buddhist proponent, or even the worldly person, accepts therein [in the case of pleasure, etc. the quality of arising impermanently and so forth.

Furthermore, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) occurs by virtue of the person being addressed (*pratipādyavaśena*), and not because of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). What kind of restriction is this? Or, if it is claimed that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum in the example is accepted by taking a probandum established merely through the desire of the person being addressed, then why is it not accepted by taking what is established merely through one's own desire? For there is no difference between one's own desire and the desire of another when they are both devoid of valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇabhūta*).

If it is asked, "What fault is there in accepting this?"—there is none at all. However, because a reason (*sādhana*) imagined according to one's own whim would lack pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the intended probandum (*sādhya*), just as the probandum itself [lacks it], the inclusion of the word "object" (*artha*) in the definition of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) as "that which reveals an object perceived by oneself" would be meaningless. If it is then asked, "In that case, how could there not be faults such as the 'lack of continuity' (*niranvaya*) since the pervasion of the reason with a probandum established merely by the whims of oneself or another is not proven?"—it is for this very reason that even if something is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason is rendered useless because its absence [in the subject] is thereby established.
Nor can there be the exclusion of a conceptual construction (vikalpa) imagined to be meaningless regarding what is already perceived, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga);
for such a conceptual construction cannot be connected with an object that is both that [perceived] and not-that, and because it would be conducive to universal emptiness (sakala-śūnyatā).

If it is argued: "The waking cognition is intended to be the sublater (bādhaka), since when that exists, things like a dream-elephant do not exist as ultimate reality (paramārthasat); rather, although they are non-existent in that way, they are falsely conceptualized as existent, and thus worldly activity proceeds"—this is not so, because the opponent does not admit that it is a sublater of that.

Even if [the absence of ultimate existence] were admitted, its absence in the case of pillars and so forth during the waking state would mean that there is no lack of ultimate existence [in those things].

Or, even if for some reason that absence were established in those cases, it does not follow from this that it is established everywhere. This is because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against its presence there.

Indeed, no one has ever seen a cognition that has entered the path of seeing the ultimately real being subverted by anything—just as, for example, the quality of being a speaker is not seen to be subverted in the case of an omniscient being; likewise, because such a thing is never observed in anyone who exists.

Nevertheless, there is no groundless animosity toward the Mīmāṃsaka on the grounds that [the reason] "being a speaker" and so forth lacks probative force (*gamakatva*) for proving the absence of that [omniscience] therein;

or else, how could the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason in the case of [ordinary] vision be avoided? Furthermore, even a contradiction does not directly subvert the existence of that [quality] therein, because the two types of contradiction regarding the reason cannot be established through non-perception (*adṛṣṭa*), as in the argument:
"The eyes and other [faculties] are for the sake of another, because they are composite, like the parts of a bed or a seat," and so forth.
The example would be established as accepted within the definition of the thesis if the word "itself" (svayam) were included.
It should be observed— in the *Pravāha* [of the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*], verse 4.30... in the case of a jar and so forth.
"Neither self-will nor non-will" means "the will of another," because there is no distinction [in that regard].
In this context, the definition of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) according to the Teacher is: "the manifestation of an object perceived by oneself."
"In that regard, inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) is the manifestation of an object perceived by oneself"— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 467.
For the proponent of the non-duality of appearances, there is no sublation of waking cognition.

If it is argued that non-existence is indeed contrary to ultimate existence merely by virtue of its non-perception, and thus the reason (*hetu*) is pervaded by that [non-existence], and therefore there is a contradiction due to the removal of the intermediate term; [we reply: if the pervasion of one by the other were established because their coexistence is observed somewhere—just as the pervasion of "being an effect" by "having an intelligent cause" is established because their coexistence is observed somewhere—then since such observation of coexistence exists here as well, a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is equally difficult to find elsewhere.

Or, let it be granted that there is some way in which this [reason] is excluded from the counter-example; nevertheless, even if it is accessible through clear perception, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason for ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*) remains unremoved. Therefore, this [argument] would be trivial.

Just as in the case of a jar and so forth, a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the reason of "being an effect" is difficult to find in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), so too in other cases, even when the reason is accessible through clear perception, such a subversion is difficult to find. Now, one might ask: "Does the Buddhist not establish or negate anything at all? Why then [is this said]? Some maintain: "It is merely that a person engaged in conventional practice—who establishes the ultimate reality of waking pillars and the like based on appearances and so forth—is refuted by the fact that those [appearances] are shown to be fallacious in a hundred instances such as dreams, since he himself accepts that [ultimate reality] is absent there."

In that case, does the proof become fallacious (vyabhicārin) simply because it is accepted by a person who lacks valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*)? If so, then every property such as existence (*sattva*) would likewise be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the proponent accepts it in permanent entities like space (*ākāśa*)—just as he accepts impermanent things like jars—and if appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and the like are inconclusive, how can there be an establishment of the ultimate reality of external objects? For the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) cannot arise with certainty from a proof whose deviation is doubtful, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If there is doubt regarding the object, what is the fault? What is the use of resorting to that which is useless for practical activity (*vyavahāra*)? Furthermore, what is that reality (*tattva*) which ought to be resorted to by abandoning [the doubtful]? If you say it is "mere self-awareness" (*svasaṃvedanamātra*); well, that too is established through appearance and so forth, and since that has been shown to be fallacious by your own admission, this is nothing at all. If a distinction is admitted here by the opponent, then that same distinction must be admitted elsewhere as well;
and the fallacy of one thing does not entail the fallacy of another, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As it has been said:
"These defects arise from the acceptance of [the existence of] *sattva*."
"Those whose eyes are as fickle as those of a Caṇḍāla, a cowherd, or a child produce delusions regarding Indra’s net and the like, and nothing else. — *Nyāyabindu*, Verse 51.

Now, if it is argued that this establishes the existence of external objects, it is replied as follows: Just as the operation of cognition toward grasping itself occurs without abandoning its concomitant grasp of an external object, and the operation toward grasping an object located in a different place occurs without abandoning its concomitant grasp of itself, so too, because the grasp of an effect occurring at a different time is established without abandoning its concomitant grasp of the cause, the causal relation is proven to be ultimately real. And since that is established, the previously stated objection—that "because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the relation of cause and effect between speech and intellect, the intellect cannot be inferred from speech"—is refuted, just as in some cases fire is established by the sight of smoke, so in other cases consciousness is established by the perception of speech.

Furthermore, because the relationship of cause and effect is not established in the case of cognition, even when speech is observed in the presence of cognition, it does not follow that [cognition] exists everywhere and at all times solely from that [speech]. For instance, although a water-lily (*sālūka*) is seen to arise from a water-lily, its appearance from cow dung is also observed; thus, the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not removed. Therefore, some ask: "How can speech be an inference for cognition? These people are even more wicked than the Cārvākas, for they themselves accept that a certain thing arises from a certain thing at one time, yet later assert the opposite.

And how can it be established for those who speak thus that all cognition is self-apprehending (*svagrāhin*), whereas [otherwise] there would be apprehension by another (*paragrāhyatā*)—from which the exclusion of the Mīmāṃsakas and others would follow?
For perception is not capable of performing so many functions, since it does not operate upon what is not its own object, and because a single statement cannot simultaneously negate duality.
Furthermore, that which is not self-apprehending is not cognition at all.
Why is this so? Because of the mention of "its own" (*sva*) and because there is no other characteristic for it.
Why is that also so? Because it is observed to be thus. [Objection:
But if it is observed to be thus in one instance, how can it be so in all cases? For even when the nature of a tree is observed once, its deviation from that nature is not thereby excluded.

Even this being the case, knowledge never abandons its own nature, whereas an effect abandons its cause—this is the behavior of a tyrannical king! Therefore, it was rightly said: "No one ought to disagree with the statement 'of living beings'";
for by demonstrating the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it follows that knowledge must be apprehended by another.

And how, for those who speak thus, is it established that all knowledge is one? The connection [of the sentence] is: "because of the negation of its non-duality. The sense is that there might be a suspicion of a transgression of the essential nature [of knowledge].
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the bondage of merit and demerit," no one ought to disagree.

For example, since these [pleasures] are by nature impure due to their inherent quality of manifesting themselves and others as they truly are, investigators ought to infer that even adventitious pleasure and so forth—which arise from false knowledge (mithyājñāna) and are perceived alongside poisons and the like—are produced by similar causes. Otherwise, how could fire and such be inferred from smoke and the like? However, there is this distinction: that which is the subject of dispute, such as false knowledge and so forth, is designated as "sin" (pāpa), whereas that from which pleasure and so forth arise is designated as "merit" (puṇya).

And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*) for them [the Jains] is as follows: "Pleasure and so forth, which have become the object of our current dispute, arise from causes similar to the poison and other factors associated with them, because they are transformations occurring when those [causes] are present, just like well-known false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*).

Furthermore, this too is well-said: "No one should be able to dissent from the fact that there is a bondage of merit and demerit for living beings (*jīva*)," and likewise, "no one should be able to dissent from the fact that their bondage occurs precisely through the influxes (*āsrava*) of pure and impure actions of mind, speech, and body."

To explain: regarding poison and the like, there is the notion of benefit where there is harm for oneself or others due to false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). From that arises non-restraint (*avirati*) with respect to those objects; from that, too, comes the lack of mental application toward the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding what is beneficial or otherwise. From that, greed (*lobha*) arises—the mental, vocal, and physical activity directed toward seizing it. From that, its acquisition follows—the conjunction of the self with it. From that, again, further false knowledge arises. The same should be stated for other cases as well. Likewise, in that very context, anger and the rest should be explained as proceeding from false knowledge, consisting of their respective activities, their appropriation, and so forth, beginning with a false self-view (*mithyātman*).
In the same way, the occurrence of pleasure and so forth upon the acquisition of specific medicines and the like, resulting from right knowledge and so on, is to be explained.

Thus, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, the bondage of merit and demerit is inferred; therefore, it is inferred that [bondage] comes into being. Furthermore, authoritative instruction (*ājñā*) and the like, as well as false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) and so on, are its causes.

Nor is it improper to infer the effect from the cause; otherwise, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), which establishes the conventional usage of "non-existent," would remain unestablished, since that [non-perception] is accepted as the cause of that [usage].

Even in the case of an inference based on capacity (*yogyatā*), how can that inference be free from doubt, given the possibility of suspecting a deficiency in the causal connection (*pratibandha-vaikalya*), as in the inference of cooked rice from rice and so forth?
In this regard, the postulation of a specific cause is the same in both cases;
as it has been said:
The connection is that the bondage of non-conscious karma is inferred by means of [the presence of] karma.

The self exists as the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent," having entered into bonds such as "arising" and "ceasing"; those bonds are the outflows (*āsrava*), and they are produced by anger and the like; those [defilements] such as anger are born of negligence (*pramāda*) due to the absence of vows (*avrata*).

That very same [soul], when accumulated through falsehood, becomes stained; yet, upon the attainment of time and other factors, it is gradually liberated from its association with the impurities of right-view, vows, and skillfulness— Ātmanuśāsana, verse 241.
This very self of mine carries away my merit and happiness through those bonds produced by the *āsravas*;
those [bonds] are under the sway of anger and the like, and that anger and so forth are born of negligence (*pramāda*).
Therefore, because of false knowledge, I am constantly and correctly endowed with vows (*savrata*) against them.
"The one who is capable of performing the penance of yoga that has exhausted the *kaṣāyas* is a liberated ascetic" (*Yaśastilaka*, p.

Thus, it is said that for those who speak of the destruction [of karma], there is a transition to an inferior configuration; other than that, no unseen cause for it arises, because such a cause is not observed.
As it has been said:
"Delusion regarding suffering and craving are the causes of bondage for living beings; he in whom these two do not exist does not undergo rebirth. (Prajñāpradīpa 1.83).

Furthermore, there would be "re-binding" and so forth; that is, there would again be a variation of results characterized by pleasure, pain, and so on, within the continuum of bondage, according to the respective proximity of the causal complex such as time and other factors. (10)
Furthermore, like the variations in the poison of a rat or a mad dog,
there would subsequently— meaning at another time— be a diversity of results from their bondage of merit and demerit, and likewise, there would be a difference in their effects.
"What are its characteristics? To this he says: "Pleasurable," and so forth.
In that context, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of desirable and undesirable bodies and the like.
Under what condition would these occur? To this he says: "Accompanied by bondage."

Bondage is a specific conjunction (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*) between the soul (*jīva*) and karma, not an inherence (*samavāya*), because inherence is incompatible with consciousness. Its continuity is its persistence as a stream until the attainment of the fruit. This is what is meant: if there were nothing from anger and so forth that, through a stream of connection with the self, reached the time of the fruit's realization, how could there be a variation of fruits in another birth? Furthermore, since anger and the like would dissolve at the very moment of birth, such a [bondage] is not tenable in the doctrine of absolute momentariness, because that doctrine negates the existence of a stream.

When there is immersion within a single field, the differentiation of results is characterized by mutual interpenetration. By this, the claim that "there is no differentiation of results arising from mental, vocal, or physical actions" based on the scriptural injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice a white goat" is refuted; for substances and other factors perish at the very time of the sacrifice and so forth.

Regarding the persistence of that [karmic] stream, it is better that the persistence of those karmas already arisen from them should remain, because there is no contradiction; whereas for substances and so forth, this is not the case due to the opposite being true, since even at the time when their fruit is experienced in this life, the continuity of that [substance] is not perceived.
If that [persistence] exists, how and from where could that [fruition] arise? To this, he says: "according to its own [nature]" (*yathāsvam*), etc.

The "arising" (*udaya*) of a particular karma is the ripening of its capacity to produce a fruit at the appropriate time; "impulsion" (*udīraṇa*) is the ripening of what was previously unripened. "According to its own [nature]" means without transgressing that [respective timing].

Because of the capacity [of the action] to perish, its own [nature] would [be lost]; here the intended meaning is this: if wholesome or unwholesome karma, having first arisen by way of its own intrinsic nature, were to produce its fruit even while remaining in that same state at a later time, then that fruit would have existed at the very moment of its arising.

For when there is no deficiency in the cause, there can be no deficiency in the effect; otherwise, it would follow that the effect is not produced from that cause, as in the case of substance, quality, motion, and so forth.
At the very time of the sacrifice, there is a continuous flow from the sacrificial materials and other elements.

The following might be thought as the result: "This very nature is such that its effect is seen at a later time—for indeed, it is observed that mantras, tantras, and the like, which are effective in their own country, produce their effects in another country. That is not tenable; for it would follow that those effects must coexist with the cause even at a later time.

And likewise, even for a yogin, there arises no such cognition as "this action has arisen [for him]," nor is that which lacks a cause an object [of knowledge]. This is because of the statement: "A means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is effective when it is accompanied by its object.

Thus, the claim that even that which lacks a cause is an object for a yogin is merely a fancy; for otherwise, it would follow that anything could be possible for anyone else as well, according to the principle: "For whomsoever there is a certain measure of capacity... (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 223).

[The opponent] might say: "Surely the cognition of the Lord (īśvara) is eternal and yet apprehends objects; let it be so eternally. Otherwise, how could the cognition of a non-omniscient yogin apprehend an object? [For us, it is] because that [cognition] is an effect [of that object]. [The author replies: How can two successive effects arise from a single action of a unitary nature, or from anything else? If you say, "Because of its inherent nature (svabhāva)," would that nature belong to the cause or to the effect? First, it cannot belong to the cause, because it has a single nature.

For it is not logical that the very same [nature] which operated toward the first effect should operate elsewhere; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence (prasaṅga) of there being no difference in the time of the effects.
Nor does it belong to the effect; for that is impossible given the two alternatives of being already produced or not yet produced:
it cannot belong to what is unproduced, because it would be like the horn of a donkey;
nor can it belong to what is already produced, because of mutual dependence—namely, that the produced thing has that [nature] as its essence, and that its production occurs within that [nature].
For that which lacks a cause is not an object of cognition—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 80.

Now, if it is argued: "Just as from a single [cause] of a single nature there is simultaneously an effect differentiated by space, so too, in succession, there is an effect differentiated by time"; let this be the view of the Buddhist (*saugata*), but not of the Jaina. For the latter, the difference in effects always arises precisely from a difference in the nature of the cause.

On this point, another says: "Just as a cause of a single nature possesses manifold potencies within itself, so too it should produce manifold effects by means of that very [nature]; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. This is not correct, because [this proponent] does not understand the Jaina system (*samaya*).

Indeed, it is not the Jaina view that a thing possesses some capacity by means of some extrinsic nature; rather, it arises from its own causes as being of that very nature, just like a cognition whose nature is either doubt or its opposite.

For example, according to the scripture, just as a doubtful cognition, although having the form of doubt regarding an object such as a post, is nonetheless non-doubtful in its own essential nature, so too [is the case here].

By this, that which was stated by someone—that the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are pervasive of their substratum—is refuted; for it would follow that their effects would arise everywhere and at all times, and it would follow that liberation (*mokṣa*) would be impossible, since liberation consists in the absence of merit and so forth.
Since those [impressions] are absent there [in liberation], they cannot be pervasive of their substratum, because the self exists in liberation as something devoid of them.

Or how is the absence of that [soul] determined there? Because of the absence of its effects, such as the body and so forth. But is it an absolute rule that the absence of a cause is understood from the absence of its effect? If that were so, how could there be a cognition of *dharma* and the like everywhere, given that the soul is all-pervasive? Since its effects are not observed everywhere, the absence of those effects there is due to the absence of the effect itself, and not due to the absence of *dharma* and so forth—this is not a valid answer; for otherwise, the same undesirable consequence would apply even to liberation (*mokṣa*).
Because of the existence of the self— which is empty of phenomena and so forth— in liberation, [there is no fault].
The non-existence of merit (*dharma*) and so forth is untenable, for even though their effects exist, they are not perceived.

Furthermore, if the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*), despite not pervading its own substratum, were to produce merit and so forth in the self everywhere and at all times; then merit and the like, likewise, would produce their effects everywhere despite not pervading their own substratum—so what is the use of postulating such pervasiveness? This is merely trivial.

If it is argued that its pervasiveness over the self does not mean that all its effects occur everywhere, because of the deficiency of the causal complex consisting of time and so forth, whereas when that [complex] is present, the effect certainly arises; to this he replies: "Time and so forth," etc.

Time is the first among those [factors], such as place, specific substances, and so on; these are what is meant by that expression. Their "causal complex" (sāmagrī) is simply those very factors when endowed with a specific transformation (*pariṇāma*), and not something other than them, for otherwise it would follow that the arising of the effect is from something distinct [from the cause].
Furthermore, since that which is distinct [from the cause] cannot be related to it— and because inherent relation (*samavāya*) has been refuted—
if one were to postulate a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor, then those very factors would suffice as the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) to assist the effect;
if yet another [relation] were postulated, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If its presence—that is, its proximity—is accepted, there would be a variation in the results of karmas due to the influence of their arising (*udaya*) and activation (*udīraṇā*).

Alternatively, one might consider that its proximity would be useless in the absence of any assistance rendered by it; or rather, it should be explained as follows: there would be a variation in results upon its presence because [the result] occurs only when it exists, whereas previously it was absent even though those karmas were present.

Furthermore, by the statement "there would be a variation in the fruit within the continuity of bondage," he refutes the notion that such variation arises from the visible [cause] itself, such as service and the like. This is because we observe a variation in results even among those who perform identical service: for one person the fruit appears quickly, for another after a long time, and for yet another there is no fruit even after a long time.
Now, a diversity of effects cannot arise from an identical cause, for that would entail the absurdity of something not being its own effect.
Indeed, from seeds of white lotuses, it is never the case that white and non-white lotuses are produced.
Time and the other factors constitute a causal complex that is indeed distinct [from its constituent parts].
Of the causal complex,
[namely] the cause consisting of the complex of time and so forth.

By this, the possibility of [the birth of] persons from time and so forth is refuted, because they are distinct from the objects of perception; for even from water placed in a crystal vessel through which light filters, the birth of various living beings is observed.
In that regard, the postulation of subtle, imperceptible specificities of the elements would not differ from the doctrine of karma;
for if such a specificity were to occur only occasionally and in certain instances, it would indicate a causal necessity inherent in the self.
Furthermore, if things were accidental, the distinction between false cognition and so forth would not be preceded by the influx (*āsrava*) caused by false cognition and the like.
Then, regarding the statement "it remains in its former bond" and so forth,
which concerns the differentiation of results,
he provides an illustration, beginning with "a mouse."

A genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed between the words *mūṣika* (mouse) and *alarka* (mad dog), which have been made into a copulative compound (*dvandva*), with the word *viṣa* (poison). Alternatively, that same compound may be expressed as a compound with the word *vikāra* (modification), [meaning] a compound of *mūṣika*, *alarka*, and *viṣa* which have been made into a copulative compound. Then, [the term] *tadvat* is a genitive compound meaning "it exists similarly to that modification" (*tadvikāreṇa tulyaṃ varttate*).

In the phrase "characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth," the author introduces the following verse beginning with "udayodīraṇa" in order to define the fruit of false vision and knowledge intended by the word "and so forth":

"When there is the presence of the rise (udaya) and activation (udīraṇa) of those karmas that obstruct right vision, [the states of] false vision and [false] cognition arise from the subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣayopaśama) of the karma-prakṛtis. (11)

False view (*mithyādarśana*) is the lack of faith in the true nature of the principles, such as the soul (*jīva*). Regarding the soul, this consists of either nihilism or the conceit of being a non-soul; for false view does not transcend these two forms, being either a misconception (*vipratipatti*) or a lack of comprehension (*apratipatti*).

Thus, even in the case of the *kṣāyopaśamika* (subsidence-cum-destruction) state of false view, there occurs a transformation into wrong cognition (*matyajñāna*) and so forth, due to the rise and activation (*udaya-udīraṇa*) of the karmas that obscure it.

If it is argued that stating the verse again for the purpose of illustrating what was already indicated by the word "etcetera" (ādi) would result in redundancy, and that this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) since the same would apply to the statements intended to illustrate desired and undesired fruits such as the body and so forth—[we reply: no, because those were introduced in a different manner.

For instance—the absence of restraint arises from false knowledge and so forth; from that, negligence; from this, anger and the rest; from those, the influx (*āsrava*); from that, the bondage of karma; and again, within the continuity of bondage, there would be a variety of fruits—this is the intention of the Sage (*sūri*), based on such statements as "This 'I' takes away my karma, my happiness, and my fame" (Yaśo° pṛ.

246). In this regard, if the first [cause], namely false belief (*mithyātva*) and so forth, were non-causal or had another cause, then everything would be exactly like that. To this, he says: "In the case of rising (*udaya*) and activation (*udīraṇā*)" and so forth.

The intended meaning here is as follows: even that [state of] falsity and so forth arises from another [cause], namely the force of the rising (*udaya*) and activation (*udīraṇā*) of karma; for that series is beginningless, like the series of seed and sprout.

Alternatively, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such things as transition to a desired state, and not false view (*mithyādarśana*) and so forth, because dispute regarding those has already been refuted by such statements as: "False knowledge is invalid due to its lack of correspondence" (*Siddhiviniścaya* 4.2).
To demonstrate this point once again by means of an illustration, he states the verse beginning with "udayodīraṇa" (arising and activation).

The intended meaning here is as follows: just as the poison of a rat or an *alarka* dog becomes effective as a result when its own temporal conditions and other causal factors are present or absent, so too, due to the force of arising and activation, a certain adventitious falsity—such as [the notion of] non-momentariness—is perceived; and from that very same cause, another adventitious conceptualization, such as pleasure and so forth, is likewise desired.
This occurs when there is both arising (*udaya*) and activation (*udīraṇa*).
Of what [is this the cause]? He says: "view," and so forth; [it is the cause] of those karmas that obstruct knowledge.
What would result from that? He says: "false view and intellect" (mithyādṛṣṭidhiyau); the ellipsis is that these would be false inclination and false knowledge.
If it is asked, "Is this always the case?"—to this he replies with the words beginning "karma" (action), and so forth.

When certain types of *karmaprakṛtis* (karmic natures) are in a state of subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*), then there occurs in the self a tendency toward the apprehension of objects; otherwise, such [apprehension] would be impossible, as in the case of one who is intoxicated or unconscious. Even then, when certain [other karmas] are in a state of rising (*udaya*) and so forth, there is a false inclination (*mithyārucyādi*) due to the rising or activation (*udīraṇā*) of some [karmas] and the subsidence-cum-destruction of others. Just as, for example, in the case of one who has fainted from consuming poison and the like, upon the first awakening, that person perceives a delusion (*vibhrama*) because of the subsidence-cum-destruction of certain loathsome qualities and the rising or activation of others.

Explaining the verse beginning with "jīvādi" (living beings, etc.), [the author] first explains the false view (mithyādṛṣṭi) previously mentioned, stating that because the continuum of karma, its arising, and false belief (mithyātva), etc., is incapable of producing knowledge, [it constitutes] false view.
What is it? He says: "the soul, etc.

By the word "etc.," the non-soul and so forth are included. That alone is the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*) because it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Lack of faith, that is, lack of inclination, toward that is what is meant;
demonstrating that very point, he says: "the soul, etc."

The word "tāvat" (first) denotes sequence. The connection is as follows: "atheism" (*nāstikyam*)—the state of an atheist (*nāstika*), which is false vision (*mithyādarśana*)—exists in the living soul (*jīva*), which is the self (*ātman*).

In that very context, he shows another [form of false vision]: "Furthermore, in another [object]—namely, an imagined substratum (*dharmin*) devoid of the transformation of consciousness, colored by attributes such as omnipresence and so forth—the conceit of being a living soul (*jīvābhimāna*) is also false vision"; this term "false vision" carries over from the previous statement. Why? Because conceiving something to be what it is not is of the nature of that [false vision].
Why, then, is it shown to be of only two kinds? To this he says: "Of the one with false vision," and so forth.
For one whose inclination is toward false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), how can there be non-transgression through faith? To this he says: "contrary conviction" (*vipratipatti*), and so forth.

"Contrary conviction" (*vipratipatti*) means a contrary or perverse conviction regarding the soul (*jīva*), or else it means non-conviction, the absence of conviction; the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative, and the word "thus" (*iti*) marks the conclusion of the discussion on false inclination.
It is false because it is false according to the Naiyāyikas and others.

If it is asked: "Is there not also a third alternative consisting of doubt—namely, 'whether the soul exists or not,' or 'whether its nature is that of conscious transformation or something else'? Why is this not mentioned here? The answer is: No, because that [doubt] is already included under the term "non-comprehension" (*apratipatti*), since doubt is essentially a form of non-comprehension. Regarding such a person of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), he asks: "Of what kind is his state of existence? To this he says: even for one who possesses a state arising from the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of karmas—that is, for a false-viewed person whose state exists within that destruction-cum-subsidence.

That too is the word "of that very [thing]" used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); or, if it is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), since that [word] is absent in one devoid of similarity (*vatsatā*), how could it belong to that? To this, he says: "It appears as that," and so forth.

By the word "that" (tat), the *jīva* is referred to. Of that *jīva*, there are the destructive karmas (*ghātikarmāṇi*). Although this refers to karma in general, by virtue of the context, those which cause its impairment through the obstruction of right vision (*darśana*) are understood. Due to the force of their arising (*udaya*) and premature activation (*udīraṇā*), it is not only wrong vision (*mithyādarśana*) that arises for him from this [karma], but also wrong knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Demonstrating this, he says: "of sensory cognition" (*matya*), etc. Wrong sensory cognition (*matyajñāna*) is knowledge that is erroneous regarding apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth; it is so called because it is the beginning of wrong scriptural cognition (*śrutājñāna*) and the rest. That itself is the transformation (*pariṇati*).
And the word "ca" (and) should be understood here;

therefore, the meaning is this: there is a doubt as to whether that transformation [of the soul] also occurs due to the rise and activation of those very destructive (*ghāti*) karmas, even in the case of the *kṣāyopaśamika* state.

If it is argued that doubt indeed arises elsewhere as well—just as it does regarding the living being—and since the possibility of nihilism exists elsewhere too, why is the word "first" (*tāvat*), which denotes sequence, employed only with respect to the living being and not elsewhere? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "nihilism therein," nihilism is twofold: that which exists as reality (*prajñāsat*) and that which exists as designation (*prajñaptisat*);
likewise, it refers to those who hate the self, [asserting] that the truth is either unperceived or unperceivable. (12)

Objects such as jars and pillars are seen to exist only as conceptual designations (*prajñaptisat*), because shape and so forth do not exist within their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); this is due to the persistence of the faults regarding the impossibility of their subsistence, the resulting infinite regress, and the non-existence of the gross object.
Furthermore, circularity and the like do not appear [as independent entities], since nothing exists apart from those [specific characteristics].

Cognition-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). Because things exist as mere designations according to how they appear, even for one who is deluded, neither multiplicity nor unity is possible, since there is the appearance of a distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and consciousness itself. Since a nature conceived as unitary is not established either intrinsically or extrinsically, the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) cannot establish the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanairātmya*) of all phenomena in the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even while being cast into the pit of misfortune by his own false attachment to this [self], he does not perceive it as such when it exists.

Due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one cannot maintain that there is only perception and no other reality of objects of knowledge (*prameya-tattva*); for if other means of cognition are denied, the very definition of perception becomes untenable. What, then, could one establish or deny by what? Consequently, the world would consist of nothing but the four elements.

While it is indeed well said that, from the perspective of self-cognition, the world is afflicted both externally and internally, this is so only because [the opponent] has failed to refute the systems of other schools of thought.

Having fallen into a state of total delusion, even regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), one resorts to denial because of the resulting contradiction; otherwise, one ought to explain the arrangement of the four elements based on their distinct characteristics.

Yet, such an explanation of the arrangement of the four elements is not tenable, because the reality [of things] cannot be fully understood through the definition of even imperceptible objects, as it would otherwise be impossible.

In this regard, since even the state of *akṣāyopaśamika* (subsidence-cum-destruction) is established—or held as a view—as "false vision" (*mithyādarśana*) due to the force of the arising and activation of the *ghāti-karmas*, there exists the state or the action of an atheist (*nāstika*), which is twofold, being of two kinds according to the distinction between external and internal objects; or else, because consciousness alone (*vijñaptimātra*) exists through the diversity of its objects consisting of living beings (*jīva*) and non-living beings (*ajīva*); or again, through the distinction between the objects of waking and dreaming, or through the distinction of its scope; or else, through the distinction between the means of valid cognition such as inference (*anumāna*) and their respective objects of cognition (*prameya*). Thus it is distinguished.
Alternatively, showing the distinction between that which is atheism regarding the *jīva*, he says "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth.
Therein, in the *jīva*, atheism is twofold, by way of the division between the Buddhist and the Cārvāka.
Or else, it should be explained as follows: "therein," meaning between those two—atheism and the conceit of a self other than [the body]—atheism is twofold.
What is that? He says: "existent as designation" (*prajñaptisat*), which means "existent as conventional reality" (*saṃvṛtisat*).

[Objection: But the word *prajñapti* is not established anywhere as a synonym for *saṃvṛti*; therefore, one should say "seen as existent as conventional reality" (*dṛṣṭaṃ saṃvṛtisat*), for in this way the instruction becomes clear, since *saṃvṛti* is well-known everywhere as "the concealing of reality" (*tattvasaṃvaraṇāt*) and as "the cognition of false conceptualization. [Objection continued: Nor is it appropriate to speak thus, lest the verse be corrupted. [Response: That is not so; for speaking in that manner is intended to demonstrate the distinctions between the views of other schools.

For instance: "Everything perceived is considered false by the conscious one; there is no fault in [its] non-existence, even though it appears like an illusion, a mirage, and so forth" (Pravārtikālaṅkāra 3.211). Why? He says: because of the reason that it is "conceptually existent" (*prajñaptisat*). That of which cognition (*jñapti*) has departed is called such; that which possesses existence as a conceptual construct is likewise called "conceptually existent. This applies to all things.
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for anyone that apprehends ultimate existence, since perception and so forth occur even in dreams;

thus, everything—such as pleasure and so on, or blue and so on—which exists (*sat*) as it is perceived, moving within the range of perception in the form of an exalted non-dual cognition, is not [ultimately real] in the form of living (*jīva*) or non-living (*ajīva*), according to the statement:
"And whatever blue and so on is perceived."

Furthermore, there is another view: everything seen otherwise is existent by way of designation (*prajñaptisat*), existent by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāreṇa sat*), because of the statement [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*] "validity is by way of conventional usage" (PV 1.6).
This is based on the etymological derivation: that which has a cognition (*jñapti*) that is loose and pleasing only so long as it is not investigated.

He further demonstrates his extreme nihilism: that which is unseen and unperceived—the experience of momentary atoms, or like the person (puruṣa), the absolute emptiness of everything—is what is ultimately real.
Showing yet another [view], he says "tathā" and so forth;
"tathā" means in that manner, and "dṛṣṭam" refers to seeing, that is to say, direct perception.
It must be understood as "only what is seen" (*dṛṣṭam eva*). By this, that which is unseen—such as inference and so forth, which are distinct from direct perception—is not included.
What is that? He says: "Reality" (*tattvam*).
It is called reality because its object is reality; this is a metaphorical designation of the object for the subject, just as in the *Prakaraṇavārtika* it is said: "Perception is existence" (3).

54. Or rather, the connection is as follows: the nihilism (*nāstikyam*) of those who hate the knowledge of the self—the Buddhists and the Lokāyatas who propound selflessness—is twofold; it consists in grasping that the reality of the self and so forth is "only seen," meaning it is merely made an object of perception and not made an object of inference and the like, and thus [they hold] that it is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
"Conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) is that which covers (*saṃvaraṇa*) from all sides.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is called "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) because it completely obscures the true nature of all things;
or, conventional reality is mutual co-arising, meaning that [things exist] by depending upon one another.
Alternatively, conventional reality is a convention (*saṃketa*), meaning worldly transactional usage.
And that [conventional reality], characterized by the signifier and the signified, knowledge and the object of knowledge, and so forth—
*Mādhyamakavṛtti*, p. 240— is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), which is merely a conceit of cognition in the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Convention (saṃvṭti) is said to be the consciousness of conceptual construction (vikalpavijñāna), which arises from beginningless latencies (anādivāsanā) through resolute belief (adhimukti)— *Pramāṇavārttika-bhāṣya*, p.

It is called *saṃvṹti* because it conceals (*saṃvriyate*) and covers (*āvriyate*) the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, both by its nature of obscuring and by its manifestation of what is covered;
ignorance (*avidyā*), delusion (*moha*), and inversion (*viparyāsa*) are its synonyms—*Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā*, p. 352.
Explaining the verse [addressing] nihilism (*nāstikya*), he says: "A jar, a pillar, and so forth are seen," etc.

That of which a jar, a pillar, and so forth are the beginning—that is, whatever entity is sentient or insentient—is thus described; and that is "seen," meaning it has been made an object of perception.

Now, one might ask: "When it should have been said 'a jar and so forth,' for what purpose is the mention of a pillar? This is said in order to demonstrate that the perception of the pillar is similar to that of the jar; for if even one of them were denied, that [denial] would apply to both. Indeed, just as a pillar is not seen by the sight of a jar, so too a jar is not seen by the sight of a pillar. Since their perception is asserted to exist through mutual exclusion, how can there be a negation of other continua (santānāntara), from which non-duality (advaita) would follow?

If that [nature] were the essence of a single thing, or if it were apprehended [as such], then even its sequential occurrence would not contradict that; how then could there be selflessness (*nairātmya*) or momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*)? When this is established in the demonstration of those [principles], if one were to say "the jar and so forth" (*kumbhādi*) once again, one might suspect that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), things like the *puruṣa* seen in other doctrines are included. To address this, he says: "existent as a designation" (*prajñaptisat*).
The meaning is that it is a cognition that has proceeded [toward its object]; or, it is existent according to conventional usage, like the hair-tufts seen by one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*).
In this regard, the proof (*sādhana*) beginning with "that which is a clear perception," and so forth, should be understood.
Regarding that very point, he states another argument: "Because of the absence of configuration and so forth," etc.

Configuration refers to length and the like; "and so forth" (ādi) refers to [qualities] such as substance-universals (*dravyasāmānya*) and the rest. Since these are absent in the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which are characterized by external and internal atoms—from what [could they arise]? To this, he says: "Because of the impossibility of subsistence," and so forth.

The "mode of subsistence" (*vṛtti*) is the inherence (*samavāya*) of qualities in a qualified object, of a whole in its parts, or of a genus in its particulars. Regarding this mode of subsistence, there is a dilemma: does it occur by way of a single part (*ekadeśena*) or by its entire self (*sarvātmanā*), and is it successive (*krameṇa*) or simultaneous (*yaugapadyena*)? Through such a conceptualization of difference, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) arises, whether [the relation] is in that [particular] or in that [whole].

If it subsists by way of a single part, then another distinct part must be postulated for that [part], and yet another for that one as well; thus, there is no finality regarding the parts. If it subsists by its entire self, then either the quality or the qualified object would alone remain. This should be stated similarly for other cases involving the qualified object and so forth.

That being the case, the connection is as follows: because of the persistence of that aforementioned fault— which consists in the linguistic usage [of] "qualities and so forth" and "those possessing them"— it is observed that jars, pillars, and the like are *prajñaptisat* (conceptually existent) when the apprehension [of their ultimate reality] is sublated in the presentation of jars,
pillars, and so forth.
The object of vision is to be seen as perceived by the proponent of the non-duality of the Person (puruṣādvaitavādin)—in substances, qualities, and actions (pṛ. 264, l. 7).
Even though it occurs in only one place,
this passage contained therein has been written twice.

The Jaina might argue: "Granted that qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth do not exist as something distinct from their substratum due to the aforementioned faults; however, the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself—such as a jar or a gross form—must exist. To this, he replies: "Because of the absence of the gross" (*sthūlasyābhāvāt*).

This refers to that which is endowed with magnitude (*mahattva*); it is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), and by it, the absence of length and so forth is also implied. Thus, the connection is made by changing the case-ending of the word *svalakṣaṇasya*.
Furthermore, its non-existence follows from the absence of its cause;

for its cause is the conjunction of many parts, and such a conjunction of parts—whether in its entirety or in part—is difficult to establish, either because it is relative, or because [the categories] acquire their nature by being relative to one another: the subtle and so forth being relative to the gross and so forth, and the gross and so forth being relative to the subtle and so forth.
Furthermore, phenomena that exist dependently are not ultimately real;

by this, the doctrine of non-difference is shown—this is the distinction. Because of the absence of such [ultimate reality], jars and the like are conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*); thus is the composition of the gross.
If it is argued that atoms, as conjunctions, must therefore be ultimately real; to this he replies: "Because the spherical," and so forth.

Since the spherical—the subtle partlessness which is the "beginning" (ādi) of such properties as momentary destruction—is not perceived within particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), therefore each of those [atoms] is non-existent.
If it is argued that "only blue and so forth, devoid of the aforementioned specificities, is ultimately real," he says in response: "Because of its being distinct from that," and so on.
Here, the reason just mentioned—namely, that because blue and so forth are impossible and do not appear as something distinct from the perceived gross jar and such—is to be understood.

Therefore, the meaning is this: just as circularity and the like do not exist because they do not appear [as such], so too blue and the like do not exist as distinct from that [the jar]. Thus, this is not tenable: that whatever appears in a certain way is ultimately real in that very way, just as blue is ultimately real as it appears in its blueness.

And so forth. Since there is no example of something blue [that is not momentary], even if one were to imagine such a thing, who could prevent the same [imagination] regarding circularity and so on? Thus, the statement denying that [non-momentariness] is contradicted by what precedes and follows. By the phrase "of that which is distinct from it," he shows this:

if the ultimate reality of blue and so on—which are not distinct from their nature as gross and so on—is accepted because they appear in that way, then for the proof of the momentariness of everything, the reason based on appearing in that way [is valid]; for the reason is not unestablished due to a lack of a cause for the appearance of non-momentariness, just as there is for the appearance of grossness and so on.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that blue and so forth— which are non-different from that [pot]— do not possess ultimate existence while the pot does, then the reason would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*). Therefore,
since blue and so forth cannot possibly exist apart from it, the pot and such things are "thus existent" only as conceptual designations (*prajñaptisat*).
The conceptualization of the gross is not distinct from the intrinsic nature of the gross and so forth.
Now, demonstrating another meaning of the term "designation" (*prajñapti*), he says: "mere representation" (*vijñaptimātra*) and so forth.
The connection is as follows: that which is seen, such as a jar or a pillar, is merely a specific cognition (*jñapti*); for it has been stated that "whatever appears is consciousness."
And what is that [nature]? He says: it is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is accepted as being ultimately real.

As Prajñākaragupta has also stated: "Alternatively, the illumination of an unknown object—this is the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from the ultimate perspective" (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 2.5).
The Madhyamika, refuting this, says: "Just as it appears," and so forth.

Here, the intended meaning is as follows: Is consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) imagined in accordance with how it appears, or otherwise? If the first position is held—that it is designated as existing in accordance with appearance, without overstepping what is seen—then, like external objects, consciousness-only is considered to exist as a conventional reality (prajñaptisat) that is real only when unexamined, but not ultimately real.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Even for one who is deluded," and so forth.

The intention here is as follows: by one who asserts that even though it appears variegated, cognition is indeed single—referring to such passages as *Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 3.220—one has accepted its ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*) despite its manifoldness. Likewise, for the self (*ātman*) which is manifold yet unitary, which is cognized and subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), there is ultimate reality;
this applies not only to the non-erroneous [self] of mere-cognition (*vijñaptimātra*), but also to the erroneous, transforming self—this is the meaning of the word "also" (*api*).
What follows from this? He says: "Because of the possibility of both multiplicity and unity.

He thinks as follows: that for which there is the possibility of both multiplicity and unity cannot be non-erroneous, just like the transforming self (*ātman*); and yet, multiplicity and unity are possible in the case of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

If, moreover, the opponent considers even that [representation-only] to have ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*) in the same way [as the self], what fault would there be? None at all; rather, it would be a merit.

If it is argued that because the transition to the opposite of identity-in-difference is prevented, the world would consequently not be Buddhist; I do not know how even such a thing was understood by Prajñākara regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.

If it is argued that "surely multiplicity and unity cannot exist even for a transformed self that is deluded, but they can exist for one who is undeluded and consists of that [consciousness] alone," to this he replies with the verse beginning "grāhya-grāhaka-saṃvitti" and so forth.

The words *grāhya* (the object), *grāhaka* (the subject), and *saṃvitti* (consciousness) form a *dvandva* compound, which is then joined with the word *bheda* (difference) in a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound (*bheda-śabdānām*). Thus, by changing the case-ending, the connection is made with the phrase "because of the manifestation of that alone" (*tanmātrasya*).

Regarding the second position: because that which possesses a "probable single form"—meaning a form whose nature is endowed with the number one by the exclusion of other continua, or rather, a form whose nature is probable (i.e., mentally introduced as "it exists" but not yet ascertained through means of valid cognition such as perception) in a single locus—is not established through its own self-cognizing direct perception (*svasaṃvedana-adhyakṣa*), it is not apprehended. For, even when one does not minutely consider spatial difference as one would temporal difference, no cognition appears in which the nature of blue and so forth, or the form of an atom, is otherwise [than singular].
Alternatively, [the reason] is "because of non-establishment from itself," which means because of non-production or non-origination;

for nothing whatsoever has origination from itself, as that would entail the consequence of things existing everywhere and at all times due to being causeless. Furthermore, even if blue and so forth were to arise from yellow and so forth, there would still be such a restriction [of the object] even though cognition is not produced by that object; therefore, enough with this postulation of [cognition] having the same form as its production.
Just like that restriction [of time], the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svarūpaniyama*) is also established through conceptual construction and not otherwise.

By this, the restriction of nature regarding the production of effects even sequentially by a permanent, uniform entity—which depends on auxiliary factors yet does not depend on any assistance rendered by them—is explained.
Therefore, it remains established that [the cause] is not established by itself.
Even if it were without cause, representation-only would still exist.
In the determination of arising, there is the determination of the object,
just as there is the determination of the object.

Showing that it is unestablished even from another [source], he says: "And because it is unestablished from another, i.e., because it is not apprehended. To explain: there is no manifestation of smell in the eye, which is assumed to have a single nature; likewise for other [senses]. This is because it is the locus of debate as being distinct from blue and so forth, or pleasure and so forth. Even if its manifestation were present there, since in the ultimate sense the relationship of grasped and grasper does not exist, there is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect. (Pramāṇavārttika 2)

This contradicts such statements as "cognitions are without objective support" (*Nirālambanavāda-prakaraṇa-vārtika*, p. 387) and "that which appears is cognition," because there is no contradiction in the appearance of even an insentient object being dependent on something else.
Furthermore, that [appearance] has no other experience [of itself], since the same objection would apply to that as well; therefore, it shines forth by itself.
This is the remainder [of the argument].
Furthermore, even for another entity of that same nature, its establishment would depend on something else, and that too would depend on something else, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If, on the other hand, it does not possess that nature, then what is the point of postulating that it is partless? This is what is intended.

[Objection: But if that [consciousness], being devoid of its own manifestation, is established through something else, then its very nature as representation (*vijñapti*) is lost, since that nature is characterized by self-manifestation. Therefore, how can the non-acceptance of an external object be refuted? [Reply: True; nevertheless, this is said with reference to those who establish that [consciousness] through the impossibility of other alternatives—such as the error of an apprehended object (*grāhya*)—while their own form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) remains uncertain. Or rather, it is said with reference to those who establish the state of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) based on scripture, such as the statement that "the non-dual vehicle is supreme."
And so it has been said: "Non-dual... (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 2.7).
Here is another explanation: because [the self] is not established—because there is no origination—from another, from itself, or from any other cause whatsoever.

For example: [if it is argued that] its production occurs at a time subsequent to the simultaneous [cause], then that too would be the cause of the other because there is no distinction; and if that were so, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Or, if it is held that only a certain thing is the cause or the effect, and likewise only a certain thing is the grasper (*grāhaka*) or the grasped (*grāhya*), then this has already been refuted—namely, that even blue and the like would become the grasper of cognition.

And just as its own nature (*svarūpa*) is produced by another and not its production itself, so too, when the nature of that blue and the like is apprehended, it is the nature that is apprehended and not the act of apprehending (*grahīti*) that is produced.

Therefore, this [objection] is also refuted: that if cognition were the instrument for grasping an object in its own form, there would be the instrumentality of the object in one case and an infinite regress in another;
by this, it has also been stated that its production occurs even from something at a different time.

Furthermore, if that which is non-existent at the time of the produced cognition were to arise from another, then production would occur even from the son of a barren woman, because there is no difference [between them].

Now, if it is argued that although [the effect] does not exist at that time [of production], it does exist at its own time—unlike the son of a barren woman, and therefore this fault does not apply—[we reply: surely, if its existence at its own time is not perceived in any way, just as its non-existence at the time of the effect is not perceived, then this is a mere statement and cannot serve as a solution. If, however, it *is* perceived, how can there be the cessation of the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender? Therefore, this is nothing at all. Alternatively, if the opponent thinks, "Since no one admits the arising of anything from anything else, why is this said?"—it is for the purpose of demonstrating the establishment of what is undesirable for him.

For when that which exists in such a form does not arise either from itself or from another, and for that very reason does not perish, it follows that it is eternal; thus, there is a contradiction of the thesis of universal momentariness.

Furthermore, for the proponents of consciousness (*jñānavādins*), since time does not exist, the persistence of a single entity through the three periods of time—that is, its continuity through a single moment—is their "momentariness," which constitutes a deviation from their own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), even though [the entity] is arising.

Regarding what is asserted by the proponent of the non-duality of appearance— that the arising of the external object occurs simultaneously with the primary cognition, and that the primary cognition arises simultaneously with the external object— if knowledge is simultaneous with blue and so forth as its apprehender, then why is blue and so forth not also the apprehender of knowledge?
If it is non-different from the object,
then in the case of non-difference,
or even in the case of difference, if one accepts another assistance for the sake of a relation, there is an infinite regress.
Because there is no distinction in the cause at the time of the effect.
To the objection, "Let that [non-existence] then remain unestablished;

what of it?", he says: "By its own nature (*svabhāvena*), that is, by its very essence (*svarūpeṇa*), there is the selflessness (*nairātmya*)—the essential emptiness (*svarūpatucchatā*)—of all entities (*sarvabhāvānām*); [this follows] from the non-establishment of that [existence]. This is the construction of the words. Thus, having caused the Proponent of Cognition (*vijñaptivādin*) to fall by means of the Proponent of Emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), he now himself strikes down the Proponent of Emptiness with the words beginning with "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).

The connection is as follows: because of the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth—which serve as the instruments—the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) cannot apprehend the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanairātmya*).

For one for whom everything is empty, there is also the absence of means of valid cognition; thus, if that [selflessness] were to be apprehended by him through that [absence], then that [absence] would also have to be apprehended by this [means of cognition], and that too by another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is what he thinks.

Or rather, if [the self] is understood through its absence, what is the point of seeking further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) elsewhere? If it is argued that one cannot understand its absence because the very means of valid cognition that establishes universal emptiness is sublated by the appearance of blue and so forth, or pleasure and so forth— meaning that in the absence of a means of valid cognition, one cannot understand the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nairātmya*)— then this is explained as being [the case] precisely within emptiness due to the absence of a means of valid cognition.
Regarding the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) within the absence of means of valid cognition,

Prajñākaragupta says here: "The very appearance [of an object], because it is devoid of conceptual constructions such as cause and effect, is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by way of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), just as a bare ground is the emptiness of a jar."
And since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) exists there as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can it be said that "in its absence, one cannot apprehend that"? To him, he replies:
"And even if [it exists]"—that is, even if one accepts the existence of a means of valid cognition characterized merely by appearance, or the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of intrinsic nature.
What [is the reason]? He says: "Therefore, this," and so forth.
Therefore, because of that state of being, this Prajñākara and the others do not perceive, even while being acted upon? Even while being made to enter?

What is it? He says: "The pit of misfortune" (*anarthagarta*). Because one accepts it as misfortune (*anartha*) by oneself, it is a misfortune; that which is characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth is like a pit because of its nature, and having entered that pit, one does not extricate oneself from it even in a thousand yugas. What is this "pit of misfortune"? He says: "The self, the living being" (*jīva*).

By what means? He says: "By false attachment" (*mithyābhiniveśena*). False (*mithyā*) means unreal; attachment (*abhiniveśa*) is the insistence on [theories such as] non-self (*nairātmya*) and so forth. That [insistence] occurs within that which appears as a single manifold [consciousness], and thus it is so described. By that [attachment], by oneself—that is, by one's own self.
Alternatively, if it is argued: "Even when the self is being cast into the pit of misfortune—the pit of total emptiness—it does not perceive itself;

how much less, then, would this [other] not perceive itself? To this it is replied: It is not possible to establish that [non-perception] either in the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or when they exist, because [of the following].

Why? He says: "Perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the means of valid cognition"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]; there is no other, such as inference (*anumāna*) and so forth. This is the point.
"Is it only this that ought to be understood in such a way, and not anything else? To this he says: "Or rather, the reality of the object of knowledge (*prameyatattva*).

By indicating this alternative view with the word "or," he means that there is one thing to be determined by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), namely the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*) and so forth, which constitutes the reality of the object of knowledge, and nothing else.

And why is this so? Why is it that in the absence of that [other means], one cannot apprehend it? To this he says: "By another means of valid cognition," and so forth. That which is other than the means of valid cognition *pratyakṣa*—namely inference (*anumāna*) and the rest—is "another" (*antara*). When there is a negation or exclusion of that [other means], the definition of *pratyakṣa* becomes untenable.

For the definition of *pratyakṣa* is clarity (*vaiśadya*) accompanied by non-confusion (*aviplava*), and that [clarity] resides in every individual instance of it; yet it cannot be apprehended without another means of valid cognition, because *pratyakṣa* has a restricted scope.

Furthermore, because it lacks a defined characteristic (*akṛtalakṣaṇatvāt*), there can be no comprehension of it from that [source]; and in its absence, one cannot possibly comprehend it—this is the connection [of the argument].
Thus, the Cārvāka's claim that "it is not so" appears to be meaningless.
Inference is the manifestation of direct perception accompanied by non-confusion and clarity.

This is another explanation based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): when it is necessary to negate other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the definition of direct perception is mentioned because that negation is not possible through anything else.

For direct perception alone—and nothing else—is capable of performing such extensive functions as establishing that "other means of valid cognition do not exist in every respect"; therefore, in the absence of that [definition], one cannot comprehend [the negation].

Regarding the negation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the author of the *Tattvopaplava* says: "The Cārvākas have deliberated well [on this matter]: 'The fact that those [other means] are impossible by their very definition is not a fault for them; rather, they accept perception only in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)'. To this, he replies: 'What by what? and so forth.

Because of the impossibility of that [definition], what—namely, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and other defects of the definitions of perception and so forth belonging to others—could the Cārvāka possibly apply, and by what means? By nothing at all."

Indeed, even that [definition] cannot be established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it would be well said that Bṛhaspati’s aphorisms are devoted solely to the refutation of others.
What is that [which is to be defined]? It is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and so forth; by what could one refute it? For from the affirmation or negation of something the world arises.

Of what nature is it? He says: it consists precisely of the four elements (*cāturbhautika*), because it is perceived as being composed of the four elements, earth and the rest, just as a house is understood to be made of bricks.

Or rather, he thinks: "In the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), by what could one establish or negate the earth and so forth, as well as the soul and so forth? For both affirmation and negation would be impossible.
He states this very point: "Because, from whatever affirmation or negation [is made], the world would consist of only the four elements; it would be composed solely of the four elements."

This is what is meant: by the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if one were to reject the elements (*bhūta*) just as one rejects the self (*ātman*) and so forth, it would result in the fallacy of universal emptiness (*sakala-śūnyatā*). Conversely, if one were to accept the self and so forth just as one accepts the elements, there would be no distinction from worldly convention (*vyavahāra*); for why then would [the world] consist of only the four elements, given that the opposite state [of non-elements] exists? Therefore, this [position of yours] does not surpass that of the Buddhist (*saugata*). Thus, he demonstrates [this] with the words "that this... and so forth; for in that [Buddhist system], perception or any other means of valid cognition is denied—since the non-sublation of the apprehension of those [objects], or any other defining characteristic of such [cognition], exists even in a dream.

Since it is impossible to know that [the cognition] has been produced by non-defective causes—because the defectiveness of the sense organ, whether it be transcendental (*atīndriya*) or otherwise, cannot be known through perception, and even if it were known, the aforementioned objection would not be resolved—and because if one were to again postulate that this [second cognition] too was produced by non-defective causes, the same objection and the same response would apply, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*);

furthermore, if its validity is understood from the validity of the cognition itself, there is a circularity (*anyonyasaṃśraya*). For instance, once its validity is established, the fact that it was produced by non-defective causes is established; and from that, the establishment of its validity follows.

Therefore, there is no external means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever; rather, the affirmation or negation of anything occurs by the power of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). Thus, for some, even according to this *Tattvopaplavagrantha*, its author Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa [holds that] there is no such result as heaven and so forth. And it has been said even by those who know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*): "The worldly path must be followed..."

Regarding worldly convention, "the fool and the wise man are alike," and so forth—surely, if [reality] is thus obscured, what relevance does this have to the principles (*tattva*)? Now, therefore, we shall explain the principles: earth, water, fire, and air are the principles; the designation of body, sense-faculties, and objects applies to their collection, and so forth. No; for that has a different purpose.
For what purpose? For the sake of reflection.

But what is it that is reflected here? The principles (tattvas) such as earth and so forth are well-known in the world; yet even these, when subjected to investigation, do not remain established—how much less others?
Thus, while the principles are indeed thus submerged in error, all worldly transactions are possible as long as they are not subjected to critical inquiry.
Page 125— *Tattvopaplava*.
This is cited from *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, page 69 and 74.
The Cārvāka [is the proponent] of the definition of the means of valid cognition regarding the earth and so forth, as well as living beings.
Or, regarding the validity of knowledge, it consists in the thorough cognition of its non-defectiveness, that is, its being produced by non-defective causes.

Furthermore, because it causes a fluctuation regarding reality, the "victorious host" might speak while relying on the Buddhist doctrine; to this he replies with the words "svasaṃvedane" and so forth.
"Svasaṃvedana" means the cognition or apprehension of itself by itself. By "upekṣayā," meaning by way of acceptance—if indeed [this were the case], then there would be dissatisfaction.

Such being the situation, that which is externally subverted and internally otherwise, the Buddhist doctrine itself has its scope eliminated; thus, it is called the "Cārvāka" system, wherein perception alone is said to be the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The connection is with the words "yadi nāma" (if indeed). In that regard, he states a speech intended as a derisive retort: "This is indeed well-spoken," because even what is poorly spoken is designated as "well-spoken"; and because of the departure from other systems [of thought] and the abandonment of one's own entire system, there is not even a trace of being well-spoken—this he indicates by the particle "eva" (indeed). Why is it poorly spoken? Because this is laughable. He says "svasaṃvedane" (in self-awareness), etc., anticipating that a Buddhist, perhaps out of partiality for his own side, might say so.
Here too, the word "api" (also/even) is to be understood;

therefore, the meaning is as follows: not only externally, but even in one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because of the perception of *apralāpa*—that is, the perception of *pralāpa* (nonsense) and *nihnava* (denial)—this [statement] is indeed well-said. This is the connection.
Having done what? He says: "having reached the absolute state of delusion" (*vibhramaikāntam upetya*).
Since this [error] has already been examined there as well, as if it were external, it is not examined here again.
