Now, it is true that even there, the perception of denial exists, because in this world consisting of the self born from many lifetimes, the occurrence of dispute cannot be prevented even there. However, although that denial is being perceived, it is excluded by reasoning (*yukti*); thus, the connection is that there is the perception of that very exclusion of the denial.
Nor is a non-contradictory affirmation the excluder of that [denial], for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is asked, "How can there be an absence of that? he says here: "Otherwise," and so forth.

"Otherwise" means by another way in which there is no contradiction; [the phrase] "due to mutual contradiction" refers to a conflict between them, and this depends upon the perception of that [contradiction].
For instance: if there were a contradiction between perception and negation, then when self-awareness exists or when it is absent, even the mention of self-awareness would be difficult to find.

Nor is it the case that there is coexistence in this way, nor is there any apprehension of contradiction; for perception— whether simultaneous or otherwise— is not contradictory to that [object], due to the same fault as in the case of the apprehension of an object.

Furthermore, how could contradiction even be understood as real within a false monism that is not "this" (i.e., not an object of experience)? Nor can it be known through inference, because [inference] is not admitted;
otherwise, there would truly be a contradiction with the thesis of self-cognizing direct perception (*svasaṃvedana-adhyakṣa*).

This is another explanation regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*): first of all, there is no exclusion of that [object] by means of self-awareness, because there is no contradiction between it and that [object]; otherwise, there would be a conflict with another means of knowledge—namely inference—in the manner of excluding it, since that [inference] perceives it.

For example: if its exclusion is by means of inference (*anumāna*), how can self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) alone be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? And how could that [self-cognition] exclude it by means of that [inference]? If it is argued that there is no fault because one resorts to inference in conventional practice (*vyavahāra*); then what is this so-called "conventional practice"? If it is argued that it is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of people regarding its existence even when the means of knowledge called inference does not exist; no, for in this case there is an absence of a means of knowledge.

It is not a matter of self-cognizing direct perception (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*); for therein one does not accept an absolute falsehood, since there is no denial of what is perceived. Nor is it established by itself as the basis for the establishment of another, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is it inference (*anumāna*); it is sheer audacity to claim that its establishment proceeds from that very thing which does not exist. Even if its establishment were by means of that which is conventionally established (*saṃvṛtisiddha*), it would be of the same nature; according to the maxim: "As is the Yakṣa, so is the offering."
The conventional usage based on self-cognition is indeed inference.
"As the fool, so the Yakṣa" (Pra-vārtikālaṅkāra, p.

293). But another says: "The absolute admission of error in self-awareness is not tenable on the basis of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for that [self-awareness] is not established through error."

If you argue that this is not correct because [the object] is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), etc., we say no; for in this case, the establishment of the external object would remain unavoidable. Lest there be a fault, one might then claim that perception is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even regarding the mere external elements such as earth and so forth. To this he says: "The arrangement of the four elements," etc.

The "arrangement" (*vyavasthā*) of the four elements—earth and the others—is their existence (*sthiti*) free from confusion (*saṅkara*) or intermixture (*vyatikara*). One ought to explain those very elements by their distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*), namely, through their different functions of supporting (*dhāraṇa*), moving (*īraṇa*), and flowing (*dravaṇa*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: likewise, another person, though being led by his own false attachment into the pit of calamity while perceiving himself to be alive, does not realize it.

To explain: just as the earth and other elements are mutually distinct throughout the three periods of time due to differences in their intrinsic natures such as solidity and so forth, so too is the self distinct from them—despite the rule of simultaneous perception—due to the difference in its nature as conscious and incorporeal; thus, the absolute delusion [of identity] is unestablished.
The statement "those very [qualities]" is redundant here;
for the earth, the characteristic is support; for air, motion; for water, fluidity; and for fire, heat—these are the characteristics derived from the primary elements.

Now, one might object: "As was previously stated, 'he ought to understand,' so too should it be said here, 'he ought to speak. Why then was it said, 'he ought to tell'? It is replied: "He tells" means he causes another to understand (*pratipādayati*). And that [other] who is to be caused to understand must be one who has already attained consciousness (*caitanya*); otherwise, stones and the like would have to be caused to understand, which they are not because they lack consciousness. If it is argued: "But how is consciousness established even in that which is intended as the object to be understood? Is it through direct perception (*adhyakṣata*)? No, for perception does not operate there [in the object].

An other [person] cannot perceive the pleasure, pain, and so forth of another; otherwise, there would be no negation of an omniscient being. [If you argue that] one perceives only consciousness (caitanya), how else could there be the cognition "he lives" from the sight of the body? For there can be no cognition of a qualified object when its qualifier is not apprehended, just as there is no cognition of a person with a staff when the staff is not apprehended—if this is your claim, we say: no. Because consciousness is non-different from pleasure and so forth, it is not logical to apprehend consciousness—which is non-different from them—while pleasure and so forth are not apprehended. Otherwise, even when the lump [of clay] and so forth are not apprehended, there would be an apprehension of the substance "clay."
The Śaiva [tradition] holds that [the self] is opposed to consciousness in its transcendent state.

If it is argued: "Just as when the staff is not perceived, the person holding the staff is not perceived, so too when the modes (paryāyas) such as 'staying in a lump' are not perceived, why should there not be a perception of the substance (dravya)—just as in your own system, even when the moment-to-moment transformation is not perceived, there is a perception of the substance, or as at a distance, even when the specific qualities are not perceived, there is a perception of pure existence (sanmātra)"? We say: no; because that transformation is not perceptible to ordinary persons.

If it is argued that the non-perception of their specific qualities is due to extreme distance, whereas pleasure and so forth are not like this because they are the opposite [of being distant], and that these [pleasures] have self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as their sole nature—then from what [source] is this known? If it is from their non-perception by a sense organ, then from what is this [non-perception] known?
Because there is doubt regarding pleasure and so forth in another person, that [doubt] applies equally to consciousness (*caitanya*) as well.

If, due to distance, the pleasure and other states of another are not perceived by the sense organ, then the experience of pleasure and so forth would occur upon mutual contact; however, since pleasure and the like are not experienced when they enter within the body, this would lead to the undesirable consequence [of such experience] even in the case of pure consciousness. Alternatively, the experience would have to occur through something entering into that [consciousness].

Therefore, according to the Jaina school, there is no apprehension of that [soul] through perception; rather, the cognition "this one lives" arises because the specific form of the body is not seen, just as the cognition of fire arises in a certain place from seeing smoke. This is intended to demonstrate that [the soul] is established by means of inference, thereby refuting [the claim that it is] a separate means of valid cognition.
Because the transformation of form through successive prior and subsequent states is extremely rapid,
by a person who effects entry into another's body...

If, on the other hand, it is argued that its establishment cannot be stated by means of its own differentiation, to that he replies: otherwise, because of the consequence of infinite regress through that mode of stating it even in the absence of such [differentiation], there would follow the non-existence of the four elements due to their persistence;
for in the absence of a difference in defining characteristics, there can be no determination of a difference in the things defined.
Or it should be stated that [the distinction] arises from its being other than that reality, because otherwise it would follow that [the two] are identical.
If it is argued, "In that case, one ought to explain the distinction based on their difference," the author replies here: "And not... and so forth.

That is to say, it is certainly not the case that the status of being the speaker of the arrangement of the four elements is thus justified or established by perception acting as the instrument, in the manner of a distinction in characteristics.

Why is this so? He says: because of the knowledge of the characteristics—namely, the nature of *dhāraṇā* and so forth—not only of those [elements] such as earth that are perceptible, but also of those that are imperceptible;

or else, because at the time of describing their systematic arrangement through perceptible differences in characteristics, they are subsequently seen to possess those same characteristics even when they are imperceptible.
Nor is it logical that such [an object] is [established] by perception;

for it cannot be said that smoke, when perceived in another location and so forth as being preceded by fire (*dhūmadhvaja*), has its status thus determined by a previous perception, because even imperceptible things are [known] in that form through inference (*aṅganāt*). Why is this so? He says: "Because of the comprehension—that is, the ascertainment—of the principles (*tattva*) such as earth and the rest, in their entirety and totality; otherwise, if it were not so, they would be untenable even in the case of imperceptible things due to the absence of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This is the connection [of the sentence].
Because the existence of the four elements is accepted,
even those that are imperceptible [are established].
Or rather, [the objection is raised]: "How is it that this is so, given that even things beyond the senses are seen in such a way? To this he says: "In their entirety," and so forth.

This is because there is no other way for the reality of the nature of earth and the other elements to be apprehended—either as "this" or as "not this"—than through repeated perception; otherwise, their non-appearance in that very same manner would be untenable.

That being the case, it is difficult to establish the position that the earth and other elements do not possess the nature of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), nor the nature of consciousness that persists into the next world, nor the nature of specific pleasure, cognition, and so forth.

Alternatively, the sentence beginning with "in its entirety" (*sākalyena*) should be explained in connection with the following verse: because the realization of the reality (*tattva*) of earth and the other elements—which consists of the nature of cause and effect such as satisfaction and so forth—is otherwise impossible, that is, impossible through any other mode than the absence of internal knowledge (*ādhyātmikajñāna*), [it follows] that internal knowledge exists; this is the ellipsis. Since internal knowledge is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the weight of the elements is real;
whether it be real or unreal, let it be so, for the elements are fivefold. (13)

Having established the distinction between the intrinsic natures of earth and so forth, how can one who rejects the distinction between the intrinsic natures of cognitions—such as the various forms of joy, sorrow, and so on, which are directly perceived within—be considered a person of discernment? Furthermore, if direct perception of real entities were a distinct principle, the enumeration [of principles] would be contradicted;
for if one were to conceive of them as being included within consciousness, there would be only a single principle.

For instance: when, due to some particular instance of earth or other [element], the cessation of suffering such as hunger is once perceived, and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established—that "whatever is of this kind is the cause of the cessation of that [suffering] for a specific living being after such a duration of time"—then, upon seeing that same thing or something similar, there arises a recollection of the relationship, followed by recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), reflection (*cintā*), and finally activity toward the object being seen, based on the comprehension of its nature as the cause of that [cessation]. This is generally the case;
as it was said in this very work: "Sensory cognition... (Siddhiviniścaya 1.27), and so forth.

And this [process] is not possible for earth and the other elements, because we observe that a preceding cognition transforms into the form of a succeeding cognition, just as a lump of clay transforms into the form of a pillar;
let that be so, let it remain—there is no need for further deliberation.
Why? He says: "Because it is directly perceived."

Indeed, the reality that is directly perceived as being augmented by the qualities and modes (guṇaparyāya) impossible for earth and the other elements cannot be subject to the investigation of whether it is distinct from earth and the others or otherwise; for that consequence would apply to those [elements] themselves in relation to one another.
What, then, is to be investigated? He says: "having the elements as its object," etc.;
the meaning is that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is knowledge having earth and the other elements as its object, i.e., sensory cognition.
[The text says: "Food and so forth are the preventers of the affliction of hunger and so on.

Now, one might object: "Is this not already prevented by the removal of that [affliction] through spiritual knowledge (*ādhyātmika-jñāna*)? Why then is this stated separately? True; nevertheless, the distinction is that what was previously stated in a general sense is here stated in a specific sense.
In this regard, there are several views held by others: one is that it (the world) has the nature of the elements (*bhūta*);
another is that it is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of those [elements];
yet another is that it is a reality distinct from them, like water in a mirage; and the final view is that it is a reality [in its own right].

Because it is an effect of that [perception], it is included within that very category; thus, there is no need for multiple separate statements regarding it. If the elements such as earth and so forth are of the nature of elements, and if knowledge whose object is the elements were to be considered perception, then let it be sufficient with that—why [is this said]? He says: because it would be non-existent (*abhūta*), since it would possess a non-existent nature (*abhūtasvabhāva*).

For all beings do not perceive themselves as having the nature of consciousness, because that would entail the absurd consequence that the entire world consists of living organisms; furthermore, the hypothesis that there is some manifestation or disappearance of consciousness in certain cases is even more wretched, as it would make no distinction from the Sāṃkhya view. Thus, for the Cārvāka, the arrangement of the elements must be of the very nature of the elements themselves.
Sensory cognition exists only in the real,
according to the Sāṃkhya school's conception.

Likewise, if it is argued that this [unreal thing] has a transformation consisting of a slightly real form because it possesses a nature that undergoes transformation in some way, then let that too be unreal; for in that case, it would not possess a real form in any way whatsoever, due to the contradiction between the insentient and the transformation into the sentient. Furthermore, if that which is unreal were different from the real, it would be non-existent by its own nature, like the water in a mirage.
The word "if" (cet) should also be connected here;
let that be so,
for it has been stated that, consequently, there is neither an affirmation nor a negation of anything.
If that which has arisen from the unreal form is the ultimate reality, then let it be the fifth principle (*tattva*); this is the implied conclusion,
because there is no other possible way for that which exists to be other than this— so he thinks.

Likewise, there is this other [objection]: if it is argued that the non-existent (abhūta) arises from the existent (bhūta) because the effect is distinct from its manifest cause, like a cloth from its threads; even so, if it is existent in the form of an element (bhūtarūpa), then because it is included therein as an effect—just as a cloth is in the earth—let this also be considered:
everything would be non-existent (abhūta), devoid of elements, because there would be no fixed order of elements due to their mutual inclusion within the relationship of cause and effect.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that there is no fault because fire and so forth arise from wood and the like which already contain fire within them, he replies: "Let there be a fifth principle, because of the existence of consciousness within earth and the rest"—this is the intended meaning of the explanation; however, fire does not arise from wooden material such as wood, nor does earthen pearl and the like arise from water.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Earth, etc.

Having accepted through cognition the difference in nature—that is, the diversity of essential form—of earth and so forth, one accepts the difference in nature of cognitions belonging to distinct mental continua, that is, their diversity of form. The mention of "cognition" (*vijñapti*) is for the purpose of negating the [permanent] Self (*ātman*) of the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas. The mention of "difference in nature" is for the purpose of refuting all forms of non-dualism (*advaita*).
Of what kind is this? He says: "Joy," and so forth.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "Internally," and so forth.
By this, he shows [the self] to be like a lamp [inside] a house from the body;

because he rejects—that is, refutes—that [the self] is an object of direct perception through one's own reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), how could one be a discerning person? Moreover, with the words "And furthermore" (*api ca*) and so forth, he states another objection right here: if sensory cognition whose object is the elements (*bhūta*)—such as earth and the rest—is a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) from those elements, namely earth and so on, then the enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) that there are exactly four principles (*tattva*) would be contradicted.

He shows their distinctness with this further explanation: "If it is argued that *tattva* (the principle) is distinct because it is internal as the effect of earth and the other elements"; to this he replies: if one were to conceive of consciousness—which is characterized by the apprehension of self and others and consists of the sentience of direct perception of the elements—as being included within those very elements due to its having their nature, then *tattva* would be only one, and its fourfold division would be lost because of their mutual inclusion.

Now, if it is argued that this is not so because earth and the other elements appear as mutually distinct, then [we reply]: since cognitions appear in exactly that way as being distinct from one another, otherwise the world would consist merely of living beings—lest even the subject under discussion (the fourfold nature) be lost. Thus, there is no loss of the fourfold character by virtue of their mutual distinction.

If, however, there is no inclusion therein because of having that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather because of being a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of it, he says in response: "It would be a synonym," and so forth; [this refers to] among the primary elements (*bhūta*), by way of being a synonym for the primary elements.
There may indeed be a transformation of earth and so forth into water and so forth; however, the conscious cannot [become] the unconscious, nor can the unconscious [become] the conscious.

(14) The subtle substance of *pudgala*, having undergone transformations such as hardness and so on, receives the designations of "earth" and so forth; yet it is observed to transform extensively into other states. For example, the moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*), which is of the nature of earth, melts at the rays of the moon; likewise, semen and blood undergo a transformation of form and so on until they reach the state of ash or clay, and the same applies to pearls and other such things.
Wood and the like become fire through contact with a forest fire and so forth;
however, the conscious does not undergo transformation by abandoning consciousness, nor is the unconscious observed becoming conscious.

Thus, how can this "Beloved of the Gods" (Devānāmpriya)—who unifies the two principles of the conscious and the non-conscious, and who establishes the substance of the *pudgala* as fourfold through the divisions of earth and so on—be considered sound-minded? His intellect is perverted, for he utterly disregards direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

First, regarding this present life, the initial and final minds of living beings stand in the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*) with respect to other intervening minds, because they are of the nature of mind; just like the intermediate mind.

Furthermore, there is indeed a *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability) here: because a newborn infant exhibits a continuity of memory from previous practice and manifests fear and so forth, the objection regarding deviation—namely, that [the first mind] is like a flame preceded by another flame in the case of a traveler’s fire—is refuted, since in that case there is a contradiction with its being preceded by a material cause of fire.

Since a conscious being, transforming by its very nature as consciousness, does not depend on any other cause, its manifestation occurs spontaneously and without delay; because it is not caused by external conditions, unlike the insentient, the second [moment] must necessarily follow. If, however, the final moment lacks the power to become the subsequent [moment], it would prove its own non-substantiality—that is, the absence of a continuity of its own material cause—since a real entity is defined by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
To say that it does not produce its effect is contradictory;
for while the occasional nature of dissimilar effects produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is well-established, this is not the case for the subsequent state of the entity itself.
Furthermore, this observation of destruction at the end is unproven, and the observation of persistence in the middle would also establish stability, as there is no deviation from this fact.

If the conscious were to evolve into an unconscious form, as in the case of falling asleep and waking up, then since the state after death (pretyabhāva) would be established, how could this not be irreproachable? [To this we reply: It is utterly illogical to conceive of a confusion or a mixing between the two natures—consciousness and its opposite—which are established by their own inherent nature, for that would involve abandoning what is observed and imagining what is unobserved. Furthermore, the opponent [who argues] that "living beings are like bubbles in water" and "consciousness is like the power of intoxication," having seen bitterness in the *arka* plant, applies it to molasses.

If, despite the specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*) and other distinctions of representation (*vijñapti*), the existence, producedness, and so forth of [mental states] were to have the nature of the primary elements (*bhūta-svabhāvatva*)—on the analogy of the power of intoxication and the like—then for that very reason, another [opponent] could likewise establish that even the primary elements do not transcend being transformations of intellect and consciousness (*buddhi-caitanya-vivarta*), just as pleasure and so forth are self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*). Thus, through this "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) fallacy, one would overstep the established order of means and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇa-prameya-vyavasthā*) due to a false dogmatic adherence.

Comparison: "Living beings are like water bubbles; for just as bubbles, devoid of any regulating unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), arise from the ocean and so forth by the power of the inherent capacity of things and thus come to possess various designations, so too do living beings come to possess the variety of pleasure and pain."—*Nyāyakumuda*, p.
342. "Consciousness is like the power of intoxication."—*Nyāyakumuda*, p. 342;
*Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkara-Bhāṣya* 3.3.54.
3.53 Nyāyakaṇikā, p. 437.
"Consciousness is like the power of intoxication"—Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, Prastāvanā, p. 93; Prakaraṇapañcikā, p.
146. For comparison: "Just as [intoxication arises] from the combination of the ingredients of liquor, so does the knower [arise] from the combination of the elements"—Yuktyanuśāsana, verse 35.

The essential point here is as follows: if consciousness were included within [the categories] by virtue of being a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the elements, something undesirable would be established and something desirable would not be established.

First, he demonstrates the establishment of the undesirable: "Whose transformation (*paryāya*) or evolution (*pariṇāma*) could there be, and what [could it be]? To this he says: "Of earth and so forth, water and so forth."
He will explain the meaning of this himself in the commentary (*vṛtti*), so it is not stated here;

the sense is that [the opponent’s] intention—that water and the other elements are included within earth and the rest—is thus shown to be unestablished. Demonstrating this lack of proof, he says: "In that way," and so forth.

In the same manner as the earth and so forth have water and so forth as their modifications (*paryāya*)—according to the mode of following positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—likewise, consciousness (*cetana*), such as apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth, is not at all a modification of the insentient (*acetana*), which is devoid of the nature of consciousness, nor is the insentient earth and so forth a modification of the sentient; such is the connection [of the terms].
By this, it is established that "all this is indeed the Self" (*ātmaivedaṃ sarvam*). (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25)

This and other such [objections] are also refuted, because one observes the arising of *īhā* from *avagraha*, of *avāya* from that, of *dhāraṇā* from that, and then of memory (*smṛti*), recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), this [inference], and reasoning (*tarka*) from that;
for the transformation of one thing cannot belong to another, as that would lead to a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*). This is what is intended.
Regarding these beings, the author Akalaṅkadeva [states] in his own commentary (svopajña-ṭīkā):

It might be thought: "If the unconscious does not belong to the conscious, or the conscious to the unconscious, how can there be the state of sleep following the waking state, and from that, the state of awakening, since it is then that the occurrence of *avagraha* (perception) and so forth is possible? Regarding this, the resolution offered by some is: "In that state, there exists non-conceptual vision (*darśana*), and from that comes awakening. For others, it is: "That [awakening] arises from waking-consciousness. For yet others, it is: "From the Self devoid of cognition."
The latter alternative [that memory belongs to something other than cognition] is not possible as a solution.

For even if it is granted that those elements which constitute effects are momentary—and thus memory, recognition, and so forth would not be possible [if they belonged to them]—nevertheless, such phenomena are possible because they belong to their causes, the primary elements (*bhūta*), which are eternal. Even if their forms and other qualities are not perceptible to those like us, they are nonetheless perceptible to Buddhas and others, despite being dependent upon those [elements]; just as sound, though dependent on space, is perceptible even though the "supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattva*) and other qualities of space are imperceptible.
If it is argued that there is no transformation for that which is insentient,
then [we reply] because of the perception of non-conceptuality.
The awakening of Prajñākaragupta and others, and that of the Naiyāyikas and others.
The meaning is that consciousness [does not arise] from the elements because they are insentient, like [inanimate] objects;
this refers to the elements in their form as effects.
The meaning is "of the atoms which are the causal nature of the elements";
[it refers to] the visible forms and so forth residing in the atoms that constitute the causal nature of the elements, even though they are dependent upon those elements.

As for the one who maintains that [the intellect] is supported by space, he argues that if the intellect were supported by the body, then because the body is momentary, there would be no recognition of it in another place and so forth. This might indeed be the case if the cause were not conjoined with that which is conjoined with the effect; but this is not so, because we observe the conjunction of the threads with that which is conjoined with the cloth, and because the intermediate body serves as the cause of awakening [of the intellect], since [the intellect] exists when that [body] exists and is absent when it is absent.
It does not belong to the waking mind, because that [mind] exists only when the former is absent;

nevertheless, if that [mind] were its cause, then a widow’s pregnancy would result from her long-deceased husband rather than from a man currently present, and thus she would not be subject to punishment for the body.
The waking consciousness is the cause of awakening for the awakened consciousness.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction in the waking mind imitating [the state of] the body when the latter is the cause of awakening—that too is easily resolved; for since imitation can occur even from the cause of a cause, there is no contradiction.

To explain: that body is the cause of the mind, just as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are; from that [body], another body arises again, just as the vital breaths arise from the previous one; the vital breaths represent the final stage, and from that, an awakening corresponding to them occurs, like a son resembling his father.

For example, from the father’s emission of semen and so forth, through a specific transformation thereof, there arises a body for the offspring that conforms to the father; or alternatively, the body is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of consciousness, while the mind is its cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). Furthermore, the effect of another [cause] conforms to its cooperative cause; otherwise, how could cognition conform to its object? Nor is it a valid answer to ask how something occurring at a different time can be a cooperative cause, for others accept that even for one bitten by a snake and rendered unconscious, the previously conscious mind remains a cooperative cause for the mantra and other factors, despite their temporal difference.

Furthermore, the first [alternative] is simply not considered; for if one admits that consciousness is momentary even during sleep and so forth, one must state its distinction from waking. If it is argued that this is because, in that state, there would be no superimposition (samāropa) such as "momentary destruction" and so on—which are established by perception and serve as causes for activity and the like—just as in death, we reply: no, because those [causes] are absent there;
otherwise, if they were perceived, there could be no such thing as a state of deep sleep.
However, that non-perception does not refute these conceptual constructions (kalpanā), as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 127, and elsewhere.
Furthermore, if you claim that the specific feature [of perception] is the absence of certainty (*niścaya*), that too is not tenable. Let there simply be that absence;

why would the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) and so forth—which were experienced—be considered unexperienced, such that the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding them would not occur? If you argue that what was experienced by non-conceptual [perception] is equivalent to what was unexperienced, then the state of deep sleep and the like, in which all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn, would not differ from other states; thus, it would be the same elsewhere as it is there.
The waking mind indeed exists,
because [the objects] arise and pass away without being communicated [to it], such that even though they are real, they would remain unperceived; this is the remainder of the sense.
Just as in sleep and other states,
even when one remains with the inner self stilled by withdrawing all thought from every side,
the cognition produced by the eye perceives form; that is sensory perception.
As it is said in the *Pravacanasāra* (2.124): "It floats [there]";

for even though conceptual constructions such as "blue" and so forth exist there, there is no awareness of them from that [state], because the conscious is not the object of the conscious, nor is the unconscious a synonym for it. If you argue that this is not tenable—on the grounds that "the conscious is certainly not [the object] of the unconscious," and so forth—we reply as follows: *Pravacanasāra* 2.124: "It floats there. Even though conceptual constructions such as blue and so forth exist there, there is no awareness of them from that state, because the conscious is not the object of the conscious, nor is the unconscious a synonym for it. If you argue that this is not tenable—on the grounds that "the conscious is certainly not [the object] of the unconscious," and so forth—we reply as follows:
Because we always accept the consciousness of both determination and its opposite,
this fault does not arise for us as it does for the exclusively Buddhist position; rather, since awakening could not otherwise occur, it is inferred to exist in the interval.
Why do the Jains not hold that even non-conceptual consciousness is always self-evident?
Otherwise, how could this relationship of cause and effect be restricted?
It would follow that it is either causeless, caused by something else, or caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

If consciousness during sleep is unperceived and thus awakening is without a cause, then clouds and the like would likewise be without a cause since they too are unperceived in their material substratum; consequently, everything that is occasional might be suspected of being causeless.

Or, if [awakening] has another cause, then clouds and the like must also have a cause of a different kind; thus, the established order of the four elements would be undermined, because we observe that things arise only from earth and the other [elements] of their own kind. Furthermore, even if it were unseen, one could infer that a layer of water and so forth has a cause of its own kind.
If it is argued that, like awakening, [the world] is without cause—
that is, causeless—
then earth and the other elements themselves must be its cause.

By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: "Just as from non-conceptual sleep there arises conceptual waking, so too from the insentient there arises the sentient"; for how so? Because the same consequence would apply elsewhere, for it could indeed be said: "Just as from subtle elements such as earth there is the state of those gross elements, so too from water and the rest there might be the state of earth and the rest," and thus earth and the others would not be distinct principles (*tattvāntara*).

[Objection: But just as the earth and other elements are of different classes from the self (*ātman*), how can the earth and so forth be synonymous with water and the rest? To this, he says: "The substance *pudgala*, etc."—the substance possessing color, taste, smell, and touch is the *pudgala* substance. What would it be? He says: it would bear the designations of earth and so forth; this is the ellipsis.
Regarding this, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), water and so forth are included.
Having done what? He says: having attained—that is, reached—what? Having attained the transformation of the vowels (*svaravivarta*), [the earth] comes to possess the designation "earth."
This should be applied elsewhere as well;

what is meant is this: earth and the other elements are not of different classes, because they are modifications (*paryāya*) of a single substance, just like a lump of clay and so forth, and thus [they are] exactly like the self (*ātman*).
Pudgalas possess touch, taste, smell, and color.
— Tattvārthasūtra 5.23

If it is asked: "Is there something other than the perceived earth and so forth that bears that designation? We say: No; for just as with a cloth, since the gross is invariably preceded by the subtle, the existence of threads is established.

Even so, let there be an inference of a cause of such a nature for the earth itself, which possesses its own color, taste, smell, and touch; however, if it is argued that for water, fire, and air—which respectively lack smell, taste, and color—one must instead infer another corresponding cause, we reply: No; because even in those cases, since they possess touch, the inference of smell and the rest is not refuted.
What, then, is that? He says: "Furthermore, otherwise," and so forth.
Furthermore, subsequently, the substance *pudgala* is observed to transform extensively in another way—that is, in a manner distinct from earth and the other elements.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning with "just as."

The word "yathā" (just as) is used here to illustrate an example. [An objection is raised: "How is it that the moonstone, which by its hardness has the nature of earth, becomes water? To this he says: It is not the stone itself that liquefies, because that is not observed; rather, some say it is the lunar rays, which consist of water, that come into contact with it.

What fault is there in their rapid movement? If you say it is "non-perception," no; for even though the parts of a fragrant substance move in all directions at all times, they are perceived in exactly that same quantity. Why, then, would the rays of that [jewel] not also be non-perceptible? As for the distinction that "the successive arising of other [moments] belongs to the series and not to that jewel"—by what is this distinction established? [The opponent asks: Semen and blood are liquid in form; through the sequence of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth, they undergo transformation into a female body and so on.
What kind of element is this? To this he says: "Ashes," and so forth.

In the compound *bhasmamṛttikayoḥ*, a *dvandva* has been formed; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), a *bahuvrīhi* is implied, where the word "etc. includes lumps (*piṇḍa*) and so forth. Furthermore, by the word "limit" (*paryanta*), that same [category] is to be enjoined;

likewise, by that very method of application of specialized medicinal substances and the like, [substances such as] pearls (*muktāphala*) and so forth are included, while by the word "etc. snow (*hima*) and the like are encompassed. The term "melts" (*dravati*) is understood to follow.
Alternatively, the connection is that the substance of the *pudgala*, having attained a transformation of moisture (*snehavivarta*), undergoes a modification into pearls and the like.
Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the transformation of *statakā* and so forth into pills and the like is included;
and by the word "etc. in the phrase "wood etc.," grass and so forth are meant, which become like fire. Why? To this he says: "the fire-drill" (*araṇi*), and so forth.
From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [it follows] that due to the conjunction with specific substances and so forth, it is established: the substance *pudgala*, and so on;
water, fire, wind, and the rest, being endowed with smell, taste, and color, possess touch, just like earth.
Air, first of all, possesses color and other qualities because it possesses touch, like a jar and so forth...
Water possesses odor because it possesses touch, like earth;
fire likewise possesses taste and odor because it possesses color.
— Sāṃkhyasūtra 5.3:
[This refers to] the moonbeam.

If it is argued that new rays of light are produced every moment, then let the gem also be produced as something entirely new in each instance—this being a case of a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).

In that case, just like that, it would be the conscious spirit (*puruṣa-cetana*) that transforms in such a way, and not the substance of the person (*pudgala-dravya*). To this, he replies: "Not again"—meaning it is certainly not the case that the conscious Self, which is Brahman, undergoes transformation into the form of earth and so forth by abandoning its nature as consciousness, which is the state of illuminating both itself and others.

This is what is meant: just as the substance *pudgala* undergoes transformation into the form of earth and so forth because the continuity (*anvaya*) of those forms and qualities is perceived therein, if the *puruṣa* were likewise to undergo transformation into that form, then the continuity of consciousness (*caitanya*) would be perceived there; but since it is not so, [the opponent asks: "then perhaps the insentient transforms into the form of the sentient? To this, he replies: "If the insentient earth and so forth were to become sentient, it would be observed as such."
The word "not" (na) is understood from the previous context.

By the phrase "that is perceived," he shows this: if the insentient were transformative and the sentient were its transformation, then that [sentient nature] would be perceived as persisting through the form [of the insentient];
however, that is not the case, because there is the manifestation of the internal sentient principle which is devoid of form and the like.

Nor is it better to assume that color and the other qualities do not manifest therein; for if one assumes that the characteristics of the elements do not manifest within one another, then it would be illogical to explain their distinction based on those characteristics when they exist as earth and so forth within earth and the other elements.
In each and every conscious being, there is the establishment of the four elements, beginning with earth.
Concluding [the argument], he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore this very selfhood (*svatva*), characterized as the substance of the *pudgala*, being endowed with the number one, is established in four ways—that is, by four modes.
By what? He says: "By the division of earth and the other [elements]. How is it established? "Abiding in itself" (*svasthaḥ*); the meaning is that it is possessed by the elements (*bhūtagṛhīta*).
Why? He says: because his intellect is perverted (*viparyasta-buddhi*).
Just as one who establishes the single moon as being two possesses such a kind of intellect, so too does this person.

If it is asked, "But since the mental states of others are difficult to discern, how is it known that he possesses such a kind of intellect?"—to this he replies: "O you who are dear to the gods" (*devānāṃ-priya*), and so forth.

Since he is beloved by the gods who are fools, he is not identical with that [reality] merely by virtue of his existence, for that would lead to an over-extension; rather, because he teaches the absence of protection from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because their minds have been nurtured on pleasure, they do not enter into the domain of the means of valid cognition. Therefore, he is understood to possess such a notion.
If it is asked, "From where is his teaching of such a reality also known?", the author says here: "Of perception," and so forth.

Is he unwell because he is overstepping the bounds of either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or its object (*prameya*), and presenting them in a completely different way? No; thus he says: "Unifying the reality of the sentient and the insentient.
How so? "Both," meaning both [categories] remain as multiple [entities], just as in the previous case.
The Cārvāka possesses a distorted intellect;
he is one of distorted intellect.

For the Cārvāka, since it has been established through the complete presentation of immediate subverting arguments against the contrary—that "only that which is sentient becomes sentient during the intermediate state"—he states the following to demonstrate what is thereby proven: "Of living beings in this life," and so forth.
"Living beings" (prāṇinaḥ) refers to those who possess the ten vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) as enumerated in the scriptures. Of them...

By this, he demonstrates that all related initial and final moments of consciousness (*citta*), being taken as the subjects (*dharmin*) of the inference, are established by means of inference due to the existence of [their] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; otherwise, since they would not be apprehended by perception, one might suspect that the reason (*hetu*) in the inference would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Nor is it intended here to prove those very minds of the self (*ātman*) themselves in that manner, because of the plural designation "minds" (*cittāni*);
furthermore, the occurrence of many minds at the beginning and end is not possible within a single self.

To this, the following is said: the statement "of living beings" (*prāṇinām*) is for the purpose of making known that the beginning and end minds of all sentient beings are to be delimited by [the mind] itself.

Even so, since those beings are without beginning or end, a beginning and end mind are impossible for them; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). For that which has no preceding mind would be the "beginning," and that which has no subsequent [mind] would be the "end"; and this is not logical if the continuity of living beings is without beginning. To this, he says: the word "here" (*iha*) refers specifically to this present birth, while the repetition [of the word] is intended to demonstrate the sequence of the means [of proof] even regarding previous births.
In what manner are those initial and final moments of consciousness? To this he says: "In consciousness," and so forth;
those for which another moment of consciousness exists as their material cause (upādāna) and effect (upādeya) are described in that way.
The word *bhūta* is connected with each [term];

therefore, this is the meaning: the initial moments of consciousness (*ādicitta*) are those that constitute the material cause (*upādāna*) for subsequent moments of consciousness, while the final moments of consciousness (*antyacitta*) are those that are the effects (*upādeya*) produced by other moments of consciousness—or rather, it should be understood as "those which constitute the relationship of material cause and effect between one moment of consciousness and another."

For instance, the initial moments of consciousness are the effects (*upādeya*) of the interval between the death-moment of a previous existence and [the next], while the final moments of consciousness are the causes of appropriation (*upādāna*) for the first moment of consciousness of a future existence.

Even so, it should be stated that "moments of consciousness are related as cause and effect of appropriation"; what is the purpose of using the word *antara* (interval), since the distinction is already established by the very statement that they stand in the relation of appropriator and appropriated? Otherwise, it would be untenable. If it is argued that this is like [the case of] a single self (*ekātman*), we say no; for such a formulation is used precisely to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) for the Sāṃkhya opponent.

For the Sāṃkhya, who maintains the absolute non-difference between cause and effect in all cases, might think that the argument "because they are the material cause (upādāna) and the product (upādeya) of the mind" is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā). Why? Because those [elements] are of such a nature. To this he says: "Because they are of the nature of consciousness (cittatvāt). Some hold that since the particular (viśeṣa) is the probandum (sādhya) and the universal (sāmānya) is the probans (sādhana), the reason is not unestablished as being a part of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñārthaikadeśāsiddha). Others hold that even if there is this relationship of probandum and probans between two particulars or two universals, this fault does not apply.
Otherwise, [the fallacy] would also occur in cases such as "sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of sound" (śabdatva).
To show an example for this, he says "just as," etc.;
the meaning is "just as the middle mind."

The five vitalities of the senses, the three vitalities of strength consisting of mind, speech, and body, and the vitalities of inhalation, exhalation, and life-span— these constitute the ten vitalities. — *Gommaṭasāra Jīvakāṇḍa*, Gāthā 129.
The beginning and the end of the initial and final moments of consciousness are birth.
The statement "it must be said thus" appears meaningless,

because in the absence of difference, the relationship between material cause and effect is impossible, and because a universal must reside in its particulars; furthermore, the fault of total non-continuity (niranvaya-doṣa) does not apply either.

But surely, since the subject (*dharmin*) is a particular cognition and the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is the universal, there is no fallacy of being a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*)—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.
387; *Hetubinduṭīkāloka*, p. 396.
Prameyaratnākara, p. 41–42.

[Objection: Is it not the case that for a Jaina, a reason is not made known by a mere example—as in [the argument] "A diamond is scratchable by iron because it is earthy, like wood"—but rather by *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of being otherwise)? And since that [impossibility] exists here, he says: "In this case," and so forth. Here, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) refers to excellence; "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means in the manner of the absence of the probandum; "impossibility" (*anupapatti*) means non-occurrence. By the use of the particle (*eva*), he asserts that there is not even the slightest possibility of its [the probandum's] occurrence.
Why? He says: "His birth," and so forth.
[The child] is born indeed from the very beginning, or even prior to that, due to the continuity—meaning the non-interruption—of the memory of drinking from the breast and so on in a previous life.

This is what is meant: if the reality of the final moment of consciousness at death were not invariably connected to the awakening of the subsequent birth and so on, then, in the absence of the impressions deposited therein, there would be no continuity of memory for one who has been born.

If it is argued: "How can another person, who is merely a human being like oneself, understand [the state of mind], given that the mental fluctuations of others are difficult to trace? To this, he replies: "Through fear and so forth," etc.

This means: because of the perception—that is, the ascertainment—of fear and other states such as desire through facial distortions and the like. Otherwise, we might imagine an absence of perception regarding specific mental fluctuations of another;
but this is not the case. Therefore, from facial distortions and so forth, there is the perception of fear and the like, and from that, the perception of its cause (the underlying emotion).
The logical reason (*hetu*) is characterized by "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*);
this is illustrated by the comparison with an infant born on that very day, who, due to the continuity of memories from previous practice, experiences joy, fear, and sorrow.
— Nyāyasūtra 3.1.19

Even if there were a continuity of memory (*smṛtyanubandha*) during existence, the objection that the logical reason in the statement "because of the continuity of memory practiced in a previous life" is unestablished in its essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) is thereby refuted.

[Objection: "Granted that in the case of a middle consciousness, consciousness-ness is observed to be accompanied by the property of being produced by another consciousness; nevertheless, this is not tenable for the initial and final consciousnesses. Otherwise, since a fire is seen to be preceded by a flame, one might infer that even the fire of a traveler's camp is likewise preceded by a previous fire because it possesses that same nature.
If you argue that there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in other cases as well, [the author] replies here with the words beginning 'of the traveler's fire' (*pathikāgneḥ*).

By this [statement], the word "this" (*ayam*)—because it is placed at the end—is to be understood as following immediately after "like the fire of a [previous] fire" (*pratyagnivat*), and should be read in its proper place.

The meaning of this is as follows: "of the traveler's fire" (*pathikāgneḥ*) refers to the fire belonging to a traveler; the mention of "traveler" is intended to indicate that its status as such is remote due to the traveler's lack of permanence, or rather, to indicate the possibility of its being preceded by another flame or otherwise. For although it is possible for his fire to have been preceded by another flame—which is the probandum (sādhya)—the reason (*hetu*) here should be understood as "because it is a traveler's fire. He states an illustration: "like a fire facing [another]," (*pratyagnivat*).

A certain traveler, afflicted by cold, having kindled a fire either from the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇi*) or from elsewhere, became free from cold and departed for some other place. Then, another person who considers himself a scholar arrived at that very spot, kindled a counter-fire (*pratyagni*) from that [original] fire, and formulated an inference: "The traveler’s fire was preceded by another flame, because it is a fire, like the counter-fire;

yet this is not the case [for the traveler’s fire]. Thus, the objection regarding the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of your inference has been refuted by this subsequent passage, because the definition of a valid reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) applies to the subject at hand, whereas its opposite applies elsewhere.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "The cause of fire," and so forth.

The cause of fire is the substance *pudgala*, as described immediately prior; because there is no contradiction in its being preceded by that [substance] in the case of the fire on the traveler's path—due to the absence of opposition—it does not have another flame as its antecedent. [The opponent objects: "But surely, according to the principle stated regarding consciousness, there is no contradiction in its being preceded by that [substance]."
The second fire produced from fire is preceded by flames,
because it is fire.
This is for the purpose of making known that it is preceded by the fire of the traveler,
because the traveler possesses the nature of fire.

Then, let the minds of travelers and others everywhere and at all times be preceded by those [virtuous] thoughts, for they surely accomplish what is desired. [Objection: But surely the final mind at the moment of death [is not so established], due to a lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[Reply: In that case, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) belonging to one who perceives only the proximate part is incapable of performing such an extensive function, because it arises through the power of its immediately present object.

If it is argued that there is no inference [of consciousness] because of the absence of a probans (*liṅga*), since its non-existence follows from the absence of a mark, and furthermore that the existence of "cittatva" (the nature of mind) cannot serve as a probans because it is unestablished; we say: no. For would that [probans] be an effect, a cause, or neither? In that regard, it cannot be an effect, because it exists even prior to what is intended to be the material cause (*upādeya*). Some hold that water and so forth are the effects of bathing and the like because they exist even before those acts; but for them, what does the collection of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) that is to be attained do [for the water], such that it becomes the cause of the water? This is impossible for something that performs no function, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that it is not logical for an effect to exist without a cause, [we reply: But how can that which is unarisen and non-existent—equal to the horn of a donkey—produce existence for anything? [Objection: There is no fault, because it exists at its own time. [Reply: If it exists at that time even prior to the arising of the effect, then by implication the cause has already occurred (*pūrvabhāvitva*), and thus its "future-ness" (*anāgatatva*) is lost. If it exists later, once the effect has already arisen, it is of no use, since it is impossible to produce what has already been produced (*kṛtasya karaṇāyogāt*).
In that case, there is neither an effect nor a cause; for when an effect is not perceived by one of limited vision, its specific nature cannot be ascertained,
and when it is perceived, inference is redundant.

Nor is that alone a valid logical mark (*liṅga*), because of the possibility of a deficiency in the necessary connection (*pratibandha*); since there is no connection for that which is neither [of the two], it lacks the status of a logical mark.
To this, he says: "Of an existing conscious [entity]," and so forth.

From the context—"of that which exists, of the conscious [entity], in its final state"—this is obtained. By this, he says the following: it has been established that, in the interim, the existence of the conscious [entity] or anything else is pervaded by its capacity to produce subsequent transformations, just as it is pervaded by its capacity to perform distinct functions. Therefore, if that [existence] were to occur even in the absence of that [capacity for transformation], it would follow that it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); how then could there be reality or otherwise for anything? Otherwise, because of the suspicion that every pervaded thing might exist even in the absence of its own pervader, the entire world would become non-inferable.

Because that conscious being arises from one whose nature is consciousness and whose form is consciousness—transforming and evolving without depending on any other cause—therefore, there exists no other cause distinct from it; for that which has no dependence upon another, or that which does not depend [on anything else], lacks both existence and non-existence of such a cause. Here, however, the impossibility of any other explanation (*anyathānupapatti*) certainly exists; this is the connection with the phrase "our direct perception" (*asmadādipratyakṣam*).
The mind is not cultivated because it lacks the nature of being a cause.
Performing that which does not exist as a reality.
The subsequent mind is merely a cause, being distinct from both the effect and the cause.
"Is it not the case that, even if there is no dependence on inference, there will be no transformation into that form? To this he says: "By itself," and so forth;
because the manifestation occurs spontaneously, by its own nature, without delay, and instantaneously.
Whence is this [known]? To this he says: "Because it is non-contingent" (anaimittikatvāt), and so forth.
He anticipates a further objection—that [the world] might be causeless like insentient things such as the earth—and in order to refute that, he says "the second," and so forth.
To this, he states the reply: "That [moment] necessarily," and so forth, because that second moment exists by necessity.
Then, he states the refutation for one who does not accept [the sequence], beginning with "If," and so forth.

The word "punaḥ" (again) serves to indicate an alternative position: the final moment, which is the mind at death, lacks the capacity for subsequent existence—that is, it lacks the power for further transformation. [The opponent asks: "Since the final moment is a non-entity (*avastutva*), what could it possibly do? To this, he replies with the words beginning "svopādāne" (in its own material cause).
By the word "sva" (its own), the final moment is referred to; [the argument is that] it would establish the absence of the continuum of its own material causes.

Why? To this he says: "The object," and so forth (verse 237). Since an entity is characterized by the performance—that is, the production—of its effect, its causal capacity is its defining characteristic. If it is argued that this capacity exists even for that moment which does not produce the effect due to the absence of auxiliary conditions; to this he replies: "The capable," and so forth.
It is contradictory to say that [an entity] is capable when produced in its final moment and yet does not act;

for instance: if it is capable, how can it not act? If it does not act, how can it be capable? Otherwise, one might think that even if something is eternally capable, it would never act due to a deficiency of auxiliary causes.

If you ask: "Why is it not suspected that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or the capacity for it is not the definition [of existence], but rather the connection with being (*sattā*)? [The answer is: because it is non-pervasive, because it is absent in universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, and because it has already been refuted.

If it is argued that one should not suspect that [the entity] lacks reality simply because it lacks the power to become its own successor, despite possessing the power to produce something of a different class; we say no. This is because there is no such intention regarding a single purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and because the total annihilation of the elements (*bhūta*) is not admitted.
For this very reason, it has been stated: "like the insentient," meaning [it possesses] the capacity for purposeful action.
The characteristic of things,
the characteristic of things, the characteristic of things.

The relation to existence (*sattā*) for all three categories—substance and the rest—as maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas... [is rejected] because they possess existence inherently (*svataḥ-sattva*), and because there is no relation to existence in the case of universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*). (Praśastapādabhāṣya; Vyomavatī, p. 121)

[Objection: "But just as for a conscious being there are no [mental states] such as *avagraha* (perception) after death, nor before death, so too [there are none] after [the final moment]; To this, he replies: For those various dissimilar effects whose production depends on a complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there may be occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*), as in the case of bracelets and other ornaments made from gold. However, one must not consider the occasional occurrence of the subsequent arising [of consciousness] to be like that of an insentient thing. Furthermore, for one who attempts to prove that the final moments of consciousness are not the material causes (*upādāna*) of further moments of consciousness, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), just as there is for one who attempts to prove that sound is inaudible.

If it is argued that [the soul perishes] because its destruction is observed at the end; to this, he replies: Therefore, on account of the reasoning already stated, that which is asserted by the opponent—the observation of the destruction of the conscious being after death—is unproven and uncertain. This is because its destruction is not established there.
Furthermore, the mere non-perception [of the soul] is due to the lack of capacity for such apprehension in one whose life has ceased;

and this non-perception is not sufficient to subvert the subject (pakṣa) of the argument. Otherwise, the non-perception of eternality in the case of sound would also have to be a subverter of it—so he thinks.

And for this reason, he says that [the existence of the self] is unestablished: "The observation of stability in the interval between birth and death—that too is not established by the logic already stated; rather, the connection is that it would establish stability only at the end.
Why? He says: "Because of non-deviation, i.e., because of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva).
For instance, if the state of the endurer did not exist at the end, it would not exist in the middle either, since there is no distinction [between the two]; such is the Buddhist position."
As it has been said:
"In the end, because of limited knowledge."
For it is held that birth alone is the cause for the destruction of entities; thus, that which has arisen and is not yet destroyed would have to perish later together with its causes.
"Once this [birth] has been extracted... birth itself would perish; later, by what could it be [reinstated]?—*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-vṛtti*, p.
12. Now, if there is stability in the interim, then since its form is exactly that [same as before], by what could subsequent stability be prevented?
This too has been stated:"
If he were to remain for even another single moment after having arisen in one moment in the midst,
then surely he would remain likewise for thousands of millions of moments.

Now, if the view is that even that which is stable in the interim perishes when confronted by a subverting cognition such as "this is perishable," that too is not tenable; because, like the ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, such a thing cannot be subject to that [perishing], and because it has been stated that the absolute destruction of an existent thing is impossible,
there can be no destruction of that which is eternally stable.

Having become a follower of the Sugata’s doctrine, a Cārvāka might at some point argue that the non-perception of staying in the middle—that is, the non-observation of staying in the middle—is due to its non-establishment, and not merely because of non-deviation [from the conclusion], such as the phrase "the observation of staying in the middle" and so forth;
by this, the non-establishment of the observation of staying in the middle is refuted.

If it is argued: "Let the observation of staying in the middle establish the staying of consciousness at the end, but let it do so in the form of insentience; therefore, the reason is contradictory," to this he says: "If... and so forth.

If that which is conscious were to evolve in the form of the unconscious, and then again evolve in the form of the conscious—just as in the case of sleep and waking, since the establishment of rebirth after death (pretyabhāva) is like the establishment of becoming again after having died—how could this not be in some way faultless?
What is it [that is faultless]? To this he says: "The other," and so forth.
This refutation was stated by accepting [the opponent's position], whereas in reality this is not the case.
Recalling what was stated in the passage beginning with "the conscious [entity] does not, however, abandon consciousness," he says: "Of the conscious and the other," and so forth.

The conscious is the living soul (*jīva*); the other is the unconscious, such as earth and the rest. The "confusion" (*saṅkara*) of these two is their occurrence in one place; the "interchange" (*vyatikara*) is their mutual entering into each other's domains. The apprehension of these two is indeed improper.
Of what nature are they? He says: "established by their own nature" (*svabhāvasiddhayoḥ*), meaning established in their respective essential forms by the exclusion of one another.

Or rather, [if one asks], "From what [source] do the two [entities] arise, being produced from an entity of their own kind? He says: "Because of the abandonment of the perceived difference between those two, there is the destruction of everything. This shows that [the distinction] does not belong to non-existent things—since even the perception of blue and so forth, or pleasure and so forth, is accompanied by that [distinction]—and because of the conceptualization of the admixture (*saṅkara*) and so on between those two, which is unperceived and not made an object of direct perception.

By this also, he demonstrates that for another [opponent], there would follow the consequence of yet another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), because without that [prior cognition], it would be impossible; [thus] there is the loss of stability.

Now, let it be that there is the postulation of the unseen (adṛṣṭa); however, it would not be without a means of valid cognition (apramāṇaka), because an inference establishing their non-difference is accepted through worldly convention (vyavahāra).

And that inference is as follows: "The conscious [self] is a transformation of the elements (bhūta-pariṇāma) or has their nature, because of its existence and so forth, like a water bubble or the power of intoxication [in wine].
He states this very point with the words beginning with "jala" (water).
"It exists like bubbles in water"—to whom does this apply? He says: "the living beings (jīvas).

This is what is meant: just as bubbles, consisting of the elements such as *sattva* and so on, which are of the nature of water, arise and perish right there [in the water], so too do the living beings [arise and perish] within the earth and other elements. Thus, they exist in a manner similar to intoxication (*mada*) produced by the consumption of liquor. Such is the meaning.
What is that? It is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is the intended meaning here: just as the power of intoxication, which is inherent in the fermented juice (*bhaṭīkivodini*), is manifested and then again disappears within that very same substance, so too is consciousness [manifested] by the elements (*bhūta*).

To this, he gives the following answer: "In this way, another person, having merely seen the bitterness in *arka* juice, attributes it to molasses and other substances—claiming that molasses and the like are bitter because they come from the same source as the *arka*."

By this, he shows that just as there is a contradiction of the thesis (*pakṣa*) by perception (*pratyakṣa*) here, so it is in the present case as well; thus, while refuting the reason (*hetu*), he says "of cognition" (*vijñapteḥ*), etc., which connects to "if one were to prove" (*yadi sādhayet*).
"Of cognition" refers to the transformative consciousness (*pariṇāmicetanā*). The syntactical connection is: "if one were to prove [it]."
What is it? He says: "the elements," and so forth.
Why? He says: "the arising of beings," and so forth.
By what example? He says: "the power of intoxication," and so forth.
"Even when what exists? He says: "of its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*)," and so forth.

Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), distinctions such as synonyms (*paryāya*) and so on are included; he shows the absence of any obstruction to that [specific characteristic] and states its refutation: "from that very [source], existence, being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth, prove [the conclusion]"—this is the connection.

What is it? He says: "Intellect" (buddhi) and so forth. Intellect is the first transformation of primordial matter (pradhāna), known as the Great One (mahat); consciousness, however, is the Person (puruṣa). The "transformation" (vivarta) of these two is their modification. Of whom does this non-transgression apply? He says: "even of the elements" (bhūtānām), not merely of anything else.
And of what? He says: "pleasure and so forth," etc.
[This refers to] pleasure and so forth, and self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); "like those two" means similar to them.
Who is he? He says: even the Sāṃkhya—because of the statement in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (v. 21): "From that [group of sixteen], from the five [tanmātras], the five gross elements arise."

Because of the statement in *Ṛgveda* 10.90.2 and elsewhere that "this [universe] is indeed the Puruṣa," the proponent of the non-duality of the Puruṣa is not only the Cārvāka; this is the meaning of the word "also" (*api*). For this reason, the inconclusive contradictory reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) consists of such properties as existence, origination, and being produced; this is to be connected by changing the case-ending [to the genitive]. It is of such a nature that it does not deviate from the contradictory probandum (*sādhya*), because, just like the transformation of the elements into consciousness, these [reasons] also establish a transformation other than [the one intended].
Alternatively, "contradictory" (viruddha) means that which is non-deviant from a contradictory probandum—that is, its inseparable concomitance (avinābhāvin) with it.

To explain: consciousness’s possession of existence and so forth during the intermediate state has been established as being non-deviant from being derived from a conscious cause, because—according to the logic just stated—the presence [of the reason] in the heterologue (vipakṣa) is refuted. Furthermore, just as external pervasion (bahirvyāpti) is ineffective when internal pervasion (antarvyāpti) is unestablished, so too is it ineffective even when it is established.

As he will say: "The Self exists because of the synthesis of the means of knowledge" (p. 104). And in that regard, [the Self] does not exist as something insentient, for that would lead to an undesirable conclusion and the means of proof would be futile; nor does it exist as something purely sentient, because if that were proven, the reason would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) due to its presence even in earth and other such things. This is because the reason must be qualified. This is another explanation, beginning with "from that very [reason]," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of [other] beings as well" (*bhūtānām api*): this word *api* (also/even) is displaced in its order and should be understood immediately after the term *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the non-deviant contradictory).

Consequently, the meaning is as follows: not only is there the non-deviant contradictory, but there is also the deviant (*vyabhicārī*), because even during the intermediate state of consciousness (*vijñapti*), although it does not transcend the transformation (*vivarta*) of sentience (*caitanya*), one observes such qualities as existence, arising, and being produced.
The Cārvāka [asserts] the non-difference between the conscious and the unconscious,
[claiming it exists] in water alone.
By the word "etcetera," properties such as having an origin and being produced should be understood;
[these are to be excluded] from the group of sixteen consisting of the collection of the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*),
specifically from the five subtle elements characterized by form, taste, smell, touch, and sound.
Internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is the pervasion between the probandum and the probans within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself.
As for the comparison: "If internal pervasion is not established, the external [evidence] is useless" (Pramāṇasaṃgraha, p.
111); thus, it is not without purpose.

With the words "iti" and so forth, he states the conclusion: in this manner, by means of the immediately preceding method, one would overstep the established order of the means and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇa-prameya-vyavasthā*) due to false attachment—that is, due to an insistence on what is unreal. Since the designation emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva-pradhāna*), "the establishment" refers to the very clarity, the state of non-delusion, within cognition; one would overstep that and lead it to utter dissolution.

For instance: if perception—which sees consciousness as entirely non-different from the elements—is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then how could the cognition of a double moon and so forth not be [valid]? For by following the worldly distinction between perception and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*), one would become a materialist (*laukāyatika*). Alternatively, if it is not a valid means of knowledge, then like the cognition of a double moon, everything would be without distinction, because the nature of that which is non-different from the elements would be grasped by everyone as being different from them.
Indeed, no cognition perceives itself as consisting of form and other qualities, since the identity of form [between the cognition and its object] has been denied.

Nevertheless, if one were to assume that such an object is perceived in that way, then it would follow that the entire world possesses omniscience; this is the connection [of the argument], because [the theory] has already refuted the existence of the form of the object within the cognition. Thus, "the world would become non-materialistic (alaukāyatika) regarding valid cognition" is the syntactical link.

Furthermore, if all cognition were to manifest as being of the nature of that [object], then every contradiction would have been already chewed over by the Cārvākas; so what is the point of composing this treatise? For instruction regarding blue and other such objects is not meaningful for one who is already perceiving them.

If it is argued that [the qualification] "that" is for the purpose of excluding error (*bhrānti*), we say no. For if even the cognition of error appears as having that very nature, the fault remains as it was.
