Consequently, since one would be grasping a nature that is both non-different and different from that [object], what indeed could be called non-erroneous perception that might serve as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? If it is argued that it is non-erroneous with respect to the mere nature of the primary elements (*bhūtātman-mātra*), this might be so if the existence of that alone were perceived from some source; however, because perception contradicts that [existence] by not perceiving it, and because a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) is difficult to find even in this case, [the mere nature of the primary elements is not established].
If, then, that [object] appears as distinct from the elements (*bhūta*), some maintain that it exists exactly in that way;

yet others hold that even so, if there is no difference between it and those [elements], then there would be no distinction of anything from anything at all, and thus neither the establishment of perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the establishment of its objects (*prameya*) would be possible.

But there is another view: it is true that [consciousness] is distinct from those elements which are intended as its causes, because it appears as such and because the effect is different from its cause. Nevertheless, just as a cloth produced from earthen threads, though distinct, is itself earthen, so too consciousness, being derived from a body composed of elements, is itself elemental. That is incorrect, because the similarity between the threads and the cloth in terms of having color and other qualities does not exist between the elements and consciousness, since consciousness lacks color and the like.
Even in that case, if one were to conceive such [an inference], it would not be perception, because other means of proof have been excluded;

nor would it be inference, as this would overstep the established order of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vyavasthā*) by implying that perception alone is a means of knowledge and nothing else. Furthermore, if one were to establish the possession of color and so forth in the elements by using the example of earth—despite the fact that existence and the like are already established for each individual element through that very same [inference]—one would thereby overstep the established order of the objects of cognition (*prameya-vyavasthā*), even though the [resulting] cognition arises as something distinct.
There exists a means of valid cognition that establishes [the object] through its similarity [to other things], because of [its] existence and so forth.

It has already been explained that atheism (*nāstikya*) is a false view (*mithyādarśana*). Now, desiring to explain the other [false view], namely the conceit of being a living soul (*jīvābhimāna*), he says: "And likewise," and so forth.

"And likewise, the view that the self (*ātman*) is an agent through its qualities (*guṇa*), yet remains unchanging with respect to other objects, and is an enjoyer—this is false; for it is a conceptualization of a pervasive [self] as having spatial dimensions. (15)

Since benefit to others is possible only for that which is inherently active and possesses manifold forms, to abandon that and instead claim agency (*kartṛtva*) for an immutable entity based on the inherence of effort and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and to further claim enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*) based on the inherence of pleasure, pain, and so forth— this is like beginning to describe the excellence of the valor and other qualities of the son of a barren woman.
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the defining characteristic of a real entity.

Likewise, another [author] distinguishes the true nature of the soul (*jīva*)— characterized by consciousness, agency in the transformations of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and the state of being an enjoyer— as the conscious person (*puruṣa*), who by his very nature is himself a non-agent; he asserts that the insentient *pradhāna*, which consists of the cause and its effects, possesses those functions, such as pleasure and so on,
because it is only through the *pradhāna* acting spontaneously that the benefit of the body can occur.

In that same manner, by means of qualities—characterized as effort, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth—which serve as instruments, the self (*ātman*) acts as the agent. Of what nature are these [qualities]? They are "distinct entities," meaning they are absolutely different from it.

Furthermore, of what nature is the self? To this he says: "even though it is unchangeable"—that is, even though no excellence can be added to it nor any deficiency removed—it is held [by others] to be the enjoyer through those qualities such as the intellect (*buddhi*), which are distinct entities. This is false; for although the self is unchangeable and, like space, does not undergo transformation because its nature consists in the experience of pleasure and so on, it is nonetheless claimed to be the enjoyer, which is false due to its contradiction with reason.

Having thus demonstrated the conceit of a self in other systems such as Vaiśeṣika, he speaks [the following] to demonstrate that of the Sāṃkhya, beginning with the words "the enjoyer" (*bhoktā*), etc. The meaning therein is as follows: the Self, which is the *puruṣa*, is the enjoyer—that is, the experiencer of objects presented by the *guṇas* (sattva, rajas, and tamas), which serve as causes and are distinct entities dependent upon *pradhāna*. [The Sāṃkhya claims] that although it is unchanging (*avikārī*) and devoid of any transformation consisting in the direct perception of those [objects], this is false;
for that which has not undergone such a transformation cannot become [an enjoyer] in that way, because it would involve a contradiction.

If that [Being] were always of that same nature, there would be no distinction between waking and sleep, because it is impossible for the existent object of perception not to be perceived when there is seeing; therefore,
even the postulation of its manifestation and concealment is not tenable for that which is changeless.
By this, it is stated that everyone perceives everything whose form has been presented by the cognition of another person;

for unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is not the regulator of perception, because it is uniform in nature, nor is the perceived object [the regulator], as that would entail its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Furthermore, for those who hold the same view, it is false to say that while one thing is visible, another is not seen;

likewise, it is false to claim that the enjoyer is a non-agent, because there is a contradiction between being an enjoyer and being a non-agent, since non-agency is characterized by the absence of all causal power.
Now, demonstrating the falsity common to both of these, he says: "The pervasive," and so forth.

The conceptualization of spatial extension and the conceptualization of partlessness for the all-pervading self (*ātman*) are false, because of the contradiction between the two; this will be demonstrated [in the section] where it is stated that "the alternatives beginning with 'all-pervading' are [false]. Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), partlessness and so forth are included. That [conceptualization] is also false: because there is a lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it in one case, and because in the other case it would entail the consequence that [the self] does not pervade the body.
If the self, according to the Naiyāyika,
were by nature a faculty of vision.
Manifestation occurs at one time and concealment at another,
because the eternally immutable Puruṣa is always of a single uniform nature, whereas the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) is not.
Because the status of being an enjoyer belongs only to the agent of the act of eating,
[there is a contradiction] for both the Naiyāyika and the Sāṃkhya regarding [the soul's] all-pervasiveness and partlessness.
In the case of being omnipresent while being partless.

With the verse beginning with *svataḥ*, he states the meaning of the *kārikā*: because benefit to others is possible only for that which proceeds from itself (*svataḥ*), namely the self (*ātman*), while undergoing a subsequent transformation that does not abandon its prior form; and because the assistance (*upakāra*)—meaning either the production [of effects] by others who are distinct from the self, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, or the excellence (*atiśaya*) produced through auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)—is possible only for such a [transforming entity], therefore, setting that aside, the Naiyāyika begins to describe the perfection of qualities such as valor in the son of Vyāsa (Arjuna), asserting that agency belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*), which is essentially immutable and eternally stable, due to the inherence (*samavāya*) of effort and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); and furthermore, after the attainment of desired objects drawn in by effort and unseen merit, enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*) arises due to the inherence of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Thus the Naiyāyika commences his exposition.

This is what is meant: just as it is not logical to proclaim the perfection of qualities such as valor for the son of a barren woman because he cannot benefit others, so too, since an unchanging [Self] cannot benefit others and lacks both effort (*prayatna*) and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), agency is not logical by virtue of inherence in that [Self]. In the absence of those two, how could agency exist? Since there is an absence of the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth, the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) through inherence in that [Self] is likewise non-existent. Thus, the mention of effort and unseen merit together is for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of a causal relationship between them.
For it is held that the unperceived [effect] arises from a specific effort, and from that specific effort [the effect arises];
in this regard, since even for a single unchanging entity there is no production [of a second], the absence of a second is easily established.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the presence or absence of the relationship between the example (dṛṣṭānta) and the thing exemplified (dārṣṭāntika)—for by that, the status of being an example is attributed to effort, while the status of being the thing exemplified is attributed to the unperceived.

For example: "Animals and the like are drawn toward Devadatta by his quality of effort (prayatna), because they possess the property of being its auxiliaries while being effects, just like food and so forth. In that case, if the status of effort as an unchanging quality is denied, how could the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) possibly be a quality of it?

Since it is impossible for an auxiliary benefit produced by another to be deposited [in the self], and since there is an absence of agency characterized by such [deposition], how can there be assistance rendered by another?
Of the self by means of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) according to the Naiyāyika.

Bodies and the like are effects produced by the elements impelled by the specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of Devadatta and are appropriated by him; for, while being effects, they are instruments for his enjoyment, just like a house—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī*, p.
149. [This establishes] the state of being a quality of the self that is not subject to modification (*avikāryātmaguṇatva*).

If it is argued: "Granted that there may be no correct description of qualities such as valor for the son of a barren woman who is absolutely non-existent, yet for the Self, even though it is changeless, a description of agency and so forth is appropriate because of its existence," to this he says:
"The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a thing (*vastu*), i.e., of an entity (*bhāva*), is what? He says: transformation (*pariṇāma*)."
In the absence of that [change], the status of being a real entity (*vastutva*) is impossible;

therefore, having abandoned the characteristic of a real entity—which is characterized by change—one must again [attribute it] to that which is non-changing, meaning precisely to that which is devoid of the transformation that constitutes the characteristic of a real entity, for the non-existence of the characterized (*lakṣya*) necessarily follows from the cessation of its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The rest is as before.

Having thus refuted the Nyāya position in the absence of transformation (*pariṇāma*), he speaks as follows—beginning with "tathā"—in order to refute the Sāṃkhya position: "In that manner" (*tathā*) means by that method; "the other" refers to the Sāṃkhya, who "divides" (*vibhajate*)—that is, attributes to—the "reality" (*tattva*), the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the living being (*jīva*), the self (*ātman*), characterized by consciousness, pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as agency and enjoyership.

"How is it like an elephant? To this he says: "Having been assimilated," and so forth. "Assimilated" (*pratipanna*) means made one's own through some form of non-difference. Of what [is this said]? He says: "Of the *pradhāna*. [This refers to] that whose nature (*ātma-svabhāva*)—the nature of each preceding cause such as *mahat* and so on—is [assimilated] by each succeeding effect.
Of what [is this said]? He says: "Of the *pradhāna*."
Of what [is it the state]? He says: "of the insentient.
Its functioning as pleasure, pain, and so forth is its transformation (*pariṇati*).

By the words "it is established" and so on, if the Puruṣa, like the Pradhāna, were also established as having the nature of cause and effect, what fault would there be by which his changelessness (*avikāritva*) is postulated? Nor can that [changelessness] be abandoned without a fault, for that would result in the Puruṣa being an irrational agent (*aprekṣākāritā*).

Or there might be a fault regarding perception and so forth if [the qualities] were perceived as belonging to that which is unchangeable; however, [the author] shows by means of the words "pleasure" and so on that this has already been answered.
For this has already been answered by [the passage]: "There may be a transformation of earth and so forth," *Siddhiviniścaya* 4.14, and so on.
The reality of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva) would be accepted as belonging to the person (puruṣa).

If it is argued: "This might be so if pleasure and the like were established as conscious, but they are not," [we reply: how then is the person (*puruṣa*) conscious? [We say] because it is accepted [as such]. This [consciousness] does not exist even in the case of another's pleasure and so forth, nor is there any distinction based on whether it relates to oneself or another; for that [distinction] is irrelevant. By this, the argument "from scripture" (*āgama*) has been considered.
If, on the other hand, it is argued that it is conscious because it perceives itself, and that pleasure and the like must also be conscious for the same reason—
since there is no other person who directly perceives them either— then, if one likewise postulates another perceiver for that [perceiver], there would be an infinite regress.

The non-perception of another [quality] occurs in both cases because, being transformations of the insentient *pradhāna*, pleasure and the like do not possess the nature of apprehending themselves, just like earth and other elements. This is a sublation of the subject (*pakṣabādhanam*) by perception, like the [alleged] inaudibility of sound;
furthermore, one must consider how those [pleasures and so on] can be its transformations.
Because there is no grasping of a self [in pleasure, etc.], there is mutual dependence [between the self and pleasure].

Some maintain that because they arise and are distinct, pleasure and so forth are insentient, like a jar and other such objects. In that case, since the self exists [alongside them], the self too would be insentient, just like them. To this we reply: just as even though *sattva* (the quality of goodness) is common to both, one thing is sentient while the other is otherwise, so too, despite the lack of distinction in their arising and other characteristics, [the self] may be different [from pleasure, etc.].

In this regard, others raise the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); but that is not so, because the designation "arising" and so forth applies to "becoming otherwise" (*anyathābhāva*), which is accepted even by the Sāṃkhyas, and because no other entity fit for such a designation is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even for the Buddhist.
Therefore, it is intended that just as pleasure and the like are conscious, they are said to be transformations of consciousness.

Thus, the conscious person (*puruṣa*) is himself, by his own nature, a non-agent; he is called an agent only figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) due to the superimposition of agency upon *pradhāna*. This is shown by the word "himself" (*svayam*), meaning by his own essence (*svarūpataḥ*) and not figuratively.

The reality of the *jīva* is analyzed as follows: it is the "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*) because of its direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the objects presented by perception (*darśana*). He thinks thus: just as the state of being an enjoyer, so too the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is appropriate only for a conscious being acting with deliberation, and not for anything else; otherwise, since all human goals would be accomplished by that [consciousness] alone, what purpose would the postulation of a [separate] *puruṣa* serve for the Jaina?
The person [is so called] because, in the Jaina scripture, pleasure and other qualities are described as being conscious by virtue of their admission [as such].
If this is argued, [the answer is] no, because pleasure and so forth are not apprehended as being the self.

If pleasure and so forth are not grasped as being the self, then the transformation of the insentient *pradhāna* is established; and once that is established, the non-grasping of the self is established—just as in the case of earth and the other elements.
Thus, it is like earth and the rest.
It has been explained that the pervasive notion of space is false, by means of such arguments as "the insentient [world] arises from the intelligent Pradhāna itself" and so forth.

For instance: for the Supreme Being who acts by Himself and simultaneously pervades all the limbs of the body with His own limbs, support—such as holding [the body] and so forth—is possible; therefore, there is no dependence on a location, unlike the indivisible consciousness (*avibhāga-citta*) imagined by the Buddhists.
This has been considered by the author of the treatise in the *Cūrṇi* regarding the proof of the soul (*jīva*) in the *Laghu-ādi*; this too should be understood.
Why is this so? He says: "The characteristic of a non-entity," and so forth.
Transformation is the becoming otherwise of an entity, whether simultaneously or sequentially;
the remainder is as before for that which is partless.

The Sāṃkhyas and Naiyāyikas argue: "Indeed, just as the final moment (*caramakṣaṇa*) of a mobile living being (*trasajīva*), such as a leech or an ant, is real because—though it does not perform its own purposeful action—it is identical to that which performs the purposeful action for another, so too should the self (*ātman*) be real. To this they reply: "That is not tenable, because [the self] lacks that [capacity], and so forth. To this [objection], he says: "The final," and so on.
If the self were an entity at the moment of the final consciousness,

it would therefore be a non-entity, since it is like that [final moment] in being indistinguishable from a non-entity. If a permanent self and the final moment of cognition were real entities on account of some similarity to a causal agent or the like— despite being themselves ineffective and incapable of performing any purposeful action— then, precisely because they lack causal agency, their lack of reality is evident, owing to their similarity to non-entities.

That which is both the end and a moment of consciousness—that very thing would be a self (*ātman*), a person (*puruṣa*), or a non-agent (*akāraka*). How could it be an entity (*bhāva*) or a real thing (*vastu*) if it were not performing an action?
For it must be an agent; since it possesses the same properties as another agent, the word "if" (*cet*) indicates the intention of the opponent.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: the connection is that "the self would be as clear as non-existence.

Therefore, because of its lack of form—due to non-existence—and because there is no distinction (aviśeṣataḥ), meaning an absence of specific difference, the example is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama) for the Jains;
thus, [the author], brushing aside both the example and the subject of the example with a single blow of the palm, says "eternal," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the eternal, unchanging self and of the final moment of cognition imagined by the Buddhists"—the word "and" (*ca*) here functions as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).

[The author asks: "If some kind of reality is admitted for that which acts for itself nothing at all, which performs no purposeful action (*anarthakriyākārin*), from what [source] would such reality arise? He answers: "Because of its similarity to an agent" (*kārakasādharmyāt*).

Because of the commonality with a causal factor (*kāraka*), characterized by being knowable (*jñeyatva*) and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including such properties as being a real entity (*vastutva*)—[the opponent objects]:
"But is not 'knowability' the production of a cognition having itself as its object? Therefore, if that [property] belongs to it, it contradicts the claim that 'it is itself incapable of acting.

Furthermore, if one attempts to prove its status as a real entity based on the commonality of being a real entity and so forth, it follows that the very same thing is both the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*)."

Regarding that, if it is argued: "As for what he will say concerning the state of being knowable and so forth—namely, 'because of similarity with non-entities' (avastusādharmyāt)—that too is not consistent, because there is no similarity with things such as a donkey's horn," we reply: No, because the intention is otherwise.

For example, just as by another [opponent] the reality of the final moment of consciousness or of the self—which are themselves incapable of acting—is established according to the view of the *kārikā* by means of some property existing in both cases, then, in order to point out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of this reason, he says: "Furthermore," and so on.

Furthermore, immediately following this application [of reasoning], the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is: "[it does not arise] from another cause," precisely because of its lack of causality, and thus because of the absence of any similarity with a causal factor (*kāraka*).

Indeed, for that which is itself incapable of performing any action, even if a similarity with a causal factor existed through some attribute, it could not be known; for there is no possible means of knowing such an attribute.

What follows from this? He says: "Manifestly," that is, in such a way that it becomes evident, there is the non-substantiality (*avastutva*)—the absence of any proof for substantiality (*vastutva*)—of the subject under discussion.
He says "this, however, must be certain," beginning with the words *avastu* (non-entity), and so forth.

Because of its similarity (*sādharmya*) to a non-entity such as a donkey's horn—that is, because of its resemblance to being incapable of any action (*akiñcitkaratva*)—its status as a non-entity, or lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), is evident.

When the opponent desires to establish the reality (*vastutva*) of this [subject] which is incapable of action by imagining a similarity to an agent (*kāraka-sādharmya*), then the counter-proof (*pratipramāṇa*) is stated, beginning with "precisely because of its non-agency," and so forth.
The Naiyāyikas, Sautrāntikas, and others maintain that the self is an object of knowledge.

Demonstrating that the reason—namely, "precisely because it is not a causal agent"—does not deviate from the probandum (*sādhyāvyabhicāra*) according to the logic accepted by the opponent, [the author] says: "If it pervades existence," and so forth.
If [the final moment of consciousness] pervades existence, then the very existence of the effect itself is its own causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Through succession and non-succession, [the capacity for causal efficiency] would cease upon the cessation of the immutable [entity];
thus, we do not perceive any causal efficiency apart from its existence.

Furthermore, that [causal efficiency], by means of succession and simultaneity, would pervade the existence of an entity; therefore, as it itself turns away from the final moment of consciousness or from the eternal, it would cause that existence to cease.
If there is no restriction on the exclusion [of the reason] from non-pervaders,

then how could that [reason], such as existence (*sattva*), be non-deviant? For it is only by pervading existence— that is, being present— that momentariness would be established as ultimately real, provided that [existence] does indeed pervade it.

What is it? He says: "Causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*). By itself, what is this causal efficiency? He says: "The very existence of an effect is the capacity of its cause," because that [capacity] is about to be defined. That causal efficiency, too, is pervaded by succession and simultaneity; the word "if" (*cet*) is understood here, and the verb "pervades" (*vyāpnoti*), which has undergone the transformation of the suffix *kṛt*, is connected to this context.

If causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) were to cease upon the cessation of its own existence in that which is immutable, immovable, and eternal (*kūṭastha*), then it would cause existence itself to cease; or else, by changing the grammatical case of the word "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyām*), the connection is made with the phrase: "succession and simultaneity cause their own cessation to cease. For it is clearly established that the final moment of consciousness is non-existent because it lacks causal agency, and thus shares the characteristics of a non-entity. This is the logical construction.

The word *vyāpnoti* ("it pervades") ends in a verbal suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*); the form *vyāptā* ("pervaded") is what is connected here. The term *dvivacanatā* is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*).
But here, the word *arthakriyām* (purposeful action) is connected as an accusative case ending.

Now, if it is argued: "Even though the final moment of consciousness does not produce an effect of its own kind (*sajātīya*), nor does it produce an effect of a different kind (*vijātīya*) such as the cognition of an object, my reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*); however, yours is unestablished because [the final moment] is simply non-productive (*akārakatvāt*),"—this objection is answered by the phrase *na paramārthataḥ*. It is understood that "existence" (*sattā*) means the presence of a subsequent transformation following itself; "its absence" (*vyatireka*) means its non-existence. Thus, the meaning is: "without that [subsequent transformation]."
We do not perceive causal efficiency as the production of something heterogeneous; rather, we perceive it precisely along with that [homogeneous effect].

He thinks as follows: just as, having observed the nature of being a tree in a *śiṃśapā* in one place, its nature as such is established even in other locations and so forth—otherwise, it would follow that it lacks a nature—so too, since the capacity of an entity to produce effects both homogeneous and otherwise is frequently observed from that very [nature], why is that [capacity] not established at all times? For there is no distinction. Otherwise, all inference would be destroyed.
(The text here is fragmentary.)

If it is argued: "Granted that, since [the effect] stands before it by virtue of [its] existence, it may indeed possess that nature; nevertheless, it will not produce something of its own kind"—this is contradictory, like [the claim that] something eternal is capable yet does not act.
Furthermore, because the material cause (*upādāna*) exists, there is no contradiction in the non-perception of that which is derived from it (*upādeya*).
Now, if the existence of an entity is pervaded by its being an effect, then even in the absence of an effect belonging to a different genus, that [existence] is not contradicted.
Why is this so? Because it is observed to be so; and that is the same in the other case as well.

If bondage consists in the production of a dissimilar [effect] even when a similar one is not produced, then likewise, there must be the possibility of producing a similar [effect] even when a dissimilar one is not produced; thus, how could there be an absence of doubt regarding the so-called omniscience of the Sugata or anyone else? Furthermore, for those who argue in this way, how can a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) be productive, such that the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.18), "that which depends on a single causal complex," and so forth, would be easily established?
Therefore, let there be the production of the similar just as there is of the dissimilar.
The existence of an entity consists in its nature of producing both that which is of the same class and that which is otherwise;
the point is that all objects should produce only a subsequent moment of their own kind, and not a dissimilar omniscient mind.
For in that case, having produced a subsequent moment of the same kind, one can account for [the production of] a moment of a different kind simply by postulating its status as a cooperative cause.

One might ask: "Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "If that aforementioned causal efficiency (arthakriyā) were to pervade the existence of a real entity (vastusattā), in what manner would it do so? To this he replies: "By means of succession and simultaneity."

What follows from this? He says: "Exclusionary causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would exclude the existence of those two [the final moment of consciousness and the eternal], whether from the final moment of consciousness or from the eternal.

Why is this so? To this he says: "By itself," that is, by its own nature. When there is an exclusion of the non-pervasive, there is no necessity for the exclusion of the non-pervaded, because such exclusion is not invariably concomitant; this is the implied meaning. It might be argued: "Let causal efficiency be excluded from the final moment of consciousness, yet existence does not thereby cease, because there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*. To this he replies: "And that," and so forth.

How could existence (*sattva*) and so forth not be a non-deviant reason? It is thought that they are not a reason at all, because even in the case of an eternal entity—which performs no purposeful action—the presence of that [existence] cannot be ruled out.

Since there is deviation, only the momentary would be established as ultimately real, because there is no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between existence and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

If it is argued: "Indeed, the existence of a thing is not pervaded by the existence of its effect, such that upon the cessation of the latter, the former would also cease; rather, it is pervaded by the capacity to produce it. And since that capacity exists in the final moment due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), there is no non-existence [of the cause]," to this he says: "The causal complex" (*sāmagrī*), etc.—[meaning] that upon the cessation of the effect, the capacity to produce it [also ceases].

Even in the production of an effect, the causal complex (sāmagrī) is the cause, not a single [factor]; for if a potent entity, having obtained the causal complex, necessarily acts even though it is eternal, why then [is this not accepted]? (19)

The cessation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) does not entail the cessation of the existence of the entity itself. Furthermore, it is incorrect to argue that while the final moment possesses the capacity [for action], it does not perform it due to a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) or because of its similarity to what is capable; for even in the case of a permanent entity, although it always possesses the capacity, the consequence would follow that it performs or does not perform an effect depending on the completeness or deficiency of the causal complex. Moreover, specifically, a permanent object might perform an action when the causal complex is present, but the final moment does not, because it is absolutely non-existent.
Furthermore, the very occurrence of an entity in some way when its auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) are present is the defining characteristic of existence;
therefore, scripture is not capable of subverting this through reasoning, because the necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.

The meaning is that the cause which produces an effect is simply the totality (*sāmagrī*), the completeness of the efficient causes (*upādāna-hetu*) and auxiliary causes that are capable of producing the qualities of the effect; it is not that one among those [causes] is the cause.
The opponent considers that the final moment is singular;
the word "yadi" (if) indicates his intention.
He recites the following reply, beginning with "śaktimān" (the possessor of power), and so forth.

A potent entity—one that is always capable and eternal, whether it be the self or something else—produces effects upon encountering the causal totality (*sāmagrī*). What is meant by this? Just as a momentary thing, though capable in its final state, does not produce effects due to the absence of the causal totality, yet produces them at other times because of its presence, so too an eternal thing, though always capable, produces [the effect] only at the time of the causal totality and not otherwise; thus it is the producer of the effect.

In order to explain the verse beginning with "not causal efficiency" (*nārthakriyā*) at the penultimate moment and so forth, he says: "Causal efficiency"—that is, the existence of an effect—when it ceases, does not cause the existence of the thing itself to cease, because the latter is not pervaded by the former; such is the meaning.

Furthermore, regarding its capacity (*sāmarthya*)—that is, its excellence (*sauṣṭhava*)—if it is asked: "Since the final moment possesses [this] capacity, why does it not produce the effect? He replies: "Because of the deficiency of the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaikalyāt*), that is, due to the absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāripratyaya*).
If it is further asked: "How is it known that [the capacity] exists even when the effect is not produced? He replies: "[It is known because it is] capable," and so forth.

In this context, that which has performed the action is understood as "capable," because anything else is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, due to the similarity of some aspect existing in both cases, worldly people distinguish [the capable] from another thing that is also capable by virtue of its similarity to the one that has performed the action of dying.
To this, he provides the following answer: "This is incorrect."

Why? He says: because there would follow the consequence that even for an eternal entity—not only for a momentary one—there would be the production or non-production of an effect depending on the completeness or incompleteness of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
In what being present? He says: "even when its capacity (*sāmarthya*) exists.
When? He says: "at all times" (*sarvadā*).
He also demonstrates the distinction of this [final moment] from the preceding ones by means of the words "especially" (*viśeṣataḥ*) and so forth.

"Distinction" (*viśeṣaḥ*) means that, compared to that [preceding] moment, there is an excellence (*atiśaya*). Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of this excellence, he says that even an eternal entity (*nityo'rthaḥ*) acts; not only does it not fail to act, but what kind of [entity] is it? He says: "from its possibility" (*saṃbhavāt*), meaning the presence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī-sannidhiḥ*).

"Because of its occurrence, there is the presence of a causal complex for it"— by this word "occurrence," he demonstrates that even though nothing at all is produced by the auxiliary for it, nevertheless, it occurs together with it because they perform the effect simultaneously, just as in the case of the theory of momentariness;
such is the meaning regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Even the substantial existence of a thing is poison because of its substantial existence.

If it is argued that the final moment also acts in that same way, and thus there is no distinction between this [final moment] and others, the author replies: "But not even the final moment acts"—this is the connection.
Why? He says: "In every respect," meaning in its entirety, and not because it is absent at the time of the effect's production;

for that which is non-existent does not exert itself toward the arising of an effect. Otherwise, one might suspect that even from a long-dead person, there would be the direct production of breath and so forth in the body; consequently, even by virtue of being a continuum of mental moments, the living body would lack a self (ātman).

If, on the other hand, it is maintained that the eternal cause performs its function at its own [specific] time, even that is not tenable; because, although it was previously capable, if the effect does not subsequently exist, there is no negation of the nature of the eternal object. Likewise, since the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender is not prevented, it follows by this that its operation does not extend to anything else either; thus, what was "stuck" to the opponent's position regarding the eternal has been refuted.

Even in that case, since the effect arises according to the gathering of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) despite the prior existence of capacity, surely no entity—whether the final moment or any other—is observed to produce an effect while persisting for more than a single moment; certainly not an eternal object. If it is asked, "How then is this [entity] distinguished from that [eternal one]? he says here: "The auxiliaries," and so forth.

When a dissimilar effect arises, that which acts as a cooperative cause—whether in its presence or proximity—does not function by its own nature in every respect, but rather through some specific aspect; for it is observed that the very movement toward a subsequent form is the defining characteristic of an entity (*bhāva*), which is the true nature of the thing.

Thus, having established that the final moment of consciousness (*antya-citta-kṣaṇa*) is not a real entity, it has been well said: "The final moment of consciousness is the self," and so forth, regarding the eternal.

It might be thought that the statement "it exists" (sannivāva) here is redundant; for according to your own scripture, the self is non-agent, devoid of qualities, pure, and an enjoyer. To deny that very [self] would contradict the scripture. Nor can the scripture be set aside by this reasoning, because their subject matters are different.
As it has been said:

This [self] has been extracted: "In the Sāṃkhya system, the self is formless, conscious, an enjoyer, eternal, all-pervading, inactive, a non-agent, devoid of qualities, and subtle" (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
"In the Sāṃkhya system, the self is a non-agent, devoid of qualities, and an enjoyer" (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, Bṛhatī-vṛtti, p. 41;
Sūtrakṛtāṅga-ṭīkā, p. 21).
The non-agent, devoid of qualities, pure—*Nyāyakumuda*, p. 112; *Yaśastilaka Upaniṣad*, p. 250:
"The non-agent, devoid of qualities, pure, eternal, omnipresent, and inactive."
In the teaching of Kapila, the Self is formless, conscious, and the enjoyer—*Ātmānuśāsana*, verse 137.
For comparison: "And because of this [nature's] reversal, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established."
Isolation, neutrality, the state of being a witness, and the state of non-agency—
[these belong to him] whose [nature], beyond the senses and imperceptible, is seen by the final prophetic eye. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 19)
"Those entities which are not sublated by inference," *Vākyapadīya* 1.38.
And it has been said by Bhartṛhari—*Sanmati-Ṭīkā*, p.
753: Regarding this, he says "that is not so," and so forth.

That scripture (*āgama*) which propounds a self that is non-substantial and unchanging is not capable of subverting or refuting the reasoning just mentioned; rather, that very reasoning is capable of subverting it, because its scope remains unimpeded even with respect to supersensible matters.

Or if it is thought that, since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished, how else could inference (*anumāna*) proceed? In that case, the scripture is capable of subverting such a conception of the self only when it is presented in that specific manner, not by its mere existence, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, that scripture does not produce the cognition of the self in the primary non-conscious *pradhāna*, just as it does not do so in jars and the like.

Nor does it nourish any purpose [to speak] of a person who is devoid of such modification and is beyond perception, even though he exists; for if [the self] were known through one's own consciousness, then since it is established for all individuals by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what would the scripture accomplish? Furthermore, there can be no delusion regarding that which is changeless, which is what reasoning removes.
This is because of the nature of reasoning itself.
Practice is an error;
by this it is established that even though the non-duality of the Self is negated, the scripture is not capable of subverting it.
Therefore, the established position is as follows: [the objection] beginning with "that is not so" and so forth is a refutation by means of reasoning.

Now, if activity in some sense is indeed the defining characteristic of an existent (*bhāva*), and that [activity] exists in the *pradhāna*, then it is a real entity; consequently, the Sāṅkhya would not be refuted in an absolute manner like others. Furthermore, since there is the presence of proofs such as the "limited magnitude" (*parimāṇa*) of diverse manifestations (*bheda*) therein, even the suspicion of its non-existence is not logical. To this, he says: "In the statement 'the *pradhāna* exists,' etc."
The evolution of subsequent stages occurs because of the finite measure of distinct entities, their commonality, their activity due to potency,
the distinction between cause and effect, and the non-separation of the manifold universe.
— Sāṃkhyakārikā 15.
Regarding the doubt concerning the absence of proof for the claim "Pradhāna exists," there are [arguments] such as the persistence (anvaya) of differences and so forth.
Otherwise, they would arise in a manner entirely different [from what is intended], like the properties of an entity in isolation (ekānta-bhāvadharma).

If it is to be proven that diverse things (bhedāḥ) are preceded by a single cause, [the argument] is indeed contradictory—just like [proving] permanence and so forth—because of the existence of a cause for the manifold nature (vaiśvarūpya); for it is only the transformation of the causes of the manifold nature and so forth that is possible, since a single self (ātman), being of a single nature, cannot itself be admitted to possess a manifold nature.

Since there is no contradiction in the production of modifications—which possess the nature of both the universal and the particular—in accordance with their own inherent nature, it is certainly not the case that even when the cause is expressed as a universal, the conscious power (*cicchakti*) acts as a cooperative cause, because it is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*).
[Objection: If this were so, it would follow that everything else is non-existent.

Regarding the thesis that "Pradhāna exists," the reasons stated by the opponent—such as "concomitance" (anvaya), which is the following along [of effects], and those beginning with "limited magnitude" (parimāṇa) and so forth, of which this is the first—what are they like? He says: they would be established only in the manner of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), and not even slightly in the manner of its presence; therefore, they are not "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), but rather precisely "contradictory" (*viruddha*). This is the meaning of the particle *eva* ("precisely").

Regarding this, he states an example: when the one-sided positions of eternalism or momentariness are to be proven (*sādhya*), [the reason] exists like a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*). Here, "entity" (*bhāva*) means existence (*sattva*); this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which [qualities] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) are included. Because it is dependent on another, it is "similar to that," i.e., it exists as a property. Thus, since the Sāṅkhya has demonstrated the existence of the subject (*dharmin*)—namely, that "the Omniscient One himself exists"—he has not pointed out a fault in the proof of that [subject], because it is favorable to the establishment of his own position; rather, he has merely revealed its contradictory nature (*viruddhatā*).
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "If [the world] were preceded by a single cause," and so forth.

"Single" means unique, without a second; that which is the cause called *pradhāna*—if it is to be proven that [the world] is preceded by that, meaning caused by that, of what things? Of the "diversities," namely *mahat* and the others.

Now, an objection is raised: in the *kārikā*, "Pradhāna exists" is stated as one thing to be proven (*sādhya*), whereas in the *vṛtti*, the fact that differences have a single cause as their antecedent is stated as something else. How, then, is there consistency between the *vṛtti* and the *sūtra*? If it is argued that the *vṛtti* must conform to the *sūtra*, some here offer this resolution: because the fallacies of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) are seen when attempting to prove the existence of the subject Pradhāna through properties belonging to existence, non-existence, or both, they claim that such a statement [in the *vṛtti*] was made precisely to demonstrate that even if another such probandum were formulated, the fault of contradiction would still persist. By them, the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even in the case of having a single cause as antecedent" (*ekakāraṇapūrvakatve*) is to be understood; for it is not only in the case of "Pradhāna exists" that [the reason is] contradictory, but also in the case of its being preceded by that [single cause]. This is so that the meaning may be understood accordingly. Furthermore, in the *sūtra* itself, the phrase "Pradhāna exists" should be explained as a mere illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Otherwise, how could the inconsistency between them be avoided?
The commentators [state]:
with respect to a subject consisting of a primary essence (*pradhāna*),
[the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) when proving existence, contradictory (*viruddha*) when proving non-existence, and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when proving both properties.
A property of existence does not exist in what is unestablished; a property based on both [existence and non-existence] is inconclusive;
and a property of non-existence is contradictory. How, then, can that "being" (sattā) be proven? — *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.186.

This is another explanation: "the single cause" (*ekakāraṇam*) is a designation for *pradhāna* (primordial matter) having the sense of "another" (*aparama*). And because that [cause] exists prior to the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the others, it is "prior" (*pūrvaka*). Thus, when its existence—that is, its reality—is to be established, the term "of the differences" (*bhedānām*) from the previous explanation is to be connected here as well, just as before.

Since, in this very subsequent [section], the various differentiated entities such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest constitute the cause of manifoldness (vaiśvarūpya), one might object that they are indeed contradictory.
To provide an illustration for this, he asks: "How can there be 'eternal' and so forth? He replies: "Because transformation (pariṇāma) alone is possible."

"Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the modification of a substance through its own qualities and modes, not through the qualities and modes of another, because [modification] occurs only therein; this applies to the various forms, effects, causes, and so forth. This is the connection, with the case ending changed [to the genitive]. Why is this so? To this he says: "of the causes of the universal form and so forth. Here, "form and so forth" refers to taste and the rest. "Universal" (*viśva*) means without exception. It is not "partial," like the form and so forth of the causes accepted by the Naiyāyikas, such as the substance *pudgala*. According to their view, "pudgalas possess color, taste, smell, and touch" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.24).
Because of this statement, [the phrase] "since only transformation is possible for those causes such as Viśvarūpa" is understood to follow.
What is meant is this:

that which has no other, second thing beyond it—its state is *aparamatva* (the state of having nothing superior); that which has this as its meaning is *aparamatvārthaka*. The sense is that the Pradhāna is one alone, not a second.

Just as in the system of the Naiyāyikas, taste and smell are not admitted in fire, smell is not admitted in water, and color, taste, and smell are not admitted in air, so too here there is no deficiency; for *pudgalas* possess touch, taste, smell, and color—according to the *Tattvārthasūtra*: "From primordial nature (*prakṛti*) comes the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the I-principle (*ahaṅkāra*); from that, the group of sixteen."

Therefore, based on the statement in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (Kārikā 21), "From that group of sixteen, five [arise] as the five elements," it must be stated as follows: just as the elements possess form and other qualities, so too do their causes, which are designated as the five *tanmātras*; this applies up to *prakṛti*, because an effect cannot arise from something of a different genus (*vijātīya*).

By the phrase "of the causes," he demonstrates the plurality of the *pradhāna*—which has another name, *pudgala*—in relation to its specific manifestations. Why is this so? To this he says: "by itself, of the one," and so forth.
This refers to the non-acceptance by the Sāṃkhya himself of that which is called "the universe," namely, an effect such as earth and so on, which possesses a complete form and the like.
To whom does it belong? He says: "Of the self, that is, the person.
Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates an alternative position.
Of what nature is it? He says: "Of that which has a single nature."

He thinks as follows: "Of one whose nature is characterized by consciousness (*cetanā*) and not by characteristics such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth"—just as for a person who is devoid of form and the like, there is no effect consisting of form and the like, so too for another [principle] that is essentially nothing but a person, this [consciousness] belongs to the person alone; what then is the use of postulating a separate reality?
Furthermore, of what kind [of being]? To this he says: "of one," meaning of that which is endowed with the number one.

The intended meaning here is this: just as it is illogical for that [Pradhāna] to have multiple effects consisting of form and so forth—which are distinct in terms of place, time, and nature—so too it is illogical for a single Pradhāna [to produce such diversity].
Furthermore, demonstrating that the production of the various forms of the universe and so forth is possible only in that [Pradhāna], he says "of the modifications" and so on;
[this refers] to the modifications, which are specific effects, and not to the unchanging Pradhāna.
Of what nature are they? [They are] "of the nature of both the universal and the particular.

What of them? To this he says: "Their own-nature," and so forth. The connection is as follows: because there is no contradiction in the arising of another modification corresponding to that which is their own-nature (svarūpa)—that is, their essential character—therefore they are possible in that very state.
That is not correct—
for the subtle elements (tanmātras), namely form, taste, smell, touch, and sound,
are the fundamental causes.
In relation to its effects, everything that is an effect— consisting of the Great One (mahat) and so forth— is called Pradhāna.
The activity of the Puruṣa consists of the transformations.
"Root nature is not a modification" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3.22), and so forth...
"The seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both natures and modifications;
the group of sixteen is only modification; the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification."
This is the remainder [of the argument].

Now, one might ask: "In the absence of a fundamental cause (*mūlakāraṇa*), from what do those transformations arise? [The answer is: Because of the beginningless contradiction that "those [arise] from other transformations, and those [in turn] from others," they are possible precisely within that [process]; thus, that succession pertains to the sphere of relations. This is not the Sāṃkhya view of realization that has been stated—namely, the absolute [view of] permanence, momentariness, existence, origination, and so forth. That is not tenable, because that [Sāṃkhya position] is unestablished.

For he maintains that when "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth are adduced as a reason to prove the absolute permanence of a thing, there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because existence is present in the Great One (*mahat*) and other evolutes which are subject to transformation—just as it is in the permanent Puruṣa. Furthermore, even if [the reason] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) were present there, it would be partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*) because it does not exist in either Prakṛti or Puruṣa.

On the other hand, when momentariness is being proved for everything, since existence is present in the permanent Puruṣa, that same fallacy of deviation applies; likewise, "being produced" and the like remain partially unestablished and are not contradictory (*viruddha*).

Now, if both of those [properties] are established as belonging to *pradhāna* alone, then there would be a contradiction for [the reason] "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, since these exist only in *pradhāna* and the like which are subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*); however, this is not the case for "existence" (*sattva*), because it exists even in the eternal *puruṣa*.
The reading enclosed within these marks was written twice;
here, "not" (*na*) is redundant.
Now, [it might be argued that] these defects do not apply because the Puruṣa is also subject to transformation; to this, he says: "Not at all," and so forth.
Indeed, even when the term "cause" is used in its general sense, a transforming cause is not what is intended here.
Why? Because of the power of consciousness (cicchakti). (Yogabhāṣya 1.45)
Because of this statement, the self (*ātman*) is not a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), since that power is non-different from it.
Therefore, the meaning is this: the self is by no means a transformative cause (*pariṇāmika-kāraṇa*) of the power of consciousness, which is the capacity in the form of sentience.

"Why? he says: "Because of its non-transformability," that is, because the self is devoid of transformation; this is the connection [of the reason] through a change in case-ending (*vibhaktipariṇāma*).

Thus, the follower of Kapila (*kāpila*) maintains that existence (*sattva*) and so forth are contradictory to the thesis when the absolute [positions] of eternalism or momentariness are to be proven, but rather [they are contradictory] as previously stated.
The Teacher, refuting this, says: "But if it were so," and so forth.

The word "nanu" is used for the sake of inquiry. The sense is: if it were as stated—that is, if [the Self] were not the cause [of cognition]—then the consequence would follow that the existence of the Self would be [impossible]; this is the connection.
But this is not the case. Therefore, by one who desires its existence, its capacity for transformation must be admitted; thus, how can the illustrative example be considered unestablished?

This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the power of consciousness (citiśakti) is unchanging, non-transmigrating, does not manifest objects [by itself], is pure, infinite, and consists of the quality of sattva.
— Yogabhāṣya: of the self, of the self.
If it is argued that the self (ātman) is therefore the cause of that power, the author replies here with the verse beginning "buddhyā" and so forth:

"If the power of consciousness (cicchakti) were to arise from the person (pums) by itself regarding what has been determined by the intellect (buddhi), then why would cognition and the rest not belong to the conscious being alone, since they are its very functions? (21)

The transformation of consciousness (*cetanā*)—characterized by its manifold nature (*vaiśvarūpya*) and so forth—is established, because no activity of consciousness is perceived apart from pleasure and the like.

Therefore, the power of vision (*darśana-śakti*) is independent of any external effect, just like the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the intellect (*buddhi*); for it is the Self (*puruṣa*) that perceives the object as determined by the intellect, since both possess the possibility of manifold nature and so forth. Why then would the unchanging power of consciousness conform to the transformations of the intellect?

"Through such a process as 'the senses perceive the object once it has been determined by the intellect,' the *puruṣa*'s power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—which is the capacity for that perception—possesses the forms of objects grasped [by the senses] inherently and not from another source. By connecting this with the singular form obtained through the word *vṛttiḥ* (understanding it as 'the modification'), there is a connection with the phrase 'it would be so' (*tathā syuḥ*), where the singular form is likewise obtained. Thus, the word *syāt* means 'if it were to be so. Here, he states the refutation of the opponent's position, beginning with the words 'knowledge and so forth' (*jñānādayaḥ*)."

Those things of which knowledge is the first—namely pleasure and so forth—are thus described. How could they not be? They are indeed the modifications (*vṛtti*) or transformations (*pariṇāma*) of the conscious principle alone, the *puruṣa*. This is what they [the Sāṃkhyas] maintain: just as the various distinctions such as omniformity (*vaiśvarūpya*) and others do not have a single cause, otherwise, like the body and so forth, there would have to be some other single cause for the *puruṣas* as well, who would then be subject to transformation; such is the Sāṃkhya view. The same applies to the various distinctions such as jars and so forth.
[Thus it is said: "The senses perceive the object, the intellect (*buddhi*) determines it, the mind (*manas*) wills it, and the self (*ātman*) is conscious of it."

In this way, the sequential functioning of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the eye (*cakṣus*) is observed: the eye sees the form, the mind conceives, the ego identifies, and the intellect determines.
To explain the verse [from the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*], he says: "Of the conscious one," and so forth. (Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti, p. 47)

From what is the transformation of consciousness established? To this he says: "from its manifold nature" (*vaiśvarūpyāt*), by which the word "etc. includes the relationship of cause and effect and so forth.

Why is this so? To this he says: because no activity of consciousness—that is, no transformation of consciousness—is perceived apart from pleasure and the like; rather, the meaning is that each such activity is perceived as being of the very nature of pleasure and so forth.

Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, by the immediately preceding reasoning, [the author] states that it is not from the power of perception of the elements," beginning with the words "kārye" (in the effect), and so forth.
This word "kārya" (effect) has the state of being as its primary meaning; the sense is that, regardless of the specific object being an effect, it is indeed an effect.
Here he provides an illustration: "like the determination of the intellect."
The determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is the ascertainment of both self and other—is like that [determination];

just as that determination does not depend upon being an effect (*kāryatva*), so too its capacity (*tacchakti*) does not depend upon being an effect. Since the eternal person (*puruṣa*) perceives—that is, sees—the object determined by the intellect because of that capacity (or, in response to the objection: "because he perceives"), in the absence of that [capacity], he would not perceive at all.

That is not correct; for it has been extracted from the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (verse 50, page 50) that "the Puruṣa is neither nature (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*)," [as stated] in Sāṃkhyakārikā 11, regarding the function of consciousness (*caitanyavṛtti*).
Āptaparīkṣā, p. 164; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
100; Nyāyakumudacandra, p. 190.
The cause is [found] on page 235 of the Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa-prakaraṇa and on page 233 of the Syādvādaratnākara.

If the effect is indeed the determination by the intellect (*buddhy-adhyavasāya*), then since that [determination] does not exist in something independent of being an effect, what has happened to its capacity (*tacchakti*) such that it too would belong to that [effect]? If it is argued that "the property of one is not necessarily the property of another," to this he replies:
"Because of the possibility of manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya*)," and so forth; he considers this according to the stated principle.

To whom do these belong? He says: "Of both"—namely, of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*) and the determination of the intellect (*buddhy-adhyavasāya*). Even though there are distinctions between them, [the Self] eternally perceives the object as determined by the intellect.

And by one who speaks thus, it must be admitted that the person (*puruṣa*), like the intellect (*buddhi*), assumes the form of the object; otherwise, even if devoid of form, he would perceive an external object independent of the intellect—so what is the use of postulating the intellect? If it is maintained that the person also possesses that form, to this he replies: "From what [reasoning]? For from no reasoning whatsoever does the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi-vivarta*) conform to—that is, imitate—the modification of the intellect into the form of the object.
What is it [that imitates]? He says: "The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
Of what nature is it? He says: "Unchanging (*apariṇāminī*)."
The sense is that, by conforming to that [object], it would become subject to transformation like a mirror or similar objects; thus,
the Puruṣa is also the power of consciousness.
This is another explanation: for what reason is it that she, though unchanging (*apariṇāminī*), nevertheless conforms to that transformation? Here the word "even" (*api*) is to be understood;

[the sense is: if she conforms to the object by herself, then for that very reason she would conform to the object through its infinite transformations, and thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) within that [process]. This is what is being considered.

Likewise, there is this further point: how could the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is unchanging and eternally of one form, conform to the transformations of the intellect (*buddhi*)—namely, the successive or simultaneous transformations consisting of the reflections of various objects such as blue or states such as pleasure? It cannot be identical [to them], for it would not be similar to them due to contradiction;
for instance, if it were always of one form, then it could not follow the transformations of the intellect; and if it follows those transformations, it is not of one form.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the subject to apprehend the object without a multiplicity of powers to apprehend it, as is the case with the multiplicity of objects; the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that [if there were no such multiplicity], a single nature would not be able to produce multiple effects, just as [the argument] has been explained.
Thus, it would not be manifold.
If the power of consciousness (cicchakti) conforms to the transformations of the intellect (buddhi),
it is the apprehension of objects.
Since it has been established in this way that knowledge and the rest are indeed the functions (vṛtti) of that very [Self], he says— beginning with "knowledge"— to show what is thereby obtained:
knowledge and so forth belong to the non-living, embodied [entity] which is distinct [from the Self].
"Knowledge is either false for the soul, or it is manifold and thus non-self.

[The opponent] asserts a distinction fabricated by themselves—claiming that knowledge is a "modification" (*vṛtti*) of the insentient and "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) of the sentient—because no specific difference is perceived and because such a view leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Likewise, the other [opponent] asserts that for a substance which is inherently devoid of consciousness, consciousness is a distinct quality (*guṇa*) arising from a connection [with the self].

Even if [the soul] exists substantially, since that [consciousness] is absent, how could an ignorant being be called conscious? For if consciousness were a separate entity, it would lead to an over-extension;
likewise, the views that consciousness is material or that knowledge is non-self are false perspectives.

The mention of "knowledge and so forth" (*jñānādi*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of pleasure and the rest; therefore, knowledge and the like constitute the modification (*vṛtti*) of the non-living (*ajīva*), the insentient *pradhāna*.

Of what nature is this [non-living]? It is "embodied" (*mūrta*), meaning possessing form and other qualities. That which is knowledge is false, according to the reasoning and statements already explained. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "of the living being" (*jīvasya*), and so forth.
Alternatively, the word "iva" (as if), which will be mentioned later, should also be connected here;
from that, this meaning results: of what kind is the soul, the self? Of one that is "vyatirekin"—absolutely distinct from cognition.

The qualification "of that which has form" (*mūrttasya*) is not connected here because it is impossible; for the opponent admits that even such a self (*ātman*) is formless (*amūrta*). [In this context,] "cognition" (*jñāna*) refers to a function (*vṛtti*);
thus, just as the cognition under discussion is false, one might ask:
"In what way is this also false? To this he says: "devoid of self-nature" (*anātmakam*).

That which has no self is "selfless" (*anātmaka*); thus, the knowledge that "knowledge is [the property] of the self" is false. Just as that [notion] is false, so too is the knowledge that "knowledge is a function (*vṛtti*) belonging to a soul (*jīva*) distinct [from it]" false.

This is what is meant: just as knowledge consisting of something other [than the self] is without a substratum and cannot be the quality of anything, so too [knowledge] would not be a quality of a distinct [soul], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that it is indeed a quality of the self due to inherence (*samavāya*) therein, we say no; for since inherence is without distinction, there would be no distinction [in the relation], and furthermore, inherence lacks existence due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If that [subsequent cognition] were a quality (*guṇa*) of that [preceding one] because it arises from it—such that each subsequent cognition is a quality of each preceding momentary cognition—then the proof of another substratum (*guṇin*) distinct from it would be entirely out of place.

Furthermore, just as it is difficult to establish the causality of a momentary entity when it performs its effect at the very time of its own existence (since this would result in the simultaneity of cause and effect), so too is it for a non-momentary entity. This is because, due to the qualification by the time of the effect, if the preceding and succeeding forms are in every respect non-different from that [non-momentary] nature, then that [entity] consists of nothing more than those [forms].

Or rather, just as it is difficult to establish that [the cause] performs that [action] at the time of its own existence because it is itself non-existent at the time of the effect, so too is it for the other [the effect], because the subsequent is in every way non-different from the preceding form characterized by prior time; otherwise, there would be nothing at all, not even a single thing.
Furthermore, there is no simultaneous pervasion of multiple places and times by another self, because of its partlessness (*niraṃśatva*), like a mind devoid of self-nature.
Thus he states the conclusion: "or manifold"—the phrase "false cognition" (*mithyājñāna*) is understood to follow.
It is entirely distinct from the Sāṃkhya [system],
because it lacks any substratum.
Because the object is one and the same for all, there is no distinction among them.
If inherence were a quality of the self.
The Buddhist replied: "From its own nature,
there is [the relation] between that which exists in the preceding moment and the nature existing in the succeeding moment."
The connection is that causality is difficult to establish in the absence of difference; [thus] the effect belongs to the momentary.
Causality belongs even to the eternal by virtue of its own nature.
The connection [of the sentence] is that causality is difficult to establish because of its uniform nature (*ekarūpatva*).
Even if there is non-difference, he states the meaning of the verse— namely, "the activity of the insentient," and so forth— in order to explain how unity might be absent despite such non-difference.

What is the function (*vṛtti*) of the insentient instrument (*karaṇa*), which is transformation (*pariṇāma*)? [The Sāṃkhya says: "Knowledge" for the sentient person (*puruṣa*), and "perception" (*upalabdhi*) or "vision" (*darśana*) is the function. Why does the Sāṃkhya state such a distinction—which is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is thus unfamiliar? He says: because no difference is perceived between the specific qualities of knowledge and perception.

If it is argued that this reason is inconclusive because there is a distinction between a glowing iron ball and fire even when no difference is perceived, [the author] replies here: "Because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), for it would follow that there is also a distinction between the person and consciousness.

It could be said that consciousness is indeed different from the person, and that the determination of non-difference arises from their conjunction—just as there is no actual difference between the iron ball and the fire.
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇe).
He states that the conceptualization of difference was merely self-contrived due to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

thus, for one who maintains the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavādin*), no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) is established. Demonstrating this over-extension because the iron ball undergoes such a transformation, he says "in the same way," and so forth.

Just as the Sāṃkhya proponent states the difference between intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness (*caitanya*) by means of his own specific method, so too does another, the Yauga (Yoga), [state it] regarding substance (*dravya*).

Although the term used is general, it is understood from the context to refer to the "self" (*ātman*). He asserts that for one who is inherently devoid of consciousness by its very nature—that is, for the insentient—there exists a distinct quality (*guṇa*) that is a separate entity (*arthāntarabhūta*); this is not to be accepted as a valid view.

Why? He says: because of "sambandha," that is, inherence (*samavāya*). And thus, just like cognition, consciousness (*caitanya*) is not the nature (*rūpa*) of the person (*puruṣa*); therefore, this [claim]—"consciousness is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the person" (Yoga-bhāṣya 1.9)—is not logical.
This is what the Jainas and others believe.

Because it undergoes transformation into fire through contact with fire, he asks: "Why is it said 'in that way' (tathā)? For by the force of what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do I declare all this?

To this, he replies: "Even though there exists a relation between the substance and consciousness—which are absolutely distinct—in the form of inherence (*samavāya*"; here the word *api* expresses possibility, because in reality, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition, that [inherence] does not exist).

Since there is no cognition such as "the whole exists in this part" when there is the appearance of different classes [of entities] both externally and internally, and because of the absence of a substratum (dharmin), inference whose object is that [substratum] does not occur;
how then could the conscious self, which is of the nature of existence, be called "conscious"? Not at all.
Why? He says: "from a different object, from consciousness distinct from that."

Why should this not be the case? He says: because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even the sky and so forth would then become conscious; thus, the status of intellect and the like as "specific qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇa*) and the enumeration of substances as "nine" would be undermined, since their connection [to consciousness] is universal and thus indistinguishable even in those cases.

If it is claimed that despite the lack of distinction in the connection, a distinction between the two related entities is intended—this is not so, because it would result in the connection being rendered purposeless.

For by whatever proximity that distinction is desired despite the lack of distinction in the connection, by that very same [proximity], there would be no fixed rule for the designation "this belongs to that."
The Naiyāyika [maintains that] because consciousness is distinct [from the body],
color, taste, smell, touch, natural fluidity, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are the specific qualities (vaiśeṣikaguṇa).
—Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 39.
In that regard, the substances—earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind—are said to be exactly nine by the designation of "generality" and "particularity"—Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 3.
Because volition (cetanā) inheres [in the self] even in space, despite the lack of distinction in the relation [between the two].
A distinction between the two related entities is admitted;
what then is the use of postulating a relation?
Furthermore, if consciousness were perceived in the self alone, that would be logical; however, this is not the case, for there is no perception of such a self.
Nevertheless, if one were to postulate that [consciousness] exists there [in the object], let it exist elsewhere as well, since there is no distinction;

or alternatively: this word "object" (*artha*) refers to objects such as jars and the like. Therefore, if something other than that [object]—being distinct from it by its very nature and thus graspable by a separate cognition—were to become another object (*viṣayāntara*), how could that which is itself insentient (*ajña*) be called conscious (*cetana*)? Why? He says: because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for even in the case of a connection with effort (*prayatna*) and so forth, it would have to be considered conscious.

Now, since cognition consists in the apprehension of an object, it is conscious only through its connection with that [object], not through a connection with anything else, because such a connection would be of a contrary nature. It has already been stated that if there were no apprehension of itself, the apprehension of the object would also be impossible, just as in the case of a jar or similar things; thus, [consciousness] is something distinct from the self.
Because, due to the very inherence of the knowledge of another's qualities, there is an absence of the intrinsic nature of grasping an object.
Showing once again the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of knowledge according to the Sāṃkhya, he says: "In that way, moreover," and so forth.

In that way—by that method of Sāṃkhya conceptualization—and furthermore, after the conceptualization of the Sāṃkhyas and others, there would be the knowledge of consciousness (*caitanya*) as something corporeal (*mūrta*), such as the fourfold [elements] beginning with earth; by this, the opinion of the Paurandaras is demonstrated.
Alternatively, there is the view that "the Person alone is all this," as stated in Ṛgveda 10.90.2 and elsewhere.

Alternatively, in this context, "of the embodied" (*mūrttasya*) should not be connected with "one's own view" (*svadarśanam*). It should not be said that the occasional incorporeality (*amūrttatva*) of the Jaina conscious being is irrelevant here; rather, it refers to the other, the insentient (*acetana*), such as the earth and so forth, which are corporeal. By this, the system of Aviddhakarṇa is shown. Furthermore, while the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is already present [in the compound], its repetition is for the sake of indicating an immediate connection—that it is separated by nothing else—so that it may be connected here as well: "cognition is non-self (*anātmaka*), meaning devoid of a self (*ātmaśūnya*)."

The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction; thus, this being the case, the remainder [of the meaning] is that false views are connected with those who propound extremist doctrines (*ekāntavādin*).

Although the systems of the *Yaugas* and others have already been mentioned, they are presented again immediately after the system of the *Kāpilas* for the purpose of demonstrating the excessive extension (*atiprasaṅga*) therein, [specifically] regarding that which is characterized by consciousness (*caitanya-viśiṣṭa*).
The Jaina perspective regarding the Cārvāka [position] during the state of being bound by karma.
