Now, as for what was stated in the very first verse of this same section—namely, that "false cognition [arises] from the manifestation of an obscuration belonging to the knower who exists by his own nature," and so forth—that is incorrect. For there can be no connection between the formless self and that which is considered an obscuration, which possesses form, just as there is none with a liberated self;
nor can there be an obscuration that is unconnected, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
He states this very point in the words beginning with "How? and so forth.
[Page 321] If it is asked: "How, moreover, can there be a connection with action for that which is formless?"
A ruby or similar gem is certainly not a material form that serves as the cause for its association with impurities.
Likewise, the soul, though formless by nature, becomes bound by impurities due to its own defects.
Even if one were to imagine a material form for the soul, another internal defect must be postulated as the cause of its bondage by karma, just as in the case of a ruby.

Furthermore, how can there be natural causes of bondage—such as false view (*mithyādarśana*) and so forth—for that which is formless and conscious? Moreover, how can there be a connection between that which is formless and matter (*karman*), which is corporeal?
If it is asked, "Is it not true that 'by means of the corporeal' is not explicitly heard here; how then is it obtained? [the answer is: from the statement "of that which is formless."

If action (*karman*) were also formless (*amūrta*), then that statement [of the Sūtra] would be meaningless; for there is no contradiction in the conjunction of two formless things, and because of the expression "by means of action" (*karmaṇā*), it is impossible for anything else to possess the nature of action.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the conjunction of the corporeal and the incorporeal; therefore, [the Sūtra] is stated because it is relevant to the context.
The word "if" (*ced*) indicates the intention of the opponent;
here he states the reply: "by impurities, by nature"—this is a statement regarding the formless.

If it is asked: "Has this not already been established by the passage beginning with 'avidyādeḥ nanvetat parasparavilakṣaṇāv api', and has the cause of that bondage also been stated by the passage beginning with 'śubhaiḥ'? Why, then, is it stated again? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of supporting that very point by means of another method.

For instance, even regarding the concluding statement beginning with "by means of mental, vocal, and physical actions," which no one can reasonably dispute, someone might say: "Skipping over the passage beginning with 'like the five aggregates,' [one might argue that] gold and the like are indeed corporeal (mūrta), and being observed to be connected with other corporeal things such as blackness and so forth, corporeality itself is the cause of bondage. Since that [corporeality] is absent in the Self (ātman), there is no bondage for it. To him, it is said: "By the impurities... and so forth.
It is certainly not corporeality that is the fundamental cause of bondage.
Why? He says: "A ruby (māṇikya) and the like would be bound... [if corporeality were the cause].
By what? He says: "by impurities," such as dross (*kiṭṭa*), tarnish (*kālikā*), and so forth;
the connection is with the word "embodied" (*mūrtaḥ*) by changing the case ending.
And he thinks that this is not so, because it is observed otherwise as well.
Page 254,
Page 255,
Page 255.
Because there is an absence of a formal manifestation (mūrti) through [the powers] such as Kālī and so forth,
he says here: "And another [objection] from the standpoint of defects."

Or rather, its own defect—characterized by being produced from a corrupt source and so forth—by means of that [defect], the ruby (*māṇikya*) and other such gems might be bound [with flaws]. Why? "By nature" (*nisargāt*), that is, by their very essence.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: a flawed ruby and the like are bound with [other] gems, but others are not; for it is due to their inherent nature (*svābhāvyāt*) and because they are observed to be so.
He states the answer to that: "The individual soul (jīva) is formless.

Although the word "also" (api) has been elided here, it should be understood as present; thus, the individual soul is not only [like] a ruby and so forth, but what is it like? He says: "formless," meaning its form does not exist.

Explaining the verse that describes the nature [of the soul] as being subject to impurity, he says "of the jīva," and so forth, because it is produced from a source (khāni) associated with impurities due to its own faults— namely, its inherent nature (nisarga), its disposition (svabhāva), and its personal defects such as false belief (mithyātva).

Even after postulating a form for the soul, another internal defect characterized as *bhāvakarma* (psychic karma), which serves as the cause for the bondage of *dravyakarma*, must be postulated—just as in the case of a ruby or similar object. Therefore, by that logic, he asks: "Of what [unembodied entity] are the natural causes of bondage? and answers: "Of the conscious one (*cetana*)."

Who [is the agent]? To this he says: "false view" (mithyādarśana), and so forth. Now, one might object: why postulate a connection between the formless [soul] and material karma? For even if it were formless, there would be no fault in its inherence in the qualities and so forth of that [soul]. As it has been said: "The specific quality of the self which bestows the fruit upon the agent, which is opposed to its effect, and which is born of conjunction—this is *adṛṣṭa*; *dharma* is also explained in the same way. If this is argued, he replies here: "by way of genus" (jātyā), and so forth.

When [dharma] is accepted as that which is called *adṛṣṭa*, it is a quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*), the cause of what is pleasant, beneficial, and liberation for the agent; it is supersensible (*atīndriya*), opposed to the consciousness of final bliss, and born from the conjunction of the person and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) when there is a pure intention (*abhisandhi*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 138.
If objects were distinct from the universal (jāti) by virtue of that universal being inherently existent in itself,
then why would substance not likewise be distinct from other things— namely, qualities and actions?

(23) Although the word "by the universal" (jātyā) is used in a general sense, it is understood here as referring specifically to "existence" (sattā), because of the statement "they would be [distinct]."
For objects do not exist through something else;

by what kind of thing? By that which is distinct—that is, absolutely different from substance and so forth. To the question "By what [is this difference]? he says: "Substance, quality, and action are the object (artha) in relation to substances, qualities, and actions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8).
From this statement,
"syuḥ" means they would be, or they would exist as real entities.
Why not? What is the connection with this which is about to be stated?
For that which is not of such a nature by itself does not become so through another; otherwise, things like color and so forth would likewise [become] taste and so forth.
Furthermore, the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) of objects with such a universal (*jāti*) will also be refuted in this very treatise.
"Artha" refers to substance, quality, and action— according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, [it is that which is] distinct from the possessor of form.

Furthermore, whether in the case of a grammatical formation (*vṛtti*) or a verse (*śloka*), if even the universal (*jāti*) is non-existent, how could anything non-existent become existent by means of it? For it is not the case that the son of a barren woman becomes existent by means of a garland of sky-flowers;
and if [you argue] it is by means of another universal, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If [it exists] by itself; regarding this, the opponent says: "Would the universal *jāti*, namely *sattā* (existence), be existent (*satī*) by itself, through its own nature (*ātmanā*), from objects (*arthebhyaḥ*)? This connects with the word "would be" (*syāt*) which is to be stated later.
He thinks that in the same way, objects (*arthāḥ*) themselves would also exist [by themselves].

By this, [the view that] dharma and so forth are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self is rejected, because of the absence of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*); and [the view that they are] produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga-ja*) is also rejected, because of the absence of quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*).
For there can be no conjunction in the absence of action, since this [conjunction] is preceded by that;

or rather, the Jaina demonstrates that the inference of dharma and so forth from animals and the like approaching Devadatta is untenable, because— according to the opponent's own admission— there is an absence of action in those animals.
Tranquility (śānta) is a quality of the person—
a quality of the category of quality and of the category of action— [as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 138.
[That which arises] from a pure intention born of the conjunction between a person and the internal organ— this is refuted [by Praśastapāda] on page 138 of the *Praśastabhāṣya*,
because it is preceded by action (*kriyā*).

The body and other such effects are produced by the elements impelled by the specific quality [of consciousness] belonging to Devadatta, and they are appropriated by him; for, being effects, they serve as the instruments for his enjoyment, just like a house. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī, p. 149; Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p.
Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 88)

Or, however the properties of another may be, he speaks thus to demonstrate the fault: "By means of other properties (*arthāntara*) that are absolutely distinct from substance, the substance—earth and so forth—would become white, or [possess] number and so on; and what would it become? He says: "By means of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*";

specifically, by qualities such as color and so forth, and by actions such as motion and so forth, respectively: by qualities it would be white, possess number and so on, and by actions it would be a mover and so forth."
The phrase "what [is the point]? should be connected here as well; otherwise, even the self (ātman) and so forth would [be agents], since there is no distinction.
What follows from this? He says: "devoid of action," and so on—either the possessors of qualities (guṇins) are devoid of action, or the causal factors (kārakas) are without qualities.

The occurrence [of these] through inherence (*samavāya*) is, in that very same way, difficult to follow. [The phrase] "having departed from actions" means they are "devoid of action"; this is used as an emphasis regarding speech. The connection with what has already been stated is: "the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, which are the substrates (*guṇin*) or substances (*dravya*), would exist even without all their qualities (*guṇa*). It is thought that they would thus remain entirely unconnected to one another.

[Objection: "But this is not a fault, because although there is a difference between the universal and its possessor, the quality and its possessor, and the action and its possessor, the universal and so forth reside in their possessors by way of inherence (*samavāya*). [Reply: To this he says: Is it that inherence itself does not reside [in its own substrata] by means of inherence? It does not reside at all, or else its residence is defective; for if inherence were to reside in its inherent substrata (*samavāyin*) by means of another inherence, the cognition "inherence resides here" would have to be based on yet another relation. If that too were based on another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Otherwise, even the cognition "the cloth is in the threads" and so forth would not be a proof for inherence, as it would be subject to the same deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

If [the universal] does not reside in them, then no entity whatsoever could have a relation [to it], because it would be independent [of its locus], like space. For this very reason, its being the agent of the notion "here" (ihapratyaya) is likewise difficult to maintain, just as in the case of space; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that this would apply even to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) despite the absence of a relation. Thus, what is proclaimed by the Vaiśeṣikas is contradicted by reasoning and is therefore meaningless.
In the case of substances and so forth, there is another relation; here, among inherent things, it is by the very cognition "this is inherence" [that it is known].
If there were no relation of inherence among the inherent entities, or [if there were no relation] of inherence itself.
It should be understood that the objection regarding the consequence of [the karma] being a relation—
even in the absence of a relation with its own correlates—
is refuted by this [statement], as well as the claim that it is contrary to the effect yet bestows the fruit upon the agent.
The meaning is that its effect— consisting of results such as pleasure and pain— is contradictory [to its own existence],
for it is understood that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) perishes after having produced its own effect.
It should be understood as "dharma"—[see page 308, note 3]. (Note:
Although there is a reference to a footnote in the book, the corresponding footnote is not present.)
Thus ends the Fourth Chapter, the Proof of the Soul (*jīvasiddhi*), in the *Siddhivinischaya-ṭīkā* composed by the bee at the lotus-feet of the venerable Vibhadra, Anantavīrya.
The Fifth Chapter: The Proof of Debate (*vādasiddhi*).
Thus, by means of the two preceding topics, the hearing of recollection and so forth, which is the application of the wordless, has been explained.

It was stated previously that "that which is joined with words other than [the subject] has been heard"; the occasion for explaining that has now arrived. And since that [hearing] is for the sake of another (*parārtha*), some proponents of extremist doctrines (*ekāntavādin*) are observed to attempt to join even a proponent of logic (*nyāyavādin*) with defeat under the pretext of censuring his speech when he employs such [words] for the purpose of communicating to another. To refute this, the author introduces the *Vādanyāya* and states at its outset the summary verse beginning with "by the establishment of the thesis" (*pakṣasthāpanayā*), etc., regarding what is heard when the employment of words must be performed.

One does not defeat an opponent in a formal debate (vāda) by refuting their position when the subject matter has already been discarded; for one who has established their own thesis through the statement of reasons and the pointing out of faults in the opponent's arguments, yet remains silent once the subject matter has been refuted, cannot be defeated by such means.

Or if he speaks something else, he is equal to his opponent in failing to achieve his own purpose. The "proposition" (*pakṣa*) is that which has its definition about to be stated; its "establishment" (*sthāpanā*) is its support. In what [context] does the proponent or the opponent defeat [the other] or triumph? In debate (*vāda*).

What [is it]? He says: he whose position (*pakṣa*)—the object (*viṣaya*)—has been refuted is called "one who has cast aside the subject"; the proponent (*vādī*) makes the opponent (*prativādī*) recognize him as such. He says "no," and so forth;

by the word *svākūta*, one's own position (*svapakṣa*) is referred to. *Utsarga* means abandonment; this is an adverbial modifier. Thus, he does not defeat [the opponent] in such a way that his own position is abandoned.

The meaning is that one who lacks the establishment of a position does not defeat [the opponent]. By means of what? To this he says: "By the utterances of non-essential members of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*). That which is not a member of the proof is a "non-essential member of the proof"; its utterance is so called. Alternatively, "non-fault" (*adoṣa*) refers to that which is not a fault; its mention is "utterance of non-fault. Or rather, "utterance of non-fault" (*adoṣokti*) is the non-articulation of a fault even when one exists. The "enumerations" (*saṃkīrttana*)—meaning the manifestations (*prakāśana*)—of these two, namely the utterance of non-essential members of the proof and the speech of the debate (*vādokti*), are by means of those.
Whom does he not defeat with those [arguments]? He says: one who has accomplished his own purpose.

Of what nature is he? He says: "one whose objects have been destroyed" (*astaviṣaya*), meaning one whose position (*pakṣa*) has been refuted. Now, has this matter not already been stated by the phrase "abandoning his own intention" (*svākūtojjham*)? Why is it stated again? True, it has been stated; nevertheless, it is stated again for the purpose of demonstrating that previously, when he had not yet adopted a position, he did not defeat [the opponent].

As it has been said: "Since the proponent must perform both—establishing his own position and refuting the opponent's position—the one who has resorted to a position does not defeat [the opponent] if his subject matter has been refuted. This is the distinction.

Here is another explanation: he defeats the knowledge of [his own] intention, and not one who has established his own goal through its proclamations; [he is one] whose subject matter has been refuted, meaning whose subject matter has been obstructed by the great earth of unestablished [reasons].
The failure to state a member of the proof by means of other tactics such as quibbling while one is speaking.

A caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) who desires victory must perform both: establishing his own position and refuting the opponent's position—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 87. Furthermore, "one whose subject (*viṣaya*), that is, the thesis (*pakṣa*), is obstructed or occupied by that unestablished great king, the great sovereign (*mahābhūpāla*)," means "one whose thesis is unestablished" (*asiddhapakṣa*).

[Objection: "Granted that he does not defeat one who has established his own position, but what if he defeats one who remains silent? To this, [the author] says: "Regarding 'one who remains silent,' etc. Here, the first alternative is intended: Does the opponent defeat him while establishing his own position, or does he defeat him by saying, "Even though you were authorized to state a proof, you said nothing at all and merely practiced silence"—thus speaking the truth that it was useless for the accomplishment of his own purpose, or by remaining silent himself? Regarding the first case, it is said: "By the establishment of a position," and so forth.
The second [alternative] says: "He remains silent"—the connection is that he does not [speak]. What is he doing? "Speaking" (*bruvan*);
that is, manifesting silence while speaking, or else a person prattling something else that is irrelevant.
Of what nature is he? He is "exactly equal" (*sama*) to the opponent who is to be refuted; the particle *eva* (only/exactly) should be understood here as preceding [the word *sama*].
Under what condition is he equal to him? To this he says: "in the non-achievement of his own purpose" (*svārthāsādhane*).

For just as there is no accomplishment of one's own purpose for one who remains silent and fails to state a proof, so too there is none for one who merely points that out or speaks something else entirely.

For one's own purpose is not accomplished merely by pointing that out; the remainder of this will be explained in the third [chapter]. Regarding this, he says: "When one speaks, saying 'this is to be proven,' the other remains silent; yet even he, though remaining silent, does not defeat the speaker."
For what reason? He says: "By means of that which is to be proven, acting as the instrument.
Indeed, it was stated that one defeats [the opponent] in debate merely by saying, "You have become silent"; so, what is this "debate"? To this, he says: "A statement that is capable," and so forth.
The wise know that *jalpa* (disputation) consists of four components, including "competent speech" (*samarthavacana*).
"Competent speech" is debate (*vāda*);
it is the presentation of arguments and refutations by two parties desiring victory in one place before witnesses, with the aim of establishing the subject matter at hand.
—*Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 111; *Tarkabhāṣā*, p. 280; *Prameyaratnamālā*, 6.
47 Pramāṇanaya° 8.1
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 2.1.30.
The fruit [of debate] extends up to the determination of the position, which is the illumination of the path.

(2) Without the proponent’s capacity to establish the truth, the illumination of the path through the clearing away of wrong paths is not possible; likewise, when the assembly lacks the capacity to report the faults of the truth as they truly are, one observes those who—though themselves proponents of logic—reject the opponent through their actions and speech merely to conceal their own arrogance. Therefore, [the fruit is as stated].
The distinctions and definitions of the *chalas*, *jātis*, and *nigrahasthānas* are not elaborated upon here.

According to the definition provided by some that "debate (*jalpa*) is the means of proof and refutation through those [elements]," debate consists of exactly four limbs. Furthermore, there is no confusion regarding the speech itself; it culminates solely in the determination of the truth or its opposite regarding one or the other, and does not merely indicate the intention of the speaker.

If it is asked: "Since the establishment of proof, refutation, and their fallacies depends upon the connection with the actual nature of things (*vastutattva*), and since the statement intended merely to indicate the speaker's intention is indistinguishable in all cases and lacks such a connection, how can words convey their own objects?
[The answer is: They know—that is, they understand—*jalpa* (disputational debate) to be speech that is capable [of establishing its point].
Who are they? He says: "The wise," meaning the learned ones such as Samantabhadra Svāmin and others.

If that is so, then why has the logic of debate (*vādanyāya*), characterized by *jalpa* (disputation), not been specified for them, just like other systems of logic (*nyāya*)? And if it is not specified, how can their thorough knowledge of it be understood? If you argue that the specific states of the speakers' minds are known through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of their speech for those who are not omniscient; who says that it was not specified by them? For indeed, there is the thorough knowledge of *jalpa*.
The discourse of Samantabhadra and others is a designation according to its true meaning; you yourself are the Sage Sumati, by whom your own doctrine has been established through excellent reasoning.

And since, according to the reasoning of the Lord [Utpaladeva] set forth in verses such as *Bṛhat-sva-bhāṣya* 17, the establishment of the reality of all actions and factors of action does not exist in the remaining systems,
it is understood that those who praise the awakening of people to be instructed have everywhere accepted that very same [reality].
Furthermore, because [the means of knowledge] such as quibbling (*chala*) are not mentioned in some parts of their own treatises— just like the *kaṇacara* and others—

and because one who himself does not act improperly yet applauds another who acts properly is understood in the world to be "one who performs the desired proper action," just like the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas.

If it is asked, "How then is he his son? it is said: Why is the sage Sumati (Good Intelligence) so named—that is, why does he possess a name whose meaning corresponds to its reality? He says: "By which [reason]"—the word "by you" is to be supplied as an ellipsis—your own position (*svapakṣa*) was led by well-reasoned, uncontradicted logic consisting of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not by that which consists of quibbling (*chala*) and the like; it was brought to the person seeking [truth], meaning he was awakened by that reasoning. They state the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposite case with the words "And since," and so forth.

Therefore, let the investigators consider whether it is appropriate that the proponent, by stating "then, by establishing the position," etc., has declared that both [the proof and the refutation] must be performed;

why was the *vādanyāya* not stated by them? And it is the intention of those very venerable authors of the Sūtras—which is not understood by ordinary people—that is being revealed in detail by the learned author of the Vārttika, namely the author of the *Tattvārthavārttika*. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, even the root verses contained within the present treatise are referred to by the word *vārttika*. Regarding the question posed by its author, "What then is *vāda*?", the answer "Why do they know *jalpa*? is stated. This is because there is a distinction between *vāda* and *jalpa*, and the answer must correspond to the question; otherwise, it would be as if someone asked about his own back and another were to describe his wife.

Now, if there is no difference between the two, even so, it must be stated in accordance with the subject at hand, because it is expressed thus according to the intention of the nine verses [of the *Vādanyāya*]: "They know debate (*vāda*)... This is for the purpose of dispelling the delusion regarding their difference among those of small intellect.

For this very reason, *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is also not a separate type of discourse (*kathā*). If *jalpa* (wrangling) is not different from *vāda*, how could *vitaṇḍā*—which is a particular form of that—be distinct from it?
For the Naiyāyika says: "The specific qualities of a jar, such as its earthen nature, are not distinct categories of objects (padārthāntara);

or rather, they know [these] in debate (vādam). Here, the word *vāde*, which follows from the previous context, is connected to this [sentence] by changing its grammatical case; thus, he maintains that debate (*vāda*) is something other than mere wrangling (*jalpa*).
In order to dispel the confusion regarding the distinction between *vāda* (formal debate) and *jalpa* (wrangling),
[it is stated that] *jalpa* is a specific type of *vāda*.
"Do the specific jars know that speech? To this he says: "Effective speech.
Or, what kind of speech or debate do they know? To this he says: "Effective speech."

If the statement is capable, or rather, if the statement is capable in this debate, then what indeed is a "capable" statement? That by which one's own intended meaning—whether in the form of a thesis (*sādhya*), a proof (*sādhana*), or the characteristics of contradictory refutations—is communicated to another through speech; that is called "capable."
And how speech functions as a communicator of meaning will be examined;

by this, he refutes the absolute position that a statement consisting of a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) or a five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) alone constitutes a formal debate (*vāda*),
[arguing] that its employment for the sake of instructing another is not done out of mere habit.

In this regard, since a statement is sufficient insofar as it accomplishes the understanding of that [meaning], what is the need for a restrictive rule? By this, the definition from the *Nyāyasūtra* (1.2.2)—“*jalpa* is a debate consisting of the establishment [of one's own position] and the refutation [of the opponent's] by means of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)”—is rejected; for quibbles and the like are statements that lack efficacy.

For those [fallacies] do not establish one's own position when employed by oneself, because that would entail the futility of the proof (*sādhana-vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*); nor do they refute the opponent's position when pointed out against another, because that would be a contradiction. Even when they are employed, there is no obstruction to the establishment of the probandum for one who states a valid proof. Therefore, performing a single instance merely for the sake of deluding the opponent is useless, like closing one's eyes in both cases; likewise, the pointing out of unestablished (*asiddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons is exactly the same. Thus, in such a debate (*jalpa*), there is an absence of the wrangling (*vitaṇḍā*).

For it is said: "Vitaṇḍā (cavil) is that kind of disputation which lacks the establishment of a counter-position" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.3). In this context, if "lacking the establishment of a counter-position" means being devoid of the support of one's own position, then it would not be a "sustained argument" (*samarthavacana*); how, then, could it be a form of *jalpa* (disputation), from which *vitaṇḍā* is distinguished? If, on the other hand, it is argued that the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) necessarily strives to refute the opponent's position, and therefore his words of refutation are called a "sustained argument," that too is without substance. For, in the absence of the establishment of one's own position, there can be no negation of the opponent's position.
As it has been said: "If you argue that vitandā (cavil) is the self-defeat [of one's own position], then let this fault belong only to the other [party]— namely,
the Buddhist who accepts what is favored by the Naiyāyika."
An example (udāharaṇa) is an illustration (udāhāra), meaning a statement; it is the communication of understanding to another, such as through quibbles (chala) and so forth.
Even when employing quibbles and other such tactics, it is still *jalpa* (wrangling), because there is no contradiction with the opposing side.

Where one who desires victory engages with another who desires victory, seeking gain, honor, and fame for the sake of victory or defeat, that is "discourse between those desiring victory" (*vijigīṣukathā*); this is designated as *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*—*Nyāyasāra*, p. 16.
*Nyāyakalika*, p.

13: If it is thought that [the definition] would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to explanations and the like because a competent statement is also a form of chatter (*jalpa*), he says in response: "consisting of four components" (*caturaṅga*).

Or else, how can *jalpa* alone be *vāda*, since there is a difference in their objects? For *jalpa* has as its object one who desires victory, whereas *vāda* has as its object the learned and so forth. To this he says: "consisting of four components."

There are four constituent factors characterized by the proponent, the opponent, the audience, and the strength of the assembly; these are not "members" (avayava) of the speech, because speech does not possess such members.
Among these, what is called *vāda* (debate) is that which one speaks with another after having taken up a position according to the scriptures;
that debate is twofold in brief: *jalpa* (contentious debate) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
—Carakasamhitā, p. 262:

"The adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis by the proponent and the opponent constitutes *kathā* (discourse). It is of two kinds: discourse for those free from passion (*vītarāga-kathā*) and discourse for those desiring victory (*vijigīṣu-kathā*)."

Where one who is free from passion engages in proof and refutation together with another who is likewise free from passion for the sake of determining the truth, that is called "discourse of those free from passion" (*vītarāgakathā*), using the technical designation of "debate" (*vāda*).

Debate (*vāda*) is defined as a collection of statements consisting of the employment of proof and refutation based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), preceded by the formal adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis by two parties free from passion, and concluding with the determination of one side. (Nyāyasūtra-bhāṣya, p. 15)

And it is said in the *Nyāyakalika* (p. 13): "Those who know their own system and the systems of others, who are of noble birth, who stand on both sides, who are patient, and who are devoted to the paths of debate—such impartial persons are declared to be the arbiters (*prāśnika*)."
—Nyāyapraveśavṛtti, p. 14; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, p. 63;
Nyāyatātparyaṭīkā, p. 158.

In the second interpretation, however, the word *aṅga* can signify a "component part," based on the statement from the *Vādiprativādi*: "They know debate (*jalpa*) as discourse involving skill in the four components. This shows that in [the other] interpretations such as *vyākhyāna*, it is not "discourse involving skill" that is called *jalpa*, because those [components] are absent there.

Furthermore, the mention of the "assembly" (*sabhā*) and the "president of the assembly" (*sabhāpati*) indicates that this [debate] has as its object one who desires victory; otherwise, like the other interpretations, its inclusion would be useless.
Since this alone constitutes the nature of a debate that is subject to defeat, how can there be a difference in their respective domains?
[The author] demonstrates [the answer] by means of the absence of proponent and opponent.

By this [definition], even if one were to conceive of a distinction between the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*) within *vāda* and *jalpa*, it is stated that such speech is not *jalpa*.

If it is argued that if that speech were *jalpa*, it would lack a conclusion because there is no mention of the causes for its restriction, such as the "non-establishment" (*asādhana*) and so forth, he says here: "until the determination of the thesis" (*pakṣanirṇayaparyantam*).

The term *pakṣa* refers to the subject matter that is the object of dispute; its *nirṇaya* (determination) is the finality (*paryanta*) consisting in its establishment through the removal of conflicting views. Thus, it is so described; the meaning is that it does not extend to the enumeration of the merits and faults of the proponent and the opponent.
A statement that is [merely] "capable" (*samartha*) is one that is incomplete.

Now, if it is understood that the non-occurrence of *jalpa* (wrangling) lasts until the determination of the thesis (*pakṣa*) belonging to the proponent, then [the objection holds] because such determination has not yet occurred; for one employs the reasons for that [thesis] in order to produce a certainty in another, just as one has oneself attained certainty. Otherwise, like a cowherd, how could there be any proficiency in *jalpa* for him? By this, the view that [the non-occurrence of *jalpa* lasts] until the determination by the audience (*prāśnika*) is also considered refuted, because of the statement "of those who know both systems," since only those who have ascertained both sides can serve as an audience.

Furthermore, not every king, like [an ordinary] king, is himself capable of reaching a definitive conclusion on that matter; thus, it is difficult to ascertain whether the debate must continue until such a conclusion is reached by him.

Nor is it logical to say it must continue until a conclusion is reached by the opponent, for even an opponent who maintains a firm delusion instilled by his own false scriptures may reach a conclusion regarding the matter he is addressing.

If it is argued that this is not tenable because [the proof] must extend until the determination of the thesis (*pakṣanirṇaya*), we say: this is not well-stated. For, by the presentation of a reason (*sādhana*) that is inseparably connected with the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvi*), even those who are conceited are seen to abandon their deep-seated delusion and recognize the opponent's position as being defeated, just as those who are ill take a supreme medicine.

Furthermore, even those of dull intellect who do not understand [the truth] for themselves—taking them into account—the determination of truth arising from the presentation of that [argument] occurs as a realization based on the words of others by those who have known both sides of the case; otherwise, since there would be a total lack of discernment regarding the merits and defects of the proponent and the opponent within one's own mind, how could there be a state comparable to a touchstone upon which such dependence could rest?
This is because the position of the proponent has been determined.
The comparison is: "The wise produce in others a certainty that is like their own certainty."
"Measurement for the sake of another is called 'statement' by way of metaphor"—
*Nyāyāvatāra*, verse 10—
[this applies] in the absence of a determination of one's own position.
The adjudicators (*prāśnikas*)— who are impartial, wise, conversant with both systems of tenets,
and refuters of fallacious arguments— are like the reins that control the debate.
And such arbitrators as these—
[as stated in] the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*,
p. 649— the king, established in the position of presiding over the assembly (*sabhāpati*).
Therefore,

[the cognition] produced by the application of a probans that is invariably concomitant [with the probandum], ending with the determination of the opponent's position by the president of the assembly, [is valid].
From the comprehension arising in the minds of the judges and others from the speech of the proponent...
The stone known as *kasauṭī*, which is used for testing gold, depends upon experts and others;
what, then, is its fruit? To this he says: the phrase "the fruit of discourse" (*jalpasya phalam*) is understood to follow here.
What is this? He says: it is the *prabhāvanā*, or manifestation, of the path consisting of right knowledge and so forth.

Now, the *adhyavasāya*—that is, the determination or personal ascertainment of reality (*tattva*) such as the Self—is its fruit; namely, the protection of that [ascertainment] from "robbers" such as the Buddhists and others. For the purpose of protecting the ascertainment of reality, debate (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*) are employed, just as one uses a covering of thorny branches to protect the growth of seeds (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.50).

If it is argued that this is because of the scriptural statement [to that effect]; if its protection is by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then you are acting favorably toward the domain of valid cognition, since the manifestation of that [protection] necessarily follows from that very engagement.
If, however, it is from something else; that is not tenable, as will be explained:
even if bandits refute it by means of valid cognition—and not through deceptive speech or other non-authoritative means—impartial judges who know the truth consider that to be its protection.

If [the path] is based on valid means of knowledge, then it is protected by that very [validity] itself; what is the use of the effort of employing quibbles (*chala*) and the like? For the *kiṃśuka* trees, which are naturally red, by whom indeed could they be dyed? What purpose would there be in using quibbles and the like for the illumination of the path?
The preservation being performed consists of the firm determination of the reality established by oneself.
If the Buddhists and others refute reality by means of statements supported by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one might object:

"Surely the proponent must convince the opponent, the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*), and not the presiding judge (*sabhāpati*) who possesses only a delicate intellect; therefore, what is the use of him? Let it be that debate (*jalpa*) is known to have only three components. To this, he says: "The proponent," and so forth.

This is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the proponent’s capacity to demonstrate reality to the opponent and the members of the assembly; by this, the capacity of both the opponent and the members of the assembly to demonstrate reality is also included. Without that—specifically, without the manner in which there is an absence of understanding in the person to be instructed and in the instructor—it is not possible to illuminate the path through the cleansing and removal of the wrong path (*unmārga*) and the one-sided path (*ekānta*), according to the method to be described hereafter.

Thus, for King Pariṣadvala, an authoritative command must be issued according to what is appropriate and fitting regarding truth, such that when the plaintiff and defendant report their faults to the king, he says: "You must remain thus," and "You and the members of the assembly must report exactly what has occurred. If there is no capacity for this, then purification through that [command] would not occur;
why? To this he says: "Having himself extracted," and so forth.

From what [evidence] do we see those who reject even a proponent—who speaks according to logic and possesses such qualities of character—as a debater? He says: from their actions and speech. Why [do they act] with such self-importance? He says: for the sake of concealing [their own faults] by themselves, on their own part.
[Objection: "But surely the members of the assembly (*sabhyāḥ*) are the ones who prevent such [abuse], since they cast out one who transgresses them.
If you think that the *Nyāya* treatise itself is therefore the regulator, then [the author] says here: "Quibble" (*chala*), etc.
Quibble (*chala*) is the subversion of speech (*vacanavighātaḥ*) by means of the fabrication of an alternative meaning (*arthavikalpopapattyā*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.10)
Fallacious refutations, however, are the *jātis* (Nyāyabindu 3.140);
and misconception and lack of comprehension are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.19).

2.19 Some say that their distinction and definition are not elaborated here for fear of prolixity; rather, they should be seen elsewhere. That [category] in which there is proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upālambha*) is thus described.

What is it? He says: "debate" (*jalpa*). This is because debate has a definition distinct from formal discussion (*vāda*) according to certain Naiyāyikas and others, and because one observes those two [proof and refutation] being employed against opponents [in debate]. This is the connection [of the words].
By the king, the lord of the assembly, commanding.

The elucidation of the path by the Naiyāyikas is as follows: "Speech (jalpa) is the demonstration and refutation [of a position] through quibbles (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti), and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), established according to the rules as stated. — Nyāyasūtra 1.2.1.
2.2 It is considered that because [actions such as] kicking and so forth are equivalent to verbal abuse, slapping with the palm, and the like.

For instance, when it is stated, "This man is wealthy because he possesses nine blankets," the opponent raises the objection: "He does not have nine blankets, but only one; therefore, the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha). In this regard, it must be considered: does the opponent incur defeat by raising that objection at the outset during the correct application of a proof, or rather when the situation is reversed? Regarding the first position, the proponent (vādī) already defeats the opponent simply through the establishment of his own thesis; what need is there for anything else? If it is argued that even by raising such an objection one wins—on the principle that "what is doubly bound is well-bound"—that is untrue. For once the opponent has been refuted by logic, further efforts are futile; it is like those who, having killed a snake with poison, would then apply a mere light slap to kill it.

And how is there this distinction that a "different reason" (*hetvantara*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), whereas the mere pointing out of another defect is not? For otherwise, the disputant would simultaneously incur both victory and defeat. Therefore, since the intended meaning of the reason—such as "having nine blankets" (*navakambala*) and so forth—is [the fact of having many blankets], this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

In the case of words that have multiple meanings, the intended meaning must be determined through context and other such factors; otherwise, since all words possess multiple meanings, every reason (*hetu*) and so forth would be fallacious, because even in a usage such as "there is no smoke here from that fire," there would be the possibility of pointing out such a fault. Thus, this [objection] should be refuted, but one should not be defeated by that alone; for otherwise, the employment of a valid proof would be rendered futile, and in that case, victory and defeat for the proponent would occur only once.

But then, should one who speaks thus not point out that [fallacy]? We say: no, it is not for the purpose of defeat, but rather with the intent of prevention, because of the fault inherent in the subject matter.
What is the fault if it is not pointed out? None at all, provided that one establishes the reason.

Others maintain that [the defeat of the proponent] consists in "refutation" (nigraha); however, that is incorrect. For, if the failure to point out a quibble (chala) employed by the opponent were the basis for the proponent’s defeat, then one would have to establish that he is defeated because of "overlooking what ought to be censured" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa), thinking: "Alas, this very quibble was employed by me, yet it was not pointed out. In that case, if he himself points it out, he is merely exposing his own fault.

Is there then any difference between the state of a fault existing inherently and the state of its being pointed out? Indeed, we see even thieves and others being defeated by faults they have exposed themselves.
Since there is the saying, "Who indeed would expose his own private parts? and because it is improper for him to disclose that himself, [one might argue]:

"Then let the members of the assembly (sabhyas) do so. If it is argued that just as their failure to point out that [defect] establishes his defeat, they should likewise establish victory based on the statement of a valid proof—such that both victory and its opposite [defeat] should coexist—then let this further fault belong to the mere chatterer alone.

Now, if the validity of the proof (*sādhana*) were to be compromised by the fault of failing to point out those [defects], then let that fault also not exist! Oh, how impartial are the judges (*prāśnika*), since they consider even a great merit to be invalid due to a minor defect, yet do not consider a minor defect to be non-existent due to that merit! This is not so; for in the first case, when a valid proof has been employed and a quibble (*chala*) is subsequently pointed out, the proponent (*vādī*) emerges victorious.

[Objection: "If it is argued that for the sake of protecting the truth (*tattva-rakṣaṇa*), the virtuous (*sadbhiḥ*) must indeed employ *chala* and the like, whereas those desiring victory (*vijigīṣubhiḥ*) may use them; [Response: Then one would have to say that they might likewise use clawing, slapping, blows with weapons, setting fire, and so forth.
Therefore, this is not a superior means for protecting the truth. — *Vādanyāya*, p. 71.
Because even the disparagement [of someone] by means of sticks, slaps, and so forth is invariably connected with the purpose of protecting the determination of reality—
*Nyāyakumuda*, p. 338—
the expression "this boy has nine blankets" (*navakambalo 'yaṃ māṇavakaḥ*) is employed.

In this case, the speaker’s intention is "this man has a new blanket" (*navaḥ kambalo 'sya*); however, while there is a distinction in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), there is none in the compound (*samāsa*).

Here, the quibbler (*chalavādī*), disregarding the speaker’s intended meaning, imagines another sense—the unintended one—thinking: "By you, it was actually stated that 'he has nine blankets' (*nava kambalā asya*)."

Having imagined [the existence of nine blankets], one denies it on the grounds of impossibility, saying: "He has only one blanket; how could there be nine? This is a quibble regarding a word with a general meaning, known as *vākchala* (verbal quibble); this is its refutation:
such a censure of another’s statement by imagining an impossible meaning is not tenable.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2.12
Carakasamhitā, p. 266; Upāyahṛdaya, p. 15; Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī, p. 16.
The purpose of raising quibbles and the like, *Nyāyakalikā*, p. 16.

When the opponent has refuted a reason that was stated without qualification, the proponent’s desire for a qualification constitutes "another reason" (*hetvantara*), because the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and other such tactics against the opponent would otherwise be futile. (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.6)
2.6 On the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna).
When the term *śikhin* is employed in the sense of *agni* (fire), someone might object by raising a *chala* (quibble), thinking that the word *śikhin* refers to a peacock,
merely because of the use of a word with multiple meanings.
The Naiyāyikas would then be exposing a mere fallacy (chalodbhāvana) if...
The opponent [is defeated] by the opponent or by the proponent.
Overlooking an opponent who has reached a point of defeat constitutes "neglecting the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa)
— Nyāyasūtra 5.2.1.
Even when a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) has been established, it is [the fault] of the opponent alone because he does not say, "You have been defeated."

Regarding the exposure of one's own fallacies and the like, the *Tulanā* states: "When questioned by the assembly as to whose defeat this constitutes, it must be declared [by the respondent]; for indeed, one who has incurred a point of defeat would not expose his own private parts.
— *Nyāyabhāṣya* 5.2.19.
2.21 The disputant points out [the opponent's] failure to state the quibble and so forth.
In that case, for the Naiyāyika proponent who accepts the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and so forth in debate (*jalpa*), [what follows]?

Nor [is there victory] in the second case through the excellence of the proof (*sādhanaguṇa*), because since both [parties] are equal, whose victory would it be? Or rather, would there not be defeat for the other as well? For just as the employment of a quibble (*chala*) by the opponent is a fault, so too is the employment of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) by the proponent.

If it is argued that the proponent (*vādī*) must likewise point out [the opponent's faults], otherwise he alone would be the loser if the proponent is not the winner— since victory and defeat exist through their mutual dependence— then in that case, the proponent’s neglect of what is to be questioned (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) is not being pointed out. If, on the other hand, the opponent also wins by not pointing out the fault, then once again,
if both victory and defeat are pointed out, it is said that the proponent alone loses because of the manifestation of his own fault.

Now, if the judges (prāśnikas) consider the failure to point out a fault in the proponent's argument to be a defeat for the opponent, or if they consider the proponent's use of a fallacious proof (sādhanābhāsa) or the opponent's use of a quibble (chala) to be so, then the situation remains such that there is a simultaneous determination of victory and defeat for both parties.

Now, they establish the determination of victory or defeat by waiting for the other to point out a fault in their respective positions; what then is the status when no such fault is pointed out? If it is argued that there is a determination based on equality between the two, from where does this arise? If it is argued that it is because neither side has established its own position, then let that same state remain even when a fault *is* pointed out, since there is no difference [in the outcome]. Even if there is a distinction in the pointing out of each other's faults, the subject at hand—the reality (*tattva*)—remains unestablished.
Furthermore, the fault is not that victory or defeat is individually attained or avoided.
The opponent should bring forth a fallacious proof for the sake of victory and defeat.
Let the judges determine the defeat [of the opponent] upon the manifestation of faults.
Let there be an establishment [of the matter] through the equality of the proponent and the opponent.

Furthermore, when a proponent of the absence of proof (*sādhanābhāvavādin*) has pointed out a quibble (*chala*) against an opponent, what has been lost for that opponent such that [the proponent] establishes victory? If you say it is because [the opponent's position] is rendered invisible by that pointing out, then why would the pointing out of a flaw in the proof not likewise be "as if lost" due to its rendering [the proof] invisible? This being so, if that flaw were pointed out by the respondent (*prativādin*), what would happen to the respondent? If you say that the non-pointing out of an existing flaw constitutes a point of defeat (*nigraha*), then it follows that either that [flaw] belongs to him or it does not; for one who desires victory for the proponent by pointing out some other flaw, there arises the contingency of "overlooking the censurable" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) in part.

Even when both faults are pointed out, it has been stated that pointing out one [fault] is no different from pointing out the second; thus, one who employs various forms of quibble (*chala*) is understood to be a proponent of fallacious arguments (*sādhanābhāsa*).
The pointing out of a flaw [in the reason] is also a defect of a fallacious proof;
the sense is that otherwise, nothing at all would be established.

Now, what is the outcome when the one employing *chala* (quibble) points out a fault? If it is argued that there is the attainment of victory or defeat [only] once, provided the proponent (*vādī*) points out the quibble; then even for the proponent, two faults arise upon revealing that [fault], namely: the failure to reveal the quibble and the statement of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).
And the refutation regarding this has been considered immediately below.
Therefore, even one who employs fallacious arguments does not defeat a speaker who uses quibbling (*chala*).

By this, the view that the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) is defeated by the opponent when employing quibble has been considered; for the same fault applies to the two aforementioned alternatives.
Now, quibble is of three kinds: verbal quibble (*vākchala*), general quibble (*sāmānyachala*), and figurative quibble (*upacārachala*).

Regarding that, the explanation of the first [type] is as follows: "Verbal quibble (*vākchala*) is the imagining of another meaning from the speaker's intention when a meaning has been stated without qualification" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.12).

This is its meaning: when a meaning has been stated by a general term expressing a number without distinction—as in the reason "because of having nine blankets" (*navakambalatvāt*)—the imagining of another meaning, namely the sense of being possessed of the number nine, based on the speaker's intention at that time regarding the acquisition of new blankets, is verbal quibble.
For instance, when it is said, "Because this [man] has nine blankets," the objection, "How can this man, who has only one blanket, have nine blankets?
constitutes the threefold quibble (*chala*), namely: quibble regarding a general term (*sāmānyachala*), and quibble regarding a metaphorical usage (*upacārachala*)—*Nyāyasūtra* 1.2.13.
2.11 *Pratyagram* means new.

The aphorism defining *sāmānyachala* (quibble regarding generality): "Quibble regarding generality (*sāmānyachala*) is the imagining of a non-existent meaning through the connection of an overly general [term] with a possible meaning" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.13).

When a possible meaning is being heard, because of its connection with an overly general term—that is, its connection with an inconclusive generality—one imagines a non-existent meaning; by means of that, one imagines a cause for that which is not a cause, consisting of many such generalities. When speech is explained in this manner, it is a quibble (*chala*). It is not [truth].
For example, when it is said, "This Brahmin is endowed with learning and conduct," someone says, "It is possible for a Brahmin to possess the perfection of learning and conduct"—this is praise.

Then another says, "If being a Brahmin were the cause, the indicator, or the producer of that perfection, then even an outcaste would be endowed with it. That which reaches and yet exceeds the intended meaning is an over-common generality (*atisāmānya*).
Just as the status of being a Brahmin sometimes attains and sometimes transcends the perfection of knowledge and conduct— Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2.8.
Praise of the Brahmin, even though unrefined.

The definition of quibble in respect of metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*)— “Quibble in respect of metaphorical usage is the denial of the actual existence of a thing when there is an instruction based on a figurative application of a term” (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.14).
14. This is the meaning here: when a figurative sense is expressed, the contradiction of the statement arising from the assumption of a primary sense is "quibble" (*chala*).
For example, when it is said, "The platforms are crying out," [the opponent argues] that the platforms do not cry out, but rather the persons situated upon them do.
Thus, all three types of quibble are merely quibbles and do not lead to a point of defeat (*nigraha*), as has been stated.
By this, *jāti* (the futile rejoinder) is also explained.
But what is this *jāti*? *Jāti* is an opposition [to an argument] by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.18)
18. Regarding that, "an objection (*pratyavasthāna*) is a futile rejoinder (*jāti*)"—this is the general definition of a futile rejoinder.

Some say that an objection is merely an opposition and that such mere opposition is a fallacious refutation (*pratiṣedhābhāsa*); this is untrue. For there is a contradiction in the word "objection," which expresses a general category of reply, being applied to its fallacious counterpart when there is no actual meaning or object involved;
yet that [contradiction] does not exist here.
The passage contained herein has been written twice.

Regarding the example stated here in the *uttarābhāsa* (fallacious rejoinder): when the Vaiśeṣika has stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," someone says: "Just as the state of being produced is observed in a jar while it possesses impermanence, so too [is it observed] even in the absence of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*); therefore, this also follows: 'Sound is not a quality of space because it is produced, like a jar. This is merely a counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*). Why? Because, although the non-quality-status (*anāguṇatva*) is refuted by way of an irrelevant form (*aprastutākāra*), the impermanence itself is not refuted.
"Some say there is also sublation by scripture (*āgamabādha*);
that is not a well-spoken word from a Vaiśeṣika, for in every case of sublation by scripture, scripture itself is the thesis (*pratijñā*). (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.1)

Because this contradicts [the definition], it cannot be considered an "admission" (*āgama*) by way of distinction; for otherwise, there would be a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) even in other cases, since this does not undermine the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the previously stated reason. Others say that it is merely that [reason itself]; for them, since the determination of victory or defeat arises from the very same prior reason—which is unimpaired in its attainment and capable of proving the point at hand—this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Otherwise, it would be futile.
Even if [the opponent] were refuted by these two [arguments], it has been stated:

how is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) not destroyed by this? For even if one states that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—which is concomitant with the absence of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatvābhāva*)—is present in a jar and so forth, if the pervasion of that [producedness] with impermanence (*anityatva*) were not established, such would be the intention of the opponent;
thus, for the Vaiśeṣika, there is nothing other than the observation of co-presence (*sahadarśana*) that establishes pervasion.

Since a jar is not a quality of space, as for what was further stated—that if space were not apprehended, the subject (*pakṣa*) would have an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), whereas if it were apprehended through its having sound as a quality, there could be no negation of that [quality], and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) does not exist by virtue of the absence of being a quality of space, and therefore this is not equivalent to the previous case—that is not correct. For it will be demonstrated that even if space were apprehended, it is not apprehended through sound; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
[Nyāyasūtra 1.1.35: "For the sake of its division, [the definition of proof is stated] by means of similarity and dissimilarity."

2.18 The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates an objection raised against the reason (hetu) stated by way of similarity: "The reason is that which establishes the probandum through similarity with the example" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.34).
1.35 Thus, the remainder [of the definition] is that a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is an opposition based on the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of the example (*udāharaṇa*).
In this regard, the example is: "The self possesses action (*kriyāvān*), because it is endowed with qualities that are the causes of action, like a clod of earth."

Here the opponent says: "If the self is thus established through its similarity to a substance possessing action—namely, through its connection with a quality that is the cause of action—then let it follow that it is devoid of action because it is a substance, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]. This is a poor rejoinder, because it does not refute the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the original reason; this is merely an illustration, for by this, any counter-argument based on similarity to the example is also a futile rejoinder (*jāti*).

For example: "The self is inactive because of its omnipresence, like space. To this, an objection is raised: "The self is active because it possesses qualities that are the causes of action, like a clod of earth; for there is no distinction [between the two cases].
This too is a fallacious refutation (*asaduttara*) for the very same reason.

It demonstrates an objection based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) when the reason has been stated by way of similarity (*sādharmya*). The remainder is that this is a "futile rejoinder" (*jāti*), which is an objection based on the similarity of the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*) to the claim that "the reason is that which establishes the probandum through the similarity of the example."

Just as grass and the like are not sentient because they lack breath and so forth, whereas that which is a sentient locus is seen to possess breath and so forth, as in the case of a living body—if, on account of its dissimilarity to a living body, [grass] is deemed non-sentient, then by virtue of its similarity to it—namely, its materiality (*mūrtatva*)—grass and the like ought to be considered sentient, since there is no specific reason [to the contrary].

This is an illustrative example; therefore, when one objects that "the reason is the proof of the probandum through dissimilarity to the example," such an opposition based on dissimilarity to the example is a *jāti* (futile rejoinder).

An example of this is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; for whatever is not impermanent is not produced, just like space. When this is said, the opponent replies: "If sound is impermanent due to its dissimilarity with the permanent—namely, its being produced—then let it be permanent due to its dissimilarity with the impermanent—namely, its lack of tangibility. This is what is called a *jāti* (futile rejoinder).
As for the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), they will be discussed right here at the appropriate occasion.
A *jāti* is an opposition [to an argument] based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with respect to a genus (*jāti*).
— Nyāyasūtra 1.2.18.

2.18 When a conclusion is drawn by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), and because the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is established, an opposition based on similarity itself— which is not distinct from the original reason for establishing the thesis— is the "counter-argument of similarity" (*sādharmyasama*).
The illustration is: "The self possesses action because it is endowed with qualities that are causes of action for a substance;
a clod of earth is a substance endowed with qualities that are causes of action and thus possesses action; likewise, the self [is so]; therefore, the self possesses action.

When this has been concluded, the opponent objects by means of similarity alone: "The self is devoid of action because it is an all-pervading (vibhu) substance, and an all-pervading substance is devoid of action."
Space is all-pervading and inactive, and likewise is the self; therefore, [the self] is inactive.

But there is no specific reason [to conclude this], for while it must be active due to its similarity with that which possesses activity, it is not [necessarily] inactive due to its similarity with that which lacks activity. Because of the absence of a specific reason, this constitutes a "balancing the similarity" (sādharmyasama) refutation.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 4.1.22.
The quality that is the cause of action is the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
The author of the Bhāṣya is one who acts because of the prior cause, precisely due to the non-frustration of pervasion.
And in the case of a conclusion based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa upasaṃhāra*), one might object: "The self is inactive because it is all-pervading;
for a substance possessing action is seen to be non-pervasive, like a clod of earth, and the self is not like that; therefore, it is inactive.
Or, by way of dissimilarity: "An inactive substance is seen to be devoid of qualities that cause action, such as space (*ākāśa*); the self is not like that; therefore, it is inactive."

Furthermore, there is no specific reason why, because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action, it must be inactive rather than active simply because of its dissimilarity to that which lacks action; thus, due to the absence of a specific reason, this is "balancing the dissimilar" (*vaidharmyasama*).

Now, regarding "balancing the dissimilar": a clod of earth is seen to possess action because it is endowed with qualities that are the causes of action and is finite, whereas the self is not so; therefore, it does not possess action like the clod of earth.

Yet, there is no specific reason why, because of its similarity to that which possesses action, it must be active rather than inactive simply because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action; thus, due to the absence of a specific reason, this is "balancing the dissimilar."
— Nyāyabhāṣya 5.1.2
Misapprehension and non-apprehension are points of defeat— Nyāyasūtra 1.2.6.

Concluding [the section], he says: "Therefore, they know that speech which consists of the four factors and so forth is *jalpa* (disputation)," as has been stated. This is a statement establishing the point.
In that regard, what is its similarity [to perception and inference]? He says: "Even of verbal testimony," and so forth.
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "even of verbal testimony, not only of perception and inference, does there exist capacity.
Of what nature is it? He says: "Other than that," and so forth.

By the word "that" (tat), the reality under discussion is referred to as being present for both the proponent and the opponent. Therefore, the determination of either one of them—whether it be the status of the proponent or that of the other—is what constitutes its "conclusion" or "limit"; this is what is meant by the term [tad-avasānam]. The sense of the particle "eva" is that it is not something else imagined [by others].
If it is argued that this [determination] is merely indicated by the intention of the speaker, to that he replies: "But not... (na punaḥ). It is not at all an indication of the speaker's intention;
here too the particle "eva" is to be understood, or the word "punaḥ" is used here for the purpose of emphasis.
Why? He says: "The proof," and so forth.

Proof (*sādhana*), refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), and their fallacies (*tadābhāsa*) constitute "proof and refutation alone" (*sādhanadūṣaṇamātra*). Their "establishment" (*vyavasthā*) is a state consisting of verbal designations and conceptual constructions (*abhidhānavikalpātmikā sthitiḥ*). Because of its dependence upon reality (*vastutva-pratibandhāt*), the meaning of this is as follows: reality (*vastu*) is that which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*); because of its dependence—that is, its being contingent—upon that true nature of proof and so forth.

This is what is meant: conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the means of proof (*sādhana*) and so forth as its object; otherwise, if [the object] were established from that [conceptual construction] in some other way, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of those [means] would be abolished, because conceptual construction is not denied [as the source]. Even if it were not denied, [the object] would not be established from that [conceptual construction] either; for otherwise, even from something like "that which does nothing" (*akiñcitkara*), that [object] would be established, such that one could even say: "Sound is produced because it is impermanent, like a jar. Furthermore, since [these arguments] arise from conceptual construction, they are all the more dependent on that [construction] as their object. Thus, this [notion] has been refuted: "Words have conceptual construction as their source," and so forth.
That which has an entity as its object [is valid] with respect to an entity,
because the entity is established.
The establishment of reality occurs through non-conceptualization; conceptualizations are the source of words.
There is no mutual connection between them; these words do not touch upon the objects themselves.
This is the remainder [of the sentence]—*Nyāyakumuda*, p. 537, note 7.
With the words "the speaker’s intention" and so forth, he raises an objection based on the opponent's view in order to refute it.

The "indication" (*sūcana*) is that by which the intention (*abhiprāya*) of the speaker—the proponent of the proof (*sādhana*) and so forth—is indicated or expressed; the "denotation" (*abhidhāna*) is the same. These two form a copulative compound (*dvandva*) characterized by their collective totality (*samāhāra*). This [compound] applies everywhere because there is no distinction between the presence of the proof and so forth and their absence.

Why is this so? He says: because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—between the indication of the speaker’s intention and the means of proof (*sādhana*) and so forth. For that reason, how could there be an indication by means of words? (Note: "indication" is used here as a term of art). If it is argued that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) convey their own objects, characterized as means of proof and the like; in this regard, he states the verse beginning with "nothing unestablished is to be introduced," etc., in order to demonstrate the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) on the part of the opponent:
"Nothing unestablished is to be introduced anywhere, nor is anything [already established] removed."
If it is argued that the member [of the syllogism] is indicated by speech, how can the speaker be free from confusion?

How can one whose words are not to be heeded be a proponent when stating that "words are the means for someone"? Since he relies on the establishment of reality produced by those [words], the statement of the reason—whether by expressing a member of the proof or by pointing out an actual defect—indicates what is capable even though it is itself incapable; however, the statement of the probandum is not sufficient even indirectly, according to the opponent who possesses only ordinary capacity.

Comparison—[the opponent argues that] one relies on the establishment of the object produced by that [inference], and not on its being the denotable [of a word]; this is merely a view based on one's own scripture (*svadṛṣṭirāgamamātra*), because it entails the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasāhasrī*, p. 130.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): Even indirectly, the statement of the thesis (*pakṣokti*) is not sufficient, because it merely expresses what is yet to be proven (*sādhyābhidhānāt*).
The statement of a reason, though itself incapable, indicates that which is capable. — Pramāṇavārttika 4.17.

In some cases, when sound or the like is the subject (*dharmin*), a certain property such as impermanence (*anityatva*) that is unestablished (*asiddha*) is neither to be introduced (*upaneya*) nor presented (*upaḍhaukanīya*) by means of speech—that is, by the word "impermanence. Otherwise, he considers the proof (*sādhana*) to be purposeless.

For that very reason, from sound or the like, a certain property such as permanence (*nityatva*) is neither removed (*apanīyate*) nor refuted (*nirākriyate*) by speech, such as by the statement "it is not permanent."
This has been stated in the *Viniścaya*: "In that case, how can someone's [statement] be a means of proof (*sādhana*) for another by adding or subtracting something somewhere?

What, then, is accomplished by it? To this he says: "The mark (*liṅga*), which is a member of speech, is indicated for the sake of others; inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is the illumination of an object perceived by oneself" (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 4.1).
According to this statement, how can such a speaker be unconfused? He is indeed confused, because his utterances are contradictory from beginning to end.

The phrase "by speech" (*vācā*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, it is also indicated that [the object] is pointed out even by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Or, it is an elliptical indication that it is also determined by speech.
The meaning of "what is seen by oneself" (*svadṛṣṭa*) is that which has been seen by oneself by both the proponent and the opponent, or by the one who explains and the one who understands.
If there are judges, the removal of their disagreement is established by implication from their very authority; by this [statement],
the matter perceived by oneself is made known to another.
And that form consisting of bodily and vocal intimation is the "object seen by oneself" (*svadṛṣṭārtha*) therein; it is the threefold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*). — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 4.169.
In order to explain the first verse, he says: "Words," and so forth.

How can a Buddhist (*saugata*) whose speech is to be heeded when he asserts that words are not a means of proof for anything in any way whatsoever? Why? He says: because he relies upon the establishment—that is, the determination—of reality (*tattva*) produced by those very words. This is the reason.

He asks, "Why is this so? and replies: "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*); its "limb" (*aṅga*) is the cause, namely the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*). Alternatively, it is called "means of proof" because that by which something is proven is the means of proof. Or, [the compound] may be connected by changing the case ending: "from the statement"—that is, from the presentation—of the "members" (*avayava*) of this [proof], such as the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), etc., by means of words;
or [it is so called] because of the "exposing" (*udbhāvanā*) of an existing defect (*doṣa*), such as unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), etc.

The intended meaning here is as follows: if one does not establish that [point] by means of stating a proof or a refutation, then the proponent incurs defeat due to the non-statement of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), the failure to point out a fault (*doṣa*), and the utterance of meaningless speech;
whereas if it is established, this fault is merely incidental to the speaker.
In the case of not stating the categories consisting of proof and refutation.

It might be thought: "Nothing at all is established by that [word], nor does anyone actually understand anything; rather, like two people with ophthalmia, the cognitions of both the speaker and the listener arise through delusion such that they think, 'This has been communicated by me through words' and 'I have understood it. This is not sound, because how could one who knows this for oneself subvert the linguistic convention of words, as one would the convention of conjunction and so forth? Just as this person, having perceived that a mark such as conjunction is fallacious due to the absence of an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) and has therefore abandoned it, he should likewise abandon the word.

Now, if one cannot live for even a moment without abandoning that [inference], then let it be abandoned. Furthermore, in the case of inferring a future cart and so forth from the rising of the Kṛttikā star and the like, let there also be no abandonment of the rising of the Kṛttikā;
thus, the inference that "the sun will rise tomorrow because it has risen today" would not exist, as deviation is possible.

If, however, a worldly person understands a logical mark (liṅga) and so forth even from such a word, then its acceptance is for the sake of that [worldly practice]; for this very reason, let the acceptance of the "conjoined" (saṃyogin) and other types of relations also stand.

Therefore, this [person] understands the logical mark (*liṅga*) from a word even though it is not [intrinsically] connected [to its object], but does not understand the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) from such a mark; this is the natural capacity [of words]. Even one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), once he has recognized that his cognition is false due to the ophthalmia, does not engage in worldly activity based on it. Otherwise, Prajñākaragupta’s establishment of three positions regarding erroneous cognition would be untenable: "One who has recognized the deviation [of a means of knowledge] does not proceed from it, but rather from inference; for another who has experienced deception, the other [means] is a valid authority" (ŚV Śabda 112).
Thus, [the point is] from the word.
By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: "How can one engage in activity for the sake of awakening another in non-duality?
For, since the distinction between self and other is unestablished for him, it is merely his own self-awareness that arises in the form: "This is another, I am not another."
