In this context, there is no division from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Both [the questioner and the respondent] experience a cognition colored by their own respective forms; there is no actual division, just as in the case of a dream-cognition or the ravings of a madman.

[Objection: If that is so, then how can the proponent (*vādī*) be considered "mad," given that even the realization of non-duality (*advaita*) arises from it? [Response: Indeed, this proceeds as the dissolution of all cognitions; here, there is no emergence of a [dualistic] cognition at all.
What, then, is to be done by the opponent or another? Is anything being done that is observed? — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vārtikālaṅkāra*, p.
293. [The categories] accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas are: conjoined (*saṃyogi*), inherent (*samavāyin*), inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*), and contradictory (*virodhi*).
— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.1.9
In the absence of invariable concomitance,
if one were to abandon the word [“reason”], one might as well infer that a cart will appear from the rising of the Kṛttikā constellation.
"Tomorrow the sun will rise," or there will be an eclipse— just as one determines the proximity of Rohiṇī by observing the rising of Kṛttikā (Laghīyastraya, Verse 14).
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 351;
[this refers to] the Buddhist view regarding even that which is deviant (vyabhicārin).

However, cognition such as that of a yellow conch shell, being devoid of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all, because it lacks the attainment of such purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
When the accomplishment of purposeful action consists merely in the [perception of] shape, another cognition— namely inference— is the valid means of knowledge.
For instance: an appearance of such a nature is not devoid of configuration;
this is an inference because it has been observed so elsewhere.
And thus, one for whom no deviation has ever been perceived is indeed deceived by a contradiction regarding what was intended.

But he who perceives the possibility of error proceeds after deliberation: "First, only the configuration is obtained; regarding the other [the object], there may be doubt or error. Thus, there are these two cognitions—the inference regarding the configuration and the doubt regarding the other—which are both valid and invalid means of knowledge.
However, cognition whose object is a word is a valid means of knowledge because it communicates the speaker's intention. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p. 5)

Now, for one who considers that from a word (*śabda*) there is a cognition of a real entity (*vastu*) and from that [cognition] the attainment of it, would that knowledge not be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Let this very fault be his; therefore, it is established that just as with a logical mark (*liṅga*), so too by one who conducts worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) through a word, a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between that [word] and the true nature of the real entity must be admitted, just as in the case of a logical mark and the like. Thus stands the position regarding the word.

"Let this be so; nevertheless, if it is argued that the word indicates the logical mark (*liṅga*) and not the probandum (*sādhya*), to this he says: 'the indication of that which is capable,' and so forth.

What is the indication of the capable—that is, of the logical mark which is competent to make the probandum known? To this he says: 'the statement of the reason (*hetu-vacana*), which is a sentence expressing the three-fold logical mark.'"

Of what nature is it? He says: "Even though powerless," meaning even though it is incapable of making the probandum known by itself—that is, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya-vacana*). Of what nature is this? He says: "The expression of the probandum" (*sādhyokti*), such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) "Sound is impermanent. Furthermore, it is not only because the establishment of the probandum comes from the proof (*sādhana*) that [the proposition] is insufficient; rather, like the verbal expression itself, it is also indirectly (*pāramparyeṇa*) not capable of conveying the probandum, nor is it competent for the communication of the probandum. Thus, the opponent considers that its power is ordinary (*prākṛta-śakti*); that is, its power is ordinary or belongs to the ordinary, because it lacks the capacity to convey the probandum as something possessing [intrinsic] power.

If it is argued that, just as with the logical mark (*liṅga*), the statement also possesses the capacity to establish the probandum (*sādhya*), and therefore the probandum is established from that very [statement] alone, rendering the reason (*hetu*) useless; to this he replies: "When correctly investigated," and so forth—meaning that when the various formulations of the sentence are correctly investigated, they themselves come within the scope of reality.
"It is to be accomplished by those who perceive it, yet it is generally unknowable by those of ordinary intellect.

[Objection: "If it is argued that this entire process of inference and the object of inference proceeds according to the principle of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) as mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and does not depend on external existence or non-existence; then how can there be a comprehension of an object from a sign (*liṅga*) which is itself an object? And how is it that the distinction between property and property-bearer is merely imagined by the intellect and not an actual object, given the admission that conceptual constructions do not touch upon real entities?"

Since [inference] has a real entity as its basis, if it has a real entity as its object, how could the statement of the reason—which is impossible without a reason that is invariably concomitant with the probandum—not have reality as its object?

To the question, "What are those which, when properly presented as proofs invariably concomitant with the probandum, having been deliberated and examined, lead to the domain of reality? he says: "The conceptualizations of meaning (arthavikalpa) which are the effects of sentences."
Alternatively, one should understand that the mention of "sentences" (*vākya*) implies both sentences and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
The mention of "sentence" is for the purpose of demonstrating its utility in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) exclusively apart from individual phonemes and words;
the mention of "conceptual construction" is for the sake of providing an illustrative example.

Just as conceptual constructions (vikalpas) that have been correctly investigated according to the stated method have reality as their object, so too do sentences; for words such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth have no objective referent because they originate from conceptual construction, like words such as "primordial matter" (*pradhāna*). This is intended either to point out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason in this case, or [to establish] the sentence itself as being accepted by the Sāṃkhyas.

By all of this, the following is stated: even when it is being demonstrated that "sound is impermanent," they do not understand it—either because they rely on their own tenets (*svasamaya*) or because of the similarity of other sounds which are non-momentary. It is for their sake that the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is presented. If it is asked, "In that case, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the reason alone, what is the purpose of stating the probandum?", he says here: "Generally" (*prāyaḥ*), etc.

Generally—that is, for the most part—it is not by its nature as sound and so forth, but rather in the form of momentariness and so forth, that the sound and so forth which are the probandum (*sādhya*) and the object of inference (*anumeya*) are "unknowable" (*ajñeya*), meaning uncomprehended.
By whom? He says: by those of ordinary intellect, namely the Buddhists (*saugata*).

Their knowledge is entirely non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). Since even conceptualization, like its own nature, does not exist externally—because it is contradictory for a single thing to possess two forms—what do they do? To this he says: "by seeing," meaning by directing the sense faculties toward that [object]; the sense of the phrase is that [the object] would not be graspable by the senses due to their attachment to their own [erroneous] views.

The meaning is that it is impossible for a single conceptualization (*vikalpa*) to possess two natures—namely, non-conceptuality with respect to its own nature and conceptuality with respect to an external object—because these are contradictory.

This is what is being said: just as a reason (*hetu*), when establishing a probandum (*sādhya*), assumes a verbal formulation in order to convey its cognition, so too does the operation of the eyes and other senses; since there is no distinction [between the two cases], what difference is there such that the sense organ would be useless and a fault, whereas the verbal expression alone would not? Rather, it is the verbal expression itself [that is the cause].

If, however, even when the object is already understood through a logical mark (*liṅga*), the operation of the sense organ does not cease, and even upon the arising of the cognition, there is no further futility of that [operation], then—since it is effective with respect to the mere substratum (*dharmin*)—this fault does not apply. One must consider this: that which is a merit in one case may be a merit in all cases, and what is a fault in one case may not be a fault in another. Thus, [the objection] regarding momentariness and other such properties is to be examined.

If it is argued that, fearing this fault, one must avoid the sense-faculty (*indriya*) there just as one avoids the statement of a proposition (*pratijñāvacana*), lest there be a failure to establish the property of the subject (*dharmyasiddhi*); let this be another fault of his,
provided it exists.

Without providing an explanation for the latter half of the verse concerning the operation of the sense faculties—since that is easily understood—he states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to support the first half: "All indeed," and so forth.

All this practice of inference and the object of inference, or the practice of the sign (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the sign (*liṅgin*), which is being perceived through either the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) or the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), [occurs] by means of what is mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and appears as conceptual construction.

By what [is this established]? He says: *dharma* refers to [qualities] such as *sattva* (purity), and *dharmī* refers to [substances] such as sound; the *nyāya* (logical principle) regarding these two is [the rule stated in] *Sarve bhāvāḥ svabhāvena...* (*Pravāhaṇavāda*, 3.39) and so forth, as well as [the rule concerning] the exclusion or non-exclusion of other properties (*dharmāntara*).

If it is argued that, in that case, because that conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) has a real entity (*vastu*) as its basis, its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is ultimate (*pāramārthika*), he says here: "That conventional usage does not depend on anything external."

What is it? He says: "The existence and non-existence of both the attribute and the substratum"—this is what is expected [as the object], because he considers that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is without an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*);
the phrase "if" (*cet*) indicates the intention of the opponent.

Regarding this, he states the refutation: How is it that the cognition—that is, the understanding—of fire and so forth arises from the object itself, which is a real entity (*vastubhūta*) such as existence (*sattva*) or smoke, and not from a conceptualized [property] such as being either the subject (*pakṣa*) or a similar instance (*sapakṣa*)? For, according to the opponent’s own statement that "an object indeed makes an object known," why should that cognition not arise from the latter? It is replied: When the conceptual distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is without a real objective basis, then the property-bearer—the sound—and its properties—existence and so forth—are not distinct from [the mere fact of] being either the subject or a similar instance. Thus, there is no real object to serve as the basis for the inference.

And thus it has been stated by Ācārya Dignāga in his *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* (1.3): "Indeed, this entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference is based on conceptual construction; it is [distinguished] through a distinction between property and property-possessor as mounted upon the intellect. He says "and thus" (*tathā ca*) and so forth, because this was also stated by him—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 24.
Because they are established in their own intrinsic natures,
they partake in the exclusion from both intrinsic and extrinsic natures;
this is the remainder [of the sense].
The existence of the property and the non-existence of the substratum [are established] from the object, because the cognition of the object [arises] from the object— *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.15.

If it is argued: "Surely it has been stated that the comprehension of an object arises from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); here, the distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is merely imagined by the intellect, and not even the object itself [is real]," to this he replies: "And how... and so forth.

The state of being [the relation] between the property (dharma) and the possessor of the property (dharmī) is "thatness" (tattā); the distinction that exists by virtue of that is itself imagined by the intellect (*buddhi-parikalpita*), and does not exist in the object (*artha*). Furthermore, the relationship characterized as the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is not merely a distinction based on thatness; how could it not be imagined by the intellect? Rather, it is indeed imagined by it.
Why? To this he says: "of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpānām*), and so forth.

The intended meaning here is as follows: according to the method stated, no object—whether internal or external—can exist as partless; for if it has parts, it falls within the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And since the Buddhists admit that conceptual constructions do not touch upon real entities, based on their statement: "Conceptual construction is a manifestation of the non-real, a corruption arising from contradiction," it follows that even the object is merely a mental construct. Thus, one should observe the view of Prajñākaragupta, who holds that reality is mere manifestation (*pratibhāsa-mātra*), transcending all conceptual constructions.

It must be considered whether its [the conceptual cognition's] properties such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth are also conceptualized as having the nature of an object (*artharūpatayā*). If they are, how could this [cognition] conform to the statement of Dharmakīrti, "For an object makes an object known"? If it is argued that these [conceptual cognitions] must therefore have real entities (*vastu*) as their objects, to this he replies: "Since those [conceptual cognitions] have as their basis, cause, and support an entity (*bhāva*)—whether external or internal—that consists of parts (*sāṃśa*);

that is, if it is accepted that conceptual cognitions have real entities as their objects (the word "of conceptual cognitions" being understood from the context), then in what manner (*kena prakāreṇa*) would they not have reality (*tattva*) as their object? They would necessarily have reality as their object.
What [is it]? He says: "The statement of the reason.
Of what kind is it? He says: "That which is untenable without a reason.
What kind of reason? He says: "The probandum," and so forth.
"Conceptual constructions arise from the object; therefore, it is thought that the word [denotes] that [object].
By this, the first half-verse is supported.
Furthermore, it has been said: "Conceptual construction is a distortion because it appears as a non-entity and because it is deceptive."
—*Praśamaratiprakaraṇa*, Kanda, p. 190;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 500;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 82.
"When examined, indeed everything falls apart; there is no reality other than non-duality"—*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra*, p. 31. *Dharmasaṃgraha*, p. 134; *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p. 44.

Thus, by demonstrating that certain conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) have external objects as their domain, Prajñākaragupta has likewise demonstrated that the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*) arising from them also has those same external objects as its domain.

Now, having raised as a prima facie argument the claim made by the opponent— that because [the cognition] arises from the desire to speak (vivakṣā), its object is that [desire]— he refutes it, saying "The desire to speak," etc.,
[concluding that] the word has the external object as its domain.
For the Buddhist,
[the word] also conveys the intention.
The object that appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker's activity— that is where the authority of the word resides; it does not depend upon the actual state of the thing itself.
A sentence, which has its power derived from the speaker's intention, is not obstructed in its own meaning.
How can there be an establishment of reality through a mark (liṅga) indicated by that [statement]?
Objection: Since a statement indicates merely the intention of the speaker without distinction, one would not attain reality from it even indirectly;
nor do they indicate the speaker's intention with absolute certainty, because [the meaning] is established otherwise in cases such as corrupted speech.

The reason (hetu) is that which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds due to the necessity of inseparable connection (avinābhāva). All others are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
— Hetubindu, Verse 1.

Since one can apprehend even an object that is not personally intended by means of such [words], and since among multiple possible meanings, by whom has this specific meaning been distinguished—such that the speaker’s intention alone would be the meaning?

If, due to occasional discrepancies, there is no confidence in words themselves, what is the point of urging the critique of the deviation of verbal conceptualization through such a trivial hypothesis; why not reject cognition itself?

The term is so called because its origin or cause is the very desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), according to the etymology "that from which something originates" (*prabhavati*); or else, it is that from which the desire to speak originates, as it originates from that.
What is it? He says: "Why is that sentence not composed? To this he replies: "It is not obstructed."

"Where? he asks. He replies: "In its own object"—that is, in the object which belongs to the proponent (*vādī*) in the form of the logical reason (*hetu*). Here, the meaning should be understood through a rhetorical question (*kāku*). To this, he provides the answer: "By what [is it indicated]?"—by that which is indicated by the statement; by what sign (*liṅga*) is the intention (*vivakṣā*) considered to have ascended into conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?

Since others do not accept that it indicates anything else, how could there be an establishment of reality—such as the desired momentary destruction—in any way? What is meant is this: the logical mark (*liṅga*) mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which is indicated by that [inference] has no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with reality; and that which has a necessary connection with reality is not what is indicated by it. Furthermore, when one thing is indicated, there can be neither comprehension nor activity regarding another; otherwise, if the word "horse" were uttered, there would be such [comprehension or activity] regarding a cow.

Now, if it is argued that because the purpose is not accomplished by one who has mounted that [vehicle], the [purpose] must occur elsewhere; that is not so, because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Furthermore, if it is held that even though it was not indicated by him in reality, there is nevertheless the cognition that "the three-featured logical mark (liṅga) was indicated through error"; that too is not tenable, because it is impossible for even an erroneous cognition to occur with respect to what is not its object. Otherwise, from the word "horse" (aśva), there would be a cognition of a cow (go).

If it is argued that [conceptual cognition does not have the object as its domain] because of dissimilarity, then what indeed is the similarity between the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) and the intrinsic nature of the object (*arthasvabhāva*)? If such similarity exists, then why is it not prevented—just as in the case of direct perception—that conceptual constructions have the object as their domain? For even in the case of direct perception, there is in every respect an absence of that [intrinsic nature], yet the real entity (*vastubhūtārtha*) is expressed by words.
Practice [is impossible] regarding an object that has become a real entity, because of the absence of similarity.

As for the one who thinks: "Even in the absence of that [external object], there is such a cognition due to the force of internal disturbances"—that too is not a vision of reality; because whatever is the effect of something indicates that very thing through an invariable connection (*pratibandha*), just as smoke indicates fire, and a sentence is the effect of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

Furthermore, whatever is not the effect of something does not indicate it even through error, just as that same smoke does not indicate what is not fire, and a sentence is not the effect of the [external] object.

If, however, even so, that [cognition] produces a cognition of that [object] there due to some proximity, then for that very reason, in the ultimate sense, something that is not a cause would produce a cognition; and that cognition would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object for one who has the conceit of non-discrepancy, just as the cognition of a jewel through the hole of a keyhole is a cognition whose object is a jewel that is not the cause of the effect of fire.

It might be thought: "A sentence does not produce knowledge of an object in any way whatsoever other than through the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); rather, only another conceptual construction (*vikalpāntara*) arises from the sentence such that the object is cognized. This is not so, because there is no perception of such a sequence—first a conceptual construction of the intention from the sentence, and then a conceptual construction of the object. Therefore, it remains established: how can the determination of reality (*tattvavyavasthiti*) occur through a sign (*liṅga*) indicated by that [intention]?
Here is another explanation: the word "also" (*api*) should be understood here [in the phrase] "even that which originates from the speaker's intention."

To the question, "How is a sentence constrained by its own object—that is, by the thing it expresses?"—the answer is: "Because the determination of reality [occurs] through the mark (liṅga) indicated by that [sentence]. Explaining this verse, he says: The Buddhist, by making a general objection and thereby encompassing the position that "a sentence indicates an object merely as the speaker’s intention," would not understand the reality—the object to be established—even indirectly from the sentence, let alone directly.
Or rather, [he might think]: "From the sentence there is a mark, and from that, reality"; thus, it would become an inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna). This is what he considers.

The second commentary on the verse has been shown by this very means through the method of negation (*vyatireka*). Having accepted that a sentence indicates the speaker’s intention, a refutation was stated; now, showing that even that is not the case at all, he says: "And [they] do not" (*na ca*), meaning they certainly (*ekāntena*) and necessarily (*avaśyambhāvena*) do not indicate the speaker's intention, nor is it indicated. He says "is heard" (*śruti*), etc.;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of "shifting to another meaning" (*arthāntaragamanam*) is intended.
Where there is the reading *śruti-dṛṣṭy-ādeḥ*, there, by the word "etc.," the inclusion of "defects such as conceptualization" (*kalpanā-duṣṭa-ādi*) is intended.

Since defects such as those involving corrupted hearing (*śrutiduṣṭa*) are established from other sources, he speaks—citing the meaning obtained by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—beginning with "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*). Here, "subject" (*pakṣa*) refers to the locus (*dharmin*), because the term for the whole is metaphorically applied to its part. Its "property" (*dharma*) is that which belongs to it; "by a portion of that" means by a portion of that subject, namely the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), and not by a mere part of the subject itself, since the word "subject" does not denote the aggregate. It is "pervaded" (*vyāpta*) due to its connection with pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And pervasion (*vyāpti*) resides in the pervader (*vyāpaka*); that is, it exists only where this property of the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*) is present, not where it is absent.
It resides in the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only where this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is present, and not elsewhere.

Why is this so? He says: "Furthermore" (*punar*)—this is used for emphasis (*vitarka*). The meaning of the particle "only" (*eva*) is that the reason itself is never, even in the slightest degree, a non-reason (*ahetu*).
As for the question, "Of how many kinds is it?", he says: "For that reason is indeed threefold. Why? He says: "Because of the mark [liṅga] such as 'contradictory' (viruddha), etc."
The "subject" (*pakṣa*) is the locus of the property (*dharmin*), because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part—*Hetubindu*, p.

52. For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) there [in the subject], or the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only there [where the pervader is]—*Hetubindu*, p. 53.
Where there is the existence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), there can never be its non-existence;
in that very place, there is the existence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
Here it is objected: if it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), how can it be unestablished (*asiddha*)? It is called "unestablished" when it is itself, or its locus (*āśraya*), is in doubt.

And at that time, for no one would there be the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) if it were not pervaded by that part [of the subject]; how then could it be contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)? For by the statement of its pervasion by that part—which expresses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—those [fallacies] are excluded:

for that which exists in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) and is absent from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is contradictory; that which exists in both, or is possible in both, is inconclusive; and this [reason] does not have such pervasion by that part. [Reply: No, because it is stated thus from the perspective of another.

For the opponent accepts the presence of existence (*sattva*) and so forth in the subject (*pakṣadharman*) and its pervasion by a part of that (*tadaṃśavyāpti*); how, then, can there be validity for such a person who maintains non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*)? It is said to be "unestablished" (*asiddha*) because the occurrence of existence and so forth is not possible for him anywhere; or rather, his own [doctrine of] non-absolutism is contradicted by you, since this [reason], like the absolute momentariness imagined by the Buddhist, is also inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) regarding the absolute non-momentariness. As he will say:
"Because of the refutation of the contradictory and the inconclusive, the Buddhist..."
For the Buddhist, it is unestablished (*asiddha*);
for Siddhasena, it is contradictory (*viruddha*); and for Devanandin, it is [unestablished].
"There are two kinds of causes for the certain accomplishment of the Samantabhadra [result]" (Siddhiviniścaya, Chapter 6).

Therefore, other [fallacious] reasons such as *ariṣṭa* and so forth—distinct from the "effect" (*kārya*) and other reasons postulated by others—are not valid reasons when proving death and the like; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Why? He says: "Because of the restriction of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-niyama*)."

The explanation of this very point begins with the words "thence" (*tataḥ*) and so forth. Regarding the second explanation, he says: "Thence follow the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), such as the *sādhya-sama* (equal to the probandum) and others," which were imagined by Prajñākaragupta, a proponent of the theory of future causes (*bhāvikāraṇavādin*).
Why? He says: "Because of the rule of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvaniyamāt*).

This is its meaning: the rule of non-existence without that which is to be produced (*vinā bhāvyam antareṇābhāvyaniyamaḥ*), that is, the rule of non-existence when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent. Furthermore, it is stated that there is no occurrence [of the reason] even when the probandum is absent; thus, it is said that [the reason] does not exist in the case of the absence of the probandum. Therefore, what follows from this? He says: "By itself," that is, by its own nature, there is the comprehension of an object—even one not intended—not only of an intended thing, from words; this is the connection, with the change of case ending (*vibhaktipariṇāmena*).
Furthermore, words do not invariably indicate the intention of the speaker; thus, those [words] imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas are dependent [on that intention].

Now, if it is argued that although the *bhāvanā* is explained in this way—namely, that while this is not its [intrinsic] meaning, rather the meaning is the speaker’s intention—to this he replies with the words beginning "In reality," and so forth.

Thus, since words have multiple meanings, by which person or by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has this meaning being indicated been distinguished—that is, separated—so that by such a distinction the meaning would be nothing other than the speaker’s intention? The sense is: by no one at all. By this, the letter (*patra*) is also considered; for a written statement indeed possesses multiple meanings.

Now, one might ask: "Since [the word] occurs even when the object is absent, are words meaningless? To this he says: "Not in every case, because of contradiction and deception. By whom? He says: "By words. Even when there is agreement, since there is frequently no confidence produced by oneself—that is, by the Buddhist himself—what is the use of such a trivial conceptualization? He explains what kind: "That [conceptualization] in which there is the pointing out (*codanā*) of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of words, that is, of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)."

Then what would the opponent do? To this he says: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*)—because it is mentioned immediately after the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), the word "knowledge" here refers to perception (*darśana*). That alone [is rejected], not the conceptual constructions of words, because by the rejection of that [perception] itself, those [constructions] are also rejected, since they are rooted in it. Thus he thinks: why would one not reject them? One would certainly reject them externally, because perception occurs even in dreams and the like despite the absence of an external object; so say some.

That self-awareness by which knowledge comes to be known as "knowledge" is what is called "knowledge. Why would one not reject that very [self-awareness] as well? For, just like the appearance of duality, there is no confidence in that [self-awareness] either, due to the objection of its deviation;
this is because conceptual constructions are rooted in perception.
The proponent of the non-duality of appearances (pratibhāsādvaitavādin),
demonstrating this very point even regarding self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), says:

For it can indeed be said: "No conceptual construction whatsoever is capable of directly indicating, even through a causal chain, that perception is sufficient for the apprehension of the probandum. (6)
If cognitions were directed solely toward the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there would be no basis for their engagement with objects that differ according to various conventions (*samaya*).
[Objection: If there is an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why does one not reject cognition itself?
Or, if it is argued that there is no proof of rejection, this is equally true even regarding the rejection of a sentence.
Regarding the realization of reality, speakers excel by means of specific sentences when inference functions; it is not otherwise.
Just as there is the capacity to convey meaning despite the deviation of its effect, so it is with the word.
For it is possible to say, etc.;

that is to say, because it is possible to say what? He replies: "Because of the apprehension of the probandum"—that is, the apprehension, vision, or direct realization of the probandum, namely momentary destruction, which is self-cognized and not cognizable by anything else; perception, which is of four kinds, [namely] non-conceptual vision, is not capable, not sufficient [to establish it].
How so? He says: the word "api" (also) should be explained here according to the principle of a change in the sequence [of thought], meaning not only directly, but also indirectly.
For instance, it is not direct, because [the cognition] proceeds even when there is an absence of ultimate reality, as in a state of cognitive distortion (*upaplava*).

This being the case, whatever appears is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), just like the clusters of hair perceived by one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*); and the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of knowledge and so forth does indeed appear.

Nor should it be thought that because the clusters of hair and the like are of the nature of cognition (*jñānātmaka*), their existence would render the example devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for the similarity of form (*sārūpya*) is denied, the distinction between the forms of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakākāra*) is perceived, and there is no contradiction in one thing being apprehended by another, just as in the case of production.
In the absence of this [external object], there would be a lack of inference for the Proponent of Cognition (*vijñānavādin*).

For that [cognition] is held to be produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics. How could one who accepts its non-existence state such an inference as: "Whatever appears is cognition, just like pleasure and so forth; and blue and so forth appear"? If this [inference] were merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), how could the existence of blue and so forth as cognition be established from it? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If you say: "As is the Yakṣa, so is the offering," and thus that [inference] is not accepted as being real for that reason; then what is blue and so forth in reality? If you say it is "cognition," from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this known? If you say "from this very [inference]," then alas, you are defeated, because it contradicts your own fundamental position.
If this inference is not connected to that [object] even through a causal chain, how can it be non-deviant with respect to it? Nevertheless,
its existence is established by means of inference, which is divided into sensory perception, mental perception, self-awareness, and the perception of yogis.
The objection—“How can there be any activity even when non-duality exists from the perspective of ultimate reality?”—has been refuted;
for how could it be consistent to say, “As is Bali, so is Yakṣa”? What connection is there between the two?
If it is argued that [this is so] from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), [the response follows].
Inference regarding its own object does not deviate from that object.

"Thus, because the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) are indirectly connected to the real object, there is no deception even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.82). If, however, one argues that this fault does not arise because [the cognition] is accepted as the effect of that [object] through a causal chain, then all inference would consequently be non-deviant; therefore, there would be no such thing as a "semblance" (*tadābhāsa*) of it.

If it is argued that, because there is no obstruction in that case, there is no non-deviation (avyabhicāra), and therefore its establishment does not occur through perception; we say no, because it lacks the capacity for such an operation. For this [perception] cannot apprehend that "all this is cognition of blue and so forth," since that would entail the consequence of grasping other things as well.

Furthermore, there is no logical justification for the claim that everything—such as blue and so forth—is external to your cognition; for in this regard, nothing other than that [blue] is excluded from your mere non-perception, since your mere non-perception is equally applicable to proving the non-existence of that [external object]. Otherwise, suffering would be non-existent due to the non-perception of pleasure, because it is indirectly its effect.
If it is argued that "perception [is known] by another perception"—

that is, surely my own perception does not cognize the nature of all blue and so forth as being identical with cognition, but rather only that which has itself been made an object— [we reply: no, because there is dispute regarding that point.

For instance: who perceives that "your perception perceives blue and so forth as its own nature"? If you say "that very same [perception]"; then [we reply]: that perception perceives something other than itself as distinct from it, and thus, while perceiving that object in such a way, it does not perceive itself as being that very same thing. Therefore, the proof of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) is not established. How then can he communicate this to another? In what manner? Because your perception cannot be a cause for another's understanding, and because it would follow that any other cognition would be useless.

If it is argued that [the cognition of one thing] serves as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the cognition of another, then—since there would be no proximity or distance between them with respect to anything—the [cognition] of everything would arise [from everything], and thus there could be no dispute at all.
Nor is this the case for the Jains.

Furthermore, how could the relationship of cause and effect not exist? For, just as in that case, the apprehension of one by another would be contradictory, and likewise, perception (*pratyakṣa*) would similarly become the cause for the cognition of another.
If you say, "It is not mine," then it is the same as saying, "It does not belong to another"—
for the Jaina, this is not established even by inference, due to the faults already mentioned.
Blue and so forth [arise] from four conditions: the causal condition, the object-condition, the immediate condition, and likewise the dominant condition; there is no fifth condition.
—Madhyamakakārikā 1.2.
For comparison: "For the mind that appears as blue, its state of having the form of blue arises from the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) which is the blue object."
From the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), there arises the nature of consciousness;
from the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) of the eye, there is the specific determination of grasping form;
and from the causal condition of light as a cooperative factor (*sahakāripratyaya*), there is the clarity of the object.
— Brahmasūtraśāṅkarabhāṣya, Bhāmatī commentary on 2.2.19.
Because there is a counter-argument:

as for this claim that—due to the non-difference of blue and so forth from the intended perception—the cognition perceives that very thing as its own self-nature, and thus its non-difference from it [is established]—how can there be a grasping of it by that [perception]? For example: whatever is grasped by something is grasped by it as its own self-nature, just as one's own form [is grasped by itself]; and blue and so forth are indeed grasped. However, this was not stated as a formal inference (*anumāna*).
If it is argued that there is no means for him to communicate this [to another] because of the absence of another, and thus he is not communicated with, then this is the same in other cases as well.

For another can also say: "I perceive blue and so forth as distinct from themselves, yet there is no other cognizer who is being communicated with by me; you raise objections against me, but our own position is established through the refutation of the opponent."
"Blue and so forth are perceptible" means that blue and so forth are apprehended by perception; this is an application of the term "difference."

As for this further objection: "How does that [object], which is distinct from cognition itself, become cognized by it? And how can that which is non-distinct be cognized? [The answer is: "Because it is perceived as such. This applies equally elsewhere;
therefore, it is not logical that things such as the mass of hair [seen by one with cataracts] are of the nature of cognition.

Furthermore, if that which exists externally were to possess ultimate reality, then the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be purposeless for the sake of establishing "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
By this, the state of being free from the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence regarding reality has also been considered.

Therefore, one who accepts that [position] must admit the non-existence of external things such as the hairs seen by one with cataracts; thus, the example is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
If it is argued that [perception consists of] blue and so forth,
[the response is: "Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous"— in this regard.

[Objection: But if existence, consciousness, and so forth appear in perception, why is there no apprehension of them? [Response: If you say it is because perception lacks the capacity for that, we say no; for what is intended here is apprehension in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
For this very reason, the term "probandum" (*sādhya*) is included;
if what is erroneous were the probandum, it would result in nothing but mere conceptual difficulty.
Because each [means of knowledge] is capable of directly apprehending its respective object of proof (*sādhya*), perception is capable [of this];

for that very reason, it is indirectly so by virtue of generating an inference whose object is that [perceived thing]. Since no such [inference] arises through error in any way whatsoever, it is held that perception is not incapable of apprehending the object of proof.

If it is argued: "Surely, if there is an error even regarding the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) just as there is regarding the form of the object (grāhyākāra), then even the error itself is not established;
therefore, let there be only that [intrinsic nature]," to this he says: "Of the capable," and so forth.
It is some conceptual construction (kalpanā) that indicates—that is, makes known—the capable logical mark (liṅga), not every [conceptual construction], nor is it real (sat).
That is to say, "having that as their object" means they are capable of directly indicating it;
the mention of "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which "word" (*śabda*) is also included.
Alternatively, because of the metaphorical application of the cause to the effect, or the effect to the cause, the word is referred to by the term "conceptualization."

This is what is meant: just as there is error regarding something else despite no difference in appearance when one's own nature is abandoned, so too there is error regarding words such as "Pradhāna" despite the abandonment of the indicative word and conceptual construction;
thus, perception is erroneous with respect to the external object, which is its cause.

Regarding that which was stated—"being solely intent upon the ultimate reality" (*paramārthaikatānatva*) and so forth—he states the refutation therein: "If being solely intent upon the ultimate reality," and so on.

The "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If it is accepted that there exists the state of those [cognitions] whose "sole intent" (*eka-tāna*)—meaning their primary focus—is a connection such as identity (*tādātmya*) with that [particular characteristic], then:
Of what [cognitions]? Of "intellects" (buddhi).
What would happen to that? To this he says: there would be—i.e., there could be—an activity, a proceeding;
where? Toward objects.

In what kind of things? In those that break the boundaries of other systems (*samayāntarabhediṣu*). Here, "system" (*samaya*) refers to the philosophical view (*darśana*), not any other, as that is not the subject at hand. This view holds that externally the objects of perception are momentary, partless atoms with mutually distinct bodies, while internally there is non-dual cognition; anything other than this is "other than that" (*tadantara*), meaning those things which, by being established as different from the Buddhist system, have the nature of being stable, gross, common, and so forth.
Why are [cognitions] such? He says: they are "without basis," meaning they are devoid of an objective support (*ālambanarahita*).

From this we conclude: since there is no uniformity in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-ekatānatva*) of cognitions (*buddhi*) whether external or internal, for one who wishes to establish the objectlessness (*nirviṣayatva*) of words, that [objectlessness] has fallen away from those cognitions; and thus, it follows that even that which was attached to the *piñjana* (the bundle) has fallen from the ultimate unity of objects, leaving words without a basis (*anibandhana*).
There would be no engagement with objects that differ according to different conventions— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.206.

Having refuted through the very *pūrvapakṣa* the view of Prajñākaragupta—who, thinking that the non-existence of anything internal or external follows from the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus the proof of its non-existence is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)—the author states the intended meaning of the two verses, beginning with "The absence of means of valid cognition," etc.
The meaning of this is as follows: regarding what was said—"Why would he not reject cognition itself?"—[the response is:]...

In that regard, the rejection of that [object] implies the rejection of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the means of valid cognition is of the nature of knowledge; or, if such [knowledge] exists, the rejection is unestablished, for the refutation of this or any other [entity] is unestablished. Just as the establishment of ultimate reality, the establishment of its rejection is also not possible without a means of valid cognition. As it was said in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*: "The means of valid cognition, while making itself one's own... (*Nyāyaviniścaya* 1).

49. If one thinks, "Therefore, let there be mere sensation (vedana-mātra)," then [the author] says here: even in the refutation of the sentence—that is, even in the rejection of the sentence having an object—it is not only [the case for] cognition; it is the same, that is, similar.
Showing that there is no haste regarding the sequence, he says "tattve" and so forth; that is,
regarding the occurrence— that is, the operation— of inference toward the apprehension of reality (*tattva*), such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*).
One should transcend common perception;
the implication is that this applies not only to specific instances within the continuum of erroneous cognition.
If it is objected: "But surely that very cognition is inference; how then can this be said?"—[the answer is: No; for by the term "inference" used figuratively, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is denoted.

By what [means]? To this he says: "By specific statements," namely, by the utterances of the three-featured mark (*trirūpaliṅga*). What is its purpose in that regard? He says: "In order to communicate"; even commentators rely upon this, and not otherwise—that is, not by any other means.
The intended meaning here is as follows: For one who seeks to establish that "every sentence is devoid of an external object," perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard.

Furthermore, if there were an inference such as—"whatever is not connected to something does not produce a correct cognition of it, just as smoke [does not produce a cognition] when there is no fire; and every sentence is unconnected to an external object"—then the thesis (*pratijñā*) of this statement would contradict its own words in establishing the logical mark (*liṅga*). If it does not establish that [mark], how could another person have a cognition of the logical mark?
Mocking the opponent’s thesis that "the sentence is merely the comprehension of reality and does not convey an external object," he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.

Just as fire and other such things, though produced from causes such as wood, are still indicative [of their causes] even when their effect is seen to deviate [in the presence of a magnet or other factors], so too is the case with sound despite its occasional deviation;
demonstrating this, he says: "From various causal complexes," etc.—meaning, when fire arises from diverse causal complexes such as wood and the like.

Since reality is realized [through it], why should one abandon the verbal [expression]? ...Because reality is realized through it, the verbal [expression] is seen to be employed even in inference for oneself; otherwise, it would indeed be improper.
From what kind of causal complexes—meaning from assemblages of causes—are they produced? From diverse ones, meaning from those of different classes;
and again, from what kind? From wood and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), gems and other materials are included.
By this, he shows that it is only the wood and so forth that are specifically designated by the term "causal complex" (sāmagrī), and not something else distinct from them;
for if there were such a thing [as a separate complex], he would have said, "If there were a causal complex of the wood and so forth."
Furthermore, if this very [intrinsic nature] were the cause of the production of the effect, then fuel and other such materials would be useless.
Nor is it logical for an effect produced from one thing to belong to another, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If you argue that it is related to that [fuel], and thus, by virtue of being related to it, that [fuel] is also a producer, then its relationship to that [fuel] must also be established.
Why? Because it inheres [in them].
If it is omnipresent, one must consider why it belongs to only some [substances] and not others.

Furthermore, even if no distinction is made regarding the relation of inherence, if you still maintain that there is a distinction among the related entities, let it be so; however, a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not thereby established.

If it is argued: "By whatever proximity [certain things] possess certain causal complexes (sāmagrī), even though inherence (samavāya) is non-distinct [in all cases], let those very things produce that effect by that very [proximity]; what is the use of inherence?"—if you say this because [the effect] is not related to inherence due to its being an effect, then why do firewood and the like not produce that [effect] in their own nature? What is the prejudice against the effect such that they do not produce it? If you say it is by another complex of causes, that is the same fault, and there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).
The word "api" (even) in the phrase "even in the presence of fire" should be understood as expressing possibility.

For smoke, like fire, cannot have an effect as its mark (*liṅga*) in the absence of something of a different class; yet even when such [a cause] is possible, the effect serves as a mark, according to the principle that "a well-discriminated effect does not deviate from its cause. Does this not apply to sound as well? The word "mark" (*liṅga*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
Of what nature is it? He says: because from that word a Buddhist understands either reality characterized as a *liṅga* (logical mark) or something else;
for instance, the word which exists when the object exists is one thing, and that which exists in its absence is another.
Thus, "a well-discriminated effect does not deviate from its cause"—this has not been chewed by the flock of crows that are Buddhists.

Nor is this objection valid: "The very same word 'jar' which is observed when the jar exists is the same one observed in its absence; how then can it be a logical mark (liṅga)? For their identity is not established, since both differ in terms of location and other factors.
Thus, similarity is not precluded elsewhere either, due to the causal complex (sāmagrī).
The totality of the totality.
The effect [arises] from the totality of conditions in the absence of an external object.
Regarding the absence of the jar,

it might be thought that there is no similarity between the sound produced from wood and so forth and that produced from a gem and so forth, due to the dissimilarity of their causes; it is not [similar] to such [a cause].

For that which is produced from such [a cause] must be of such [a nature], and not otherwise; if that which is produced from such [a cause] were of a different nature, there would be no fixed distinction between "such" and "otherwise.
This same response applies equally to the case of sound as well.

Just as people everywhere consider the word "pot" to be the same, so too do they consider fire produced from wood and fire produced from a gem to be the same, because they observe similar practical usage;
[this reading within the text has been rewritten].

As for one who thinks: "Fire is produced from fuel; that fuel, like wood, is also a gem; therefore, from such [a cause] arises such [an effect]"—in that case, what is this "fuel"? If you say it is "a substance capable of producing fire," then smoke, being produced from the head of Śakra or similar things which are capable of producing it, would likewise be [fire] arising from such [a cause]. Yet, by this much, the head of Śakra and so forth do not become fire; otherwise, wood would be a gem, as there is no distinction [between them].
Because smoke is produced from an anthill,
there is no distinction in its capacity to produce fire.
However, there is another view: the word resides in the speaker, while the object resides in another place and so forth; how then can that [word] be a logical mark (*liṅga*)?
For a great mountain possessing smoke is not a logical mark for a fire in the great ocean.

How then [is it a mark] in cases such as when leaves and the like in another place indicate a fire there? Or how is it that the awakening of a mind elsewhere—such as at a different location—from one who was asleep elsewhere occurs, since for Prajñākaragupta there would be no awakening without a material cause (*upādāna*)?

And he himself desires the inference of the moon and so forth from the moon reflected in water and the like; if this view were established, then this [objection] would be trivial. [The opponent objects:

"But surely, if the effect deviates from the cause, let there be no inference of it from that. To this he says: when fire arises from various collections of causes such as wood and the like, the effect as a logical mark (liṅga) is not necessarily a mark for that [specific cause].

To this, he states the reply: "The word," and so forth. From which word the Buddhist or the Cārvāka understands the reality—the intended object—is that word what? The intention here is this: even while abandoning inference due to the aforementioned defects, one cannot abandon the word, for that would result in total muteness. If one does not abandon it, then if it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one could not understand reality from it; otherwise, how could a discerning person act, or why would they seek another means of valid cognition? If it is a means of valid cognition, then our desired conclusion is established.
And for this reason, the word "ca" (and) [is used];
why [is there] a general statement regarding perception and the rest, which have become invalid means of knowledge?
He states the purport of the first half of the verse with the words "from the realization of reality" (tattvapratipatteḥ) and so forth;
he states the purport of the second half with the words "verbal" (śābda) and so forth.

If it is argued that the reason is unestablished because there is no comprehension of reality from words, he says in response: "Even in inference for oneself," and so forth. The meaning is that it is not only in inference for others, but even in inference for oneself, the observation of the application [of words] is otherwise—that is, in a manner other than the absence of comprehension of reality through another means—which would be entirely improper due to the lack of purpose. This portion of the text has been rewritten. Showing that this [other view] is likewise improper, he says: "Regarding reality," and so forth.
The proponent wins by communicating the truth, while the opponent also wins by exposing a real defect, since both outcomes are possible simultaneously.

If one accepts that a word indicates the speaker’s intention, the proponent is defeated because he has failed to state a constituent of the proof in reality; likewise, the opponent is also defeated if he fails to reveal a real defect.

For one who does not establish the reality (*tattva*) by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the opponent points out the fault of stating what is not a constituent of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*); thus, there is a simultaneous attainment of defeat (*nigraha*). Since victory arises from this, there is no such thing as "victory" for anyone without the establishment of one's own position; for victory is characterized by the manifestation of the path [to truth] through the rectification of deficiencies. Therefore, the very state of having one's position refuted is the ground of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

If one remains silent while the other has not yet been defeated by that much alone, who is refuted by whom? For when either a proof (*sādhana*), a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), or their respective fallacies (*tadābhāsa*) is thus being pointed out, silence can also occur simultaneously.

However, because the truth—which consists of the form of the reason (*hetu-rūpa*) or else the form of the probandum (*sādhya-rūpa*)—is communicated, the Buddhist (*saugata*) triumphs over the opponent; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Not only does the proponent (*vādī*) [triumph], but the opponent (*prativādī*) likewise triumphs over the proponent; this is the connection made by changing the grammatical case.

Having done what? He says: "The fault of the real [proposition] (bhūtadoṣa)—that is, the fault of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*)—should be pointed out; otherwise, it would be entirely improper. This follows [from the context], because otherwise, in the manner of a lack of comprehension, the communication of the truth and the pointing out of the actual fault would be absolutely impossible.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Simultaneously" (*yugapat*), etc., because of the simultaneous occurrence of those two, namely victory and defeat.

For instance: just as in the case of a Buddhist who possesses a valid proof while his opponent is the reverse and thus suffers defeat, so too might the Buddhist suffer defeat, because he fails to state that proof even though it exists;

and just as a Vaiśeṣika or other proponent of a flawed proof is subject to defeat, so too would the Buddhist opponent be defeated for the same reason—failing to point out the flaw even though it exists. Alternatively, this verse should be read after having first presented the opposing position.

If the word itself were the reason (*hetu*), then since the probandum (*sādhya*) would be established from that alone, the further employment of [qualities] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would constitute the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "another reason" (*hetvantara*).
By this, the claim that verbal testimony (*śābda*) is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) has also been refuted. To this, he replies with the words "In reality," etc. [Objection:

But this has already been capable of being refuted by the passage beginning with "This has been properly examined," so why is it stated again? [Response: It is for the purpose of demonstrating another refutation; thus there is no fault.

The Jaina proponent is victorious; why [is he not defeated] by the opponent? To this he says: because he causes the understanding of reality—such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth—through statements consisting of correct means of proof, propositions (*pratijñā*), and the like. Furthermore, does the Buddhist opponent not also defeat the proponent? By what means? By failing to point out the actual fault—that is, the ultimate refutation—in the statements of the proposition and so forth.
And he considers this to be untenable;
why? He says: "Because of the simultaneous occurrence of those two, victory and defeat.

For instance, at the very moment the proponent, having established his own position through reasoning, triumphs over the opponent, at that same moment the opponent might put forward a futile proposition and so forth; and thus, there is a possibility of both occurring at once.

In the argument "Sound is impermanent because it exists," if the probandum is established by the single reason "existence" alone, the employment of a second reason constitutes the point of defeat known as *hetvantara* (another reason).
When a reason has been stated without qualification and that reason has been refuted, the proponent's desire for a qualification constitutes "another reason" (hetvantara).
— Nyāyasūtra 5.2.6.
The connection is that [the treatise] "conquers the proponent," as stated on page 6, line 322.
Explaining the verse for the sake of others, he says: "The intention of the speaker," and so forth.

Regarding the acceptance of that which is the indication of the speaker’s intention—the making known [of it] by means of the word as an effect-reason (*kāryaliṅga*)—the Buddhist proponent is defeated by the Naiyāyika and others.
Why? He says: because of the factors of proof (*sādhanāṅga*), such as the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

Alternatively, [one might ask]: "How is the connection made by changing the case ending as follows: 'Either the means of proof (*sādhana*) itself is the member (*aṅga*), being the cause for the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*); or rather, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the means of proof, and its member is its cause; [this is so] because of the non-statement by the proponent'? To this, he says: "In reality (*tattvataḥ*), that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthena*)."
For, in reality, one thing cannot be indicated by that which indicates another, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Likewise, in that manner, the Buddhist opponent is also defeated; this is understood from the context.
Why? He says: "Because [the reason] is real," and so forth.
Because he does not reveal the defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) even though they exist in reality,
he says "Thatness" (*tattvam*) and so forth, desiring to explain that [fallacy] by means of the second sense of the second [term].

Does one point out an actual fault in the Buddhist’s statement of the proposition and other members of the proof—which fail to establish reality through valid means of cognition? This should be explained with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), or the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood here. Why? He says: because of this reason, there is a simultaneous attainment of defeat for both parties.

Why? He says: [the word] "simultaneously" (yugapat) is understood from the context as "because of victory. Since victory for the proponent necessarily follows from the demonstration of reality—just as defeat follows from a flaw in the argument—he considers this and states the conclusion:
"Since it is thus, therefore, for whom is there such a thing as 'victory' without [something else]? He says: "one's own position," and so forth.
By what means? To this he says: "deficiency," and so forth.

Why? To this he says: because of the state (bhāva), that is, the reality (tattva), of that which has the characteristic of the manifestation—that is, the illumination—of the path consisting of right vision and the rest.
Of what? Of victory.

Since this is so, therefore, "the state of having a refuted position" (*nirākṛtapakṣatvam*)—that is, the very condition of one whose position (*pakṣa*) has been refuted—is the [ground for defeat], and nothing else such as a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, applies to either the proponent or the opponent.

The point of the verse is that this [refutation] exists even for a Jaina who employs an incorrect proof, when he brings forward the statement of a proposition and so forth against a Buddhist; thus, it is he alone who is defeated.
By this very [argument], the following [objection] of the Sugata is also refuted: "The [syllogism] consists of five members" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.32).

In this regard, the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that a deficiency, inversion, or excess of members [of the syllogism] constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). An opponent objects: "This is being said too much; only the state of having one's position refuted (*nirākṛtapakṣatva*) is a point of defeat. If it is argued that even silence (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*) is such a point, he replies here: "When either a proponent (*vādin*) or an opponent (*prativādin*) falls silent, by that mere silence there is no victory for the other—the opponent or the proponent. Who, then, is defeated by whom, and why? Thus he says: "Simultaneously," and so forth.

It is not only that the simultaneous occurrence of the pointing out of a proof, a non-proof, or a member of the argument such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) is possible; rather, because even remaining silent can occur simultaneously, this is what is meant: if the debater suffers defeat due to silence, since that [silence] might also occasionally occur for the opponent, both the winner and the loser would exist at once. Thus, debate (*vāda*) consists in the acceptance of a thesis and its counter-thesis, wherein means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) are employed for proof and refutation, which is not contrary to established tenets (*siddhānta*), and is endowed with the five members [of a syllogism]. (Nyāya-sūtra 1.2.1)
2.1 Thus, regarding the definition of debate (*vāda-lakṣaṇa*),

by this [rule], it is permitted to point out the fallacies of deficiency and excess: that which is deficient by even one of the constituent members (*avayava*) is "deficient," and that which has an excess of reasons (*hetu*) or examples (*udāharaṇa*) is "excessive."

By the inclusion of the phrase "not contradicting the tenet," it is permitted to point out the fallacious reason called "contradictory" (*viruddha*)—defined as that which, having accepted a tenet, contradicts it; thus, in formal debate (*vāda*), these three points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are to be pointed out.

Others say: "It is contradictory that only the *hetvābhāsa* (fallacious reason) is cited as a point of objection (*codya*) in debate, and not the *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) and so forth; how can this be justified? [The answer is: Because of the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya* that "the *hetvābhāsas*, which are taught separately from the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), shall be cited in debate," and because the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) implies its constituent parts (*avayava*), it follows that when the refutation of those parts rooted in fallacious means of cognition is established, the exposure of all *hetvābhāsas* therein is also accomplished.

"By the inclusion of [the condition] 'not contradicting one's own tenets,' the point of defeat called *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of tenets) is raised in formal debate (*vāda*), defined as 'the occurrence of a debate due to a lack of restriction once one has accepted a tenet'—see *Nyāyamañjarī*, *Prameyakhaṇḍa*, p. 150.
This is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Victory [is also achieved] due to the silence of the opponent.

[Objection: "Surely, the fault does not arise for another merely because someone remains silent, but rather for one who proclaims [the fault] in that manner; and since that [fault] does not exist when both remain silent, [the objection is invalid]. To this, he says: "In the proof," and so forth.

The word "that" (tat) refers back to the proof and the refutation—such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) and so on. "Appearing like that" means appearing as if it were that [actual fault]. And "appearing as such in reality" refers to the unestablished nature and so on being proclaimed as such through their mode of appearance. The connection [of the sentence] is: "[this occurs] because of the simultaneous possibility of those two."

The proponent thinks thus: "When one of the faults of proof, such as 'unestablished' (asiddha) and so forth, has been employed by the opponent, the other party does not point out that specific fault, but rather points out something else. In that case, who wins or loses? Neither, for otherwise victory and defeat would simultaneously belong to both. Equality alone is logical;
who then establishes this? If you say 'the assembly,' why? Because neither has established the truth—since one has stated a faulty proof and the other has pointed out a different fault."

In that case, even when merely indicating silence, since there is no establishment of any desired goal for someone, one ought to establish the equality of those two [the rejoinder and the silence] by way of their lack of utility as a means of proof (*sādhana*).

However, if it is argued that the other party is the winner because the proponent has exposed that fault, let this matter rest for now, as it will be examined by the verse beginning with "not a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅga*) and so forth;
for its exposure is indeed present.
The opponent is the adversary of the proponent.

Some maintain that when the assembly itself points out the manifestation of another's faults, then the proponent wins; but by whom is this pointed out? If you say "by the proponent," then both would win simultaneously, because by that very act he reveals his own fault just as he does the other's;
by this, the position of the "assembly" is refuted, for if the assembly fails to perceive a fault even when it exists in the proponent, it follows that they are not impartial.
Showing another refutation against the opponent on this very point, he says: "The statement of what is not a member of the proof," and so forth;
[these two] are the non-statement of a member of the proof and the non-pointing-out of a fault.
If points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are accepted, what then is the use of the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*)?

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The failure to state a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*) constitute the two points of defeat; any other [point of defeat] is not tenable, and thus it is not accepted."

—Vādanyāya, Verse 1. If it is accepted that the debate concludes with a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) due to the proponent’s silence and the failure to state a member of the proof, then [the opponent’s] silence—the non-utterance of a member of the proof—and the failure to point out a fault—the non-revelation of a fault even when one exists, i.e., indifference—are points of defeat for the two parties, the proponent and the opponent respectively. If this is so, what is the point? [The word] "by means of" (*sādhyaiḥ*) and "by means of proofs" (*sādhanaiḥ*), understood as being known, must be supplied. Thus, the sense is: "What is the use of things known? and "What is the use of proofs known? if they lead only to defeat?
The plural number in both instances is used with respect to the meditators (*dhyātṛ*).
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a deliberation (*vitarka*);

the intended meaning here is as follows: if that thorough knowledge were for one’s own sake alone, then because it would be impossible to communicate it to others, how could there be compassion in anyone toward anyone else, such that the relationship between disciple and teacher (*śiṣyopādhyāya-vyavasthā*) could exist?
Alternatively, one must consider how anyone could have full knowledge of that [truth] in the absence of a teacher.
If you say it is "by oneself," then everyone would possess such knowledge, and the composition of treatises would be useless.

If you say it is for the sake of others, then why is someone who has become silent [after realizing the truth] restrained? He should be instructed until he realizes the reality; otherwise, why is it said: "One should speak only so long as the person to be instructed understands"?
Thus, how could this be a well-spoken statement?

For those who do not understand what has been proposed by another, why is it repeatedly propounded [by them], yet their own proof is not? What is this restriction—that everyone else is propounded [to understand], but neither the proponent nor the opponent [is]?

If you say it is because of "banditry" (dasyutva); how is there banditry? Because of entering into another convention (samaya). Precisely for that reason it is propounded, so that by abandoning the immersion in that [other] convention, there may be an immersion in the convention of the proponent.

If it is argued that some followers of other paths are indeed seen there [in the Buddhist system] due to the force of specific instructions, even though they are attached to other systems (*samayāntara*), yet not all are so;

we reply: in that case, no one at all could be a person to be instructed (*pratipādya*). For even when being instructed, another person does not abide solely within the desired system, since we observe that some do not engage with it while others do engage with a different system.

How is it that one who is a learned person (*śiṣṭa*) and so forth does not become a bandit (*dasyu*) at the time of engaging in debate, given that [the state of being a bandit] is present then? Otherwise, how could there be engagement in that [debate]? If you say, "It is never [the case that he is a bandit]," then how can there be certainty that even another [person] is always such [a non-bandit]? By this, it should be understood that even the student who raises the objection would be a bandit. Furthermore, if it is argued that [he is a bandit] because his engagement is motivated by the intent to defeat [the opponent], then it has already been stated in response: "If [this were so], then the learned person and others would [also be bandits]."
In debate, it is solely for the purpose of entering another system that one enters into one's own [opponent's] view.

Furthermore, if the opponent remains silent and, due to his thievery, does not respond, he is merely not defeated [by being silenced]; in that case, the proponent himself must not awaken the other from this very state by means of a correct proof. Rather, he should either observe silence toward him or say something at random. If it is argued that under such circumstances the opponent is indeed defeated, then the employment of the *ṭhaka* (the "thief") should be made so that he turns away; and those who wish to engage in debate should employ *ṭhakas* for the sake of understanding that [turning away], not for the sake of understanding the proof of a proponent of truth.

If it is argued that, because he has become "faceless" (nirmukha) through that application, he should be addressed and even subjected to cross-examination with the words, "I have been ignored by you, therefore you are defeated," and thus there would be an injustice; [we reply: no, for such [procedural requirements] do not apply in the case of suppressing bandits, whereas in other cases they apply equally to the opponent.

The mute [author] provides this further explanation through the application of the term *ṭhaka*: "If the statement of that which is not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) and the pointing out of that which is not a fault (*doṣa*) are both accepted as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then what need is there for the thesis (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*)?"

For instance: when the proponent has been defeated after the opponent has pointed out a real defect in his statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, or in his statement of an unestablished reason (*asiddha*) and so forth, the opponent’s repeated effort to prove his own position would constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Likewise, when the opponent has been defeated by the proponent after the latter has pointed out a non-existent defect, the proponent’s subsequent proof of his own position in that same manner would likewise [be a point of defeat] for both the proponent and the opponent.

To refute the opponent's position, the other [the respondent] further objects as follows: "No one indeed strives for the sake of establishing their own position after the time of defeat, because there is no purpose [in doing so]. Rather, it is said that both the proof of one's own position and the refutation of the opponent's position must be performed by the proponent; this, however, is for the sake of establishing a rule regarding the proponent's activity."

For it is not just anything that must be spoken by the proponent (*vādin*), but rather the establishment of his own position and the refutation of the opponent's position; this is because of the mention of "by the proponent," otherwise he would incur defeat (*nigraha*).
