That [objection] is not sound; for a contradictory proof (*viruddhasādhana*) is not what is understood here as a non-member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), since it is a member of the proof insofar as it establishes the thesis (*pakṣasādhana*), and its defeat is therefore accepted [by us]. Thus, according to the statement that "the state of having a thesis refuted (*nirākṛtapakṣatva*) alone is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)," rather, the statement of an unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or other such [fallacious] propositions and their arguments constitutes the proponent’s defeat, as it is a statement of a non-member of the proof.

*Vādanyāya*, p. 66: From where is this [known]? If you say, "Because his position is not established," then does the opponent have an established position by virtue of which he would be victorious? And there can be no such thing as the defeat of the other without his victory, because victory and defeat are mutually dependent.
One does not overcome the opposing debater by establishing one's own position, but rather solely through the defects in the opponent's statement.
If that were so, one might as well overcome [an opponent] by wriggling one's eyebrows and the like, for there would be no distinction [between the two means].

If it is argued that the establishment of the opponent's position follows from that [admission], we say no; for that is impossible due to the mere presence of the other fault [of contradiction]. Otherwise, what would be the use of those means of proof which are invariably concomitant with the probandum? And how, in this case, would the proponent's own "unestablished" (asiddha) reason be distinguished from the "contradictory" (viruddha)? Therefore, one who desires victory must establish his own position and refute the position of the opponent. — *Vādanyāya*, p. 72.

The statement of a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa)— whether it be unestablished (asiddha), contradictory (viruddha), or inconclusive (anaikāntika)— which is not a constituent part of the proof for establishing [the thesis], is also a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) for the proponent, because he has employed what is incapable [of proving the point]—
*Vādanyāya*, p. 66— since he has merely pointed out a fault in the proponent's own position.

From this it follows: if the statement of a disputant that lacks a constituent of proof is intended to be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then what is the use of proofs for establishing the thesis?
Likewise, the pointing out of a non-fault as a fault by the opponent should be considered a point of defeat;

for when the disputant has presented a flawless proof and the other party points out a fault where there is no fault, if he were defeated on that account alone, then what would be the use of the proofs set forth for the sake of establishing the thesis? Nothing at all [would be achieved] by those proofs.
He thinks that its presentation is for the sake of refuting the opponent, and that it has arisen from something else;
surely, in the absence of that [refutation], the failure to point out a fault would not even be recognized, since the opponent understands it otherwise.
The presentation of a proof [is established] precisely by the non-pointing-out of faults when there is an absence of a proof.

Furthermore, when an opponent does not point out a flaw during the application of a valid proof, how can he be defeated? If you say it is "from that very application," then let him be defeated even when no flaw is pointed out; for that application at that time is not the same as the original application. Otherwise, even the non-pointing-out of a flaw would be difficult to follow. Moreover, if defeat comes from something else, what is the use of that [original] proof? And if defeat occurs from that alone, what is the use of anything else? The logic is the same.
Therefore, he says: "But what [is the use] of the probandum and the means of proof?

The meaning of this is as follows: if the failure to point out a fault in another's argument is accepted as a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then what is the purpose of the probandum and the means of proof? The word "accepted" (*iṣṭam*) is understood to carry over from the previous context; thus, he considers that if [the opponent's position] is accepted, then the failure to point out a fault is rendered pointless.
At that very moment, the opponent [is defeated] due to the application of a correct proof.

It might be thought: "Even if the opponent does not point out a fault that exists, and the proponent likewise does not point out a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then the proponent alone is defeated because he has neglected what ought to be questioned (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇāt*), since his own position has been refuted.

If it is argued that this is the same even when the fault is pointed out—since both are intended to be grounds for defeat—let this matter rest for now, as it will be examined later [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*] under the section beginning with "When the proponent states multiple reasons" (siddhivi॰ pari॰ 5).

Another disputant says: "The failure to point out a fault when a correct proof has been employed is not intended as a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); rather, it is so when there is an employment contrary to that. To this he replies: "What then [is the role] of the probandum and the proof? The intended meaning here is this: when a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) has been employed by the proponent and no fault has been pointed out by the opponent, the proponent does not defeat the opponent; for one who perceives a fault cannot be victorious, and without him (the proponent), there can be no defeat of the other.
If that were the case, the opponent too might defeat the proponent; thus, victory and defeat would occur simultaneously, and consequently, it would be more appropriate for them to be equals.

Nevertheless, since the members of the assembly (*prāśnikas*) establish [the proof] for the opponent alone, how can they be considered impartial (*madhyastha*), given that they rely on such debate? Why, then, are there members of the assembly who, by means of those proofs of the probandum (*sādhyasādhana*), establish what is to be proven?

[Objection: "Surely equality would obtain if the proponent did not manifest the opponent's failure to point out a fault; but if he does manifest it, then his position does not hold. To this, we consider the following: Does he manifest that [fault] by revealing his own fault, or otherwise? In that regard, the latter alternative is not possible; for if he does not reveal his own fault, he is unable to know that "the fault employed by me has not been pointed out by him," and thus his purpose is not achieved. Nor is the former alternative possible; for it has already been stated that by revealing his own fault himself, he alone incurs defeat (*nigraha*).

If, moreover, victory were to arise from exposing the actual faults of another, while defeat would likewise arise from manifesting one's own actual faults, then [one might argue]: "Since this fault is not a fault because it is set aside by the merit of exposing the other's actual faults, how can this [self-exposure] be a merit? [The opponent asks: "Why? [The proponent replies: "Because it is set aside by that [merit]. [The opponent asks: "By whom is it set aside? [The proponent replies: "By the disputant."
He should bring to light the opponent's failure to point out a fault in that opponent [of the proponent].
Furthermore, there is defeat for the opponent;

moreover, if one's own defects were to lose their status as defects within oneself by revealing the defects of another, then one would have to say at the very moment of uttering any of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), such as the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth: "Although I employed this unestablished or other reason, its fallacious nature was not pointed out [by you]."
And she said: "Of the disputants," and so forth.

"Of the disputants" means those who hold a prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*). "From silence" refers to the failure to state a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*). A member of the proof for one's own or the opponent's position is that which does not exist, such as a proposition (*pratijñā*) and so on that is unestablished; it is from the statement of such [unestablished things]. It is not, however, to be explained as "from the non-statement of a member of the proof" (*na sādhanāṅgavacanāt*) or "from the statement of what is not a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacanāt*), because that is already covered by the phrase "from silence.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

A point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs at the conclusion of a debate or discussion, or rather, when there is the inclusion in a statement of proof of that which is not a constituent part of that very proof—such as the proposition (*pratijñā*), application (*upanaya*), or conclusion (*nigamana*)—because such inclusion constitutes a useless utterance by the proponent; [Vādanyāya, p.

Alternatively, "sādhana" means proof; that which is a factor of such proof is a "sādhana-aṅga," namely the property (dharma) belonging to the object under dispute—the very subject that serves as the cause for initiating the debate. To introduce or to suppress another, unintended particularity by means of resorting to treatises or other pretexts—whether for the purpose of deluding the opponent or for the purpose of obstructing his ability to restate the argument—is also the "statement of what is not a factor of proof" (*asādhana-aṅga-vacana*), which constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent because it is an irrelevant statement. — *Vādanyāya*, p. 66.

If it is argued that, just as with the proponent, when the opponent remains silent or speaks nonsense, there is no conclusion because both parties are equal [in failing], the author replies here: "Having exposed the actual fault... and so forth. Since he has won by exposing the real defect, how can the proponent be defeated merely because the debate concludes otherwise? (11)
That is not well-said—that one who desires victory must perform both: establishing one's own position and refuting the opponent's position.
[The author asks: "Having exposed the actual fault, such as silence or other ultimate faults, how was it exposed? He says: "He has won" (jitavān).

Or rather, having exposed that [fault], the proponent has won; because of that, subsequently—in the sense of a further deliberation (*vitarka*)—the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is used... [thus] the opponent is defeated because he is unable to establish his own position.
Why? He says: because by that alone—by the mere pointing out of the fault in the [opponent's] argument—the defeat (*nigraha*) of the proponent is completed.

Otherwise, how could the proponent be defeated by one who, through his wisdom, does not complete that [refutation]? In no way. For instance, regarding that [refutation], there are four positions concerning the proponent’s effort: (1) for the sake of defeating [the opponent]; (2) for the sake of awakening [him]; (3) for the sake of awakening [him] when he is already virtuous; and (4) simply as a debate (*vāda*). Thus there are four positions.

In that regard, in the first case, that [refutation] would be futile, because the defeat [of the opponent] occurs through something else, since even silence and so forth constitute the application of a *thaka* (a technical term for a fault). In the second case, however, it is untenable for silence and so forth to constitute a defeat;

for teachers do not employ pupils in defeat merely on account of a fault when they have already made an effort to instruct them, and judges do not [do so] toward one who knows both systems of tenets (*siddhānta*).

Even the report of the third alternative is not tenable; however, in the fourth case, the speaker would be a proponent of incoherent speech. For the opponent strives before the witnesses to demonstrate his own superiority, thinking that if he were not made fully manifest at the conclusion of that [struggle], he would be perceived as lacking splendor; therefore, let that very [struggle] be undertaken for the sake of establishing one's own position.

Now, [the opponent might argue] that once that [debate] is concluded, no one exerts effort toward establishing their own position. To this, he says: "That is not so," and so forth. Why is it not well-spoken? He explains: "Whether it be the proponent (*vādin*) or the opponent (*prativādin*) seeking victory, both must perform two things: the proof of one's own position and the refutation of the other's position."

For instance—the connection is as follows: it is not merely that which must be done by the opponent (*prativādin*) who desires victory; rather, he must render the proponent (*vādin*) something other than a human, such as a Piśāca, and likewise, the proponent must also render the opponent in such a manner; this is what must be done.

By this, the point that "there is no pointing out of a fault" is also explained. Therefore, it is established: if the reason or the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were verbal—such as [the argument] beginning with "the silence of someone"—then since the probandum would be established by the mere statement "sound is impermanent," what would be the use of [the reason] "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth? If that [probandum] is already established, then stating such [a reason] constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Right here, he states another objection: "If the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established in its entirety," and so forth.

Only when the invariable concomitance is established in its entirety does the reason become proven; therefore, just like the proponent of existence (*sattva*), the proponent of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) [is also required]. 12.

Since the reason (*hetu*) has already been stated as being pervaded in its entirety (*sākalyena*), does the subsequent statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) become identical to the statements of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the application (*upanaya*), or not? Having set aside your attachment to the Tathāgata, close your eyes or open them and consider this for a moment: is the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*) identical when both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) are stated together? If it is identical, why [use] the statements of the proposition and so forth? For the thorough understanding of the capacity of the proof is the same in both cases, provided that the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been established and ascertained in its entirety and without exception.

Of what? For that very reason, from that same cause, [the proof] is established; for when the probandum exists, there would be one who asserts its existence, and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the application (*upanaya*) and so forth is intended—it should be supplied that there would also be one who asserts the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
The meaning is that the proponent of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) would be similar to the proponent of existence (*sattva*) and so forth;
for we perceive no difference between the statement "sound is impermanent" and such statements as "sound exists" or "sound is produced.
By the word "api" (also/even), one who asserts a sentence such as "whatever exists or is produced is impermanent, like a pot; and sound exists or is produced" is included.

For one who asserts the simultaneous employment of both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) in the formulation [of a proof], there is no distinction from [the opponent] regarding the application [of the reason]; this will be examined in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) during the discussion on the operation [of the reason].
In order to explain the verse (*kārikā*), he says: "In its entirety," and so forth.

Regarding the statement such as "Whatever is existent or produced is impermanent, like a jar," which expresses a reason that is pervaded in its entirety: why is the subsequent statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) similar to that? He says: "It is similar to the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the application (*upanaya*)," and so forth.

Whether it be "it may or may not be so," or "the passion of the Tathāgata" (the Sugata’s acceptance), or likewise, by that same principle, a statement such as a "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*), or the statement of the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*); having set aside all such passionate attachments through this method—whether by closing or opening one's eyes—one should reflect upon the similarity and dissimilarity together at once: "Whatever exists is impermanent, like a jar; sound exists; if it were permanent, it would not exist even though it is [perceived], like space; and sound is thus. One must state everything, including whether the proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*) such as "whatever exists is entirely impermanent, like a jar; and sound exists" is valid or not, and so forth.

Alternatively, the inclusion in a proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*) of that which is not a member of that very proof—such as the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application (*upanaya*), or the conclusion (*nigamana*)—is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent precisely because it is a useless statement (*vyarthābhidhāna*). (Vādanyāya, p.

61) [Objection: Surely, by the statement of the proposition "sound is impermanent," the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—"and sound is existent"—must be considered equivalent, since it is merely a specification of the probandum (*sādhya*) itself.

For just as the impermanence of sound is to be proven for one who holds a contrary view, so too must its existence (*sattva*) and other properties be established; otherwise, the statement of that [reason] would be purposeless. In the syllogism, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a jar; and sound is produced," the very same point already expressed by the statement "sound is impermanent because it is produced" is repeated by the statement "and sound is produced. Likewise, the very same point already expressed by the statement "whatever is produced is impermanent" is also expressed by the statement "and sound is produced."
Because of the statement of universal concomitance (*sākalyavyāpti*), because of the mention of sound’s being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and because the particular is included within the general—

otherwise, like sound’s being produced, other things would not be denoted by it, and the statement of concomitance would become meaningless— the application (*upanaya*) is the subsumption of the reason (*hetu*).
The connection is that "it should be considered equal.

By this concluding statement, "therefore it is impermanent," that which is equal to it has been reflected upon. Just as indeed the very meaning already stated by the force of the reason (*hetu*) is expressed by the conclusion (*nigamana*), so too is that which was stated by the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) [expressed] by the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*);

likewise, the statement of the reason’s presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), together with the statement of its similarity or dissimilarity, constitutes the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*). Thus, [the structure] is the same.

If it is argued: "Just as when a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been stated in a definitive manner, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and the absence of non-concomitance (*avyatireka*) are understood through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), so too, by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the existence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*) are understood through presumptive implication from the statement of the reason that is known to be pervaded in its entirety; therefore, where would a syllogistic statement consisting of the three-fold probans (*trirūpa-sādhana-vākya*) be of use?"—to this he replies: "That which is not equal" (*yadasamānam*). How so? The syntactic construction of the words is: "Why would one be defeated by the very statements of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, rather than by other statements such as the proposition? (i.e., why would the opponent be defeated by the statement of the three-fold reason itself, rather than by the statement of the thesis?).

For the statements of those [members of the syllogism], such as the proposition (*pratijñā*), do not undermine the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason, nor do they undermine the cognition thereof, from which its logical necessity (*pratibandha*) would arise. Now, it may be argued that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not only defective due to faults in the reason (*hetu-doṣa*), but also due to faults of the proponent (*vādidoṣa*); and there is indeed such a fault, namely, the failure to recognize the capacity of a proof to establish the probandum even when devoid of statements such as the proposition—otherwise, one would not employ it.

If it is argued, "For what wise person would not exert effort toward that which is purposeless, thereby only causing themselves distress?"—to this he replies with the words beginning "sādhane" (in the proof), and so forth.

The thorough understanding of the capacity of the proof (*sādhana*), such as existence (*sattva*) and the like, is the same in both cases: in the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the like, and in the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the like, according to the method already stated.
Therefore, he thinks that just like the proponent of existence and the like, the proponent of the property of the subject and the like would also be defeated.
Furthermore, regarding the thorough knowledge of the capacity of the means of proof (*sādhana*):

if the proponent were defeated on the grounds that a failure to fully understand the similarity of the means of proof in an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) constitutes a fault, then this would constitute another point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the Buddhist (*saugata*). Demonstrating this, he says: "Precisely because of existence," etc.;
[the opponent] is defeated regarding the momentary duration, arising, and so forth, precisely because of existence.
Because of the statement regarding the predominance of the property (*dharma*), the proponent [commits a fault] through ignorance of its capacity.

Since even a mere entity has the capacity to prove destruction—either because it arises again or because it is produced (*kṛtakatva*)—the introduction of a qualification (*upādhi*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). This is because those [reasons] are characterized by an operation that depends upon both self and other; for one does not necessarily become defeated by that which must lead to a point of defeat, since students are to be instructed [by means of such arguments].
For even if that which is pure is a means of proof (*sādhana*), it is not logical for it to require further limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

[The word] "because" (*iti*) has the sense of the particle *eva* (only/necessarily), meaning: because it exists (*sattvāt*), because it is present (*vidyamānatvāt*), and because it is devoid of any limiting condition that is either different or non-different. When the momentary destruction of some subject (*dharmin*)—at the place of the "moment"—is established and ascertained, then when that [reason] consisting of origination and so forth (where "origination" is the first among such properties as being produced) is employed, the disputant is defeated; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
[This refers to] the qualification.

Now, is it not the case that by the word "origination" (utpatti) one expresses existence characterized by the acquisition of self-nature for that which previously did not exist, and by the word "produced" (kṛtaka) one expresses that very same state of depending on the operation of another? The same should be said regarding "immediately following effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva) and so forth. Therefore, just as there is no defeat when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because of its existence" (sattvāt), so too there is no such defeat when it is stated, "because of origination," "because of being produced," or "because of immediately following effort. Thus, [the objection] is not tenable.

If it is argued that "the same thing being expressed by another word does not constitute a point of defeat (nigraha), for otherwise even 'smoke' would become one when expressed by that [other] word," the author replies with the words beginning with *dharma*. The connection is made by transforming the case endings (*vibhaktipariṇāma*) in both instances: [the relation is] "because of the statement of an additional [quality] through a property (*dharma*)—in the form of prior non-existence, the operation of another, and so forth—which serves as a qualifier that is both different and non-different from the entity; and because of the statement of existence through arising and so forth.
What is meant is this: if that very pure existence (*sattva*) which is denoted by the word "existence" were also denoted by the word "arising" and so forth, then this fault would not arise.

And when that [existence] is spoken of, for the sake of instructing the disciple, it is designated by words such as "existence," "producedness," and so forth— distinguished according to the divisions of pure and impure, and according to the distinctions of differentiated and non-differentiated qualifiers; thus,
even when production and other states are expressed, they float within the word "existence" itself by means of another term.
Comparison— just as whatever is existent is all momentary, like jars and so forth, and sound is existent (Hetubindu, p.
55)— the essential nature [of the probans] may depend on a distinction of conditions, or it may be absolute.
It is said: "For the sake of establishing the probandum, [the reason] is like 'being an effect' or 'existence' with respect to destruction" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.185,
In some cases, it occurs through the inclusion of a property that constitutes the very nature [of the subject], as in that same [work]:
"Whatever exists is all impermanent, like a jar, etc."—this is the formulation of a pure essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti, p. 349).
The formulation of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) by way of a distinction between essential properties is as follows: "Whatever has an origin is impermanent.
The formulation by way of a distinction between adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) is: "Whatever is produced is impermanent.
In this same manner, [formulations] such as "being differentiated by the differentiation of conditions" are to be understood.
By this, [the arguments] such as "being differentiated by the difference of conditions" (Nyāyabindu 3.11–13, 15) are explained.

Furthermore, in words such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), there is reliance on mere convention (*saṅketa*) and not on [intrinsic] understanding (*vyutpatti*). This being the case, how can "being immediately subsequent to effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) be a property that pervades only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣaikadeśavyāpakatva*)? Or, if that were the probandum (*sādhya*), why would "impermanence" (*anityatva*) be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)? For it is impossible for that [inconclusiveness] to apply to pure existence (*sattva*). By this [statement], is it meant that it is qualified by that [effort] and not by production (*utpatti*) and so forth? What is the basis for this distinction, given that there is no difference between existence and "being immediately subsequent to effort" and the like?
By this [argument], it is refuted that "being subsequent to effort" does not state a different meaning (arthāntara) when [the probandum] is "existence" (sattva).

[Objection: "Granted that there may be a designation of a 'being' (sattva) possessing attributes such as dharma by way of its production and so forth, even so, how could one be defeated in that regard? To this, he says: "That," and so on. By the word "that" (tat), the being (sattva) is referred to. Its "capacity" (sāmarthya) is the power of proof belonging to it alone. Through "ignorance" (anabhijñā)—that is, through a lack of full understanding—one thinks thus: "If pure being possesses the capacity for proof, what is the use of other qualifiers? Therefore, the employment of those [qualifiers] is not a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna)."

Others, however, say: "Momentariness is not established for arising and so forth in any [entity] from an ultimate standpoint (*paramārthatas*), because such [momentariness] does not exist ultimately; rather, it is because they appear as such, according to the statement, 'It is just as it appears,' and so on.

And that very appearance is existence (*sattva*), according to the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (3.54): 'Apprehension is existence. Therefore, this is not a fault. To them, too, this is the very same reply.

For example, if the momentariness of all things were established, certain, and accepted simply because of the appearance of momentariness in such things as sentient beings, how could the Buddhist be refuted? To this he says: "Because of the statement regarding *dharma* and the *adhika*.
That is, because of the statement concerning both *dharma* and the *adhika*.
The property of all entities—that is, their appearance as strictly momentary—is established neither by perception nor by inference.
It is not established by perception first, because that [momentariness] does not appear therein.

Indeed, there is no certainty that entities appearing with momentariness appear in the cognition of the eye and other senses; for it is determined that in those [cognitions], things such as snakes appear as persisting through successive states such as being coiled and so forth.
Prajñākaragupta and others, who maintain the doctrine of non-dual appearance, hold that in perception there is only the act of appearing.

Comparison: Therefore, by abandoning both [extremes], the person (puruṣa), whose nature consists of exclusion and inclusion, must be accepted— just as a snake [is perceived] in relation to its coils and so forth— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Ātmavāda, verse 28.
It is to be directly experienced, like a snake in [the coils of] a bracelet and so forth— Nyāyaviniścaya 2.116.
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (verses 223–24),

contradictions and other such objections have likewise been answered; the extremist conceptualization of difference and non-difference between a quality and its possessor has been refuted by means of non-absolutism (*anaikānta*).

In this regard, Arcata’s presentation of an infinite regress appears to be self-defeating for his own position, because even when the three-fold nature of a logical reason (*hetu*) is ascertained, that [infinite regress] remains possible; for he accepts there two aspects: the expressible and the other (the non-expressible). Otherwise, in the absolute monism of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-ekānta*), since the relation of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmin-bhāva*) would be absent, there could be no establishment of even the *Hetubindu* by means of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, those two things would have to be entirely distinct entities, and that...
If it is argued that for the sake of establishing the non-difference of those two— which are distinct from one another—
there is another non-distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva) stated [to exist] so that their non-difference may be proven; |||

Another nature would have to be imagined, and thus there would be an infinite regress—Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 105. For even though it is conceptual with respect to the form of the object, it is non-conceptual with respect to its own nature.

If it is argued: "But surely, the perception of a preceding moment does not function with respect to a succeeding moment, nor does the perception of that [succeeding moment] function with respect to the preceding one; so how can the persistence of anything be cognized by means of it?"—then [we reply]: in that case, since that [perception] terminates in its own nature alone, how could it be the apprehender of other things, such that the manifestation of momentariness could be established? For the cognition of a property (dharma) is invariably concomitant with the cognition of the substratum (dharmin). Thus, how is the reason established? For this very reason, there is no inference either, because in the absence of that [cognition], it too is absent.

If, however, you seek the establishment of the reason by accepting that all appearances of momentariness are established conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), then the opponent may likewise establish the unestablished [nature of the reason] in that very same way— namely, by accepting that the appearance of a single entity persisting through the three times is conventional— since there is no difference in their status as occurrences of subsequent perceptions.
By means of perception, there is the perception of the substance which is the locus.

Even for the Jaina, in the absence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one must then establish that all things possess the property of appearing as momentary by perceiving that property in an entity currently being apprehended. Here too, the same objection applies: by what means are they so established? Not by direct perception, nor by inference, because of the faults already stated.

If that [momentariness] is established conventionally, then momentariness itself would also be conventionally established; thus, there is no determination of the ultimate nature of entities. How skillful indeed is the Buddhist in defining the nature of entities!

Or rather, what is this momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) in regard to entities that are themselves being perceived? If you say it is the state of being severed by successive limits (*koṭi*), then if a perception—preceded by the grasping of those limits—were to grasp that severance for anyone, then the grasping of continuity would not be refuted, because, just as with the severance, its opposite (continuity) could likewise be grasped by another [perception]. Otherwise, it would follow that one would grasp the persisting nature in exactly that same way. Thus, it has been stated that just as with spatially separated objects, the perception of temporally separated objects is also not contradictory, since the denial of similarity (*sārūpya*) has been rejected.
If it is argued that there is no lack of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta), we say no; for its presence as a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) is not established through perception,
nor through inference, because this [inference] is preceded by that [perception], and in the absence of the latter, the former cannot exist.

Or, let it be granted that its establishment [of momentariness] occurs from some source; even so, since the probandum is established by the very establishment of the reason (*hetu*), inference is redundant. To explain: if there is an appearance characterized by the severance of preceding and succeeding moments, this is an appearance of momentariness. Since that which is uncertain cannot function as a reason, if that [momentariness] is certain, then what is uncertain that remains to be established by inference? If you say it is the "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*) regarding it, we say no; for such usage is of the nature of certainty itself.
Thus, this follows: even for one who ascertains the ground as distinct from a jar, there is no ascertainment of the absence of the jar.

And how could inference function for the sake of practical activity regarding what is grasped by conceptual perception for one who speaks thus? Or how can those who do not accept momentariness in entities yet accept their appearing in such a way [as momentary]—since the apprehension of an entity is inseparable from the apprehension of its properties, and appearing in such a way is a property of momentary entities; otherwise, who indeed, desiring a property of an entity, would not desire the entity itself? (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 2).
"193. Is this well-spoken? How so? Just as those who do not accept momentariness are seen [to speak], so too is the manifestation [of things] established from that;
once the reason is proven, the probandum is established, and further inference is useless—this very point constitutes a ground for defeat (nigrahasthāna).
He states this because of 'excessive speech' (*adhikokti*): one would be defeated by stating an inference in excess of what is necessary once the reason has been ascertained."
The point is that the uninterrupted continuity of following after the preceding and succeeding [moments] can be apprehended by another perception.
Whether it be the case that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by direct perception,

or else that all things are momentary because they appear as such— if, on the other hand, those things appearing as such were not actually so, there would be a state of formlessness (*nīrūpatā*), because the determination of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is grounded in consciousness (*saṃvit*).
If the matter at hand were established by this much alone— namely, "like blue and so forth"—

then for one who maintains the doctrine of the non-duality of the Self (*puruṣādvaitavādin*), there is no other means for establishing [the probandum] even through an example, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, momentariness cannot be the probandum for such a person, as there would be no distinction from the point of contention.
If one were to state an example that exceeds [the scope of the thesis], one would be defeated;
for [in that case] momentariness would result in being a mere nothingness.

Or, if one imagines another means [of proof], this is the absolute rule: that whatever appears in a certain way exists as such in ultimate reality. If that were so, then pillars and the like, appearing with a nature that is both gross and manifold, would exist exactly as they appear; thus, even if they are appearances like those of a magical illusion or a mirage, there would be no fault. Thus it floats [in the argument] in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra* (3.221).

If even in a sequential manner, as in the case of non-sequential [cognition], there arises doubt regarding the existence of a single object, how can the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) be possible? Furthermore, if that appearance is negated, it would entail the negation of everything; thus, inference cannot arise because the property (*dharma*) and so forth are unestablished.

If it is argued that [the reason] is not universal (*asāmanta*), then the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by virtue of those very [properties], and one would be defeated by the statement of that [inconclusiveness].

To this he says: "By the mention of an additional property" (*dharmādhikokti*). This is a compound meaning "that which is both a property (*dharma*) and additional (*adhika*). Since the qualifier and the qualified may be placed in either order according to one’s preference, the additional element (*adhika*) is here the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
Furthermore, [the opponent] would be defeated because the property of being a subject (*pakṣadharma*) belongs to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) as well;

likewise, since existence itself is established in arising and so forth—just like momentary duration—if the Buddhist were to accept this, he would be defeated by stating a reason that is "non-deviant yet contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
In the phrase "in arising and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes both duration and destruction.
By what reason would he be refuted? To this, he says: "That," and so forth.

It refers to that capacity which belongs to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the reason for the probandum; or else, it refers to that [capacity] of the reason which is devoid of an example; or again, just as with its own cause, so too with the cause of another;
or it is due to ignorance of that [capacity], or due to the non-existence of that reason, or due to ignorance of its capacity.

He explains the verse containing the word *adhika* with the words "of the mere," etc. The word *api* (also/even) is used in a different syntactical order; [it means] "even of the mere," not only of smoke and so forth. "The mere destruction" is the proof (*sādhana*). "From similarity" (*sādharmyāt*) means from the cause. Furthermore, in the case of a reflective consideration (*parāmarśe*), [the word *punaḥ* refers to that].

Because of the non-employment of a qualified [subject] in the statement beginning with "of that which previously did not exist through a limiting condition" (*upādhinā prāgasataḥ*), the term "of an entity" (*bhāvasya*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
How so? He says: "either because of arising or because of being produced" (*utpatteḥ kṛtakatvādvā*).
What follows from that? He says: "it is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent"; this is the remainder [of the sentence].

[The opponent objects: "Surely, by means of a qualification, just as a mere entity (*bhāva*) is expressed by the word 'existence' (*sattva*), so too [is it expressed] by words such as 'origination' (*utpatti*) and so forth. To this, he replies: "In relation to self and other," and so on. That which has a dependence upon the two operations—of itself and of another—or which depends upon those two, is "dependent" (*tadapekṣa*). And since that is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of those [states] such as origination and so forth, [they are not mere entities].

Arising (*utpatti*) is defined as an entity (*bhāva*) that depends on its own operation; for it is stated that "arising is the acquisition of self-nature by that which previously did not exist. Thus, an entity whose qualification is non-distinct [from itself] is described in this way. However, properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) are defined as entities characterized by dependence on the operation of another; for it is declared in the *Nyāyabindu* (3.14) and elsewhere: "An entity that depends on the operation of another is 'produced' (*kṛtaka*)."
By this, it is considered that when a pure [entity] itself is expressed with a distinct qualifier, there is no mention of its properties because another word is not employed;
in some places, the reading is "there is dependence on the operation of self and other."
In that context, it should be explained as "existence" (bhāva) with respect to that [capacity].
If it is argued that the mention of that [capacity] as qualified [by existence] is for the purpose of establishing the capacity of the pure [entity], he says here: "Not indeed," and so forth.

He thinks thus: one who is prompted [to act] by that [fault] will inevitably fall into a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna); therefore, students should not be instructed by him, because he does not apply himself to their benefit.

For by the word "origination" (utpatti), that which possesses a state of requiring an operation for the completion of its own nature is "produced" (kṛtaka). Therefore, this term "produced," although denoting the intrinsic nature (svabhāva), implies an extrinsic condition (paropādhi).
—*Pravāha-svabhāva*, p.
348: Because there is no favoring of disciples with respect to the activity for the sake of oneself and others.

This is another explanation: the existence (*bhāva*), which is the being (*sattā*) of a solitary moment—distinguished from its own and other classes and devoid of parts—or rather, the apprehension of that entity (the term "object" being applied metaphorically to the subject), does not alone possess the capacity for destruction by another as accepted [by the opponent]. For whatever meets the conditions for perception and is not perceived in a certain place, that does not exist there, just as a jar of such a kind is absent in a particular location; and the preceding and succeeding moments meet the conditions for perception during the middle moment, yet they are not perceived therein.

Alternatively, [the argument] "whatever appears as such... and so forth depends upon a formal syllogism (*prayoga*); therefore, why would this constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? To this he says: "Because of its arising, or because of its being produced"—here, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "as if" (*iva*).
Or rather, it is the middle moment [of existence] that exists between the preceding and succeeding moments.

What is meant by this is as follows: according to Prajñākaragupta, a proponent of partless non-duality (*niraṃśādvaitavādin*), nothing whatsoever arises that was previously non-existent, nor is there anything produced (*kṛtaka*) that depends upon the operation of another; nevertheless, for one who asserts such a cause, there is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). This is because no entity or perception of it is established, since it is sublated by the appearance of something gross, stable, and singular—which is contradictory to its own nature. Likewise, due to the capacity of that very [appearance], to subsequently qualify that same [entity] with a limiting condition (*upādhi*)—namely, its existence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*)—is a point of defeat.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the "adjunct" (*upādhi*) consists of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), presence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣe'sattvam*); because the reason (*hetu*) is taken as qualified by these. Thus, the connection is as follows: since their nature (*rūpa*) is characterized by the existence of those two—the application of the proof (*sādhana-prayoga*)—which are the operations of the respective proponent and opponent, [the mention of] "non-occurrence" and "destruction" as reasons [for defeat] constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) according to Prajñākaragupta.

It can be stated that whatever is perceived there in such a manner as to meet the conditions for perception exists in reality exactly so—as in the case of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) with respect to its own forms—and likewise, such an entity is perceived in some way within its own successive states (*svaparyāya*) which occur sequentially; furthermore, whatever appears in an uncontradicted cognition exists as the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*) in that very way, just like self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and everything indeed appears as consisting of origination, destruction, and persistence—this may also be expressed by the principle: "whatever is independent of something else," and so forth.

The phrase "even of a pure entity" (śuddhasya api bhāvasya) is understood to carry over [from the previous context], meaning that even for an entity devoid of a reason (*hetu*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), [the following applies]: when it serves as a means of proof (*sādhanatve*), it is devoid of a reason; and when it is a mark (*liṅga*) that establishes the probandum (*sādhya*), it is devoid of an example. Furthermore, regarding that mark which requires the presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), it is so described. It is logical, appropriate, or fitting that the "limiting condition" (*upādhi*)—namely, the requirement of its existence in the similar class (*sapakṣasattva*)—should apply to the mark.
According to Prajñākaragupta, an entity that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) [is the subject].
It is restricted by that very nature; for example, as the final causal complex is restricted to the production of its own effect.

Furthermore, showing another refutation regarding that same previous position, he says: "Without a pronoun," and so forth—without a pronoun there is no sentence, and without a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) there is no word.

Comparison: When perishability is established by the mere fact of existence (*sattva*), the mention of "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*) or "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth constitutes the statement of an extraneous qualification; and in cases such as "produced" or "following immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*), the addition of the suffix *ka* constitutes the statement of a non-essential part of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*), which leads to defeat. — *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 86.

How is it that the statement of the reason "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) involves the mention of the suffix *-ka* used in its own sense (*svārthika*), which demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent"—and yet this would not be the point of defeat called "the superfluous" (*adhika*)? For even without that [suffix], the meaning is understood; and since the meaning might be understood from the mere use of the word in its function (*vṛtti*) everywhere, what purpose does the statement of the entire sentence serve such that it would not be "superfluous"? ... [Tattvasaṅgraha, verse 291] Otherwise, in your own formulation as well, there is likewise a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) used in its own sense.
Furthermore, there would be a fault regarding that [conclusion], because it would be established as having a meaning already known [from another source]:
"Whatever is produced is indeed seen to be impermanent, just like a jar and so forth;
and sound is produced"—for from this much alone, the probandum is determined.
Therefore, you must condense [the text] even without [my] words;
otherwise, it would result in defeat. This has been stated in the *Siddhiviniścaya*:
"A sentence is [defective] without a pronoun, and a word is [defective] without a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)."
One who does not fear the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) regarding the summary of the meaning should condense [the argument].
— *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Book II, pp. 237–38:
"One who does not fear the points of defeat regarding the summary of the meaning should condense [it]. (14)

The statement that "whatever is existent, possesses origination, is produced, or follows immediately after an effort" should be condensed as "the existent has originated," and so forth, or simply as "the existent is impermanent.

This is because once the pervasion (vyāpti) is established through the force of a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) that sublates the presence of the reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa), an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is of no further use;
thus, this pervasion would be contained within the thesis (pratijñā) itself.

Therefore, it would be better for the Buddhist to state the original proposition as "sound is perishable. How should that statement which is intended to establish the logical mark (*liṅga*) be abbreviated? He says: "without the use of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnā vinā*).
The connection is as follows: even that word which [occurs] in that very sentence, apart from the employment of that specific word, should be condensed;
how so? He says: "without a secondary derivative (taddhita)."
By what [means]? To this he says: "equal," and so forth.

That whose meaning is directly perceived by one word through another word is described as such; by that [word], there is a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna). In that regard, it is not [a point of defeat] for the Buddhist, nor for anyone else, without that secondary suffix—such as *ka* added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*)—and so on.

The sense is that in the phrase "kṛtakam," one should have used simply "kṛtam"; thus he explains the verse: "That which is existent, possesses origination, is produced, and follows immediately after effort," and so forth;
therein, even though there is a difference in the formulation of the counter-reason (*pratihetu*).
The singular number in the word "sentence" (*vākya*) refers to the genus [of sentences].

Furthermore, if the word "and" (*ca*) is connected with each [term] individually—such as the sentence "whatever is existent is impermanent, like a jar; and sound is existent"—this should be applied in all cases.
The mention of "sentence" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, individual words such as "existent" (*san*) and so forth are also included.
"What, then, should be done? To this he says: "It should be condensed.
How? To this he says: "That which is existent is arisen," and so forth;
"the existent is impermanent," meaning "that which has arisen is impermanent. In this manner, it should be applied everywhere.

Now, it was stated that a statement should be abbreviated by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and not without an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); so, should an example be mentioned? To this he says: "Always," and so forth.

The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the preceding reason. Thus, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that what is existent is impermanent, what is produced is impermanent, what is made is impermanent, and whatever is permanent is impermanent—is established and ascertained through the force of the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the presence of the reason in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the example is of no utility; therefore, the connection is that it should be abbreviated in that manner.

If one asks, "What is the fault in such a concise formulation? he replies: "And thus, by that very manner just mentioned, this very proposition (*pratijñā*)—in the form 'existence is non-eternal' and so forth—would itself be the pervasion (*vyāpti*). For there is no distinction between the two states of "sound is non-eternal" and "existence is non-eternal"; consequently, there would be no logical reason (*hetu*) here at all—this is the meaning of the particle *eva*. To explain: if "existence" and so forth were again employed as the reason, it would result in the fallacy of the reason being merely a part of the subject matter of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).

If, on the other hand, [the reason] were to indicate that impermanence itself exists eternally, then because it would exist at all times, the object of proof (*sādhya*) would be cognized from it at all times; thus, there would be no dispute. Let the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself be so—what is the fault? To this, he says: "Therefore," by the aforementioned logic, it is better to maintain the original position under discussion—that sound is perishable. For even if one were to beat one's head and cry out, the original proposition does not cease; such is the thought.

If it is argued: "In the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), what is the use of the proposition (*pratijñā*)? And in its establishment, what is the use of the reason (*hetu*)? To this he replies: "If [it is established] by 'perishable' and so forth... If, according to the logic already stated, it is established that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is ineffective, then the statement of an uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*) such as "the nature of being sound" (*śabdatva*) is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Demonstrating this with an example, he says: "Perishable...": the fact that an entity is perishable is established by the reason alone.
When internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is not established, external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is not a proof.
(15) For comparison: "When internal pervasion is not established, the external factor is useless"—*Pramāṇasamuccaya-vṛtti*, p. 111.
"Since the probandum is established by internal pervasion alone, an external example would be useless;
the experts in logic know that this remains so even in its absence.
— *Nyāyāvatāra*, verse 20.

Whether the reason (hetu) possesses the power to convey the probandum (sādhya) through internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) or lacks such power, the presentation of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is useless. Internal pervasion is the pervasion of the probans with the probandum within the very subject under consideration (*pakṣa*); external pervasion, however, occurs elsewhere, as in: "An entity consists of multiple aspects because existence is established for it in that very way," or "This place possesses fire because it possesses smoke; whatever is thus is so, like a kitchen."
—Pramāṇanaya [tattvāloka] 6.35, 36; Dharmasaṃgrahaṇī-vṛtti, p. 82.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 12:

"The capacity of a reason [to prove its conclusion] lies solely in the fact that it cannot be otherwise [than the probandum] (anyathānupapatti), because the presence of the reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is excluded by a subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa).
Therefore, just as the existence of sound is not possible if it were eternal, so too is its nature as sound [not possible]."

The word *vā* has the sense of *iva* (like), because particles have multiple meanings; it is to be understood immediately after the phrase "existence is perishable. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: since there is the statement that "whatever exists is perishable" and "the existent is impermanent," just as the proposition "the existent is impermanent" is not established by the mere thesis but rather by a reason (*hetu*), so too the proposition "sound is perishable" is established by a reason alone. He thinks thus: just as there is no fault for one who states a reason after saying "the existent is impermanent," so too there is no fault after saying "sound is impermanent."

If it is argued: "Indeed, I do not establish through a logical reason (*hetu*) that 'all that exists is pervaded by impermanence'; rather, it is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for that [object] is perceived as being directly impermanent itself," to this he replies: "When internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is unestablished, there is a pervasion of the probans (*sādhana*) by the probandum (*sādhya*) in the locus of dispute. When that [pervasion] is unestablished in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) due to the force of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), then pervasion in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is 'external pervasion' (*bahirvyāpti*); it is not a proof of the probandum—this is the remainder [of the sense]. Therefore, the point is that for one who desires the establishment of internal pervasion, that [external pervasion], though remote, must also be proven by the logical reason alone, just like the [subject] possessing the probandum."

In the second introductory section (*pātanikā*) of this position, the commentary on the verse explains: how is that which was proposed—that sound is perishable—established? To this he says: "by *dhvani*. This designation is one in which the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant; thus, it is to be understood as following after the word "sound" (*śabda*), meaning "by the very reason that being *dhvani* is being *śabda*," and not by any other reason.
He states an illustration:
the word "or" (*vā*) is to be understood from the preceding passage, and the particle "iti" is to be joined here as well;
thus, just as an entity (*bhāva*) is established as perishable by the very reason that it is an entity, so too is the subject at hand [established].
For there is no other reason (*hetvantara*) for establishing the pervasion of an entity by impermanence;

this is the intended meaning here: just as in the case of "sound is impermanent," because the exclusion of non-sound has already been stated by the term *dharmin* (the subject), one cannot further say "because of being sound" (*śabdatvāt*), so too, in the case of "that which exists is impermanent," because the exclusion of the non-existent has already been expressed by the word *sat* (existent), it is impossible to say "because of existence" (*sattvāt*).
Now, since it has already been stated by the principle "whatever exists is impermanent" that all non-existence is excluded, the statement "sound exists" is likewise of that same nature;
let this be another fault of his, and it need not be further discussed.
The Buddhist might think: "The property of being a sound (*śabdatva*) is not a valid probans because it lacks an example. To this, he says: "Internal," and so forth;
this is easy to understand.
Revealing the meaning of the verse as being devoid of presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), he says: "In the dissimilar class," and so forth.

When there is the exclusion of that valid cognition which sublates the existence of the reason in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), then the efficacy of the reason—the capacity of the mark (*liṅga*) to make known its own probandum (*liṅgin*)—is established.

From where does that [necessity] arise? He says: "Otherwise"—that is, by another mode [of proof], namely the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), there is the "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) of the mark (*liṅga*), which is its impossibility; it is from this alone, and not from "presence in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and "presence in similar instances" (*sapakṣasattva*). This is the meaning of the particle *eva*. Therefore, just as when the capacity of the reason has been demonstrated through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), yet for one who has not understood it, a statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is given even without [the other members], so too, for one who knows that it would not be understood without it, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is considered necessary for the sake of the person to be instructed (*pratipādya*).

He demonstrates the second point with the words "from that" (*tataḥ*) and so forth. The sense is this: by the logic of the operation of the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which sublates the contrary position (*vipakṣa*), just as existence (*sattva*) is not possible for sound or anything else if it were eternal, so too is "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*); thus, like "sound" itself, "sound-ness" is also a logical reason (*hetu*).

[Objection: But surely, internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is the pervasion of the probans by the probandum within the subject (*pakṣa*) alone; and that is the cognition of a relation residing in two [loci]. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra 1)
Because of such statements, [the probans] would be understood when the probandum is already established, and not otherwise.

If it is argued that the cognition of this [probandum] arises from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), and that its deficiency is due to that very [other means], then there is a circularity (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): once the probandum is established by this [inference], the establishment of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) occurs through it, and through that establishment of internal pervasion, the probandum is established.
If it is argued that, therefore, universal concomitance (*sākalyavyāpti*) is superior, he says in response: "By way of totality," etc.,
and the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhyapratipatti*) [occurs] through inference.
Through inference, the pervasion of the probandum and the probans in every instance—both in the subject (*pakṣa*) and in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—is "universal pervasion" (*sakalavyāpti*).
How could such universal pervasion exist without internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*)? 1/2

Mere external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is not the means of proof; rather, it is internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) alone that necessarily entails the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*). Therefore, the statement of the probandum is superior, as in the sequence: "...soundness... From this, internal pervasion alone is superior; for in its absence, if one were to attempt to establish pervasion through totality (*sākalya*), there would be no external example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and consequently, no reason (*hetu*) whatsoever would exist.

The formulation of a thesis is fruitful because the positive concomitance (*tadbhāva*) and the causal relation (*hetubhāva*) cannot be stated [otherwise]; so what is the use of an example that demonstrates identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) for the sake of the wise? If the proof (*sādhana*) fails to establish what has been stated, it would constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*);
in that case, it is logical that there is a point of defeat due to the defectiveness of the proof.

Even though it possesses defects, the opponent’s statement—that because the proponent has the capacity to expose the defects asserted by the other party, this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the respondent—is the mere babble of a child; for that would lead to an infinite regress.
Therefore, the statement of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not exceed the nature of a proposition (*pratijñā*).

And here, the pervasion of the probans by the probandum within the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) is what constitutes universal pervasion (*sākalyena vyāpti*). How could it not be so? That is to say, without that internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), it would not exist.

Otherwise, there would be a partial pervasion even in the subject, just as there is in the external example. If it is argued, "Let that [universal pervasion] be established by that very [internal pervasion]," then how can one avoid the reproach of self-contradiction when asserting that? Furthermore, if it is claimed that this [pervasion] is not cognized in the subject but only in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), then that cognition is not a cognition of universal pervasion, because it does not possess the nature of such [a cognition].
If, however, the application of that [reason] to that [subject] were not accepted there, how could such an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) be avoided?
He explains the half-verse concerning pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "mere external pervasion" (*bahirvyāptimātra*), and so forth.
The opponent argues: "In the proof that diamond (*vajra*) is scratchable by iron, mere [logical] evidence (*tanmātra*) is not a valid means of proof because it contradicts perception;

however, where there is no such contradiction, it is indeed a valid means of proof. [The author replies: No. Even when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) based on identity (*tādātmya*), if a contradiction with perception is possible, what confidence can there be in other cases? If sublation (*bādhā*) were impossible for that which possesses the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then that very characteristic would be undermined.
Furthermore, the existence of that necessary connection is seen precisely because wood and other such things are both earthy (*pārthivatva*) and scratchable by iron.

If it is argued that there can be no dependence on causal factors for its existence—since its existence follows from that very [nature] itself—and that this would lead to the consequence of its eternal absence, just like destruction; we say no. For there is no eternal contradiction with its potentiality (*yogyatā*).

Just as, although wood and other earthen substances are scratchable by iron, it does not follow that all such things possess that property, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the opposite case; if that is so, then you have effectively accepted a universal pervasion (*vyāpti*).

If it is argued that "it is so," to this he replies: "Pervasion in its entirety necessarily entails the establishment of the probandum, because without it, the cognition of that [probandum] is impossible. Thus, he considers that there is a contradiction with perception, given the possibility of such a contradiction with perception.

Comparison— If there were no sublation (bādhā) regarding that which possesses the defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa), then those very characteristics would be undermined, resulting in a lack of confidence (anāśvāsa) everywhere. — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.22.
*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra* 3.71:
the quality of being scratchable by iron.
Concluding the present topic because it is impossible to apprehend universal concomitance (*sākalyavyāpti*) [through inference], he says "therefore" (*tataḥ*), and so forth.

Since this is the case, for that reason, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvacana*), which is the indication of the probandum (*sādhyanirdeśa*), is superior. Otherwise, when there is an indication of a reason (*hetu*) endowed with the property of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*), the non-indication of that [proposition] would be praiseworthy; yet even more praiseworthy than that is its indication, because it serves to assist those of dull intellect. Thus, it is called "superior" (*śreyān*).

Alternatively, since the apprehension of the pervasion in its entirety implies the establishment of the probandum through the metaphorical application of the object to the subject, the statement of the probandum is indeed superior; thus, [the definition] "the non-statement of the probandum" is corrected to "the statement of the probandum."

He thinks as follows: "Even though the probandum (*sādhya*) is already implied by the pervasion of the totality (*sākalyavyāpti*), there is still a further proof of the reason (*hetu*); likewise, there is also [the need for] the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvacana*). Regarding the commendable demonstration of the proof of "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), he says "sequence," etc., [anticipating the objection]:

"But has this not already been established by the passage beginning with 'In the case of the counter-example' (*nanvetad vipakṣe*)? What, then, is being established again? [The answer is: No, because it is introduced in a different manner.

For instance, pervasion by the totality necessarily implies the establishment of the probandum, provided that the cognition of the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the entire pervaded and its pervader is inseparable from the cognition of the entire pervader.

If it is argued that this is not the case, but rather [the inference] is preceded by a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the author replies here: "The mention of 'succession' (*krama*) and so forth is easy to understand;
the mention of 'audibility' (*śabdatva*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which the apprehension of 'audibility' (*śrāvaṇatva*) and other such properties is included."
What follows from this? He says: since this is so, therefore internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) alone is superior, and not external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) or universal pervasion (*sākalyavyāpti*).

For this reason as well, that [internal pervasion] alone is superior; he says: in the absence of that—that is, in the absence of the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—if one were to attempt to establish pervasion by means of a universal and non-particular pervasion of existence (*sattva*) or other [reasons] with respect to another [subject], no [reason] would function as a valid logical mark (*hetu*), whether as an essential nature (*svabhāva*) or an effect (*kārya*), because of the absence of an external example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

As for what was stated by the opponent—that at the time of defining the characteristic (*lakṣaṇakāla*) it is the subject (*dharmin*), at the time of formal application (*prayogakāla*) it is the collection of property and subject (*dharmadharmisamudāya*), and at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāptigrahaṇakāla*) it is the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*) as the thesis (*pakṣa*)—that is refuted by this [following argument]: for it is not the case that every entity whatsoever, whether smoke or anything else, is pervaded by destruction and fire. To this, he says: "The postulation of a different thesis is fruitful."

[Objection: "Surely, since there is no external example for establishing pervasion in its entirety, let there be no search for one [at that stage]; however, because the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) operates in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and because that [pervasion] is established thereby, it is proper to search for it at the time of the formal argument (*prayoga*), since it exists then. To this, he says: "In the presence of that," etc. What is the purpose?—the ellipsis is to supply "none whatsoever. By what means? He says: "by the example."
By what means? He says: "by demonstrating identity (*tādātmya*) and causal origination (*tadutpatti*).

With respect to whom? He says: "with respect to the learned (*viduṣaḥ*)," that is, with respect to those who possess a thorough knowledge of the power of the reason (*hetu*), which is manifested through the operation of the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the presence of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Why [is this so]? To this he says: "because it is inexpressible (*avācyatvāt*)."
To the question "Of which two?", he says: "Of the state of being that [the probandum] and the state of being its cause.
Here too, the phrase "with respect to the learned" is to be connected.

This is what is meant: identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*) are not demonstrated by means of an example; for if those two are already known from another source, what is the use of them? As it has been said:
In this definition of the reason (*hetu*), when internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is absent and [the reason] is to be ascertained, the subject (*dharmin*) is the object of inference;
elsewhere, however, at the time of the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), the aggregate (*samudāya*) is the object of inference.
"But at the time of ascertaining the pervasion (vyāpti), the property (dharma) is the object of inference"— this is stated in the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* 2.8.
[The two types of pervasion are] identity (tādātmya) and causality (tadutpatti).
"For the presence [of the property] and the causal relationship are demonstrated by means of an example for those who do not know them;
for for the learned, only the reason itself needs to be stated" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.27).
To the question "By what kind of example, and for what purpose? he says: "When that which has been stated is not established by a certain example..."
Of what? Of the means of proof, the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Of what kind? Of that which has been stated, that is, uttered. It would be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). The connection is: "What [is the use] of that example?"—for it is thought that its establishment comes from something else entirely.

This is another explanation of what was stated by the opponent: "If one fails to establish the proof—which was presented by means of an example for the sake of an ignorant person and set forth in its own words—there would be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Here, the word "iti" should be understood as indicating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, he states the refutation, beginning with the words "In that case," and so forth.

In that regard, since the proof in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is faulty, it is only logical that there should be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); [the opponent argues] that this very faultlessness is revealed by means of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). [The author replies: No, because that faultlessness is revealed in other ways as well—this has already been stated. However, regarding the previous explanation, one should infer another refutation starting with the word "therein" (*tatra*) concerning faultlessness.
The opponent says: the phrase "even though the proof possesses a fault" continues [from the previous context].

In whatever manner (*yathā*) or by whatever means (*yena*) the fault was stated by the proponent (*vādin*), if the respondent (*prativādin*) has the capacity to point that out (*udbhāvanāyām*), then it is logical that the respondent’s point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs; otherwise, the respondent would be defeated either because he fails to reveal a fault that actually exists, or because he lacks the capacity to point it out in that manner—this is how it should be understood.

And this [charge] that it is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent—this explanation is to be considered; because the proof possesses a fault, and since the authority for the defeat of the proponent does not extend to others, the Teacher says: "What has been stated in this manner by the other is the speech of a child."
Why? He says: "Because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*).

To explain: even when the proponent has employed a proof (*sādhana*) stating that there is a fault (*doṣa*), if the judges (*prāśnikāḥ*) establish his defeat (*nigraha*) only after depending upon the opponent's pointing out of that fault, then three alternatives arise: he might point out that same fault, he might point out another fault, or he might not point out anything at all.

Regarding the first alternative: just as there is a dependence on the disclosure of the fault even though it has been employed, so too, once it has been disclosed, there would be a dependence on its removal, and further, a dependence on its justification; thus, an infinite regress results.

If, however, victory for the opponent were established merely by pointing out the faults of the real [objections], then the proponent could likewise establish defeat for the other merely by employing those faults, without needing to wait for a second presentation. If it is argued that the second presentation is required because the opponent's inability to point out such [faults] is not known by that much alone; then, since the other's ability to avoid them is also not known by that mere presentation, the requirement for a third presentation follows by force.
By this, the two subsequent alternatives have been examined for their faults by the judges.
By depending on the opponent's pointing out [of a flaw],
the judges always proclaim the defeat of the proponent who possesses a valid proof, thereby [establishing] the victory of the opponent.
In consideration of the opponent’s presentation of a fault, the proponent, concluding the present subject, says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"not all of that is impermanent"—does not exceed the proposition (*pratijñā*); the intention is that such a statement would be nothing other than the proposition itself. This is the statement of pervasion.

Here the opponent says: "As for what was stated—that in establishing pervasion in its entirety there is no example because of the absence of [any such thing]—the core point is that in establishing the pervasion of an entity under dispute by means of its momentariness, there is no other [entity] to serve as an example. To this he states the reply: "The non-endurance beyond a single moment... and so forth. "The non-endurance beyond a single moment is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
