Furthermore, how could that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) exist in that absolute state? (16)

From what counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is there an exclusion of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), since direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) is untenable in the case of momentariness? Therefore, by raising the charge of the fault of redundancy (*ādhikyadoṣa*), the opponent does not triumph over the proponent of ultimate reality (*paramārthavādin*); for the time of the transition between the production and the destruction of a dimension is a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*). Any persistence of an entity beyond that is its destruction; since that [persistence] is not established through direct perception, [the opponent's argument fails].
And this has been explained [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*] by the passage beginning with "perceiving the individual characteristics as one" (svalakṣaṇāny ekam siddhi-vi.
1.9); what is meant is this: if a momentary entity were established anywhere through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then by that example, any other [entity] would also be so.
And it is not thus,
by way of citing another atom as an example.

It might be thought: "The middle moment, severed from its prior and posterior limits, or those two limits themselves as distinct from it, are apprehended by perception; otherwise, the consequence would follow that [the object] lasts for only a single moment. In that case, the conventional usage of 'non-existence' is established merely through the non-perception of what is perceptible. To this, he says: "In that," and so forth. In what? He says: "In that [reality] which consists of external, internal, partless, continuous-less, and momentary atoms; in what [regard]? He says: 'In an absolute sense' (ekānte)."
What? He says: "But what is it that is not established at all?"—this phrase is supplied from the context. What? He says: "perceived," and so forth.

This is what is meant: if, in that absolute [non-existence], something were to exist that meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), then its non-perception, its absence, or the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding it would be established; however, this is not the case, as has already been largely explained.

Because that which possesses the characteristic of height is not perceived there, its absence would be established; yet that is not absolute, because even as with non-succession, it is possible for a single thing to possess multiple forms through succession as well. Thus, it is established that from the observation of the momentary destruction of some particular entity, the pervasion of all things by that [destruction] is proven, regarding the prior and posterior moments which differ from the middle moment.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Arcaṭa— that the establishment of the pervasion of existence by momentariness through its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) does not depend on the force of an external example, and that the statement of an example is made with respect to the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the specific nature-reason (*svabhāvaviśeṣahetu*)— he refutes that by saying "the object," etc.: "From what [source]?"—
from no source whatsoever, namely, from the counter-example intended to be non-momentary, is there an exclusion.
Of what? He says: "of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*).

For existence is pervaded by that [efficiency]; therefore, as that [efficiency] is excluded from it [the permanent], it would necessarily exclude existence as well. But why is it that this very [efficiency] is not excluded from it? He says: "because perceptibility is untenable in the case of the momentary doctrine."
The connection is with "of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāyāḥ*).

For when, in the case of momentariness, perceptible causal efficiency occurs through either succession or simultaneity, then upon the exclusion of those two from something [else], that efficiency is excluded.
But when, as in the case of non-momentariness, it is not perceptible in the other case either, then how could it be excluded from that very thing? This is the intended meaning.
For that [proof] consists in the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the reason when it is reversed from the probandum;

for example: "Whatever exists is necessarily momentary, because if it were non-momentary, it would be incompatible with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), and thus its status as a real entity (*vastutva*), which is defined by that [causal efficacy], would be lost" (Hetubindu, p. 54).

Because in the case of the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the establishment of identity is based on the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the contrary;
— *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 51:
"by way of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyayā*).
Causal efficacy [proves] the existence of the eternal.
Causal efficiency [does not arise] from either the eternal or the non-eternal.
Causal efficiency, whether successive or simultaneous, is possible even for that which is non-momentary.
He states the conclusion starting with "Therefore, not...

and so forth: since the objection that the supreme reality would be non-eternal and so on has thus resulted as a consequence of the summary, therefore it does not hold together that the opponent, the adversary, can defeat the proponent of the ultimate truth by pointing out defects such as redundancy.

Furthermore, showing that if an opponent were to defeat the proponent of ultimate reality (*paramārthavādin*) by pointing out defects such as redundancy (*ādhikya*), this would not constitute another valid refutation, he says: "The statement of the probandum (*sādhyokti*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*)," and so forth.

Because [the property of] being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is impossible in the absence of the word [expressing it], the statement of the probandum is the means of proof; however, an entity (*bhāva*) that has not been established is not a means of proof. (17)

For indeed, if the matter at hand were completed by this much alone, what would be the use of "existence," "being produced," and so forth? But has this not already been stated: "A means of proof (*sādhana*) that is not established is not accepted as such, because it leads to defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Soundness (*śabdatva*), however, is indeed a means of proof, because its nature pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka-svabhāvatvāt*), just like existence (*sattva*) and other properties when proving impermanence in its entirety; for it satisfies that single definition [of a reason]. Otherwise, even if there were an example, it would be non-informative (*agamaka*).

[The opponent asks: "What is this 'utterance' (*ukti*)—the statement 'Sound is impermanent,' which is both the utterance and qualified by impermanence? To this he replies: "The meaning is that the 'means of proof' (*sādhana*) is the logical reason (*hetu*)."

Why? He says: because sound is impossible when there is no cessation (*nivṛtti*)—that is, no transformation (*pariṇāma*). For this reason, the statement of the probandum (*sādhyokti*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*).

What follows from that? He says: "neither existence (*bhāva*) nor producedness (*kṛtakatva*)" is the means of proof; this is understood by ellipsis (*anuvarttate*), because the impermanence of sound is established from something other than the mere mention of its possibility.

If, however, after stating "sound is impermanent," one were to say "because of existence" or "because of being produced," then—since the previously stated "sound-ness" (śabdatva) is itself incapable [of proving the point] and its capacity is not understood—the statement of "existence" and so forth would constitute a "different reason" (*hetvantara*) and thus be a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); this is what is intended.

Now, if it is argued: "If sound is the reason, then because it exists at all times, the object to be proven (*sādhya*) would be cognized at all times; consequently, there could never be a dispute regarding the permanence of anything"; to this he replies: "It is not a means of proof" (*asādhana*), etc.—here the term "entity" (*bhāva*) or "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is understood to follow from the context.
The word "vā" has the sense of "iva" (like);
therefore, the meaning is this: just as with existence (*bhāva*) or just as with being produced (*kṛtakatva*), the sound is not an unestablished means of proof, but rather it is indeed established;
and since its establishment is not eternal, how could there be a cognition [of it] at all times? Otherwise, this would be the same in other cases as well.
He explains the verse with the words "For [there is] no [such thing as] sound," and so forth.

The implicit meaning is: if the matter at hand is concluded merely by the impossibility of sound existing without transformation, then what is the use of invoking such reasons as its existence or being produced, once the proof of the transformation of sound has been established?
If it is argued that there is no dispute because the cognition of an object occurs at all times for everyone, the author replies with the words "nanu" and so forth.

"Nanu" is used here as a gesture of head-shaking (indicating a challenge). What has been stated—that is, what has been established? He says: a means of proof (*sādhana*) that is not even supported [by evidence] is not accepted.
Why? He says: "restraint," and so forth.
Nor is there a constant corroboration of that [reason], because the cognition of the probandum occurs only in that way—this is the sense.

Now, if it is argued that its corroboration is indeed by means of an example, and that [example] is present here; to this he replies: "Audibility" or "audibleness" is itself the probans (*sādhana*), and it is not the case that it is not a probans.
Why? He says: "Because of its being that which is to be proven," and so forth.
Because of the existence—that is, the state—of that which has as its nature both the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), he asks:
"Where indeed, what [is there]? He replies: "In the proof of impermanence by means of totality, just like 'existence' (*sattva*) and the like."

Why is this so? He says: because its single defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is established; otherwise, due to the absence of the establishment of that single characteristic, there would be a lack of probative force (*agamakatva*) even when an example exists—just as in the case [of the fallacious argument]:

"This is produced immediately after effort, because it is impermanent, like a jar. Here, the identity (*tādātmya*) between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is established; otherwise, such arguments as "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced immediately after effort" would not be possible, for this [impermanence] being established as the *sādhya* does not abandon its identity [with the probans].

It is not correct to say, as Arcaṭa stated—that "that which has the nature of being immediately following upon effort is impermanent; that alone is the probans" (Hetubinduṭīkā, p. 74); for [if that were so], it would follow that all inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika*) would be abolished, since the example [would itself be such].

If it is argued that because "being produced" (kṛtakatva) exists even in the absence of "immediately following upon effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva), it does not have that as its nature (atatsvabhāvatva); and if this same situation applies to "impermanence" (anityatva) as well, then—due to the lack of identity (tādātmya)—there would be no positive concomitance (anvaya) of "immediately following upon effort" with "impermanence," nor would there be its cessation upon the cessation of the latter. How, then, could the former be cognized from the latter? This is not a fault, because impermanence is established by that [reason] precisely as the very nature of the object that immediately follows upon effort—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 73–74.

Furthermore, demonstrating the refutation that results in the defeat of the proponent of the ultimate truth by exposing defects such as redundancy, he says: "Or, having not stated that... and so forth.
That Buddhist, having not stated that [probandum], if the unspoken means of proof (*sādhana*) is established...
Furthermore, that which is other than the probandum (*sādhya*) is also to be refuted; yet it is refuted without being restated.

If one states a proof (*sādhana*) without stating the thesis (*pakṣa*), one makes the thesis implicit by the very act of proving it again. If, on the other hand, one were to prove without stating the proof—such as [the argument] "whatever is produced," etc.—then how could it not be proven when a refutation is possible without restating the opponent's proof? For there is no distinction between these two cases.
Regarding the point that a *nigrahasthāna* (point of defeat) occurs when either one [of the two] is stated, the same applies even when both are stated.

If one does not state the proposition (*pratijñā*)—"Sound is impermanent because its association is constant"—but states only the reason, one incurs defeat due to stating what is meaningless, or is it otherwise? He says: "The proof" refers to the mark (*liṅga*) such as existence (*sattva*), and "the refutation" here means that its status as unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is rendered flawless—that is, it is made free from defects. Why not? Because there is a connection between the two particles *kin* and *na*, even though they are separated.
Of what nature is it? He says: "unspoken" (*anukta*), meaning not uttered.

[Objection: But in that case, the non-binding of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) would be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); and since stating a proposition (*pratijñāvacana*) when one has already accepted its justification would also be a point of defeat, in both ways the rope is caught.
This might be the case: why is the stated proof (*sādhana*) being justified? To this he says: "Like the probandum (*sādhyavat*), like the impermanence of sound.

If it is asked, "What is the fault in justifying what has not been stated? it is replied: If there is a dispute regarding that [probandum], its justification must come from another proof; if that too is unstated, it must be justified by yet another, and that too by another—thus, due to infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the employment of a proof would never reach a conclusion. Furthermore, the proponent must perform both tasks: proving his own position and refuting the opponent's position.

Your opponent is only refuted when he refutes the entire proof-statement, from the proposition (*pratijñā*) up to the conclusion (*nigamana*); and if the Buddhist proponent refutes [only a part] after having uttered that [statement], how could the employment of the proposition not result in defeat? Showing this, he says: "The object of refutation," and so forth.

"The object of refutation" refers to the proof (*sādhana*), which follows as "the lamp of another's [view]"; this serves as an illustration for the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the other members of the syllogism.
The word "ca" (and) is used here as a conjunction to include the preceding [point];
having restated and formulated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is then refuted and rejected—this is its connection with the word "kim" (why?).
[The opponent] thinks that one should not formulate a *pūrvapakṣa* either in a treatise or at the time of debate, because otherwise the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) would necessarily follow.

By this, it should be understood that the Buddhist opponent who refutes a proponent such as a Naiyāyika after having restated his proof is [already] refuted; however, if one were to refute it without necessarily restating it, he says: "And the object of refutation," etc., where "and" (ca) is used in the sense of "as follows" (yathā).
Just as a refutation is made without restating the proof, why should that which has not been stated not be established?
He clarifies the meaning of the verse with the words "without stating the thesis," and so forth:
by stating the proof without having stated the thesis that "sound is impermanent," the Buddhist makes the proof—which is being stated by himself—the very thing to be proven (the thesis).

Why? To this he says: "Because of the subsequent substantiation of that [proposition]"; that is, because the means of proof (*sādhana*) is established by being free from defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), with the words to be construed by changing the case-ending (*vibhakti-pariṇāma*).
And that [substantiation] must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, one would incur defeat (*nigraha*).
To the objection that "it is being substantiated even though it was not stated," he says: "If one were to substantiate the means of proof without stating it, just like the thesis (*pakṣa*)."

Regarding this, what is the fault? What is it that is censured? He says: "that which is produced," and so forth; [the fault is] clearly failing to restate the proof (*sādhana*) of the opponent, the respondent.

It is considered that the restatement of that [proposition], namely the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), must necessarily occur; for when a refutation is possible, there is the possibility of the manifestation of that refutation against the proof (*sādhana*). By changing the case ending, the connection is as follows:
"How could the proof, once adduced, not be supported by reasoning? It would certainly be supported."
Why? He says: "That," and so forth.

"That" (*tat*) is a particle used in the sense of "of that"—namely, of this aforementioned statement which serves as a proof for both [positions]—because there is no distinction [between them] regarding the refutation or the establishment [of the thesis].

What, then, has happened to the opponent? To this he says: "In the statement of either one of those two"—that is, when there is a statement of either one of the two, namely the proof (*sādhana*) alone without its support (*samarthana*), or the support alone without the proof—whatever point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been stated by the opponent, such as the failure to support a proof stated in one case, or the non-statement of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) in the other case—that is improper; for he considers that even when both are stated, there is no difference [in the fault]. Thus ends the sixth section, the *Sādhana*.
The genitive [case] occurs in the first alternative;
in the second alternative, [the locative case].

Regarding the reason for what was stated by the opponent—that if sound is a logical mark (*liṅga*), then since all that is desired would be established from that alone, the employment of another reason constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent—there he says: "In the case of the proponent's statement of multiple reasons," and so forth.
It is indeed held that there is defeat for the proponent when he states multiple reasons.
"The defeat of the caviller does not occur by stating multiple refutations.
(Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, Vol. 2, p. 376). This has been cited:
because [the opponent] points out only one defect in the proof and fails to point out the remainder, there would be victory and defeat for the proponent and the opponent simultaneously.

How could one who points out numerous defects surpass a proponent of multiple means of proof? By what means is the defeat (*nigraha*) of the opponent—the Jaina and others—intended by the Buddhist, and in what respect? To this he says: "When multiple reasons are stated for a single probandum (*sādhya*), since the object has already been established by one reason, other [reasons] are futile, like lighting a lamp where one is already shining. This is the view of the opponent.

In this regard, the following is considered: a proponent must perform two tasks—establishing one's own position and refuting the opponent's position. A Buddhist proponent, having stated a single reason for his own side, is defeated by pointing out numerous faults in the opponent's non-monistic (anekānta) position, such as contradiction (*virodha*), lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and non-existence (*abhāva*). If the opponent is defeated by only a single fault, then other [faults] would be useless;
therefore, he should state only one refutation in every case. By this rule, the opponent's position would be refuted in its entirety.
It is for this purpose, they say, that "it is indeed" (*kila*) is stated.

Now, because of the maxim that "what is twice bound is well-bound," even when many refutations are stated, there is no defeat; for this very reason, even when many reasons are stated, there would likewise be no [defeat].

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "There is no defeat of the proponent upon the statement of multiple refutations"—this phrase carries over from the previous context—and "there is no suppression of the caviller, not of the one who possesses a formal debate."

Alternatively, because of the statement that "the proponent is defeated when he states multiple reasons," one must say that the opponent is the victor upon pointing out those [reasons], for otherwise that would be impossible; and in that case, there is the possibility of multiple faults for the proponent. Since stating multiple [reasons] is a fault, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the same applies to the opponent's failure to state anything at all, just as in the case of stating multiple reasons. He says this very thing: "There is no defeat for the opponent upon the statement of multiple refutations."
"The rest is as before" refers to what is called contradiction in the Jaina doctrine.

Because it would be improper for the proponent to suffer defeat [under those circumstances], he explains the verse: "Since the opponent points out only one defect in the proof—or the counter-proof—put forward by the proponent, and fails to point out the remaining defects even though they exist, there would be victory and defeat for the respondent at once;

furthermore, if he were to point out multiple defects, how could the opponent surpass the proponent who possesses multiple proofs? The connection is made by changing the case-ending [of the word *aneka*].

Under the pretext of censuring the statement of the thesis and so forth, he—who, by joining even a proponent of logic with defeat, considers himself superior and mocks the opponent—says: "If a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), while pointing out a fault, were to defeat one who has established a thesis, this would be a great system of debate. (20)

It is largely trivial to claim that even one who lacks the establishment of his own position wins by raising a "fallacy" (*doṣa*)—which does not actually obstruct the proof—against an opponent who is establishing the truth through *vitaṇḍā*. For since debate occurs only between two capable parties, how could either of them possibly be considered a mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*)? Indeed, neither of them can be called a caviller, because the opponent refutes the proponent after having stated the proof, or because he himself somehow provides a reply; for if both were merely cavillers in that way, the logic of formal debate (*vādanyāya*) would be rendered complete and meaningless.

One who establishes one's own intended position (*pakṣa*) by means of a proof that is inseparably connected with the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvi-sādhana*) should not be defeated; the word "api" (even/also) is used in a different syntactical order and is to be understood after the term "vaitaṇḍika. Even a *vaitaṇḍika*—though devoid of establishing his own position—is one who [engages in] *jalpa* (disputation) that lacks the establishment of a counter-position; this is *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), according to the *Nyāyasūtra* 1.2.3.

Because of this statement, if it is argued that the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) is stated as one's own position (*svapakṣa*) according to the maxim of the elephant and the female elephant, then if there is a fault therein, this great "method of debate" (*vādanyāya*) would not be a method of debate at all, but rather a destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*);

for it is thought that, like the statement of a thesis and so forth, even meaningless things such as quibbles (*chala*) could be brought forward under the pretext of pointing out a defeat (*nigraha*).

What must he do in order to refute him? To this he says: "By pointing out a fault (*doṣamudbhāvayan*). From the statement "having established the thesis" (*pakṣaṃ sādhitavantam*), it is understood that he points out a fault that does not obstruct the establishment of the thesis.
Here, "counter-thesis" (*pratipakṣa*) refers to one's own position; for, in relation to the opponent's position, even the proponent's position is a counter-thesis.

The proponent of the counter-position (*uttarapakṣavādī*) is a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*); with respect to the position being established by the first proponent, he is called the "counter-position" according to the analogy of an elephant and its rival. He indeed accepts that [counter-position], yet he does not provide a proof for it; rather, he remains merely refuting the opponent's position. Commenting on the verse in *Nyāyamañjarī*, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 153, he says: "He wins while being devoid of the establishment of his own position"—this is essentially trivial.
Who? He says: the opponent. By what means? By cavil (*vitaṇḍā*).
What is he doing? Manifesting [the fault].

"What kind of what? he asks. He says: "A fault that does not obstruct success. "What [fault]? he asks. He says: "One who establishes the truth"—for the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), this is the only course: that he wins by any means whatsoever. To this, he replies: "Of two capable [parties]," and so forth. Only when both the proponent and the opponent are capable—that is, when they possess the power to state correct proofs and refutations—is there a debate, and not when they are incapable. This is because a debate between the capable and the incapable, or a debate with the capable for one who is incapable, is impossible, just as there can be no debate between a fierce king and a eunuch.
How could either the proponent (*vādī*) or the opponent (*prativādī*) be considered a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), given that their roles are the opposite of that?

It might be thought by one who is incapable [of understanding]: "When the proponent has employed a correct proof, if the opponent, failing to see a real fault, does not point out the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth—even though it is not an obstacle to the establishment [of the proof]—then his defeat would be absolute."
However, when that [defect] is pointed out, there arises a doubt; for if the proponent refutes it in that very manner, he suffers defeat.

But if the defect is not refuted, or if it is refuted otherwise than correctly, the proponent alone is defeated. Thinking, "A doubt is better than certain defeat," the opponent, becoming a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), raises the statement of the proposition and so forth.

Likewise, when that [objection] has been raised, if the proponent does not state a reply, then he would suffer certain defeat; however, when a mere reply is stated, there is doubt: if the opponent refutes it in that very same way, the proponent would be the victor, but if he fails to refute it or refutes it incorrectly, he would be the one who suffers defeat. Thus, since there is certain defeat [in the latter case], it is better to have doubt; consequently, the proponent also becomes a *vaitaṇḍika* (caviller) by offering a mere reply. Therefore, it is not that only the opponent is a *vaitaṇḍika*, but rather both are *vaitaṇḍikas*.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
"Not indeed" means that it is certainly not the case that only one of the two—the proponent or the opponent—is a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*); rather, the sense is that both are cavillers.
Why? He says: because [the arguments] are being repeated; otherwise, there would be the ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*).

What is it? He says: "The proof (sādhana) according to the opponent's wish. What does one do with that? "Refuting" (dūṣayataḥ), meaning rejecting by means of censuring the statements of the proposition and so forth.
Of whom? He says: "Of the opponent" (prativādinaḥ). What of him? He says: "Because of the counter-establishment" (pratyavasthānāt), that is, because of the refutation.
By what means? He says: by oneself (*svayam*), that is, by the proponent himself (*ātmanā*).

How so? He says: "by stating some kind of answer, however slight" (*kathañcit yatkiñcid uttaramabhidhāya*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), while "vā" indicates the intention of the opponent.

Here he states the refutation: "In that way," meaning by the aforementioned method, if the status of those two—the proponent and the opponent—as *vaitaṇḍikas* (cavillers) is admitted, then the logic of debate (*vādanyāya*) is merely a mockery, because it lacks completion.
The meaning is that it would be mere cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) and not the logic of debate (*vādanyāya*), because the opponent [would not be] in accordance with the facts.

Nevertheless, since uncertainty is better than certain defeat, it is logical to employ that [probative argument] as a means of manifesting grandeur when stating the thesis and other members—*Nyāyamañjarī*, *Prameyakhaṇḍa*, p.
152. Regarding the statement of the thesis and so forth:
The opponent includes this passage:
"Non-reproduction is the failure to repeat that which has been understood by the assembly and has been stated three times"— Nyāyasūtra 5.1.15.

Furthermore, if it is argued that this is unestablished—that even a proponent of a correct proof (*samīcīnasādhanavādī*) would be subject to defeat (*nigrahārha*) if he were merely a speaker of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, and how could he be a victor (*jetā*) by means of a statement of proof devoid of those [other members]? To demonstrate this with the first half of the verse and then to refute it with the second half, the author says: "In this case, the chatterer... (*kārikāṃ jalpāka ida*).
The proponent,
who speaks by means of statements such as the thesis and so forth, is victorious when establishing the object through speech that is not excessive.
"How could the opponent not be defeated by means of [the proponent's] restatement and so forth?

Since the opponent reaches a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because the proponent has stated the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), it is argued that [the opponent's silence] is thus untenable and therefore trivial. [To this we reply: Just like the restatement of the proof, the proponent who possesses a faulty proof would likewise be defeated again for stating other faults, for failing to state them, and so on. By this, [the charge of] "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*) and the like is refuted.

Since there can be no victory for either party in the event of another's misconception or non-comprehension without the establishment of one's own position, who could be defeated by whom? Furthermore, that which establishes the desired object and its proof consists of the three types of reasons characterized by the three features, such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), because they possess the certainty of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). In this regard, characteristics such as "being a property of the subject," "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), or "being prior" (*pūrvatva*) are not the actual means of proof; for how could one realize the identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between the probandum and the probans without ascertaining "the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*)? Once that is realized, what is the use of another redundant relation acting like a useless goitre?
If it is argued that the talkative disputant wins, what is he doing? To this he says: "What is he establishing? To which he replies: "His own position (svapakṣa)."
He says: "By *anadhikoktyā* (by non-excess in speech). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it refers to that [speech] which is also deficient.

If that is so, then there is victory for the proponent (*vādin*) and defeat for the opponent (*prativādin*). In what state, then, would there be a fault? Or would the pointing out of such a fault constitute the opponent's defeat?
It cannot be by non-excess in speech while one is establishing the meaning.

In this regard, too, the following must be considered: does the proponent win because he fails to point out the opponent's existing faults, or because he states a correct proof? Regarding the latter alternative, it has been stated that this would contradict [the rules of] *jalpa* and so forth; thus, that very same defeat of the opponent applies to the first alternative as well. For if that same proponent wins by himself pointing out the fault, then it is said that he suffers defeat.

If, however, it is because the opponent fails to point out [the fault] even though it has been made manifest by the arbiter, then just as the failure to point out a fault establishes the defeat of the other party, so too would it establish the defeat of the proponent regarding his own statement; thus, this argument is trivial.
By this, the time for stating a faulty proof is also determined:
in that case, the defeat of the proponent is declared by the opponent.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "By what means would the opponent not indeed be defeated? He replies: "By means of re-utterance and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of the pointing out of faults and other such methods is intended.
Explaining the meaning of the verse, the proponent says: "The proponent," and so forth.
The meaning of this has already been explained.
Why is this so? To this he says: "In the proof," and so forth.

Because the opponent reaches a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), and because [the argument] is untenable in the manner stated by the other party, it is "mostly trivial" (*phalguprāya*). Thus, like the mere reiteration of the proof, the statement of other faults, as well as non-statement and so forth—referring to those such as the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*) and the rest—it is considered that [the opponent's defeat] occurs precisely through the victory of the proponent, since he reaches that point of defeat.

If it is argued that the attainment of that [defeat] occurs through those very [reasons] and not for any other; to this he says: "Even by one who asserts a faulty proof (*sādhanavādin*), and not merely by another, the opponent would thus be defeated"—this is the connection [of the sentence].
The remainder here has been considered as the attainment of defeat (*nigrahaprāpti*).
It is not because of victory in debate that he has made this further statement— "this by that," and so forth; here,
the particle *tat* functions in the sense of *tena* (by that).

By the phrase "by that [establishment of the position]," etc., when it is said "by this," referring to that which is currently appearing as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the mind, there would be immediate comprehension; whereas when it is said "by that," it refers to something long past. Therefore, it is said "by this" (*tenaitena*).
How is it refuted and rejected? He says: "non-appearance," and so forth.
Non-ingenuity (*aprati-bhā*), which consists of the failure to provide a response (*uttarāpratipatti*) and so forth, is the first among those points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*);
their detailed exposition (*prapañca*) is not demonstrated here for fear of excessive length, and it should be understood from the breakdown of the three types of debate (*kathātrayabhaṅga*).

How is he said to have been "refuted"? [This refers to] the following: when there is a misconception on the part of some proponent or opponent, or when one who has established a supreme path otherwise grasps it otherwise, or due to non-comprehension—specifically because of the absence of that comprehension—there is no victory for the other, the opponent, without the establishment of his own position. For what reason? Because no one is refuted by anyone; for victory and defeat are mutually dependent. Thus, the failure to comprehend the answer is *apratibhā* (inability to respond)—Nyāyasūtra 5.2.18.
From this specific treatise named *Nigrahasthāna*.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "the proponent, the opponent, and the arbiter" and ending with "only thus does it have four components," the statement "the wise know [it] as having four components" has been explained. Now, desiring to establish that "speech by one who is capable—that is, one who is able to prove the point to be established—is *jalpa*," and wishing to refute the opinion of others, he introduces [the following] with the words "as for that which... and so forth;
the phrase "as for that which is the definition of debate (*vāda*)" serves to indicate an alternative position.

What is that? He says: the establishment of the desired object—that is, the object intended by the proponent—is the *sādhana* (means of proof), which is to say, the cognition of the inferable (*anumeya*). The meaning of *sādhana* is "that by which something is established," namely, the *liṅga* (logical mark).
The word *ca* (and) serves to include the preceding [definition].
*Tadaṅgam* means a member or constituent part (*avayava*) of that *sādhana*, which is the *liṅga*.

What is that? He says: "the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), its presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), or its absence from the similar instance, is included; or rather, the establishment (*siddhi*) of that [reason] is the limb or cause of the proof (*sādhana*). What are they? He says: "those characterized by the three marks" (*trilakṣaṇāḥ*). Those for which the three marks—namely, the property of being present in the subject and so on—are their characteristics are thus described. How many are they? Three, according to the distinction of effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*).

What are they? He says: [they are] either the indicators (*agamaka*) with respect to the reason (*hetu*), or those which possess the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

The "establishment of the desired object" (*iṣṭārthasiddhi*) is the proof (*sādhana*); its "constituent part" (*aṅga*) is that which brings it about; the "statement of that constituent part" (*tasyāṅgasya vacanam*)—the failure to utter that constituent part is the ground for the defeat (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*) of the proponent. And here, the "constituent part of the proof" (*sādhanāṅga*) is said to be the mark (*liṅga*) whose three forms (*trairūpya*) are certain; the "statement of that constituent part of the proof" is the communication of the mark possessing the three forms; the "non-statement," "failure to utter," or "non-expression" of that constituent part of the proof... — *Vādanyāya-ṭīkā*, p. 3.
The word "previously" is redundant;

for the three-fold nature of the logical mark (liṅga) consists precisely in its being ascertained as existing in the object of inference (anumeya), existing only in the similar instances (sapakṣa), and being non-existent in dissimilar instances (asapakṣa). — *Nyāyabindu* 2.10.
One [reason] exists in the similar class (sapakṣa): the word "sound" is written twice;
[the others are] non-perception, essential nature, and effect.
— Nyāyabindu 2.11.
This is another explanation from the perspective of the Naiyāyikas and others.

What is the limb or constituent part (*avayava*) of that immediate means of proof? He says: for a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) means of proof, it is the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), everything belonging to one's own position is included; therefore, [the types of inference are] *pūrvavat* and *śeṣavat*, as stated in Nyāyasūtra 1.1.5.
Thus the sutra is summarized:
"that which possesses" (tadvat) refers to that which has a "prior position" (pūrvapakṣa) because it was stated first among the means of proof and so forth;
and "that which possesses" (tadvat) refers to the "similar instance" (sapakṣa), which is the remainder extracted from the aforementioned "position" (pakṣa).

The property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) belongs to the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) mark; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the "generally observed" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is also included.

Thus, [the three types of inference are] "that which is like the previous" (*pūrvavat*), "that which is generally observed" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), and [the purely negative], according to the *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.5.
Thus is the summary of the aphorism:
by the word "generally" (*sāmānyena*) and through the qualification [of the term "non-perception"], the meaning is that [the reason] is not observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
For that which possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is the essential factor (*aṅga*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "the remainder" (*śeṣavat*) and "that which is observed through generality" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*) are included;
thus, the third aphorism is also supported: "The [inference] based on what precedes, the remainder, and that which is observed through generality" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.5).

Thus, the cause that is a constituent part of that proof is its "limb" (aṅga). What are the characteristics of those three types of reasons—the purely positive, the purely negative, and the positive-negative? They possess three characteristics.
This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the inclusion of those possessing two characteristics is intended.

Alternatively, they are so described because they possess three characteristics, such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth; this is an elliptical expression, and therefore those possessing two or more characteristics, such as being a property of the subject, are also included.
There are three types of causes, distinguished as cause-and-effect, non-cause-and-effect, and neither-cause-nor-effect; based on these,
the threefold inference to be described hereafter— namely, *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*— is preceded by them.
With respect to the order of utterance, the meaning is that the *pūrva-pakṣa* (the prima facie position) is stated before the reason; thus,
[the terms] "pūrvavat" and "śeṣavat" [are used].
Regarding "comparison" (*tulanā*) or "the threefold": it is as previously stated—namely, *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
That which possesses the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is *pūrvavat*.
That which possesses a remainder (*śeṣa*) consisting of something of the same class as that probandum is *śeṣavat*.
As before, [the term] "pervading the probandum" (sādhyavyāpaka) applies equally to the *pūrvavat* and the *śeṣavat*—[as stated in] the *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 46.

It is of three kinds: positive (*anvayin*), negative (*vyatirekin*), and both-positive-and-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*). Among these, the both-positive-and-negative [reason] is that which, while occurring in the intended subject and in things of its class, does not occur in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). For example: "Sound is impermanent, because, while possessing general and particular properties, it is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves, like a jar."
The positive (anvayin) [reason] is that which, while existing in the subject and in things of the same class intended [by the proponent], is devoid of the counter-example (vipakṣa);
for example, for those who maintain the universal impermanence [of all things], "sound is impermanent because it is produced," for this [reason] has no counter-example.

A *vyatirekin* [reason] is that which, while intending to pervade the subject (*pakṣa*), lacks a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and does not occur in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). For example: "This living body is not soulless, because [otherwise] it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth" (*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 46). This is because a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) reason lacks non-existence in the dissimilar instance, whereas a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reason lacks existence in the similar instance.

And thus, as before, because it arises prior to the effect, it possesses a cause that precedes it; this is "śeṣavat" (the remainder), meaning the effect remains [as the basis for inference]. This is "sāmānyatodṛṣṭa" (inferred from general observation) insofar as it is characterized generally by the absence of a specific causal relationship. Thus, the three sūtras concerning taste and so forth are followed accordingly.
By this, the *vīta* and other [reasonings] are explained.
Why is that their constituent part? To this he says: "In those," and so forth;

because there is a necessary rule (*niyama*) regarding the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) within those three reasons, namely, the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the others.
Because this is the context of formal debate (*vāda*), the inclusion of those specific terms is intended;
therein he states the refutation, beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth.

"Therein" means in that aforementioned prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). "Having the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), "priority" (*pūrvatva*), and "that which has priority as its first member"—this is what is expressed by the compound *tadādi*. That which has such characteristics is also described in the same way.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) is connected with each term—namely, *pakṣadharmatva* (presence in the subject) and the rest; its purpose is to include *tadasavyāpta* (pervasion by that).

By [the mention of] *kāryatva* (being an effect) and so forth, there is the inclusion of *svabhāvatva* (essential nature) and the like, as well as *pūrvavat* (based on what precedes) and so forth; the word "ādi" also includes *śeṣavat* (based on what remains) and the like.

"Why is that not a means of proof, why is it not a logical mark (aliṅga)? To this he says: "Otherwise," and so forth, as before. This refers to cases where an effect is inferred from a cause, such as when one infers that "there will be rain" from the rising of clouds.

The *śeṣavat* [inference] is that where the cause is inferred from the effect; for example, having observed that the river's water is contrary to its previous state—namely, its fullness and rapid flow—one infers from the current that rain has occurred.
The *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] is the observation elsewhere of that which was previously seen elsewhere, characterized by prior movement; such is the case with the sun. —Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.5.
1.5 As stated by the Sāṃkhya school.
In this regard, inference (anumāna) is first of two kinds: *vīta* and *avīta*.
That which proceeds by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and is affirmative is *vīta*; that which proceeds by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and is prohibitive is *avīta*.
Among these, *avīta* is "that which has a remainder" (*śeṣavat*). *Vīta* is twofold: "that which was previously seen" (*pūrvavat*) and "that which is observed through generality" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
In the *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī* (verse 5),
regarding the phrase "it is redundant because it was already stated before," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) [is used].

If it is argued that—by the word "etcetera" (ādi)—let it be granted that these [reasons] are for one's own benefit, nevertheless, the means of proof (*sādhana*) characterized by being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), being an effect (*kāryatva*), and so forth, is indeed [the proof] because of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) consisting of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*); to this he says: "Because of non-difference from the probandum," and so on.
Because of its non-difference from the probandum (*sādhya*), the term "probandum" refers to the essential nature as the reason (*svabhāvahetu*), due to that non-difference.

By the word "means" (*sādhana*), the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are intended; their identity (*tādātmya*) and their origination from it (*tadutpatti*) constitute the nature of the probandum (*sādhyarūpatā*), which is the attainment of its own being from the probandum. How could a follower of the Sugata not understand those two—identity and origination? By doing what? By not ascertaining, whether it exists or does not exist, the impossibility (*anupapatti*) of the reason in the manner of the absence of the probandum (*anyathā sādhyābhāvaprakāreṇa*). If this were otherwise, [the reason] would be unestablished.
This is what is meant: by the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) are pervaded;
for wise men do not consider that which occurs even in the absence of another thing to be of its nature or its effect.
Therefore, in the absence of certainty regarding that [principle], there is no certainty regarding those two [relations].

If it is argued that one merely determines that the definition consisting of "being prior" (*pūrvatva*) or "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is not a valid means of proof (*asādhana*); to this he replies: When the cognition of that [non-proof] is admitted—that is, when its determination through the impossibility of its being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) is accepted—what is the use of another relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth? Of what nature would it be? It is considered to be a useless "internal goitre" (*antargaḍu*), serving no purpose other than the establishment of the very objective already achieved by the relation of *anyathānupapatti*. Thus, the desired conclusion is established.

If it is argued that because of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), there must be identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), and that even this [impossibility] cannot be ascertained as real without another relation—[the opponent asks], "How then is it not included within those two? To this, he replies: "The establishment of a single characteristic," and so forth.
Otherwise, how could the "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) or the establishment of the "single characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇasiddhi*) be complete?
Thus, this [definition] should be applied to the *pūrvavat* and other types of inference as well; it is not a valid means of proof.

The "establishment" (*siddhi*)—that is, the determination—of that single primary characteristic of a probans (*sādhana*), namely "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*), has been made in its entirety by [the passage beginning with] "How? and so forth; this is either to be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) or will be performed in the immediately following chapter to be discussed. Thus, having first demonstrated that the Buddhist-imagined characteristics such as "priority" (*pūrvatva*) and "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) are not valid probans because they lack "inexplicability otherwise," he now says "In the same way," etc., demonstrating to the Naiyāyika that the characteristics such as "priority" are not valid probans for that same reason of lacking "inexplicability otherwise."
In that same manner, by the immediately preceding method, this [point] regarding "that which is not a means of proof" (asādhana) is to be applied.
To the question "Where [is this]? he says: "As before," and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of *vīta* and the others is intended.

For instance: [the argument] "The subject (pakṣa) and the similar instances (sapakṣa) possess the probans (sādhanavat), because they lack the impossibility of being otherwise (anyathānupapatti) like those other than them"—this would not be a valid proof.

Otherwise, one could also say: "Everything that is the subject of dispute is impermanent, because of its existence (sattvāt), like a lamp and so forth," since this would possess the characteristics of the "pūrvavat" and "śeṣavat" types of inference.

Now, [the opponent argues: "Even if there is no absence of impermanence, since existence (*sattva*) is present in the self (*ātman*) and so forth, this is not a valid proof (*sādhana*). What then would be? It is that which necessarily does not occur in the absence of that [probandum]; this is 'inexplicability otherwise' (*anyathānupapatti*). So what is the use of the redundant 'as before' (*pūrvavat*) and so forth? Likewise, regarding the statement that "the *pūrvavat* and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [types of inference] are absent in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)," even this, when devoid of that [inexplicability otherwise], is not a valid proof. Otherwise, one could also argue: "Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is a cognition of a jar and so forth, because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self; whereas that which is not self-aware is not a specific quality of that [self], as in the case of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. This would also be possible, because the property of being "as before" (*pūrvavat*) and the non-observation [of the reason] in the counter-example—whether generally or specifically—are both present.

Now, if it is thought that even in the absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), this is not a valid proof because [effort] exists as a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) therein; what then would be the case? [It would be that which] necessarily does not exist in its absence. Regarding this, it has been stated that the logical necessity (*anyathānupapatti*) is established.

Likewise, the statement that there are three types of inference—*pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*—is incorrect; for otherwise, how could such arguments as "these fruits are ripe and have such a taste because they grew on the same branch, like the fruit already consumed," or "those which do not possess these qualities did not grow on the same branch, like the unripe fruits," be considered valid? They would not be valid.

If it is argued that [the definition] is not [valid] because its object is sublated (*bādhitaviṣayatvāt*), then surely, since sublation is impossible for that which possesses the defining characteristic, that very characteristic would be refuted (as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*, p. 66). How, then, could there be confidence in other cases such that "pūrvavat" and so forth could serve as a means of proof (*sādhana*)? For non-sublation (*abādhitatva*) is also part of that definition.

If it is argued that this [reason] lacks the application of the definition [of a valid reason], then what is this "unsublated reality"? Is it the observation of [the reason] in the locus of the probandum even when the probandum is absent? Or is "unsublatedness" the necessary non-observation of it in the absence of that [probandum]? This is [simply] "inseparability" (*anyathānupapatti*). There is no distinction between these two states, because that which is devoid of inseparability is devoid of unsublatedness.
The meaning is that the specific quality of the self exists in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), which is the absence of the probandum;
[this refers to] the two conditions of being uncontradicted and being otherwise inexplicable.

Furthermore, regarding the state of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), there are three possible positions: is it due to the non-perception of a sublater (*bādhaka*), or is it due to [the inference] being "pervasion by what precedes" (*pūrvavat*), "pervasion by what follows" (*śeṣavat*), or "pervasion in general" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), or rather, is it due to a sublatting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)? Among these, in the first position, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because even when a sublater exists, its non-perception is possible due to some cause, and because it may be perceived again at another time. Furthermore, in the case of scriptures where defects were not previously seen, the observation of defects through investigation subsequently draws in internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), which consists in the non-perception of a sublation throughout the three periods of time.
In the second [case], the subject at hand is also avoided;
in the third, our established tenet is proven by way of sequence.

Furthermore, as for this [argument] that it is "uncontradicted" (abādhitatva)— namely, that it is "like the preceding" or "possessing a cause"— that too is worthless; because it would entail the consequence of the non-existence of those free from passion (vītarāga),
since [the subject] would be either a mere collection of moments or else possessed of passion like an ordinary person, even if it is intended to be one who is free from passion.

For the person (*puruṣa*) is held to be the cause of passion and the like, because it is admitted that effects such as cognition possess those as their specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). One who is admitted to be free from passion is not the cause of them; therefore, there would be no liberation for one in the cycle of existence (*saṃsārin*), and thus religious practice for that purpose would be useless.

Nor should it be thought: "The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the cause of passion and the like, not the person alone; therefore, [your argument] proves what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding the inference of that [person], and there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the person. This is because dependence is denied for that which is eternal, and thus it is impossible for that [causal complex] to be its cause.

If, however, that specific state produced by it is invariably concomitant with it, then the inference of that [state] arises from that very [cause]; thus, the meaning is that Kaṇāda taught a system characterized by a single defining mark,
namely, passion and the other causes.
Since the causal complex (sāmagrī) is the basis for inferring passion and so forth,
and since that complex is the cause of passion and the like, their production does not occur from the Puruṣa alone.
Of the person,
of the totality,
of the person.

And as for the other two types—*śeṣavat* and *kāryavat*—that too is unsatisfactory. For it is admitted by you yourselves that even in the absence of a wheel, a potter’s staff, or similar tools, a specific configuration such as that of a jar can arise from the production of qualities resulting from baking (*pākaja*).

This being the case, since there is the possibility of such a thing occurring somewhere even in the absence of an intelligent agent—as in the case of a wheel and so forth—how can one infer an intelligent cause with confidence in the case of a mountain and the like?

Now, if the perception of that [effect] were to occur at some time even in the absence of the wheel and other such factors, just as it occurs in the absence of an intelligent agent, what contradiction would there be? Or, if there were a contradiction, then since the capacity to indicate [the cause] would be established from that very fact, why [would you need] the "residual" (śeṣavat) inference,
given that [it is observed] in the production of color and so forth born from contact with fire,
even in the absence of a wheel and the like?

Furthermore, as for that other [case]—where taste and so forth are seen in color and so forth generally, by way of their being neither cause nor effect—that too is an unexamined assertion; for it would entail the undesirable consequence of cognizing anything from anything whatsoever. If you say, "In that case, the inference of that [color] from this [taste] occurs within a single substance, so this is not a fault," then one might infer color from taste in a certain fruit, or infer cognition and so forth [from the body], because their coexistence is sometimes observed there due to their inherence (*samavāya*) in it. If that is so, then inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) is the basis for being a prover.
If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the harm?", we say no. From that [perception of color], there would likewise be an inference of action, since there is no distinction between them.

Even so, if that [inference] is possible from color and so forth alone, what is the use of co-inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*)? Furthermore, if the cognition of color from taste occurs elsewhere because their coexistence is observed in some cases (such as in a fruit), then let there be the apprehension of smell and so forth from touch in water and other substances, since their coexistence is observed there as well.

If it is argued that this is not the case because smell and so forth are not observed in things of the same class as the water being inferred, then for that very reason, there can be no such inference anywhere.

Nor is this an absolute rule that [a mark] seen in connection with only what is of the same class as the object to be inferred (liṅgin) causes one to infer it; for there is no contradiction even otherwise. Otherwise, how could the position of the opponent not be established? Thus, this [argument] is trivial. As for "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa), however, it is the inference of a similar object from a mark that is neither its effect nor its cause, such as the inference of taste from color in a wood-apple (kapittha) and so forth.
(*Nyāyamañjarī*, *Pramāṇaprakaraṇa*, p. 119).
Why? [This question] is written twice regarding the result of cognition and so forth.
Because of inherence in the same object,
as in the case of color, [there is inherence] of action.
The inferential mark (liṅga) exists when there is the possibility of the fruit, which is inference.
If it is argued: "Surely, if the absence of the probans is apprehended through perception in the case of the total absence of the probandum, then the cognizer would have to be omniscient;
otherwise, there would be an infinite regress regarding inference, and there is no other means of knowledge," to this he replies: "The form is inferred by means of sound reasoning," and so forth.

The cognition of that [invariable concomitance] also arises from another inference; thus, through sound reasoning, it is inferred that the single defining characteristic of a logical reason—whether its form be perceived or otherwise—is its "unaccountability otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*). || 23 ||

For one who desires to establish an object—whether proximate or remote—in its entirety, either as "this" (*idantā*) or as "not this" (*nedantā*), reasoning (*tarka*) alone is the ultimate refuge and nothing else, because it has everything as its domain. Therefore, reasoning is the unsurpassed instruction for establishing the reality of words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). For if there were no self-awareness (*svavedana*) in all cases, cognition itself would be untenable due to the absence of any other defining characteristic. Thus, that form or nature which is inferred—that is, deliberated—by means of indistinct conceptualization, perception, and so forth, belongs to what? He says: to the cause, i.e., the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Of what kind [of being]? Of one for whom there is perception—that is, of a sentient being such as smoke, etc., which is capable of being grasped through perception—or of another, which is incapable of being so grasped.

For example, in the case of infinite knowledge being the means to infinite bliss, or in the case of that [knowledge] being the means to the absence of hunger and so forth, or in that very same case, of infinite power (*anantavīrya*).
And this is not stated with reference to people like us; rather, for another [being], everything is indeed directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

"What is that nature? he says: "The impossibility of being otherwise," meaning the necessary non-occurrence of the probans in the absence of the probandum. "What is that? he says: "That nature is the single characteristic, the primary characteristic.
"Of what? he says: "Of the reason (hetu)," which is connected by repetition.

This is what is meant: neither perception nor inference establishes a single, definitive characteristic of the logical reason (hetu), because [otherwise] there would be either omniscience for the cognizer or an infinite regress; rather, omniscience is accepted by him through mental conceptualization, as he has said:
Alternatively, if the goal to be proven is that there is an absence of hunger and so forth for one who possesses infinite bliss,

the formal argument (*tulanā*) is as follows: the Kevalin does not eat, because otherwise it would be impossible for him to possess the absence of passion and aversion and the presence of infinite vigor.

—Even though this [cessation] is of a nature free from desire, because it is of the nature of suffering, it is impossible for it to exist in the Blessed One, who possesses infinite bliss — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
The Omniscient One is held to be the knower of everything without exception; he knows the universal nature of both the existent and the non-existent.
O Jina, this is so even though you possess a human nature, so what need be said of one who possesses all-encompassing knowledge? (Pātrakesarī-stotra 19)

[Objection: Surely there is no such thing as *tarka* (logical reasoning), because it is not perceived, like the horn of a donkey; how can anything be inferred by means of that which is non-existent? Or, even if it were existent, it would be useless, since its object is established by other means. To this, he says: "That which is proximate," and so forth.

For a person who desires to establish—through its entirety and by means of its pervasion across different places and times—a proximate object (such as smoke) fit for perception by a human eye, or a remote object contrary to that, in its specific identity (*idantayā*) as impermanent and so forth, or as an effect of the nature of fire, or by its non-specific identity (*nedantayā*) as eternal and not an effect of the nature of fire; for such a person in the world, *tarka* (logical reasoning) is the supreme and most excellent refuge.
Of what nature is it? It is described as such because its object is the absence of the probandum in the case of its opposite (*anyathā*).

This is what is meant: one who wishes to establish the desired reality in its entirety by avoiding what is undesired must accept inference; and by accepting that [inference], one must accept the logical mark (*liṅga*) as having the single defining characteristic of being necessarily inseparable from the probandum (*sādhya*). Furthermore, that certainty [of the inseparability] comes from reasoning (*tarka*), and not from anything else. Thus, for one who negates [reasoning] while having accepted it, [the fault is] "desiring what is hated" (*dviṣṭakāmitā*) by means of reasoning.

As for the inference that was restated—namely, "or [the means of knowledge] are themselves useless because the other is established by something else"—to that he says: "Nothing else. This means that nothing else, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, which has been examined through reasoning (*tarka*), is a refuge; this is understood from the context.
Why is that very [reasoning] the refuge? To this he says: "All," and so forth.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says "tataḥ" and so forth.

Since it is thus, therefore the establishment of reality through words and conceptual constructions (*śabdavikalpa*) is like the inviolable command or edict of a fierce king—that which cannot be transgressed. This is the logical conclusion (*tarka*).

If it is asked: "In the context of the conceptualization of reasoning (*tarka-vikalpa*), for what purpose is the mention of 'word' (*śabda*) introduced here, which is not relevant to the subject? It is replied: Because of the statement beginning with "of the word as well" (*vacanasyāpi*), this [word] is also relevant to the context;
therefore, the term "word" is included in the phrase "of word and conceptualization" (*śabda-vikalpayoḥ*).

If it is asked: "But since there is no twofold connection between the word and those two [particulars and universals], how can the word have them as its objects?"—to this he says: "The word and conceptual cognition are capable," and so forth.

If every word or conceptual construction, being capable by its very nature through the characteristics of identity or origination, were [false] everywhere by itself, then its falsity would depend on something else, just as it is for the cognitions of the eye and other senses. (24)
If this is so, how is it that the author of the treatise has stated elsewhere: "The word is capable... (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Book II, p. 321)? [And:

"If words do not possess reality by their own nature, it cannot be established even through efforts, because perception is what is to be proven; how then can there be an establishment of reality? (25)

The sense is that "suitable" means capable; since the relationship of capability between those two [the word and the object] is like perception and nothing else, there is no fault even in its negation.
To the question "What is it? he says: "Is it some word or conceptual construction (vikalpa)? No," he says: "It is all."
Why? From itself, that is, from its own majesty. Furthermore, of what kind of object? "Everywhere" (*sarvatra*);
since it is a particle (*nipāta*), it has the sense of restriction, meaning "in every case indeed."

That is not correct—[the objection being] that if those two [words] possess the fitness for restriction, then, like smoke and so forth, their application to another object would not occur by the power of human intention. If it is argued that even in that case, because of that fitness, there would be a simultaneous comprehension of all objects from them, we say no; for in one case there is a dependence on the destruction-and-suppression (kṣayopaśama) of karma by another [person], while in the other case there is a dependence on an unrestricted convention (saṅketa).

[The opponent asks: "What is the use of that [convention] for something that is itself fit? This too is trivial; for what use is it for something that is unfit? Indeed, sand does not become oil even when subjected to pressure.
[Objection: "In that case, if the object does not exist, there would be no engagement with it. To this he says: "Falsity," and so forth.

Falsity (*mithyātva*) is the representation of one's own object in a manner other than [its actual state], belonging to both the word and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The connection [of the term] is made by changing the case-ending.
Why is this so? He says: "From something else," namely from some action, or from another [cause], such as false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
As it has been said:
"Even though there is no identity or causal relation between word and conceptual construction..."
In the case of a word that is conceptualized by a Jaina.
Of sound and conceptualization— that is, of conceptualization and the karma that obscures knowledge.
"Whether the quality or defect of a word arises from the quality or defect of its cognition, or from the quality or defect of the vocal activity," as stated in *Pramāṇasamuccaya* 2.16—
those of dull intellect who desire this are not the authors of the treatises.
This is the remainder [of the verse].
To the question "What might it be?", he says: "Like the cognitions of the eye and so forth"—this expansion is the mind by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*). (Pravāha 1)

Because of this statement, just as these [faculties], which are capable of functioning for their own sake, become otherwise due to external factors such as cataracts (*timira*), so too is it with the subject at hand; thus,
the second half [of the verse] concludes that the impurities are adventitious (*āgantuka*).
The falsity of cognitions applies to words as well.

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that a word is determined to be capable of its own meaning because it produces the effect of cognition, and since that [capacity] arises from convention (*saṅketa*), how then can there be such a determination? To this he replies: "The singular number [used for] words previously was with reference to the genus (*jāti*); here, the plural number is with reference to the individuals (*vyakti*).
If, by their own nature—that is, by their very essence—they were not capable of being conveyed, then the word would not manifest the intention of another."
Even by means of efforts (*prayatnaiḥ*) and even by means of making conventions (*samayakaraṇaiḥ*), it is not possible to produce that fitness (*yogyatvam*);

the plural number indicates that this applies not only to one or two, but even to many. For instance: whatever is inherently unfit (*svato'yogyaḥ*) for something cannot become so through efforts, just as sand and the like cannot produce oil; and words are inherently unfit for another person’s realization of reality (*tattvapratipādane*).

And it is possible to bring that about through efforts; therefore, by those [efforts], they are inherently capable. This is because one observes the concomitance of specific cognitions of color and so forth with the words "color" and so forth.
Thus it has been said: "The cause produces a specific [result] for things that undergo transformation through natural decay (*visrasā*).
So he thinks.
Regarding the phrase "even by efforts," for this very reason it was stated by the Buddhist: "The cause produces a distinction in things that are subject to transformation through natural decay."
"The hammer and so forth possess positive and negative concomitance with respect to jars and so forth"
*Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī*, p. 62.
By this, the following is refuted: "From the observation of an effect, its capacity is inferred; from capacity, the effect [is inferred]; thus there is mutual dependence.
How so? Because it is not admitted that the effect is apprehended there through capacity, since that effect is directly perceived (*pratyakṣatvāt*).

We say that the investigation as to whether [the establishment of an object] occurs solely through a necessary connection such as identity (*tādātmya*) with its effect, or through something else, depends upon "fitness" (*yogyatā*), because that fitness alone can withstand such inquiry. If that [fitness] were absent, from what source could there be the determination (*vyavasthiti*)—that is, the establishment—of reality (*tattva*), which is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? One might think it is due to the absence of any other cause for that determination.

If it is argued that this comes from non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), he says in response: since conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) for the Buddhist, it follows that [the determination must come from] non-conceptual perception.

The object of proof (*sādhya*) is unestablished, because of the statement in the *Nyāyabindu-śloka* (1.72): "the object of proof is unestablished. That which has as its object (*viṣaya*) a nature consisting of partless, momentary cognition and so forth is described as such, because everything else is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). From the existence of that [object], it is thus; or rather, from where could there be the establishment of that? Or else, it should be understood that the non-dual (*advaya*) is the object of proof, because—like the *puruṣa*—it is unestablished; for an object, by virtue of being a determiner of self and other, is no different from an insentient jar, and because of the existence of that [non-duality], due to its very nature, [there is] fitness (*yogyatā*).

The opponent might think: "In reality, whether it be conceptual or otherwise, something is accepted by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in some respect; therefore, its non-existence does not constitute a fault for the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin), nor is there a failure to establish reality.
As for that which is accepted, its validity is established through conventional usage" (Vyavahāra-prakaraṇa 1).

"Because it is so stated," that is, because of the statement [in the scripture]; regarding this, he says: "The phrase 'the reality' and so forth is redundant, because of the statement 'of the non-conceptual'."

Without the knowledge of reality, he claims to know the reality of the world as momentary destruction; yet he speaks of a cause that is beyond the scope of words—how can he establish this with non-proofs? Having taken as valid for worldly transaction a false cognition devoid of objects, such as perception and inference which have as their scope only coarse and singular forms, he desires to describe the ultimate reality. Since every conceptual construction, such as the "invariable concomitance" (*pratibandha*), lacks any excellence when not examined according to its true nature, he does not rely upon worldly consensus as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of entering into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If that [inference] were valid, there would be a sublation of [theories] such as momentary destruction;

if something invalid were to establish the ultimate reality through some means, then why seek validity elsewhere? Such seeking would be rendered purposeless. There is an obstacle to the complete entry into reality:

if one intends to demonstrate the proof of the ultimate reality by means of arguments using words that indicate the speaker’s intention, how could one not prove that reality? For what reason would the proponent be defeated on that account?

Furthermore, perceptual cognition does not establish the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) according to its true nature, because what appears therein is a single gross object common to many parts such as color-form, and merely a thing excluded from what is not of that nature; if one accepts the direct awareness of that which is unique to it [the particular], then it is impossible to deny that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) also possesses it. This being the case, the funeral libation has been offered to the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvedanādvaita*) and to the conventional practice of proof and so forth, since there is no difference between conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions regarding the absence of [such] perception.

Nor is a mere difference in appearance contradictory to the fact that cognitions have a single object; this is the meaning: partless, momentary atoms of cognition and the cognized, as well as all such successions of consciousness devoid of external objects, are entirely and in every way erroneous. The reality (*tattva*) is mere appearance (*pratibhāsa-mātra*), which is the emptiness of the *sūkala* (the conceptualized); this is the distinction between philosophical views.
