"Vitti" is the comprehension, the grasping of that [reality] according to its true nature; without that—that is, apart from it—the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have non-reality as their object. Therefore, the Buddhist knows—understands—this.
What is it? He says: the reality of the world (*jagattattva*), the essential nature of the world.
Of what kind is it? It is momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*).

This is an elliptical expression; by it, he indicates that [the world] is merely a continuum of consciousness, merely an illusion, merely an appearance devoid of all conceptual construction, and merely emptiness. By this, he demonstrates the contradiction between the opponent's own earlier and later assertions.

For instance: if one knows the reality (*tattva*) of the world to be of such a nature, how could it be said that "knowledge of reality does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth" (*paramārthataḥ*), on account of which [the author] would say, "validity [is established] by means of worldly convention" (*vyavahāreṇa*)? Or, if it does not exist, how could one know it to be so? It is precisely now that he speaks—by saying "it is like a contradiction," etc.—of what? Of the reason (*hetu*).

Otherwise, how could the statement immediately following the former [proposition]—which is intended to establish that "this is the refutation"—lead one to accept the realization of the world's momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*)? It is not otherwise. What kind [of statement is it]? He says: "That which is beyond the range of speech" (*vāgagocaram*), meaning that which does not become the object (*gocara*) of words. Thus, he considers this a contradiction with his own words (*svavacanavirodha*), because he himself states a reason that is beyond the range of speech and yet puts forward a sentence for the purpose of establishing it.

If it is argued that "the nature of the continuum of consciousness and so forth exists only through conventional usage, for you who know reality, neither the means nor the object is within the sphere of speech from the perspective of ultimate truth," to this he replies: "What could one establish, and by what? By no means of proof."

"By those which are not [valid] means of proof from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*)," he thinks: "If another were to establish reality by means of those things which are themselves not means of proof but are accepted as such by worldly convention (*vyavahārin*)—or by means of those accepted by the Buddhist, such as *vitarka* and so forth—the Sāṃkhya would thereby establish, through conventional usage, the ultimate insentience (*acetanatva*) of pleasure and the like."

Furthermore, as for what was stated here—that "as is the Yakṣa, so is the offering (bali); as are the means (sādhana), so is that which is to be accomplished (sādhya)"—that is refuted by this [argument], because when the means for the ultimate reality (paramārtha) are absent, it is impossible to have a realization of "such-and-such. Thus, the objection—"How can there be any practice even in non-duality (advaita)?"—is rejected. For how is it consistent to say, "As is the offering, so is the Yakṣa"? What has any connection with what?
Commenting on the verse at page 293 of the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, he says: "Objectless," and so forth.

Having taken as valid—in terms of conventional usage—both inference and perception (which are respectively objectless, i.e., devoid of objects, or else have discarded their objects, being false cognitions, and which have as their domain a coarse, unitary form), the Buddhist himself, while treating what is not a means of valid cognition as a means of valid cognition, desires to describe and establish reality.
And one might think: "There is no such determination [of reality] from that [erroneous cognition], just as there is no determination of real water from the cognition of water in a mirage.

To this, he says: "It might be argued..."—let it be that there is no determination of that [object] from perception, which has that [erroneous] thing as its sphere; however, it could arise from inference, because it is indirectly connected to it, according to the statement: "Even an error is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) by virtue of its connection [to reality]. To that, he replies: "Because of the lack of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), etc. and so forth.

The "connection" (*pratibandha*) is the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*). Of this [connection], which is the first among such properties as its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), there is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); the certainty (*niścaya*) that grasps it is [the means of knowledge]. For a non-conceptual [cognition] does not operate therein, since it is impossible for it to function with respect to what is not its own object. Indeed, the operation—namely, "this has arisen from that," "this is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)," or "this is its property (*dharma*)"—is its capacity; yet such an operation, consisting in the perception of atoms as causes and so forth, is unestablished for another [person], because that [non-conceptual cognition] lacks any excellence and thus lacks distinction from inference.
By what [is this established]? He says: "unexamined," and so forth. Is this [the case] for someone [in particular]? No; he says: "for everyone.

What is meant by this? If the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and so forth were false, then it would not be logical that inference has a connection with a real entity even through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*). Thus [it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* 2].
And so forth; and [the passage] beginning with *maṇipradīpaprabhayormaṇibuddhyā* (PV 2.57) [arises] from the object of a coarse, single form.
It should be observed— page 82, note 4—
that the capacity for indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) [is established] in the context of relation and so forth.
The Jaina and other systems [are concerned] with the conceptualization of obstruction and so forth, which relates to the real entity only indirectly.
The ellipsis is that there is no deception even for those two who appear as such [but are empty], because of their connection with the [actual object] for those who speak.
The remainder of the argument is that even though there is no distinction in their being false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*), there is a distinction with respect to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

If, however, this view is held—that for people there is no perception of atoms, nor of fire and smoke, nor of a tree and a *śiṃśapā*, nor of smoke on a mountain; rather, there is only the perception of a coarse unity, because it is precisely therein that the worldly transactions of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth occur—then would that [perception] be invalid (*apramāṇa*) or valid (*pramāṇa*) for you? Regarding the first position, he states the fault: "In the world," and so forth.

Why does he say that worldly consensus—consisting of the cognition of a single gross form—is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? He says: "For the sake of entering into the ultimate reality" (*paramārthāvatārāya*).
Regarding the second point, he says: "If that were a valid means of knowledge," [then] by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of momentary destruction, partlessness, and so forth is intended.

The sense is that since even through a gradual process one [cognition] can be established as having multiple forms, conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To the question, "What fault is there for one who relies on that [conceptual cognition] as invalid for the sake of entering into ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)?", he says: "Of that which is invalid," and so forth.

Or, if that worldly consensus is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then when its validity as a proof for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is admitted, why would one seek a further means of knowledge even elsewhere—such as regarding permanence and so forth? For, if it were accepted from that very source, which is itself false according to worldly convention, the search for a means of knowledge would become useless, since anything else could be established even without a means of knowledge.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In its entirety," and so forth.

For the sake of entering into reality—that is, for the purpose of penetrating such principles as the self (ātman) and the Lord (īśvara)—an inference such as "the living body is endowed with a soul" or "the body and so forth, being the subject of dispute, have an intelligent cause," is not a valid means of knowledge; therefore, momentary destruction and other such properties are not established through such fallacious inference.

If it is asked how fire is established here through the inference "there is fire," so too it is said by the opponent: "In that case, if the self and so forth are not established due to false cognition, how can momentary destruction and the like be established? If it is argued, "Just as the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between existence and momentary destruction is established from the perspective of worldly convention, such is not the case for the self and so forth based on the possession of breath and the like," it has been stated here [in the verse] beginning with "the necessary connection" (*pratibandha*). The sense is that if this were so, there would be no perception of smoke and the mountain; for [in reality], it is only in the perception of a gross unity [of the two] that [the inference functions].

If it were said that "even in the case of the eternal [self], it is based on worldly consensus," then the establishment of an eternal reality would follow even for the Naiyāyikas and others, which is redundant.
Another type of inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is also stated: "by means of words," and so forth;
this intends to demonstrate to another person the probans (*liṅga*), which is the means of proof related to a reality such as momentary destruction.
By what [means]? He says: "by words.
Of what kind? He says: "in the mouth," and so forth;
the sense is that they are unimpeded by any means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
But would it not establish reality? It certainly would.

By what means? To this he says: by means of non-proofs (*asādhana*), such as "possessing breath" and so forth, which are unestablished (*apratibaddha*). Since the establishment of reality is [effected] by non-proofs, the proponent (*vādī*) would be defeated for that reason;
or, in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepa*), it is emphatically "not at all."

"Is it not the case that there is no fault here? For, while inference and the object of inference do not exist [as separate entities], that [intrinsic nature] exists as a sequence, being devoid of distinctions such as the state of being a reason (*hetutva*) and so forth; and because it is established through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), this objection does not apply.
To him, another replies with the words "And not... and so on.

If it is asked: "It might be thought that this has already been stated by the passage beginning with 'this connection' (*pratibandha*) and so forth; why then is it stated again?"—it is true that it was stated, nevertheless:
As it is stated in the *Mādhyamakakārikā* (24.8): "The Dharma-teaching of the Buddhas relies upon two truths:

the worldly conventional truth (*lokasaṃvṛtisatya*) and the truth in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasatya*). Therefore, that [previous statement] was said with reference to worldly conventional truth; however, with reference to the ultimate truth of non-dual appearance, this is now asserted: perception does not at all establish its own nature—the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—through the directness of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-adhyakṣa*), nor does it determine it as being free from doubt and the like.

"Is it not even slightly so? To this he says: "In accordance with its definition. That which is defined as being undivided (*avibhāga-lakṣaṇa*) because it is devoid of the consciousness of the forms of the grasped and the grasper—how could that be transgressed? To this he says: "Of a single gross [object]," and so forth.

The intended meaning here is as follows: since there is no grasper of blue and so forth that is distinct from the body, pleasure, and the like, the opponent maintains that what appears is by its very nature (*svataḥ*) of the essence of cognition (*jñānātmaka*). Of that single gross object—which consists of many parts common to color-form and the rest—it is merely because it appears therein in the perception (*pratyakṣa-buddhi*) [that it is so].

For the proponent of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaitavādin*), although that [consciousness] is partless and non-dual, blue and other objects appear otherwise; thus, even though it is a single entity, it appears as if possessing succession.
As it has been said:

"Just as for those whose senses are afflicted by mantras and the like, fragments of clay and so forth appear in a completely different way, even though they are devoid of that [perceived] form"— this is the remainder of the verse (Pravāha-vārttika 2.355).
"Just as in the deserts, even a small fire appears large from afar" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.356), and so forth;
likewise, because of the non-perception [of distinctions] by those whose minds are unimpaired, the first half [of the verse] states: "Though undivided... (Pramāṇavārttika 2.357).
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," he says there: "And [it is] merely the object (vastu) excluded from what is not that form (atadrūpa-parāvṛtta), because that single gross [form] appears therein.

This is what is meant: when a reality imagined by others is established through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) either prior to or subsequent to its manifestation—just as elephants and the like [are established] prior to the appearance of a pillar and so forth—then it is logical that it manifests in that way.
But this is not the case, because that very [nature] appears until the attainment of the path to enlightenment;
nevertheless, even if there is the occurrence of its appearance, nothing would have been apprehended in its own form, since one might at some point imagine another thing appearing in that same way—
thus [it is said] by those whose vision is distorted regarding the nature of cognition.
The ellipsis is: "it appears as if possessing the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.
Now, [one might argue that] the gross is postulated in relation to the subtle, and the one is postulated in relation to the many.
Nor do phenomena become ultimately real through dependence, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

It is not the case that a single gross object appears in a perceptual cognition, but rather in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); if it is argued that what appears therein is the atoms of cognition (*jñāna-paramāṇu*), to this he replies: "That is uncommon," and so forth.
This refers to the acceptance of the awareness of that which belongs to another—that is, the uncommon [atom] which is excluded from everything else.

What [is the consequence]? He says: "Even of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and not merely of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), the acceptance of that—namely, the acceptance of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) which is unique to itself and others—is impossible to deny; for acceptance does not differ from mere desire.

This being the case, the funeral libation has been offered to the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvedanādvaita*) and to the practical discourse of means and ends (*sādhanādi-vyavahāra*), because [conceptual construction] has as its object a mentally constructed universal (*kalpita-sāmānya*).
Thus, regarding direct perception:

Now, if it is thought that [the object] is not accepted because it does not appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the author replies with the words "having perceived" (*pratītya*) and so forth:

since there is no distinction between conceptual and non-conceptual [cognition] regarding this absence of a unique perception (*asādhāraṇapratītyabhāva*), when this is the case, everything beginning with the substratum (*dharmin*) is unestablished in such statements as "that which appears in perceptual cognition despite the absence of a unique perception" and "in whatever manner something appears."
In that regard, if one accepts the cognition of those [two], then even in the case of conceptualization, there would be such a cognition for both oneself and others; thus,
in the first case, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
while in the other case, it is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Since the apprehension of both the preceding and the succeeding [moments] by a single [consciousness] is not contradictory— just as the apprehension of both self and other is not— it follows from this that [the statement] "without the knowledge of reality," and so forth, applies when there is an absence of the perception of uncommon [specific] cognition.
For in perceptual cognition, the ultimate reality of the object of conceptual construction is established;
indeed, its establishment [is thus secured].
"Because it does not appear in the mind as something distinct from the word, [the word] is the cognizer of that object which is not indicated by it, just as when that [object] is seen.
This verse was extracted from the *Apohasiddhi* (p. 6), treating it as a scriptural authority (*śāstra*).
Sanmati-Ṭīkā, p.

260: If it is asked, "How can it be said that 'the reason (hetu) must be expressible within the range of speech'—that every word or every conceptual construction (vikalpa) applies everywhere?"—to this he replies: "And not," and so forth;
and it is certainly not merely a difference in appearance (pratibhāsabheda).

Of what [cognitions]? Of cognitions (*buddhi*). [The opponent objects: "There is a contradiction because they have a single object. [The author replies: Even if there is a single object, that alone is possible; however, the distinction between them consists in their specific qualifications (*viśeṣa*), and thus it is not contradictory. He indicates this by means of the word "alone" (*mātra*). Showing the difference in appearance with an illustration, he says: "Distant, near, etc. and so forth.
Just as the appearance of a single object perceived through the causal complexes of "distant," "near," and so forth differs, so too do the appearances in perception and non-perception differ.

(24) If you maintain that visual and other cognitions, though occurring toward a single [object], experience a difference in appearance, then why would perception and the others not have a single object despite the difference in appearance caused by the difference in their causal complexes? By asserting that conceptual construction lacks an object because it apprehends something as what it is not (*atasmiṃstadgraha*), you are defeated, for you have stated something that is not a constituent part of a valid proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).
Since a relation is invariably of a non-essential nature,

and reality is defined according to how it is perceived, how could the establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta) not follow from the impossibility of [absolute] reality otherwise? We shall explain immediately after this that its definition consists in independence from anything else.

The words *dūra* (far) and *āsanna* (near) have the state [of being far or near] as their primary meaning; therefore, "that which has distance and proximity as its beginning"—by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of "further distance," "greater proximity," and so forth—or alternatively, the inclusion of "having dim vision" and so on—those [causes] are thus described. Those [perceptions] which possess such causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) are also thus described. Furthermore, those which are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) and which are cognitions of a single object (*ekārthasaṃvid*): the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) of these is "distinct" (*bhinna*) according to the manner—whether clear or otherwise—of perception and non-perception, that is, of sensory cognition and verbal cognition. "In that way, the manifestation is distinct" is what follows [as the conclusion].
Explaining the verse, he says: "The eye and so forth," etc.

If it is maintained by the Buddhist that the cognition of the nose and so forth—which have the eye and so forth as their [causal] basis—experiences a difference in appearance regarding a single object, namely, a distinction between a clear and a non-clear manifestation, then from what [cause does this arise]? It arises from a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
"How could it not be so? It certainly must be so. To this he says: "the state of having a single object.
Of what [is this true]? To this he says: "of the perceptions," and so forth.

"In what [case]? He says: "Even when there is a difference in appearance, this is refuted by that [following argument]: two cognitions which have different appearances do not have a single object, just like the cognitions of color and taste; and the verbal and sensory cognitions have different appearances.

Likewise, those two which have a single object do not have different appearances, just like the two persons' cognitions of that [same] blue object when it is present; [the objects of] the two are a single object, and they are not [mutually] independent."

Thus [it is asked]: how so? Because there is a deviation [in the argument], since even when the object is one and the same, we admit a difference in the manifestation of the cognition for two people with weak and keen eyesight, as in the case of two persons having cognitions of blue.

As for the one who says: "Because the object of that [cognition] is not established in relation to another, and because even there, due to the lack of a clear manifestation, there is no single object—since otherness is absent and because of the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*)—therefore, even though the object is an undivided unity, the difference in the manifestations of color and so forth in visual and other cognitions arises from the specific difference in their causal complexes"; he is not a person of discernment. For, if cognition were indistinctly manifest, it would follow that the Buddhists could never engage with objects in pairs.

For a discerning person does not act toward that which has arisen [in consciousness] while knowing it to be objectless, because that would entail the absence of any examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in all cases;
furthermore, one who acts would not experience non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*),
yet such discrepancy does indeed occur, as is observed in the case of scripts and the like.

"This appearance of mine is such," [as stated] in *Prakaraṇavārttika* 1.1 and elsewhere; because of such inference, they engage with that object due to its indistinct manifestation, and not from the collection of sense-faculties—this is a great deafness! Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress regarding inference;
therefore, that is nothing at all.

Now, one might argue: "Since sensory cognition and its opposite are both clear in their respective ways, let there be identity of object between them based on having the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as their object; however, this is not the case for perception and indirect cognition (parokṣa), because the latter has as its object a non-real universal (sāmānya). To address this, he says: "Conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), etc. [The opponent objects: "If you understand that conceptual construction is without an object because it grasps that [universal] which is not the particular, then why was such a position already refuted by us previously? To this, he replies: "Because it is not a constituent of the proof" (*asādhanāṅga*), etc.

This is what is meant: when a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has as its object a universal (*sāmānya*) that does not exist as a real entity (*avastusat*), then the speech arising from it also has that same [non-real] object. Consequently, it does not have as its object a factor for establishing ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, because one is defeated due to the non-statement of such [a real object], [the opponent argues]: "The Arhat is not killed"—because this conceptual construction is indirectly connected (*pratibandha*) to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the speech arising from it is also [connected] to that [particular characteristic]. To this, [the author] replies: Because the relationship—which is a mutual inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)—is by necessity and definitively of a non-ultimate nature (*atattvarūpatva*), it is non-ultimate because it is of a non-real nature (*avasturūpatva*).

Since the specifically characterized nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) imagined by others is not established from any [valid] source, how could there be a real connection (*pratibandha*) for anything with respect to that, whether directly or otherwise? If it is asked, "If that is unestablished, what then is reality (*tattva*)?", he says here: "Reality," and so forth.
The sense is that it is according to appearance, without overstepping the mode of perception, such as the gross and so on.
What follows from this? He says: "Otherwise," and so forth.

Otherwise, since there is no establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta) through any other mode than the impossibility of reality [in a single nature], the establishment of non-absolutism occurs by means of that impossibility;
regarding this, the opponent asks the Master with the words "How? and so forth. Being thus questioned, he says: "Its definition," etc.

The establishment of the definition of that reason will be discussed in the section to be stated immediately following; therein, we shall explain the disregard for other factors such as the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatva).
An appearance that is of such a nature is not devoid of configuration;
because it is observed to be so elsewhere, it is likewise an inference— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 2.173.
Since the universal is a non-entity, because its object is that [universal],
it has a non-entity as its object.
The connection with the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) belongs to that which originates from conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Bound to its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
thus, having analyzed the nature of verbal expression (*jalpa*), he now says "by means of *syādvāda*" and so forth, demonstrating the purpose of presenting it in an assembly.

When all one-sided doctrines concerning the nature of all things have been refuted by the presentation of discourse through the doctrine of manifold aspects (syādvāda), the logical intelligence of the wise becomes unified.

Adhering to the true meaning of reality and attaining incomparable conduct, it is definitively determined to be the direct cause of the great fourfold infinity. (28) The particle *syāt* has the sense of "praiseworthy."

And by what kind of *syādvāda*—that is, by what kind of excellent discourse—is it characterized? It is one whose object is all things (*samastavastuviṣaya*), meaning its object is entirely (*samastena*) and completely (*saṃpūrṇena*) all things; that which has this as its object is so described.
To the question "What [is destroyed]? he says: "In those things that have been demolished (*abhidhvasteṣu*), that is, refuted (*nirākṛteṣu*)."

"In what [contexts]? he asks. He replies: "In the doctrines of absolute monism (*ekāntavāda*)," that is, in the various types of discourse related to absolute monism; for by the use of the plural, all such discourse is encompassed.

When these exist, what happens? He says: "It is made one-faced," meaning it is turned away from other discourses and rendered fixed upon noble conversation. Thus he says: "it is directed toward that."
Of what nature is it? It is "logical" (naiyāyikī), meaning established by reason.
Of whom? To this he says: "of the wise" (matimatām), that is, of the intelligent.
Why is it so? To this he says: "in reality," and so forth.
Only that which is intent upon the true meaning becomes endowed with logic;

what is it doing? He says: what is it attaining? It is attaining conduct (*cāritra*), namely impartiality toward the positions of the proponent and the opponent. Because it is incomparable yet comparable, as if by two [sides], the reason (*hetu*) and the mark (*liṅga*) are determined.
To whom does this systematic arrangement—purified of the stains of all conflicting views—belong? He says: "Of the Great One, who possesses the fourfold infinity.
Now, one might object that the cause of fire and other such things must also be determined; this is true, yet effort expended regarding the primary principle also applies to other cases.

For this very reason it is said, "of the Great One" (mahataḥ); or rather, this is a preamble intended as an introduction to that which is about to be expounded, even though [the term] is used in a figurative sense.

Since there is likewise a dispute regarding the cognition of the inferable even when [the reason] functions as a cause, that too must be determined. To this he says: because it is stated that even though [the reason] is manifested by the *syādvāda*—the teaching of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) which encompasses all objects—it is not possible without non-absolutism itself, the absolutist doctrines such as those of the Buddhists and others are thereby refuted. Having thus unified [the discussion] toward non-absolutism, the remainder is as before.
Therefore, it is the reason alone that is determined, and not the cognition of the inferable.

If it is argued: "Since that [inference] functions as a cause for the occurrence of debate even regarding his own statement, why is that not also determined by you, just as it is by others? We say: no; because this has been examined immediately following [the previous point], and for this very reason, there is no mention of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
If it is questioned what the fruit of the manifestation of the path is, [the answer is:

by means of the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness), the intellect disciplined by the logic of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*)—that is to say, right knowledge—is directed toward the true meaning;
it is conjoined with a predilection for the true meaning, and results in incomparable conduct (*cāritra*), which is the cessation of sinful activity.
Attaining immediately the infinite quartet— of infinite knowledge and so forth— it is determined that it is the cause, the great instrument; thus,
even the causal statement [is established] as having the characteristics of infinite knowledge, vision, bliss, and vigor.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the *Jalpasiddhi* (Establishment of Debate), in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by the sage Anantavīrya, who subsists at the feet of the venerable Vibhadra.
Chapter Six:
The Establishment of the Definition of the Logical Reason (*Hetu*).
If it is asked: "Since the reason has already been determined by the wise themselves, why is it being determined here once again?"—to this he replies: "O you," and so forth.

The fool, who is a harsh and noisy person lacking discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, is generally confused and deceived; he is not capable of awakening to the stainless state of the Lord which has been tasted [by the wise].
By accepting [the world] as it is, he does not merely defile it with false and one-sided views;
rather, we shall clearly demonstrate how he curses and reviles those who teach the Dharma of the virtuous.
Like a child, because of his natural aversion toward his own path, the outsider—such as a follower of the Sugata and others—is like a fool; by this, [the author] shows his innate delusion.

Of what nature is he? To this he says: "The *heya* (that which is to be abandoned) consists of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth; the *ādeya* (that which is to be accepted) is the impossibility of [the probandum] otherwise (*anyathānupapannatva*). The *viveka* (discrimination) of these two is their discernment, that is, their mutual separation. In this regard, one who is both *kāhala* (confused/indistinct) and a *khala* (wicked/vulgar)—such a person is *kāhalakāta*, meaning a wicked person terrified by the difficulty of such discrimination. Even when having that discrimination explained to him by another, he does not understand it himself; such a person is first deceived (*pralabdha*) and then bewildered (*ākula*) by it for the most part (*prāyeṇa*), or in abundance (*bāhulyena*). By this, they indicate that [the error] is produced by mental impressions (*ābhisaṃskārika*)."

What is that? He says: "Not capable" (*nālaṃ*), meaning not able; "able" (*alam*) means excessively, or even slightly capable—this is the sense, according to the statement in the *Hetubindu* (verse 1): "Because of the rule of invariable concomitance.
What is he not capable of doing? To this he says: "To awaken," that is, to know.

What? He says: "The term" (*pada*). Why? Because of the context: it is a "term" (*hetu*) because by means of it the object to be inferred is reached or understood, according to its etymological derivation.
The expression "intrinsic nature as the path" is here meaningless,
because falsity is innate due to its inherent depravity.

Because it arises from the instruction of another, false view is [excluded]; the reason is that which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds.
Because of the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), others than these are pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). —
*Hetubindu*, verse 1, chapter 1, section 3.

If it is argued that "surely that [knowledge] belongs to the Tīrthaṅkara at all times, and therefore its non-apprehension does not constitute a fault," the author replies here: *amalālīḍham*— that which has been tasted (*ālīḍham*) by the stainless ones (*amalaiḥ*), such as the Gaṇadharas and others.
"They do not paint what is defective; for whom would there be a loss of purity? To this he says: "By our own master, Pātrakeśarin"—so say some.

Why is this? If it is argued that it is because the subsequent commentary was composed by him as a refutation of the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇaka*) regarding that subject; [we reply: in that case, it would belong to the venerable Sīmandhara Bhaṭṭāraka, the Tīrthaṅkara who has direct perception of all things.

Therefore, first the commentators—desiring to demonstrate that this [definition] is not merely a product of their own intellect, but is established by the supreme tradition (parāgama)—state the *Anyathānupapattivārtika* which was obtained from the assembly (*samavasaraṇa*) of the Lord Tīrthaṅkara Bhagavān Sīmandhara through the grace of the Gaṇadhara-deva, brought forth by the goddess Padmāvatī, and presented to the venerable Pātrakeśarin: "The state of being otherwise impossible... (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Vol. 2, p. 177).
The definition of the reason (*hetu*) was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* as follows: "The state of being otherwise impossible" (*anyathānupapannatva*). (Tattvasaṅgrahaślokavārttika, p.
205; Pramāṇaparīkṣā, p. 72;
Jaina-tarkavārttika, p. 135).

In the *Sūtrakṛtāṅga-ṭīkā*, folio 225a, and the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, folio 40, [the author] raises the objection regarding the view of Pātrasvāmin with the words "otherwise... and so forth; [as it is stated: "...not being otherwise impossible... and "...being otherwise impossible..."—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, folio 560.
Nyāyadīpikā, p. 32:
As it was stated by Pātrasvāmin—"The state of being otherwise impossible... Syādvādaratnākara, p. 521:
"Where the impossibility of [the probans] existing otherwise is known, what is the use of the [other] three [criteria]?"
— *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 104.
This was stated by Pātrakeśarin: "The state of being otherwise impossible... — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 9.
If the property of "inseparability from the contrary" (anyathānupapannatva) is present, what is the use of the three [characteristics] there?
If inseparability from the contrary is not present, what is the use of the three there?

If it is asked, "How is it known that this was done?"—is it not the same as asking, "How is it known that the *Trikalalakṣaṇakadarthana* was composed by Pātrakeśarin? It is also the same in both cases that [the authorship] is established through the renown of the teacher; moreover, there is a great and well-known tradition regarding this matter.

If its validity depends on its being composed by him, then what confidence can there be in establishing that [authorship]? If you say it is "his" because he composed it for that purpose, then the entire scripture and its subject matter would likewise be his alone; consequently, it would be designated as not composed by him even for his own disciples, or perhaps it would not even belong to Patañjali himself, since he too composed it for another purpose, and that other person for yet another—until no one could claim this scripture was theirs.
In the *Ārādhanākathākośa*, regarding the verse on "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) being composed by Sīmandhara:
It is well known as "composed by Pātrakeśarin";
it was for the sake of Pātrakeśarin,
that is, for the sake of his own disciples.

Because this [work] is the cause for the continuous composition regarding that subject, Pātrakeśarin thought: "This is [the work of the Blessed One]. For, if it were by some other author, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a lack of designation [by the tradition].
Therefore, it is determined that this is the reason for the Blessed Tīrthaṅkara who taught after having directly realized [the truth] in its entirety;
and this has been stated as the reason for its being untainted (*amalālīḍhatva*).

"Surely even he accepts the definition of the *sūtra*, since he admits that in the absence of the probandum there is necessarily an absence of the probans; so why is it said, 'in order to awaken the fool'? To this, he replies: the phrase "the fool accepts the position" (*padam*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

"How does he make it turbid? He says: "By means of false exclusives (*vitatha-ekāntaiḥ*). Even such things as "the property of the subject exists only in the similar instance" (*sapakṣe sanneva*) are likewise false exclusives;
by these, having rendered what is stainless turbid while attempting to establish [his position], he perceives that [position] just as one who sees two moons perceives the moon. Thus he thinks.
By this, he demonstrates the state of childhood and the deception regarding the time for discerning what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted;
now, showing the agitation caused by being deceived by that very [childhood], he says: "Not only that," and so forth—meaning it not only defiles that, but it even cries out.

Whom? To this he says: "the masters who instruct well," meaning those who compose replies that do not contradict what is seen or what is accepted; here, this phrase—understood through the transformation of case and number—is connected [to the previous statement].
By this very [phrase], those who are shameless... (Pra.vā. 3).
From such statements as these, it is understood that he "curses";

indeed, it is only one who is agitated by being deceived by a wicked person who curses them, and no other. For this reason, we shall examine that state clearly and precisely—whatever it may be—that is improper and agitated.
They prattle on, [but] that too is rejected because it occurs only in one instance;
this is the remainder [of the argument].
"By what will its locus be made manifest, or by what will it be expressed? To this, he says: "The position," and so forth.

That which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by a part of it (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*) attains the status of a logical reason (*hetu*). [This is] the comparison: "The reason is a property of the subject that is pervaded by a part of it... (*Hetubindu*, verse 1).
Otherwise, if this [reason] is not characterized by the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapanna*) through reasoning (*tarka*), [it is not a valid reason]. (Verse 2)

In inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), the subject (*dharmin*) whose specific property one wishes to know is the "thesis" (*pakṣa*); in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), however, it is the subject whose specific property one wishes to make known. Because one adopts a thesis in order to produce a certainty in others just as one has attained certainty oneself—and because there is a desire to know on the part of the other—the designation "thesis" applies to that which the proponent intends to demonstrate, due to its proximity to the speaker's intention, just as the term "inference for others" is used.
The property of such a subject (*pakṣa*) in its primary sense, which is pervaded by that part (*tadaṃśa*), is that very part itself;

for that property is a single portion of it. Since the word "subject" (*pakṣa*) denotes the whole, if one were to use the term "subject" metaphorically to mean the locus of the property (*dharmin*), then even the status of being its property (*taddharmatā*) would not be established.

For it is not the case that the property [of being a product] is intended to be proven there [in the example], because otherwise everything would be every property due to the unrestrained nature of desire; and if that [property] were not excluded, there would be doubt as to whether the property is intended to be proven. Otherwise, the statement of the reason would be purposeless.

If a subject-property (*pakṣadharma*) belonged to one whose property is doubtful, how could there be the figurative designation of "subject" (*pakṣa*) applied to it? For, desiring a doubtful property, one might suspect the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason, which is why this [author] resorts to the figurative usage.

Furthermore, if the reason (*hetu*) were pervaded by the subject (*dharmin*) of a metaphorical position (*upacaritapakṣa*) without doubt, then even "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth would be a valid reason for the permanence of sound, being pervaded by "existence" (*sattva*), "knowability" (*prameyatva*), and so on, rather than by that [actual] subject.

Furthermore, it is not logical that after a term has functioned through a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) to a single part, it should again be referred to by a pronoun and then used as a collective term for the whole; for since the word *pakṣa* does not denote the whole but denotes only the locus (*dharmin*), the statement "its property (*taddharma*), like its part (*tadaṃśavat*), is not a part of it" would be well-said. Otherwise, this [metaphorical usage] would be a transgression of the primary meaning of words, following the logic of eating a *karkaṭī* fruit out of fear of bathing in the Gaṅgā, because of the very same fault.

Pervasion (vyāpti) is either the necessary presence of the pervader (vyāpaka) there, or the presence of the pervaded (vyāpya) only there; in this regard, it is solely the impossibility of being otherwise (anyathānupapatti), and not any other form.

If not, what would be the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and what the pervader (*vyāpaka*)? If you say that the cause is [the pervader] of the effect and the nature (*svabhāva*) is [the pervader] of the entity (*bhāva*), then how can there be such a thing as "pervasion" for a momentary cause that does not reach the time of its effect? Furthermore, if there is an absolute difference between those two natures, what could be pervaded by what? If one establishes the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*) based merely on the intention of the conventional user (*vyavahartṛ*) without examining the reality, it would follow that this [intention] is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādaka*). If it were contradictory, then relying upon it would be an act of irrationality, as it would be useless for the matter at hand.

In that case, regarding this rule of necessary concomitance (*pratibandhaniyama*), how could the far side of the moon be inferred from the observation of its near side? There is no relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between these two, as they exist simultaneously;

nor is there identity (*tādātmya*), because their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ. Enough with this! Is the inference based on "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) not therefore faultless? How else, indeed, would it be accounted for? Surely, entities do not deserve to be subjected to such questioning. If there were identity, what then would be the reason for saying that a *śiṃśapā* has the nature of a tree, or that smoke is the effect of fire? [Otherwise] there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To this, too, the same answer applies.
In this context, the object of inference (anumeya) is the subject (dharmin) whose specific property one desires to know— Nyāyabindu 2.6.

Comparison— Now, it might be argued that the Master’s statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) is indeed intended, as he said: "With the desire to produce in others a certainty similar to one's own certainty,
there is the exclusion of anything else [than] the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the connection (*sambandha*), and the probandum (*sādhya*)."
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 487:

"The production of certainty in others, just like one's own certainty, is declared by the wise to be inference for the sake of others (*parārthamāna*); the verbal expression is so called by way of metaphorical designation."
"For that part is indeed its very property" (Nyāyāvatāra, verse 10);
"the subject is the property-possessor, because the term for the whole is metaphorically applied to the part" (Hetubindu, p. 52); "for that part is indeed its very property" (Hetubindu, p. 53).

For at that time, by virtue of the speaker's intention, it is not a part of that [whole]—that is, a "portion" (*tadaṃśa*)—which is called the "subject" (*pakṣa*), because the term "subject" does not denote the whole;
for its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) therein. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti, p. 16)
Or rather, the existence of the pervaded (vyāpya) in that very [locus]—[Hetubindu, p. 53]. Compare: "The cognition of the moon in water and so forth is likewise inference."
— Laghīyastraya, verse 13;
likewise between the dewlap and the horn, and between the near and far sides of the moon—
Nyāyaviniścaya, 2.

By this reason, form is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends it; [this] demonstrates that even if that [means of cognition] is not accepted, the thesis— whose definition will be stated hereafter— still exists for those who hold it.
The word "api" (also/even) is connected with each term:

"dharma" (the property), and by the word "api," it is also [connected with] "pakṣadharma" (the property of the subject). This [property], such as existence (*sattva*) in the case of sound, or the rising of the Kṛttikā constellation in relation to the rising of the Pleiades (*śakaṭa*), when perceived through direct perception, attains the status of a logical reason (*hetu*) in its capacity as a means of cognition (*gamakatva*).
Likewise, by the word "api" here as well, even that which is not pervaded by that [subject-portion] attains that [status].
The example for that is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because of its existence, like a pot," or "because of its audibility.
The term *tadaṃśa* (that-part) will be defined in this very commentary.
To the question, "In what manner does it go toward that [the probandum]? he says: "Otherwise, in the manner of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), it is unestablished (*anupapanna*)."
Does everyone of that kind attain that [state]? No; thus he says: "It is observed"—that is, ascertained—if this [reason] is otherwise inexplicable.
By what? He says: "By tarka" (logical reasoning).

He states the fault in not accepting this [definition]: "If this [reason] does not attain the status of a logical reason (*hetutā*) because it is not otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapanna*), then even such [arguments] as 'he is dark-skinned because he is his son' would follow [as valid reasons]. Likewise, if a reason is not perceived by means of *tarka* (reductio) as being 'otherwise impossible'—even if it is ultimately otherwise impossible—it does not attain the status of a logical reason; otherwise, one who has come from Nālikera Island might, upon seeing smoke somewhere, arrive at the cognition of fire.
Or, if it is perceived by *tarka* as being otherwise impossible, then surely it attains the status of a logical reason; indeed, it certainly does."
When the non-eternality of sound is to be proven,
[the word] "nanu" is used in the sense of a deliberation (*vitarka*).
He explains the verse beginning with "for one's own sake" (*svārthe*) and so forth:

regarding that inference which is for one's own sake, what is the subject (*dharmin*), i.e., the thesis-locus (*pakṣa*)? It is that whose specific qualities are desired to be known (*jijñāsita-viśeṣa*).

Regarding the inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the phrase "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates an alternative position; the term "subject" (*pakṣaḥ*)—defined as the locus (*dharmin*) whose specific property one wishes to make known—is understood to carry over [from the previous definition].
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "If [one considers] one's own ascertainment," and so forth;
here, by the word "and" (*ca*), the proponent (*pratipādaka*) is referred to.

Certainty (*niścaya*) is the comprehension of the inferable (*anumeya*). That which functions similarly to that is "like that" (*tadvat*). For the sake of producing certainty—and thus generating the comprehension of the inferable—in other persons who are to be instructed, the proponent adopts a subject (*pakṣa*). Because of this cause, that [subject] is called the "particularity intended to be made known" (*jijñāpayiṣitaviśeṣa*), for it is precisely that wherein a property (*dharma*) not yet established for the opponent is desired to be demonstrated; it is in that sense that it is so described.

Now, even if one adopts a thesis (*pakṣa*) in order to produce a certainty in others similar to one's own certainty, if the person intended to be instructed has no desire to know (*jijñāsā*) that property (*dharma*), how can that be a "specific feature intended to be made known" (*jijñāpayiṣita-viśeṣa*)? If it is argued that "the specific feature desired to be explained to one who wishes to know that specific feature is called the 'specific feature intended to be made known'," to this he replies: "And when [there is]... and so forth. Only when there is indeed a desire to know on the part of the other—the person to be instructed—is the subject (*dharmī*) called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) as the specific feature intended to be made known.

[Objection: "If he [the listener] were to have an inquiry regarding that [subject], then just as in an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) the designation 'subject' (*pakṣa*) applies only to one who possesses that [reason], so too in an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the designation applies to another who possesses it. Thus, the connection with its merits and defects belongs only to that other person, not to the proponent. To this, he says: "Of the speaker’s intention alone," etc., and the phrase "even when" (*satyām ca*) etc. follows. Therefore, the meaning is this: even though there is an inquiry on the part of another, [it refers to] the proponent who intends to explain a matter not yet understood by him. This is the sense.

The term "designation by the thesis" (*pakṣavyapadeśaḥ*) means the designation [of something] as the thesis; that is to say, it belongs to that [intention] which is the thesis, and not to anything else. Why? To this he says: because of the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of the speaker—the proponent’s intention, which is the resolve to communicate a meaning not yet understood—[the thesis belongs] to that alone and not to any other intention. For instance: first there is another's desire to know the truth (*tattva*), followed by the communication of that [truth], then the proponent’s intention to communicate it, and finally the adoption of the thesis (*pakṣaparigraha*). Thus, there is a proximity of the speaker’s intention toward the adoption of the thesis.
He states the illustrative example established in both cases: "like the designation for the sake of another," for one who possesses the desire to know,
for one who possesses the desire to know.
The meaning is that it is well-known only to the person for whom the argument is being established (*pratipādyasya*).

Having thus explained the definition of the *pakṣa* (the subject), he states the formal application (*prayoga*) while demonstrating it: "It is a property (*dharma*) of such a *pakṣa*—that is, of the subject as previously described—because [the probandum] is dependent upon it."
In this context, no consideration has been made regarding the restriction of the prior or posterior limit, because the absence of defects in both cases will be demonstrated later;
the connection is with the word "reason" (hetu), and what kind of reason? It is "pervaded" (vyāpta).
In that regard, it is called "pervaded" (*vyāpta*) because of its connection with pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And pervasion consists in both the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*):
[the pervasion] residing in the pervaded is the existence [of the pervader] only there; [the pervasion] residing in the pervader is the fact that the pervader exists only where [the pervaded exists].
By what? He says: "by a part of that. By the word "that" (tat), the subject (*pakṣa*) is referred to.

And although, according to the literal function of words (*śābdī vṛtti*), the subject is subordinate as a qualifier of the property (*dharma*), nevertheless, its predominance follows from the logic of the actual meaning (*ārthanyāya*), because the property is dependent upon it.
Thus, "by a part" means by a constituent portion (*avayava*) of that [subject].

By all of this, he shows that this [reason] possesses the three-fold form characterized by being a property of the subject (pakṣadharma), positive concomitance (anvaya), and negative concomitance (vyatireka).
Of what kind [of reason]? To this he says: "of the non-figurative," which means "of the primary.

For pervasion (vyāpti) consists either in the presence of the pervader (vyāpaka) only there [in the locus of the pervaded], or in the presence of the pervaded (vyāpya) only there [in the locus of the pervader].
—Hetubindu, p. 53:
When the pervader (vyāpaka) is the probandum (sādhya), [the reason exists] only when that [probandum] is present, but not in the absence of the pervader for the pervaded (vyāpya).
When the pervaded exists,
there is necessarily existence [of the pervader] and never non-existence;
this is according to the compound formation following grammatical rules (*vyākaraṇa*).
In the expression "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), [the word *dharma*] refers to the subject because it is dependent upon the subject.

By this, it is stated that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), as well as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), are each ascertained by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
[this constitutes] presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*). — *Hetubindu*, p. 53.

"Non-existence in the non-concordant class (asapakṣe 'sattvam)" means exclusion from the discordant class (vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ). He explains the term "part of that" (tadaṃśa): "A part of that [subject] (pakṣa) is 'that-part' (tadaṃśa). He states a synonym for "part": "its property" (taddharmaḥ).

Again, he states the point following that: "If it is a part of that"—surely, if it is a property (*dharma*), it is not its location (*deśa*); if it is its constituent part (*avayava*), it is not its property (*dharma*).

If it is argued that "it is both that property and a part of that" is a mutual contradiction because of the difference between the two—just as Dharmakīrti stated: "That property is not a part of that" (*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 17)—this is not sound; for such a statement was made with the intention that there is no difference between the property and its part.

For when the object of knowledge consists of both difference and non-difference, its various distinctions are understood through this [treatise] by means of synonymous terms such as "attribute" (*dharma*), "part" (*aṃśa*), "portion" (*ekadeśa*), "distinction" (*bheda*), or "modification" (*paryāya*). Since the object of knowledge is composed of that [duality], the meaning is that reality consists of substance and modification. This is because we observe worldly usage such as "an entity is the substratum of real attributes" and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.44), "What other part could there be that has not been seen?", every quality has indeed been seen; as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3).

Having stated this, and also saying "as property and property-bearer" (*dharmadharmitayā*) [in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*, p. 24], he says this in order to show that those who speak of a difference between two parts of a single property (*dharmaikadeśayoḥ*) are speaking in contradiction to their own words:

"If it is argued that 'that property' (*taddharmaḥ*) is a part of that [whole], meaning it is a part of the property-bearer (*dharmi*) which is a metaphorical extension (*upacarita*) of a part of the position (*pakṣa*) as a whole (*samudāya*)," to this he replies: "This has already been established by the fact that the word 'position' (*pakṣa*) denotes the whole."
The meaning would not be "a part of that" for the term *tadaṃśa* if the word *tadaṃśa* were taken to mean a "part"; for in that case, that part could not be expressed by the term *taddharma*.
Comparison between the property (*dharma*) and its constituent part (*avayava*): by the word "that" (*tat*), the subject (*pakṣa*) is referred to, not the property (*dharma*),
because a property cannot possess another property.

Furthermore, "part" (*aṃśa*) refers to the property (*dharma*), not a single portion (*ekadeśa*), because the word "side" (*pakṣa*) denotes the locus (*dharmī*) alone; thus, it is not a part of that [locus], since for it there is no single portion—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 17.
Dharmakīrti [states] that the distinction between the property (dharma) and the property-bearer (dharmin) is created by the form of the cognition— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*.

Thus, while the primary [meaning] is what is to be communicated to another, why resort to a figurative interpretation (*gauṇakalpanā*)? In the *Vārttika-hetubindu-śāstra*, [the author], demonstrating the refutation of the position that is metaphorical (*upacarita*), attributed to others (*paropacarita*), or shown by others (*paropadarśita*), says: "The subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus (*dharmin*)," and so forth.

If one accepts such a metaphor—that the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is the locus (*dharmin*) alone—or if one accepts a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) in the ultimate sense, whereby the collection of both property (*dharma*) and locus (*dharmin*) is [taken as the subject] because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) with its part, the locus (*dharmin*), despite the absence of that [collection] in its other part;
then what [follows]? He says: "That," and so forth.

That which has the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) as its attribute is "that-possessing-a-property" (taddharmaka); the state of being such is "property-ness" (taddharmatā). That too is not established.
Thus, the word "of the subject" (dharmiṇaḥ) is connected [to the preceding] by changing the case-ending;
by the use of the word "also" (api), it is indicated that not only is the state of being a part of that (tadekadeśatā) unestablished.

For just as a partless subject (*dharmin*) cannot have a single part [as its locus], because that would entail it being a collection (*samudāya*) in itself, so too its property (*dharma*) cannot possibly exist; for otherwise, one could not avoid the consequence that the subject and property together constitute a collection.

Otherwise, how could it be said at the time of formal application (*prayoga*) that the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) is the collection of property and subject? Thus it is thought [in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*, p. 12].
The "side" (pakṣa) is the subject (dharmin), because the term for the whole is metaphorically applied to its part—Hetubindu, p. 52. [Note:
the phrase *paropacaritaḥ* is written twice; it is the genitive case.]

In that context, when the characteristic of the reason (*hetulakṣaṇa*) is to be ascertained, the subject (*dharmin*) is the object of inference (*anumeya*); elsewhere, however, at the time of the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhyapratipatti*), the aggregate (*samudāya*) is the object of inference;

but at the time of ascertaining the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the property (*dharma*) is the object of inference—*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, p. 97. Now, it may be asked: "How can it be said that [the reason] is a part of the subject? For not only would its being a part of it fail to be established, but its being a property of it (*taddharmatā*) would also not be established. True; this should not be stated in this way, for it was stated from the perspective of another [system].

If it is argued that, just as with a single part (*ekadeśa*), even a property (*dharma*) of the object is not possible there [in a partless entity], yet it is desired to be established therein; to this he replies: "No," and so forth. Indeed, in that case, that property—which is the property of that subject (*dharmin*)—is not intended to be established in a partless subject. For a real entity (*bhāva*) does not become otherwise by the power of human desire, thinking, "let its state of being a single part (*tadekadeśatā*) be otherwise."
Showing another refutation, he says: "And thus," and so forth.

In that manner—by the phrase "the property desired to be proven therein"—every object such as blue and the like would be "possessing that property" (*taddharmā*), meaning it would possess every property such as yellowness and so on; thus, for that which is partless...

If it is argued that this is not a fault because people desire to prove eternality in the case of sound, but not yellowness and so forth in the case of blue and other colors—[we reply: because there is no restraint, since there is no one to prevent it, of what? He says:
of desire; for there is no one to prevent someone who seeks to prove that the flock of crows, cuckoos, and so forth are yellow because they exist, like gold.

If it is argued that there is a sublation of the subject (*pakṣabādhaka*) for that [inference], whereas where such sublation does not exist, the property desired to be proven (*sādhayitum iṣṭas taddharmas*) [is established]; to this he replies: "In its non-sublation"—that is, when the property desired to be proven is not sublated by perception or other means of knowledge (*pratyakṣādinā*), and when its non-sublation is accepted as the condition for the property being desired to be proven, there would be doubt. The connection [of the words] is: "in its non-sublation" (*tadanirākṛtau*).

He thinks as follows: even in cases such as "sound is impermanent because of its existence, like a jar," the non-refutation [of the reason] by that [opposing proof] is not determined at the very time of the proponent's desire [to state it]; and if it is not determined, it does not constitute a valid definition. Therefore, he states the refutation regarding the absence of doubt: otherwise, since the statement of the reason would be useless through another mode of doubt that is not refuted by that [opposing proof], there would be doubt regarding the reason. This is established by the construction of the words; for instance, if the probandum were already ascertained in that subject (dharmin), then the ascertainment of its non-refutation would not eliminate the doubt. Furthermore, if that [probandum] were already ascertained prior to the presentation of the reason, what would be the use of it?
When there is certainty regarding the probandum through the reason, [it arises] from desire.

It might be thought: "The cessation of doubt regarding the probandum does not arise from the ascertainment [of it]; rather, even that ascertainment occurs there through the perception of a mark (liṅga) that is invariably concomitant with it. This is not sound, because in reality, that property (dharma) belongs to that [locus] only in this way; otherwise, there would be no perception of a mark invariably concomitant with it there, nor is such perception possible in a partless [entity]. Furthermore, it is not the case that the property to be proven is not desired [to exist there], for there is no such principle as: "A region possessing smoke would not be 'with fire' for one who does not desire fire, but becomes 'with fire' for one who desires it."

And it has not been determined that there is no such thing as a partless entity, nor will it be determined here that this very object would be the case. If it is argued: "In that regard, the property is neither sublated nor certain, but rather doubtful"; to this he replies: "If one, regarding that subject (*dharmin*), employs the designation 'subject' in a figurative sense while desiring a doubtful property, how could one suspect it to be unestablished (*asiddha*)?"

Of what? He says: "of the reason" (*hetoḥ*). One might ask: "In what case should one not entertain such a doubt? He says: "when the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is accepted as a constituent of the reason. Of what kind [of subject]? He says: "of that which possesses a doubtful property" (*sandigdhadharmiṇaḥ*), meaning that for which the property to be proven (*sādhya*), such as impermanence and so forth, is still in doubt.

This is what is meant: just as the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) is desired by means of a property (*dharma*) that is itself doubtful, so too should the subject (*pakṣa*) be accepted as the aggregate of the property and the locus (*dharmidharmin*) which is both doubtful and established. This is not correct; for if the aggregate were already established prior to the application of the reason, what would be the use of the reason? And if it is not established, the reason’s possession of that property (*taddharmatā*) is unestablished. Thus, [the definition] by means of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)...

Comparison: Even when the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is formulated as "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), if the "subject" (*pakṣa*) were understood as the whole (the aggregate) which is the object of inference, then every reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*); or, if it were established, inference would be redundant. Thus he says, "The subject is the locus of the property" (*pakṣo dharmī*). (Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 17). What kind of non-establishment? How is there non-establishment? How might one suspect it? To this he says: "Because, due to the suspicion of that non-establishment, this Kīrti would resort to a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) by means of the statement: 'The subject is the locus of the property, [whereby] the whole is metaphorically attributed to its part. (Hetubindu, p. 52).

Or, [the word] "yataḥ" is used in the sense of an objection: for who that is not insane would desire the pervasion of the reason by a property that is doubtful, rather than by the whole [collection]? Thus, [the phrase] "how is it unestablished? is written twice.

Dharmakīrti: "But surely, just as a collection [of reasons] with a doubtful property is not accepted by me, so too pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason is not accepted [with a doubtful one], but rather with one that is certain. To this he says: "If," and so forth.

If it is asked, "Has this not already been refuted by the statement 'Otherwise, the statement of the reason would be purposeless' (*anyathā hetuvacanānarthakyāt*), after having raised such a doubt? Why is it doubted again? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of demonstrating an additional refutation.

The word *yadi* at the beginning indicates the opponent's intention, while *punaḥ* indicates an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*). Of which [position] is this a figurative application? It refers to the subject (*dharmī*), not to the aggregate (*samudāya*). The phrase "by an unambiguous and certain property" (*dharmeṇa*) follows from the context; the ellipsis to be supplied is: "the reason (*hetu*) is held to be pervaded."

The refutation here is as follows: if the eternality of sound—that is, its being unproduced—is the probandum (*sādhya*), then "being produced" and so forth (the word "and so forth" including arising and the like) would be a logical reason (*hetu*); it is thought that [such a reason] would not be contradictory (*viruddha*).
This is because [the reason] is for the sake of another's perception, according to Jaimini’s Sūtra 1.1.18.
The meaning of the word "api" (also) is that [the reason] is exactly of this nature.

Of what kind is it? By what is it pervaded? To this he says: by existence (*sattva*), being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), and so forth; not by a property of that subject (*taddharmin*), that is, a property of the subject of the thesis (*pakṣadharmin*).
For "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and the like do not exist apart from "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth; thus, it is said that [the reason] is pervaded by that.

Now, if the reason were pervaded only by that which one intends to prove and not by anything else, it would not be free from doubt; for it has been stated that the statement of the reason would result in pointlessness because its purpose is for the sake of another, [in the argument]: "Sound is eternal."

It might be thought that the intention is to prove that "the repeated utterance of what is impermanent is not possible," because [the reason] is beyond doubt in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) but not in the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus it is said that it will be established for that [subject] because it is intended to be proven there. This, however, is not sound; for since that [reason] will belong to that [subject] once the whole (*samudāya*) is established, let it be stated as belonging to that very thing even before [the establishment], and not merely to the substratum (*dharmin*).
For example, someone, having observed another person cooking, asks: "Whose rice is this? Being thus questioned, he replies: "It is rice.
At that moment, it is not yet [rice], because that would entail the absurdity of the effort being fruitless;
nevertheless, such a designation does exist.

Therefore, we consider that since the designation "of this" will apply to the rice once it has been produced, it must first be designated by means of that [rice]; thus, the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the subject (*pakṣa*) to the locus (*dharmin*) is redundant,
for what is to be proven is rather the cooker of the uncooked rice.

Accepting that metaphorical usage, he states the refutation, beginning with "And not," and so forth: "And not" means indeed not; it is not improper for there to be a function within a collection. Of what? Of the word "collection"—that is, of the word "position" (*pakṣa*), which denotes an aggregate of properties (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*).

Of what kind [is that]? It is that which functions—meaning its occurrence—is by way of metaphorical application (*upacāra*) upon a single locus (*dharmī*), which is a part of the whole (*samudāya-ekabhāga*), by itself (*svayam*) or through its own nature. Furthermore, of what kind is it? He says: "Again, subsequently, by the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) 'that' (*tat*) as a part of it" (*tadaṃśena*). Here, by the word "that" (*tacchabdena*), [the subject] is referred to; because that function is untenable, "a part of it" (*tadaṃśaḥ*) refers to its property (*taddharma*), not a single portion of it (*tadekadeśaḥ*). Why? Because the term "subject" (*pakṣa*) does not denote the whole, but denotes only the locus (*dharmī*). Thus, it is well said that [the definition] would not be valid at all.

He thinks as follows: when the application of a term denoting a whole (*samudāya*) by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) to that which resides in only one part of it does not contradict its application to the whole, then the reference to that very [part] by means of that word—as in "that portion" (*tadaṃśaḥ*) or "one part of it" (*tadekadeśaḥ*)—is not contradictory.
To this he provides an example: "staying in the village," etc.
[This refers] to the village as a whole, not to every single part of it; otherwise, the statement "I, staying in a certain part of it, saw [something]" would be untenable.
By this metaphorical usage of the word "village," he states that [the term] functions with respect to a part of it.
To the question, "Where was I standing when I saw the burning? he replies: "Standing in a part of that [village]."

By the word "that" (tat) here, there is a reference to the primary village as a whole, and not to a single part of it; for such usage occurs [only] when one is situated in a portion [of the village], as in the expression "he stands in that [village]" (*tad-sthaḥ*). This is for the sake of the illustration:
just as in the case of saying, "I saw [something] while standing in a part of that village."
Concluding the point already stated, he says: "Therefore this," and so forth.

Since it is thus, for that reason, what is this which is being performed by another? He says: "The transgression of the primary meaning of words"—that is, both the primary [nature] and the meaning of the word.

To explain: the primary worldly meaning of the word *aṃśa* is "part," while the word *pakṣa* refers to the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmī*). What does its transgression—that is, its overstepping—do? To this Dharmakīrti replies: it follows the maxim of eating the *karkaṭī* fruit out of fear of bathing in the Gaṅgā.

[Objection: But surely, due to fear of that [transgression], there exists a fault such as execution or imprisonment for the carving of a *karkaṭī* fruit; it does not exist in its transgression. If you ask, "How then can it be said that he follows that principle?"—to this he replies with the words "In that very case," and so forth.
The meaning of the particle *eva* is that because there is a fault in transgressing it, there is no transgression of it.
Therefore, it remains as previously described— beginning with "that which is desired to be known" (*jijñāsita*) and so forth— and not as "the subject is the locus" (*pakṣo dharmī*) and so forth,
for fear of [falling into] the ritual bath at the Gaṅgā.

Having thus explained these two points—the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and [the reason's presence] through a portion of that [subject]—he explains the term "pervaded" (*vyāpta*) with the words beginning "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), the intended meaning here being: it is called "pervaded" because of its connection with pervasion (*vyāpti*).

And that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is based on both the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*); it belongs to the pervader insofar as that pervaded property exists in a given locus (*dharmin*). However, it does not belong to the property itself [as a separate entity], because there is no other property therein; rather, the pervasion of the pervaded is simply its existence (*bhāva*), as the term "existence" continues to apply. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*): wherever the pervading property exists in a locus, there alone is its existence, and not elsewhere.

What follows from this being so? To this he says: "In that case," meaning when that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is accepted, there is "otherwise" (i.e., in the manner of the absence of the probandum) no "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) of the reason, nor is any other form [of the reason] stated—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

By this, it is established that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) attains the status of a reason when it is pervaded by a portion of that [probandum], provided that it is characterized by reasoning as being "otherwise inexplicable" (*anyathānupapanna*). This is pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Dharma abides in dharma;
its existence is indeed real, and it is never non-existent.
Showing the fault in not accepting that [principle], he says: "If not," and so forth.
If there were no "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), what would be the probandum (*sādhya*)? Of what would the probans (*sādhana*) be the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)?

Thinking that [the opponent] might believe that even in the absence of something considered the probandum, another thing could exist, the opponent—feeling as if he were being questioned himself—says: "The cause, such as fire, [is the pervader] of the effect, such as smoke; the nature, such as 'treeness,' [is the pervader] of the entity, such as 'śiṃśapā-ness'"—thus the word "pervader" (*vyāpaka*) is understood to follow.
The word "cet" (if) indicates the opponent's intention; showing the response to that, he says: "Of the momentary," and so forth.

If the cause is held to be the nature of the effect—that is, if the nature of an entity is necessarily pervaded by its cause—then in the absence of that [cause], the [effect] must necessarily not exist; thus, the very principle of "inseparability" (*anyathānupapatti*) is established.
And since that [non-existence] occurs only in the case of the non-unique (anekānta), he shows this by the phrase "of the momentary" (*kṣaṇikasya*).
This was stated according to the opponent's own intention regarding a cause that perishes without leaving a trace immediately after the time of its arising; in reality, however, that is not a cause.

Of what kind [of cause]? Of one that does not reach the time of the effect, having already perished even before the production of the effect—how then could there be anything called "pervasion" (*vyāpti*)?
For pervasion belongs to the cause, which is the pervader; it means that wherever the effect exists, the cause must exist.
However, this [pervasion] cannot be obtained for that which has already perished.
For if it were so, how could one prevent that effect from being causeless when its [the cause's] absence occurs? The meaning is that the rest of the argument has been stated here.
The Buddhist [holds that] when the pervader is absent,
the pervaded is [absent].
Existence is momentary in the absence of a cause.
