Refuting the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: If an absolute non-difference between the entity (*bhāva*) and its essential nature (*svabhāva*), and between existence (*sattva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), is admitted, then what could be pervaded by what, since the pair of the pervaded and the pervader would be absent?
And in that case, just as there is an absence of universal and particular, this [logical relation] is contradicted in their absence.
In the case of an absolute non-difference, the pervader would reside in both that and what is other than it, or the pervaded would reside exclusively in that; thus,
[the definition] applies whether the pervaded exists or the pervaded is absent.
The pervaded (vyāpya) must necessarily reside within the pervader (vyāpaka); it can never exist in the absence of the pervader.

As for the claim that "the imagined permanence [of the universal] is pervaded by the imagined existence—which is itself a conceptual exclusion of non-existence"—that too is difficult to maintain in an absolute sense. For if there is an absence of conceptual construction (vikalpa), such a conceptualization is utterly impossible;

yet if such conceptualization does occur, then because the expressible form and its opposite are in some way contradictory, their coexistence in a single locus would mean that the *Apohavārtika* has been given a final farewell.
For this reason, it was stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* within the "Chapter on Apoha" that there is no difference in the case of absolute non-duality (*abhedaikānta*).

Regarding this, Prajñākaragupta says: "The nature of a cause is not the nature of its effect, nor is the nature of an entity non-pervasive, because both [the cause and the pervasion] would be absent due to the lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

As for the statement that the effect and so forth are causes with respect to the cause and so forth, that [is asserted] on account of the intention of the person engaged in linguistic convention; its validity [is established] by means of such convention. (Pramāṇavārttika 1)

"Because of this statement," he says in response: "By virtue of the intention of the conventional user (*vyavahartṛ*): worldly people, who are devoid of the refinement of the scriptures, have one intention, while the Naiyāyikas and others, who possess that scriptural refinement, have another. Even though for those conventional users there is an absence of cause and effect as ultimate realities—that is, an absence of the intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*) of things—their intention is that 'smoke arises only from fire' and 'the *śiṃśapā* tree exists only as a tree. In the same way, when that determination of identity (*tādātmya*) and causal origination (*tadutpatti*) is being made, having done what? Having failed to examine [the matter]."

What? Is it the reality (*tattva*)—the ultimate nature—of cause, effect, and so forth; or is reality perceived as the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaita*)? If that were perceived, since such a state would be untenable, what [would follow]? He says: that intention (*abhiprāya*) would result in another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), a means of valid cognition distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
First of all, there is no inclusion [of this cognition] within perception, because it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
Even in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), others call that which is non-conceptual "perception";
if it were included therein, its establishment would depend on perception, and thus its conventional nature (*sāṃvṛtatva*) would be untenable.

Nor is it established through inference, because [inference] consists of conceptual construction (vikalpa) which is itself a concealment (saṃvṛti) by means of the concealment of reality (tattvasaṃvara). This is due to the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*);
for instance, inference exists when there is a determination of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), and thus the establishment of those [relations] depends upon it.
It is not non-pervasive, but rather pervasive with respect to the conceptual intention regarding the effect and the essential nature.
In the case of direct perception, [it functions] by concealing the reality of conceptual construction.

Furthermore, since it has been stated that "that which does not exhibit a correspondence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is not a cause, and that which is not a cause is not an object [of cognition]," inference, being the effect of that determination, is the determiner of it; and that effect exists because of the intention toward it, and that [intention] is inference. In that case as well, the same objection applies and the same answer follows, leading to an infinite regress.
Therefore, it should be understood that it is established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)—p.
188, note 7.
If it is asked:

"Is that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) not indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it lacks the defining characteristics [of a valid cognition]? How then can it be distinct from those [two types of valid cognition]? To this he replies: "Because it is non-discrepant (*avisamvādaka*); because its establishment as such is non-deviant."

If it is argued that this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the opponent accepts that "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge" (*apisaṃvādakaṃ ca jñānaṃ pramāṇam*, *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.3) and thus maintains that [the Buddha's teaching] is a valid means of knowledge; to this he replies: if one were to accept his intention—that there is a lack of non-contradiction, i.e., a state of contradiction—then by resorting to that [intention], the acceptance of that intention would constitute the irrationality of the Buddhist.
Why? He says: because of its lack of utility for the subject at hand;
that is, because it is of no use for the determination of the matter under discussion.

For instance, whatever is non-concordant (visaṃvādin) is not useful for the intended determination even in practical activity (*vyavahāra*), just like the cognition of water in a mirage; and that intention [of yours] is non-concordant.

Whatever does not serve as a basis for a particular determination is not accepted by one seeking that determination, just as water is not accepted by one seeking fire; and this intention [of the subject] does not serve as a basis for that determination. Thus, if that intention were non-erroneous with respect to its object, it would follow that there is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the opponent; otherwise, since it would not be relied upon, the conventional usage based upon it would be destroyed—this is established regarding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Because it lacks the defining characteristics of a means of valid cognition,
it is not a separate means of valid cognition according to the Buddhist.
If it is argued that this too is not a fault for the conceptual [cognition] intended by the user of conventional discourse, because it is accepted [as such]; let this matter rest for now.
Something else is stated: even if that established rule exists, he says "tad etasmin" and so forth, demonstrating precisely this lack of pervasion (*avyāpakatva*):

if that aforementioned restriction of concomitance (*pratibandhaniyama*), consisting of identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth, were accepted as residing in that [other], how could the far side be inferred from the observation of the near side?
Of what? Of the moon and so forth. How so? To this he says: there is no causal relationship between these two—the upper and lower parts—because they exist simultaneously.
Nor is there identity [between the two], because their characteristics differ.

If one asks, "How then can there be inference from that? he says: "Enough! [Do not think] that inference would be non-concordant because of 'otherwise-unaccountability' (anyathānupapatti). To this he replies: "[Inference is] faultless and non-deviant."
The Vijñānavādin says:
"Because two co-existent things lack mutual dependence, there is no relationship of cause and effect;

why then [is this so]? and so forth, raising the opponent's objection. If it is asked, "What is the reason that the front part is established in a manner other than the absence of the back part? the answer is: "Indeed, these [parts] do not deserve such an inquiry, 'Why does this happen for you? Rather, they must be accepted by those with discerning wisdom exactly as they appear to consciousness through the cognition of their non-contradiction."
If it is argued that this would result in a mere "stretching out of the feet" (an absurdity); to this he says: "In the case of identity," and so forth.

What, then, is the reason for [stating] that the nature of a tree is the *śiṃśapā*, or that smoke is an effect of fire? For such a consequence would follow. To this, too, the same answer applies: "Entities indeed do not deserve to be subjected to questioning.

If it is then argued: "Let it be that the front part is the cause of the back part precisely because it is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*"); to this he says: "The back part," and so forth.

By postulating that the posterior part possesses an essential nature (svabhāva) of inseparable connection with the anterior part, why would one not include [this reason] within the category of essential nature (svabhāvahetu) or effect-reason (kāryahetu)?

Therefore, for one who postulates that the anterior part has an essential nature of inseparable connection with the posterior part, it is logical to understand that smoke’s capacity to indicate [fire] arises precisely from its essential nature of inseparable connection with fire; what is the use of [postulating] "origination from that" (tadutpatti)? And if that were the case, the relationship of signifier and signified (gamya-gamaka-bhāva) would exist in all respects, because the relationship of produced and producer (janya-janaka-bhāva) exists in all respects.

It would follow that there is a relationship of produced and producer between parts of entities; otherwise, for whose sake would the proponent postulate the "inseparable connection" characterized by "the impossibility of being otherwise," [if not] for the sake of the front part?

What should one do? To this he says: why should one not include both the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) within "the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*)? One should indeed include them. To explain the verse, he says: "of its near side," and so forth. The moon and other such objects are its near side; its essential nature consists in its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the far side—that is, its non-deviating form. It is logical that not only for this [moon], but also for smoke, there is the capacity to indicate fire because of its essential nature of being inseparably connected with fire. Thus, it is proper to understand its status as an indicator of that fire.
What follows from this? He says: "Nothing"—the connection is that nothing [is established] by the production of smoke from that fire.

Now, if it is argued that smoke is an indicator (*gamaka*) of that [fire] precisely because of its production from it, he says in response: "And if that production is accepted as the sole basis for being an indicator, then there would be a relationship of indicated (*gamya*) and indicator (*gamaka*) between fire and smoke in every way, by every possible manner"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Just as fire is cognized through a general mode such as its capacity for burning or cooking, so too could it be cognized through a specific, uncommon [mode] that is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes and is restricted by place, time, and form. Thus, inference would have the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object just like perception; there would be no distinction [between them]. If it is argued that the distinction lies in the lack of clarity (*avaishadya*), this too is untenable; for if the particular were the object, that lack of clarity would be impossible, and the opponent does not admit such a thing. If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be two types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on the two types of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), given the overlap of objects?"—let this be another fault of his position.
For the Buddhist, [the existence of] fire is established through direct perception.

Since two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operate upon a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇaviśeṣa*), that which was stated—namely, "the determination of a specific smoke is admitted to be inseparable from that [fire]; fire is in every way inferable, because its cognition is observed when one discerns smoke produced by saffron, sandalwood, or agalloch"—is refuted by this. For even there, there is an inference of general properties such as saffron and so forth; otherwise, since inference would have the ultimate particular (*antyaviśeṣa*) as its object, how could there be doubt regarding it? Furthermore, the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the inference of a particular must be considered;
this will be examined immediately hereafter.

Likewise, since smoke is an indicator in every respect, it might be so by way of a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*)—such as the modification of the throat and eyes—but it might also be so by way of a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth. Thus, even if there is doubt regarding the smoke itself, let there be the cognition of fire from the ascertainment of its existence and other such general properties. Therefore, he considers the proclamation of "unestablished due to doubt" and so on to be worthless, because one observes the cognition of fire from sandalwood, agallochum, and the like, despite their specific differences.

It might be thought: "Only the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of fire are the producers, and therefore it is cognized by those alone; whereas only the specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) of smoke are the produced, and therefore it is the cognizer by those alone. To this, he says: "In every way," meaning in all possible manners, because the relationship of producer and produced is not accepted [in that manner], he states the fault [of such a view] with the words beginning "of entities" (*bhāvānām*).

The use of the plural number is for the sake of encompassing all [aspects] in every way; otherwise, there would follow a relationship of producer and produced only in part or by way of a single component—just as fire is a producer by means of general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) and not by specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*), while smoke is produced by means of specific properties and not by general properties—and thus it would apply to all entities. In that case, even the relationship of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) would be based on that [partiality] and would exist only in cognition; therefore, this is not tenable, as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.42): "Of a single nature of an object... and so forth.
Since perception itself exists by means of specific properties alone, what other unperceived part could there be that would need to be examined by other means of valid cognition?
This is the remainder [of the argument]:

if it is held that the relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*) and the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) are accepted in every respect, and thus there is a determination of a specific quality produced by that [cause]; to this he replies: "What is this specific quality produced by that (*tajjanyaviśeṣa*), which is intended as something other [than the cause]? etc.
"Because it cannot be otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) applies even to another [reason] that is intended [as valid].

By stating that only the pervaded (vyāpya) possesses the capacity to indicate [the probandum], despite there being no difference in their identity (tādātmya), he establishes that [the reason] has only one defining characteristic, since it does not depend on [factors such as] being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva).

That which has this intermediate distinction residing in the smoke—namely, being "produced" (janya)—is described as such; and that specific distinction residing in the fire is the [distinction] belonging to the fuel.
Who? The connection is that nothing whatsoever is intended by the Buddhist himself as being cognizable.
Of what nature is it? To this he says: "para" means existing; "apara" means that from which there is no other distinction, i.e., the unique (asādhāraṇa).

Is it not intended at all? To this he says: "except otherwise it would be impossible" (*anyathānupapatteḥ*). Without "otherwise being impossible," it is indeed intended, because its being cognizable is accepted without a formal example (*nidarśana*).

Regarding "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), there is this further explanation: that which is produced by that fire is "produced by it" (*tajjanya*); and that very thing, characterized by the property of being smoke (*dhūmatva*)—namely, existence (*sattva*) and so forth—is the "particularity residing in smoke" (*dhūmagato viśeṣaḥ*). What other distinct particularity is intended by the Buddhist himself? None other than "inexplicability otherwise," for that same [principle] is intended even in the case of what is accepted.

To explain: although existence (*sattva*) and other properties are no different from "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*) in being effects of fire when smoke is the locus (*dharmin*), only "smokiness" is the indicator (*gamaka*) because of the impossibility of its otherwise [existing], and not the other. Thus, the theory of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*) is refuted.
Now, while refuting identity (*tādātmya*) as the basis for existence and so forth, he says: "Even though there is no difference in identity..."

By stating that "between the pervaded and the pervader," it is the pervaded alone—such as existence (*sattva*)—and not the pervader—such as impermanence (*anityatva*)—that possesses the capacity to prove (*gamakatva*), the opponent [the Buddhist] establishes that there is only one defining characteristic [of a valid reason]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "dependence on being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), the Buddhist includes the apprehension of the pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*).
If it is objected that a reason (*hetu*) is not valid in the absence of either a similar (*sādharmya*) or a dissimilar (*vaidharmya*) instance, the author replies here: "That," and so forth.

Since external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is not established whether [the instance] is proven or unproven, the proof [must consist] of universal pervasion (*sakalavyāpti*), because [otherwise] one cannot avoid both faults. 5.

The establishment (*siddhi*) of that internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) consists in its cognition or its acquisition of its own nature; its non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is the opposite of these two. When those two exist, external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*)—which is pervasion elsewhere than the subject (*pakṣa*)—is rendered ineffective due to the absence of proof (*asādhanāt*). Relying upon that [external pervasion], nothing becomes a proof.

Alternatively, it is because of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyabhāvāt*) in that [external pervasion], or because of its lack of being a proof (*asādhanatvāt*); the meaning is that it is not a proof.

If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) consists in universal pervasion (*sakalavyāpti*), to this he replies with the words "universal," and so forth. Universal pervasion is the pervasion [of the reason] both in the subject (*pakṣa*) and elsewhere; since that [pervasion] does not escape the two aforementioned faults, he establishes that very point. For instance: universal pervasion does not exist without internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*). If that [internal pervasion] is established from some source, what is the use of another [external pervasion]? If it is not [established], then what is universal pervasion? Likewise, without external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*), that [universal pervasion] is also not tenable, because it would be merely nominal.
The meaning is that external pervasion (bahirvyāpti) would be established because it is unestablished (asiddhatvāt).

It is true that there is universal pervasion (*sakalavyāpti*); for instance, from seeing the near side of the moon and so forth, the far side is inferred. However, this is not due to the impossibility of another explanation (*anyathānupapatti*), but rather because they depend upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatayā*). Refuting this, he says: "If there were identity between the delusion of the mind and self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), [it would be] by means of distinct [characteristics]," and so forth.
Things that are perishable must be perceived through their own inherent natures as imperishable. Delusion is thus defined: it is the apprehension of something as what it is not.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyāsa*), and so forth are included. Self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is direct perception through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedanādhyakṣa*), and this too is an elliptical indication; thus, [the point is that] if there were identity (*tādātmya*) between the mind (*citta*)—which includes non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpakapratyakṣa*) and so on—and its erroneous self-awareness, then they would have to be perceived as distinct (*vilakṣaṇa*), dissimilar (*visadṛśa*), and as objects of the senses (*indriyagocara*).

To the question "Of what [things] by means of what?", he says: "Of perishable things," that is, of those which are fragile and subject to destruction at every moment, "[by means of] imperishable ones," that is, by means of those that remain stable.
Of what kind? "By means of natures," that is, by means of essential forms.
Is this by means of all [natures]? No; he says: "By their own," that is, by their respective natures, and not by those belonging to another cognition.
He explains the verse with the words beginning "error" (*bhrānti*), and this has already been explained in the first section.

Although the term "error" (*bhrānti*) alone would have sufficed to express "misapprehension" (*viparyāsa*), both terms are nevertheless employed for the purpose of demonstrating the two types of delusion: that which pertains to external objects and that which pertains to internal [consciousness].

If this is so, what is gained? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth; that is, by means of both the perishable and the imperishable nature of things, the realization of reality according to how it is perceived is not transgressed.

The identity of subtle things that are distinct is perceived through their own natures— which are gross and non-distinct, visible or even invisible— as well as through properties that cannot otherwise be explained, just as it is understood in the world. (7–8)
A trunk (skandha) as a single entity, consisting of its lower, upper, far, and middle parts, can somehow be inferred by someone from something else, just like color, taste, and so forth.

Otherwise, how could one who accepts that identity with a contrary nature is established through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*)—while imagining an inference that has an exclusively distinct object, which contradicts experience, is non-conceptual, and is without an object—establish the proof of reality? What could be more illogical than this, since it transgresses the very principle of "otherwise-unaccountability"?

Furthermore, another [proponent] posits a restriction of concomitance (*pratibandhaniyama*) between co-existent factors—such as the posterior part of color (*rūpa*) and so forth—with the anterior part of taste (*rasa*) and so forth; this contradicts his own position. For, if color is established through the power of its material cause (*upādānaśakti*), which is inferred from the experienced taste, it would transcend both perception and its own logical mark (*liṅga*) and number. Moreover, having accepted that the material cause of that [color] possesses a cooperative nature (*sahakāritva*) in the production of color and so forth from the experienced taste, he then perceives the effect, namely color and the rest.

Without the activation of the potency of its own material cause (*svopādāna*), there is no production of taste; that [potency] alone is the cause of color and so forth. Therefore, this is the sequence of cognition: one infers past [colors] from a single present [taste], but not future ones, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Why is this? Because there is no such conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

Thus, the inference of an effect from a cause, and the inference of color and so forth from a simultaneously existing taste through an indirect succession (*pāramparya*), does not merely set aside established cognition; rather, it establishes the necessity of the invariable concomitance (*pratibandhaniyama*) of what is being inferred.
According to the manner of observation— that is, without deviating from what is observed— there is indeed a realization of reality through reflection; it is neither transgressed nor rejected.
What is its nature? To this he says: the word "perceiving" (*pratī*) should be understood here as "identical with" (*tādātmya-mati*).
Of what things? To this he says: "of the subtle ones.
Of what kind? "Diverse," meaning mutually distinct.

By what [means]? To this he says: by "gross" ones. Of what nature? "Indivisible," meaning common to many constituent parts. Furthermore, of what nature? "Well-examined. By what kind of examiners? To this he says: "by those for whom [the probans] is otherwise inexplicable" (*anyathānupapanna*).
"By their own," meaning by those belonging to themselves; not only by those [visible ones], but also by the visual organs— this being an elliptical expression for the sense organs—
and by the non-visual [organs] as well— this too is an elliptical expression.
By what [means]? By those that are "capable of being perceived by touch" (*spraṣṭavyaiḥ*). The word "also" (*api*) is to be supplied here after the term "visual" (*cākṣuṣāṇām*);
and by the phrase "as it is understood in the world," he demonstrates that there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) established by common experience.
If it is asked, "What is the utility of this in the present context? he says here: "The trunk [is perceived] by its front part," and so forth.

The aggregate (*skandha*), such as the moon and so forth, is a whole (*avayavin*). Of what nature is it? It is a *dvandva* compound of "front" (*arvāk*) and so on; furthermore, it is a *karmadhāraya* with the word "part" (*bhāga*). That which has these as its constituents is "that-constituted" (*tadātmaka*); and that which is singular is "one-constituted" (*eka*). Just as it is perceived in the world, in that aggregate, some part such as the middle would have to be inferred by someone through some front part.
By whom? By the wise investigators.
He provides an illustration: "like color from taste.

Just as, due to some kind of identity (*tādātmya*), color and so forth are inferable from taste, yet it is not the case that there a certain part is inferred from a certain part on the basis of dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*); such is the meaning of the illustration.

Without commenting on the three verses beginning with "In the *mātuliṅga* there is color [etc. from taste," which concern the objects of all the sense faculties and are easy to understand, [the author], desiring to establish the illustration, says "the adversary" (*pratyanīka*), etc., and so forth.

The two natures that are antagonistic and mutually contradictory—namely, conceptualization and non-conceptualization, or erroneous perception and direct perception, or contrary perception and doubtful perception—their identity (*tādātmya*), their oneness, is established, determined by valid cognition, and logically tenable in certain cases such as consciousness. Accepting this, by what means? To this he says: "Otherwise," and so forth;
that is, by the impossibility of those two natures existing in any other way, namely, in the absence of such identity.

For instance: if there were an absolute distinction between the nature of the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and the nature of the conceptual (*vikalpa*), how could there be the cognition of that [non-conceptual state], from which its conceptualization would arise? For if one were to conceptualize what is not known, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And thus, since "conceptualization is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression" (Nyāyabindu 1.5), even this conceptualization cannot be obtained; far removed, therefore, is any talk of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

If you say [it is known] by itself (*svataḥ*), then the consequence remains that the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*); how then [is this] consistent with the principle stated in *Nyāyabindu* 1.10, "of all minds and mental factors," and so forth? Otherwise, even in that case, the postulation of another nature distinct from that [nature] would incur the aforementioned fault and lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if [you argue that] there is a perception of something else by means of a nature other than the nature of non-conceptuality—that is, a formless perception (*nirākāra-darśana*)—and that there is a perception of that [object] despite its being non-existent, then there would be an identity (*tādātmya*) between the self and the other, which are mutually exclusive. In this case too, within the extreme of difference (*bhedaikānta*), the original point is not maintained; thus, there is a circularity (*cakraka*).
By this, the remainder should also be considered;
therefore, their identity must be investigated.
To establish [the object] as being dependent upon that—what could be more unreasonable than this? This very thing is what is unreasonable.
"What kind of thing is it? Having become what, from where, and what does it establish? To this he says: "Having conceptualized the non-conceptual (avikalpa), what [is there to be established]?
He says: "In an absolute state," and so forth.
Of what nature is it? It is contrary to experience (pratītiviruddha).

For it is not observed that a form terminating in each individual atom has ascended to the level of direct perception, because that would entail the non-existence of the perceptible (dṛśyānupalabdhi), due to the absence of two objects associated within a single cognition. If it is asked, "How then can there be a perception of 'gross,' 'long,' and so forth, even through delusion, from which the determination of mountains and such things arises?"—let this other fault remain; to say "it is refuted" here is meaningless.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "the self-awareness of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*)—namely, the awareness of the very nature of conceptual construction—is *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition); this would be the well-stated [definition] in the *Nyāyabindu*."
The word "ma" (not) here is meaningless, because conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*), which are by nature opposites, [cannot coexist].

Furthermore, if a single visual perception were to have multiple atoms as its object and possess a mental aspect (*sākāra*), what would be the consequence? To this, it has been stated: "[it would be] opposed," and so forth.
And having postulated that inference is without an object,
the phrase "contrary to experience" (pratītiviruddha) follows here as well.

In some cases, when one accepts the identity of two things of contrary natures as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the identity of eternality and non-eternality, or of being produced and existence, and so forth— these being of contrary natures— is established in the case of sound, one considers that [inference] to be contrary to experience and without an object.

Regarding the question, "How can it be improper to claim that the establishment of reality [comes] from non-conceptual perception and from inference—which is its opposite and lacks a [real] object?"—the author says: "Otherwise," and so forth.

The meaning is this: since the Buddhist accepts identity between two things of opposing natures on the grounds of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise), for him to then establish the establishment of reality based on that very [identity] is a contradiction; therefore, the idea that there is no identity between those two in any case is indeed improper.

The intended meaning here is precisely this: since there is an absence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) when flavors and other momentary atoms are isolated, how could there be an inference even if it were devoid of an object, such that a determination of reality (*tattvavyavasthā*) would occur? If that [inference] exists, then the identity (*tādātmya*) of two things whose natures are respectively opposed—conceptual and non-conceptual—is established in some cases; since that [identity] also exists for flavors and the like, there is no lack of proof for the example, namely, their identity within a single substance.

However, as for one who thinks that from the near portion of a conjoined object, color and other qualities situated in the far portion are inferred through inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*), and not through identity (*tādātmya*) or any other relation—even he is refuted by this [argument]. For it could be said that the Vaiśeṣika and others, while accepting identity or some other relation between two things of opposing natures—such as capacity and incapacity, or any other pair—on the grounds of its being otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*), nevertheless postulate a conceptual construction (*parikalpya*) that contradicts experience: namely, that substance, quality, and action possess absolutely distinct natures, are momentary, subject to destruction, partless, and restricted to a single substrate. Since inference is preceded by such [conceptual] constructs, it is rendered devoid of a real object (*nirviṣaya*).

"The rest is as before," says the Vaiśeṣika. Now, one might argue: "Even if there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the near and far parts, or between color and so forth and taste and so forth, nevertheless, the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) does not arise from that identity being otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*); rather, it arises through the inference of a previously qualified cause, because identity itself exists precisely through that. To this, he replies: "Different from that," and so forth.

Therefore, because identity cannot otherwise be accounted for (*tādātmyānyathānupapatti*), no other [factor]—neither by the Buddhist himself, nor by the world, nor by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—has been devised or constructed.
By this, he shows that the [Buddhist] has independence regarding the matter at hand.
He asks: "Who [is there]? and answers: "The restriction of the necessary connection (*pratibandhaniyama*)."
The word "and" (ca) implies that it is not only perception and so forth [that are excluded] from the context of the near and far parts, or of color-form and taste;

or alternatively, it should be explained as follows: "other than" (aparaḥ) means different from that which is established through the constraints of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), namely, that characterized by dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*).
Why is that [dependence] established? He says: because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring co-existent things.
Of what things? He says: "of the posterior parts of form and so forth.
By what means? To this he says: "by the anterior parts of taste and so forth.
Of what nature is that [perception]? To this he says: "it destroys its own doctrine."
By the word "sva" (one's own), the reference is to the Buddhist; as to why he is the destroyer of his own doctrine, he says: "by means of the employed flavor," and so forth.

The capacity or efficacy of the substrate—which, through the transformation of the consumed and tasted flavor, acts as the cause for the transformation of the flavor and its co-existent color-form—is the "substrate-capacity" (*upādāna-śakti*) of the flavor with respect to the production of flavor, and the "co-operative capacity" (*sahakāri-śakti*) with respect to the production of color-form; likewise, the capacity of the color-form is the "substrate-capacity" for the production of color-form and the "co-operative capacity" for other [qualities]. Therefore, when the establishment or inference of color-form is being performed, the Buddhist would be overstepping common experience and worldly consensus.

Indeed, there is no common worldly understanding of a successive sequence such that one first infers a specific causal complex from the tasted flavor, and from that [complex] one infers the color; for in that case, the inference of color is understood directly from the tasted flavor itself.

Nevertheless, if one were to postulate such a process, the refutation—beginning with the words "for it is possible to understand the essential nature as the reason" (*svabhāvahetu*)—will be set forth.

If it is asked, "But if this transgresses common experience, how does it contradict his own position?"—the answer is that the refutation regarding this has already been stated and will be further examined.

When the consumed taste and its coexistent color— which serve as the transformative cause— themselves undergo transformation by way of becoming the nature of a subsequent taste and the nature of a subsequent color, [this occurs] upon the production of that subsequent taste.

Furthermore, regarding that which is called "reflection" (*manana*) in the world as an inference based on the world, and that which was proclaimed by Dharmakīrti—what of it? For it would transcend the scope of cognition. To show another defect in establishing that [position], he says: "It would transcend its own gender and number, as well as the domain of effect, essential nature, and non-perception," [stated] by Dharmakīrti.

Thus, by accepting the mark [of inference] as the cause, he explains the verse beginning with "from the consumed taste" (*rasād upayuktāt*) and so forth: from what kind of taste? From one that has been consumed; what did the Buddhist or the world perceive? To this he says: "the state of being a cooperative cause" (*sahakāritvam*).
Where? He says: in the production of color and so forth.

Of what nature is it? He says: it has the nature of its material cause (*upādāna*). That is, it has the nature of the material cause of that [substance] whose rasa has been consumed. Furthermore, subsequently, there is its effect; that is, the effect of that [material cause] which possesses that nature as a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) therein.
He says that very thing: what does that [object], such as form and so forth, do? He says: "it cognizes. From where [does this arise]? He says: "by its power," and so forth.

The activity of power (*śakti*) is its operation toward the effect; without it, there is no production of rasa, nor the attainment of the essence of the rasa that has been employed. To the question, "Whose [attainment] would it be without it?", he says: "Of its own material cause" (*svopādānasya*), that is, of the material cause of the employed rasa. But what follows from its activity and the production of that [rasa]? He says: "That very thing"—namely, the activity of that power—is the cause of form and so forth; for this reason, there is the cognition (*gati*) or apprehension of those [causes] belonging to one and the same past time, but not of those yet to come.
Why? Because of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*). The word "iti" marks the end of the opponent's position; therein he states the refutation: "What is this? and so forth.

Since the flavor previously experienced [leads to] the cognition of the flavor that was the cause of its production—which acts as a concomitant cause for the color—and subsequently the cognition of the color follows, what sort of sequence of cognition is this being asserted by the opponent? The meaning is that it is contemptible.

Why? He says: "Because there is no such conventional usage," or rather, because of the understanding that the movement [of time] belongs to past and present times alone, and not to future ones; thus, what is this sequence (*krama*), this order (*paripāṭi*), this non-transgression of logic? To this he says: "In the same way," and so forth.

In the same way, it should be understood that for the Buddhist (*saugata*), there is no cognition of past things belonging to a single time [in relation to others], nor of future things, because of the absence of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) in that very manner— as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.12— and because conventional usage occurs otherwise;

for he himself accepts that, by means of the taste already experienced and the taste inferred therefrom, there is a non-erroneous cognition of future form (*rūpa*) and so forth in relation to that [present experience].
He states another refutation: "And thus, by that very method imagined by the opponent, the inference of the effect from the cause— 'of rasa,
it is theirs'— is here meaningless."
Without the activity of power (śakti), there is no essence (rasa); that very [power] is the cause of other things.
Thus, the cognition of past and future times arises from the mark of their effects.
...the movement [of inference] pertains to things of a single past time, not to future things, because of the possibility of deviation— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.12.
The first rasa of the Pravāha-svavṛtti,

The meaning is as follows: although the inference of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) from the taste currently being tasted—which involves the prior taste and prior form contained within a single causal complex—is technically an inference of the cause from the effect, it is nonetheless an inference of the effect from the cause; for the prior form, having produced its own subsequent form of a similar kind, enters into the causal complex that produces the subsequent taste. Thus, from the prior form within a single complex, there is an inference of the subsequent form, which is indeed an inference of the effect from the cause.

As for one who thinks, "The cause is yet to be," and according to this view maintains that there is inference of the cause from the effect, but not inference of the effect from the cause—he contradicts his own statement regarding the [inference of] fame (*kīrti*). For him too, the apprehension of a preceding rasa by means of a consumed rasa would constitute an inference of the effect from the cause;
if this were not admitted, then statements such as "that which depends on a single causal complex" (*ekasāmagryadhīna*) in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.18) and so forth would be meaningless.

Prajñākara has explained that if there were a state of mutual cause and effect, there would be a mutual dependence; thus, by this [argument], one would overstep both the cognition and the gender and number of its own logical mark (*liṅga*).
Prajñākara [states that] for Dharmakīrti,
there is the cognition of form and so forth— which depend on a single causal complex— from taste.
By means of inferring the nature of the cause, just as [one infers] the transformation of fuel by means of smoke— *Pramāṇavārttika*,
[now], showing the fault of the acquisition of what was not previously done, he says: "And those that coexist with the cause," and so forth.

"How can there be an inference of form and so forth at the same time as the taste, given that [the taste] has the nature of coexisting with the form and so forth that are being inferred? To this he says: "By way of succession," in the manner previously described.
What does that do? He says: "It not only obstructs, but also refutes the established consensus of cognition."

By this, the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) is shown; however, how does it contradict the rule of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*)? Because it is described that even in the absence of identity and so forth between the taste and the form being inferred, the former is an indicator (*gamaka*) due to another type of necessary connection.
By this, the acceptance of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyupagama*) is stated.

It might be thought that because of their identity in having a single object, it is not intended that, from an ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), the former is the cause of the latter, nor is the latter the mark (*liṅga*) of the former—such that there would be this fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth; rather, it is merely inferred by a conventional practitioner who follows that doctrine, and that very [inference] is being restated here.

Regarding this, another says: "In that case, why was it rejected when one actually perceives form from taste? If you say it is because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them, then what is the connection between the preceding and the succeeding [moments]? If you say it is 'causality' (*tadutpatti*), then since this is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is it said to be accepted only by those engaged in worldly practice (*vyavahārin*)? For that which is established by *pramāṇa* ought to be accepted by both parties; otherwise, if you argue that it is accepted by the practitioner because it is validated by something else (*parataḥ prāmāṇikatva*), then for that very reason, let there be some other necessary connection."
And this logic is not appropriate for those who follow reason, simply because it is established by the acceptance of something that lacks valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*).
If it is argued, "Let that be so," [the author] replies: "And of those that coexist," and so forth.

It is only from a taste that coexists with it that there is an inference of color and so on at the same time; it does not merely refute the indirect pleasure accepted by the Buddhists, but rather, the word "refutes" carries over to mean that it also refutes the rule of invariable concomitance (*pratibandhaniyama*).

Since another type of necessary connection (pratibandha) is established between two co-existent things, as in the case of blue and its cognition, then their causal relation (tadutpatti) should be understood [as the basis for that connection]— p. 263, note 11.

Thus, when the example has been cleared up, the opponent says: "As for what was stated—that there must be identity (*tādātmya*) between error and perception—that is not sound; for error, which consists in the manifestation of variegated forms, is distinct from perception, which is of the nature of self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*), due to the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). To this, he replies: "If each its own part... and so forth. The word *svam* (its own) is written twice [in the verse].
If consciousness (*saṃvitti*) were [divided] into its own parts, why would the external object of cognition (*bahirvedya*) not be likewise?
They would differ because of the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), since the cognitions of a person [differ] in this way.

If it is argued that for a single person, there is a difference in the appearance of cognitions such as form (*rūpa*) due to the difference in the causal complexes of the eye and so forth—just as in the case of consciousness (*vijñāna*)—then even if one imagines that to be an error, the objection remains the same, because one does not transcend the two forms [of subject and object]. [The self] does not take itself as its own object by dividing itself into parts in the form of existence, sentience, and so forth, but rather in the form of a distinction from the aspect of error; for if it were so, it would follow that error is non-existent, since cognition (*saṃvitti*) would be making itself its own object. If "cognition" (*vitti*) means "intellect" (*buddhi*), [the same fault applies].
Regarding that, the refutation is as follows: "Why is there no cognition of external objects such as jars in their fragmented parts?"—this is the construction of the words;
for [the opponent] considers that [cognition] occurs in that very way because it is perceived so.
To the question, "How could that cognition of them be in fragmented parts? he says: "The causal complex," and so forth.

Since they would be divided—that is, distinct from one another—by virtue of being perceived as discrete fragments? To this he says: "The cognitions of the person (*pudgala-saṃvidaḥ*)," meaning the cognitions of jars and so forth consisting of form, taste, smell, and touch;
"from what [do they arise]? To this he says: "From the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī-bhedāt*)," that is, from the difference in the collection of causes such as the eye and so forth.
The meaning is that [the cognition] has that single [object] as its domain;

since the first half of the verse is easy to understand, the author does not comment upon it, but explains the second half: "Of a single *pudgala*—such as a jar consisting of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth—which possesses a nature common to its own qualities (*guṇas*) and modes (*paryāyas*), and which is not of the nature of parts and a whole as conceived by others to be absolutely distinct from color-form and so on—there is only a difference in the appearance of the cognition of color-form and the like, but no difference in its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Why is this? He says: "By the eye, etc. and so forth.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Of consciousness alone," and so forth.

The Buddhist conceptualization is that form and the rest are indeed absolutely distinct ultimate realities (*paramārtha*); the Vaiśeṣikas (*yauga*) conceptualize that the part and the whole are absolutely distinct.

If it is asked: "But since the verse was composed based on the premise that cognition is distinct from the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*), how can this [present statement] be said?"—it is not so; for this is stated with the intention of showing that there is no contradiction in the possibility of an external form, just as there is no contradiction in the possibility of something being both visible and invisible within a single entity.

If it is thought: "There is no difference between cognition and the forms of the apprehended object and so forth, nor [is there a difference] from the perspective of ultimate reality; rather, that [cognition] consists of those very forms, because that which possesses those forms is erroneous and thus cannot be defined as either identical to or different from them.
As it has been said:
"This conceptual construction, in accordance with the object, perceives a distinction within the thing itself."
This has been cited— *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, second chapter, page 14;
*Prakaraṇavārttika*, 2.355,
etc.— just as in the case of [the perception of] shards of clay and so forth.
The ellipsis is that they appear in one way even though they are devoid of that form;
as in *Pravāha* 2.354, "even though undivided," and so forth.
Although the nature of cognition is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinctions of the grasped object, the grasping subject, and the act of awareness to those whose vision is distorted;
regarding this, he says: "That illusion," and so forth.

When the conceptualization of error is applied to that cognition—which possesses the distinction of appearing as the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and so forth—it does not transcend either of two modes, because, in relation to its own nature and the nature of another, it does not bypass the mode of non-error and the other mode [of error]. Thus, the objection remains: "How can one thing have a manifold nature?
[The opponent argues: "Its own nature has the mode of non-error, while the nature of another has the mode of error;
or else, like the nature of another, even its own nature is held to be erroneous. To this, he says: "Just as for itself," and so forth.
If it were not for the self-cognition of the intellect according to its own nature,
then even an inferential cognition would be established as an error due to the delusion regarding its own form.

Since the self-nature of perception and inference would otherwise be subject to delusion, and since even perception cannot be established as cognizing its own object without the possibility of uncertainty, the reality [of the distinction between them] is well-established!
If there is no [self-awareness] of cognition, what would be the consequence? He says: self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) is the knowledge of its own nature.

Is this in every respect? No; he says: the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) according to their respective natures is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (Nyāyabindu 1)

The nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), for it is stated [in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* 1.210]: "This mind is luminous by its very nature. It exists otherwise, however, without deviating from that [nature].

Why? He says: "Due to the delusion regarding its own form. The "own form" (*svākāra*) of the cognition is its self-nature (*svātmīya*), which is its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*); [as stated in the *Prakaraṇavārttika* 2.327: "it manifests by itself.

Because of the delusion (*vibhrama*) regarding that [form] therein, what follows? He says: "The cognition of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be established as being of the nature of an error (*bhrānti*)."
By what means of valid cognition? By none whatsoever, because it is not established by perception itself, which is inherently erroneous, just as the external object [is not].
If it is argued that it is established by inference; to this he says: "erroneous," etc.
The word "also" (*api*) has a displaced position; even inferential cognition is erroneous.
There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of it;
due to the absence of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, it shines by itself— *Prakaraṇavārttika*.
Showing the meaning of the verse, he says: "Direct perception," and so forth. [The opponent argues:
"All well-established reality is entirely erroneous; this statement is merely a mockery.
If it is argued that self-cognizing direct perception alone is non-erroneous," to this he replies: "Without the doctrine of manifoldness (anekānta)," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: Is that self-cognizing perception—"I know blue"—of the nature of the cognition of both the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, or is it something else? In the first case, since self-cognition of its own object is untenable without non-absolutism (anekānta), not only for inference but even for perception, the principle that "the object is itself" remains well-established.

As for the second case, what would be the status of pleasure, blue, and so forth? If you say they are erroneous, [we reply] no, because nothing else contrary to them is observed, and thus [the latter] does not exist.

The same objection applies even regarding perception; therefore, one might think that the very same point [remains] because the true nature of things is well-established through the erroneous nature of both perception and inference—[namely, that] although an object does not manifest itself in its own form due to being devoid of the discrimination of error, it nevertheless manifests itself through the grace of consciousness, such that for the other [the cognizer], there is an absence of error. To this, he says: "Clearly manifested," etc.—a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) pervades both its own manifestation and its concealed nature.

If a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) pervades both the cause and the effect, then the subject-object forms of cognition are merely errors, because that [particular] itself is devoid of duality. If those two are errors, what would be non-erroneous such that it could be direct perception? For they are of the nature of that [particular], since no absolute [entity] is perceived apart from them.

If, despite some manner of perception occurring, there is no perception of its distinction [from other things], then what obstacle is there to the successive causal and logical pervasion of the two natures—the manifest and the other—of that very mental *svalakṣaṇa* which is perceived only conventionally (*saṃvṛti*)?

Some hold that the "manifest" (*vyakta*) is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), consisting of the nature of consciousness (*bodha-svabhāva*), while the "concealed" (*saṃvṛta*) is its opposite, namely the distinction between the forms of the object and the subject (*vedya-vedaka-ākāra-viveka*). Others maintain that this has various meanings, such as "if it perceives itself in parts," and so forth.

Therefore, just as cognition manifests in the form of true volition and so forth, it also manifests in the form of the discernment of error; however, the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*) arising at a subsequent time merely imagines a veil of non-existent objects such as the grasped (*grāhya*) and so on, and thereby conceals that discernment, but not its other nature.
As it has been said by someone:
"Though the nature of cognition is undivided, those whose vision is perverted [perceive it otherwise]."
"It appears as if possessing the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.354).
Regarding the statement that "it is determined by conceptual construction," he says: "It is clearly manifest," and so forth.

The manifest (*vyakta*) is unobscured (*asaṃvṛta*), having consciousness and so forth as its intrinsic nature; if that were obscured, there would be a cessation of intellectual discourse, just as in the case of momentary isolation (*kṣaṇaviveka*).
Thus, the obscured (*saṃvṛta*) is shown [as distinct]. In the absence of that [obscuration], because there would be no delusion (*vibhrama*), scripture would be purposeless.

Furthermore, by the statement, "If the single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the object of cognition, pervades both the manifest and the obscured selves and consists of them," he demonstrates the opponent’s own admission.
In this context, it should be understood as follows:
a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) pervades both the nature of the cause and the nature of the effect.
Thus, since succession and non-identity are established, the negation of the causal relationship for a single entity destroys the Buddhist doctrine.

Since a stainless consciousness that is free from the aspects of the apprehended and so forth is not possible, [the author], demonstrating this through [the arguments] beginning with "not by means of awakening" (*na buddhatyādinā*), composed this verse while provisionally accepting that [consciousness]. Thus, explaining the verse with the words "in some way" (*kathañcit*) and "distinct from the manifest" (*vyaktetara*), he says: "Not of the intellect," and so forth.

The meaning of the particle *eva* is that the aspects of the apprehended and the apprehender do not belong to the intellect; they are merely constructed by the error of mental conceptualization and are not real.

Why? To this he says: because the Buddhist's own absolute position—that all cognition is undifferentiated—would be abandoned; for [if that were so], those two [the apprehended and the apprehender] would exist as real entities within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Otherwise, how could his well-stated verse be possible: "Even though the nature of consciousness is undifferentiated, it is perceived by conceptual construction as if it possessed the distinction between the apprehended, the apprehender, and self-awareness" (PV 2.354)? For such a distinction exists only within conceptual construction, not in that absolute [undifferentiated] state.

Nor is it the case that even he [the conceptual construction] exists without that [object]; this too is a mere report. For if one were to imagine it to be so even there, it would lead to an infinite regress.

If one considers, "Conceptual construction is the reality of the object, and nothing else—what is the basis for this distinction?"—he states another refutation regarding that very point: If those two cognitions, having the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender, are erroneous, being superimposed by conceptual construction upon a partless cognition, then what is non-erroneous? There is nothing devoid of those forms which could be non-erroneous perception.

The intended meaning here is this: if the undifferentiated nature of cognition were ever established, then those two [distinctions] could be superimposed upon it by conceptual construction; otherwise, it is not so.

For if the mother-of-pearl is not established, the superimposition of silver upon it cannot be established. If those two were established in the same way that "silverness" is established in silver—or if they were established in the conceptual construction itself—it would be so;
but such is not the case.
The forms of the apprehended and the apprehender [are present] in the non-dual cognition as the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender.

[Objection: "But surely that non-differentiated nature [of consciousness] always appears [to you], and those two [aspects] are mounted upon conceptual construction (vikalpa). To this, he says: "How indeed can those two—the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender—be the very self, the essential natures, of that which is of the nature of cognition? He explains: because of the non-perception of that which has as its ultimate property (anta-dharma) pure consciousness alone, which is absolutely devoid of the apprehended and so forth, being distinct from them—that is, distinct from those forms. Having granted the perception of that [consciousness], he states the refutation with the words beginning "in some way" (kathañcit), etc.

When there is perception in the form of sound and so forth—and not in the intended form—and when there is ascertainment through the exclusion of doubt and the like, yet there is non-perception of the distinction between them; and when, even though that distinction exists, there is non-perception of that error (*vibhrama*)—that is, when the distinction is not perceived despite being present in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)—what [is the consequence]? He says: "Of what [consciousness] would there be a simultaneous pervasion of the natures of both the manifest and the other? [The answer is: for the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of consciousness, what obstacle is there to its successive pervasion of its own cause and effect?

If it is objected: "Indeed, cognition exists in the effect, not in the cause, because at the time of the cause it is absent; for this very reason, it exists in the cause but not in the effect. Therefore, how can there be a realization of the pervasion of the particular characteristic of consciousness by its own cause and effect? For what kind of constraint (*pratibandha*) could there be in that regard?"—to this he replies: "It indeed conceals," and so forth, because at the time of the cognition, the cause of cognition—the effect—is non-existent.

Just as cognition, by its very nature, conceals the absolute difference between its own object and the particular [aspect] that produces the result, so that this difference does not manifest by itself;
in that same way, through proximity, there is a sense of identity between error and perception.
This very point was stated by the gods themselves in the *Siddhiviniścaya*:
"By means of that proximity through which there would be identity between erroneous cognition and direct perception,
so too, even though there is a distinction between the part and that which possesses it, reality is therefore of a dual nature."
—Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, Prastāvanā, p. 168: "The identity of its own cause and effect is therefore the reality consisting of the three natures.
If there were the possibility of absolute [identity] in some cases, this cognition of non-absolutism (anekānta) would not be produced."
To the extent that the cognition of one's own object occurs in fragments rather than in its entirety, to that same extent it is a manifestation of blindness;
it merely conceals and merely obstructs [the object] from one another.
What is it? He says: "the function," which is knowledge.
Of what [objects]? He says: "of the particulars, the aids, and the exclusive fruits. Of which two? To this he says: "of one's own self and of the object."

By what [means] does it [cognize] itself? To this he says: "by means of the universal [consisting in] the oneness of the preceding and succeeding [moments] of its own object"—that is to say, even here, it is that which grasps cause and effect as having the nature of a universal which opposes the absolute [view of] difference.
If it is asked, "Is this merely imagined by you, or does it indeed appear so?", he says: "it would appear," and so forth.

Just as there is an inference of the word "thus" from hearing the word "just as"—due to the constant connection between "that" (yad) and "this" (tad)—the meaning is as follows: in whatever manner a cognition is perceived in the world, it should appear in that same way;
and since in the world a particular is perceived through its universal with respect to its own object, it therefore appears in that very manner.

Nor is it contradictory for a cognition that has arisen from a cause to be oriented toward grasping its fruit; otherwise, it would be contradictory for something that has arisen in relation to itself to function in relation to another, and thus the proof of the momentariness of all things would be premature.
However, this much is the distinction: in one case there is a difference of place, and in the other, a difference of time.

If it is argued that since the causes, fruits, and the generalities [of these] appear as three distinct entities mutually separated, they cannot be of a single nature—otherwise, the world would not be both manifold and non-manifold—the author says here: "In close proximity," and so forth.

How could there be identity—that is, oneness—between two things, characterized by appearing in such-and-such a way due to their being sublated, or characterized by arising from their own causes in such a way as to be incapable of being distinguished? To this he says: "Between error and perception.

For instance, that very cognition of a yellow conch which is erroneous because it lacks the stability of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is nonetheless non-erroneous with respect to its own nature, or with respect to the mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*), because there is no contradiction therein.

Nor can there be an assumption of non-contradiction for another cognition in that case, precisely because of seeing that [object]; otherwise, it would not arise from anything else either, since it would be assumed from yet another, leading to an infinite regress (*avyavasthā*). For just as in the case of the cognition of yellow in a conch shell, there is an absence of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) related to yellow, so too in the case of the shape (*saṃsthāna*), there is an absence of the purposeful action consisting in the form of a common, indistinct inference. If it is argued that "the person engaged in conventional practice regarding a universal entity does not think in this way," [we reply: in the cognition of yellow, when the appearance of the shape is present...

If it is argued that their identity exists in conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), then the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth applies to that very [conventional] level. But what of their identity when the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is also being considered? To this he says: through that proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there is an identity between its own cause and effect;
from that identity, reality (*tattva*) consists of a triad, having the nature of arising and so forth.

The cause is the prior mode (*pūrvaparyāya*), the effect is the subsequent mode (*uttaraparyāya*), and the substance (*dravya*) is the commonality (*sāmānya*) inherent in those two; these are the three entities.
Desiring to explain the first verse by way of negative concomitance (*vyatirekamukhena*), because they possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), he says: "In some cases," and so forth.

Whether in some external or internal context, or in error, or elsewhere in empirical usage, or in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), when the possibility of exclusivity—the possibility of an exclusive position against all other opponents' doctrines—is established by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what kind of cognition would be produced such that one could say, "This is it"? To this he says: "It is non-exclusive," and so forth. [The opponent argues: "Since that possibility exists, its denial [by you] is untenable. To this he replies: "Insofar as... and so forth.

The perception of its own two objects—that is, the apprehension of cognition in its parts—is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). If [it is argued] that this is not by way of form—that is, not by way of a nature that distinguishes error—this is the view of Dharmottara and others.

Likewise, it is not by way of the nature of cognition as connected to a subsequent causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because of such statements as: "the awareness of a relation residing in two [terms]" (*pra.vārtikālaṃkāra* 2.1), and so forth.

Otherwise, since the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) would be cognized at the very moment the cognition of the means of proof is apprehended, its further examination would be a mere child’s play. If, however, its validity were doubted because it is grasped as such [only through subsequent confirmation], then even though it has been apprehended, it is not yet ascertained by the observation of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). In that case, it is not truly apprehended; for a person engaged in practical activity does not consider what has been apprehended to be "apprehended" if it remains unascertained.
And you follow that [position], because even though in the ultimate sense there is no causal relation between effect and cause, you accept it by virtue of [the Lord's] will.
Furthermore, when an external object such as color-form (*rūpa*) is perceived, an internal aspect consisting of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth is experienced simultaneously;

yet it cannot be said that the perceived aspect, such as blue, is experienced as having the nature of pleasure, for it is not determined that the blue is experienced as being of the nature of pleasure.
— Nyāyabinduṭīkā 1.10: Examination of the Nature of Valid Cognition (pramāṇatā)

"The conventional nature [of things] is not undermined by the desire of worldly people through non-conceptualization of the ultimate; however, if that [conventional nature] is grasped, let its grasp occur through conceptualization. Thus [it is said].

The Sautrāntika maintains that the producer of cognition (*prajñākara*) likewise does not produce the apprehension of an object as "blue" and so forth by way of its having been produced; for [if it did], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no dispute [between us] regarding the substantiality (*dravya*) and other [categories] being of that nature. Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika and others have stated that even if power (*śakti*) were absolutely distinct from that [substance], [the same fault would apply].
What does one do when being born? To this he says: "In its entirety," and so forth.
As long as the mind is impartial toward the examination of reality, there is a suspension of dispute; however, this is not the case when it comes to [the proclamation of] that specific realization.
Explaining the second [point], he says: "mutually," and so forth;
all of this is easy to understand.
Furthermore, showing another example that follows from the same principle, he says: "mutually," and so forth.
The two ends of a scale, namely the lowering and the raising, are mutually inseparable;
for the weighing— the simultaneous occurrence of the lowering and raising of the scales and so forth—
does not imply that name and form are the cause [of the weighing], nor is there any deviation from that [simultaneity].
But identity could only exist in some way; therefore, it does not [exist] between the two ends of a scale.
(Nyāyaviniścaya 2.338)
If such a mark [of inference] exists in a pot or similar object, why then is not every effect [likewise a mark]?

(15) By observing the lowering or raising of one end of a scale, there is an inference of the other; and by inferring the shadow and so forth from a tree and so forth, one who considers this to be an inference based on an effect (*kāryaliṅga*) blocks the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
For it could be argued: "An existent thing, whether being produced or already produced, produces only that which is imperishable;

therefore, through the inference of the nature of its own cause, there is the cognition of the essence of the cause. Alas, what a wretched man this is! For even though he beats his own breast and cries out, the world does not desist [from its course]. To illustrate: a tree and the like are neither the nature nor the effect of its shadow and so forth.
And there is no contradiction here; the cognition of the moon and so forth in the water-moon and so forth is likewise an inference,
for the moon and so forth are neither the intrinsic nature nor the effect of the water-moon and so forth.
*Laghīyastrayā-svavṛtti*, verse 12–13:
"The sinking and rising at the two ends of a scale are inferred as being mutually inseparable"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"Sinking is inseparable from rising, and rising is inseparable from that [sinking], because otherwise it would be impossible"—this is understood to follow.

In the phrase "in a vessel, etc.," the word "etc. includes the perception of the moon in water and so forth; the supplement is that when a substance such as a cloud exists, [the rain] is inferred. Here too, the connection is made by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*). Now, previously it was stated that this [effect] is the result of a prior causal complex (*pūrvasāmagrī*); therefore, that very complex is what is inferred. To this, he says: "of such a kind," and so forth.
If such an effect were the *liṅga* (the logical mark), then why would [the qualities] such as *sattva* not also be an effect?
Explaining the portion beginning with "such" (*īdṛk*), he says: "of the two ends of the scale," and so forth.

From the observation of either the descent or the ascent at the two ends of a balance scale, there is an inference of the other—either the ascent or the descent. Likewise, there is the inference of a tree from its shadow and so forth, or the inference of a tree by means of its related shadow and so forth; this is an effect-reason (*kāryaliṅga*). The Buddhist (*saugata*), asserting "possibility" (*sambhava*) as a [separate] reason, obstructs—that is, rejects—the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*); he would call that very thing an effect-reason.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For it is possible," and so forth.

For it could indeed be argued that when an existent entity produces an effect—whether that effect be produced, or whether it depend upon the operation of another thing—it produces it as something momentary, non-eternal, and of a permanent nature, because such is observed in the case of jars and the like; this is what [the opponent] thinks.

What follows from this? He says: because of that reason, or from this mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the inference of the nature of its own cause—from the inference of the nature of the cause of an entity, whether it be a produced thing (*kṛtaka*) or otherwise, which has the nature of being perishable and consists in the production of an effect; through the inference of that [nature] belonging to the cause-essence or the produced thing, there is comprehension. The point is that perishability as existing at that very time is not inferred directly.

Now, if it is argued that when there is an inference of the nature of its own cause from this [effect], then the effect is "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth, whereas when perishability—which is its very nature—is inferred, then it is a "nature" (*svabhāva*); then, in that case, when there is an inference of the nature of taste and so forth, it would be "being an effect," but when there is an inference of color and so forth occurring at the same time, it would be a different type of mark (*liṅga*).
If you say that in the present case the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) does not exist here, we reply: here too, the capacity (*yogyatā*) is the same.

Just as there is a lack of confidence in all cases regarding two distinct things that are neither cause nor effect—since even when they are not seen together at some place or time, they may later be seen together again, and conversely, even when one is absent, the other may still be seen—so too, even if identity is observed between two non-distinct things in some instances, because that identity is observed otherwise elsewhere (as in the case where "mango-ness" exists even in the absence of "tree-ness"), there would be a total lack of confidence everywhere;
and if the world were examined in this manner, its everyday practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would collapse.

And this position is not tenable for you because you have accepted it; how then could it be tenable for a Buddhist (*saugata*)? For he too has accepted this. Just as the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth is established prior to the entry into non-duality (*advaita*) based on worldly [consensus], let there also be the establishment of the relationship of "inseparability" (*ayathānupapatti*) among co-existent qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest, since there is no difference [in the logic]. Thus he says, starting with "suffering" (*duḥkha*): the connection is that "he lives in such a way that suffering occurs. The word *vata* expresses dejection; this Buddhist is a poor, wretched fellow.
What is he doing? He says: "In the world," and so forth.

Why? He says: "Because for that Buddhist, even though the world is weeping and crying—this is an adverbial phrase denoting the manner of action—the [suffering] does not cease; therefore, [the existence of the Buddha] is established through the worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) which proceeds from the impossibility of any other explanation. This is the connection.
