For an entity whose own nature is being brought to completion while depending upon the operation of another is "produced" (kṛtaka)
— *Nyāyabindu* 3.12.
Showing another example of this very point arising from the *āmralatā*, he says: "In the same way," and so forth;
likewise, there is an inference of a light that has arisen from among other lights.
From what cause would it follow that "the cart will rise" [in conjunction] with Kṛttikā and so forth?

Regarding the enumeration of necessary connections (*pratibandha*), what is the proof for the statement "the cart will rise because of the rising of Kṛttikā"? Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) here; otherwise, the enumeration of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃkhyā*) appears to be undermined by the enumeration of necessary connections.

For one who does not accept that the knowledge of future results, such as the rising and setting of the luminaries, is inference (*anumāna*), there would follow the consequence of [it being] another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Since [the past and present] are connected by identity (*tādātmya*), there can be no cognition of future [results] from some [past or present sign], because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*, p. 49. Thus, by rejecting the very [principle of] pervasion (*vyāpti*), he not only shatters the seal of inference, but also destroys the entire system of means of valid cognition and their objects.
[As for] comparison (*tulanā*): "One may infer the future cart from the rising of the Kṛttikā [star]."
"Tomorrow the sun will rise," or "There will be an eclipse"—
this non-contradictory cognition concerning the future obstructs both the enumeration of logical relations (*pratibandha*) and the enumeration of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
— *Laghīyastrayasvopajñavṛtti*, verse 14.

Just as, due to the impossibility of it being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), there is an inference of one from the perception of the other between rising and falling, or an inference of a shadow and so forth from a tree and so forth—in exactly that same manner, such would be the inference; this is the connection [of the sentence].

From where, and where? To this he says: "If [it is argued that] among the luminaries, one who has risen [is known] by means of a sign (*liṅga*) such as the constellation Kṛttikā, and thus [the fact] that another luminary such as the Big Dipper (*śakaṭa*) will rise is established by the Buddhists (*saugata*); to this he replies: "Why should it not be so? If there is no cognition (*pratipatti*) of past things belonging to a single time [as being present]—that is, if [you say] it is not because of the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) regarding future things—then even for those who follow worldly convention (*vyavahārānusārin*), there would be a destruction of that convention.

For the inference of the future Big Dipper from the rising of Kṛttikā does not occur [directly], but rather [it is inferred] from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of both [constellations], according to some."

The simultaneity of those two [is necessary]; otherwise, even for taste and the other [sensory objects], it would not occur, which would be meaningless—[as stated in] the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*: "The cognition of things belonging to a single past time...

Furthermore, even if they depend on the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), if there were no simultaneity between the two, that which is the object of mental perception (*mānasādhyakṣa*) could not be an auxiliary to sensory cognition, as in the case of the rising of the Kṛttikā star and the rising of the Pleiades constellation (*śakaṭa*).

The meaning is that the object immediately following the object of sensory cognition, acting as a cooperative condition for that sensory cognition, produces mental consciousness; [if this were not so], that [mental consciousness] would not exist.

Now, even if one infers the nature of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in some way, there is no comprehension of the future rising of a cart from past or simultaneous factors. This contradicts the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*: "He alone knows who says such things.
Others hold that even the effect is a cause, and thus the rising of the cart is inferred from the rising of the Kṛttikā star.

In their own treatise, they state: "The sun will rise tomorrow; today, that [sun] has already risen. This discourse, which negates inference, is inconsistent with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If neither [of these two] is accepted, how could the cessation of what is not yet present be certain? Furthermore, if the effect were to exist prior [to the cause], then according to the Sugata’s teaching on the nature of the Sugata, all preceding states would be of the nature of effects, while subsequent ones would be of the nature of causes; consequently, one would engage in activity for the sake of that [prior state].

And thus, in this context, the Blessed One’s status as an authoritative source (*pramāṇabhūtatva*) is expressed through praise by means of the perfection of cause and fruit. Therein, the cause is the perfection of intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*), with respect to conventional authority (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*). Intention is the desire for the welfare of the world; application is the state of being one who acts for the benefit of the world. The fruit is the perfection of one's own purpose, which consists of the state of being a Sugata. (*Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1)

All of this [the aforementioned argument] is incorrect. If one explains it thus with reference to conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*), then it would follow that when fire is not habitually experienced, one acts toward its effect upon seeing the mark of its cause—namely, that fire is the cause and burning or other purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is its effect. Even so, if that very action were the cause, then the burning of the creeper would be the cause of the mass of leaves and fruits; therefore, the inference of that burning from the cause would be an inference of the effect from the cause.

If it is argued that the cause for being a Sugata (Well-Gone One) or a Protector (Tāyin) in this way must be intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*), and that their fruit would not exist [without them], then the previous contradiction remains as it was; why is this so? Because in the absence of being a Sugata, there is also an absence of the perfection of intention and application; in the absence of those, there is no Sugata-hood. Alternatively, if they were to have one another as their cause, then because they would be mutually dependent, neither of the two would be established.

Based on worldly convention (*saṃvyavahāra*), one desires the relationship of cause and effect everywhere; otherwise, one would not accept the rising of the constellation Kṛttikā as the cause for the rising of the constellation Rohiṇī, even though that [latter] is impossible otherwise and is free from those defects, because it relies on something other than that [convention]. This is true for those whose wisdom is hidden from others.
By this, the inference of death from portents (*ariṣṭa*) and so forth has been chewed and re-chewed by Prajñākaragupta, who maintains the doctrine of real causes (*bhāvikāraṇavādin*).
Comparison: Therefore, that which is stated by Bhaṭṭa—“The sunrise that is yet to be is not accompanied by today’s sunrise;
nevertheless, it is inferred from today’s sunrise that it too will occur tomorrow”—is refuted, because the reason (hetu) exists as previously described, being conjoined with the probandum (sādhya).

And as for the inference of tomorrow’s sunrise from today’s sunrise— that is not a valid inference because it lacks a determining mark (*liṅga*), like inferring tomorrow’s sunrise from seeing a donkey today— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*,
"Tomorrow the sun will rise," or "There will be an eclipse"— [these are examples]. (Laghīyastraya,
Verse 14) Because it constitutes the subject matter of the treatise,
it is the Blessed Lord himself who is established here as the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 1. And here, at the beginning of the treatise, the praise of the Blessed One is expressed by way of his being "one who has become a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇabhūta*) through the perfection of cause and fruit, for the purpose of generating faith.

In this context, the "cause" consists of the perfection of intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*); "intention" is the desire for the welfare of the world, and "application" is the state of being a teacher (*śāstṛtva*) due to instructing the world. The "fruit" is the perfection of one's own welfare.
The perfection of one's own welfare consists in being a Sugata, based on three kinds of meaning:
the sense of being a teacher, like one who is handsome;
the sense of non-returning, like one whose fever has been completely cured; and the sense of being exhaustive, like a well-filled jar. — *Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstravyākhyā*, Chapter 1.
Because that [nature] exists even in the absence of being a Sugata, despite the absence of the perfection of intention and application.

Prajñākaragupta, meaning "one whose wisdom has perished," explains the meaning of the verse beginning with "the connection" (*pratibandha*) and so forth: when an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the connection—that is, the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*)—is being made, such that the connection consists only of the forms of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) and no other, he asks: "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the [inference] 'The cart will rise [in the east] because of the rising of the Kṛttikā [star]'?"
It is not perception, because it relies upon a logical mark (liṅga);
nor is it inference, because it occurs even in the absence of another person's obstruction.
The implication is that it must therefore be a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).
Alternatively, it should be explained as: "Why is it not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another?

If it is argued that "it is not a means of valid cognition because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)," he replies here with the words beginning "And not here," etc., meaning that among the deviations characterized by the apprehension of distortions in place, time, and form, not even one exists; such is the apprehension of some.
From where is this [known]? To this he says: "The Kṛttikās," and so forth.
Or rather, from where is that authority? To this he says: "By what has been done," and so forth.

But how is it known that its non-occurrence otherwise is impossible? If you say, "Because it is not observed when the intended rising of the cart is absent," that is not so; for the non-observation of an omniscient being would imply the absence of the object everywhere, but not for anyone else, because of the possibility of error—since we observe those very same *sakaṣāya* myrobalan fruits at one time to appear differently on another occasion.

If it is argued that this fault does not apply to the Buddhist position because the necessary connection—such as identity (*tādātmya*)—which serves as the basis for that cognition exists, this is not sound. For, just as the nature of being a tree is understood to be invariably concomitant with the *śiṃśapā* at all times and in all places due to the frequent observation of the *śiṃśapā*’s nature as a tree (otherwise it would never possess that nature even once), so too the rising of the Kṛttikā constellation, being observed to have the nature of being invariably concomitant with the rising of the Rohiṇī constellation in many instances, is understood to have that nature at all times and in all places; otherwise, its possession of that nature even once would be impossible.

In this case, why is there no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the *śiṃśapā*? And just as its existence even in the absence of a tree constitutes its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), so too, in the absence of that very nature of being inseparable from it, the rising of the Kṛttikā remains equally lacking in intrinsic nature.
Nor should the objection be raised here: "From what does its having that nature [arise]? For this is the same in the case of the *śiṃśapā* as well;
it is not the same because [the latter] arises from its own cause.
In this case as well, let this very same response suffice: if it is argued that there would be the consequence of [inferring] that [tree], then the same applies to the *śiṃśapā* tree;
moreover, no inferer exists who perceives everything, for that would render inference useless.
Since sweet things are observed even in another place, at another time, and in connection with other substances,
the understanding of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)— whereby the term "etcetera" includes origination from that (*tadutpatti*)— is established.
The logical connection is that a *śiṃśapā* has the nature of a tree because it arises precisely from that which has the nature of a tree.
The consequence of [the fallacy of] inferring from a cause has already been given as a rebuff to the essential nature (svabhāva) reason; now, why offer a libation of water [to dismiss it]?
For the Buddhist says that there is no other mark (liṅga) than this.
Showing another refutation on this very point, he says: "In the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: since [the object of knowledge] is included within inference (*anumāna*), the enumeration of the means of valid cognition as "two" would be like a contradiction to the restrictive enumeration [of the types of relation]. [The opponent might argue: "There are only two kinds of relation"; thus, that restrictive enumeration would appear to contradict the restrictive enumeration of the means of valid cognition.
By using the word "as if" (*iva*), he shows his disregard for such an argument.

Why? To this he says: "The knowledge of that fruit which has as its beginning the future rising and setting of the luminaries—the planets and so forth—is [an inference] for one who does not accept [it as such] because of the aforementioned restriction; otherwise, there would be the consequence of it being a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, it is understood that for one who does accept it, there would be the consequence of having to accept other [invariable] relations (*pratibandha*), such as the inference of the rising of the constellation of the Big Dipper (*śakaṭa*) and so forth."

Since this would entail the acceptance of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) consisting of the nature of preceding and succeeding moments, distinct from identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), he says again, "by way of identity," etc., to demonstrate that:
through some inferential mark (*liṅga*), there is the cognition of past things belonging to a single time, but not of future ones.

Why? Because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Thus, he does not merely shatter the seal of inference; what is he doing? He is rejecting *vyāpti* itself, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps it—this is the intended meaning.

For instance: at the time of the rule of its causal connection, an object that is not a cause cannot be the object of cognition; nor can everything—past, present, and future—be the cause of that cognition which has universal pervasion as its object, because it is accepted that only that which has immediately preceded is a cause in all cases. Otherwise, it would have to produce its own effects in other locations and so forth;
thus, according to the rule that [cognition] grasps pervasion:
The cause of cognition would produce its effect in another place and at another time.
Others say: "For us who maintain the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*), that distinction of seals does not constitute a fault, because it is based on scripture.
To this, he replies: "Something" (*kiñcit*);
however, rather [than being a fault], it follows that it even shatters the established order of all means and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇa-prameya-vyavasthā*).

Because that [distinction] would be impossible in the absence of inference; otherwise, the establishment of the general categories of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its opposite would be rendered meaningless, as would everything else, due to the impossibility of establishing the system of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and their objects (*prameya*).

For when there is a general establishment of both valid cognition and the semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), the distinction between "this is valid cognition" and "this is not valid cognition" occurs precisely through inference based on the cause of non-contradiction.

"Because there is a cognition of something else, there is the existence of another means of valid cognition; and because of the negation of some [other means], this remaining [means exists]"—this verse was cited in the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* (p. 8) on the grounds that Dharmakīrti also stated this, and it is cited in the *Pramāṇaparīkṣā* (p. 64), the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 180), the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 261), and so forth.

If it is argued that even though there is a difference in their respective arrangements, the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*); to this he replies with the words beginning "directly perceived": direct perception is exclusively distinct from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
False inference has an unreal object; the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the primary characteristic.
[Verse 17] We perceive that which is clear... [and] at another time... as a cognition consisting of the delusion of the conceptual construction of grasped and grasper, but not as something absolute;
for its characteristic must be established by pervading other locations and so forth.

The intended meaning is that it is not possible [to establish that] by means of self-cognitions (*svasaṃvedana*) that are themselves uncharacterized; this is logical—if the definition of the fourfold perception were stated in its entirety, [it would be possible], but it is not so because of its absence. If it is argued that, conversely, it is precisely self-cognition that is said to be established by perception (*pratyakṣasiddha*); to this he replies: "Perception," etc.—whether it be that which is called self-cognition or something else.

"What is its nature? To this he says: [It is] that which is distinct from, dissimilar to, or turned away from the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) of the Sugata—which is characterized by a single, unique, and unassisted end (*anta*)—if it is argued that the establishment of that [object] occurs through inference. To this he replies: "How can inference be false or non-concordant? To this he says: [Because it would be] devoid of a real object, objectless, or purposeless, since the non-duality of appearance is accepted as being self-established.

Alternatively, [one might ask]: "What follows from the fact that its objects, causes, characteristics, and means of knowledge are non-existent? To this he says: "The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the primary characteristic belonging to another. By this, he provides the etymological derivation (*nirukta*) of the term *svalakṣaṇa* for perception (*pratyakṣa*).
How, moreover, can self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) be a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) distinct from that [external object]? To this he says: "clear" (*viśada*), and so forth.

Just as the simultaneous apprehension of a single gross object is possible, so too is it possible for an object persisting through another interval of time; to this he replies with the words beginning "at another time" (*kālāntare*).
By this, he demonstrates the perception of a contradictory [reason] (*viruddhopalabdhi*) in the proof that it is not perceived:
"If you desire non-duality in that which is distinct from its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then let that [non-duality] reside here in this grosser [object]."

"If you think again that 'you are in every way already liberated in the eastern and northern parts [of the body],' then that non-duality (advaita) is distinct from that [liberation]; regarding this, he says: 'Just as in consciousness,' and so forth. We perceive consciousness in such a way that the two conceptual distinctions—the grasped and the grasper—are themselves dualities; by means of those two, [consciousness] is of the nature of delusion."

He thinks as follows: "If that non-dual entity, being distinct from pillars and the like, were to exist as a body [of consciousness], what would become of those pillars and so forth? If they do exist, does their manifestation arise from themselves or from another? If from themselves, then the error of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) would follow.
If from another, then our desired conclusion is established; for you yourselves perceive even a single [indivisible] whole. To this, he replies: "But not... and so forth.
Because a pillar and so forth cannot logically possess the nature of a pillar and so forth, since it would follow that they are of the nature of self-cognition; this is the meaning.
When the pillar and so forth appear [in that way], then...

Thus, since non-absolutism (anekānta) is established both externally and internally, [the author], showing what follows from this, says: "Intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is also conventional usage," and so forth.

For those who perceive non-absolutism, intrinsic nature is the cause even for conventional usage because it functions as reality; however, for those who are dogmatically attached to that [false view], it is false. (18)
Through the application of reasoning based on the cognition of words such as "contradictory" and so forth,
the perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvopalambha*) arises;
from that, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) whose object is non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is to be established.

In that regard, since one observes a subject who has not yet apprehended an object when that object is being apprehended, it is not logical [to claim] that "this is not the essence" or "it is not the effect," and so forth;
furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is the means for establishing the linguistic usage of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Thus, this person, perceiving multiplicity both externally and internally yet being averse to the vision of reality, is led— either by reliance on his own tradition or through the application of reasoning—
to engage in that conventional discourse because of the non-perception of [absolute] existence and so forth;
for just as it is within, so too is external existence of a manifold nature, since an absolute [nature] is not perceived and because otherwise it would be untenable.
The particle *api*, though its placement is displaced, should be understood as following immediately after the word *svabhāva*.

Thus, it means that not only is non-perception (*anupalambha*) a cause, but also intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and even the perception of the non-exclusive (*anekāntopalambha*) is a cause—that is, a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Where? To this he says: "in practical discourse" (*vyavahāre*); from the context, it is understood that this refers to the non-exclusive (*anekānta*).

[Objection: "But surely, since the non-absolutism (anekānta) is established directly from that very perception, how can this [perception] be the logical reason (hetu)? To this, he says: It should be understood as having the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) included within it, because it causes [the understanding] to proceed toward the reality whose nature is non-absolutism.
Of whom? He says: "even of those who perceive" (*saṃpaśyatām*); the word "even" (*api*) is to be understood here as well.

What [is the purpose]? He says: "It is for those who have a false adherence to non-absolutism (*anekānta*). This means: for the sake of removing that false adherence—which is an adherence to absolutism—directed toward that non-absolutism. What is meant is this: just as even the *svabhāva*-reason (*svabhāva-hetu*) is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*) when it is distinct [from the other two] because it is not different from the probandum (*sādhya*), so too this apprehension of essential nature (*svabhāvopalambha*) is distinct from both the effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*) and the pervaded-essential-nature reason (*vyāpya-svabhāva-hetu*). Thus, there are exactly three types of logical marks (*liṅga*). (Nyāyabindu 2)
11. Thus [the argument] is refuted; thus is shown by him himself the sublation (*bādha*) of the thesis and the reason employed by the Proponent of Cognition (*prajñākara*).
Furthermore, there are only three types of logical marks (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*).
In the case of proving an indivisible, absolute [unity], how can that reason be valid therein? It is as stated: "it is contradictory to that," and so forth.

By the word "that" (tat), the non-absolute (anekānta) is referred to; or by the phrase "contrary to that" (tadviruddha), the absolute (ekānta) such as permanence and so forth—which is contrary to the non-absolute—is meant. Those things which have these two as their beginning are thus described.
The word "beginning" (ādi) is connected with each [term]—namely, "those beginning with that" (tadādayaḥ) and "those beginning with what is contrary to that" (tadviruddhādayaḥ).

In this context, by the first word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of non-exclusive causes, effects, concomitants, and so on; by the second, there is the inclusion of exclusive causes and so forth. Of these, respectively, there is "word" (*śabda*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Through reasoning (*tarkeṇa*), by means of the employment of logical reasons that refute the existence [of the probandum] in the counter-example (*vipakṣe sadbhāvabādhakahetuprayogataḥ*), and through their application—that is, the utterance of the sentences that establish them—an extensive elaboration [is possible], though it is not stated here for fear of making the book too voluminous. It should be understood by wise and intelligent people from the work named *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*.
It should be observed—expounding the verse on page 104 of the *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, he says: "The apprehension of the intrinsic nature," and so forth.

"Apprehension of the intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvopalambha*) means that the intrinsic nature itself—the object of knowledge which is the manifold state of being—is apprehended; this is according to the etymological derivation that it is both the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the apprehension (*upalambha*).

Alternatively, if it is established that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist when it is perceived—since the term "object" is applied metaphorically to the object of perception—it is called the "intrinsic nature of its perception.

What follows from this? He says: "From that intrinsic nature, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) has a non-exclusive object (*anekāntaviṣaya*); [therefore] existence, cognition, and so forth are to be proven (*sādhya*).

If it is asked: "But surely, since that [existence, etc. is already established upon the perception of the intrinsic nature, how can it be 'to be proven'? To this he replies: "In that case," and so forth.

In that case, if there is a cognition of the object and its apprehension within the context of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), yet the subject [of that apprehension] remains uncognized by the Buddhist and others, then—due to their doctrine—the non-apprehension consisting of that apprehension would be non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). Consequently, even when that [object] is cognized, it would be logical that the subject remains uncognized. This is not the case for you, because the apprehension of non-absolutism is of the nature of a determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*), and there is no further linguistic transaction (*vyavahāra*) to be established beyond that. If this is argued, it has already been stated here: "In that case," and so forth.
For it is observed that even for one who possesses the apprehension of non-absolutism, there occurs the superimposition of the contrary.
And there is no such thing as what is perceived being logically untenable;

for this very reason it was stated [in the *Ślokavārttika*] that "it is from perception. Furthermore, it was stated in the first chapter that the perception of the bare ground is non-conceptual; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
What happened after that? He says: "Therefore, this is not the essence," and so forth.

Since it is thus, he asks: "What is this? and answers with "the non-perception of the effect," and so on. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*): [it refers to] the perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvopalambha*), which is the means for establishing the positive and negative linguistic conventions (*bhāvābhāvavyavahāra*) by means of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and its corresponding linguistic usage; for it is considered to be a means for such linguistic usage.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.

Since it is thus, for that reason, this proponent of an extremist view (ekāntavādī), such as a Buddhist and others, while indeed perceiving non-absolutism (anekānta), where [is he]? He says: "both externally and internally."

What is that? He says: [it is] being turned away from, or averse to, the vision of reality—that is, of the non-absolutist (anekānta) nature of the soul and so forth. The sense is that even while perceiving reality, one thinks, "I do not see. Why is this? He says: "Due to adherence to one's own tradition" (samaya), which means due to the obsession with the dogmatic grasping of one's own scripture, or for some other reason. What is done by that [adherence]? He says: it obstructs the practical application of the meaning. By what means is this done? He says: by the employment of logic (tarka)—that is, by syllogisms rooted in logic. Showing these, he says: "In existence," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of all reasons well-known in both one's own and others' systems;
by this, [the phrase] "through the application of knowledge and reasoning" (*jñānatarkaprayogataḥ*) has been explained.
Now, in order to explain "the application of ignorance and fallacious reasoning contrary to that," he says: "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), etc.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is of a non-absolute (*anekānta*) character, whereas its opposite is the absolute (*ekānta*) such as permanence and so forth; this is what is indicated by the term "indicated" (*upalakṣyate*). This is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), and by it, [the category of] "and so forth" (*ādi*) is included, because that [opposite] is not perceived. Thus, the connection is: "in that very same way, by that very same manner, an entity is like one whose nature is non-absolute.
If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); to this he replies: "because even externally, the absolute is not perceived."
If it is argued: "This has already been considered;

surely there would be a non-perception of that [nature], nor is an entity (*bhāva*) of a manifold nature (*anekāntātmaka*), because there is no contradiction; thus, the reason (*hetu*) has a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)," then he replies here: "Otherwise"—that is, by way of another mode, namely the absence of the manifold nature of the entity—[the reason] would be untenable, and in that case, there would be a non-perception of it. To explain: is this non-perception of it the cessation of perception, or the perception of something else? The first position has already been answered, as it is not accepted, since [the entity] would be non-existent due to the non-existence of its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the second [type of non-apprehension] does not occur without indetermination; and the non-apprehension of certainty,
which consists in the apprehension of something else, cannot be established without indetermination.

Regarding this, he says: "The proponent of the absolute delusion of external objects [argues that] the perception of the absolute delusion of the external is unestablished as a reason (*asiddha*) in that case. Anticipating that view and refuting it, he says: "If [the external were] of a nature consisting solely of perception, stable, and gross, then those who are not negligent would not perceive it as having a nature that is absolutely delusive. (19)

Because the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are in contradiction with a nature that is visible, unitary, stable, and gross; because if they were distinct, there would follow the faults of the dilemma regarding subsistence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*), infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and so forth; and because when external objects are refuted, the same applies to cognition (*vijñapti*) as well—since it is impossible for the cognized, the cognizer, the delusion, the awareness, the conceptual, and the non-conceptual to be identical in any way whatsoever—no cognition could be erroneous.
For if they were distinct, their mutual relationship would be unestablished, just as between different mental continua (*santānāntara*).
Furthermore, it is not logical to establish the selflessness of entities in their entirety, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a claim;
this is because it would contradict the acceptance of those very means of valid cognition, just as in the case of the absolute negation of the counter-position.

"One, stable, and gross" constitutes the compound *ekasthirasthūlāḥ*; these are their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and one must further form a *karmadhāraya* compound with them. By means of these [intrinsic natures], entities cannot exist.

Of what nature are they? If they are "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*), meaning mutually dissimilar, then from what [source do they arise]? To this he says: "Because their nature is exclusively erroneous" (*ekāntabhrāntasvabhāvāt*). That is, because their very nature is exclusively—that is, necessarily—erroneous; for that reason, by that cause. Alternatively, the expression emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva*): it should be understood as "because of the state, the reality (*tattva*), of those whose nature is exclusively erroneous."

For instance: these [entities] cannot be accepted by the wise as having real intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), because their intrinsic nature is exclusively erroneous, like the intrinsic nature of a king seen in a dream.

And their intrinsic nature is exclusively erroneous because they appear as being co-referential with the perceived object, or because of contradiction in a single locus, like the intrinsic nature of hair that is distant and sparse;
this applies only to the opponents.
Having thus presented the opponent's view, he states the refutation here: "By those who are not negligent.

This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here: if one accepts that things which are unitary, stable, gross, and of distinct natures possess a nature that is exclusively erroneous, then a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought to establish that [erroneous nature]; otherwise, because that [nature] would not be established, there could be no manifestation of it therein, since through such [an invalid means] that delusion would not be apprehended—just as when one apprehends the object of another's mind, one does not apprehend that [other person's] single [subjective] object.

And in its investigation, for that very reason that non-existent things appear there as having that nature, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); and for that very reason that it is the cognizer whose nature is exclusively delusion, it is therefore not a valid means of knowledge. Furthermore, even by those natures such as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the like—of which "slight validity" (*īṣat-pramāṇa*) and "invalidity" (*apramā*) are the first—it should not be constituted.

This is what is meant: the absolute identity between the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its opposite would be of a delusive nature, just like the identity of parts with their form, or the identity of prior and posterior portions in a stable object, or the unity resulting from the conjunction of many parts in a gross transformation.

And thus, not only would the distinction between dream and non-dream states be impossible externally, but even the distinction between knowledge and its object within consciousness would be unattainable.

Regarding what was stated there—that the second [position] is certain that "it is not [the case] without indeterminacy"—if it is argued: "If even a single, stable, gross nature were established by perception in one place, just like multiple, momentary, subtle natures, but this is not so because such an analysis is impossible, and therefore only the imagined [nature] exists, which for that very reason is erroneous"; then, demonstrating and refuting this very point, he says: "By perception alone... and so forth. The connection is: "[it] should not be conceived," both externally and internally.
By what? He says: "by those [natures] that are perceived as singular, stable, and gross."
Because of the qualification "perceptual," it is understood that [the object] must possess a conventional, unitary, stable, and gross nature;
otherwise, the mention of "one" and so forth would be made in a general sense.
He states the refutation with the words "by those of different characteristics," and so on.
The word "also" (*api*) should be understood here [in the phrase] "even though they are distinguished by being excluded from everything.
To the question "by what kind of things?", he says: "by non-validity and so forth" (*apramā-ādibhiḥ*).

"How is it that there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) for those [things] whose nature consists of cause, effect, and so forth, as indicated by the word 'etcetera'? To this he says: "Because their nature is exclusively erroneous. This is what is meant: just as things such as unity and so forth are accepted as being conceptual (*kalpita*), even though they appear with clarity, so too should the distinct particularities (*viśeṣa*) and absences (*abhāva*) be accepted.
The sense is that [the objects] must indeed be accepted as merely imagined (kalpita).

To explain this verse, he says: "Because of the contradiction with the nature of being external, particular, unique, stable, and gross" regarding *svalakṣaṇānām* and so forth; that is, because of the contradiction with the nature of being external, particular, unique, stable, and gross, there is the rejection of external objects (*bahirarthanirākṛtau*).

In this regard, he states another reason: "If there were a difference [of the universal] from the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and its own nature were admitted to be distinct [from them], then because of the consequence of faults such as the dilemma regarding subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*) and infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Here, the word "and" (*ca*) is to be understood as serving to conjoin the reasons.
The dilemmas regarding subsistence are such as: does it subsist by way of a single part, or by its entire self (*sarvātmanā*), and so forth?

[Objection: "Surely, because of the contradiction with its own nature and because of the consequence of those same defects, let there be a refutation of that very nature [of the object] as being external, but not of the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why then is it stated without distinction, 'in the refutation of external objects'? [Response: He thinks thus: "If, by the two aforementioned reasons, even that which has such a nature and is perceptible (*dṛśya*) is refuted, what confidence can there be in anything else? And for this reason, the term 'perceptible' was included in the previous section. Furthermore, since there is no perception of those things characterized by a nature other than that [of the object], what [confidence] could there be in them? Thus he says: "Even of cognition (*vijñapti*)."

Not only is the external object [absent], but every refutation—both that which has been stated and that which has not been stated—is equally applicable and common [to all positions]. Thus, by means of the passage beginning with "the object of cognition" (*vedya*) and so forth, it is both established and being further established: the *vedya* is the apprehended form such as a pillar, and the *vedaka* is the form of cognition capable of apprehending it. These two alone constitute the error (*bhrānti*), and that [error] is the very nature of consciousness (*saṃvedana*). This applies to those things beginning with the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized (*vikalpyāvikalpyādi*), of which these are the first.

Alternatively, by the word "the object of cognition" (vedya), forms such as blue and so forth are expressed; by the word "the cognizer" (vedaka), there is the cognition which possesses that form and apprehends it.
And as for this which was stated:
"And because of the difference in the forms of the objects, there is a difference in the cognitions."
"Because that [object] exists only when this [cognition] exists, the nature [of the object] is understood by itself," as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.6.

By the word "error" (*bhrānti*), the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness within cognition is grasped, according to such passages as *Pravāhaṇa-vāda* 2.355; and by the statement "though undivided, the nature of cognition... (*Pravāhaṇa-vāda* 2.354), non-dual awareness is understood through the term "self-awareness" (*saṃvedana*). Regarding these [terms] joined in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) should be treated as a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) referring to those [cognitions] that grasp conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth. Of these...
Of what kind [are they]? He says: "mutually," and so forth.
Because, in every way and by every means, identity (*tādātmya*) or oneness (*aikya*) is impossible for this [consciousness], no erroneous cognition could exist.

This is the intended meaning: if there were absolute oneness between the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the subject (*vedaka*), and the awareness of error (*bhrānti-saṃvedana*), then either consciousness alone or error alone would be the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Alternatively, if there were an absolute identity between the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*), then only one of the two would exist; thus, a single cognition would not be variegated (*citra*). Likewise, even in the case of a mere blue [object], upon examination it would not be non-variegated either; therefore, it must be explained that no cognition whatsoever—whether variegated or non-variegated—would exist.

Similarly, regarding the cognition of an error (*bhrānti-saṃvedana*), if they were identical in reality, only one of them would exist; thus, nothing else could be perceived as an erroneous object (*grāhya*). (Page 388, Note 4)

It should be observed—see page 388, note 5—if it is argued that there is a distinction (*vyatireka*) among them despite their identity (*tādātmya*), [the author] says here: the term "connection" (*saṃbandha*) follows from the phrase "in the case of a distinction, i.e., a difference between them. For the same reason that no connection is established between different mental continua (*santānāntara*), as in the case of those [external objects], no cognition whatsoever would arise; thus, this verbal formulation is empty. [For it has been said: "The self-nature is known by itself" (*pra.vā. 1*).
Thus, nothing would be erroneous;

and as it is said in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.7), "validity [is established] by means of worldly practice," for that [practice] would be impossible in the absence of erroneous conceptualization (*bhrānti-vikalpa*).

If it is argued that, because reality cannot be established when examined elsewhere as well as externally, there is therefore a total emptiness—as stated in the *Prakaraṇavārttika*: "Thus this [world], having become such a body, has surely come to be like an illusion" (2.209) and so forth; to this he replies: "And it is not at all proper to maintain [this]."
What? Selflessness, which is the absence of intrinsic nature. Of what? Of entities.
How? To this he says: "in its entirety," that is, by way of totality, even by way of its own nature as if it were another nature.
Why? He says: "Because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is the selflessness (nairātmya) of that [entity]. The connection is made by changing the case-ending.
Here he provides an illustration: "as in the case of the extreme of the opposite," meaning as in the case of the extreme of [the existence of] entities (bhāvaikānta).
Regarding the acceptance of a means of valid cognition for that [position], he states the refutation: "tatpramāṇa... and so forth.
Because that which is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that selflessness (*nairātmya*), or regarding it, contradicts its own acceptance;
for instance, if there were no selflessness of phenomena in their entirety, that means of valid cognition would not exist, as even the investigation itself would be untenable;
yet if that [means of valid cognition] exists, then selflessness must also exist.
Furthermore,
this is something that follows from the very nature of things, as the wise say:
"In whatever way objects are analyzed, in that same way they fall apart."
— since even the investigation into the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is absent, if indeed such a means of valid cognition exists...

It might be thought: "No one asserts that selflessness (*nairātmya*) consists in the total absence of all appearances. There is no fault even if [appearances] are non-existent, like the appearances of a magical illusion (*māyā*), a mirage (*marīci*), and so forth," according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* (3.211): "Because there exists the mere appearance of pillars and so forth, which is erroneous, yet devoid of both delusion and its opposite. To this, he replies: "In the case of the absolute falsity (*mithyaikānta*)... and so on, [meaning]:
because of the stream of diverse cognitions that are non-beneficial and unstable due to the intellect’s conviction in absolute falsity.
One does not perceive an external reality that is like the fierce planet of Death (Kṛtānta).

For an appearance, such as the manifestation of a variegated butterfly, cannot share a single destiny (yogakṣema) [with its object], because it does not negate the difference in nature [between the appearance and the object]; otherwise, it would follow that the mental continuum is a single entity. Even regarding external objects, one does not admit a single nature for individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), precisely because there is a difference in their natures.

The term *mithyā* (false) is a designation in which the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant; therefore, it refers to the nature (*tattva*)—that is, the essential form (*svarūpa*)—of that very cognition which possesses the quality of being exclusively false (*mithyātvam ekāntaḥ*). [The author] states that the Buddhist knows this, because it has been said: "Since delusion is not established due to delusion, he holds the heterodox view (*kṛtānta*) like a malignant planet.
Furthermore, demonstrating that others likewise fail to grasp this, he says: "It is useless," and so forth.

The meaning is that there exists no external object to be grasped by that [cognition], whose capacity [therefore] has its own form as its objective support (*svarūpālambana*). It is not stable; "unstable" means momentary (*kṣaṇika*). It is both "objectless" (*anartha*) and "unstable" (*asthira*). That [is] the cognition (*dhī*), and of that [cognition], there is "variety" (*citram*), which is its "variegatedness" (*citratvam*), because the designation emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāva*). Or rather, by that [variety] there is a continuum (*santati*); one should know its "reality" (*tattvam*) to be oneness (*ekatvam*).

This is what is meant: by one who asserts the non-existence of cause, effect, and so forth, that [non-existence] must be stated in its own nature, since there is no other way to negate the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That [nature] too consists of a single, variegated manifestation; otherwise, everything would be a total void.

It has been stated that even this manifestation is inseparable from the unity of preceding and succeeding moments. Thus, he does not perceive the reality in external objects such as jars; this too is a "grasping at a false doctrine" (*siddhāntaviṣamagraha*), because there is no distinction between the two cases, and the rest has already been covered previously.
Desiring to explain by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that one who possesses a manifold and unstable stream of cognitions does not know reality, he says "citra" and so forth.

The appearance of a variegated butterfly—that is, the cognition having its form—is the beginning of that which consists of the appearance of a variegated carpet and so forth, or the appearance of perception and other means of knowledge; thus it is described. In this context, there is no "unity of acquisition and preservation" (*ekākayogakṣematva*): *yoga* is production, and *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been produced. This applies to one who experiences [these appearances]; for in the case of unstable cognitions, there is an absence of such preservation.

Alternatively, *kṣema* means non-destruction; since the word for that [non-destruction] is conventionally applied there—just as the word "bhadrikā" is used for those who are disliked—the state of having a single, undivided *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation) does not negate the difference in nature of the appearance, namely the cognition of a variegated butterfly.

Why? To this he says: "because it would entail the consequence of the unity of the continuum (*santānaikatvaprasaṅgāt*)," meaning because it would entail the consequence of the oneness or non-difference of the continua.

For when a single cognition arises or is experienced, at that time the cognitions of other mental continua [are also experienced]; otherwise, the world would consist of nothing but a single stream of cognition. This being the case, everything that has been asserted by someone—that "self-awareness alone is the one direct means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) and no other, while the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) exists merely out of deference to those to be trained (*vineya-jana*)," and so forth—all of that collapses, because there would be no beings to be trained.

Therefore, since the arising of another cognition must be admitted at the time of the arising of one cognition, the "commonality of acquisition and preservation" (*ekayogakṣematva*) of the mental continua would eliminate their difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). Thus, once again, this is not a resolution of the aforementioned fault.
Nor is it the case that [the fault is resolved] in this way; therefore, it is considered that [the claim of commonality] is ineffective for eliminating the difference in intrinsic nature.
In this context, *yoga* (acquisition) is the persistence of a property not yet obtained, while *kṣema* (preservation) is the persistence of a property already obtained.
— PRAVĀHAKA’S OWN COMMENTARY ON HIS OWN TREATISE, 1.24,
regarding "defective" (duṣṭe).

[Objection: "But surely, in cases such as the appearance of the three steps, although there is a single *yogakṣema* (shared destiny) for the manifestation, this does not negate a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*); nevertheless, [the parts] would still be one. [Response: To this he says: "Even externally," and so forth.

It is not only internally, but even externally, [the unity is negated] precisely because of a difference in intrinsic nature, and not otherwise. This is because the opponent does not admit a single intrinsic nature for the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of atoms of form and so forth. For this reason, he negates that [unity] of theirs.
This is what is meant: just as there is no unity among external atoms due to the difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), so too it would be [the case] internally.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because of such statements as, "How could there be variegation in a single [entity]? It would not exist," etc. (*Pravāhaṇa-vāda* 2.210), to this he replies: "Unestablished" (*asiddha*), and so forth.
Even in that view, if this [cognition] itself finds pleasure in objects on its own, then what are we [to say]?—this is the remainder [of the argument].
Thus, for Siddhasena, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*); for Devanandin, it is contradictory (*viruddha*).

In the case of establishing [the existence of God] with absolute certainty, that [reason] of Samantabhadra is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the immovable Self (*acalātman*), such as [the qualities of] existence (*sattva*) and so forth.
— *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 114.
The reading in the present text is found at *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, second part, page 181:
"The unestablished (*asiddha*)... the contradictory (*viruddha*) [is] according to Mallavādin... — *Jainatarkavārttika*, page 107.
In the *Ratnākara* (p.

1032), it is stated that the property of being a real entity (*vastudharma*) such as existence (*sattva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is not established in its entirety for either the absolute momentary or the non-momentary;
furthermore, it is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it proves the non-exclusive (*anekānta*) nature through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*).

Furthermore, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of [reasons] such as existence (*sattva*) when proving momentary destruction and so forth arises because those who have not examined the true nature of reality rely upon worldly consensus as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the reason exists in both the proponent’s own position and its opposite, since it is possible for an effect to arise at its own specific time—without distinction—even from a cause that was previously capable of producing it; nor would the arising of an effect through the existence of its own cause be contradictory, whereby a fault would only occur if [the cause were] non-momentary. Since this has been determined... this is well said.

If the establishment of the absolute uniqueness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) were accepted as proven, then every logical reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished for the Blessed One, who has already attained realization.

If it is asked, "How so? it is replied: By means of a subtle investigation, even internally, everything is found to be devoid of appearance (*pratibhāsa*). What, then, would be the instrumental cognition (*sādhana-jñāna*) from which there could arise an engagement with a future object to be attained through inference during practice? Or what would be the perception of a middle [moment] distinct from the preceding and succeeding [moments], by virtue of which the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)—beginning with the argument "whatever appears as such..."—could be established? Or what would be the manifestation of blue and so forth, by which the principle "that which appears is cognition" and so on could be proven? By this, [the reasons] such as existence (*sattva*) and the rest are also refuted.

Just as in the case of the absolute doctrine of non-existence (*abhāvaikānta*), every reason (*hetu*) [adduced] for the absolute doctrine of existence (*bhāvaikānta*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because that [existence] is not perceived and because there would be a total confusion (*sarvasaṅkara*) of things. Furthermore, in the attempt to prove the absolute doctrine of the non-existence of entities that are mutually distinct from one another, the opponent’s position does not differ from the immediately preceding one; for if everything were of the nature of everything else due to the absence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, there would be no relation, since the connection of one thing with another—such as inherence (*samavāya*) and the like—is denied.

And for one who speaks thus, the mutual distinction or the distinction from anything else among antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest is not established, because of the fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the absence of further antecedent non-existences and so forth. Therefore, it is well said by Siddhasena: "In establishing an absolute [position], the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*); for that which is established would not be [so]."

A certain fellow-sectarian of the Naiyāyika, from the perspective of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikapakṣa*), says here: "This is incorrect because Siddhasena has not stated that [the probans] is unestablished (*asiddha*) in any instance"; has he perhaps heard this?
Regarding the fault of speaking falsehoods, the Śākyas say that calculation is for one who is not omniscient;
yet for them, all [knowledge] is indeed omniscience.
Thus, those faults of false doctrine which the Śākyas and Ulūkyas (Vaiśeṣikas) allege against the Sāṃkhyas—
all of them are true for those [Śākyas and Vaiśeṣikas] in their own false doctrines.

Now, therefore, it is maintained that a single cognition is variegated (*citra*) due to its form. To this, [the opponent] says: "The reason [adduced by you], O Devanandin, is contradictory for establishing a single [unitary] entity, because there is a contradiction between variegation and oneness, whether occurring sequentially or simultaneously.

Furthermore, since things appear as momentary in some way or another, the momentariness of entities is established precisely in that manner. The same should be understood regarding existence (*sattva*) and other [reasons]."

If it is argued: "Surely, for the venerable teacher of the Vaiśeṣika school and others who maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākārajñānavādin*), there is no single cognition variegated by the appearances of blue and other objects; against whom, then, can the non-exclusive nature (*anekāntātmakatva*) of everything be established by what example, such that the reason [used] in proving their doctrine of exclusivity (*ekānta*) would be contradictory? [We reply: No; for even in his case, there exists a single mental cognition (*mānasajñāna*) consisting of multiple capacities for grasping various pervaded and pervading categories of objects pertaining to the three times for every living being.

Otherwise, from where could there be a grasp of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) in its entirety, by virtue of which inference would occur? Nor is that very capacity for grasping the past which is the same as the orientation toward grasping the present and so forth; for this would entail the identity of the objects of cognition. Indeed, in the cognitions of the eye and other senses, that very orientation toward grasping taste is not the same as the orientation toward grasping color and so forth; otherwise, the distinction between different cognitions would be rendered useless. Even in those cases, the capacities are entirely distinct from one another.

Since inherence (samavāya) is negated due to the absence of a relationship, the designation "those [qualities] belong to that [substance]" would be lost; and if one were to postulate a power of assistance for that [inherence], there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, one must accept that a single cognition consists of multiple powers.
And how can a single cognition be manifold? Therefore, it is established that [the opponent's position] is contradictory, and so forth;
as it has been said: "The proof [of the manifold nature of reality] arises from non-absolutism" (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa 1.1).
The establishment, accomplishment, or cognition of the existence of the self of words, meanings, and their relations does not arise from anything else because it is non-exclusive;
this applies even to the Vaiśeṣika in the absence of such mental cognition.

Regarding the powers (*śaktayaḥ*), another says: "I, who am a proponent of the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*), do not accept a cause in any ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). That which is accepted is accepted through conventional usage (*vyavahāreṇa*), because of the statement [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*]: 'The validity [of cognition] is by way of conventional usage' (PV 1.4). To him, he replies: "That cause of Samantabhadra is twofold for the purpose of establishing a single point."
The meaning is that [the reason] is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) because it occurs in both the similar class (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

To explain: existence (*sattva*) consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); this is impossible in reality for both the non-momentary and the momentary, since it cannot exist at a time when [the thing] itself is present or absent. However, it has been stated that through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), it is not excluded from either case;
by this, it is established that "existence is apprehension" (*upalambhaḥ sattvam*), as explained in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 231.

For just as the permanence of a single entity—its persistence through the three periods of time—cannot be apprehended from any source, so too is the momentariness that terminates in a single atom. Nevertheless, if you accept the apprehension of that [momentariness], why do you not also accept the perception of a substance (*dravya*) that persists through all states within the domain of the three times? For from this it would follow: whatever appears in a certain way, that exists in reality (*paramārthasat*) exactly as it appears; just as pleasure, appearing as such in its true nature, exists in reality as such, so too do entities appear as impermanent.

Nor is it a valid answer to say that such conventional usage applies elsewhere as well, such that everyone would be an all-seeing one; for even if one perceives the momentariness restricted to each individual atom, everyone would thereby be a Sugata. If you argue that there is no fault because the Buddhists do not accept anyone other than one who perceives things in this way as a Sugata in reality—since they desire it to be so—then let that same answer apply to the present case as well.

If it is argued that there is no established distinction between those in saṃsāra and others, then why is there not likewise an absence of the distinction between the Sugata and others? Just as he is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), so too is the other;
thus, both are established through conventional usage (vyavahāra), or neither is established from the perspective of ultimate reality.

As for this further objection—that at the time of perceiving the first moment, if one were to perceive the states of the past and future, there would arise at that very moment the cognition of oneself as both born and dead—that too is not sound. For in both cases, the reasoning is the same:

he who perceives a single atom as distinct from what precedes and follows it would perceive himself as being simultaneously born and dead. Consequently, it would follow that no one could ever engage in or desist from any activity whatsoever.

If that [perception] is admitted, who can prevent the admission of one who perceives even those things existing in all states throughout all time? Now, if it is thought that [the object] must arise and perish at the very moment of being perceived, that too is not tenable; for it is apprehended exactly according to its own timing.
If this is not admitted, what confidence can there be in anything else? Therefore, just as with the non-momentary, there is no perception of the momentary in reality;
both are [only perceived] through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Thus it was rightly said: "That [perception] is twofold according to Saṃantabhadra."
If it is asked, "Where, then, does this Blessed One state that the reasons of those who hold to one-sided doctrines are inconclusive? [the answer is: No;
rather, [it is stated] in the context of accepting both engagement and cessation within the position of eternalism.

"Those ascetics who are wide awake regarding the lapses of others, yet keep their eyes closed toward their own faults—what can they do? They are unworthy vessels for the glory of your doctrine. This is because [the opponent's objection] is raised by this verse from the *Bṛhatsvavṛtti* (verse 99).
This is its meaning: those disputants are "unworthy" (apātra), that is, not a fit vessel for what? He says: "the glory of Your doctrine" (*tanmataśriyaḥ*).

This refers to the glory of the doctrine of You, the Blessed One, who are free from passion (*arajina*)—its glory being the subject matter of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), which pervades all categories of existence. [They are unworthy] of that [glory], namely, the proponents of absolutism (*ekāntavādin*).
What could they do? Nothing at all; the meaning is that they would perform neither the establishment of their own position nor the refutation of the opponent's position.
Of what nature are they? Wretched and miserable.
Why? To this he says: "Awakened by the lapses of others," and so forth.

For the opponent, from the perspective of the Buddhist, there is the flaw of asserting eternalism; for the Buddhist, from the perspective of that opponent, there is the flaw of being unable to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to [the subject's] being neither successive nor simultaneous. Therefore, those awake observers of this [flaw], who have closed their eyes to their own defects, act as if they do not see them even while seeing their own faults.
Consequently, just as existence and so forth establish momentariness, the proof of non-momentariness is likewise equal [in its application].
With reference to the proponent of permanence (*nityavādin*), he explains the verse with the words "of existence, etc. (*sattvādeḥ*):

that which has existence—defined as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), perception (*upalambha*), or something else—as its first [property], belonging to every reason (*hetu*) associated with the proponents of extremist views (*ekāntavādin*), is described as such. Of that [reason]...

Of what kind [is the subject]? It is of a real entity (*vastudharma*). [The opponent] thinks: "Since there is no such thing as an absolutely singular entity, its property (*taddharma*) is likewise of that same nature.

[The opponent objects: "Surely, although that [property] is absent in the case of absolute permanence (*nityaikānta*), it does exist in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*); therefore, there is no fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhatva*). To this, he says: "Because [the reason], such as existence (*sattva*), is unestablished in its entirety—that is, in its totality—with respect to both the alternatives of momentariness and its opposite. This might be thought: "Let that [reason] be unestablished when examining the reality imagined by the proponents of absolutism (*ekāntavādin*); however, if one accepts it according to how it is observed, this is not a fault. To that, he says: "Because it is otherwise inexplicable," and so forth.
The contradiction of existence and so forth follows from the context;
why? He says: "Because of the proof of non-absolutism" (anekānta).
Why is this also so? He says: "Because otherwise—in the manner of the absence of non-absolutism—it would be untenable that existence and so forth [apply] according to observation."

Another, however, says: "In reality, [the ultimate] transcends all conceptual construction; conventionally, there is the proof of momentary destruction and so forth. To this, he replies: "The inconclusiveness," and so forth, meaning that existence and the like are deviant.
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is used here in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*).

When the proof of momentary destruction and so forth is being formulated, the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is for the purpose of encompassing the objects of proof (*sādhya*) of all proponents of absolute positions (*ekāntavādin*).
Why is that [proof] established? It is because of [the reason] "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth.

By whom? He says: by those who have not examined the reality of the ultimate truth (*asamīkṣitatattvārthaiḥ*). This means by ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*)—those by whom the reality of the ultimate truth, characterized as the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitalakṣaṇa*), has not been properly examined because they have failed to remove superimpositions based on error.
Having done what? Having resorted to what? To worldly consensus (*lokapratīti*), that is, to the conceptualizing intellect whose object is duality.

Regarding this, some have said: "Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory knowledge," and so forth; such a definition of valid cognition is with respect to conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*), as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (1.5).
To the question, "Of what nature is it? he says: "It is considered valid cognition from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
How is there uncertainty (*anaikāntikatva*)? To this he says: "In one's own position," and so forth.
Then, in the manner imagined by him, the reason characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) exists not only in both positions (*pakṣa*) but also in the counter-position (*vipakṣa*).

Why? He says: because even before the production of the effect—that is, prior to its arising—it is possible without distinction (i.e., without any difference) for that cause, which is capable of producing it and possesses the power to generate the effect, to produce its own effect at a later time restricted to its own specific moment; where?
In both one's own position and the counter-position, namely, in those things whose natures are respectively momentary and non-momentary.

Regarding this, it has been argued by someone as follows: "If the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is eternal and was already capable of producing all future effects even prior [to their production], he would produce them all simultaneously, and even before that, and even before that again; thus, there would be no fixed temporal order for the arising of effects."

Thus [it was argued], but that has been refuted. How so? If action, characterized by consciousness and momentary, were capable of producing its own diversity at the very time of its own existence for the sake of generating its effect, it would produce it then and there. Furthermore, whatever other effect belongs to that action characterized by consciousness, let it produce that as well at the time of its own existence; thus, even in the view of momentariness, the determination of the time of the effect's production becomes impossible, because [the cause] produces its own fruit at that same time. Therefore, [the claim of momentariness] is not tenable with respect to such phenomena as "acting after having remained still," specific configurations, and purposeful causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

"Establishing what is already accepted" (iṣṭasiddhi) is "proving what is already proven" (siddhasādhana). Having established this [in the *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.20], regarding [the reasons] such as specific activity, structural configuration,
and causal efficiency, there is either the establishment of what is already accepted, or non-establishment, or doubt in the example.

These [reasons], such as "abiding before activity" (*sthitvā-pravṛtti*) and so forth, which are intended as reasons based on the nature of an effect, are not valid reasons; for even when these are present, only that which is [already] desired is established, resulting in the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddha-sādhana*).
"And the thesis is not established"—this is from the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*.

If, however, one seeks the production of an effect at a later time even from a capable momentary cause, how else could there be conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) for one who has risen after a long sleep due to previous practice? In that case, let it be sought [that an effect arises] from an eternal cause as well; this is not tenable, because "there is no production from an eternal [cause]" (*nityād utpatti-viśleṣāt*), according to the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.9).
Regarding the logical reason "because dependence is impossible":

one might object, "Surely a permanent entity, though capable at first, may later produce its own effect; yet since that very same [entity] produces the effect, it must perform that same action again in its subsequent state—how then can there be a cessation of the effect? To this it has been said: because the production of an effect restricted to its own specific time is possible; for if it were to perform that very same action again and again, the production of an effect restricted to its own specific time would not be possible.

Even in the case of the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikapakṣa*), everything is the same. To explain: if a lamp produces cognition in the cognizer by means of that very same nature (*svabhāva*) by which it produces soot elsewhere, then it would likewise produce that cognition in the soot, or else produce soot in the cognizer. If it is argued that this contradicts the essential nature of a cause that reaches the time of the effect—whether on a wall or at a window—the author replies with the words "And not," and so forth.

And it is not the case that the production of an effect is never contradicted by the existence of its own cause; for if there were a contradiction, it would be contradicted by the existence of the cause, just as the production of cold is contradicted by the existence of fire.
If you ask why the grasping of its own cause is not contradicted, it is because neither of the two types of contradiction exists here.

For there is no contradiction characterized by non-coexistence with its existence [i.e., the cause], because one does not observe the necessary cessation of any occurrence whose causes are unimpaired when another [the effect] is present; for even at the time of the production of a cloth, its causes—the threads—are perceived. Nor is there a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion, since the cognition of a gold bangle has [gold] as its cause.
For the contradiction between entities is of two kinds: the cognition of contradiction arises from the absence of something that has its causes complete when another thing is present,
as in the case of cold and hot sensations.
Or [they are contradictory] by virtue of having characteristics that exist through mutual exclusion, like existence and non-existence—
*Nyāyabindu* 3.72–75.

If [the object] is distinct from that [moment], this objection does not apply here: "By what means is the unity of the preceding and succeeding [moments] perceived? Since the answer has already been given, he asks: "In what way does it not exist? He says: because of contradiction, it exists only as non-momentary; the fault characterized by the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would not apply to the momentary.
Demonstrating that this [objection] has already been answered, he says: "Having determined," and so forth;
and concluding, he says: "Therefore, this is well said," and so forth, regarding the two successive stages of the preceding and following [arguments].

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Arcaṭa: "Existence (*sattva*) is pervaded by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); and since there is no other mode [of action] besides succession and simultaneity for that which performs such action, and since those two [succession and simultaneity] exclude it from the non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), they in turn exclude that causal efficiency; and since that [efficiency] is existence, by the maxim of the bird not seeing the shore, it [existence] takes hold of momentariness because of the absence of any other alternative. Therefore, how can it be certain that [existence] belongs to the momentary?"—showing that this same [argument] applies equally to the other position (the non-momentary), he says: "There may be existence... [in] succession and simultaneity," and so forth.

For effective action is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity, since there is no other possible mode; therefore, because those two—which pervade effective action—are incompatible with non-momentariness, they are excluded from it. Consequently, effective action itself, which is pervaded by them, is also excluded. Thus, the absence of all causal capacities—the definition of non-existence—is drawn out by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) in the case of non-momentariness, because two contradictory properties cannot coexist in one place.

Then, when a being has turned back from that [search] and remains among only those things which are momentary, it experiences their very nature; thus, there arises the ascertainment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—in the form of positive and negative concomitance—that "whatever exists is necessarily momentary. (pp. 146–47) Therefore, regarding the phrase "like one who does not see the shore," and so forth: it is said that when merchants aboard a ship release a bird with the hope, "Perhaps it will see the shore," and when, while wandering in all directions, it does not find the shore, it returns to the ship itself; this case should be understood in the same way.
Page 193 — *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*:

"Existence (*sattā*) would be the reason [for proving momentariness] because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not perceived in the heterogeneous instance (*vipakṣa*), the non-momentary; if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). || 22 ||

Whatever exists is all momentary; because in the opposite case (the non-momentary), causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradicted by [the impossibility of action occurring] either successively or simultaneously, existence— which is defined by that [efficiency]— by being excluded from it, establishes the subject as being such [momentary],
provided that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is ascertained there through the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding one's own position.

Exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa) occurs through the presence [of the reason] in the subject (pakṣa), and the presence in the subject occurs through exclusion from the counter-example; thus, there is mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) and a circularity (*cakraka*), because the very establishment of those two would be impossible.
