But surely, in the case of a non-momentary entity, there is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); otherwise, what would be the use of inference there? Any disagreement regarding that [causal efficiency] is refuted by the application of the argument that it would otherwise be impossible.
Both of these [objections] are incorrect.
"Existence might be the cause"—where [is it the sign]? To this he says: "in a non-momentary object"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Why? He says: because, in the case of the opposite [position], namely the momentary, there is no apprehension—and thus no cognition—from any source—of existence (*sattva*), which is pervaded by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is itself pervaded by succession and simultaneity.

This [opponent] could also say the following: "Existence, being excluded from the momentary through the exclusion of its own pervader [causal efficiency], must reside in the non-momentary, as there is no other alternative," provided that succession and simultaneity are the pervaders.

It might be thought: "The non-existence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the contrary case—the momentary—would be established if that [efficiency] were excluded from the non-momentary; otherwise, being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), how could it prove its absence there? Therefore, since causal efficiency is observed in the non-momentary through either succession or simultaneity, and yet it is not found there [in the momentary], [the argument holds]. To this, he says: "The pervader," and so forth.

If it is thought that the absence (*vyatireka*)— the exclusion— from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), namely the momentary, of that non-perception of succession and simultaneity which was adduced to prove the non-existence of the momentary is established, because the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) appearing in the eternal has been determined as being [exhausted] by either succession or otherwise (simultaneity)—

then the word "only" (*eva*), used in the sense of restriction, should be understood as following immediately after the phrase "because of the mention of causal efficiency," since particles have multiple meanings.

[Objection: "Let existence (*sattā*) then be the reason for non-momentariness; even so, the Jaina's primary position is undermined. To this he says: "It might be" (*syāt*), etc.—the meaning of this has already been explained. [The objection continues: "If the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), yet that [concomitance] is not established, then in that case, the reason must pertain to the momentary, since there is no other possible mode for a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*). [Objection: "How then can there be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*)? To this he says: "It might be," etc.
Causal efficiency is non-exclusive with respect to the present, or else it exists in both the subject and the counter-example among momentary things.
The non-existence of a sentient being [is established] from momentariness, and there is the cessation of a sentient being.
If [the entity] exists, then there is the observation of causal efficiency in that which is non-momentary.
He explains the *kārikā* with the words "whatever exists, all that," and so forth:

whatever exists and is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*), all that which exists is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "as if" (*iva*); it should be understood as following the word "momentary," meaning "as if momentary."
This is merely an illustration; for it is not by means of the verse itself that its capacity to convey meaning is described.
Why? He says: "In the case of the dissimilar instance," and so forth.

The "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*), in relation to the non-momentary, is the momentary; because in that [case], there is a contradiction with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity.

For instance: first of all, there is no gradual production of an object therein; for that would mean producing one [part] and then, by that very same [cause], producing another in succession—that is what "gradual production" entails. And such a thing is not possible even for that which, like a permanent entity, possesses a single partless nature, let alone for something momentary, in the absence of a supporting example.
Even for that which is momentary by its very nature, there is sequential action.

By this, the two effects—the immediate and the long-term awakening of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—of the waking consciousness are established, as stated by Prajñākara: "For the waking mind produces the vital breaths and so forth immediately [after it ceases], and it brings about awakening after deep sleep;
therefore..."

“If that cognition is the cause, or if it is the nature of the object’s production, or its effect—in every way, by it the arising of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is made known” (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra 1.5). Regarding this, the following is considered: if it is the cause, how can there be activity toward it again through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), given that “the arising of purposeful action” refers to two successive effects? Furthermore, if activity is not desired [immediately] after [the first cognition], why was it said: “Perception is a means of valid cognition because it prompts activity when repetition occurs”? And if it is not repetition, then why was it said: “From this [perception] inference arises first, and then the arising of that [purposeful action]”?

Therefore, just as in the case of the permanent [entity], there is no production of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) from a momentary entity either successively or simultaneously. To act upon many things at once by means of one would be as previously described; and since that is impossible for a non-momentary entity—as it was stated that even spatial differentiation is not possible for another [type of entity] if it possesses a single nature—[one might ask]: "Let there be no causal efficiency whatsoever in a momentary object; what is the fault? To this, he says: "Existence, which is defined by that [causal efficiency], being excluded from the momentary, establishes the thesis—that is, the probandum—as being non-momentary. This is logical.
He raises the objection regarding the simultaneous performance of a momentary [action] according to the view of Arcaṭa, in order to refute it, with the words "If," and so forth.

If the non-perception of the two pervaders—succession and simultaneity—which constitutes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), were determined as the exclusion from the non-momentary, then it would be logical that it establishes the subject (*pakṣa*) as being existent; yet this is not the case. By what reasoning is this so? In our own position, since succession and simultaneity are present in the non-momentary through the operation of perception, their non-perception therein is sublated by the operation of perception, and not otherwise.

If it is argued that "the subverting proof (bādhaka) is excluded from that very non-momentary which is the counter-example (vipakṣa) in relation to the momentary, and for that very reason it functions perceptually within its own position (svapakṣa)," [the author] replies here with the words "from the counter-example" and so forth: The exclusion of the pervader (vyāpaka) from the counter-example results in the perceptual functioning of that [pervader] within the subject (pakṣa), namely the momentary. In that case, the observation of the pervader in the subject implies its perceptual functioning, and by means of its perceptual functioning in the subject, there is the intended functioning [of the pervader]; thus, a circularity (cakraka) like a wheel revolves, characterized by mutual dependence. Since this is so, there would be no established determination (vyavasthiti) whatsoever for either of those two.

Regarding the two points—the direct perception [of the subject] and the exclusion [of the probans] from the counter-example—the proponent of permanence (nityavādī) offers this reply: "Not [is it] momentary," and so forth.

The word *nanu* here signifies excellence; the syntactical supplement (*upaskāra*) is that there is direct perception which grasps that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—namely, the performance of a purpose through either successive or simultaneous action—in the case of what is non-momentary.
Of what nature is it? He says: it is "real" (*satya*), meaning non-false or non-constructed.

For instance, this person, perceiving an object through the senses, perceives it as persisting through the three periods of time; otherwise, he would not perceive even that which lasts for a single moment. Why then does he rely on inference in that case? If it is argued that "the object is neither perception nor inference," he replies here: "In that regard, there is a misconception among the Buddhists (*saugata*); the superimposition of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇika*) is being refuted."

Why? He says: "Otherwise"—that is, by way of the non-existence of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatvābhāva*)—there is the impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Because of its employment—that is, because of the utterance of the sentence that establishes it—the cognizer understands this other explanation: "Whatever exists, all that is momentary," according to the Buddhist; while the proponent of permanence [says] it is "non-momentary"; [and thus] it is understood from the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*).

In both cases, he says this: just as "sound is impermanent because it is one or the other of the subject or the similar instance" is a formulated [inference], so too [the arguments] such as "it exists," "because it is a mountain," or "there is a sublation in the dissimilar instance," etc., are formulated with respect to the momentary; and in relation to that, the non-momentary is the other dissimilar instance.
The remainder is as before;
the Teacher himself refutes that pair, saying "it is improper," and so forth,
which has already been explained.

If it is argued that there is indeed the operation of perception regarding the momentary, and therefore there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), to this he replies: "But there is a circularity (*cakraka*) because of the repeated occurrence [of the same argument]. What is the point of this? With the intention of asking what operation exists by which this proof of yours is established, the opponent asks: "Surely, in the case of the non-momentary, since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible, there is no perception whatsoever that could serve as a witness."
Since the word "nanu" has the sense of an objection, the Teacher gives the reply:
"That which was said— namely, that there is direct perception of causal efficiency in a non-momentary thing— is true, that is, not false."

If it is argued that the presentation of a reason (*hetūpanyāsa*) is therefore useless in that case, he says here: "Misconception" (*vipratipatti*), etc. It might be thought that [the reason] is not purposeless—because for a single entity, there is a contradiction in having multiple natures—and thus even there, that [reason] does not apply. To this, he says: "In its own nature" (*svabhāve*), etc.

In that which is by nature unerring, one perceives what is erroneous; in that which is free from conceptual construction, one perceives the conceptually constructed; in certainty, one perceives doubt; and in the eternal, one perceives the non-eternal entity.
(23) For an eternal substance, the occurrence of a non-eternal nature is impossible.

Without a single nature consisting of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), natures such as error and its opposite would be devoid of intrinsic being (*niḥsvabhāva*). If a difference in nature were to constitute a distinction [between entities], what is the use of postulating a distortion of cognition? Whether an entity is characterized by cognition or something else, such as the moon and so forth, it exists only when its own nature—that is, its essential form—is present.

In what kind of state? In that which is "without delusion" (*avibhrama*), meaning pure through the discernment of delusion; for [the object] is deluded by being characterized by the clarity of true consciousness and so forth, and thus possesses delusion (*savibhrama*) through the duality of forms such as the apprehended object and so on. Likewise, the term "conceptual" (*savikalpa*)—referring to a nature (*svabhāva*) appearing as capable of association with verbal expression—is understood here as "free from conceptual construction" (*vikalpa-kalpanā-rahitah bhāvah*).

Alternatively, the word order may be construed as: "in the conceptual," meaning "possessing differentiation," as it has manifestations such as blue and so forth, while "non-conceptual" (*akalpa*) means "undifferentiated."

Likewise, regarding the doubt "Is this a post or a person," the existence [of the object] occurs in the form of a mental representation—either as "there is no doubt regarding its nature" or "this is a present doubt"—and this is how the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) should be explained here by way of implication (*kāku*).

Alternatively, the notion that an impermanent entity is perceived or known as permanent within its own permanent nature, or conversely, that a permanent entity is so perceived within an impermanent one, is refuted by this very point—even for the Vaiśeṣika and others who maintain an absolute distinction between the natures of the permanent and the impermanent. For even in their view, there is a contradiction in the non-arising of doubt, since their position consists of either the ascertainment or the non-ascertainment of an object.

He demonstrates the meaning of the verse along with its justification: "The substance possessing the aforementioned characteristics is eternal," meaning it persists through different periods of time; thus, what is to be proven here is "transformative eternity" (*pariṇāminityatva*), because no other [kind of eternity] is accepted.
Why? He says: "Because an impermanent nature is untenable," that is, because a purely (ekānta) non-eternal form is impossible.
This is an elliptical indication; therefore, it should also be understood that "substance is impermanent because a permanent intrinsic nature is untenable.

Even while there is transformation, there is permanence; the meaning is that [permanence] consists in the nature of arising, passing away, and persistence, for an immutable permanence is not accepted.

If it is argued that because no substance other than form and so forth is perceived, it does not exist, and therefore the reason [of the argument] suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), the author replies with the verse beginning "bhrānti" and so on.

By the word "ādi" (etc.), a *dvandva* compound is formed with "bhrānti" and the others; then, by the word "svabhāvāḥ" (intrinsic natures), a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound is formed. [The meaning is: "Those [entities], such as error and the rest, would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
without what [would they exist]? To this he says: "Self-cognition" (*svasaṃvedana*) and so forth.
Without a single common nature, what would it be? It is external substance, which is perceptible—that is, graspable by direct perception (pratyakṣa).

Furthermore, what is it? It is self-cognition (svasaṃvedana); and this, although it is internal perception, is appropriately applied here as a qualification because of its non-deviation [from the object].
Why? To this he says: "In another aggregate," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: just as there is a mutual difference between form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] in a non-exclusive manner, if that same [difference] were to exist between error (*vibhrama*) and its opposite, then that undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be unavoidable.
Since reality is not established in such a way, the implication is that [these phenomena] would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
If it is argued that, therefore, there is a single entity appearing as error, its opposite, and so forth; to this he replies: "Because of the difference in intrinsic nature," and so on.

If the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) of an entity is accepted as being what constitutes its differentiation, then what [remains]—given that both internally and externally, cognition consists of forms that are both unitary and manifold? Thus, by means of the conceptualization of error, the substance (*dravya*) is established.
Therefore, that which was stated by someone—that "the apprehension of the own-form (*svarūpa*) is through itself" (Pramāṇavārttika 1)—is refuted.
Thus, in that regard, if [the object] possesses the nature of being both one and many, our desired conclusion is established;

however, if it were otherwise, then the statement "all things are devoid of intrinsic nature" would be nothing more than the babbling of a fool or a manifestation of an unknown meaning, because of the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (p. 30): "The definition of valid cognition is that which reveals an object not yet known."
"All phenomena are empty because they lack intrinsic nature"—
this is from verse 1 of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*.
Therefore, it is shown that they are devoid of intrinsic nature because they are empty of defining characteristics.
— Prajñāpāramitopadeśa 2.215;
that which was just mentioned.

Another [opponent] says: "The selflessness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-nairātmya) does not lead to a fault, because it is accepted [by us]. To him, he replies: "By which [means], 'an entity' and so forth...
if that cognition by which non-existence would be an object of knowledge does not exist in reality, [then how can there be such a cognition?]"

The establishment of one's own position would not be sublated, because no contradictory [evidence] is perceived. One cannot possibly establish the selflessness of phenomena both externally and internally through valid cognition, because that would involve a contradiction;
for in the absence of valid cognition, there can be no realization of selflessness in the ultimate sense.
Therefore, the apprehension of existence indeed occurs; this establishes non-absolutism (*anekānta*) because of the non-apprehension of what is contradictory to its own nature.

To the question, "By which cognition is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) determined? he says: "Non-existence is the exclusion of everything; and if that cognition [of it] does not exist in reality"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

In this regard, the refutation is as follows: "The establishment of its own object" means that the establishment of both [the cognition and the object]—that is, their attainment of self-nature (*ātmalābha*), which is to say the establishment of the cognition and the cognized—would not be sublated;
it would not be negated.

It is thought that even if there were the state of the apprehended and the apprehender, the establishment of the non-existence of that [state] would not be prevented; or alternatively, when the Buddhist is himself devoid of the cognition of non-existence—which he has accepted—then, like the son of a barren woman, he could not state any sublation regarding the establishment or the cognition of the two self-objects (svārtha) accepted by the Jaina. Having spoken thus, how could he not be a contradiction of his own words? Thus, the cognition of the two self-objects would not be sublated, as it is established in the world.

If it is argued that "in that case, there is no validity as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in reality, because of the statement [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*]: 'Validity exists through conventional usage' (PV 1.6)"; to this he replies: If that cognition by which non-existence is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is a means of valid cognition, it is not so in reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—but rather from the perspective of conventional usage in the form of relative truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Here, the refutation begins with the words "for its own sake" (*svārtha*), etc.

The intended meaning here is as follows: [the opponent might argue that] since the cognition of non-existence arises from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the cognition of existence would likewise arise [from such a source];
or else, [they might argue that] non-existence established by a non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is not ultimately real, and therefore existence remains in its original state.

To this, he states the reason: "because of the non-perception of the contradictory," that is, because of the non-perception—meaning the non-cognition—of the absolute non-existence of that which is contradictory [to existence].
He demonstrates the meaning of the verse with the words "externally" and so forth:
a Buddhist is not at all able to establish through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the selflessness of phenomena both externally and internally—that is, the emptiness of everything.
Why? He says: because of contradiction; that is, because there is a mutual opposition between the non-existence of everything and the existence of the means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that, therefore, it ought to be understood through non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), he says in response: since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is an absence of the realization of selflessness (*nairātmya*), in what [condition] would that occur?

He asks: "In the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what follows from that? He replies: the perception of existence (*bhāvopalabdhi*) certainly occurs; thus, the establishment of the non-exclusive nature (*anekāntasiddhi*) is achieved.

Now, it is not the case that [the existence of] an entity is established solely by the perception of its exclusivity (ekānta); for in this context, "nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth refer to the non-perception of exclusivity, which is contradictory to a nature characterized by non-exclusivity (*anekānta*).

As for what was stated regarding the "perception of an entity" (*bhāvopalabdhi*): there is indeed the perception of blue and other such things, but how can it be said that "this belongs to the entity"? Because there is no proof for its being the true nature of that entity.

If it is argued that "apprehension itself is the proof of its validity," we say no; for even in a dream, that [apprehension] possesses the same nature, and thus there is no ultimate distinction between what is real and what is otherwise.

Nor is there any difference in that apprehension caused by the presence or absence of a sublater (bādhaka) in some cases, because the absence of a sublater is established only in its entirety [in the waking state].
Nor is there a distinction based on causal efficiency (arthakriyā), because that is absent in both the eternal and the non-eternal, and because it exists even in dreams.
If it is argued that this [cognition] does not possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), how is it different from another? Because of its appearance;
for in the other case as well, the absence of sublation is the same, as is the perception of blue and so forth.
Because there is no evidence to establish that an entity possesses the nature of an entity,
whereas its perception does exist.
The nature of existence is the specific characteristic of apprehension.

Furthermore, regarding both of these one-sided views, [the causal efficiency] existing in a dream-like state— if that [efficiency] were also of the nature of an entity arising from within that [dream], there would be an infinite regress because of the requirement for another [entity] within that as well.
If it is argued that [the cognition] arises from an object, there is mutual dependence;
if it arises from itself, let jars and other things be likewise, since they too cause satisfaction; and for the same reason, let that [cognition] be so even in a dream, as there is no distinction.
"Therefore, there is no such thing as the apprehension of an entity"; to this he replies with the words "false," etc.:

because it arises from another causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the causal efficiency has the nature of an entity, and because the causal efficiency [arises] from the entity, the entity has the nature of a causal efficiency.

If you maintain that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is of the nature of an existent entity, then you— by means of words claiming to be "knowledge of reality"— are a Vidūṣaka who, alas, undermines the very proofs for illusory objects, non-existence, impermanent cognition, and variegated mental continua. (25)

O friend, for one who perceives identity between their own consciousness and the cognition of an object through delusion—addressed thus with the word "friend"—how can there be a contradiction between the produced and the unproduced, or the gross and the subtle, within that single [consciousness]? In that case, what offense has been committed by the external object against one who, through false cognition, perceives the internal object of knowledge in its entirety as either ultimately real or otherwise? Why should it be rejected? For, since the understanding of the reality of affirmation and negation is indistinguishable from contradiction in the case of an absolute false position (*mithyaikānta*).

Therefore, this person—who, through absolute delusion, desires to establish both reality and falsity internally and externally—does not defeat the proponent who asserts the affirmation and negation of the momentary and its opposite, because he fails to provide a valid proof for his position.

This is its meaning: "cognitions and words" (*jñānagiraḥ*) refers to cognitions and speech; the mention of "words" is intended to indicate external objects by way of illustration. You, my dear friend, are a reviler of those principles, of those cognitions and words, and of the true nature of those principles, objects, and meanings—since you are a follower of the Sugata (*saugata*). Therefore, you are a "reviler" (*vidūṣaka*), one who brings about subversion, because you revile the true nature of cognition as it is accepted [by us] regarding external objects;
for the same logic applies in both cases.

For instance: just as it is argued that because pillars and such appear [to consciousness], they must possess ultimate reality in the waking state, so too, by that very same logic, if cognitions possessed ultimate reality, then external pillars and such would also possess it; thus, there is no entry into the doctrine of the sole reality of cognition (*jñānaikāntavāda*). This is contradictory to the statement: "The supreme non-dual Nāga."

Or, just as objects such as jars in a dream—though their forms are superimposed by appearance—are not ultimately real, so too it is said that other things are likewise [unreal]. Thus, if waking jars and the like are unreal despite appearing, what confidence can there be in cognitions? Therefore, the abandonment of external objects is logical, just as in the case of the theory of external objects (*bahir-artha-vāda*).
And so, how could an opponent who maintains the doctrine of cognition alone (*jñāna-vādin*) remain?
All the rest here should be stated as before.

If it is argued that, like external objects, consciousness (*vijñāna*) also lacks ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), to this he replies: "False" (*mithyā*), and so forth. Those things for which there is an appearance (*ābhā*) or manifestation of an object are "object-appearances" (*arthābhāni*); they are not stable, meaning they are unstable or momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Furthermore, those which are both object-appearances and unstable, and moreover those cognitions (*jñāna*) themselves—those false cognitions whose diverse (*citra*) or manifold continuums (*santāna*) you, my dear, establish; therefore, you are a refuter (*dūṣaka*), a debunker (*vidūṣaka*), because it is impossible for them to be established as having ultimate reality if they consist solely of error (*vibhramaikānta*).
It should be understood that ultimate reality exists solely as a manifestation—
page 1, note 8.
If pillars and the like, which possess manifest forms,
are non-existent, then...
Even the abandonment of knowledge [is taught] by the Buddhist Vijñānavādin for the sake of awakening.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Of self-cognition," and so forth.

Regarding that self-cognition which belongs to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), what is its relation to the cognition of objects—that is, to the grasping of external objects? It is through a cognition that is erroneous, like a dream, having as its object non-existent things; for the Buddhist who perceives identity (*tādātmya*)—the state of having those two erroneous natures as its own essence.

This is what is meant: just as the cognition of an object—whether it be a cognition of its true nature or an erroneous one—is itself self-cognition, so too, if that self-cognition were either erroneous or otherwise [non-erroneous], then for one who perceives its identity with the cognition of the object (which may be erroneous), how could there be a contradiction between two properties such as "produced" and "unproduced," or "gross" and "subtle," regarding a single external entity? This is because, like self-cognition, the cognition of that [object] is also considered non-erroneous; thus, self-cognition is held to be non-erroneous.

Why does this same explanation not apply to the appearance of contradictory properties even regarding an external object? For one who perceives identity—that is, oneness—between self-awareness and the awareness of the object through an appearance of the external, whether erroneous or non-erroneous, how could there be a contradiction between those two in a single locus? This is because the superimposition of contradictory properties cannot be prevented even in the case of cognition. [Otherwise,] there would be the consequence of redundancy with [the statement] "In the absence of error regarding its own nature, [it is] erroneous," etc. (Siddhiviniścaya 6.23).

For one who perceives the identity of that [external object] with its erroneous cognition of the object, and who—through that erroneous internal cognition within his own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*)—perceives the internal knowable (the nature of consciousness) as either erroneous or otherwise, there is no obstruction whatsoever, nor any fault caused by an external object, on account of which the Buddhist might reject the external object; this is the connection [of the sentence], with the case-ending changed from the preceding doubt. This was stated immediately before.

By means of the preceding verse, he reflects thus upon his own self-awareness: "Let [the opponent] perceive the external object as it exists— whether as a whole internal object of cognition through false intellect, or as something ultimately delusory or otherwise— as the other perceives it, for there is no distinction [between our respective cognitions]."

One might think: "If [cognition] apprehends an external object by means of that [form], how could it be false? If it were so, it would be contradictory to say that it does not apprehend anything by means of that [form], yet it does apprehend it and is nonetheless false. To this, he says: "That," and so forth.

Regarding those two—the affirmation and negation of the internal object of cognition and the external object (meaning: the affirmation and negation of the internal and the external)—there is the realization of their reality, which is the awareness of their true nature. Because there is no distinction in the contradiction [involved] in the case of an absolute [monistic] view (*mithyaikānta*), the intention is as follows: just as in that absolute view there is no realization of any affirmation in reality, so too there is none of negation; thus, in the absence of its negation, that absolute view cannot be established by means of awareness.
If it is false, then since there is no negation of external objects, the doctrine of the exclusivity of consciousness (*vijñānaikāntavāda*) would be established.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, this [person]," and so forth.

Since it is thus, therefore this follower of the Sugata (*saugata*), desiring to establish [his position], from what [source] does he do so? He says: "From that"—namely, from the reasoning (*nyāya*) which establishes the existence of cognition (*buddhi*).
"What does he wish to establish? He says: "Both internally and externally.

The meaning of "as if" (*iva*) should be understood as occurring after the word "internally" (*antaḥ*), as if following a different syntactical order; thus, the reality (*tattva*) is "as if internal" and its ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*) is "external."

For instance—having established the lack of distinction between dream and waking states, and even while refuting external objects, one must nevertheless admit that cognition (*buddhi*) is of an ultimate nature (*paramārtharūpa*), because of the formulation of the definitions of ultimate and conventional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The sense is that once this is admitted, the logical principle applies to external objects as well; it cannot be warded off by the king’s rod [of punishment].
What does one who desires that [external object] do? To this he says: "Whether momentary or otherwise," and so forth.

The momentary and the non-momentary: he who is habitually a proponent of these two, or of their respective positions, stating their affirmation and negation respectively, does not defeat [the opponent]. Just as a proponent of the affirmation of the momentary position establishes the momentary position through his own logic, while a proponent of its negation negates the momentary position by pointing out its defects—so too is this [case].
If it is argued that, "In that case, cognition is as mistaken regarding its own nature as it is regarding external objects," to this he says: "And falsity..."

Thus, this [argument] follows the pattern of "internal" and "external"; desiring to establish [the position] by himself, through what means? Through the error of absolute [one-sidedness], the rest is as before.

However, this is the distinction: just as the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādī), while establishing his own position through conceptualization, does not abandon the opposing position, or while negating the opposing position, undermines his own position by refuting the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends permanence—so too does this [proponent].
Alternatively, "the illumination of an unknown object" is the ultimate definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
whereas "non-discrepant cognition" is the conventional one; this remains so even when the existence of external objects is accepted.

If it is argued: "The proponent of the negation of the momentary alternative has not stated a formal proof (*vidhi*) for the negation of the alternative other than the momentary; whereas for this [other] proponent, such a proof exists. Therefore, how can it be said that he does not defeat the former proponent? To this, he replies with the words beginning "In the proof" (*sādhane*).

The intended meaning here is as follows: In a system that maintains that "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) is ultimately real while external objects are its opposite, even though something other than representation—just like representation itself—is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no presentation of a logical reason (*hetu*) in proving "that-only" (*tanmātra*). This is because the thesis (*pakṣa*) is sublated by perception. As it has been said: "There is no protection for that [thesis] by means of reasons; for that which is destroyed once it has arisen [is gone]. Because the employment of the proof—the statement of the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of "that-only"—is prohibited and refuted, and because that [proof] is useless once [the thesis] has been refuted.
In the view that even "mere-cognition" (tanmātra) lacks ultimate reality just like external objects, the means of proof (sādhana) is likewise of the same nature.
For that which is non-existent cannot be a logical mark (liṅga) for that which is non-existent, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga);
consequently, one considers that there is a prohibition against employing such a means of proof, since its employment would be futile.

Alternatively, because its application is prohibited, and because that statement [of the opponent] is refuted by itself as being mere illusion, this [proponent] does not defeat the proponent of that [view]; thus,
for the Vijñānavādin,
[the external object] is not ultimately real (*aparamārthasat*).
The object is also representation-only,
and representation-only is also [representation-only].

Regarding this, another person says: "It is not the negation of consciousness itself that is being stated with respect to what appears as consciousness—which would result in this fault—but rather, it is only the superimposition of ultimate reality upon things such as jars, which are the subject of dispute, that is being refuted by means of the example of the hairs seen by one suffering from ophthalmia. This [objection] too is refuted by the following.

For instance: if the ultimate existence of such things as the hairs seen by one with cataracts were established in some way from the perspective of ultimate reality, then that very [example] would constitute a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) for the reason intended to exclude them; thus, because the application of the proof is prohibited due to such deviation, the proof cannot be employed.

If, on the other hand, it is not so established, then there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of any proof by that [reason] in that case, and the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Therefore, he says: "In the proof," and so forth.
Because a means of proof that is not pervaded by the probandum is unfit for application,
[this is known] through valid cognition from its appearing as consciousness.
If, by means of valid cognition, there is no ultimate existence of the hairs and so forth perceived by one with cataracts, then,
in the case of those hairs and so forth seen by one with cataracts—

The absence of that [object] is accepted therein by the conventionalist (*vyavahārin*) who possesses his own object of proof; therefore, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that [absence] by it. If so, then for the Buddhist (*saugata*), since perception is pervaded by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which is accepted as ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*) among cognitions, whatever is perceived is ultimately real, just like self-awareness. And since the external object is perceived during the waking and dreaming states, [the Buddhist] would be a proponent of the absolute truth of external objects. Now, it might be argued: "He does not accept that self-awareness is ultimately real"; [we reply: it is the same, for even the conventionalist does not accept the absence of that [self-awareness] therein.

If it is asked, "How is there a distinction between that which is real and that which is otherwise? [we reply: How is it that for the other [the unreal], there is no difference in the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding both ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*)? Or, if that [cognition] lacks ultimate existence, how is it distinguished from external objects such that the external object is abandoned but not that [cognition]? This [proponent] relies on the establishment of the absence of all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), yet does not accept its ultimate existence; otherwise, even if the awareness of another were not ultimately existent, the external object would still be established through it.
By this, the claim that the pervasion of the reason is established by an example accepted by the opponent is refuted; rather,
it is accepted by those engaged in conventional discourse.
Self-awareness possesses ultimate reality;
even if it were not ultimately real, the desired conclusion would still be established from it.

Furthermore, even if a practitioner were to accept the non-existence of that [external object] in a particular case without relying on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this does not entail its non-existence everywhere; for since the suspicion of ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*) regarding some external object would not have been removed, how could the mind of an intelligent person be fixed solely upon the Buddhist doctrine? Otherwise, just as one might accept the absence of omniscience in a certain individual and thereby conclude its absence everywhere, so too would one's animosity toward the Mīmāṃsaka position be groundless.
Thus he says, "In the proof," and so forth.
For the Buddhist, the term "that" (sa) is meaningless, because the application of a proof is precluded by the fact that its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) is doubtful.

[Objection: "If the object were perceived just like cognition, then it would be correct that both exist or do not exist without distinction; however, since it is only cognition that is perceived—because blue and so forth are necessarily perceived together with it due to their being of the same nature as it—[the object does not exist]. To this, he says: "Simultaneous perception," and so on:
"Because of its being of the nature of cognition, and because of the necessity of simultaneous perception, there might be a difference between blue and the cognition thereof."
If it is argued that non-simultaneous perception is unestablished because they are seen separately, [we reply:

in the proof of absolute non-difference based on the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), since either error or direct perception would be absent, no erroneous cognition could ever exist; for it would follow that direct perception is by nature invariably free from error, like deep sleep.
Furthermore, since blue and its cognition are observed both externally and internally, how is the rule of simultaneous perception established?

If [the reason] is "because those whose vision is fixed on a single object simultaneously perceive that object even when they do not perceive another's cognition," how can there be such a restriction? For if there were a rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) for things existing in a single moment, it would follow that the entire world constitutes a single continuum (*ekasantāna*), since they arise through their own self-cognition.

Furthermore, if the reason is "the rule of being perceived by a single cognition," it is unproven (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because it is possible for blue to be perceived simultaneously by multiple cognitions, and because there is no prohibition against many substances being perceived by a single cognition.

If, on the other hand, it is an "unperceived non-existence" (*asahānupalambha*), what is the distinction? It would be a mere non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) that neither establishes the probandum nor the probans, like [the non-existence of] a hare's horn or a donkey's horn. Because the definition of the comprehension of one object through another belongs to cognition—just as in the case of a single, constant error—there is a rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), which is a rule of perception occurring at the same time, between blue and its object, or between blue and the cognition of blue. This rule has been put forward by the opponent for the sake of cultivating the notion of their non-difference. From this logical mark (*liṅga*), there would be difference—that is, distinctness or manifoldness—between blue and the cognition thereof; thus is the connection [of the argument], by way of repetition.

Because that restriction, when analyzed through reasoning, results in a state of difference; therefore, since its establishment follows from that, this [argument] is considered a contradictory means of proving non-difference.
For it is not logical that there could be a simultaneous perception of blue and yellow when only blue is perceived. Thus, in the case of unity, the sevenfold [analysis] does not apply.
For a Buddhist Vijñānavādin, by what means can the distinctness of an object from its cognition be established, given that the object is necessarily perceived simultaneously with the cognition?

For there is a simultaneous perception of the object, such as blue, together with the cognition, and not separately from the cognition—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 3.388. Here, the subject (*dharmin*) consists of the form of blue and its cognition; their non-difference is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); and the reason (*hetu*) is the aforementioned rule of simultaneous perception.
In the Master’s formulation, it is precisely such a meaning of "reason" (hetu) that is intended;
[the term] "in difference" (bhede) is therefore redundant. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 567)
Because of the necessity of simultaneous apprehension, there is no proof of difference [between the object and its cognition].

If it is argued: "Surely, even though there is no difference between the two moons, that restriction [of simultaneous perception] holds; how then can this be pervaded by difference?"—it has been stated here that "there would be no simultaneous perception, as in the case of other things. Having explained that the word *saha* means simultaneity, and having raised an objection regarding an alternative meaning for that term, he says [in response], refuting it: "If it is non-perception without [the other]... (*asahānupalambhaśced*).

This is its meaning: "non-apprehension together" (*sahānupalambha*) means apprehension separately (*pṛthagupalambha*) by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). This [separate apprehension] is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*), which expresses a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and not an exclusion, because the former would entail the aforementioned consequence. When there is a connection [with the negative], "non-apprehension together" is the absence of separate apprehension; it is "apprehension together" (*sahopalambha*), since the word *saha* has multiple meanings—the word "if" (*cet*) indicating the intention of the opponent.

Regarding this, the refutation is that the reason—defined as "simultaneous perception"—is unestablished (*asiddha*) for this point. Why? He says: because of the observation (*īkṣaṇāt*) that the blue object and the cognition thereof are seen separately;
for instance, in the cognizer, cognition is perceived through the assertion of "I" (*ahamahamikayā*), whereas elsewhere, objects such as a jar are perceived even at the same time.

Likewise, when an object is remembered at one time and the memory occurs at another, if that memory were without an object, there would be no inference [of the object], because the relation was not grasped at that [present] time;
and since the relation was grasped previously when the object existed, it would follow that the object must exist even at the time of the old man's [memory].
In the case of inferring future death and so forth from signs such as *ariṣṭa*, the manifestation of the inference and the object of inference as distinct in time is already established,
even though there is unity in the case of erroneous cognition.

Regarding the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), the venerable Śubhagupta says: "This reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because in common usage the word 'together' (*saha*) never occurs without another [thing];
therefore, this reason is contradictory if there is simultaneous cognition."
Again, he himself says: "If the word 'together' (saha) means 'identical,' then the reason is unestablished (asiddha).
For instance, in the case of watching actors, the moon, or wrestlers, there is certainly not apprehension by one person alone;
for even when blue is apprehended, the apprehensions of that [blue] belonging to other mental continua (anyasantāna) are not apprehended."

And when all moments of consciousness of all living beings are perceived by the Omniscient One, how then could the rule of "cognition by one [person] alone" (ekopalambha) be established? Furthermore, the restriction to cognition by one is established only if there is a negation of cognition by others;
however, such a negation of cognition by others is impossible, because affirmation and negation cannot apply to that which is remote by nature (svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa).

Now, if the word "simultaneous" (*saha*) is intended to mean "at the same time," then the reason is in every respect inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the Buddha’s object of knowledge, the mind, and the mental factors (*citta-caitta*). For instance, it is well known that although there is a rule of simultaneous perception between the mind of another continuum (*santānāntara-citta*)—which is the object of the Blessed Buddha’s cognition—and that Buddha-cognition itself, there is nonetheless a difference (*nānātva*) between them. Likewise, even though mental states and mental factors are perceived simultaneously, they are not one and the same; therefore, the reason is inconclusive.

...It might be argued: "Even if presence in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is not certain, it is nevertheless doubtful; therefore, the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika) because its exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful" (*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 567–69). [Thesis:
There is no non-difference between blue and the cognition thereof, because they are necessarily perceived together.
Because [the reason] is contradictory, unestablished, doubtful, lacking negative concomitance, or lacking positive concomitance— Nyāyabindu 3.83.
Śābarabhāṣya on Bṛhatī,
Pañcikā 1.1.5.
Śāṅkara Bhāṣya on the Bhāmatī, 2.2.28.
Yogasūtra-tattvavaiśāradī 4.14; Nyāyakaṇikā, p. 264.
Aṣṭaśa° Aṣṭasa° pṛ 242; Prameyaka° pṛ 79;
Nyāyakumu° pṛ 122.
In a place such as the ground, etc., [as stated in] *Sanmati-ṭīkā* p. 352 and *Syādvāda-ratnākara* p. 152.
Of recollection regarding the past and the present.
Inference would not arise because of this [lack of a relationship];
by this, the rule of simultaneous perception is also considered, since it is absent everywhere.

Now, if it is argued that the activity of cognition does not occur apart from its own nature, and therefore this fault does not arise—[we reply: it has already been stated that its activity is observed elsewhere as well, such as in external objects like a jar. Furthermore, if the non-difference between blue and its cognition were not made an object of experience by that very [cognition], what would be the point of adducing the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*)? Moreover, the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*) has also been considered by us elsewhere.

The claim that there is no difference between the subject (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), and the inference itself—on the grounds that their non-distinct cognition establishes a separate apprehension—is refuted by this [argument]. This is because the word "together" (*saha*) denotes a single object; thus, the restriction to the apprehension of a single cognition alone is what constitutes the "restriction of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyama*). Alternatively, since both [subject and property] are apprehended, the particle *syāt* here functions as a conditional; therefore, it includes the remaining faults such as those concerning the logical reason (*hetu*) and so forth.
Explaining the verse concerning the cognition and the object, he says: "Simultaneous apprehension," and so forth.

Regarding the question—"What is the connection with the words 'of the blue and its cognition' (*nīlataddhiyoḥ*) which will be mentioned later, when the absolute non-difference is being established on the basis of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*), that is, the rule of simultaneous apprehension?"—he says: "By the word 'error,' etc.

By the word "error" (*bhrānti*), even error is included because of the statement that [cognition] is valid (*pramā*) by virtue of its connection [to reality]; thus, a delusion (*vibhrama*) is understood to exist within the object of inference (*anumeya*) for the inference of the absolute non-difference of the blue and its cognition.

Since it is stated in the *Nyāyabindu* (1.10) that "in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is direct perception and non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*)," there would be no erroneous cognition—whether of one of those two [the object and its cognition] or of the direct perception itself—due to the absence of error when they are not distinct, or when [error occurs] elsewhere. Consequently, for one who desires gain, there is the destruction of the very root;
for one who seeks to establish their distinction by means of inference, inference itself is lost.

Why is there an absence of that? To this he says: "By its absolute... and so forth. Because of that restriction—namely, that absolute distinction (*tadekānta*) between error and direct perception, which is an absolute difference—the nature of direct perception, which is self-cognizing and immediate, is established as being distinct and free from error through its common, indistinct manifestation; for this reason, the following is stated: when error is non-different from direct perception, then it is that very [perception] itself.

Whatever is non-different from something else becomes that very thing, just as, for example, the nature of direct perception itself; and since error is non-different from that [perception], it follows that there would be no erroneous cognition anywhere because of the absence of such [a distinct error]—this being the reason for the consequence that error would be excluded from direct perception. To illustrate this point, he says: "like deep sleep."

One who is overcome by deep sleep is in a state of *suṣupti* (deep slumber); it is just like that, and one thinks in this way: [if] there were no distinction between error and direct perception, then that very [error] would be that [perception]. It would follow that there is merely a common, clear form, devoid of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and lacking the protection of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And such is not the position accepted by the opponent.

The meaning is that, because inference is accepted [as a valid means of knowledge], there is indeed a distinction between erroneous cognition and direct perception; since the rule [of their co-existence] exists [only for the latter], the logical reason is contradictory (*viruddha*).

By this, the explanation should be seen as follows: "Because of the necessity of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*), there would be a distinction between blue and the cognition thereof" (p.
82, note 4).
Because of the simultaneous perception of erroneous cognition.
Error is indeed directly perceived through direct perception.
Showing that perception is indeed an error, he states "blue," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the meaning obtained from the particle *eva*.

To the question "Where is this seen? he says: "Of blue and its cognition, externally and internally"—meaning blue is external and its cognition is internal. By the word "and" (ca), he indicates that at other times there are the remembered object and the inferred object, and at other times there are remembrance and inference.
To the question "What follows from this? he says: "From what," and so forth.
The meaning is that the reason—namely, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*)—is not established from any [valid] means of knowledge (*māna*).

Demonstrating its lack of establishment by another method, he says: "For those persons whose gaze is fixed—that is, directed all at once (*sakṛt*) and simultaneously (*ekahelayā*)—upon a single object such as a dancer (*nartakī*), even though they do not perceive the cognitions of others, but rather only perceive those specific persons, since they see both those persons and their objects, how could there be a rule of simultaneous apprehension?
The word *syāt* is supplied by the particle *iti*.

[Objection: But if that cognition is not perceived, how is it known that "this is its object"? [Response: Because of such statements as, "The perception of a relation residing in two [terms]" (*Prakaraṇapāda-vārtikālaṅkāra* 2.1), or because people are seen to act toward it, it is determined that this object has been made the object of that cognition. If that is so, then by inference it is understood that whatever is perceived by one person is likewise perceived by another; and thus, from the observation of similar activity in both, the perception of a common object is established.

If it is argued that because inference has a universal as its object, there can be no perception of a single individual object—otherwise, from the sight of a body covered by a cloak of horripilation, there would be the apprehension of a single pleasure [in all men]—that is incorrect. For even animals are seen to perceive a female animal desired by themselves as being desired by others, and they are observed to associate with them based on the understanding: "She is of the same kind as she who is desired by us, so she is desired by others. Such an understanding would be impossible if there were no perception of a single object.

If it is asked, "How do they understand it in that way? the answer is: "Because of the determination of a specific effect. Otherwise, how could the statement, "In every respect, the relationship between the signifier and the signified is indeed accepted when there is a determination of that specific [effect]," be appropriate? Nor is this an absolute rule that only a universal is to be inferred based on similarity with the example (*dṛṣṭāntasādharmya*), for it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.26): "The wise person should state only the reason (*hetu*) itself."

Or let it be that there is no certain cognition to the effect that "whatever object this person perceives, another person perceives that very same one"; nevertheless, since there is no denial by another of that perception, the restriction [of the object] remains doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*). If it is argued that the restriction is established because the cognition is devoid of any perception of another [observer], then [the objection follows]: in that case, when a sprout is perceived as distinct from a seed inside a rat-hole, the operation of that [seed] is not [perceived] there;

therefore, just as the operation of a cause might be possible for an effect even though it is unseen, so too might the operation of another's cognition be possible regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Furthermore, if one does not accept the existence of a causal relationship between them, then an inference of the non-difference between the blue object and its cognition based on that necessity is untenable;

for while such a distinction might be accepted in conventional practice, that very acceptance leads to the conclusion that the necessity [of their identity] is unproven due to doubt. Thus, this argument—that [the identity] follows from the awareness of a single form—is trivial.
The ellipsis is "when there is the apprehension of the two natures, there is the cognition of the relationship";
for those who do not perceive it [the relationship] in the example, [it is established] through the states of being that and having that as its cause.
"They are made known"—
this is the ellipsis— [in the case of] the sprout.

It might be thought that, because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*), this form belongs to cognition itself and is known by it alone, not by anything else. That is not so; for from what is the fact of its having that form established? If you say "from that very rule," then there is circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*): once the fact of its having that form is established, the rule is established, and from that, the fact of its having that form is established.
If it were from another source, then that knowledge would be rendered useless by this very [present] knowledge.

Even if the fact that [the cognition] possesses the form of that [object] were established by some means through the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*), nevertheless, the same fault remains even if the Sugata perceives it. Furthermore, if he does not perceive that [cognition], how could the Sugata be omniscient, since ordinary beings perceive that object separately? If he does not perceive it, how could the Sugata be omniscient?
The reading contained within this [manuscript] is written twice;
however, another [reading] is considered as follows:
"Its apprehension is not to be grasped, nor is it graspable by another cognition, for it is likewise empty of that."

Nevertheless, because of the statement that "the light consisting of knowledge was likewise [present] for the position of direct perception," his omniscience is not that of knowing everything without exception, but rather the knowledge of his own nature. This too is not correct, because there would be no distinction from others, and it would result in the futility of [statements] such as *pramāṇabhūtāya pramāṇasamu°* (Pramāṇasamuccaya, verse 1).
Even if that is designated according to conventional usage, it has already been stated that for that very reason the logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Having bowed to the Sugata, who seeks the welfare of the world, to the Teacher, the Sugata, the Protector;
for the sake of establishing valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that which was scattered throughout his own works is here composed as a compendium— this is the sense.

Having prostrated to the Sugata, the Protector who seeks the welfare of the world, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is here set forth according to rule out of compassion for people bewildered by fallacious reasoning.
This is the remainder [of the argument]: *Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 1.

And if such a being has not been apprehended from any source whatsoever, how can he exist, such that he is praised in that manner? Thus it follows: just as there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*) regarding the eternal Lord (*īśvara*), so too there is an absence of any means of valid cognition regarding the Sugata.
Alternatively, if he has been apprehended, then you yourself must know the Sugata, and nothing else beyond him; this is sheer folly.

Therefore, for one who accepts either its existence as a reality or its specific distinction, how is it that the aforementioned fault is not incurred? Thus, it remains established: "From what [source] does the restriction arise?"
The Sugata is the authority, as expressed in the form "to him who has become the authority," and so forth.
The Sugata, having established the term "syāt," speaks further to demonstrate its meaning, beginning with "tadeka" and so forth.
This means: of those cognitions belonging to other continua that arise in a single moment—namely, those whose nature it is to exist at one and the same moment as that intended cognition of blue.

"From what [reason] is that [simultaneous perception] established, given the rule of simultaneous apprehension? To this he says: "Because of its arising through the cognition of itself or of the self.
Then [the opponent asks]: "What follows from that? To which he replies: "The entire world [is consciousness]."
But this is not the case; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*). This is the intention (*bhāva*) of Samantabhadra. However, his view is that for those two...
[text fragment]

...By the passage beginning with "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*), [the author] states that since there is no difference between them, there is no restriction of the relationship of apprehended and apprehender; and if the apprehended were different from what is intended as the apprehender, its apprehension by the latter would not occur because of the rule that [an object] must be known by another [consciousness], rather than appearing by itself. Nevertheless, because of the necessity of simultaneous apprehension, they are non-different, and thus it was said, "that one [is the same]," and so forth.

Others resolve this as follows: even if there is no difference between the blue and the cognition thereof, there is no identity, but rather a similarity by virtue of both being cognitions; just as one cognition is like another cognition, so too is the blue, because of the necessity of their simultaneous apprehension.
Thus...

"...there is no deviation of the reason [from the probandum] because it does not occur in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). They are not acting correctly; for if whatever is perceived together with a cognition were itself that cognition, then other cognitions existing at the same moment as the cognition of blue would necessarily be perceived together with it, and thus they would incur the nature of being blue.
Furthermore, if the cognition which is its effect were also blue, the same fault would remain, and since that fault remains in the same state, the entire world would then be nothing but blue.
Thus he says "tadeka... and so forth.

Because that cognition of blue, existing in a single moment, does not arise by itself from its own [nature], it demonstrates that even the perception [of the object] occurs simultaneously with it—as if they were co-existent—due to the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*). Consequently, it would follow that the entire world constitutes a single continuum (*ekasantāna*) or a similar continuum; yet this is not accepted by others. Therefore, the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*).
In that regard, the cognition "this is blue" is not understood merely from that rule of necessity, but rather because it manifests itself inherently, just like the cognition itself.

If it is argued that the cognition of the Omniscient One does not manifest as blue in the same way as a restricted cognition of blue—lest there be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)—then let it simply be that "blue is cognition because it is self-luminous," like that very cognition; what is the use of this restrictive rule which is subject to deviation? If it is argued that "let it be just that," we say no; since its manifestation is established as being solely extrinsic, it would result in the consequence of [the object] becoming blue.
From the mere necessity of simultaneous apprehension, by means of the necessity of simultaneous apprehension,
there is the appearance of blue.

As for the view of the opponent, because they accept non-dual knowledge (*advaya-jñāna*), they maintain that the entire world is a single cognition (*eka-jñāna*); however, it is not a single continuum (*ekasantāna*) because such a thing does not exist, and thus there is no deviation from their position by that [argument]. That is not well-stated; for even one who perceives only blue would face the undesirable consequence of perceiving the variegated nature (*citratva*) of the entire world. Otherwise, it would have to be said that "the many are one," and since that consequence would follow both simultaneously and sequentially, he says: "the entire [world]," etc., [ending with] "due to the absence of a continuum."

Having thus analyzed the word *saha* (together) in the sense of simultaneity for the purpose of showing that the manifold is indeed of a single form—since particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings—he now analyzes its meaning as "one" by saying "if," and so forth.

The word "if" indicates the opponent's admission; "again" refers to an alternative position. "The necessity of being perceived by a single cognition" means that there is the perception of a single cognition, not of an object; or rather, that there is the necessity that blue is perceived by one cognition and not otherwise—that necessity is the reason. The meaning is: "if there is the necessity of simultaneous perception."

Regarding the first position, he states the refutation: the connection is with the phrase "the reason is unestablished" (*asiddho hetuḥ*), because the object is also perceived. Regarding the second, he says: "and it is inconclusive" (*anaikāntikaśca*); "inconclusive" means deviant (*vyabhicārī*).
And by the word "ca" (and), he shows that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), stating: "of the blue," etc.
This has been explained as [referring to] something belonging to a dancer or the like, occurring simultaneously with a word; for it is possible to perceive [it] through multiple cognitions.
By this, he demonstrates the fallacy of being "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*).
This has been examined immediately above.
He now states the fallacy of being "inconclusive" (*anaikāntikatā*): "not only of one, but even of many substances."

By this, he refutes the formulation of that as the subject (*pakṣa*); for the oneness of living beings (*jīva*) and so forth does not follow merely from their being formulated as the subject of a single cognition, because such a claim is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It might be argued that since these [modes] are one in relation to the substance (*dravya*), they could indeed be formulated as the subject;
however, the apprehension by a single cognition—that is, the perception—cannot be denied, for there is no negation of the observation of being apprehended by a single cognition.
Otherwise, it would be "total emptiness," as it has been stated; thus, the word *saha* is indicative [of this].
He raises another objection in order to refute [the previous argument] with the words "yadi" (if), etc.

If the reason "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*) were instead "non-apprehension without [the other]" (*asahānupalambha*), then the refutation is: "What is the distinction? There is no difference between this and the previously stated meaning. To explain: by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*), "non-apprehension without" means "apprehension separately"; when this is connected with the negative particle (*nañ*), it results in "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*) through that same function [of exclusion].

Now, if there is an expectation for a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) here, then let the probandum (*sādhya*) also be of that same nature, since otherwise the connection [between them] would not be established.

If you say "it is so," he replies with the words beginning "non-presuppositional" (*prasajya*): the mere non-presuppositional negation is neither a probandum nor a probans; that is to say, it does not function as the thing to be proven, nor does it function as the means of proof.
To the question "Of what two things [is this like]? he says: "Like a crop," and so forth.
To the question "Why? he says: "Because of the observation of the characteristic of the cognition—that is, the apprehension—of an object such as fire from another object such as smoke;
or else, by relying on that which is the characteristic related to the object, namely the scriptural teaching that 'an object indeed consists of objects'."

In the negative compound *asahānupalambha*, the meaning is indeed of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), because the understanding of the object follows from the sense [of the compound]— *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.193.

[The opponent] says: You have stated that there is the apprehension of a single cognition possessing the form of blue, but not of the object; therefore, the reason—that the restriction [of the object] is unestablished elsewhere because the object is also apprehended—is not tenable. If you argue that this is incorrect because no one perceives an object existing at its own time of presence or absence, and because a single entity cannot function in both respects simultaneously due to contradiction—then, to this he replies: "Of cognition," and so forth.
This has been discussed extensively and does not merit further deliberation;
for an object existing at the time of cognition lacks causality with respect to that cognition, since there can be no relationship of cause and effect between two simultaneous entities.
The point is that if that which is non-existent at the time of cognition were the object of apprehension, it would follow that everything past and future could be perceived.

The example "just as in the case of a single delusion" is presented; however, having introduced that very single delusion, he refutes it with the words beginning "those with impaired eyes": "Just as the cognition of those whose minds are afflicted by ignorance appears falsely due to their respective conditions," this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Cognition arises with a false aspect, like [the perception of] floaters and so forth.
— *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.217.
Thus, the dull-witted have concluded that this applies everywhere.

If one attempts to prove the objectlessness of all cognitions that have become subjects of dispute—cognitions which, being themselves not made objects [by another], would thereby establish their own objectlessness—this would constitute a contradiction that destroys one's own position (*iṣṭavighātakṛd-viruddha*) by transgressing the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*). Furthermore, since there is no distinction from external objects, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) could not be established; for if there were an absolute non-delusiveness, it would contradict the fact of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*), whether together or separately, just like the appearance of two moons. Moreover, if one seeks to prove the absence of both difference and non-difference simply because blue and its cognition are not perceived as distinct, the establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would be contradicted.

That cognition whose sense-faculties are "disturbed" (*vipluta*) is so described; it refers to cognitions such as those of a person with jaundice or other defects affecting the senses. Just as it appears in that manner—either through the mode of activity involving the grasped and the grasper, or otherwise—it manifests as having an unreal object. Likewise, in that same manner, in all cases regarding both one's own and another's nature, or alternatively, in both the waking and dreaming states, whatever cognition has an unreal manifestation, why would it not indeed have an unreal manifestation? This is because the intended meaning is understood through the double negation (*pratiṣedha-dvaya*).

He refutes this as follows: "In this way, the dull-witted and wisdom-deficient followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) have come to believe—that is, they have understood—that the cognition which appears in the supportless sky in the form of hair, the form of a floating mass [of clouds], or the form of mosquitoes and so forth," while explaining the verse, he says: "Regarding the misconception," and so on.

Regarding this, he states the refutation: "All," etc. The intended meaning here is as follows: by means of this inference, would the objectlessness (*nirviṣayatā*) of those cognitions that have become the subject of dispute be established, or would there be the exclusion of the superimposition of having an object (*saviṣayatā*), since there is no other possible alternative? In the first case, if these cognitions—the subjects (*dharmin*)—are not themselves apprehended, then their property of being objectless cannot be apprehended, just as Devadatta’s dark complexion cannot be perceived if Devadatta himself is not grasped. Consequently, the logical reason (*hetu*) is ineffective.

Thus he says: for all cognitions—that is, those sensations which have become the subject of dispute—whose object is not apprehended by the proponent himself through inference regarding the self, there is no proof of their being "objectless" (*nirviṣayatā*). This [reason] subverts what is desired from the cause; it is the destroyer of the proponent’s desired [conclusion]. Therefore, it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*);

specifically, what here is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*)? It is "contradictory" because it is obstructed and encompassed by "inefficacy" (*akiñcitkaratva*), which is the opposite of "efficacy" (*kiñcitkaratva*).

In this analysis of those [cognitions], their status as objects is established; however, in the same way, the status of other [objects] as objects is also established by means of the appearing object (*pratibhāsin-artha*). Otherwise, even for this [present cognition], it would not exist, and thus its incapacity remains as it was.
This is precisely what he says: "Because the lack of an object is established for all cognitions that do not themselves take anything as an object"—this is the intended meaning.

It is a "contradictory fallacy" (*viruddho hetvābhāsaḥ*) because it subverts what is desired; for the Buddhist, what is desired is that waking and dream cognitions are devoid of objects, and this [reason] acts as a subverter of that.
For instance—the wise maintain that a "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reason is one that is not pervaded by the [property to be proven], yet produces the illusion of being so pervaded;

and in the present inference, it is established that the nature of being a cognition of the apprehended and the apprehender, or whatever else [is cited], is pervaded by the state of having an object (*viṣayatva*). Therefore, it must be stated as follows: "The cognitions of the waking and dreaming states possess an object, because they have the nature of a cognition of the apprehended and the apprehender, or for some other reason [cited] by the opponent, just like the inference under consideration."

If it is argued that there is the fault of contradiction with common consensus (*prasiddhi-bādha*) and so forth in proving that dream-cognition has an object, [the response is: this is equally applicable when proving that waking cognition lacks an object; in what respect would it be contradictory? To this he says: "In the transgression of *syādvāda*..."—that is, if one transgresses or abandons *syādvāda*, which holds that some cognition has an object while some is otherwise, and that even this is "in some way" (*kathañcit*). Thus, the translation is as follows: If it is argued that there is the fault of contradiction with common consensus (*prasiddhi-bādha*) and so forth in proving that dream-cognition has an object, [the response is: this is equally applicable when proving that waking cognition lacks an object; in what respect would it be contradictory? To this he says: "In the transgression of *syādvāda*..."—that is, if one transgresses or abandons *syādvāda*, which holds that some cognition has an object while some is otherwise, and that even this is "in some way" (*kathañcit*).
