He thinks as follows: "Just as the Buddhist establishes the falsity of all cognition by using the example of false dream-cognition well-known to the opponent, so too might the opponent establish the truth of all cognition by using the example of true inference well-known to the Buddhist. In that case, there would be a contradiction.

However, if the opponent then relies upon the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects) and argues—just like the inference under discussion—that even though dream-cognition is false, some cognition must possess an objective basis (*sālambana*) because it possesses that [dream-object's] form, then the reason is the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."
Obstructed by the contrary, it is "contradicted";
this applies not only to this [feeling] alone, but to those feelings that have become the subject of dispute.
The meaning is that it would be established as being devoid of its pervasion, or as causing an illusion regarding its pervasion.
Even though the nature of consciousness consists of the forms of the grasped and the grasper,

if the proponent of consciousness (vijñānavādin) further asserts that there is an exclusion of superimposition (samāropavyavaccheda), it is said in response to that: "Superimposition is the conceptual construction of objectivity in regard to things that are devoid of objects."

Since no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates with respect to that [object] prior to that inference, how can its lack of an objective referent (*nirviṣayatā*) be established, such that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would be a superimposition (*samāropa*), and the inference would become purposeful by way of excluding it?

He says this very thing: [the point is that] for all cognitions—whether they be dream-cognitions or other types of awareness—their lack of an object (*nirviṣayatā*) is not established, whether by the Buddhist himself or by another who attempts to take them as objects. Under what condition? He says: "In the transgression of *syādvāda*. *Syādvāda* is the capacity of a single cognition to grasp both its own nature and the nature of others; "in the transgression of that" means in the position where cognition is restricted solely to its own nature. Because of the establishment of their lack of an object, the phrase "self-subverting" (*svayam iṣṭavighātakṛt*) follows. That which is "desired" (*iṣṭa*) is the superimposition (*samāropa*) accepted by the proponent; its "contradiction" (*vyāghāta*) is its non-existence, and "making that" (*tatkaraṇam*) refers to bringing about that contradiction.
What follows from this? He says: "Contradictory" (viruddha) is a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa), as before, being ineffective.
Now, suppose one were to desire all of this for those very objects that have been made the subject of inquiry; regarding that, he says: "All," etc.
The explanation here is the same as in the second explanation previously given.

However, this is the distinction: by that very perception through which one establishes that all cognition is objectless, the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—namely, the contradictory and the inconclusive—are to be applied as before.
By means of the inference under discussion, the superimposition (*samāropa*) of having an object is excluded. Regarding this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he states the refutation:
the superimposition would take the form of a conceptual construction of having an object.
The point is that this perception possesses an object because its object is the state of being objectless (*nirviṣayatā*).

Now, if it is argued: "But even that perception is indeed objectless, and therefore this fault does not arise," [the author] replies here: "Because there is no distinction from external objects," and so forth;
the word "itself" (*svayam*) also carries over here.

For the Buddhist himself, not only is the establishment of cause and effect in another mental continuum impossible due to the lack of distinction from external objects, but even self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) would not be established.
And if that were so, how could delusion or anything else be established? This is the intended meaning.

Therefore, just as self-awareness alone exists and not the external object despite the lack of distinction regarding the external object, so too, despite the lack of distinction between the appearances of dreams and other states, it belongs only to the waking jar and such; thus, how can the reason (*hetu*) be unestablished (*asiddha*)?
Regarding this, Prajñākaragupta states: "The existence of objects in a dream is just like that of jars and other things in the waking state;
as it has been said:"
"This [distinction] between truth and untruth is merely conventional;
when the true nature [of things] is directly realized, such things as 'truth' become untenable" (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra 2.37).
To this, he replies: "In the case of their non-erroneous singularity"—that is, if the non-erroneous singularity of both of those, namely self-awareness and external objects, is accepted.

The intended meaning here is as follows: what is the sense in saying that "being a speaker of truth" is difficult to establish? If everything were unreal, or if it were devoid of the distinction between the real and the unreal; regarding that, it was stated previously [in the verse] beginning with "because there is no difference from external objects," and so forth.

Now, if it is held to be real, then this is said: the reason is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because it is contradicted by the fact of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*); for even in the case of a double moon and the like, the very existence of simultaneous perception implies only difference (*bheda*). This is the underlying point.

Alternatively, regarding what was stated—that because there is no distinction from external objects, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) would not be established—the opponent argues that in this context, self-awareness is established through its manifestation, whereas the external object is established through the opposite. To this, he replies with the verse beginning "that which is non-erroneous and absolute," and so forth. Here, is that self-awareness dualistic, partless, and momentary, or is it a single variegated entity? Regarding the second alternative, the refutation to be stated later begins with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

The first objection: By the word "that" (*tat*), self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is referred to. Regarding that [self-awareness], it is non-erroneous, unitary, and independent. This is because, if one were to admit [the existence of] both subject and object (*dharmin* and *dharma*) in all respects, there would be a contradiction with their simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha*). This is due to the impossibility of a single cognition having the form of blue, or because of the contradiction in the apprehension of one thing by means of only one [cognition], whether externally or internally, since independent apprehension is negated. The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "simultaneously (*saha*)"—meaning either at once or separately through a difference in time and so forth—is used in a conjunctive sense. The meaning of the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "non-apprehension of blue and its cognition" is that there is simply no perception [of them as separate]; it is not because of their simultaneous apprehension. However, if one accepts the proof of the absence of either difference or non-difference between blue and its cognition:
He states an illustration: "like the appearance of two moons.

Just as there is neither difference nor non-difference between the appearances of two moons—because those two [moons] are grounded in a real entity (*vastu*), whereas their appearances are not real entities—so it is with the two subjects under discussion. Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Because of non-apprehension" (*anupalabdheḥ*). If this is put forward as the reason for proving the non-existence of difference and non-difference, then the establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—the proof or determination of its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), which consists of existence—would be contradicted; for that [non-apprehension] exists even in the case of partless self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Furthermore, Prajñākara maintains that a reason whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not ascertained cannot be a means of cognition,
especially in the case of that which is partless (*niraṃśa*).

If it is argued that "the two appearances of difference and non-difference, like the appearance of two moons, are certainly not accepted as being exclusively erroneous in nature, but rather they are non-erroneous regarding their own essence while being otherwise regarding the form of the object to be grasped," to this he replies: "But surely... and so forth.

The rule of the simultaneous apprehension of cognition and its object is an error resulting from the one-sided adherence to the falsity of reality; for where could there be a cognition of an internal object of knowledge as a real entity? (28)

And without non-absolutism (anekānta), there can be no rule of the simultaneous perception of the blue object and the cognition thereof; for without that [non-absolutism], the reality of the knowable—which is internal—would not exist even externally. Within the framework of some form of non-absolutism, absolute oneness of the cognition with respect to its own perception and the perception of the object cannot be maintained, whether by accepting the absolute grasping of reality according to their respective order, or the absolute grasping of falsity. If such were accepted, where would the rule of simultaneous perception be? Nowhere at all.

Since the perception of an object is impossible in the absence of an experience of partless cognition, it is held that for one whose perception is not directly perceived, the vision of the object cannot be established;
for if that [cognition] were experienced, even a false construction would be real,
and thus there would be knowledge of reality within the knower.
Even though there exists the experience of partless self-awareness (*niraṃśa-saṃvedana*), he explains the verse regarding that very experience with the words beginning "And not" (*na ca*).

The meaning is that there is no rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) between the blue object and the cognition thereof without the possibility of non-identity—that is, not in the case of absolute identity—because the very apprehension of those two would be absent;

for even when that [object] is apprehended, without it [the cognition], the reality of the internal object of knowledge does not exist by itself. This is the construction of the words "na ca" (nor), because even that which is external and internal is non-existent [in isolation].

If it is argued that there is non-absolutism (anekānta) both internally and externally, to this he replies: "If one accepts that both cognition and the object possess the nature of being both one and many, why not [accept this] in some respect (*kathañcit*) rather than in every respect (*sarvathā*)? He says: "No," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: even if there is a fixed rule regarding difference and non-difference internally or externally, there is no absolute unity (*naikāntenaikatvam*); likewise, this applies to the blue object and its cognition as well.

Furthermore, if—despite there being no difference in the nature of apprehension—one maintains that in the case of self-apprehension there is an absolute certainty of grasping reality (*tattva*), whereas in the case of the apprehension of an object there is an absolute certainty of false grasping (*mithyāgraha*), then this constitutes a non-absolutism (*anekānta*) in some respect regarding both the waking state and the dream state (the rest being as before). Alternatively, if one holds a non-absolutism such that "knowledge is erroneous with respect to its own form and also with respect to the object," then the reality of external objects exists in some respect as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of both perception and inference.

By this [argument], he demonstrates the partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhatā*) of that [opponent's] restrictive rule: for although that [object] exists in the form of consciousness and blueness, it does not exist in its nature as momentary destruction and so forth.

If it is argued that even if there is a rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), the false form of cognition is not its own form but rather the form of another, and therefore this fault does not apply; to this he says: "In the establishment of self-cognized and non-cognized knowledge of the self," and so forth—it is not established.
The object (*artha*) is a single entity consisting of both the perceptible and the imperceptible, differentiated by time and other factors.

(29) If the diversity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were not the differentiator of an entity, what would be the use of this baseless conceptualization of "exclusion from others" (*anyavyāvṛtti*), which—by obstructing many "gaps" such as the relationship between cause and effect, the continuity of the stream, the connection between action and its fruit, and the recollection of those objects—is impossible to close?
This is the intended meaning: for the opponent, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) appears as something distinct from pleasure and so forth, or from blue and so forth, or from the body.
Nor can there be identity with that [object] by means of the imposition of contradictory properties such as plurality and unity;

therefore, even though there is difference, the appearance of identity is due to error. Otherwise, it would result in the fallacy of non-exclusivity (anekānta), as has been stated. Thus, when the establishment of that cognition—which is characterized by having its own nature both perceptible (*svapratyakṣa*) in the form of consciousness and so forth, and imperceptible (*parokṣa*) in its distinction from forms like pleasure and pain, and which possesses those two selves, namely the perceptible and imperceptible natures—is accepted, what is not established? Indeed, everything is established. Why is this so? He says: "A single object."

Of what nature is it? By what means [is it so]? He says: "By the distinction of time and so forth," that is, by the distinction of time, space, and so on. Thus he thinks: since consciousness is a single entity consisting of both the perceptible and the imperceptible, therefore the one self consisting of the perceptible and the imperceptible is established.

And because that rule [of simultaneous perception] is unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddha*)— since it does not exist even in the case where knowledge and its distinction are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) due to their non-difference— therefore, the object is established;
such is the rule of simultaneous perception for self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

With the words beginning with "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature), he states the meaning of the verse: If that very multiplicity of the intrinsic nature of cognition—which exists in the form of both direct and indirect [perception]—were not the differentiator and the bringer of multiplicity for that entity itself, then what would be the use of a non-consequential conceptualization (*niranvaya-kalpanā*) based on the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of an entity from others, whether of the same class or of a different class? To the question "Of what kind [is this conceptualization]?", he says: "Effect," and so forth.
Effect (*kārya*), cause (*kāraṇa*), continuum (*santāna*), action (*karma*), and latent impression (*vāsanā*)—the latter being mental action (*cetanā-karma*). [Abhidharmakośa 4.1]

Because of this statement, the fruit consists of the transition to another body and so forth, and the connection between those two is their production. Furthermore, by means of the word *prabhṛti* (etcetera), there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its referent is memory and so forth. Its "many" aforementioned gaps are the defects; the inability to cover them is the rebuttal, which is itself the "inability to ward off the undesirable" (*anartha-nirvāra*). That [rebuttal] is that by which the mental action—consciousness—is [defined]. —Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya.

[Objection: "Surely the nature of cognition is not non-meaningful (*anarthavat*) or erroneous. Nor does it possess the nature of being both non-erroneous and otherwise with respect to its own and other forms, nor does it possess the nature of the form of its own apprehended object, nor does it possess the nature of something else in dependence upon the distinction from the form of its own apprehended object—such that this fault would arise. Rather, it consists precisely of the forms of pleasure, blue, and so forth, and the body, because of their necessity. [Reply: Anticipating a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from this [position] by means of the cognition of a Buddha and its objects, he says: "Even if there is a necessity [of their coexistence], if there is a difference between those two due to the necessity of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*), then [your argument] is inconclusive (*anaikānta*)," proving this with the words beginning with "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
Even if there is a rule of simultaneous perception between the cognizing mind and all the objects grasped by it,
even if that rule exists despite their difference, otherwise [your] proof of non-absolutism would be undermined.
The object consisting of the middle part and the near side is directly perceived by that [consciousness] itself;
its being beyond perception is due to its prior parts, its further side, and so forth, just as in the case of a cognition of a Buddha.
Not only do the moments of a single continuum possess that restriction, but by virtue of that very restriction, they belong to one and the same continuum, whereas other continua do not.

If the Buddha were the cognizer of both the mental continua (*santānin*) and other continua, then because of that single apprehension, the continuum would not exist, as it would result in their becoming one with that [cognition]. Furthermore, if consciousness is restricted to being non-different from its object, how could there be an instruction consisting merely of the conceptualization of "one's own" and "another's" continua without false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*)? How could those false conceptual constructions—which possess a nature of manifoldness (*anekāntātmaka*)—not exist in a middle form that is perceivable, given that their prior and posterior limits are unperceivable by nature?
The visible object... enough of this digression;
therefore, reality cannot be apprehended as being exclusively either external or internal through false [views], nor even by means of direct perception.
But has this not already been stated by us—that it was not said by the author of the treatise?

[The term] *pratyakṣa* refers to that whose front portion (*arvāgbhāga*) has a middle form, meaning it possesses a middle nature; and that [portion], along with its object (*sacā sāvarthaśca*), constitutes the "hiddenness" (*parokṣatā*) of the self’s own nature (*ātmanaḥ svarūpasya*). By whom is this hiddenness [perceived]? To this, he says: "By those who are prior," and so forth.
Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth is intended.
He states an example: "like the cognition of a Buddha" (*buddhabuddhivat*); that is, like the cognition of the Sugata, and likewise [in other cases].
And this illustration is made with respect to the manifold nature [of objects], not with respect to visible and invisible forms.

For the Buddha’s gnosis is perceived simultaneously with all objects, yet it does not possess identity (*ekatva*) with them; thus, "simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambha*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), meaning it is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*).
Explaining the verse, he says: "Not only... and so forth.

This is its meaning: when the Sugata perceives—either does he or does he not—the moments of his own continuum (*ātmasantāna*) and the past and future infinite moments of those continua, as well as the moments of other continua? In the first case, not only is there the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) for the moments of a single continuum, but by that very cognition through which they are perceived, there is a rule of simultaneity with it; thus, there would be the state of being a single continuum (*ekasantānatva*). "Single" means non-different; "continuum" refers to those whose nature is a continuum. Furthermore, there would be the state of being a single continuum for other continua along with the Sugata’s cognition—this is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied. This is so if the Buddha is the knower of the possessors of the continua (*santānin*) and of the other continua.
And likewise, in other cases as well, [the cognition] would appear in the form of both the visible and the invisible;
or else, that cognizer would perceive them according to their respective places and times. The meaning is that the reason [proffered by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Now, fearing these two faults, if it is not accepted that they are absolutely identical with it, then he says: "That one," and so forth.

Because that Buddha perceives by means of a single, non-distinct cognition (*atanajas-jñāna*) what is intended to be expressed, there would be no continuity (*santati*) of those possessing a continuum (*santānin*) nor of other continua.
Why? To this he says: "Because of the consequence of their becoming one with that"—that is, because of the consequence of those [objects] becoming one with that perceiving cognition.
Now, if it is argued that the Buddha is not the knower of them because [the cognition] terminates in its own nature alone, to that he says: "Furthermore," and so forth.

Furthermore, after this fault, there is a connection with the word "of the Buddha" (*buddhasya*) through a transformation of the case ending (*vibhaktipariṇāma*), following the subsequent realization of knowledge.
If the restriction that [the Buddha] is not cognizable by another is accepted, what follows? To this he says: "self and other," and so forth.

"One's own" and "another's"—these two are the continuums (*saṃtāna*). The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding them is the distinction between momentary destruction and so forth; that very [distinction] is expressed by the term "mere" (*tanmātra*), which indicates the non-existence of external objects. How could there not be an instruction on that? [The answer is: Not at all. For one who does not perceive something himself cannot instruct others correctly regarding it, just as a man in the street cannot instruct others on the meaning of a treatise. And the Buddha does not perceive that [external object], since it is mere conceptual construction. This is a non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).

That is not tenable—the point is that here the Blessed One himself is established as the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūta*) with respect to the Dharma and other matters (*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 1).
The repetition of the word "continuum" (*santāna*) appears redundant;

however, here, at the beginning of the treatise, the praise of the Blessed One is expressed as the very subject matter of the work because he is established as an authoritative person (*pramāṇabhūta*) through the perfection of cause and effect. For it is the Blessed One alone who is proven to be the authoritative person in this [treatise].
— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*:

It might be thought that, according to the statement in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.6, "The cognition of its own nature occurs by itself," there is no actual distinction between the cognition and the object within cognitions whose own nature has been fully determined.
"Furthermore, the instruction regarding that alone [is possible] because nothing else to be considered is applicable. To this, he says: "It is false," and so forth.

How is the word connected to both [sides] by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (the *kākākṣagolakanyāya*)? The sense is: how can the instruction of that [object] be possible for either a Buddha or anyone else without a false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*), since such consideration is impossible through non-conceptual [cognition]?
If it is argued that "that conceptual construction certainly exists," to this he says: "That is false," and so forth.

Regarding those two— the Buddha and others— there is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, only the teaching that false conceptualizations are merely the conceptualization of one's own and others' mental continua.

If it is argued that even when it is stated, "Indeed, the falsity of conceptual cognitions such as those of Kapila and others is obtained because they possess that nature [of being conceptual]," the statement "that [conceptual cognition] is false" is redundant; we reply: some maintain that for the Sugata there is a conceptual cognition not produced by a logical mark (aliṅgaja).
If that were to be in accordance with reality, it would constitute a separate means of valid cognition, since it is not included within perception.

Or, if it were included therein, then that [conceptual cognition] would also be a conceptual perception; since it apprehends what has already been apprehended, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is asked how it could be distinct from that [non-conceptual perception], [the answer is: just as in the case of non-conceptual [perception], since a conceptual [cognition] can also function within a continuum (*saṃtāna*), let the non-conceptual [perception] be invalid because it apprehends what has already been apprehended by that [conceptual cognition]. Or else, there is no fault, because it is designated as such only in relation to another [cognition].

If it is argued, "Let there be this very nature of manifoldness (anekāntātmakatva), which consists of being both erroneous and non-erroneous; what is the fault in that?"—to this he replies: "How," and so forth. How could a thing whose middle nature is perceivable not exist? It certainly does exist; where? At the prior and posterior limits (koṭi).
By what? By that which has an invisible nature; because conceptual constructions (vikalpa) possess a false form, it is conceptual cognition.

The qualification "false" has been provided specifically with reference to the Buddhist position, because [the object] is apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) through conceptual construction (*savikalpa*).

Having thus established the non-absolutism (*anekānta*) regarding succession, he speaks—saying "the visible," and so forth—in order to explain the non-absolutism regarding non-succession within the aggregate (*skandha*).
The connection [of the words] is: "how is it not [so]?
Thus, enough with this digression.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Since this is so, for that reason (*tat*), one cannot apprehend a reality (*tattva*) either externally or internally.
By what means? He says: by the Buddhist views (*darśana*) which are exclusively false (*mithyaikāntaiḥ*) and by conceptual constructions (*vikalpaiḥ*).
If it is argued that "just as this [perception] is so, you too ought not to accept the non-absolutist reality (anekāntatattva)," to this he replies: "Even by perception," and so forth.

Indeed, even for the Jaina, perception consists in the grasping of only the present moment; it is not an object [of such grasping] because it would entail the consequence of perceiving the prior and posterior limits [of time].

If it is argued that, likewise, in this case, the perception of the near side is submerged and does not see the far side and so forth, and therefore it does not cognize their unity; and for this very reason, there is no inference either, since one does not establish that anything possesses both a visible and an invisible nature— then to this he replies with the words beginning "seeing," which refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Perceiving the identity between the prior and the posterior, the living being [realizes] that he alone is one, the mere existence; and by the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible," he thoroughly understands that very same [reality]. || 31 ||
"Intellection (mati), memory (smṛti), recognition (saṃjñā), thought (cintā), and discernment (abhinibodha) are not different things" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.13).
By this, the author of the Sūtras states that the relationship between intellection and the others is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*);
for if there were an absolute non-identity even with respect to one of them, the comprehension of an object would be impossible, just as in the case of a different mental continuum (*santānāntara*).

The teacher Umāsvāmī states that the living soul (*jīvātman*) "comprehends" (*abhinibudhyate*), meaning it knows the oneness of the preceding and succeeding moments from all sides; he says "it [is not]" and so forth to show that this is not as accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
The meaning is that this has already been established previously in this very context.

Now, if it is argued: "But since this [Self] consists of cognition, and because cognitions are absolutely distinct, he too must be distinct," the author replies: "He is one," meaning he is common to all his own preceding and succeeding states (paryāyas).
By what reasoning? He says: "By *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise).

That is, by that impossibility—according to the stated method—of the existence of either the living being (*jīva*) or the non-living (*ajīva*) in any manner other than [the one under discussion] (i.e., in the absence of oneness).

If it is argued that he perceives [all] merely as existence, such that everyone would possess omniscience; to this he replies: "Perceiving mere existence," meaning making it the object of his vision as something common to both the conscious and the unconscious.

For instance: the determination of a general property such as "sentience" or its opposite must be preceded by the perception of another, higher-order generality, because it is a determination of a particular, just like the distant determination of a post's nature (as a post or something else).
Now, there is no generality higher than existence (*sattā*), for if there were, it would lead to an infinite regress.

If, on the other hand, one argues that the determination of a particular occurs even without the perception of a generality when one is close at hand, then the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*); this is not so, because in that case, although the distinctions such as apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth do exist, they are simply not perceived.
Each individual soul (jīva) is distinct from one another; furthermore, there is a universal (sāmānya) known as existence (sattā).

If it is argued that even so, there may be mere existence because of apprehension, but not a specific distinction because of the contrary [state of doubt], to this he says: "Conceptualizing"—that is, conceptualizing and determining that very same generality of existence as differentiated by specific distinctions such as being conscious or unconscious, through knowledge beginning with *avagraha* and ending with *dhāraṇā*; and having previously and subsequently remembered it thus, having recognized it, and reflecting upon it, one "comprehends" (*abhinibudhyate*)—in the form of *avagraha*, *īhā*, and *dhāraṇā*.

This is another explanation: one perceives—that is, infers—the invisible nature of the preceding and succeeding limits of that which is perceived as having a middle form, as well as the imperceptible taste, touch, and so forth of its near and far parts.
By what means? He says: "Otherwise," etc.;
that is, by way of the impossibility [of the observed state] if the invisible nature did not exist at the perceptible preceding and succeeding limits.
What is this that has been described? He says: "perceiving," and so forth;
this has already been explained.

Explaining the *kārikā*, he shows that the author of the *sūtra* forms a single syntactical unit with it by means of the word "self" (*ātman*), using the passage beginning with "the intellect" (*mati*) and so forth.

He explains the term "not a different thing" (*anarthāntara*) as follows: by this phrase, he states that there is a relationship between the intellect and the others characterized by identity—a nature of oneness in some sense—and not merely synonymy, because that would contradict common experience. To the question "Why is this so?", he replies with the passage beginning "one of those [others]" (*tadanyatama*).

Among those [faculties] such as perception (*mati*) and the rest, if there were an absolute difference—meaning not merely a lack of identity among all of them—then the cognition of an object, whether it be a jar or the like, or an inferable entity such as fire, would be impossible. This is because there would be no perception of even a single atom, despite its being active in relation to everything;
for, just as another continuum (*santānāntara*) is invisible to another person, so too would atoms be invisible to everyone.

Nevertheless, why should there be such hostility toward the postulation of perceptibility in another continuum, such that someone would claim its inferability or its absence based on non-perception? Because neither cognition nor inferential awareness is established in another continuum—as in the case of "it is like that"—just as, for example, because another person does not see smoke while one does, because another does not remember it while one does, because one person lacks recognition of the other, and because the other lacks the necessary reasoning (*tarka*), there is no inference regarding another continuum; so too in the present case, according to the author of the *Tattvārthasūtra*.
The Cārvāka [attributes the origin] of atoms, and [the Sāṃkhya,
that of] the person (puruṣa).
The meaning is that recognition does not occur.

If, however, it is argued that this fault does not arise because—due to some proximity within a single continuum and not elsewhere—the subsequent operation of memory and so forth proceeds from prior perceptions and so on; that is not so. Because even if there were a fixed rule of cause and effect in that case, it would follow that there is no distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*) and other types of causes.
For that which transforms itself into a particular form is the material cause of that [form].

If it is argued that this [definition] does not apply to difference, nor is there any other form of it—namely, that the cause of the cause of the continuum is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)—then what is this so-called "continuum" (*santāna*)? If it is said to be a flow of cause and effect, no; for it would follow that the Sugata and another person belong to a single continuum.
If the Sugata were [the cause] of another, he would necessarily be the latter's defiled [cause].

The claim that "the stream [of consciousness] is similar" is also not a valid answer; for if there were similarity by virtue of being cognition (*jñānatva*), then the states of cause and effect would fall under the same single continuum (*ekasantāna*) as the Sugata.
If there is similarity through the nature of cognition, the fault in question is not avoided:
when the Sugata knows the mind of another person, then the mind of that other person becomes the cause of the Sugata’s mind, and consequently, the two would result in having a single continuum.
The continuum [of the object] would result in being a single continuum with the Sugata’s cognition that cognizes both the preceding and succeeding moments of the jar; likewise,
the cognition of an ordinary person and the Sugata’s cognition that cognizes it would result in being a single continuum, because of their similarity by virtue of both being cognitions.

Now, if it is maintained that there is a continuous series of moments consisting of the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), this is precisely what we wish to investigate: in the case of absolute difference, what is the material cause and what is the other? If, however, within a single continuum the preceding moment is the material cause and the subsequent one is the other, then the establishment of the material cause and the other depends upon the establishment of the continuum; and the establishment of that continuum depends upon the establishment of the material cause and the other. Thus, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

Now, that which undergoes transformation through the transformation of another is the *upādāna* (material cause), and the other is the *upādeya* (the effect). What is this so-called "transformation of one thing through the transformation of another"? It is the arising of a similar mind from a mind refined by scripture and so forth. Why, then, does the knowledge of a yogi not become similar to that [refined mind], such that what is intended to be known would thereby be the *upādeya*?
The arising of conditioned mind occurs from conditioned mind within practitioners.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that only the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) arises: it is not logical to say that the mind, being first conditioned by scripture and so forth, arises from a preceding state that was unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Nor is the reply—that "by whatever modification [it arises], that itself is its conditioning"—a valid solution, because it leads to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, that which transforms into the state of being adopted is the material cause (*upādāna*) from the mind.

Now, one might object: for a sleeping person who sees a dream, the waking consciousness—which does not transform into the form of awakening—is nonetheless its material cause; thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This has been addressed in this section.

And from what [source] does that [waking consciousness] have its material cause (*upādāna*)? Because we observe the awakening to that very form; for you yourself accept that the Sugata’s gnosis is also of that same form, and thus it follows that his gnosis would be the material cause and the Buddha-gnosis the effect.

If you argue that this is not so because of a difference in location, then in the case where one who was asleep in one place awakens in another, the waking consciousness could not be the material cause of the awakening.
By the statement that one who has fallen asleep in one place awakens elsewhere in another country,
this [position] refutes the idea that the body and mind of the dream-state are derived from those [waking ones].

Now, if it is maintained that the mind— just like the body of the sleeper— travels to another place because its continuum is not interrupted, then let the travel over time be examined as well, since there is no distinction between the two cases.
Therefore, it is well said that "appropriation" (upādāna) alone is logical— namely, the phrase beginning with "other than that" (tadanya)—
just as the body experienced in a dream [is affected] by fear, leaping, and running (*Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 2).

Thus, having first demonstrated the absence of a logical reason (*hetu*) in the case of a false absolute position through the passage beginning with "asiddhaḥ siddhasenasya," [the author] now states—beginning with "ekalakṣaṇa"—that such a reason is absent everywhere in the absence of even a single characteristic:
"By the power of a single characteristic, the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are excluded."
Contradictory, inconclusive, unestablished, unknown, and ineffective [reasons], etc.

|| 32 For comparison: "The unestablished is that which is not recognized; the contradictory is that which is established otherwise; and the inconclusive is that which is applicable here in more than one way."
— Nyāyāvatāra, verse 23:
Due to the absence of the impossibility of [the probans] existing otherwise, that [reason] is remembered as being manifold,
through the extensive categories of the contradictory, the unestablished, the doubtful, and the ineffective.
—Nyāyaviniścaya, verses 365–366:

That [reason] is contradictory because of its being otherwise; it is unestablished because of its total absence; it is deviant because it exists even in the dissimilar class; and when [the probandum] is established, every [such reason] is ineffective.

"A reason that is not ascertained through the impossibility of its existence otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) is the prover; thus, fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—such as those characterized by being unknown, doubtful, unestablished, lacking negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or lacking positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—are excluded.
(Pramāṇasamuccaya, vv. 48–49). Thus, the fallacious reasons are refuted.
How so? It is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it is established in one way; it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it is established in another way;
and it is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is possible in yet another way.
Furthermore, if that [reason] is not known, it remains unknown and is thus ineffective;
likewise, the example [is ineffective].
For is a three-featured [reason] not a means of cognition in the absence of even one of its features? [The answer is: Non-apprehension...
Whence is this? First of all, the perception [of the object] is manifold and indeed impossible to determine.
How so?

Because of the power of having a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—which are counterfeits of a reason—are excluded by virtue of the majesty of the "inseparability from the probandum" (*anyathānupapannatva*); they are set apart from the power of a valid reason.
What are they? He says: "contradictory," and so forth.
Having formed a *dvandva* compound of "contradictory" and the others, a *bahuvrīhi* should be constructed with the word "etc. (*ādi*);
therein, by the word "etc.," the inclusion of the "doubtful" is intended.
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "Otherwise," and so forth.

Otherwise—that is, by that necessary non-occurrence (*anupapatti*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent—the object determined [as such] is the reason (*hetu*), the indicator; thus, by implication, fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) such as the contradictory (*viruddha*) and others are excluded from being valid reasons. Another asks: "How so? The Master replies: "In a different way alone"—that is, by the very mode of the absence of the probandum, or rather, by its occurrence in the opposite of the probandum—it is contradictory (*viruddha*).

And likewise, by way of the presence of the probandum (*sādhyabhāva*) and otherwise by way of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it deviates (*vyabhicārin*). Likewise, by way of being possible otherwise, it is unestablished (*asiddha*);

that is, when there is ignorance of it—meaning when that reason, though existing, is not known due to doubt and so forth and is thus not determined—it is "unestablished through ignorance" (*ajñāta-asiddha*), which follows from the previous context.

Alternatively, if that characteristic of the reason (*hetulakṣaṇa*) is unknown in the subject (*pakṣa*) or elsewhere, then being unknown, it is ineffective; by this, [the categories] such as "doubtful" (*saṃdigdha*) and so forth are explained.

To the question, "What is the example for this?", he says: "In exactly the same way"—that is, the example stated in the passage beginning with "asiddhaḥ siddhasenasya" and so forth is to be understood here.

If it is argued that contradictory reasons (*viruddha*) and the like are excluded not because they lack a single characteristic, but rather because they lack the characteristics such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), the author replies: It is not the case that a thing possessing three characteristics—that is, a mark (*liṅga*) whose characteristics are the three [features] beginning with being a property of the subject—is a signifier (*gamaka*) merely through the absence of one characteristic; rather, it is only when those [characteristics] are present that it is so.

He thinks as follows: "If the state of being a prover (*gamakatva*) is pervaded by the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*), then this [proving power] would exist when those [characteristics] are present, but would not exist in their absence. However, [the proving power] would simply not exist in their absence even with only as many characteristics as are required for pervasion; so what is the use of the three characteristics? What is that 'three-characteristic' mark (*liṅga*)? To this, he says: "Non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*), and so forth.

From where does this [conclusion] come? From where does the opponent—the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*)—say that "in the absence of those [characteristics], that [mark] is a prover"? He says: "Apprehension," and so forth.

The word "tāvat" expresses sequence; the opponent considers that the variegated (*citrā*)—meaning manifold in form—is indeed impossible to ascertain, and that what is unascertained cannot be a means of comprehension.
He asks, "How?"—in what manner is it impossible to ascertain?
Furthermore, the three characteristics of the logical mark (liṅga) are: its existence only in the object of inference (anumeya),
and its existence only in the similar instances (sapakṣa).
And its non-existence in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa) is definitely ascertained.
—Nyāyabindu, Chapter 2.
To this, he states the reply: "Not [the case] when the conditions for being perceived are met," and so forth;
that is, not when the object possesses the characteristics of being both perceptible and imperceptible.
Since the establishment of their respective intrinsic natures consists in mutual non-existence (parasparābhāva), in that case,
the fulfillment of the conditions for perception (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti) requires both the completeness of all other causal factors for perception and a specific nature.

For neither the completeness of the other causal factors for perception nor their absence is itself the fulfillment of the conditions for perception, such that there could be a determination [of one] through the form of the mutual non-existence of the other.
The definition of the "visible" (dṛśya), which is about to be stated, applies to those two; thus they are so described. To the question "What are they not?", he says:
"The visible," and so forth, because the definitions of both the visible and invisible objects result in their meeting the definition of the visible.
What is this? He says: "mutually," and so forth.

It is the absence of that which is characterized as invisible within that which is characterized as visible, or conversely, the absence of that which is characterized as visible within that which is characterized as invisible; this is "mutual non-existence. By means of this, there is the establishment of their respective intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). Because these two characteristics serve as the cause for such establishment, the term "establishment" (*vyavasthiti*) is used to denote "ascertainment" (*nirṇaya*).
"Established as having the nature of mutual non-existence" (*parasparābhāvasvabhāvavyavasthitaḥ*) is an alternative reading.

The meaning is: established and determined by its own form, the perceptible object (*dṛśya*) is here [defined] by its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while its non-existence is established elsewhere; thus, there is neither confusion nor intermixture.

The intention here is this: when the characteristic of a perceptible object is determined, then the attainment of that characteristic is perceived in some cases, and from non-perception, its absence would follow; yet such is not the case.

Regarding the definition of an object as that which is not perceived, the opponent here says: the definition of a perceptible object is its capacity to produce a cognition of itself when all other conditions are complete;
and since this [capacity] is not a separate entity—out of fear that it would result in the non-substantiality of the object—it appears when that [object] appears. (Pramāṇavārttika 3)
Because of such statements as these,

how could the totality of other conditions— such as those accompanying a jar— which possess the characteristic of being visible, not be distinct from the prostrations and so forth? Since [the result] would be obtained by excluding that which has the characteristic of being visible, the characteristic of an invisible object would likewise be merely the opposite of that.

It is also not tenable to say that [the negation] has the nature of the aforementioned state by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), because [it is said] "not [of that which] meets the conditions of perceptibility," and so forth.

Or, let there be the definition of a perceptible object; even if the final [negation] does not meet the conditions of a perceptible object, nevertheless, its denial of identity with anything else is not contradictory, provided that the collection of other causes for perception—distinct from the counter-positive—is present.
Since the jar is itself directly perceived, what other part of it could there be that is not seen and must therefore be examined by means of other instruments of knowledge?
Thus [is] the remaining [definition of] mental attention (*manaskāra*): it is the "turning toward" (*ābhoga*) of the mind—that is to say, its application.
This passage, contained within this [definition], has been written twice.

To this, the following reply is given: The specific nature [of the object] and the completeness of other conditions consist in the capacity of the object and the other conditions to produce the effect that is the cognition of color and so forth.
And this [capacity] does not possess the characteristics of being perceptible, because the power of a cause is for people like us always to be inferred from its effect;
otherwise, one who perceives the cause would have no doubt regarding the effect. Thus, the inference of a future life is not purposeful.

As he will state [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*]: "And because the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth does not admit of a perceptible characteristic" (6.35). Nor is that statement dependent on that alone, since it applies without distinction elsewhere as well.

The non-contradiction consisting in the similarity to the perceptible has already been stated; furthermore, the definition of the imperceptible object is the absence of that [perceptibility] which is its fitness for perception. Moreover, it is not the case that the imperceptible has attained the definition of the perceptible, nor is it logical that there is an absence of the properties and so forth belonging to the perceptible as having attained that [definition].

Thus, since both are imperceptible, there is indeed no establishment of mutual non-existence or of their own-nature as existing apart from each other— just as there is none between an atom and a ghost;
for this very reason, there is also no negation of identity, because the existence of one [the ghost] is admitted only in relation to a perceptible object.

Now, [it might be argued that] because of contradiction, there is an absence of the characteristic of an imperceptible object within the characteristic of a perceptible object; but even that is not so. For it is only things that have a perceptible nature which are admitted by the opponent to be contradictory, as stated in such passages as "of those very things that have a perceptible nature which are contradictory to them," and so forth. Furthermore, if it is sought to establish the non-existence of the other through the capacity (yogyatā) that is to be inferred from its effect, that too will be shown to be a mere wishful thinking in the passage beginning with "of the imperceptible" and so on.
In this context, "attaining the conditions for perception" consists of the completeness of all other conditions for perception and a specific nature [of the object]— *Nyāyabindu* 2.14.
Capability is of the nature of power;
since the direct perception of the soul that migrates to the next world has occurred, its capability is also directly realized,
as it has attained the characteristic of being perceptible.
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "In that regard, 'perception' (*upalabdhi*), etc.

Herein there are two positions: [the first is] the fulfillment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), which consists in the completeness of the other causal factors for perception (*upalambhapratyayāntarasākalya*) and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), or else being an object of sight (*darśanaviṣayatā*).

Regarding the first position: in that context, "non-apprehension of what has reached the conditions for apprehension" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānupalabdhi*) is the reason for non-existence, according to the text *Hetubindu* (p. 64). Here, "reaching the conditions for apprehension" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) means that when certain factors are present, an apprehension—that is, a cognition—is characterized; the "reaching" (*prāpti*) refers to the completeness (*sākalya*) of the other conditions for apprehension, such as the sense organs and so forth, relative to the conditions for the jar, as well as the specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) of the jar itself, and its capacity (*yogyatā*) in that regard—the word "and" (*ca*) serving to conjoin these.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "For there is no apprehension," and so forth.

For it is not the case that there is no completeness of the other conditions for perception; this [mention of completeness] is an illustration, by which the specific nature [of the object] is also grasped, whether it be its presence or its absence, because of its own being perceived. Since it has reached the state of being perceptible (*lakṣaṇaprāpta*), there would be a determination of those two—completeness and incompleteness—in the form of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Or, the word "since" (*yataḥ*) may be used in the sense of an objection.
If it were not so, what would follow? To this he says:
"And thus, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of both the effect and the essential nature is not established," and so forth.

Since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between two things pertains to all three periods of time, if the non-perception of that which is perceptible were of the nature of a simple negation (*paryudāsa*), then for no one would there be any certainty regarding the past or the present. How could one who does not know that "a *śiṃśapā* will not be a non-tree" or that "smoke is not born from non-fire" be a knower of pervasion (*vyāpti*)? Furthermore, how could he then perform an inference based on it? Therefore, this is not a certainty: namely, that the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions of perceptibility is the means of proving non-existence.

And because of the word "and" [in the definition of non-perception], the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established; that is, the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established.

This is because, regarding two types of objects characterized as perceptible—namely, those that have attained the conditions for perceptibility and those lacking them—the one characterized as perceptible but devoid of the other conditions cannot be determined. Thus, the character of being perceptible is not established in the cause, the effect, the presence, or the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Consequently, since the cessation of the cause or the presence is not established in any instance, how could there be a cessation of the effect or the essential nature preceded by that [cessation of the cause]? This is what is intended.

If it is argued that even if the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not occur, the capacity of the effect and so forth to indicate [the cause] exists through mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone; to this he replies with the words "having as its object the three times," and so on.

The intended meaning here is this: if negative concomitance is not established, positive concomitance is also not established, because the opponent accepts a mutual inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between these two.
Consequently, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), such as identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth, which is based upon that [concomitance], is also not established.
Only the perception of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the probandum and the probans establishes the necessary relation (*pratibandha*); since that [perception] is absent here,
it appears that a portion of the text has been lost, as this [subject] lacks the characteristic of being an imperceptible object.
That which establishes the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) of positive and negative correlations in their entirety.
He explains the verse with the words "perception" (*upalabdhi*) and so forth;
this is easy to understand.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore"—that is, for the reason stated by the aforementioned logic—there would be no single cause among those such as the "effect" (*kārya*) and others that possesses absolute non-deviation (*aikāntika-avyabhicāritva*).

Having thus demonstrated that the other [opponent] lacks the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) and that there is a refutation when those conditions are met, he now asks in order to refute non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) as a means of establishing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "If cessation consists in exclusion (*paryudāsa*), whose is this cessation? He replies: "Of that very perception which perceives the absence of *śiṃśapā*-ness when there is no tree, or the absence of smokiness when there is no fire. Of what kind of perception? He says: "Of past or present perception, not of the perception of a specific person."

The word "ca" (and) is to be understood here as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), because even if another [term] were excluded, the exclusion of the positive entity (*bhāva*) would not be established; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Not a non-tree," and so forth.

One who does not know that "it will not be a *śiṃśapā*" [is called] a non-tree; and one who does not know that "it will not be smoke" in such a way—what kind of person is he? He is one for whom birth from fire does not exist (*anagnijanmā*), meaning one for whom there is no arising from fire.

How could such a person be a knower of pervasion (*vyāptijña*)? Not at all; for the state of being a knower of pervasion consists in knowing the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in its entirety. Thus, the Buddhist (*saugata*) is not [a knower of pervasion].
Furthermore, one might later perform an inference regarding that tree or fire; how so?
Because for one who does not know [the object], there is the application of that [inference].
He states the conclusion: "Therefore, this is not an absolute rule," and so forth.

Therefore, this is not an absolute conclusion for whom? This is an illustration of "perception" (upalabdhi); thus, it is not an absolute rule that non-perception—whether of that which meets the conditions for perception or of its opposite—proves non-existence.
Who [is it]? He says: "Of that which has reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya*);
the particle *eva* (only) is to be understood here.
Non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), consisting in another entity distinct from the form of the object to be negated and its cognition, is the means of proving non-existence (*abhāvasādhanī*).

The meaning is that there is the establishment of the absence of tree-ness and so forth by means of the invisibility of future time and so forth, through the invisibility of being a *śiṃśapā* and so forth;
for one who does not know the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no possibility of performing an inference.

Regarding this, it has been raised in the *Hetubindu*: "Is it not the case that one does not prove the absence of an effect and so forth through the absence of a cause and so forth in another location and the like? Rather, because the absence of that [cause] there is not ascertained, it is merely stated as a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum): 'If there were no tree, there could be no *śiṃśapā*, for that would entail the loss of its own nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); and if there were no fire, there could be no smoke, for that would entail being causeless. To this, it has been said: "This is not so, because when neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is ascertained, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not ascertained."

And how is it that the *śiṃśapā* has the nature of a tree, such that it would not exist in the absence of that [tree-nature]? Because it is seen as such. If this is so everywhere, then the cognizer would be omniscient. If it is only in some cases, then the fact that the impermanent has the nature of being immediately preceded by effort—because it is seen so in the case of a jar and the like—is not its essential nature, since it is seen otherwise in the case of forest flowers and the like. Therefore, the claim that "the *śiṃśapā* will not exist in the absence of a tree" is likewise not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By this, smoke is explained:

because it is absent when that [fire] is absent, its nature consists in being that [fire]. But this involves mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): once its nature as that is established, its absence due to the absence of that [fire] is established, and from that, its nature as that is established; thus, this is nothing at all.

If the non-perception of the cause and the pervader establish the existence of their respective opposites through the proof of the presence of something else, thereby establishing the positive linguistic usage (*sadvayavahāra*) regarding them, and if that [non-perception] establishes the negative linguistic usage (*asadvayavahāra*) only when the objects in question meet the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), then how can those two types of non-perception—the non-perception of the cause and the pervader—be employed with respect to an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*)? They cannot be so employed as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not ascertained.

These two [types of non-apprehension] are employed in certain cases solely for the purpose of demonstrating that when the cause and the pervader—whose relations are already established—are absent, the absence of the other [the effect or the pervaded] must necessarily and invariably follow.

For when the relationship—characterized either as "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*) or as "identity" (*tādātmya*)—has been established between the cause and the pervader by means of the aforementioned proof that establishes the causal relation and the proof that establishes the relation of pervasion and pervaded, then wherever there is an absence of those two whose relationship has been established, there must necessarily and invariably be an absence of the other, whether it be the effect or the pervaded; otherwise, the consequence would follow that [the effect or the pervaded] is without a cause...
— *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p.
203–4, regarding another location and so forth.
It must be otherwise; otherwise,
there would be no invariable concomitance.
The accomplishment is established even in the absence of a tree, for it is observed to be so.
If it is argued that there would thus be such a perception even in the absence of effort, namely, that they are seen to be impermanent;
Because, even in the absence of a tree— which is impermanent— the nature of being a *śiṃśapā* is still possible;
[this refers to] the *śiṃśapā*.
If it were the nature of a tree, then because of the absence of trees, there would be an absence of the *śiṃśapā*.

Now, one might argue: "Granted that there is no attainment of the characteristic of the perceptible within the definition of both the perceptible and the imperceptible objects; nevertheless, since the effect consisting of the cognition of color and so forth is observed when conditions such as the opening of the eyes are present, in some cases the perceptible object is cognized as distinct [from others], and because that is not observed, the imperceptible object is cognized as distinct from the other. To this, he says: "Of the imperceptible," and so forth—just like the non-perception of a perceptible object that is itself imperceptible and not subject to inference.

Comparison: It is incorrect to say that non-existence is not established due to the non-perception of the invisible, because doubt would arise regarding the cessation of another's consciousness, leading to the undesirable consequence that those who perform consecrations (*saṃskartṛ*) would incur sin; for it is frequently observed that even when something is imperceptible, such as a disease, its cessation is determined. (Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p.
52). Ordinary people understand the non-existence of invisible things such as the minds of others.
Because its specific form, modification, and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable—[as stated in] Laghīyastraya, verse 15:
"How could there not be non-existence, given that the causes for the absence of inference are impossible? (35)

Just as the non-existence of an object of perception is established through non-apprehension when the causes for its non-perception are absent, so too, when the causes for the absence of inference are absent, the non-existence of the inferable—such as another's mind—is established; otherwise, the cognition of another's insentient body would be impossible. Thus, this [position] triumphs even over the proponent of the identity of the elements and consciousness (*bhūtacaitanyavāda*) by sheer audacity, because it entails the total abolition of inference, the denial of perceived objects, the lack of any stable consistency anywhere, the mere grasping at the refutation of others' positions, and the rejection of one's own position.
How so?

If, however, this insistence is maintained—that because distant things cannot be proven non-existent, then no reason (*hetu*) would be valid since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "smoke" with "perishability" and "fire" respectively would remain unestablished—then this is detrimental to the followers of Śauddhodani (the Buddhists), as it would entail the total destruction of inference (*anumāna*).
—*Aṣṭaśatī*, p. 52.
Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti, verse 15;
Pramāṇasamuccaya, page 108: "Of the invisible," meaning that which has an unperceivable nature.
Of what kind [is it]? Of that which is not inferable—that is, not determinable by inference—meaning, of that for which the effect and so forth have not been shown.
What [is the consequence]? He says: "How is its non-existence not cognized? It is indeed cognized.
Under what condition? He says: "When there is an impossibility of the causes of inference."

The absence of inference is its non-existence; the cause of that is the absence of the inferrer and so forth. It might be thought: "If, in the case of its impossibility—that is, when it is non-existent—there is an absence of the person performing the inference as well as an absence of the logical reason (*hetu*) and so on, then how can anything established as being invariably concomitant (*pratibaddha*) with that [object] be proven, if the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is always invisible? Furthermore, the non-existence of one thing cannot be determined by the non-existence of its effect and so forth; otherwise, the non-existence of smoke and *śiṃśapā* trees would entail the non-existence of fire and trees."

If it is argued that this is not so, the author replies here: "Like the non-apprehension of the perceptible" (*dṛśyasya-anupalambhavat*). "Of the perceptible" means of that which is endowed with the characteristics of a perceptible object. "Apprehension" (*upalambha*) means that which is apprehended, i.e., the perceptible; or else, it is that by which something is apprehended. "Non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*) is the absence of apprehension. "Like that" (*tadvat*) means similar to that. This is what is meant: just as when the causes for the absence of perception are absent and the observer and other factors are present, there is an absence of apprehension despite the [object] meeting the criteria for perceptibility—meaning that while the object possesses the characteristics of being perceptible, its apprehension is absent—so too should the absence [of the object] be understood in the case of the subject under discussion, even though it is imperceptible.
The meaning is that there would be non-existence; [this applies] to the perception of the seer or of light and so forth, provided they exist.

As for what was stated regarding the visible object serving as the substratum—namely, "how can there be a necessary connection (pratibandha) for anything with that which is invisible"—that is incorrect. One must consider: if the power characterized by visibility is itself invisible, how can there be an obstruction to its perception? Furthermore, as for the other point—that the absence of fire is known from the absence of smoke—that too is easily refuted. For, if the perception of an effect such as a jar is absent, how can the absence of the jar be established anywhere? Indeed, it could be argued that causes do not necessarily possess their effects.

Nor is it a valid answer to say that "the accomplishment of that [effect] necessarily occurs for one whose capacity is unimpeded," because since capacity is imperceptible, one cannot determine the distinction between that which has an impeded capacity and that which does not; furthermore,
The accomplishment of the effect by means of the cause.

Furthermore, since there is no certainty regarding the absence of every capacity— even those whose efficacy is restricted— in every instance, the apprehender or the causal agent would face the consequence that they could neither proceed toward nor turn away from anything whatsoever due to the suspicion of its presence.
He explains the verse with the words "Just as" (*yathaiva*) and so forth, out of concern for the possibility that there might be an obstruction to its capacity:
just as the non-existence of a perceptible object is established through non-apprehension, that is, from the absence of perception.
Under what conditions? He says: "In the absence of perception," and so forth.

The non-existence of perception is its non-arising; the cause of that is the deficiency of other causal conditions (*pratyaya*). Its impossibility means the completeness of other causal conditions. This is what is meant: even when there is completeness of other causal conditions, when the perception of a jar on the ground does not arise, then its absence is cognized. By demonstrating the establishment of the appearance of the perceptible object and thereby showing the presence of the causes of perception, that very [absence] is admitted.

In the same way, the non-existence of that which is inferable—that is, capable of being inferred—such as another's mind and so forth, is established under what condition? To this he says: "when there is no possibility of the causes for the absence of inference.
The cause of the absence of inference is the absence of the inferrer, the subject (*pakṣa*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth; "in its impossibility" means that these [factors] are present.

If it is asked, "How can there be the establishment of its non-existence when that [inference] exists?", the reason here is to be understood as "due to non-perception" (*anupalabdheḥ*), because there is an absence of inferential perception.

If it is objected, "But inference is an effect of the object to be inferred; therefore, in the absence of this [object], how can there be an absence of that [inference]?", he replies with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth: otherwise—that is, by the other way [of establishing non-existence], namely the manner in which its non-existence is not established when it exists—there would be no possibility of cognizing another insentient body, and thus the non-existence of the object to be inferred is established.
The absence of a jar [is established] when there is the existence of the subject, the example, and so forth, for the cognizer,
[but not] for another's mind and the like.
The relationship is that in the absence of the object of inference, there is an absence of inference.

It might be thought: "Since activities such as movement and withdrawal—which are effects of consciousness—are not observed in another's body, the absence of consciousness in that other body is established. Nor does the absence of an effect entail the absence of its cause, because the suspicion that the cause’s capacity is obstructed or that there is a deficiency of some other auxiliary cause has not been removed; therefore, since the cognition of another's body as being devoid of consciousness is untenable, what you seek to prove is already established. To this, he says: "That, this," and so forth; here, the word *tat* (that) carries the sense of *saḥ* (he).

Thus, this Buddhist, by defeating the Sāṃkhya—who asserts that consciousness is inherent in the elements (bhūtacaitanyavāda)—through his audacity, surpasses even those who assert that what has not existed in the three times does not exist;

for just as the former accepts everything as unperceived everywhere, so too does this [Buddhist] accept the existence of everything everywhere, because he admits that consciousness, whose capacity is restricted to its own cognition, exists everywhere like consciousness whose capacity is restricted to another's body.
Or rather, it should be understood that he likewise defeats even the proponent of the view that the elements themselves are consciousness.
Just as he maintains that consciousness, though unmanifest, exists in the elements, so too does this [opponent] maintain that "everything exists everywhere.
How, then, is he defeated? To this he says: "In every way," and so forth;
that is, in every manner.
The Sāṃkhya proponent’s discourse consists of speech with the Cārvāka.
If it is argued: "Surely inference exists for the Buddhist; how then does he prevail through mere audacity? To this, he says: "Because it would entail the abolition of inference.
Why is this so? To this, he says: "It is observed," and so forth.

It is an observed fact that smoke and the like arise from fire and the like, and that the *śiṃśapā* tree possesses the nature of a tree and so on. This is because the Buddhist denies not only other things, such as God (*īśvara*), but even this [observed fact].

For just as in that very body, consciousness—though its nature is an unperceived effect—is suspected to exist, because of the statement that "the absence of an effect implies the absence of a cause whose capacity is unimpeded," so too, the existence of smoke, *śiṃśapā* trees, and so forth, which have the unperceived effect of cognition, is suspected to exist either before or after fire, trees, and so on; thus, he considers that the connection (*pratibandha*) is not established. Why is that? He says: "In some cases," and so forth.
In some cases, because there is no fixed determination regarding place and so forth, and because the entity is not restricted to that very location, he states another reason: "The other," and so on.

This refers to the position of the opponent, such as the Jaina, who maintains that the self exists in the living body but not in things like jars; therefore, upon the cessation of the self, there is the cessation of the living being. This is the refutation—that is, the rejection—of that position.

For instance: the Supreme Self, whose characteristic is consciousness that persists through prior and subsequent states, cannot be established as non-existent on the grounds that it is not perceived by direct perception in objects such as jars, for this would lead to an over-extension of the argument;

nor can its absence therein be proven because its effects are not observed, as in the case of a dead body, such that the cessation of breath and so forth would necessarily follow from the cessation of the Self.

That very [absence] is "only that" (*tanmātra*) because of the insistence (*abhiniveśa*) and attachment (*āgraha*) therein, and because of the rejection of one's own position (*svapakṣapratikṣepa*). When fire has ceased, the absence of smoke from walls and such things constitutes the exclusion (*vyatireka*) from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). The "rejection of one's own" (*svapratikṣepa*) refers to the refutation (*pratihati*) of the Buddhist's own [position]. For example, just as it might be conceived that consciousness—though its capacity is obstructed in a body considered dead and thus not performing its own effect—might still exist, or as it might be conceived in a jar and so forth, so too might fire be conceived in a wall and such things. Therefore, the absence of smoke does not necessarily follow from the prior cessation of fire; for this reason [the Buddhist position is rejected].
The word "na" (not) serves as a conjunction with what precedes,
[referring] even to that which is observed by the Cārvāka.

Comparison—causes do not necessarily possess their effects; therefore, from the non-perception of the effect, what must be established is the absence of those [causes] whose capacities are unobstructed, and not of others. (Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā 2.32)
Those things such as smoke, *śiṃśapā* trees, and so forth, for which the unperceived effect known as "cognition" [does not arise]—
that is, those smoke, *śiṃśapā* trees, and so forth, which do not even produce a cognition of themselves when they are unperceived; this is the meaning.
The establishment of inseparable concomitance is the existence [of the cause],
[determined] by the non-perception of the effect.
In the case of a jar and so forth,
[the existence] of the jar and so forth [is dependent] upon the wall and so forth.
Not understanding the Master’s intention regarding the wall and so forth, another asks, "How? In response to him, the answer is given: "Invisible," and so on;
[the meaning is that] due to the non-perception of what is invisible, one would not perceive this in isolation.

Having considered this very point, it has been stated elsewhere by the gods: "In a solitary place where there is no perception of the invisible, the cognition consisting of the conceptualization of the visible and the invisible is [expressed as]: 'I am not a Piśāca. (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, Vol. 2, p. 26).

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the nature of mutually distinct, momentary atoms, whether it be its own form or another form, excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes because it is established in its own intrinsic being.
