For one who perceives this, how could there be a perception of an entity excluded from that [specific characteristic], if the nature of partless objects—which have reached the condition of non-apprehension—is not established? In the absence of that, since the distinction between the nature of the perceptible and the imperceptible would not be established in its entirety, the entire world would be as if in a deep sleep.

If it is argued that this has already been stated in the passage beginning with "and not [in the case of things] which have attained the characteristics of being visible" (*na ca na dṛśyalakṣaṇaprāpte*), we reply: the "attainment of the characteristics of perceptibility" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) was stated there as consisting of the completeness of other causal conditions (*pratyayāntarasākalya*) and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*); however, here it is said that "attainment of those characteristics" means being an object of vision (*darśanaviṣayatā*). Would a Buddhist or others not perceive this? To this he says: "I am not a piśāca, nor do I exist."
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, one should not characterize [the self] as "the conscious is not unconscious" or "the unconscious is not conscious.
The same should be stated regarding blue and so forth.

Of what nature is he? He says: he is one for whom there is no cognition (*dhī*) of distinction—that is, of difference—between the visible and the invisible; that is to say, he is like one who [perceives] molasses and milk as a single substance.
Under what conditions? He says: "When there is doubt and exclusivity regarding the non-perception of the unobservable.
This means that when there is doubt and exclusivity based on the non-perception of the unobservable, which constitutes the fulfillment of the conditions for perception.
Explaining the verse, he says: "The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)," and so forth.

The particular characteristic is the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), which are mutually distinct; its own form (*svarūpa*) is its essential nature (*ātmasvabhāva*). What is its other form (*pararūpa*)? Whether it be the nature of the object (*arthasvabhāva*) or not, he asks:
"Of what kind is it? and answers with "of the same class," and so forth.
Why? He says: "Each its own," and so forth.
What is that? He says: "What has happened to the Buddhist who sees? and he says: "How," and so forth.
How is there no perception at all? It is because there is no perception of that nature which is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes.
Under what condition? He says: "non-perception," and so forth;
when the nature of that partless object—which has reached the conditions for non-perception and is beyond the range of vision—is not established.
It is not the case that the absence of such atoms of [other] colors as yellow and so forth is established in invisible atoms of [a single color] like black;
therefore, that is not tenable—[as stated in] the three verses beginning with "All entities... (Pra.vā. 3.39).
In specific cows such as Khaṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and in all things such as white horses and the like,
everything exists by its own nature through the establishment of its respective self-nature.
Since things participate in exclusions from both their own-nature and other-natures,
therefore, based on whatever [other] things there is an exclusion of objects, conceptual distinctions of universals are constructed which penetrate those specific differences.

Therefore, that specific quality by which a distinction is perceived cannot be established by anything other than that; thus, the distinction is determined by its difference from others. — *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.165.

If it is argued that there would be no harm even if that perception did not exist, to this he replies: In the absence of that—meaning in the absence of that perception—the distinction between the perceivable and the imperceivable natures cannot be established in its entirety or without exception. Because of the failure to establish that distinction—that is, the separation or division such that pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth, are of a perceivable nature, while Īśvara and so forth are of an imperceivable nature—the world would be as if in a deep sleep;
there would be neither practice nor non-practice, and likewise no non-dual cognition.

It might be argued that if there were liberation from the protection of pride (mānatrāṇa) through emptiness, the world would be well-established; for I do not accept atoms anywhere, since I accept reality in accordance with conventional discourse, and thus this fault does not apply. To this, the Vijñānavādin replies with the words beginning "direct perception" (pratyakṣam), and so forth.

If one were not seeing [the object] directly as distinct from everything else, how could one perceive the absence of the nature of an invisible object within the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

Just as one who perceives a single thing necessarily perceives the absence of the nature of other objects, so too [must one perceive the absence of others] regarding that which has reached the conditions for perception; otherwise, the perception of an unmixed nature would be impossible.
And thus:
a Buddhist person would not proceed to consume curd and the like,
suspecting that there might be an invisible Buddhist body within it.
"Even when curd and such have been eaten, one might think, 'I have not eaten sour gruel and the like'—thus he either knows this or does not know it; yet the Buddhist body has not been consumed.

Thus, when diseases, spirits, planets, the sense organs, and so forth are excluded in isolation, how can there be the establishment of engagement or withdrawal? For how could another causal condition—whether complete, deficient, or otherwise—be set in motion, given that the power of mantras, medicines, and the like lacks any perceptible characteristic?
Nor is this an absolute rule that the power of the perceivable object is itself perceivable; enough with this digression.
Regarding the question, "What would perception do, which, depending upon the agent and the entire universe, is established [as such]? he says: "perceiving the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."

Of what nature is it? If it is excluded from others—whether of the same class or a different class—then how is it not a perception of the absence of the nature of an unperceivable object? Why would it not be a perception of the absence of the nature of an unperceivable object? It certainly is so; otherwise, how could perception see that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is excluded from others?
Revealing the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) through the verse, he says: "Just as one," and so forth.

Just as—in whatever manner of acting according to people's inclinations—the Buddhist (*saugata*), seeing a single [locus] such as the ground, necessarily (*niyamena*) perceives the absence of the nature of other objects that have met the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*); in that same manner, [it is established].
What does he do? He says: "perception," and so forth; the connection is that they "see.

For he does not perceive the absence of earth and the other elements by means of these very [cognitions] when they have attained their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather [he perceives the absence] of an invisible collection of atoms.
He states the refutation regarding this non-acceptance: "Otherwise," and so forth.
By this, [it means] because of the impossibility in the manner opposite to what was stated;
of what? Of the perception of an unmixed intrinsic nature (*asaṃkīrṇasvabhāvopalabdhi*).
And thus:
a Buddhist person would not engage in the consumption of curd and the like for the sake of eating it.
Suspecting that his Buddhist body there was invisible,
he consumed his food along with milk-rice and the like, yet he did not consume the sour gruel and such.
"He knows that [the offering] is produced from curds and so forth, or he does not know; he has not eaten the body of a Sugata"—
thus says the monk who consumes [the offering].

He states another refutation, beginning with "disease" (*vyādhi*) and so forth: when this [theory of] absolute chance (*ekānta*) is examined, how can there be the establishment of the existence or non-existence of the engagement and withdrawal of diseases, spirits, planets, the senses, and so on? It cannot be established from anything at all; for, from what source could one apprehend the completeness, deficiency, or otherwise of other causal conditions (*pratyaya*) for that establishment? Furthermore, he states another point: "And how can there be the establishment of the engagement and withdrawal of the power of mantras, medicines, and so forth?"—this is the connection [of the argument].
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because that [nature] is perceptible, he says here: "perceptible," etc.

Nor is this an absolute rule—that the inherent power (*ātmaśakti*) of a perceptible thing must itself be perceptible—because it is subject to deviation due to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Enough of this excessive digression; he states another refutation for the series of refutations.

If it is argued: "Indeed, momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), although constituting the very nature of perceived things such as jars, remains unperceived; and in worldly practice, the non-perception of the unperceivable has been stated to be a cause for doubt. Let this fault apply there [in the case of the jar], but not to the non-duality of manifestation (*pratibhāsādvaita*), because even that which is unperceivable—such as the thoughts of others—is negated therein"—to this he replies: "The nature," and so forth. Furthermore, non-perception regarding remote objects, characterized by the cessation of perception and inference, is a cause for doubt.
— Nyāyabindu 2.47:
Regarding the nature of cognitions that are manifold yet unitary and partless, when they are spatially remote...
How is momentariness established? From the non-perception of existence.

How can the reality of cognitions—which is partless and invisible—exist, and how can it not exist? Because of the remoteness of its own nature, for that very reason, its exclusion from both self-nature and other-nature cannot be established.

Since there is no perception of that which is not directly present, how could the existence of an external object be possible? Nor is an inference for its existence logical; for the point here is this: is that consciousness, which consists of partless, single atoms, variegated or unitary? In the first case, since it is not perceived like other existing things, it does not exist; so from what could its momentariness be established? From nothing at all.
Of what [things]? He says: "of those whose consciousness lacks parts.
Why? He says: "because of the nature's remoteness from its own being, due to non-apprehension";
the sense is that by means of non-apprehension, there is the very non-existence of that existence.
To the question "In what [does this occur]? he says: he provides the commentary on the verse beginning with "sva" and so forth, starting with "of cognitions" (*saṃvidām*) and so on.
He considers that the reality (*tattva*), which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of cognitions, is partless, invisible, and unperceivable; therefore, he thinks that it does not exist.
What happened after that? To this he says: "How," and so forth.
"And how not? is the question of the opponent;
the reason for that is stated as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and so forth.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: for this very reason—namely, due to the remoteness of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviprakarṣa*)—the exclusion from both self-nature and other-nature would not be established for cognitions (*saṃvidām*).

Now, one might object: "Since a false apprehended form is observed, its existence is inferred; so how can it be said that it does not exist? To this, he says: "From where could there be the perception of an external object? From a perception that is itself unperceived (*apratyakṣopalabdhi*), the reality of cognitions might be conceived."

He states another refutation: "Nor indeed is existence [sattā] measured by inference for the Buddhists; for when existence is the probandum (sādhya), every reason (hetu) falls into the threefold fault," according to the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* (1.193). The sense is that it is not logical to say "existence is inferred," because of the absence of a reason (hetu).
Here too, it should be explained as: "since existence would not be possible without inference."
Regarding the phrase "because perception is not direct," it is written twice [to indicate the following]:

when existence (*sattā*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), a property of existence (*bhāvadharma*) as a logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharma*) is contradictory (*viruddha*); and a property common to both is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, they bear these respective names.
He states the concluding verse beginning with "The nature of the visible" (*dṛśyasvabhāva*), etc.:
"The nature of the visible does not exist at all in isolation, neither internally nor externally, anywhere.
Whence could there be an entity, and where? Where, then, could the conventional usage of non-existence occur? (39)

Since even doubt, whether external or internal, cannot be established, what could be determined by what? Thus, for one who asserts the four elements alone, this is the most wretched of positions: how could there be a visible or perceivable nature anywhere, either internally or externally? From what has anything arisen? To this he says: from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is the perception, and where is existence (*bhāva*), since that [existence] is dependent upon perception?

Since it does not exist in the absence of that [perception], where is the Buddhist who establishes the conventional usage of "non-existence," given that the perception of another— which is the basis for that conventional usage— is absent when there is no perception of existence?
He explains the verse regarding the perception of another object with the words "outside or inside," and so forth.

If it is argued that, in that case, there would be doubt; to this he replies: because even doubt—not only anything else—is impossible to establish through cognition, since it too is a form of knowledge and, being partless, is identical to any other [cognition].

Alternatively, if it is argued: "Since establishment—that is, completion—is impossible, and because there is no perception that is common to both the existence and non-existence of that which serves as its basis, let there be the voidness of everything; moreover, even that is precisely what the Buddhists intend," [the author] replies here: "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would this voidness be established? By nothing at all, by anyone. Since this is so, therefore this Buddhist is worse than those who maintain the four elements, for he has negated the very self (*ātman*) perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas this [other school] has negated everything. Thus he thinks.

Let it not be that, according to the Cārvāka, emptiness is merely the absence of all appearances and lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*); rather, Prajñākaragupta maintains that appearance itself is devoid of properties such as unity or plurality, and that causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is likewise merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). To this, he replies with the words "perceptibility" (*pratyakṣatva*) and so forth, [arguing that] it is conceptual (*kālpānika*).
The perceptibility of absences, as well as their status as cause and effect,
would likewise follow for those very [absences], because there is no perception of partless [entities] due to the non-apprehension of what exists in ultimate reality. (40)

Since perception and inference in their entirety have non-entities as their objects, and since the [two] logical reasons—the effect and the essential nature—are themselves of the nature of non-entities, how could anything be established from them? Furthermore, it is not reasonable for this partless reality to be apprehended by conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*), because that would contradict experience and because such a thing is impossible in an absolute sense. Consequently, even the status of being perceptible, the objectivity of perception, the causal relationship between fire and smoke, and the relation of cause and effect would absurdly apply only to those [non-entities], and not to real entities.
Why is this so? He says: because neither a partless reality (*tattva*), which is a consciousness transcending all conceptual constructions, nor anything else, is perceived;
that is, because they simply do not exist.
To the question "How is this so?", he replies with the words "of that which exists in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthasata*) and so forth.
Why is there no perception of the ultimate reality, which is a non-dual variegation consisting of partless atoms? To this he says: "In perception," and so forth.

This is because perception, like verbal testimony, has as its object coarse forms that lack objective reality; and because inference has as its domain such [coarse] universals; and because [perception does not grasp] them in their entirety or without parts.

If it is argued that, just like sound, inference— though having a non-entity as its object— is nonetheless a means of establishing a real entity because of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) therein, [the author] says here: "In the case of an effect," and so forth.

Because the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) are non-entities— either because they lack the nature of existence like water in a mirage, or because, due to their partlessness, they lack the status of being real entities through non-perception— the following is stated: if the reality of the effect and the essential nature were [established] from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), then, owing to their necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), that class of inference would also be possible.

And why is it not so? For what reason would anything accepted by the opponent be established by those two—namely, the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)? It is for no reason at all.
Or rather, the term "by perception and inference" (*pratyakṣānumānābhyām*) should be understood [to apply here].

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "Just as for a worldly person, through those very two [means]—whether due to habituation or lack thereof—the future object is established because there is no other means, so too is my proof of partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) established. To this, he says: "And this is not so," and so forth.

And is it not the case that it is not at all proper or possible for conventional means of knowledge (*sāṃvyavahārikapramāṇa*) to conceive of or rely upon a partless reality as an agent? To this he says: "Because of the subversion of cognition.
Why? He says: [because] of the subversion of cognition.

Just as conventional cognition exists both before and after [an object] because reality is understood through its opposite, and its establishment follows that cognition; so too, in the case of a real entity, there is no perception of an impartite [whole], and what is perceived cannot withstand analysis— therefore,
even for the reasons of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Reality [is established] by means of the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) and the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) alone;
there is no fault even if the mere object is non-existent, like the appearances of a magical illusion, a mirage, and so forth— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.156.
If this is argued, [the author] says here: "In that case," and so forth.
The connection is with the phrase "because of its impossibility" when a one-sided view—that is, an exclusively false view—is accepted, as stated in the passage beginning with "its being perceptible."

If it is argued that [the distinction] is not established because of error; the answer to this is shown by the verse beginning with "through internal occurrence" (*antarvṛttena tādātmya*) and so forth:
"We, who know the single characteristic, perceive identity and so on; for those who know both the simultaneous and the successive, there is a single self-awareness through reasoning. (41)
Since reality is such that, through its connection with both the perceptible and the non-perceptible simultaneously, it exists as a composite of those very constituents;
how then could there ever be a "possessor of qualities" (guṇin) that is distinct from the collection of qualities (guṇasamudāya)? It is an absolute impossibility.

That is to say: this identity between the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*), characterized by some form of oneness—such as the oneness or difference of cause and effect—between the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the attainable (*prāpya*), is not to be transgressed by other people. Who are we that perceive it thus?
He says: "We Jains, who know the single characteristic. Why? He says: "From reasoning (*tarka*), that is, from inquiry (*vicāra*)."

If it is asked: "How can we perceive identity and so forth between that which possesses the occurrence of a subsequent mode immediately after a preceding mode has ceased? To this he replies: "Simultaneously," and so on.

We perceive through reasoning that there is a single, non-different self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)—where "self" (*sva*) is another name for the cognizer (*ātman*)—of those who perceive simultaneously, such as the apprehensions of qualities like color and taste, and of those who perceive sequentially, such as the apprehensions of modes like the lump of clay, the jar, and the pot.
When? At the same time. Of what two? Of perception and its opposite (non-perception).

Just as we understand it from the very nature of its perception, so too, by virtue of their connection—that is, their conjunction—of what? Of the constituent parts, such as the hands, feet, and so forth, which lack individual integrity; that which is the aggregate designated as the "body" is also perceived as a reality, as a single unity. This connection is established by adapting the case ending and number [of the pronoun]. Just as [the body] is merely an arrangement of atoms, in the same way, the aggregate of qualities such as form and so forth is perceived as a reality.
Regarding its synonym, he says: "Because it is possessed of qualities (*guṇin*)," for this reason, where indeed could absolute exclusivity (*ekānta*) possibly exist? Nowhere at all;

because, if absolute exclusivity were possible, then this perceived nature of one's own specific characteristic (*svalakṣya-ātma-lakṣaṇa*), which consists of non-absolutism (*anekānta-rūpatva*), would have to be transcended by others—the Jains.

The lump of clay, the small clod, the mushroom-shaped mass, the thick paste, the husk, the sheaf, and the jar are successive states (*paryāya*) of the clay as it is oriented toward becoming the form of a jar— namely,
of those aggregates (*skandha*) which have become conjoined and unified in the form of constituent parts.
This concludes the sixth chapter, "Establishment of the Characteristics of the Cause," from the *Siddhiviniscayaṭīkā* composed by Anantavīrya.
The Seventh Chapter: The Establishment of the Treatise (Śāstrasiddhi)

Like perception and the other means of valid cognition, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is also a means of establishing an object; and since there is no disagreement regarding this, he says "the treatise" (*śāstra*) and so forth, in order to explain its nature:
having observed through various forms of reasoning and scripture that even with respect to objects that can be examined, every treatise is deceptive and stained by the one-sidedness of falsehood.
The teaching of the virtuous, characterized by the truth of the word "syāt" (may be), is to be accepted;
for those whose intellects are capable of investigation, the use of the particle "kāra" here is sufficient—enough with the audacity of those who hold to one-sided views.
A scripture consists of either extensive [treatises] or intermediate statements; it is not a mere syllable or a single word, because such things are of no use in conventional discourse.
What is that? The meaning is that one must adopt, rely upon, and treat as authoritative [that which is sound].

How so? He says: "For those whose intellects are capable of critical examination, [the suffix] *ktvā* is used after a verbal root denoting the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.21). This refers to the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows.
Thus, some say that even regarding that which is capable of being examined by those whose intellects are able to investigate reality— thus [it is said].

Is it possible to examine only some specific [scriptures] among those such as the *liṅga* and so forth, rather than only those objects that are absolutely beyond perception? No; thus he says: "all," meaning all that has been composed by anyone other than the Omniscient One.
Of what nature is it? He says: "the word 'syāt'," and so forth.

That which has "syāt" as its suffix—that is, the syllable "syāt"—is called *syātkāra*. That [word] is also "heard there," meaning the sound itself; that which has this very [sound] as its true, non-erroneous mark (*lāñchana*) is described as such.
Why? He says: because it is the teaching (*śāsana*)—that is, the expounder—of existing things (*satām*) such as the living beings (*jīva*) and so forth;
or alternatively, because it is the indicator of the Exalted Ones (*arhat*), being their effect.

If it is argued that its state of being thus is doubtful, he says in response: "Whose doubt is there here regarding the teaching of the wise, who are experts in time? To this he replies with the great sentence beginning with "parīkṣaṇa" and so forth, which constitutes both an intermediate sentence and a major statement within the treatise.
The sixth case (genitive) occurs in connection with a *kṛt* suffix, denoting either the agent or the object— *Siddhāntakaumudī* 2.3.65.

If it is asked: "We have heard that the Blessed One is an Arhat; however, since there are indeed faults here resulting from the application of extremist views, how can this [teaching] be accepted? To this, he says: "Extremist," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: "Enough" (*alam*) means "it is sufficient" with respect to those who hold extremist views regarding objects (*viṣayiṇi*), because they metaphorically apply the term "extreme" (*ekānta*) to the object itself; thus, there is no need for the delusions of those who propound such views, since their faults have been refuted. Having considered this, he asks: "By what means? and says: "Having perceived [the teaching] to be contradictory," and so forth.

This refers to having seen and known that [the doctrine] is contradictory, being stained by false extremism (*mithyaikānta*); here too, the phrase "the scripture" (*śāstra*) and so on is to be connected.

By what means? To this he says: by means of reasoning (*tarka*) and scripture (*āgama*). By "reasoning" is meant the discernment between what is logical and what is otherwise, even regarding that which is already perceived; and by "scripture" is meant the words of the Truth (*tattva-vākya*), which are derived from logic (*nyāya*).
Of what nature are they? To this he says: "by many doors," meaning by many varieties, [serving] to refute the faults employed by those who maintain extremist doctrines (*ekāntavādin*).

If it is asked, "The scripture is indeed to be accepted; since all objects are established by means of empirical perception and inference alone, for what purpose is the scripture to be accepted?"—to this he says: "Scripture (śruta) is the path to the highest good for men who are cognizant and subject to transformation," and so forth.

The purpose of the instrument [of knowledge] is not to indicate the intention of the speaker, but rather the reality of the means and the goal. As the person hears, grasps, retains, understands, reflects upon, and becomes firmly convinced of the reality of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* as the means for the absolute and final cessation of beginningless suffering, so does the conscious, unchanging *puruṣa*—perceiving this demonstrated state of detachment and experiencing isolation (*kaivalya*)—attain liberation; thereafter, the instrument no longer presents itself to him.
And some maintain that a noble person does not fall away from the cessation of longing.

Not tolerating that reality of the means and the end, the Naiyāyikas [ask]: "How can there be activity on the part of an insentient instrument, given the risk of over-extension? Or how can there be perception by that which is insentient? How could an instrument see without another instrument? And how can there be perception even for a sentient being who is not an agent? Furthermore, how can there be a conjunction between the two pervasive entities—the seer and the object of sight—given their respective natures and states? Thus, the Naiyāyikas declare that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the abiding of the self within itself, free from all attributes, once birth has ceased due to the impossibility of further activity; this occurs because defects do not arise when false knowledge is removed through the knowledge of the principles (*tattva*), such as the self.

This grasping at "self" and "mine" is the cause of saṃsāra; since it arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*), how can it lead to liberation? Those followers of the Sugata (*saugata*) who assert that a permanent entity is simply impossible, and that the means for its realization is the cultivation of the Four Truths resulting in Nirvāṇa—which consists in the total cessation of the continuum—must be confronted with this objection: Since the false cognition produced by words that set forth the Four Truths lacks a real object, how can there be a realization of reality (*tattva*) from it? Furthermore, how can there be both the knowledge of reality and Nirvāṇa arising from the culmination of the intensification of the cultivation of what is not reality?

If there is no distinction between the positions of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and its opposite, since they are equally characterized by being exclusively false, is there any difference at all? Furthermore, regarding the presence or absence of the relationship between perception and its fallacious causes, as well as their conceptualizations, there is no distinction because their objects are equally false. Since the definition [of reality] is according to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since it excludes other classes of characteristics that are dissimilar to the specific characteristic, how can there be an understanding of reality? Moreover, since you admit that even the statement of a proof does not express reality, what kind of teaching on reality could the Sugata possibly have?
Thus, through the cultivation of reality, there arises—without remainder, free from error, pure, and absolute—the knowledge: "I am not, nothing is mine, and I do not exist."
Knowledge consists in the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*; this is the meaning.
Upon the dissolution of the body, because its purpose has been fulfilled, the *pradhāna* ceases its activity.
One attains both the certain and the absolute isolation (kaivalya).
Thus, because of the absence of the threefold suffering through its absolute cessation and non-recurrence, one attains isolation, which means liberation.

"Upon the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the removal of each subsequent one, resulting in liberation. — Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭhara-vṛtti;
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.2.
Alternatively, they are called Noble Truths because the noble state is established through their full realization.

As it has been said: "Monks, because he has fully awakened to these four noble truths as they really are, the Tathāgata is called the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.433; Visuddhimagga 16.20–22).
The certainty regarding this is as follows: "like the vision of the four noble truths.
They are called *āryas* because they have gone far away (*ārāt*) from evil states;
for that very reason, they regard these [truths] as true, and thus they are their "truths" (*satyāni*).
Because they are fourfold, it is said that there are "four.

The five aggregates of affliction, which have become the fruit, constitute the single truth called suffering (*duḥkha*). Those same aggregates, when acting as causes accompanied by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), constitute the second truth called origination (*samudaya*).

The third truth, called cessation (*nirodha*), is the state of the mind free from afflictions (*niṣkleśa*); the fourth truth, called the path (*mārga*), is a specific state of mind characterized by aspects such as selflessness (*nairātmya*) which serves as the cause for attaining that state—*Nyāyabinduṭīkā* (Dharmottara-prakaraṇa), p. 67.
Scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) alone is not [the means], for perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) have limited objects.

"The highest good" (*śreyaḥ*) is liberation; its "path" (*panthāḥ*) is the way. Because of the instruction regarding that path—namely, right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth—it is the "path to the highest good.
For whom? He says: for persons (*puṃsām*), that is, for souls (*ātmanām*), and not for momentary streams of consciousness (*kṣaṇika-citta-santati*), because [liberation] is absent in them.

If it is argued that [the scripture] would be useful for those who are absolutely distinct from knowledge, the author replies: For other perceivers—those who know both their own and others' natures—even if they have heard the scripture, it is useless. Just as with jars and the like, even when there is hearing, comprehension of the meaning, its subsequent practice, and the fruit thereof which is liberation, it is not useful for them.

Furthermore, for those whose nature is distinct from knowledge, such utility does not exist, just as it does not for space and so forth. Therefore, the conceptualization of a self is not fruitful on the path to liberation.
Right view, right knowledge, and right conduct constitute the path to liberation— Tattvārthasūtra 1.1— because of the absence of a [permanent] continuum.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because cognition belongs only to those things distinct from cognition— namely, the heard word and the self— and not to space and so forth, then how is this not a fault? For, since the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) has been refuted, existence itself would be indistinguishable everywhere.

Furthermore, when a distinct self is perceived, there is no cognition here in the form "knowledge is in the self" by which inherence (*samavāya*) might exist in this case; otherwise, one could even have the cognition "knowledge is in a donkey's horn," despite [the self] being existent, all-pervading, and unitary.

Now, suppose the view is that knowledge must reside in a substance because it is a quality, like color and so forth, and that there is a distinction between a quality and its possessor, since otherwise that [relation] would be impossible. That too is not tenable; for that [distinction] could only exist if one were to perceive a substratum distinct from the knowledge, the color, and so forth, but as has been stated previously, such a thing does not exist.
Even if one were to assume the perception of such a substratum, one would have to assume another substratum for that, and yet another for that, leading to an infinite regress.

If it is argued that the entire teaching of the Śākyas [Buddhists] is thus reduced to a mere plurality of forms and so forth—neither a self nor a composite aggregate (skandha) such as a jar—we say: no. This is because we establish the nature of the self as a single cognition existing in a temporal sequence (pūrvāparībhūta), and likewise because we establish the status of a jar or other aggregates through the unity, in some sense, of specific qualities such as form and so on. Furthermore, the reason (hetu) for proving that such a cognition depends upon another substance is unestablished (asiddha), since its quality-ness (guṇatva) is not established. For a quality is defined by the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.16) as: "A quality is that which resides in a substance, possesses [other] qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent [of other causes]."

16. Thus, the definition of a quality (guṇa) does not entail its dependence on a substance (dravyāśrayitva); nor is there any lack of distinction between substance and quality because of their connection through the difference between prior and posterior cognitions.
If it is argued that the nature of the prior and posterior states constitutes "quality-ness" and "dependence upon that," the response here is as follows:
Because it is impossible for [the object] to be a quality (guṇa),
the observation of the substratum belongs to a single cognition that is sequential in nature (pūrvāparībhūta).
In the Jaina view,
the self would not be distinct from knowledge; likewise, cognition and inherence, as well as the cognition of that which inheres in the same object, [would not be distinct].

To this, the following verse is appropriate: "For those who understand... Even so, if it is argued that this [consciousness] might belong to the Sāṃkhya Puruṣas because of the statement in the *Yogabhāṣya* (1.9), "And thus consciousness is also the own-nature of the Puruṣa," he says here: "Of those that undergo transformation."

[Objection: Is it not the case that for the Sāṅkhya, the Puruṣa is the desired goal, whereas for the Buddhist, the Pradhāna [is the goal] because of the transformation into consciousness? If it is asked, "How then can such a doubt be raised?", [the answer is]: No; because there is no distinction between consciousness and seeing, as they are non-different.
Intellect, apprehension, and knowledge are synonymous— Nyāyasūtra 1.1.15.

It might be thought: "The eternal Vedic revelation would be the means for their path to the highest good (*śreyas*. To this he replies: "Having as its object the reality of both the means and the goal" (*sopāyopeyatattvārtham*).

Here, "means" (*upāya*) refers to the cause—namely, falsity (*mithyātva*) and so forth for *saṃsāra*, and right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth for *mokṣa*. "Goal" (*upeya*) refers to the fruit—namely, *saṃsāra* and *mokṣa*. That which exists together with the means is "with the means" (*sopāyam*); that which is both such [a means] and the goal is the "reality" (*tattva*), which is the "object" (*artha*) or subject matter of the scripture. Thus it is described.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the eternal Vedic revelation does not provide such [a teaching].
If it is argued that their path is indeed called the *piṭaka-traya* (the three baskets), to this he replies:

"The word of the Sugata, which indicates the intention of the person [who spoke] and is not merely the literal expression of the speaker, is the path to the highest good (*śreyas*); the Mīmāṃsaka does not say so."
The Buddhist replied:
"The three collections— the Sūtra-piṭaka, the Vinaya-piṭaka, and the Abhidharma-piṭaka— are for men."

Refuting the path to the highest good (*śreyas*) of the Sāṃkhya and Naiyāyika by means of the Naiyāyika, and that [path] of the latter by means of the Sugata’s [teaching], he himself explains the verse by way of negation (*vyatireka*), beginning with the words "the instrument" (*karaṇam*).

In this regard, he first presents the Sāṃkhya doctrine: "The instrument [of cognition], such as the ear and so forth, in whatever manner hears, grasps, understands the meaning of the scripture that has been heard, retains it—bringing it to the state of being an object of memory and retention at a later time—discerns it, becomes transformed by its meaning, reflects upon it, deliberates whether 'this is correct' or 'this is otherwise,' triumphs, and becomes intent upon it; why does it do so? He says: 'The qualities (guṇas),' etc.;
the qualities are sattva and the others; the persons (puruṣas) are the souls; the interval between them is their distinction, and that very thing is the reality (tattva)."
In what form? As a means (*upāya*), as a cause (*kāraṇa*).
Of what? To this he says: "of the cessation of beginningless suffering.
Of what kind [of cessation]? He says: "certain" (*aikāntika*), and so forth.
To whose [state] does it belong? He says: "of the person" (puruṣasya). Seeing in such and such a manner, what [does he attain]? He says: "disgust and detachment" (nirvedaṃ vairāgyaṃ ca).
Of what nature is it? He says: "This is shown as being demonstrated by the instrument.
Who is it? He says: "The Puruṣa.
Of what nature is he? "Conscious."
Furthermore, what is its nature? Being unchanging, what does it do while perceiving? To this he says: "It attains liberation.
What is it doing? Experiencing what? Kevalya (isolation).

If it is argued that the Buddhist analysis implies that even one who is liberated might return to saṃsāra, he says in response: "He does not show himself again"— the word "again" (punar) being understood as "afterwards" (paścāt).
Nor does the noble person ever cease [to exist].
Why? To this he says: "Because of the cessation of longing"—thus some followers of Kapila [argue].
Refuting that with the perspective of the Naiyāyika, he says: "That," and so forth.

What is that which pertains to the Sāṅkhya? The connection is that the Naiyāyikas, unable to tolerate the truth regarding the means and the goal [as held by the Sāṅkhyas], have declared their own view of liberation. To the question "How is it tolerated? he says: "How," and so forth.
How could there be cognition—which consists of hearing and so forth—in something that does not function?
He asks: "Of what? and replies: "Of the insentient instrument, which is a transformation of *pradhāna*.
Why? He says: "Because of the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," meaning that such cognition would then follow for jars and other such things as well.

Or else, by what means—through what mode of perception or inference—is there apprehension or comprehension of that which is insentient and imagined by others? It is not by any means, because that [apprehension] is absent therein; thus it is stated: "How could there be an instrument? and so forth, because apprehension is absent in the *puruṣa*.

If it is objected: "But if that [instrument] does not exist, how could the person see what has been shown? To this it is replied: How could an instrument see without another instrument? Otherwise, one might as well see the object in the same way; so what is the point of postulating an instrument? If one were to postulate yet another instrument for that [first instrument], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, he states the fault in such a postulation: because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), for in that case, one would have to postulate [instruments] for everything else as well.
Therefore, that [instrument] is not tenable as a cause, and so forth.

Regarding what was stated by the author of the *Karaṇa*—namely, "seeing," and so forth—he replies: "How can there be perception even for a conscious being who is not an agent? Because that would lead to an over-extension [of the principle].
This refers to the Puruṣa who is a non-agent; in the system of Kapila, the Puruṣa is a non-agent, devoid of qualities (*aguṇa*), and pure.
Because of this statement, how can there be apprehension? If it is the direct realization of an object by the conscious self, [we reply:

for that which was previously unengaged in seeing the object—even when the object was present—is not logically capable of seeing it later; if it were previously unengaged, it would remain so as before. If it abandons its prior state, how is there no agency? For, just as with the action of an instrument, there is an inherent agency through the action of seeing as well.

Now, if it is argued that the Puruṣa, being eternally indifferent, perceives whatever object is present at any given time—just as [an image appears] in a mirror—that is incorrect; for such perception is impossible so long as indifference is not relinquished.

Furthermore, if it is claimed that he perceives everything at all times, the author replies: "Because of the over-extension [of the consequence]," meaning that it would follow that everyone would perceive every object everywhere at all times.

And it is said: "In the Sāṃkhya system, the Self is formless, conscious, an enjoyer, eternal, omnipresent, inactive, a non-doer, devoid of qualities, and subtle" (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhadvṛtti, p. 42).
It was written again that what was previously stated is not logical,
because even the observer is merely the agent of the act of seeing, since the state of being an observer is untenable if it does not consist in the nature of being the agent of seeing.
The Puruṣa states another objection: "In the case of the visible and the seer," and so forth.

How can there be a conjunction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, which are all-pervasive by virtue of their natures as the visible and the seer? Or rather, the word "or" (vā) is intended to include the contingency [of their being distinct].
If it is argued that there is no fault because those two sometimes attain different states, to this he says: "of those two states" means of those two immutable [states].

If it is argued that this is incorrect because the *pradhāna* is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), so that it is improper to speak of "those two states"; [the reply is: No, for by that logic the *puruṣa* would also incur the consequence of being subject to transformation, as there would be no distinction between them.
This is because [he believes] that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would never cease.
Thus, by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), it has been explained that Nature and Spirit are subject to transformation,
just like the Pradhāna.
Now he presents the view of the Naiyāyikas in order to refute it through the Buddhist perspective, beginning with the words "the self" (*ātmā*) and so forth.

That collection of categories of which the self and so on are the primary elements—that alone is reality (*tattva*). Through knowledge of that, when false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is removed, defects (*doṣa*)—namely passion (*rāga*) and the rest—do not arise. Because they do not arise, activity (*pravṛtti*) is impossible; because of the impossibility of activity, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the effects of passion and the rest, are impossible. Upon the cessation of birth, the Naiyāyikas declare that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the abiding of the self, devoid of all qualities, within its own nature.
As it has been said:

The attainment of the supreme good results from the knowledge of the truth regarding the means of valid cognition, the objects of cognition, doubt, purpose, example, tenet, members of a syllogism, reasoning, ascertainment, discussion, sophistry, cavil, fallacies of the reason, quibble, futile rejoinder, and points of defeat. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1)
Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the non-existence of each preceding one; thus, liberation [occurs]. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.2)
Thus, because that which immediately precedes it does not exist,
the Buddhist states this refutation, beginning with "So 'yam" and so forth.

To the question, "Who is this one who, though measured by the Sāṅkhya, is being addressed as a Naiyāyika?", he says: "How can the grasping of 'self' and 'mine' lead to liberation? If one asks why, he replies: "Because it is the cause of *saṃsāra*.
Furthermore, it is not logical that the very cause of *saṃsāra* should be the cause of liberation, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Why is this so? He says: "Because improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) is [the cause], and because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is without an object.
This is what was stated:
The meaning is that one is deluded;
when there is the notion of a self, there arises the conception of "other," and from the division between self and other, grasping and aversion follow.
"All defects arise when bound to these two" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.221). Having stated this, he sets forth another refutation beginning with "of the eternal": "Of the eternal," etc.
By this [statement], the possibility of an eternal thing—one whose nature is unchanging—being a real entity is thus excluded.
This too has been explained.
Now, he introduces the Buddhist doctrine in order to refute it himself: "The four truths," and so forth.

The four truths are those known as suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). Those who speak of that which has the means for the cultivation (*bhāvanopāya*) of these as its cause are the followers of the Sugata (*saugata*).
"What is that? he asks; [the answer is] "nirvāṇa," which is "mokṣa.

Of what nature is it? He says: "sakala" and so forth—[meaning] having the form of the total destruction of the continuum of all things (*sakala-santāna*). [The opponents] might thus "stand their ground" or "be subjected to inquiry."
If one asks, "How so? he says here: "How so," and so forth.

Knowledge concerning that [truth] produced by words that set forth the Four Noble Truths is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), because its object is not the [actual] thing (*artha*)—due to the lack of a necessary connection (*apratibandha*) with the thing—and because the word does not arise directly from that [thing], since the connection between them is not admitted. Therefore, how could there be no understanding at all of reality characterized by the Four Noble Truths?
If it is argued that even so, liberation would occur for those who cultivate whatever is understood from that [word], he says here: "How so," and so forth.

How could there be knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)— namely, the knowledge of the four truths and *nirvāṇa* arising from that [meditation], which is born from the culmination, the limit of excellence, and the final stage of meditation upon an object that is not reality? [If one were to argue] that it would be like knowledge afflicted by desire, grief, and so forth, and thus would be merely non-reality knowledge (*atattvajñāna*),
that is not tenable—
[because it arises] precisely from the objects themselves.
"From verbal testimony [comes knowledge] of the path to heaven and liberation; the person who distinguishes [the means] is the authority.
Even if another [person] lacks full understanding, that [authority] may still belong to him. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra 2.31)

In that very context, he states another fault: "The false absolute," and so forth. Just as there is no distinction between the knowledge of the meaning of a treatise that propounds an eternal self and the treatise that propounds the Four Truths—since both are equally characterized by the false absolute (mithyaikānta)—when that is the case, is there any distinction whatsoever between the two positions of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and its opposite? *Nairātmya* means the state of being devoid of a self; "the other" means the state of possessing a self. Between these two positions, or between these two propositions, is there any difference? The meaning is: there is no difference whatsoever. Consequently, one thinks: just as liberation results from the cultivation of the [notion of] a self, so too does it result from the cultivation of selflessness.

Regarding the Nyāya and Buddhist treatises, one might ask: "Is it not said that there is no difference between the two? If you argue that since both possess positions such as the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth—provided that a certain position exists and not another—and that liberation belongs only to those proponents of selflessness who, having understood the meaning from scripture, further investigate and meditate upon it through perception and inference; to this, he replies with the verse beginning "perception," etc.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the logical reason (*hetu*), as well as their fallacious counterparts (*tadābhāsa*), constitute "perception, reason, and their fallacies. These are themselves the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and their divisions. Their "connection" (*sambandha*) is the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) with the object; the presence or absence of that [connection] pertains respectively to the conceptual constructions of perception and reason, and to the conceptual constructions of the fallacies of perception and reason—the absence of connection with the object in the case of the fallacies of perception and reason. Now, regarding these two positions—selflessness (*nairātmya*) and its opposite—is there some distinction between them? This is the connection [of the argument]. Since perception and the other means of knowledge are negated in both positions, he considers that through conceptual construction, that [negation] is equal in both cases.

Why is this so? To this he says: "false," and so forth. The state of being the object of those two is their "object-nature" (*gocaratā*); because that is without distinction, why is that also so? To this he says: "according to its definition," and so forth.

If it is argued: "Let it be that in this way, according to its definition—that is, without overstepping its characteristics, being 'as-it-is-defined'—and since that object imagined by proponents of other doctrines such as non-self (nairātmya) is of a different character, dissimilar, and of a distinct genus from that [true nature], therefore, in the view of non-self, the knowledge of reality leading to nirvāṇa is not logical," to this he says: "From what? and so forth.
The realization of reality through some means of valid cognition— whether by the Sugata or anyone else—
is thus first refuted as the accomplishment of one's own welfare for the Sugata under the position of the doctrine of a self (ātmavāda).
Now, refuting the accomplishment of the welfare of others in some way—whether eternal or non-eternal—he says: "In the proof," and so forth.

This refers even to the statement of the proof, that is, even to the statement of the three-fold mark (trirūpaliṅga), such as: "Whatever exists, all that is impermanent" (*Vādanyāya*, p. 6); not only [the injunction] "One should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice" (*Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad* 6).

Since the Buddhists admit that such [teachings] as these do not express reality, he asks: "What follows from that?"—namely, "Of what nature is the teaching of the Sugata, the speaker? and so forth. This means:
of what nature is the teaching of the Sugata? It is of a nature that is true.
That is not tenable—
for it has been said: "One who possesses knowledge is sought after so that one may practice what he has taught,
by those who suspect deception when an ignorant person attempts to give instruction" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.32).

Even when [the speaker] possesses knowledge, reality is not understood from their words; rather, there is only the apprehension of the speaker’s intention. Furthermore, since this occurs even from the words of others, it must be stated as follows:
[this apprehension] is possible even from the words of the Naiyāyikas and others.

"A person possessing knowledge is sought out for the sake of practicing what he has taught; those who suspect deception do not seek one who merely provides instruction. Thus, the realization of reality by people occurs either through the presence of the Sugata himself, or teachings [emanating] from walls and other such things.

Thus say some; that is incorrect, because the realization of reality through its proximity must be either perceptual in nature or conceptual in nature. In the first case, it follows that for all living beings, omniscience arises simply as a means of being in its proximity.
This would imply that one who knows only the Four Truths is omniscient, which is the position of the opponent;
as it has been said:
Due to the momentum of his accumulated provisions, teachings issue forth from even walls and other such objects according to his desire, like those from a wish-fulfilling gem—
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 3680.
By his mere presence... [of] the world, Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.1.38.
Merely by being in the presence of the Sugata, one becomes a knower of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with their means:
that which is to be abandoned is the truth of suffering; that which is to be adopted is the truth of cessation; and the means for these two are the truths of origin and the path.
Whether he sees far or not, let him who is authoritative see only that which is desired as the truth;
for if one who sees far were the authority, we would worship vultures.
Come here,
O birds who see from afar and hear from afar!
As stated in *Prajñāpradīpa* 1.34–35 and elsewhere,
the practice of reality would thus be rendered purposeless.

Regarding the second alternative: would it consist of mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or would it be of the nature of inference (*anumāna*)? In the case of the first alternative, the fault already mentioned applies, namely, that it is "the cultivation of what is not reality" (*atattvabhāvanā*), and so forth. Furthermore, if its object were held to be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this would be contradictory, given the principles stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* (3.1): "There are only two means of valid cognition," and "conceptual construction is the appearance of a non-entity," and so on.

Regarding the second alternative: if the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) arises from the mark (*liṅga*), and if the mark itself is apprehended by oneself, then the realization of the probandum (*sādhya*) must also occur by oneself; so what is the use of its [the probandum's] presence? For it is of no use to one who is already cognizing fire from smoke.

Now, if the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) is like that of the probandum (*sādhya*), then it must arise from that very same [cognition]; and if that [cognition of the mark] is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), then—despite there being no distinction in their both being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)—why is there this division such that it is perceptual with respect to the mark but not with respect to the probandum? If it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), how can the apprehension of the mark arise from it, since it would then lack the nature of inference (*anumāna*), and if it were an inference, the same problem would recur, leading to an infinite regress?
Therefore, there is no apprehension of the reality of anything through the proximity of that [mark], because it consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpātmaka-bhāvanā*).
There are only two kinds of valid cognition— [as stated in] the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*—
and the presence of the Sugata makes that presence meaningful.

Regarding what was further stated on account of the Sugata’s presence— that "teachings [issue] even from walls and so forth"— if teachings can arise from those things even when they are devoid of consciousness (jñāna), how can it be well-said that [they issue] "from walls and so forth"?
Regarding the reading *kuṭyādibhyaḥ*, the meaning is "from the root-gandhakuṭī. [As for the verse: "Words have conceptualization as their source; conceptualizations have words as their source.
Because of their mutual connection, these words do not touch the objects. Is this so?

Now, if those sounds which occur even in the absence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are entirely different [from the mind], then that mind must also be something else which could exist even in their absence; in that case, how is the existence of another world established? Furthermore, if this were so, how could there be a perception of consciousness in another body through speech and the like? And why would it not be so? Is it because Dharmakīrti and others say that [speech arises] from mere material elements due to the proximity of someone—like a wall or such—or do they say it of their own accord? Since this doubt has not been resolved, [the proof fails] because [speech] would arise from mere matter even in the absence of consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding the Sugata: if no one attains the realization of reality through his teachings, what is the use of them? If there is [such realization], then it is established that sound denotes meaning.

If you argue that, just as in that case, another [sound] also [denotes meaning] due to its proximity to that [realization], then other [sounds] would also [denote meaning] due to the proximity of others, because there is no restriction on the capacities [of sounds].
The teachings of Kapila and others would also be indicative of reality;
however, as for this [objection]: that which arises dependent upon the speaker’s intention (vivakṣā) could only convey that very intention.

Thus [it is said]. Even in that case, those [cognitions] arising in connection with walls and so forth would cause one to infer the walls and so forth, and since that [inference] depends upon their proximity, the realization of reality would either be remote or obstructed.
Therefore, it remains to be established what kind of teaching of reality this is;
in this very manner, the passage beginning with "by this, the means and the goal" has been explained.

If it is argued that since words are teachings, even the Sugata must possess conceptual construction (vikalpa), and therefore [the teaching] consists of phenomena (dharma) and so forth; to this he replies: "That which includes both the means and the goal," and so on.

If the Buddha, having ascertained the reality of both the means and the goal, were to cause others to ascertain it through expressive words, then conceptual constructions would have reality as their domain. [Objection:

He, while ascertaining reality through conceptual constructions that do not touch ultimate reality, causes others to ascertain the object of conceptual construction by means of expressive words that do not denote reality. Who is capable of bearing such a burden of contradiction, other than one who is utterly deluded?
The Buddha, the Sugata, having ascertained [the nature of reality] and brought it within the scope of conceptualization, does not ascertain it through non-conceptualization;
by this he shows that since the pure, non-conceptual state of awakening exists for the Buddha, no verbal activity proceeds from it, and thus the conceptualization of "Buddhahood" is purposeless.
By this, the following argument advanced by Gadādharakīrti is also refuted:
"Those poets who conceptualize the words of the Sugata, the Sage conceptualizes even those conceptualizations;
because they do not exist apart from that [conceptualization], the fault shines forth. Therefore, they [the poets] effectively utter praises through their words of praise."

How so? In the absence of such speech, what is the use of that which is meaningless and merely nourishes [the notion of] objects? The rest has been considered immediately above: "Now, non-duality is free from impurity. Therefore, everything stated there is improper; because of the absence of the meaning of such speech, whether the activity of speech or its object were to be perceived from it, in either case, words would have only particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their domain.

If it is argued that this might apply to the Buddhists (*saugatas*), we say no; for since that [perception] is not denied in other cases as well, it would not be restricted solely to the object itself. This is because others also accept it for themselves, and there exists a perception of extreme proximity, as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, page 233: "to whatever extent... etc.

It is not logical that the speech of anyone arises from a conceptualization other than [the conceptualization] of another; otherwise, smoke might also arise from fire in one place, yet from something else in another.
Just as [the cognition] of an object is [produced] by the Sugata in one way, so too would the speech of a Buddha arise from something other than a stable [state].
Having determined what? He says: "With means," and so forth.

By whom, and what would he do? To this he says: If, by means of expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*), he were to determine the Supreme—which is other than the self (*ātman*) and unknown during the day—then what would have occurred? To this he says: "Conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) based on words would have their range within reality (*tattva*)," meaning they would have the well-defined characteristics (*sulakṣaṇa*) as their object; this is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied.

He thinks as follows: If that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the Sugata has birth and so forth as its object, then—just like any other conceptual construction—if his speech were bound to that [object], then that very [object] would be understood from it; thus the same fault applies to the statement of the proof (*sādhana*), and so on.

Alternatively, if it has the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, then the conceptual construction of "blue" and so forth does not have a real entity as its domain, because of that [fact of being a conceptual construction], just like the conceptual construction of water in a mass of mirage-rays.

Furthermore, the statement that "conceptual construction (vikalpa) is a distortion because it appears as a non-entity and is thus a cognitive affliction" is merely a verbal assertion; for even the word of the Sugata does not prevent that [appearance], and consequently, the word originating from him also has that [non-entity] as its object.
Thus, from the word of the Sugata...
Thus, non-conceptual [cognition] is the fault of ordinary people.
Just as the word of the Sugata is meaningful for us and others, so too is that of another.
Because the words of the Sugata are conceptual, even though they are connected with the meaning.
He explains the verse by way of negation (*vyatirekamukhena*), beginning with "the ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) and so forth.

This aforementioned ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which consists of the principles of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, is not touched by those things that are beyond its scope; he asks, "by what kind of things? and answers: "by conceptual constructions" (*vikalpaiḥ*).
Doing what? To this he says: "ascertaining," that is, determining.
What? "Reality" (tattva). Who? This very Buddha causes his disciples to ascertain it.
By what means? By words (*vākya*). Of what nature are they? They are those that do not denote real entities (*tattva*).

What [is the object] like? To this he says: "The object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has a clear and common form; this is the real entity (*tattva*). Who is capable of bearing this burden of contradiction, this burden of the fault that leads to self-destruction? Only one who is capable of bearing the burden of absolute certainty (*ekānta-viniścaya*), because [the opponent] is devoid of any consideration of what precedes and follows.

[The opponent argues: "It was written again [in the verse] that he is capable of understanding; surely the disciples do not realize the reality (*tattva*) directly through the words of the Sugata, but rather his intended meaning (*abhiprāya*), and then they themselves realize the reality through reasoning. To this, [the author] replies: "If [it is] verbal," and so forth.
If the investigators, having understood the speaker’s intention through words...
Why could they not likewise realize reality through the eyes and other sense organs?

Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between objects seen and heard regarding the realization of what is real or unreal through the examination of what is logical or illogical; for if only sensory cognition—such as that of the eyes—had reality as its object, then non-conceptual cognition would lack validity, since its validity consists solely in the exclusion of superimpositions. Otherwise, it would follow that all other cognitions would likewise possess validity.
That [intention] would exist only from the perspective of conventional reality and so forth;
however, that does not exist for the Sugata, the speaker, once one has understood his intention— that is, his desire to speak.
By what means? He says: "by words.
Who are they? He says: "the examiners," that is, those who contemplate reality. What should they do? He says: "they should understand."
What? Reality. By what means? By reasoning, if it be of the nature of perception and inference. If...
He states the refutation: Why indeed would the investigators not thus comprehend reality through the eyes and so forth?
The mention of the "eyes" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the other sense organs, and by the word "and so forth" (ādi), inference is included.

This is what is meant: if, even when one engages with the word of the Sugata, there is no realization of reality from that [word] alone, but rather through reasoning in the form of perception and so forth, then—since reality is the object of perception and so forth—the realization of it would come from those very sources; what, then, is the use of the word of the Sugata? Thus it would be useless. [But this is not the case,] for one realizes the speaker’s intention through words, [namely] from the word of the Sugata.

Since the commentary on the *kārikā* is easy to understand, he has composed it using words that convey the speaker’s intended meaning; yet, regarding this very point, he states another objection—beginning with "naravī" and so forth. [The opponent asks: "When that cognition is being produced, by what means? He replies: "By the examination of what is logical and what is illogical (*yuktāyuktaparīkṣayā*)," meaning by that examination which determines, "This is logical" or "This is illogical."

What is it? He says: "Is there some excellence, or is there none at all? Of which two? To this he says: "Of two objects. Of what kind? "Perceived and heard," that is, those apprehended by the senses and by words.

He thinks as follows: "If, having apprehended a reality, investigators were to apprehend that very same reality through reasoning after examining the underlying intention, and likewise, having apprehended a reality from verbal testimony, they were to apprehend that very same reality through that [reasoning] without [examining] the intention—then what kind of distinction would there be between the two? There is no superiority. To this he says: Because there is no such superiority by which the cognition of the eye and other senses alone would have reality as its object, whereas the cognition derived from hearing (śruta-jñāna) would not have reality as its object; that superiority does not exist.

If it is argued: "But even when scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) has been set in motion regarding its own object, it does not exclude superimposition (*samāropa*), because even when it is stated that 'sound is impermanent,' the cognition of permanence is not removed; otherwise, the means of proof would be useless, as the instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which excludes such [superimposition]," to this he says: "That," and so forth.

The superimposition of that [non-existence] is the superimposition of objects seen or heard; inference is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that. It is thought that if the validity of that very exclusion alone is accepted—and not the validity of the knowledge derived from hearing (*śrutajñāna*)—then non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*) would not possess validity, because it lacks the quality of being an exclusion of that [superimposition].

How could it not be so? To this he says: "In every way," meaning by the very mode of excluding that [superimposition], and also by the mode of grasping the object, for fear of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [validity] applying to something else as well; or rather, just as by the mode of momentariness, so too by the mode of blue and so forth, since even here there is a dependence upon conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Whether by way of non-repetition or even by way of repetition, since there is still the superimposition of identity between the perceived and the attainable, how could perception otherwise be a means of valid cognition regarding what is yet to come? If it is asked, "In that case, to what would it belong?"—to this he says: "Conventional," and so forth. It is called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) because it conceals (*saṃvaraṇāt*) distinctions; it is the cognition of a whole (*avayavin*) and so on. By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), recollection and other such cognitions are included. If it is argued, "Let it belong to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); what is the harm?", to this he says: "And that," and so forth.
The intended meaning is that [otherwise] there would result the absence of any restriction on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus,
[inferences such as] "sound is momentary because it exists" and so forth serve to exclude superimpositions (*samāropa-vyavacchedaka*).

Having thus established in general that the Sugata’s teaching of reality consists precisely in the exclusion of superimpositions (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*), [the author] now says "by means of reasoning," etc., demonstrating what kind of teaching of reality consists in the specific negation of the path characterized by selflessness (*nairātmya*) as taught by him: "By means of reasoning... and so forth, as spoken by the Sugata.

Nirvana is attained when the doubt regarding selflessness has ceased, through a non-conceptual state of consciousness that is distinct from others, wherein successive existences have mutually receded and merged into a single identity.

Whether by itself or through another, even when there exists an excellence of similar or dissimilar transformation among one's own or another's cognitions, this living soul (*jīva*)—being individually experienced within each person and being distinct from any confusion or intermixture—is itself that which reveals the status of being the object of a cognition whose scope is the general nature of an unerring identity among one's own and another's cognitions; thus, it utterly refutes the one of wicked intellect who denies it. What need is there for further deliberation on this? If [this is not so], it is merely the manifestation of darkness.

Apart from a soul (*jīva*) whose nature consists in the transformation of the sequence of conceptualizations of one's own and others' views, the absolute particulars (*ekāntaviśeṣāḥ*) are not observed and their momentary existence is untenable; thus, what has been brought to its end—that is, to non-existence? He says: "the doubt regarding selflessness" (*nairātmyaśaṅkā*). By what means? He says: "by means of the self that is both free from conceptualization and otherwise" (*nirvikalpetarātmanā*).
It is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and its own conceptualization (*svavikalpa*); that is, it is that whose nature (*ātman*) or essence (*svabhāva*) is conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).
This has been stated in this very work, in the first chapter, in the passage beginning with *siddhivi° 1.10*: "In the case of the restriction to a single appearance," and so forth.
Of what [things]? He says: "simultaneous," and so forth.

Those which arise through both simultaneous and successive [processes] are "simultaneous-successive-arisen" (*sahakramabhavāḥ*). And these, being mutually and reciprocally excluded (*vyāvṟtta*), yet again belong to those various [cognitions] that are of a single nature, belonging to a single continuum, and are cognitions (*saṃvid*); such is the meaning in the text.

Others read: "of the cognitions of a single self (ātman) regarding successive states and mutually exclusive [states] such as pleasure," and in that case, the meaning is as follows: "of those cognitions belonging to a single self or individual soul (jīva) with respect to states that are both successive and mutually exclusive, such as pleasure"—thus, by virtue of the established nature of the word itself, the two [terms] here are appropriately joined.

The commentators might think: "Since the forms of conceptual and non-conceptual cognition are observed to be one in certain instances, it is improper to establish the unity of successive cognitions; otherwise, why not establish pungency in molasses simply because it is observed in the arka plant? Furthermore, there is the contradiction of direct perception regarding the establishment of unity for those who maintain succession, just as there is regarding pungency."

Apart from their unity and the nature of consciousness, no other form of these [cognitions] is accessible through perception; and since that nature exists even in relation to other mental continua, all selves would possess the same single essence.
Thus, even for the intended cognitions, there would be no distinction of space and so forth, and consequently, the existence of distinct selves is not established.

If it is argued that by this [explanation] the second interpretation has been considered, he says here: "From itself or from another," and so forth. "Its own" (*svāni*) refers to those [cognitions] falling within its own continuum; "others" (*parāṇi*) refers to those belonging to other continua, such as the cognitions of a son; and "those" (*tāni*) refers to the cognitions themselves. Even though they exist (*vidyamāne*), why would there be dissimilar or otherwise transformations—meaning an excellence of dissimilar transformation—with respect to the object? To this he says: "From itself," meaning from its own material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), or "from another," meaning from a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*); the word "or" (*vā*) is used in a conjunctive sense.
As it has been said: "Whether by itself or from another, it evolves; thus cause and effect proceed in succession" (Siddhiviniścaya 3.19).
Even though that [Self] exists, from what, doing what, and who does what? To this he says: "In the confusion," and so forth.
Regarding the living being (*jīva*) who is the object of the direct perception of self-awareness, whom indeed does he disregard? To this he says: "The Buddhist and the Cārvāka of dull intellect."
What was he doing? Rejecting what?

He says: he was making [the self] the object of a cognition whose scope is the non-failing generality of identity for his own cognitions; he was making it the object of a cognition of non-failing identity for those [cognitions] of others; and he was proclaiming its status as the object of a non-failing cognition of generality in relation to others—at that time, he did not achieve renown.
Why? He says: "Because of confusion," and so forth.
