In the case of confusion (*saṅkara*), within one's own minds there is the state of being the object of a cognition of identity, just as there is the state of being the object of a cognition of generality; and in the minds of others, there is the state of being the object of a cognition of generality, just as there is the state of being the object of a cognition of identity. Furthermore, "interchange" (*vyatikara*) refers to the presence of such a cognition of generality in one's own minds and the state of being the object of a cognition of identity in the minds of others. "Intermixture" (*vyatikara*) is the absence (*abhāva*) of those two [states] in their respective places. Therefore, having reached that [intermixture], of those successive cognitions (*krama-saṃvidām*)...
The nature of volition belongs to cognitions that occur sequentially;
the simultaneous attainment of all [cognitions] is confusion.

If it is argued that "intermingling" (vyatikara) is the mutual entering into each other's domains, and that since the single Jīva does not indeed stumble anywhere, [the objection] beginning with "it is not logical from its own nature" is incorrect; to this he replies: "separately" (pṛthak).

What is this "separate" [self] like? It is "to be personally experienced" (*pratyātmavedanīya*). Since this principle holds true here, what is the use of our concern with inference regarding the living being (*jīva*)? If you ask, "For what purpose, then, will [the author] later state such things as 'the perception of succession there'?"—to this he replies: "And not... and so forth.
If it is merely the manifestation of darkness, that is, ignorance (*ajñāna*), then what is the use of our concern?
It is accepted as such because of its manifestation; the sense is that it is for the purpose of distinguishing it [from others].
To the question "Of what? he says: "Of the one," and so forth, meaning "proclaiming the state of being its object for both one's own and another's consciousness."
From what [source] is this known? He says: "Of one's own and others," and so forth.

Perception (*darśana*) of both self and other, as well as apprehension (*avagraha*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), recollection (*smaraṇa*), and so on—these alone constitute sequential transformation (*kramapariṇāma*). That which has this very [transformation] as its nature (*svabhāva*) is thus described as the soul (*jīva*), the subject matter of another category. How could these be seen without it? To this he says: "Of absolute particulars" (*ekāntaviśeṣāṇām*).

Substances and the other categories are called *viśeṣas* because they are distinguished (*viśiṣyante*) from one another; for this very reason, the proponent of them is called a *Vaiśeṣika*. "Exclusively particular" (*ekāntaviśeṣa*) means those that are exclusively particulars. The phrase "of these" refers not only to them alone, but also to their momentary existence—the word "and" (*ca*) should be understood here in this sense. He states another reason with the words "because of non-perception" (*adṛṣṭeḥ*), meaning "and because of its impossibility" (*anupapatteśca*).
The connection is with "of absolute distinctions" and "of momentary duration";
thus the Vedāntin says regarding the individual soul (jīva).
In the following verse,
inference is [referred to as] inference.
The proponent of the category of particularity (*viśeṣa*), demonstrating its untenability, says: "Because of the rule of sequential perception," and so forth;
"there might be non-difference among self-cognitions due to the restriction of their sequential perception."
Just as there is a rule for simultaneous perception despite the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth, so too,
even in the case of absolute difference, the identity of the arising and perishing of a momentary entity is established because of the rule of sequential perception;
for it is accepted that the destruction of the cause and the arising of the effect are perceived at the same time.

Nor is the very persistence of an entity its destruction, on account of which there would be a rule of simultaneous apprehension; for a rule results in both affirmation and negation, and it is untenable that perception and non-apprehension— which have momentary persistence as their object— should have a single nature as their domain independently of external factors.

And likewise, because of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there would be identity between the destruction of the cause and the arising of the effect; for there is neither deficiency in the former nor isolation in the latter. Furthermore, it is contradictory that these two, which possess mutually exclusive natures, should have any kind of identity (*tādātmya*). How could one who accepts the identity of birth and destruction with persistence through the determination [of cognition] reject the perceptible existence of an entity that pervades pleasure and so forth, even when there is a difference in time and other factors? For the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is defined by mutual exclusion, and thus possesses three characteristics at every moment.

Comparison: That which belongs to another isolated region—namely, its *kaivalya*, its state of being alone (*ekākitva*), its lack of companionship—that very thing is the "deficiency" (*vaikalya*) or absence of another counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar;
this is stated in the *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 188.

[Regarding] "one's own" (*svasva*): it refers to one's own cognitions (*saṃvid*), that is, one's own individual cognitions (*svasaṃvidaḥ*), and not to the cognitions of others (*parasaṃvidaḥ*). Of these...

What [is meant]? He says: "If non-difference is intended as identity, then the self of everything would consist of only a single moment, because [everything] enters into that [moment]. To this, the Buddhist replies: "It may be so in some respect, but not in its entirety."

It might be thought: "Because of the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth, there is indeed a distinction among those cognitions. To this he replies: "Even though there is a distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth, what [is there] regarding the non-distinction of cognitions? If it is asked, "Since difference and non-difference are defined by their mutual exclusion, how can there be identity between them? he says here: "Like the rule of simultaneous observation. This means: just as the rule that two things cannot be observed simultaneously in the same place establishes their mutual exclusion, so too do difference and non-difference appear to be mutually exclusive. However, in the case of cognitions, they are observed together; therefore, despite the apparent distinction of their objects such as pleasure and pain, there is no real distinction in the cognitions themselves. Thus, their identity is established.

"Vi" refers to various (*vicitrā*) perceptions (*īkṣā*, *dṛṣṭi*, *vīkṣā*) having diverse forms such as delusion and so forth. "Niyama" is the necessity (*avaśyambhāva*) of that perception; otherwise, as it has been stated, there would be total emptiness (*sakalaśūnyatā*). Thus, "niyāma" and "niyama" have the same meaning, just as in the case of the necessity of simultaneous perception. Now, if it is argued: "A probandum is not established by a mere example due to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), but rather by a logical reason (*hetu*); therefore, let that very reason be stated," he replies with the words beginning "krama" (sequence), etc.

First, there is the perception of the material cause (upādāna), and then the perception of that which is produced from it (upādeya); this is "perception in succession," and [the argument follows] from the necessity of that.

[Objection: "Granted that although the perception of a jar and a cloth may sometimes occur together, their identity is not established because there is no rule [of simultaneous perception]. Nevertheless, just as there is a deviation [from the rule] regarding the necessity of simultaneous perception among moments of consciousness belonging to different mental continua—which, though distinct, coexist—likewise, since there is a necessity of sequential perception even for those same [moments] when they occur sequentially despite being distinct, the deviation remains exactly as it was in the case of night and day. [Reply: It is said: By the word "sequence" (*krama*), due to the context, the sequence of the perceptions of self and other, consisting of the relationship between material cause and its effect (*upādāna-upādeya*), is understood. The "rule" (*niyama*) is the non-existence [of such a sequence] otherwise than this; therefore [the argument holds].

This is what is meant: since there is a sequential perception of self-consciousnesses, wherein each preceding one serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for each subsequent one, and each subsequent one is the effect (*upādeya*), this sequence cannot otherwise be accounted for; therefore, there must be non-difference (*abheda*) among them.
For this very reason, it is improper here to require an external example, as the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "as if" (*iva*).

On the other hand, other teachers, taking the sequence of cognitions as undifferentiated based on the context, state the reason "because of the necessity of their being perceived together" (*tadupalabdheḥ niyamād avaśyambhāvāt*), and they offer the example: "like that which is necessarily perceived together, though not necessarily [perceived] simultaneously. How can they avoid the aforementioned fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? For even in the absence of a necessity for sequential perception, there is no non-difference [of the objects]. Furthermore, how is there not a deficiency in the example (*sādhanavikalatā*), since the entire probans is absent even if there is merely a necessity of perception?
Furthermore, it is not proper to accept what has been repeatedly refuted by oneself for the sake of establishing one's own position;
moreover, there is the fallacy of the probandum being absent (*sādhyavikalatā*) with respect to the proponent, because he does not admit the non-difference between the cognition and the blue object.

If it is argued that this is an illustration from the perspective of another [opponent], then for him too there is the fallacy of the probandum being absent, because he does not admit non-difference even in some sense (*kathañcit*).
Therefore, this is of no consequence;
the commentators [assert] a common sequence, but not one based on the relationship of material cause and its effect.
"Because [the object] is perceived sequentially by cognitions occurring in succession within another continuum"— thus [the opponent states] the complete reason for the proponent.

With reference to the Vijñānavādin, [the author] explains the verse by stating "even in the case of absolute difference" (*bhedakānte’pi*) and so forth, in order to show that the opponent must also accept the identity (*tādātmya*) of the arising and destruction of a momentary entity for this very reason.

It is not only in the case of non-difference (*abheda*), but even when absolute difference is accepted—pertaining to the Buddhist and Vaiśeṣika positions—it is established that there is some form of oneness (*kathañcidekatva*) between arising and destruction, which are the two characteristics of a momentary entity; this is an illustration, and by it, all impermanent things are included. Just as with destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), the identity of arising and destruction is proven.
Why is this? He says: "Because of the rule of sequential perception.

This means that prior to its arising, there is the perception of its transformation—that is, its destruction—and because of the necessity of that [perception], if the arising were something other than the thing being produced, then, due to the absence of a relationship between them, nothing would possess that [arising]; consequently, nothing at all would arise, and nothing would perish, like the horn of a donkey. Otherwise, since the self (*ātman*) and so forth would also have a relationship with that [arising], they too would arise.
By pointing out a refutation based on the rule of successive perception, [the opponent] asserts that [the object] is distinct.

If it is argued that the self and so forth also possess origination, and that origination is either the inherence [of the effect] in its own cause or the inherence of existence (*sattā*) in what was previously non-existent, and that this does not apply to the self and so forth because they exist at all times—then from what [is it prior]? If you say "prior to origination," then of what is there origination? If you say "of the jar and so forth," it has already been stated in this regard: how could [origination] be distinct from that [jar]? Otherwise, it would not belong to the self and so forth either.

And since that [inherence] cannot be without a substratum, how could there be its perception prior [to the production of the effect]? For something that has not yet acquired its own form—like the horn of a donkey—what kind of inherence could there be with its own cause or with existence (*sattā*)? If its own form has been acquired, that itself is "production"; therefore, enough with the conceptualization of a distinct production consisting in the relation of the effect with its own cause and existence, for the conventional usage is simply that "the effect exists" by virtue of that [cause] being existent—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 129.
If origination, even though distinct [from the object], were designated as "of the jar" and so forth,
then it would simply be the state of having attained its own nature (labdhātmarūpatva).

Likewise, if destruction were distinct from the entity, there would be no connection between the two; how then could the entity be said to have "perished"? This would lead to an over-extension of the principle. If it is argued that the entity is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and non-existence is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and therefore the relation of qualification exists because of that [non-existence], [we reply]: the relation of qualifier and qualificandum is logical only when the qualificandum exists at the time of the qualifier. But how can there be non-existence while the entity still exists? For Devadatta does not die while he is still alive;
furthermore, the simultaneous perception of two entities is like that of a blue lotus.

Because it is concealed by the destruction of the object (*artha*), there is no perception of the entity (*bhāva*); therefore, there is no perception of an entity colored by that [destruction]. Furthermore, destruction is not a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*);

for a qualifier is said to be that which, being colored by itself, produces a cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Whether it be blueness or that [destruction], if it is colored by that [entity] in its cognition, it does not conceal it.

If, moreover, there is no existence of the entity at the time of its destruction, how could there be the non-existence of one thing at another time unless that [non-existence] were to cease by itself? Otherwise, there would be the non-existence of a jar at the time of the production of a cloth.

If it is argued that this is not so because of a lack of connection, then what is the connection between the entity and its destruction? If it is said to be the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*), it has already been stated in this regard: since that [qualifier-state] is distinct from those two, how can it belong to them? If another connection is postulated, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that even in the absence of such [a further connection], that [state] belongs to those two, then qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth would belong to their substratum even in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*) and the like, as there would be no distinction.
Nor is "it belongs to nothing" a valid reply; for that would entail its non-perception by direct perception, since there is no sensory contact with it.
Even if there were contact, it could not be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because it is not a substance (*adravyatva*);
nor can it be inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) and so forth, because its independence would then be lost.

In the case of direct perception (*sākṣāt-sannikarṣa*), the same applies even to pleasure and the like; therefore, enough with the postulation of a "relation of relations" (*sambandha-sambandha*) in that regard.

Some maintain that the destruction of an entity is not distinct from its becoming a non-qualifier (*aviśeṣaṇībhāva*); however, this too is not tenable. For, just as cold is removed by fire, an entity is removed by that [destruction]; nor is what is called "opposition" (*virodha*) merely a property that causes cessation, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, if there were a cessation of this [destruction], the consequence would be its differentiation from the object as before, leading to an infinite regress;

yet if there is no differentiation, then the destruction being produced by destruction would not be distinct from it, nor anything else—thus a distinction is not tenable. Therefore, it is well said: "the perception of succession," and so forth.
The connection with destruction is not [possible] for an entity;
this has been written again.
"Colored by destruction" means "destroyed";
this also applies to the state of being a qualifier colored by [the quality] blue.
Even in the absence of a relation with existence and destruction, origination is a qualifying attribute.
Since conjunction occurs only between substance and substance,
inherence in the conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya) and other relations belong only to those things that are dependent, such as qualities, actions, universals, and so forth.
The relation of the relation [of inherence] consists in conjunction-inherence (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), because pleasure and the like inhere in the self which is conjoined with the mind.

Now, one might argue: "Let it be granted that for a momentary entity, identity between its arising and perishing is established; however, this is not due to the rule of sequential perception, but rather due to the rule of simultaneous perception. To this, he says: "The cause," and so forth. "Cause" means the instrument (*kāraṇa*); "fruit" means the effect (*kārya*). This is because the arising and perishing of these two are admitted to be perceived at the same time, respectively.

For instance: at the very moment that the destruction of the lump of clay is perceived, there is the perception of the *śivaka* (the first stage of the pot), and not [a temporal sequence] between the destruction of the cause and the arising [of the effect]. Otherwise, since production and destruction are mutually contradictory, if they were to exist in the same place at the same time, there would be no relation of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*), he thinks.

[He further maintains that] destruction is the state of being distinct from the nature of the fruit, and that this is perceived at the very time of its arising. That is untrue, because such an admission [leads to an absurdity].
For just as the absence of the cause is perceived at the time of the effect, so too is the absence of the effect at the time of the cause—its absence being merely of the nature of non-existence.

This very point he states with the words "And not," etc.: "And not" means that the very persistence—the state of remaining at the time of origination—is not the destruction of the entity, nor is it the cessation of its own-nature; for since there is a rule of simultaneous perception, persistence itself would be the destruction, [which is absurd].

The word "yataḥ" may be used in the sense of an objection: "Since there would be a rule of simultaneous perception, [it] could not be so at all, because by that [rule], existence would sublate destruction.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because of affirmation," and so forth.

When there is the perception of the cause’s arising, that is the primary means—the principal method—of its negation; it is not of the form where the arising occurs first and the destruction follows later. That [negation] is described in such a way, and that which has that [negation] as its fruit is also described in the same way.
What is this? He says: "The restriction," for the word "hi" (indeed) is used in the sense of "because."
Showing that there is no positive injunction here, he says: "Because of the impossibility of the two—perception and non-perception—having a single nature as their object," and so forth.

Regarding the "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) imagined by others, its "abiding" (*sthiti*) is its acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*). Of that [abiding], there are perception and non-perception, which are seeing and not seeing. Since it is impossible for these two to have a single nature as their object—the state (*tattā*) of those two whose object is a single nature—it is impossible. [The author asks: "In the absence of what? He replies: "In relation to the external."

The meaning is that perception occurs at the first moment, while non-perception occurs from the second moment onwards, independent of anything external; for it is impossible for perception and non-perception to occur simultaneously.
The sense is that neither production nor destruction could exist, because destruction would be sublated by production, or production by destruction, since these two function sequentially.

It might be thought: "Let it be that, with respect to external objects, the perception and non-perception of momentary existence are established as having a single nature; and what would follow from that? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.
And thus, in that manner, there would be a unity—somehow an identity—between the destruction of the cause and the arising of the effect, because of the rule of simultaneous perception.

Why? To this he says: "Because of the deficiency (vaikalya), i.e., the absence, of the preceding cause, and the isolation (kaivalya) of the subsequent effect. By this, he negates a separate non-existence.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the destruction of the cause is of the nature of cessation (*pradhvaṃsa*), whereas the arising of the effect is the acquisition of its own-being from a previously non-existent cause, having existence as its intrinsic nature? Therefore, how can there be identity between these two, which possess mutually contradictory natures? To this, he replies: "And not... and so forth. Of what kind are these two—destruction and arising? He says: "Mutually... and so forth.
One might think that there is no contradiction whatsoever in the identity (*tādātmya*) of two things whose natures are mutually opposed, because such [identity] is perceived;
thus [the author] provides an example, beginning with "if one were to accept... and so forth.
Then, if the opponent were to accept the oneness of cause and effect—that is, of destruction and arising—what fault would there be? To this, he says: "birth," and so forth.

The Buddhist, asserting the identity between the arising of the fruit and the destruction of the cause, by what [means] does he do so? By what co-existence (*sahasthityā*)? He asks: "By what co-existence? He replies: "What would he accomplish by co-existence? He asks: "How could he reject existence (*bhāva*)? Of what kind [is that existence]? It is "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), meaning cognizable by direct perception.
Again, of what kind is it? He says: "Pleasure," and so forth.

[The opponent objects: "Surely, since effects such as pleasure and pain falling within a single continuum are non-different from the sentient being that pervades them, if [the cause] is said to belong to that [single continuum], then it should also be said to belong to those belonging to other continua, because there is no difference in that regard. Or, if you say that this is not so here because of differences in time and so forth, then let it not be said in the other case either, for there is no difference. To this, he says: "Time and so forth," etc.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of place (*deśa*) and so forth is intended. This has already been considered in the passage beginning with "Whether from itself or from another, [the cognition] of one's own or another's minds," and so on. If it is asked: "How could this refute the entity (*bhāva*) postulated by the Sāṅkhya, which is all-pervasive (*tadvyāpin*)?"—to this he replies: "The specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), etc.

Regarding the phrase "that which has its own self as its characteristic," why is it so called? To this he says: "Because it has mutual exclusion as its characteristic. That is to say, it is that which has mutual differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*) as its defining mark.
The term "perception" (pratyakṣam) should also be applied here;

for how could one reject that [perception] which belongs to the Vaiśeṣikas and others? To this he says: perception is characterized by the three marks at every moment, because there is no difference [between them] in terms of existence and consciousness.

But surely, for self-cognitions residing in different mental continua, there is a restriction regarding their sequential perception due to the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and because they belong to a single continuum (*ekasantānatva*), and not because of non-difference (*abheda*). Therefore, since the reason is established otherwise, why is it said: "If it is argued that non-difference among self-cognitions would follow from the restriction of sequential perception"? To this, he replies: "The state of cause and effect," and so forth;
for momentary things, there is no causal relationship, so where is there a continuum?

How could there be similarity among them, given their lack of continuity, as is the case with other objects? (7) The proponent of the selflessness of phenomena (*bhāvanairātmyavādin*) rejects that which is not contradicted by the experience of a single common cognition—consisting of the various forms of the grasped and the grasper manifested as the transformations of existence, form, configuration, and so forth—and which exists as cause and effect due to the difference between preceding and succeeding natures. Thus, he directly oversteps the momentary nature of things.
For if the effect were to exist while the momentary cause still persists, then this world would be momentary, yet devoid of sequence and lacking any continuum.
If that [cause] does not exist, how could there be for you a rule of its arising immediately thereafter, such that its arising would not occur at an undesired time?
That cause, being always capable, would forcibly produce the effect at the very moment of its own existence.
If the timing of the effect's arising were determined by its own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*), how could there even be the status of "effect" for something independent?
If the restriction of production were based merely on immediate succession, then since there would be no distinction between all things in all cases, how could there be any restriction at all?

If the restriction of the production of a substance were due to its own cause as material (upādāna), nothing would be over-extended. Furthermore, if it were dependent on other conditions, there could be no establishment of either production or continuity for entities that lack persistence (niranvaya), because such production and continuity are observed even when those conditions are reversed.
In the view of absolute difference (*bhedaikānta*), similarity dissolves the more it is investigated, just as [the notion of identity] dissolves in the case of a cognition appearing as blue.

For momentary entities, there is no relation of cause and effect; since that is absent, where could there be a continuum (*santati*) or a stream (*santāna*), either externally or internally? Since the latter consists of the former, how can even its absence exist? To this, he says: "Because of the lack of persistence" (*niranvayāt*).

Since momentary things dissolve in every respect at the time of their own fruit, even though the relation of cause and effect exists, the similarity between the preceding and succeeding moments—which serves as the basis for the designation of a "single continuum" because there is no other alternative—would [otherwise] exist; however, that is not the case, as he demonstrates: "From what cause, or by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is there similarity—that is, the state of having an identical form—for those momentary things?
He provides an illustration: "Just like other objects."

If it is argued that because the continuum consists of the nature of cause and effect, there would also be an absence of the causal relationship [in the ultimate sense], and thus this fault does not apply to the Buddhists due to their acceptance of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*) and non-dual appearance without parts (*niraṃśapratibhāsādvaita*); to this, he says: "In the form of existence," and so forth.
It is incorrect to reject existence (*bhāva*), for one considers that in rejecting it, there would be an impossibility of rejecting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Of what kind [is this existence]? He says: "directly" (*samakṣam*);
by this, he demonstrates the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) in its rejection.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? To this he says: "of the nature of existence" (*sadrūpa*), and so forth.
The term *sat* (existent) is a designation emphasizing the state of being (*bhāva*).

Thus, that whose form, configuration, and so forth have existence as their essential nature (*svarūpa*) or intrinsic character (*svabhāva*)—whereby the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes all external properties arising in succession—is described in that way. By the phrase "of the nature of existence," he negates the imagined nature (*kalpitatva*) of the configuration and other such qualities. That which has such a manifestation (*vivarta*)—such as a jar and the like—is described as "that [which is] of such a nature."

The two "variegated" (vicitrau) forms are the various modes consisting of the apprehended and the apprehender; that which is one and common to both is "common cognition," and this too is described as such. Furthermore, there is a dvandva compound of these two, and the experience (*anubhava*) of them is "by that. By this [term], he shows that even non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣabādhita*).
For that very reason, showing that even the non-absolute nature of succession (*kramānekānta*) is not contradictory, he says: "In cause and effect," and so forth.

Whence is this? If it is argued that [the relation] exists both before and after, [the author] says: "Because of the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*)," meaning that because there is an absence of identity of essence (*svarūpatva-abhāva*), there is no relation;
who denies this? And so forth—this refers to the Buddhist (*saugata*) when he says "existence" (*bhāva*) and so on. This is the meaning.
The point is that the means by which its negation is performed must itself be of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*).

Now, if it is argued: "It has been stated that [the mind] transcends the directly perceived momentary entity, because that [momentary entity] is the basis for all conventional transactions regarding cause and effect, whereas anything else is the opposite"—to this he replies with the words beginning "If it exists" (*sati*), and so forth.

If an effect were to arise when a momentary cause—existing for only a single moment—is present, then this world accepted by the opponent would, upon investigation, be of what nature? To this he says: "momentary.
Of what nature would it be? To this he says: it would be "simultaneous," meaning it would be established in a single moment.

And thus, he considers that the proof of the next world and so forth would be contradicted by the opponent's own words; what, then, would such [an entity] be like? He says: "Devoid of a continuum" (*niḥsantāni*) means those moments which constitute the relationship between material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeya*). That from which or by which they have departed or been discarded is "devoid of a continuum. This is because, like the left and right horns of a cow, there is a contradiction in the causal relation between things that lack succession (*akrama*); this is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, the meaning is that precisely because there is no succession, it would be devoid of continuity and lack even mere tranquility; for in the absence of prior and subsequent cause and effect, it would necessarily follow from the very nature of causality.
Nevertheless, this does not negate [the existence of] universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, provided they exist.

The following is what is meant: at the very moment of its own arising, the cause is momentary; thus, at that same time, when the effect exists, there is the simultaneity (*samasamayatā*) of cause and fruit. Alternatively, the present effect produces its cause either prior to or subsequent to itself at its own time; that [cause] also produces its own cause at its own time, and that [cause] likewise its own cause at its own time. Because there is no persistence through the time of arising, this is an indication of non-succession (*akrama*); by this, it may also be non-simultaneous (*asahabhāvi*).

If an effect exists when its cause is momentary, then because all subsequent moments that constitute effects would have transmigrated into the time of each preceding cause, the entire world would exist for only a single moment;
and even if it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), [it would follow that it is unreal].
Whether the cause is eternal or whether it is occasional, it produces the effect— whether contemporary with it, prior to it, or subsequent to it— at its own time;
thus, it is indeed a cause at the prior time.
But the "subsequent" [cause] is stated with reference to a future cause, whether preceding or following [the effect];
or else, lest this fault occur, a cause existing at the same time as the effect is accepted. To that, he says: "In its absence," and so forth.

When that momentary cause is absent—whether in the past due to its destruction, or in the future because it has not yet arisen and lacks existence—and when it is non-existent at the time of the effect, from what cause could the arising effect come? From nothing at all, so the reflection concludes. Thus, there is a rule of immediate succession: either the rule that the effect arises immediately after that cause, or the rule that it arises in the time immediately following that cause.
For [it is argued]: "Why would that not occur due to that restriction? and so forth;

namely, that the production of that effect at an undesired time—where what was intended to occur earlier occurs later, or what was intended to occur later occurs earlier—would mean that the conventional usage of inference and so forth would not be restricted. This is what is being considered.

As for what was stated by the opponent himself: "If there is a cause, there is causality; and for that which is without a cause, there is no restriction of place and so forth," as in *Prakaraṇavāra* 1.182 and elsewhere, namely, that there would be either eternal existence or non-existence.
This is accepted because a cause that lacks a [further] cause does not depend on anything else.
For it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible—this is the remainder [of the argument].

It might be argued: "This fault belongs to the effect itself when it arises at a later time, not to the cause; for even a cause situated at a different time, like one situated at a different place, remains a cause, since its status as such is established according to what is observed."
Furthermore, at the time of awakening, even that waking cognition which was non-existent [previously] is seen to be its cause; regarding this, he says: "Only that which exists," and so forth.
Only that which exists—meaning that which is final, capable, and fit for producing an effect—would be the cause, the agent, and would produce the effect.
At what time? He says: "At the very time of its own existence," that is, at the very time of its own being, "forcibly" (prasahya), meaning by sheer necessity.

The intention here is as follows: just as it is said that a permanent entity, being inherently capable at all times, must produce its effect by force whenever it is so capable; likewise, even a momentary entity, if it were previously capable, would produce its effect precisely at the time of the effect because of its very nature of being momentary. Thus it has been stated regarding the permanent entity as well: "Whenever an effect is about to arise... (*Siddhiviniścaya* 3).
11. Such [an argument] is not tenable—that the production of an effect is pervaded by momentariness—because there is no distinction in other cases either.
Now, if it is argued that even when the cause is capable at its own time, the effect arises later by its very nature; to this he says: "By its own inherent tendency" (svarasataḥ), etc.

If one accepts the necessity of the time of production—that is, the rule that an effect arises immediately after something else at one time, while it arises at another time after yet another—then how can there be the status of being an "effect" for that which is independent (*svatantra*) and self-sufficient? It is thought that this would be like the position of [the opponent's] eternalist view.
For an effect is dependent (*paratantra*); it necessarily arises when another [cause] is capable.

However, the other's [i.e., the opponent's] view is that the preceding immediate cause is the "prior" and the subsequent is the "effect. To this, he replies with the words beginning "nairantarya... (due to the lack of continuity).

The "immediacy" (*nairantarya*) of cause and effect is the absence of any intervening space; if the determination of the arising [of an effect] were based on that alone, then from what would there be a restriction regarding cause and fruit? It would be from nothing at all. Why? To this he says: "Everywhere," and so forth.

Prajñākara has stated that since immediacy is possible everywhere—in every effect and elsewhere—without distinction among all causes and other factors, from what indeed could there be such a restriction?
of a Buddhist [cognition] that has arisen without a cause.

If it is argued that "surely this fault applies everywhere in the case of the causal relation between what is immediately preceding and what follows, and thus it would not exist [in our view]," the author replies here with the words beginning "of the substance" (*dravyasya*).
If the necessity of the origination of a substance, such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth, is accepted, no further undesirable consequence follows immediately.
Of what kind [of substance]? To this he says: "by its own causes," and so on.
When? To this he says: "in the subsequent [moment]," and so on.
The state of having another external condition as its auxiliary cause— that is the nature [of the effect];
this has been discussed [under the heading] of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

"A substance that is without beginning or end, which is about to arise, which is stable yet perishable, may evolve by itself or from another, sequentially, in the form of cause and effect" (Siddhiviniścaya 3.19). To this [objection] one might say: "This restriction [of the relationship between cause and effect] does not arise from mere immediate succession, but rather from similarity; that is, the preceding similar [moment] is the material cause (*upādāna*), while the other is the effect (*upādeya*). To this, he replies with the words "And not," and so forth.

Nor can there be, for those things that are entirely without continuity—that is, devoid of any underlying connection—any establishment of "arising," which means the causal relationship or the continuum (*santati*, *santāna*), on the grounds of "similarity," meaning their having an identical form; from what [source] would this be established? To this, he says: "That... and so forth.

The connection is as follows: even in the case of its opposite—that is, even in the absence of similarity—not only when there is no absence [of similarity], but because things are perceived in such a manner through the process of their origin and continuity.
For instance, there is perception in that way even in the absence of similarity between wood and ashes, or between inferential knowledge and the Buddha’s cognition;

or alternatively, even in the case of its opposite—that is, even when the origin and so forth are reversed—because things are perceived in such a manner through the mode of similarity, as in the case of twins and the like.

This was stated while accepting similarity; however, [the author] says "similarity, moreover," and so forth, demonstrating that in the extreme view of difference (*bhedaikānta*), that very thing does not exist at all.

The word "ca" (moreover) is used for the accumulation of refutations. In whatever way—by whichever mode such as difference, non-difference, and so on—it is investigated, in that very way it falls apart.
Where? In the extreme view of difference.

One should consider how the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*) could apply to similarity, just as it applies to permanence, in the case of Prajñākaragupta’s view? For just as perception, which grasps only the middle moment, does not grasp the preceding and succeeding moments and thus does not grasp their identity (*ekatva*), so too it does not grasp similarity;
regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Blue," and so forth.
That which has a blue appearance—that is, a form—and is also a cognition, [is the subject]; "of that very thing" means "like that."

The meaning is that the restriction of cause and effect consists of the cultivation born of hearing (*śrutamayī bhāvanā*), which takes the form of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), and the cultivation born of reflection (*cintāmayī bhāvanā*), which takes the form of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*); from these two forms of inference, non-conceptual yogic cognition arises—
this is precisely what constitutes similarity.
Since there is no apprehension of the similarity between the preceding and succeeding [moments] of a single entity that exists across both,
he says "attained," etc., demonstrating what is established when selflessness has thus been refuted.
The individual soul (jīva), which attains manifestation and concealment at every moment, is established as being beginningless; yet, through its nature of sleeping and waking, it abandons saṃsāra.
This is because it is impossible to deny the infusion of new qualities into that which has substance as its substratum.

Manifestation and concealment occur at every moment, for such a sequential process is not prohibited; otherwise, sleep and awakening would be inexplicable. Furthermore, this continuum is beginningless, since a fixed order of succession is impossible without something that undergoes transformation.
Because of the exclusion of otherness, the one established soul—the *jīvātman*—is proven and certain, whether in *saṃsāra* or *nirvāṇa*.
Of what nature is it? To this he says: it is that by which manifestation and concealment occur upon attainment; thus it is described.

Where? At every moment—that is, at each and every instant—for instance: having attained the state of manifestation in the form of existence, consciousness, and so forth, and having attained concealment in the form of momentary destruction and so forth;
yet, as has been established, there is no contradiction between the natures of being perceived and not being perceived in a single locus.

If it is argued that if the invisible form were non-different from the visible, it would necessarily be visible itself; this would indeed be so if acts of perception depended upon the objective existence of things. However, since perceptions depend upon the capacity of the person, if a person is capable, he perceives something even with that which is absolutely different, as when one perceives one's own finger along with the moon; whereas if he is otherwise, he does not perceive even what is different, such as one who sees the moon and a mountain joined together failing to perceive them as distinct from one another.

Now, if the perceptible were identical with the imperceptible, it would follow that it is identical even with a donkey’s horn. If, then, the perceptible cognition of a blue form were identical with the perceptible yellow form, everything would be so because there is no distinction; for it has been stated that in the absence of identity, there is the non-existence of everything. If you argue: "Just as the identity of a certain cognition of blue with a certain yellow form is perceived, yet this is not the case for everything with everything; therefore, just as [identity] exists between the moon and a mountain through their exclusion [of others], but not with a donkey’s horn—it is the same [in our case]. [Response: This is the same [as the previous fallacy]. If identity with a donkey’s horn does not occur because of its exclusion, then why should identity with a yellow form not likewise fail to occur? Since the reason for the non-occurrence of identity is the same, the example is irrelevant. Furthermore, if identity is established by the exclusion of others, then since the exclusion of all other things from a single cognition is equal, everything would again become identical to that cognition. Thus, the argument remains unrefuted.

If it is asked, "How is there non-apprehension? [we reply: It would be so by way of being apprehended by another person; otherwise, even if momentariness were cognized through inference, there could be no unity for sound and the like. Or, if it is asked, "By what means is the form of what was previously apprehended apprehended later by oneself? we say: because it is so perceived. For it has been established that just as with the non-sequential, so too with the sequential, there is the grasping of a single variegated object.
Therefore, it is logical that there is the manifestation and concealment of its individuality (*vyakti*).
Cognitions [arise] from object to object.

[Objection: "But surely, if the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*bodhasvabhāva*), then because it is always of that form, there would be no such states as sleep and so forth. To this, he says: "That living being (*jīva*) is one for whom sleep and awakening are two aspects of the Self.

He thinks thus: just as even in the state of being essentially awakened, manifestation and concealment occur simultaneously due to the force of obstructing causes, so too do sleep, awakening, and so forth occur both simultaneously and sequentially.

As for one who thinks that because there is no perception [of the self] during sleep and so forth, it must be absent—then for that very reason, there would be an absence of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) everywhere.

If it were perceived during sleep and so forth, why would the living being not be perceived? [If you say] its absence exists here [during sleep], then its absence exists elsewhere [in waking]; [but this is not so] because of the absence of inference and other means of knowledge [at that time], since [the self] is of the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpa*).

If it is argued that since there is no perception of persistence through moments, there is an absence of a living soul—just as there is a logical mark such as existence (*sattva*) that establishes momentariness, yet there is nothing whatsoever that establishes a self (*ātman*) in that regard—we reply: "Awakening" (*prabodha*). This is our position.
For there is no example admitted by both [parties] regarding an effect that arises when its material cause has long since passed away;
for everything is such a material cause for everything, and as for the argument that the material cause has long since perished,
the response has already been given regarding similarity.
Therefore, it is appropriate [to state] "at the time of sleep," and so forth.
Furthermore, if this is the opponent's view— that the soul (jīva) is established as existing only from conception until death, and not as beginningless and endless due to a lack of evidence,
and that even if such a soul were established, it would be of no consequence for one who maintains the doctrine of the next world— [then the following applies].
Regarding this, he says: "It is beginningless" (*anādiḥ*), and by implication it is also "endless" (*anantaśca*).

For instance: whatever is a substance (*dravya*) is of the nature of being both beginningless and endless, just as the substance of the *pudgala*, the substances such as earth, and the living soul (*jīva*).
The soul (*jīva*) is a substance because it consists of qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*), just like [other substances];
therein, qualities are said to be knowledge and so forth, while modes are said to be pleasure and so forth.
Furthermore, the soul is not a mode of earth and the other elements, because that has been denied.
The remainder has been considered here; we shall now speak of sleep and so forth.
For the Cārvāka, any purpose whatsoever has long since perished.
Is this living being (jīva), like the earth and other elements, of the nature of saṃsāra or otherwise? In the first case, there would be the abandonment of nirvāṇa;
in the second, the removal of saṃsāra.

If it is argued that [the soul] sometimes takes the form of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and at other times otherwise, and if it is further argued that "impermanence" means the absence of that [transmigratory state]; to this he replies: "He abandons transmigratory existence.

Transmigratory existence refers to the wandering through the womb and so forth, as well as its causes—namely, active karma (*bhāvakarma*) and substantial karma (*dravyakarma*). He abandons or relinquishes these by virtue of a specific collection of conditions.
Furthermore, for the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādins*), some degree of impermanence is not undesirable.
The absence of a soul;
passion and so forth consist of matter (pudgala).

If it is asked, "From where does this [liberation] of the soul arise?", the author replies here with the words beginning "dravya" (substance), etc.: from the quality characterized by transmigration, the quality consisting of liberation—which is its distinct nature—is established as its own substratum through right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth; for that [establishment] cannot be negated.
Of what kind [is it]? He says: "having substance as its locus" (*dravyāśrayasya*), meaning that for which substance is the locus.
By this, he shows the possibility of refuting that which is imagined by the Buddhists, Naiyāyikas, and others to be without a locus;
for it is not logical that its self (*ātman*)—being of a permanent and unitary nature—should be its locus.
Therefore, if that which is dependent is not distinct [from the self], then either liberation or saṃsāra alone would be absolute;
if it were distinct, the two would not belong to it, because there would be no connection and because inherence has been refuted—
or even if that were not refuted, it would lead to over-extension, since that [inherence] too would be distinct from it.
And why is it impossible to deny [this]? He says: "At every moment," and so forth.

Because for the soul (*jīva*), which exists as a succession of moments and experiences manifestation and non-opposition at every single instant, there is likewise no denial [of this] as long as it is not distinct from the eternal substance.

[Objection: "Surely, because there is no relationship, even for inherence (samavāya). For in that state of awakening where there is manifestation, there is no concealment; and in that state of sleep and so forth where there is concealment, there is no manifestation. Therefore, since it is not perceived there, [one might conclude] that the entity does not exist there. To this, he says: "In sleep," and so forth.
This has been established;
what follows from its lack of logical inconsistency? He says: this *jīva* is beginningless and is perceivable through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
It is thought thus: just as one who was in a state such as deep sleep becomes awakened again, or one who is awakened enters that same state, so too is the *jīva* beginningless.

If it is argued that the soul (*jīva*) is not beginningless, but rather a continuum of moments of cognition (*jñānakṣaṇasantāna*), and that the distinction between bondage and liberation resides in that very continuum; to this he replies: "Of the continuum also," and so forth.

Not only in the case of bondage and liberation, but even for a continuum, a restriction is impossible without a transforming entity (*pariṇāmin*); for every continuum would belong to everything, since there is no deviation from that which governs such [restriction], such as its origin and so on. Thus, whether in *saṃsāra* or *nirvāṇa*, a single [governing principle] is established.
Because sleep and awakening would otherwise be inexplicable,
that subtle entity which pervades states such as sleep is one and the same in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; therefore, since there is no distinction between them, there would be non-duality.

If it is argued that whatever is non-different from the non-different is itself non-different—just as its own nature (svarūpa) is—and since both saṃsāra and mokṣa are non-different from the non-different [Self], they must be one; to this he replies: "Upon the exclusion of otherness" means that because there is an absolute exclusion of otherness—that is, of plurality—between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, a single entity is established therein. Thus, there is neither absolute identity nor absolute difference between them. Otherwise, due to the absence of a common substratum for saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, nirvāṇa would be without a material cause (anupādāna); such is the intended meaning.
From the living being, [there is the non-duality] of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; from the living being, [there is the non-duality] of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Now, one might object: "Are not only the moments, existing as cause and effect, directly perceived, and not some 'self' (ātman)? Furthermore, the cognition of them as a single entity is a deception—arising either through the perception of a similar subsequent moment or through superimposition—and its object is merely projected, like the case of twins or a magical illusion; therefore, these moments alone are ultimately real, and there is no such thing as unity. To this, the author replies with the words beginning "akramaṃ" (non-sequential), and so forth.

Even though he perceives that impermanence in the moments that constitute cause and effect, the person of dull intellect does not ascertain it; for he is either deceived by the apprehension of a persisting entity, always suspecting its continued existence, or deceived by the production of a subsequent similar [moment]— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 2.208.

In some cases, there is a lack of full comprehension of that [object] because another similar thing arises; this is due to delusion for one who does not perceive the difference, like the [failure to distinguish between] separate illusory balls.
Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 120:
Through ignorance, that which is non-successive appears as having a successive birth and so forth, whether existent or non-existent.
Others know that even difference, like reality itself, is not ultimately real, appearing as if it were so through the existence of internal and external forms;
for even in the absolute doctrine of difference, the status of either an agent or a knower cannot be established.

Nor is there, either externally or internally, the perception of difference at every moment in the ultimate sense as it is described, because direct perception is subject to contradiction and inference is devoid of a real object;
indeed, no cognition ever deviates from the reality of pure existence (*sanmātra*), for deviation occurs only among [apparent] differences.

If there is an absolute distinction [between things] due to the false appearance of the conceptualization of one's own and others' mental continua, how can that [distinction] be established? Furthermore, if the cognitions of activity and so forth deviate from mere volition, why would there not be a non-deviation from action even through a causal series, such that the external object could not be established? [The claim that] "the reality transcends all conceptualizations because the conceptualizations of one's own and others' sequences consist entirely of ignorance" is untenable, as there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Just like the absolute distinction [between things], existence (*sattā*) does not appear [to us], because the description is primarily concerned with the state of being (*bhāva*).
Of what nature is it? He says: "without sequence," meaning devoid of the sequence of cause and effect and so forth.
With what does it shine? He says: "with non-existent things," meaning with those that are not present.
For what reason does it appear as such through them? He says: "by means of ignorance."
By "ignorance" (avidyā), it is meant false knowledge (mithyājñāna), and not the mere absence of knowledge (vidyā), because the latter cannot function as a cause,
nor can anything else; for there is no other entity besides knowledge characterized by existence,
whereas ignorance, being a non-entity (avastu), is therefore inexpressible as being either identical to or different from that [knowledge].
In this regard, he states an example well-known among the Buddhists, beginning with the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*):
the particle *yathā* (as) is used in the sense of "just as";
just as reality, characterized by cognition, appears through ignorance (*avidyā*) by means of existing external and internal forms, so it truly is.

Therefore, just as non-difference is not ultimately real, so too difference is not ultimately real; thus other Buddhists, who maintain the doctrine of the absolute unity of existence (*sattaikāntavādin*), understand it in this way.

This interpretation is excellent, as the author will state in the commentary (*vṛtti*): "Indeed, no cognition deviates from the reality of pure existence (*sanmātratattva*), for deviation occurs only among [the particulars of] difference.

Or else, as it has been said: "In the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no single perfected one (*siddha*) free from duality"; that is true, but he would be merely a conceptual construction based on the transformations of all individual souls (*puruṣa*).
As it has been said: "Puruṣa alone is this [all]" (Ṛgveda 10.90.2), and so forth.

Or perhaps the conceptualization devised by the proponents of philosophical systems might be as follows: "The universe, though consisting of pure existence, manifests here as a single substance through various functions"; or alternatively, that Brahman alone is the ultimately real, appearing as such through the power of inferior knowledge (aparavidyā).
This has also been stated:
the word *iva* in the context of the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*) has the meaning of "just as" (*yathā*).
In this very verse,
just as in the previous verse:
"Just as a person afflicted by cataracts [perceives] the pure sky..."
Just as one perceives a single object as if divided by various distinct measures,
so too this stainless Brahman, though free from conceptual construction, appears to have attained a state of impurity through ignorance and assumes a form of differentiation.
Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, Bhāṣya-vārttika, 3.5.43, 44.
Showing this, he says: "Others, the proponents of the Puruṣa, know that reality shines forth as being without succession," and so forth.
Of what nature is it? It is "without succession" (akrama), meaning it is itself devoid of arising, destruction, and so forth.
By means of what does it appear? To this he says: "by those characterized by successive birth and so forth.
Of what nature are these? To this he says: "by those that are unreal" (asadbhiḥ).
The word "by the wise" (*sadbhiḥ*) is connected here [to the verb].
If it is asked, "How can that which is without sequence appear as having sequence?", he says here: "externally," and so forth.

This is its meaning: just as the principle of consciousness (*vijñānatattva*), though without sequence, appears to those who maintain the doctrine of duality through external and internal forms by means of the wise, so too does the subject at hand.
By this, [the verse] beginning with "The person is the Ṛg-veda" is shown.
Likewise, by what does reality appear as being without sequence? By means of the birth of sequence and so forth.
By what kind [of things]? He says: "by unreal ones" (*asadbhiḥ*).

Since the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is possible [here], the qualifier "by ignorance" (*avidyayā*) is connected with this very term [“unreal ones”] and not with the preceding one [“external,” etc.].
“External,” etc., serves as the illustration.
"By means of ignorance (*avidyā*), reality (*tattva*) appears both externally and internally.

Now, if reality is merely existence (*sattāmātra*), one might ask: "How is there the perception of distinctions such as the factors of action (*kāraka*)? To this, he says: "Even in the case of absolute difference," and so forth.

It is not only in the case of absolute non-difference or absolute existence; rather, even in the case of absolute difference, because the relationship between cause and effect is denied, the status of the factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and the means of cognition (*jñāpaka*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), but only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
And conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) occurs elsewhere as well, namely, the perception of difference among factors of action (*kāraka*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth.

If it is argued that "since absolute difference (*bhedaikānta*) is the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its existence there is ultimate (*paramārthataḥ*)," [the author] replies here with the words beginning "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*).
"Is there no perception of difference even from moment to moment?

Where [is it]? To this he says: 'Whether externally or internally, how could it not exist? To this he says: in the manner in which the perception of difference is described by the Buddhists—that is, in the form of momentary, single atoms—in that very manner [it does not exist]."
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because perception," and so forth.

Because perception—that is, the cognition defined by others as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)—is the object of disagreement, meaning it is a subject of dispute;

for it is not established without contradiction by both the proponent and the opponent. If something were established by that [perception] such that there would be no dispute, then the Buddhist should not state a proof for its absolute nature (*ekānta*).
Nor is anything established by means of another conceptual construction; otherwise, why would the very establishment of the difference between cognition and consciousness not occur in this way?
For the status of the producer and the indicator is such that perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous—*Nyāyabindu* 1.1.
The Sāṃkhya doctrine is based on the absolute [view] that [everything] is momentary.

It might be thought: "Let there be no establishment of perception, nor of the object, based on each individual atom; however, it may arise from conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), and from that, the apprehension of difference (*bhedopalabdhi*) may also occur. To this, he says: "The cognition of perception is either contradictory or manifold; because its object is thus, there is no apprehension of difference as it is described. If it is argued: "Let there be no apprehension of that through perception, but let it come from inference (*anumāna*)," to this he says: "And because inference is without an object (*nirviṣayatvāt*)."
"Inference has the universal as its object; that which is other [than the particular] is the universal, and that is the object of inference" (Nyāyabindu 1.16–17).

According to this statement, for the opponent [the Mīmāṃsaka], the universal is nothing at all. Therefore, just like the cognition of water in a mirage, no real entity is established from it—this is the connection [of the sentence], with the case-ending and verbal form understood according to their future application.

This is what is meant: if perception were to have as its exclusive object difference both before and after [the production of an effect], then it would be logical that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [effect] because of its arising from that [cause] and its non-deviation from it; however, this is not the case for the Buddhist, due to [his reliance on] inference.
The word *bhā* is the third case ending (*tṛtīyāvibhaktiḥ*).

Furthermore, regarding this view of another [opponent]: "Even though there is the manifestation of non-difference as well as difference both externally and internally, nevertheless, difference alone is ultimately real because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārāt*), whereas non-difference is not, because of the opposite"; to that he says: "Not at all, nothing," and so forth. Indeed, no perception or any other cognition deviates from the reality of that [consciousness] alone (*tanmātratattvam*). Where, then, does its deviation occur? He says: "Because of deviation only with respect to differences (*bhedeṣu*)," [meaning] of the cognition.
For instance— the cognition of two moons and so forth deviates from duality;
therefore, just as difference is not established, neither is non-difference established for anyone, according to the Buddhist.

If it is argued: "But if reality is merely existence (*sattāmātra*), then, due to the absence of the distinction between the one who explains and the one who is explained, how and by whom could reality be explained? To this, he says: "One's own," and so forth.

One's own is the proponent (*vādī*) and the other is the opponent (*prativādī*); regarding the continuum (*santāna*) of those two, because of the false appearance of the distinction—whether it be conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*), or actual difference—even if there were an absolute monism of difference (*bhedaikānta*), how could that absolute monism of difference be established?

For instance: direct perception of one's own mental continuum cannot be the object of dispute; inference lacks a [corresponding] objective reality; and regarding the mental continuum of another, even in the absence of such [an external object], there is the occurrence of signs such as activity (vyāpāra) during dreams. This is the intended meaning. Now, if it is argued that in the waking state the speech and so forth of another’s mind are [the cause] directly, whereas in a dream they are through a mediated succession, and therefore there is no deviation (vyabhicāra), the author replies with the words "activity" and so on:

if it is accepted that there is no deviation in the case where the cognition of activity and so forth consists merely of the volition (samīhā) or effort (ceṣṭā)—that is, if it is held that the cognition is nothing more than that itself—[then the following applies].

In what manner? He says: "Even indirectly"—by the word "even" (*api*), it should be understood that [the cognition] must be non-deviant from that [object] even directly. Here, "non-deviance from action" (*kriyā-avyabhicāra*) refers to action consisting of activity and verbal expression; the mention of "action" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which a jar and so forth are also included. Why would there not be non-deviance from that? [The answer is: there certainly would be, because of the cognition of that [object]; for if there were no such non-deviance, the establishment of an external object would not occur. This is the connection [of the words].

He thinks as follows: just as in a dream, even in the absence of objects, forms, and functions, there is the perception of their appearance, so too in other circumstances, even in the absence of those [objects], there is the appearance of them; thus, the existence of external objects is not established. Likewise, since in a dream there occurs a cognition manifesting activity and speech even in the absence of any actual striving, so too in other cases, such a cognition occurs even in the absence of another continuum; therefore, the existence of another continuum is not established by inference, even when no such continuum exists.
Even in the waking state,
even in the absence of causal efficiency,
even in the waking state.
Even in the absence of another continuum,
there exists the presence of activity, speech, and so forth;
by this, one who imagines the body experienced in a dream to be non-illusory should be refuted, because the external object has not been negated.
In this context, Prajñākara raises the objection of the view of Prajñākaragupta in order to refute it, beginning with the words "one's own and others," etc.,
[stating that] reality transcends all conceptual constructions.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because it consists entirely of ignorance.
Of what [does it consist]? To this he says: "One's own," and so forth.

One's own (*sva*), another (*para*), and the intermediate (*kṣama*)—the causal relationship (*hetuphalabhāva*) among these constitutes their conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), that is, determination (*vyavasāya*).

By thus demonstrating that these [objects] fall within the scope of direct perception, he points out the refutation of that [position] with the words "due to the absence of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāvāt*) and so forth; that is,
the impossibility of that reality which is beyond all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is its "impossibility" (*anupapatti*).
Why? Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain:

perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a valid means of cognition in that regard, because it is not perceived apart from things such as jars, which consist of multiple attributes such as pleasure and so forth. Nor is inference (*anumāna*) [possible], because of the absence of the conceptualization of property and subject (*dharma-dharmin*), and because of the absence of a nature that is either conceptual or otherwise.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "as if possessing difference" (*bhedavat*) means just as there is a plurality of blue and so forth, or of pleasure and so forth; "like that" (*tadvat*) refers to that very [plurality].
In this way, the verse is explained according to its first meaning.

This is another explanation: regarding the passage beginning with "even in the case of absolute difference" (*bhedaikānte’pi*), the sense is that the status of the causal and the cognitive (*kārakajñāpaka*) does not exist—not only in the case of absolute non-difference (*abhedaikānte*), but even in the case of absolute difference—certainly not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), but rather according to the doctrine of the transformation of the person (*puruṣapariṇāmapakṣa*).
By this, the statement "the non-sequential appears as if sequential through such things as birth" is explained.
If it is asked, "Why is this so? he says here: "At every moment," and so forth;
this is easy to understand.
If it is further asked, "Why is even this so? he says: "Of perception," and so forth.

Since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—which consists of the distinction between the cognized object and the cognition—is a subject of dispute; since sensory perception (*indriyapratyakṣa*) is also a subject of dispute regarding objects composed of multiple parts, forms, and so forth; and since inference (*anumāna*) is either without an object or has as its object only its own internal aspect (*svāṃśamātra*) constructed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*), how can there be the establishment of the absolute difference [of the soul] from perception or inference? It is thought that for the proponent of transformation (*pariṇāma*), this very [soul] would be established.
Thus it is said: "It appears as if it were an external reality, both within and without. Indeed, this is certainly not the case.

What is it? It is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the reality of pure existence (*sanmātratattva*); it is sentience (*saṃvedana*), the reality of mere awareness; "existence" (*sat*) means the awareness of being, because the root *sad* has the sense of going and the sense of knowing. It does not deviate from all selves, for in relation to sentience, there is oneness of self; thus, the meaning is that the Self alone is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).

Where, then, does the deviation (vyabhicāra) occur? He says: "In the very particulars (bheda), namely in pleasure and so forth, because of the deviation of cognition"—the meaning is that this is the "residence" or the "going" [of the deviation].

Now, if it is asked: "Since there is a distinction between one's own and another's continuum (saṃtāna), how can it be said to be 'mere person' (puruṣamātra)? To this he says: "One's own and another," and so forth.
By this, it has been explained that [reality] appears through ignorance as non-existent things such as succession and the birth of succession;
now he states the conclusion with the words "one's own and other," etc.: the reality which is beyond all conceptual constructions and devoid of all differentiation is the nature of the Puruṣa.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To this, he states the reply: "Because of the absence of valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇābhāvāt*), and so forth;
[this refers to] the logical establishment that the self (*ātman*) consists of all transformations (*pariṇāma*).
And of what, and like what? He says: "Like that which possesses difference.
Difference (*bheda*) is the exclusion of everything from everything; its "extreme" (*ekānta*) is like that, and [the world] is like that.

Why? He says: because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). There is an absence of the means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*), regarding the claim that "everything is a transformation of a single person."

For it is not the case that, as in the instance of pleasure and other sensations occurring within a single continuum—where there is an unerring cognition of oneness due to a competitive impulse (*ahamahamikā*)—so too is the cognition "this is a jar" or "this is cloth" regarding all such things like jars and cloths a cognition of oneness; rather, that cognition has a common transformation (*samānapariṇāma*) as its object, not oneness, because it is not experienced in that way.
Nor is the establishment of one thing possible through a cognition of another; otherwise, from the cognition of blue, the establishment of yellow would follow.

Consequently, there is an absence of direct perception here; and because of that absence, there is also an absence of inference, since the latter is preceded by the former. Furthermore, nothing in the world is untenable except on the assumption of the transformation of a single self, such that one would need to postulate it;
for everything arises solely from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*).
Furthermore, even conventional transactions such as self and other, giver and receiver, or the bound and the binder are difficult to establish here;
therefore, its existence is not proven through inference in the case of cloth and the like, nor in the case of pleasure and the like.
In the case of inference,
when the root [gam] is used in the sense of "existing" (sad-gamana), it accepts a transformation within a single self.

If it is argued that [the claim] "because of the absence of valid means of knowledge" is unestablished, since there exists scripture such as "This [universe] is indeed the Person" (Ṛgveda 10.90.2), we say no; for this is not scripture because it is sublated by direct perception, like the Piṭakatraya and similar texts, and because other [scriptures] exist.
Alternatively, if there is an impossibility of that stainless, non-conceptual Brahman-atom, of what [kind] would that impossibility be? To this he says: "like absolute difference" (*bhedaikāntavat*).
That which is differentiated from everything else is "difference" (*bheda*); [it refers to] partless cognition. "Like that" means like that [absolute difference].
Why? Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Even that [lack of proof] follows because perception has a subject of disagreement as its object, because it has the distinction between the sentient and the non-sentient as its object, and because inference lacks an object in this regard.

Regarding that [inference] as well, this must be asked: "From what is the establishment of the absolute non-difference [of the self and the world] proven? If scripture (*āgama*) is also not different from that [self], then it is likewise unestablished.
Nor can that very same thing be both the object to be established and the means of establishment, because of contradiction;
or, if in this system the cognition of that [object] is simply the comprehension of scripture (āgama), then what is the utility of scripture therein? Of scripture...
Furthermore, because there exist other scriptural authorities that establish difference,
[the doctrine of] the non-difference of Brahman [is untenable].
The cognition of Brahman [arises] because of the non-difference between those two;
furthermore, does one who has realized Brahman through scripture perceive that very nature of Brahman, or someone else? In the first case—the nature of non-difference.
If one knows Brahman as devoid of its own cognition, then how could it be said that "the Self was previously like a jar"? Thus everything has been explained.
This distinction between knowledge and ignorance is projected upon that which is devoid of cognition in the world.
"No," he said; therefore, it remains devoid of both measurement and protection.
If its self-cognition is eternal and if that already exists even prior [to scripture], then scripture is rendered useless for it; how can there be any action for that which is already established?
If this [self-awareness] is established by scripture, how can its permanence be asserted?
Since self-awareness is impermanent, it follows that the self itself must likewise be impermanent.

If [the certainty] were other than the non-dual, non-conceptual self-awareness because of its dependence on scripture, then how can its status as being essentially identical to that [awareness] be asserted here as permanent?
