Nor does anyone perceive the Self through another consciousness that is devoid of self-awareness;
otherwise, the futility of the Self would be immediately apparent.
Therefore, the Self does not know its own nature by itself; hence, it is Brahman.
If it were perceived by something else, how could that non-duality exist?
(7) And how could that which is created by ignorance perceive [itself]?
For the form of Brahman does not destroy thirst through the delusion of water. (8)

If another [consciousness] also knows that self, how indeed could it be real? For when it is known by another, its [status as a subject] is not prevented; nor is there an infinite regress, since for that other [subject], there is likewise the grasping of consciousness by yet another.
If that [consciousness] were itself the very existence of the manifestation of Brahman,
then tell me, alas, what can be said regarding its being produced by ignorance?
If it were said that its cognition is by Brahman in reality, [then...]
If, upon the realization of one's own self within Brahman, the nature of being either knowledge or its opposite were attained, then for no one would there be the realization of Brahman; therefore,
that [position] is not tenable.
"The words of those who perceive, through the vision of the Ṛṣis, entities that are beyond the reach of the senses and inference, are not contradicted by inference" (Vākyapadīya 1.38).
This is because, for such a person, there is simply no [empirical] perception at all.
If the scripture were different from that [non-dual reality], how could non-duality be maintained?
Consequently, in the cognition of it, the system of the grasped and the grasper would necessarily follow.
If there is no cognition of it, how can the scripture be established in reality?
If you consider even that [scripture] to be ignorance, then how could reality be understood from it, or by whom could that scripture itself be understood? From scripture? [No.]
Scripture is that which is not commonly recognized as such; it must be stated either as something other or otherwise,
whether as distinct or non-distinct.

"How can ignorance (*avidyā*) be spoken of by the wise as being [the opposite] of knowledge (*vidyā*)?"—from this it follows that [ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge], because there is no such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and so forth.
Furthermore, demonstrating that objects are neither exclusively different nor non-different, he says: "consisting of both difference and non-difference," and so forth.
Difference consists of non-difference among objects because it would otherwise be impossible;
likewise, non-difference consists of difference. Therefore, reality is not absolute from either side.
For the world to attain the path, valid cognition is like a staff for the blind.

If that [cognition] consists of ignorance (*avidyā*), by what means does it perceive its own counteragent? Since even the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*) consists in the non-perception of reality (*tattva-apratipatti*), how could one perceive reality? If these two do not differ from one another, such that the absence of ultimate existence (*paramārtha-sattva*) is perceived, then this establishment of the fruit of valid cognition would not be merely according to appearance, but rather from the perspective of ultimate reality; for otherwise, the acceptance of ultimate reality would be untenable, leading to the consequence of total instability. Thus, in the view of absolute difference (*bheda-ekānta*), since a perceived form cannot exist without an unperceived aspect, there would be no error anywhere at all.
Since it is impossible for a cognitive error to conceal any aspect of consciousness— just as it is impossible for it to conceal its manifest aspect—

the establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result is made according to how things appear, even though the distinction between the apprehended, the apprehender, and the cognition itself does not exist.
— *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.357:

Because of the context, [the reference is] to objects such as pleasure belonging to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*), and not to other continua (*santānāntara*), since non-difference (*abheda*) is not admitted in that case.
"Differentiation" means manifoldness;
what is that? He says: "It consists of non-difference," meaning its nature is some kind of unity.
Why so? He says: "Because it cannot otherwise be accounted for."

Otherwise—that is, by way of the impossibility of difference being of the nature of non-difference—the phrase "of the difference of things" (*bhedasyārthānām*) may be construed. For just as for those [things], in the absence of difference, there is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, so too in the absence of non-difference, there is nothing that consists of difference. Thus, by that mode of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), non-difference is the reality through manifoldness (*anekāntataḥ*). Therefore...
The meaning is that, according to the context, there is no non-difference between the pleasure and other states residing in different mental continua.

If it is objected: "Since all objects of apprehension are non-existent—like the hairs seen by one with ophthalmia—the phrase 'of objects' (arthānām) is incorrect," he says in response: "The means of valid cognition" (pramāṇam), and so forth.

To whom do the means of valid cognition, such as perception and so forth, belong—being like a blind man’s staff? To this he says: whatever is accepted by someone as a means to liberation is considered that person’s path;

and for the follower of the Sugata, the unreality of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) is accepted as the means to *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, that alone is his path, because it is through the realization of that [unreality] that one proceeds.
For that [cognition] is not established without being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like its object;
for whom is it thus? To this he says: "of the world," meaning of the people born from the Tathāgata.
Then what follows from that? To this he says: "If that... and so forth.

If that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is considered to be of the nature of ignorance (*avidyātmaka*) and indeed erroneous even in its own essence— since one observes that objects such as jars in a dream are of the nature of ignorance, and at other times their reality is likewise asserted by others— then because reality is seen in both cases, why should this Buddhist world not also accept that the means of valid cognition itself possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*)? For what reason does he stubbornly maintain the opposite view regarding the entire [world]?

The proponent of Consciousness-Only (Vijñānavādin) says: "The meaning is that they are not [established] by anything; for in the absence of an ultimate means of valid cognition (paramārtha-pramāṇa), even the counter-position is not established."
The unreality of the objects of cognition consists in their being of the nature of ignorance even during the waking state.
He states that having ignorance as its essence—
that is, being of the nature of ignorance— is the opposite [of knowledge], as if it were imagined by a blind man.

[Objection: "But surely the Buddhist does not establish the non-existence of anything in any respect by way of ultimate reality (tattvataḥ), such that this fault would apply. Rather, when there is an absence of ultimate existence, whatever superimposition (samāropa) of existence—whether external or internal—is made by another, that very existence is refuted by inference, even though [the inference] itself is of the nature of ignorance (avidyā). To this, he says: "Superimposition," and so forth. Even in that which is devoid of ultimate existence, the cognition of ultimate existence is "superimposition" (samāropa). Its "exclusion" (vyavaccheda) is its removal, or the inference directed toward that [removal]. This [inference] also [is not a means of valid knowledge], not only perception, because it consists in the non-comprehension of reality.

If it is argued: "Reality consists in being of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*); since [the object] is of that nature, there is no apprehension of reality. For just as there is no apprehension of reality through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too there is no apprehension of reality through its exclusion (*vyavaccheda*); therefore, reality is not cognized even from that," [the author] replies here with the words beginning "From what... (*kutaḥ*) and so forth.
The meaning is that reality would become falsity because error would be unestablished; for this reason,

when the absolute positions of difference and non-difference, or substance and mode— which consist in the apprehension of reality— are investigated, they do not surpass one another, since the absence of ultimate existence is perceived by the proponent of external objects.

If it is argued that [the object] exists as ultimate reality because of the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is itself an inference consisting in the exclusion of superimpositions (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*); to this he replies: "That is not so," and so forth.

That is to say, from that self-awareness—which consists in the cognition of the absence of all conceptual constructions—this establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result is not merely according to how things appear.
[Pravāhaṇa 2.357] How then is that? He says: "But rather... (api tu). From what [perspective] is this so in the ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ)? To this he says: "In the ultimate sense," and so forth.

Because the acceptance of ultimate reality—which possesses a nature consisting of all delusions and so forth—is otherwise untenable, that is, impossible through any other mode than the non-existence of the establishment of means and objects of knowledge in terms of true reality (*tattvataḥ*); therefore, the connection is that "in true reality" it is so.
This means that the establishment of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results occurs according to conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) following [the dictates of] perception.

"Is it not the case that there would be an acceptance of that [existence], yet no real establishment of it? To this he says: "Because of the consequence of a lack of settled order" (*avyavasthā-prasaṅgāt*).

This means that if one accepts that only things such as delusion exist and not [qualities] such as permanence, then the absence of such a settled rule (*avyavasthā*) would follow; because of the consequence of that lack of settled order, the phrase "real establishment of it" is established by the words "of objects" (*arthānām*).
And the establishment of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results involves the acceptance of all conceptual fluctuations.

Now, let it be that objects exist both externally and internally; nevertheless, how could their nature be both difference and non-difference, or non-difference and difference? If you say it is because of contradiction, to this he replies: "Difference," and so forth.

In the case of an absolute difference (*bhedaikānta*), if one accepts that there is a total cognition (*saṃvedana*) of an entity—whether it be a conscious being or something else—that has been made an object by a cognition, then that aspect which is uncognized (*asaṃvidita*) at that very time by that same cognition, characterized by the capacity to produce its own specific effect, the distinction from the aspects of other objects, and so forth, would be impossible. The meaning is that if such [an uncognized aspect] were admitted, then because everything would be cognized in its entirety, there would be no error whatsoever, whether external or internal; the force of the particle *eva* (only) is that if there were error anywhere, it would have to exist everywhere.

Likewise, in the case of the extreme of difference (*bhedaikānta*), since consciousness—whether of itself or of another—is not perceived as having the nature of existence, sentience, and so forth, and since that which is unperceived consists of ignorance and a lack of discrimination, no error whatsoever could ever occur. Why is this? To this he says: "Because of the concealment of the cognition," and so on. For it would be impossible for there to be any delusion (*vibhrama*) that conceals some aspect or form—such as momentariness and the like—of cognition, which is the knowledge whose objects are both self and other.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "just as [the cognition] has a manifest form.

And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: For whatever person a certain object is not concealed (*asaṃvṛta*), there is no error (*bhrānti*) regarding it for that person; for example, in the case of the intended consciousness with respect to the forms of existence, sentience, and so forth. And since the form of pleasure and so on, which is the subject of no dispute, is not concealed from cognition, inference is not accepted by the opponent as having the exclusion of error as its result.
Furthermore, error is indeed admitted by the opponent. Therefore, we conclude: [cognition] possesses a cognized form.
By this, it has been established that difference consists of non-difference, and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "Even in your own system, how can error be possible for a soul whose nature is to grasp all objects exactly as they exist? To this, he says: "Of the soul," and so forth, even according to the Jaina doctrine.
The adventitious karma of the living soul (*jīva*), which is consciousness (*saṃvit*), is the cause of its delusion, like liquor and such; its manifestation (*prapañca*) is held to be beginningless.
(12) This has been extracted from *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, page 179.
Praṇidhiprakaraṇa, p.

71: The soul (*jīva*) has knowledge as its intrinsic nature (*jñānasvabhāva*). This is because the negation of a soul that is either insentient and unchanging or sentient and unchanging would result in the failure to establish selflessness (*nairātmya*). Its transformation [into a different state] occurs through connection with another substance (*dravyāntara*), like intoxication and so forth. If, on the other hand, there were a beginningless continuity of agency and enjoyment belonging solely to the karmas, then [the world] would not differ from being soulless, since no other inherent nature (*svabhāvāntara*) could be discerned, as in the case of momentary destruction and so forth.

If it is argued that, without such a transformation of the self (*ātman*), the status of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for effort, pleasure, pain, perception, and cognition would be untenable and useless, [we reply:
for the conscious being, that very *karma* is the direct cause of *saṃsāra*, and not the transformation of the living being (*jīva*) characterized by effort;

this is because we observe modifications such as false view (*mithyādarśana*) arising through the influence of the emergence and intensification (*udaya-udīraṇā*) of connections with other substances. Consequently, liberation (*mokṣa*) results from the total destruction of that [karma].
Even for one who postulates a Lord (Īśvara) and so forth, this leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga):

that Lord too would be the cause of saṃsāra, since he is not distinct from the individual soul (jīva). Alternatively, if he were to act according to the connection with karma—or conversely—his supreme sovereignty (pāramaiśvarya) would be untenable.

Of what kind is the *jīva*, whose other name is *ātman*? To this he says: it is "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), which is "correct" (*samīcīnā*)—meaning either having the form of grasping all objects exactly as they exist, or existing in the form of each respective object because it cannot be a cause of delusion; otherwise, since any error could arise from any action whatsoever, there would be nothing that is non-delusory.
If it is asked, "Why is that not [the cause] for him? the author replies here: "Like wine and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), intoxicants such as *madana* and *tvaca* are included.
For just as wine and the like are the cause of Devadatta's delusion, so too is karma for him.

Now, if it is argued that even a solar eclipse and the like—which do not belong to that [object]—are causes for its misapprehension, because a cognition of yellow is observed in a white cloth [during such an eclipse], and therefore there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); we say no. For when there is a connection with that [eclipse], the rays of light belonging to it (the sun) become properties of that [cloth]. Thus, other frivolous objections should likewise be considered, otherwise.

If, indeed, there is no loss of its own nature for the individual soul (jīva) even when connected with karma due to the agitation caused by desire— just as during a solar eclipse— then that [connection] is not an illusion; consequently, there would be no distinction between the liberated and the non-liberated.
The claim that the self possesses perspiration and is constantly sweating is a non-existent [position],
for this is not accepted by the proponent of that [self].
Thus it has been said:
If there were a loss of its own nature, how could one who holds the self dear desire [its] destruction? (Prajñāpradīpa 1)
If this is argued, he says here: "Of the living being," and so forth;
like wine and the like, that karma is the cause for the delusion of the heart.

This is what is meant: just as in connection with liquor and the like there is some kind of transformation (*anyathābhāva*) in him—otherwise, he would be indistinguishable from one who is not intoxicated, or there would be a difference in the continuum (*santāna*)—so it is also in the case of connection with karma. Even for one who thinks that there is no transformation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the liquor and so forth because it is eternal, but rather that a state of intoxication arises as something distinct from it—the reply to him is this: if that state were distinct from him, then he would not be intoxicated, just like another person, because that state is not experienced by him. If it is argued that he is intoxicated because that state is experienced by him, then how could a yogi not be [considered intoxicated] in the same way?
Since there is no inherence (*samavāya*), there can be no distinction [of the effect] from that [cause];
if it is argued that the state [of the cause] is the effect because it is produced by it, then let this be said of God and others as well, since there is no difference.
Furthermore, the causal relationship between cause and effect has already been refuted regarding eternal entities; therefore, this argument amounts to nothing.
If it is argued that because one is intoxicated during the state of intoxication, there can be no [perception] from that state, and therefore, due to the direct experience of that state,
there is no inherence (*samavāya*) of that state in the yogin;
Because inherence (*samavāya*) is eternal and all-pervading, there can be no distinction [of karma] arising from it, since it is without distinction everywhere.
To this, one might think: "What is the proof for the existence of that karma? To this, he says: "Of the soul," and so forth.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "That which is the delusion (*bhrānti*) of the soul—which has the nature of illuminating both self and other—is perceived as that karma, like wine and the like."
If it is asked, "What, then, is that [cause] from which this [delusion] is inferred? he says here: "The cause.

Since action (*karman*) is the cause of the one-sided delusion regarding permanence and so forth—just as with liquor and the like—therefore, that [delusion] is understood from that [action]. To explain: the one-sided delusion of living beings regarding permanence and so forth is preceded by a specific other substance associated with it, because it is such [a delusion], just like the delusion regarding direction and so forth in one who has consumed liquor and the like.
That specific quality of another substance which exists there is, for us, action; such is my view regarding that action, [though it arises] from delusion.

Others say that for us Jains, the word "me" (mine) is meaningless; they argue that while errors regarding stones and the like may sometimes occur, preceded by specific substances as their cause— since such is observed— the error of the absolute [view] of momentary destruction and so forth must be preceded by a true error, because no other cause, such as the karma of another or any other factor, is observed.
[Objection: In that case, even a sprout whose seed is not perceived would not be preceded by it. [Response:
If you argue that its being preceded by such a [seed] is inferred because we observe that things of its kind are preceded by such [seeds], then this is the same in the present case as well.
Furthermore, just as sensory errors are perceived, so too are mental errors perceived in one who is intoxicated due to contact with another substance.

Furthermore, even from an instruction that is not distinct [from ordinary perception], such delusions are observed; these too arise solely from karma acting as a concomitant cause for that instruction, just like wine and the like. Moreover, if a delusion were possible from that very delusion, how could it occur for one who has just awakened from a long, deep sleep? This is because there is no mental delusion at the onset of sleep and so forth, and because one does not subsequently remember it in that same way. Even if one were to admit that in that state, the condition of having withdrawn all conceptual constructions would be impossible for anyone, since not even a mere cognition of that [state] is admitted there. And it has already been stated that a remote cause is not [effective].

If it is argued that, because its cause is karma, there is no cessation of that error as long as it is eternal; to this he replies: "It is adventitious," meaning that because the error regarding its effect is occasional, it too is occasional.
For it is not logical that a constant effect should be occasional;
as it has been said:
"The illusion of yellow in a blue lotus arises from the disturbance of bile and other humors."
If non-existence [is established] because of non-perception, then the sprout would have the seed as its antecedent.
The delusions of the mind of the living being arise from karma; thus it has been written again.

The intention of Prajñākara, the author of the doubt, is that since even prior error ceases during sleep and similar states, one cannot admit even mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) during sleep and so forth.
"If the eternality of action is accepted, how could there be a cessation of their effects as long as the cause— the action— has not perished? (Nyāyaviniścaya 1.103).
If it is asked: "Even so, how can there be a connection with karma for one who was previously pure and subsequently liberated? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth.

The stream of the manifestation (*prapañca*) of that karma is held to be beginningless, because its continuity as an effect has been established as being without beginning. Explaining the meaning of the verse, he says: "Knowledge," and so forth.

From what [source] is it that the soul (*jīva*) has knowledge as its intrinsic nature (*jñānasvabhāva*)? To this he says: because of the negation—that is, the refutation—of the soul conceived by the Sāṅkhya as insentient and unchanging, and of the soul conceived by the Vaiśeṣika as insentient and unchanging; and because of the non-establishment of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

If it is asked, "How can there be any alteration in that which has knowledge as its intrinsic nature?", to this he says: "That alteration" means the soul’s alteration, or its state of delusion (*bhrāntatva*), due to connection with another substance. That is, from a substance other than the self-substance (*ātmadravya*), namely the substance of karma (*karmadravya*), through connection with that [substance].
He provides an illustration: "Intoxication," and so forth.
Just as intoxication and the like result in a change of state through their association with something else, so too is the case here.

[Objection: But how can there be any change of state for that [Self], since it is eternal and thus lacks a substratum and possesses no excellence that could be removed? [Response: It is merely because of the agency [of the Self]—due to its being the cause of the manifestation of pleasure, pain, and so on, by means of the instruments such as the body and senses, which are specific transformations of primordial matter (prakṛti)—that it is designated as an "enjoyer" (bhoktṛ).

If it is argued that the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) belongs to the person (*puruṣa*) only figuratively because he is not an agent (*akartṛtva*), whereas in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) that [status] is absent; demonstrating this very point, he says "if" and so forth. The word "if" (*yadi*) indicates the opponent's view. As for the meaning of the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "but again... of actions alone, not of the self," he asks:
what is it? He replies: it is the continuity (*prabandha*) of agency and enjoyership.
"What is its nature? To this he says: "It is held to be beginningless"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Refuting this, he says: "It would not differ from the selfless [position]"—the meaning is that this position would not differ from, nor be distinct from, the view that there is no self; for even if a self exists, it would be indistinguishable from non-existence insofar as it is devoid of agency and enjoyership. Thus the Sāṃkhya speaks.
The meaning is that because the soul possesses no excellence that can be added or removed, no excellence whatsoever can be imparted to it or taken away from it.
Because it is equal to non-existence.

Now, if it is thought that the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) consists in a change of state produced by connection with a different substance, that does not exist for the Self; however, consciousness characterized by the experience of pleasure and so forth, which are distinct entities, is indeed the essential nature (svarūpa) of the Puruṣa. (Yogabhāṣya 1.1)
If it is argued [that this is so] because of such a statement, here [the author] says: "From its own nature," etc.

Apart from the nature of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), which consists in the experience of pleasure and so forth whose essence is consciousness (*caitanya*), there is no other nature consisting in the perception of something eternal, non-eternal, or partless; for that other [nature] is not apprehended—that is, it is not ascertained—just like momentary destruction and so forth. Indeed, only one nature, which is consciousness manifesting as joy, sorrow, and so on, is experienced, and nothing else.

In that case, some maintain that agency belongs to the self because of the inherence (*samavāya*) of effort, and the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) belongs to the self because of the perception of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and not to the *karmas*.

To those [who hold this view], he replies with the words "of the self," and so on. "Of the self" means of that which has "jīva" as its other name. "In that manner" (*tathā*) refers to the mode of transformation consisting of the perception of effort, pleasure, and so forth. Without such a transformation—where "effort" includes pleasure, pain, and so forth (the word "and so forth" including desire and the like), "perception" includes the cognition of effort and the like as well as form and the like—the state of being their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) would be untenable. Thus, the construction of the phrase is: "because of the impossibility of that [inherent causality], there must be a change in that [self]."

Why is this so? He says: "Because of lack of utility," meaning because of transformation into the form of effort and so forth; the sense is that only a transformative cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) can logically be an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Furthermore, he writes: "The state of being subject to modification is eternal."
Comparison: We perceive this single reality alone as manifesting in various forms such as joy, sorrow, and so forth; let names be assigned to it as one pleases—*Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* 3.277.
Because of their adherence to inherence,
the Vaiśeṣikas fail to fully understand the distinction between inherence, the inherent cause, and the efficient cause, due to their one-sided insistence on the difference between cause and effect.

If it is argued that "that in which an effect is produced is its inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*), then what is meant by "in which [it is] produced"? If this means "that which is related by way of inherence," we do not perceive any other entity situated between the pot and its parts apart from them. Nevertheless, rather than postulating such a perception, it is better to accept the non-disputed fact of some form of identity (*tādātmya*) between part and whole, quality and qualified, and genus and its possessor, as observed in experience.
And thus, the faults of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) are avoided;
for it is not only their identity that is contradictory, but even the perception [of them] is so,
since the nature of a thing is its being perceived as such through some form of identity with that which was previously unperceived.

Nor is there a contradiction with anything in its own nature, for that would entail the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Now, the establishment of inherence (*samavāya*) does not indeed proceed from perception, but rather from its effects.
And what is that effect? He says: "If you say it is the cognition [of] 'the whole in its parts,' no; for that is possible even if there were identity (*tādātmya*).

What is the meaning of 'the cloth is here in these threads'? It means that it exists in them through some form of identity, since, by virtue of intention, one also perceives 'the threads are in the cloth.
Thus, since inherence (*samavāya*) is not established, it has been stated: 'wherein it is interwoven.'"
By this, the view that [the cloth] has as its non-inherent cause the non-inherent cause of its own cause is refuted.

Furthermore, the production of a cloth devoid of color and other qualities is not perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), such that the colors and other qualities of the threads could serve as its non-inherent causes; for we observe only the production of that which is already endowed with color and the rest.
As for the claim that "because of rapid occurrence, there is merely the conceit of perceiving it thus," that is trivial; for if that were so, the same consequence would apply everywhere.

Then, in the passage beginning with "sthitam ātmanaḥ," the form of the cloth is grasped by the word *sva* (itself); its cause is the cloth; and among the causes of that [cloth], the form of the threads—which is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*)—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) with respect to the form of the cloth.
The form of the cloth...

Now, suppose the following view is held: "Let it be granted that for the self (*ātman*), such a transformation (*pariṇāma*) is possible through the agency of inherent causes such as effort (*prayatna*); nevertheless, what is established for the Jaina? To this he says: "Of the conscious one," and so forth.

For the conscious one, who undergoes transformations consisting in the perception of effort, pleasure, pain, and so on, that very same thing which exists in the form of a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), namely *karma*, is the direct cause of saṃsāra and the cause of desirable and undesirable bodies and the like; for subsequently, the appropriation of a low state is observed, just as a drunkard appropriates an impure place.
Furthermore, the transformation of the soul (*jīva-pariṇāma*) does not possess the same nature as effort, because that [transformation] lacks a cause.

If it is argued that this is because one observes that the desire for reaching a particular place and so forth is preceded by a wish, and that [desire] is the cause of that [action], we say: no, because there is a deviation in the case of one who falls into an impure place while intoxicated. This is the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*).
Why is this so? To the question, "Why is that very *karma* the cause of that? he says: "By another substance," and so forth.

A distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) has been explained; by its means, there occurs the arising (*udaya*) of a relationship, which consists of the granting of results according to the time, as well as *udīraṇā* (activation) and *apakvapācana* (the ripening of the unripe)—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) by another substance is intended. By the power (*vaśāt*) of that [substance], through the influence of false view (*mithyādarśana*) and so forth—by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is intended—the transformation (*vikāra*), which is the modification (*pariṇāma*) of the soul (*jīva*), is observed. From this, one concludes as follows: the adventitious pleasure, pain, and so forth of the transmigrating soul arise due to the power of the arising and activation of bondage by another substance; because they are adventitious, they are like false view and the rest.

As for the third argument stated by the opponent—that the pleasure, pain, and so forth which constitute the subject of dispute are produced by a quality of the transmigrating soul that shares the nature of effort, because while being an effect, they are beneficial to it, like food—this is refuted:
if [the production] is through a causal chain, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*);

if, however, it is direct, then even though the modification of that [quality] is seen directly due to its connection with another substance, to postulate yet another cause would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is argued that "let that very thing be the cause of *saṃsāra*," [the author] says here: "Liberation results from the destruction of that, i.e., from the destruction of karma.

For instance, whatever has a specific cause does not exist in the absence of that cause, just as a sprout does not exist in the absence of a seed; and *saṃsāra* has karma as its cause. This is the comparison: bodies and so forth are effects produced by the elements impelled by the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of Devadatta and are appropriated by him, because, being effects, they are the instruments for his enjoyment, like a house.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī, p. 149:
The meaning is that there would be a lack of determinacy due to the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
The opponent said: "This living being is ignorant and not master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by God, it may go either to heaven or to the pit."
Thus, in the *Mahābhārata*, *Vanaparvan* 30.28,
it is said: "The Lord is the cause of that."
Based on such statements as "Time ripens all beings" (Mahābhārata, Ādiparvan 1.273–75) and others, time is the cause; thus, "time creates beings, and time destroys creatures."
Time again subdues Time as it withdraws all creatures;
Time transforms all states of being, both auspicious and inauspicious, in the world;
Time contracts all creatures and emits them once more.
Time keeps watch while others sleep; for Time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Time moves through all beings, unrestrained and impartial—through those that have passed, those yet to come, and those that exist in the present.
Having understood them to be created by Time, you should not abandon your consciousness—
the Supreme Person alone— Mahābhārata, Puruṣa-sūkta 10.
Because of such statements as these— "The Person is the cause;
the Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be"— (Ṛg Veda).
Based on such statements as "From Prakṛti comes Mahat" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 22), Prakṛti is the cause, and not karma alone;
from Prakṛti comes Mahat, from that comes Ahaṃkāra, from that the group of sixteen,
and from five of that group of sixteen come the five elements.
—Sāṃkhyakārikā.
Regarding this, he says:
"The Lord and so forth are the cause of transmigratory existence"—this is understood to follow [from the previous context].
By this phrase "even while imagining," he demonstrates that according to the aforementioned method, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein; it is merely imagination alone.
Showing the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would follow from the absence of that [cognition] and the consequent absence of action, he says: "of that too," and so forth.

It might be argued that such [agency] would belong to other liberated souls (*muktātman*) and transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*) without distinction; however, it would also belong to that Lord (*īśvara*), for He too would be the cause of *saṃsāra*.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of non-distinction from the individual souls (*jīva*)," meaning because the Lord is non-different from the individual souls.

For just as this [ignorance] is the cause of saṃsāra for souls who are devoid of karma, so too might such pride (abhimāna) be [the cause]. Now, because He is omniscient, He does not join the self with suffering; for that very reason, He would not join it with anything else that is faultless, since He is free from any association with impure causes. Thus is the Lord.
By this, play (*krīḍā*) therein is prohibited for him; if that [play] were caused by her, it would also apply to the Self (*ātman*).
For indeed, we see those who are full of longing and those who are filled with desire directing their consciousness toward the Self.
Nor has this been refuted by the claim that "it is by its very nature the cause of that";
nor is it logical to make a distinction that its nature as such exists only in another and not in itself when it is not being perceived;
or else, for that Īśvara as well, other individual souls (jīvas) would be the cause of his transmigratory existence.

Why is this so? To this he says: because there is no distinction among living beings (*jīva*) due to their lack of action; for, by virtue of qualities such as omniscience, there is no difference between those living beings who are free from karma.
This is [the case] through sport (*krīḍā*).
The Lord of the creator of the net of Indra, the Lord.

Now, one might ask: "Why is it said that [the Lord] is absent in that case, when indeed, in its presence, He is the cause of it? To this, he says: "In accordance with the connection to karma," and so forth.

Herein is the intended meaning: neither does karma do anything to the Lord, nor does the Lord do anything to karma; rather, there is merely an operation toward the effect by these two as mutual auxiliaries.

Or is it that the Lord, impelled by karma, produces the effect—unlike anything else—or that karma, being insentient, is impelled by the Lord like an adze? Regarding the first position, [it is stated]: "In accordance with the connection to karma," and so forth.
"Except in the case of the opposite," and so forth;

for whichever living being has a connection with karma—whether it be of beautiful form or otherwise, whether it yields fruit immediately or otherwise—it proceeds according to that connection with karma. If it is admitted that the Lord acts toward the production of effects by relying on such auxiliary factors as those connections, then His supreme sovereignty is untenable due to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); this [point] also follows here.
The connection is thus: "that very karma is the cause of *saṃsāra*."

For instance: if that [Lord] possesses supreme sovereignty even while performing an effect with the assistance of karma, then time and other factors would also possess it, since there is no distinction [between them].

If it is argued that the Lord produces the collection of causes and effects as an effect because of his being both knowing and unknowing, whereas time and the rest do so otherwise, and therefore this is the distinction; then from what source is the establishment of his such thorough knowledge? If you say "from production," then there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of time and the rest.

Even the response "because he produces [them] while possessing selfhood" is not a valid answer, for there is a deviation by means of one who is in deep sleep, who is the cause of the activity and speech of himself [but lacks the required qualities].

If it is argued that this is because of the absence of all delusion (*sarvavyāmoha*); from where does that [absence] come? From omniscience (*sarvajñāna*). This results in a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): the establishment of the absence of all delusion depends upon the knowledge of that [omniscience], and the establishment of that [omniscience] depends upon the former.
Therefore, this is not a distinguishing feature of this [omniscient being] over time and so forth.
Or, let there be such knowledge of that; even so, it does not distinguish this [omniscient being] from others, because such knowledge is ineffective (*akiñcitkaratva*) in this regard.

For indeed, the thorough knowledge of one who, having recognized that an ignorant person is engaged in what ought not to be done, impels that person toward what ought to be done, is fruitful; however, in this case, if [the Lord] were to impel [beings] in that very same way according to their connection with karma—as if by chance—then supreme sovereignty, characterized by qualities such as omniscience, would be untenable; therefore, karma alone is the impelling cause for that.
Because [the opponent] holds that God is ignorant, [they claim] karma-relatedness is the auxiliary cause of God.
If [it is argued that it arises] from the production by Īśvara, then [it must be asked] of Īśvara:
The Lord of time and so forth, the Lord of the Lord.
The connection here is that [the Lord] "sets that [karma] in motion.
Regarding this, the objection of "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*) need not be considered;

for instance, if karma—even though insentient—is capable of producing its effect at the proper time, then since that [effect] is accomplished from that very [karma], what is the use of a Lord who knows it? For that which is incapable of producing [an effect] in such a way does not produce it through the proximity of another; otherwise, a barley seed would produce a rice sprout when placed near someone who knows how to do so.
Furthermore, it is impossible to deny that knowledge is a cooperative cause [of action],
whereas the Lord is not so.

Now, if that capacity is produced by him [the Lord], then since the action (*karman*) is produced by the Lord and not the effect (*kārya*), how does he, as its auxiliary, produce that [effect]? If you say that both are produced by him alone, from what [source] is this known? If you say it is because an action capable of producing such [an effect] cannot arise from anything else, then from where has the Lord’s capacity to produce that pair of effects come? Is it without cause? If so, it would exist everywhere; otherwise, why postulate a restriction of the effect to a specific cause even in other cases? If you say there is no fault because that capacity is eternal, we say no, for that has been refuted.

If you say [the world arises] from its own cause, then since action (*karman*) also arises from that very same cause, what is the use of a Lord (*īśvara*)? Thus it is established—starting with "as... and so forth. Now, if it is maintained that the Lord is impelled by action, or that action is made effective as a causal agent by him; regarding this, he says: "Or in the case of the reverse," and so forth. "Reverse" (*viparyaya*) refers to a sequence other than the one previously stated. And that [reverse sequence] is possible only immediately within the doctrine of those who maintain both the Lord and action. Furthermore, since supreme lordship (*pāramaiśvarya*) would be untenable if such [action] were the initiator, action alone must be the cause of that [world].
For instance, if he were impelled by karma like an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and thus engaged in activity, there would be no distinction between that karma and [the action] of a Lord (īśa).
The Lord is the effect; indeed, the Lord alone [is it].

If [the Lord acts] without a cause, then what need has the Lord [of such a cause]? Let that ordinary person himself perform the action, impelled by him; what is the use of the Lord’s impulse? Furthermore, if even that insentient thing impels the Lord, how is the distinction made that "it is not his knowledge" [that impels him]? It is illogical to say that one thing impels the Lord who was already impelled by another, for that would lead to an infinite regress.
In that case, action does not impel the Lord, nor does the Lord [impel] action; for supreme sovereignty would otherwise be untenable.

To explain: it would be better if he had simply performed the effect itself—what is the use of impelling an action? It is highly implausible that one who lacks the capacity to produce an effect should possess the capacity to impel it.
Or let that [agency] belong to karma alone; what is the use of a karma that impels karma?
The ordinary person [is subject] to the power of karma.
Let it be granted that [the soul] possesses the capacity to produce effects through the impulsion of karma.

Now, if that [soul] were insentient, it would certainly engage in action toward its effect only when impelled by something else, like an axe or similar tools. How then could its presiding agent—knowledge and so forth—be sentient? If you argue that it must be sentient like ourselves, this is incorrect; for it has already been refuted by the argument concerning the collection [of atoms]. Furthermore, if there is a difference between us and that [presiding agent], then it does not possess sentience.

If it is argued that consciousness arises from the inherence of knowledge [in the Self], we say no; for that [inherence] has been refuted, and since [the Self] exists as omnipresent, there is no distinction [between one part of it and another], so where would knowledge reside? If it is claimed that even though the relation is non-distinct, a specific relation is nevertheless accepted [for the Self alone], from what does this follow? If you say "by its own nature," then from what does that nature arise? If you say "because it is observed to be so," then this is logical only if knowledge were observed in Īśvara alone, to the exclusion of space and other things.
If you argue that "He alone sees," this must be accepted only after drinking from the vessel of the ordeal (*kośapāna*).

By this, the Yoginīs are considered to be [established] by their very nature; what, then, is the use of *samavāya* (inherence) for the restriction of relations? Even the cognition "here" will arise from that very [nature];
therefore, there is no other conscious being who could be its presiding controller.
If there were no difference between knowledge and its possessor, then even in other cases the absolute distinction between quality and the qualified would collapse.

Consequently, since a non-omniscient being whose nature consists of non-eternal knowledge and so forth possesses the status of being an effect, by that same analogy it would follow that the Lord (*īśvara*) is also an effect; thus, he too would have another intelligent creator, and from that, his supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*) would be untenable. This is the argument regarding action (*karma*).
Primal matter, atoms, and karma function only when presided over by an intelligent cause prior to their initial activity, because they are insentient, like an axe or similar tools—[Nyāyavārttika, p.
[This concerns] God.
If it is stated by way of an example that which is unestablished,
[it is so] because of sentience or because of knowledge,
due to the refutation of inherence.
If it is argued that knowledge is the very nature of the Lord, this being said enters the intellect only through the drinking of wine.
From the very nature of karma,
as illustrated by the example of ourselves and others.

Furthermore, regarding the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*): if there is the absolute rule that everything insentient (*acetana*) proceeds toward action only when presided over by a sentient being (*cetana*), then for whatever [effect] belongs to a particular [agent], that very agent is its presider; thus, the postulation of a Lord (*īśvara*) is redundant, for his presiding power does not consist in anything other than his mere presence (*sannidhāna*) therein.
If it is argued that [the Self] possesses the quality of being an impeller (*prerakatva*), let that also belong to another [the Lord];

for even in the absence of knowledge of that [other], how could this be? This is not a valid answer, because it has already been answered by the observation that even in a sleeping person who lacks such knowledge, there is the movement of his own limbs and body parts; thus, it would follow for the Lord as well.

If this objection is raised— that even for someone like us, there must be an impeller, and furthermore, how can one who is bodiless prior to the connection with a body be its controller?— the author says "The application of the soul," etc., showing that this is equally applicable to the Lord as well.
The desire of the omnipresent Lord is inferred from the bodies, organs, and so forth, which serve as the instruments for the experience of living beings;

for how could a being who is about to arise—being currently devoid of a body and organs and thus experiencing no connection with them—possess the capacity to produce that which is fit for the soul's enjoyment? Therefore, it cannot be maintained that the production of the [body] occurs once it has already been acquired.

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that God (*īśvara*) is the cause. But how could it be possible for Him, who is devoid of body and organs, to create by His mere will a body and other instruments suitable for the experience of a living being (*jīva*)? [The answer is: Because of the specific nature of that production (*tadutpatti-viśeṣāt*). Furthermore, even if one accepts His transformation (*pariṇāma*), since He remains as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), and because activity and so forth are possible only for that which undergoes transformation, how could the defects characterized by instigation (*pravartanā-lakṣaṇā doṣāḥ*)—which are the causes of His birth—not exist? For this very reason, the connection with karma is logically established.

Having observed that some things produced by volition are suitable for experience, why would the agency of a body and instruments not necessarily follow in every case of conceptualization? And thus, there would be an infinite regress.
Furthermore, when there is a deviation from what is observed, it is more reasonable to postulate the capacity of its own karma.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (also) and, being a separate syntactical construction, should be understood as following immediately after the word "īśvarasya" (of God).
Not only for another who is non-Īśvara, but even for the Īśvara himself— of what nature? Of the bodiless (vitanoḥ)—
what is inferred?

By what [means]? He says: "by the body, the instruments, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the worlds and other such things are included. Through the metaphorical attribution of identity (abhedopacāra), the properties residing in those [worlds], such as being an effect (kāryatva) and so on, are called the "body, instruments, etc. By what kind [of means]? He says: "by their connection with the application of the individual soul" (jīvāpāyogayogaiḥ). Here, "individual souls other than the Lord" (anyajīvāḥ) are understood, because of the mention of "that Lord" (tasya īśvarasya). Their "application" (upayoga) is the activity of producing them; "suitable for that" (tatra yogyaiḥ) means that just as they can be produced by the Lord, so too can they be produced by others. What is inferred of him? He says: "the will," that is, the desire to create (sisṛkṣā).
Of what nature is it? He says: "Its cause"—meaning the cause of the causes of the body, the instruments, and so forth.
Just as that [unseen] cause is inferred for another who is bodiless, so too it is for Īśvara; such is the sense.
Alternatively, the word *ca* (and/but) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*): what else could be inferred except for Īśvara?
Regarding the question "Who?", the response "The cause, etc. is written again redundantly.
If it is argued that just as the Lord possesses the capacity for that creation, another does not, this would be correct only if such were observed to be the case.
For there is nothing that is impossible when it is observed.

If it is argued, "What need is there for anything else, since everything is produced by God?"—this too would be reasonable if it were established from some other source; however, since God himself is inferred from the observation of effects such as bodies and so forth, and since those effects are of various kinds, they lead one to infer a corresponding agent of the self, just as in the case of jars, cloth, cities, gardens, and the like.

Now, by whom is it said that "one [agent] is inferred because the instrument of one [agent] is observed"? Let it be so inferred, provided there were a correspondence of that knowledge with the effect; but this is not the case. Regarding the word *śabda* (sound), another [opponent] says here: "The entire world is a single composite whole (*avayavin*); even though its construction might involve many agents like a palace, there must be a single agent, equal to a master builder (*sūtradhāra*), who knows the entire collection of causal factors. That too is incorrect; because even for a single object, such as a body or the like, multiple master builders may be involved in the production of the effect part by part.
In order to explain the verse beginning with "of that which has no body as its cause," [the author] first introduces the passage beginning with "body and sense organs.
The meaning is that the transmigrating being experiences the connection with the body and so forth by itself—that is, by its own self—and not by means of a Lord or other external agent.
Of what kind of being? He says: "of one whose body and organs are not yet perfected. How so? Not in any way whatsoever, because the capacity to produce what is fit or unfit belongs only to the Self.
"Why? he asks, and says: "Because of the grasping of that," and so forth.

[The opponent argues: "It is not the procreator who possesses the capacity to produce that [offspring], but rather the parents who possess qualities contrary to that [procreator]. To this, he replies: "Because of the completed [act]," and so forth, due to their engagement in sexual intercourse.

And that very [action] is not the exclusion there, because it would follow that offspring would be produced at every act of sexual intercourse; such is the sense. If it is argued that "the exclusion there is due to karma," and so forth, then the production of the body, senses, and so on would not be possible;
for why and by whom would that [production] be possible? To this he says: "By the method of elimination (pāriśeṣyāt)," and so forth.

When that which is possible has been negated, the establishment of the remaining alternative is *pāriśeṣya* (the method of elimination). Therefore, God is the cause. For instance: the body, which is an effect, is invariably concomitant with a cause; and since, by the aforementioned reasoning, no other cause for it exists, God alone remains by way of elimination—thus say the Vaiśeṣikas and others who are [allegedly] refuters of reality.
He states the refutation of that [position]: "of one who lacks body and organs," and so forth.
The connection is made by changing the case ending to "of the Lord (īśvara) who lacks body and organs.
Furthermore, the word "punar" (again/furthermore) is used in the sense of deliberation (vitarka).

How could the production of a body and so forth by means of desire—that is, by will—be possible? To this he says: "The experience of the living being," and so on. Otherwise, if [the body] were produced spontaneously by itself, its production through desire might be conceivable; but from where is such a desire of his known? From where is that of God known? From the accomplishment of the effect; this is the same in other cases as well.

Nor can it be answered by asking why the world is not produced at will after its birth; for since the production of all effects is governed solely by the will of God, there is no evidence for such a thing, and thus no obstacle could be conceived even if the world were produced directly from Him. Consequently, that [will] would not arise again with respect to that [world].
"His works," such as the *Tattvadūṣaka* and others, were written again;
they consist of the form of instruments for [constructing] the body and so forth.

It might be thought: "There is no one's desire to bring about the soul's connection with a body and so forth; or, if such a desire exists, why is it not remembered by everyone now? This is not sound, because even if that object [the desire] were not remembered, its non-remembrance would not preclude [its existence]. Furthermore, the capacity [to produce the effect] remains doubtful in both cases. With this in mind, he says "tad" and so forth:
"And that very [desire], because there is no distinction in its production, belongs to God."

If it is argued that for this very reason of distinction, it is better that [the world] was created by Īśvara, since dharma is established through his worship; to this he says: "And it is prohibited," and so forth.
Regarding the word "arises" (*utpadyate*), which refers to origination (*utpatti*):

surely my purpose is merely to establish an intelligent cause. Let that cause be Īśvara, or another, or even just a transformative (*pariṇāmī*) one. To this he says: "The inherent cause (*samavāyin*)," and so forth.

Even if one were to admit that this Lord or another undergoes transformation—the word "even" (api) indicating an alternative position—why would such an admission be made? To this he says: "Because [it is] the inherent cause," and so forth. That is to say, because the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*), as well as "subsisting while acting" (*sthitvāpravṛtti*)—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including the status of being an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇatva*) and the rest—is possible only for that which is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).
Regarding that, the refutation begins with "pravartanā" and so forth:

how could the defects characterized by incitement, such as passion (*rāga*) and the rest, not exist? [The question] "How so? is answered as follows: "They are the causes of its birth. That is to say, they are the causes of that "birth," which is characterized by connection to a body, sense organs, and so forth; the meaning is that for him too, there would be *saṃsāra*, just like other living beings.

If it is asked, "What is the proof for the existence of that defect? [the author] says here: "Those things whose characteristic or mark is *pravarttanā*—that is, the impelling of living beings who are engaged in activity—are so described. For instance, he who joins a person to an action that is most desired is called 'passion' (*rāga*) and so forth, just as a magnet [draws iron]; and since the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*) likewise joins [beings to their actions], his impelling them is not contradictory even in the absence of passion and the like; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this, the reply will follow in the words beginning with "because of the creation of the body and so forth" (*tanv-ādi-karaṇāt*).

Even though he possesses them, passion and the like are not the cause of his connection with karma because he is a specific deity, just as the poison of a peacock is not a cause for intoxication; therefore, since the occurrence of a connection with karma would follow from the mere existence of these defects, why would they not be the causes of that birth? Otherwise, one might think that for Īśvara, there would be a state of connection with those [defects] for everyone as well.
Due to the absence of defects, there would be an absence of connection with karma;
thus, first of all, his state of being a transmigrator is demonstrated by his own reasoning.
Now, demonstrating this through another argument, he says: "created by a conscious being," and so forth.

Something such as well-prepared soup and the like may be created by a conscious being, but not everything is so, because—as has been established for the opponent by the passage beginning with *bhūtā bhavyāḥ* (Siddhiviniścaya 3.8)—there is a lack of valid proof [for such a claim].
Of what nature is it? He says: "suitable for enjoyment," meaning that which is fit to be enjoyed by living beings.

Having done what? He says: "having thoroughly observed" (saṃprekṣya), meaning having seen; the connection is that [this applies] to the state of being created by a conscious agent when the conceptualization of suitability for enjoyment is applied everywhere, to everything.

And so is the formal argument of another: the kingdom and so forth are fashioned by some conscious being, such as a king or a lord, and are then enjoyed, because they are objects of enjoyment, just like soup and other such things.

Regarding the question, "Who is this Maheśvara who possesses a body? the refutation is as follows: [If he were] one whose activity involves a body and organs, would it not follow that he must possess a body and organs? And in this case too, the same argument applies, and the example is indeed a cook. Thus, his own body and so forth would be enjoyed by another, and that other by yet another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); such is the sense.
Or, if it is held that he is without a body or organs, or that he enjoys a body and so forth provided by another; [we reply]: no. To this, he says: "Perceived," and so forth.

The production of soup and the like suitable for another’s enjoyment, or the giving [of such food] to a cook and the like who possess a body and sense organs, or [the act of eating] by one born [already] provided with them—when these are observed, what action [could there be] in the absence of those? When [such actions] are being performed, it is logical to postulate that capacity of the enjoyer's own karma which consists in the capacity to produce the instruments (bodies and organs) suitable for the enjoyer's enjoyment;
for just as such capacity is not seen in an insentient thing unguided by a conscious agent, so too it is not seen in a sentient being who lacks a body and organs.
The point is that this same logic applies equally elsewhere as well.
The Supreme Self is the Lord of the Lord.

[Objection: "The capacity for the instruments [of action] to be fit for enjoyment is indeed observed only in a living being who possesses a body and instruments, and not in one who is devoid of body and instruments; for when moving into those [instruments], there is an absence of another body and instruments. Therefore, that [capacity] must be seen as a deviation from the rule. [Reply: It is said: Even for one in states such as deep sleep, though lacking consciousness, there is no deviation from the rule.
For in that state, consciousness is not admitted by the opponent, on account of which the person (*puruṣa*) would then be conscious.

At other times, even if it exists, it is useless because of the acceptance of the Jaina doctrine; therefore, since its existence [is asserted] only through that very acceptance, the *kārmaṇa* body, which is another body, would be established as the cause of its movement for everyone. Now, if God is the cause of its movement while it is in that state, then this fault does not arise. In that case, He alone—possessing a body, organs, and vital breath—is the cause of its movement; for a lack of body and organs is never observed to be a cause of movement, so how could there be a mover of that which is insentient? This is because such is never observed, even in the case of one who possesses a body and organs.
Therefore, no one at all undergoes that transition into another body in the next world while being devoid of the body and other constituents belonging to the previous existence.
Even when one is in states such as sleep, according to the Buddhist [view], it exists.

Since the self migrates from this world to another body in the next world, regarding this migration to another body, the opponent objects: "The defects that cause birth do not belong to the Lord, yet even one devoid of them is the cause of saṃsāra. To this, he replies: "Because of its true nature," and so forth.

Why would an intelligent person otherwise join beings with the afflictions of existence by creating bodies and so forth for one who is free from defects or devoid of a body and such, and who does not himself commit any act of malice? (14)
This [restraint] should not be applied by an intelligent person toward those who do no harm; for this was stated elsewhere by the gods:
"Because of the production of the body and so forth... (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Book II, p. 231).

Or, for living beings who possess karma, the cause of their bodies and so forth is the activity [of action] impelled by the will of God; [but] can there be such activity within a living being without God?

(15) For God necessarily requires karma as its own impeller even for liberated souls (*muktātman*), who do not experience the suffering of bodies, organs, and so forth; since He merely brings that [karma] into proximity through His will, He could thereby produce the body and so on—what need is there for the will of God? It would be better [to say] that God alone [is the cause].

And because he is the creator of those [beings] and so forth, for what reason—why, from what cause—would the Lord (*īśvara*) join living beings (*prāṇin*), who themselves commit no harm or offense, with the afflictions of existence (*bhava-kleśa*), that is, with the suffering of *saṃsāra*? For he is called "wise" (*buddhimān*) because his wisdom is invariably present in every soul, as stated in such passages as: "He is perceived by creatures through a faultless intellect that encompasses all objects," and so on.

Now, [the opponent might argue that] he joins even those who have committed no offense with those [sufferings]; for in that case, the meaning of the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) would be that he joins even those who have committed an offense in a different way, which would result in the impossibility of his acting with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakāritā*).

If it is argued that he joins them with those [sufferings] for the sake of the continuation of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), thinking that if he did not join them with those [sufferings], there would be an absence of cyclic existence; to this, he says: "The affliction of existence," and so forth.
The sense is that [the Lord] is not such a foresighted agent whose cause is the affliction of existence.
The Lord of beings is the Lord.

If, however, it is thought: "The Lord does not himself join beings who have committed no offense with the miseries of saṃsāra; rather, such actions have been performed by the beings themselves, and being impelled by them, He is unable to remain indifferent in joining them [to those results]"; to that he says: "Or [it would be] of those possessing karma," and so forth.
What would be the cause for the activity of beings who possess karma—indeed, not of those without karma—in the actions of the body and so forth? Activity [would be impossible].

Of what? [It is] of the will of God (īśvarecchā). Here, the objection is considered to be: "Because these [beings] lack the karma that impels them. To this, the refutation begins with the words "residing in living beings" (*prāṇistham*) and so forth.

The connection is as follows: why is that which resides in living beings—the cause of the body and so on—not [produced] without God? That is to say, without God (*īśvaram antareṇa*), [it would follow that it arises] for those who possess karma.
He thinks as follows: "By whatever proximity (*pratyāsatti*) actions impel the Lord, by that same [proximity] they impel the body and so forth. (This has been written again).

Now, if it is argued: "The previous position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) was established that the activity of the Lord’s will is the cause of the body and so forth, whereas the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) speaks instead of the Lord himself; and a refutation must follow the previous position"—we reply: No. Because of the principle "that which belongs to what belongs to something" (*tadāsthātātsthyāt*), the word for that [will] is used [for the Lord]. Thus, the Lord acts through the will, and by means of that [will], the effect is accomplished; therefore, there is no fault.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Of the liberated selves," and so forth.

For the liberated selves, from where could there be the production of suffering such as that of the body or the sense organs? Because they are devoid of karma; the meaning is that [the organs] produce [effects] only for those who possess karma.
The word "there" (*tatra*) is to be supplied, meaning "in that [state of having karma]."

What follows from this? He says: "By itself," and so forth. [The opponent argues that] God necessarily requires an impeller for himself, or else, by the very power of karma, a conscious being is necessarily [impelled] in such a manner.

Since, by that very power—that is, by the mere will of the Lord alone—it brings [the material] into proximity, why should the insentient body and so forth not be produced from that very majesty? Without the will of the Lord? He states another objection: "That is better," and so on.
Now, if it is argued that he is not impelled by anyone for that purpose, but rather acts out of sport (*krīḍā*); to this he says: "Even for liberated souls," and so on. [This refers to] the Lord.
Even though his self is liberated, he may act through a body and so forth for the sake of sport; otherwise, how could an intelligent being join living beings together by the power of destiny?
If...

Not only for those with karma, but even for the liberated self (*muktātman*) who is without action, there may be the performance [of acts] while sporting with the body and so forth; it is not otherwise. If it is argued that a king, by inflicting punishment such as execution or imprisonment upon one who has committed an offense, is called "sporting" (*krīḍana*), yet this would not be considered sport for the liberated self when performing such acts—[we reply: what is the nature of sporting?
If it is argued that he creates even that [the body] by means of her (Buddhi), to this he says: "Is the Intelligent One not indeed a player?"—this is the connection. Furthermore, regarding play:

if Maheśvara, being a player, fashions bodies and so forth for embodied beings, then he would join even those who perform auspicious deeds with hell and the like, and even those who perform inauspicious deeds with heaven and the like; thus, their worship and so forth would be useless. He states this very point in the words beginning with "yojayet" (he would join).

The connection is made by changing the case ending [from *yojyate*] to *yojayet*, as in "he would join living beings with bodies and so forth. Why? He says: "By the power of destiny (*bhavitavyatāvaśāt*), and not by the power of auspicious or inauspicious karma. How so? The meaning is: "He would not join them through a mere confusion [of results]. Clarifying the meaning of the verse, he says: "If," and so forth.
The meaning of all this has been understood:
by means of this, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that [Self] in producing the body and so forth has been considered to be like the sun, which is the cause for the blooming of lotuses;
for otherwise, it would entail the fallacy of imagining such an intrinsic nature to belong either to karma or to the transmigrating living being (*jīva*).

Indeed, the constituent parts that originate the body and so forth of the Lord Sūrya must be dependent upon an intelligent being, because they possess their own causal activity, just like threads and the like.

Likewise, if it is argued that bodies and so forth have an intelligent cause because they possess a specific arrangement of their own constituent parts, because they are derived from non-conscious material causes, and because they are effects—just like a cloth and the like—the [author] replies here: "The four great elements, having existed [first], then proceed to act... [they are] preceded by an intelligent being, because they are effects... because they possess parts (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
54; Praśastapādavyākhyā, p. 301).
"According to the Vaiśeṣika Upaskāra, page 62:
'That which arises independently of a body is preceded by an intelligent agent, because it possesses a cause...'—Praśastapādabhāṣya with Kiraṇāvalī, page 97; Nyāyalīlāvatī, page 20."
*Nyāyamuktāvalī*, p. 23:

The manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, which serves as the cause of pleasure, pain, and the like, is presided over by an intelligent cause, because it possesses form and other qualities, just like a chariot and such.

Likewise, merit and demerit, being instruments, bring about the experience of the person while being presided over by an intelligent cause, because they are instruments, just like an axe and the like.

The great elements, ending with air, proceed in their respective functions such as supporting and so forth, being presided over by an intelligent cause because they are insentient—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 457–67.

The subjects under dispute, such as atoms, trees, mountains, and so forth, have as their agent a maker who is cognizant of their material causes, because they possess the quality of having an origin, or because they have insentient things as their material causes.
As in the case of a palace and so forth—*Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 597;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 194.

The omniscient and immutable [Lord] is to be established by means of the design of effects, maintenance, and so forth; from the word, from cognition, from scripture, from the sentence, and from a specific number.
— *Nyāyakusumāñjali* 5.1.103.

In that regard, Āviddhakarṇa sets forth two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the Lord (*īśvara*), stating: "That which possesses a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts," and so forth.
That which possesses a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts...
Whatever is understood through an intelligent cause, such as a jar and the like,
whether it is perceptible by two sense organs or imperceptible— such a subject of dispute is preceded by an intelligent agent; by this dissimilarity (vaidharmya), atoms are considered [not to be so].
The taking up of threads and so forth is presided over by an intelligent agent, because they possess color and other qualities;
just as observed threads and the like, being possessed of color and other qualities, produce their own effects— Tattvasaṃgraha, verses 47–49.
If persistence, directed activity, specific structural arrangement, purposeful efficacy, and so forth were possible through other means alone, then they would not have the Lord as their cause.

(17) Furthermore, neither "persistence and activity" nor "the capacity for purposeful action" can serve as a reason for the fact that bodies, sense organs, and the like have an intelligent cause, because these reasons are inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).

Since eternal entities such as the self (*ātman*) are themselves accepted [as existent], the fact that they possess a configuration of constituent parts that initiates them would be a reason for their being preceded by an intelligent cause, just like a jar or similar objects which possess bodies and instruments;
indeed, the mere fact of being preceded by an intelligent cause is precisely what others (the opponents) desire to establish.
Regarding the phrase "because of the lack of a body" (*vitanukṛteḥ*):

if it is asked, "But why is this proof for establishing God (Īśvara) refuted again, when it was already refuted previously by the passage beginning with 'by means of those suitable for the use of a living being' (*jīvopayogayogyaiḥ*)?"—the answer is: No; there is a distinction. Previously, the capacity of another [being] to produce a body and other instruments was denied; now, the proof for that [capacity] itself is being refuted. This is the division.

Activity (pravṛtti) after abiding, operation (vyāpāra) after ceasing from an action, specific configuration (saṃsthānaviśeṣa)—which is a particular arrangement of the constituent parts that originate it—and causal efficiency (arthakriyā), as well as those things beginning with being an effect (kāryatva) and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) including such properties as being produced—these would be established in a manner entirely different [from what they actually are], namely, in a way that excludes God; therefore, they are contradictory [to the existence of a bodiless creator]. (Page 477) [This refers to] one who is devoid of a body.

[Objection: Surely a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) is that which exists only in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); however, this [reason] exists even in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar, and thus would be "inconclusive" (*vyabhicārī*).

Or, if it is called "contradictory" because it exists in the "transforming" (*pariṇāmin*), which is opposed to an eternal God, then how can it be contradictory when proving that very [God]? [If you say: "Because it contradicts the proposition (*pratijñā*) of eternity," [we reply: No; for even for you, in proving that the world is indeed uncreated (*akṛtrima*), there is a contradiction [with the proposition].
Furthermore, that proposition does not belong to the Sāṅkhya proponents who maintain the existence of God.

If it is argued that the Lord alone is indeed uncaused—[as stated in] Mūlāgama Gāthā 712—and that if He were subject to transformation, He would be an effect and thus preceded by another Lord, leading to an infinite regress; otherwise, the reason [for His existence] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—then let this very fault be accepted, what is the use of anything else? No; for there is another way of explaining it.

The particle *eva* has the sense of "even" (*api*) because it is a grammatical indeclinable (*nipāta*). Therefore, the meaning is: "Even otherwise [if they were produced] by something else, they would still not have God as their cause.
Alternatively, there will be the following commentary: "Neither the body nor the instruments," and so forth.

Or rather, regarding one who says, "The eternal, bodiless Maheśvara is the cause of the body and so forth"—in relation to that person, the particle *eva* is used for restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
