Otherwise, the very existence of things would not be possible; therefore, [the world] does not have God as its cause, because [such a claim] is contradictory.
If the inclusion of the term "Īśvara" (God) were thus purposeless, otherwise he would have used the term "intelligent agent" (*buddhimad*);
here, the commentary begins with "his own constituent parts," etc., regarding Īśvara.
Explaining the verse, he says: "The state of being composed of a body and sense organs," and so forth.
Why is "abiding" or "functional activity"—that is, the capacity for causal efficiency—not the probans? Because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
From where does this [follow]? He says: "In eternal things," and so forth.

Because [the existence of] persistence and causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is accepted by the proponent of God (*īśvaravādin*) himself as being through the self (*ātman*), he demonstrates by the mention of "eternal" that there is an absence of an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇa*) therein; and by the mention of "self," he shows the absence of non-conscious superintendence (*adhiṣṭhita*) over its own effects, otherwise there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
The reason [for its being a body] would be "being the cause of the arrangement of its own constituent parts"; this term "reason" (hetu) is understood from the context.
To the question "Of what? he says: "of the mind-body complex (mātṛtanu-karaṇa).
To the question "Like what? he says: "like a jar and so forth."
By this, it is stated that [the reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of the desired probandum;
by this, [the status of] "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth has been examined,
as has the case of an eternal Lord (*īśvara*) being presided over by another conscious being.

If that is so, how can there be a fault for one who maintains that God is the cause [of the world] while possessing a body and having non-eternal knowledge? To this he says: "Of others," and so forth.
Is this merely desired by the Jains? He says: "The mere fact that bodies, organs, worlds, and so forth, are preceded by an intelligent cause"—this is the connection.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate all the previous objections.

He thinks as follows: If the instruments of the Lord—namely his knowledge, body, organs, worlds, and so forth—arise from his own karma, then they must arise from that very same source for another being as well; what, then, is the use of a Lord? If it is argued that [the world arises] from that which is presided over by him, this too has not been established by him.
If it is argued that [it arises] from the Lord himself, that contradicts [the premise] and constitutes a doctrine of no-karma (*akarmavāda*).
The claim that the omniscient Lord possesses knowledge of all instruments and so forth has been refuted in the *Pramāṇasaṃgrahabhāṣya*,
as has [the claim regarding] the action of the Lord and that of other people.
Furthermore, if in the act of creating his own body and so forth he were to depend upon whatever else is supreme, then he would be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) just like others.

If, on the other hand, he does not depend [on anything], then what is the point of depending [on anything] even when creating another's body and so forth? Even one who is himself bodiless produces a body and such for himself, but not for another; this is indeed a great exercise of foresight! Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In the act of creating a bodiless [body]," etc., and concludes with: "Therefore," etc.
Now, demonstrating the contradiction with his own words of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda— who both assert that God is the sovereign cause of the body and so forth— the author says "saṃsāra" and so on,
stating that [liberation] consists in liberation through the destruction of the experience of worldly pleasure.
If God were the cause of the body and so forth, the scripture would be contradicted.

The author of the Sūtras stated that the attainment of the supreme human goal, which is the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), results from the knowledge of the reality of the self and other principles; he thus indicates that there is indeed a cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), since the body and so forth have God as their cause.

Since these two are mutually contradictory, how can the author of the Sūtra be considered intelligent? What discerning person would compose a treatise concerning that which is understood to be liberation and yet characterized by insentience, on the grounds that God is not intelligent? That is not so, because no other [cause] is possible. He is called "the Lord" (īśvara) because He is the master of the entire aggregate of effects, beginning with the body; if He is eternal and all-pervading, then the statement of Kaṇāda and others in their Śāstra is contradicted and sublated. Doing what? He says: "speaking," that is, declaring.

What is this? He says: "From liberation, how [can there be] liberation?"—this is the meaning. Why? He says: "Because of the cessation of the experience of worldly pleasure (*saṃsārasukhasaṃvitti*). *Saṃsāra* is the continuous succession of birth, death, and so forth. The mention of "pleasure" (*sukha*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes pain and the rest. *Saṃvitti* is cognition (*buddhi*). Since it would follow that those who perceive pain and so forth are also included in the term "cognition," their separate mention is intended to demonstrate that [liberation] is not appropriate for them. [Liberation occurs] through the cessation of those [experiences].

This is what is meant: when the Lord (*īśvara*), who is of a single nature, eternal, and all-pervading, is the cause of all things that arise, then everything would always belong to everyone without distinction, such as bodies and so forth; thus, there can be no liberation through the destruction of those [bodies]. This has been stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*: "The term 'distinct cognition' (*pṛthaksaṃvitti*) is employed."
"How can there be a cessation of their effect when the cause of the experiences of worldly pleasure has not perished? (Nyāyaviniścaya 1.103).
Thus, how is there a cessation of the effect?—Nyāyaviniścaya.

If it is argued that since an eternal entity cannot exist, whatever dependence there is for a particular excellence must have that [non-eternal cause] as its cause, and therefore how could such a cause be untenable? [We reply: For one who desires liberation and the entry into the city of Nirvāṇa from the city of Saṃsāra, God (Īśvara) must not be accepted as the cause of that [liberation], just as Primordial Matter (Prakṛti) and the like are not.

The meaning is that liberation would occur even while in the state of transmigratory existence, because the efficient cause is present; and if it is explained in this way— that the Lord is the cause [of bondage] with respect to the body and so forth— then [liberation would likewise follow].
What was he doing? What was he saying? What kind of scripture was it? To this he says: "called liberation," meaning that in which liberation is present.
Why is this so? To this he says: "in saṃsāra," and so forth.
In that case, there is a contradiction due to mutual inconsistency, and the [opponent's] position is refuted as follows:

while always maintaining that the self is the agent of the body and so forth, one who desires liberation speaks a scripture that teaches liberation, yet that very scripture declares the absence of such agency; this is the contradiction.

Now, if it is argued that that scripture was not composed by him because it originated from another source—that not everything is created by God—then that is incorrect, because [the opponent's own position] would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Or rather, [the author] addresses the objection raised by others—that the author of the treatise might be under the sway of *karman*—or as it has been said: "How can one who is subject to *karman* surpass other transmigrating beings or even his own self? Suspecting that this is an argument for his intelligence (*buddhimattva*) based on another's perspective, he refutes it by saying "In saṃsāra," and so forth.
The phrase "If God were perceived as the cause of the body and so forth" is to be supplied [to the text].

Having done what is He their cause? To this he says: "Due to the cessation of the experience of worldly pleasure. This means by relying on that cessation—that is, by relying on the experiences of pure bliss. And the mention of "worldly existence" (*saṃsāra*) is for this very purpose; otherwise, he would have simply mentioned "the experience of pleasure. Doing what, and relying on what, is He perceived as their cause? To this he says: "Speaking the scripture whose essence is liberation. The mention of "liberation" is intended to indicate all the other principles known through it.
Here the refutation is being set aside, namely: "The Lord [is the cause].
For instance—if pure bliss and consciousness are intended as the Lord, then that very same [nature] must be attributed to others as well, and not the body and so forth;
if, on the other hand, it were not the body and such, then he would likewise produce those very selves.

Now, since the auxiliary causes of an action exist elsewhere, one might argue that the action should be performed right there and not upon the self, because the opposite is the case [for the self]. However, the action must also be enjoined upon the self as something desired; otherwise, if it were not its cause at that time even in another locus, how could there be any non-deviation among causes? Alternatively, this should be explained as: "the scripture is contradicted by a means of valid cognition. Regarding this, the commentary will proceed with the words, "what discerning person," and so forth.
Regarding the view that for other living beings, karma is not the cause but rather God is the cause.
In order to explain the verse concerning "being an effect" and so forth, he says: "The author of the Sūtras," etc.
The author of the Sūtras refers to Akṣapāda and others; he states the supreme human goal.
What? The attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), which is the acquisition of *nirvāṇa* characterized by the complete destruction of all specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*).
From what? He says: from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) regarding the self (*ātman*) and so forth, not from God (*īśvara*); otherwise, that [worship of God] would be futile.
By this, he demonstrates that while God exerts himself to produce the knowledge of reality, one might as well simply grant liberation.
That very author of the Sūtra indicates that saṃsāra is surpassed by liberation (mukti);
why? He says: "The body and so forth are caused by the Lord"—the word "iti" should be understood here—and thus he speaks because of this.
Concluding [the argument], he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Since this is the case, for that reason, how could the intelligence of the *Sūtrakāra* be postulated given the mutual contradiction between these two statements of the *Sūtrakāra*?
Or alternatively, if the *Sūtrakāra* were Maheśvara, because everything is preceded by him, the other [statement] would be as before.
However, this is the distinction: how can the possession of intelligence be attributed to Īśvara?
Alternatively, one may explain by splitting the sentence as "the body and so forth indicate [the existence of] the one whose nature is Akṣapāda," or there is also the reading:
"Īśvara is the cause of the body and so forth."

In that case as well, there would be such a split in the sentence; how then could the intelligence of these two—the author of the *Īśvara-sūtra* and the author of the [other] *Sūtra*—be postulated? He raises an objection to refute [the opponent's view], asking: "What discerning person, perceiving supersensuous objects—an epithet for liberation and by extension for the entirety of the principles beginning with the self—[would accept this]?"

Of what nature is it? It is perceived as *acaityanya*, which is the state of being devoid of consciousness (*cetanārahitatva*). Would anyone compose a treatise concerning that [state]? No, because the Sugata and others do not speak of things unrelated [to their own experience], and because for Kaṇāda and others, the desired goal is accomplished through such instruction. Regarding the objection—"Is there no intelligent being (*buddhimān*) who has realized that [state]?"—or "Why is there no intelligent being?", he states the refutation here with the words "No" (*na*), and so forth.

As for what was said—that [liberation] does not occur from that [source]—why? Because they maintain that another mode of liberation is possible, as follows: just as for the Lord, who possesses the nature of infinite knowledge, when karma—which obstructs that [knowledge]—is removed, there is omniscience and never a lack of consciousness; so too for another, this very same distinction would apply: for one, the removal of that [obstruction] is innate, while for another, it results from a means. Therefore, some strive toward liberation by other means.
Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impressions are the specific qualities;
[if these were eternal], knowledge of reality would be useless, because [the world] would have been preceded by Maheśvara.
This must be explained solely through the instruction of the Lord;
demonstrating this very point, he says: "The attainment of the Self," and so forth.

They know liberation to be the attainment of the self's own nature through the destruction of the internal impurities of the soul. As for the comparison: it is not insentient due to the destruction of qualities and so forth; it is not a void due to the destruction of the qualities and the possessor of qualities; nor is it a non-enjoyer due to the absence of objects of enjoyment—[as stated in] Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti, verse 76.
At that time, there is the abiding in its own essential nature for the person whose karma has been utterly exhausted.
It is neither non-existence, nor is it insentience, nor is sentience purposeless—*Tattvānuśāsana*, verse 234:
"Neither non-existence, nor insentience, nor is sentience purposeless. (19)

Indeed, we do not maintain that *nirvāṇa* is a non-existent entity devoid of self, lacking all qualities, or that it possesses a self while being devoid of both the seen and the seeing—like some other distinct substance.
What then? It is the soul’s attainment of its own nature through the destruction of impurities, like a gem;
otherwise, effort would be in vain.

This being the case, God is not the intelligent one, because liberation is defined as the total absence of all qualities; nor is Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and the like, because they engage in discourse for that purpose. Since their assertions are mutually contradictory, they are comparable to the Buddha.
Therefore, O seekers of liberation, uproot the view of a self (*sattvadṛṣṭi*), which has its seeds in a beginningless continuum of similar types.
— Pramāṇavārttika 2.256.

In that regard, because the entire multitude of afflictions, such as ignorance and passion, has been abandoned without remainder, it is considered *nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
In this context, "substratum" (*upadhi*) refers to that in which self-attachment is deposited;
by the word "substratum," the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), which are the causes for the conceptual designation of a self, are meant.
It is called a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) because it remains (*śiṣyate*).
It exists together with a remainder of the substratum (*upadhi*), thus it is "with-remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).

What is that nirvāṇa? It is simply the mere aggregates (*skandhamātra*) alone, devoid of the thieves of afflictions such as the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); it is like the state of a village remaining after the entire band of thieves has been slain—that is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

But where in nirvana there is not even a mere aggregate (skandha), that is nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), because the remainder of the substratum (upadhi) has departed from it; and with reference to that very state, it is said—by way of analogy with the destruction of a village when the entire band of thieves has been slain: ...
With a body not withdrawn, he dwelt within the sensations;
his mind was liberated like the extinguishing of a lamp—Mādhyama-āgama-vṛtti, pp. 519–20.
Liberation is the absolute cessation of the nine qualities of the self— Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 638—
as long as all the qualities of the self, such as latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, have not been destroyed.
Indeed, until then, the absolute cessation of suffering cannot be conceived;
for in that state, what kind of self remains? It is established solely in its own essential nature, abandoned by all qualities (guṇas).
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 508;
Praśastapādabhāṣya-kanda, p. 287;
Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī, p. 6.

Comparison: "Therefore, that perception of the object which arises from its conjunction with that [Purusha] is experience (bhoga); whereas the perception of the Seer's own nature is liberation (apavarga)" — Yogabhāṣya 2.23.
They know liberation (*mokṣa*) to be the soul’s attainment of its own nature, that is, the attainment of its innate nature consisting of infinite knowledge and so forth.

From what does this attainment arise? To this he says: "From the destruction of internal impurity. Internal impurity is the soul's alteration from its true nature; from its destruction, [liberation occurs].
By implication, this also states the destruction of material impurity (*dravyamala*), because in the absence of the latter, the former cannot exist.

They do not know the liberation of the soul (*jīva*) to be non-existence, because that [non-existence] lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatva*); nor do they know its lack of consciousness, that is, its being devoid of sentience.
What then do they know? They know liberation to be precisely this: therefore, consciousness is not purposeless or empty of an object to be grasped; they know it to be such for him.
In the absence of an obstruction to that which has the characteristic of illuminating both itself and others, there is rather the complete manifestation of that characteristic, not its non-existence;
for the sun does not abandon its nature of illuminating both itself and others when the veil of clouds dissolves, even though its substantial activity [of shining] may cease.
In the absence of internal impurity, form, and karmic matter,
there is [only] the soul of the soul.
Explaining the *Mokṣakārikā*, he says: "By no means at all is there a disciple who has attained nirvāṇa; what kind of state is it? It is merely the non-arising of the sun."
He states the distinction from the Vaiśeṣika conception of *nirvāṇa*: "And likewise, *nirvāṇa* is not without self.
What kind of state is it? It is the reality (*tattva*) consisting of consciousness and the rest, which is devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
He states the distinction of this [system] from the Sugata’s [Buddhist] view: "It is endowed with a self.
To the question, "Whose deficiency is that, if not [the Buddhists']? he says: "Like other substances.
A substance other than the living-substance (jīvadravya) is earth and so forth; that is the "other" (antara), and it is like that [living-substance].
Just as there is no total deficiency of qualities in earth and so forth due to the fear of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), so too for the living being (*jīva*);
by this, he states the absence of a supporting example for the other's [claim] regarding that deficiency: "In the same way, we do not teach Nirvāṇa."
"What is it like? he asks, and says "the visible," and so forth.
"Then what do you, sirs, say it is? he asks, and says "but rather," and so forth;
"but rather," however, we teach that Nirvāṇa is the attainment of the self for the living being whose nature is consciousness.
Why? He says: "Because of impurity," and so forth.
Whose [impurity]? He says: "Like a gem," and so forth.
Regarding the consequence of not accepting that, he says: "The state of being a fault otherwise," and so forth.

The sense is this: liberation for those seeking release would otherwise be a fruitless endeavor because it is impossible to destroy that which possesses intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and because there would be no purpose [for such destruction].
Thus, demonstrating what occurs for the Supreme Being when the soul attains liberation characterized by the acquisition of its true self (*ātma-lābha*), he says: "That being so," and so forth.

In that manner, if liberation—characterized by the soul’s attainment of its own nature—exists, then the Lord is not omniscient, because liberation is described as consisting of the total absence of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Nor is the creator, such as Brahmā and others, omniscient, since they act for that purpose [of liberation] based on scriptural injunctions.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "mutually," and so forth.

Abiding in one's own self consists in the soul’s lack of all qualities; if that were the case, it would result in the non-existence of that [selfhood]. Yet even that [non-existence] is contradictory to its abiding therein, because of the scriptural teaching of it.
He states the illustration: "We say 'like a Buddha' (buddhavat) because it functions in the same way as a Buddha," [this is] for the Vaiśeṣika.

Those purified by the vision [of the Guru] worship that which is auspicious, undecaying, free from disease, inexhaustible, and unassailable; which is devoid of sorrow, fear, and doubt; and which is the stainless, ultimate abundance of bliss and knowledge. — *Ratnakaṇikā*, verse 40.
In the *Sarvārthasiddhi*, on page 1,
the word "iva" is used in the sense of "like," as in the case of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, and others.
For the sake of liberation,
according to the word of the Lord, when there is a deficiency of all [other] qualities.
There would be an absence of abiding in one's own self,
which is the deficiency of all qualities due to not abiding in one's own self.
Showing that [the opponent's position] is contradictory and that the Buddha lacks intelligence, he says "tattvam" and so forth:
"That which is the reality (tattva) of things is emptiness; those [things] are without self (nirātman)."
How could nirvāṇa be distinguished [from this], and for what purpose should one practice austerity for its sake?

(20) Nirvāṇa, characterized by the non-rearising of the five aggregates, is established by its own nature; for what purpose would one perform austerity, since the continuum is unconditioned and non-existent?
Since the final moment of consciousness is non-substantial due to its lack of causal efficacy, the causal series leading up to it would likewise be non-existent.
Therefore, the defining characteristic of substantial continua is precisely the progression from cause to effect, as they consist of mutual conditions;

otherwise, how could the definition of "effect" and "cause"—namely, that when X exists, Y necessarily exists, and when there is a modification in X, there is a modification in Y—be established? Nor is there any other definition of mutual perception.

If, however, nirvāṇa is the attainment of a mind purified by the discernment of error through the cultivation of wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) alone, that too is not possible within false meditation, just as [it is not possible] for selflessness (*nairātmya*) to exist in those states such as desire, grief, fear, or madness.
To the question "To whom do these [states] belong?", he says: "Of the Selfless One"—meaning, of the Buddha who possesses a mind according to the Sautrāntika and other schools.

Those entities—such as form and the rest, the five aggregates, the mental continua devoid of external objects, or even total emptiness—their reality or intrinsic nature is empty and devoid of self-existence (*niḥsvabhāva*), because, according to the method already described, the establishment of such a reality is impossible. If that were the case, what would follow? He says: "What would saṃsāra be? and "Nirvāṇa [would be the same]"; that is to say, there would be no distinction between the two desired states.
He states another objection for that reason: "For that purpose..."
What? You practice austerity, and that person [practices it] as well;
the word "ca" (and) serves to include the opinion of those who hold such a view.
Showing the meaning of your verse, he says: "Five," and so forth;
thus, Nirvāṇa is established.
What is its nature? He says: it is characterized by the absence of rebirth.
Why? He says: because there is no rebirth in the absence of anything whatsoever, even by its own inherent force (svarasataḥ), without any cause; such is the meaning.

If it is argued that for the sake of which, for the cause of which Nirvāṇa, one performs asceticism—that [Nirvāṇa] is established by itself; to this he replies with the words "santāna" and so forth. Since a continuum (saṃtāna) does not exist—whether as distinct from or non-distinct from the members of the continuum (saṃtānin)—because it is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), therefore an effort for its cessation is as fruitless as [trying to remove] the redness of a *kiṃśuka* flower; such is the meaning.
Showing that for this reason as well effort is not for the sake of its destruction, he says: "The final," and so forth.

That mind which will never again have another mind of the same kind is the "final mind. Since it is incapable of performing any action (*akiñcitkaratva*)—that is, because it does not perform any purposeful activity (*anarthakriyākāritva*)—it is non-existent (*avastutva*). Given its non-existence, the causal series leading up to it is likewise non-existent in that same manner of being non-existent. Therefore, since there is no continuum to be destroyed, one performs ascetic penance for the sake of destroying the continuum.
If it is argued that there is no fault because there is no cognition of a different kind (*vijātīya*) by the yogi [to perceive such a final mind], he says here: "One's own," and so forth.

The meaning is that its own cause and fruit consist of its own material cause (*upādāna*) and its own effect (*upādeya*). To the question, "Of what things does activity proceed from these two? he says: "Of the continua of substances (*dravya-santāna*). Substances possess qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*); the very activity of those continua of substances is their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because it is observed to be so. Furthermore, that which is the defining characteristic of something cannot exist in the absence of that thing; just as knowledge would not exist in the absence of self-awareness (*svavedana*).

Therefore, just as the establishment of the cognition of that [object] follows from knowledge, so too the establishment of its activity follows from the substance (*dravya*); for the sake of demonstrating this once again, the term "substance" is employed.
Furthermore, their activity arises precisely from that [substance]; thus he says: "mutually," and so forth.

"Mutually" means one another; "condition" (*pratyaya*) means cause—this is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus. Because they have that very thing as their essence (*ātman*), that is, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their activity arises precisely from that reality (*tattva*).

He thinks as follows: Just as for a yogin or for anyone else, the final moment of consciousness (*acaramacitta*) serves as a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*), because otherwise its status as an object would be impossible; so too must it be for the final consciousness (*sacittasya*). Otherwise, although color might be a cooperative cause for taste, taste would not [be a cooperative cause] for that [color]. Thus, the principle that "even a single factor dependent on [the causal complex] flows forth" (from *Pravāha-vāda* 3.8, etc. holds true. If that were the case, what could prevent another effect from arising, even one of a different class, when the primary material cause (*upādāna-pratyaya*) and the cooperative causes (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) are present?
The meaning is that [it] is non-existent because it is devoid of the triad beginning with arising;
for it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
O monks, of the conditioned, arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and alteration of duration is also discerned."
And that which does not exist, such as the horn of a donkey, possesses no characteristic such as birth and so forth—from the *Madhyamakavṛtti*, p. 145.
From the moments.
For the purpose of the cessation of the continuum,
it is logical that there is simply the proceeding of the state of cause and effect.
The cause is the state of being the material cause (upādānakāraṇatva) with respect to the subsequent flavor.

The understanding of taste from form and so forth occurs through the inference of a causal property (*hetudharmānumāna*), like [inferring] a modification in fuel from smoke; this is the remainder [of the argument].
By this, the deficiency of the capacity for appropriation (*upādānaśaktivaikalya*) in the wind is refuted, as that would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to other cases as well.
Furthermore, it might be argued that because it follows after its own kind, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is also a cause for it; however, due to the absence of such a connection, there is no continuity for us.
As it has been said:
"Because of the absence of the connection of craving."
"Non-continuity" (*ananusantāna*) means the absence of continuity hereafter;
one who possesses neither the perverted cognition regarding suffering nor craving—which causes bondage—for living beings, does not undergo rebirth. (Prajñāpradīpa 1.83)

If this is argued, it is not so; for the rebirth of beings in inferior states is the effect of that [craving], since such rebirth does not occur in its absence, whereas mere consciousness is not its effect, as it exists even in one who possesses craving but is absorbed in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Now, if it is thought that for those of pure intention there is no state of existence due to the power of great compassion, it has been said: "Those whose great compassion is vast remain indeed dependent on others" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.209).

"But for those who have severed the continuum, because that [continuum] is absent, there is perpetual non-abiding. This is incorrect; for even in the absence of that [continuum], just as in the case of insentient things, the series does not cease due to its own causes.
Therefore, it is established: "Because they consist of mutual conditions," [this is so] due to the absence of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

It might be argued as follows: even if the final moment of consciousness possesses both capacities, since such is frequently observed in other cases, it is logical to postulate an unseen factor (adṛṣṭa) corresponding to that; otherwise, how could it be established that cognition manifests itself without parts? Furthermore, an objection has been shown elsewhere—that there would be no perception of color from taste—and thus it is said that an effect of the same class does not arise from itself just as one of a different class does not. How then can it be asserted that "the activity of substances consists solely in the sequence of their own causes and effects"? To this, he replies: "How otherwise," and so forth.

By means of its production (*tatprabhava*), [the cause is established] otherwise: when that which is intended as the cause exists, and not when it is absent, the existence—that is, the very arising—of that which is intended as the effect must be determined. Furthermore, regarding transformation, it should be understood that when there is a modification of something, that is its "modification" (*yadvikāra*). This refers to the derivative (*upādeya*); previously, this was the definition of the effect in general. It should also be understood that "that is its effect," and conversely, "the other is its cause. How then could the definition of cause and effect not be established in some way? For just as that which is intended as the final mind, though capable, does not arise by itself, so too [an entity] might arise by itself even while this [cause] exists. Just as there is the production of a dissimilar [effect] even by one who is not producing a similar one, so too there would be the production of something else even by one who is not producing a dissimilar one; thus, the effect is not produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Or, at some time, both might simply not arise by themselves. Therefore, the point is that if the final [moment] exists even while not producing an effect, then the same would apply to an eternal entity as well.
"That which arises only when something else exists, and which undergoes modification when that other undergoes modification—
that they call its cause. — *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.40.
The effect is of the same genus.

If it is thought that [the donor] is a being of a different genus— [that is,] that the assistance rendered by the auxiliary cause (sahakārikāraṇa) to the material cause (upādāna) consists not in producing an excellence in the gift, but rather in the operation of all [causes] toward a single effect, and that this is not contradicted even for the final [cause]— to that he says: "And not," and so forth.

And there is nothing other than what has been stated, characterized by mutual dependence; rather, it is this very [point] that has been explained: for that which is existent, eternal, and capable does not depend upon another. By this, the existence of the final sound at the time of the non-commencement [of the series], as well as its partless nature and its relation, have been considered.
[The opponent objects: "But surely, [the word] 'one's own' (sva) is redundant.

Let it not be that nirvāṇa is the cessation of the mental continuum; rather, let it be the opposition to the outflows (āsrava) and the arising of an outflow-free mind. To refute this very point, [the author] shows with the words beginning "if," etc.: "If, moreover, nirvāṇa is the attainment of a mind purified by the discernment of error..."

"What are they doing? he asks; [the author] replies: "Those who cultivate—that is, practice—wisdom (*prajñā*) consisting solely of reflection (*cintāmayī*), which takes the form of inferences such as impermanence and so forth, and no other.
Regarding that, he states the refutation: "And that," and so on;
"even that *nirvāṇa* is not possible," as has been stated.
How so? By means of the passage beginning with "cultivation of what is not reality" (*atattvabhāvanā*), he asks:

under what condition does that [realization] not occur? He says: when there is the cultivation of false [notions], inference regarding everything else is false. For when there is the cultivation of that, true knowledge of reality does not arise from the practice of false knowledge, just as in the cases of lust, grief, fear, madness, and so forth.
Nirvana consists of causes and effects; therein, ignorance and the other [links] are considered bondage, while liberation is held to be their cessation, which is the stainlessness of the intellect.
...as it has been said: "The mind itself, when permeated by the afflictions such as passion and the like, is indeed saṃsāra;
that very same [mind], when liberated from them, is called the end of existence"—Tattvasaṃgraha Pañjikā, p. 184.
Established in moral conduct and possessing [the wisdoms] of hearing and reflection, one applies oneself to meditative cultivation;
the cognitions arising from hearing and so forth have as their objects names, both [names and things], and the ultimate reality.

Wisdom arises from hearing and the other [stages]. Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas maintain that wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) concerns the name and its referent; wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) concerns both the name and the referent; and wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) concerns the referent alone.

For wisdom consisting of hearing is the certainty born from the authority of a reliable person (*āpta*); wisdom consisting of reflection is the certainty born from the investigation through reasoning (*yukti-nidhyāna*); and wisdom consisting of cultivation is the certainty born from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
—Abhidharmakośa-ṭīkā, p. 161.

Another Buddhist says: "Just as even when one is not actually the son of Vinatā (Vainateya), the thought 'I am Vainateya' brings about the removal of poison through false imagination, so too in the present case, there is the removal of defects. [Reply: No; because that same consequence would apply even to the imagination of a self and so forth, and because the illustrative example is identical in both cases.

Nor is it tenable to claim that there is no fault even if [the initiation] is false because of its connection with a real object (*vastu*), for this has already been answered by the statement that "it is not established because of the absence of that [object].

By this, he demonstrates that liberation (*nirvāṇa*) is logically possible through [initiation] itself, and not through its cause. Having refuted one who attempts to prove that initiation is the cause of liberation by means of the analogy of castration (*nirbījīkaraṇa*), he now seeks to prove it by means of the illustration of the removal of poison; thus, he acts improperly.
Even when Garuda has been pierced, I am Garuda;
[those] overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, madness, thieves, dreams, and so forth—
They perceive even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them—
*Pravāhaṇa-vāda*, 2.282.
Now, there is no capacity for initiation and the like to produce [results] if they were to occur after death; such a distinction does not exist...
because of the lack of decrease or increase in the nourishment of the opposing side and one's own side.
"Defects, being a continuum of their own seeds, are not prevented even in one who has been initiated"— *Pravāha-vārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 160.

Therefore, whether it be real or unreal, whatever is intensely meditated upon results, upon the completion of that meditation, in a cognition that is vivid and free from conceptual construction— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.284.

286. [Objection: "But surely, even though falsity is common to all things, since it has been stated that 'all is suffering and impermanent,' and because it has been stated that detachment from sense objects is like [the sight of] urine on one's own thigh, and because it has been stated that there is no self-knowledge, therefore the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*) alone is the limb of liberation. To this, he says: "Detachment," and so forth.

The intention here is as follows: even if it is stated that the Self is one, without beginning or end, and of the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*), and that passion (*rāga*) and the like, as well as old age and so forth, are merely adventitious to it—nevertheless, detachment (*vairāgya*) arises in the knower of reality (*tattvavid*) regarding those [adventitious states]. This is just as a person of noble character, having been led toward an improper act by some cause, feels detachment upon being reminded of his lineage, heroism, and other virtues. Conversely, for one who does not know the truth, even when told that something is "the opening of the anus," he does not feel detachment; for we observe that he continues to engage with it even when seeing it as a hole in the neck or elsewhere. Furthermore, even when the opposite is said—that it is "the private parts" (*varāṅga*)—he still perceives it as "that" (*tat*) or "this" (*yat*).
Dispassion arises in one who does not know reality.
For one who knows reality, detachment is the most excellent limb.

The word "yat" here is either meaningless, or it means that in my position, since [reality is] false conceptualization, nirvāṇa is not possible; however, in the doctrine of the self (ātmavāda), the practice for that purpose is likewise [possible]. Thus:
The connection is that [it] is not possible.
For one who perceives a self, there arises therein a constant attachment of "I";
from attachment, one thirsts for pleasures; and from thirst, one conceals the defects.
If it is argued as in Pra.vā. 1.219, he says here: "I am conscious," and so forth.

"I am conscious; my knowledge is my true nature; [this] deficiency [of mine] is due to the enemy that is karma"—thinking thus, one should strive by means of the proper methods for the sake of isolation (kaivalya), because the attainment of the object occurs through a succession of inferences.

Who, indeed, not knowing the reality of the self and what belongs to the self, would—though afflicted by suffering—exert themselves toward the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, like one who is intoxicated? However, when through some means one realizes through the knowledge of reality that the essence of the self is consciousness characterized by infinite knowledge and so forth, and that the objects to be attained are that [consciousness] while the objects to be abandoned are the karmas such as *mithyātva*, then, like one desiring to make oneself or another free from disease, one would naturally apply oneself to the means for that end; otherwise it would not be so, because in a doctrine of absolute [non-existence], the attainment of the highest good for oneself or others is utterly impossible. Thus, the conscious being thinks: "I am the knower of myself and others."

Why? To this he says: "Because my consciousness (*jñāna*) is my very nature (*svarūpa*); otherwise, like a jar or other objects, that [consciousness] would be impossible. If it is argued: "The conscious being (*cetana*) exists through a relation with consciousness, not because consciousness is its nature," [we reply: if there were such a relation, then upon abandoning its original non-conscious nature, the postulation of that relation would be purposeless, since consciousness would be established by its very nature alone. If, however, that [non-conscious nature] is not abandoned, it would not be conscious; it might at best be "possessing that" (*tadvān*).

If it is argued that Devadatta does not become a staff simply through a connection with a staff—just as one might say "the bow enters"—we reply: no. This would be a mere metaphorical usage devoid of firm conviction. And how could there be a distinct cognition of that [staff] otherwise? Thus, the establishment of the relationship [is required].

If it is argued that [the designation] is due to metaphorical application (upacāra), from what does that [application] arise? From a connection with that [object]. This results in mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
The Naiyāyika says: "Because it is the very nature of the self."
Because, in the inherence of cognition, there is a figurative designation [of the self as cognizing] without abandoning its own insentient nature.
Furthermore, how can cognition itself possess sentience when it is devoid of self-apprehension, such that—by virtue of its connection with that [self-apprehension]—it might become sentient?
If it is argued that [cognition is sentient] because it apprehends objects, we say no; for in the absence of self-apprehension, that [apprehension of objects] is impossible.

It would be better to postulate that the self alone possesses the illumination of both itself and others; what need is there for another cognition? From this, it follows that "my cognition is my own nature.
If it is argued that because the apprehension of objects is impossible, everyone would necessarily be all-seeing, to this he replies with the words beginning "by karma," and so forth.

Of what use is that karma? It is an enemy because it destroys its own true nature; it is an adversary because it causes a "distortion" (*vikalpa*) of that [nature]—that is, because it consists of an incomplete manifestation of the nature of knowledge. For the sake of *kaivalya*—the state of being solitary (*kevala*), meaning the condition of the Self when devoid of karma—for that purpose.
One should strive and exert effort by adopting and relying upon right vision and the other [limbs of yoga] through skillful means;

for what person of knowledge, indeed, having perceived his own enemy as being susceptible to destruction by such means, would remain indifferent even because of the snare of a mere fragment of adventitious pleasure produced by that enemy?
Such being the case:

In order to explain the *kārikā*, he says: "The self," and so forth. Here, the intended meaning is as follows: would one who does not know reality (*atattvajña*) but perceives a self fail to strive for its sake, or would one who knows reality do so? Regarding the first position, he states that it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), asking: "Who here would not strive? What [would they not strive for]? He says: "The reality of the self (*ātmīyatattva*)," which consists of infinite knowledge and so forth, because it exists as long as the substance [endures], as will be demonstrated; it is not the body and so forth, nor the pleasure and so forth arising from them, because of the opposite being the case and because of their dependence on another. To whom [does it belong]? He says: "Beneficial," and so forth.
Beneficial is nirvāṇa and its means of accomplishment; harmful is saṃsāra and its cause. Of these two, there is respectively their attainment and their abandonment.
To the question "What is it like? he says: "Like one intoxicated," etc.—this is the reality concerning one's own self.
As long as there is no self-substance (*ātma-dravya*), so long does the body and so forth not exist,
because [the latter] are dependent upon the sense-faculties and so on.

If it is argued that one might still engage in activity toward that [body] even while being unaware of it during the experience of suffering, the author replies with the words beginning "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and so forth.
For even a child tormented by hunger does not proceed toward boiled rice [alone] while knowing both the rice and its means of attainment;
rather, in the second case, one who perceives the Self proceeds for that purpose. Thus he says: "When," etc.;
the word "again" (*punar*) indicates an alternative position—that a person might understand [the Self] through some means of valid cognition, such as inference.
What is it? He says: the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), that is, the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*).

What is that? He says: consciousness (*caitanya*). [Objection: But everyone always perceives that; therefore, why would anyone strive for its sake? To this he replies: "possessing infinite knowledge," and so forth.
What else is that which qualifies consciousness? He says: "If, moreover, the goal (upeya) were to be attained [in that way], what [would happen]? He says: "Action (karman)."
Of what nature is it? By what is it to be abandoned? To this he says: "By the knowledge of reality," and so forth;
and how it is [abandoned] regarding reality, that will be explained accordingly.
Furthermore, what is its nature? To this he says: "false," and so forth.
Arising from that and having that as its essence, consciousness—like wine consumed by one [already intoxicated]—does not [arise] from anything else.

From what does that arise? He says: "By nature" (nisargāt). Who indeed would be called a fool regarding its means—the means to liberation? He says: "The self," and so forth; the meaning is: like a physician who desires to make either himself or another free from disease.

Just as a physician who perceives reality, even while seeing his own self, engages in emetics and other treatments for the sake of removing what afflicts both himself and others—considering the resulting state to be a superior happiness—so too does the person under discussion. Otherwise, one would not apply oneself to that [remedy] in any other way. Why? He says: because in the view of absolute permanence (*nityaikāntapakṣa*) and the view of absolute momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikāntapakṣa*), the attainment of liberation, which is the supreme good for oneself and others, is absolutely impossible; [this is so] regarding consciousness (*caitanya*).
The statement "consciousness and action [belong] to this" is also useless; why is that? He says: "the mind," and so forth.
For those who fear a confusion of actions due to the lack of a fixed distinction between the difference and non-difference of one's own and others' mental continua, [it is said]:
"Self-awareness alone is the defining characteristic of the mind; otherwise, the self-cognition of all minds and mental factors would not be possible. (22)

Nor is there absolute self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) of the mind, because that would entail the non-existence of error; for [the mind] possesses a manifold nature according to how it appears. Furthermore, the realization of reality as it truly is cannot occur either through itself or through another, because another cognition does not have that [reality] as its object, due to the rule that [cognition] is known by nothing else, and because there is no contradiction in apprehending even a manifold nature [of the mind].
Therefore, there is no distinction between one's own mind and another's mind,

because the differentiation of the object's form— which cannot be cognized by itself— would entail the status of "otherness," and because even another's mind would, through such arguments as simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*), result in attaining its own nature.
From where could there be a continuity of minds? Since an effect [arising] from self or other [is impossible], when that [cause] exists, it would be like the horn of a donkey;
nor can there be a continuous succession of effects from that. Thus, it should be understood that the status of being an effect for that which is absolutely non-existent is refuted.

But how can that which already exists be an effect? [The opponent argues: "Because it is produced, like a cause. [To this we reply: By not accepting an absolute [position], you act in a way that is favorable [to our view].

For just as the effect exists, so too it cannot arise because it is already accomplished; and just as it does not exist, so too its arising is absolutely impossible, like a sky-flower. This has already been answered.

There is no view of absolute certainty (ekāntadarśana) by relying upon which the establishment of non-absolutism (anekāntasiddhi) could be challenged through doubt and the like; for if that [view] were denied, where and of what would there be "doing" (karaṇa) and so forth? Furthermore, since there is no distinction between the continuums of self and others when such a distinction is not perceived, and since the distinction between self and other continuums exists [only if perception occurs], how could this person—who, due to the lack of perception by another and the non-perception of effects, lacks the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and thus somehow fails to know virtues and faults—cultivate friendliness and the other [immeasurables] according to their respective objects?

The mind is of two kinds: that which is momentary and pervasive as imagined by the Sāṅkhya, and that which is eternal and pervasive as favored by the proponents of Sāṅkhya and Vedānta. Furthermore, there is the "self" (*tattva*), whether internal or external, and the "continuum" (*santāna*), which is a series of similar causes and effects; in its absence, a dissimilar continuum is utterly excluded because it depends upon that [similar one]. Moreover, the "difference" (*bheda*) among those [factors] such as atoms is their manifoldness, and "non-difference" (*abheda*) is their unity; the connection is that these are untenable due to the lack of stability in the case of an absolute position (*ekāntapakṣe*).
For instance: no partless entity, even if it exists, is perceived by the mind through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
for this very reason, it is not perceived through inference (*anumāna*) either; since the manifold transformations consisting of joy, sorrow, and so forth are experienced by oneself.
This has been examined, and will be further examined.
And since that [the Self] is not perceived, even the distinction between "one's own" and "another" is difficult to establish;

not only is the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*) absolutely impossible therein, but even qualities such as friendliness (*maitrī*) are impossible. Demonstrating this, he says: "Friendliness and so forth," etc. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), not only is compassion (*karuṇā*) and the like included, but initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other such things as well. The sense is that such a person does not exist anywhere—whether among the learned or elsewhere—because there is no one who possesses the necessary practice (*anuṣṭhāna*).
He states another argument—beginning with "viśeṣeṇa" (specifically)—and demonstrates it according to the view of Nyāyātireka:

action (*kriyā*) consists of activity, speech, and so forth; its "confusion" (*saṅkara*) refers to the occurrence of such activity in one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), or the occurrence of the conduct of one with passion (*sarāga*) in that [state of being free from passion]. What then of the ethical precepts (*śīla*) of the Buddhists?

Where could there even be loving-kindness toward those who hold false views? Because it is impossible to know such a person as they truly are; or rather, [it is impossible] for the Sāṅkhyas who suspect such a thing, for they, asserting that "everything exists everywhere," would not fail to suspect even an object of equanimity within the sphere of loving-kindness.

By this, the Vaiśeṣika and others should also be considered: if there were an absolute difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality, then the restriction that qualities such as "well-bred" (*śiṣṭa*) reside in a specific substratum would not hold; furthermore, in the case of one free from passion (*vītarāga*), there would be no perception of a partless consciousness.

Relying on the Sāṃkhya doctrine, [the author] says "one's own self-awareness alone," etc., in order to explain the meaning of the verse [from the *Prakaraṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 180]: that everything exists everywhere.
This very particle *eva* (only/itself) is to be understood in three places—as "self-cognition alone," "the characteristic alone," and "of the mind alone.

If it is asked: "But does it not also have cognition by another? Why is that [cognition by another] not stated as its characteristic? [The answer is: Because it is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), since it is absent in pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth.
If it is further asked: "Why is that alone its characteristic?"—to this he says: "All... and so on.

The meaning is as follows: since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the very definition of the mind itself, otherwise—by way of its absence—self-awareness, which is the grasping of one's own nature, would not be possible. This is because if that [nature] were grasped by a subsequent cognition that arises in immediate succession and is conjoined with it, yet is incapable of having the same object, or by means of presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
By this, it is stated that "this is indeed its definition.

Of what things? He says: "of all minds"—that is, of cognitions of blue and so forth, and of mental factors (*caitta*) such as pleasure and so forth; this is to be understood as a restriction, for otherwise there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it applying to something else as well.

If it is argued that, in the absence of self-awareness (*ātma-vedanā*), there can be no establishment of specific distinctions—and that this very [absence] is the defining characteristic of your [position]—to this he replies: "No," and so forth.
It is not the case that self-cognition is an absolute self-grasping of the self by itself; rather, the meaning is that it occurs in some way or other (*kathañcit*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of delusion," and so forth.

According to the Sāṅkhya, if the conscious *puruṣa* perceives itself as being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and so on—just as it perceives its own dissolution (*svalaya*)—and if that perception occurs while [the self] is distinct from *prakṛti*, then since there would always be a thorough knowledge of the reality of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, from what source does this delusion regarding the self arise?
By means of a second cognition inherent in that very self, compared to the Naiyāyikas and compared to the Mīmāṃsakas.
Otherwise,
[it would result] from the thorough knowledge of the distinction between primordial matter and the spirit through their distinct natures.
"Therefore, through association with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears here as if it were sentient;

and likewise, while the qualities (*guṇas*) are the agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 20). From this, how could transmigration arise? For even if there were a conjunction of those two—which are partless—there could be no possibility of such a metaphorical delusion regarding their activity.

If it is argued that this error belongs to *prakṛti* and not to the *puruṣa*, then how can such a distinction be established when the nature of *prakṛti* itself is unknown? For the insentient cannot cognize for itself: "I am mistaken here.
If it is argued that it is known through the cognition of the *puruṣa*, then the postulation of a *puruṣa* is useless, since such a distinction is impossible if the *puruṣa* does not know *prakṛti*.
If it is argued that the *puruṣa* does indeed know it, we say no; for that is impossible as long as he lacks knowledge of *prakṛti*.

Just as in the case of sensation (*vedanā*), there is for that very [sensation] a perception of itself as primary which is consistent with reality, so too let there be an inconsistent perception of it from some cause. Why then, in the case of the *prakṛti* being imagined as deluded, is there not the conceptualization of one thing as both deluded and non-deluded? How could this apply to the *pradhāna*? Because of its capacity for transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). If such a conceptualization were applied to the *puruṣa* as well, what contradiction would there be? Therefore, it is established: "Oneness [of the self] does not exist through that [perception], because of the consequence of the absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) and the absence of error" regarding both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
In the self-awareness of "mine," one's own nature is the apprehension of one's own cognition.
In the hypothesis that the single Puruṣa is subject to transformation.

By this, the doctrine of the proponent of Brahman (brahmavādin) is refuted; for if Brahman were absolutely capable of self-awareness, how could this delusion of cities, gardens, and so forth arise from its non-perception of them? [Otherwise,] if Brahman were to perceive [them] itself, it would entail a deficiency in Brahman.

As for one who thinks: "Cognition, which exists for multiple moments and is not momentary, inheres in the self, and therein exist existence (sattā) and particularity (viśeṣa)," he too is refuted by this [very argument]. For, since the grasping of that [cognition] occurs by its own nature—even though it is related to multiple moments—just like the form of the apprehension of an object, how could there be any error therein? Consequently, the composition of a treatise for the purpose of excluding such [error] is shattered; this is the meaning.
By this, the inherence of existence and the other categories in that [cognition] within the self has been examined.

Furthermore, regarding cognition: if existence and so forth were distinct from it, what would be its nature by which it might cognize, and with what would it be connected? If you say it is "the grasping of an object," then the grasping of an object is cognition (*buddhi*). (Nyāyabhāṣya 3.2)

Because of this statement, why should that [object] not also be distinct from that [cognition]? For even there, the cognition of difference exists. If it is argued: "What is the grasping of this object by this cognition? Since there is the state of 'this belongs to this,' the cognition itself is of that form—just as blue is the very form of blue, and a universal (jāti) is the very form of a universal"; it is said in reply: What then is this cognition? If you say it is the grasping of the object, then the same fault recurs again and again, resulting in a circular argument (cakraka).
Furthermore, [it cannot arise] from knowledge...
If the apprehension of the object were also known by that very same [cognition], how could there be error?
Furthermore, in the absence of a cause for it, how could there be a cognition of relatedness therein?
Furthermore, existence and the like, being devoid of a relation, cannot be related by that [cognition];
for even the perception of its own nature is capable of being conceptualized.
If [the object] were not grasped in its own nature, there would be a further delusion.
Even for that [cognition], the refutation remains in the same state when it is cognized in its entirety;
therefore,
this Buddhist position is trivial, because the distinction between cognition and the appearance of the object is not perceived (Siddhiviniścaya 1).

Having discussed this with the words beginning "Thus," and showing that for this reason as well there is no absolute consciousness of the mind in the view of absolutism, he says: "In accordance with perception" (*yathādarśanam*), and so forth.

This means without overstepping what is perceived; because reality—the nature of the mind—is of a non-absolutist character, its own nature is not apprehended by itself in any way whatsoever, according to the intention of others. Why? Because the apprehension of a nature by itself [is impossible]. (*Pravāḍa-vāda* 1).
6. By this—

this state of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result is established exactly according to how it appears, even though it does not exist as a separate triad of grasped, grasper, and consciousness.
By the words "as intended" (*yathākūtam*) and so forth, he demonstrates that even such passages as *Pravāhaṇa* 2.357 are possible only within the framework of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).

Since the existence of another person's dharma is not established—due to the absence of inference and other means of knowledge—how can there be such things as "cultivation consisting of reflection" (*cintāmayī bhāvanā*)?
It might be argued: "There is no self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) of any cognition, because it is contradictory for an action to operate upon itself;
nor is there awareness through another, because [the cognition] would then be an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), like a jar or similar objects. To this, he says: "And from another," and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of conjunction;

it indicates that not only is there no self-apprehension of reality according to its intended nature, but apprehension is indeed possible from another source as well—whether through subsequent perception, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), or other means.
Why is this so? He says: "of another cognition," and so forth.
Other than the intended cognition, perception and the rest are "other" (*tadantara*) because they have that [intended object] as their limit, since they have partless consciousness as their object.

What is meant is this: because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself, there is no manifestation of cognition therein; nor is there a manifestation of the partless in another [object]. Thus, [the theory of] the destruction of all things [is avoided].
He states another reason: "not cognizable by another," and so forth.
Because there exists no other object of knowledge for it, nor is there any other [subject] whose object of knowledge it is—this being a rule;

or else, if that object of knowledge were something other than it, then by that very rule, it would be grasped by cognition as such. Furthermore, because of its connection with that [object], the nature of the self is not manifold, since even the nature of the self would otherwise contradict its own apprehension.

Otherwise, how could there be the apprehension of objects existing in a jar or similar things? It has been stated that this [cognition] is a means of proof even for that which lacks a similar instance (asapakṣa), just like the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth.
The meaning is: because [consciousness] is not distinct from the object of knowledge within its own self, that is, because it is of the nature of cognition;
this is due to the rule that [otherwise] there would be no necessity for another [cognition] to cognize it.

When there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the term "ananyavedya-niyamāt" (due to the restriction of being cognizable by nothing else) establishes that [the opponent's] conceptualization of another cognition regarding the perception of partless consciousness— which is devoid of any similar instances (*sapakṣa*)— is untenable.

"Otherwise, that [self-cognition] would be entirely useless, since the accomplishment of the effect [of cognition] occurs through another [means]. By this he shows, or rather, the restriction regarding the object of another: knowledge is known only by another knowledge, not as something self-known, nor as something remote, because in those cases there is no apprehension of the object; therefore, the restriction of being known by another is the restriction of not being known by itself. Hence...

The first two [alternatives] are untenable because they involve discordant defects; otherwise, what would be the purpose of the second alternative? Furthermore, regarding what was stated by the Sāṅkhya—that the intellect (*buddhi*) is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) while the person (*puruṣa*) is imperceptible (*parokṣa*)—he replies: "Because of the rule of being known by none other. Since the person is not known by anything other than itself, it is "known by none other" (*ananya-vedya*); because of this rule, and because it is not apprehended either by itself or by another, there would be a total lack of apprehension, just as with another mental continuum (*santānāntara*). Thus, the claim that it is "imperceptible" is meaningless.
By this, the Vedānta position has also been considered;
concluding [the discussion], he says: "In that regard," and so forth—since it is thus, therefore there is no establishment of one's own or another's mind.

It might be thought: "That which is to be known within is not unconsidered, nor is it even imperceptible, because it is itself directly perceived by its own nature as consciousness and so forth. To this, he says: "The distinction from the form of the object," and so on. "Distinction from the form of the object" means the absence of gross forms such as pillars and the like; or alternatively, the "object" (viṣaya) is primary matter (pradhāna), and its "form" (ākāra) consists of agency and so forth—the distinction from that. Of that [distinction]...

Of what kind [is it]? He says: "not subject to questioning from its own side," meaning that it is beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*). For if it were not present within consciousness (*saṃvit*), the consequence would be its being something other than that; thus, the establishment of that [object] therein [would be impossible]. Furthermore, if it were distinct from that [consciousness], there would be the consequence of identity between consciousness and the form of the object. This is another explanation: the object—such as "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) and so forth—is known by cognition; therefore, because it is distinct from that, there is a discernment (*viveka*) from it.
"The rest is as before" means [the attributes] such as "being knowledge" and so forth; by this, the distinction of Brahman from ignorance (avidyā) is also explained as being devoid of meaning.
By this, the view [of some]—that "the nature of cognition is undivided" (Pra.vā. 2.354), and so forth—is refuted.

That is not correct; for there is no consciousness other than the form of the object, because the very form of blue and so on is that [consciousness], as established by the necessity of simultaneous perception and other arguments—so says a certain Buddhist. To this, he replies: "Even of another's mind," and so forth.

It is not only the form of the object, but because even the mind of another attains its own nature—that is, attains the form of the intended cognition—the respective determination [of object and subject] occurs;
by what means? He says: "Because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension," and from the word "gadi" (and so forth), [it follows] "by simultaneous arising, and so on."
To those whose vision is perverted,
it appears as if possessed of a distinction between the cognition of the apprehended and the apprehender— *Prakaraṇavārttika*.

If it is argued that because the form of the object consists of consciousness itself, the single cognition cannot be manifold; let this fault apply to that [position]. Furthermore, showing that there would be no distinction between one’s own mind and another’s mind, he says "of many," and so forth.

From where does the continuity of minds arise by means of the mind? From where would it not arise? To this he says: "The effect," and so forth. What follows from that? To this he says: "One's own and others'," and so forth.
Showing its impossibility, he says: "When that exists," and so forth.
If it is argued that its production arises from a cause that has already perished, to this he says: "Like a human horn," and so forth.

It is not the case that its non-production occurs when the cause is either existent or non-existent; if one asks, "What is the example for this?", he says: "And not... and so forth, because even for an imperceptible alternative course, it is logically impossible for it to depend on place and other such factors.
If it is argued that [the cause] is immediate; to this he says: "Therefore, there is no continuity," and so forth.
Since a non-existent thing, like the horn of a donkey, how can it possess causality? Therefore, why is continuity untenable? To this he says: "The effect," and so forth.
The point is that there is no distinction whatsoever between that which has perished immediately after and that which has perished long ago.

However, a cause that has long since perished is eternal and undifferentiated, and thus it is not required; for that reason, [the effect] does not arise from what is non-existent, nor is it the effect itself. Demonstrating this, he says: "And so," and so forth.

And thus, in that same manner, it should be understood that the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is denied for that which is absolutely non-existent—that is, not existing even at the stage of the cause—just as in the case of a donkey’s horn; this [comparison] follows [from the previous argument]. If it is argued: "Granted, let there be no causal status for a donkey’s horn, which is always non-existent; however, for things such as a jar, which possess prior existence (*prāgbhāva*), there may well be such a status," [the response is: this would result in mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*).

Is [the effect] that which has already arisen, or that which has not yet arisen—like the horn of a donkey—or does its arising occur in relation to something else? Furthermore, there is no such thing as "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva) established by any means of valid cognition apart from the entity itself, by virtue of which the effect could possess that [non-existence].

If it is argued that the very existence of the cause constitutes prior non-existence, this is not correct; for since the cause itself is not yet fully known, a cause existing prior [to the effect] would not be of such a nature, and thus everything would become [a cause], resulting in the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

If it is argued that "that whose positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) the effect imitates is the cause," then what is this imitation of positive concomitance? If it means "the effect's coming into being when that [cause] exists," then a logical consequence follows: there would be the contingency of simultaneous production.
For only if the status of being an effect is established can its prior non-existence be established, and from that, the status of being an effect [is further established].
Therefore, the basis [for causality] is the fact of following the positive and negative concomitances.

Regarding the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—as stated previously on page 68 of the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*—the same fault applies. What, then, is "conformity with the absence" (*vyatirekānuvidhāna*)? If it means "not occurring when that [cause] is absent," how can there be conformity with that [cause] for something that occurs only when the cause is absent? If you say, "it exists at its own time," that too is untenable, because everything exists at that time.
Therefore, that which is non-existent cannot possess the status of being an effect, because it does not conform to the variation of its cause.
The opponent asks: "But how could that which exists—meaning that which is already present prior to its production—not have the status of being an effect? It has it in no way."

Why? To this he says: "Because of being produced" (*kṛtatvāt*), that is, because it has already been brought into existence prior to the operation of the cause, just like the cause itself. Now, it might be argued that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is defined as the state of having its existence dependent on the operation of another; thus, the meaning would be: "because of being produced, [the effect] exists even prior to the operation of the cause. Alternatively, since the root *kṛ* denotes action in general, one might explain it as "because of being made" (*kṛtatvāt*). Or else, how can that which is an effect (*kāryatva*) be said to exist again [prior to its production]? Thus it should be explained.
Alternatively, how is it understood that "the effect-ness of that which exists [is established] because it exists like its cause"?

To this, one might object: "Surely, effect-ness does not belong to what is non-existent because it is produced, but rather even to what exists because it is manifested, just like a jar and so forth. To this, he replies: "It is accomplished by 'like its cause'"; the ellipsis to be supplied is "because the refutation has already been made."
In every respect, just as that which already exists cannot be produced, so too it cannot be manifested; thus he provides the answer with the words "tadekānte" and so forth.

The meaning is: the "one-sided view" (ekānta) is the position that an effect must be absolutely pre-existent; since you do not accept this, you are acting favorably toward us, for even the Ketus do not admit that such a thing is an effect.
Showing that there is a refutation even if the effect exists in some way, the opponent says: "Just as," and so forth.
That is to say, if the effect already exists in the causal state in a certain manner, then it ought not to undergo production in that very same manner;
why? Because it is already accomplished, just like the cause—this is how the argument should be construed.

And in whatever manner and by whatever means that which is non-existent cannot possibly arise—because it is absolutely impossible, like a sky-flower—the word "iti" marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument; he states the reply to that: "And this [objection] has already been answered."
What answer has been given? He says: "At every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*), from the *Siddhiviniścaya* [1.10], and so forth;

therefore, this [position] has already been refuted by the statement, "Everything is incapable," from the *Prakaraṇavārttika* (2.4), because it is contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that consciousness or anything else is established for both parties as having a non-exclusive nature (anekāntātmaka), and thus there is no such thing as an exclusive view (ekānta) because of the existence of this [non-exclusivity], then the author replies: "No," and so forth.

Nowhere—whether externally or internally—is there an exclusive view (*ekāntadarśana*) by relying upon or depending on which [exclusive view] the establishment of non-exclusivity (*anekāntasiddhi*) regarding substances could be challenged. To this, he says: "Doubt," and so forth.
The meaning is that doubt and the like do not arise regarding an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If it is argued that just as the one-sided (*ekānta*) is seen, so too is the many-sided (*anekānta*) seen in some cases, [the author] replies with the words "that" and so forth:
if there were a denial of that many-sidedness which is directly perceived, then nowhere—meaning in no place—would there be the production of anything by anyone.
Why is this so? To this he says: "In the non-perception of one's own and another's," and so forth.

The meaning is that since there is no perception of one's own partless consciousness (*niraṃśacitta*) nor of another distinct continuum (*santānabheda*), there can be no inference regarding another [mind] either, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) connected to that [object] is not observed.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the absence of a distinction between sentient beings" (*sattvabhedābhāvāt*).

If it is argued that this has already been covered by the passage beginning with "nanu svapara" (surely [the distinction] between self and other), because there is no distinction among living beings such as being superior in qualities and so forth—which would otherwise be subject to refutation—[we reply:

No; by that [previous passage], the non-existence of the very nature of the distinction between their mental continua was stated, whereas by this [present passage], it is stated that even though there exists a distinction between the mental continua of self and others, there is no distinction among sentient beings characterized by superiority in qualities and so forth, due to the lack of valid cognition [for such a distinction].
Demonstrating this very point, he says:

"Even when there is the established distinction between self and other," and so forth. This means that it is not only when such a distinction is absent; even when it exists, how can this follower of the Sugata cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the like toward objects such as those superior in qualities, without transgressing their respective domains?
What should he do? He says: "Without having apprehended them as [real] entities" (*apratipannakāntataḥ*), meaning in no way whatsoever.
To the question "How [and] which ones?", he says: "Thus," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "The supreme," and so forth.
