and so on, in the manner of demonstrating the absence of the possibility of multiple meanings, providing a counter-explanation for every commentator against every commentator.
When there is a disagreement regarding the agent of the communication,
the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes the injunction to cultivate [the practice] and so forth.

In such passages as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the phrase "one should perform the Agnihotra" could mean "one should eat the *utra*— that is, the flesh— of an *agniha*, which is a dog that kills fire (*agniṃ hanti*).
Consequently, the Vedic injunction "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra" [would be contradicted].
Regarding the statement "one should eat dog-meat," what is the proof that this is not the intended meaning? — *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.318.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that Jaimini does not understand the meaning from the Veda through inference (*arthāpatti*), but rather realizes it directly for himself because he is free from passion (*vītarāga*), and teaches it to others by means of the Veda? To this, [the author] says: "If, however," and so forth.

For whom—whether for Jaimini or for Brahmā—is this the characteristic of one who perceives reality as it is, namely, being free from passion and the like? If that were the case, then from such a person, being devoid of passion and the rest, there would be the comprehension of the Vedic meaning for another—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
How is the refutation intended here? And so forth.
The sense is that [the reason] is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) because of the example of me; for I have taught [the Veda] not for the sake of gain, and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that there is no fault because even he (the author) is made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), he says in response: "Even if he possesses passion and so forth," and so on.

If someone were to know, or were to speak, the reality of the intended meaning of that [Veda]—that is, the reality of the meaning of the Vedas—which is to be known immediately thereafter, what else could that be? Why would the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of a human statement not exist [in such a case]? It would certainly exist.
Why? He says: "Because of passion and so forth," and it should be understood that this continues up to "because of the knowledge of reality.

The opponent says: "We do not say [he is incapable] because he possesses passion and so forth; rather, we say that one who disregards the instruction of another might know [the truth] or might speak [of it]. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the opponent's position.
Regarding that, the refutation begins with "But who, moreover," and so forth:
by whose teaching Upavarṣa and others [follow],
and from whom Kapila and others [differ]— whereby Upavarṣa and others would be distinguished as proponents of reality (*tattvavādinaḥ*), while Kapila and others would not.
Who is that other, or who is superior to the seers (ṛṣis), or distinct from them? None at all;
why? To this he says: "Because of the vision of its meaning," and so forth—that is, because of the vision of the meaning of the Veda.

If it is argued that even another person, being dependent on the instruction of another, understands his own purpose and would speak [of it], and that other [person] likewise depends on the instruction of another—thus this tradition of instruction is beginningless and non-contradictory; to this he replies: "Because of the possibility of its having multiple meanings, for what reason [would] another [person] not [speak]? This is the construction of the words.
He asks: "What [is the reason]? He says: "Reality," etc.
One should not say "this" either as a form intended [by the speaker] or as a form not intended, because the Veda would be distinguished from human speech by the establishment of reality [through it].

He thinks as follows: if that [word] had only one meaning, it would be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and being ultimately real, it would be fixed. In that case, since it could not be made otherwise even by a hundred imaginings, the realization of the truth might indeed arise from the succession of teachings regarding its beginninglessness and so forth. However, when multiple meanings are possible, who among them is beginningless and who is imagined? Without knowing that, how can there be the conviction that "this is the meaning accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and is beginningless"? If it is argued that "the learned one is the Brāhmaṇa," it has been stated here: "because of the lack of certainty regarding that. For that very reason, even if the meaning were manifold, it would still be the meaning of that [word], because there is no distinction [between them].
The Mīmāṃsaka teachers [hold that] this passage within it has been rewritten or fabricated.

Furthermore, according to the Buddhist doctrine, why is the consumption of dog-flesh—not being an eternal Vedic injunction—not considered the meaning of the Vedas? It cannot be a later interpolation, as there is a lack of evidence for such a claim.

If he [the one consuming dog-flesh] is not a "wicked twice-born" (dvija-dhusta), then who is? If you say he is a Brāhmaṇa because of his connection to yoga; then how is it that he lacks that very connection? If that were the case, how could he have been a Brāhmaṇa prior to following that [Buddhist] path? For a white horse that lacks the connection to the genus "cow" can never be called a cow.

If it is argued that even then he is not a Brāhmaṇa, then who is a Brāhmaṇa now? If it is argued that he is one who is never associated with the duties of another [caste] throughout the three periods of time, then who could possibly understand this? For Devadatta and others, who are perceived as performing the duties of the twice-born, would then no longer be Brāhmaṇas at those times, whereas upon entering into those duties they would become so—this being the opposite of the current view. If this is said, has the nature of being a Brāhmaṇa (*brāhmaṇatva*) been destroyed? If it has, then the universal (*sāmānya*) is not eternal; in which case, a shaven-headed person sitting in the middle of a herd of cows would not be a cow. If, on the other hand, it has not been destroyed, then he remains a Brāhmaṇa even upon entering into those [other duties].

If it is argued that [the status of a Brahmin] does not exist in the Vedas due to the absence of devotion (*bhakti*), then is that devotion itself the state of being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇya*), or is it something else? In the first case, it cannot be a universal property (*sāmānya*), because devotion is a specific quality (*jñāna-viśeṣa*);
consequently, even if one kills someone in a state such as deep sleep, there would be no fault such as *brahmahatyā* (killing a Brahmin).
In the second case, even in the absence of that devotion, the status remains as it was, and thus that same fault [of over-extension] persists.
If it is argued that he is known [as such] precisely because of devotion to him, we say no; for that state exists even among Śūdras.

If it is argued that [the knowledge] is not recognized in a Śūdra even though he lacks the recitation of the Veda, then from what source is the knowledge of his being twice-born (*dvijatva*)? If it is argued that it is from [knowledge of] his lineage (*gotra*) and so forth, then the same applies elsewhere:
there is a connection with Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇatva*).
Prior to adopting the doctrine of the Sugata, Śvetāśva was a proponent of other [non-Buddhist] doctrines.
Even while standing in the midst of horses with a shaven head, one enters the doctrine of the Sugata through the acceptance of the Sugata’s teaching.
Devotion to the Vedas alone [is sufficient], even if it involves the killing of a twice-born man.
Even in the absence of devotion to the Veda,
[this occurs] because of the presence of devotion to the Veda through devotion to the Veda.
Even though devotion exists in a Śūdra who is devoid of the qualification for Vedic recitation, [it is not effective].
By this, the performance of those [Vedic] rites by a Brāhmaṇa is refuted.

For instance: is that very [birth] what constitutes being twice-born (*dvijatva*), or is it something else common [to all]? If it is that very [birth]; then an infant, being devoid of it, would not be so.

Even so, if that [status] were accepted at that time, how could it arise from the performance of those rites at another time? If you argue that even another person might [attain it], but not this one because he lacks that [status], from what does this follow? If you say "because he is not a twice-born (advija)," then that would apply to the subject under discussion as well. If you say that he becomes a twice-born through the performance of those rites, there is a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): the status of being twice-born depends on the performance of the rites, and the performance of the rites depends on that status.
The twice-born [should] indeed practice the meaning of the Vedas;
even though he is devoid of practice during childhood, his status as a Brāhmaṇa is accepted.
Even one who is not twice-born (advija) may become twice-born (dvija) by performing the duties prescribed in the Vedas during stages of life such as youth;
by this, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) and other matters are also considered.
If it is argued that [the status of] being a Brāhmaṇa is a universal (sāmānya), then even in its absence, that [status] remains as it was, and thus one is not a non-Brāhmaṇa.

If it is further argued that the meaning accepted by the Brāhmaṇas is not the same as that accepted by many people, we say no; for even if there are many, they have accepted that very same [meaning], just as in the case of eating together in a common assembly, it is indeed that which is accepted by the many.

If it is argued that because it was fabricated out of hatred, it is therefore not the truth, [we reply: it is the same in that another [text] was also fabricated by the twice-born out of devotion. Thus it is established: "that which has many meanings," and so forth, refers to the state of being twice-born (*dvijatva*).
Even in the absence of the performance of Vedic rites,
one who follows the doctrine of the Sugata possesses the status of a twice-born.

To refute the argument stated by others regarding the authority of the Veda— namely, that it is accepted by many people in the form of sacrifices and so forth— the author says "The Veda," etc., while demonstrating [the following].
If it is argued that the Veda is authoritative because it is eternal and its author is not remembered, then why would others not likewise deny the existence of the author of their own scriptures?
It has already been stated that the mutability of sound, or of anything else, is established.

Furthermore, even in the absence of transformation, it is not logical that the collection of syllables is non-human (apauruṣeya), by virtue of which the Veda would be intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*); for this [reasoning] would apply by extension to other scriptures as well, since there is no distinction [between them] and because the author is not remembered. Moreover, if this [non-remembrance of an author] were a valid ground for authority despite being fallible, then other scriptures would also possess authority, or else the Veda itself would not.

Would there not be no validity whatsoever for phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*), since the comprehension of their meaning arises from convention (*saṅketa*)? In that case, there would be no distinction between the collection of sentences under discussion and any other [text] with respect to another person. Furthermore, if human expression were intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), it would be a source of valid knowledge even for one who has not observed the convention.
Even if no author is remembered, the lack of beginning for these compositions might still exist;
yet, how could there be validity for that collection? It would be like the conventions of barbarians.
That is not so, because even in the case of something non-human (apauruṣeya), trust arises when meaning is understood through the power of convention.

Even the non-interruption of tradition might serve as a means to dispel disagreements regarding that which is of human origin, since those who perceive its meaning repeatedly re-establish it whenever it has been lost;
but how can the Veda possess authority? To this he says: "Because of its eternity, because of its being non-human in origin."
It is reasoned as follows: in the case of verbal testimony, defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, which cause invalidity, are seen to arise from the mind;
and since these passions and so forth reside in the person, when the Veda is removed from the person, it is removed together with its substratum, the passions and the like.
And when the passions and the like are removed, the invalidity dependent upon them is also removed, whereby the validity that is the natural rule (*autsargika*) remains established.
For instance: whatever is without a basis does not occur in the absence of that [basis], just as smoke does not occur in the absence of fire;
and since the lack of authority in verbal testimony is based on passion and other such factors, it does not occur in the Veda because of the absence of those factors there.
As it has been said:
"Because of the absence of passion and other such qualities in an unfaithful man."
It is established that the arising of defects in a word depends upon the speaker;
therefore, the absence of such defects is proven in certain cases by virtue of being spoken by a person possessing excellence.
This refers to the absence of defects.
"Because it is impossible for [the defects] of those who are inferior in their qualities to be transferred into the word"— this is the ellipsis.
"In the Veda, because there is no speaker, we have no suspicion of defects" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanā, verse 62).
If it is asked, "How can there be eternity in that case? he says here: because no author is remembered.
For instance—that whose author is not remembered is eternal, like the sky; and so is the Veda, provided the word [is used] to indicate the intention of another.
The refutation here is as follows: "Of the author of one's own scripture," etc.

Is not the memory of the author of one's own scripture—the *Amṛtāgama* and so forth—whoever that author may be, such as Jina and others—is that not denied by others? Indeed, it is denied by the Jainas and others. The intended meaning here is this: just as in the case of the Veda, let there be no recollection of its primary author; let that [lack of recollection] be the reality. For even in that case, in the Veda, Hiraṇyagarbha and others are indeed remembered.

If that [authorship] were denied in other cases as well, there would be no distinction between what is Vedic and what is otherwise; for even in non-Vedic texts, one would have to say "it must be remembered.

Therefore, by those who employ the Veda in practice, the author of the relationship [between word and meaning] must necessarily be remembered, as must the author of the linguistic usage itself. For this reason, we understand that the Vedas were not composed by anyone after having established a relationship [between word and meaning] for the sake of usage. Consequently, the relationship between a word and its meaning is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5

And when a word conveys its meaning because it was composed by a reliable person (*āpta*), rather than by its own inherent power (*svaśakti*), how could that reliability not be remembered at the time of the cognition? (Bṛhatī, p. 177)

Therefore, since the author of the Vedas and their grammatical relations must necessarily be remembered, and since their non-existence is determined through the non-perception of something that would otherwise be perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*), the eternality of the Vedas and their relations is established; thus he says: "It is seen... (*dṛṣṭa*... — *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verses 123 and 130;
*Nyāyaratnākara*.
But how is it that the Vedas lack human authorship? Because no human author is remembered—[Prakaraṇapañcikā, p.
140]; and because no author is remembered, they lack human authorship—[Bhāṭṭadīpikā, p. 33].

"Because there is no recollection [of an author] despite the fact that [the Veda] ought to be remembered, and because inference regarding an author is impossible since he has been ruled out by the non-perception of a fit object (*yogyānupalabdhi*), and because the application of names is based on oral transmission, the Vedas are not of human origin"—
*Śāstradīpikā*, pp. 69, 616.
The quality of being authorless or eternal applies to the teaching just as it does to the Teacher.
In the *kārikā*, demonstrating that permanence (*nityatva*) is unestablished, he says "of sound" (*śabdasya*), and so forth.
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "as if" (*iva*).

Just as with something else such as gold, it was stated that for sound, this [permanence] exists only through non-exclusivity (*anekānta*); thus, its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) is established, just as in the case of Kumārila—this is the illustration.

If it is argued that "transformational eternity" (*pariṇāma-nityatva*)—and not "immutable eternity" (*kūṭastha-nityatva*)—is the reason [for the Veda's authority], and since that [transformational eternity] is unproven for both [the proponent and the opponent], the reason is therefore not "unestablished" (*asiddha*); to this he replies: Even if transformational eternity is accepted, the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the nine-syllable [Vedic] corpus is not tenable—that is, its lack of a human author is not logically consistent—by which means the Veda might be intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*) due to the absence of defects inherent in a person.
Why is it not tenable? He says: "Of other scriptures as well," and so forth.
This is because of the consequence of that [non-human origin]; that is, due to the consequence of non-human origin, transformational eternity would also exist there [in those other scriptures].
But this is not the case; therefore, the meaning is that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*).

Now, if it is argued that there is no fault because the reason is qualified as "because of its eternity while possessing the quality of being difficult to pronounce" and so forth, the author replies: "And because of the absence of a distinction. This is because there is no distinction in the Veda that excludes other [texts], since it is possible for all such distinctions to be produced elsewhere as well.
The word "ca" (and) is used here for emphasis; he states the following—beginning with "of the agent"—to refute the opponent's reasoning that establishes permanence there:
"This reason, too, is inconclusive."

He states another objection with the words "by that much," and so forth. By that much—namely, by the mere eternality of the author due to the non-remembrance of him—if the Veda were to possess the status of a valid authority (*pramāṇa*), then other scriptures as well—not only the Veda—would likewise possess the status of a valid authority, because their authors such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others are similarly not remembered.
By this, the latter part [of the verse] is explained.
Now, even so, another treatise lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); to this he replies with the words "from scripture" (*śruteḥ*) and so forth,
[stating] that its status as a *pramāṇa* [is derived] from another treatise.

Furthermore, setting aside other treatises, there are the following positions regarding whether the authority belongs to the phonemes (*varṇa*), the words (*pada*), or the sentences (*vākya*) of the Veda. Regarding these, he states the refutation of the other two positions: [if it were the phonemes], there would be no authority for phonemes or words anywhere; rather, it would exist even in the case of ordinary speech and the like. This is because, through the double negation, one arrives at the understanding that it refers to perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For in neither common usage nor the Veda is there any distinction between the phonemes and words [of one and the other], such as "fire" (*agni*) and so forth. Regarding the third position, is there a dependence on conventions established by humans, or are they otherwise? He states the refutation of the first position: "convention," etc.

There is no distinction whatsoever—whether based on validity or its opposite—between this collection of sentences under discussion and the collection of Vedic sentences, in relation to that collection of human-authored sentences.

Under what conditions? He says: "If there is the comprehension of that meaning from convention (*saṅketa*)," [it follows that] a person possessed of passion and so forth would establish the convention; thus, he considers the convention to be restricted to that [person].
He states another refutation: "There is no distinction whatsoever between the mass of sentences under discussion and other human sentences.

[He argues that] the manifestation of that mass of sentences—which always exists—is their *vyakti* (manifestation), not a convention regarding their meaning, because this has already been stated by the words beginning with "not a convention regarding its meaning" (*na tadarthasya saṅketa*).
And that manifestation is human in origin; in its nature as consciousness, there is no distinction whatsoever between that collection [of words] and anything else regarding the validity of sentences.
Thus ends this section on the validity of sentences.
"Duality" (dvaita) means that two alternatives will be stated;
[it refers] to the mass of Vedic sentences in relation to the mass of human-authored sentences.

He thinks as follows: just as there is no fixed meaning for a collection of sentences that does not exist when it is not produced by one possessed of passion and other defects, so too, even though the present collection of sentences exists, if it is manifested by such a person, its manifestation would be otherwise; thus, the same defect applies to the collection of Vedic sentences being manifested by one possessed of passion and other defects.

[Objection: Manifestation would indeed be contrary to what is desired, for manifestation occurs according to the nature of the object to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*), as is observed in the case of a jar and the like. [Reply: No, because in the case of a bedstead (*khaṭvā*) and so forth, the manifestation of the face and other parts is seen to occur otherwise.

Furthermore, no one can manifest that mass of sentences (*vākya-rāśi*) which is spread everywhere in a manner different from its true form, lest they incur public censure and become untrustworthy. Even if someone, through delusion, manifests it incorrectly, he will be excluded from that community once his error is recognized.

If it is argued that for this very reason, even today, those learned in the Vedas recite the text together during the festival of Indra while correcting it; it is replied: what proof is there that this same practice has existed everywhere in this manner throughout all of infinite past time? It cannot be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because no one living at present has witnessed that time.
If it is argued that if such a witness did exist, it would be appropriate for someone from that time [to testify]; then [the only recourse would be] the drinking of the ordeal-water (*kośapāna*).

Nor is there inference [to prove it], because such [inference] does not exist. If it is argued: "At that time, the Veda was indeed present everywhere because it is of the same nature [as what we see] now, just as it is today," then how could it be that the Bharata and other works were not also present at that time? If you say, "Because they are sublated by the work of Vyāsa," we reply: No; for here too there is the sublation of specific instances of gold (or the text), and its disappearance elsewhere—what confidence can there be in this case? If it is argued that the established tradition that "the Veda existed just as it does now at other times" is the proof here, then the established tradition that "at other times it was composed by Hiraṇyagarbha and others" is equally present.
Nor is there scriptural authority [for this], because such does not exist;
for there is no scripture of the opponent that establishes the self as being spread everywhere at all times, since they accept it only insofar as it pertains to its functional effects.
When a sword is extended, its edge is seen to be extended; thus,
the Veda is so called because it possesses such forms as extension.
Because the Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, and so forth are Vedas, [it follows that] in past time...
Just as the *Mahābhārata* is well known to have been composed by Vyāsa,
so too is it well known that the Veda was manifested by Hiraṇyagarbha,
even in the past.

The sense is that the Veda itself contains the same [notion], as seen in such passages as "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning" and "He who indeed imparts the Vedas," through which it is well known that the Veda was created by Hiraṇyagarbha.

This is because its authority is accepted only in respect to the injunctive portion (the *vidhyaṃśa*) with the words "one should do. By this, the authority of the Veda as it has been transmitted in future times has been considered.

Thus, since its continuous flow is established at all times, it is possible that it might sometimes manifest otherwise; therefore, there is no distinction between this [Veda] and that which is not of human origin.

Now, as for what was said—that "the understanding of its meaning occurs by virtue of convention"—that is incorrect. By virtue of that convention, the meaning of a *pada* (word) is understood, but not that of a *vākya* (sentence), because we observe the comprehension of the meaning even upon hearing a previously unknown verse whose word-meanings have already been grasped. And if it is argued that the meaning of a sentence is the meaning of the Veda, to this he replies with the words beginning "svataḥ" (by itself).

If [the Veda] were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by its own nature—that is, by its own majesty—due to its independence from anything else, then even one who has not observed the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) would become a means of valid cognition regarding the comprehension of its own meaning;

consequently, upon hearing that collection of sentences, everyone who understands the individual word-meanings would have a realization of its meaning through instruction by another. But this is not the case; for even a learned person does not understand another's poem correctly merely through such instruction, but rather by virtue of the linguistic convention.

It might be argued that [the opponent's position] follows merely from their own instruction, as it was stated: "There is no distinction whatsoever for one person regarding a mass of sentences composed by a human being that has not been previously established. That is untenable; for even its manifestation is eternal, occurring again and again, rather than being something new produced at some time by someone, because there is no recollection of its author.
To this, he says: "Even in the absence of remembrance of the author," and so forth.

The word "api" (even) is used in the sense of possibility. If it is argued: "Even if there is no recollection of the author of that manifestation, because the beginninglessness of the tradition is established through that manifestation, it does not follow that [the scripture] is necessarily eternal," the author replies with the words "tathāpi" (even so), and so forth: "Even so, in that manner of the beginninglessness of the tradition, how can there be validity for that collection [of scriptures], like the conventional usage of barbarians?"

Comparison: Since the linguistic practices of barbarians and the like, as well as their atheistic utterances, are also beginningless, they likewise possess that same status [of being non-human] due to the continuity of prior impressions;
even if such authorlessness were established, what benefit would there be?
—*Pravāhaṇavāda*, 3.245–46;
*Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, p. 238.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.

Even in the case of a collection of sentences that is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), how can there be confidence when the comprehension of meaning occurs by virtue of convention (*saṅketa*)? This is because the establisher of the convention is possessed of passion and other defects in this present age.
Or, if it is argued that its production is otherwise possible—just as in the case of individual [words]—to this he replies: "Of that which is of human origin," and so forth.
"What might be the means for removing the contradictions found in human speech? To this he says: "The continuity of the tradition is the means, not merely its majesty alone.
And why is that? To this he says: "By those who perceive its meaning," and so forth.

Just as there is the manifestation of a tradition through those who perceive the meaning of the treatises by repeatedly reviving what has been lost again and again, suppose the following view were held: "Let even a human-authored treatise not be a means of valid cognition regarding its object, because—unlike that which is authorless—it lacks any necessary connection such as identity (*tādātmya*) with the object. To this, he says: "The treatise," and so forth.

The scripture is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by its own nature, encompassing all objects in their specific and possible forms; it would be established as such through the minds of the omniscient teachers. Otherwise, who else could proclaim these words? For if speech were devoid of the distinction between the known and the knower, how could it exist?

Reality is established by the force of the thing itself; how could a treatise be an authority for one of dull intellect, such as a disciple of Śuddhodana? To this he says: [it is known] from itself, by virtue of its own capacity, and not through identity or other such relations, just as the rising of the Kṛttikā star indicates that the cart will appear.
If it is argued that "everything [would be so]"; to this he says: "only a certain restricted [thing], not everything.
What is that? He says: "the possible," and so forth.

The "possible" refers to its own nature, and the "particular" refers to the form of perception and so on. That whose object or range is "entire" (aśeṣa) in respect to that is described as such; that is to say, it is that which is corroborated by other means of valid cognition and the like.

Since the past and the future do not exist, that cognition occurring with respect to them would lack an object and thus be invalid. To this, he replies: this cognition is considered to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the same way as the cognitions of the Omniscient Ones—even though those cognitions of the Omniscient Ones operate upon the past and so forth, they are valid in their ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Therefore, if it were the case that words could denote neither a universal (*sāmānya*) nor an individual (*vyakti*), then the past and the future could not be denoted by words. That objection is refuted, because even that which has ceased is apprehended there through the power of the Omniscient One's knowledge.
In the case of a future [action], the past or future [agent] could not be designated, because that [past or future state] has perished in terms of its actual meaning— *Pravāhaṇa-vāda* 2.18.
Furthermore, as for this [objection]:
"If [cognitions] are fixed upon objects that are past or even future by means of their connection with universals (sāmānya),
how could there be a true dharma?"
Pra.vā. 2.34:

Even with respect to past and future objects, verbal expressions (śruti) based on and supported by the universal (sāmānya) are applied and established—such as "the jar was" and "it will be," and so forth.

And thus, it would have to be said that the universal (*sāmānya*) is a property (*dharma*) of a non-existent jar; yet how could that universal, being existent, be a property of a non-existent thing such as the past and so forth? For sharpness does not belong to a rabbit's horn—*Pramāṇavārttikamanorathanandinī*. To this, the following is considered: why is it not a property of the past and the future? Because they are non-existent.
When is there non-existence? At its own time; yet even that which is present is connected to it, since that too depends on multiple times—past and future.
How then could words directed toward an omniscient being be without an object? For even in their case, the object must be either the universal (*sāmānya*) or the individual (*vyakti*);
in both instances, the same logical consequence as for [other] words follows.

If [the universal] exists at another time, then since sound would be present at its own time, how could that property—the universal—be a non-existent property? If it is argued that it is called a non-existent property because the past and so forth do not exist at the present time, then in a single variegated cognition (*citraikajñāna*), the blue form would have yellow and other colors—which are non-existent—as its non-existent properties while they are present; thus, this is difficult to overcome even for all cognitions. Furthermore, if the past and so forth appear in their own nature, how can they be "past" and so on? That is illogical.
For how can that which has been seen in its own nature be [designated as] past and so forth?
Indeed, from what is unperceived, no form such as the past and so on can be conceptualized. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra 3)
If it is argued [that this is so], we reply: this is not true. For why would that which appears in its own nature to the omniscient ones be non-similar across the past and so forth?

If you say, "Because everything appearing to them must be present," we have already stated in response to this: there could be no cause for those [appearances], since you do not admit that they are present.
In all the cognitions of the omniscient one, in all the cognitions of the omniscient one, [of] all the cognitions of the omniscient one.

The meaning is that [the Sugata] does not accept [the preceding moment] as a cause, because he accepts only the immediately preceding [moment] as the cause. Furthermore, if the Sugata perceives his own causal state, how can he be omniscient? If he perceives it by means of himself as being present, how could he know or speak of his own self as having the state of practicing reality (*tattvābhyāsa*) as its cause? Otherwise, one would perceive a color perceived at the same time as being the cause of taste; thus, Dharmakīrti, in making an inference of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) from taste, did not understand the Sugata’s doctrine.
If, however, [the object] exists as the prior state of the self, then its appearing in its own nature would not constitute presentness.

If it is argued that the Sugata does not perceive anything other than its own nature— on the basis of such statements as "there is no other object of experience for the intellect" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.327)— then how is it that the yogi, who rejects the authority of scripture (*āgama*), is not far removed from this very point?
That is not correct. If it is argued that the definition [of perception] is "the yogic perception produced by the intensification of the cultivation of the real nature of things" (Nyāyabindu 1.11),
and thus refers only to yogins who perceive the essential nature [of things], then everyone would be such [a yogin], since there is no distinction.
And how could the conclusion that [the world] consists of nothing more than its own nature be established for anyone? This has already been stated.
Furthermore, the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaita*) has been examined.

If one accepts the establishment of that [non-duality] for anyone at all, then the establishment of it for the Sugata himself would also be unavoidable; thus, just as with the omniscient ones, there is the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) that words [referring to] the past and so forth would also be unprohibited. Therefore, this is closely connected with the [position of those who claim to be] omniscient.
Because it serves as the cause,
there is no other experience of that state of the practice of reality.
Because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] shines by itself;
this is the remainder [of the sense], and thus they would be yogis.

If the scripture of the Omniscient One is indeed an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object, then there is no distinction between verbal cognition and sensory cognition. As it has been said: "How can there be a cognition with diverse appearances arising from that same single form of sound and so forth? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.24).

Alternatively, it has also been stated that because the meaning is understood from that [word] alone, the collection of sense organs would be rendered useless—namely, that if the cognition of the manifested form arises from the word, the utility of that very collection [of organs] would be nullified. To this, he replies: "by the speakers," meaning those who cause others to understand the supreme state.

This is what is meant: if people understand reality through the word of an omniscient being by its very nature, how is the aforementioned twofold fault not incurred? If they do not, then what is the purpose of postulating an omniscient being? For this well-spoken verse applies: "One who possesses knowledge is sought... (Prajñāpradīpa 1.32) and so forth.

If it is argued that [the understanding] takes the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), how could that be so for one whose birth is unconditioned by such [concepts]? Furthermore, it is not tenable to say that there is conceptual construction regarding omniscient beings, because the answer to that has already been stated.

For instance: if conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object regarding those [universals], the previously mentioned fault is not avoided, because that fault is not prevented in other cases either. Nor is there a fixed determination of the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it has a non-real universal (*avastusāmānya*) as its object; let there be error (*bhrāntatā*) regarding them—this is of no consequence.

If it is argued that [this occurs] "together with the omniscient ones such as Māna and others," to this he says: "It might be," and so forth. That very cognition (*mati*), which consists of both manifest and non-manifest appearances, would have diverse appearances arising from a single-natured object such as sound—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), smell, taste, and so forth are included—from what [source]? Furthermore, it is a contradiction for something to have a single-natured object and yet possess diverse appearances—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, Manorathanandin.
"From the word alone, some [attain] that which was taught for the sake of comprehension..."— this is the latter portion.
The meaning is that, among the omniscient ones, the enumeration of the two types of valid cognition is established because the objects of knowledge are of two kinds.

If it is objected: "Since there is an absence of both the means of knowledge (*vedaka*) and the objects of knowledge (*vedya*), how can any scripture whatsoever be intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "Who here," and so forth.
Who else but Siddhauḍuṇi Śikādigrāda could utter such words? And is it not he himself? He says: "the speech."

Of what nature is it? He says: "In which [view], the object of cognition (*vedya*) such as a jar, the cognizer (*vedaka*) which is knowledge, and speech which is the designation of the jar and so forth—all these are empty, meaning they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
By this, he demonstrates the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) for the opponent.

For instance: if nothing at all exists, how can there be this statement that establishes [that very thing]? If it does exist, how can it be said that "nothing exists"? If it is argued that it might be like a dream and so forth; how is that possible? If it is argued that it is through delusion (*bhrānti*); it has been stated in this regard that [this is not so] because such delusion is not established in the case of absolute error.
If it is argued that [the Self] is beyond all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it has been said in response to this:

"Of what kind? He says: "[It is beyond the concepts] of those of dull intellect (*jaḍadhī*), whose minds are averse to the knowledge of reality, whether through the notion of 'this-ness' (*idantā*) or 'not-this-ness' (*anedantā*);
[it is not contradicted] even by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-adhyakṣa*)."

If it is argued that emptiness is thus established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and that meditation transcends all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then how can it be said that "it is experienced by itself"? To this, he says: because the reality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other entities is arrived at through the power of the thing itself (*vastubala*), it is said to "exist."
If it is said that "something exists," [the opponent] shows that this is unestablished even for one who has fallen away from [right view].
Thus ends the seventh chapter, "The Establishment of the Scripture," in the *Siddhivinischaya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vibhadrapāda, whose prowess is infinite.
Chapter Eight:
The Establishment of the Omniscient One.
If it is argued that one should not say "by the omniscient ones" because of their non-existence due to a lack of proof, the author replies here: "The object is established," and so forth.
Because of the non-existence of [such] omniscient beings, the entire object—pertaining to the three times and consisting of the principle of manifoldness (anekānta)—is established.

In the ultimate sense, the nature of cognition attains clarity regarding its own object through the abandonment of excessive obscurations—just as, for example, one perceives the moon with eyes from which cataracts have been removed;
it is the cause for liberation from karma, but it is not heard of in the world as a cause for the liberation of a substance. 1.

The object (*artha*) is an entity that illuminates both itself and others; cognition (*buddhi*) is that very thing, which is the self (*ātman*) or the living being (*jīva*), and not something other than cognition, because [anything else] would lack the manifestation of that [cognition], as established and determined by the aforementioned reasoning.

If, however, it were other than that, then even for a potter there would be no connection with it, and thus [the potter] would not be the cause of the perception of jars and so forth. How then, on the strength of that [connection], could there be the agency of some conscious being over the body, the world, and so forth, by virtue of which his thorough knowledge of the entire range of causes and effects would be established?

Now, if it is argued that cognition is said to belong to the self because it is its effect, then let it be said of the jar and so forth as well, since they too are admitted to be its effects by virtue of being objects of cognition (*prameya*).

If it is argued that [the jar] is not [its effect] because it is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), then [cognition] would belong to the conjunction with the self, because that is its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). If it is argued that it does not [belong to the self] because [the self] is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), then no; for it is impossible to establish the rule of causality through the relation of inherence when there is an absolute distinction between cause and effect.
Distinct from the intellect, yet distinct by means of the intellect.
From the example of the pot,
[there is the inference] of a creator of the body, the senses, the world, and so forth,
namely, Īśvara.

Now, that in which an effect inheres—such as a pot—is its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). What is the meaning of "inhering"? It means existing by way of inherence (*samavāya*). What is this so-called inherence? If it is argued that inherence is the relation between two inseparable things (*ayutasiddha*) standing in the relationship of container and contained, which is the cause of the cognition "it is here," [we reply: no, because the cause of that cognition is adequately accounted for by the specificities of cause and effect themselves.

If it is argued that there is indeed the cognition "cause" with respect to a cause, and likewise the cognition "effect" with respect to an effect, but not the cognition "non-cause," then [we reply]: in that case, there would also be the cognition "here" with respect to inherence (*samavāya*), but there would not be the recurring cognition "this is a universal, this is a universal. Why is it that inherence is the cause of the cognition here, whereas for the aforementioned cause and effect, there is no such cognition as "this is the cause"?

[The answer is: Inherence is that relationship which, being between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and standing in the relation of the supported and the support, is the cause of the cognition "here."
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 5;
the reading "iheti-pratyaya" (the cognition "here") is missing from this text.

Furthermore, if inherence (*samavāya*), while remaining unconnected with its own substrata (*samavāyin*), produces for a yogi or anyone else the cognition "this is inherence" and "the cloth is in the threads" by its own majesty—unlike space and so forth—then the cloth too, while remaining unconnected with the threads, would produce the cognition "this is the cloth" and the cognition of "here" (*iha*) for that very same reason. Consequently, this is another position: that there is a relation between the two, because of the perception that "this is on the branch. Therefore, there must be a connection between both.

If it is argued that, just as from the branch there arises the cognition "the tree," so too at that time there is the cognition "the branch" [in relation to the tree]; we say no, because this would entail the absurdity that the branch is the constituent cause (*ārambhaka*) of the tree. If it is argued that what is prior is the constituent cause and the branches are prior [to the tree]; that is not sound, because their state of being prior is not observed. If it is argued that they are inferred to exist prior to the cloth, like the threads [prior to the cloth]; then let it be inferred that the tree exists prior to the branches.

Because the subtle is seen even within the gross—as in the case of potsherds and the like—it is not the case that the non-perception of something that exists and is visible constitutes a prior sublation; for this [argument] applies equally elsewhere, and thus it amounts to nothing. Furthermore, no cause for the cognition "there are jujubes in this bowl" is established here as being necessarily connected with the bowl and the jujubes, such that one might imagine a similar relation elsewhere.

If it is argued that their relation is inherence (*samavāya*); and if the cognition "inherence resides in the inherent things" is based on another inherence, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is not so based, then this very [cognition] constitutes a counter-example (*vyabhicāra*) to the proof of that [inherence], by its own power alone.
Regarding the comparison with a tree: these expressions such as "the cloth is in the threads" and so forth are self-composed;
in common worldly usage, one would say "the horn is on the cow," whereas "the cow is in the horn" is unworldly.
"Branches are on the tree, and stones are on the mountain"— such is the common worldly understanding. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.350)
Furthermore, the knowledge that "those [objects] are in those [cognitions]" is said to transcend the world—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 267;
*Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti*, p. 14.
In this case, [the relation] is "being produced from a tree" [as in the case of a pot], whereas in the instance "cloth here in these threads," it is [the relation of inherence].

It might be thought: "The cognition of that [relation] is based on a connection consisting in the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*). That is not sound; for if universals (*jāti*) and so forth were also qualifiers of substances and the like—just as inherence (*samavāya*) is—then it would follow that they too are based on that [inherence] in all cases.
Furthermore, even regarding the state of being a qualifier, the same consequence as in the case of inherence must be considered. Therefore, there is no such thing as inherence.
Regarding universals and so forth, as well as the state of being a qualifier, they must be either connected or unconnected with their respective relata, and so on.
Now, if it is argued that inherence (*samavāya*) exists there because the self undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of cognition, then it follows that cognition is the self.

If it is argued that this would result in the Buddhist position, he says in response: "In non-absolutism (anekānta), that [object] is established in reality as having that nature; thus, 'non-absolutism' is that whose essence (tattva) or own-nature (svarūpa) is such.

If it is argued that this is a fallacy because the state of a single entity possessing multiple attributes is merely conceptualized, he says in response: "The object is established; by the method described, it is established as having a determinate scope; therefore, there is no end to the dispute. If it is argued that [the object] has the three times as its scope, he says in response: "It has the three times as its scope."

Objects established in the three times are also expressed by the term "three times" (trikāla), meaning that which has the three times as its object. In the absence of such [an omniscient being], since universal pervasion would be unestablished, there could be no inference whatsoever;
nor would the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) convey any object pertaining to the three times—for it is said, "For the Vedic injunction... (*codanā hi*, Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2).
1-2. Such well-spoken words would arise from the Buddha's wisdom.

Regarding the absence of a living being (jīva) as the subject of the three times, the Śābarabhāṣya states: "For it is the Vedic injunction (codanā) alone that is capable of making known such objects as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, the hidden, and the remote; nothing else, such as the sense organs and so forth, can do so."
Reflecting with his beautiful eye upon everything as being devoid of an omniscient being, that Cārvāka was led for a long time to a "colorful execution" (destruction) by this very path.
The Vaiśeṣika says: "Someone indeed might be so"; to that he replies: "Every one without exception"—for it is not only some particular self that is conscious.
If it is argued that pervasion must be known in its entirety; then there would be neither the other [means of knowledge] nor inference,
for it has been established that even one who is unborn does not live without inference.

If it is argued that even an omniscient being would be established [as such] because he possesses the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as his object, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); for it has been said:
"He has the three times as his object."
"If he were [known] through the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), who could deny that he is omniscient? (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra, verse 110); thus says the Mīmāṃsaka.

But by whatever single means of valid cognition an omniscient being is postulated, he must surely perceive all [objects], such as tastes and so forth, with that very eye— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra, verse 111.
Regarding this, he says: "In its own object," and so forth. [The objection is:

"Since the omniscient one (*sakala*) has attained clarity regarding his own object—which consists of the three times—he is connected to that very [object]. This is not the case, because it would contradict the subsequent text;
for by the mention of "his own" (*sva*), there is a negation of restricted omniscience.
Indeed, it is not logical that unobstructed knowledge, whose object is everything, should be restricted in its manifestation, like the orb of the sun;
as it has been said:
"How could the Knower be ignorant regarding the object of knowledge?"—thus [it is] with respect to the obstructer.
"Fire is a burner; it would not be a burner if there were no obstructer," as quoted from *Yogabindu*, verse 431— this is cited in *Jayadrathayāmala-prabhā*, page 66.
*Yogabindu*, p. 50: "If there were no obstacle, how could it not be unobstructed?

Furthermore, what was stated here by Prajñākaragupta—that clarity is established when the self is unobscured while possessing all objects as its domain, and once that [clarity] is established, its having those objects as its domain is established—this is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).
Thus, that [objection] has been refuted by the statement "it has as its object the three times.
It has been stated that for that [consciousness], there is no life even in the non-duality of manifestation (*pratibhāsādvaite*) without inference;
and that [inference] also does not exist without the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigrahaṇa*).
By the mention of "grasping an object," clarity such as that found in desire, grief, fear, and so forth is excluded;
for inference does not possess clarity regarding its object.
It has been stated that [meditation] consists of conceptualization regarding the objects of meditation such as desire and so forth.
Now, one might object: "The mental cognition of another person regarding objects of the three times is not perceived;
how then could that [cognition] be either vivid or accurate? For, in the absence of a supporting example or logical reasoning, it remains unestablished.
As it has been said:
"Just as charcoal, even when being tolerated, never attains whiteness, so too agreeable cognition, through repeated practice, never attains the state of having a real object. Thus [it is said].
For a glowing coal, even when being rubbed, never becomes white; the contact with one's own inherent nature cannot be prevented by anyone.
— *Pravacanavārtikālaṃkāra* 2.169b–170a.
Regarding this, he says:

"The darkness has been removed," and so forth. This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for dust, mist, and the like; that whose [darkness] has been removed is described as such. One whose sense organ (indriya)—the eye—is thus [clear], the perception of form and so forth, beginning with the perception of a tree, is also described in that way; "like that" means similar to that.

He thinks as follows: Just as the cognition of the moon and so forth is, due to the influence of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), indistinct or incorrect with respect to its own object and not so by its own nature, so too is mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); and just as that [sensory cognition] becomes distinct and correct therein upon the removal of the obscuration, so too is mental cognition. This would indeed be your position if that [mental cognition] were of the nature of grasping what is indistinct and incorrect, or if it were eternal; but that is untenable, because of the statement that reality is manifold (*anekānta*), and because we observe in dreams and the like the perception of things that are unreal, indistinct, and incorrect.

Nevertheless, since that [cognition] has that [object] as its intrinsic nature, even the cognition of two moons and so forth has that as its intrinsic nature; thus, invalidity is not extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
And just as a cause such as ophthalmia is perceived in this case, so too is a mental cognition inferred.
Furthermore, for the Mīmāṃsaka, inference is not an invalid means of knowledge, because it would otherwise follow that the eternity of the Veda could not be established.

If it is argued that the cognition of two moons and so forth arises from a defect, and if its nature were such [by itself], then there would never be a perception of an object as it truly is or in its clarity; if this is said, then the same applies here.

Furthermore, if in a true dream that cognition possesses truth and clarity due to something else, then for the cognition of the moon and so forth as well, it must be the case that invalidity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Thus, the consequence follows.
The non-perception of anything else is the same in both cases regarding cognition; this has indeed been written twice [in the text].

If it is argued that, like the perception of that [object], there is no reason for it to achieve clarity (*vaiśadya*) with respect to its own object, he says here: "Excellence (*atiśaya*) is the cause."

If it is asked, "Of what is this excellence (*atiśaya*) or pre-eminence (*utkarṣa*)? it is said: By stating that [the cognition] "attains clarity (*vaiśadya*) regarding its own object, like the perception of the moon by an eye from which the cataract has been removed," it is effectively stated that the cataract of the obscuration (*āvaraṇa-timira*) has been abandoned.
Therefore, the excellence of the obscuration is the logical reason (*hetu*) or mark (*liṅga*).

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The abandonment of obscurations among persons reaches its ultimate limit in some cases, because it is a matter of degree (*atiśaya*), like the abandonment of cataracts and the like.

If it is argued: "But since this abandonment is observed to be non-ultimate, like the abandonment of [the defect] *dṛṣṭiprāha*, then for this [obscurational ignorance] as well, there would be non-existence [of the ultimate], just as in that case; and since this is not accepted, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)," [the author] replies: "The liberation from karma," and so forth.
Liberation from karma is the removal of karmas away from the self; the cause is for that purpose, and not for the sake of their absolute non-existence.

Why? He says: "Furthermore," [it is] not at all that the destruction—defined as absolute non-existence—of a substance, whether it be the soul (*jīva*), matter (*pudgala*), or anything else, is observed; for it has already been established that there is no absolute annihilation of that which exists, and thus it is not stated again.

Therefore, the sense is that just as there is liberation of the self from its own attributes, so too liberation from what is not-self is possible for that [soul], and thus there is no deviation [from the rule].
Alternatively, an excellence of knowledge or truth is apprehended.
Just as there is the abandonment of obscurations, so too is vision knowledge;
[this applies] to vision as well.

If it is argued: "Just like space and so forth, which possess obstructions, even if [the Buddha] is established as being present in his own domain, he—or anyone else—is not established in a specific form [as the Sugata], because there is no reason connected to that [specificity]," to this he says: "Because he is heard," and so forth.

In the world, that which has been brought within the range of hearing through scripture—namely, in the context immediately following, either the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness), that mass of statements marked by the word "perhaps" (*syāt*), or else the excellence consisting in the specific relationship between actions and their fruits—is the means of accomplishment; "its excellence" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Since there is no denial of the establishment of the excellence of the speaker from the excellence of the speech, [the doctrine] is indeed invariably concomitant with that. If it is argued: "But was not the *syādvāda* also taught and postulated by the Sugata? Therefore, as it attains clarity therein, it too would be established"; to this he replies: "In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*)."

It might be argued that the clarity of cognition arises from the operation of the sense organs upon what is imagined based on what has been heard; and since the operation of the sense organs occurs only with respect to what is present and proximate, how could one who attains such clarity therein be established as omniscient?
And it has been said:

"Being of the nature of cognition, it perceives what is present and immediate; knowledge arising from the eye and other [senses] does not arise with respect to the past or the future. Thus [it is said].
If it is argued that "the eye and other [senses] perceive what is connected and present" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.4,
verse 84), to this he replies with the words beginning "cognition" (*dhī*), etc.,
because of [its] being observed.
If wisdom does not exist for men regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses, then from where could this [knowledge] have been extracted?
...If it is said to be from scripture...
(Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa chapter, verse 12).
If it is argued that the non-contradiction of astrological knowledge [proves the existence of a creator] because it is heard in scripture, then there must be another means of proof.

Comparison: "By whom all the movements of the planets and so forth—which are the causes of pleasure, pain, and the like—have been directly perceived, by him what part of the world has not been directly perceived?"
— Nyāyaviniścaya 3.414:
[This is so] because of the observation of correspondence [of predictions] regarding lunar and solar eclipses and the like.
Even regarding that which is not perceptible, such as sin and so forth, it is not tenable that [the scripture] lacks authority—
Śāstravārtā 2.3.

Parokṣa-jñāna (indirect knowledge) is indeed accepted [by us]. How, then, is there non-contradiction regarding the specific details of future objects in astrological knowledge? This is because their nature (*svabhāva*) and effects (*kārya*) have not been previously perceived; because the authority of scripture (*śruti*) is not admitted in that regard due to its restriction to matters such as injunctions (*vidhi*); and because there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If, however, scripture is held to have the three times as its object, it follows that indirect knowledge belongs to persons. If this is not so, then the intellect (*buddhi*), which was just mentioned as being of the nature of consciousness, would attain clarity (*vaiśadya*)—provided that it does not [otherwise] exist.
Regarding an object that is absolutely beyond perception, such as dharma and so forth,
it should be understood that [knowledge] arises "from itself" (*svataḥ*), in order to exclude [the need for] signs (*liṅga*) and the like;
for it does not arise from any means of valid cognition whatsoever.

Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) here should be understood as having the sense of repetition—repeatedly, throughout beginningless and endless time. "Non-contradiction regarding the knowledge of the luminaries" (*jyotirjñānāvisaṃvādaḥ*): the luminaries (*jyotīṃṣi*) are the planets, constellations, and so forth; their "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the determination of their rising, setting, and continuous movement, along with their results, causes, substrata, qualities, and the like, as well as the specific locations of living beings. "Non-contradiction" regarding that means its absence of error; since there would be no other cause for such non-contradiction in its absence, [the author] asks:
"Of whom? He replies: "Of men" (*puṃsām*). And since this non-contradiction exists separately from others, there is therefore an intelligence (*dhīḥ*) regarding that matter.

If it is argued that any instance of non-correspondence [with reality] arises from a failure to understand the relationship between the subject matter and its presentation, or from a lack of knowledge regarding the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), just as there is non-correspondence in the cognition of an object of inference due to ignorance of that relationship; and that once that relationship is fully understood, non-correspondence is no longer observed, therefore there exists a scripture that is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), and from that [scripture] comes non-correspondence [with reality]; To this, he replies: If the non-correspondence [of reality] is derived from the heard scripture, then this form of scripture is another means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) distinct from the other means consisting of the propitiation of the Omniscient One through superior qualities. Thus, this scriptural form is a separate means of accomplishment.

The meaning is that for those who are not omniscient, [knowledge] regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses is impossible, because such knowledge would otherwise be non-contradictory, and without [an omniscient being], that non-contradiction would be absent.
Since there can be no lack of contradiction in a treatise without the establishment of an omniscient being,
he says— while commenting on the verse— "knowledge of the imperceptible," and so forth.

[Objection: Surely, by whom is it maintained that the knowledge of dharma and so forth—which is imperceptible (parokṣa) in relation to persons such as ourselves and is separated from us by space and other factors—is exclusively inference (anumāna), such that this [objection] is raised? It is not by a follower of the Sugata (Buddhist) and others who profess omniscience, because they also accept that such knowledge is perceptual (pratyakṣa).
Nor is it by a Mīmāṃsaka, because he also accepts scripture (āgama).
Nor is it by a Lokāyatika (Materialist), because he does not accept the validity of either inferential or any other kind of knowledge. [Reply: We say: "By the Buddhist."

For instance: since the apprehending cognition of a thing is of the same form as that from which it has arisen—even for the Sugata—therefore, that imperceptible object which imparts its form is inferred by the Sugata just as it is by people like us, because [otherwise] that object would not be determined by him through either perception or inference; otherwise, he would be even more wretched than an ordinary person, or rather, we say, even than a Cārvāka.

Therefore, one who desires worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) based on the scriptures of the non-omniscient and so forth must accept inference even regarding things that have perished and the like, just as in the case of another's consciousness; otherwise, there would be no accomplishment of complete worldly transaction,
because of the rule that [such] depends upon indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*).
The meaning is: "because otherwise, cognitions having that form would be inexplicable.
If the proponent who rejects the authority of the scriptures of the Omniscient One should say, "Let it be exactly so," [the author] replies here: "How could it be future? and so forth.
Regarding the question of how there could possibly be no contradiction in the knowledge of astrology concerning future specific objects such as eclipses and so forth—why is this so?

To this he says: "Because of those," and so on. Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*) of those specific future objects have not been previously apprehended, it is impossible to reach a prior determination regarding the eclipse and so forth.

He thinks thus: if the intrinsic nature of those [objects] were determined along with the Sugata, how could they be future objects? Or, if there were a determination of the cognition of that form, or even of its effect, such as the questioning [of the object], then that same fault would apply.

If it has been established that the future is not a [valid] cause, or if—in the case of those who maintain a restriction to one or two means of valid cognition—it is observed that the operation of inference is impossible because a certain determination of the unknown cannot occur, then [the opponent might argue]: "Since there is also scripture (āgama) as a source of knowledge regarding the imperceptible, this fault does not arise. To this, he says: "And because of scripture," and so forth.

"Scripture" (*śruti*) is the knowledge of an object not present to the senses produced by scripture; and since its authority is not admitted in that regard for things such as those yet to come or those already destroyed, the following is the intended meaning [of the opponent]: "When neither perception nor inference regarding a future object exists for the Sugata or anyone else, then scripture—which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeyī*)—must be accepted as the means of valid cognition there; and since it was not composed by him, its authority is accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas. To this, he replies with the words beginning "vidhyādi," etc.

If it is argued that the injunction (*vidhi*)—which is the beginning of [the category] consisting of *niyoga*, *bhāvanā*, and so forth—is itself the object because it is restricted to that [injunction], and that even the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept the authority of the Veda (*śruti*) in that regard, and therefore another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must exist there; to this he replies: "In the means of knowledge," etc., meaning that no other means of knowledge exists there apart from the means of knowledge already established.

Now, if it is maintained that scripture (śruti) without distinction has as its object all three times, he says "If, however," and so forth. To that, he provides the answer beginning with "It follows," and so forth, regarding both the Cārvāka who maintains there is only one means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the Buddhist who maintains there are two.
The Veda is accepted as an authority regarding the future.

If it is argued that since the Veda itself reveals an imperceptible object regarding the future and so forth, what is the need for knowledge in that regard? To this he says: "The reality whose object is the three times," and so on; to whom would the Veda communicate such a reality?
If a person does not know [the truth] because of the absolute and inexhaustible veil [of ignorance], then— just as this has been cited in the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* (p.
12)— such persons, due to their lack of desire to sever that veil of ignorance, are not capable of understanding it, for there is no obstacle to the excellence of that [ignorance].

The Veda is not inherently authoritative for anyone, because it cannot be ascertained; therefore, it could not establish reality for anyone at all. Rather, the intention is that [the Veda] has the three times as its object, yet it is insentient.

Like the eyes and other sense organs, it would produce cognition therein regarding its own appropriate object for everyone, or else for no one at all; in that case, the convention [of teaching] would be useless. Would he not communicate something by some means? To this, he says: "If, due to the absolute obstruction of imperishable veils, a person does not know reality as it is—encompassing the three times—in a clear manner, then he could not communicate that knowledge in such a way, because of the absence of any distinguished person capable of establishing the convention.
If it is argued that there may be someone who directly knows the meaning of the Vedas, but not everyone, to this he replies: "The persons," and so forth.
Announcing that they are capable of knowing because of the removal of the veil of defects regarding that object, he says: "From any cause whatsoever," and so forth.

It is not only from themselves; rather, because of some cause such as right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and the like, there is the destruction—that is, the removal—of both [the attachment to reality and] the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*). Since this is desired, they are capable of knowing; thus, their object pertains to the three times.
If it is argued that there is no complete severance of those obstructions for ordinary persons, whereas such exists for the Omniscient One, the author replies with the words beginning "that" (*tat*):

because the excellence—that is, the intensity—of that severance is established through both omniscience and non-omniscience, it follows that the knowledge of supersensible things belongs to [the Omniscient] Person;
this has been discussed immediately below.

Is it not true that, for those whose obscurations have been severed, persons are indeed incapable of understanding the meaning of the Veda; yet the Veda, being authorless (apauruṣeya), proclaims its own meaning by itself?
Regarding this, he says: "The Veda," and so forth.
Another asks, "Of what is it the authority?
To him, he replies: "It is not the authority of anything, for it is well-spoken."
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of that," etc.

The sense is that there is no one who knows the true nature of the meaning of the Veda, because—due to being a human being—one lacks personal certainty regarding it, like a man on the street; or because the Veda itself is insentient and thus cannot produce certainty therein.
This is established by the inference: "There is no one who knows the true nature of the meaning of the Veda, because he is a human being, like a man on the street."

Furthermore, all speech is produced, and the communication of meaning is observed to depend upon a person; yet, if even Vedic speech—which is seen to reside within itself—were suspected of being otherwise, then the clear knowledge of meaning in persons would exist even in the absence of that [Veda], despite being perceived through the senses.
These two [speech and its meaning] are therefore without human authorship (apauruṣeya) and eternal.

If it is argued that, whereas in the case of the Veda there is the proof consisting in the non-remembrance of an author despite the absence of sense organs, such [proof] does not exist here, we say: no; for even in this case there is an excellence of knowledge, as he shows by saying "of living beings," and so forth.

A learned person does not disagree with the sequence by which those who know the meaning of the scriptures— such as the living beings, the senses without assistance, and so forth— possess an excellence of cognition that establishes their non-human origin.

No one can reasonably disagree regarding the progressive excellence of intelligence among the multitude of living beings, from stationary objects up to those who know the true meaning of the scriptures; except perhaps for the disciple of Śauddhodani, who maintains that there is doubt even regarding remote objects, and for those who know the scriptures but claim otherwise.
For those who know the meaning of the scriptures, the excellence of their knowledge of that meaning certainly exists in every respect, due to the gradations in their natural aptitude and practice.

How so? Regarding the connection... likewise, if someone were to possess a proficiency in supersensuous knowledge that is independent of the meaning of the scriptures, what contradiction would there be? For if excellence were impossible, the Veda itself could not be a means of valid cognition;

just as the Veda, despite no difference in its being a verbal testimony, conveys its own meaning through its own inherent power, so too, despite no difference in their being human beings, some particular person might apprehend supersensuous objects independently of the senses.

What kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the world could establish the non-existence of an omniscient being? Since perception and the other [means of knowledge] are contradictory to having non-existence as their object, and since it is not accepted that a "means of knowledge of non-existence" (*abhāvapramāṇa*) would otherwise result in futility, there exists a scripture uncontradicted by reasoning which states:

"The omniscient being does not exist, because he is not perceived, like a sky-flower. To this, it is replied: if "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*) is either the cessation of a proving means of knowledge or a self devoid of that [knowledge], then the absence of self (*nairātmya*) would follow for each accordingly.
For one who does not perceive everything cannot directly realize all the specific qualities of every self;

for that very reason, it is impossible to infer those individual specificities because no probans (liṅga) exists, since the reality of things— which consists of multiple natures— is established by means of that [probans] without such specificity.
For what reason? Because if that [self] were established, then even its own nature—which is inseparable from the specific qualities not yet established—would likewise result in being non-self;
consequently, there would be no apprehension of anything at all, leading to the non-existence of everything, since this same consequence would apply even to what has been heard.
For indeed, since the accomplishment of the human goal depends upon having a specific object [of knowledge], otherwise the scripture would simply be unworthy of attention; thus,

this cessation of the cognizer’s means of valid cognition— which pertains to all things— is impossible to comprehend, and it therefore establishes not only the non-existence of an omniscient being, but also the exclusion of all objects whatsoever.

If that is so, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence? We say it is scripture (*śāstra*), because it establishes its existence and describes the fourteen stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*).

How is this [scripture] authoritative? If you ask how the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is authoritative, it is because of its eternity; let the same apply to the teaching (*pravacana*) for that very reason.
How is the eternity of the teaching established? It is as it is with the *codanā*.

But how, then, is the eternity of the *codanā* established? [It is] because no author is remembered. If you argue that for that very same reason, authors—namely the *tīrthakaras*—are remembered for the supreme scripture (*paramāgama*), [we reply: do not the followers of Kaṇāda and others remember an author of the Veda?

Furthermore, if the recollection of Kaṇāda, Bhikṣu, and others were invalid, there would be no distinction whatsoever regarding the validity of the recollection concerning other [authors] and the subject matter of the supreme scripture (*paramāgama*).

This teaching is thus authorless (*apauruṣeya*); since both the omniscient one and the scripture are accepted as eternal due to the continuity of their tradition—whereby the Tīrthaṅkaras merely re-establish the lost teaching—how could there be such mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) in this case?
Therefore, it is established that neither inference nor the scripture proves the non-existence of an omniscient being.
Nor is it the case that the teaching of non-absolutism (anekānta-śāsana), which establishes the manifold transformations of living beings, is invalid;
