nor is there any counter-evidence against it, because its subject matter is sublated by the doctrine of conditional predication (syādvāda), just as in the case of the Three Baskets (piṭakatraya).
For that [opposing] absolutism is impossible, or else it would be devoid of a subject matter; thus has this been established as a royal road.

If, on the other hand, you argue that they are not omniscient because of their being speakers and so forth—due to their being speakers, their being human beings, and their possessing passion and the like, just like a man on the street—then how could Jaimini be a knower of the Veda? Indeed, it is not logical to conclude that everything is exactly like something else based on some commonality, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, these reasons such as "being a speaker" are non-probative (*ahetu*), because they lack the condition of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*) and because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the contrary case.

As for the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "an omniscient being does not exist because he is not perceived," one's own perception is unestablished (*asiddha*) in that regard, since the perception of both self and others is possible for all those who possess valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). ... [of] all omniscient ones.
This has been extracted... [regarding] the excellence of cognition... *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, Book II, page 252.
For comparison: "In this way, that kevalajñāna which is manifested through inference would not be established without scripture, and without it, scripture [would not exist]."
It is true that the excellence of a person is considered to arise solely from the power of the [ultimate] reality; however, its human composition is held to be beginningless— *Nyāyaviniścaya* 3.
Comparison: "But in the case of the negation of an omniscient being, speech and so forth are doubtful" — *Nyāyabindu* 2.2.12.

Comparison: If an omniscient being does not exist, then both one's own non-perception and the non-perception by all [others] are unestablished as grounds for doubt, because even that [non-perception] is not apprehended by those of limited vision.
"Non-perception by all [is] doubtful; non-perception by oneself is inconclusive. (Nyāyaviniścaya 3.406)
Because of the existence [of things] even when they are not perceived, such as the dūrvā grass within the hollows of the Vindhya mountains—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 65;
*Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 100.
*Tattvasaṃgraha* (verse), p. 13; *Ātmatattvaviveka*, p.

94: That which has no companion is "without companion" (*asahāya*), namely, the sense-faculty (*indriya*) which is beyond reasoning (*atarka*). Therefore, regarding the gradual increase of consciousness among living beings (*jīva*)—that is, sentient creatures—from those with only one sense-faculty up to those who know the meaning of the scriptures, the learned man does not indeed disagree. This is just as there is an increase in dimension starting from the dimension of an atom up to the dimension of space (*ākāśa*).

Surely this point will be established by the [following] counter-argument beginning with *siddhivi° 8.8*: "Omniscience would be established through the excellence of knowledge. Why, then, is it stated here? Therefore, it is explained otherwise: a learned person (*vidvān*), who is skilled in examining what has been said and what has not been said in the scriptures, does not disagree that there is an excellence of sensory cognition (*akṣavijñāna*) regarding the capacity of knowledge to grasp objects beyond the senses (*atīndriyārtha*).

Of whom? He says: "Of the knower of the meaning of the scriptures" (*ā śāstrārthavidaḥ*). One who knows from all sides (*ā samantāt*) the meaning of the entire scripture—whether the Veda or the science of light (*dyotiśāstra*)—which is beyond the senses, is a "knower of that meaning" (*tadarthavit*), that is, the omniscient one. Whence could there be any excellence superior to him? He says: "Because of the presence of the senses" (*akṣakṛt sahākṣābhāvāt*). Now, if it is asked: "In the absence of the senses, whence could he [be omniscient]? To this he replies: "Successively" (*kramāt*), that is, from perception and so forth as they have come down through tradition (*āmnāya*).
The genitive case in "jīvānām" is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

The intended meaning is: how could one who is himself learned and understands the sequence of the subject matter by reflecting upon the scriptures contradict another person who knows the meaning of the syllables without assistance?
The word "pratinā" is written twice.

Now, although there is disagreement among the established doctrines regarding the excellence of that [perception], since there is no other possible means of cognition for that which is absolutely imperceptible and beyond the reach of the senses,
it has been said regarding supersensuous knowledge: [atīndriyajñāne]...
Such a non-perception is said to be non-conclusive;
it is said to be non-conclusive regarding the determination of the existence or non-existence of objects that are beyond the senses. Such is this non-perception.

Therefore, there is no certain determination of existence or non-existence regarding things that are absolutely beyond the senses; rather, it has been stated that non-apprehension (anupalambha) concerning such supersensible objects does not produce certainty, because it can occur even when the object is actually present.

Consequently, for things that are absolutely beyond the senses, there is no certainty regarding their existence or non-existence, since the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is absent even when the object exists.
"Because even when the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are absent, the non-existence of the object is not established"— Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī 2.94.
The Buddhist [cites] Prajñāpāramitopadeśa 2.94; regarding that, he says: "of stationary beings and so forth," and so on.

Of what [group] is this? It says: "of the mass of living beings (*jīvarāśi*). By this, it is explained that [the group begins] with stationary things such as trees and ends with those who know the true essence of the meaning of the scriptures.

Among these, he who possesses a progressively superior excellence of intellect even beyond the next [level] is so described; no one is able to disagree with him regarding what is about to be said, except for the disciple of Śauddhodani (the Buddhist).

Of what kind [is he]? To this he says: "one who speaks with doubt regarding what is near and what is far," and so forth. Only such a person is capable of dissenting, because doubt is the basis for dissent.
If it is asked, "Why is another not capable of dissenting? to this he replies: "and for those who know the meaning of the treatise," and so forth.

The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also/even). Those who know the meaning by means of a treatise are "knowers of its meaning" (*tadarthavidaḥ*). For them, as well as for others who are subjects of dispute, there certainly exists in every way—that is, in all respects—an excellence of knowledge regarding that meaning, which is a preponderance of knowledge concerning the treatise's subject matter.
Why is this so? To this he says: "By nature," and so forth.
Because of the intensity of that [knowledge] which has as its primary factors both natural acuity and practice—such as [the effects of] medicine, military training, and the like.
To the question "How so?", the answer is provided by the words "upanibandha" and so forth.

For who indeed, while understanding the meaning of a treatise for themselves, would understand it elsewhere [without it]? By this, it is established that he is a learned person (*vidvān*). Likewise, if some particular individual were to possess a proficiency in supersensuous knowledge independent of the meaning of a treatise—attained through the practice of natural acuity in that very same manner—then nothing at all would be established [as valid].
By this, the rest is excluded;
however, non-apprehension whose object is remote— characterized by the cessation of perception and inference— is a cause of doubt (*Nyāyabindu* 2).
The meaning is that the remaining portion of the verse has been explained by the Buddhist.
He states the refutation of not accepting that [position] with the words "In that case," and so forth:

because, according to the Jaiminīyas and others, due to a specific distinction from ordinary [speech], the Veda would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by itself, independent of a person; rather, it would certainly be so.

Therefore, this is established: just as the Veda alone—despite there being no difference in its being speech—communicates its own meaning independently of a person, so too, despite there being no difference in their being persons, only some [individual] perceives an imperceptible object independently of the senses.

If it is objected that in this way no distinction would have been made between one's own position and the opposing position, and thus the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of the Veda would not have been refuted; to this he replies: "Among those in whom excellence is possible" means among those exceptional persons who possess the vision of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*). The connection is that the Veda would not be self-evidently authoritative; the sense is that its status as an authority depends precisely upon them—namely, upon those who possess knowledge of supersensible things.

It might be thought: "In the case of the Veda, which is independent of anything else, there exists no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to establish its meaning; however, in the case of a person who is independent of the senses, it is simply impossible for him to apprehend an object, and this impossibility serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*). Therefore, how can there be equality [between the two]? To this, he says: "The means of knowledge," and so forth.

The inclusion of the term "in the world" (*loke*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since [the non-existence of an omniscient being] is already established in some part of the world. What kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is there? The meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the Cārvāka does not accept [any such proof], on the grounds that the fivefold set of means of valid cognition—perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth—is contradictory to having non-existence as its object and would result in the futility of the means of valid cognition consisting of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*); we say: no. For one who maintains perception as the sole means of valid cognition, it is improper to prove the non-existence of [an omniscient being] everywhere in the world, because he himself would then incur omniscience, and because inference (*anumāna*) and the other means of knowledge do not exist for him.

The reply that "it belongs to him because of the opponent's admission" is not a valid answer; for that would entail the consequence of [the opponent] possessing supersensible knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*).
If it is argued: "Just as the opponent has no linguistic convention regarding that [object] without inference, so too let that [inference] be indistinct without supersensible knowledge";
we say no. Since inference exists, that [indistinct cognition] cannot be denied even if it were distinct—let this matter rest for now.
Non-existence is the means of proving that; as it has been said:
"For one who personally knows through direct perception that there is no omniscient being anywhere because of the absence of knowledge beyond the senses, [he himself possesses] omniscience."
And the worldly discourse of the Cārvāka proceeds solely on the basis of the opponent's own admission.
Inference, too,
is knowledge of supersensible objects without knowledge of pervasion.
Supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*) is that which has no negation; "non-negatable" (*aniṣedha*) means it is impossible to negate.
It is that in whose nature as a real entity the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish the non-existence of an omniscient being find no footing.
If it is argued that "the non-existence [of a means of knowledge] serves as the proof for that [non-existence] in order to realize the non-existence of the object" (*mī.
ślo. abhāva. ślo.

1*), we say no; for that [non-existence of a means of knowledge] would also be the proof for [the non-existence of] dharmas and so forth, since perception and the other means of knowledge do not operate with respect to them, just as they do not operate with respect to an omniscient being.

If it is argued that the absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there [in the case of the omniscient being] is unestablished because scripture (*āgama*) exists [to prove it], we say: no, for that [scripture] exists regarding the omniscient one as well. Thus he says: "In the absence of that"—meaning in the absence of an omniscient being—there is scripture for us; therefore, even in this case, the means of valid cognition called non-apprehension (*abhāva*) is considered unestablished with respect to supersensuous things such as *dharma* and so forth.
Non-existence is the establisher of non-existence with respect to phenomena and so forth.

If it is argued that the scripture is authoritative because it was spoken by an omniscient being, and the existence of an omniscient being follows from the authority of that scripture— thus resulting in a circular dependency— the author replies: "There exists that scripture which is not subverted by reasoning and not subverted by any means of valid cognition."

That scripture is not authoritative by virtue of being spoken by him; rather, it is understood that the scripture is authoritative as a scripture because it is free from contradiction, just like perception and other means of valid cognition.

[The opponent objects: "But surely the scripture [is authoritative] in that case. [The author replies: The scripture is unestablished because it is sublated by reasoning, since there exists a non-perception that sublates it.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "It does not exist," and so forth.

Regarding this [proof of] omniscience, some raise the following objection: if the omniscient person, who is the subject (*dharmin*), is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*);
if he is established, then a negation is untenable because it would be sublated by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends him; furthermore, the logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished.
There is no non-perception of that which is established, because that would be a contradiction.

For what purpose, then, has this inference been presented? Some say it is merely a restatement of another's view; but this is not so, because for the opponent that [inference] does not exist, nor does its existence arise from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since its non-existence is being proven by that very means. Furthermore, a discerning person does not state another's view if it is incoherent. To this, it is replied: what has thus been described is the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), not inference.

To explain: how does the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) arise regarding the claim that "there is no omniscient being"? He says: from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), that is, from the absence of the five means of valid cognition.
What is it like? To this he says: "like a sky-flower."
Alternatively, this is an *arthāpatti* (presumption) independent of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*);

or else, from the perspective of the Jaina doctrine, it is an "inference by another" (*parānumāna*) stated [by the opponent], for their view is as follows: "An omniscient being exists, because there is a well-ascertained means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that precludes the possibility of any sublation, just like pleasure and so forth."

Regarding this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the following is said: if there were a cessation of the means of proof (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*)—that is, the cessation of the means of proof that establishes an omniscient being—or if the self were devoid of such [a means], then the non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) would entail the consequence of selflessness (*nairātmya*) for each respective case.
Why? To this he says: "The self of all," and so forth;
demonstrating that very point, he says:

If it is argued that one who is not all-seeing cannot directly perceive those specificities of all things that are established in such a way, but rather cognizes them through inference—to this he replies: "Not that very [thing]," and so forth.

Precisely because he is unable to directly perceive them, for that very reason inference is impossible; this expression (*asatyatram*) is a term where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent.
Of whom? He says: "within each individual," and so forth.
Why? He says: "the sign," and so forth, [referring to] the Omniscient One.

If it is argued that because there is no omniscient being, the Jaina’s [doctrine] cannot be known through inference from another person, and therefore [all things] must consist of both the universal and the particular—that is not correct. If it is then asked why inference is impossible regarding the specific qualities of individual selves (*pratyātma-viśeṣa*), he replies: "Because of the non-distinction of that," and so forth.
The particle *tat* functions in the sense of *tasmāt* (therefore);

therefore, from that inference which establishes the reality of an object as consisting of multiple natures—in what manner? He says: "without distinction," that is, by way of generality (*sāmānyena*).

It might be argued: "The specific qualities of another self are not cognized through inference because they are not conjoined with any particularity; for if they were, it would follow that perception and inference are indistinguishable, and thus inference would be impossible regarding the specific qualities of individual selves. To this he replies: "From some [particularity]," etc.

If there is a cognition of those [qualities] from some particularity such as specific behavior, and if there is a cognition of the specific qualities of the individual selves, then [it follows that] there must be something inseparably connected (*avinābhāvin*) with those unperceived specificities.

It is thought thus: even the cognition of anger and so forth, due to specific factors such as outward behavior (*vyavahāra*), is indeed inference. Furthermore, that [inference] takes anger and the like as its object through a subordinate generality (*avāntara-sāmānya*), and not by way of a restricted particularity.
For it is not impossible for inference to apprehend the subtle particulars of the momentary nature of anger and so forth;

otherwise, their non-perception would entail their non-existence. This is not correct, because it would follow that the generality of anger and so forth—which, by its very nature, does not exist without a particularity that has not been cognized, and which is thus invariably concomitant with an unperceived particularity—would likewise lack self-nature (*anātmakatva*).

For instance: in relation to the subtle distinctions that perish at every moment, there exist general and particular qualities belonging to the self; in the absence of those [distinctions], even they would not belong to it. Furthermore, since the self is not perceived as something distinct from them, its non-existence would constitute *nairātmya* (the absence of self).
If it is asked, "What fault is there in that?"—to this he replies with the words beginning "thence" (*tataḥ*).

Therefore, because there is no apprehension of anything due to selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is no apprehension of anything whatsoever; thus, due to the absence of apprehension, there would be a total non-existence of everything— just as in the case of an omniscient being—
and this includes verbal expression, speech, and inference.

The word "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) is written twice; thus, there is no fault, as specific individualities are understood from what has been heard. To this, he says: "Even of what has been heard," and so forth;
for not only in the case of perception and the like, but even in the case of what has been heard, there is the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*).
Why? He says: "For not... and so forth.
Why is that? He says: "Because the accomplishment of the human goal has a specific object.
Now, if it is argued that the scripture does indeed take [the goal] as its object, he says in response: "Otherwise... and so forth.
Concluding that, by this method of making [the object] its domain without exception, the scripture itself is indeed not to be attended to, he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.

Since it is thus, therefore (*tat*), for that reason (*tasmāt*), this aforementioned cessation of the cognizer’s means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the cessation of the cognizer, the Mīmāṃsaka, of the means of valid cognition such as perception regarding the omniscient one—is impossible to apprehend even though it pertains to all [cognizers].

The mention of the "cognizer" (pratipattr) establishes not only the absence of an omniscient being, but furthermore establishes the exclusion of all things and the non-existence of every entity. This is because in states such as sleep, intoxication, and fainting, that [omniscience] is absent in all cases. As for the claim that others do not see everything at those times—what is the basis for this? Moreover, if one were to see him by means of that very same [knowledge], what would be distinguished in the case of seeing an omniscient being in another life? Or else, for the proponent of the absolute doctrine of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), there is a cessation of that [knowledge] everywhere.

And just as there is no absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*), namely non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), regarding dharma and so forth when they are understood from scripture (*śāstra*), so too is everything [to be understood in this way]. To demonstrate this, he addresses himself to the opponent with a question: "If that is so, then what is the proof for the existence of the Omniscient One? To that, he says: "We state that the scripture is the answer.
Why? To this he replies: "Because of that," and so forth;

because it establishes the actual existence of that Omniscient One by describing the fourteen stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*), and not merely by mentioning [his] supernatural attainments (*labdhi*).

If it is asked, "How is the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of this scripture, which establishes the existence of that [Omniscient One], established?"—this is the position of the opponent. To this, the reply is: "Then how is the authority of the *codanā* [established]? Here, *codanā* refers to the Vedic statement that establishes *dharma* and so forth; how is its authority established? [The opponent thinks: "If both lack authority, there would be the disappearance of *dharma* and the rest.
Thus, the existence of the Omniscient One is established through the attainment of falsehood (*mithyātva*), the destruction of karma (*sāsādana*), and so on, up to the stage of the *ayogakevalin*.

The opponent says: "Because of its eternity, that [scripture] is authoritative. [The author] replies: "Precisely because of that eternity, let there be authority for the *pravacana*—the scripture which sets forth the stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*).
How so? Thus the opponent asks regarding the *pravacana*; the answer to that begins with "Just as," and so forth.
An attendant asks: "In that case, how is the eternity of the injunction established? The Vedic scholar replies: "Because its author is not remembered.
The Teacher says: "Precisely for that reason," and so forth—that is, the eternity of the supreme scripture follows from the very fact that its author is not remembered.

If it is argued that "the Tīrthaṃkaras are remembered as the authors of the supreme scripture"—this is the objection raised by the opponent; here is the reply: "Of the Veda," etc., [stating] the Mīmāṃsaka's [position on] authority.
The Mīmāṃsaka objects: "But surely they remember that the Vedas have authors, and their remembrance is not a valid means of knowledge. To this, he replies: "Kaṇabhakṣa," and so forth.

Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas, Buddhists, and others maintain that there is no difference regarding the authority of the memory concerning the author of the supreme scripture (paramāgama) held by other Mīmāṃsakas compared to that of the Veda and the supreme scripture.

If it is argued: "In the case of the Veda, that memory belongs only to the opponents (paravādins) and not to the proponents (vādins); therefore, it is not authoritative. However, in the case of the well-established teaching (pravacana), that memory belongs to both parties, and thus it is not unauthoritative"; to this he replies with the words "tadetad" and so forth.

If it is asked: "When this scripture, which establishes the Omniscient One, is examined, it is non-personal (apauruṣeya) and eternal; if it is non-personal, what do the founders of other sects (tīrthakaras) do therein that leads to such a conception?"—to this he replies: "The founders set it in motion; they manifest the scripture as it has been handed down. If it is asked why [the Jains say this], it is because they accept the eternity [of the scripture] due to the eternal continuity of the tradition of the Omniscient One and his scripture.
How, then, is there the complete cessation of that twelvefold [scripture]? It is like the Vedic scriptures;
just as in their case, the recollection of these [twelve] states by teachers is not the cause [of their authority]. Thus, the recollection of an author is established in every respect.
It has been lost in the teaching of the Mīmāṃsakas.

The teachers who are disciples of the Jaina [tradition] state what is obtained when this is the case: "From what [cause]?"—that is, from no cause whatsoever. Since the principle is established in that very way, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*) which would render this [argument] untenable.
"Then it would not be established through scripture, nor would there be scripture without it" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanā, verse 142).
Showing also that which is obtained from the subsequent [verse], he says: "That is not so," and so forth.

The meaning is this: since scripture is indeed an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), therefore no inference whatsoever can establish the non-existence of everything, because inference does not operate within the domain of scripture.
As it has been said by some:
"They perceive with the eye of the seers (*ārṣa*) those things that are beyond the senses and imperceptible."
"For those whose statement is based on [direct] experience, it is not sublated by inference" (Vākyapadīya 1.38).
If it is argued that he is not the subject of the treatise, to this he replies: "And the teaching," and so forth.
Thus, it is established and certain that he is omniscient.

If it is argued: "Granted that there may be no inference [to prove this], yet there might be another scripture that establishes it, since they possess equal force," to this he replies: "There is no such intention regarding what is to be known"—that is, the teaching of non-absolutism (anekānta) is not one that fails to demonstrate the manifold transformations of souls.
For if something is the proponent of a certain state, it is contradictory for that very same thing to be its negator.
And if you say it is something else, we reply: nor is there any other scripture that serves as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) to contradict it.
Why? He says: "Because its object is not sublated by the *syādvāda*," and so forth;
he provides an illustration: "like the *Piṭakatraya*," which is a proof for the non-existence of an omniscient being.
Rather, it is precisely that which establishes [the truth], namely the three baskets known as the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, which are prohibitive.
[Objection: But how could the scope of the *Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama* be sublated by the *syādvāda*, given that the *syādvāda* itself has its scope sublated by it? To this, he says: "For that," and so forth.

For that [doctrine] being propounded in the *Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama*—because (*hi*) a single-sided (*ekānta*) view is not possible—what [is it]? And so forth; or [it is said to be] "without an object" (*nirviṣaya*), and so forth. Thus [he explains].
How is this not possible? To this he says: "This has been made into a royal road," by which he shows its status as a mere substitute.

For instance: since [inference] would be without an object (*nirviṣaya*), what could be established from that false cognition (*mithyājñāna*)? Indeed, no establishment of reality (*tattvasiddhi*) can come from such a [cognition] devoid of an object, just like the cognition of two moons and so forth.

If it is argued that there is a deviation [from the rule] because, through inference, one attains the realization of reality even from a false cognition—such as the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel (where the cognition is indeed false)—we say no; for that [inference] is included within the category of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, if inference were indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*), then it would have to be free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*); thus, there is no deviation by means of it.

If it is argued that for one who, by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), believes "the very same jewel seen is the one now obtained"—and thus for him that [recognition] is perception (*pratyakṣa*)—then for a Mīmāṃsaka or similar proponent who likewise considers the single recognition "this is that very same person" to be non-contradictory to what arises from the senses, that too would have to be perception. Therefore, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not twofold simply because objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are twofold; for even if this [recognition] were perception, its object would still be a universal (*sāmānya*), which contradicts the absolute [definition] of perception as being free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*).

And how could this statement— "Whatever appears as what it is" and so forth— be well-said for one who speaks thus [denying momentariness], given that momentariness is established by direct perception?
For if, upon investigation, this [momentariness] were not perceived directly, then for that very reason, let there be no direct perception of the subject at hand either,
just as in the case of two people running toward the light of a jewel or a lamp while perceiving it as a jewel.
Even though there is no distinction among false cognitions, there is a distinction with respect to causal efficiency— Pramāṇavārttika 2.57.
Therefore, let it be understood that all cognition which arises— whether before or after the contact of the sense organ with its object, or even from memory— is perception.
— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 4.236;
recognition as well.
Regarding recognition,
perception is indeed non-conceptual;
such is the case for recognition.
Because it consists of deliberation (*vicāra*),
by this [reasoning] the status of being perception (*pratyakṣatva*) has been considered with respect to a future object to be attained.
Furthermore, if perception were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding a future object, there would be a contradiction of two logical constraints (*pratibandha*).
And since a future cause has been refuted, this [position] is thereby rejected:
that "even though there is a discrepancy with one's intention, there is still validity because of the absence of error."
"Furthermore, wind is seen otherwise, and this [argument regarding] the subject has already been answered" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.56).
This might be the thought: "If perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to what is yet to come, then it would not be a valid means of knowledge at all;

but if it were [valid] with respect to the present, what fault would there be? Nor is it appropriate to apply [the charge of] deviation everywhere simply because deviation is observed in some instances of the present, for that [charge] would then follow even in the case of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)," as has been stated.

Furthermore, if inference is non-erroneous (*avisaṃvāda*), how can it be without an object? If you argue that this is because its object is a universal (*sāmānya*) which is not a real entity (*avastu*), then perception (*pratyakṣa*) would likewise be so. In that case, by what means could the non-erroneous nature of the inference of a gem based on the luster of a gem be recognized? For it has been stated that the perception of the gem to be reached does not grasp partless atoms (*paramāṇu*); therefore, this argument amounts to nothing. Indeed, even in perception, one thing is seen while another is obtained.

Now, as for what was said—that "the Tīrthaṅkaras set forth the teaching"—let that be true; however, they are not omniscient because they possess speech and other such qualities, just like an ordinary man on the street. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "If, moreover," and so forth.
He states the refutation therein: "If [my words] were not otherwise," and so forth, [arguing] from the reasons of being a speaker, being a human being, possessing hands, feet, and so on.

[Objection: "But surely, omniscience has been observed in other persons where speakerhood and so forth exist, and since speakerhood and so forth are also observed in the Tīrthaṅkara, let that [omniscience] exist in him too. Otherwise, how could there be the cognition of impermanence from the property of being produced (kṛtakatva) and so forth? To this, he says: "Not indeed," and so on. It is certainly not logical to conclude that because of some similarity—namely, the similarity of speakerhood and so forth—between the Tīrthaṅkara and another person, everything such as non-omniscience must likewise exist in that same manner as the speakerhood and so forth. This is because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga): if one were to see that a speaker is foolish, then everyone would have to be so.
If, however, that person is seen to be wise only occasionally, then it would be the same even in the case of an omniscient being; thus,
let there be non-omniscience in the fool.
The speaker, concluding [the argument], says: "Therefore, these," and so forth;
since it is thus, therefore these—namely, the qualities of being a speaker and so on, which are asserted by the opponent—are not valid reasons.

If it is asked, "Why? [the author] shows by means of the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth that [the reason] lacks the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), because it lacks identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth. This has been established by the statement "because of its presence here.

[One might ask: "How can it be devoid of that [identity], since an omniscient knower perceives them at all times? [The answer is: Because there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary case (*vipakṣa*).

If it is argued that there is a contradiction—such as that between being produced and so forth—which acts as a sublater, we say no; for there is an absence of any means of apprehending such a contradiction.

For if a decrease in that [omniscience] were to occur upon an increase in cognition, then a realization of contradiction might exist; but since this is not the case, non-apprehension is the sublater in that instance. Thus he says: "The omniscient one," and so forth.

If one accepts that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum—namely, "an omniscient being does not exist because he is not perceived"—is being established, the author states the following refutation:
"If [it is argued] that 'he is not perceived by anyone'... and so forth; and regarding this, he says: "In respect of all means of valid cognition" (*sarvaprāmāṇya*), and so forth.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Of all omniscient beings," and so forth;
[this refers to] the fact that identity and the other [logical reasons] lack the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).
In the case of an omniscient being, there is a depreciation of the status of being a speaker for one who perceives a contradiction.

If it is asked: "Since omniscient beings exist, how is it that they do not perceive themselves or another as omniscient? To this, he says: "In the case of doubt regarding the existence of an omniscient being," and so forth;
[the meaning is that] when there is doubt regarding the existence of an omniscient being, non-perception (anupalambha) is not established [as proof of non-existence].
Consequently, there would be a mutual dependency among all these reasons.

Just as there is a mutual dependency in the argument "there is no omniscient being," so too is the proof of the universal presence of passion and the like refuted— namely, that "all persons other than those on the street are possessed of passion and the like, because they are speakers, etc., just like him"— insofar as the non-perception of an omniscient speaker is itself dependent on that same premise.

Likewise, since the means of proof for that [omniscience]—such as the words of Jaimini and others—are themselves to be proven, the Veda is not a valid authority while other [means] are; thus, regarding the existence of omniscient beings which is asserted by the opponent, non-perception (*anupalambha*)—that is, the non-perception of all [omniscient beings]—is not established. Furthermore, if one who perceives both self and others were to prove their non-existence through the non-perception of those [beings], the same fault remains, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) or a circular argument (*cakraka*), as they consider.

Now, if it is thought: "He who perceives both himself and another is called omniscient"; and if it is argued that he is not omniscient because, being a person (*puruṣatva*) and so forth, he is like a man on the street—then it has been said in response to this: these are not valid reasons because they lack the condition of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*).

If it is argued that the non-perception of the state of being a person, of speech, and of omniscience constitutes the intended pervasion (*vyāpti*), then that same [fallacy] recurs, resulting in a circular argument (*cakraka*).
Furthermore, is this non-perception one's own or of everyone? And so forth.

Now, it might be argued that by establishing the absence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), properties such as "being human" or the like establish the existence of an omniscient being somewhere; however, this is not the case, for [the reason] must be pervaded by that [omniscience]. But if there is doubt regarding the non-existence of an omniscient being, how can that pervasion (*vyāpti*) be established? If you say that the absence of doubt regarding that [omniscience] follows from that very [pervasion], then there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).
For instance: once the pervasion is established, the absence of that [omniscience] is established; and once that is established, the pervasion is established.

Thus he says: "Therefore, because non-perception (*anupalambha*) is unestablished, there would be a mutual dependence among all reasons—such as 'being human' and so forth—in establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being or in establishing the pervasion."
He states the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in order to explain the verse: "There is no omniscient one," and so forth.

Just as there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*)—wherein the perception of the non-existence of all things is established only if the non-existence of the omniscient one is established, and the non-existence of that [omniscient one] is established only if the perception of the non-existence of all things is established—exactly the same mutual dependence applies when the non-perception of the speaker who is omniscient is being proven.

For instance: once the non-existence of an omniscient being has been established, the fact that no speaker who is omniscient is perceived constitutes the proof of his absence; thus, the non-perception of an omniscient speaker is the proof for the non-existence of an omniscient being.
Extending this [argument] to other cases, he says "by this," and so forth.

By this, the proof for the possession of passion (*rāga*) and so on by the person under discussion is refuted. In what form is that proof? He says: "in its entirety"—that is, all persons other than the man in the street possess passion and so on, because they possess the quality of being speakers and so forth, just like him.

If it is asked, "How is this refuted?", it is said: likewise, when proving that [the Vedas are authoritative], even for Jaimini and others, the Vedas are a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in one case and not in another; otherwise, if only a specific person were to prove it, then Jaimini or someone else might be the opposite of that. Thus, there is an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) of the reasons.
The rest here is the same as before.
Having thus established the lack of authority for the statement that urges [the Arhat] toward reality in the proof that the Arhat possesses passion and so forth, now—
Because it is a statement, the statement of an injunction (*codanā*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like any other statement;

in that regard, the cognition of a previously unknown object (*apūrvārtha*) is established as being free from sublation and is recognized by the world as a valid cognition produced by non-defective causes. Thus.
Demonstrating that very point through the logic of another school, he says: "The means of valid cognition [is] of sensory perception... and so forth;
this was cited from the Bhāṭṭa [tradition]—Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 33.
Pra° Parī° pṛ° 63;
Ta° Ślo° pṛ° 173; Prameyaka° pṛ° 611.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 318; Nayopadeśa, p.
33: "If the validity of sensory cognition [is established] through the ascertainment of non-sublation..."
"It is a rash assertion to claim that an omniscient being does not exist when the impossibility of sublation has been determined.

If the validity of visual and other types of cognition—or any other—is established by its own uncontradicted object-domain, then it is likewise logical for the [omniscient] Teacher’s teaching to possess validity.

Therefore, an omniscient being exists, because there is no valid means of knowledge that can definitively establish his non-existence, just as in the case of pleasure and so forth, or blue and so forth."

In this context, that which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is well-ascertained and for which no sublation is possible is [established] through the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*). The mention of "sensory cognition" (*akṣabuddhi*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), and thus the cognition arising from Vedic injunction (*codanā*) and so forth is also included. If its validity is determined by the very manner in which it has arisen—provided that the impossibility of sublation is ascertained, meaning it is so described because the impossibility [of sublation] has been determined—then [the claim] that [this applies] to an omniscient being is mere audacity; such is the sense.
To explain the verse, he says: "Of the cognition of the eye and so forth," etc.

If the validity of another cognition or injunction were established by itself, through its own nature, by what means would it be known? It is by having an uncontradicted object; therefore, by virtue of having an uncontradicted object, the validity of the teaching—even the scripture that establishes the existence of an omniscient being—is also logical. He states "therefore" and so forth to show that [the omniscient one] is free from defects in this context.

Therefore, on the basis of the authority of the teaching (*pravacana*), [the author] asks: "How does it follow that there is an omniscient being? He replies: "Because of the state of—that is, the reality of—that which possesses such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as is well-ascertained and free from any possible sublation;
he provides an illustration: 'pleasure and so forth,' etc."

If it is argued that two examples are presented here by way of distinguishing between external and internal objects—namely, that while perception and other means of knowledge possess well-ascertained and non-occurring sublation (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding pleasure and so forth, or blue and so forth, this is not the case regarding the Omniscient One, and therefore the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*)—to this he replies with the words beginning "well-ascertained" (*suniścita*). The phrase "well-ascertained and non-occurring sublation" refers to what has been stated by the opponent regarding the Omniscient One; the word "refuted" (*pratyukta*) is understood to follow.
Why? To this he says: "On account of the authority of the scripture"—that is, on account of the authority of the Āgama that establishes it according to the stated principle.
The comparison is: "That exists, because there is no possible sublation [of it], as is the case with pleasure and so forth" (Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti 1.4).
*Tattvasaṃgraha* verse 185;
*Āptamīmāṃsā* verse 109;
*Aṣṭaśatī* on page 44 of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*.
Praṇamya-mīmāṃsā, p.
14; Prajñā-nīti, p. 29; Ṣaḍdarśana-samuccaya-bṛhaspati-vṛtti, p. 14.

Others read "because of the lack of authority of the treatises" (*śāstrāprāmāṇyāt*); for them, has the very support of its own authority—which was explained immediately before—been forgotten, such that they read it thus? For the commentators, the phrase "its own authority" (*mevatprāmāṇyam*) is written twice here redundantly.
Now, for the justification of the authority of scripture:
let it be understood that the validity of all means of valid cognition is intrinsic.

Relying on two positions held by others— namely, "A capacity that does not exist inherently cannot be produced by another" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.4), and "Valid cognition is that which is produced by non-defective causes, as is commonly accepted in the world"— he establishes the authority of that [Buddhist] teaching, saying: "In the Omniscient One exists," and so forth.

The Mīmāṃsaka position is that the cognition "the Omniscient One exists" is valid by its very nature, because it lacks causes possessed of defects and because there is no possibility of sublation. (7)
The cognition that "the Omniscient One exists" is not non-authoritative in itself,

nor does it have a defective cause; furthermore, since the scripture that establishes him is also not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) is indeed established by one's own perception...

Since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be established without the non-perception of something, it would follow that the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) is futile;

for the cognition of existence occurs entirely independently of signs (*liṅga*), sense organs (*indriya*), and so forth. Therefore, there is a contradiction in the cognition of the non-existence of an omniscient being.
Consequently, the cognition that arises regarding the object of an omniscient being—namely, "the omniscient one exists"—is valid by itself (*svataḥ*) and not from any other cause.
He states another reason: "Because of the absence of a faulty cause.
The word "api" (also/even) shifts the grammatical sequence and is to be understood immediately after this [phrase].
Why is that? He says: "Because of the impossibility of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*)."

Immediately after [the statement] "from scripture" and "due to the absence of a faulty cause," he speaks while explaining the verse, beginning with: "The cognition that 'it exists in the omniscient one'... and so forth.
Whence is this? To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
Now, if it is argued that its inherent validity—which is its natural state—is set aside by the fact of its being produced from causes possessed of defects; to this he says: "And not," and so forth.
And it is certainly not the case that the cognition under discussion has as its cause something possessed of defects—that which has such a defective cause.
Why? He says: "That," etc.

Because that [scripture]—the scripture that establishes him, namely the one that establishes the Omniscient One—is not merely Vedic, but is *apauruṣeya* (authorless), and thus devoid of any person who could be a locus of defects.

[Objection: But surely its cause may possess those defects, just as there is the cognition of yellow in a white conch-shell; and furthermore, the cognition regarding the Omniscient One is indeed sublated. To this he replies: The absence of any subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is already established.
By this, he states that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
If it is argued that non-perception (*anupalambha*) is the subverting proof (*bādhaka*), he says in response: "one's own perception," and so forth.

If it is argued that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is the subverting proof, he says in response: because without the non-perception of someone—whether it be the non-perception of a certain omniscient being or of anyone else—the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be established; and since the non-existence [of the probandum] would not be established, it would follow that the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is futile.

If it is argued that "otherwise, while the non-existence of that [object] might not be established through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), it would be established through perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) would be redundant," the opponent replies: "That is indeed accepted, because that [perception] is not distinct from [ordinary] perception."
He replies to that: "In its entirety," and so forth.

In establishing the non-existence [of duality] through perception, does duality exist in some respect or in its entirety? The first position is not suspected as being subject to refutation because it is accepted; for the existence of all things is accompanied by its opposite.

As for the second position, does duality arise from the sense organs or from something else? Here too, the first position is not suspected [as being untenable] because it is unacceptable to the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), since the operation of the eyes and other senses extends only to what is present.
Only two positions remain regarding the two types of dualism (*kevala-dvaita*);

therein, because it is a contradiction for a Mīmāṃsaka or similar proponent—who is himself (*svayam*), by his own nature (*ātmanā*), and entirely (*sākalyena*) independent of signs, sense organs, and so forth—to have a cognition of existence while simultaneously having a cognition of the non-existence of an omniscient being, the implication is that such a cognition [of the latter] must exist.
For instance: if someone were to have a cognition of the non-existence of that [omniscient being] by himself and in its entirety, he himself would be omniscient; thus, there is a cognition of him.
If that is not the case, then [the claim] "he is omniscient" is not a cognition of him;
or else, because there is a contradiction with such a cognition of him, [there is] non-connection (*asamprayoga*), according to Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.4.

Since the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) for such [statements] is already established, the existence of the Omniscient One has thus been proven through scripture—just like *dharma* and so forth—by means of what is accepted by others. Consequently, the objection beginning with *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 1: "The five means of knowledge do not arise regarding that nature of a thing... and so forth, is refuted.

The means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) has two alternatives because it depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratipakṣa*), just as existence depends upon non-existence.
That which is connected and present is apprehended by the eye and other [senses]— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sūtra 4, Verse 84;
[this concerns] the non-existence of an omniscient being and the cognition of an omniscient being.
The realization of the non-existence of an omniscient being must be complete; for if it were not a realization of the non-existence of an omniscient being,
then perception would be defined as "that cognition which arises in a person when there is contact of the sense organs with an existing object" (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.4).
The remainder of the sense is that "the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*abhāvapramāṇatā*) is for the purpose of realizing the existence of a real entity (*vastusattā*).
Now, having established that [existence] through inference and then refuting it, he says: "Of knowledge," and so forth, [referring to] the existence of an omniscient being.

The treatise on the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), beginning with the five types and including non-apprehension (*abhāva*), establishes that omniscience is achieved through the excellence of knowledge, just as [the measurement of] magnitude is established. This is the comparison: for that which is increasing in this manner reaches its limit where it is unsurpassed; he is the omniscient one.

There is an attainment of the ultimate limit for the seed of the omniscient one because it is capable of exceeding [all others], like a measurement; he in whom there is this attainment of the limit of knowledge is the omniscient one—
*Yogabhāṣya* 1.25.
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 12: "Clarity [of cognition] arises in some cases from the removal of the stains of defects, as in the case of the eye [cured of] cataracts (timira).
Just as... clarity [arises] from the destruction of the two obstructions (varaṇa), due to the removal of stains, as in the case of [the eye freed from] cataracts..."
Where would the sovereignty of knowledge—characterized by the direct realization of all objects of knowledge—be established?

And why [would it be established] in a person who has reached the limit of the cultivation of the antidote to impurity? To this he says: "Because of the increase due to excellence," that is, of knowledge.
Of what [is this said]? He says: "like that which undergoes transformation" (*pariṇāmavat*).
By this, the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the Sugata and others is also explained;
the word *vā* has the sense of "or" (*iva*).
If it is argued: "Granted that he possesses such sovereignty, yet there would be neither a clear nor a complete cognition of all pervasions," to this he replies: "Clarity," and so forth;
the phrase "due to the excellence of cognition" is understood to carry over, meaning "due to the excellence of those two."
Regarding this, he states the following in order to explain the verse, just as for one whose vision is cleared of cataracts; the passage beginning with "just as" is easy to understand.
If it is asked, "Whence comes its clarity?"—to this he provides the illustration beginning with "there is no defect" and so forth: "in the absence of darkness," etc.
It might be thought: [this occurs] due to the destruction of defects and obscurations.
If it is argued that even in this case there is no absolute destruction because its [impurity] is seen to persist in some instances, to this he replies: "Of the ruby and so forth," etc.
Just as the removal of impurity from a ruby and such is indeed preeminent—that is, absolute—so too is it for a certain soul.
For there is no deviation anywhere due to the cause being excessive;

thus, the absence of consciousness certainly exists [in some cases]. Due to ignorance... for one who does not know the scriptures, in the case of *māṇikya* gems and so forth—the word "and so forth" including gold and the like—an excessive, increasing removal of impurities such as rust, dross, and the like, becomes indeed absolute for someone who possesses the excellence of applying the remedy against those impurities. Just as that is so for them, so too does such a [removal] certainly occur for the self as well.

If it is argued that for one whose character is characterized by the excellence of effort in the means of purification, even the ultimate cessation of cognition is seen to possess a degree of excellence, and thus that [cessation] might also be ultimate in some cases—otherwise, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) of the reason—the author replies here: "For not in this case... and so forth.

Indeed, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) here regarding the reason "because of the absence of excellence [in the self]"; for just as there is an absence of insentient action in the self, so too there is an absence of the insentient in some cases within the self. Since this is included within the probandum (sādhya), there is no deviation.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In some cases," etc.;
for in matter (pudgala) in the form of a clod of earth and so forth, there is indeed an absence of insentience.
Why? He says: "Because of ignorance," and so forth.
Why [is this so]? He says: "Until one knows the scripture.

Now, one might object: for a Jaina, a reason is not a means of knowledge merely through an illustrative example (*nidarśana*), but rather by the force of a sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding its presence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); and there is no such sublation against the excellence of knowledge in the absence of omnipresence (*vibhutva*). To this, he replies: "Knowledge," and so forth.
If knowledge were not incomparable [and] all-pervading by its very nature, how could one know the uncreated Vedas, which are devoid of any omniscient author? (10)
This has been established:
therefore, cognition necessarily pervades its own object as a substance and as an intrinsic nature; any error regarding it arises from external causes such as cataracts.

Since the diminution of passion and other defects is observed when their antidote is present, the attainment of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)—which is the release from the veil of defects through the excellence of its application—is simply the perception of one's own nature, and not a transcendence of that nature.

Therefore, even the analogy of jumping and so forth does not obstruct the attainment of the ultimate limit of the excellence of the nature of knowledge, because of the disparity between the two cases.
If it is asked, "If knowledge does not exist, what would it be like? he says: "It is incomparable, beyond further impurity, transcendent to the senses, pure, and uncontradicted."

Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "all-pervading" (sarvagata), meaning capable of discerning all objects. Since its own great self is independent of the senses and so forth, by what means of knowledge (pramāṇa) does the Mīmāṃsaka or the Lokāyatika know or perceive the worlds (loka)—that is, the universes? He says: "devoid of omniscience."

Or should one view all people in the world as being devoid of omniscience? From where would one know the Vedas to be uncreated and without beginning or end? For it is not possible to know them without such knowledge, since sensory perception lacks the capacity for that, and there is an absence of inference;
"stainless" (nirmala) means that which transcends impurity.

Now, if it is argued: "Is this not the case—that the space and time under dispute are devoid of an omniscient person, like space and time that are currently non-existent? We say: no. It has already been stated here that these are not valid reasons because they lack *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of the reason being true otherwise). Otherwise, why would all [reasons]—such as the perception of a certain place or time as devoid of a learned person by one who lacks the perception of his own mother’s marriage—not likewise prove [the absence of an omniscient being]? Furthermore, what prevents another person from seeing him at a different time? This is because scripture (*āgama*) is not a means of valid cognition regarding his non-existence, and because [scripture] concerns subjects such as supernatural knowledge (*vidyā*).

Furthermore, analogy (*upamāna*) is utterly excluded [from proving an omniscient being], because it is impossible for there to be any relationship between an object of comparison and its counterpart when neither has been directly perceived in terms of their actual nature, place, or time.

As for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it is likewise untenable, because no phenomenon is observed that could not exist without the state of an omniscient being. Alternatively, one might argue: "The past time was devoid of an omniscient being, because it is time, just like the present time."

—Mīmāṃsā-sloka-vārttika, Tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 75: Because of [the absence of] place or because of the absence of time, [one infers] the lands of the Persians to be devoid of the marriage of one's mother, and certain times to be devoid of scholars.
Gradually, over time, even someone who was not a scholar becomes a scholar; for in the absence of an omniscient being,
the Vedic scripture possesses authority regarding matters of duty (*kāryārtha*), but not regarding its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
By this, the beginninglessness of the Vedas is also considered;
for there is no inference regarding them, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*),
while [arguments] such as the non-remembrance of an author have already been answered.

If it is argued that the non-artificiality [of the Veda] is established merely by the existence of other scriptures (*āgama*); from what, then, does the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of those [scriptures] derive? If you say "from those very [scriptures]," there is a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): once their non-artificiality is established, their authority follows, and from that authority, their non-artificiality is established.

Furthermore, there is no other such statement by which, through similarity with it, the non-artificiality of the Veda could be established. Nor is there anything perceived apart from that which would be otherwise inexplicable (*anupapanna*), such that its non-artificiality could be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Only direct perception remains;
if that is incapable of taking as its object a time that is beginningless and endless, then how can there be any cognition of it? [The answer is:
Precisely because it is uncreated (*akṛtrima*).
To explain that there exists a knowledge which is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), incomparable, and all-pervading, he says: "This has been done," and so forth;
"this" refers to what has been determined.
What is it? He says: "arising," etc., concluding with "therefore," etc.—by this reasoning, cognition, as the agent, necessarily pervades; that is, it necessarily takes [the object] as its domain.
What [is it]? What kind of substance? To this he says: "its own nature," and so forth.

If it is argued that because it is non-distinct from everything, it would pervade all things; to this he replies: "in the form of the illumination or non-illumination of its own object, there arises its opposite. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the opposite—characterized by non-occurrence, lack of clarity, or falsity—arises for that cognition."

Why? He says: "From something external, such as cataracts (timira) and so forth. Here, [the question is] from what does the accomplishment characterized by their destruction arise? He says: "From the counteragent," and so forth.

The antidote to defects (*doṣa*) and obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) is right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and the rest; for when these exist, we observe the diminution of passion and other afflictions, the perception of objects never before seen, and the initiation of that which has no other author, such as the composition [of this treatise]. Furthermore, in the absence of the removal of obscurations, knowledge cannot be directed toward its own object, as is observed in the case of one whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts. Its application is its completeness; because of the excellence of that [completeness], the defect (*doṣa*) consisting of passion and so forth has been explained in the *Pramāṇasaṃgrahabhāṣya*. An obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is karma that veils knowledge and the rest; from their separation, the attainment of isolation (*kaivalya*) occurs.

Of what nature is it? He says: it is simply the perception of one's own nature, because the existence of one's own nature belongs to all souls, and because there is the perception of a completely new object in every respect.

It might be thought that for one who is not omniscient, the postulation of omniscience would constitute a transgression of his own nature (*svabhāva*). To this he replies: "But not" (*na punaḥ*), meaning there is no transgression of the soul's nature of being a knower of some things (*kiñcijjñatva*) when that [omniscience] is postulated; for if one were to postulate a transgression of its nature, the soul would cease to exist because of that very nature.

Because that is its very nature, once omniscience has been established as having such a nature as the self (*ātmasvabhāva*), [the author], demonstrating the established result, says "Therefore... and so forth. Since, due to the excellence of knowledge, omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is the nature of the self and—because it is to be accomplished through the destruction of impurities—it is not to be accomplished by further effort; therefore, by the word "etc. in the phrase "transgressing [limits] and so forth," the heating of water is included. [The opponent] obstructs—that is, refutes—the pervasion of the ultimate limit of the excellence of the nature of knowledge, because the example is dissimilar to that [reality].

If it is asked: "Since he has attained the ultimate limit of the excellence of the nature of knowledge, what is his cause? Is it simply the perception of his own nature, or rather some non-existent quality belonging to him? To this, he says: "Not so," and so forth;
for it is not [the case], because it is impossible to produce that [nature] by means of the senses, logical marks, and so on, by oneself.

Knowledge would pervade its own object, and not otherwise. Otherwise, one could not apprehend anything at all due to distance and so forth. For it is impossible for that [knowledge] to arise through the senses, inferential marks, and so on—the word "and so on" (ādi) including scripture, repeated practice, dharma, and the like—unless knowledge pervades its own object along with its characteristic of being accompanied by the non-existent (asadagra). It would not be possible otherwise, namely, through the removal of defects and obscurations from within itself.

For it is not the case that space and so forth—which lack the capacity to be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition and the like—are produced either inherently or by something else as possessing that capacity; for otherwise, there would be the consequence of the collapse of the established nature of things.

Now, if it is argued that the power residing in the self—which produces the cognition whose nature is the apprehension of all objects—is not produced by anything other than the self itself (because that would entail the consequence of the self being an agent), but rather that cognition itself is produced [by something else], we reply: If that [self] produces a distinct cognition by means of an inherent, supreme power, let that very [power] be the grasper of the object; what is the use of postulating a separate [cognition]? Or, if it is argued that there is no apprehension of that [object] without a distinct cognition, then let there be no production of it without a distinct power.

If it is argued that this is so; then it is logical here that there is simply an absence of knowledge regarding power (*śakti*), and that very [absence] is what produces that [effect]. Thus, the self would be a non-agent. Furthermore, since inherence (*samavāya*) has been refuted, power does not inhere in it. Even if it did exist there, since it would be indistinguishable [from other powers], why would it not belong to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth as well? If, on the other hand, it is maintained that although the relation is indistinguishable, a distinction exists between the relata; from what is that [distinction] held to arise? If it is said that power is "inherent in itself," then if that too is distinct from it, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If there is no difference [between existence and the categories], let it remain exactly as it was from the beginning; what is the use of imagining that difference? This is the same fault.

The "group of existents" (*sadvarga*) consists of substance, quality, and action, which possess a connection with the universal *sattā*; the "group of non-existents" (*asadvarga*), on the other hand, consists of the universals, particulars, and inherence, which are devoid of a connection with *sattā* and are existent by themselves (*svataḥsan*).
This is the meaning according to the second [interpretation].
If the self were distinct from cognition,
The term "object" (artha) refers to the transformation into the nature of cognition;
this is the capacity (śakti).
Furthermore, since inherence (*samavāya*) is uniform,

if power (*śakti*) were distinct from it and yet eternal and all-pervading, it would not be the case that knowledge does not arise everywhere and at all times; thus, the argument— "the self is omnipresent because its qualities are perceived everywhere"— is not tenable.
If, on the other hand, that [cognition] is produced by someone else at another time and place, how can it be produced by one who is devoid of it? Otherwise, it would also exist in space and so forth.

If you say "no" because of [the self's] lack of capacity, then what capacity for that does the self possess? If you say it is distinct [from the self], then there is an infinite regress; therefore, since it is eternal and all-pervading, what is the use of a self? Since its effects are established from that [cognition] alone, if you say that cognition itself is the self, then let the production of the continuum of cognition and the grasping of its objects occur through that very [cognition].

If, however, the apprehension of "cognition-ness" (jñānatva) is distinct [from cognition], then the power (śakti) would be distinct and not the producer of that [cognition]; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of further powers, or a circularity (*cakraka*) regarding another power. If that other power were eternal and all-pervading, then that power—which is the capacity (*yogyatā*)—would not be distinct from the Self (*ātman*).
The second [case ending] is used for that which lacks capacity,
by means of capacity itself.

If it is argued: "But if that [consciousness] alone is the apprehender of the object, then since it would be without distinction for everyone, everywhere, and at all times, everyone would be an omniscient seer"; we reply: No, because by that same logic, it would follow that the cognition of that [object] would also arise for everyone, everywhere, and at all times. If it is argued that even in the opponent's position this same fault applies, yet it does not occur there because of the deficiency of auxiliary causes (*sahakāra*); then just as that [consciousness] does not produce cognition due to the deficiency of those [auxiliaries], so too it does not apprehend the object due to the deficiency of the veil (*āvaraṇa*).

What is done by its obstruction? And what is done by its deficiency? If you say "nothing," then [we ask]: why does the cognition not grasp the object even when there is an obstruction? If you say, "It is because it is not a producer [of the cognition] like knowledge itself," that is the same [point]. Now, if you say that its nature (*svabhāva*) is such that it does not produce [the cognition] due to the deficiency of that [cause], but rather produces it through the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), then let its nature be such that it does not manifest the object when an obstruction is present, but does so when there is a deficiency of that [obstruction]; for the power of an entity (*bhāvaśakti*) is inconceivable.

If [the cognition] does not [arise] due to the veil of reality (*tattvāvaraṇa*), what is the point of its destruction? If it does [arise], then it is the Buddhist position. If [you say] that nothing is produced for it by the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*), then this is the very same fault:

just as it acts through the proximity of that [auxiliary], so too, in the presence of the veil, why would it not reach the pinnacle of excellence in its cognitive nature in some other way? How else could it be understood?
He says: "None at all."
The Sugata states the reason for this: because of remoteness and so forth, due to the intervention of intrinsic nature and other factors,
and due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes.
Due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes for itself, its power [is obstructed].
If it were to fall into impermanence,
there would be no dependence upon auxiliary causes through the proximity of those auxiliaries.

In order to refute in another manner the objection—found in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 826, in the *pūrvapakṣa* section—that "there exists a space of ten cubits [separated] from the object immediately following [the body], such that one who leaps might go through the air," he states the verse beginning with "yadi nāma" (if indeed): "yadi nāma... [and continues with] "adhikāṃ daśahastāntaram" (an additional space of ten cubits), and so forth.
"Those like you cannot leap even ten cubits;
why then should the king of birds not leap a thousand yojanas?

(12) Because of the excellence resulting from the destruction of the obstructive karma of vigor (*vīryāntarāya-karma*), there is the realization of an excellence in powers such as leaping; since there is no restriction until the level of Garuḍa, the existence of persons possessing excellence is established.
This verse, taken as the opinion of Kumārila, is cited in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* as "stated by Kumārila" (*kumāriloktam*);
its second half is: "One is not able to travel a hundred yojanas even through hundreds of repetitions."

If those like Ambhava do not leap even ten cubits into the sky, why indeed would they not leap a thousand *yojanas*? For it is impossible to prevent a being from leaping up simply because it belongs to a different species; otherwise, one might as well see a human with honey. If it is argued that the leaping of a thousand *yojanas* is unproven because Vainateya (Garuḍa) is not seen [doing so], we say no; for since we observe that Bheruṇḍas and others possess a superior capacity for leaping compared to other birds, such a feat must be admitted as possible for Vainateya. Thus it has been stated.
The *garuḍa* belongs to the class of birds, whereas the other belongs to the class of humans; thus, there is a difference in species (*bhinnajātīyatva*).

Now, one might argue: "The leaping of the *bheruṇḍa* is innate (*sahaja*), as it arises solely from its species, whereas the excellence of knowledge in a human being is produced by practice (*abhyāsaja*), like jumping; therefore, it is logical that [the latter] is restricted in that manner. To this, he says: "Obstruction of vigor" (*vīryāntarāya*), etc.

Vigor (*vīrya*) is capacity; its obstruction (*antarāya*) is a specific karma that acts as a veil even over existing [capacity]. The excellence of its destruction (*kṣayātiśaya*) is the increase resulting from its removal. Its mastery (*vasā*) consists in the attainment of excellence in powers such as jumping.
He says "ākūta" (intention): because there is no obstruction [to progress] up to Garuḍa, there is the attainment of a superior person; this is "sātiśayopapatti" (the proof of superiority).

He thinks thus: the leaping of Garuḍa is not innate, but rather born from the destruction of karma that obstructs it; so too might it be in the case at hand—how is it understood that this [power] is due to karma and the like? If it is argued that potency (vīrya) exists eternally in the self and is merely manifested through the destruction of something that had suppressed it, and does not come into being as something previously non-existent like birth and so forth; [we reply: no, because it is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) of the self, just like knowledge (jñāna).

Is it not true that vigor arises from what was stated—that the attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*) results from freedom from the obscurations of defects? Since freedom from those defects is impossible in any speaker, even in an omniscient one, the proposition [of such a speaker] is sublated by the inference of passion and so forth arising from the mark of speech; for speech is indeed the effect of one possessing passion and the like. To this, he says: "Speech is the effect of one possessing passion and the like"—how so? (426) [The opponent asks: How is it that speech is the effect of one possessing passion and the like? (426) *Ka*? (How? [End of verse 426]

And this reason called "the state of being a speaker" (vaktṛtva), which is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "whose characteristics are knowability, provability, substantial existence, and so forth," is precisely that which is implied in the proposition regarding freedom from defects (*doṣavimuktipratijñā*).
— *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 881.

If every word is an effect produced by one possessed of passion and other defects, how can *codanā* (Vedic injunction) be an authoritative means of knowledge? What would the speakers of those [words] accomplish through their eternity? (13) Since every speaker is necessarily possessed of passion and other defects due to the very nature of being a speaker, if [their words] were invalid without distinction, how could the Veda possess authority? If sentences were eternal, the activity of the palate and other organs would be rendered futile; otherwise, it would be established that what is produced is a manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and not the sentence itself—how could this be so? Furthermore, even though there is no difference in the nature of the words, Vedic sentences would not be defiled by the defects of the speaker, which is why the oral transmission (*pravacana*) distinguishes it from others; it could not be otherwise.
Nor is speech the effect of [mere] desire, since it is observed even in states such as sleep;

rather, speech is caused by the proficiency of the instruments of cognition.
