And that proficiency of cognition would distinguish its own effect from another [cause], so that speech would not be eternal; for otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of an absence of disagreement regarding its interpretation.
Since other types of sentences possess the property of being invariably concomitant with consciousness, whereas Vedic sentences do not, let there be no transgression of their inherent nature;
therefore,
it is only the proficiency of the instrument of consciousness that constitutes the most effective means of accomplishment.
—Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 73

Here, this is investigated: Is every statement the product of one possessed of passion and other defects, or is some of it not? If some of it is not, then how is it known that those [statements] which have a visible author are likewise [the product of one possessed of passion]? If you say it is because of their similarity to those whose authors are invisible, from what does that similarity derive? If you say it is from the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, then since these phonemes and so forth are the same everywhere, it is incorrect to say that some [statements] are not [the product of passion], because they are recognized as such. If you say it is because they express non-existent objects, then a statement whose object is a non-existent thing would be the product of one possessed of passion; thus, the fact that its author alone possesses passion and other defects is established, and [your argument] proves what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*).

Furthermore, if every word— that is, every utterance— is the effect of one who possesses passion and so forth because it arises from the totality of reality (sarvatattva), and if the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) are likewise words, how can they be authoritative? For, by virtue of being verbal in nature, they would be the effect of one possessing passion and so forth, just like those [other words], since they share that same causal status.

If it is argued that, because it is a verbal testimony and because it is an effect of one possessed of passion and so forth, all such effects are said to have a universal creator, whereas the *codanā* (Vedic injunction), being eternal, is without a creator— here he says: "Eternality," and so forth.

What could an author do for those injunctions whose eternity is inherent? Furthermore, because such an author cannot be ascertained due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he does not exist; for that eternity is not determined by perception even if it were present, since that would entail the [absurd] consequence that the perceiver must be omniscient.
As it has been stated in this very context: "Knowledge is incomparable," and so forth.
It is not established merely by the non-remembrance of a creator; for even that is subject to deviation (vyabhicāra) due to old wells and the like, as has been stated.
Or rather, it is rejected because [the reason] exists in cases such as sacred scriptures (*pravacana*) where there is deviation.

Alternatively, it is considered otherwise: would the reason be immutable eternity (*kūṭasthanityatā*) or transformative eternity (*pariṇāmanityatā*)? The first position is untenable, because it has been refuted.

The second [argument] also applies to gold and so forth, because even in that gold and so forth, there is the efficacy of the letter *ka* and others; this was discussed in the context of [the opponent's claim of] eternity.
The non-recollection of an author applies even to the case of eternal transformation.
To explain the production of synonyms such as "bracelet" (*kaṭaka*) and "earring" (*kuṇḍala*), the author states: "Every speaker," and so forth.

Every speaker without exception—meaning one who possesses desire and the like due to the very nature of reality—is connected to the phrase "speech has all genders" through the transformation of gender (*liṅga-pariṇāma*).

If, for that very reason—namely, because of possessing passion and so forth—the speaker is invalid without distinction, then how can there be validity for the Veda? If you say that the Veda has no author, to this he replies with the words "of sentences," and so on:

[otherwise] the operation of the palate and other organs would be fruitless; otherwise, is it not the case that manifestation is produced, rather than the sentence itself? Why has this been established? This has already been explained:
precisely because of being a speaker.
Regarding the word "speech":

[the opponent argues] that Vedic words denote their meaning by themselves alone and not from a person; therefore, because they are artificial (kṛtrima), they lack authority. To this, he replies: "And not," etc. It is not at all the case that Vedic sentences would be tainted by the defects of a speaker; rather, they would indeed be tainted, even though there is no difference in their being preceded by a person (*puruṣapūrvakatva*).

It is not only by the previously stated method that this is so; for if the statement of the specific quality of eternality were indistinguishable from other Vedic knowledge, one would establish its distinctness as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) on that basis, and not otherwise. If [the Vedas] were to express their meaning through a person, then has it not already been said:
"Every word is an effect of one possessed of passion and the like, because desire is a particular form of passion"? And yet, [you claim] "it is not a sentence," and so forth.

Why is this so? He says: "In sleep, etc."—by the word "etc.," he includes states such as when the mind is directed elsewhere. Even otherwise, because [the action] is observed even in the absence of effort produced by an immediately preceding desire, what is its cause? He says: "Intellect, etc. Since intellect is established as present even in sleep and other such states, there is no deviation [from the rule]. Now, if one asks: "Since everything is equally preceded by that [intellect], how can there be mutual difference among the various traditions (samayas)? To this he says: "And the proficiency of knowledge"—that is, the proficiency of knowledge regarding the soul and so forth—does not distinguish its own effect, namely the teaching, from that of others, such as the teachings of the Sugatas and others.
For a distinction is indeed observed among the words of those who know the truth and others based on their being true or otherwise;

if it is argued that proficiency in that [truth] would eternally distinguish the sentence from another by its own function, to this he replies: "That eternal sentence would not, therefore, distinguish itself from that [other]; why? He says: because it would follow that there is an absence of conflicting interpretations."
He thinks as follows: "If permanence were to establish its own meaning by itself, this would be logical; but it is not so.
Therefore, the statement is made primarily because of the absence of any contradiction [regarding that permanence]. Why would the sentence 'permanence' distinguish it from anything else?
To this he says: 'Because of being explained,' and so forth."

Regarding that which was stated—that there would be a rule that a sentence is necessarily preceded by cognition—if it is argued that this is not well-said because Vedic sentences are otherwise, [the author] says here: "In the case of consciousness," and so forth.

The state of being invariably concomitant with consciousness, or the state of being preceded by intelligence, belongs to the sentences of men, such as those of the Vedas. How then could there be such an invariable concomitance for the Vedic sentences imagined by the Śākyas, given their lack of constituent parts? Thus, the opponent—who, while asserting that the proponent of an omniscient and dispassionate being has committed a deviation from the nature of things (svabhāvātikrama), himself speaks of this deviation as a fault—should not [be allowed to] do so.
Why? He says: "That very... and so forth.

Therefore, since [the Veda] is produced intentionally at the beginning of sleep and so forth, the Veda is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) and possesses parts, because its production is established by that [intentionality]. Even in the absence of effort impelled by an immediately preceding desire,
and even in the absence of proficiency in the instruments of cognition, there occurs the manifestation of speech characterized as utterance, because it is partless (*niṣkala*).
Even though the scriptures are preceded by the proficiency of the instruments of the intellect,
they [are presented] part by part.

The Mīmāṃsaka might argue that "being a sentence" (vākyatva) would necessarily entail "having consciousness as its cause" (caitanyanāntarīyakatva), and thus it would prove the human authorship of the Veda; however, [the opponent] says that this is not a valid reason because there is doubt regarding its exclusion from the contrary case (vipakṣavyāvṛtti)— namely, "a superior person (puruṣātiśaya) is established," and so forth.
In the same way, the excellence of the Person is established;
it is inferred from the fact that the cognition of the non-existence of an omniscient being would otherwise be inexplicable.
Even for those who claim that the Veda is eternal, an omniscient one free from defects is established.

Why? Because there is no recollection of an author for the entire [Veda] at the appropriate time; and because the Veda’s status as a source of knowledge and its status as a statement of belief are indistinguishable in terms of their eternity, [the same logic applies] and not everywhere...
How can an omniscient being be known by those who are not omniscient, such that one desiring spiritual practice would adopt his teaching?
That same difficulty applies elsewhere as well;
for [the omniscient being] is inferred from hearing "just as" (tathaiva), since there is an eternal connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*.

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as, despite the lack of distinction in being "other," the eternity of the scripture—the Veda—is not [established] for another [person], yet despite the lack of distinction in being a speaker and so forth, the excellence characterized by omniscience, freedom from passion, and so on, is established for a person; likewise, otherwise, let there be no eternity even for that [Veda], since there is no distinction. If it is argued that there is a distinction because the validity of the Veda has its basis in eternity, whereas for a person there is the opposite, having its basis in excellence; we say no, because it will be demonstrated right here that [the Veda's validity] is based on such excellence.
The claim that "the absence of an agent is based on his eternity" is likewise [untenable];
for an omnipresent Lord who pervades the entire range of space and time cannot be cognized without a superior [cognition],
and if he is not cognized without that [superior cognition], it is equivalent to saying nothing at all.

For if the mere existence of an object were pervaded by the sight of any living being whatsoever, and that sight were further pervaded by memory, then this [argument] would be correct; but it is not so.
Therefore, even the eternity of the Veda is established because its authority cannot otherwise be accounted for; thus, "the Veda is eternal."
The eternity of the Veda and the absence of an author [are established] without any excellence on the part of a person.

It might be argued: "Since an omniscient being does not exist, he cannot be the author of the Veda; because it is impossible for one who is not present to compose such a vast literary work that serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding supersensible matters, its eternity is established. To this, we reply: "The excellence of the Person is established through the fact that the existence of an omniscient being cannot otherwise be accounted for. Thus, the claim that "he is the author of the Veda because of the non-existence of an omniscient being" is like a dense cloud [obscuring the truth]. For if the non-existence of such a being were determined in its entirety, then doubt would not persist; otherwise, even that determination of non-existence would itself depend upon an omniscient being. This is the intended meaning.
The omniscient one [is established by] the eternity of the Veda in the absence of an omniscient one.
If that non-existence were not certain, then there would likewise be no certainty regarding the total non-existence of an omniscient being.
In order to explain the verse, he says "nityam" and so forth.

Even for those who assert that the Veda is eternal—not to mention others—an omniscient being free from defects is not established; this is because [the status of] being a speaker and the like is subject to defect, just like the nature of speech itself.
Thus, he asks "kutaḥ" (why? in order to demonstrate another logical argument.
He says this in the passage beginning with "sakaletya" and so forth;

by this, he demonstrates that [the Veda] is established as omniscient. With the words "yathā samayam" and so forth, he shows it to be free from defects. If it is argued that because of its very permanence, the Veda is not subject to the same status as the statements of atheists and the like—which are impermanent—[the author] replies here: "because the author is not remembered," and so forth, since there is no difference in the permanence of the Veda and the statements of atheists.

Alternatively, [the opponent might argue]: "The Veda is a valid authority because of its eternity, whereas others are not because of the opposite. To demonstrate that the reason [eternity] is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) in this case, he says "nine," etc.
By this, he shows that even things such as the marriage of one's mother—which are not valid authorities—are eternal, just like the Veda.
If that [marriage, etc. were also a valid authority, then it would follow that it must be practiced, just like the meaning of the Veda.

If it is argued that its author is remembered, to this he replies: "In all cases," and so forth. Granted, let the Veda be authoritative; indeed, let there be an omniscient being. However, it is impossible for one who lacks the knowledge of the knower of truth—that is, the knowledge of the omniscient one and his objects of knowledge—to arrive [at such a conclusion].
As it has been said:
"How indeed can this person be known as omniscient even at that time by those who desire to know him, yet lack the specific knowledge of his cognition and its objects?"

In the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, verse 134 of the *Codanā* section, it is stated that [the omniscient one] is known by an omniscient being; for according to his view, it would follow that there must be another omniscient being.
This too has been said:
"And many omniscient beings would have to be postulated by you;
for he who is himself not omniscient does not understand the omniscient one" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanā, verse 134).
He says this very thing: "How," and so forth.
If it is asked, "Let it not be known; what is the use of knowing that? he replies here with "Since," and so forth:
since one desires to engage [in activity] based on knowledge, one should therefore accept that teaching as the teaching of the Omniscient One.
If it is argued that this has been stated [in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Codanāsūtra, verse 136] beginning with "By whom the omniscient one was not known," etc., to this he replies: "That," etc.;
that objection raised by the opponent is the same even in other cases, namely, regarding the doctrines of others as well.
If the omniscient one is not understood by someone,
then for that person his words do not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge, because their source is unknown, just like the words of another— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In the knowledge of the Self of all," and so forth.

If one were not discerning the reality that is both knowable and unknowable by the knowledge of the Self of all, how could one himself be a knower of the absence of omniscience in that [omniscient being]? (15)

If one were to think that [the opponent] does not know it himself due to a deficiency in the knowledge of that which is to be known, this is not the case; for even in the case of proving the non-omniscience of a particular person on the grounds of his commonality with speakers and others, the same [objection] applies, because its absence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished. The Mīmāṃsaka will demonstrate that he would indeed be omniscient: all selves (*ātman*) or living beings (*jīva*) residing throughout the entire world—including stationary things and so forth—possess various cognitions. By discerning and knowing through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) both that which is to be known (*vijñeya*) and delimited, and that which is unknowable and undelimitable, the Mīmāṃsaka would be omniscient, since no other [person] has any operation regarding those [objects]. This is what will be established.

For just as the knowledge of an omniscient being, or his state of being an omniscient knower, cannot be known by anyone as "this person is omniscient" unless that [knowledge] itself is known—since he too is omniscient only through the knowledge of that [knowledge]—so too, if one does not directly perceive the reality of the objects of those knowledges in their entirety, or the nature of that [reality], how can one understand the absence of an omniscient being in its totality? For if one knows it, one is oneself omniscient.
And thus, with regard to Dharma, the Vedic injunction alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and nothing else such as the sense organs and so forth. (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2)

Thus, if one praises the Bhāṣya by saying that [the author] knows himself to be omniscient, and [argues] that another person likewise knows themselves in that same way, then since the non-perception of such an object is established,
who is there? Furthermore, the very existence of an omniscient being would be known through this [Bhāṣya], which is the same fault.

If that were the case, then omniscient beings would also have to be postulated; this applies equally to the opponent's position as well, since the means of valid cognition [depends] upon a person (mī॰ ślo॰ codanā॰ ślo॰ 135, etc.).
Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction— Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.2.
"Only *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to *dharma*—this has been established [in the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].

For *codanā* alone is capable of making known such matters as what has been, what is, what will be, the subtle, the hidden, and the remote; nothing else, such as the sense organs and so forth, is capable of this"—Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2.4.

Furthermore, his knowledge would be completed at some point in time; and since it follows that the selves and their cognitions are limited to only that much, how could they be beginningless and endless? Who now could perceive their beginninglessness and endlessness—either he himself or someone who reads his work? For on what basis could their existence be conceived? If, even upon its completion, those [selves and cognitions] were not limited to only that much, then, because their nature remains unbounded by him, there is no proof of the limited knowledge of Time.

If, on the other hand, it is not admitted that this [process] reaches completion anywhere, then—even over many thousands of aeons—the discernment of the reality of all things, whether knowable or unknowable by the knowledge of the self, would remain incomplete; for as long as there remains even one thing unknown by him, the suspicion regarding his omniscience does not cease, and thus the status of being omniscient would still be lacking.
This is the connection [of the argument].
Even though the Veda contains the complete knowledge of the omniscient one, it [does not contain] the knowledge of the selves or of individual cognitions.

However, because non-existent things also possess existence due to their being time—just like the present time—the sense is that the absence of omniscience which is sought to be proven [by that argument] does not hold. Since he perceives each thing exactly as it exists, this is not a fault; for another omniscient being would likewise perceive them in that same way, and thus there would be no such defect in his case.
It is improper [to say] that another’s misconduct should likewise be considered;

surely this fault would arise if he were to discriminate between the reality that is knowable and unknowable by the knowledge of all beings, since he does not do so. To this, it is said: "If not"—that is, if he himself, by his own self, were not a knower of the absence of omniscience, how could this not have been established?

Furthermore, regarding the communication of the state of omniscience, if one holds that *codanā* alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the Dharma, then the proof of the validity of *codanā* by means of excluding connection with anything else is baseless. For, by the exclusion—which is the absence—of any connection with the validity of another omniscient being distinct from the Veda, what [is established]? Moreover, if there is doubt regarding the non-existence of such [an omniscient being], the authorlessness of the Veda remains doubtful; how then could it establish its own validity? For how could one who desires to act proceed from that [Veda] which is not of human origin, since the suspicion of the existence of an omniscient being—who is invisible to people like us and who could be its author—has not been removed?

Even non-recollection does not establish the non-existence of that [object]; for recollection is the effect of experience (*anubhava*), not the effect of the object of cognition (*prameya*), because otherwise it would follow that everything [would be recollected] from that [experience] without distinction. Therefore, the absence of the object of cognition does not result from the absence of recollection; otherwise, the absence of smoke would entail the absence of everything.
However, if [the absence of recollection were to establish the absence of the object], it would be due to the absence of its cause, namely experience.
Furthermore, our experience is not the effect of all objects of knowledge such that, in its absence, there would necessarily be an absence of the intended object of knowledge;

therefore, for one who desires the Vedas to be authorless, their non-existence cannot be known when there remains doubt regarding the non-existence of an omniscient being. Thus, the stated defect is not avoided.
The absence of an author for the Veda also [proves] the non-existence of a creator of the Veda.
There is an absence of an agent, even for those such as the Jains, because there is no recollection [of such an agent].
The phrase "due to the absence of an object of cognition" (prameyābhāvāt) is written twice redundantly;
for if there were an absence of a non-cause even from a non-effect,
then [the absence of the effect] would follow from the absence of memory.
In the absence of experience, which is the cause of recollection, there would be an absence of omniscience.
Now, regarding the point that one might understand the absence of that [omniscience] without even discerning it, he says "yadi" (if), etc.

The knowledge of all that is knowable is its object; the knowledge regarding that object—due to a deficiency in that [knowledge], there is all the more a lack of omniscience in all beings. He states the sequence here: that one would not oneself perceive, "I am not omniscient. To this, he says "nahi" (not indeed), etc.

This would be a point already explained if the non-omniscience of all persons were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); but this is not so, because it is perceived through inference (*anumāna*). To this, he says: "In the case of a person," and so forth.
This applies not only to the proof at hand, but also to proving the non-omniscience of specific individuals such as the Sugata and others.
Why? He says: "Because of being a speaker," and so forth.

Regarding that generality of being a speaker and so on which belongs to the Sugata, the Rathyāpuruṣa (the man in the street), and others—what follows from that? He says: "This inference is the same [in both cases]."

Since the non-existence of the qualities of being a speaker and so forth is not established as the opposite of omniscience in the case of the non-cognition of all things— whether they are knowable through self-awareness or not—
the rest [of the argument] regarding the non-existence of an omniscient being should be understood by the discerning eye itself through its own effort.
Demonstrating the result obtained when proving the omniscience of another while one’s own [lack of] omniscience remains to be established, he says "nara" and so forth:
"A person"— meaning an embodied being or a speaker— "knowing the world, [is] not all-knowing."
Therefore, there would be an omniscient being; hence, there is no proof for the non-existence of an omniscient being.

(16) Even though the commonality of being a person (*puruṣatva*) and so forth exists, just as some [people] know that the world is devoid of an omniscient being or that others possess passion and so forth, while others do not, in the same way, if some were to be omniscient, why would that not be possible? For what reason would there be no omniscient being? A man, a person, an embodied being, or a speaker—whether knowing everything or not knowing everything—might know the world and thus be omniscient. Therefore, there is no proof for the non-existence of an omniscient being, because the proof for such [non-existence] is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by that [possibility]. This is the intended meaning.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Even though [it exists]," and so forth.

Even if the universal property such as "personhood" (*puruṣatva*) exists—not only if it does not exist—just as some, such as the Jaiminīyas and others, perceive the world as devoid of an omniscient being, and how could they perceive the possession of passion and so forth by someone like the Sugata, who is beyond their perception, while others, such as common street-people, do not? In that very same way, if there were some who were omniscient, why would that not be possible? Since it is impossible [for them to perceive it], there would be no omniscient being anywhere at all.
[Objection: This fault would indeed apply if some perceived the world in that manner through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, [they perceive it] through inference (*anumāna*).

For instance: all cognitions that are considered to be direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), which have become subjects of dispute, are produced by the contact of sense-faculties with their objects and possess restricted objects, because they are [cognitions] of such a nature; here, the state of being a direct perception is established in this way, and likewise, the objects under dispute are objects of direct perception through sense-faculties restricted to specific objects, because they are of that nature, just like the intended object.
This is correct.
Jaimini and others [hold that it is] because of its being perceptible and because of its being an object.

Just as in the case of jars and other objects, whatever kind of perception of whatever kind of object is observed by people at present through various means of valid cognition, it was exactly the same in another time as well.
If it is argued [as stated] in verse 113 of the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika* on *Codanā*, we say no; for this is subject to deviation by way of true dreams (*satyasvapna*).
Indeed, that cognition of a true dream understands an object that is not in contact with the senses and is even obstructed, as has been established in the *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*.
The Lord himself is unassailable and shines forth with perfect clarity through the light of his own purpose, like a true dream (*satyasvapna*)—*Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p.

99. If it is argued that, just as there is a sublater (*bādhaka*), there must also be a doubt regarding the existence of an omniscient being due to the absence of a prover (*sādhaka*), he says this very thing in the passage beginning with "the prover" (*sādhaka*).

It is incorrect to say that there should be doubt regarding an omniscient being because of the absence of both proving and refuting evidence; for while doubt might occasionally arise from the absence of both proving and refuting evidence, in this case, since a refuting evidence is impossible, the existence of proving evidence alone is established. (Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 49) [Verse 17]
By what means is the determination of the non-existence of that duality [established]? In this regard, it is due to the determination of the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*);
for from that very fact, the validity of perception is also established, since there would otherwise be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of accepting reality merely according to how things appear.

Therefore, there is no so-called "proof" other than the complete absence of subverting evidence; for, due to the absence of both proof and subversion regarding that [omniscience], doubt would arise concerning its omniscience, since proof and subversion are characterized by mutual affirmation and negation.
To this, he states the refutation: "Because of the impossibility of a subverter," and so forth.

From what is omniscience established in a particular person? To this he says: "Because of the impossibility of a sublater (*bādhaka*). By this he means the following: the absence of a sublater is pervaded by ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), because such is observed in the case of the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of pleasure and so forth. Furthermore, in the absence of ultimate reality, there is the cessation of the absence of a sublater for the perceived forms of mirages and the like. That which necessarily ceases upon the cessation of another is pervaded by that [other]; for example, the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) is pervaded by self-awareness. And since that [omniscience] ceases when its existence ceases, it follows that [the absence of a sublater] is pervaded by ultimate reality.

It might be argued that there is no sublation [of the cognition] when the ultimate reality of the sentient being ceases, because even in the absence of such a sentient being, that [cognition] is absent in the case of jars and so forth seen in dreams; thus, it is not pervaded by that [sentient being]. [To this we reply: it would follow that there is no distinction between the forms grasped by their respective self-cognitions, since those forms would be presented [identically].
Therefore, one who maintains that the form apprehended in dreams and the like is non-existent must admit the existence of a sublater [of that cognition]; for even in the absence of ultimate reality,
there would otherwise be no sublater.

Others maintain that there is a pervasion (vyāpti) between ultimate existence and the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*); they argue that in cases such as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), even though ultimate existence is absent because it lacks a relation [to being], there is still an absence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, they claim there is no relationship of pervaded and pervader between these two. This is not so; for it has been shown that when non-existence is distinct from existence, there exists a subverting proof against it, or else there is a relation to existence.

Therefore, since the certainty of existence arises precisely from the impossibility of a subverting factor, those of deluded intellect speak of "there" (tatra) and "here" (iha) [regarding that sound]; thus,
even in the absence of ultimate existence,
there is the absence of a subverting factor and ultimate existence.
[Objection: Surely, doubt regarding that [omniscience] is not admitted to arise from its mere nature alone, but rather from that [nature] accompanied by the absence of a means of proof;

for the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), which consists in the presence of a proving means (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*), brings about the existence [of the object], and that [proving means] does not exist in the case of an omniscient being. [Response: To this he says: "Because such a thing is possible for one who possesses a means of proof. This [term *vyatirecaka*] is a restrictive [qualification] and should be understood as following immediately after the word *siddham*.
Since a practitioner exists, omniscience is possible; and since that possibility has already been demonstrated, it is not shown here again.

Furthermore, if there is a scriptural cognition—free from sublation—that asserts that a particular state of some person exists which directly perceives all objects, then that constitutes a valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for its existence, because there is no sublation.
The particle *eva* functions as an exclusive delimiter (*vyāvartaka*) by itself.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Dharmakīrti—"In that case, let there be doubt due to the absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.32)—to that he replies: "By what means of valid cognition is the determination of the non-existence of those two—the pair of proving and refuting means of valid cognition—established? By none whatsoever. This has already been explained.

He considers it thus: regarding an omniscient being, the proof of doubt must be established by a reason (*hetu*), and that reason must itself be proven; otherwise, it would be impossible to establish [the subject] through it, because it would follow that one is stating something that is doubtful and unproven. For comparison: "And here, the mere absence of proving and refuting means of valid cognition is indicated by doubt."

— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 4.91. Thus, it is established that when there is an absence of both proving and subverting means of valid cognition, this perception of a common property, existing at a single moment together with the non-perishing state [of the object] and the recollection of its specific [distinguishing] features in their state of perishing, is the cause of doubtful cognition.
—*Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 247;
*Nyāyakusumāñjali*, Chapter 2, p. 8:

"From the ascertainment of the proving and refuting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no dispute regarding existence and non-existence; from the lack of such ascertainment, doubt would arise."
—Aṣṭaśata, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 49; Laghīyastrayasvavṛtti, p. 2; Pramāṇanayatatvāloka, 1.
11 *Prameyaratnamālā* 3.29
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 5: Because it is impossible for a reason to establish doubt regarding an omniscient being.

If it is argued: "Granted that there may be no definitive determination of the non-existence of those two, let there at least be doubt"; [the author replies: "In that case, the doubt would arise from that very [cause], not from the non-existence of those two. If it is further argued: "Let it be that the doubt arises from that very cause"; here [the author] says, beginning with the words "bādhaka" (the sublater), where the word "tatra" (there) denotes sequence. The sense is: "Therefore, the doubt regarding that [object] does not arise from the doubt regarding those two."

Nevertheless, if there is still doubt regarding that very point, he says here: "Precisely from that," and so forth. From what [does this certainty arise]? He says: "Even of perception—not only of scripture—it is precisely from that [absence of sublation] that its validity arises."
In the case of an omniscient being, there is a twofold absence of both proof and disproof, due to the doubt regarding the absence of proof and disproof.
It might be thought: "Its validity [is established] from appearance, not from that [subsequent cognition]. To this he says: "In accordance with what is seen," and so forth.

If the apprehension of validity were accepted as occurring upon the apprehension of reality, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all cognitions would be valid. Furthermore, this very object of cognition would also be free from doubt, because of the determination that no sublater exists.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, etc.

Since this is so, for that reason, there is no other "proving means of knowledge" (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) apart from the exclusion of subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa-vyāv� omniscience*); rather, that [exclusion] itself is the prover. For, because of the existence of another prover, and because of the absence of both proving and subverting means of knowledge regarding that omniscience, doubt would descend upon omniscience. Why is this so? He says: "The prover," and so forth.
Because of the existence—that is, the very nature—of those two whose characteristics are the mutual injunctions and prohibitions of the prover (*sādhaka*) and the subverter (*bādhaka*).

To explain: the prohibition of the subverter is itself the injunction of the prover; the prohibition of that [prover] is itself the injunction of the subverter. Likewise, the injunction of the subverter is itself the prohibition of the prover; and the injunction of that [prover] is itself the prohibition of the subverter.

Otherwise, the negation of selflessness (*nairātmya*) in a living body would not be possessed of a self (*sātmaka*); or, for Dharmakīrti, the absence of the absence [of the reason] when there is no counter-example (vipakṣa)—such as the reason of being produced (*kṛtakatva*)—would not be of the nature of a presence. Thus, there would be neither the cessation of the subverting factor (*bādhaka*) nor the actual existence of an omniscient being, because of the lack of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Since the exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful, the proof is "like the remainder" (*śeṣavat*), which is merely a negation of the prover.
The procedure for the practitioner,
demonstrating this very point, says: "How," and so forth—
how can there be the cessation of obstacles when that [obstacle] exists at the passing away of the omniscient one?

Whether there is a deficiency in the knowledge of the entire world or its presence, the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), being present, would indeed establish the existence of an omniscient being; of this there is no doubt.

For it is not the case that in the absence of anything at all, the subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) itself would not exist; rather, in its absence, the establishing means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) also does not exist.
Why does this very same [inference], being certain, not establish the actual existence of an omniscient being? Because the exclusion of the prover (sādhaka) is impossible;
for even other objects of cognition exist precisely because they are known by uncontradicted cognition, and this is true for the omniscient one as well.
In the absence of both proving and refuting evidence, let there be no doubt either; [otherwise] it would be like deep sleep, as in the case of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Enough of this digression.

If the absence of an omniscient being in the world—which constitutes the opposite of the probandum—is present, how can the cessation of its sublation be a reason for its existence, that is, a reason for the existence of an omniscient being? To this, the answer is: "The cessation of the sublation," etc.; when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established, it should be understood immediately following that [statement]:
the cessation of the sublation occurs only when [the omniscient being] exists.

Under what condition? He says: "Upon the disappearance of the omniscient one," that is, in the absence of an omniscient being; the word "only" (eva) has the sense of an exclusionary indicator (*vyāvartaka*), because the cessation of that [omniscience] is pervaded by its existence.

If it is argued that the absence of sublation [of the omniscient being] follows from the existence of an omniscient being, then how can there be a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by that [omniscience] when its existence is not yet established? If you say that the establishment of that [omniscience] follows from the absence of sublation, then there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

For instance: [if one argues that] the existence of that [non-omniscience] is established by the establishment of its pervasion by the absence of that [omniscience], and then by that [existence] the pervasion with it [omniscience] is established—this is not so; for this is the same even when the pervasion of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth with the non-eternality of sound is being established. Now, if it is claimed that here the pervasion is not intended to be established in the subject (*dharmin*), but rather in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) such as a jar; [then we ask: is the pervasion established in the subject—the omniscient one—by the presence of non-omniscience, or rather in the similar instance, such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, where its [omniscience's] existence is absent? If [you say] it is when the non-eternality of sound is [established]; [we reply: no.
In this case, there is pervasion by way of the generality of impermanence (*anityatva-sāmānya*); elsewhere, there is pervasion by way of the generality of existence (*sattva-sāmānya*).
It is for this very purpose that it was stated: "Even of perception," and so forth, regarding the failure to establish the actual existence of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*).
From the removal of subverting factors follows pervasion;
from the removal of subverting factors follows the existence of an omniscient being.
Due to the removal of obstacles by means of the existence of an omniscient being,
[this applies] to pleasure and so forth.
If it is argued that the existence of an omniscient being constitutes the pervasion when the impermanence of sound is the property to be proven;

[Objection: "In that case, external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) would have been accepted by you; and by this much alone, [the mere presence of] the reason would become a means of proof (*gamaka*), because even [the reason] 'being his son' and the like would result in being a means of proof, since internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is admitted as the basis for its being a means of proof, and that [internal pervasion] is apprehended in the subject (*dharmin*), and this is not the case when [the reason] has ceased. To this, he says: "When it exists," and so forth.

The phrase "therefore, at all times, the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*) would establish the existence of an omniscient being; one must not entertain doubt regarding this probandum (*sādhya*)" is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

Otherwise, there would be doubt regarding the existence [of the omniscient being] even in the case of the eyes and so forth, because—aside from the absence of a subverting factor—there is no other defining characteristic [for its existence], and mere non-perception (*adarśana-mātra*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).

In the case of a reason such as "The son of Maitra in the womb will be dark-complexioned because he is the son of Maitra," there is [fallacy] by virtue of mere external pervasion (bahirvyāpti) in the similar class (sapakṣa).

Is this not an inference based on internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) regarding the definition of existence? How then can it establish the probandum when its object is sublated by that [other] internal [cognition]? For instance: "There is no omniscient being, because there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes such a person with absolute certainty," and so forth.

If it is admitted that [the proof] has been refuted by someone else, or that there is an absence of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) according to the method stated, then there would be no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the omniscient being. However, moreover, if his non-existence were to be proven, there would be no establishing evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*); rather, there would be an absence of establishing evidence.

It is certainly not the case that there is an absence of establishing evidence regarding the non-existence of an omniscient being, because it is impossible to ascertain such an absence, since either he himself or another possesses the establishing evidence for him.
If you argue that it is "not so" because of the absence of that [evidence], then from what does that absence arise? If you say "from another," then this [other] is futile.

If it is argued that [the non-existence of the omniscient being is established] from this [perception], there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): if its non-existence were established, then perception would not fail to be a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing that [non-existence]; and if that [means of knowledge] existed, then the establishment of its non-existence would follow. Therefore, this is trivial.
The non-existence of the omniscient being cannot be established by another inference.

Summarizing, he says: "Therefore, this exclusion by subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is itself [the proof], and nothing else has been done. He asks: "Being certain, what does it do? and answers: "He is omniscient," and so forth.

"Why does the exclusion of the prover not establish its non-existence? To this he says: "Because the exclusion of the prover is impossible, since in the absence of an omniscient being, its determination is impossible"—this is the sense. Showing the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposing position (*vipakṣa*), he says: "Even for another object of cognition (*prameya*) in the form of pleasure and so forth—not only for the object of cognition that is the 'knower of all'—is there the nature of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), which is the reality of the other side [the subject], simply because it is known by an uncontradicted cognition?

If it is argued that this is because what is merely shown is fallible, and [the proof lies] in its being the cause of purposeful action (*arthakriyākāraṇa*); [we reply: no, because if that [purposeful action] does not appear [in the cognition], then the notion 'that [action] arises from that' is untenable."

Even regarding manifestation, it has been stated that its establishment [as real] follows from an uncontradicted manifestation; by this same reasoning, the claim that [reality] is established elsewhere through causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is refuted, as there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because even in that case one would have to depend on another [instance of] it.

Some say [validity arises] from the connection with existence (*sattā*). [Objection: Why is there no [validity] in the water of a mirage? [Reply: Because of sublation (*bādhana*). If you say this, then you have fallen into my own teaching regarding the nature of things (*dharma*). Furthermore, the function of the particle *eva* has been shown; the meaning is that validity does not consist merely in being an object of perception (*darśanaviṣayībhūta*)—this is the sense of "existence" (*sattva*).

It might be thought: "The state of being an object of uncontradicted cognition is unestablished in the case of an omniscient being. To this he says: "That state of being an object of uncontradicted cognition exists even in the omniscient one. This has already been explained. Since that is not well-stated—because there is an absence of both proving and subverting evidence regarding him, resulting in doubt—he states another refutation beginning with "In the proof," and so forth.

The proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) is the cognition whose object is the omniscient one; the subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is that which has his non-existence as its object. If it is admitted that this [subverting means] is absent—that is, if it is devoid of the cognition having him as its object—then even doubt would not arise. For doubt is not tenable when there is no apprehension of even the mere substratum (*dharmin*). He states an illustration: "like selflessness," "as in the case of the five [aggregates]," and "similarly."
The meaning is that knowledge might sometimes be doubt, like emptiness; the meaning is that it might be like one who is dead.

If it is objected: "But surely all cognition is dependent upon the self; since that [self] is absent in the state of the five [elements], how can there be such [cognition]? To this he replies with the words beginning "while asleep," etc.
By this, the objection regarding the non-establishment of the locus (*dharmyasiddhi*)—which was previously directed against the Buddhist and subsequently against the Mīmāṃsaka—is refuted.
Showing that there is more to be said on this matter, he says: "Enough of this digression" regarding emptiness.

Secondly, [the opponent asks]: "Granted that an omniscient being exists, why is it that only the Arhat is omniscient and not another? That which was said—'well said, well said'—is written again without purpose."
"If the Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not?
If both were omniscient, how could there be a difference of opinion between them?
(Tattvasaṃgraha, Verse 3149, in the *pūrvapakṣa*).
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Even though," and so forth.

"Even though [the truth] exists, those who do not perceive the reality of what they have experienced themselves—would omniscient ones be postulated by investigators as proponents of an extremist doctrine? (19)
To this, he provides the following reply: "Of the proponents of one-sided views," and so forth.
Sugata and others, failing to discern—that is, failing to ascertain—the reality (*tattva*) which is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of what?

Of an object (*vastu*) such as pleasure or blue, which is experienced as having a manifold nature (*anekāntātman*), because they characterize it as having a one-sided form (*ekāntarūpatayā*), why should an omniscient being be sought by investigators? Not at all.

It might be thought: "Since the mental fluctuations of others are difficult to discern, how can it be understood that they do not perceive that [reality]? [The answer is: because they speak otherwise; for the most part, they are like those who have strayed far from the path.
Even in that regard, for everything that exists, the nature of persistence, origination, and dissolution is established.
In some cases, a certain mode of being (*vṛtti*) arises from one or another aspect of the self.

(Verse 20) "Arising" (*utpatti*) is the acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*); "subsistence" (*sthiti*) is existence (*sattva*); and "destruction" (*nāśa*), moreover, is the falling away from its own nature (*svabhāvapracyavana*). How can these three be of a single identical essence? Even for an object that is unchanging—whether it be momentary or persisting through other phases—that which constitutes its very self and exists in such a way, it always possesses that [nature]. Furthermore, arising, subsistence, or destruction would not be possible apart from these three aspects of the self, because the persistence of its own nature is characterized by the exclusion of any other substance.

For an object that is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), the very loss of its prior nature and the subsequent attainment of another nature constitutes its transformation; because the transformative cause does not depend on anything else for its own manifestation as its effect,
there is the deficiency of the former and the deficiency of the latter.
The visible middle form of a real substance is existent in some way; otherwise,
because it would be impossible for it to assist others— since it does not attain any subsequent transformation occurring within its own continuum—
it would be entirely...
Because substances mutually induce and inhibit one another, characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),

and because decay is observed at their end, one who desires to see decay even before that time may, upon observing stability in the middle, ascertain that there is stability of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) at both the prior and posterior limits as well, since there is no difference;
[thus] a single entity consisting of both the visible and the invisible, like the perceptible and the imperceptible, or like a *pudgala* possessing manifest color, touch, and so forth.

Furthermore, since that which has the nature of direct perception can somehow be established as inferable, there is no contradiction [in our position]; otherwise, it would follow that even consciousness itself does not exist. Moreover, those who are dogmatically attached to the absolute unreality [of all things] will be refuted later on.

If it is argued that, unlike the nature of being manifold (anekāntātmakatva), a single entity does not possess the nature of persistence, arising, and passing away at every moment, nor do [the states of] the neck and so forth arise and pass away in such a way, and furthermore, the persistence of the final and intermediate moments is perceived; to this he says: "of everything indeed," and so forth.
This means "of everything indeed"—not of some restricted portion—of the existing, i.e., present, category of both sentient and non-sentient things.
Of what kind [of thing]? To this he says: "having persisted," and so forth.
What of that? He says: what is "established" (siddhā)? He says: "ascertained" (niścitā). What kind of "functioning" (vṛtti) is it? He says: "arisen" (udbhūtā).

Is this so everywhere and in every way? No; he says "in some places, in some manner. Among the triad of persistence, origination, and destruction, [he considers] that which consists of one of these, or has one of these as its nature—such as that which consists of persistence in the case of transmigrating souls (*saṃsārijīva*), or that which consists of all three.
To explain the verse, he first sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), beginning with "origination," etc.

What is origination (*utpatti*)? It is manifestation (*prādurbhāva*). To this he says: "attainment of self" (*ātmalābha*), meaning the attainment of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). The sense is that it is not the inherence in a cause (*kāraṇa-samavāya*) or the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) for something previously non-existent.

For instance, if origination were inherence [in causes] of what already existed inherently from before, then it would follow [absurdly] for the self (*ātman*) and so forth, as well as for their omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and other qualities.

If you say it is because of non-existence (*asat*); then even things like a hare’s horn would exist, since they too are non-existent both before and after [the production]. If you say "no" because of that non-existence, what is this non-existence? If it is the absence of a relation to that [cause], then from where does that [absence] come? If it comes from non-existence itself, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*). For instance: once the absence of the relation to that [cause] is established, the non-existence of those things follows; and from that non-existence, the absence of the relation follows.
Thus, since the cause is absent, those things are non-existent; and in that case, this very point must be stated.

For example, from where does that absence of a cause arise? Because it is of the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), from where could it come? [If you say] "from the absence of a cause," then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*).
Furthermore, how can a non-existent destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) exist, such that the efficacy of a hammer or other instruments is rendered meaningful?

If it is argued that for that [sound], neither an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) nor a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) is accepted, but rather a causal condition (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) exists; then why is this not the case elsewhere? If you say "because it is not observed," then for that very reason, the self (*ātman*), space (*ākāśa*), and so forth, could not be the inherent causes of cognition (*buddhi*), sound (*śabda*), and the like, for they are not perceived in the manner described by the opponent.

If it is argued that there would be a lack of a substratum (*nirādhāratā*), let it be so; what is the fault? If it is argued that there would be a lack of form (*nirūpatā*), no; because this is contradicted by the case of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*).

If it is argued that there is an absence of the quality of being a quality (*guṇatva*), what indeed is this so-called "quality-ness"? To say it is simply its own nature (*svarūpa*) is no answer, because the same consequence would apply even to destruction. By this, the absence of being a quality has been considered.

If it is argued that [a quality] is "dependent on a substance" (*dravyāśritatva*); from what, then, is that established? If you say "because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*), this is stated [as a circular argument], for there is mutual dependence: its being dependent on a substance follows from its being a quality, and its being a quality follows from that dependence. This would apply even to things like a rabbit's horn, which are non-existent.
If this is argued,

then since its nature as absolute non-existence is established in the absence of a cause, why would that [absolute non-existence] not have both an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)?
The fact that sound and the other [qualities] reside in a substance is established solely from their non-perception [independently].

Furthermore, as for this argument: "Intellect and the rest are qualities because, while they lack the status of being substances or actions that are subject to negation, they are related to existence (*sattā*), like color and so forth"—that too is not sound. [Objection: It is not inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) because of the counter-example of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*); if you say that this is because destruction lacks a relation to existence, [we reply: no, for even if it were related to existence, there would still be no fault in our position.

Otherwise, how could there be the cognition that "destruction exists"? If it is argued that this is metaphorical (*aupacārika*), from what [source] is this known? And from what is the absence of a relation with that [existence] known? If it is argued that it is because the cognition of it is metaphorical, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, if the cognition of existence regarding destruction is metaphorical—on the grounds that it has substance (*dravya*) and so forth as its object, and because it is a cognition of such [an object], like the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth—then from what is its having that as its object known? If it is from the metaphorical nature of the cognition, then again there is mutual dependence.

Now, if destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) does not depend on anything other than substances and so forth because it is not perceived as such, then for that very reason cognition and the like would also not exist; thus the same point recurs, resulting in the fallacy of a circle (*cakraka-prasaṅga*).

As it is said in the comparison: "Sound is a quality (*guṇa*), because, while being distinct from substance and action, it is related to existence (*sattā*), like color and so forth" (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p.

If the cognition "it exists" (sann iti) were merely figurative, there would be an absence of its connection [to the object]; and if that connection were absent, the cognition "it exists" would be figurative.
Thus, to state again that the object of the cognition "it exists" is substance and so forth, as being figurative, is redundant.
This is because the cognition "it exists" has substance and so forth as its actual object.

If it should be thought: "In the case of a connection with non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), its nature as non-existence (*abhāvatva*) is lost"; [then we ask: why is it not lost when there is its production or its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? Therefore, just as that [nature] is not lost even though there is no difference in that [production or efficiency], so too it is not lost even though there is no difference in its connection [with destruction]; thus everything is well-established.

Furthermore, if there were a distinction between the existence and non-existence of substances and so forth despite the non-difference of their relation to that [universal], then non-existence itself would also be differentiated; for it is impossible to deny a subordinate universal even in the case of absences.
Otherwise, the conformity of the cognition and designation of "non-existence" therein would be difficult to maintain.
Therefore, since qualities such as cognition and so forth do not possess the same nature as destruction, the existence of an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is not established.

Now, if it is argued that the occasional nature of cognition and so forth implies an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), this too is not particularly elegant, as it is subject to deviation by the case of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). For even though destruction is a non-entity (*abhāva*), some entity (*bhāva*) likewise arises in such a manner, since the natures of entities are diverse. Furthermore, if cognition and so forth lack an inherent cause, from what would they arise? Why could they not arise from an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), just like destruction? Otherwise, destruction itself would not occur either.

If it is argued that in the case of non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsabhāva*), which is causeless, the absence of the effect is not necessitated by the absence of a cause; and if it is further argued that this is because [destruction] is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*); to this it has been said: Furthermore, from what [source] is it known that for jars and the like there exists a cause, namely a relation with "Being" (*sattā*)? If it is argued that since they exist by their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), that [relation] is also known; then both [the jar and its relation] would have arrived at self-nature (*svātman*). If it is argued that neither is so; then why should there not be some other such category [of entity]? For otherwise, how could the restriction on the number of categories be established?
If it is argued that [the effect does not exist] because it is not perceived [prior to its production], that is the same in other cases as well.
Therefore, since it possesses the nature of an entity and yet occurs only occasionally, its "origination" (utpatti) is simply its acquisition of self-nature (ātmalābha).
He states that there is persistence even in the absence of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) by means of the words beginning with "sthitih" (persistence) and ending with "punaḥ" (again).

By the word "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature), he negates [the idea that it] is distinct from its own being. By the phrase "pracyavanam" (falling away), he indicates the disappearance of the existent; and this has already been explained.
This triad of origination and so forth has a single referent—its essence or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—which is mutually identical; that is what is meant by the term "thus described.
How is this so? Providing the explanation for this verse, he says: "Even though [it] is unchanging," and so forth.
"Even though [it] is unchanging," etc.
Not only those that undergo transformation, but even those that are unchanging—the word [is applied] in this cultivation;
of what [object] is it? He says: of an object—of what kind? Of one that is momentary, or of one that persists through other times, that is to say, of an eternal one.

What follows from this? He says: for whatever—whether momentary or eternal—the nature (*ātman*) or intrinsic character (*svabhāva*) is as it truly is, whether momentary or eternal, that object always obtains its own nature and never otherwise; there is no such distinction. Otherwise, if everything everywhere were always momentary, or if the self and so forth were always eternal, then even an object possessing that very nature would always obtain it. This [consequence] he negates.

If it is argued that this might be so because an object could consist of three aspects due to the occasional attainment [of its causes], to this he replies: "Not so. "Three-naturedness" (*tryātmyam*) means the state of having three natures; its "absence" (*vyatireka*) is non-existence. Therefore, there is no arising [from such a cause].

For things like a donkey's horn, which lack the nature of arising, do not possess arising due to the absence of a cause; whereas a jar and the like do not follow this pattern because the opposite is true. To this it is said: "Three-naturedness" (*tryātmyam*) is the existence of the three-natured, meaning the state of consisting of the triad beginning with arising.
Furthermore, because the cause exists, if it is argued that an existent substratum does not produce that which is by nature unarisen— otherwise, it would destroy that which is indestructible,
and thus nothing could ever arise— it has already been stated in this regard that the wheel and other such things would be rendered futile.
Likewise, there is no persistence apart from that [cause];
for indeed, that which is censured by its own nature of persisting cannot possibly remain stable from any cause whatsoever.
For an action that has already yielded its fruit cannot be made to persist even by Īśvara, as it is contrary to the nature of an effect (vaiśeṣika-sūtra 1.1.1).
1.14 Because of this contradiction,
if it is argued that the Lord lacks the power to establish those [distinctions], then how could it be otherwise? Otherwise, the Lord would possess a dual nature.
Just as one who lacks the capacity [to act] is not an establisher, so too that which is devoid of the power of persistence does not persist from any cause;
by this, the establishment of that [object], being devoid of the nature of destruction, is likewise refuted.
The meaning is that it is devoid of anything other than the threefold nature;
"unseen" (adṛṣṭa) refers to merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), and so forth.
Action that is opposed by its effect— meaning action is contradicted, or destroyed, by its own effect, which is the fruit;
this refers to the state of being either capable or incapable in the production of the body and so forth.

If it is argued that "stability is not necessitated by the nature of stability, because we observe the destruction of jars and other things even while there is an absence of the hearing or application [of a cause for their destruction]," we say no; for that [jar] possesses a perishable nature.
If it is asked, "Why then does its destruction not occur at all times?"—who says that it does not? It is simply not perceived due to concealment, like the sensation of heat in gold.
Rather, it is the power of destruction itself—which arises occasionally due to a difference in causes—that persists as the very nature of stability.
Just as when a jar or similar object is present, the manifestation of hot touch does not occur in gold, which consists of the substance of light.
Likewise, apart from that [nature], neither transformation nor destruction is tenable;
for there can be no destruction of anything belonging to the category of general properties (sāmānyadharma) that is devoid of that [specific] nature.
If it is argued that there is no destruction [at all], then it would follow that a jar or the like could still be perceived in its shards and so forth.
If it is argued that [the definition does not apply] because of concealment (*tirodhāna*), that is untenable because such concealment is impossible for this [definition].

Demonstrating this very point, he says "in a substance" (*dravye*) and so forth. The ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied is: "because of the state of being a reality (*vastu*)," that is, because of the fact of its being a thing whose definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from other substances—such as earth and the rest—from those [other] substances.
Why is this so? He says: "By its own nature," and so forth.
The meaning is that all things exist by virtue of their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*); otherwise, everything would be of the nature of all things and both beginningless and endless.
As it has been said:

The meaning is that, because concealment is impossible in the case of a potsherd and so forth produced immediately after the destruction of a jar, [the object] would be "consisting of all things" in the absence of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*); it would be "beginningless" in the absence of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which is the absence of arising; and it would be "endless" in the absence of destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

"Who would not desire all this to be real from the fourfold perspective of its own nature and so forth? It is unreal only through error; otherwise, it is not established [otherwise]. — Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 15.

[Objection: "But surely the persistence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) exists only in things that are momentary, for it has been said: 'All things [arise] by way of their own nature' (*Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* 3.39), and so forth. To this, he says: "Of that which undergoes transformation," and so on.

The word *ṣu* is used here for emphasis. [The opponent asks: "How is it that one obtains that very object which is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) as being always thus? To this, he says: For the Buddhist (*Saugata*), the destruction of the existing prior nature is precisely what is intended;

furthermore, either the subsequent attainment of another nature is that [destruction], or rather, the attainment of that [other nature] itself is its destruction, and not some other kind of annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*).

In this regard, if one asks: "Let this be so when the subsequent effect occurs immediately; but what happens when it does not occur at that time? To this he replies: "Because of transformation," and so forth.

Since the transformation (*vivarta*) of the evolving cause—the material cause—into the nature of its own effect is independent of anything else, the departure from that [cause] and the attainment of that [effect] is a mental construction (*bauddha*).
It might be thought that the attainment of another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is itself the falling away from the previous intrinsic nature.

If it is argued that the attainment of that [new nature] is not itself its falling away, but rather that non-existence (*abhāva*) is something distinct; to this he replies: the deficiency of the former is its non-existence, while the isolation of the latter—its being devoid of the form of the former—is the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of that [former state], not something existing apart from it.
If it is asked, "In that case, does it not exist at that time? And if so, how [can it be said to exist]?"—to this he says: "Because of being transformative," and so forth.

This means that because the transformative cause—the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)—is independent of anything else with respect to its own manifestation (*vivarta*), [the effect] is perceived through that.
If it is then argued, "In that case, it follows that 'subsistence' is merely the destruction of the prior form and the arising of the subsequent form"; to this he says: "And not," and so forth.
"Abiding in that" means *tatsthaḥ* (situated therein). Concluding [the discussion on] what occurs in the prior state, he says: "Its arising," and so forth;
thus, the infinite regress (*anavasthā*) consisting of that very nature which was propounded by others is refuted.

Now, if it is thought: "Let the apprehension of stability occur where a continuous series of three parts is obtained; but how can this be where there is only a middle form? To this he says: "Of the existent," and so forth.

That middle form which is visible of an existent substance is indeed existent in some way at its prior and posterior limits, though not in its entirety. Why? He says: "Otherwise," that is, by way of its non-existence [at those limits].
To the question, "How is the remainder one's own scripture? he says: "In every way," and so forth, as is perceived.
If it is thought: "Previously, that [entity] was eternal because there is no perception of its cause arising, but later, why [is it not eternal]?"—to this he says "svam" and so forth:

because for that which exists as belonging to its own continuum and attaining subsequent transformations, assistance by another is impossible, and thus a cause of a heterogeneous effect is impossible, since such is not observed; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of being unable to infer color from taste.
"Let there be no benefit even in that case"; to this he says: "The whole," and so forth.
From where is this understood—that for one who does not undergo transformation into that [benefit], such benefit is impossible? To this he says: "Mutually," and so forth.

Mutual engagement (*pravṛtti*) is production by way of a capable form; mutual withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) is cessation by way of an incapable form. *Anvaya* is positive concomitance (*anugama*), and *vyatireka* is negative concomitance (*vyāvṛtti*). Because of the state of being—that is, the fact of having—those two as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Of what? He says: "mutually," etc.
Of which things? He says: "of substances.
The implication is that this is because they are perceived at different times.
Because production from a cause is contradictory, [the effect] is non-existent, like a donkey's horn; otherwise, it would be existent.
This being the case, showing what is established, he says "that" and so forth.

Since this has just occurred, therefore—at the end, at the time of the production of a dissimilar effect, or at the time when no effect is produced—the destruction of substances is established because their decay is observed; thus the Buddhist, having seen stability in the middle, ought to determine the existence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in the prior and posterior limits as well.
Now, if there is sublation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here, there was [sublation] previously; thus he says: "because there is no distinction."
It has already been stated that the demonstration of its abiding in the middle [is established] here; thus, it is not discussed further regarding the position of its stability.

Now, one might ask: "Since there is a distinction between the natures of the visible and the invisible, how can one thing possess both the form of the visible and the other (invisible)? To this, he says: "The visible," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), forms such as moving and non-moving are included.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "In perception," and so forth;
this has been established [in the following]: "Because no distinction is perceived between consciousness and the appearance of an object" (Siddhi-viniścaya 1).
With the words beginning with "ityādinā," he provides an illustration for those such as the Vaiśeṣikas: "udbhūta" and so forth.

Those whose primary qualities are visible form (*rūpa*) and touch (*sparśa*), both manifest (*udbhūta*) and unmanifest (*anudbhūta*), as well as odor (*gandha*) and the rest, are described as such. That which possesses these manifest and unmanifest forms, touches, and so on, is the referent of the compound; "like that" means similar to that very thing.

For instance: on earth, all qualities beginning with color (rūpa) are generally manifested and visible; however, with respect to specific distinctions, they are divided in two ways: in water, odor (gandha) is unmanifested while the others are not; in fire, odor and taste (rasa) [are unmanifested]; in air, only touch (sparśa) is manifested—the meaning is that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound referring to color, taste, and touch.

If it is asked: "How is there a cognition of the existence of smell and so forth in water and other substances when they are unmanifest? If it is argued: "Because they possess touch, as in the case of earth;
otherwise, manifestation would occur in something of a different genus," we say: No, for since that [manifestation] exists in earth, there is no fault.

How does it possess that same class-nature? How does it possess the class-nature of gold? The possession of the class-nature of gold by fire is due to its being a substance of light (*tejodravyatvāt*); [the argument] "because it is a person (*pudgalatvāt*)" is the same.
How is it so in that case? [One might ask: "How is there luminosity in the *hotṛ* priest? Indeed, there is no other [means of cognition] there, for that would result in the absence of dispute;
its apprehension arises from the sense organ aided by instruction, and this is the same even regarding its being a person.

The perception of a radiant form is inferred from that [color]; let it be inferred if there were an invariable concomitance between them, but this is not so, because such a form is seen in a cloth crushed by a smooth stone that is yellow, odorless, and stainless.
Likewise, since tactile sensation is also observed, one might infer the nature of *pudgala* (matter) [from color] without distinction.

If it is argued that earth and the other elements are likewise specific substances (pudgala-dravya-viśeṣa) because they are seen to undergo transformation and appropriation— just as water and so forth become pearl-oysters and the like— and that for this reason they are said to be "material" (mūrta) like the *pudgala*, [we reply: they possess the nature of fire (*tejas*).

If it is argued that in gold, because of the difference between the possessor of qualities (the substrate) and the qualities themselves— such as its luminous form— it would not follow that "it is seen" while "that [form] is not seen," we say no; for this position has been refuted.

Even if there is a difference [between the substance and its qualities], the same logical consequence (prasaṅga) applies: the substrate would not be perceived as related to the qualities that appear [in cognition].

If that [substrate] were also perceptible, there would be a grasping of all its qualities; in its absence, there would be no perception of its being related to them, because [the relation] is not perceived otherwise than through the perception of the qualities currently appearing. If it is argued that the cognition of its being related [to qualities] occurs even when only the qualities appearing [in cognition] are grasped—[but] how could that be? If it is due to a relation, then there must be yet another "being-related-ness" for that relation, and yet another for that, leading to an infinite regress (anavasthā).

Therefore, it is logical that the single entity consists of both the visible and the invisible, since there is no absolute difference between quality and the possessor of qualities regarding its connection with other qualities.
