In the absence of the perception of qualities, it is logical that the connection with those qualities also resides in that very [substratum]; regarding this, he states another argument: "In perception," and so forth.

The connection [of the reason] is appropriate only with respect to that whose nature (svabhāva) is directly perceived, such as sound and so forth, and not with respect to any other subject (dharmin), because [the latter] is unestablished and because its status as an object of inference is logically untenable. This is established by the passage beginning with "visible, invisible, etc. Therefore, it was written again in vain. Now, one might ask: "What is the point of making that very nature an object of inference? To this he says: "In some way," namely in the form of sound and so forth, and not in the form of momentary destruction and so forth; for if it were in the latter form, there would result the futility of inferring that very nature.
If it is argued that [the cognition] does not exist because there is no certainty regarding what is uncertain, that is the very same fault—namely, the dual nature [of the object].
Furthermore, the refutation of the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) has already been established;
otherwise, the inference of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣayānumāna*) would be rendered useless. This is the intended meaning.

If it is argued: "But when the nature of the visible object is present and another thing is not seen, how can there be identity between the two? It would be like [the non-perception of] a different object that has arisen," [the author] replies here: "Not indeed," and so forth.
Why? To this he says: "Because of consciousness," and so forth;

for not only is there no external object, but even from the word [itself], there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of consciousness itself—that is, of mere cognition.

If it is argued that because of momentariness, the non-production of subsequent effects, and the non-appearance of everything, all things are included within mere illusion (vibhrama), and thus nothing anywhere is capable [of action]—since existence and non-existence are established through the superimposition of contradictory properties such as visibility and invisibility, and since there is no appearance of anything else, a single entity cannot possess both visible and invisible forms; to this he replies: "That is a false absolute," and so forth.
That even "mere consciousness" (saṃvittimātra) must be regarded as false—that is an obsession with an absolute [view]. In reality, [entities] such as one's own self and others are apprehended.
The remainder is easy to understand.
Furthermore, with the words "Moreover" (kiṃca) and so forth, he states another fault: in that case, [the opponent's view] is destroyed because the Sugata will be refuted later.

Refuting the Vaiśe� omniscience of the Vaiśeṣikas and others by showing that neither momentariness nor the capacity to produce a subsequent effect can appear [in their cognition], he says: "By virtue of being born from contact with the existent," and so forth;
omniscience is contradicted by the fact of being born from contact with the existent.
How could one who was previously non-omniscient become omniscient later? [And] how could that [omniscience] belong to an eternal being through anything else?

(21) How can there be knowledge of everything without remainder from the contact of the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects? Even if there is the power of asceticism (*tapas*), because the senses do not transcend their conjunction [with objects], they have restricted domains; and since the mind is atomic, if one were to imagine a clarity of contact with external objects by the force of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), then the non-simultaneity of cognitions would no longer be a valid mark for the existence of the mind.
The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind—
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.16.

But surely he also possesses eternal knowledge; therefore, why is that not considered non-contradictory, such that it is not suspected here as a point of refutation? If [you say] "no," then indeed it ought to be suspected. If you argue that it is not suspected because it was already refuted during the refutation of God (Īśvara), then by the same logic, since the negation of any other [entity] follows from the negation of momentary and partless entities, that too should not be suspected.

If it is argued that this is for the sake of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); and if it is further argued that even an eternal entity is likewise [subject to such proliferation], we say no. For the investigation of the properties (*dharma*) of an existent entity occurs because of its existence, not of a non-existent one. If it is asked how there can be a lack of existence [for the eternal], [we reply] it is due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Perception does not apply there, because it does not function with respect to that which is beyond the senses;
nor is there inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*);
the nature of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) is not the logical mark, because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by the cognitions of persons such as ourselves.
If the omniscience of the Lord, or of the Vaiśeṣika, is considered contradictory;
Even the knowledge of the Sugata is a valid means of cognition because it lacks eternal knowledge.
By this, [the argument] that "eternal cognition is like omnipresence, being a specific quality of an omnipresent substance" is refuted.
If it is argued that [the definition should be] "being an object of all things," [we reply: no, because of the case of the cognition of other yogis.

If it is argued that [the reason] must always have that as its object; if that very thing is both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the qualification of the reason (*hetu*), then it is worthless, for the opponent's impermanence is not established here,
nor is there an illustrative example (*nidarśana*),
due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
It might be argued: "The knowledge of God is eternal because, while existing, it is not produced by causes such as merit (dharma) and so forth, just like His omnipresence (vibhutva).
However, God possesses no merit or the like; since those causes are absent, His knowledge cannot arise from them.
Nor can that knowledge be produced by the merit or other qualities of another person, because the qualities of one self cannot be the cause of the qualities of another self.

Furthermore, does the knowledge of the Lord accomplish nothing at all? If that were so, from what would the production of all effects arise? If it arises from the Great Lord himself, then there is no distinction between such a person—who acts toward an effect independently of intellect—and an insentient agent;
for even if intellect exists, it would be useless.

Now, if [it is argued that] through the grasping of the object-entity (*padārtha*), the operation of every cognition (*buddhi*) pertains only to that [grasping] at the time of its own birth, and not to the production of the effect, then there would be a collapse of conventional usage such as "this was done intentionally" or "this is an unintended action. If, on the other hand, it is said that [the action] is "done by the person together with that [cognition]," and thus figuratively called "done by the cognition," then what contradiction is there in that cognition also being the instrument of that [action]? [Otherwise,] there would be another self (*ātman*).
The absence of distinction is the operation [of the cause] in the production of the effect,
occurring precisely at the time of the apprehension of the object.

Furthermore, by means of the intellect itself, accompanied by the intellect—if it were not [an effect] of another self’s quality, how could there be a cognition of another woman in one person due to the meditation of a counselor? If it is argued that even for another person, that cognition belongs to their own self; we say no, because it would follow that qualities such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth are useless everywhere, since [the result] would arise from the self alone.

Now, if it is argued that the minister’s meditation is a cause of mental transformation, and that the knowledge of God might likewise be such a cause—let it be so, what is the harm?—then, in the same way, other factors such as religious merit (*dharma*) and so forth would also be its causes. Thus, the absence of a cause is unestablished (*asiddha*);
therefore, there is no inference here.

If it is argued that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause for the arising of the knowledge of God—just as in your own system, whether the Omniscient One is known by that [means] or without it—then in my system, that very knowledge itself cognizes the eternity of the Self, either through that [means] or independently; [we reply: no, because this would result in the cognition of [the Self and the knowledge] as one and the same, making the postulation of God useless, since its purpose is accomplished by that much alone.

Just as there is no distinction in their being cognition (*jñānatva*), yet only that [particular cognition] is eternal; so too, although there is no distinction in their being qualities (*guṇatva*), only that [particular quality] is without a substrate (*anāśraya*).

Thus, the two observations—of non-eternality and eternality—are stated with respect to one case, while the fault mentioned in the other case is addressed by [the fact that it] arises from contact with the existent (*satsamprayogaja*) and so forth.
Therefore, it remains that knowledge is not eternal,
[being known] by itself and by another omniscient being.
In response to the doubt— "Since there is no other cognition of the Lord, how indeed can cognition exist without a substratum?"— he says:
The meaning is that within the general category of knowledge (*jñānasāmānya*), there are only two alternatives: namely, the knowledge of God (*īśvarajñāna*) itself.

In this context, "contact" (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the conjunction with an existing object; if knowledge were produced from that [contact], then the omniscience of the soul asserted by Kumārila would be contradictory, because he has not avoided all the faults [previously mentioned]. This is the sense.
He states another refutation: "From what cause does the eternally existent self possess omniscience? From none at all, because it would contradict its eternity.
If it is argued that "this [omniscience] is innate," he says in response: "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this understood?"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

If it is argued that because the nature of the self is seen as possessing excellence, omniscience (*sakalajñatā*) is produced by a cause as a distinct cognition whose object is everything, and that [omniscience] belongs to him due to its connection with that [self]; to this he replies: How could that [omniscience] belong to one who was previously not omniscient once knowledge has arisen later? For it is not logical that something [like omniscience] should come from another to one who is himself devoid of the inclination toward grasping objects.
The omniscience of the eternal self is omniscience.
In order to explain the verse, he says: "One's own," and so forth.

From the contact—consisting of conjunction and other types—of the self (ātman), the sense organ (indriya), the mind (manas), and the object (artha), how can there be knowledge of everything without exception?
If it is argued that such knowledge of all objects arises from the power of austerity (tapas); to this, he replies: "The power of austerity," and so forth.

The power of asceticism (*tapas*) is a specific capacity; even when that exists, cognition does not arise solely because it cannot transcend the contact of the sense organs [with their objects]. For in that case, cognition is not independent of contact; this is established by the opponent's own position. Furthermore, the phrase "because of the non-transcendence of the contact of the sense organs" should be explained accordingly.

Indeed, it is not the case that while that [divine eye] exists, the sense organs fail to apprehend an object with which they are in contact; for otherwise, there would follow the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reasons that establish sensory contact.

If it is argued: "The eye of people such as ourselves perceives an object with which it is in contact, because, while lacking its [the divine eye's] power, it is a sense organ, like the sense of touch (*sparśana*)," we say no. This is because the absence of that [divine power] is unproven, since it is not excluded in other births;
furthermore, because the qualification "to whatever extent" is missing from the reason, the reason is non-probative, and because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, by the power of that [internal organ], the sense organs are known to be of such a nature that they become fully accomplished in relation to all their respective objects. Regarding this, he says: "restricted," and so forth.

For, by the power of that [internal organ], the tactile organ and the others do not wander toward every object, leaving the body behind. If they were to wander along with it, then, even though the rays of the eyes reach everywhere, there would be the apprehension of form alone in its entirety, and not of taste and the other [objects].
If that [object] were apprehended by that [mind] alone, then the other sense organs would be rendered useless.
To this he says: "restricted," and so forth.
If it is argued that the mental [cognition] of the yogi has the entire range as its object, whereas that born of the eyes and other senses does not, to this he replies: "of the mind," and so forth.

If one asks, "From what [source] does the conception of clarity arise when there is contact with external objects from the perspective of the subtle mind? he says: "By the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), aided by merit (dharma) and so forth. The sense is that, because the mere [mind] possesses the capacity to be the cause of clarity in the cognition of those [objects], just like the mental cognition of the past and so on, there exists the possibility of a connection independent of sensory contact, namely, the potentiality of austerity (tapas) from a previous birth.
By the power of austerity,
even taste and the other [objects] are perceived by the eye alone.

If it is argued that the clarity of cognitions such as dreams belongs to the mind alone, [we reply] that it would belong to others as well, since there is no difference in that regard. Furthermore, if from that [mind alone] the yogin possessed clarity regarding the knowledge of all objects, then because of the non-difference between every connection and its related object, this would be the case for everyone;
but it is not so. Therefore, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) must be admitted.
To the question "What [is there] in that [instance]? he says: "The non-simultaneity of cognitions," and so forth.

The meaning is this: even when all sense-objects are present, the fact that cognitions do not arise simultaneously would not be a valid mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of the mind (*manas*), because—just like the clarity of those cognitions—their non-arising also occurs solely due to unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
The mind is conjoined with the self, and all objects are [conjoined] with that [mind]; thus, because there is no distinction in this indirect relationship,
[the self] possesses clarity regarding all objects without exception.
Demonstrating this very point through the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions, he says: "That," and so forth;
and because of that variety, for some there may be simultaneous cognition, otherwise not.
Even if this were the case, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that multiple memories arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, because the soul is atomic and independent [of parts], there is no distinction between its spatial location and the object; therefore, [the soul] would be rendered a non-entity. Thus: || 22–23 ||
For one who asserts that there are six categories of existence, what object could there be that is distinct from those [categories],
such that it might have a conjunction with another mind?
Furthermore, since it would be distinct from substance (*dravya*), there would occasionally be a memory arising from disjunction (*vibhāga*).

Nor can selfhood be inherent in the [bodily] parts, for that would entail the consequence of [the self] being manifold; nor can it belong to what is not-self, because of the lack of contact with each individual [part]. Furthermore, if there were a difference between the parts and their possessor, pleasure and other qualities could not properly reside in the self.

If external objects were known through the contact of the self, the mind, and the senses, why would cognitions not arise simultaneously? If the mind were unitary, there could be only a single cognition at once, because it is impossible to restrict its connection to each individual self [if there were many].

If, for that purpose... [there were] a sequential connection of such a [mind] with cognition in some instances, then omniscience would follow; how much more so for one who does not abandon his non-omniscient nature? Furthermore, prior to that, it is impossible for something devoid of a connection to the nature of cognition to be either an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

By the word "that" (*tat*), the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the cause of that clarity is referred to; due to its diversity as a cause, consciousness would arise simultaneously for certain beings such as Īśvara, both externally and internally, whereas for those lacking the power of austerity (*tapas*), it would otherwise be established in a sequential manner.

[Objection: But surely, since that which is to be known through inference cannot be non-existent in this way, otherwise there would be the futility of a cause even when its effect is observed everywhere, precisely because that [effect] has been produced. [Response: No; for its mark (*liṅga*) is not seen to be invariably concomitant (*pratibandha*) with it in any instance, or else one must admit that what is unperceived is itself the mark; therefore, it would not be a valid mark. Thus he says:
He states another refutation: "Even when," and so forth.
Not only when [the mind] is absent, but even when the mind exists, the simultaneous arising of memories would follow as a consequence, solely from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
From where is this [known]? To this he says: "That is its self," and so forth.
That [self] is the mind (*manas*), and the person (*puruṣa*); from what does the dependence on their conjunction arise? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.
Alternatively, it should also be explained that there would be a simultaneous arising of that [cognition] and the contact with its own self.
Why? He says: "Because they are independent," and so forth.
Of what? He says: "Of the atom," and so forth.
If the non-simultaneity of memories is accepted, what [follows]? Here he says: "In a location," and so forth.
Now, since the opponent also does not accept the simultaneity of visual and other cognitions for that very reason, one should have said "of cognitions in general" (*saṃvittīnām sāmānyena*).

And the word "memory" (*smṛti*) is not a term denoting generality, because it denotes a specific instance of it. Therefore, if you say that this [reference to] "memories" is not logical; [we reply: there might sometimes be simultaneity even of visual and other cognitions, for we do not infer [simultaneity] from their appearance, as there is a reversal [of that inference] in the case of conceptual cognitions (*savikalpa*).

Or else, let the statement "it exists" be [understood as follows]: since there is no distinction between the locus (pradeśa) and that which possesses the locus (tadvat)—both being of the nature of a conditioned locus—there would be a mutual difference; yet if there were such a distinction, only one of the two would exist. Why is this so? Because the parts (pradeśas) would lack substantial reality. To this he says: "The six categories," etc.;
the sense is that the opponent does not admit any category other than those [six].
In the absence of a distinction in consciousness,
according to the Vaiśeṣika.
Some maintain that even those [categories] distinct from that [substance] are real; that is not so, for what is the meaning [of "real"]? And so forth:
substance, quality, and action are the objects (arthas); [the definition of object is] "that which exists in substance, quality, and action" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.2).

If it is argued that "the categories exist" because of the statement [in the *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha*], "Existence (sattā) is that which makes the three categories existent," since existence—which possesses a distinct nature from those [categories]—cannot have inherence (samavāya) with them due to the impossibility of its inherence [in them]; to this, he says: "Substance... and so forth.

The conjunction of those spatial points of the self with the mind, or with another body, and so forth, arises from the action of one of the two factors; how could it be produced by conjunction? Nor indeed could there be disjunction, because that [conjunction] is preceded by conjunction, and in its absence, [disjunction] would not exist—even though they are distinct from the six categories.
The claim that "inherence belongs to what is distinct" is redundant;
for the comparison [to existence] holds because that "existence" (sattā) resides in substances, qualities, and actions.
— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.38

"If there is an absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), how could [the qualities] not exist? To this he says: "Because they are distinct from substance," meaning because they are different from substance. And without that [substance], how could there be a quality such as conjunction? If it is argued that "because of some conjunction, such as an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) acting as a concomitant cause, they are not distinct from substance," to this he replies with the words beginning with "for you" (*tava*).

The intended meaning here is as follows: If the spatial parts (pradeśas) that are distinct from the self were a substance—just as potsherds and the like are substances distinct from a jar—then would they be the substance of the self itself or something different from it? Regarding the first alternative, because the universal "selfhood" (ātmatva) inheres in them, they would be a substance of the self, just like the primary self. But that is untenable due to a contradiction with reasoning;
thus he says: "And not at all," meaning that the subordinate universal "selfhood" does not inhere in the spatial parts, for there is no difference [between the self and its parts].

From where do the parts of the parts come? To this he says: "Pratyātma" means with respect to each individual self; because of the consequence of differentiation within each self, there would follow a state of multiplicity.
He thinks thus: [If there were] multiplicity of selves within a single self, there would follow the consequence of its having parts and so forth.
Furthermore, if they were not all-pervading, there would be an abandonment of the absolute thesis that the self is all-pervading.

Moreover, when those [selves] come into contact with the mind, the inherence of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) would also belong to them alone, because it is produced by their contact; for it is stated that since that [contact] is produced by conjunction, the *adṛṣṭa* produced by that conjunction is "produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind."
Furthermore, that which is produced by conjunction with one thing cannot inhere in another, because that would entail the same [inherence] in other sentient beings as well; moreover,

since it is stated that "the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) which yields fruit should reside in those very [beings] who are the agents," they must possess activity when traveling to other worlds, and if they did not descend [to earth], there would be the destruction of the distinctions within saṃsāra.
Furthermore, if the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of one [person] were to cause the transmigration of another, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Regarding the second position—that [the soul] is not omnipresent—since there is no contact with substances in other locations, how could there be an attraction by that unseen force? This must be considered.

Moreover, the conjunction of a spatial point with the mind is flawed, just like the conjunction with an atom. Thus, if the soul were not omnipresent, there would be the aforementioned difficulties; if it were omnipresent, there would be the same problems as in the first case, including the impossibility of its being in a state of contraction or expansion.
Alternatively, the conceptualization of that [space] would be futile; for since the production of the effect occurs from the very first [moment of] being a non-self, that same fault recurs.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate a further spatial part to avoid that fault, the same [problem] would recur, resulting in a circular argument (*cakraka*). Thus, this [position] is not tenable at all.
Showing the fault in the second alternative, he says: "Nor from what is not a self," and so forth.

Even according to the other alternative suggested by the sūtra, pleasure and so forth cannot arise as memories from the contact of the mind with a distinct substance that possesses spatial extension (*pradeśa*) and is of a similar nature; why? To this he says: "In the self," etc., and states another refutation beginning with "of the part and the possessor of the part," and so forth.
It is easily understood that,
when there is a multiplicity of spatial units (*pradeśa*), there is a corresponding multiplicity of those spatial units themselves.
The reading included within this—"the arising of dharma from the conjunction of the self and the mind"—is redundant; [as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 638:
"in the regions of the self."
"It is the cause of the beloved, the beneficial, and liberation for the agent"— [from] *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, page 637.
Furthermore, regarding the position that "it is after that," [the text continues with] "again, in its majesty," and so forth.

"The self (ātman) is joined with the mind (manas); the mind with the sense-organ (akṣa); and the sense-organ with the object (artha). Given this contact—the relationship consisting of conjunction and so forth—between the self, the mind, the sense-organ, and the object, why would simultaneous cognitions not arise when there is the production of knowledge of external objects?

If it is argued that because the mind is unitary, there can be no simultaneous connection of all the sense-organs with their respective objects by means of it, [the author] replies here: "Of the minds," and so forth.
If the mind were unitary, there would be only a single cognition at once.
But this is not the case, because [you] do not accept it; for by that very [reasoning], there would be the undesirable consequence of no cognition arising in other selves.

If cognition arises from that very [cause] even in one [self], then the simultaneous arising of multiple cognitions in a single [self] would be unavoidable. Since [the cause] is the same for the production of many, what determines the distinction that it occurs in only one?
When knowledge arises within the inner self through the mind and the senses.
It might be argued that even though there are many [minds], only one mind at a time is conjoined with a single soul; to this he replies with the words "pratyekam" (each) and so forth.

The sense is that because it is impossible for each individual mind to have a necessary and inevitable connection with each individual soul—since that would contradict the omnipresence (*vyāpitva*) of souls—the hypothesis that the conjunction of what is seen by Kṛṣṇa acts as the regulator is corrupted by the aforementioned defects.
Now, as to how the fault of having parts can be attributed to a self that lacks spatial extension, he says: "If," and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says: "For that purpose," and so forth;
[this refers] to that self.
He states another refutation with the words "tādṛśa" and so forth.

The connection is as follows: for such an immutable entity (*kūṭastha*), omniscience is impossible because of its association with knowledge occurring sequentially—that is, successively and repeatedly—in some particular state.
If that were the case, even when there is such an association, its orientation toward grasping objects would remain as before.
The meaning is "hard," referring to the self which is partless, immutable, and eternally fixed.
Since [the self] is eternal even when connected with knowledge, just as in its prior state,
he states another argument, beginning with "What more," and so forth.
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates that the previous refutation has not been resolved.

For one who does not abandon his non-omniscient nature, how can there be omniscience? This [question] follows from the connection [of the argument]: Is his nature such that it does not face toward previous objects, like space and so forth, or is its nature such that it faces toward them? In the first case, the previous statement [applies]; in the second case as well, is his nature facing toward all objects or facing toward only a few categories of things? Regarding that, in the first alternative, there would be omniscience for every living being;
in the second, [the same applies to] the second [alternative].
The ellipsis is "it arises from its connection with cognition";
for even when there is such a connection, one must state the refutation that the tendency toward grasping the object does not remain as it was before.

If it is argued that omniscience is impossible for any living being whatsoever, and that even in the case of subsequent cognition, this [self] possesses only the status of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) directed toward its object and nothing else, and that due to a particular auxiliary cause (*sahakāriviśeṣa*), it may at some time produce such-and-such a cognition— regarding this, he says: "Previously," and so forth.

Prior to the arising of the cognition that exists as before, there is no connection with the nature of cognition; rather, for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that very cognition is its nature, and that alone is the connection. Therefore, for the non-conscious conceptual construction, its being an inherent cause—that is, its being a cause through inherence in that cognition—is impossible. For instance, earth and other such substances, which lack the nature of cognition and the connection [to it], are not inherent causes of that cognition; and likewise, according to the opponent, the self lacks those [two]. Otherwise, even earth and the like would become its inherent cause. Thus, [the status of] being an inherent cause [is untenable].

If it is argued that if the earth and other elements were the causes of their own effects, there would be a loss of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) because the body and so forth are impermanent; and if it is further argued that this [loss] would apply to atoms because they are not perceived—[we ask]: is there, however, a non-perception of the self (*ātman*) as postulated by others? If that is so, let it be for the atoms;
since cognition is a quality (*guṇa*), its substrate alone is established, but there is no certainty as to whether that substrate is the self or the atoms.

If it is argued that those [qualities] are not perceived by people like us because they are the causes of cognition, just as their forms and so forth are not perceived; then why would the self also not be unperceived, even though it is its cause, given its omnipresence? In this case, the diversity of qualities is not a reason for such a distinction, since [the self] would be the inherent cause of knowledge if it were of an impermanent nature.
The cause is merely the support for the atoms of earth and so forth.
The phrase "exists" is to be supplied when [the atoms] are the cause of cognition; furthermore,
if atoms possessed the quality of consciousness, they would be all-pervading like space.

For instance, if it is argued that atoms are all-pervasive because, while being eternal, they are the substrata of qualities perceptible to people like us—just like space—we say no; for there is a deviation [from the rule] by the case of jars and the like, since absolute eternity is denied everywhere.
Therefore, just as atoms are not the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of those [qualities] due to their lack of connection with them, so too let the self not be [the inherent cause].

If it is argued that it would be an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause); to this he replies: "And [the status of] being an *asamavāyikāraṇa*... and so forth—all of this is impossible. Regarding the connection with cognition:

what indeed is this *asamavāyikāraṇa*? If it is said to be "that which is other than the *samavāyikāraṇa* (inherent cause)," then the *nimittakāraṇa* (instrumental cause) is also other than that; consequently, even something deficient in that [quality], like the eye and so forth, could be its cause, and thus the negation [of such causality] is untenable.

Now, it is said that for a subsequent sound, the preceding sound is its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) by way of inherence in its own cause; or, as in the case of a cloth, it is inherent in the cause of its own cause; or, as in the case of cognition, it is inherent in the cause of the cause, namely the conjunction of the self and the mind. This is incorrect, because the conjunction of the self with the body is not admitted in any instance.

If it is argued that [the opponent's] assertions are maintained [as valid], it is replied: regarding the production of recollective cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*), the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is accepted by the opponent as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because of the statement that "the latent impression is born of cognition and is the cause of cognition," and because it inheres in its own cause. Yet even that is impossible for something lacking those [qualities], for just as an insentient thing is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the sentient, so too it would follow that the sentient must inhere in it;
[but this is not the case, as the inherent cause must be distinct from the non-inherent cause].

Space, although devoid of any relation to the intrinsic nature of cognition, is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition and the cause of the subsequent sound; therein it is the inherent cause.

The cause of the color of the cloth is the cloth; its cause is the threads. Among these, the color of the threads—which exists as an inherent cause (samavāyi-kāraṇa) by way of the relation of inherence—is one cause of the cognition. Another cause is the self (ātman), and the third is the contact between the self and the mind (ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga), which exists in both [the self and the mind] by way of the relation of inherence.
Thus, the inclusion of the term "of that" (tasya) is redundant.
The comparison regarding the arising of a mental formation (*saṃskāra*): "born from knowledge...
— *Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 3.
The cause of recollection is the self, in which the mental impression (saṃskāra) is inherent;
[this refers] to a self that is devoid of the nature of cognition.
Suppose it is argued that the spatial parts (pradeśas) of the self exist and that they are somehow distinct from it. To this, he says: "If, however," and so forth.
If, moreover, the identity between the parts and their possessor were not perceived by this cognizer—
One might conquer the Buddhists through boldness regarding the reality of substance and modification:

even though there is a difference between the self and so forth, and their respective spatial locations (pradeśa) and the possessor thereof, they possess a form of identity (*tādātmya*) in some respect by their very nature, because no other relation exists;

whereas for qualities and the qualified, or for universals and their possessors—which exist simultaneously—there is no identity in any respect. Thus, desiring to establish this reality as such through one's own ingenuity, one triumphs with audacity over the disciples of Śauddhodani, who, due to the delusion of fallacious reasoning, reject the transformation into identity between the object and its mental form.

If it is argued that the locus (*pradeśa*) and that which occupies it (*tadvat*) do not possess independence like a jar and a cloth because inherence (*samavāya*) is impossible—and since they cannot be other than identical (*tādātmya*), even if there is some form of identity between the locus and its self, here [inherence] does not exist; to this, he replies: "If there were oneness of the locus and that which occupies it" (*tadvad eṣa tadvadaikyaṃ cet*), and so forth. The meaning is that if this Naiyāyika, who has accepted the oneness of the locus and that which occupies it, were not to perceive it as such, he would not perceive the reality (*tattva*) of substance and mode (*dravyaparyāya*) as being both unity and multiplicity (*ekatānātvam*); rather, he would have to perceive it as such.

Expounding upon the verse, he says that one may overcome the Buddhists—who fail to perceive the identity between substance and its modes—by means of boldness: "The self and so forth"; by the word "and so forth," movement and the like are included. Even though there is a difference between the locus and that which occupies it, how is there a certain degree of identity? He asks: "By its very nature. To this, he replies: "Because of the relations," and so on.

Because there is no relation other than the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), there can first of all be no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between those two; for if there were, it would follow [absurdly] that they would be like the mind (*manas*) and its conjunctions.

Furthermore, in that case, the self (*ātman*) and so forth would not exist in those [objects], otherwise even jars and the like would [exist in them] due to the lack of distinction in their conjunction.

Even for objects such as pots, there would only be conjunction with their own constituent parts, whether through inseparable inherence (*ayutasiddhatva*) or otherwise; this is equally true for the case at hand.

Nor can it be inherence (*samavāya*), because that would entail that those [parts] are themselves composed of further parts, and consequently, like pots and the like, they would be non-eternal. Furthermore, by virtue of being characterized by the specific arrangement of their own constituent parts, even God would necessarily have been preceded by another God.
For that very reason, [relations] such as inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) are cast far aside;
there is no identity whatsoever between a quality and its possessor, but rather only difference.
To the question "Of what kind are these two?", he says: "Together," and so forth.
Furthermore, of which two? He says: "jāti" and so forth;
and "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Thus, desiring to establish reality (*tattva*) through his own arbitrary intellect as being exclusively of the nature of difference—identifiable as "this"—and not as having a non-exclusive, momentary, and other such forms, he [the opponent] triumphs over the disciples of Śauddhodani with impudence.

Doing what? He says: [doing so] while rejecting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a transformation consisting of identity (*tādātmyapariṇāma*), due to the delusion of fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*).
How do they reject it? He says: this has been discussed at length in the passage beginning with "the form of its own object" (*svārthākāra*).

If it is argued that there is no identity (*tādātmya*) even between a location and that which occupies it, he says here: "For locations and their occupants cannot possess independence like a jar and a cloth"—this is the intended meaning.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the existence of inherence (*samavāya*) and other relations, he says: "Inherence," etc.
Is it impossible for that [identity] to exist in every respect? To this he says: "Elsewhere," etc.
If a relation other than identity were desired [between the part and the whole], that would be impossible; however, if identity is accepted, it is indeed possible for the parts and their possessor,
as it would be for the self and its attributes.
Since it would belong to the various regions, there is no independence.
Showing that inherence is impossible, he says: "Conjunction," and so forth;
[it is] like an all-pervading substance, other than conjunction and inherence.

Apart from identity with its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it does not establish itself [as related] anywhere. Thus, setting aside transformation (*pariṇāma*), no other relation—whether conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)—can be postulated;
for in their absence, there would be no obstruction to all-pervading entities existing within their own locations.

If it is argued that in the case of an absolute difference between those two, the relation here is the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) through the occurrence of inherence (*samavāya*), [we reply: let this very same relation apply everywhere; it is certainly not otherwise. For how could a relation be established elsewhere—among things that are mutually distinct—apart from their own nature and identity (*tādātmya*)? He provides an example: "like all-pervading substances" (*vibhudravyavat*).

If it is argued that [the relationship] is established through conjunction (*saṃyoga*); to this he replies—stating the meaning of the verse—that it is not established through conjunction or inherence (*samavāya*). He says "everywhere," etc., meaning that apart from transformation (*pariṇāma*)—specifically inseparable transformation (*avinirbhāga-pariṇati*)—no other relation between the self (*puruṣa*) and the staff can be postulated.

What is this? He says: it is conjunction (*saṃyoga*). However, it must be conceived in such a way that conjunction exists in some manner as the identity (*tādātmya*) of two things; otherwise, it would follow that the person and the staff are its parts and [the self] is the whole (*avayavī*), just like a jar and its potsherds. And thus, from the pulling of one, there would necessarily follow the pulling of all, even in the case of the self and the body, because there would be another whole [distinct from them]. But this is not the case.

Having thus explained the transformation of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—that is, their transformation as identity (*tādātmya-pariṇāma*)—he asks: "What other relation could be postulated? He says: "Inherence (*samavāya*).

Why? To this he replies: "In its absence"—that is, in the absence of such transformation—since there would be no obstruction to the existence of all-pervading entities like the self (*ātman*) within their own spatial locations, there would be a lack of relation; therefore, such transformation must be postulated.
"In what [case]? he asks. He says: "In the case of the absolute distinction between those two, there would be an absolute plurality between that location and its possessor;
thus, inherence would be the connection. To this, he replies:
"If it is argued that the occurrence of inherence is due to inherence itself... To this, he replies: "Of inherence," and so forth.
There would be a conjunction; the relationship between those two would consist of conjunction.

Some maintain that inherence (*samavāya*) is a non-connection. For them, the relation between a quality and its possessor is called a "connection" because it generates the cognition "it is here"; yet this is not possible for something non-existent, as it would be contradictory for such a thing to generate a cognition like any other distinct category (*padārthāntara*).

If it is argued that it possesses a capacity (*śakti*), then, by virtue of possessing that capacity, it would be so [a connection], just as a substance is white by virtue of possessing the quality of whiteness.
Furthermore, if the capacity is distinct from that [inherence], the establishment of a connection is not achieved.

Furthermore, if one postulates *samavāya* (inherence), there is no end to it; moreover, since the relation of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*) exists, let that alone be the connection—what is the use of *samavāya*? If it is argued that qualities and so forth are indeed qualifiers of substance, yet there would only be a cognition colored by the quality and not the cognition "it is here" (*ihapratīti*), [we ask]: how then does the cognition "there is inherence" arise? This very relation of being a qualifier is the cause of the cognitions "it is here, it is here," and nothing else—this is truly the sport of the Lord! If one postulates yet another relation for that [inherence], there is an infinite regress.

Furthermore, what would the state of being a qualifier do for the entity? Since it is impossible for that which does nothing to be a real thing, if it does something, then everything remains in that same state.
If it is argued that the capacity (śakti) is non-different from it, then by that same logic, qualities and so forth would also not be distinct from the possessor of those qualities.

If it is argued that [the expression] "the color and so forth of the jar" would not be possible, then how could there be the expression "the power of that which possesses it"? If it is argued that because there is no difference between quality and the possessor of quality, the apprehension of one entails the apprehension of all, then why is there no apprehension of *sattā* (existence) when there is the apprehension of substance and so forth? If that were the case, from where would doubt and the like arise regarding mantras and such? This objection against the view of others is dismissed with the words beginning with "navai," wherein the word "tat" refers to the Self (*ātman*).
"Non-connection" (asambandha) means that no other connection exists for this;
[it refers to] inherence in relation to inherence.
If one were to postulate another relation for substance and so forth, it would result in an infinite regress from inherence.
Does [the property] such as "possessing qualities" (guṇin) exist?
Regarding that, he states the refutation: "partless," and so forth.

If memory were produced from the conjunction of partless atoms and the self, it would follow that memory is eternal, just like the atoms themselves; and if you claim that the sixfold group of memories is perceived simultaneously, [we reply]:

since the conjunction of the self and the mind is impossible given their absolute partlessness, and because [the self] is non-occasional, all-pervading, and co-existent with its substance, how could a specific quality arising from them—which is independent of anything else—be occasional, such that memory occurs only at certain times?
If the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) were the cause, the mind would be without a cause;
furthermore, even when the atomic mind exists, there would be the simultaneous arising of six or seven memories for the self, just as [multiple] atoms [can exist together].

Thus, this instrument—the "other self" (*ātmāntara*)—which is taught in that scripture as a distinct substance, even though it exists, proves to be of no use whatsoever when examined, whether internally or externally.

"Aṇu" is a designation for the mind. [The opponent argues: "Memory is eternal (nityam), always present, due to the cause which is the conjunction of the two partless entities—the self and the atom. This is merely an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa); thus, it would follow that memory occurs everywhere.
Indeed, when a capable cause exists everywhere and at all times, the effect cannot be occasional; for that would entail the fallacy of the cause not being the true cause (atattvārthatva).

[The opponent replies: "This fault does not apply, because conjunction does not subsist throughout the entirety of a substance. For the conjunctions of atoms do not exist by pervading their entire extent."

Regarding this, he says: "If it is held to be like an atom," meaning that just as conjunction existing in atoms does not always reside within their own nature because it does not endure as long as the substance itself, so too [the conjunction] of the self and the mind might be intended [not to be permanent]; to this, he states the reply: "Let the sixfold set of memories be observed simultaneously [arising] from the conjunction."

He thinks as follows: For the self (*ātman*), which is all-pervading and situated in the midst [of everything], there must necessarily be conjunctions with the atomic mind (*aṇumanas*), since that [mind] exists as long as the substance [lasts] and because it is connected to that self through its own nature by means of the six directions (*ṣaḍdig*). And thus, those two possess that very same quality of having parts (*sāvayavatva*); otherwise, how could [the mind] have a mode of existence in specific locations (*pradeśavṛttitva*)? Now, if it is argued that just as for the Jaina there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) in the state of atoms being in immediate proximity (*nairantarya*), so too for me there is [conjunction] between the self and the mind; this may be correct, but conjunction is not a quality (*guṇa*), because [otherwise] the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) [of the self] would be abandoned due to [its restriction to] the location of the mind.

If it is argued that let there be six simultaneous conjunctions for him, but from them only a single memory arises—just as a single cloth arises from threads or from their conjunctions—that is not so, because the intention is otherwise.

For instance, although the mind is a single entity, just as six conjunctions inhering in it with the self arise simultaneously, so too do the six memories; thus, the oneness of the mind is not the cause for the oneness of the memory. It follows [that they are distinct].
Explaining the verse, he says: "The self," and so forth.

If the absolute partlessness and unity of the self and the mind are accepted, then because a conjunction of the self and the mind—i.e., their contact—or any other relation between them is impossible, and because [such a relation] would have to exist as long as the substance exists (yāvaddravyabhāvitva), like the omnipresence of the self which is not occasional, how could there be the arising or production of that specific quality from that contact? That is to say, how could there be the production of that specific quality, such as cognition and so forth, which has its origin (*prabhava*) in that contact? It is that very thing which is the specific quality, such as cognition and so forth.

If it is argued that [memory] occurs only occasionally because its auxiliary cause (sahakārin), which depends on that [past experience], is itself occasional, the author replies: this has already been examined under the discussion of "depending on various other things" (*anyānyapekṣin*);
for since that [auxiliary] is occasional, memory would likewise occur only occasionally—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Therefore, that which was stated—"Cognitions such as pleasure and dreams are produced by the sense organs because they possess the nature of being cognitions, like cognitions of color and so forth produced by the eye and other organs; that which is the sense organ is the mind"—is refuted.
Consequently, [the opponent] considers it improper for those [cognitions] to be occasional if [the mind] exists [as their cause].
Thus, while accepting the occasional nature of the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force), he points out the fault in its being the cause of those [cognitions], saying "adṛṣṭe" and so forth.

The mind would be causeless and devoid of any mark; [this is the] comparison for the auxiliary [argument]: or else pleasure and so forth must be produced by an instrument, because they are objects of apprehension, like color-form and the rest.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 425: The cognition of pleasure and so forth is produced by the sense organs, because it is a direct cognition...
[and] memory is produced by the sense organs, because it is a cognition.
—[PRAŚA° KA° p.

90] If [visual cognition] arises from the mind, then surely visual and other cognitions would arise from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); since they would be produced from that alone, the eyes and other [senses] would be useless.

If it is argued that [the mind is not useless] because its cognition occurs from that [soul]; and if it is further argued that the mind is also not useless for that very reason, since its cognition follows immediately after inference—[we reply: no, because there is deviation from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and because that [self-awareness] has already been established. Now, having provisionally accepted the mind, he states the refutation: "Even though" and so forth. Even though the subtle atom-like mind exists—not merely when it is absent—and even though the soul possesses spatial extension (*pradeśavattva*), the six or seven types of memories would still arise simultaneously with the soul due to their connection with the soul.
Why? To this he says: "like an atom," and so forth;
because the cognition of color and other qualities arises from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) alone.

It might be argued: "In your view as well, the mind exists; that too would thus be without a cause. If it is replied, "No, because it is known through scripture," then [we respond]: "Let my [mind] be likewise.
If it is argued, "No, because its purpose is established through the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)," then [we reply]: "The same applies to yours as well."
"The conceptualization of both [is applied] in both places. To this he replies: "This very identity," and so forth.

This, when investigated, is "incapable of accomplishing anything"—that is, it is unable to effect even the slightest thing. Of what nature is it? It is "even though existing," meaning that although it exists merely as a recitation from scripture.

If it is objected: "Since it performs an action for another purpose, how can that which is ineffective toward its own object be considered a 'means' (sādhana)? [The author replies: Even when performing the effect of something else, because it is of no use—just as a defective sense organ is useless for the experience of pleasure and so forth—it is designated in this way. But what kind of thing is it? In what form is it a "means"? To this he says: "The self," and so forth.
Furthermore, in what sense is it a different object? To this he says: "it is another substance" (*dravyāntara*). A substance other than the perceived substances such as the eye is "another substance.
Where is it ineffective? To this he says: "both internally and externally."

Regarding the internal self-awareness of pleasure and so forth: it is not the case that there is no other sensory cognition [besides the awareness of pleasure] itself; otherwise, the distinction [between types of cognition] would be untenable. As for external objects such as a jar, since multiple cognitions—such as visual perception and other experiences—are present therein, the grasping or non-grasping of the phonemes and so forth is caused by the strength or weakness of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), just as in the case of a human’s grasping or non-grasping of the grammatical derivation of a word.

By the phrase "even though [it exists]," he shows that [the self] is accessible through scripture (*āgama*); by the phrase "it is ineffective," he demonstrates that even in the Jaina system, it is not inferable because it lacks any unique effect (*asādhāraṇakārya*) of its own. This is due to the specific differences in the destruction and subsidence of the veils (*āvaraṇakṣayopaśama*), which result in the self being either more firm or otherwise.
The phrase "tadetadāgama" is the opening of the commentary (*vṛtti*) that is about to be stated; since it is of no consequence [to the argument],
the expression "raparasyānubhavāde" has been written twice.

If it is argued that its establishment [as a substance] follows because the functional sense-organ (*bhāvendriya*), which consists of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the obstruction to the spatial points of the self (*ātmapradeśa*), depends upon a material instrument (*dravyakaraṇa*); then, where does it depend on that? If you say "in respect of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth," then since the eye and other such instruments exist there as logical marks (*liṅga*), this is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, you seek to establish something else even beyond that, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), as in the Sāṅkhya system, regarding that which consists of the subsidence-cum-destruction of the obstruction within the spatial points of the self.
The functional faculty (bhāvendriya) depends upon the substantial faculty (dravyendriya),
because [the latter] is accepted as consisting of eleven faculties.
Furthermore, if all cognition regarding an object of knowledge (*prameya*) were dependent on another [sense organ] when the sense organ is active, how could there be perception?
If you argue that this applies to future pleasure and so forth, we say no; for it has already been stated that this is contradicted by the case of mindless pleasure and the like.

Moreover, for one who speaks thus, why would it not follow that everything is perceptual and born of the senses, since they possess the nature of being such? If you say "because of the lack of the impossibility-otherwise-ness (*anyathānupapatti*)," then let us remain in agreement, as this deficiency is the same in the other case as well.
If it is argued that [the soul is omniscient] because of its presiding over [the mind], then let it be so;

yet whether it be the mind or the cognition as imagined by the opponent, even so, according to the Yoga school, there is no such thing as omniscience, nor is there an omniscient being. Demonstrating this, he says: "By itself," and so forth.
Nor is there omniscience; nevertheless, according to the Yoga school, this has been written twice [in the previous argument].
Furthermore, since consciousness cannot manifest by itself as something non-existent, how could it exist ultimately through another, given that this would lead to an infinite regress? (30)

Even though there is contact with all objects, there is non-omniscience because an entity consists of both existence and non-existence; for this person, whose sense organs and body are produced by yoga, might see or recollect all things in various ways through his own power and by his own nature. However, since consciousness (saṃvit)—that is, knowledge—cannot manifest when it is not functioning within its own nature (svarūpa) due to the absolute absence of that nature, and because there is no appearance of such [consciousness], how could there be omniscience? This is because one would not even perceive one’s own intellect.

That is not tenable—the argument that "the category of existent and non-existent things is the objective support of a single cognition because it is one, like the five qualities"—because this is contradicted by the cognition of that [cognition] itself. If it is argued that its manifestation occurs through another cognition, he says: the connection is that its manifestation cannot occur from something else, i.e., from another cognition, because there would be no apprehension of even a single object due to the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
It might be argued: "Since this self, being in proximity [to all objects], would perceive all things when under examination—of what nature is it? To this he says: "Yoga," and so forth.
When what exists? To this he says: "The perfected ones," and so forth.
How and in what manner? To this he says: "In many ways," and so forth; or likewise, "one should recollect," and so forth.
The word "yataḥ" (since) is used here in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepa*): one should not even recollect [the object].

Now, even though consciousness exists within the self, the proponent of contact (*sannikarṣavādin*) demonstrates the absence of omniscience by another method, saying "even though," and so forth; the word "api" (even/though) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhava*).

Even for a yogin whose sense-faculties and body have been transformed through yoga (*yoganirmitendriyaśarīra*), because there is an absence of actual contact between the mind or the eyes and their objects—due to the cessation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) after they have arisen and perished before [the present moment], and due to the absence of contact with those [objects] that will arise later—nevertheless, it is said: even if there were contact with all objects from all sides, what would be the consequence of a connection established by the transformation of grammatical case-endings such as "this belongs to this" (*asyāyam iti*)? It would be non-omniscience (*asarvajñatva*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of being of the nature of existence, because of being of the nature of non-existence, and because of being both of the nature of existence and non-existence.

Of what? Of the "entity" (*vastu*), that is, of substances (*dravya*) and so forth, there is the nature of existence; and of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, there is the nature of non-existence.
This is stated with reference to others;

this is the intended meaning: let there be apprehension by that [sense-organ] of those objects which possess an existent nature (*sadātman*) through contact with the sense-faculties; but how can there be apprehension by it of those which have a non-existent nature (*asadātman*), such as the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar and so forth? For such [non-existence] is not conjoined with the sense-organ because it is not a substance (*adravyatvāt*), nor is it inherent (*samaveta*) in it; for if it were, it would follow that there would be a cognition of it even when the object itself is absent.
For this very reason, even the relation of the relation is difficult to establish from the perspective of ultimate reality, because the sense-contact has perished.
In the future time, immediately after the manifestation of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*),
due to the conjunction of substance and substance.

Whether it be through conjunction-cum-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence-cum-inherence (*samavetasamavāya*), and so forth, or through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), such [a connection] is not possible, because that [relation] exists only between two things that are already connected.

It might be argued: "The jar and so forth are in contact with the sense organ, and by means of that [jar], its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so on are [connected]; therefore, like color and other qualities, this [non-existence] is apprehended. That is incorrect, because since non-existence is not a substance, there can be no conjunction of the jar with it, nor can there be inherence; for [conjunction and inherence] are absent at the time of non-existence.
For this very reason, no other relation either can be connected with non-existence.

If it is thought that because the jar is non-existent, there is for the sense organ in contact with the jar a relation of being a qualifier of the conjoined (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇībhāva*) with respect to the absence of the jar; a relation of being a qualifier of what is inherent in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamaveta-viśeṣaṇībhāva*) with respect to the absence of color and so forth; and a relation of being a qualifier of what is inherent in what is inherent in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavetasamaveta-viśeṣaṇībhāva*) with respect to the absence of color and so forth—and that this should be stated similarly for action and the rest—that too is incorrect, because it contradicts well-established tenets. For that very thing which is the direct relation of the jar with its prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and its posterior absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is itself its impermanence.

What is the point of this [argument] that "non-eternality is the existence of both [the entity and its absence], as stated in the *Nyāyavārttika* (p. 284)? One [thing], sound, is inherent; another, color, is inherent in the jar which is in contact with the sense organ; and non-existence is the qualifier of that [color].
One word, "inhering" (*samaveta*), is redundant:
in a jar conjoined with a sense organ, "color" (*rūpa*) inheres; therein "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) inheres; and its qualifier is "non-existence.
For comparison: [the definition] "that which expresses a relation of existence delimited by both ends..."

The hearing of the term "impermanence" (*anityatāśruti*)— as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 2.111— is intended for those such as the Naiyāyikas who hold that the relation of existence (*sattāsambandha*), which intervenes between the prior and posterior limits of both [beginning and end], is what expresses impermanence;
for the *Nyāyavārttika*, impermanence is that existence of an object delimited by both ends.

Furthermore, if the relation of the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) is not apprehended, how can there be the cognition that "this is the qualifier of that"? For it is not reasonable to have the awareness that "this too is conjoined with that" when conjunction itself is not apprehended. If it is argued: "Just as there is the cognition 'this is inherent in that' even when inherence (*samavāya*) is not grasped, so it is here as well"; [we reply: No, because the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) is equivalent to what is to be proven (*sādhyasama*). For the cognition "it is inherent" is dependent upon inherence, just as the cognition "it is conjoined" is dependent upon conjunction.
And that [cognition] is not possible without the cognition of that [object], otherwise there would be the cognition "this is white" even without the cognition of whiteness;
yet it is not perceived as such.
If you say, "That [object] is also perceived," then what is its relation to the sense organ? If you say, "It is the state of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇībhāva)," then there is an infinite regress.

Moreover, at the time of the contact between the sense organ and the jar, neither prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) nor destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) exists. Therefore, how can there be an indirect relationship (*pāramparyasambandha*) of the sense organ with that [non-existence]?
For there is no relationship between an existent and a non-existent, just as there is none with a donkey's horn.
If it is argued that this refers to the existence of the jar prior to and after [the contact], then at that time, there is neither the jar nor the contact with the sense organ.

Furthermore, an absence that is not apprehended cannot serve as a qualifier, just like a staff [if it is not perceived]; if it were apprehended, it could not be so while coexisting with the jar, because at that time the absence does not exist,
nor could it be apprehended alone, because there is no means for its apprehension.

For this very reason, even when it is being recollected, it does not function as a qualifier; for in the absence of the perception of conjunction or inherence, there can be no cognition such as "it is conjoined" or "it is inherent."
That which exists both before and after a conjunction or an inherence is "existing before and after" (prākpaścātstha),
such as at the time of the jar.

The proponent of non-existence (abhāva) says that because non-existence is not a positive entity, it is a "supreme non-existence": when a jar is in contact with a sense organ, existence (*sattā*) inheres in it, and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth serve as its qualifiers; thus, there is the state of being a qualifier of what inheres in that which is in contact. This too is without substance; for it is impossible for that [existence], being eternal, to have such qualifiers, just as in the case of the Self (*ātman*) and other such entities.

Furthermore, regarding existence (*sattā*): at the time of a jar, its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) perishes, and thus that [prior non-existence] also has a subsequent destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). Likewise, when there is the existence of a subsequent destruction that was previously non-existent, there is a prior non-existence of that [destruction]; yet there is no such apprehension or denial in that case. This is because, due to the absence of inherence (*samavāya*) with existence, there is no designation of non-existence as being impermanent, since it lacks a connection with existence delimited by both ends [of time].

If you say it does not exist [in the word], then what confidence can there be regarding the beginning of a word? If you say that it exists there by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then it would follow for other cases as well, since there is no distinction. If you argue that its status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*) is established through attention (*avadhāna*), then what connection could there be between that [attention] and it, by which its apprehension would occur? If you say it is the status of being a qualifier, then what is this "status of being a qualifier" distinct from the thing itself? If you say it is so [distinct], then it would be *samavāya* (inherence) as well, because the cognition of the inherent is non-different [from the cognition of the thing]. If you say it is not so, then the argument is the same: even the cognition based on that [inherence] would not be differentiated.

Therefore, since there is no sensory contact with that which has a non-existent nature, there is no apprehension of it; thus, it is established that the proponent of sensory contact (sannikarṣavādin) cannot be omniscient.

The meaning is that even for prior absence (prāgabhāva), there is an absence of a relationship with existence (sattā) which resides between its own prior absence and its subsequent destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva).
That is to say, that which arises and perishes is itself the impermanent;
it is not a qualifying attribute, because there is no difference [between the two].

Even though [the proof] is based on the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*), nevertheless, in order to show that even for the Buddhist (*saugata*)—just like for the Naiyāyika—the acceptance of omniscience implies that something [previously] admitted by him is lost, he says: "Perception," and so forth;
perception has all things as its object, including those at different times, such as the future.
If it is argued that the validity of cognitions does not indeed depend on their similarity to an object—[then we reply:

if a cognition produced from some object is considered perception only when it conforms to that very object, why would it not also be perception regarding a future object? Since there can be an excellence of similarity to that [future] object and since it is produced from it, to postulate its status as perception leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Enough with this postulation of an untenable grasp, for it leads to an over-extension. Regarding two perceptions of which... [it is enough].

For just as it is utterly illogical for you to maintain that an independent effect exists when its cause is absent, so too, if the capacity to discern [an object] from some consciousness were to arise through the perception of the specific characteristics of its own effect and cause, it would occur only at the time the object is being cognized;
this is because the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between the perceived object and the perception always exists.

Just as this substance is characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*) by its very nature, so too must it be understood to be essentially living (*jīvātmaka*) and inherently characterized by consciousness (*jñānasvabhāvaka*) by its own nature; for it is only because the powers of acting and knowing exist inherently that the attainment of specific auxiliary effects through external transformation is possible. Therefore, nothing that is non-conscious by nature can become a "knower" through a connection with consciousness, like a jar or similar objects.

This very self, which by its own nature possesses the illumination that grasps everything, being itself the essence of consciousness, when freed from defects and veils, would perceive its own specific characteristic—the infinite knowledge and so forth—alone;

that direct perception (pratyakṣa) would have all things as its object. Of what nature is it? It is "anāgata," meaning future; this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), by which the past is also included.

What does that do? He says: "If [consciousness] knows objects belonging to different times—past, present, and future in their entirety"—then its validity as consciousness would not arise from its conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*), but rather from some other excellence (*atiśaya*). For even for a yogin, knowledge of the future does not arise such that it would take on the form of that [future object]; otherwise, he would have to exist at the very time of every future event, and thus it would not be known that he exists here, at this time of the effect, and not at the time of something else. Likewise, this [consciousness] occurs even at the time of the effects of all beginningless objects.

It should be stated as follows: likewise, two effects occurring at different times from a single [cause] do not arise from a non-sequential [agent], because that would contradict such statements as *Pravāha* 1.45: "Sequential entities do not [arise] from a non-sequential [cause].

Now, if one were to argue that for the yogin everything is strictly present—such that nothing is its cause, nothing is its effect, and nothing imparts its own form to the cognition thereof; and if both the cause and effect of tranquility, as well as the cognition thereof, were to exist in that very same way [as being merely present].

Now, if cognition does not grasp that which does not produce its effect or does not possess its form, then let it be so for everything— each according to its own extent— and thus there is no lack of distinction among all things. Therefore,
for the Buddhist,
that [cognition] does not indeed arise from that object through such a consciousness.

Indeed, not all objects—whether future or past—are causes with respect to the cognition intended to arise, because causality is admitted only for that which is present at the time of the effect; otherwise, visual cognition would be produced in the location of an object even if the eye were not present there, or fire and the like would produce upward heat even if they were not present in their own location. Thus, [the soul] does not possess the quality of being omnipresent.
With respect to both of these,
it follows by implication that [the offering] belongs to Agni.
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "from something" (*kutaścit*) and so forth:

if a cognition produced from some object—whether immediately preceding and past, or future, or simultaneous with the cognition itself—is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), i.e., a direct realization of the object, under what condition does this occur? He says: "only upon its transcendence" (*tadatikrāntau*). The transcendence (*atikrama*) of that object from which the cognition has arisen is its passing away; it is precisely upon that [transcendence] that, by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatayā*), the reality (*tattva*) becomes the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and thus that [cognition] is a direct perception of it. The sense is that it is because of having arisen from that [object] that it is a direct perception.

"Even in the future"—by the force of the word "even," [it is implied] "even in the present"—why would it not be so? The term "perception" (pratyakṣam) carries over from the previous context, and the fault therein has already been stated.
Showing the sublation [of the opponent's position] regarding the counter-example (vipakṣe bādhā), he says: "That," and so forth.

Because there is the possibility of an excellence of similarity (sārūpyātiśaya) with that object of cognition (prameya), and because of its arising from that object of cognition, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in the conceptualization of perception toward that [object].

In this regard, showing that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one were to postulate [the existence of an external object] based on a mere excellence of similarity, he says: "Of which two perceptions," and so forth;
this is easy to understand.
Showing yet another refutation in this very context, he says: "Enough," and so forth.

The intended meaning here is as follows: when the very capacity to produce a cognition is said to be what makes something an object (*grāhya*), then it would follow that its status as an object (*grāhyatā*) arises from that very capacity; therefore, enough with the useless conceptualization of an unreal object.
Why? He says: "Because of over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgāt*).
Showing that there is an over-extension in assuming such a conceptualization because [the object] arises from that [cognition], he says: "For just as... and so forth.

For by whatever manner [you explain] the two characteristics—namely, the absence of a cause and the presence of an entity—of that which is being produced, what kind of thing is it that comes into being? It is utterly illogical for that which is independent to possess the nature of an effect;
and this has been stated by the Naiyāyika as well, in response to the Saugata.

In the same way, it is considered utterly illogical to perceive that which does not exist at the time of the cognition of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its respective cause; for instance, according to the Buddhist, if a destroyed cause does not operate toward the production of the effect, or if the effect is not designated as "belonging to" that cause, then likewise, that which does not exist at the time of perception cannot be endowed with the power of being grasped, nor can perception be accompanied by the capacity to grasp. Otherwise, the relation of cause and effect between two things existing at different times would become indistinguishable from the relation of the grasped and the grasper.

Alternatively, it is utterly illogical for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is the cause of cognition—to be the object of that cognition; because this [cognition] is a specific effect, and since it arises even when its cause has ceased, it cannot be designated as "belonging to that" [cause], just like [the offspring of] one who has ceased [to exist].
