"In that case, just as a cause produces its effect only when it already exists at the time of the effect's production, so too cognition grasps the object of knowledge (prameya) only when it already exists at the time of the object, because it is the result thereof," says the Naiyāyika. To this, he replies: "If the capacity for discernment belongs to consciousness by virtue of some relationship characterized by 'origination from that' (tadutpatti), then the capacity for discernment would belong to the object only at the very moment of such a cognition, and not regarding what is past or future. Thus, how could anyone possess omniscience? This is the intended meaning.
Or, if it is held that the past or the future is the cause of cognition, then its capacity must reside therein;

for the similarity between the past and the future is not established by anyone other than through the determination of a false cognition regarding the object of perception. If it is asked, "How can that which belongs to a different time be an object of apprehension?", those who know [the truth] understand its status as an object of apprehension.
Those who know the reasoning [of logic] maintain that causality alone is capable of imparting its own form [to the cognition];
this is the conceptualization of its being perception (*pratyakṣa*). — *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.124ab.
The phrase "in the case of a characteristic of an entity" (bhāvalakṣaṇe) is redundant; the object of cognition (prameya) is simply the effect (kārya).

If it is argued that at present there is no connection between the seer and the seen because of the absence of mutual benefit, to this he replies: "Because the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor exists between the object and the act of seeing at all times, even throughout the three periods [of past, present, and future]. Regarding the claim of another that omniscience is merely the awareness of one's own nature and not the awareness of all things—based on such statements as "the object is not grasped by it, nor is it grasped by that"—to this he says: "This very substance," and so forth.

Therefore, for that reason, by the logic already stated, this substance being perceived is itself—due to its non-differentiated transformation (*pariṇāma*)—characterized by transformation (that which has transformation as its characteristic), and likewise consists of the nature of the living soul (*jīvātman*). This distinction arises from itself alone and not from anything else; it is of the nature of cognition and consists of the modes (*paryāya*) of apprehending both self and other. This is to be understood because there is no contradiction in a single, manifold form having the nature of apprehending both self and other.

If it is argued: "If its possession of that nature [of cognizing self and other] were due solely to the operation of the eyes and so forth, then [it would follow that it is not inherently cognitive]," to this he says: "The agent," and so forth.

The agent (*kāraka*) consists of the doer (*kartṛ*) and so forth; the cognizer (*jñāpaka*) is the Self (*ātman*). It should be understood—[as stated on p. 419]—that the nature of knowledge belongs to both of these because their capacity exists inherently (*svataḥ*), and because even for external factors such as the eyes, it is possible to obtain specific benefits through transformation (*pariṇāma*).

If it is asked, "In the investigation of the knower, for what purpose is the mention of the *kāraka* (the causal factor), which is irrelevant here?"— it is for the sake of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*). Just as the power of a *kāraka* exists inherently in things like rice seeds, yet it also acquires a specific assistance through transformation from external factors, so too it is not the case that the power to produce a rice sprout is imparted to a barley seed by manuring and the like.
Concluding [the argument], he says: "Therefore" (*tanna*), etc.

For that very reason, in some cases, the self or another [entity] whose nature is ignorance—that is, which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of knowledge—is not called a "knower" due to its connection with knowledge, just like a jar or similar objects.

If it is objected: "But even a jar or such things have no connection with that [knowledge]; how then can it serve as an illustration? [The reply is: No, because the all-pervading *samavāya* (inherence) is non-distinct everywhere, and because [such a connection] has been refuted.

If it is argued that if cognition were by its very nature self-evident (*svata eva jñānasvabhāvatva*), then everyone would be an all-seeing seer (*sarvadarśitva*); to this he replies: "By its very nature," and so forth.

Because there is a connection with other objects, the awakening of the capacity [to perceive], and even the illumination that grasps everything, it is for this reason that this very self, which is the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanādhyakṣa*), is by its own nature the essence of consciousness (*saṃvidātmā*). The meaning is that there is no difference between the self and the awareness of the self.
And of what nature is he? To this he says: "in the form of pleasure, etc. and so forth.

Because of being free from the obscuration of defects (*doṣāvaraṇavimukta*), due to the absence of the obscuration of defects, he attains his own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is his own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*)—namely, infinite knowledge and so forth, which is absolute (*kevala*) and unaided (*asahāya*). For this reason, there is the sovereignty of his own nature (*svabhāvavibhutva*), and thus even the inherence of knowledge (*jñānasamavāya*).
"Let it be then that the spatial points (pradeśas) are of the very nature of the self"; to this he replies with the words "Just as," and so forth:

"Just as the self would be connected by itself with infinite spatial points, so too would the object [be connected] with infinite modes (paryāyas); therefore, objects are not inherent (samavāyin). (32)
In some way...

just as the expansive self and so forth would be connected with infinite spatial points (*anantapradeśa*) by their own nature and not through the force of inherence (*samavāya*) and the like, so too is the object of cognition, such as a jar, connected with infinite modes (*paryāya*). To explain the verse regarding those objects of their respective means of knowledge being inherent and possessing inherence, he says: "in some way," and so forth.
Everything is easily understood.

Furthermore, he states the fault [that arises] in the absence of spatial parts (*ātmapradeśa*): "That," and so forth; even if there is a metaphorical designation of those parts, the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions would follow.
Just as for those who maintain a single-sided [monistic] doctrine, there is the hearing of sound from a distance; so too,
if space were devoid of spatial differentiation (*pradeśanānātva*) in ultimate reality, it would follow that the cognition of each individual form and so forth would occur [simultaneously],
and how could the ear-cavity of space [be established]?
Furthermore, because the distinction of the cause is indicated by the absence of the effect—
since even fire that is superimposed does not burn, as that would entail the non-existence of the primary object—
if one were to admit a restriction to a particular location for some reason, that distinction [of the cause] would necessarily follow.

There would be hearing even of sounds from distant locations, because the cause for perception—namely, inherence in that which is conjoined [with the sense organ]—is present; this is due to the omnipresence of both the self and space, and because the mind possesses activity.

Even if one were to set aside the mind as the regulator through unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), since the self is in fact partless despite the metaphorical attribution of spatial divisions, simultaneous cognitions would still be possible even upon accepting those metaphorical parts.
He states another refutation: for the Naiyāyikas who maintain the doctrine of absolute unity, there is the hearing of sound from a distance.

Demonstrating the meaning of the verse, he says: in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), that is, without figurative attribution (*anupacārataḥ*), if there were no plurality of spatial locations (*pradeśanānātvābhāve*), it would follow as a logical consequence (*prasajyeta*) that the cognition of form and other objects would occur simultaneously for both earth and space.

For when the mind is conjoined with any one of the sense organs, such as the eye, it is conjoined with space as well; therefore, through the relation of inherence in that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), at the time of perceiving color and so forth, there would be the perception of all sounds inherent in space.

If, however, it is argued that even though there is conjunction with space, this does not occur for the ear, [the author] says: "Of space," etc., and introduces the opponent's view regarding the ear in order to refute it.
Regarding this, [the opponent asks] "How could there be a refutation here? and so forth;
[the author] replies with the words beginning "In the effect" (*kārye*), asking "Why would they indeed exist? and so on.

If it is argued that sound, its cognition, and [the quality of] being produced are properties of space (*ākāśa*), and that because of the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of these—namely their non-existence everywhere—the diversity of the causes of space (i.e., the plurality of spatial points) is metaphorically designated, and from that diversity of points follows the diversity of auditory perceptions; to this he replies: "Indeed, fire... and so forth. Why does it not burn at all? To this he says: "Even though superimposed... and so forth.
For otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that this [fire] which is directed toward a boy (*māṇavaka*) or even toward water and other things would not burn them.

The meaning is that since metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) can be applied everywhere, and because there is no distinction in the absence of hot touch due to the [mere] relationship [of contact], even fire itself is inherently devoid of hot touch; it becomes hot only through its connection with heat. This is the sense. *Saṃyoga* (conjunction) [is the cause].
From this, fire also, being naturally devoid of hot touch, becomes hot solely through its connection with heat. This is the meaning.

If it is argued that those regions [of space] exist in reality, the author replies here: if one accepts a restriction of regions based on some effect that is invariably concomitant with it, then—given the acceptance of a restriction such that "one region is enclosed by the ear-cavity" while "another region is different and contrary to it"—a division of that space necessarily follows;

and thus, the unity of the sky (*gagana*) becomes difficult to maintain. Furthermore, the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) as in the case of the soul's regions (*ātmapradeśa*) should be considered.
Moreover, he states the refutation again regarding its being without parts (*niṣpradeśatva*): "In a remote [place]," and so forth.

Wherever all sounds are inherent in space, there the mind is conjoined; therefore, because of the presence of "conjunction-inherence" as the cause of apprehension, that [space] is the veiling [obstructor]. If this is so, then even when one is near, this very [space] would be the cause of hearing.

It might be thought: "Sound is perceived by the mind when it reaches a portion of the self conjoined with the mind, because—while being a specific quality of an all-pervading substance—it is perceptible to us and others, just like pleasure and so forth; therefore, there is no fault [in our position]. To this, he replies: "Because the self and space are all-pervading and the mind is mobile, there would be the hearing of sounds even from distant locations.
Thus, space is an all-pervading substance, and sound resides in space.

He thinks as follows: the mind possesses action (*kriyā*), whereas sound is inactive (*akriya*); therefore, having reached the location of the sound, it manifests it—just like the rays of the eye—and thus the perception of distance and so forth postulated by the Buddhists is not contradicted, while the effort of sound’s movement is avoided through the analogy of waves and ripples.

How can there be a perception of proximity when hearing things from distant places or far-off regions? How is it that the moon is perceived as being near? [The answer is: It is due to the rapid functioning of the sense organ (*indriya*). In this case as well, the mind (*manas*) functions with equal rapidity in the apprehension of sound. Now, if it is argued that the mind does not leave the body to go elsewhere, how then does the eye travel? The non-perception of movement would apply equally to both;

the view might be that the eye, having gone to the location of the object, illuminates it because it is composed of light (*taijasa*), like a lamp. The mind also, by virtue of being a sense organ, is similar to the eye. Thus, the two cases are the same.

Now, as for those sounds that are heard, their movement is restricted to that specific location and not to any other place; by what has this been caused? If it is argued that it is by *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen force of karma), the author replies with the words beginning "by the unseen" (*adṛṣṭa* ityādi). The meaning is as follows: if the restriction [of sound] is governed by the *adṛṣṭa*, then let the mind (*manas*) be dispensed with, since the purpose of that [mind] is accomplished by the *adṛṣṭa* alone; thus, that which was stated by the opponent in the *Gandhakaika* treatise—that the soul (*ātman*) is omnipresent because it simultaneously comes into contact with all corporeal things—is untenable when that [omnipresence] is refuted, and therefore it should be abandoned.

As he said: "Whether spatial divisions exist or not, the omnipresent [substance] would be connected simultaneously with infinite modes; likewise, the self [is connected] repeatedly by its own nature. (34)

Whatever number of conjunctions there may be with the all-pervading self or another [substance], consisting of embodied entities that are mutually distinct, those conjuncts—being themselves mutually distinct in nature—establish through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) that many distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāvabheda*). Furthermore, whether they possess the designation of spatial extension (*pradeśavyāpadeśa*) or not, the entity would be connected to them by its own very nature through identity (*tādātmya*).
By this, [the argument for] the mode (*paryāya*)...
In the absence of a distinction in conjunction, if there were a disjunction of even one among them, it would follow that all would disjoin simultaneously;
and thus, when any one part moves, every composite substance would move at once, because a single conjunction is established throughout.
Likewise, like an all-pervading substance (*vibhudravya*), an atom would inherently possess infinite modifications (*paryāya*).

"Let there be spatial divisions (pradeśas) or let them not exist; even so, the all-pervading, omnipresent essence of an entity would simultaneously connect with all corporeal forms. Anticipating this [objection], he says: "By means of infinite modes (paryāyas), the self would be crowded together within itself, both repeatedly and successively."

He explains the verse: With how many things are there conjunctions of the all-pervading (*vibhu*) Self, or of anything else such as space? He says: "With those that possess form" (*mūrtimadbhiḥ*). Form (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading; with those possessing that [form], of what nature? He says: "Of the other," and so forth.

Of what nature are they? He says: those conjunctions, whose natures are mutually exclusive, establish as many distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāvabheda) in the self and so forth as there are conjuncts. For what reason? He says: "Because otherwise it would be impossible" (*anyathānupapattyā*). "Otherwise" means by way of the absence of those [many] distinct intrinsic natures; "impossible" refers to their non-occurrence. If that single atom were connected to space by one and the same intrinsic nature through which it is joined with one atom, then by that very same [nature] it would be joined with all substances. This is because it would follow that everything would enter into the intrinsic nature of that atom with which it is conjoined.

It is not the case that these differences in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) do not exist; furthermore, whether or not they are designated as occupying specific locations during this deliberation, an entity such as space would be connected with those differences in intrinsic nature by its very own nature, without depending on conjunction or other relations.
Why? To this he says: "Because of identity" (*tādātmyāt*).

If it is argued that a single atom is conjoined with six [other atoms], yet it does not possess as many distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāvabheda), and therefore there is a deviation from the rule, [the author] replies here: "By this," etc. To the question "Why?", he says: "Succession" (paryāya), etc. If it is asked what would follow from the impossibility of that [succession], he replies: "In the absence of a distinction in conjunction"—that is, if all parts were to have a single conjunction—then upon the separation of any one of those atoms which constitute the effect-substance, since the conjunction would be absent, it would follow that all the atoms must separate simultaneously.

What would happen in that case? To this he says: "And thus, for all [atoms], by way of their division, when some atom in a cloth or similar object moves, every effect-substance would move simultaneously. Why not? To this he says: 'In all places,' etc.; because of the occurrence of a single conjunction among all atoms, when one atom moves, every effect-substance would move simultaneously."
The opponent states that the claim "it is distinct from those [atoms] located in the eastern and other directions" is redundant;
he says: "From action comes disjunction; therefore, when action occurs in one atom, that [disjunction] is joined to that very [atom] and not to another."

It is not the case that the disjunction of the staff from Devadatta must belong to everyone everywhere; how then can it be said that "there would be the consequence of disjunction for all [others] because of the disjunction of any one of them"? That is not so, because disjunction is the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and since conjunction is unitary, its destruction is also unitary. For there are not many annihilations (*pradhvaṃsa*) of a single jar.
If it is argued that the destruction of conjunction results from disjunction, but that [destruction] is not itself [the disjunction], we say no; for it is not perceived as such.

Indeed, there is no cognition of conjunction [in that case], because it [the object] exists; for if such a cognition were present due to its being the destroyer of that [conjunction], then there would arise the cognition "it is repeatedly conjoined and disjoined from the staff," but this is not the case, because of the contradiction.

For it is not the case that a person becomes "the one with a single staff" at the very same moment he is "the one with a staff. Now, if it is argued that there is no such fault because the disjunction occurs when the conjunction is in a state of perishing; if that state is the conjunction itself, then the same fault remains. If, however, it is something else, and if it exists at that same time, then there would be a simultaneous perception of three things: the conjunction, its state, and the disjunction.
If [disjunction] occurs at a time subsequent to that [conjunction], then there is no conjunction [at that time].

If it is argued that this is so because disjunction causes the destruction of conjunction, and that its [conjunction's] destruction occurs prior to [the disjunction], then there is mutual dependence: disjunction arises from the destruction of conjunction, and its [conjunction's] destruction [arises] from that [disjunction].
There occurs a disjunction that has the nature of the destruction of that [prior] disjunction.
The destruction of conjunction is disjunction;
disjunction.
The state of destruction of a conjunction arises from a conjunction.

The opponent says: "The state of being on the verge of destruction (vinaśyadavasthā) is the completeness of the causes of destruction. At that time, if conjunction exists, the same fault remains—namely, the simultaneous perception of both conjunction and disjunction—because disjunction alone is the cause of its destruction. If it is argued that there is no perception of it at that time because it is obscured by the destruction produced by disjunction, that is incorrect. How can a destruction occurring at a later time than those two [conjunction and disjunction] act as an obscuration of the prior conjunction? Indeed, the expansion of the sun, which is not present at night, cannot act as an obscuration of the darkness of that form.

It might be argued that at the time of disjunction, there is a perception of conjunction—namely, that because the occurrence of the destruction of disjunction and conjunction is so rapid, they are determined to be simultaneous; therefore, even at the time of disjunction, the existence of that [conjunction's] destruction is present through superimposition, and by that, it [the disjunction] is obscured. But that too is not sound, because the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is denied to what is merely superimposed.
Furthermore, there is the refutation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*):

because the side of existence (*bhāva*) is stronger, it is logical that destruction is set aside by conjunction with an existing entity; otherwise, in the case of an interruption by cognitions—where the stream of sounds such as *vaṃśa* would be interrupted during the interval between cognitions—the perception [of the sound] would not occur.

Furthermore, what is this "disregard" (tiraskāra) by that [separation] toward that [conjunction]? If it means "causing destruction," then, since there is no [other] division [of the parts], the destruction of conjunction would not result from separation; rather, its destruction would follow from the absence of conjunction itself, not from separation. Moreover, even if that were admitted, it is only logical that the nature of the visible object remains unimpaired;
therefore, separation does not occur at the same time as conjunction.

If it is argued that it might exist again; [we reply: it would have to exist at the very moment of its destruction. Thus, the destruction is not caused by disjunction (*vibhāga*), because they coexist.

From what, then, does destruction arise? And from what does disjunction arise? If it is argued that it is produced [by an action]; for that very reason destruction occurs, as such is observed. Furthermore, at the time of that destruction, no disjunction is perceived.
Then it was stated: "Disjunction is the destruction of conjunction; and since that [destruction] is one, disjunction is one.

Thus, having refuted the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), he says—"In that manner," etc.—to show what follows: when that refutation has been established in that way, the proof of infinite modes (*anantaparyāya*) for the atom, just as in the case of all-pervading substances (*vibhudravya*), occurs by its own nature.
Because it perishes through destruction,
it is said to "abide therein" (tatstha).
It is said: this which is being stated by way of metaphor expresses the conclusion— beginning with the words "therefore" (tataḥ), and so forth.
Then,
by gradually experiencing the reality consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, consciousness [realizes] its opposition to the distinction between saṃsāra and its opposite. || 35 ||

Knowledge is not something other than that [object], because it is identical with its own self through a transformation consisting of identity-in-difference; for [otherwise] there would be no relation, as it would lead to an infinite regress.
This occurs either at the time of the destruction of that [object] or at the same time as it.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "By gradually experiencing oneness with reality (*tattva*), it becomes a substance (*dravya*).

To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "Consisting of consciousness," meaning that the substance is of the nature of consciousness (*cetana-ātmaka*), whereas the other is of the nature of non-consciousness (*acetana-ātmaka*).
If it is asked, "From what [source] is it conscious by nature? he says here: "Consciousness," and so forth.
If it is asked, "How is there the distinction between saṃsāra and its opposite? he says here: "The adversary," and so forth.
Since this is so, cognition is not something other than the self.
Why? He says: "Because of the universal," and so forth.
Why is that also so? He says: "Because of transformation through identity.
Why is this also so? He says: "Because of the lack of finality in relation to a connection; for if one were to postulate another connection, the regressus ad infinitum would not cease."

He asks, "From what does its cessation arise? and replies with the words beginning "from itself" (*svataḥ*), meaning that it arises solely from the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) and not from anything else. Concluding the subject under discussion, he says with the words beginning "therefore, this" (*tadayam*).
Therefore, this conscious knower, whose nature is pure awareness, becomes omniscient and a seer of all objects at every moment when his connection to those [objects] is severed.
Otherwise, since [the senses] do not function by reaching their objects, how could there be a grasp of pervasion (vyāpti), from which [omniscience might arise]? 1/2.37–38ab.

Since this is so, therefore, is that which is directly perceived [the Self]? Is it a jar or the like? No, he says—[it is] consciousness (*cetana*). If it is argued that "it is so because of its connection with consciousness," to this he replies: that whose very nature (*svabhāva*) is consciousness is "one whose self is consciousness" (*saṃvedanātmā*).
If it is argued that [the Self] consists merely of non-existence, he says "no"—the meaning is that the Knower knows both himself and the other.
What is that? He says: the Omniscient One.
Under what condition? He says: when there is the dissolution of the obstruction to that.
Why? He says: "Because it pertains to all objects," and so forth.

If it is argued that at some time the omniscient one might again become otherwise [i.e., non-omniscient], he says "no"; the sense is that this does not occur because there is an absence of obstructing causes at every moment.
If it is argued that he knows only what is proximate and not what is distant, he says in response: "Because the mind acts without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*)."
Otherwise, how could there be the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), from which [would arise] either inference or the thorough knowledge of the meaning of the Veda?
The intention of the one raising this doubt is that the conscious being would be void, because it would be a mere appearance (*pratibhāsa-mātra*).
Showing the refutation of the opposing view, he says: "If the Omniscient One," and so forth.

"If the Omniscient One—whose intellect transcends the mediation of the sequence of sense organs and whose defects and obscurations are utterly exhausted—does not [perceive], then who indeed would illuminate [the truth]? (38)

Comparison: As Akalaṅka said: "If cognition were not possible regarding a subtle, obstructed, or entirely imperceptible object, how then could there be non-contradiction in astrological knowledge (*jyotirjñāna*)? For even astrological knowledge is indeed set forth by an omniscient being; therefore, from this non-contradictory astrological knowledge, the existence of an omniscient being is established. As it has been stated: "If the intellect of men does not [function] regarding an entirely imperceptible object, then from where would there be non-contradiction in astrological knowledge? If [you say it comes] from scripture, then there must be another means of proof (*sādhana*)."
Thus—“Therefore, the omniscience of anyone else does not exist while [the Buddha] exists”—this is a well-spoken statement (subhāṣita). (Dharma-paryāya, p. 246)

The instruments are the sense-faculties; "succession" means sequence, that is to say, order; "obstruction" refers to impediment by way of space and so forth; he whose intellect (*dhī*) is of such a nature as to transcend these is thus described. From where [does such a one arise]? He says: "If not, because of the exhaustion of the obscuration of defects and the radiance [of knowledge], then who is omniscient? If such a person does not exist, then no one is omniscient.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), time and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are included.
Showing the intended meaning of the verse, he says: "Therefore, not from another," and so forth.

Since it is thus, therefore (*tat*), omniscience does not belong to anyone—whether from another [source] such as a distinct cognition, or from the eyes and other senses, or from someone such as Īśvara.
Why is this? To this he says: "Being," and so forth.
The phrase "Thus has this been well-spoken by me" is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

Having thus refuted the omniscience [of the Buddha] in the Yoga and Sautrāntika systems, and desiring now to refute that in the Sāṃkhya doctrine, he introduces their system with the words beginning with "by means of the divisions," etc.:
"by means of the divisions of ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), consciousness (caitanya), and so forth."

The Sāṅkhyas declare that the activity of the self is merely [the reflection of] the insentient intellect (citi). The followers of Kapila, assigning functions thus—"the sense organs perceive their respective objects, the mind conceives, the ego-principle identifies, and the intellect determines"—[assert that] the person perceives only that object which has been determined by the intellect. If this were the absolute case, no one would be an all-seeing knower, because perception occurs through the intellect when the eyes and other senses have ceased [their own specific operations].

If, however, the cognition of a person were exactly like that [of the senses], then why would one postulate distinctions such as *ālocana* (indeterminate perception) and so forth? Because of the multiplicity of designations for specific types of knowledge beginning with *avagraha* (apprehension), the enumeration [of the senses] would be contradicted, since those specific functions belong to the domains of *mati*, *śruta*, and the rest.

[The compound] *ahaṅkārādīnām* is a *dvandva*; with the suffix *-tasi* applied after the division (*vibhāga*), it means "from that" (*tataḥ*). Thus, from that [division], there is the function (*upayoga*)—the specific activity—of the self (*ātman*) or living being (*jīva*), which consists of the characteristics of *ālocana*, *manana*, *saṅkalpanā*, and *adhyavasāya*. [This applies] to that which is otherwise insentient (*acetana*).
"Why is that not so? he asks, and replies: "Because [it belongs] to another than the conscious spirit (cit), namely the Puruṣa"—this is the meaning.

Thus the Sāṅkhyas declare; and according to their established doctrine, the sense organs perceive the objects, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) conceives of them as "mine," the mind (manas) forms intentions, the intellect (buddhi) determines, and the Puruṣa is conscious.
Thus,
the meaning is that this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
It should be observed (p. 99, note 4):

By this [statement], he shows that the followers of Kapila are of deluded intellect, as they superimpose the attributes of the conscious self—such as perception and so forth—upon the unconscious *pradhāna*.
For one who knows the attribute of one thing to belong to another is not sound-minded; otherwise, one seeing yellowness in gold while looking at a white conch shell would be considered sound-minded.

If it is asked, "In what way are those [qualities] properties of that [self]?"—how, for example, are color and other qualities properties of a jar? It is because they are perceived as such. This is the same elsewhere: because perception and so forth are observed to be permeated by consciousness (*cetanā*), and because the self is characterized by knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). Now, if it is argued that consciousness appears to be superimposed upon those [qualities] and not present there primarily, then where does it exist primarily? If you say "in the person (*puruṣa*)," we say no; let it be figuratively attributed to that very [person]. If it were primary elsewhere, then the person would be perceived as something distinct from those perceptions and so forth, and would possess consciousness. But this is not the case. Therefore, consciousness is primary in the self.

Now, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that [absence of sublation] belongs to the person (*puruṣa*) alone because he is free from sublation, and not to those [mental states], because they are the opposite [of being unchanging]. But what is the sublater (*bādhaka*) of their independence? If you say, "It is the consequence of consciousness (*cetanā*) undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*)," then what is this "transformation" unestablished for the Sāṅkhya? If you say, "It is so [that it is established]," then it is not logical to say that the primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is non-transforming—given such statements as "From the pre-eminent *prakṛti* comes the Great One" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 22) and so forth—which show that *prakṛti* is transforming while consciousness is not. What is the basis for this distinction? [The answer is:
They are the attributes of the Self (*ātman*).
If this is argued, [we reply that] for those things pervaded by consciousness, it is consciousness [itself].
The Person alone possesses consciousness in regard to perception and so forth.

It might be argued that [the term] "supreme" (prakṛṣṭha) in relation to insight (ālocana) and so forth is redundant; for even if primordial matter (prakṛti) is subject to transformation, the Person (pums) is not, because that is the very nature of entities. Otherwise, water would also be a carrier [of fire], just like fire.

This might be so if, by excluding *pradhāna*, an unchanging nature were established in the *puruṣa* from some source—just as the hot nature of fire is established by excluding water—but this is not the case, for it is established through scripture (*āgama*), as it says: "The *puruṣa* is neither a primordial cause (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*)" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 1.23). Therefore, this is not a valid answer, because the same [lack of proof] applies elsewhere.

Furthermore, what is the cause and what is the effect? Who understands such a person [as you describe]? If you say it is *pradhāna*, how can it be insentient? Otherwise, even a person who perceives an object determined by the intellect (*buddhi*) would have to be insentient.

If you argue that it is the *puruṣa*; yet if his self-realization, brought about by scripture (*āgama*), were merely occasional, then that itself would constitute his being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). Consequently, the Vedas and scriptures would be rendered futile, and even the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of an eternal entity has already been refuted. Thus, this position of yours is trivial.
The connection is "he understands.
To explain the verse, he says: "the function of consciousness," and so forth.
The followers of Kapila (*kāpilāḥ*), by employing—that is, making it perform—the function of consciousness, namely its transformation into perception and so on, for the insentient *pradhāna*.
In what manner? To this he says: "For its own sake," and so forth.
What do they do? To this he says: "Only," and so forth.
Showing another defect in this very context, he says: "Determined by the intellect," and so forth.

Since determination (*niścaya*) is also of the nature of cognition (*gamana*), the word "only" (*eva*) excludes the external [object]. If there were the absolute necessity (*ekānta*) that a person perceives only the object—that is, the form of the object as determined by the intellect (*buddhi*)—then no one, whether Kapila or anyone else, would be all-seeing.

Why? To this he says: "Because of the cessation of the activity of the eyes and so forth. Why? To this he says: "Because of perception," meaning because the intellect is directly realized by the person.

The Sāṃkhya maintains this very view: "If the Puruṣa does not perceive the intellect (buddhi), how could it perceive that object? For when a mirror is not seen, there is no perception of the face or other things reflected within it."—thus says the Teacher.

Furthermore, if the intellect (*buddhi*) is not perceived by that [Puruṣa], how can its existence be established, or the establishment of its determination of objects? If you say it is from the Puruṣa, that is contradictory—since he does not perceive it, its establishment by him is untenable due to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If you say it is "by itself" (*svataḥ*), there is an entry into the Buddhist doctrine (*saugata-mata*), because the Buddhists accept the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of the form of the object.

If you then argue that its establishment is necessary because the apprehension of an object cannot be established without an instrument (*karaṇa*), we say no; for the eyes and other organs are already established as such instruments. If one imagines something else beyond them, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—for one would have to imagine yet another beyond that.

If it is argued that [the self] sees, then it is logical that it perceives objects through the process beginning with visual apprehension (*ālocana*) and so forth. If it is further argued that this is not the case because of the absence of other sense organs such as the eyes, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), then it is well said that it perceives the object in that very same [internal] locus—namely, "determined by the intellect" (*buddhy-adhyavasita*), and so on. Therefore, it is well stated that "because of the observation of the cessation of the eyes and other organs," the Person (*puruṣa*) is distinct from the intellect.
The accomplishment of the intellect (buddhi) arises from the Puruṣa alone, for the intellect is merely an instrument.
Because the apprehension of objects is established even without the eyes and so forth,
others recite: "because seeing is observed from the functioning of the eyes and so forth."

In this regard, [the opponent] is incapable [of providing a valid argument]: because an object is perceived through the operation of the eyes and other senses, it is that very operation which stands in a relationship with that [perception], whereas the Puruṣa perceives only the reflection in the intellect (buddhi) and not the object itself, as the Sugata [teaches]. Thus say the commentators, [arguing] that [the perception belongs to] the operation of the eyes and other senses alone.
The author anticipates the opponent's objection with the words "If, however," and so forth.

Here, "if" indicates the intention of the opponent, while "however" signals an alternative position. The connection with what precedes is as follows: "Just as someone might be all-seeing, in that very same manner, by that same means of perception—without the intervention of reflection and so on—the cognition of another person would exist."

The intellect indeed determines—that is, ascertains—the object; by using the particle *eva* (indeed) in this way, [the author] shows that there is no determination of any object whatsoever that does not depend [on something else]. Refuting this, he says: "What is there... and so forth.

In this regard, concerning that aforementioned opposing view (*paramata*), what is the use of postulating distinctions such as "observation" (*ālocana*) and so forth? What is gained by saying, "the senses observe their own objects," and so on? Just as the *puruṣa* perceives the intellect (*buddhi*) without the postulation of such distinctions, or as the intellect perceives the object, the senses perceive its observation, the mind its conceptualization (*saṃkalpana*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) its self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and the rest of the senses their respective functions—all without further postulating other instruments—so too does he perceive the object. Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and consequently, no one would be an all-seeing witness; thus, the sense is that he perceives the object even without the distinctions of observation and the like.

Now, in order to show that cognition (*buddhi*) is not other than consciousness (*caitanya*), [the author], demonstrating a case where its logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), says: "In the cognition of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth," and so on.

The intended meaning here is as follows: If one were to take the difference in designation—that consciousness is *buddhi*—and likewise, because there is a multiplicity of specific cognitions such as apprehension (*avagraha*) and the rest, then the enumeration that "consciousness is *buddhi*" would be contradicted, resulting in a plurality of principles (*tattva*).
This might be the thought [of an opponent]: "That multiplicity of designations is merely imagined according to the Jaina's own whim"; however, the same applies to the Sāṅkhya as well.

This might be [argued]: "In both cases, there would be worldly consensus; for specific cognitions such as *avagraha* (perception) and so forth are merely distinctions of the intellect (*buddhi*), and therefore the multiplicity of their designations is simply a multiplicity of synonyms for the intellect itself. To this, he replies: "If [it were so], etc. Because that Self possesses specific modes of application (*upayoga*), these are its specific applications; the cognition consisting of *avagraha* and so forth is *mati*, while *śruta* is verbal knowledge, and the term "etc. includes these. Since these have those [specific applications] as their objects, because of that state of affairs—that is, because of that reality—the enumeration [of the types of knowledge] would be contradicted.
He thinks as follows: just as apprehension (*avagraha*) and the other stages are included within cognition (*buddhi*), so too they are included within the self (*ātman*);
thus, let there be a diversity of designations for specific types of knowledge such as apprehension, while maintaining the non-difference between cognition and consciousness.
If it is asked, "What is the fault in that? he says here: "There is no knowing-ness," and so forth.
There is no knowing-ness in *pradhāna*, nor in the *puruṣa*, who is insentient and unchanging; indeed, there is no one at all who is omniscient and yet not of a dual nature. (40)

For just as the conscious being is designated as "possessor of a body" due to its connection with a body, or as "possessor of breath" due to its connection with breath, so too it might be designated as "possessor of ego" or "knower" due to its connection with something else, such as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth. However, if this were the case, it would follow that consciousness is distinct [from the self], and consequently, perception and so forth would belong to the insentient [self]—just as they do to a jar or other objects—which is incorrect;
therefore, it is not so, otherwise.
Even if [the Self] exists, it is not joined [to cognition] because of its lack of knowledge and lack of intelligence; who then is omniscient?
The intended meaning is this: consciousness consists of the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*), and it does not belong to either the *pradhāna* or the unchanging *puruṣa*.
The Pradhāna, being insentient, possesses no consciousness;

nor indeed is consciousness admitted by the Sāṅkhya for the Puruṣa, because he is unchanging. Thus, according to Kapila, there exists no one at all who is omniscient, as neither [the Pradhāna nor the Puruṣa] possesses both qualities, and because nothing other than the nature of the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa is accepted as distinct from these two.

Alternatively, [the author], demonstrating the meaning of the verse— that what kind of self (*ātman*) could be omniscient given that its nature is distinct from the nature of those [faculties]— says "Just as indeed," and so forth.

Just as, for the Jaina school, the designation "living being" (*jīva*) is applied to consciousness due to its connection with a body, and "possessor of breath" (*prāṇin*) due to its connection with breath— wherein the body and so forth are not essentially different from the self, but [the designations arise] only through that connection and not by itself— likewise, if the Sāṃkhya [proponent] were to designate the conscious [self] as "possessor of ego" (*ahaṅkārī*) or "knower" (*boddhā*) due to its connection with something essentially different such as the ego-faculty (*ahaṅkāra*), [the term] "conscious" (*cetanaḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
Refuting this, he says: "Vision," and so forth.

The meaning is that for the Naiyāyika—not for the Sāṃkhya—vision as well as consciousness (caitanya) alone, and not merely the ego (ahaṅkāra) and so on, would result in being something separate and distinct from the Puruṣa. Thus it is thought.
But this is not the case; therefore, like the perception [of objects], the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth must be admitted as non-different from that [consciousness].
Since this is so, [the opponent's position] is untenable.
Of what? He says: "Of the insentient," and so forth.
What is it? He says: "perception," and so forth.
Of what is it like? He says: "like a jar," and so forth.
Concluding the present topic, he says: "therefore," and so forth.
He states the refutation of the opposing view: "Otherwise," and so forth.

If it is argued that [the effect] would belong to the Person (puruṣa); to this he replies: even though it exists, according to the Sāṅkhya, it is as if non-existent because it lacks any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Nevertheless, it is said: "Even though the Puruṣa exists, why is he not conjoined? To this he says: "Because of ignorance and lack of intelligence.
If it is argued that "another [being] is omniscient," to this he replies with the words beginning "Who... and so forth; the two previous explanations apply here as well.

Now, refuting the opponent's proof for the existence of the person (*puruṣa*)— which is based on the designation [of agency] as proceeding from the person— the author says: "The sentient and the insentient," and so forth.

For the Sāṅkhya, everything—whether conscious or unconscious—is inferred to be conscious, because it exists for the sake of another due to its being a composite, just like the eye and other sense organs; thus, agency [is attributed to the conscious principle]. (41)

If it is argued that "the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another because they are composite, like the parts of a bed and so forth," this is not a valid reason (*ahetu*), because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the existence of composites of sentient beings and composites of both sentient and insentient things that do not exist for the sake of another.
For the "compositeness" of the eyes and so forth is nothing other than their specific arrangement;
since there is no difference in this regard even in other cases, and since there is no delusion [regarding their purpose], [the reason fails].

The two subjects (*dharmin*) are "everything that is conscious" and "everything that is both conscious and unconscious"; however, one should not state "everything that is unconscious," because that would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), as such an admission has already been made by the opponent. From that [subject], the purpose of another (*parārtha*)—that is, the aim of another—is inferred.
By what reason? He says: "Because of being a composite (*saṅghātatvāt*), like the eye and so forth."
Every conscious being possesses agency; otherwise, even the eyes and other sense organs would not possess it, for they too have no purpose other than to serve another.
Furthermore, [if this were not so], statements such as "the self is a non-agent" and "it is devoid of qualities" would be contradicted.

Now, if it is not inferred [that there is a creator], then there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with that very same proof for a person (*puruṣa*). If you argue that there is no inconsistency because that [person] has been made the subject (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), then he must be distinct from the class of sentient beings or the class of insentient beings—that being the one for whose sake this entire world exists as its cause.
This is not so, because the probandum would never be established, since another and yet another means of proof would be required even in that case.
The agency [of the self] is to be inferred— page 299, note 6.

In order to explain the *kārikā*, he states the opponent’s formal argument (*prayoga*); then, refuting it with the words beginning "in the case of consciousness" (*cetane*), etc., he says: [The reason] "because of being a composite" (*saṅghātatvāt*) is not a valid reason because it is non-exclusive (*anaikāntika*), since there are composites that are not for the sake of another—such as a collection of conscious beings, a collection of persons, a collection of conscious and unconscious things, or a collection of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. The property (*dharma*) to be proven is "they are for the sake of another," as in:
"the eyes and so forth are for the sake of another, because they are composites, like the parts of a bed or a seat."

If it is argued that there is no deviation [from the rule] because the nature of being a composite (*saṅghātatva*) as it exists in the eye and so forth does not exist in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the author replies here with "Not indeed," and so on.

For the reason that the nature of being a composite belongs not only to the subject at hand but also to the eye and so forth—distinct from its mere "abiding together" (*samavasthāna*) or its "occurring inseparably" (*avinirbhāgavartana*)—but rather is that very same thing;

and even if that were so, if it is further argued that this is not the case for the counter-example, the author replies: "That abiding together exists elsewhere too, even in the counter-example under discussion."

If it is argued that the eye and other [senses] do not possess either plurality or unity, and that there is no lack of distinction between sentient and non-sentient things because of that, [the author] replies here:

"Because there is no distinction," as stated in Sāṅkhya-kārikā 15, "because of the finite measure of differences" (*bhedānāṃ parimāṇāt*). The sense is that since it is possible to establish the distinction of a single measure for color and so forth, and since distinction can be established everywhere, [the opponent's argument] is thus useless (*vyartham*).

The remainder [of the aphorism] is: "Because of the existence of the cause in the effect, because of the activity of power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the multiform."

As for what was further stated—that it is like the limbs such as the bed and so forth—this is now considered: what is the "other" there, for whose sake that [body] exists? If you say "the body," no; because that would entail its being the enjoyer.
For this very reason, it cannot be the intellect either.

If it is argued that it is the *puruṣa* [who perceives], then who is it that perceives each respective object? It cannot be answered that it is the *pradhāna*, because that has already been refuted. If it is argued that it is that very *puruṣa* himself, because he is of the nature of self-luminosity and luminosity for others (*svaparaprakāśarūpa*), then why is there an inference regarding the eyes and other sense organs, given that he alone perceives his own objects through those organs? [The reply is: "For the purpose of eliminating delusion (*vyāmoha-vyavaccheda*). If it is argued that this is so because delusion exists in cases such as sleeping and the like, then that would entail the fallacy of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the necessity of further examples.
Furthermore, when the instruments such as the eye do not act upon one another, it is the Person alone who acts;

moreover, the capacity of the Person to illuminate both self and other is not incompatible with his undergoing transformation, for that [capacity] would be impossible if he were of a single, unchanging nature.

Because it is impossible for [consciousness] to illuminate both itself and others, [one might object]: "If its utility as a cause were like the perception of light and other things, what would be contradictory? Nothing at all. However, there would be no state of non-agency (*akartṛtva*);
moreover, in the apprehension of the self, if it were to depend upon [another factor] such as sensory perception (*ālocana*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*).

Otherwise, why would that [cognition] depend upon an object? If it were to cognize itself, then things such as beds for that purpose would not be cognized; for the cognition of those [objects] is invariably concomitant with the cognition of both [subject and object]. Thus, all this is unestablished. Otherwise, by this very [argument], the non-establishment of the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth is also demonstrated.
Therefore, in the system of Kapila, there is no one who is all-knowing, nor is there anyone who is liberated;
he states this very point as follows: "Of the visible and the vision," and so forth—how can there be liberation for the visible and the vision, which are eternal and all-pervasive?

As it has been said elsewhere: "Because one may be liberated from suffering through [the knowledge of] the seen and the seer, for that purpose one should practice austerity" (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇaprakaraṇa, p. 232). "For the sake of being liberated from suffering, a person should exert effort. (42)

Neither does the *pradhāna* nor consciousness (*caitanya*) ever transcend transformation; otherwise, it would follow that the *pradhāna*, whose nature is invisible, would become visible. Thus, by this [argument], the claim that "the activity of *prakṛti* is for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*" is refuted, since the liberation of the *puruṣa* is already established even before the cessation of *prakṛti*.
For this very reason, no one would strive for liberation from suffering;

for in the absence of a single person whose nature consists of perceiving defects, making efforts to eliminate them, and exerting effort toward their causes—just as in the case of momentariness—how could there be any engagement with what is to be abandoned or what is to be adopted? That is not so... [end of fragment]
For the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception and for the sake of liberation of the Pradhāna, there is a conjunction of both, like that of the lame and the blind; from this conjunction, creation arises.
— Sāṃkhyakārikā 21.

The object of perception is *pradhāna*, and the subject of perception is the *puruṣa*; how is the liberation of these two [achieved]? Of what nature are they? To this he says: "impermanence," and so forth.

For what purpose would one strive—that is, for which [liberation] one might be released from suffering, namely from the threefold suffering—or for whom would one strive? For the sake of that, or for the sake of liberation from suffering; who [would strive]? The *puruṣa*.
Or, the word "yataḥ" (from which) is used in the sense of an objection. Or, he states the meaning of the verse according to his own view with the words beginning "pradhāna" (the Pradhāna), etc.

Now, [an opponent might argue: "The Pradhāna is subject to transformation, not eternal. To this he says: "Not of the Pradhāna," where the particle "api" indicates that even this [claim] is merely an accepted tenet (*abhyupagama*). In reality, there is no transformation of it, because everywhere it is admitted that there is only manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and disappearance (*tirobhāva*).

If it is argued that this very [consciousness] is also subject to transformation because its manifestation is admitted to occur upon the cessation of its conjunction with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and thus there would be no transgression against it, whereas for the person (*puruṣa*) there would be a transgression of the power of vision; to this he replies: "Or rather, of consciousness... and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Otherwise... and so forth.
If it is argued that the *pradhāna* abandons its visible nature, to this he replies: [the *pradhāna*] would then possess an invisible nature, and so forth.
How could there even be the state of being seen? To this he says: "visible," and so forth.

In this regard, if it were to abandon its nature as an object of perception in every respect, then this fault would indeed arise. Otherwise, for one who is devoid of the form of fearlessness, there would be the consequence of being like the breast of a barren woman. However, while there is the abandonment of that nature with respect to the liberated self, there is the opposite with respect to another. If it is argued that, consequently, the entire world would attain liberation along with Kapila, that is incorrect; because at that time, wherever that state of being an object of perception exists, all things possess the nature of being perceived by all persons.
For such a distinction is not observed among jars and other objects which possess the same nature of being visible, occupy the same location, and are perceived simultaneously.

Now, if it is argued that just as there is the relinquishment of the visible nature of *prakṛti*, so too there is the relinquishment of the seeing-nature of the *puruṣa*; to this he replies: "In that way," and so forth, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
The primary cause (pradhāna) is that which transcends transformation.
If one were to abandon it in every respect, then the nature of the visible would be non-existent, like the son of a barren woman.
If there were an abandonment of the nature of being an object of perception even with respect to a transmigrating self,
then it would also apply with respect to liberated selves.

Extending this refutation to the liberated one with respect to the transmigrating being, he says elsewhere: "Liberation cannot be produced for the seen and the seer, for how [could it be produced] for those that are eternal and all-pervasive," and so forth. This—that the activity of *prakṛti* is for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *puruṣa*, meaning liberation for the *puruṣa*—has been refuted and rendered powerless.
For if both were all-pervading and eternal, the activity of anything would not be logical; indeed,
nothing of such a nature ever proceeds or ceases from anything, because that would entail the loss of the all-pervasiveness of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

Furthermore, since [the Self] is all-pervading and eternal, what is the purpose of its activity? It is not for the sake of producing a conjunction [with the intellect], because that [conjunction] exists at all times, and there is no cause for what has already been produced. Moreover, the conjunction of that [intellect] with the Self is exactly like the conjunction of the Self [with other things]. By this, it is shown that the activity of the conscious [Self] is desired to be occasional. To this, he replies: even prior to—that is, before—that activity, which is the cessation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Person (*puruṣa*) would not be established; thus [the objection] is refuted.
For one who is liberated, there is no such thing as transmigratory existence, because that would lead to an over-extension [of the principle],
since primordial nature exists for the sake of the liberation of the spirit.
He states another fault: "For this very reason, what [is the purpose] prior to the attainment of liberation? He says: "Not anyone," and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says: "From heat," and so forth.
Explaining this very point, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
If it is argued that a person should therefore strive for a happy rebirth, he says in response: "Upon seeing the defects," and so forth.

The vision of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, the removal—that is, the destruction—of those defects, and the means for that [destruction], namely right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth, constitute its very nature. Since this [nature] belongs to a single person, in the absence of that [person], how could there be activity, and where? To this he says: "Regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted"—this is the conclusion, beginning with "Therefore, not... and so forth.
Some say that the one who knows the vessel of his own nature is omniscient;
regarding this, he says "omniscient," etc.—the omniscient one [knows] all objects... by virtue of cutting through the veil of all defects without exception.
It may be that, due to the lapse of time, the sequence of words occurring immediately after [his] effort is not perceived;
yet it is to be understood as distinct from other things, like the clusters of great celestial lights. || 43 ||
"What kind of being would he be to be omniscient? To this he says: "Sakala," etc.
The meaning is that since the mere awareness of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is common to all [beings], one is not thereby an "all-knower" (*aśeṣajña*).
If it is argued that he [the Lord] exists by his very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*); to this he replies: "Because of the cutting away of the veil of all defects.
By what means? To this he says: "By the instruments" (*karaṇa*), and so forth.

If it is asked, "Where would this occur? he replies: "Because there is no further rebirth" (*apunarāvṛttitvāt*). Now, if he is intended to be omniscient (*sarvajña*) while still in the state of a *vattin*, then there is no severance of all defects.

Now, if it is argued that [the speaker] is not [an authority], what is the use of such a non-beneficial person? To this he says: "Of those things occurring immediately after effort," and so forth; the meaning is that [the cognition] would otherwise occur even during sleep and so on.
If it is further objected that every speaker is always defective, like the man of today, he says here: "The object of knowledge," and so forth.

The nature of the Great Ones, who possess complete knowledge, should be understood as distinct from others and distinct from previous persons, even in their false cognition, just like the calculation of the luminaries.
Even in the absence of the intention to speak—
thus ends the eighth chapter, "The Proof of the Omniscient One," in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by Nantavīrya, who relies upon the feet of Raviśrībhadra. Śubham.
The Ninth Chapter:
9. The Establishment of Sound.
Now, if the activity of speech deviates from its immediate succession [to the cognition], then what is the status of speech? To this, he says: "From association," and so forth.
Atoms, having undergone transformation through association with the desire to speak, become the objects of verbal cognition;
their differentiation is the expression itself, consisting of phonemes, words, and sentences, which is established by its own nature.

Having approached Siddhārtha, people ask, "What does he say? and thus he is proclaimed; for like the word *akṣa* and others, the person who knows the general meaning has no desire for a specific distinction regarding his own purpose. [This leads to] the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

The objects within the range of *śruti*, that is, the sense of hearing, are sounds; not all things such as jars and the like are "sounds" [in this sense], for if they were, they would have to be transformations (*pariṇāma*) of sound.
As it has been said:
Those [objects] such as jars, and words— which are of the nature of sound and are synonyms for the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman)—
are that beginningless and endless Brahman, the imperishable reality of sound (śabdatattva).

If it is argued that "the process of world-origination evolves in the form of objects" (Vākyapadīya 1.1), we say no; for it would follow that they [the objects] must be perceived as being of the same nature as that [source], just as a jar or similar object is perceived as being of the nature of a house [if it were its source].
Indeed, jars and other such things, though transformations of clay, are not perceived as being non-identical with it, but rather as being identical with it.

Otherwise, for one who has come from the Coconut Island (*nālikeradvīpa*), there would be no cognition of that designation, just as there is none of fire; thus, the convention (*saṅketa*) would be useless everywhere.
Therefore, the claim that [the word] is not so because its essence is sound (*śabdātmakatva*) is pointless here.
If jars and other such objects were of the nature of sound rather than being composed of clay, then,

just as fire is not perceived by one who has come from the Coconut Island (Nālikera-dvīpa), there would likewise be no perception of the denotation; this is an example of a negative instance (*vyatireka*).

Now, suppose it is thought: "Just as for you colors and other qualities do not exist manifestly in sound, so too for me sound does not exist manifestly in jars and the like. This is without substance, because it will be demonstrated in the following verse that in those cases, the manifestation of those [qualities] which were unmanifest is seen through inference. Furthermore, there is no such inference regarding the existence of sound in jars and the like, because its cognition occurs there only due to convention (*saṅketa*); nor is the notion that "it was there even before" tenable, because even then there is no cognition of it there, since sound is cognized in the speaker and the axe-handle is cognized on the ground.

Nor can there be a relationship of transformation (*pariṇāma*) between two things perceived in different locations, because that would entail the same for a jar and a cloth that are merely co-present.

If it is argued that their appearance is an illusion—like the appearance of two moons or like the moon [reflected] in water versus the moon in the sky—then, since even the appearance of the word and the jar is illusory, as in the case of dreams and so forth, what could be the transformation of what? Furthermore, the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) applies equally elsewhere, in the case of the word as well.
A word [denotes] its object even through convention.
Because the word is not perceived,
there is also no manifestation of a jar that consists of the word itself within the word and its object.

If it is argued that since those two [the self and the body] are distinct in terms of their location, how can they have grammatical co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the case of a pot and a cloth? And yet, such co-referentiality exists, because of the cognition "this is a cow. If this were so, then from the cognition "I am fat," the self would not be distinct from the body; or, from the cognition "men with spears enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*), where spears are perceived as men due to association, if you claim that here there is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) because there is no sublation elsewhere, then the same logic applies [to your position].

Because of the very identity between cause and effect, there occurs a figurative treatment of their mutual non-difference, as in "he sees with the eye" or "food is indeed the vital breaths. How much more so, then, would this not occur between the signified and the signifier? They would not be distinct within the word.

Furthermore, since there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that is, the application of two words with distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) toward a single substratum—it is logical that identity belongs to those two words themselves, not to the word "cow" and its referent, because such [co-referentiality] is absent between them.
For their application is not for the sake of expressing oneness, as nothing else exists besides them.
If it is argued that this [identity] consists in having the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktikatva*); then it would apply to a pot and a cloth, since we have the cognition "pot-cloth" (*ghaṭapaṭau*).
If it is argued that there is identity (*tādātmya*) between them, that is unestablished for the two; moreover, that very thing is both the probandum and the probans.

Therefore, this word is applied to it through metaphorical attribution (*abhedopacāra*): "this lump of flesh is named 'cow'," as well as through distinction, such that the name "cow" is used in grammatical coreferentiality (*śabdasāmānādhikaraṇya*) with this lump of flesh.
This [is the relation] between the two words "śabda" and "go," and between the word "go" and its referent, the cow.

Others might offer this rebuttal: "The term *gośabda* [‘cow-word’] is a compound of words (*padasamudāya*) whose intermediate members have been elided, such that the usage is simply *gauḥ*, just as in the case of *bhīmasena*. However, their position is not tenable, because if one were to apply such a construction universally to all technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*), then even terms like *bhīmasena* would not exist, but rather [the full forms] like *bhīmasenaśabda* would have to be used."
But this is not the case, because such usage is not observed among grammarians;

for there is a cognition of isolated word-meanings being joined to their designata (*saṃjñin*). Otherwise, even the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) in the expression "one whose [name] is the word 'cow'" would not exist, since that is seen only when the two [the word and the object] are established separately and independently, as in the case of "Citragu" (the owner of brindled cows).
Therefore, it is established that jars and other objects do not have the nature of words.

In the case of the word *bhīmasenaḥ*, which is called a "name" (*saṃjñā*) because its name is the word "Bhīmasena," the word "word" (*śabda*) is elided; likewise, in the case of *gauḥ* as well, one should understand that the word "word" is elided in the analysis "that whose [name] is the word 'cow'. This applies to words that express names.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that because we observe *bahuvrīhi* compounds where the meaning of another word is predominant, words must be the objects of the Vedic revelation (*bhavati-śruti*), and therefore they must be eternal. To this, he replies: "They have undergone transformation" (*pariṇatāḥ*). This means they have passed away from their form which is not the object of the revelation and have attained the form which is its object; thus they are said to be "transformed. Otherwise, as before, how could there be any hearing of them afterwards? If their nature were such that they were not the objects of that [revelation], there would be no hearing of them even prior to the operation of the palate and other vocal organs.

If it is argued that, since the nature of the object belongs to that [sound], it would be heard even before by one whose mind is directed toward it and who possesses the sense organ— due to the absence of a manifestor— we shall set this aside for now, as it will be examined elsewhere and will also be briefly examined here [in the passage] beginning with "these atoms.
Furthermore, [the word] must be eternal because its perception is for the sake of another.
Sound ought to be eternal;
why? Because its manifestation is for the sake of another.
"Manifestation" means utterance, and that is for the sake of another, in order to convey a meaning to another.
For if a sound perishes as soon as it is uttered, one sound could not convey its meaning to another; therefore, it would not be uttered for the sake of another.
If, on the other hand, it does not perish, then it is logical that the meaning is understood because it has been perceived many times—Jaimini-sūtra, Śābara-bhāṣya 1.1.6–23.
1.8 Śāstradīpikā, pages 540, 559, 568.
*Nayaviveka*, p.
242; *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdanirṇaya section; *Bhāṭṭacintāmaṇi*, p. 26.
Tantrārthāvatāra, page 26;
Bṛhatī, 1.1.1.
Others maintain that sounds, being qualities of space (ākāśa), exist even prior to the operation of the palate and other vocal organs.

To this he says: "Atoms" (paramāṇavaḥ) refers to extremely subtle *pudgala*s possessing color, taste, smell, and touch; those which have evolved into the domain of hearing are "sounds" (*śabda*). Sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*) and is perceivable by the sense of hearing.
"And space possesses sound; that [space] itself is the ear, and sound is its quality" — *Prakaraṇapañcikā*,
*Nyāyamañjarī*.

If it is asked: "Since there is no difference between an atom (*paramāṇu*) and space (*gagana*) in terms of being entirely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*), how can sound be established as having atoms as its cause while excluding space? The answer here is: [It will be stated later] that "the qualities of what is not a cause [do not belong to the effect]," and so forth. Let it be that space is not its cause; nevertheless, from where is it established that atoms are its cause? It cannot be established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because [atoms] are not perceived by it.
For when things are perceived by direct perception, this [inference] occurs: "this has arisen from that," just as smoke [arises] from fire.
Nor can it be established through inference, because there is no mark (liṅga) for such an inference.

If it is argued that its existence is established on the grounds that, like a cloth, a gross sound must have a material cause (upādāna) of smaller dimension than itself; that too is not tenable, because we observe the production of a pot of similar [gross] nature from a lump of clay that is equally gross.
There is no contradiction in the possibility of something subtle arising even from something gross, as in the case of old gold and mercury.
It might be thought that ash is more subtle than gross gold or mercury;
for as something is perceived in a particular case, so it must be there— where grossness is seen, that is the material cause, and where the other is seen, the other is the material cause.

Furthermore, it is not observed that sound takes either of the two [atoms] as its material cause, nor is there an effect without a material cause; thus, its existence is established by the establishment of an invisible cause. This is not so, because even for something invisible, there is no contradiction with grossness. Even if it consists of subsequent transformations, a smaller cause is admitted for that very reason, until—given its nature—one reaches the atom. This is not so, because that [subtlety] is demonstrated even from the gross.
Furthermore, there is no evidence that anything arises from a state of partless atoms;

moreover, since we observe the production of sound only from two hands striking together, it is logical that it has those [hands] as its material cause, produced by the mutual clashing of the two hands.

It might be argued: "The production of the effect occurs precisely through the destruction of the material cause (*upādāna*), just as the production of a jar is not seen when the hand that produces the sound is observed, nor is the lump of clay [seen] when the jar is produced. This too is without substance, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by the moonstone (*candrakānta*); for even though its transformation into water occurs through contact with moonlight, the stone itself is still perceived to be exactly the same size. Others, however, resolve this thus: "It is not that the moonstone dissolves due to contact with the moonlight, but rather that the rays of the moon themselves liquefy. For them, substances such as camphor would, at every moment, become smaller in dimension than their own original measure.

Since those [atoms] move toward their respective forms and so forth in all directions, let there be no further entry into them; let it be the same elsewhere as well. Therefore, atoms, sounds, and moonbeams [are not composed of parts].

Or rather, they are composed of air; for thus say the authors of the Śikṣā and the Mīmāṃsakas: "Sound is air that, rising upward from the region of the navel, is struck by the throat and other organs."
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that there is no comprehension of that [atom] through inference because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—that is not so. Because the excellence of the diminution of magnitude in both the conscious and the unconscious must be grounded in something, and since that excellence exists, there must be that wherein it is grounded;
that which is the substratum of such excellence in the unconscious is, for us, the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Nor does its non-existence follow from its non-perception, because that [non-perception] is inapplicable to an object of inference and would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) is not lacking the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*); for once the existence of an omniscient being has been established, how could it be that atoms are the respective causes of those [sounds]? What, then, is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of sound, which is corporeal? Nor can there be an effect without a material cause, as that would lead to an over-extension.

If it is argued that [the cause] consists of the staff, the drum, and so forth, then what is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*)? Furthermore, in the absence of those, no effect is observed or accepted by anyone.
Since an unobserved thing cannot be an auxiliary cause, nor can it be the material cause (*upādāna*), on what basis is this distinction made?
It is because of the presence of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*).
The excellence of diminution [of ignorance] follows from the mere non-perception [of objects], since non-existence is not established by that alone;
this applies to one who possesses the excellence of the advancement of knowledge.

Furthermore, it is not perceived. Moreover, if the palate and other such organs were its material cause (*upādāna*), then upon their destruction, [the sound] would cease to exist, because a material cause is characterized by the transformation into the form of its effect. Alternatively, if one holds the view that certain invisible parts of those organs transform into the nature of sound, while other similar parts enter into them, and thus there is no spreading of the sounds in all directions once they have been produced—then our desired conclusion is established, since we designate those very parts as atoms (*paramāṇu*).
