How could it be so? If indeed the rice sprout were not to have the unseen seed as its material cause (*upādāna*), why would that be? If you say it is because no other seed is observed [there], then it is the same in the other case: for we do not observe a gross cause that was previously unseen to be preceded by a cause of a contrary nature; thus, the parts of the palate and so forth are likewise unobservable.

As for those who maintain that sound is composed of air (*vāyavīya*), their position is likewise untenable, because it does not transcend the categories of the person (*pudgala-paryāya*) and because air is a transformation of that [person]. Furthermore, in a windless place such as an underground chamber, how could there be sound from the clapping of hands? If you argue that it arises from still air, this too is equally untenable; moreover, even when the conditions for sound are present, a person born deaf does not perceive it.
In the conceptualization of its specific [parts], let there be the conceptualization of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), because there is no difference in the nature of postulating what is observed;
and thus the authors of the *Śikṣā* say: "Air attains the state of sound"—*Śābarabhāṣya* 1.1.22.
22. Of Vāyu, who was born mute from birth.
If it is argued that [the phonemes] would generally be transformed individually; to this he says: "From conjunction" (*saṃsargāt*).

Let sounds (*dhvani*) be specific transformations of atoms mutually conjoined; yet, if it is argued that the *sphoṭa* of the phoneme and so forth must be eternal, all-pervading, and formless as that which is manifested by them; to this he says: "The difference of those," and so on—the "difference" (*bheda*) is the specific distinction of those atoms that have been transformed into the range of hearing.

Of what nature is he? To this he says: "one by whom [the phonemes] have been apprehended," and so forth. One who has apprehended that which consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*) is described as such. He thinks as follows: there is no sound (*dhvani*) apart from the form and other qualities perceivable by the auditory faculty, nor is there a word-sphoṭa (*varṇasphoṭa*) perceivable by it that possesses cognitive reality.
The same should be stated regarding words and sentences.
For the proponents of *sphoṭa*, neither a sentence nor a word consists of multiple parts;
this reality of the word is devoid of all differentiation...—*Sphoṭasiddhi*, verses 29–36;
*Sphoṭabhāṣya*, p. 1.
Sphoṭa, Nyāyamañjarī, p. 1:
In reality, however, it must be admitted that the sentence itself—indivisible like the germ within a peacock's egg—is called *sphoṭa*, and it is the cause for the cognition of distinct meanings.
—Sphoṭaprakaraṇa.
Thus, the partless sentence-sphoṭa alone— devoid of the division into phonemes and words— is superior; this is stated in the *Sphoṭatattvanirūpaṇa* and the *Sphoṭacandrikā*.
Those who know [the truth] say that *sphoṭa* is the eternal word (*śabda*), which transcends the phonemes (*varṇa*), is manifested by the phonemes, and conveys meaning;

for this very reason, they explain the meaning of the word *sphoṭa* in two ways: it is called *sphoṭa* because it is "burst forth" or manifested by the phonemes (*sphuṭyate vyajyate varṇaiḥ*), thus being manifested by the phonemes; and it is called *sphoṭa* because the meaning "bursts forth" or becomes manifest from it (*sphuṭati sphuṭībhavaty asmād arthaḥ*), thus being the conveyor of meaning (*arthapratyāyaka*). — *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p. 300.
*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*, p. 294;
*Paramalaghumañjūṣā*, p. 2:

"If it is argued that this [word] is not perceived by the sense organ of hearing, but rather is cognized through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) because the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be inexplicable," he says in response: "The expression..."

That by which something is expressed is "expression" (*abhilāpa*), namely the signifier; its differentiation consists of the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth. Since the cognition of meaning is observed to arise from those very [phonemes], even so, if one were to postulate [the word] as something else, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because it would be possible to postulate yet another thing beyond that. Therefore, [it is concluded that] the *sphoṭa* [is the word].

Since each [phoneme] individually lacks the power to convey meaning, and since there is no simultaneous existence due to the absence of conjunction—given that phonemes occurring in a fixed sequence cannot act together simultaneously—and since no such cognition is observed when uttered by different speakers, or when the sequence is reversed, or when they occur simultaneously;
therefore, the cognition of meaning, which cannot arise from the phonemes alone, postulates its own cause distinct from the phonemes—the *sphoṭa*. (Sphoṭasiddhi, p. 28)

Now, if it is argued that a single entity (the word-meaning) cannot be made known by many unstable sounds—such as *gh*, *ṭ*, and the *visarjanīya*—which do not exist simultaneously, and therefore it must be admitted that [the word-meaning] exists [prior to their utterance], that too is not well-said. For if that [single entity] is unmanifest, it would be the cause of cognition at all times; thus, the utterance of *gh* and the other sounds would be useless.
If, on the other hand, it is manifest, then if it were manifested by one [sound], the same fault would apply: namely, the futility of uttering *gh* and the others.

If it is argued that [the meaning is conveyed] by the phonemes beginning with *gha*, then, by whatever proximity (*pratyāsatti*) they manifest a single expressive unit (*vācaka*), by that same proximity they would manifest the meaning; what need is there for anything else? Furthermore, it will be demonstrated immediately hereafter that nothing eternal can possess the nature of a real entity (*vastu*).
Moreover, if each individual phoneme were the expressive unit, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the utterance of the second and subsequent phonemes would be purposeless.
However, if [the letters] were individually meaningless, then under the theory of their simultaneous production (*utpatti-pakṣa*), there would be no production [of them] simultaneously;
and under the theory of their manifestation (*abhivyakti-pakṣa*), since they are manifested only sequentially, the collection [of letters] would not exist.

Furthermore, if the denotative capacity belonged to those [letters] mounted upon a single memory, then in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of no distinction in the comprehension of meaning. Therefore, the *sphoṭa*, distinct from those [letters] and manifested by sounds (*nāda*), is the denoter.
—Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya-pradīpa, p. 16; Sphoṭasiddhi-nyāya, p. 2; Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, p. 299.
In that way, the *sphoṭa* becomes manifested;

furthermore, there would be such an exhausting succession [of steps]: the manifestation of the signifier from the phonemes *gha* and so forth, and from that, the comprehension of the meaning. If the meaning were understood from those [phonemes] themselves, this [succession] would not be necessary.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple cognitions—first of the manifestor, then of the manifested, and then of the object—and yet such is not the common usage. Even if one were to assume that [the sequence exists], it would follow that in the case of smoke and so forth, something other than the smoke is first perceived, and from that, fire is known;
the same would have to be said even regarding perception.
Therefore, its differentiation is verbal expression;
he states this by saying "by itself," meaning without mediation,
[as belonging] to the *sphoṭa*.
From sounds such as the letter *gha*, [arises] the *sphoṭa*.

Someone might object: "Is not something expressed by means of that particularity, namely 'fire-splutter'? [The reply is: It cannot be a universal (*sāmānya*), because such a universal does not exist and because it serves no purpose;

for a universal is of no use in debates, discussions, and the like, since only particulars (*viśeṣa*) are useful therein. Nor is it tenable to say that activity occurs through "indication based on indication" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*); for if the universal were perceived through that [indication], the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow.

If it is argued that, since there is a specific cognition (*viśeṣagati*), let that [cognition] be the result of the existence of those [atoms], but this is not so because it would follow that the collection of sense organs (*akṣasaṃhati*) is useless, and therefore the distinction between them is purposeless; to this he replies: "Siddhārtha" means that for which the object (*artha*) is established—that is how it is described—and the distinction between them is such.

For instance—just as there is the comprehension of an object, purposeful activity, and attainment through the operation of the eyes and other senses, so it is also from a word. The remainder will be examined right here:

the universal (sāmānya) is indicated by the word; that which is indicated by it is the particular (viśeṣa). This is "indication of the indicated" (lakṣitalakṣaṇā), whose form consists of the absence of purpose and so forth.

Now, it might be thought: "In the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), how can this be a verbal expression? To explain: there is no connection between word and object in the form of identity (*tādātmya*) because they exist in different locations; nor is there a relation of origination (*tadutpatti*) because the word exists even when the object is absent; and there is no other [relation] besides these. To this, he says: "The object established by itself" (*svataḥ siddhārtha*).
"How is the object established by its own inherent fitness, and not from anything else? To this he says: "Having approached that," and so forth;
having approached—that is, having brought—that distinction within the range of hearing, he speaks, that is, he declares it.
Who is he? He says: one who is the cause [of the cognition], unmentioned, and devoid of convention.

Furthermore, what is his nature? "Having approached that which knows the universal"—this is also to be understood here; the meaning is that having heard the word, he is the knower of that [universal].
If it is argued that this is not so because of the non-existence of a universal, we say no; for a universal is established through the similar transformation (*samānapariṇāma*) found in things.
What does he say? To this he says: "What has this one said?"—that is, "What has this speaker said? in this manner.

If the universal has already been known through the initial hearing of the word, why does one speak thus? If it is argued that "once the blue object is known in its own nature, it is not appropriate to ask 'What is this? regarding its form," [the author] replies here: "Difference," and so forth.

"Difference" refers to a subordinate particularity (*avāntara-viśeṣa*) of that universal; "desire for that" means the effort to apprehend it; and "one whose mind is directed toward that" is the designator.

"Is it not the case that in the cognition of a universal there is the cognition of its difference [from particulars], since otherwise how could even the universal exist as something other than identity? Thus, reality consists of both natures; there is no need for further inquiry here.
If it is asked: 'Even in the case of identity, why would the universal alone be presented first by means of the word?'—to this he replies: 'Just as from the senses,' etc."
Where? In the case of its own object, such as a form and so forth;

for just as from a distance there is a cognition of a universal such as "humanity" through the sense organ, then again there is a desire for its differentiation, and then again, by the power of a causal complex such as proximity in space, there is the apprehension of that particularity.
This has been stated in this very work (*Siddhiviniścaya*, 2): "For one who sees [the object] equally, there is a desire for the particular."

By such statements as these, [it is shown that] from a word, there is first the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*), then the desire for its particulars, and thereafter, through the causal complex of linguistic convention (*saṅketa-sāmagrī*), the determination of the particular. It is not on this account that the word is inherently incapable [of denoting the particular]; for if it were, the same consequence would apply to sensory perception (*akṣa*) as well.
And just as there is doubt regarding one's own object from a word, so too is there doubt from sensory perception.
Even when the capacity of a cause is apprehended as being like that of a visible form, doubt is observed regarding it;
if one argues that in that case there is another cognition in the form of doubt, then the same must apply elsewhere as well—
for no person perceives that a doubt such as "the jar does not exist" arises merely from the mention of the word "jar," since that would lead to the undesirable consequence of non-action.

Now, if the cognition of an object arises from a word, why is there even a doubt? [One might argue: "Because it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*). But then, why would there be doubt even regarding the cognition of the capacity of thoughts such as giving to bring about heaven?
If you say, "Because that cognition is common to both the presence and absence of that [capacity]," then the same applies here.
That being so, how can it be said that "the word has the object as its domain"? This [objection] is refuted by this very point.

The cognition of that [object] is non-conceptual; therefore, this is not a fault. If it is argued that because [the mind] is conscious, a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) arises therein and thus [doubt is impossible], then for one who possesses mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) in the form of a definitive determination regarding color, pleasure, and so forth, doubt would be difficult to find even when that capacity [for determination] exists.
Otherwise, such [doubt] would not occur even with respect to the meaning of a word.

Even for one whose mental state is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) and indeterminate (*aniścaya*), because that [mental state] grasps the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), what is grasped by a non-conceptual [cognition] is equivalent to what is not grasped; thus, just as verbal [cognition] has a non-entity as its object because it is a cause of doubt, so too is perception for the opponent: since a universal is grasped from that sense-organ (*akṣa*), when there is a desire for a particular and an absence of a cause for determining the particular, there is doubt—just as there is from a word. This is established.
The term *vedanā* refers specifically to feeling.
The term *bhinnā* means "divided" (*bhidā*), that is to say,
it is a synonym for "separated" (*bheda*) which, by its inherent capacity, produces a cognition that causes doubt.
Doubt is the accepted view;
it is not a fault, as it is characterized by the absence of doubt.
Regarding [the property of] being conscious and so forth, for the Mīmāṃsaka and the Buddhist.
There would be an absence of doubt.

A Buddhist might argue as follows: "One understands the universal from a word only when it has been mentioned in another language [i.e., when a convention has been established], not from one for which no convention has been made; therefore, the convention itself is the indirect cause of that [cognition]. If that were so, then even from a sense organ, one would first have already apprehended the universal, and only thereafter would one again perceive the universal.
The meaning is that this is a trivial argument: that the very same sense-organ is the cause of apprehending that [object] at other times as well, and its nature is the same elsewhere too,
because it is merely conventional.

[Objection: "But what is the purpose of examining the nature of sound, which is devoid of utility? For its nature is established through common worldly experience. To this, he says: "Because of the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)," and so forth.
If one asks, "What does this mean? he says here: "Sound," and so forth.

Sound is a modification of matter (pudgala) and a composite aggregate (skandha), like shadow, light, and so forth; thus say the stainless Deva-s: "Sound is a modification of matter and a composite aggregate, like shadow, light, and so forth" (*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p.
Verbal expression, which is the specific nature of the effect of the intellect, has its own object as its domain.
Atoms [are perceived] due to the cognition of differentiation and conjunction resulting from a particular transformation of the *pudgala*.

How so? And how could it not be so? Since things that are entirely partless would each necessarily have six parts due to the distinction of spatial directions, how could there be contact? Furthermore, would they remain separate without even contacting one another? How then could there be any interval between them, since this does not escape the aforementioned dilemma? If it is argued that there is continuity by its very nature through its own causal and effectual moments, and that this indicates a distinction in the accumulation of time—then indeed, as in the case of a moment, no entity possesses parts merely because of its continuity with others; for the absence of an interval is itself the essence of their conjunction.

Otherwise, the very distinction between cause and effect would not exist by virtue of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things. If that distinction were established, how could there be a continuous connection through conjunction (*saṃyoga*)? For it would follow that those things conjoined would be indistinguishable, since it is logically consistent for a mere spatial point (*pradeśamātra*) to act as an obstruction by its own nature. Even for that which is partless, due to a difference in intrinsic nature—just like the perception of the forms of the apprehended object and so forth—these [consequences] follow...
...no, for it has been refuted;

moreover, since that quality can only belong to a transformation of that very [substance], how could a quality of something entirely imperceptible be perceptible? This is because a transformation consisting of identity with spherical atoms is logically possible.
Since air is also perceptible, that [example] is not equal [to the case at hand].

These specific manifestations of consciousness, consisting of phonemes, words, and so forth, somehow attain a fitness for connection with meaning and are brought into the sphere of linguistic usage; it is not otherwise. Sound is an entity that falls within the range of the auditory faculty, just like any other sound.

If it is argued that existence (*sattā*) might also [be non-existent]; then what is it that distinguishes it from that [non-existence] such that this would not be the case? If it is argued that it is so because it is distinct; and if it is further argued that the word "existent" is non-existent [in itself], yet becomes existent through its connection with that [existence]; then it has already been stated in this regard that, since there is no difference between the two, that [existence] alone would be the existent. To this also, it has been replied:
Since a transformation similar to that [of sound] occurs elsewhere as well,
by this [argument] the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*) has been considered;
yet sound is not a quality.
What is that? He says: it is a modification (paryāya) of the person (pudgala).

Furthermore, persons possess form and other qualities; their modification is a transformation, and persons are not themselves those modifications. Otherwise, there would be a perception of a jar or similar object by the eye and other senses through its accompaniment by sound, just as there is [perception] of existence through its accompaniment by the nature of being (sadrūpa).
Because inherence is without distinction everywhere due to sound, and so forth; "sound," "synonym," and "pudgala" are [synonymous] terms.

If it is argued that, like those who propound the *śabdabrahman*, the *pudgala* is a synonym for sound—if, that is, the *pudgala* is a synonym for matter in the form of atoms—then, just like the blackness and other qualities inherent in them, it would not be perceived by the sense organs of people such as ourselves. To this, he replies: "It is a *skandha*";
a *skandha* is a composite substance (*avayavidravya*).
Sound is a composite entity (skandha), because, while being perceptible to people like us, it possesses parts, just like a cloth;
it is corporeal (mūrta) because it possesses tangibility, just like that [cloth];
and its possession of tangibility is established by the fact that it is apprehended through perceptions such as "soft" or "hard," just like that very [cloth].
Nor is this unestablished, because it is well-known to all the world;
for instance, people describe the sound of a lute and the like as harsh compared to the sound of a victory-bell and the like.
Moreover, if that were not established, nothing at all would be established.
The proof of sound is established through its perception upon striking the ear;
this is the comparison: sound arises from a mass, and a mass is a collection of atoms.
When those [atoms] are struck, a sound arises that is inherent and produced— [as stated in] *Pañcāstikāya-gāthā* 79—
because it is a proven fact (*siddhasādhanatva*) that a single substance consisting of a *pudgala*-aggregate can serve as the substratum for sound.
—Tattvasaṃgrahaśloka, p.
422; Nyāyakumudacandra, p. 242; Sanmatitarkaṭīkā, p. 670.

Sound is a personal substance (paudgalika), because, while being perceptible to us and being insentient, it possesses action, like an arrow—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 563. Compare: Sound is a substance, because it is the substratum of qualities such as slightness of touch, greatness, dimension, number, and conjunction.
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
550; *Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 243. Of sound.

Comparison: The common experience of sound—which produces a grating sensation in the ear-cavity and generally causes injury to houses and other objects—leads to the disappearance of the hypothesis that it is intangible.
(Aṣṭaśatī on Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p.
107) Sound possesses tangibility because it is the cause of impact upon other objects with which it comes into contact, just like a mallet or similar instruments.
For it is well-established that the striking of the auditory organ and so forth occurs through the connection with sounds such as those from a bronze vessel—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
550; *Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 243.

Regarding the proof of the possession of touch (*sparśavattva*), another says: "It is the state of being the object of those cognitions [of intensity and dullness] due to its connection with the universals (*jāti*) of intensity (*tīvratva*) and dullness (*mandatva*). This is not so, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that this would apply everywhere, resulting in the non-existence of touch [in all things].
Furthermore, sound is impermanent because it is the object of [cognitions of] intensity and dullness, just like pleasure and pain.
—Nyāyavārttika, p. 290:

Some maintain that air accompanied by sound is the object of that [auditory cognition]; for them as well, there would be an infinite regress, since another air accompanied by that [first] air would be the object, and so on, regarding the objects of the cognitions of intensity and so forth.
Comparison—the increase of sound is supreme (17).

And since a great sound is perceived when many people beat drums or utter the word "cow," it is understood from this that there is an accumulation of sound-parts for each person; but this is not so, for sound is partless, as no distinction of parts is apprehended.
And because it is partless, magnitude is impossible;
therefore, it does not increase... thus, this increase belongs to the sound-complex (*nāda*), not to the word-sound (*śabda*).
— Jaiminisūtra with Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.17

It might be thought by some that the "form" (*mūrti*) of a certain invisible sound is the dimension of a non-omnipresent substance, and not its possession of touch; otherwise, the mind would lack form due to the absence of that [touch]. That is not so; since this [possession of touch] exists in sound as well, its substantiality and non-omnipresence due to possessing touch cannot be prevented. Furthermore, its dimension is well-established, as it is the object of the cognition of length and so forth.
For those who know the categories of existence (padārthavid) maintain that "form" (mūrti) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading (asarvagata)—Tattvabindu, p.
158. Furthermore, that definition is over-extensive (atiprasaṅgin), because it applies even to the self (ātman), since its omnipresence has been denied therein.
Consequently, corporeality— which is established, which is the object of direct perception for persons such as ourselves, and which is a characteristic of corporeality free from dispute— is proven.
Nor is [the argument] "because it possesses parts" unestablished; for sound possesses parts because it is perceived as having smallness or greatness, like a pillar or similar objects.

If it is argued that this perception of smallness or greatness is due to the superimposition of the properties of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) upon the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), and not inherent to the sound itself—just as the face [appears distorted] in a mirror and so forth—this might be so, provided that sound were always of a single uniform nature derived from some source.
However, the probandum is not established by a mere example alone, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, sound is a quality of the aggregate;
smallness and greatness are not perceived as functions residing in sound, nor are coarseness and subtlety observed therein.
The conception of intensity or dullness in cognition is a conceptualization of largeness or smallness;
and that [conception] indeed becomes sharp when [an object] is illuminated by a great light,
while it remains dull when illuminated by a weak light, even in the case of objects such as a jar, at all times.
Thus it is established that length and all other such qualities are properties of the sound-vibration (dhvani)—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śabdanirṇaya, p.

785. Now, if it is argued: "In that case, just as with a clod of earth or the like, [sound] would be struck by blows to the limbs of the body; likewise, it would have a fixed location of movement; having entered the ear in one place, it would not go elsewhere within it; it would travel to the ends of the world when struck by the wind; and it would be perceived by another sense organ"; to this he replies: "Shadow," and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), darkness and so forth are included; "like that" (*tadvat*) means it exists similarly to that.
The meaning of the example is: "just as those faults do not apply here [in the case of darkness], so they do not apply to sound either.
For indeed, even in the case of a mass of darkness, there is no apprehension by means of touch and so forth.
The production of one sound by another sound within the ear.

There may be this comparison: if [the sense of smell] were of the nature of a material substance (*pudgala-svabhāva*), then the objection regarding its obstructing the expansion of vision, filling the ears, or entering through a single ear would deserve to be set aside by means of the rebuttal provided concerning the odor-atom (*gandha-paramāṇu*). — *Aṣṭaśata*, *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 108.

Even though shadow has the nature of a person (pudgala), some maintain that the word consisting of phonemes such as 'ga' is not of human origin; regarding this, he says: "The cognition," and so forth.

The effect of cognition follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [object], for it is not logical that something which follows the positive and negative concomitance of another should have a different cause or be causeless, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that it is the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of that [object] which follows those [concomitances], we say no; for that would entail an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since one would have to postulate yet another [manifestation] following that [first manifestation].
And this position has already been countered;
elsewhere it was stated that "he whose very self consists of specific differences such as color and so forth" refers to that [phoneme],
by which the *sphoṭa*-self distinct from those is refuted.
Why? He says: "Because that very thing is expressed by it.
Where? He says: "In the object of its own meaning, which consists of both the universal and the particular, or in the synonym for the phoneme (*vyañjana-paryāya*)," according to the Mīmāṃsakas.
Regarding the position of the theory of sound-manifestation (*śabdābhivyaktivāda*),

in which sound— being of the nature of a particular [manifestation]— is a modification (*paryāya*) of the *pudgala*, the reason "because of having form" (*mūrttitvāt*) resides in the mind of Sādhyasūri.

The example [cited] for that has already been shown to be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) because of atoms (*paramāṇu*); for although they possess form (*mūrttitva*), they are not its modifications (*paryāya*), since there exists nothing subtler than them. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Atoms," and so forth.
Why is this so? To this he says: "From a specific transformation of the *pudgala*.

Transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the *pudgala* is its becoming otherwise; that itself is the "specificity" (*viśeṣa*), namely, the differentiation of a single gross form into various subtle forms, or the differentiation of various subtle forms into a single gross form.
Why is that [transformation] also possible? To this he says: "Differentiation," and so forth.
"Difference" is manifoldness (*nānātva*); "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*) is transformation into unity. From the perception of these two, this is what is meant:

just as it is observed that from many small dimensions joined together, something endowed with a single largeness arises—which was previously non-existent—and is thus its effect, so too, let that which is the opposite of that [largeness], such as a potsherd, which was previously non-existent, be the effect of a single thing endowed with largeness, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]. If you argue that because potsherds and the like exist even prior [to the production of the jar], they cannot be its effects, then the Sāṃkhya view is reached, for it would follow that the jar and other things also exist [prior to their production].

If it is argued that this is not so because [the threads] are not seen [in the cloth], that is the same in the other case as well. If it is argued that the threads are seen in the cloth, we say no; for at that time the cloth itself does not exist. If it is argued that otherwise the Buddhist teaching would be different from that, we say no; for this position has already been refuted.
Atoms do not exist as modes of a person, for such a person does not exist; [atoms] are manifold and possessed of minute dimensions.
If this is argued,
the proponent [refutes] the position that there is a distinction between the part and the whole.

Furthermore, if it is argued that at the time of the jar there exist shards distinct from it, and that they lack the status of being its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) because they do not arise together with it— just as they lack it in relation to one another due to their existence even prior [to the jar]— then let there likewise be a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar as well;
for the subverting proof (*pramāṇabādhaka*) applies equally to both cases.

Since that [existence of the cause] is established through inference, it cannot be sublated by perception. Why is it not accepted that even a cloth is preceded by a great cause, just like a jar? If it is argued that while a gross object is seen there [in the case of the jar], a subtle one is not seen here [in the case of the cloth], and thus the threads would be rendered useless; to this we reply that the same applies to the lump of clay in the case of the cloth.

If it is argued that, since the lump of clay is the cause of the jar, the jar existing therein must be perceived— just as cloth exists within its threads— the answer is no; for we accept that the material cause (*upādāna*) is that which has transformed into the form of the effect, such that even the threads themselves become the cloth.
Therefore, just as one [entity] arises from the combination of many, so too does the manifold arise from its separation; how then could atoms not be its modes (paryāyas)? This may indeed be so.
Here the Buddhist asks: "How so? and so forth. The Teacher asks him in return: "And what would not exist?
He replies: "In every way," and so forth. [The objection is:

Since partless atoms would each possess six parts due to the distinction of spatial directions, how could there be any conjunction in any manner whatsoever? The resolution here is this: the intention is to ask, "But why [should they] not be non-conjoined at all?"
Thus, even by that [opponent] who, while censuring conjunction (*saṃsarga*), nevertheless accepts external objects, external atoms of form and so forth have indeed been accepted—[for it is said]:
"Because of the simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], the atom would have six parts;
and because the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be no more than a single atom."
—Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-viṃśikā, p. 7;
Catuḥśataka, p. 48; Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 203.
Those other atoms which arise from the connection with different objects are said to be "aggregated" (sañcita); for they alone are the cause of the production of cognition,
since atoms do not possess that specific quality [of being perceived] without other atoms.
Because of the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (2.195–96),
"And those [particulars] are non-conjoined, being indeed devoid of conjunction."

But are they not entirely non-distinct? They are distinct in their state—that is, [the atoms] devoid of that [conjunction], whereas when accumulated, they are conjoined. Otherwise, regarding pillars and the like, there would be no uninterrupted perception of the lower, middle, upper, and lateral parts; thus, this objection against the Naiyāyika is irrelevant. For it has been said: "If it were not uninterrupted, it would not appear; therefore, its cognition occurs through the grasping of succession" (*Pravacanavākyapaddhati* 2.256). Thus, its cognition [is established].
The Buddhist says:

"But surely, the apprehension of pleasure and so forth is perceived simultaneously with the apprehension of form and so forth. [The opponent replies: "In the case of a pillar and the like, the cognition of parts is perceived as uninterrupted; thus it is the same. Another says: "Their non-interruption is not established merely because they appear without interruption, for even in the absence of such [non-interruption], that appearance occurs in the case of distant, sparse hairs and the like. For him too, since they appear in that manner, it follows that the form which appears as uninterrupted does not belong to them, while that which does not appear as interrupted belongs to them.

And if it is argued that what appears in cognition must be its own self-cognition and cannot be of a different form, because "in the absence of that [form], there would be an absence of that [cognition]," from where does this follow? If it is said, "Because that [cognition] has that form," then from where does that [fact] come? If it is said, "Because it appears as such," then this is the same in other cases as well. Furthermore, there is no sublation [of the appearance]; for we observe the appearance of something even when that thing is absent in one instance, yet we do not thereby postulate that it is so everywhere, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that atoms do not appear [in consciousness], from what then are they apprehended? If it is said "because they are the cause of cognition," then the same consequence follows for the eyes and other sense organs. If it is said "because they impart their own form [to cognition]," then since the form within the nature of cognition is distinct from one another, the imparting of that very form results in the same fault as when only the blue-ness and so forth are imparted; thus, the atoms would possess parts, and there is no distinction from the prima facie position.
Even in the absence of non-interruption,
just as hair, mosquitoes, flies, and the like, though situated at distant intervals, produce a cognition in the form of a single dense mass—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 94.
If it is argued that there is no perception of atoms;
If this is argued:
even though blueness and insentience both exist, nevertheless, there is only the presentation of blueness to cognition.

Furthermore, if those [other qualities] do not appear, what is the point of postulating them? For the cognition of blue and so forth would arise from something else entirely—namely, from the external form and other such [objects].

Since they themselves are not deficient in being uninterrupted, they produce an uninterrupted cognition, and not some other cognition that lacks the nature of form and so forth yet possesses the aspect of form and so forth—how could this be? Therefore, if atoms are admitted, their appearance must be admitted;
and since that [appearance] is uninterrupted, they too must be so. Thus it has been well said: "How much more so, then, are the atoms themselves non-contiguous?"
He raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to state another refutation: "They might be" (*syuḥ*), meaning they could exist as non-contiguous;
here the response follows: "How so? and so forth, because there is an absence of any intervening space—that is, the absence of the presence of heterogeneous entities—between those accumulated atoms.

Why is this so? He says: "The relevant alternative," and so forth. The relevant alternative consists of the conjunction or non-conjunction of the obscuring agent (*vyavadhāyaka*) and the object obscured (*vyavadhīyamāna*). The non-transcendence of that [alternative] results in either the loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) in one case, or infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the other, because of the further postulation of successive obscurations.
Alternatively, it is because the relevant alternative—namely, "in every way otherwise"—is not transcended even when there is an obscuration.

"Let it be granted that there is no interval between them; however, does this not lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the atom] having six parts? To this he replies: "Indeed, for no one," and so forth.

Indeed, for no one—that is, for no atom situated in the middle—there is a state of having parts (sāṃśatva), even though there is no interval, due to its being surrounded by other atoms situated in various directions.
Why is this? He says: because the absence of interval itself consists in their conjunction.
By the word "that" (tat), there is a reference to the atom. Why is this so? He says: "sphericity," and so forth, [referring to] the acceptance of conjunction.

If it is objected that, on the view of non-contact (*asaṃsarga*), since every absence (*abhāva*) is not of the nature of a quality (*aguṇātmaka*) whereas conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is of the nature of a quality, how can it be said that "conjunction is precisely the absence of separation"? We reply: no; for conjunction is not perceived apart from two fingers that are not separated, and the term "conjunction" is applied only to the absence of separation, as it is devoid of [independent] qualities.

Furthermore, since conjunction is not perceived [as a distinct entity], if this [conjunction] were non-different from the conjoined parts—just as the whole is non-different from its parts—then when one part is pulled, it would follow that the other parts are pulled as well, just like the foot and so forth.
This being the case, the whole would be useless, because its purpose is already accomplished by that very [conjunction]. If you say this, let this be another fault of yours.

If it is argued that this is not so because [the whole] also appears [as distinct], we say no; for among the parts of a jar or similar objects, there is an absence of the appearance of two non-distinct entities.
Indeed, only one thing is perceived, whose nature consists of the parts, their form, and so forth—whether that be a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or a composite whole (*avayavin*).

If it is argued that, since conjunction is itself a composite, the composite must be a collection of many atoms, or else a collection of Brahmins and Caṇḍālas standing in close proximity; let this same fault belong to him who maintains that a single conjunction is non-different from those [atoms or individuals], but not to us, who maintain that conjunction is merely the absence of any interval between them.

If it is argued that "it [the whole] is not distinct from these [parts]," it has already been stated here that because inherence (*samavāya*) is refuted, no relation is established; for in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
when one finger is pulled...

If it is argued that the whole (*avayavin*) also arises from those [parts], and therefore it belongs to them; here this is to be considered: do they produce that [whole] while being in immediate contact, or otherwise? In the first case, let them produce the whole itself—what is the point of producing conjunctions for the sake of a laborious succession? If it is argued that there is no fault because it is observed to be so; there might be no fault if such observation did not occur, but it is not so, for they are not perceived to first produce a conjunction and then subsequently produce the whole.

If it is argued that such a cognition occurs due to the rapidity of the process; this reply would apply if there were a simultaneous cognition of both [the sound and its cause], but such is not the case. Otherwise, it would follow that [the atoms] produce the conjunction by first generating a further [conjunction];

and in that second case as well, those situated at a distance would produce it, since the action caused by that [conjunction] is absent there too. Therefore, it remains established: "only because of the intervention," and so forth.
The statement that atoms do not undergo conjunction is meaningless.

Others say: "We do not maintain that atoms are the cause of cognition or anything else, since we ourselves have refuted them. To this, [the author] replies with the words beginning "What then? and so forth. Regarding that, he says: "Like a moment" (*kṣaṇavat*), etc.

Although the expression "like a moment" is stated in general terms, here only the moment of cognition (*jñānakṣaṇa*) is intended, because the opponent accepts that alone as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). "Like a moment" means "just as [atoms are not admitted for] a moment. Indeed, nothing whatsoever possesses parts (*sāṃśatva*), even in its continuity (*nairantarya*). Of what moment? He says: "of the experiencing one" (*anubhavataḥ*).
What is it? He says: "continuity.
By what means? He says: "by its own effect-moment and cause-moment.

By the word *sva* (own), the middle moment is taken as the subject of the illustration; its effect-moment is the subsequent appropriated moment (*upādeya-kṣaṇa*), and its cause-moment is the preceding appropriating moment (*upādāna-kṣaṇa*). By these two [moments].
Why does that [recollection] arise from its own experience? He says: "From itself alone, not from conjunction and so forth"—this is the meaning.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Time," and so on;
the differentiation of the accumulation of time is the multiplicity of the stream of cognitions, and [the recollection arises] by means of the indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that.
He states the refutation [of the opponent's position] in the absence of this [admission]: "Otherwise," etc.

In the manner of the absence of continuity, otherwise—that is, if the determination of cause and effect were not established by avoiding the confusion of the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*)—there would simply be no stability; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author includes] the confusion of functions (*vyatikara*).

It might be thought: "Just as in the case of the knowledge arising from waking and awakening, that determination [of the sequence] occurs elsewhere by the very nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*), even in the absence of uninterruptedness. To this, the previously stated answer has been given;
now, in order to state another [objection], he says: "By the nature of things," etc.

"Thing" (*vastu*) refers to cause and effect; their "nature" (*svabhāva*) is their capacity (*yogyatā*); "from that" means from that [capacity] in the determination of them—that is, in the determination of cause and effect.
For what reason is there a continuity of conjunction?

Is the conjunction by way of one part or by way of its entire self? To this he says: "Their own atoms are conjoined with those [others]. This is stated precisely because of the opponent's own admission. If it is argued that even atoms, being by their very nature momentary entities, are devoid of contact and yet sustain a single gross transformation—thus leading to the undesirable consequence for everyone—it is the same for momentary entities as well.

For it can be argued: "If waking consciousness, though separated in time, is the cause of awakening, then why does knowledge of a past previous birth not also occur? Furthermore, this [objection] is the same in both cases.

If it is asked, "Why then do threads, when situated separately, not become the cause of a cloth?", [the answer is: "Why is fire, though separated by time, not the cause of smoke, just as waking consciousness is? The fact that it is not observed to be so elsewhere is the very same answer.
He states this because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction in the determination of causes for one's own position or the opponent's.
The establishment of the relationship between cause and effect is another way of avoiding [the objection];
it means "otherness" in this sense, namely, that [the effect] is other [than the cause].

This is another explanation: although that arrangement [of conjunction] may exist even when there is some separation from that [central moment], nevertheless, how could there be a continuous connection (*saṃyoga-prabandha*) among the preceding and succeeding moments—which are conjoined with that central moment and established without separation—that flow in a stream? Why would there not be a continuous flow (*pravāha*) if there were no separation by means of conjunction? To this he says: "Because of the consequence of non-distinction" (*aviśeṣaprasaṅgāt*), meaning because of the fault resulting from the consequence of non-distinction; that is to say, because of the same fault that applies to the accumulation of space, it applies to the accumulation of time as well.
Alternatively, regarding what was stated by the opponent—"How could there be variegation in a single [cognition]? (*Pravāha-vāda* 2.210), and so forth—he replies with "From where," etc.

For that reason, why would there not be a continuous connection—a superior, uninterrupted bond consisting of coexistence—between other atoms of blue-cognition through conjunction with those intended atoms of blue-cognition, even though they possess partless existence? He says: "Because there is no distinction," etc.

It should be observed—see page 60, note 10—that one might think: "In the Buddhist doctrine, nothing whatsoever is ever conjoined with anything else. To this he replies: "By itself," etc. The intended meaning is as follows: in the absence of non-interruption (nairantarya), there would necessarily follow the state of being separated by an interval (sāntaratva); and that [separation] occurs only when there is an intervening object, not otherwise. For it is logical that a mere spatial point (*pradeśamātra*), which is partless (*niraṃśa*) and independent of anything else, can function as an intervener by its very nature. Furthermore, it is logically established that even when there is non-interruption between things, no single entity possesses parts (*sāṃśatva*). By this, he demonstrates that if such [partlessness] were not accepted, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.

If it is argued: "Even if the systematic arrangement of cause and effect does not exist, there is nevertheless no fault, because that [arrangement] is accepted by the proponent of the non-duality of appearance (pratibhāsādvaitavādin)," to this he replies: "Number and so forth," etc.

It is not only for that which has parts (*sāṃśa*), but even for that which is partless (*anaṃśa*), there is a connection [to plurality] due to the difference in its own nature (*svabhāvabheda*), as in the case of "nine" and so forth; this should be understood here as the illustrative example.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore, these... and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says: "For not... and so forth.
To the question "Why is that?", he says here: "And it has been refuted... and so forth.
The Vaiśeṣika says: Sound is a quality (guṇa), because, while being excluded from being a substance (dravya) or an action (karman), it is related to existence (sattā), like color and so forth.
Precisely because it is a quality, it must reside in a substance;
its substratum is a substance that is all-pervading (vibhu), because, while being eternal, it possesses qualities perceptible to us and others, like the self (ātman).

If it is argued that "that which is of such a nature [as sound] and serves as its substratum is space (ākāśa)," to this he replies: For only that which undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) in the manner of sound possesses the quality of sound (*śabdaguṇatva*). But space, which is accepted by you as eternal, does not have form and so forth as its nature; for even by the opponent, the quality of form and so forth is described only as a transformation of form itself. [Furthermore: Sound is dependent upon something, because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*)... — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 322.
Sound is not of the nature of substance or action, because it is perceptible by the sense of hearing, like [the universal] "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*);
sound is a quality, because, while being distinct from substance and action, it is related to existence (*sattā*), like color and other qualities. — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 649.
In the manuscript, the four syllables following "śabdādhāraḥ" are missing and excessively rubbed away, so that even another person can only read them as "pareṇāpi.
He states another objection, beginning with "And how," and so forth.

And how could sound, which is an attribute of the sky that is absolutely imperceptible, be perceptible—that is, graspable by the sense organs of people like us? For instance: whatever attribute is absolutely imperceptible is not perceptible to people like us, just as the color and other qualities of atoms; and sound, according to the opponent, is an attribute of something absolutely imperceptible. This is comparable to the fact that no attribute of an incorporeal substance—such as an attribute of the self—is ever observed to be an object of the senses.
—Tattvārthavārttika, p. 69;
Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 421;
Pañcāstikāya-ṭīkā, p. 185.
Furthermore, if sound were a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), its perceptibility by people like us would be untenable—*Nyāyakumuda*, p. 247.

Now, if it is argued that [the reason] is one whose exclusion from the opposite class is doubtful, because it would be both a quality entirely beyond perception and yet perceptible; to this he replies: because of the possibility of that very transformation, which is the state of being identical with those atoms which have that sound as their own nature—that is, as a quality inherent in them (*tādātmya*).
The sense is that just as it is not so for invisible space (*ākāśa*), so it would not be for such atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Now, if it is argued that if sound were a quality of the atom, it would be imperceptible like its color and other qualities; [we reply] that even if it were a quality of space, it would be so—just as its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) is—thus the case is the same here.

Since a variety of qualities is possible, why should there be dissatisfaction with another [explanation]? Therefore, it is not logical to say that if sound were a quality of the atom, it would follow that it is imperceptible like its color and other qualities.

As for what was further stated— that sound is imperceptible because its substratum is a substance that is all-pervading, given that it is a quality perceptible to people like us while being eternal, and thus like the self (ātman)— this has been refuted by [the argument] that it would follow that even atoms are all-pervading.

And it has been stated that [sound] does not reside in the self. This is the comparison: if space were not all-pervasive, then sound would not arise everywhere, because an effect cannot arise in the absence of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Sounds produced in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space are inherent in a single substance, because they are sounds, like the first sound being heard now.

Furthermore, the co-inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*) between the [quality] being heard and the word must be understood as being based on a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—*Pramāṇakanda*, p.

62. Now, if it is argued that while a quality entirely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣaguṇa*) is itself imperceptible, the same applies to the specific touch (*sparśaviśeṣa*) which is a quality of air (*vāyu*); to this, he replies: "It is not the same."
Why? He says: "Even of air," and so forth.

By the phrase "in the form of touch," he demonstrates that air has the specific nature of touch; otherwise, there would be no relationship between quality and the possessor of the quality (guṇa-guṇibhāva).

And how is air perceptible? [If you say] because it is not in contact with the sense organ, then it would follow that it is also perceptible through touch, since there is contact with it by way of contact with that [touch], given the admission of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).

Or rather, there is a relation between the air and that [sense organ], yet it does not produce cognition therein; for it follows that the sense organ does not produce cognition regarding that with which it is directly connected, but produces it regarding that through which it [is connected]. This has led to the situation where one’s food is like a broken bowl!
It is observed that [the cognition] arises when there is contact; therefore, it arises in that case and not elsewhere, for the opposite would not hold.

Why is this so? If you say, "Because there is the perception of contact," then does this perception not exist—namely, "The wind touches me as soft, hard, or otherwise"? If you say, "This is an illusion," then from what [is that known]? If you say, "Because even though it is not perceptible, there is a superimposition of perceptibility upon it," then from what [is that known]? If you say, "Because its perception is an error," then there is a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): once its erroneous nature is established, its imperceptibility follows, and from that, its erroneous nature is established.
The contact of touch is with the wind and the sense organ.

This point is connected as follows: it might be thought that "the bowl or vessel belonging to the one for whom food was prepared has been broken," yet the cognition arises because of the superimposition of the wind upon mere touch, not from the grasping of that [bowl]; likewise, according to the Buddhist (Saugata) view, the awareness "I see the jar" arises from the superimposition of the jar upon color-form (rūpa), not from the seeing of that [jar].

Why is this distinction made—that a jar is perceived as having form as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), whereas air is not perceived as having touch as its limiting adjunct? Now, if it is argued that a substance is perceptible when it is graspable by two sense organs, and that air is not so, [we reply]: then the moon, the sun, and other such objects would not be perceptible, since they are grasped by only one sense organ by those standing at their side. If you say there is no fault because they are grasped by two sense organs by someone standing nearby, then let there be no fault for air as well, since it too is grasped by those two by a person with special faculties. What is the proof for this? The same question applies elsewhere as well.

If it is argued that because of the absence of color and so forth in that [air], there is no such apprehension even by means of a specific [quality], then from what source is it known that touch and so forth exist in the moon and other such objects? [It is known] from their possession of color; for it is accepted that in the case at hand [air], it possesses touch.
The remainder has been considered here through the apprehension of air.
If it is argued that [this is known] by means of sight and touch, [then it is answered:
by the deity presiding over those [senses].
By the yogin, through the wind [element] and the two sense organs.
If it is held that color and so forth do not exist in air,

and if this is an absolute rule— that only what is perceptible by two sense-faculties is directly perceived— then the self would not be directly perceived, for its apprehension involves the operation of the mind alone and no other sense-faculty.
Furthermore, [this would follow].
If a single substance were not within the capacity of each of the two sense organs— the visual and the tactile— then it could not be perceived here by either organ.
If it is argued: "Why should that [sound] belong to those two [atoms], such that it is designated as such?
This is nothing of the sort.

Or rather, since atoms, like the sky, are absolutely imperceptible (*atyantaparokṣa*), their transformation—sound—likewise would not be perceptible; thus the case is the same," to this he replies: "Of those that are spherical," and so forth.

If it is argued that the objection is not equal [to our position] because the transformation into identity (*tādātmya*) and the transformation into perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) are logically possible, and thus there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to air (*vāyu*), the author replies here: "Of air also," etc.,
and concludes with "Therefore these," etc.
Since this is so, what kind of things are these words? To this he says: "consciousness," and so forth.
By the mention of "consciousness," non-human (apauruṣeya) words are excluded; by the word "particular" (viśeṣa), sounds proceeding from false cognition are avoided.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? To this he says: "The phoneme," and so forth.
What is done with them? To this he says: "They are brought into the path of linguistic usage.
Having done what? To this he says: "In some way," and so forth.

Having understood by some means of proof, what [is known]? He says: "In the object," and so forth. That is, the capacity of words which has a connection—that is, a relation—with an object such as a jar.

Now, one might object: "Indeed, there is no relation between words and an object even through capacity; nevertheless, they are brought into the sphere of linguistic usage by means of a person. To this, he replies: "Not otherwise."
Demonstrating that very point, he says: "In some way," and so forth;
he provides an illustration: "like other words," meaning like the roar of the ocean and the like, which consist of the letter *a* and so on.

[Objection: Is it not the case that fitness (*yogyatā*) is inferred from the observation of an effect? And yet, there is no effect in the form of the cognition of an object (*arthapratīti*) produced by words, because from them there arises only a cognition of an indistinct and common form. [This is said] to refute [the claim that] they appear otherwise in the sense-faculties, for two cognitions that have different appearances cannot have the same object; otherwise, this consequence would apply even to cognitions of color and so forth. If it is argued that the determination of that effect follows from fitness, then there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the determination of the effect depends on fitness, and the establishment of fitness depends on that [determination]. To this, he says: "Speech," and so on.
Or rather, the distinction between their respective effects is logical even when speech and visual consciousness have the same object as their domain,
due to a difference in appearance, just like the perception of the same object from distant or near positions. (3)

Even if there is a difference in appearance due to a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no absolute necessity for a difference in the object, as in the case of cognitions that are near and distant.
Otherwise, how could this person, seeing the object with non-erroneous cognition, not see the specific form of the mother-of-pearl? For a common form is impossible;
if such a common form were possible, it would follow that both forms would be perceived by one who is nearby.
Therefore, the claim that "this person, though seeing its unique form as if nearby, does not ascertain it due to a deficiency in the causal conditions for ascertainment" is untenable.

For there can be no possibility of a completeness or deficiency of the causal conditions for ascertainment between two cognitions—one proximate and the other otherwise—without a distinction in their clear or unclear appearance.

Furthermore, how could there not be a difference in the nature of the perception of these two, given the difference in the causal complex such as distance and proximity? Otherwise, why would one standing at a distance see [the object] just as clearly as one who is nearby? Thus, that argument is incorrect.

Regarding the cognitions that constitute the specific effects of speech and the senses, he asks: "Even though they have the same object as their domain, which one is to be joined [with the external object]? He says: "By the difference in appearance," meaning by the distinction between a clear and an unclear appearance. He provides an illustration: "In the distance," etc.;
just as in the case of the two perceptions of a single common object—such as a tree—by two persons, one distant and one near, it is so [in this case].

Just as for one who is distant, the apprehension of an object there is indistinct, whereas for one who is near, it is otherwise; so too, there is an indistinct cognition of a single object at a given moment—thus there is no fault.
To explain the verse, he says: "The causal complex" (*sāmagrī*), etc.

Because of the difference—that is, the diversity—of the causal complex consisting of words, sense organs, and so forth, even though there is a difference in appearance, there is no absolute necessity that the object itself be different.
This is merely an illustration; [the text] begins with "proximate" and so forth.

Now, one might object: the indistinct cognition of something distant must have as its object that which is not the [actual] thing, because the dense and indistinct form appearing therein does not exist in the object.
Or, if it did exist, then even for someone who is proximate, there would be the undesirable consequence of such a cognition occurring.

If two distinct forms, the clear and the other, were present, there would be the cognition of both in both cases; but this is not so. Therefore, that [cognition] which has an indistinct object as its domain is not non-erroneous (*avisaṃvāda*). This has been stated by another authority: "The appearance in my [cognition] is not devoid of configuration (*saṃsthāna*)."

If it is argued: "But the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like, which has a real object as its domain, is indeed clear even from a distance; in that case, the perception of silver and so forth is a separate mental error (mānasī bhrāntiḥ). So how can it be said [in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṅkāra* 2.1, etc. that 'it is due to the causal complex' (*sāmagrī*) and so on? To this, he replies: "How otherwise... and so forth.

Otherwise, if there were an absolute distinction between objects based on a difference in the mental appearance resulting from a difference in causal complexes, then this person, seeing from a distance and apprehending the object through non-erroneous, non-conceptual cognition, would not have a perception of a single, dense form.

He presents the view that the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like by another person, even though situated at a distance, is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); following that, the delusion (*bhrānti*) regarding silver and so forth is mental (*mānasī*). Otherwise, there would be no example whatsoever for such a delusion. He shows this: "of the mother-of-pearl"—this is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication), by which the mirage-circle, the rope, and so forth are also included. The connection is: "he does not see the specific form, that is, the nature (*svabhāva*), which is distinguished and excluded from everything else. How so? The meaning is that he certainly does see it; and thus, just as when one is near, so too at a distance, there is the delusion of silver and the like.
The sense is that [the universal] does not exist when the blue [object] is perceived as excluded from others;

thus, it might be thought that this is an error—just as even at a distance, among hairs that are sparse, a blackness common to all appears despite the non-appearance of their mutual distinctions; so too, even when the specific form of the mother-of-pearl is not seen, one perceives only a certain "white-ness" common to both mother-of-pearl and silver. To this, he replies: "Because a common form is impossible."

Since, in the Buddhist view, a nature (*svabhāva*) consisting of a "common form" (*samāna-rūpa*) similar to that of mother-of-pearl and silver is impossible, it is thought that—just as in the perception of hair from a distance—the perception of a common form even in mother-of-pearl would be a mental error (*mānasī bhrānti*). Regarding that, he states the refutation in the case of its existence: if such a common form were possible, it would follow that a person standing nearby would perceive two forms; therefore, such a form is impossible.
If it is argued that one indeed perceives its very specific form, otherwise there would be an inconclusive [fallacy], [the author] replies here: "This person," and so forth.
This observer, although perceiving—as if it were near—that specific, unique form of the mother-of-pearl, does not ascertain that form.
Why? He says: "Because of ascertainment," and so forth.
"Because of the deficiency of the causal conditions for certainty"—this being stated by the opponent does not hold together.
Why? He says: "For," and so forth.

"For" (*hi*) means because there is no distinction between the clear appearance of the proximate cognition and the unclear appearance of the other [distant] cognition; that is to say, without the distinctness of the clear appearance of the proximate cognition and the distinctness of the unclear appearance of the other, distant cognition, there would be a mere destruction of the appearance. This is the meaning.

The cause of certainty is its cognition; the possibility of that [cognition] being either complete or deficient depends on experience, for experience is the means of cognizing it, and that [experience] is common to both cases. The sense is that it cannot be said that it is complete in one instance and deficient in the other.

If it is argued that factors such as the sharpness of vision are also causes of that [certainty], and that these are absent when the object is distant; to this, the following is considered: what is this "sharpness of vision" in that case? If you say it is the absence of activity [toward the object], then from what cause does the mental error of silver arise with respect to the mother-of-pearl, such that this [activity] would not occur?
It appears that the reading "śuktikāyāḥ" (of the mother-of-pearl) is missing here; otherwise, another quality would be erroneously attributed through the cause of delusion.

"Or [the appearance of] silver in mother-of-pearl [occurs] because of the perception of a similarity in form" (*Pra.vā.* 3.43). Thus, the absence of perception and the perception of a similarity in form are contradictory.

If it is claimed that this is accepted because even an existing [object] lacks the capacity to produce a certain cognition, then there would likewise be no certainty regarding mere whiteness; consequently, the conventional usage of "perception" would not apply to that either.
If it is argued that there is capacity in one case and its opposite in another, this is not so, because even that is impossible in a partless entity.

If it is argued that there is capacity in one respect and its opposite in another, this is not so, because it would entail the negation of permanence and because two distinct forms cannot exist [in a single partless entity].

Furthermore, since the very capacity to apprehend itself is the capacity to apprehend another, there is no prohibition against the apprehension of external objects. If, however, "indistinctness" (avaiśadya) means "lack of proficiency" (apāṭava), then this follows: when there is a specific lack of clarity in the manifestation of another cognition, a deficiency in the ascertainment (niścaya) may occur. Thus, even for one who possesses [the capacity] through repeated practice and so forth, if an object is situated at a distance, that ascertainment does not arise; therefore, that deficiency is not the cause for the absence of such ascertainment in that case.

If it is argued that proximity (*adūratva*) is also a factor in the cognition of certainty, and therefore for one situated at a distance there is the possibility of a deficiency in that cognition; to this he replies with the intention of the passage beginning "And how..."—just as, despite no difference in the experience of the form of the mother-of-pearl between those who are near and those who are otherwise, there is certainty and non-certainty due to the difference in the cognitions of proximity and non-proximity, so too, even when the object is the same, why should there not be a difference in the nature of the perception—a distinction of clarity and lack thereof—due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) such as distance and so forth? It would certainly be so; for if there were no difference in the nature of the perception, then like one who is nearby, one situated at a distance would see [the object] clearly.

Or, if [the word] "yataḥ" is used in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepa*), then if one were not to see [it at all], even when standing far away, one would see the specific, clearly defined form [of the object] on the mother-of-pearl just as one does when nearby. In that case, one would likewise see the form of distant, sparse hairs in the same way, yet one would simply fail to ascertain them due to a deficiency in the cognition of certainty (*niścaya-pratyaya*).
Thus, atoms—like distant, sparse hairs—would be the causes for the appearance of a dense, single [object]. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra 2)

92. Thus, the statement of Prajñākaragupta floats against Dharmakīrti; for it is possible to say that the cognition of two moons is produced by the sense faculties—first there is the single perception of it, and immediately thereafter, the conceptual construction of it as two.
If it is asked, "How is there clarity for this? [the answer is: How could there be clarity for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a single gross object such as a jar?
For you, [clarity] would depend on whether [the object] is near or distant.
Just as hairs, mosquitoes, flies, and the like, even when situated at a distance from one another, produce a cognition in the form of a single dense mass...—
this is the connection [in the phrase] "it floats" (*plavate*).
Furthermore, this [point] is that the sense organs (*akṣāṇi*) are also the cause of cognitions such as blue or a double moon.
[Pramāṇavārttika 2.294] But has it not been stated here [in Pramāṇavārttika 2.138] that because the two minds function simultaneously?

133. Thus, what has been said is true—but that [objection] is not a valid challenge, namely: "How can there be conformity with the presence and absence of the sense-faculties elsewhere as well? For this [conformity] remains the same even when [the object] is conceptually differentiated from them.

And yet, that [object] is not non-existent therein, because worldly convention functions in exactly that way; as it has been said: "Sense-perception is non-exclusive (anekānta), because [its object] is unestablished and not refuted" (*Pramāṇasaṃgraha* 1.4).

If it is argued that the conformity [of the cognition] to the presence and absence of the sense organs is merely an error regarding them, because it occurs immediately after a perception produced by the senses; and as it has been said:
"Because it functions in close proximity to direct perception, it is sometimes a cause of error"—that too is exactly like that.

As for that which was stated—“In other cases, it would depend upon the recollection of what was previously seen” (Pramāṇavārttika 2.298)—that too is refuted by this very [argument]; for that conceptual construction does not depend upon such [recollection], since we do not admit the perception of that [external object] anywhere.

If it is argued that “the conceptual construction arises from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that [object],” [we reply: no, because that [conceptual construction] would exist for everyone at all times.
If it is argued that [the object] is obstructed, and that even in the conceptualization of those two [aspects],

there would be an absence of external objects— just as in the case of the affliction by desire and so forth— it is for this very reason that, although the form of a double moon is within the scope of conceptualization, just like the coarse single form of cognition itself, it cannot be communicated to another mental continuum by means of words.
Furthermore, a person with cataracts does not perceive the specific form of the moon and such, nor does one standing at a distance perceive that [specific form] of mother-of-pearl and the like.
Nevertheless, demonstrating that this very [term] "having an object which is a real entity" applies here as well, he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.
Indeed, a universal (*sāmānya*) appears in verbal cognition within another continuum.

If it is argued that this form [of difference] does not exist as something distinct from the object because of contradiction, and therefore that [conceptual cognition] is without an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*), to this he replies: "The word," and so forth.

There would be a distinction of the external object through a single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that manifests as something else capable of being associated with words; therefore, reality (*tattva*) consists of both natures.
For indeed, if [the object] were ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), it would appear in verbal cognition (*śabdabuddhi*).

However, if this stable and gross form is non-existent, how could it be perceptible, or how could it perform its own causal function (*svārthakriyākārin*)—from which worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) proceeds? Likewise, the fact that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses both that nature and a non-that nature would be established, even though it is undesirable.

And thus, why is the status of some external object as the domain of sensory perception, words, and cognition not accepted, such that the absolute falsity of words and conceptual constructions is determined?

And this is not tenable, because for someone who lacks rightness (*samyaktva*), it is impossible to apprehend that [object] as exclusively false; for if there is the possibility of conceptualizing its true nature, how can all conceptualization be false? Likewise, because non-conceptual cognition contradicts determination (*nirṇaya*), there is either a connection (*saṃsarga*) or a relation (*sambandha*) of the word with that [object]; one [form] is suitable for that, while the other is unsuitable. These two forms appear [in cognition], and one among them is the common conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
If it is argued that even that [cognition] is indeed non-conceptual because it is submerged in the unique particular (asādhāraṇarūpa), let this be for now.

Just as that [particular] is so, there would likewise be a distinction of the external object from that [cognition]; therefore, reality consists of a dual nature, namely, the nature of both the universal and the particular.
In order to explain the *kārikā*, he says: "Just as indeed," and so forth.
He states the conclusion with: "Therefore," and so forth;
since this is so, therefore that which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*)—and not that which exists conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*)—would appear in word and cognition.

If it is argued: "But surely the form intended as being capable of association with verbal expression—which belongs to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conceptual construction—is not distinct from that [particular characteristic], and thus it is the particular characteristic itself; therefore, the example is not established," to this he says: "If, however," and so forth.

If this currently perceived, stable, and gross form denoted by words were indeed non-existent—that is, entirely absent—then how could it be perceptible, grasped by the direct evidence of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), such that this statement of Prajñākaragupta would be tenable: "The twofold nature of the objects of cognition is established through the twofold nature of the means of cognition, as is known from direct perception"?

The object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is within the range of immediate experience; and thus, the particular characteristic alone is the object of cognition (*prameya*), and in that regard, direct perception alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), leaving no room for a second means of valid cognition—this is the intended meaning.
The twofold nature of objects is established by direct perception itself—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* 3.2.

It might be thought that [the term] "like a cognition" (prameva) would be redundant—[the opponent arguing] that "that very form, when superimposed upon particulars, is the universal; therefore, this fault does not arise. To this, he replies with the words beginning "And how," etc.:
