How can this form of conceptual cognition—which is the operation of words, the operation of inference, and the performance of causal efficacy—be non-existent? The word "or" (*vā*) is used as a conjunction of refutations, since from it arises the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consisting of activity and so forth.

Because it performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), this is the intended meaning here: Is this form superimposed upon the particulars by that very same conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or by another conceptual construction? Regarding what Prajñākaragupta says—"That very form, though indistinct, whose body is not separate from that [particular], even when being superimposed upon a distinct fragment or the like, is a universal (*sāmānya*)"—in the first case, the capacity of the conceptual construction for association with verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃsarga-yogyatā*) is established; in the other case, because one must accept the nature of the superimposed object, even if it is erroneous.
Nor is this the view of the opponent;

by this, the second alternative is also considered. To explain: even in the second alternative, if one were to superimpose the form of the first alternative elsewhere and say "it is not its own," then that too would not abandon its nature as either erroneous or otherwise.

Or, if one were to superimpose that [first alternative] upon it (the second) because it is its own form, then it would be a *svalakṣaṇa* (particular); here too, the same fault applies, beginning with the question: "How can that which is non-existent be its own... and so forth.

Furthermore, if one were to superimpose that [universal] upon it through another conceptualization, there would be an infinite regress because yet another conceptualization would have to be postulated.

Since form and so forth are themselves without distinction the universal that is the object of inference, for if individual instances are not excluded, the individuals themselves are called the "universal."
—the meaning is that there would be the occurrence of a dual nature; this refers to another conceptual construction (*vikalpāntara*). (Pra.vārtikālaṃkāra, p. 192)

Furthermore, let the first [cognition] alone project its own form elsewhere; what is the need for a second? Even if that were so, since the distinction between error and non-error would not cease in one case, let the first cognition itself be such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Nevertheless, your desired conclusion is not established, because the projected form is non-existent. If you argue that even in the case of manifoldness (*anekānta*), it would be so because you accept manifoldness in terms of the ultimate form (*paramārthākāra*); to this he replies: "Of the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇasya*), etc.

That is to say, the state of being both that and not-that—consisting of the projected and the other (non-projected) forms—of the particular characteristic of the conceptual construction would be established in that manner, by the method just described.
What kind of thing? He says: even that which is undesirable—that is, not intended—by the Sugata;
for even if one who maintains the doctrine of absolute partlessness were deluded, there would be no second part [of reality] that could lead to happiness.
The word "api" (even/also) is to be understood as following immediately after the word "tathā" (so).

And likewise, why is it not accepted that for some external object such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) admitted by the Jains—and not for another—there is the status of being an object of sensory perception and verbal cognition? The point is that if, in one case, there is no contradiction between two forms—one erroneous and the other non-erroneous—then the absence of contradiction between two forms, one common and the other otherwise, is also difficult to avoid. For, by accepting this, the absolute falsity of words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is established;
this was stated having assumed the existence of the form of a conceptual construction and its connection with verbal expression.
Now, demonstrating that [the object] exists therein, he says: "And this is not tenable," and so forth.

Nor is it tenable—that is, logically consistent—that this [object], namely the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conceptual construction, has the nature of that [superimposed form], i.e., the nature of a superimposed aspect.
Why? He says: "Of anything," and so forth.

If it is argued that because it is impossible to realize the absolute falsity of those conceptual constructions (vikalpas) without some conceptual construction being correct—that is, possessing correspondence with reality—there must indeed exist such a correct conceptual construction, since there is a cognition of that absolute [falsity]; to this he replies: "In that case, its reality," and so forth. If that conceptual construction, for which that absolute falsity is the reality (tattva)—meaning the ultimate truth (paramārtha)—is possible, how can there be the falsity of all conceptual constructions? [The opponent might argue: "Conceptual constructions under dispute are false because they possess [conceptual] reality, like the conceptual construction of God (Īśvara) and so forth"; thus, the cognition of that [absolute falsity] arises from inference.

And that [cognition], although having a non-real object, is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory; for even that arises from the real entity through a succession of causes.
Thus it has been said: "Because it is conceptual."
Inference,
although having a universal as its object,
is also non-contradictory.

"For two people who run toward a jewel and the light of a jewel-lamp respectively, both perceiving them with the cognition of a 'jewel,' although there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a difference regarding causal efficacy. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.57)

How then can it be said that [the object] arises from that? That too is untrue; because if inference has for its object what is not the reality (*atattva*), then reality cannot be established through it. Otherwise, it would follow that reality could also be established from conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as *pradhāna* and so forth, since this [inference] is no more restricted to the real entity than they are. If you say "no" [to the latter case] because there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*) with the thing, then the cognition of water in a mirage would also establish reality, and thus that too would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since it too is indirectly connected to that [reality].

For instance: "The perception of that [water] arises from mirages; therefore, there is the conceptual construction (vikalpa) of water"—if you argue that this should be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) based on such statements as *Pravāha* 3.43 and so forth, then it would be a distinct means of knowledge.
It is not perception, because it is conceptual;

nor is it inference, because it is not produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*); otherwise, there would be an infinite regress of inference and that which is inferred (*anumānānumānika*). (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1)
8. By this [it is shown that] "it is sufficient"—this is the designation for the conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) of delusion;
thus [the claim] is meaningless.
For the apprehension of non-existent water is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely inference (*anumāna*); therefore, there is the apprehension of the self (*ātman*).

The world does not think in this way; for if that which [the world] considers authoritative were indeed authoritative, what could possibly be non-authoritative? Otherwise, the cognition of yellow and so forth regarding a white conch-shell would be authoritative with respect to a contradictory cognition. If you argue that, therefore, the production of an inference in that case is improper, it is said in reply: commentators indeed analyze it in this manner, according to the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* (1.72); thus, for them, that [cognition] would not be authoritative, as is the position of the Sāṅkhyas.
Because it would follow that the conceptualization of [causes] such as *pradhāna* would result in the establishment of reality (*tattva*) regarding the entity.
If another quality were not joined [to the object] by means of a cause of error—
as the form of silver is [joined] to mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance— [as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*].

Cognition of error, cognition of conventional reality, inference, that which is derived from inference, recollection, and verbal expression— these, along with that accompanied by visual impairment, are pseudo-perceptions. — *Pramāṇasamuccaya* 7.3ab.

The teacher Dignāga has stated the divisions of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as follows: erroneous cognition, such as perceiving water in a mirage; cognition of a substance and so forth that exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*); inference, which is the cognition of a mark (*liṅga*); that which is derived from inference, which is the cognition of the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*); recollection, which is memory; and that which is associated with verbal expression (*ābhilāpika*). — *Pramāṇavārttikamanorathanandinī* 2.288.

It is the commentators alone who analyze in this manner, not those engaged in practical activity; the latter, however, regarding their own objective support as indeed capable of causal efficiency, proceed by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.72.

Now, if it is argued that even though they [the senses] do discern, they nevertheless proceed because there is no other alternative and because of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized; then, since one who is far away—even if their intellect is capable of discernment—proceeds [to act] due to an indistinct appearance, the situation remains the same: the production of inference would be useless.

If you ask, "Let it proceed; what contradiction is there? or "Let it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) like inference," we reply: What indeed? If you say "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), then inference too would be perception.
If it is argued that [mental perception] is not [a distinct means of knowledge] because of its lack of clarity (*avaishadya*), then the same applies here [to inference]:

it is not [distinct] because it is born from a mark (*lingaja*). If that is so, then the difference between means of knowledge (*māna*) arises from a difference in their causes (*kāraṇabheda*), not from a difference in the objects of knowledge (*prameyabheda*);

for if that were the case, mental perception and the like would be distinct means of knowledge from that which is born of the senses, and thus there would be no fixed rule regarding the number of means of knowledge.

It may be argued that there is a distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): since it has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, non-conceptual [perception] is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, let inference and distant cognition be considered a single means of valid cognition, because they share the common feature of having an indistinct object.

Now, if inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for commentators, how do they themselves realize reality or awaken others to it, such that Dharmakīrti, Prajñākaragupta, and others could be considered commentators?
If you think that their activity proceeds by means of an inference established only for others (*paraprasiddhānumāna*), then they are no different from the Cārvākas;
therefore, that is not tenable, because [the distinction between] what is a means of knowledge and what is otherwise depends upon the establishment of a commonality [of the reason], and so forth.

Furthermore, not desiring inference for themselves, what would they mean by saying "all cognitions are without an objective basis" (*nirālambana*)? How could they say, "they have their own form as their basis" (*svarūpālambana*), given that perception does not function there [in that case]? Moreover, non-duality has already been refuted. Now, if they claim that inference has an object as its domain, then even for them, the cognition of water in a mirage is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, they too have come onto my path; therefore, it was well said: "the falsity of all conceptual constructions."
The linguistic convention of "awakening" [from sleep] exists because one's cognition is understood to have reached another state;
furthermore, there is the existence of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) due to the negation of something.

Thus, another [author], Śeṣa, says: "Inference is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by way of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), because of the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.5): 'Validity is established by way of worldly convention.'"

"If conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is abandoned, that [conceptualization] is abandoned, just as when a vessel is discarded, its whiteness is also discarded; yet reality (*tattva*) is established through non-conceptual direct perception (*avikalpādhyakṣa*). To this he says: "From non-conceptual consciousness" (*avikalpasaṃvṛtteḥ*), and so forth.
Why? To this he says: because it contradicts the determination that "in that way, all conceptualizations are false. That is to say: "from non-conceptual consciousness" (*avikalpasaṃvitteḥ*).
For instance:
Since it imitates conceptual constructions, how can it be non-conceptual?

For those who desire the cessation of that [conceptual] nature through such [non-conceptuality], there is no determination of those [objects]. Otherwise, if there were cognition of similarity [to the object], [that similarity] would fall away without a basis.
Therefore, when there is cognition of something other than its own nature, there can be no non-conceptuality;

for how could that [cognition] possess non-conceptuality once the falsity of that [nature] has been determined by inference, since [the doctrine of] momentary destruction is established by means of it?

Some maintain that determinate cognition (*niścaya-jñāna*) is not perception; this has been refuted by us in the text because it is subject to the same defects. Alternatively, [it is refuted] because, according to the principle that "all conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna*) is false," there is a contradiction with determination (*nirṇaya*) arising from non-conceptual awareness (*avikalpa-saṃvitti*).
This has already been examined in the *Siddhiviniścaya* (1.6) and elsewhere with the words, "Because of non-difference, [it is established] through a similar recollection," and so forth.

If it is objected: "In the perception of that [object], there is no such thing as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because such a construction is impossible when there is only the cognition of its own nature (*svarūpa*)," we reply: It has been stated in this regard that [conceptualization occurs] "due to the appearance of a single gross form."
Even so, if it is non-conceptual, then "conceptual" would merely be another name for it.

Alternatively, if this form belongs neither to cognition nor to the object—since, like a forest and so forth, it is untenable when analyzed—it appears solely through the power of ignorance. To this, he says: "The conceptual [cognition] having its own apprehended form," and so forth, [would have been] established.

Consciousness, by concealing its own deficiency in the form of the apprehended object, conceals [the distinction] from itself; for even when there is difference, it grasps them as non-different. Therefore, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the mind appears in some way as the appearance of both the object and the self, because it possesses the forms of the apprehended and so forth. Consequently, it is not tenable that perception and the like have partless objects, nor that conceptual cognition is without an object.

The deficiency or absence of the aspect of the apprehended object—that is, the gross aspect—is itself the very nature of cognition. This [cognition] is "concealing" (saṃvṛti) because it conceals [the true nature], not bringing the [gross aspect] itself into the state of being an object by its own power, even though it exists. Otherwise, there would be no appearance of the gross aspect.
For when blue is being experienced as distinct from [the cognition], there is no appearance of blue even through delusion; furthermore,
it is contradictory to claim that "it knows itself as distinct from that form," because no experience other than the body of blue and so forth appears,
since no other form of cognition is perceived apart from blue, pleasure, and the like.

pṛ. 345: Since there is no other cognition in this world apart from pleasure, blue, and so forth, it is logically certain that blue and the like are self-cognizing, just as pleasure and the like are—*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 454. Furthermore, if this form (*ākāra*) were distinct from cognition, how could it appear? If [it appears] by itself, then it would be another cognition, and the same fault already mentioned applies: namely, the establishment of a single entity characterized by the superimposition of contradictory properties. There is no fault even if [the form] is non-existent, like the appearances in a magical illusion, a mirage, and so forth—*Pravārtikālaṅkāra*, 3.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with this [statement], namely that even if it is a cognition, it is non-existent; we say no, because it would contradict the definition of ultimate reality [given] in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra* (1.5): "The illumination of an object not previously known."

If it is argued that this is due to error (*vibhrama*), then the establishment of error itself is not possible, because if there is again a distinction from cognition (*saṃvedana*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, in the appearance of ignorance (*avidyāvabhāsa*), a single entity would possess both the nature of error and its opposite.
Now, if it is argued that this form is superimposed there by conceptual construction (vikalpa), we say no; for that would entail the consequence of its appearing with clarity.
Furthermore, if it were to appear as distinct from the cognition itself, there could be no illusion of "having a form" (sākārabhrānti);
for when yellow appears as distinct from blue, no one experiences the delusion of having the form of blue therein.

Now, [it may be argued that] the delusion of non-difference arises from the superimposition of non-difference; from what, then, is this held to come? From the subsequent conceptualization. [But] it would not exist in the state where all fruitless conditions have been withdrawn, nor [could it arise] from that very cognition for one who proceeds through practice. If it is argued: "Indeed, in that case, there is no other operation of that [cognition] toward that [object] than the grasping of non-difference, and it is thus"; then, since non-difference is also grasped even when there is difference, it is well said that [the cognition] conceals that [difference]. If it is argued: "Let it be so"; to this he says: "The nature," and so forth.
To the question, "Of which two does it conceal even its own natures, such as momentariness? he says: "Of its own [nature] and its object," referring to the state of non-conceptualization.
The connection is "it would not exist.
Commenting on the verse, he says: "the specific characteristic of the mind," and so forth.

The term "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) is employed for the purpose of demonstrating that the mind is partless (*niraṃśatva*), because the opponent accepts that very [mind] as the specific characteristic; [otherwise], it might appear in some way, but not in every respect.
What is the reason? He says: "of its own [nature] and its object," and so forth.

What is it doing? He says: "in some way," that is, in the manner of being existent, conscious, and so on, and not appearing through any other property. Why is this so? He says: "the apprehended," and so forth.
"Since [it is so]," what is it that is therefore not tenable? He says: "Whence [can there be] perception and so forth? He says: "[Because it is] partless," and so on.
Thinking that "conceptual [cognition] is without an object" is like non-conceptual [perception] because it too has a unique (asādhāraṇa) domain, [the author],
refuting the opponent's argument which seeks to establish that perception has a unique object, says: "Perception," and so forth.
If perception were to conform to the form of its own object due to its own objective capacity,
it would become conceptual due to the capacity of conceptual mental activity.

Consequently, because of the resulting predicament of [all things] being one, there would be no established distinction between anything whatsoever regarding sequence, simultaneity, continuity, distance, and so forth.
Perception is cognition that is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).

Of what nature is it? To this he says: its own object consists of atoms of form and so forth; and if it were to conform to that, why would it be so? To this he replies: by virtue of the power (*sāmarthya*) of the capacity of its own object.

Regarding this, he states the refutation: "By the power of the capacity for conceptual mental attention (*savikalpamanaskāra*), there would be conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*)," which follows from the context. To explain: Buddhist perception arises by taking as its material cause (*upādāna*) conceptual inference (*anumāna-savikalpaka*); likewise, there is the affliction (*upaplava*) of desire, grief, and so forth. Since both of these lack a basis (*nālatvāt*), how could there be a mutual exclusion between them by virtue of which a distinction in designation (*vyapadeśabheda*) might occur?

Now, [it might be argued that] cognition exists by virtue of the object being unknown, and the object exists by virtue of its insentience (*jaḍatva*) relative to that [cognition]. Why is this so? It is said because even though each has a nature dissimilar to the other, one is absent in the other; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of them being either identical or different.
Furthermore, if the nature by which they are distinguished from non-causes and non-effects were the same as that by which they are mutually non-causal, then those two would be one.
Moreover, when the two forms of cultivation—consisting of hearing and reflection—are in the form of inference, upon reaching the culmination of their excellence, the knowledge of the Sugata arises.
The wisdom of the Sugata is the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the affliction by desire and so forth is its semblance (*tadābhāsa*);
thus, there is a distinction in appearance.
By this, the exclusion of that which is not the material cause and that which is not the effect is also considered.

If the atoms that receive the designation "pot" are distinct from the atoms of Mount Meru by that very nature [of being a pot], then there is no collection [of them]. If the Sugata’s cognition—by the form in which it is distinguished from its own causal moment—is [distinct] from its own subsequent effect-moment, then it possesses only the status of being an effect (*upādeya*), not the status of being a cause (*upādāna*).

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "And therefore," that is, because of the consequence of [all things] being one, there would be no sequence between any causal moment and any effect-moment, nor any non-sequence between any [quality] such as taste and any [quality] such as form; furthermore, there would be no immediate proximity (*nairantarya-pratyāsatti*) between any waking consciousness and any preceding cognition, nor any remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) caused by the intervention of sleep; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), qualities such as insentience and its opposite are included.

Alternatively, if there were no fixed arrangement of atoms in a jar—such as the immediate proximity (*nairantarya*) of one atom with another, or the distance (*viprakarṣa*) from other constituent atoms—then that very order would not exist.
By this, the second position is also considered;

for instance: if a variegated cognition (*citra-jñāna*), by whatever nature it is excluded from a cognition of pure blue, were to be [distinguished] from other cognitions by that same nature [as yellow], then it would be yellow alone. How, then, could it be called "variegated"? This should be applied here previously as far as possible.
In the view that consciousness is a collection of atoms, it should be stated as being like a collection of atoms of an object; however, there would be a distinction in meaning. But...
Now, as for what was stated—"In that case, every quality of an object perceived is indeed perceived" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.44)—that is insubstantial.

For it is impossible for a perceived [object] to possess an unperceived nature, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, there is no relationship expressed by "its" (*tasya*), just like the horn of a hare;
for one does not employ the designation that "the unperceived horn of a hare belongs to the perceived jar."

If it is argued that [the identity] is subsequently perceived right there [in the object], we say no; because there is a lack of evidence for this. To this, he replies: "Even though there is a distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible natures," and so forth.

Even though there is a distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible natures, the identity in tastes and other such qualities is directly [perceived], just as in the case of the distinct manifestations grasped by one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). 7.

Even though there is a difference in nature between that which is perceived and that which is not perceived, there would be identity—that is, oneness—in a single substance, as in the case of self-awareness;
where [would this be]? He says: "In taste and so forth."
He provides an illustration here with the words "his own" (*sva*) and so forth:

"his own" refers to that which is the consciousness itself, as well as the distinction from the appearance of the object to be grasped; this is the beginning of those [factors], namely the forms of variegated cognition such as blue and so on—those are what have been described thus. "In them, as it were" (*tadvat*) means just like those, "directly" (*añjasā*), that is, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthena*).
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "in a single substance" and so forth.
Here, the illustration is given with the words "self-awareness" and so forth.
Showing the fruit that has been obtained, he says "from that very [source]" and so forth.

Therefore, the faults such as infinite regress, which follow from the distinction or non-distinction between the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*), serve as reasons for its non-absolute nature.
Furthermore, regarding this point: if there were an absolute distinction between the limiting adjunct and that which possesses it, their relationship would not be established.

Even when there is assistance [to one attribute] by means of that single attribute, since the substratum (*dharmin*)—which is a single essence that is the constituent part of the assistance of all attributes—is apprehended, there is no recurrence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If one were to postulate a mutual difference among the capacities that assist those [attributes], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*);

lest there be such an infinite regress, one must postulate their non-difference. From where, then, does this entire proof of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) arise? [The answer is: regarding the substratum qualified by a single attribute, even when it is cognized, there is still another means of valid cognition, because that same substratum as qualified by other [attributes] has not yet been cognized.

Because that which consists of resolute determination is an initiator, perception—which arises through the efficacy of an object—replicates only the form of that object, as in the case of what follows immediately after it. This is not an absolute rule, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the nature of consciousness;
rather, within this non-absolutism, due to the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), it assumes forms such as conceptualization (*savikalpa*) and so forth.
For what reason? Precisely because of their identity (*tādātmya*). To this he says: "limiting adjuncts" (*upādhi*) and so forth.

Limiting adjuncts are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), and those possessing them are the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Regarding these, there would arise—due to their absolute mutual difference and non-difference—the defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), by which the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes contradiction (*virodha*) and the rest. These [defects] would occur; they would come to be.
Of what nature are they? To this he says: "They have that as their non-exclusive reason" (*tadanekāntahetavaḥ*).
Expounding upon the verse, he says: "And this which... and so forth; the word *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Furthermore, as stated by the opponent: if an absolute difference between the attribute and the possessor of the attribute is accepted, a relationship cannot be established,
because any other relationship— such as inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth— is denied.

Comparison: Even for one who thinks that the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are indeed distinct from one another and from their substratum, and that the scriptural statements based upon them also apply only to that very substratum—thus making this [objection] irrelevant—for him too, when the self is grasped in its entirety as non-different from the powers that constitute the factors of assistance for the various adjuncts, what difference could remain undetermined for the object of assistance? Since there is a relation between those two within the self, both are grasped in a single cognition.
If there were a difference in the powers of assistance to the attributes (*dharma*), what would happen to that [self]?
Consequently, there would be no benefit for those [other aspects], and likewise, there would be an infinite regress;
for if only one benefactor were to be apprehended, there would be no other benefits [to be apprehended].
When that which is seen is apprehended, those [benefits] which are unseen are also apprehended; thus, upon the apprehension of that, there is the apprehension of everything.
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti*, p. 132–38:
"But in that case, would that [relation] not also fail to be established between fire and smoke? To this he says:
"If there were no assistance"—if there were an absence of assistance between those two, then it would not be established; but if there is assistance, it is certainly established.
If there is assistance [rendered]; regarding this, he says: "Even in that assistance," and so forth.

Even when there is mutual assistance of one by the other, under what condition is there the non-operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? He says: "When there is the apprehension of the substratum (*dharmin*)."
By what means? He says: "by way of its single limiting adjunct" (*tadekopādhidvāreṇa*). Of that subject (*dharmin*), there is one limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) or qualification; by way of that.
Of what kind is that subject? He says: "of that whose singular, undivided self-nature (*ātman*) is the cause (*aṅga*) for the assistance provided by every limiting adjunct.
That is to say, of that whose nature is one and non-different, serving as the instrumental cause for the assistance rendered by every single adjunct.

The opponent thinks as follows: "The possessor [of attributes], being perceived through the medium of a single attribute as having the nature of the power to assist all attributes, causes all attributes to be manifested; for when that [single attribute] is not grasped, they are not grasped. Thus, how could there be the operation of another means of knowledge?

Now, if it is argued that the powers of assistance are distinct, and therefore this fault does not arise, to that he replies with the words "tadupakāra" and so forth: regarding the conceptualization of the difference among those powers which assist those attributes.
Why? He says: "From each other," and so forth.
For instance: if there were an absolute difference between power and the possessor of power, a relationship would not be established if there were no mutual benefit;
even if there were such benefit, the same [objection] as before must be stated.
Furthermore, if one were to conceive of a distinction between those two, that same fault would apply, resulting in an infinite regress.
To refute the Sāṃkhya position, the opponent raises the objection beginning with "mā bhūt" (let it not be so).

For the sake of avoiding this infinite regress, when the Sāṃkhya proceeds to conceive of non-difference between the attribute (*upādhi*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), what follows? He says: "kutaḥ" (from where?), and so forth.

Refuting this himself, he says: "Why is all this, which is being asserted by the opponent, a proof for non-absolutism (anekānta) without exception? He replies: "Because of the limiting adjunct" (upādhi), and so forth.
Then, what follows from that? He replies: "That very same limiting adjunct," and so forth.

Therefore, because those two are in some way identical (*tādātmya*), even when there is the cognition of a subject (*dharmin*) qualified by one limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) still operates—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Why? He says: "Because of that," and so forth;
that is, because that [subject] qualified by another stated limiting adjunct is not yet cognized.

The Buddhist might think: "How is it known that the form [of the object] is not apprehended by that which has already been apprehended? To this he says: "Because it consists of determinate cognition," and so forth.

Because [perception] consists of determinate cognition and has as its object a thing characterized by both the universal and the particular, it is an instigator [to action]. Therefore, sense-cognition—which rests upon each individual atom, is non-erroneous, and is non-conceptual—is not an instigator to action for anyone, even in cases of repeated practice.
By this, the experience of pleasure and so forth by Prajñākaragupta and others has been explained;
that too is produced by habituation for another.
Furthermore, there is no habituation for that which is non-conceptual; and visual and other sensory cognitions arise from within a long-continuing stream of purely conceptual cognitions,
so that their non-conceptual cause does not exist as something previously present nearby, having long since perished, and the [simultaneous] material cause (*upādāna*) has already been refuted.
And since those [cognitions] are conceptual, those belonging to their continuum are likewise; by this, mental perception is also considered,
which is also of that same nature as conceptual direct perception.

If, however, that mental attention (manaskāra) is merely an imitation of the form of the [external] object and not an imitation of something capable of being associated with verbal expression—since such is observed [in the case of perception] due to the inconceivability of the power of entities (*bhāva-śakti*)—then it follows for that very reason that from atoms there arises only an imitation of the form of blue and so forth, and not an imitation of their mutual distinction. And in that case, atoms would possess parts (*sāvayavatva*). Furthermore, perception would have a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, because it imitates a form common to many. If you say that this form does not exist there, how then does it appear? If you say it appears even though it is non-existent, then perception is an error (*bhrānta*).
If you say, "It is so"; then the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in the definition [of perception] is useless, because of the absence of such an object.

If you say, "That [term] is for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*"); no, for then even that which is the domain of inferential cognition and verbal cognition would possess the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, the claim that "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are twofold because the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are twofold" is hollow, as it cannot withstand scrutiny.
If you say, "It is not so [for inference and words]"; for that very reason, it would also not apply to that which is the domain of the eye and other senses.
If it is argued that [the existence of atoms] is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); [we reply: the original point has not been answered.

Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of inference and the like, because it appears otherwise to the sense faculties. Nor is the gross form (*sthūlākāra*) the particular characteristic, because it appears otherwise to the cognition of a yogin.

Otherwise, how could atoms be established, such that it is said: "Atoms are the cause of the appearance of grossness, like hairs that are distant and sparse"? If it is argued that their establishment comes from inference; [we reply: this is the sharpness of a sword's scabbard—that which is not perceived by the yogin, yet is understood through inference.
Thus,
it is precisely conceptualization that arises.
In the definition of perception, it is precisely conceptual [cognition] that is of the nature of conceptualization.
Cognition is twofold because the objects of cognition are twofold—*Pramāṇavārttika* 2.1.
Just as hairs, even when not actually joined together, appear to be densely clustered when at a great distance, so too it is with atoms; thus, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, like others, the yogin would be subject to error and conceptualization (*savikalpaka*). If you argue that while this form may not be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) for the yogin, it will be so for someone else; then we reply: let it not be the form capable of association with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsarga-yogya*) for the commentators, yet it will be so for those engaged in worldly discourse (*vyavahārin*).

If you say "no," because it does not perform a causal function (*anarthakriyākāritva*); then we ask: does that form perform a causal function? If it does, then the postulation of atoms (*paramāṇu-kalpanā*) is rendered useless.

If it is argued that for those engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*), he (the object) is indeed the producer of that [cognition]; and if it is further argued that the commentators do not consider there to be a difference between the expressible form and the objects of verbal and sensory cognitions— then, in following that [position], emptiness (*śūnyatā*) alone is the refuge.
In this regard—the learned declare that there is neither conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) nor non-conceptual construction (*avikalpa*).
By whom has such a learned person been taught who would possess conceptual constructions regarding non-duality and so forth?
Upon the cessation of that [duality], the wise one becomes free from doubt through its negation.

Therefore, it is established from the perspective of conventional practice that both verbal cognition and sensory perception have universals as their objects, for those engaged in practical activity [seek] that which performs a causal function.
The wise declare that in emptiness there is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization;
by whomsoever the conceptualizations of non-duality and so forth have been studied, he is truly wise.

The learned one, being free from doubt regarding that [negation], speaks—showing the reasoning of another—to establish the non-conceptual nature of the knower when [the object] has passed away: "For the sake of which," and so forth.
Perception, having arisen through the power of a particular object, assumes only the form of that object and does not imitate [the universal of] genus and the like.

This is merely an illustration. The objection here is that [the object] immediately following that object which produces the perception would be like the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object to be apprehended; [to this we reply: "This is not an absolute rule.
Why? He says: because it would follow that perception would lack the nature of consciousness (*cit*).

For instance: just as that [reflection] imitates the blueness of the object, so too does it imitate its insentience (*jaḍatā*), like a second moment of the object; otherwise, the consequence of insentience would result.
Furthermore, this [theory] would refute the fact that objects possess parts, for if the cognition of an object arises from a word, the coordination of the sense organs would be rendered useless.

If it is argued: "Just as a child, though imitating the features of its parents, does not imitate them in every respect, so it is with this [cognition] regarding the object," to this he says: "In its absolute [identity]," and so forth.
If that object is admitted to be manifold (anekānta), what follows? He says: "With conceptual construction," and so forth.

This is the intended meaning: even if [the object] is manifold, this fault occurs because [the cognition] arises from it and imitates its form; it would not occur otherwise. This is explained by the passage beginning with "with conceptual construction."
In this regard, the statement "it is so" is meaningless,
for direct perception here concerns the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the object.
If that which is being predicated as the agent were to be insentient, it would be so.
Regarding what is being stated,

[the opponent's] comparison is as follows: "That is not a real entity because it is expressible, and because it results in the fruitfulness of the collection of sense-faculties" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.1).

If all [particulars] were perceived through a cognition of the universal, then, because the entire nature of every individual would be understood by that cognition of the universal which arises from the word, it would follow as a consequence that the coordination of the sense organs is rendered useless—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 192.

It might be thought: "Just as perception imitates the blueness of an object but not its insentience, so too, due to that mental attention (*tanmanaskāra*), verbal cognition grasps only the aspect of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*) and not the ineffable form. To this, he says: "Because of the difference in causal complexes" (*sāmagrībhedāt*), etc. The intended meaning here is this: just as, due to a certain proximity, perception imitates only the blueness of an object and not its unconsciousness, so too verbal cognition grasps only that [aspect] of it and not its clarity (*vaiśadya*).
Therefore, what was stated— that whether an object is clear or otherwise, it should appear in exactly that same way in both cases— is refuted; for, except in the case of a defect,
perception would conform to the conceptualizing mind.

Just as the exclusion of an object from being non-conscious is either different or not different from the exclusion of non-blue from blue—otherwise, in the imitation of blue, the imitation of insentience would necessarily follow—so too, since an entity is excluded from everything else, there would result as many exclusions as there are forms in relation to those [other] entities. Demonstrating this, he says: "Of one," and so forth:
"By virtue of one thing's exclusion from all others, it possesses infinite forms; therefore, every quality of a perceived entity is indeed perceived. (9)
For nothing is excluded from anything else, as that would entail the consequence of their being one and the same.

Furthermore, when non-conceptual perception and another [type of cognition] arise simultaneously, how could there be a subsequent arising [of the latter], given that the determination (*vyavasāya*) of that object to be grasped by it is already established?
For this very reason, sense-perception, verbal knowledge, and [other forms of] cognition have, in some sense, a single ultimate reality as their object. This is perception...

By what means does a single entity possess the nature of being "immediate" (anantara)? He says: by exclusion (vyāvṛtti). The singular number is used with reference to the genus (jāti); the meaning is "by exclusions.
Why by that [exclusion]? He says: from everything else—both from the similar (sājātīya) and from the dissimilar (vijātīya), from whatever other than itself.
What then follows? He says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.

Because of that very reason, this is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a perceived entity; it is not [limited] to the perceived alone—this too is an illustration of the inferred and the one expressed by words. Every quality (*guṇa*), such as insentience (*jaḍatā*), belongs to the inferred alone, because there is a contradiction with anything else that is unperceived.
Herein lies the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): therefore, every quality of a perceived entity is indeed perceived.
— In order to explain the verse (kārikā) 3.44, he says: "Of someone," and so forth.
He states the refutation of not accepting that [position]: "For it is not from one," and so forth.

For the Sautrāntika and the Yogācāra, the view is that by whatever intrinsic nature (svabhāva) something is excluded from one thing, by that same nature it is also excluded from another; this is because there is no distinction between these two for them.

In that regard, concerning the first position: for what reason is no entity excluded from a single thing considered to be consciousness? He says: "Because of the consequence of their identity. By the word "that" (tat), those things from which [the entity] is excluded are grasped; because of the consequence of their identity—that is, their state of having an identical form.

For instance: just as [consciousness] is excluded from insentience by taking up sentience within cognition, so too would it be excluded from insentience by other means; consequently, that insentience would not belong to it at all—it would reside in only one place.
Or, if the thought is that just as insentience exists in one place, so it must exist elsewhere; then, just as it is excluded from one thing, it must likewise be excluded from another.

Furthermore, if the very exclusion from non-blue that constitutes the intrinsic nature of both the cognition of blue and its object were identical for both, then just as the cognition—which is excluded from non-blue—is designated as "blue," so too would it be designated by that same term when it is excluded from the external object, and not by any other designation, because the cause for such a designation would be absent.

Now, the exclusion of non-blue from those two [the blue and the cognition] occurs by way of its being blue; it does not [occur] for the cognition [itself] by way of its being the object blue. Why? Because when conceptual perception and other means such as inference have already functioned, there is subsequently at some point a further functioning of that which is of the nature of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*) toward that very same [object].

How is this possible? He says: "Of that," and so forth—that is, because a determinate judgment is established regarding that perception or the other [means], and regarding the object to be grasped by them.

Furthermore, this same point should be understood here as well; by the phrase "because of logical consistency" (*upapatteḥ*), he shows this: just as a single variegated cognition occurs simultaneously with respect to its own manifestations, so too does it occur sequentially. Therefore, by the immediately preceding reasoning, it is established that the cognitions of the sense organs, words, and [mental] cognitions have, in some sense, a single ultimate object (*paramārtha-ekaviṣayatva*); this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Why? He says: "In perception," and so forth.
The designation "cognition of blue" would apply to the cognition of blue solely by virtue of its exclusion of what is non-blue.
Then, demonstrating that very point, he says: "of perception," and so forth;
likewise, [the same applies] to the prior and posterior limits of sound and the rest.
The continuum of its own causes and effects is like that between sleep and waking.
(10) A middle form is also somehow perceivable at the two extremes of the prior and posterior [moments], because of the non-perception of what is contradictory to its nature;
for we do not conceive of a single part of a pillar or the like as being of a visible nature alone, since that would entail the non-existence of even mere consciousness.

Since the performance of a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is impossible in that [single] unity, it is precisely through the perception of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*) that this very substance would characterize its own visible and invisible co-existent natures non-confusively by way of its own pervasiveness, based upon its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For, since the establishment of a false continuum (*mithyāsantāna*) is based on such a [single] characteristic,
how could one establish the unity of a continuum when that [notion] is refuted by the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as falling asleep and waking up?

He states that while direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—namely, sense-born cognition—is clear during its middle state, it is likewise indirect (*parokṣatā*) at its prior and posterior limits; he provides an illustration for this: "the continuum of its own cause and effect. Just as the continuum of its own cause and effect—that is, the moments of the material cause (*upādāna*) and the produced effect (*upādeya*)—is direct when perceived through such modes as [immediate] cognition and so forth, yet becomes indirect, so too is the case with the subject under discussion.
"Where is he who has become thus? To this he says: "In sleep and waking.

For in sleep he is indeed imperceptible (*parokṣa*), while in waking he becomes perceptible (*pratyakṣa*); conversely, there [in waking] he is perceptible, while in sleep he is imperceptible. Thus, in waking...
In order to explain the *kārikā*, he says: "That which is perceived," and so forth.

[The objection: Let that which is perceived be of a middle nature, not only in the middle but also at the prior and posterior limits. If it is argued that it must then be either the prior alone or the posterior alone; to this he replies: "in some way" (*kathañcit*).
Why? He says: "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), etc.

By the term "intrinsic nature," the absolutely uniform (*ekānta*) essence is referred to; its opposite is the absolute [nature] such as permanence (*nitya*) and so forth. The non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) of that has been well-demonstrated more than once by the passage beginning with "not indeed" (*na hi*), and he shows this very point here.

For indeed, we conceive of a single entity, such as a pillar or other composite form, which consists of nothing but the visible, established as existing both simultaneously and successively, since there is no contradiction in its being somehow invisible [at other times].
Why is this so? He says: "Because of consciousness," and so forth;
for that too consists of nothing but consciousness, because otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the external object alone.
Why is that so? To this he says: "In the absolute monism of that," and so forth.

In the absolute monism (*ekānta*) of consciousness alone, or of anything else whose nature is exclusively that of the visible (*dṛśya*), the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is untenable; for it has already been examined how the action of an object—that is, the production of a subsequent effect—is impossible [under such conditions].
Now, one might argue that this untenability of action is accepted only in the case of a view consisting of mere consciousness.

If it is argued that "everything is incapable [of action]," according to the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (2.4), and that because this is untenable, there is no absence even of what is perceived as mere consciousness; to this he replies: "Contradictory," and so forth.

Non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is the direct opposite of that absolutism (*ekānta*). Its effect is characterized by the subsequent transformation of the preceding state; the perception of that very effect is indeed not non-perception.
Even by one who accepts mere consciousness, a manifold unity must be admitted; and that [manifoldness] is not contradictory to it, so he thinks.
Because causal efficiency is otherwise untenable, he states the conclusion with the words beginning "That," and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore this perceived substance, such as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, should be characterized—that is, marked—by what? To this he says: "By its own pervasiveness," meaning by that pervasiveness which belongs to its own form, and not by inherence (samavāya).
By what [does it characterize]? To this he says: "Its own natures," and not by another, such as God (Īśvara).
Of what nature are they? He says: "together," and so forth.
Again, of what nature are they? He says: "visible," and so forth.
By what means? He says: "without confusion," and so forth.
Why? He says: because the Buddhist establishes a false continuum by not relying on a substance (*dravya*) as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the fault in not accepting that [substance], he asks "Why? and so forth:
for what reason, or from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), does the Buddhist understand the unity of the continuum? Not from anything at all.

By what? He says: "by the objection of over-extension"—that is, the objection of over-extension regarding that substance [would arise] if everything were of both natures, as stated in *Prakaraṇavārttika* 3.181;
by that [objection], where? He says: "in sleep, awakening, and so forth."
Because its specific distinctions have not been excluded, [the rule] "when told 'eat curd,' why does one not run toward a camel? is the implied conclusion.

If it is argued: "Since consciousness is not perceived at all during sleep, it does not exist; therefore, how can the state of being both visible and invisible be established for a single entity by using that as an illustration? To this, he says: "Invisible," and so forth.
"An object that is invisible, momentary, infinite, atomic, variegated, and spherical would [otherwise] be visible, stable, unitary, and gross, because of its clear perception. (11)
For [the object] is not clearly manifest; because if that [manifestation] were transcended, the distinction between the visible and the invisible would be untenable.

Even going to the furthest extent, since there is no rejection of either the mind—which is of a single nature consisting of both the visible and the invisible—or anything else, by what could an object be cognized? It would simply exist [as such].
Of what nature would it be? To this he says: "That which has as its object the color and circular form of infinite, momentary atoms, perceivable by the senses, is so described.

Again, of what nature is it? To this he says: "Its essence is perceptible... It is both perceptible and stable, persisting through time, singular, common, and its very nature is the Self; and why is it gross? To this he says: "Because of its clear manifestation."

The meaning is that because a gross object, which is stable and unitary, appears clearly in perception, it is not an indistinct conceptual construction (*aviśadakalpa*). Therefore, if there were no perception [of such an object], there would be an absence of consciousness during sleep; for that very reason, there would be an absence of momentary, infinite atoms, colors, and circularity (*parimaṇḍala*) of the object—this is the view of the Sautrāntika. [Otherwise,] one would be perpetually overcome by sleep; otherwise, the reason would suffer from multiple fallacies (*vyabhicāra*). Now, if that very circularity were indeed perceptible, then let there be consciousness even during sleep.

If it is argued that there would be an absence of sleep [in that state], what indeed is this thing called "sleep"? If it is said to be a state of torpor devoid of consciousness (*caitanya*), how can there be an absence of consciousness when it is imperceptible? For the non-perception of the imperceptible cannot be a means of knowledge (*gamaka*) for establishing anything, as it does not produce any practical transaction (*vyavahāra*). If it is argued that he considers that state to be one devoid of the experience of dreaming, then it follows that he likewise considers that entire state—encompassing all its parts and occurring throughout the entire duration of time—to be devoid of the perception of its circularity; thus, the situation is the same.
Otherwise, how could there be a dispute, such that the composition of a treatise (*śāstra*) for that purpose would be necessary?

If that were the case, it might be thought: "Since we do not accept [the existence of] a conventional agent (*vyavahārin*), there is no absence of the perception of atoms; likewise, let there also be no absence of consciousness during sleep. For if no sublation occurs regarding that which possesses the defining characteristics, then those very characteristics must be considered flawed" (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p. 226).
Thus, if you argue that [consciousness] would be refuted by means of the conventional agent, then the same resolution applies to action as well.

And just as for you there is no fault even in that case because the proof of atoms remains unrefuted, so too for me there is the proof of the self because it is not contradicted. Or, if that [proof] is refuted, then it is the same for me as well, since I too am an agent of conventional practice (*vyavahārin*); and "that" belongs to you as well, so it is equal. For you too are an agent of conventional practice regarding external atoms, according to the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "Validity [is established] by means of conventional practice" (PV 1.5).

Now, if it is argued that the conventionalist’s determination of atoms as being stable, unitary, and gross—occurring in a conceptual cognition subsequent to the perception of them—is false; we say no, for the refutation has already been stated here: "because [the perception] is clear.
If it is argued that this is the fault; [we reply: no.

Furthermore, the Buddhist [argues]: even during sleep, one perceives consciousness because of the observation of self-awareness (*svavedana*); however, due to the absence of ascertainment regarding it at that time, the false conceptual cognition (*mithyāvikalpa-buddhi*) arising later determines its non-existence. During the state where conceptualization has been withdrawn, those [objects] are "seen" because they serve as causes for knowledge; the mind in the state of sleep is "seen" because it serves as the cause for awakening.

If it is asked, "How can one thing be the object of perception for another?"—then how is this explained in the case of atoms? Furthermore, you do not accept that [the cognition] takes on the form of those [atoms], since even your opponent admits the appearance of multiple forms.

If it is argued that atoms are inferred because blue-cognition does not occur everywhere despite the presence [of objects], then let consciousness be inferred in deep sleep because awakening is not observed in a dead body despite the presence of the final moment of mind, nor is awakening observed in one who was sleeping.
If it is argued that the awakening of that [consciousness] occurs from the waking mind, [we reply: the appearance arises from the gross [object]; thus, there is no proof of atoms.
If it is argued that they are atoms, let it be so.
The statement "because it is not seen upon waking" is redundant here, as it has already been written.

Furthermore, since that cognition is observed even with respect to hairs that lack that [atomic] form, its establishment is not achieved; for even in the absence of atoms, cognitions such as those of the *kāmalika* (jaundiced) person regarding hair and so forth are observed, so the defect remains as it was.
This is because, just as in the case of cognition, there is no contradiction in the object also possessing a gross form.

Nevertheless, you postulate that atoms alone are the cause of that [perception], while I postulate that it is the mind which is the cause of the awakening of one's own sleeping consciousness. If you say, "But the mind exists," then how is it invisible? If you say, "If it is invisible, how can it be called 'mind'? It is replied: If atoms are the objective support (*ālambana*), how can they be the cause of a cognition that does not possess their form? If they were so, how could they be the cause of the objective support? Otherwise, yellow would be the object of the cognition of blue.

If you say that the atom is not the cause of that objective support, then something else must be stated as such; and if that too has the nature of an atom, something else must be stated again—thus there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because atoms are the causes of a cognition having their own form merely by virtue of being blue, then one must apply the following reasoning: since they are in some sense perceptible, just as the self— though imperceptible during sleep— is perceptible upon waking, everything would be perfectly established and the atoms could serve as the objective support (*ālambana*).
Another says: "If it is argued that the mind is perceived even during sleep, that too is refuted by this [same reasoning], because it would entail the perception of that [mind] as being spherical.

If it is argued that this is not a fault for the Proponent of Cognition (Vijñānavādin); [we reply: no, for when a stable, unitary, and gross cognition is possible, the reality of things is established according to how they appear. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that for a single entity, its being both visible and otherwise is not contradictory."
The impossibility of that [permanent self] would result in no distinction from the Sautrāntika school;
therefore, he provides an explanation of the verse regarding the impossibility of a stable, unitary, and gross cognition, beginning with the words "For not... and so forth.
How, then, does it appear there? He says: "Clearly" and so forth;
this is an adverbial modifier, which connects with the verb "appears" by changing the verbal form [to "appearing clearly"].
"Transgressing that" and so forth...
If there were a transgression of that appearance in the form described above, then the distinction between the visible, such as a jar, and the invisible, such as Īśvara, would be untenable;
it appears that something is missing here.

[Objection: One should rather say that "the establishment of the visible is untenable," because there is nothing else besides that which is invisible, and not that "the establishment of the invisible is untenable," because for everything else besides that, the establishment of the visible is untenable. [If you argue: "If another thing of that same circular shape were admitted to appear, then by the same logic, even things like the sky-lotus would have to be admitted [to appear]; thus, let there be no distinction between the visible and the invisible, since one has admitted the total voidness of everything. To this, he says: "Even very far away," and so forth.

The state of total emptiness (*sakalaśūnyatva*) is extremely remote because it is established only at the furthest limit of the Sugata’s entire system of thought. Even that [notion of] "fragrance" is not merely near; for by what means of valid cognition, such as direct perception, could emptiness and so forth be established for the intellects of the Sautrāntikas and others? By none of them.
Why? To this he says: "Non-existence," etc. Under what condition does this occur? He says: "In the case of rejection."
Of what? Of the mind, or of something other than that—namely speech—or else of something external;
and of what nature is it? It is of a single form consisting of both the visible and the invisible.

If it is argued: "Since the mind has the nature of grasping all objects exactly as they exist, how can there be a connection with another whose nature is invisible? If they were identical, then one of them alone would be so; and if their natures were distinct, the other would be of no consequence to this one. Thus, the mind remains as it is, grasping both self and other in their entirety," to this he replies:
"This very mind, or whatever else it may be, [is related] to its bond mutually."

Even in the case of identity, just as gold and its dark color [differ] by definition, it does not abandon its manifoldness characterized by transformation; for that [manifoldness], while conforming to the universal (jāti), does not fail to appear in the cognition of the object. (12–13)

If exclusion (*vyapoha*), which is devoid of attributes such as color, shape, and dimension, were itself differentiated in nature, then— due to the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following the superimposition (*samāropa*) [of those attributes]—
it would follow that sensory cognition does not have an exclusively real object, since it would be admitted that perception has a past object.

Since even a conceptual construction (vikalpa) evoked by a word is a form of self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), how [is this so]? This very mind—though otherwise insentient—is, as a functional entity, bound to another through a specific conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*). Even though they are one, they are not non-distinct in terms of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), just as gold and its blackness are distinct. Without abandoning or relinquishing that [nature], it thus conforms to and assumes a birth characterized solely by transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇā*)—which consists of the nature of being both visible and invisible—and not otherwise. It accepts [this] as its own attainment of self-nature (*ātmalābha*).

Why? He says: "Because [it does not appear] in that cognition," and so forth. Because it does not appear in the cognition that apprehends what is other than mind—that is, in the cognition [of the person]—[he asks] what [relation] that [person] has to the entity other than mind. He says: "Color" such as blue and so forth; "shape" such as roundness and so forth; "dimension" such as this much and so forth; and the elements such as earth and so forth—those whose properties follow the non-mental [substratum] are referred to as such.
By these, the "devoid self" is the *pudgala*-natured karma, such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and so forth.

If it is argued that "the object is not within the scope of words by way of being conscious or unconscious; rather, because verbal cognition consists of exclusion (*vyapoha*), its object is exclusively non-existent," [the author] replies here with the verse beginning "of exclusion" (*vyapohasya*), etc.

"Exclusion" (*vyapoha*) means the act of excluding (*vyapohana*), i.e., the turning away from what is undesired. If it is accepted that this [exclusion] has the nature of that [particular], meaning it has the nature of the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), then the connection [of the sentence] is: "what would be cognized by what? (i.e., no cognition would be possible).

If it is argued that when superimposition (*samāropa*) is excluded by means of a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is thereby cognized through valid cognition (*pramīyate*); to this he replies: "Superimposition," etc. [The opponent asks:

"Whence does that [exclusion] come? He replies: "By non-conceptual [perception]," etc. [The opponent asks: "Whence does that [non-conceptual perception] come? He replies: "From the arising of conceptualization (*vikalpa*)."

Concluding with "That is not so," etc., he asks: "Why is it that sensory cognition (*akṣavijñāna*) does not have an exclusively existent object? He replies: "Because perception (*pratyakṣa*)," and so forth. This is an elliptical expression; by it, the phrase "because of the admission that [perception] has past objects" is also understood, as well as "because of the admission that it has future objects. Therefore, the intended meaning is that even verbal cognition (*śabdavijñāna*) possesses an exclusively non-existent object within conventional discourse.

Even for a conceptual construction (vikalpa) evoked by a word—not only for direct perception—there is, because it is a self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), a predominant operation upon itself just as there is an operation upon the object. Otherwise, that conceptual construction would become one [with the word] through the nature of being produced by that [word] or not produced by it. Or else, its nature as self-cognition [would arise] from the preceding cognition. Why is this so? If you say, "Because [the cognition] exists when that [word] is present," then the same applies to the word as well.
If it is argued that [conceptual cognition] does not exist in the absence of that [word], this objection applies equally here as well.

For conceptual cognitions do not acquire their own nature in the absence of words, because that would entail the consequence that they are not produced by them. The claim that "conceptual cognitions have words as their source" remains unshaken. Now, if it is argued that the nature of self-awareness exists in perception even in the absence of words, and thus [perception] is not produced by them; then the nature of being a conceptual cognition—which occurs when there is a word based on linguistic convention—would likewise not be produced by that [word], since that word is absent [in such a case].
If it is argued that "that [other] is different," the same reasoning applies elsewhere as well.
If it is argued that "both arise from that," then both would be unreal, or neither would exist at all;
yet he does not think it is so.
In the absence of prior cognition, it is the same regarding sound; in the absence of sound, it is the same.
It should be understood that [it] would follow as a consequence that it is not an effect of sound—
see page 319, note 8;
[it is] produced by sound.

It might be thought: "Since perception arises from a past or future object through its identity (*tādātmya*) with that object's own nature, it has that as its object; but a word does not have the object as its object because the reverse is the case. To this he says:
"How so? and provides the rebuttal beginning with "yathārtha" (as it is):
"The absolute certainty of non-delusion regarding the object would not be established, because [perception] itself is a delusion."
Likewise, because there is no necessary connection with the object, it has been said that "everything spoken is false.
When external objects are rejected, all cognitions would be exclusively erroneous;

and just as error cannot be established if there is exclusively error, so too the non-denotation of objects by words in their entirety [cannot be established], because there is no necessary connection with the object.

Even if external objects exist, since the exclusivity of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) as being exclusively erroneous is unestablished—given that non-conceptual [cognition] is not of the nature of determination (*nirṇaya*)—how can there be a distinction between the true and the false regarding the exclusive object of one's intended expression, from which the distinction between victory and defeat could be postulated? This is the intended meaning: if words were indeed devoid of objects because they lack a necessary connection with objects, then the employment of words to demonstrate that very objectlessness would not be beneficial. For instance, just as in the manner in which there is the exclusivity of error regarding objects—the exclusivity that all cognitions of pillars and so forth are entirely illusory—[so too must the status of words be considered].
Alternatively, why would the intended absolute delusion regarding objects not be established by conceptual constructions? To this he says:
"Because of delusion; for there is no establishment of delusion through delusion."

Now, let it be established that the entire speech of the Buddhist, spoken in that manner and without exception—since the word *uktam* (spoken) is derived from the sense of "that which was said"—is also proven to be false (*mṛṣā*) or untrue (*mithyā*).
Why? Because here, there is no necessary connection (*apratibandhatvāt*) with the object.

Here, the object refers to the falsity of all words as accepted by the opponent; since there is no such connection, the words that purport to establish that falsity cannot even be uttered, namely, "all words are false," because they do not denote that [intended] object.

Nevertheless, it might be thought that in such discourse, the statement of a non-essential member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the speaker, on the grounds that all speech is false. [The opponent argues: "The practitioner of worldly convention (*vyavahārī*) does not accept the falsity of all speech; therefore, like one suffering from ophthalmia being awakened by another who is not so afflicted, he is enlightened by means of false words. This is without substance, because while there may be some way to proceed in cases such as "Bring the jar," when it is stated that "the reality is beyond the range of words," if he were to understand it thus in its entirety, the reality would not have been communicated.
For one who understands the falsity of all words from a word does not understand that [word] itself as having been established as true;
for one who understands the falsity of all words from a word does not indeed understand it, because of contradiction.
To explain: if that [word] were understood from it, then there would be no falsity of all words.
If it is argued that he does not comprehend it [the object], we say no; therefore, he ought to comprehend it.

For no one, while knowing the falsity of a word or anything else, can simultaneously know its existence. If you argue that he knows the object because he knows it from that [word], yet does not know its [falsity] from that same source—how is this so? It is because of his thorough knowledge of it; for just as one comprehends a cloth or the like from the word "cloth" and so forth, it follows equally that he does not comprehend its [falsity] from that same source.
For a person engaged in worldly activity does not, on the basis of a false cognition, understand from that which is understood as being exclusively false that all cognitions are exclusively false;

and thus, the thesis that there is an exclusive state of delusion regarding objects would not be established because of such delusion. If it is argued that this must be accepted out of necessity—that it is known through perception—let that matter rest for now.

Now, if words do not have external objects as their referents because there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*) between them—just like fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—how is this understood? And why is there no such connection? If you say it is known through perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no, for that has already been refuted. Let this matter rest for now. If you argue that activity occurs even in the absence of [an object], we have already provided the answer to this previously: that there is a distinction [between valid and invalid cognition] because sensory cognition (*akṣajñāna*) also proceeds even in the absence of [its object]. This applies to both cases alike.
If it is argued that [the ultimate] arises from false conceptualization, as it has been said:
"It is beyond the range of words" or "all words are false";
if this is the objection—
Even in the absence of an object,
there is one kind of cognition that functions despite that absence, and another which brings about activity when the object is present;
words have their source in conceptual construction, and conceptual constructions have their source in words.
"These words touch upon those objects which are mutually related to one another";
regarding their mutual relation, see *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
158; regarding their absolute relation, see *Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 243.
"There is a causal relationship among them; words do not even touch upon objects"—Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā, p. 44;
Ratnākara-avatāra, p. 9; Syādvādamañjarī, p. 175.
The mutual relationship between these [is explained] in the *Nyāyakumuda* (p.
537) and the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p.
701). Now, if all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are exclusively false, then even this [distinction] is difficult to ascertain.

For this very reason it is said: "The absolute unreliability (*vibhramaikānta*) of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding an object cannot be established because they are themselves erroneous.

Furthermore, would the word [intended to prove this] be necessarily connected with the falsity of all words, or would it be a word that establishes the opposite? In the first alternative, our desired conclusion is established, since—just like that [word]—other words can also be possible as being connected to their own respective objects. In the second case, such a word would not be employed.

The Buddhist does not, simply by knowing a thing that is not invariably concomitant with the probandum, establish a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) based upon it; for that would result in a loss of his status as a prudent person (*prekṣākārin*).

If you argue that he establishes it out of necessity, even though he lacks such prudence, then what is the point now of postulating that [the object] is produced by that [cognition], whether it be perception or something else? How can one who himself acts toward a convention based on something that is not inherently concomitant, yet becomes angry at another who acts toward it based on that very same thing, be considered sane? If you say that there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between that [convention] and the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the answer to this will follow in the passage beginning with "by the distinction between existent and non-existent things," and so forth.
Therefore, he says: "Because it is not connected with an object," and so forth;
that is to say, the employment of words in the form "everything is false" should not be made.
Even by a word that is not connected to a real entity,
production [is understood] from the word itself by implication.
For the Cārvāka, conventional usage [proceeds] from sound or from a reason that is unconnected [to reality].
