In order to explain the verse regarding the intention of the word, he says: "In the rejection of external objects," and so forth;
that is, when the rejection of external objects is being carried out by the Yogācāra, who is without [external] conduct.

What [is the consequence]? He says: because there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of rejecting even the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of all cognitions—just like the external object—in the case of the absolute certainty of error; for, just as in the case of its own nature, the object also appears [in cognition]. Having considered this, he asks:

"What follows from that? and he replies: just as error is not established through the absolute certainty of error, in exactly the same way, the non-denotation of objects by words in their entirety is not established.
Why? He says: "Because there is no obstruction of the object for words in their entirety.

Or, just as for the Sautrāntika, even though external objects exist, because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are exclusively erroneous, the exclusivity of that error is not established—here the word "that" refers back to the conceptual constructions—the phrase "for you alone," etc., applies here as well as before.
If it is argued that its establishment comes from non-conceptual [cognition], he says: "Of the non-conceptual," and so forth.
The meaning is that otherwise, its existence [as a real entity] would follow.

If it is argued: "In the intended sense that 'all words are without objects,' there is a counter-argument regarding my own word; therefore, this is not a fault," he says in response: "tadvivaktā" and so forth.

The claim that "all words have objects" or "all words are objectless"—that is, the state of having as its object the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*)—how can it be true in its absolute sense? For if one says "all words are devoid of external objects," that statement is true; yet if one says "they possess such objects," that is false. How then can there be a settled distinction between these two, from which the determination of victory and defeat could be established? There is a deviation from the speaker's intention; furthermore, since the meaning is not communicated in either case, the phrase "all words have objects" is redundant, as if written twice over.

In both cases, the following might be thought: "My intended meaning is connected to the object through a causal chain, not otherwise; therefore, there is a fixed determination [of truth]. That too is favorable to my own position, because such a connection exists even with respect to external objects.
Showing another refutation regarding this very point, he says: "Whether the thing be existent or non-existent," and so forth.

Because there is no regard for the speaker’s intention regarding the distinction between existent and non-existent entities, that entity is investigated in which the arising of the result is contingent.
Disregarding the speaker’s intention regarding the word-meaning, everyone who seeks purposeful action should examine only that word-meaning which is capable of it; [one should act] only therein...
Therefore, one who engages in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) and the study of treatises (*śāstra*) ought to act solely for the purpose of establishing that object, and not otherwise.
Nor is it the case that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of cognitions everywhere depends exclusively on a connection with an external object;

for in some cases there is the manifestation of mere form (*rūpa-mātra*). Even though there is no distinction in the lack of connection with color, taste, and so forth, [the cognition] arises from that [object] and possesses its likeness (*sārūpya*); yet since both of these—arising from that and having its likeness—are unreal, they cannot be established in any way whatsoever. Let that very [connection with the object] be the basis elsewhere, because of the construction of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

If this is your insistence—that an object of cognition cannot be without a cause—then how is inferential knowledge a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in some cases, and not in others? Since the specific nature of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established through perception, how can it be a valid means of knowledge when that connection is not established elsewhere? [If you say] "by way of generality," what then is this "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*)? If one postulates an inference for that, there would be an infinite regress;
thus, its comprehension cannot occur without another means of knowledge, and in other cases as well, the postulation of a means of knowledge would be useless.

Without a universal characterized by similarity (*sādṛśya-lakṣaṇa-jāti*), how could fire and the like be cognized as a single entity while being excluded from others? Since the exclusion of other things from the intended object of cognition is indistinguishable in all cases, that which is not a cause cannot be the object [of cognition]— *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 2.257.

That object is reflected upon and examined—that object upon which the arising of the result, the attainment of the result’s own nature, depends. [The phrase] “because it is not the object of words” is to be supplied [to the end of the sentence]. How is it reflected upon? He says: as existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent; that is to say, as being and non-being. And what is that? It is the distinction between those objects. Why is the intention not reflected upon in this form: “For which word does an external object exist, and for which does it not exist? He says: because of disregard for such intention.

For the result, such as the fetching of water, is not tied to that [mental image]; otherwise, no one would act externally, or else everyone would act everywhere because the connection to a result exists for all, since the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is absent in every case.
And if the word-meaning were the speaker’s intention, activity would occur only with respect to that [intention] and not toward an external object.

For indeed, when there is comprehension of one thing from a word, there can be no activity toward another; otherwise, there would be activity toward a horse upon hearing the word "cow. Now, if it is argued that the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is bound to the object, and therefore activity toward that [object] occurs through the comprehension of that [intention]; [we reply: in this way, for the Mīmāṃsaka, the occurrence of the higher universal (*parāsāmānya*) in the particular (*viśeṣa*) would not be contradictory, provided it resides in the speaker’s intention.
"It may be" [is used] with respect to the object by means of the comprehension of the object.

It might be argued that [the cognition] functions with respect to that [particular] through error, by superimposing the intended object upon its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). This is not sound, because it would follow that everything could function with respect to everything due to such superimposition.

If it is then thought that the superimposition occurs only upon the particular itself—where the intention to speak regarding a cow has mounted—due to similarity, and not elsewhere because of the opposite [lack of similarity], then it is established that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the intention to speak has the external object as its domain.
For even in the case of perception, there is nothing other than that [intention] which arises from similarity.
In every respect, complete similarity is difficult to find anywhere; [therefore],
the status of being an object within the external domain [applies] to horses and so forth.

If it is argued that errors have restricted occurrences, and therefore some occur only in certain places and not everywhere—whence is this known? For it is observed that a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs only where its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been awakened through a causal lineage. How then could conceptual constructions, whose birth is tied to objects of such a nature, not be such that the words originating from them function in that same way? If it is argued that they do indeed function in that way, yet their objects are not those [external things], then perception would not have those things as its objects.

If it is argued that [the cognition is valid] because of its conformity (*sārūpya*); from what does that [conformity] derive? If it is argued that it derives from the production [of the cognition] from that [object]; it has already been stated that if the production of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were also [possible] from a non-conceptual [cognition], then those [cognitions] arising from conceptual constructions would be bound to the object.
Having the object as its domain means that having the object as its domain is similarity.

However, since [the conceptual construction] arises from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) through a non-sequential process, if the conceptual construction is one that determines that [particular], then it would have to determine the eye and so forth as well. If you argue that this is not the case because of their unsuitability (*ayogyatva*), then from where does its suitability regarding the particular characteristic come? If you say it is from arising from the experience of that [particular], then from where does "the experience of that" come? If you say it is from arising from that, then it would also apply to the eye and so forth;
and the reply that "it is not [so] because they do not have that form" is no answer, for the same [objection] applies equally to the particular characteristic as well.
Then it was argued: "If the comprehension of the speaker's intention arises from the word, there would be no activity toward the object";
[this is rejected] because it is observed that even from the eyes and other senses, that [comprehension] arises through a causal series.
He states the meaning of the verse according to its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) with the words "the meaning of a word," and so forth:
whether that meaning of a word exists or does not exist because of its non-existence— [this refers to] the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), that is, the desire for an object, without exception.

Who? One who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as one seeking to fetch water and so forth; he should examine only that which is capable of such action—that is, only that which is fit for purposeful action.
Why? To this he says: "In that very [context]," and so on.

Since this is so, therefore, whether it be the Sugata or someone else, while engaging in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) and composing treatises (*śāstra*), they ought to act solely for that purpose—namely, for the sake of communicating what is capable of purposeful action—and not otherwise, nor by any other mode of communicating intention (*vivakṣā*), because even if that were communicated, there would be no utility.

"But how can there be a comprehension of an object from a word whose production is not tied to that object? To this very point, he states the refutation once more: "And it is not the case," and so forth. What is this absolute rule? He says: "In all cases, the validity of cognitions of objects [arises] precisely from their connection with the object.
Why is this so? He says: "The sense organ," and so forth.
Showing another argument on this very point, he says: "In some cases," and so forth.

This is because in certain instances of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), there is the appearance of mere form (*rūpa*); by the word "mere" (*mātra*), it is indicated that specific qualities of form, such as momentary destruction and so on, do not appear. Furthermore, although there is no distinction in the obstruction of color, taste, and so forth... [the visual consciousness does not apprehend them].

...it is not [known] through a specific quality of the sentient being, nor by following upon something distinct [from itself]; for doubt and other such cognitions occur even in the absence of an object. Furthermore, although the eyes and other [faculties] are present and functional, there is an absence of cognition when the object is absent;

this following upon [the object] is not perceived by that very cognition, because at that time [the cognition] is absent. If it is argued that it is perceived by another [cognition], then that [other cognition] must apprehend both states [presence and absence], otherwise it would be impossible for it to grasp that [absence].

That [similarity] would also have to be produced by its own cause, and for that to be perceived, there would have to be a perception of its conformity to yet another [cause], leading to an infinite regress.

Therefore, it is established: since that person (the object) exists as a real entity, and because similarity is in every way untenable in him—since it would otherwise entail the undesirable consequence of consciousness being insentient and lacking determinate nature—let that [object] itself be the causal constraint (*pratibandha*). For similarity is not possible in any respect whatsoever, either in its entirety or in any partial manner; therefore, let that [object] alone be the cause.
Alternatively, it should be understood that [the object] is not established by any mode of perception or inference;
for instance, when both the cognition and the object are perceived, there arises the certainty "this is similar to that," as in the case of twins;
however, there is no perception of another's object, except through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

That too is not tenable, because [it would imply] that after previously seeing two things, there is subsequently the superimposition of seeing another thing similar to one of them—just like the superimposition [of seeing Caitra] upon seeing Maitra—or that when seeing two things, the mind takes on their form. In either case, the same fault remains, leading to an infinite regress.
If, however, it is established through delusion that [the object] is perceived in that form, then our desired conclusion is proven.

Therefore, the phrase "iti nirarthakam" [is] here; on page 486, folio kha, two lines are left blank and unwritten, and page 487, folio ka, is entirely blank; furthermore, on page 487, folio kha, one line remains blank for the Yogācāra.
Moreover, perception always cognizes the self as devoid of forms such as blue;
therefore, the similarity between cognition and its object is not established anywhere.
"I clearly perceive a jar and so forth, distinct in space."
Thus, since in the world this conventional usage is observed without contradiction, without dispute,
and based on the notion of "I," no other consciousness is perceived; this is our view.
That similarity which the followers of the Sugata claim is endowed with both measurement and protection would be established through perception; similarity is not established by means of inference.
A thesis contradicted by perception does not attain proof through any other means.
Seeing both by means of one [cognition] is not contradictory, because it has been seen; likewise, another [effect] would arise from that same [cause].
Otherwise, the wise should reflect upon the latent impression (*vāsanā*) as the cause of cognition.
That [consciousness] must also be joined with all the faults involved in grasping external objects; furthermore,
it has been established that even for one who holds that consciousness is causeless, unitary, and unpolluted, the cognition of objects is not contradictory.

The doctrine of a single partless cognition has already been refuted previously. Since that [cognition] is entirely devoid of the conceptual alternatives of being one or many, and since similarity (*sārūpya*) is in every respect impossible therein, let that very [relation of] causal dependence (*pratibandha*) suffice; why then insist on the unreality of both "being produced from that" (*tajjanma*) and "similarity" (*sārūpya*) in every respect? "No," he says: "Because of the construction of conceptualization elsewhere. That is to say, in another case—namely, the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—there is reality because of the construction of conceptualization; however, due to the absence of such construction, there is indeed reality [in the sense of non-conceptual presence]. This is the meaning.

If it is argued that, since it has been stated [by Dharmakīrti] that "validity is established by worldly practice" (*prāmāṇyaṃ vyavahāreṇa*), those very same faults apply to the Buddhist because of that conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), we say: no; for the intention is otherwise.

To explain: just as in the case of the production and similarity [of cognition], because of the construction of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), cognition is indeed formless (*nirākāra*) with respect to the object, yet it functions exactly so in worldly practice.

Furthermore, by means of a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), he states another refutation regarding that very point: "If this [text] beginning with 'this bond' [means that] the object is not the cause of the cognition's form, but rather the cause itself... [the opponent asks: "How is it that inferential cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in some cases, such as when fire is the probandum (*sādhya*)? The other asks: "And why is it not so? He provides the answer: "Insofar as it is cognized," and so forth.

If it is argued that "the specific relation characterized by 'origination from that' (tadutpatti) is known through perception—that is, it is apprehended through direct experience—because it is established by perception in the case of fire and so forth associated with a kitchen, and therefore that [perception] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [relation] in other cases, but rather a means of valid cognition elsewhere," to this he replies: "In other cases," and so forth. How can there be a means of valid cognition in other cases—that is, in what is beyond the reach of perception (*parokṣa*)? Why? He says: "Because the relation is not established in other cases."

It might be thought that inference occurs thus: "The universal of smoke is pervaded by the universal of fire; having been apprehended once, it is indeed apprehended at all times. To this, he says: "By means of the universal," and so forth, questioning the opponent with the words "But what," and so on.
The opponent says: "Exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is the universal," and so forth.

He thinks that exclusion of others means either exclusion from what is different—i.e., from the dissimilar—or the exclusion of something else, or that in this form of conceptual construction (vikalpākāra), something else is excluded;
thus, because it would have exclusion as its object like other conceptual constructions, perception would consequently become conceptual.
Now, if it is maintained that the cognition of that [universal] arises from inference, he says: "In the case of that inference," and so forth.

Since there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) when one postulates an inference for that universal—which is itself an exclusion (*apoha*) of the pervaded and the pervader—how can inferential knowledge be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) in any instance? To explain: the universal is cognized through inference, and that [inference] likewise arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*). In that case as well, there must be a perception of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by means of a universal, and regarding that too, the same must be said until one reaches a point where there is no further regress.

It might be thought that inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of cognition because it apprehends the relation of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); regarding this, he says: "Without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no apprehension of that exclusion (*apoha*). This is the apprehension of it.
Why? He says: "Even elsewhere," and so forth.

Even in other cases where [the object] is intended to be perceived or inferred, the postulation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is useless; for, as in the case of the *sāmānya* under discussion, even another [object] is cognized without it.
If its utility were established by conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then let the cognition of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) be likewise [useless].

If it is argued that yogic perception exists [to establish this], it has already been stated here that such perception does not arise from anything other than its own object; otherwise, since the probandum would be established by that very perception, what would be the use of inference? Furthermore, he states another objection: if the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is grasped through a universal (*sāmānya*), then that perception is conceptual (*savikalpa*). He says "in similarity," etc.: without a universal characterized as a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*), how could fire and so forth—which are excluded from others and distinct from heterogeneous things—be perceived as one, that is, without difference? It could not be perceived in any way.

The point is this: since a thing itself is distinguished from others by virtue of its similarity—given the existence of a universal (*jāti*) characterized by a similar transformation—what is the use of a "universal as the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha-sāmānya*)?

Why would it not be cognized in any way at all? To this he says: "the intended," and so forth. The entire cognition that is intended is that very object denoted by the word; its exclusion from other things, such as cloth (which is not cognition), is common to everything, including jars and the like.
And likewise, just as cognition— which is excluded from cloth due to ignorance— is denoted by the word "cognition," so too should a jar or the like be [denoted by that same term].

Now, if it is argued that it is cognition itself which, being excluded from those [other objects], is said to participate in that designation [of "jar"], then this is correct— [namely, that the word applies] without such means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as "it is similar" and so forth.
The phrase "because of its being so apprehended" is redundant here;
for by means of yogic perception alone, the object denoted by the word "pot" would be established.

But is it not the case that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even such similarity does not exist as a universal (*sāmānya*)? Rather, it is simply because cognitions are the cause of a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*) that there is non-difference among those cognitions; and due to that non-difference, there is non-difference among the individual manifestations (*vyakti*).
As it has been said: "Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness, cognition is non-different;
and by virtue of being the cause of a single cognition, the individual manifestations are also non-different."
Thus [it is stated] in *Pratyabhijñāvṛtti* 4.108.
Regarding this, he says: "By means of similarity," and so forth;
because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*), cognition is non-differentiating.
"By virtue of being the cause of a single cognition, even individuals possess non-difference" (Pramāṇavārttika 4.108);

for, indeed, by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), even in the absence of similarity, the cognizer himself distinguishes between objects that are causes of that [cognition] and those that are not. (15)

Without that single unifying reflection—that is, without similarity, which is to say without a similar transformation—of what [could there be such a thing]? Of objects, such as fire and so forth; by the power of recognition, whether it be a Buddhist or someone else, the cognizer distinguishes objects, establishing them through differentiation.

Of what kind [of things]? Those which have that cause and those which do not have that cause (*tadataddhetūn*). "Those having that cause" refers to jars and the like, which are the causes for fetching water and so forth; "those not having that cause" refers to cloth and the like. The word "kila" (it is said) expresses a lack of conviction, because when there is an absence of similarity (*sādṛśya*), even recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is difficult to obtain.

For it does not exist even in the case of hair that has been cut and grown back again; otherwise, from seeing grass one might think, "These are the very same hairs. Thus, he considers that recognition exists without similarity.
In order to explain the verse, he says: "Of the single reflective awareness of those," and so forth;
the meaning of the remainder [of the verse] regarding that single reflective awareness of those fragments and so on is already understood.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "The object," and so forth.

"In this way, the very distinction between object and subject is indeed destroyed everywhere, because the cognition of letters and so on is produced by the recognition of those same letters and so on. (16)
...one might establish [the distinction] by some means; however, since that [distinction] is caused by cognition, the possession of color and so forth is like similarity.
Therefore, what is the cause of what, or what is the effect, from which this conventional usage proceeds?
There is no establishment [of the distinction] through perception of color and so forth, because that which has a similar nature is perceived.
The establishment of objects of cognition does not proceed from the act of cognition itself; for if it did, then even the establishment of colors and so forth would not exist.
Indeed, that single, massive form, situated before one's eyes, appears with perfect clarity;
if that were not perceptible, there would be no object of perception whatsoever.

The object (*viṣaya*) is form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and the subject (*viṣayin*) is the consciousness thereof; the established distinction between these two, both externally and internally, would indeed be entirely destroyed. The word "kila" (indeed) is explained by this [following passage]. Why? He says: "Because of the recognition of color, etc. Color refers to white and so forth; that which has form as its beginning includes taste and the rest. The "recognition" (*pratyabhijñāna*) of that is a specific kind of mental conceptualization (*mānaso vikalpa*). Because of the production (*kṛti*) of that [recognition], the cognitions of form and so forth would be the cause of the cognitions of color and so forth; [conversely], color and so forth would not exist apart from those [cognitions].

Now, if it is thought: "In the absence of phonemes and so forth, there is no cognition of them, like a donkey's horn; and in their absence, there can be no recognition of them"—this is equally true in other cases as well. While explaining the verse, he says: "Furthermore, [the question] 'what' and so forth—why would one not establish [it]? To this he replies: "To the extent that," and so forth.

The existence of phonemes and so forth is established through the recognition of phonemes and so forth, because the cognitions of those [phonemes]—the cognitions of phonemes—are the causes of the [subsequent] cognitions of phonemes and so forth; they do not possess phonemes and so forth by way of their own nature, just as [they do not possess them] through similarity. This is the illustration.

Therefore, because there is no establishment of the reality of entities, what is conscious or unconscious could be the cause or the effect of what? The meaning is that nothing belongs to anything. For it is from such a causal relationship that this worldly convention proceeds.
The intent of the passage beginning with "varṇādiḥ" and so forth is to raise an objection from the perspective of the opponent in order to refute it:
namely, that the determination of phonemes and the like is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and not through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
The refutation of this begins with "na" and so forth.
"No"—this is a negation of the opponent's position.
Why? He says: because the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, which possess a similar nature, are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For instance, in one who lacks linguistic convention (*samaya*), whose mind is directed elsewhere, or who perceives a headless corpse (*khaṇḍa*) or a shaven-headed person (*muṇḍa*) and so on, there arises the cognition "these are similar. If this [cognition] were denied, all cognition would be abolished.

The opponent says: "The status of an object is not established by its cognition; otherwise, the status of water in a mirage would follow from the cognition thereof. This is refuted by the following: for in that case, the status of phonemes and so forth would likewise not exist, since one could say, "Their status is not established by their cognition, just like the water in a mirage," provided there were no sublation (*bādhaka*). If [the opponent replies] that this is not so because there is a sublation, [we ask]: what is the perceptual sublation of the cognition of similarity? Does it sublate itself? If [you say] it is merely a cognition of similarity, then [our position] is the same: it is merely a cognition of difference.
Because of recognition; for that [recognition] exists in the other case as well,
since there is a recognition of similarity devoid of convention.
If it is argued that the establishment of the social classes and so forth is based on direct perception;

Furthermore, it is a great mark of discernment [on your part] that something which, in its own nature, admits of two forms—one sublated and one not—cannot tolerate two distinct natures, one similar and the other dissimilar, elsewhere! Moreover, what is the sublation of that [nature] by that [cognition]? If you say it is non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*), that is unproven, because it would follow [absurdly] even for the mere color and so forth;

for if those were not apprehended, there would be no perception at all. Furthermore, the claim that this [cognition] indicates an apprehension of "that" in what is "not-that" elsewhere is refuted by the case of color and so forth, as there is no such cognition elsewhere either.
Therefore, perception is not a subverting proof;

for that very reason, inference is also not one, since [the universal] does not exist in the absence of that [particular]. If it is argued that its non-perception apart from the individual constitutes a subverting proof, then what indeed is the perception of the phoneme and so forth apart from that [individual]? If it is claimed that the phoneme itself is the individual, then let there likewise be similarity.

If it is argued: "The Jaina does not accept a universal distinct from the individuals as the Naiyāyika does; rather, the individuals themselves [constitute the universal]," then let them be so—what loss is there for us? If it is further argued: "Since we perceive partless atoms, it is not logical that those individuals possess both similar and dissimilar natures, but are merely similar to one another," to this he replies: "For that one... and so forth.
Regarding that color and so forth, what is the single common element in the process of contemplation? He says: the form;
of what nature is it? It is most gross (sthavīyān).
Furthermore, of what nature is it? How and in what manner does it exist "in immediate presence"? To this he says: "It manifests in such a way that it is perfectly clear.
He states the refutation should this not be accepted: "If that were not perceptible—that is, if that form (*ākāra*) were not perceptible—then nothing whatsoever would be a perceptible object."
This has been examined in many ways and is not stated again;
it is considered thus: if this form were substantially real in many [objects] such as sugar-cubes and the like, there would also be a similar transformation even in the absence of direct perception.
Because inference also does not arise [from it], [the universal] is distinct from the individuals and [resides] in the individuals.

Pra jñā ka ra gu pta says: "The establishment of an external object as having that form does not follow from the perception of that form, because there is deviation [in the case] of such things as distant or sparse hairs, where there is an appearance of that form. He should be asked: "Is this said with reference to an external object, or to mere cognition, or to mere delusion, or to mere emptiness? In the first case, even the established order of external colors and so forth would not exist, because there is deviation in the case of the appearance of yellow in a white conch shell.

It is not the case that yellow light exists in gold and so forth simply because there is an appearance of it; for this is inconclusive due to the appearance of bitterness in sweet milk by one suffering from a bile-fever (*pittajvara*).

Since bitterness exists in the *nimba* tree and other such things precisely because there is an appearance of it, this principle should be applied everywhere. Thus, the establishment of identity based on similarity (*sārūpya*) is sound; furthermore, the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) applies elsewhere as well.

In the second alternative, it must be considered how that form exists even in cognition, as if it were external. If you say it does not exist [externally], then what is cognition other than blue and so forth? If you say it is thus [identical], then what is blue and so forth? If you say it is nothing at all, then let cognition be likewise; for if one denies perception, every discourse becomes impossible, and in this way, the cessation of afflictions is most easily achieved.
If it is argued that [the cognition] is erroneous, then, because of that deviation, the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of anything cannot be established on the basis of its appearance.

If it is argued that blue and so forth are indeed the cognition itself, how could its form (*ākāra*) therein be ultimate (*pāramārthika*)? Otherwise, it would have to be so for the object as well. If it is further argued that, due to the deviation seen in the case of distant, sparse hairs, the form is not thus in that instance; then for that very reason, it would not exist in the case of cognition either.

Now, regarding the position of [the Yogācāra] who maintains that [consciousness] is cognition (*jñānapakṣa*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to those [non-existent] hairs, because they do not exist; but how could such a deviation be asserted by them in the case of the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*), where those [hairs] are non-existent? If it is argued that it is "due to the opponent's own admission," then why is that same form (*ākāra*) not also established for the object (*artha*) by you, just as it is for consciousness, based on your own admission? If it is argued that "there would be doubt," namely: "Is this form existent in the object just as it is in consciousness, or is it non-existent like those hairs?"—that is incorrect, because doubt remains unremoved even regarding consciousness itself.

For example, regarding a cognition that possesses an aspect such as a pillar or the like, there might arise for the proponent of external objects this doubt: "Is this aspect existent, like the pillar and so forth, or is it non-existent, like fingernails, hair, and so forth?

If it is argued that this is not so because smoke is accepted as being free from error, we say: no; this argument lacks substance. For just as a doubt is produced in the opponent by taking up an instance of error admitted by him, so too must it be produced in oneself; for only in this way would one be impartial.

Or when another says this: "Just as in the external world, so too in cognition, because of that very same deviation (*vyabhicāra*), this form is not real"; then what should you say? If it is argued: "That deviation follows precisely from his own admission, and that admission is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)," we reply: No, for it is impossible to produce conviction based on what is not a valid means of knowledge.

If it is argued that the opponent must somehow be addressed, and for that very reason he is made to fall into the pit of doubt; and if it is further argued that the Buddhist, too, must somehow be addressed by the opponent, and thus—disregarding the scope of the deviation—one establishes the reality of the object's form just as one does for consciousness, because "abandoning what has been accepted" is a fault; we say: no. For even when something is abandoned, there is no fault in abandoning that which, upon its abandonment, allows a much greater portion of one’s own position—which brings about the destruction of the opponent's position—to be established.
As it has been said:
The phrase "it is not so" should also be applied here;
that aspect is ultimately real.
Regarding the charge of infidelity, the Buddhist says:
"One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village."

One should abandon a village for the sake of the country, and abandon the earth for the sake of the self. [Objection: If that [self] is also not ultimately real even when known, then, because of that deviation, let it be the same for caste and so forth as well;
thus, the second position is also not superior.

Now the third [position] is examined: if it is argued that the appearance [of an object] cannot be real because it deviates from reality due to error, it has been stated here— "because error is unestablished"—
thus the fourth position was reduced to a fifth, as previously prescribed by rule.
The position that there is merely emptiness has met its end and reached destruction because it is contradicted by valid cognition; therefore, entities exist as they have been described.

[Objection: "But surely, by whatever proximity (*pratyāsatti*) certain entities accept a certain similarity, by that same [proximity] they themselves, though not of the nature of that [similarity], will appear as such. To this, he says: "They accept," and so forth. If objects accept qualities through a certain power (*śakti*), why would those things which lack qualities not produce cognitions of them? If they were distinct [from the cognition], how could there be a single cognition [of both]? (17)
This has been cited—*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p. 408:

"Just as it would not be logical that those particulars assist that universal [as a single entity] but do not produce a single cognition, so too a single reality such as a jar bears touch and other qualities within itself but does not produce cognitions having the very forms of touch and the rest; thus, it would not conform to the nature of a jar. Consequently, the object would be formless."

If objects such as jars, which are themselves devoid of qualities (*aguṇa*), possess that power by which they accept qualities such as color and cognition, why would they not, by that same power, produce the cognitions of those qualities? [The opponent might argue: "If objects are distinct and mutually different, how can they have a single cognition (*ekasaṃvit*)—that is, a single cognition belonging to them all?
To explain this verse, he says: "That universal," and so forth.
That universal—the universal of similarity—is one and common to all individuals such as *bāhuleya* cows; it either assists them, maintains itself within them, or manifests them.
Which ones? The individuals, namely the specific instances such as broken pieces and so forth.

Furthermore, these individuals do not produce a cognition of themselves as "cow, cow," nor do they produce the notion that they are merely individual manifestations (*vyakti*). This is because such a mode of producing cognition would be illogical; rather, it is logical that they produce only a single cognition, since their capacity is observed to function precisely in that way. In the same manner, the single, indivisible reality of the jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth bears qualities such as touch within its own nature (*ātman*); yet it does not simply produce cognitions in the form of touch and the like. Thus, it does not conform to [the literal nature of] the jar; rather, even though it does not possess those qualities [as its essence], it produces cognitions of them, and thereby conforms to [the conventional notion of] the jar.
From that very principle [of immediate succession], the object must be formless;
for, having thus established the object as being without form, the author, wishing to explain this further, says "jīva" and so forth:
by whatever power the soul (*jīva*) undergoes the modifications (*paryāya*) of pleasure and the like.
Just as one possessing power might appear to be that very power itself, so too would the intellect of variegated cognition (*citrabuddhi*) appear [as such].
By what [power]... then, in the absolute state of difference, how could perception, recognition, and so forth ever enter the path of practical discourse?

The *jīva*—the self—goes to or attains various states (*paryāya*) such as pleasure and the like; by whatever power or capacity it may have, it would be characterized as "possessing power" (*śakta*) through a conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*) following upon experience, but it is not grasped by direct experience (*anubhava*) alone.

He states an illustration established by others, beginning with "Just as a painting" (*citrāh*): just as a cognition, though itself non-variegated, appears as variegated when directed toward a variegated object such as a cloth or a perceived form; and just as even a variegated [object] is perceived as variegated; and just as that which is painted twice [appears so].
He states the commentary on the verse, beginning with "By which," and so forth.

He asks: what arises from that? He replies: "From that"—that is, from that reasoning—where, whether externally or internally, would perception, recognition, and so forth not somehow cross over into the path of practical discourse (*vyavahāra*)? Where would they fail? [They would fail] in the case of the absolute doctrine of difference (*bhedaikānta*).

Having stated the refutation by accepting a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) within the extreme view of difference (*bhedaikānta*), he now says— "The objects," and so forth— showing that [in that case] it is precisely the unifying cognition itself that is not caused by the objects, as they have not been made its object.
Therefore, since there is no necessary connection (*avinābhāva*) for that [recognition], it is not inferential.

For recognition does not itself reflect upon things that have not been made objects of its own cognition; furthermore, because it would entail the consequence of being a separate means of knowledge due to the addition of a new object of cognition (*prameya*), how could there be inference when the necessary connection is unestablished therein and universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) is likewise unestablished?

Objects such as jars and the like—which are of the nature of momentary atoms imagined by others—are not the causes of this reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*); that is to say, they are not its cause. Why is this? He says: because they have not been made into objects of cognition, meaning they have not been perceived. Consequently, due to their being non-causes, there would be no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between those things existing as the mark (*liṅga*) and the thing marked (*liṅgin*), and thus there could be no inferential cognition (*laiṅgika-anumāna*).

With the words "Not so" (*na hi*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse: Indeed, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) does not reflect upon an object that has not been made its own object by the recognizer—that is, one not previously experienced—because such recognition does not arise with respect to such an object; otherwise, it would arise everywhere.
[The opponent] might think: "But what if it reflects upon even those things not made its own object? To this, he replies: "In the case of the object of knowledge" (*prameye*) and so forth.

Since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) besides perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)—the latter being born from a non-conceptual mark (*liṅga*)—there follows the consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that [other means], namely, the existence of such a thing [as recognition]. Thus, [recognition] would be a [separate] means of valid cognition.
The connection with the words "not indeed" (*na hi*) and so forth is as follows:
to the question "Why?", he says, "And because of the surplus of objects of knowledge" (*prameyādhikyāt*).

This means it is so stated because of the engagement with objects of knowledge that are not within the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), due to the surplus of objects of knowledge.
And because it is not born from a mark (*liṅga*) that is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose essence is sound,
[recognition] does not [apply] to that which has not been experienced by the agent of recognition.

Demonstrating the resulting conclusion, he says: "Therefore, since there is no reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*) by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding that partless reality which has not itself been made an object [of perception], and since the logical mark (*liṅga*) lacks a proven connection—its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) being unascertained—from what [source] could there be inference from a logical mark? From nothing at all.

Or, let us grant that there is a reflective awareness by means of recognition when [the object] is present and has been made an object of perception; even so, because that [invariable concomitance] is absent in its entirety, there is no inference. Demonstrating this, he says "in its entirety," etc.;
the word "and" (*ca*) is to be understood here [as implying the aforementioned point].
Furthermore, since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established in its entirety, how can there be inference?
Some say that such pervasion is established through sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*),
while others say it is established through the perception of yogins (*yogi-pratyakṣa*).
Some say "from the mind" (mānasāt),
while others say "from inference" (anumānāt);
the meaning is "from the non-perception of the pervader" (vyāpakānupalabdheḥ).
Regarding this, he says: "From perception," and so forth;
the Naiyāyikas [hold that this occurs] through the extraordinary perception (*alaukikapratyakṣa*) based on the cognitive proximity of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇāpratyāsatti*).
The first perception is the observation of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin)—
*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 44—
and pervasion (vyāpti) is to be understood through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) of two general properties (*sāmānyadharma*).
The distinction [between the two] is known through the elimination of difference in certain cases of specific qualities— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Anumāna-pariccheda, verse 12.
By the force of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), the apprehension of non-deviation is achieved between fire and smoke, even when there is deviation regarding place and other factors.

"Therefore, just as one discerns the true nature of a variety of precious gems, we consider it logical that the sense organ itself—aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation—is the grasper of the natural relationship (*svābhāvikasambandha*) between smoke and fire and so forth.
— *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, p. 167.
*Tātparya-ṭīkā*, page 697;
*Praśastapāda-bhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī*, page 295;
*Praśastapāda-bhāṣya-kandali*, page 209.
*Tattvacintāmaṇi*, Anumāna section, page 210.
For comparison: Others, however, assert that at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the cognizer possesses a complete knowledge of all objects, as if he were a yogin;
otherwise, there would be no recollection of the pervasion in the form, "All smoke does not exist without fire."
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.
570: Its apprehension occurs through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), aided by direct perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).

Having perceived with the sense organ that smoke is concomitant with fire, and having known through non-perception that it is excluded from non-fire such as water and the like, one determines by means of the mind that "smoke does not deviate from fire."
—Nyāyakali. p. 3; Nyāyamañjarī p. 121, 123:
"In some cases, pervasion is known through perception; [if it were known] through inference, there would be an infinite regress."

And the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is not established when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished. [The opponent argues: "As much as..."—by establishing the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through a name that has not been critically examined, the connection is well-established! However, in the conceptualization of that inference, since the pervasion by momentariness is unestablished, the non-perception of the pervader is also not established.
But has this not already been examined: "All entities—past, future, or present"—Siddhi-viniścaya 3?

If it is asked, "Why is this stated again?"—the answer is that in that [previous] context it was stated by way of defining inference (*anumāna*) directly; here, however, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that if a word were non-informative due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the same would apply to a logical mark (*liṅga*) as well. Thus, there is no fault.

In some cases, whether external or internal, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established through perception (*pratyakṣa*) based on either effect (*kārya*) or essential nature (*svabhāva*), nor does it fall within its scope.

If it is argued that [momentariness] is established through inference, he says in response: if inference is thus accepted, there is an infinite regress. If it is argued that the non-perception of causal efficiency—which is the pervader of existence—is not perceived in the eternal, and this establishes the pervasion of existence by momentariness; to this he replies: the non-perception of the pervader is not established, for even the non-perception of causal efficiency, which is the pervader of existence, is not established in its entirety regarding the non-momentary.

Indeed, it is not possible to perceive everything that is non-momentary as being devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such that the absence of the latter would entail the absence of the former—just as the absence of a tree entails the absence of a *śiṃśapā* tree. If you argue that causal efficiency is not observed there because of the absence of momentariness, [we ask] why? If you say, "Because it is not seen when that [momentariness] is absent," then for the Mīmāṃsaka as well, the cessation of perception would negate the existence of an omniscient being. Thus, it has been rightly said: "The Sugata is not omniscient, because he possesses qualities such as being a speaker, like an ordinary man on the street."

Now, if [it is argued that] there is no omniscient being because of the non-perception of all [such beings], then since it is possible for an omniscient being to perceive [others] either by himself or through another omniscient being, how is the non-perception of all [omniscient beings] established in the present case? [The Mīmāṃsaka replies: Because no one in this world perceives such a person. [The opponent replies: That is the same [for you as well], because even the Mīmāṃsaka does not perceive anyone who perceives everything. Thus, the situation is identical.

If it is argued that he would possess omniscience; if it is argued that let him also possess it; if it is argued that for the opponent as well there would be a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding the Vedas; [then this applies] to your inference as well.

If it is argued that for an omniscient being, there is nothing to be communicated to another through inference, [we reply: for the other person as well, because they possess knowledge of everything by mere wish,
[inference] would lack the capacity to communicate.
Regarding the non-momentary,
by the Mīmāṃsaka,
[in reference to] the non-momentary.
If the Mīmāṃsaka were a perceiver of the Omniscient One— who is the direct witness of all that is not seen—
then the Mīmāṃsaka would have to accept the existence of the Omniscient One.
Indeed, there would be a lack of purpose [for the inference].
For if someone were a perceiver of the non-momentary, would he perceive it through sensory cognition? That is not possible, because that [sensory cognition] has only the present as its object.

Now, [it might be argued that it is known] through inference; that is not so, because [the object] is absent when that [inference] is absent, and it is not from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If this is asked, how is it understood that all sensory cognition has only the present as its object?
Regarding sensory cognition...

In the absence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it might be thought: "All sensory cognition has a present object as its domain because that is its nature. [If this were so,] one could also say: "The Sugata is not omniscient, nor is he free from passion, because he is a human being, like a man on the street. Now, even if there is no distinction in being a human being and so forth, if someone is postulated to be omniscient, what contradiction would there be if sensory cognition also perceived some single object persisting through the three times, by virtue of which the non-momentariness of all things would be established? That is not so; for momentariness is not negated by non-perception.

Only the deficiency of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāvaikalya*) remains; yet, since that too has not been demonstrated, it is unestablished (*asiddha*) according to the logic already stated. If it is argued: "Causal efficiency is pervaded by momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*); and because of contradiction, that [momentariness], when excluded from the non-momentary, excludes itself along with that [efficiency]; and that [efficiency] is the very essence [of the thing]," to this he replies: "In the absence of the establishment of pervasion, the pervasion of causal efficiency by momentariness is not established"—that is, in the absence of its proof, it is not established by the aforementioned method.
Momentariness is that very capacity; thus, it is redundant here to write "causal efficiency" twice.
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "as much as" (*yāvān*), etc.

Here, the opponent says: "The Buddhist does not claim that the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) for anyone by anything occurs from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), but rather from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*); and conventional reality is the non-occurrence of critical inquiry. To this he replies: "By the unexamined," etc. This means: by a nature (*ātman*) or essence (*svabhāva*) that is unexamined—that is, incapable of withstanding inquiry—and which is imagined through conventional reality. The phrase "not by its own nature" (*nātmanā*) expresses dissatisfaction [with the opponent's view]. Thus, the Buddhist establishes the "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), or the logical bond (*pratibandha*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*). This is a sarcastic remark [implying] that such a logical bond is poorly established.
The intended meaning is that the same would apply to the word and its object as well.
If it is argued that their establishment occurs through inference, he says in response: "In the postulation of such an inference," which is the sense of the phrase.
If it is argued that their establishment occurs because of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), he says in response: "By way of momentariness," and so forth.
Then it was established: "If a logical mark (liṅga) were not established as a necessary concomitance (pratibandha) in its entirety, then even a word would be a [valid] mark.
To this very point, the Buddhist states another argument, beginning with "immediately following" (samanantaram), and so forth.
Immediately thereafter, one might propose another restriction as the cause for the presentation of its own nature [in cognition], namely that cognitions are restricted to their respective objects.

Even though there exists a relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*), because the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is not made an object, it is logical that the restriction is such that whatever cause is restricted to a particular object is precisely what makes that object its domain. Thus, the restriction is established.
This [distinction] is ultimate (pāramārthika) even with respect to the word, the cognition, and the object of cognition, because it is impossible to negate it.

Now, is this not the very point already stated by the words, "And this is not an absolute rule; the validity of cognitions everywhere arises solely from their connection with the object"? Why then is it stated again? Some say it is for the sake of a summary (upasaṃhāra); others say it is not so, because of a different interpretation.

"Immediately preceding" (*samanantaram*) does not refer to the material cause (*upādāna-jñāna*), because that has already been explained; rather, it refers to something similar—namely, blue—which is like the cognition of the form of blue, and which is "immediately preceding," meaning proximate and prior. What kind of thing is it? He says: "the cause by the conferring of its own nature. It is the cause by means of conferring its own nature; thus, even though it is not the [direct] material cause, it is its material cause. For example, for Devadatta’s cognition of blue, everything blue that exists in the immediately preceding moment and all that is immediately preceding is such.
What is it? He says: "unknowable," meaning not determinable by perception, invisible, and existing in the present; this is the meaning.
For instance—in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which occurs through the principle of "I-am-ness," cognition is perceived as apprehending a jar even though it does not possess the form of the jar.

Therefore, as for what was stated—that such an apprehender is not perceived apart from the blue [object], the primary [subject], and so forth—that is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). What, then, could one do about that? To this he says: one should declare another connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya*) for cognitions; [a connection] restricted to each respective object, fixed for every single object.

For just as when something like a *sālūka* (a type of mushroom) arises specifically from cow dung and the like, even though they are dissimilar, it indicates that capacity resides in that very [cow dung] and not in everything;

for one cannot say in that case that "everything of a different class is its cause" or "nothing at all is," because such a claim is contradicted by experience (*pratīti*). In the same way, since a specific object such as a jar is perceived as arising from a specific, simultaneous, and restricted cognition—even though they are dissimilar—it suggests that the power to grasp itself resides in that very [cognition].

As for what was stated— that the capacity of a cause is inferred from the observation of its restricted effect, but that effect of the capacity is not [inferred] because it is beyond the senses, and that there would be mutual dependence in inferring one from the other— that has been refuted by this very point: because the inference of another necessary connection (pratibandha) arises precisely from the apprehension of a restricted present object.
The commentators [explain] by means of a sentence,
[and] by means of a word.
And just as there is no consciousness other than pleasure and so forth, so too it is inferred that there is none other than blue and so forth— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 409.

By this, the following point is also considered: since pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) is undifferentiated everywhere, it would follow that everyone is omniscient; however, this is refuted by the fact that we perceive the observation of restricted objects.
Now, if the observation of an object were a property of the object—just like blueness and so forth—how could it possibly belong to the object?

If it is argued that, by this same reasoning, it is considered not to be a property of either [the subject or the object], it is replied: if the production of an effect were a property of the effect, such as blueness and so forth, then everything would be the cause of some effect.

For just as its blueness belongs not to one person alone but to everyone, so too its being produced belongs only to that by which it is produced; this is the same in other cases if it is a property of the cause. If [the universal] were a property of the object, there would be the same consequence as in the case of the perception of the object; by this, its being a property of both is rejected; and its being a property of neither is explained by the refutation of that [opponent's] position.

Now, if the relation of cause and effect is not accepted in any case at all, what is it that is accepted? If you say it is "mere self-awareness" (*svasaṃvedanamātra*), this too is exactly the same [as the previous position]. For instance, just as the nature of being a cognition of blue applies to all cognitions, so too would your awareness of it be experienced by everyone alike; thus, it would be cognized by all. The conceptualization of a distinction would apply equally to the object as well. If, then, another cognition is not accepted, what would be the result? If you say it is a non-duality consisting in the appearance of a single individual entity, to this he replies: because that is impossible even in the appearance of a jar and so forth, which appear as if they were objects of measurement.

If it is argued that when the jar and its cognition appear simultaneously, they are restricted to being mere self-awareness (*svarūpa-saṃvedana*), why would they not be restricted to being awareness of each other’s forms (*pararūpa-saṃvedana*), given that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is unrestrained? Furthermore, if identity were to result from simultaneous appearance, then a nimba tree and a mango tree appearing together would have to possess either bitterness or sweetness [respectively]. If, on the other hand, identity does not follow from simultaneous appearance but rather from appearing in such a manner [as identical], then the jar and its cognition do not share a single nature of awareness, since they manifest as the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). Enough of this excessive proliferation.
Therefore, the following remains: "One might state another obstacle for those whose intellects are fixed upon opposing objects" (sapīti)—this is redundant here;
"miti" means cognition (*saṃvedana*), and "sa" [in sapīti] means "like that," i.e., like cognition. This is the meaning.
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "those two, namely identity and origination," etc.

"Those two" refers to identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*); these two constitute the relationship. Even when that [relationship] is accepted, the meaning is that because there is no making of an object out of the immediate (*anantara*), i.e., the contiguous (*avyavahita*), similar (*sadṛśa*) cognition which is the cause, and because there is the making of an object out of the dissimilar (*asadṛśa*) present [cognition], what follows? To this he says: "in the cause," etc.
Demonstrating that very point, he says: "In which," and so forth.

In which object of cognition (*prameya*), whatever *mati-jñāna*—that is, the awareness of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so on—or *śruta-jñāna* there may be, what is its nature? To this he says: "For the sake of which," and so forth.

"That very cognition takes that very object as its domain"—this logical connection holds; yet, how can that same ultimate connection exist even between the word-cognition and its object of knowledge (the *prameya*)? He says: "Because it is impossible to deny."

Having raised the objection that this reason is unestablished (*asiddhatā*) by means of the first three quarters [of the verse], he states the rebuttal with the fourth quarter: "Because they would be fruitless" (*aphalatvāt*), and so forth.
Because they would be fruitless and because of incapacity, words would not be conventionally designated (*saṅketita*) upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Since it is said that "the word 'cow' is not conventionally designated," this is a proof of non-conclusiveness (*anekāntasādhana*). || 22 ||

Words do not convey that which has not been subjected to convention (*saṅketa*). Furthermore, one who establishes a convention, or one who desires to understand from it, must act or understand with a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in mind. Nor can the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself be the object of convention, for it does not persist until the time of practical usage (*vyavahārakāla*). Moreover, it is impossible to establish a convention regarding a word and its referent if they have not been apprehended; nor is it possible once they have been apprehended, because they are apprehended by different sense faculties. Thus, a convention cannot be made with respect to a particular characteristic.
Since the connection "this is that" is impossible without mental conceptualization,

and because [the universal] is not established by mental conceptualization either, there can be no convention even for a universal; for it does not appear in perception, and even if it existed, it would lack the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

The convention (*saṅketa*) has that exclusion (*apoha*) as its object; the verbal cognition having that as its object, through the power of delusion, unifies the perceived and the conceptualized and engages the person in worldly transaction. How can this [exclusion], which consists of the exclusion of non-causes and non-effects of what is conventionally designated and possesses the nature of performing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), be exclusively non-existent? For the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Follower of the Buddha) is wise in such a way that he relies upon the purposeful action performed by things like a sky-flower, yet does not rely upon their actual ontological reality (*bhāvatattva*). Thus says the Tathāgata-prajña.
Since consciousness cannot function without a transformation that is either identical to or different from itself, there can be no fixed rule regarding the relationship between cause and effect;
if such a rule were possible, why would it not also exist externally?
Furthermore, words and sounds would not be subject to conventional designation.
Where? In the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Why? He says: because of the fruitlessness of making a convention; that is, because of the absence of a result.
For instance, since the object of a convention is already the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no utility for a convention in that regard.
Because that [convention] is absent elsewhere,
they would not establish a convention there for this reason either; thus he says, "and because of incapacity," where the word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the reasons.

For example, there can be no convention (*saṅketa*) regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of word and object when they are not yet cognized, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

nor can it be established when they are already cognized by sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*), because such perception lacks the capacity for the reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*) that "this is the denotatum" or "this is the denoter";
nor can it be established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since its object is not a real entity (*avastuviṣaya*).

If it is argued that words do not denote an un-conventionalized object, such that people would not agree upon it there; to this he replies: "They do not speak of what is un-conventionalized," because otherwise the instruction of others would be rendered futile regarding objects beyond the scope of perception.
Because there is no conventional usage [for such a compound],
this is another explanation of the sensory cognition: that even without the word "ca" (and), the conjunction of reasons is understood.
The word "ca" (and) is used out of its usual sequence and should be understood immediately after the term "svalakṣaṇe" (in the particular characteristic). It serves to aggregate what has been stated;
therefore, the meaning is this: words would not be conventionally designated not only for the particular characteristic, but also for the universal (sāmānya).
Why? He says: because of the fruitlessness of speech in that regard.

For even a universal (sāmānya) expressed by a word is not capable of performing purposeful action (arthakriyā), such as carrying a load and so forth, because it would follow that the conceptualization of particulars (viśeṣa) is futile.
He states another reason: "due to incapacity" (aśakteḥ), because it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (saṅketa) for it, and because it is not an object of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Now, if the view is held that from the word the universal is understood, and from that, the particular is also understood; to this he says: "they do not say [it is] un-conventionalized" (asaṅketitaṃ vāhuḥ na).

This is its meaning: that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in which no conventional universal (*saṅketita-sāmānya*) exists is "non-conventional"; nor do words express it, for there is no universal in that [particular] by means of which activity toward a specific object could occur. To this, he states the reply: what is thus asserted by the opponent is a proof of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).

Regarding the universal (*sāmānya*), he states the meaning of the verse beginning with "Not for the Mīmāṃsaka" (*na hi*): "For words do not denote that which has not been conventionally designated (*asaṅketita*); they denote that which has been conventionally designated (*saṅketita*). If this is argued, he says in response: "And the one who establishes the convention (*saṅketakārī*), or the one who desires to understand it (*pratipitsu*)—that is, one who wishes to grasp the convention from that [word]—is capable of acting or understanding only by aiming at causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), otherwise there would be the consequence of acting without foresight (*aprekṣākāritā*)."
If it is argued that this is the case for both [the particular and the universal], he says here: "It is the particular itself," and so forth.
If it is argued that the convention (*saṅketa*) applies to that very [particular], he says here: "And not... and so forth.
Why? To this he says: "The convention," and so forth.

If it is argued that there is the comprehension of that which is not conventionally designated because the characteristic of the time of linguistic usage is itself not conventionally designated; to this he replies with the words "again," etc., because it is impossible to comprehend the meaning of a word that is not conventionally designated after a convention has already been established; otherwise, one would have the cognition of a horse from the word "cow."
By this, it is explained that because it is fruitless,
[the teaching] is unfit for comprehension by either the recipient or the instructor.
To explain the second reason, he says: "And this [is not so]," and so forth.
Why? To this he replies: "Because a convention is impossible for word and object when they have not been made objects of cognition.
If it is argued that it would be possible if they have been made objects of cognition, to this he replies: "And because it is impossible even when they have been made objects of cognition."
Of what nature are they? He says: "of those perceivable by different sense organs," because they are perceivable by different sense organs;

for the cognition of the auditory organ terminates in sound alone, while the cognition of the visual organ and others terminates in form and so forth, and since they do not take each other's objects, there can be no synthesis such as "this belongs to that," just as in the case of different mental continua (*santāna*).

From what, then, does convention arise? To this he says: because connection is impossible without mental conceptualization (*manovikalpa*), and because it is impossible to establish a relationship such as "this belongs to that" [without it], the meaning is that it arises from mental conceptualization alone.

If it is argued, "Let it be so from that very source"; to this he replies with the words "And in mental conceptualization," etc., [stating] that this convention cannot be established with respect to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Summarizing, he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth;
the meaning is that when there is no mutual objectification, [it occurs] through mental consciousness alone.
Explaining the second point, he says: "Not only with respect to a particular (svalakṣaṇa), but even with respect to a universal (sāmānya) entity, there is certainly no convention;

why? He says: because that universal does not appear in perception—that is, in sensory cognition—and for this reason, being incapable [of causal efficiency], even though it exists and is present, it lacks the capacity for purposeful action (arthakriyā); therefore, there is no convention even with respect to a universal."
Since this is so, therefore convention has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object.
If it is asked, "Even in that case, how does activity [of the mind] toward the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) occur from the word?"—to this he says: "That which has that as its object," and so forth.
That exclusion is the object of the verbal cognition; thus it is so described.
What does that [subject] do? He says: "It employs the person in worldly transactions.
Having done what? He says: "The visible," and so forth.

The "visible" is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) is the form of verbal cognition. Having unified these two—[the visible and the conceptual]—it acts.
Why? He says: "by the power of delusion.
To this he gives the answer: "of this," and so forth.
How can even this exclusion (*vyapoha*) possess the state of being exclusively non-existent, or the state of being exclusively formless (*nīrūpa*)?

Of what kind [is the object]? It is that which effects the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, of what kind? He says: "that which has the exclusion of those things which are not its cause or effect," and so forth. Those things which are considered heterogeneous and for which that intended cause-and-effect relationship does not exist are "those which do not have that as their cause or effect" (*atatkāryakāraṇa*). From them, there is an exclusion (*vyapoha*); this is the exclusion of those designated things which do not have that as their cause or effect, such as a fragment of a pot and so on. That which has this as its single form is [the object]. Thus [he means].
Nevertheless, he states the refutation regarding the extreme position of non-existence: "of the sky-flower," and so forth.
Furthermore, even while treating *apoha* as the object [of negation], he mocks the Buddhist with the words: "that which is produced by that," and so forth.

He relies upon the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) produced by that [exclusion], which consists of removal, but he does not rely upon the reality of its nature—that is, the non-existent form of that exclusion.

Who is he? To this he says: "one whose wisdom is directed toward the Tathāgata. This means one who possesses wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding the Tathāgata, the Sugata; such is the description. Alternatively, it should be understood as: "one whose wisdom has gone—that is, been destroyed—in that manner," and for this very reason, he is "dear to the gods" (*devānāṃpriyaḥ*).
If it is asked, "From where then does his reality as an entity derive?", he says here: "Of consciousness," and so forth.

Without that transformation of consciousness—which is both non-identical to the object by virtue of its being blue and distinct from it by virtue of its being non-insentient—it would be impossible for a person engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*)—this term is to be supplied—to proceed either through perception and other means, or through the mode of determining the identity between the perceived and the attained.

While saṃsāra proceeds, there is the occurrence of successive appearances of fire and so forth due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of preceding fire and so forth; since that [succession] would otherwise be impossible, what would be the basis for it? To this he says: "Similar," and so forth.

For instance, between two cognitions of preceding and succeeding fire—which stand in the relation of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*)—there is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) that is similar in its luminosity, and another that is different by virtue of the suitability of the material cause and its effect. Even in the Vijñānavāda, such a similar transformation does not constitute a fixed rule of causal relationship.

If it is argued that non-duality is discarded because consciousness (*saṃvit*) undergoes transformation, whereas the object does not—here he replies: "In the event of its occurrence" (meaning) in the event of the occurrence of a corresponding transformation of consciousness—the word "consciousness" (*saṃvidaḥ*) carries over [from the previous context]. Why then would there not also be such a transformation externally?
To say "it is not so" is meaningless.

Regarding what has been stated by the opponent—that cognition is not insentient while the object is insentient, and that it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) with respect to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—he states the refutation of that point: "He says [it is] 'inexpressible' (*aśakyasamaya*);
words express that which has been conventionally designated (*saṅketita*), for that is remembered as being for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*)."
At that time, there is no convention regarding the particular characteristic; therefore, it does not exist therein— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.91.
Form is incapable of being conventionally designated, just as objects do not possess otherness; form is incapable of being seen, just as objects do not possess otherness.

Just as the nature of an object is such, so too it is impossible to see it, because the cause is not an object of perception due to the difference in time and because of the perception of a similar form.
In the determination of its objective domain, that universal (*sāmānya*) would have to be the object in its entirety;
