yet this perception does not merely imitate the form of its own cause, for sometimes it also imitates the form of its own material cause (*upādāna*), since a certain degree of similarity between the material cause of its own cause and other things cannot be ruled out, and because imitation in every respect is impossible.

Because there is no direct production [of the cognition] from that [object], it is incorrect to say that the object does not appear [in the cognition]; for otherwise, it would follow that cognitions such as dreams are non-erroneous.
What is meant by "that in which a convention (saṃketa) is impossible"? It means its nature (rūpa), that is, its intrinsic character (svabhāva).
Of what [objects]? He says: "of objects" (*arthānām*). In what manner? By the manner just described.

Of what nature [is that form]? It is "not shared by others" (*ananyabhāk*), meaning unique and impossible to perceive—a form characterized by momentary atoms (*kṣaṇika-paramāṇu-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, having already deliberated on the phrase "the form not shared by others" regarding objects, he explains the verse, saying: "just like the form of the object," and so forth.
Why is it impossible to perceive in that very same way? To this he says: "Because of perception," and so forth.
If it is argued that the cause must be an object [of perception], he replies here: because even the cause is not an object of perception.
Why? He says: because of the difference in time; by excluding the time of perception, the time of the object is established.
This should be applied similarly elsewhere as well, and for the opponent, there can be no relationship of grasped and grasper across a difference in time.

If it is argued that "it is the grasper of that [object] because it imitates its form," to this he replies: "When there is a similar [form]," and so forth. When the determination of making something an object occurs through the perception of a form of cognition that is similar to that object, the word "that" (tat) refers to the object.
The connection is as follows: "the vision would have as its object that generality"—namely, the generality of a similar transformation—both externally and internally in its entirety.
The meaning is that, as in the case of knowledge and the object of knowledge, it is impossible to negate their commonality elsewhere;
by this, the latter part of the verse has been explained, while the former part was not, because it is easy to understand. Knowledge...
Of the object, by means of that word "tat" (that),
[there is the cognition] of the universal consisting in a similar transformation.

And as for what was further stated—that since connection is impossible without mental conceptualization (*manovikalpa*), and because the appearance of an object vanishes when there is no mental conceptualization—the author replies with the words "Nor is this," and so forth.
Here, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of *api* (also); it is displaced from its original position and should be understood immediately after the word *dṛṣṭiḥ* (perception).

This is the meaning: perception is not only mental conceptualization; this [perception] which is accepted by the opponent as non-conceptual (*avikalpikā*) does not arise from its own cause alone. By the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*), even though it is a general term, the specific "objective cause" (*ālambanakāraṇa*) is intended due to the context.
From its own term [the word *svabhāva*], one asks: why does it imitate the nature of the immediately preceding cause? To this he says: "In some cases," and so forth.

In some instances, such as with a white conch-shell and the like, it imitates the form of its own material cause (*upādāna*), that is, its immediate antecedent cause, by itself and not through a lineage of transmission. Not only does it not fail to imitate it; for in those cases, each subsequent cognition of yellow imitates the form of each preceding cognition of yellow, and not that of the external object, because that object lacks such a form.

The intended meaning is as follows: since it is observed that mental conceptualization (*manovikalpa*) functions even in the absence of an object in certain cases, if there were a cessation of the appearance of real entities (*vastu-pratibhāsa-pratyastamaya*) in all such instances, then because even perception (*dṛṣṭi*) would lack the imitation of the form of an object (*arthākārānukaraṇa*), there would be a cessation of the appearance of all real entities. Thus, the phrase "even in some cases" (*kvacit*) applies here as well to the imitation of the form of its own causal material (*svakāraṇopādāna*).

In some cases, when rapid rotation or the like is perceived, the immediate preceding moment is the cause of that perception in the subsequent moment; and there is a dual compound (dvandvaikavadbhāva) referring to both that [moment] and its direct or indirect material cause (*upādāna*). If it is argued that even if it were to imitate the form of those two, the cognition would not appear as a single wheel-form by imitating the form of its own cause alone—since that would lead to the undesirable consequence [of such a cognition] occurring at all times—then how can there be an imitation of a form belonging to a different time? For if that were so, how could there be an imitation of a form belonging to a different location, whereby a dense and unitary cognition would arise regarding hairs that are actually distant and sparse?

Now, if it is argued that as many successive visual perceptions as there are moments of the firebrand's whirling are postulated, and that the cognition of a wheel—like [the cognition] of another continuum—is not a sensory perception but rather mental, we say: no; because it is vividly clear, like the vision of two moons.
Therefore, it also imitates the form of its own material cause.
The connection is that "appropriation" is understood from the context; [this refers] to its cognition by the mind.
The thought might then arise that the phrase "the immediately subsequent moment" is redundant here;
for in that case, there would be a mere imitation of luminosity, not an imitation of every aspect of its form. To this, he says in a single place: "in some way," and so forth.

Since similarity (*sārūpya*), which consists in some degree of luminosity alone and not in every other aspect, cannot be excluded even from that cognition which is claimed to be perception (*pratyakṣa*), this has already been established.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "In every way," and so forth.

If [the opponent argues that] there is imitation even in the form of oneness and so forth by means of the very form of blue, then there would be imitation in every respect; this is because it is impossible for that [form] to have its own cause as its [own] cause, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between cause and effect. Now, the opponent might say—even though he has been refuted—“Cognition imitates the form of only that which is directly perceived, not that of anything else. To this, [the author] says: “Directly,” and so forth.

Since there is no production from its own material cause without an intervening [obstruction], it is incorrect to say that it does not manifest that [cause]—that is, it does not manifest its own material cause.
Why? He says: "from its own [cause]," and so forth;
here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the disturbances of desire, grief, and the like are included.
For in that case, the object is not the direct cause of the cognition, because it would otherwise follow that the cognition is non-erroneous;

nor is the cognition itself possessed of the form of that object, since the appearance of the object is perceived even from a cognition possessing that form which has been separated by a long period of time.

If it is argued that the object itself is the material cause (upādāna) of that cognition, then an object separated by time would likewise be the cause of its cognition; thus, cognitions such as dreams would not consist of mere mental impressions (vāsanā).
And how could knowledge such as that of *timira* (visual impairment) be without an object for one who speaks thus? For even in that case, it is possible for a distant object to be the cause;

since there is no object in immediate proximity, if [the cognition] were objectless, why would it not also be without a material cause (*anupādāna*), due to the absence of an immediately preceding material cause? [The Buddhist:
In that case, the cause for dreams and so forth is the cognition of dreams and so forth.

It might be argued as follows: "Just as redness appears in the fruit from a cotton plant-series (kārpāsasantāna) that has acquired a potency through the application of lac-dye to its flowers—even though there occurs in the interval a dissimilar blue leaf and so forth—so too, from a mental continuum (cittasantāna) that has acquired a potency through the cognition of blue and so forth, there arises in a dream the cognition of blue and so forth, even when there is a dissimilar intervening consciousness. To this, [the author] raises the objection against the opponent's view with the words "Because of error" (bhrānteḥ), etc., [arguing]: If in that case also a cause of a different class (bhinnajātīya) which has been infused with a latent impression (vāsanā) by a cognition of the same class were the material cause (upādānakāraṇa), then the [dream-cognition] would not necessarily replicate the form of the immediate cause, since it would be replicating even that which is separated [in time].

If it is argued that there is no fault in [the claim that] the self is perceived even in dreams and the like due to delusion, then how could there be non-delusion elsewhere as well? Since there is no distinction between the existent and the non-existent, and because [perception] is characterized by grasping both that and its opposite, how is it not indeed a fault that this characteristic deviates from its definition? This is truly strange.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the error in dreams and the like has a cause, and thus the undesirable consequence of the non-appearance of objects does not apply—on the grounds that even what is not a direct cause imitates the form [of the object]—the response to this is stated: "How," and so forth. How could there be non-error for the Buddhist even in other cases, such as waking cognition? Why? He says: "Of the self," and so forth, meaning of the self's own nature (*svarūpa*).
Of what kind [is it]? Of that which exists;

of what? Of an object such as a jar, etc., which is non-existent. Since there is no distinction in the cognition [of them], and because the manifestation is identical in both cases, how can there be error in one case and not the other?
He states the conclusion regarding dreams and so forth: "Therefore," and so on.

Since this is the case, therefore—because its characteristic is the non-apprehension of that [object]—there is no apprehension of that [object]; because of the state of being that which has such a characteristic, for that very reason, there is in any way only a defect in another [theory].

"Under what conditions? He replies: "Even when there is no deviation from the [perceived] characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and even when there is similarity in its arising (*tadutpatti-sārūpya*), the perception of an external object (*bahir-artha-darśana*) [occurs]; yet, even when that [similarity] deviates, [the perception occurs]—this is strange. By this, he demonstrates that for the Sautrāntika, every perception consists of both error and non-error. Regarding the claim that "that which is directly perceived imitates the form of that very [external object]," he states the following refutation: "In the imitation of that form," and so forth.

The reason for the imitation of that form is its direct birth from it, not because of an invariable concomitance with transformation, as in the case of the forms of the embryo, the father, and so forth.
Indeed, the embryo, though produced directly from him, does not imitate the form of the father.

Because there is no direct production [of the cognition], it is rather a transformation (*pariṇāma*) characterized by the imitation of that form, since the imitation of the forms of the grandfather and so forth is logically established.

Thus, just like perception, memory, recognition, inference, and so forth, because they imitate past objects, the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) applies to the real entity (*vastu*), and not to the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because the latter is formless like a sky-flower;
for the existence of the entity resides only in the transformation of that very entity, without contradiction.

Furthermore, because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), convention (*saṅketa*) is fruitful only with respect to that [particular], and not elsewhere, since even at the time of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), that [efficiency] exists there and not otherwise;
for otherwise, even perception and inference would be useless,
as their object cannot be something that is not a cause, and a cause cannot possibly exist at the time of practical activity without falling into the error of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatā*).

If the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) were to arise from a non-entity (*avastu*)—a unity of the perceived and the attainable constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*)—then what use would there be for the perception of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? Even if that [particular] were its cause... why is it not simply the state of being born directly from that intended [object], when its intended form is being replicated? He says: "Because of the inseparable connection with transformation (*pariṇāma*), in the replication of that form."
He states an illustration— beginning with "in the womb"—
and explains the meaning of the verse beginning with "the form of the father," by which he demonstrates that the effect imitates the form of its remote cause.

If it is argued that a child is not the direct offspring of the father because [the child] arises from semen and so forth, and therefore even for that [semen], there is a resemblance to its own form; to this he says: "Directly," etc. Indeed, the embryo, which is the union of semen and blood, does not resemble the form of the father.
"What is its nature? he asks, and says: "That which has a direct origination from that [the first], and also a direct origination from that [the second].
To explain the second illustration, he says: "Because of not originating directly," and so forth; this has already been explained.

If that [cause] does not directly produce the birth of the cognition by imparting its form, what then would it be? To this he says: "In that way," even when the effect is separated [from the cause], transformation (*pariṇāma*) itself—in the manner of imparting that form—is the indicator that the cognition takes on the form of the intended object, characterized by its imitation of that form;
for we observe that the imitation of the form of a grandfather and so forth is possible.
Even if this be so, what is established regarding the matter at hand? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.

Therefore, by that same manner of imitating the forms of their causes, and because perception—as well as memory, recognition, inference, and so forth—imitates past objects due to their causal nature, the convention (*saṅketa*) pertains to the real entity (*vastu*), and not to its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Why? He says: "Because exclusion is formless (*nīrūpa*)," like a sky-flower; this is well said. If it is asked, "Since that [exclusion] exists as a positive entity (*bhāva*) among the things to be excluded (*apohya-vastu*), how can it be formless? To this he replies: "The entity," and so forth.

That [cognition] is both the real entity (*vastu*) and its transformation (*pariṇāma*), which consists in similarity; this is because it exists in that very entity, such as a sugar-candy and so forth, and not in the "exclusion" (*apoha*) or other constructs imagined by proponents of extremist doctrines—this is the meaning of the particle *eva*.
Why is this so? He says: "Because there is no contradiction," meaning because there is an absence of sublation by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He states another proof: "Causal efficiency," and so forth.

The meaning is this: only in that very case of similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*) is convention (*saṅketa*) fruitful, because it exists even at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahārakāla*); elsewhere it is not fruitful, for the opposite is true. Furthermore, as for what was said: "Words express that which has been conventionally designated; that [designation] is remembered for the sake of usage. At that time, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist; therefore, convention does not apply to it."
Regarding this, he says in the *Pravāha* (3.91): "Otherwise," and so forth.

In another way, by means of the absence of convention regarding an object, not only is verbal expression devoid of meaning and fruitless, but even perception and inference would be so. He says this very thing: for (*hi*) because the object of those two—perception and inference—is not a non-cause, but rather precisely a cause. If it is argued that this is stated from the perspective of others; to this he replies: at the time of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), a cause is simply not possible, because that would entail the fallacy of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatā*).

For instance: according to the earlier Buddhists (*pūrvasaugata*), a cause exists at a prior time, and even a yogi is unable to engage with it there, nor can he do so with respect to the present; because that [present] is not a cause, it is not an object for him.
Nevertheless, one would not be acting on the basis of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the activity;
nor is there the attainment of that very object when it is spatially distinct,
for fire is not attained at the very moment it is inferred from smoke.

If it is argued that there is no engagement [with the future object], we reply: that is not a valid reason, because just as with a conventional designation, there is engagement with what is similar to it in the future;

thus, there is engagement even with that [future object], just as there is engagement with Yajñadatta when he resembles Devadatta. If it is then argued that engagement with what resembles the designated object must be either an error or a metaphorical usage, [we reply] that the same applies to perception and other means of knowledge regarding the future.

If it is argued that it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely because it is an error, then let the word (*śabda*) also be so; and in that case, how could there be two distinct means of knowledge? Furthermore, [it is not the case that they are distinct] because the objects at the time of the convention and at the time of its practical application belong to different continua (*saṃtāna*); for there is no absolute difference between the continua, since both the convention and the practical application are observed within the single continuum of Devadatta.

Because of its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), comparison (*tulanā*)—which consists in the existence of the object and so forth—is the proof of that which possesses a form (*sākāra*). (Nyāyaviniścaya 1)
"Words express that which is conventionally designated; this [designation] is remembered for the sake of practical usage.
At that time, the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not exist; therefore, there is no convention with respect to it. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.91)
From the Buddhist perspective,
there is no object that is without a cause— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* 3.406.
And how can an object be without a cause? [The *Pravāha-vāda* states:
"An object is not without a cause"—[the *Manorathottara* 2.257].
The term "prior" (pūrva) is meaningless,
because that which exists at a prior time is not an object of cognition.
If it were to function with respect to what is similar,
then perception would be erroneous.
Furthermore, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Moreover, how is the determination of the single continuum (*ekasantānatā*) between the two causes—namely, the [object] reached and the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—established? If it is argued that this is due to similarity (*sādṵya*), we say no, because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

If it is argued that this is due to the relation of cause and effect (*hetuphalabhāva*) as determined by twins (*yamalaka*), we say no, because of deviation in the case of the cognitions of the Sugata and others.

Furthermore, if the preceding [moment] were the cause, there would be a suspicion that something else similar to it might be present due to some proximity; thus, this [definition] would be difficult to understand, for it is not the case that only the immediate effect or its similar [successor] is the cause, since otherwise everything of that kind would result in being a cause.
Therefore, it is well said: "At the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), a cause does not exist at all."

The intended meaning is that when activity occurs, there is a determination of the identity of a single continuum between that very object perceived through perception and other means—which serves as its own cause—and that which is to be attained by it;
this is the sense of "due to similarity" when the causal relationship exists.
The point is that the qualification "due to the relation of cause and effect" should be added to the reason "due to similarity."

When the Sugata knows the cognition of an ordinary person, then by means of that Sugata-cognition, there exists a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) with the cognition of the ordinary person insofar as it is its object; furthermore, since similarity (*sādṛśya*) also exists by virtue of both being of the nature of cognition, the implication is that the two would belong to a single continuum (*ekasantānatva*). Consequently, the doubt does not cease: "Was the taste not previously present, yet arising from that [cognition], could it perhaps be something else, or could it be a similar taste belonging to a different continuum?"

The cause of those two [the cognition and the word] arises one after another at that very time when the body exists. If even for a word the object existing at the time of linguistic usage is the cause, what is the fault? If it is asked, "How can something that occurs long afterwards be a cause?", [we reply: how is it that death and the like, being of such a nature, are the cause of omens (*ariṣṭa*) and so forth, by which the inference from them is born from the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅga*)? If it is asked, "How can something separated by space, such as hell and the like, be the cause of a word in another location?", it has been said in this regard: "How is it, for you too, that the dream-body [arises] in another location from the sleeping body? Or how is there awakening from the previous consciousness of one who has been led to another location from sleep? etc.
Prajñākara is a proponent of the theory of real causes, [asserting that] death omens and the like exist long before they manifest.

If it is argued that the word arises from some object within the waking consciousness of a person, and that in the absence of such an object it would not exist, yet it does exist otherwise; it is replied: if the word were born from a perceptible object that could be reached, how could it arise in a circle of mirage rays? For in that case, there is no water to be reached for bathing or other purposes.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is erroneous, [we reply: the same applies elsewhere; there is one and the same word for both the existence and non-existence of the object. Why is this? Because of the commitment [to the convention]. For this very reason, there would be one and the same appearance of water for both the presence and absence of effective action upon reaching it; yet the conventional user does not conceive of it so. Thus, the situation is the same in both cases.
Therefore, there is nothing at all for this [consciousness],
even in the absence of an object, even in the absence of an object.
The cognition of water would be a future erroneous cognition.
How can a single word be employed [in this way]?

If it is argued that there is indeed a single determination (*ekavyavasāya*) between the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the attainable (*prāpya*), and that this exists even at the time of the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of the perceived; to this he replies with the words beginning "vikalpa" (conceptual construction), etc.:

the identity between the perceived and the attainable is constructed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, [the word is applied] on account of that which is constructed by conceptual construction.

Of what kind [is this cause]? It is from a non-entity (*avastu*). If the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) were admitted [to arise] from such a thing, where would the perception of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) be of any use? Nowhere at all, because activity always occurs solely from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, how can one be composed who, while desiring conceptual construction to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that which arises through direct perception by way of determining the identity between the perceived and the attained, nevertheless desires it to be non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) during repeated practice?

Furthermore, if there is a complete superimposition (*āropa*) of the object to be attained onto the perceived object from some source, how could there be activity directed toward that [perceived object] alone, such that its practical application (*vyavahāra*) might be easily established? Since the perceived object would be as remote (*parokṣatā*) as the object to be attained, there would be that very same absence of activity;
for what is superimposed upon a remote thing does not become otherwise in any way, nor is the opponent’s objection undesirable.

Now, if it is argued that non-conceptual [perception] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause of conceptualization, to this he replies: "Even though it is its cause," and so forth.
Furthermore, this vision does not merely imitate the form of its own cause;
rather, it is simply the visible object itself.
Since there is nothing whatsoever worthy of being attained, even that which is visible is entirely a superimposition.
If it is argued that this is a matter of direct perception,
he states yet another argument: "Cognition [is] by means of blue," and so forth.
[Verse 26: "Knowledge, through its similarity with the blue, would manifest its own form; if it did not, then this [manifestation] would be entirely a false apprehension of other blue objects.

How can it be possible that this cognition, consisting of color and so forth, accepts absolute similarity with its own object, but not even with its causes or other blue objects? For the object itself, which possesses no distinct parts and is unique, must be the object of perception.
Or, because cognitions conform to the form of that [object], the word "only" (*eva*)—used for emphasis—is to be understood after the word "by the blue" (*nīlena*).

Thus, by the blue alone—that is, by the direct cause alone—the cognition would manifest its own similarity (*sārūpya*), which is its own form (*rūpa*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This would have to be in every respect, not merely through blueness, but also through momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) and so forth. If it were not so—if the cognition did not manifest the similarity of its own form to the blue, or if it manifested the form of other blues as being similar to the blue—this would be an exclusion of the other, an adherence to a dissimilar form (*virūpābhiniveśa*).

He states the meaning of the verse: This cognition, which is the object of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), is for the Sautrāntika either the external knowledge of a jar and so forth, or a reflection of external form and so on consisting of color and the like. It assumes an absolute similarity—that is, a resemblance in every aspect—with its own object (*svārtha*), which is its own direct cause, namely the specific [object] such as blue; it does not assume similarity with other blues.
Of what kind [are those others]? "Even of their causes and so forth.
By the word "that" (*tat*), the specific [object] such as blue, which is the object of the cognition itself, is referred to.

How could it be possible that the cause of those [cognitions]—namely, all other [objects] falling within their continuum, or others besides them—is also [the cause] of those [subsequent cognitions]? Not at all;
for, by virtue of such a possibility, the unique, non-common nature of the object would become the domain of perception—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Thus he thinks: it is certainly not said that cognition grasps the form of its own object like an heir grasping wealth.

And if that similarity with all blue objects consists solely in its similarity with its own object, then the worldly designation "Citra is a mimic of Mitrā" would not occur— this is the [objection] of the Yogācāra.

If it is argued that cognition is indeed perceived as assuming only the form of its own object and not that of other blue things, and therefore it is said [to be self-cognizing]—to this he replies: "having that form," and so on;
because cognitions conform to the forms of those other blue things.
Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Perception," and so forth.

Perception has as its object a universal (sāmānya) consisting of both existence and non-existence; likewise, memory, recognition, and conceptualization (vitarka)—the convention (saṅketa) regarding which [the universal] would not exist if that [universal] were absent. (27)

With respect to that which has the nature of both being and non-being, perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while in other cases there is recollection and so forth, because otherwise the linguistic usage [of those objects] would be inexplicable;
for conceptual constructions of word-meanings have that [reality] as their object,
and it is possible to establish a convention (*samaya*) therein, which is also fruitful, since such [a reality] has the three times as its object.

Otherwise, since purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) would be impossible, how could any worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) proceed from anything, such that its validity (*prāmāṇya*) might be established? For in the absence of purposeful action, that [validity] is absent.
[The author asks: "What is the nature of that perception, the cognition of the eye and so forth? To this, he says: "existent," and so on.

Knowledge (*vijñāna*) is real because it is apprehended by itself—according to the *Prakaraṇavārttika* (3.54), "apprehension (*upalambha*) is existence (*sattā*)"—whereas its causes, causes of those causes, and so forth, are unreal because they are not directly perceived. Thus, "real-and-unreal" (*sadasat*) refers to their form or nature (*rūpa*, *svabhāva*), which is neither a mere exclusion (*vyāvṛttimātra*) nor something distinct from them; and that universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*) is the object (*artha*) of which [the cognition], and thus it is so described.

The point is this: just as when an object is not seen, one cannot say that its blueness or other qualities have not been seen because a cognition similar to it is observed, so too, even when a spotted cow (*śāvaleyādi*) is not seen, because a fragment (*khaṇḍa*) similar to it is seen, let it be said that the universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of a similar transformation has been seen. Furthermore, by this [argument], the objection raised by Arcata and others—namely, "At the time of perceiving a single individual, since the others are not perceived, how can the universal residing in them be cognized through perception?"—is refuted.

"Let it be that perception has that [object] as its referent; what follows from that? To this he says: "In that manner, memory has as its object a universal (sāmānya) consisting of both existent and non-existent forms; likewise, recognition has that as its object, and so does deliberation (vitarka). And convention (saṅketa) pertains to that—[not to exclusion (apoha), but] to the real entity (vastu), provided that such a principle exists, and not when it does not. Explaining the verse here, he states: "With respect to a real entity whose nature consists of existence and non-existence, i.e., which is of the nature of both being and non-being, perception is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); elsewhere, memory and the rest are the means of valid cognition."
Why? He says: "Because its linguistic usage," and so forth.
This has already been explained: because the linguistic usage of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would otherwise be inexplicable.

Now, one might object: "Let direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be the means of valid cognition for that distinctness; however, is it not the word or the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from it that is the means of valid cognition there, since its object is something else? To this, he says: "The word," and so forth.

And the conceptualization of the word’s own meaning is not the conceptualization of Īśvara and so forth; for those two have that [the object] as their domain, since they have as their scope a reality consisting of both being and non-being.
Thus it has been said:
"In a reality whose nature consists of both being and non-being..."
Born of sound,
this [speech] instructs that "this is that very thing," through its connection with both existent and non-existent universals.

"If [the teaching] were not true, how could there be an instruction on the meaning of reality through false words? (Āptamīmāṃsā 1.110). What follows from this? He says: "Convention" (*samaya*) means a linguistic agreement; it can be established regarding an object whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence. Not only can it be established, but it is also fruitful.
Why is this so? He says: because such an object, consisting of both being and non-being, has the three times as its domain.
Why is this also so? He says: "otherwise," etc.;
for otherwise—in the manner of the absence of the object having the three times as its domain—the performance (kriyā) of the subsequent effect or of experience would be impossible.
What [is the consequence] of that? He says: "How," and so forth.

Since the engagement in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) proceeds from some form of perception or inference, how can there be validity—that is, the status of being a means of knowledge such as perception—for those who maintain extremist doctrines (*ekāntavādin*)?
[Objection: Even if that [engagement in practice] is untenable, what follows regarding its validity, such that it would not exist? To this he says: "Purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*), and so forth.

Having thus established that words have a convention regarding real entities and that they are effective therein because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is otherwise impossible, [the author] now addresses and refutes what was stated: "Words, being produced by the connection with the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), would indicate that very intention. He says, beginning with "of sentences" (*vākyānām*), etc., comparing it to: "The object which appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker’s activity..."
In that case, the validity of the word is not dependent upon the actual state of the object— *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.4.
If there were no distinction between sentences that express what the speaker intends,
there would be no established distinction between the true and the false, because both would appear as either real or unreal.

(28) In the case of sentences that indicate the speaker’s intention, without a distinction— that is, without their having reality as their object— the establishment of the true and the false is not possible, just as it is in the case of perception.

Since conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) consists exclusively of falsity, how could there be the attainment of truth through its conceptualization, by which a proponent might be victorious? For even one who experiences the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is mutually inclusive internally and externally at every moment, where else could there be [truth] except for the arising and activation of the knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa-karman*) in cases such as visual perception affected by cataracts? Furthermore, in the case of absolute non-continuity (*niranvaya-ekānta*), how could there be the cognition of error? It has been stated "of sentences" because words deviate from their referents or because they are useless for linguistic convention, and because sentences themselves are subject to error.
Of what kind are they? He says: "of those that express what is intended by the speaker," meaning those that express what is meant to be said.

By what means? He says: "without distinction," that is, in their entirety, just as the words of Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha possess the quality of expressing that [reality]. To this he replies: "the distinction between truth and falsehood"—namely, the establishment of truth for the words of the Sugata (Buddha) and the establishment of falsehood for the words of Kaṇāda and others.
That [distinction] would not exist; from the preceding verse, the word "not" (*na*) is understood to carry over.
The qualification "of those expressing the speaker's intention" and the reason "because they express that [intention] without distinction" are intended as follows:
if the establishment of truth for the words of the Sugata were due to their expressing that [intention], then it would apply to other words as well,
for even those do not function apart from what the speaker intends.
Now, because there is an absence of the presentation of reality for them, there is the establishment of falsehood; for this very reason, let it be the same for the words of the Sugata as well.
It is not so, however, because there exists a distinction produced by the presence or absence of a causal connection (*pratibandha*).
To explain: from objects arises the cognition of the Sugata, from that arises desire, and from that arise his words; such is not the case elsewhere.

If it is argued that the determination of those [cognitions] is therefore by means of inference—as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (2.57) regarding "the rays of a jewel and a lamp," etc.—it has already been said here that they are a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) like inference. Thus, how could there not be a determination of them? To this he says: "Because of the perception of true and false objects."

This is the usage of the verb *dṛś* with the causative suffix (*ṇij*) in the sense of "showing" or "establishing," because it expresses intention and there is no deviation from the actual meaning, whether that meaning be the true reality (*tattvārtha*) or the false object (*mithyārtha*).
Even regarding the statements of Kaṇāda and others,
there is simply a distinction of falsehood; the word of the Sugata alone is connected to the actual object through a lineage of transmission, and no other statement is so.
When two people run toward [an object] with the cognition that it is a jewel,
although there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a difference regarding its causal efficacy (arthakriyā).
The remainder [of the commentary] says "vākya" and so forth in order to explain the meaning of the verse: "because of the observation [of the word]."

Is the distinction between truth and falsehood not tenable in all statements? No; he says this: "In some of those [statements] as well, which indicate the speaker's intention, that [distinction] exists. To this, he replies: "Without distinction."
"What is it that cannot be established [without it]? To this he says: "In reality," and so forth.
Here he provides an illustration: "In perception," and so forth.

[The opponent objects: "That determination [of the object] does not exist there from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), but rather from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*); therefore, to prove its absence there from the perspective of ultimate reality is to prove what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). To this he replies: "From conventional reality," and so forth.

Even in the absence of a definitive distinction between truth and falsehood, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of such a distinction is mere convention (*saṃvṛti*). Because this convention consists of an absolute falsehood—where "absolute falsehood" means its nature is exclusively false—for that reason, from that conceptual construction, or from the conceptualization of words, there can be no attainment whatsoever of reality, whether it be the proof of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) or anything else; for how could a proponent be victorious on the basis of a statement such as "being produced," since a reality being established by the conventional conceptualization of that [distinction] cannot be the cause for attaining [true] reality, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It might be argued: "Just as in the case of two people with cataracts seeing two moons, that determination [of error] applies everywhere. To this, he says: "In the case of cataracts," and so forth.
Not only for another person, but even for one who experiences the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no misconception—that is, no grasping of a contrary object—due to cataracts.
Of what sort [is that experience]? He says: "Mutually," and so forth.
The meaning is that it consists of both difference and non-difference.
Where? He says: "externally and internally, and at every moment. Of what? He says: "of perception.
Of what kind of perception? He says: "in the case of one suffering from ophthalmia," and so forth.
This has been explained.
To the question "How does that belong to him?", he says: "From where else? and so forth;
[the meaning is] not from anywhere else, but rather through those two—its own arising and its unfolding—it is precisely by means of them that there is the realization of that.
To whom do those two belong? He says: "Of karma. Of what kind of karma? He says: "Of [karma characterized by] knowledge," and so forth.

In what respect? He says: "In the absolute absence of continuity (*niranvayaikānta*)," and so forth—the underlying intention being that because the usage of words is seen through the delusion of two people with cataracts seeing two moons, there would be a conceptualization of that [usage] everywhere; and because even perception, whose nature has been described, is a false view since a contrary apprehension is seen in some cases, there would be a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) everywhere.

[Objection: "But surely, let there be the apprehension of an object contrary [to reality] by means of those two [karma-types] when perception is associated with karma; however, how can that [apprehension] of what is contrary to that [reality] arise from verbal testimony? To this he says: "By means of *udaya* and *udīraṇā*, etc."—namely, by means of *udaya* and *udīraṇā*.

The realization of the opposite occurs through the rising and the activation of those karmas that obscure [the truth]; and because they arise from the perception and knowledge of false objects, the falsity of words is traditionally taught. (29)

Even in the case of a state characterized by destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣāyopaśamika*), the realization of reality occurs when there is an absence of the rising and activation (*udīraṇā*) of the destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*); it does not arise solely from birth or similarity. Therefore, one who wishes to establish reality based on some [particular] view should not merely indicate their own intended position while disregarding reality, as this would not distinguish them from other positions. We perceive no difference between what is true and what is false for one who personally favors [their own view], since their activity consists merely of expressing the speaker’s intention. Thus, the falsity of words—that is, of sounds—was remembered and authorized by the former teachers.
Why? He says: "Because of the perception and knowledge of false objects.
Why is that also so? He says: "By means of arising and activation.
Of what? He says: "Of those," and so forth.

By the word "tat" (that), the vision and knowledge that constitute the cause of verbal expression are grasped. Explaining the function of the karmas that obscure those two, he says: "Even of the state of knowledge which is [of the] nature of subsided-cum-destruction," and so forth.

Of what kind [is it]? Even that which is of the nature of subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣāyopaśamika), even that which has subsidence-cum-destruction as its purpose—what of it? To this he says: "the realization of reality" (tattvapratipatti).
When does this occur? To this he says: "the destructive [karmas]" (ghāti), and so forth.
The meaning is: "when there is an absence of the rise (udaya) and activation (udīraṇā) of the destructive karmas (ghātikarma).

If it is argued that [the soul] exists by virtue of its birth and similarity [to the previous state], he says in response: "Not merely its birth," etc., concluding the subject at hand by saying: "By this," etc.

Since this is so, therefore, this follower of the Sugata (Saugata), desiring to establish through some statement—whether related to the Sugata or related to something else—the reality characterized by the Four Noble Truths and so forth, or the object characterized by the three-fold mark of the logical reason, must state only what he intends to convey. Why? Because it is improper to suggest that which is devoid of reality (*nirastatattva*) through a statement. Such is the connection [of the argument]. Otherwise, one who wishes to communicate a cow would also be justified in suggesting a horse, as there would be no distinction between the two cases regarding their being irrelevant to the subject at hand.
If it is argued that this is a hint [of the correct view] because there is no other alternative, we say: no, for its existence has already been established.
Furthermore, what should a virtuous person who is incapable of performing what is good do? In that case, indifference alone is his proper course—this is the intended meaning.
Why is this so? To this he says: "In the other alternative," and so forth.
The position of permanence and so forth follows immediately after the Buddhist position because it does not surpass it; for there is no difference in the indication of that [position],
since it is identical in merely indicating the speaker’s intention, as is the case with a virtuous person.

[Objection: "In the Buddhist position, although there is indeed a lack of correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) regarding the sentence in the context of the absolute [view] of momentary destruction, consciousness, and illusion, nevertheless, this is not the case regarding form (*rūpa*) and so forth, because those are cognized from that [sentence] by way of the speaker's intention (*vaktrabhiprāya*). In other positions, however, there is a lack of correspondence everywhere. Therefore, how can it be said that [the Buddhist position] is not superior to the other positions? To this, he says: "Of the true and the false," and so forth.
That which is true regarding form and so forth, and false regarding the absolute [view] of momentariness and so forth, is the "true-and-false scripture" (*satyānṛta-śāstra*); of that...

Of what kind [is this]? Of that which is itself accepted and admitted by the Buddhist; for even from a falsehood—that speech uttered by the Saugatas with the intention of communicating a real object (though it is unreal) because it fails to communicate that [real] object—one does not perceive any distinction from that which is absolutely non-existent, such as momentariness, when it is uttered with the intention of communicating it, because it is a falsehood of falsehoods. The meaning is that [there is no difference] from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

And that [external object] does not exist for another [person], because its operation is admitted to consist merely in the speaker’s intention; for even though form and so forth exist externally, if they are not communicated by the word, they are no different from what is non-existent—this is the sense.

If it is asked: "How, then, can there be knowledge of reality from a word that lacks a connection to reality, even on your own position? To this he says: "The relationship between the signified and the signifier," and so forth, [starting] from "from that which is unconnected."
In the Jaina position, for that which has no relation,
how could there otherwise be any doubt regarding the relationship between the signifier and the signified?
Even though there is an infinite variety of denotable objects that have not been previously established by convention, when words are heard,

a relationship between the signifier and the signified is somehow established by itself through a particular transformation (*pariṇāma*), just as in the case of the eye and visible form. Otherwise, how could a doubt regarding a specific denotable object— such as "What is he saying?"— be possible for one who has not perceived the form, just as it is impossible for one who has not perceived a specific color?
How so?

The denoted is the jar and so forth; the denoter is the word "jar" and so forth; the relationship between these two is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), which arises spontaneously from its own inherent power.
The meaning is that [the connection] does not arise from mere convention alone.

Otherwise, how could doubt—meaning uncertainty—arise through any other way, namely, in the absence of an intrinsic relationship? To this he says: "Even upon hearing words"—that is, even when there is correct listening of sounds—not only when there is no hearing at all.
Where? He says: "In the infinite variety of un-conventional denotata.

By this, he shows that there is no convention regarding the particularity nor the universal; thus he explains the verse: "The relationship between the signified and the signifier—between the jar and its word—is intrinsic."
If it were produced from itself, it would be so;
however, the relationship between word and meaning is innate (autpattika). (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.5)
The meaning is that [the relationship] is innate (*svābhāvika*);

and such is the position of the Mīmāṃsakas, as it has been said: "The relationship between word and meaning is eternal" (*vākya-paṭala* 2.23), and so forth. To this, he replies: because of the absence of that specific transformation of both the signifier and the signified—since if there were no specific transformation, neither would exist—the relationship is established, accomplished, or determined in some way through its necessity regarding teaching and so forth.
He states an illustration: "like the eye and form.
This means that just as it is with the eye and form, so it is here;

this is an elliptical expression intended to include the ear and sound, etc. It is due to their specific connection that the eye alone manifests form alone, and not the nose or other organs, nor taste and other objects.
The Mīmāṃsaka says:
"The relationship between a word and its meaning was proclaimed therein by the great seers" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra).
The ellipsis is "by the authors of the sūtras, along with their commentaries (sānutantra), and the bhāṣyas."

It might be argued: "In the case of the eye, a certain excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced in it through its serial continuity (*santānavṛtti*) by means of the visible form (*rūpa*); thus, it does not manifest that very same [form] [simultaneously]. But this is not so for the word with respect to its object. Therefore, how can there be similarity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing to be illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*)? This is incorrect; for, what is this "manifestation" (*prakāśana*) of the form by the eye? If it is the production of a cognition [of it], then that cognition produces the momentary form existing at the same time as itself. Otherwise, how could that which has the form as its characteristic be grasped by the cognition as its cooperative cause (*sahakārī*), given that what is not a cause cannot be an object (*aviṣayatvāt*)? Nor is an excellence produced in the eye by that momentary form occurring at the same time.

For that [effect] is its cause precisely because it produces it, and there is no other causal relationship between two things possessing a single characteristic; this [relationship] results in the destruction of the continuum.
Therefore, although the eye does not produce any excellence (*atiśaya*) in the form by acting as a cooperative condition, it nevertheless illuminates that [form].

Now, if it is argued that the assistance rendered by means of that [form] is said to be "produced by it" with reference to the continuum (*santāna*), that too is not sound. For in that case, it would follow that [the cognition] is produced by taste and so forth as well;
for just as that [form] is the producer of the form which grasps it, so too is it the producer of the taste and so forth existing at the same time.
Otherwise, how could those two be dependent upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*)?

If it is argued that [the relationship] is not by way of being the material cause (*upādāna*), we say no; for it has already been demonstrated that the existence of "material cause" versus "other than material cause" lacks validity when there is an absolute distinction (*bhedaikānta*), since the operation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is indistinguishable in all cases.

If it is then argued that let there be assistance from that [cause] even for taste and so forth, we say no; for that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that taste too must be manifested by it.
If it is argued that this is not so because of its lack of capacity (*ayogyatva*), then let capacity alone be the basis for manifestation—what is the use of postulating such assistance?
A certain excellence is produced by the moment of form;
this is the production of excellence.

If there were a causal relationship between two things existing at the same time, there would be no continuum (*santāna*), because all [moments] would arise in a single moment and perish immediately thereafter; thus,
the assistance rendered by the preceding moment of form to the eye by means of the present moment of form as its material cause (*upādāna*) [would be impossible].
The previous form [is perceived] by means of the present form,
as in the case of color and taste.

Furthermore, by means of the eye, even though these atoms possess a prior and posterior form and belong to a single continuum, it would manifest their insentience (*jaḍatā*) just as it manifests their blueness, because that [insentience] also assists them; otherwise, there would be a partial relationship of produced and producer,
and such is not the case.
Therefore, it was rightly said that "let there be fitness alone," just as in the case of the eye, visible form, and so forth;
for the eye [is the locus] of insentience.
Here, the word *prati* is omitted; he states the fault in not accepting that [connection] with the words beginning "How otherwise," etc.:
how else—that is, by any other manner in which there is an absence of intrinsic connection—could it be established or be possible?
"What is it? he asks; [the answer is] "doubt regarding a specific denotation.
Of what nature is it? He says: "What does this person say?
Why [is there such doubt]? He says: "because [the meaning] has not been understood."
He states an illustration: "For a person who perceives form, just as there is a specific form possessing its particularities," and so forth;
he anticipates the opponent's objection in order to refute it, asking "How?
and so on, and therein provides the answer beginning with "Just as... and so forth.

Just as the various distinctions of perception have their determination dependent upon convention (*samaya*), so too the various distinctions of word-meanings have their determination dependent upon linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).

(31) Just as those who possess proficiency in determining conventions regarding the specific features of self-nature, other-nature, and so forth— features that have been made objects of perception— discriminate among those perceived features through their own experience, others do not.

Nor does this mean that the others are entirely unperceived; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence that even when a convention (*saṅketa*) exists, one would not understand [the meaning] in that way.
Thus, for those who perceive the word and its object, the convention is the cause for determining their specific distinction.

Furthermore, how could an inherent connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) be altered by convention? For the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things are not reversed by human will, as that would entail their becoming devoid of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). However, in cases such as the words *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) or *ṣaṇṇagarī* (six cities), the speaker determines them as expressive according to his own intent; thus they may be reversed, disregarding any external referent.

This is not so; for from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of confusion and intermixture regarding their relationship and designation.

An object cognized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is "perceptual"; its "divisions" are its intermediate distinctions. These may exist by way of one or another mode of capacity (*yogyatā*), or otherwise. Of what nature are they? To this he says: "those whose determination depends upon convention" (*samayāpekṣanirṇayāḥ*). Here, "convention" (*samaya*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the proficiency of vision and other such factors are also included.

In the same way, the distinctions between word-meanings would be determined only by depending upon convention (*saṅketa*). This is what is intended: just as perception, although inherently capable (*yogya*) of determining the distinction of its own object, does not have that capacity produced by a determination—since that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), nor does it produce a determination there by its mere existence, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) [of determination] even in cases such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)—but rather depends on auxiliary causes such as convention; likewise, a word also, being inherently capable, produces a determination regarding its specific meaning only by depending on convention.
For this is observed to be the case, and the principle is equal in both instances.
Explaining the verse precisely because of its suitability, he says: "By perception," and so forth;
[this refers to] those things made objects by perception, namely, by the seeing of the eyes and other senses.

In what [objects]? In the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) such as color and so forth belonging to both self and other—where "self" refers to direct perception and "other" refers to external objects like jars, and these are considered according to their respective possibilities. Those who possess proficiency in determination (*niścaya-pāṭava*) regarding those specific qualities through convention (*saṅketa*)—that is, those for whom there is proficiency in determination by means of that which has been established as a convention—are said to be such; they distinguish and ascertain the specific qualities experienced by themselves, whereas others do not, because they lack proficiency in convention. It is not, however, on this account that those other specific qualities are unperceived by them; rather, they are indeed perceived.

Why? He says: because even when there is a convention (*saṅketa*), there is the consequence of not apprehending [the object] in that way. "Convention" (*samaya*) is the linguistic agreement regarding the perception of word-meanings; it is the cause for determining their specific distinctions and the reason for ascertaining the difference between words and meanings. Another [opponent] asks: "How? and so forth.

Furthermore, how could an essential relationship between the signifier and the signified—characterized by a natural fitness (*yogyatā*)—be established through convention in a manner different from its actual mode of conveying a meaning?

This is the opponent's intention: Is that relationship of the word with respect to all meanings, or only with respect to a specific one? In the first case, there would be a simultaneous cognition of all meanings;
in the other case, due to a contrary convention, there would be no application toward the other meaning.
Now, if it is argued that its capacity to convey a different meaning arises from a different convention; to this he replies: "Not so," and so forth.
For (*hi*) the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities (*bhāva*), such as words and their referents, do not undergo transformation by human will, nor do they arise otherwise [than they are].
Why? He says: "Because those things which come into being would then result in the loss of their own intrinsic nature."
If it is argued that even the nature of a word undergoes transformation according to convention, the author replies here: "Indeed, speech... and so forth.

Just as in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) and *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the six cities), speech is regulated by speakers as a signifier (*vācaka*), so too is that speech transformed regardless of external objects. This is to be connected with the phrase "by means of a transformation already produced. Examples for this include *dārāḥ* and *ṣaṇṇagarī*.
Refuting this, he says: "This is not so," and so forth.
This statement formulated by another is not thus from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Why? He says: "Because of its lack of connection with that," and so forth.

The relationship between those two—the signified and the signifier—and their designation, which is the demonstration that "this is the signifier of this" and "this is the signified," [are discussed]. Their confusion (*saṅkara*) is the occurrence of all [the types of exclusion], such as the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and so forth; their intermixture (*vyatikara*) is the mutual entering into each other's domains. Because of the consequence of these two, [the following] is interrupted here, [and] interrupted here.
Here it has been shattered; here it has been shattered; here it has been shattered.
Comparison: Whatever is designated by speakers as expressive in a particular way,
that word is expressive in that way, regardless of any external referent—
such as in the cases of *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) and *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the six cities)— [Pramāṇavārttika 3].
65, 66. Here it has been broken off; here it has been broken off.

If it is argued that there is indeed such a contingency [of over-extension], he says here: "In the case of a qualifier," and so forth. The comparison is as follows: "The particle used as a differentiator excludes the non-connection of a property with its locus, its connection with others, and even its absolute non-connection."
Whether expressed along with the qualifier, the qualified, or the action, this entire meaning is understood through the speaker's intention even when not explicitly stated;
for a sentence has exclusion as its fruit, as in the case of "Caitra is an archer."
Pārtha is the archer, just as [one says] "a blue lotus"—
*Pravacanasāra* 4.190–92.

The particle *eva*, which functions as an exclusion (*vyatirecaka*), excludes from the property [denoted by the word] that which is not connected with the qualifier and the qualified, its connection with others, and absolute non-connection, but not otherwise. (32)
And by virtue of the contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*), the meaning of the two particles *eva* would indeed be understood even when they are not employed. [Objection:

It is certainly not by the speaker’s intention that in sentences whose nature is established through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and so forth—such as "Citra is indeed an archer," "Pārtha alone is the archer," or "The lotus is indeed blue"—an opposite sense might be suspected, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of such a cognition.

Therefore, precisely for this reason, even in sentences devoid of the employment of the particle *eva*, the understanding of the exclusion of non-connection and so forth occurs through contextual capacity; that understanding does not arise from the speaker’s intention, because it is the grasping of that very [contextual] state.
In the same way, even in sentences lacking the employment of the particle *syāt*, there is the comprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth.

The qualifier is "blueness" (*nīlatva*) and so on, and the qualified is "lotus-ness" (*utpalatva*) and so on; by these two, and by the action such as "exists" (*bhavati*) when it is uttered together with them, provided there is a connection (*yoga*), [the particle] excludes non-connection (*ayoga*), connection with others (*anyayoga*), and absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*).
Of what? He says: "of the property" (*dharmasya*).

Who [is this]? He says: Is every particle [an *evakāra*]? No; he says: it is the *evakāra* that functions as an exclusion (*vyatirecaka*). The meaning is as follows: when used in conjunction with a qualifier, the *evakāra* excludes non-connection with that qualifier; when used with a qualified object, it excludes connection with anything other than that; and when used with a verb, it excludes absolute non-connection of the property [with the subject]. Thus does the *evakāra* delimit the property.

If it is argued that [the exclusion] is due to human intention (*puruṣecchā*) and not due to the thing's own nature (*svasvabhāva*), to this he replies: "And not otherwise"—meaning it is certainly not the case that even when stated otherwise, that [intention] excludes its [correlative] from that [referent], because such is not observed.

For when it is said, "Citra is an archer," the exclusion of his being a practitioner of another [skill] does not become an object of cognition even through intention. Otherwise, since the intended meaning would be understood precisely according to the arrangement [of the words], the employment of a different syntactical structure (*bhinnaprakrama*) everywhere would be improper.

It might be argued: "This convention is beginningless; the particle *eva*, when employed together with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, effects an exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the like. Therefore, such a cognition arises from that [convention], not from the inherent nature of the word. Otherwise, it would exclude it in that very way only within the context of the convention, but not when it occurs at the beginning [of a sentence]. This is incorrect, because even for people who have established the convention in that manner, [the result] does not necessarily follow. Indeed, even if one were to say to someone, "Understand from the sentence 'The reason is a property of the subject alone' that there is an exclusion of non-connection," that person would not necessarily understand it in that way.
It excludes non-connection,
it excludes connection with another,
and it excludes the absolute absence of connection; therein, it merely illuminates the connection itself.
The particle *eva* [expresses] non-connection (*ayoga*) and so forth, [referring to] the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the rest.

Furthermore, because there is no contradiction in Maitra— who is related to something else and distinct from Caitra— also possessing the property of "possessing a staff" due to convention (*saṅketa*).
Right here he states another argument: "And because of its capacity," and so forth.
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *api* (also), though it is placed in a different syntactical position;
therefore, the meaning is as follows: even in the absence of application—that is, even in the absence of utterance.
Of which two? It would be these two alone.
What is it? He says: "What is to be understood? He says: "The meaning."
Why? To this he says: "By virtue of its capacity.

This is what is meant: if that meaning were understood solely from the speaker's intention (*icchā*), then how could one be certain that the intention for that meaning exists when those [words] are not employed? Furthermore, if that meaning is understood through capacity (*sāmarthya*), then [this applies] even in the absence of particles such as *eva*.
Explaining the pair of verses from the *Kārikā*, he says: "The wielder of the bow is indeed Citra," and so forth.

The specific quality (*viśeṣa*) is "archer" (*dhanurdhara*), which is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for that [subject]; the particle *eva* follows this. The referent (*artha*) and the person (*jana*) are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*); and following this, *eva* serves as the qualifier for them, namely "archer. Just as in the case of the qualified agent indicated by "the blue lotus," its action occurs; here, the particle *eva* follows this [agent]. Thus, in those sentences which exist according to their own nature—whether through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and so forth—it is not possible, nor even conceivable, for them to be otherwise or reversed by human whim.
Why? He says: "In that way," and so forth.

It should be understood that [the word] would result in a cognition in another way according to the whim of that person— thereby resulting in the apprehension of an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and so forth—
or else it would result in a cognition in the manner favored by the Buddhists;
for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing [the object] as a donkey or the like, despite its being qualified by such attributes.
Now, in order to explain the passage beginning with "and by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*), he says: "Precisely for that reason," and so forth.

Precisely for that reason—that is, because there is no possibility of it being otherwise through the will of a person—it follows by implication that there is the comprehension of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and so on.
Where does this occur? He says: "In sentences."

"In what kind of cases? To this he says: "If it is argued that there is comprehension of that [logical reason] even in cases devoid of the use of the particle *eva* by virtue of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*," then he replies here: "There is no comprehension of that by virtue of intention;
for instance: 'The property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is pervaded by its own part (*tadaṃśena*').'"

In such statements as *Pravāhaṇa* 3.1 and so forth, even if there were a different intention (*vivakṣā*), a different meaning cannot be possible because it would be contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa-bādhana*), just like a fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). Now, if there are certain sentences lacking the use of the particle *eva*, how is it understood from them that "this is the meaning of *eva* here"? For it is not possible to determine that "this is the meaning of the horn of a hare."
If it is argued that there is no perception [of the word] in either case, the author replies here: "Because of its being grasped by that.

This means that because of the existence—that is, the fact—of the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) which has as its "grasping" (i.e., its acquisition) that meaning obtained through implication (*sāmarthya*).

For just as smoke, when perceived, makes known its own cause, fire, due to its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with it, so too an object, when perceived from some source, [makes known] its own non-deviating designator.
For example, by the rule *nadu khe'ge jainendra* 1.1.18,

when the prohibition of *vo* and *evaiyoḥ* is stated, it indicates that those two stand in the relation of the modifier (*vikārin*) and the modified (*vikārya*), because if that [relation] were absent, their absence would not be possible, and thus the prohibition would be untenable.

From this it is known that [the rule] "not for all [words] in the void" applies; and that [rule], being itself understood through presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*), leads one to understand the word "partial" (*ekadeśa*). Even in common worldly usage, a statement such as "Devadatta, who is stout and robust, does not eat by day," leads one to understand that he eats at night.
Extending this principle even to the term *syāt* (the conditional particle), he says: "In the same way," and so forth;
by that same mode of logical capacity (*sāmarthya*), [this applies] even to sentences lacking the term *syāt*.
What is it? He says: "It conveys [the object] in such a way that its own nature and so forth are [manifested]"—this is the connection.
"Dhru" is the technical name for the verbal root [dhā].

Demonstrating the contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "If Caitra’s non-connection were excluded today, then his connection would be established; thus, the nature of Caitra would be proven in every respect, which cannot be for those who hate the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*). (34)

"Chaitra is indeed an archer"—this [example] is incorrect. If the qualification "only the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma eva*) is intended as an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), then [it is fine].

However, if one were to qualify the property of the subject by means of an exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)—that is, [defining it as] "the reason is the property of the subject alone"—then the reason, being dependent on that qualification, would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because it does not occur elsewhere; thus, [your position] is incorrect. How so?

The intention is this: when the non-connection of Chaitra with the bow is excluded, his connection [with it] is established. Otherwise, the formulation "Chaitra is indeed an archer" would be logically untenable.

And would that [connection] be in every way (*sarvathā*) or in some way (*kathaṃcit*)? In the first case, when the non-connection of Caitra with the bow is excluded, Caitra-hood would not be established; rather, the existence of the bow would be established.
For whom? He says: "For those who hate the *syādvāda*," meaning for the proponents of one-sided views (*ekāntavādin*).

If there were a connection between him and that [bow] in every way, there would be the consequence of it being like the milk of a female donkey; the sense is that otherwise, there would be a one-sidedness (*ekānta*) regarding those two.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated in order to explain the verse: "Caitra is indeed an archer," and so forth;
this has been explained by way of direct recitation (*nigada*).
What happened after that? He says: "That is improper," and so forth.
Because of the reasoning already stated, that [position] is improper (*ayuktam*), i.e., untenable (*anupapannam*).

What is it? He says: "The property of the subject alone" (*pakṣadharma eva*). This is a qualification by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavacchedena*). Since this would result in the identity of the subject and the property, there would be the undesirable consequence (*asatāpatti*) of the two becoming like molasses. Furthermore, he speaks in order to expose and refute the criticism made by another who maintains the position of excluding connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*): "If, however," and so forth.

The word "again" (*punar*) indicates another alternative position. By means of the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), there is a "non-connection" (*ayoga*) of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) with something other than the subject—that is, with the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). The exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) or rejection of that [non-connection] serves to qualify the property of the subject. Some commentators explain this as: "the reason is the property of the subject alone" (*pakṣasyaiva dharmaḥ hetuḥ*). Regarding the statement "the property of the subject is the reason by virtue of its being a part of that" (*pakṣadharmastadaṃśena hetuḥ*, *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.1), Kīrti states the refutation: "that qualification," and so forth. That subject (*pakṣa*) and that qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*)—whatever depends upon those two is "dependent on them"; in the phrase "dependent on that qualification" (*tadviśeṣaṇe*), it means "dependent on that qualification. Of that...
Of what? Of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
What [is its property]? He says: "Why is there uniqueness? He says: "Because of its non-occurrence elsewhere, even in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)."
Regarding this, the Master states the refutation: the phrase "what is being said by the opponent in this manner is improper" carries over;
as for the question "how?"—in what manner is it improper?
[It is so] because of its own word (*svaśabdena*).
Dharmakīrti, in the *Anyayogavyavaccheda*, page 52 of the *Hetubindu*.

If it is argued that [the reason] is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because it does not apply elsewhere while depending upon that qualification, we say no; for the qualification functions by way of exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
(Hetubindu, p. 52; this portion is fragmentary here).
Regarding the objection raised here—"It has been refuted here; it has been refuted here"—he provides the following answer: "Because of the exclusion of connection with anything else," and so forth.
In this context, [the word "only"] excludes connection with anything else; thus, [the definition] is "existing only in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*).
If that too were a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), what would be the purpose of the particle *eva*? (35)

If one were to define the reason as "existing only in the similar class" (*sajātīye sanneva hetuḥ*) by means of an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), there would be the undesirable consequence that properties such as "being produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) would not be valid reasons for the impermanence of sound. Therefore, one should qualify it by means of an exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) as "existing only in the similar class" (*sajātīya eva san*). Even when qualified in this way, if that property, while being present [in the similar class], were to transcend its exclusivity and become a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) by virtue of the nature of the thing itself, then—even though it was qualified as "existing only in the subject" (*pakṣe eva san*)—it would naturally reside in the similar class as well, because it relies on non-exclusivity (*anekānta*).
