And this is not so, because of the internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) [of the reason within the subject] and the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayoga...*).

The logical connection is as follows: by means of the reason characterized by the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), the reason exists only in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and not elsewhere, namely in that which is contradictory to it. Even if it is of such a nature, if it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), otherwise—like visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so on—it would not be a property of the subject. Being dependent upon that [subject], why would it not exist in the similar instance? If it is asked: "What is the purpose of pronouncing the particle *eva* (only) together with the qualificand? [the answer is: "Then what is the purpose in the phrase 'existing only in that which is similar' (*tattulya eva san*)? If you say it is for the purpose of excluding connection with the dissimilar (*atulyayogavyavaccheda*), then let that same [particle] be used in other cases as well."

If it is asked, "Why is there not an exclusion of the connection with what is similar (*tulyayogavyavaccheda*)? [the response is: Let there be for you too an exclusion of the connection with the subject (*pakṣayogavyavaccheda*). Others resolve this as follows: regarding the statement "existence in what is similar to the inferable (*anumeya-tattulye sadbhāvaḥ*)," having first stated the existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the inferable, the phrase "only in what is similar to that" (*tattulya eva*) does not serve to exclude what has already been mentioned. This is just as in the scriptural statement, "He begot two sons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa alone," where the expression "Nārāyaṇa alone" does not exclude Nara, because its purpose is to exclude what has not been mentioned.
In this case as well, the answer is the same: "because of the exclusion of connection with anything else," and so forth.
And for this purpose, the intention is that [the reason] must exist only in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
For when it is said, "existing only in the subject (*pakṣa*)," the opponent, having stated "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), then says "by a part of that" (*tadaṃśena*).
In this regard,

it has been interrupted here and there by the Teacher [Dignāga] in the following statement: "The presence [of the reason] in the object of inference and in what is similar to it, and its absence in what is not."
"Certainty..."—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p.
222. "And at the beginning, he himself gave birth to two sons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa"—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā-loka*, p. 247.
"The reason (*hetu*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that is pervaded by its part (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*)"—*Hetubindu*, p. 52.

In order to clarify the meaning of the verse, [the author], while indicating the opponent’s intention regarding the restriction "it exists only in what is similar" (*sajātīye sanneva*), says: "If one accepts the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) in the sense that 'it exists only in what is similar'—meaning the reason exists in what is similar and does not exist even slightly in what is dissimilar—then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [reasons] such as 'being produced immediately after effort' (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) would not be valid reasons when proving the impermanence of sound. This is because other [reasons] of that same type which subsist in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) would also be excluded. Therefore, fearing this consequence, people should qualify [the definition] by means of the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), stating: 'it exists only in what is similar' (*sajātīya eva san*)."

In that regard, it is appropriate to state the definition of the reason (*hetu*) itself as "that which exists in the similar class" (*sajātīye san*) and so forth— *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 4.189. To refute this, he states the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "in the same way," etc.

In the same way, even though that property (*dharma*) is qualified by the very method of excluding connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), when the particle *eva*—which is used as a qualifier—is uttered together with the subject (*viśeṣya*) after transcending its absolute sense, it becomes an "excluder" (*vyatirecaka*). By what does it abandon the restriction of excluding connection with anything else? He says: by the nature of the thing (*vastusvabhāva*) or by the power of the word (*śabdamāhātmya*). If it were a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), then even though it is qualified as "existing only in the subject," it would still subsist in similar instances (*sajātīya*).
Why? He says: because of the reliance on non-absolutism (*anekānta*) by its own nature (*svarasataḥ*), that is, by its very essence.

Even when there is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), it is only that which is not explicitly stated which is excluded, and not anything else; for this reason—namely, the recourse to this non-absolutism—it is observed that even when it is said "it exists only in the subject" (*pakṣa eva san*), there is no denial of its presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Indeed, one sees that in a single sentence, what was stated previously is not denied even when stated later, as for example: [The original Sanskrit text continues here.]
Supreme devotion is indeed directed toward the Jina, the Omniscient One, whose teaching is to be served by men;
therefore, when his authority is under discussion, what cause for lack of confidence could there be? This objection amounts to nothing.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that there would be a lack of commonality—he says "And not," etc., showing that this too is not a fault.
Why? He says: "Because of its internal pervasion," etc.;
this has already been examined.

Therefore, even when it is stated that "it exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*)," there remains the fault known as *asādhāraṇatā* (the reason being too narrow). Showing that this [fault] might indeed occur, he says: "The particle *eva*, which is a separator (*vyatirecaka*), when joined with an action, excludes absolute non-connection," and so forth.
Furthermore, as for what was said elsewhere: "The particle *eva*, when used with an action, excludes absolute non-connection. (Pramāṇavārttika 4).
190 Thus [it was said]; therein he states the refutation: "It follows," and so forth.
If this world, which is blue and has the singular form of a lotus, were clearly and eternally present everywhere as "this is a blue lotus," [then the following would ensue]. // 36 //

If there were an absolute restriction (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*)—that "the blue lotus exists"—then the entire world would be eternally composed of blue lotuses, governed by the constraints of its own time and so forth;
consequently, the statement "the lotus is blue" would not even be possible due to contradiction.

Otherwise, why would one not rely on the position that "it certainly is a property of the subject," since one could simply qualify it through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)? That is not the case; furthermore, there is no infinite regress in the *syādvāda* (doctrine of manifoldness), because it communicates the reality of the object as intended by itself.
If it is argued that "the lotus is indeed blue," then it follows that this entire world must be manifest as having the single form of a blue lotus at all times and in every respect.
This is the intended meaning: does the lotus exist as blue in every way, or in some way? In the first case, this fault arises;
in the other case, there is the fallacy of non-absolutism (anekānta).

Regarding the phrase "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*), he provides the commentary on the verse, beginning with "blue," and so forth: "A blue lotus indeed exists"— thus, when the extreme position of the exclusion of non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) is accepted.
What is it? He says: "its own," and so forth.

That which has time as its beginning—referring to substance and the rest—is described thus. Furthermore, this is not a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word "own" (*sva*); rather, it is a restrictive [genitive] (*niyama*). And that [restriction] is what has been transgressed by which [the world would be otherwise]. Thus it is said: the entire world might consist of blue;
would it consist of blue alone? No, he says: the world might consist of lotuses (*saroja*).
If [the lotus] were eternal and permanent because it does not transgress its own temporal restriction, what fault would there be? To this he says: "From that," and so forth.
Because of that immediate and absolute [restriction], the cognition "the lotus is blue" would simply not occur.
Why? He says: "Because of contradiction.

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): if this is blue and not of the nature of a lotus, or if it is of the nature of that [lotus] and not of the nature of blue—since these two are mutually contradictory, the word "yat" here is redundant.

If it is argued that there is no fault even in the statement "a lotus is indeed blue" because the application of a designation occurs according to the nature of things (*yathābhāvasvabhāvam*), to this he replies with the words beginning "How so? and so forth.

By this [argument], since this fault does not exist in the manner of non-existence, why would one not accept that "the reason is indeed a property of the subject" (*pakṣasya dharma eva hetuḥ*)? For, by not accepting this, one would qualify [the reason] only through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavacchedena*).
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.
[An objection is raised: "Surely the same fault applies even to the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness) of the Buddhists. To this, he replies: "And not... and so forth.

Nor is there any infinite regress in the theory of *syādvāda*; for how could there be a non-existence of things that do exist? To this he says: because it is precisely the reality of the object as intended by the Jaina himself that is communicated, words again indicate the meaning intended by the speaker; thus he states the refutation of the [opponent's] one-sided view, beginning with "the word *eva*," etc.
The particle *eva*, following its own sequence in its own sense,

[indicates] that the other [hearer] should understand the speaker’s intention exactly as it is heard. (37) Just as in the absolute view that "sounds indicate only the speaker’s intention," when the particle *eva* or the word *ca* has a different placement (*bhinnaprakrama*), if there were no inherent capacity to convey their own meaning in some way, one would not deviate from the sequence according to one's own will.

In cases of *yogarūḍhi* (conventional-derivative) compounds such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) and *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the city of six), the verbal power (*śabdaśakti*) itself must be understood as the basis for the cognition of difference.
This has been examined by the venerable Pūjyapādas, who are experts in the instruction of words, in the context of "The non-commencement of *ekaśeṣa* because denotation is innate":

if the convention [of meaning] were limited to the word-form and dependent upon human intention for the communication of its own referent, that would not be so; for linguistic usage does not occur on the basis of that alone.

When a word by its very nature conveys a qualified meaning through the proximity of another word, how can the inherent capacity of the denoter be denied? Since it is impossible to establish a restriction in every case when a single word is capable of conveying multiple meanings, absolute certainty is not established; enough of this digression.
(Jainendra 1.1.1)

The word *eva* (only) is heard in its own sense [of restriction] regarding the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and so forth; what does the Buddhist himself do by using it? He says: "Following along," meaning employing that which follows, just as in the case of [the term] *bhikṣā* and so on, he attributes the status of being an agent (*kartṛ*) to even an insentient thing.
What is it? He says: "one's own sequence"—that is, one's own (svasya) sequence (krama).
Following what? He says: "the intention of the speaker.
Where? He says: "in this [view], where the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*) is the sole object of the word."

Extending this principle elsewhere, he says: "Just as the particle *eva*, so too another [particle] such as *tā* and so forth—the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*) being intended to include the entire collection of indeclinables (*nipāta*)—may be heard following its own sequence according to the speaker's intention; yet it is not so. For even when used with an intervening element, as long as it is not connected with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the like, there is no comprehension of its meaning from that [intervening element]; this is the sense. Therefore, the word 'that' (*tam*) is redundant."

He states the commentary on the verse (*kārikā*): "When there is the absolute position (*ekānta*) that sounds indicate only the speaker’s intention and not the [external] object, then—in whatever manner (*yathā*)—the particle *eva* has a 'separated application' (*bhinnaprakrama*). This means its application (*prakrama*), or sequence of usage, is 'separated' (*bhinna*) by transcending its usual connection with qualifiers and so forth. Because of the constant syntactic connection between *tasya* and *eva*, it is understood as 'in that very way' (*tathaiva*).

It is not only the particle *ca* [that functions thus], but also the word *vā*; the word *iti* expresses the manner (*prakāra*), meaning that other words of this same kind [also function in this way]."

What, then, should one do? He says: one should not overstep the sequence—that is, the established state of its own arrangement—in the matter of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). Elsewhere, that which is designated by means of qualifiers and so forth would not be fit for connection; the meaning is that it should convey the sense as it is inherent in the grammatical arrangement. When? He says: when, in some way or another, through some manner of expression, there occurs the manifestation of its own meaning by means of what has been uttered.

By what means [is this done]? He says: by the will of the speaker—that is, by following the speaker’s intention. For if the inherent power of the word were fixed, one would have to transgress that rule; otherwise, even if the term were mentioned elsewhere, its meaning could not be understood without a connection to qualifiers and so forth.

[Objection: If its nature were thus fixed, how then is there the plural form *dārāḥ* ("wife") for a single woman's body? [And] since plurality is fixed for that term, why is there the singular form *ṣaṇṇagarī* ("the group of six cities") for a collection of six cities? [Response: Because its application is restricted to a single instance, and because apart from those six cities, no such "group" exists.
And that usage is observed; therefore, we consider that words do not have the intended meaning as their primary object. To this, he replies: "In compounds," and so forth.

Even in the case of *dhvanis* (words) that are both etymological and conventional, such as *dāraḥ* ("wife") and *ṣaṇṇagarī* ("the city of six"), it is not only in the previous cases that the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word must be understood for the cognition of plurality and unity when there is a perception of difference; it is not merely a matter of speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the singular number and so forth.
This has already been examined: "Because denotation is innate, the formation of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among synonyms) is not undertaken" (*Jainendra-vyākaraṇa* 1.2.1).

In this [verse] "1 1000," it should be understood that the Blessed Ones (bhagavadbhiḥ) are those whose feet are worthy of worship and who are expert in the grammatical instruction of words (śabdānuśāsana).
Thus,
the word *dāra* takes both the singular and the plural forms.

Furthermore, with the intention of refuting the opinion of another, he raises an objection starting with "having the word as its limit" (*padāvadhika*); that which has a word as its limit is described as such.
Who is it? He says: "Conventional usage" (*samaya*), which is the tradition of words.
What is that? He says: "The person," and so forth.

If it is argued that [the word] is dependent upon—that is, contingent upon—the intention (*abhiprāya*) or desire of the speaker, the person, for the purpose of communicating his own meaning; to this he replies: "No," and so forth.

As for what was said by the opponent—that [the object exists]—why is that not so? He says: because there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) by means of merely that much, i.e., a mere word; for it is impossible for linguistic usage, whether of the nature of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), to occur through a word alone.
Indeed, the existence of a jar does not follow from the mere utterance of the word "jar."

It might be thought: "The comprehension of a qualified meaning arises from the connection with another word, and from that, linguistic usage [occurs]. To this, he says: "In the presence of another word," and so forth.

When another word—that is, a word other than the intended word—is in proximity, if it were admitted that the communication of a qualified meaning occurs by itself, that is, by its own nature, without depending on a convention established by a person; [then...]

For not every comprehension of the meaning of a sentence depends upon convention (*saṅketa*), since we observe that some people of keen intellect perceive the meaning even from a sentence heard previously for the first time. How then can an inherent capacity (*svataḥ śakti*) be denied to the sublater [of error]? Having thus accepted that the convention which has words as its limit is dependent upon human intention, this objection was stated;
now, showing that even in that case there is no such dependence, he says: "In the case of multiple meanings," and so forth.

When it is possible to establish a single word with multiple meanings—that is, with many referents—as in the sentence "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra" (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 1.6.36), there is no restrictive rule that words indicate only the speaker’s intention. Therefore, this opponent's absolute position is not established in any way.

To explain: if words indicate only the speaker’s intention, then since the Mīmāṃsaka speaker has no intention that "fire is his own," how could Kīrti derive the understanding of its own meaning from that [word], such that he says: [The opponent's argument: "If words indicate only the speaker’s intention, then since the Mīmāṃsaka speaker has no intention that 'fire is his own,' how could Kīrti derive the understanding of its own meaning from that? [And so on.]
At that time,
because it is dependent on human will,
the dog is called "Agnihā" (the slayer of Agni); its entrails, that is, its meat, are the "agnihotra."
According to Dharmakīrti, the meaning of the word "dog" [is established] by that [usage], as in the Vedic revelation: "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra."
"What is the proof for the statement that 'one should eat dog-meat' does not have this as its meaning? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.318).

It might be argued that the "speaker" is simply one who explains [the text]; but this is not so, because even beyond the meaning stated by the commentator, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) appears to the listener when it is accompanied by reasoning. Concluding the discussion on the speaker, he says: "For this purpose, enough with this incidental discourse regarding the succession of speakers; here, the opponent has been refuted."

Now, the following objection may be raised: "Apart from atoms, there are no phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), or sentences (*vākya*); this is because they are not real entities. Therefore, how can it be said that 'the [self] which has acquired the nature of phonemes, words, and sentences' (Siddhiviniścaya 4.1)?
To this, he replies with the verse beginning "The word," and so forth.
"Just as cognition appears to itself through its own diverse forms, both real and unreal, so too does the undivided reality appear through its own distinct aspects"— thus they declare.

Since establishing the true nature of cognition according to how it is perceived leads to the consequence of manifoldness (anekānta), one must accept that reality is of a single form, which has never before been seen [in such a way].

And thus, a syllable appearing merely as a false [form], a word appearing as a false phoneme, or even a sentence whose referent has not been perceived would remain unrefuted, because there is no apprehension of sequence.
If it is argued that this results in the abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved, the same consequence applies to consciousness as well.
Since it consists of both difference and non-difference, why is there such hostility toward anything else?

The intended meaning here is as follows: if the Buddhist accepts a single, variegated cognition (*citraikajñāna*), then for the Jaina, the [existence of] phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth is established;

if he does not accept it, then for the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), it is established because of his acceptance of partless reality (*niraṃśatattva*). Thus, there is no liberation for the Tathāgata from falling into this or that side.
The term "word" (*pada*) is an illustration; by extension, it refers to phonemes and sentences. Therefore, the phoneme, the word, and the sentence appear [in consciousness].
With what [is it associated]? He says: "with forms," that is, with distinctions.
Of what kind? With its own, that is, its intrinsic;
how so? In some way, as being essentially identical to it, for otherwise existence would not be established, since relations such as inherence (*samavāya*) have been refuted.
Furthermore, by what kind [of parts] is it [the whole] constituted? He says: "by distinct [parts]," meaning mutually different.
Of what nature is that [whole]? He says: "undivided," meaning common to its own parts; or alternatively, "partless.

Furthermore, by what kind [of parts]? He says: "existent and non-existent"—existent (*sadbhiḥ*) according to the Jaina perspective, and non-existent (*asadbhiḥ*) according to the view of certain grammarians.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration, beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*):

in whatever manner (*yathā*) cognition appears through such-and-such forms (*ākāraiḥ*), in that very way some— the Jains and the Grammarians who maintain the doctrine of *sphoṭa*— proclaim the establishment of their view.

Now, where does that [object] appear? If you say "in itself," then if consciousness is perceived in something other than itself, we say no; for that has been refuted, and even if it existed, it would be restricted to the present moment alone, and thus it could not appear in inference either, since inference is absent when perception is absent. If this is argued, we reply: it appears in the self—which is manifold, consisting of the transformations of the awareness of both self and other.
This has been stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*: "By means of the self in its manifold forms" (*Nyāyaviniścaya* 1.8), and so forth.

According to some, when the recollection of the preceding phonemes occurs due to the hearing of the final phoneme—this recollection being conditioned by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the hearing of each preceding phoneme—a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) arises, and [the word] manifests therein.
That is untrue; for it is impossible for letters and so forth, which exist sequentially, to appear within that [consciousness] which has a single, partless nature.
The rest has already been considered here under the Vijñānavāda, or else there would be the consequence of [the object] attaining the nature of consciousness.
Since perception lacks the production of inference, [the cognition]—
in which the seed has been deposited by the preceding sounds— is [produced] together with the final sound.
Sound appears in the intellect when it has reached maturity through repeated practice—
Vākyapadīya 1.85.
Explaining the verse of the proponent of *sphoṭa* (*Sphoṭavādin*), [the author of the] *Nyāyakumudacandra-ṭīkā*, page 749, says: "In accordance with observation," and so forth.

If the establishment of the reality of knowledge were performed according to perception—without overstepping what is perceived—it would result in the fallacy of manifoldness (*anekānta*), because it would follow that [the object] consists of multiple aspects such as color and so forth. For this reason, reality is knowledge, which is the actual thing; of what nature is it? It must be accepted as having a single form and being partless.

Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: it has never been seen before in any way, whether through means such as direct perception or through modes such as self-aware non-duality (*svasaṃvedanādvaita*); for partless knowledge cannot be perceived, just like the *puruṣa*.

If it is argued that such a reality of cognition is indeed accepted, [the author] says in response: "And thus, by that aforementioned manner of accepting cognition, the syllable (*akṣara*) is not prohibited"—this is how the connection should be understood.

Of what nature is it? He says: "In which there appears only a false manifestation of the *mātrās*"; that is, in which there is a false, unreal appearance of the *mātrās*, such as the short vowel and so forth.
Not only is the syllable unprohibited, but the word (*pada*) as well is unprohibited.
Of what nature is it? He says: likewise, even speech that appears with unreal phonemes is not prohibited.
Of what nature is it? He says: it is that which has the ultimate reality as its object (*dṛṣṭaparamārtha*) yet manifests as unreal words.
Why is all this so? He says: because of the simultaneous realization (*akramapratipatti*), and so forth.
The opponent raises a supreme objection to refute [the argument], stating: "There would be the loss of what is perceived" (*dṛṣṭahāni*), and so forth.

If it is argued that there is a loss of the perceived distinctions such as mother and so on, and the postulation of the unperceived partless syllable (*akṣara*) and the like, [the author] says in response: "This same consequence (logical fault) applies not only to the syllable and so on, but also to consciousness (*saṃvitti*); it is not the same in that case, because it is admitted that [consciousness] has a variegated yet unitary nature (*citraikarūpatva*). Even though there is a variegated appearance, cognition (*buddhi*) is indeed one. — *Pravārtikālaṃkāra* 3.146.
If it is argued [that this follows] from such statements as "220" and so forth, to this he replies: "In that case," and so on.

If that consciousness consists of both difference and non-difference, what aversion is there toward other things such as phonemes? Why should that nature of being both different and non-different not exist in them as well—in the phonemes and so forth?

The nature of the reality of cognition is not asserted to consist of difference and non-difference in such a way that this fault would arise; rather, it is observed as such, because for that which is self-cognizing, there is a contradiction in its being imperceptible,
and yet it appears as if undivided.
As it has been said:
"The nature of the intellect (buddhi), though undivided... [Pravāhaṇa-vākya 2.354], and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "For those whose senses are afflicted by mantras and so forth" (Pravāhaṇa-vārttika 2.355),
he says therein: "undivided," and so forth.

If cognition were divided, it would manifest itself as something other than what it is; it could not transform that which is without sequence into something with sequence through ignorance. (39) Furthermore, if the atoms of cognition were entirely distinct [from one another], how could reality appear otherwise? Moreover, the form of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), being entirely different from the form of the knower (*vedaka*) and so forth, would transcend the very nature of consciousness, like any other external entity.

If the form of the knower is not cognizable apart from that [cognition], how could it be conscious such that it would possess self-awareness? Therefore, in the absolute non-difference [of the object] from cognition, there is no appearance otherwise due to delusion; for even externally, one might as well imagine that the partless word and so forth appear otherwise due to delusion. How could cognition—which is held by the Buddhists to be undivided and without distinction—appear to itself in its own nature as if possessing distinctions, given that the apprehended, the apprehender, and the awareness are otherwise [non-distinct]? It is through ignorance (*avidyā*).

What, then, would it do? To this he says: "Not without sequence," and so forth. It would make—that is, it would apprehend—as if possessing sequence that which is without sequence, devoid of order; for the root *kṛ* denotes action in general.

What [would it not do]? It would certainly not produce that cognition. What [is the object]? A word (*pada*); this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) including phonemes (*varṇa*) and the rest.
"By what? By ignorance (avidyā)," one might think—knowledge does not manifest itself otherwise, because the two [subject and object] appear simultaneously;
rather, it is only the conceptualizing intellect (vikalpabuddhi) that determines the object as if it were defiled by the distinction between the consciousness of the grasped and the grasper.

For this very reason, it has been stated by someone: "It appears as if possessing the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject" (Pravāhaṇa-vāda 2.354), yet it is not so grasped. To that, he says: "If, however," and so forth;
"if, however" (*yadi punaḥ*) is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*).

"What are the atoms of cognition (*jñāna-paramāṇu*) like? To this he says: "In every respect distinct, with bodies mutually excluded, such is the reality (*tattva*). Otherwise, because bondage would lack indivisibility (*niṣkala*), it could not be established. What follows from that? To this he says: "From what cause? From none whatsoever. This is an elliptical expression for "in some way as a unity"; [otherwise] they would appear as gross, long, or possessing parts.
For that which does not possess a certain nature does not appear in that form within a cognition that apprehends itself; otherwise, color would appear as having the nature of taste even in the eye.

And yet, that unity and so forth exists neither in the atoms individually nor when combined, and yet it does appear, because even in a state where all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn, a single gross object is perceived.
As Dharmakīrti has also said:
Although Dharmakīrti spoke of "non-duality of appearance" (*pratibhāsādvaita*), it is nevertheless observed that he said "it appears" (*ābhāti*).
"Do those atoms impart their own form to the cognition, or does that cognition appear as something gross? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.321).

How do those mutually distinct atoms impart their own form to that cognition so that it appears as gross and possesses a gross shape? That which is the true nature of the atoms is not gross, and thus it cannot be mounted upon cognition;
and that grossness which is mounted upon cognition does not exist within the atoms—*Prakaraṇavārttika-manorathanandinī*.

It might be thought: "This form does not appear; rather, that form of the object (*grāhyākāra*) is non-existent, like the appearance of an illusion or a mirage, and there is no fault in its being non-existent," according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra* (3.211). To this, he says: "The form of the cognized," and so forth. The phrase "the form of the cognized" means the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*), which is gross and of a single nature—the word "if" is understood to carry over from the previous context—and furthermore, it is indeed distinct from the forms of the cognizer and so on. [If one asks] "What is the cognizer?"—it is that by which this form of the cognized is grasped; in its absence, there would be no perception of that [object].

If it is argued that there is self-awareness (*svataḥ-pratīti*), then the status of being cognition is established, and thus the proof of the single reality of consciousness (*cit-eka-tattva*) follows; yet this is not acceptable to the opponent. Therefore, that [object] which is the "beginning" of which [the series of cognitions] must be something other than that cognition. Furthermore, if even the form of the experience (*saṃvedana-ākāra*) is absent, then that [cognition] cannot be established.

For there is no action devoid of a form; that very [action] is the form. Therefore, the nature of consciousness—the essence of knowledge characterized by self-awareness—would indeed be distinct and different, and would transcend [or exceed] [the object]; the meaning is that the form of the cognized object would be insentient.
And thus, there would be a deviation from the [inference] "whatever appears is knowledge, as in the case of pleasure and so forth," because of this [point made in the verse]:
"There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect" (Pravāhaṇa-vāda 2).
Thus, [the objection] beginning with "327" is refuted;

here he provides an illustration: "like another object" (*arthāntaravat*) means that an object other than the blue object is "another" (*antara*), such as yellow and so forth; "like that" (*tadvat*) means similar to that.
Just as yellow transcends the nature of blue, so too does the form of the object transcend the nature of consciousness;

or rather, consciousness, acting as the agent, transforms itself into the nature of the cognition of blue through the form of the awareness of the object and the specific cognition thereof, thus possessing a twofold nature (*dvirūpatā*). (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1)
By this statement, [the cognition] would transcend [its object] and thus be formless; this is the meaning.
He states the refutation regarding the form of the knower: what is the nature of the form of the knower? It is unperceivable (*asaṃvedya*).

How so? He says: "Apart from that"—that is, apart from the form of the object of cognition—in no way whatsoever, such as through perception and other means, is a partless cognition experienced as distinct from blue and the like. Furthermore, how could this conscious entity be devoid of that form? For, by virtue of its consciousness, self-awareness would belong to it.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore, not... and so forth.
Due to the distinction between the cognition of an object and the cognition of that [cognition], the intellect possesses a twofold nature;
for even at a later time, this [distinction] is not unperceived by memory.

[Objection: But surely the form of the object of cognition is not other than the cognition itself; rather, although in reality it does not possess that [form], it appears as if it possessed it. To this, he says: "In the absolute non-difference [of the two], an appearance otherwise due to the force of delusion would be a manifestation as something else. Here, the answer is: this might be imagined due to the force of delusion not only internally, but also externally.
Of what? Of that which begins with the "pada" (the state).
Of what nature is it? Precisely of that which is partless (*niṣkala*);
for even consciousness, though devoid of the form of an object, exists within the act of cognizing.

If it is argued: "Surely the phonemes and so forth are accepted as the manifestors (*vyañjaka*) of the *sphoṭa*, which is accompanied by the form of the object of cognition; and their activity consists in the act of making known (*avidyati-kriyā*), for the water in a mirage is not capable of performing any causal function (*arthakriyā*)," [the author] replies here with the words beginning "by false forms" (*mithyākāraiḥ*).
Just as a single cognition is produced by false modes [of apprehension],
so too is a sentence, which possesses a twofold nature (*dvaidhya*), manifested by manifesting words through false sequences.
(40) "Twofold nature" (*dvaidhya*) means being divided into two parts.

If a single cognition were manifested even by false objects appearing in various forms, why should a sentence not be manifested by words of false sequence? Since there is no distinction [between the two cases], just as a single, non-dual cognition is at some time abandoned of its duality through false, unreal aspects (ākāra) or parts—that is, by way of that mode of apprehension—so too is a sentence [manifested] by those whose sequence is false. This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa); by it, the phoneme (varṇa) is manifested in the word (pada).
"What by what? To this he says: "By manifestors, namely the components of phonemes, words, and sentences.
He provides the commentary on the verse beginning with "nānā" (various), etc.:

"If a single, partless cognition were manifested even by unreal objects through various appearances in the form of the cognized and so forth, then why would a word or sentence—which are manifested—[be considered] unreal due to their unreal sequence? It certainly would be [unreal]."
Why? He says: "Because of the particularities," and so forth.
Now, if it is argued that the *sphoṭa* is accepted by others as being eternal and all-pervading, and yet such a thing cannot be perceived; to this he replies: "It would not be known," and so forth.
For the proponents of *sphoṭa*, neither a sentence nor a word consists of multiple constituent parts;
this reality of the word is devoid of internal differentiation... (*Sphoṭasiddhi*, verses 29, 36).
Those who know it declare that *sphoṭa* is the eternal word, distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), manifested by the phonemes, and the conveyor of meaning... (*Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p. 300).
It should be observed—Nyāyakumuda, p. 745, note 9:
"Cognition, phonemes, words, sentences, and so forth, being essentially one, would neither be known, nor arise, nor perish; for that [cognition] is by nature false. (3.1)

In the establishment of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), nothing whatsoever is the effect of anything else, because a partless direct realization (*niṣkalasākṣātkṛti*) is impossible.

For that very reason, it would not perish; because it possesses perceptibility, it is not known, not grasped, not produced, and does not perish—the One is directly [realized] as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

What is that? He says: "Intellect, phonemes, words, sentences, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of *śabdabrahman* and other such entities is intended. For what reason? He says: "By the realization of that," and so on.

The realization (*vitti*) of that [intellect, etc.]—namely its nature as cognition, its birth, and its destruction—is "the realization of that" (*tadvitti*). By means of that which is unreal (*vitatha*), namely its essence or intrinsic nature (*ātmasvabhāva*).

This is what is meant: if cognition—even when unperceived—is said to be restricted to its own nature alone, momentary, devoid of cause and effect, and partless; then let phonemes and so forth also be accepted as eternal and all-pervading even though they are not perceived.
Since their non-existence due to non-perception is the same for cognition as well, the author, explaining the verse, says: "In perception," and so on.

When the relationship of cause and effect is accepted, of what nature is it? To this he says: "In what has occurred when [the relationship] is established through perception and non-perception? To this he says: "Not," and so forth.

Any waking cognition or any cognition such as that of sleep is not the effect of something like the eyes or mental impressions (*vāsanā*); likewise, no inflected word, or any other word or sentence, is the effect of something like the palate, space, air, or sound. Why? He says: "Because of the impossibility of the direct realization of that which is partless," and so forth; that is, because the direct realization of that which is without parts—that is, without constituent elements—such as pure consciousness (*jñāna*), is impossible.
If it is argued that even if its effect does not exist, it would nonetheless be impermanent; to this he replies: "Precisely because of that impossibility," it would not perish.
To the question "Why is this so? he says: "Because of perception," and so forth.
The implication is that, for that reason, it is indeed eternal.

If it is argued that, although the direct realization of partless consciousness (*jñāna*) is impossible, its existence is nonetheless established through inference by means of the forms of error, [the author] replies here: "Of the reality of consciousness," and so forth,
referring to that which is undivided (*avibhāga*).

There is no identity whatsoever between the manifestations of the reality of cognition and [the objects], yet because they arise from that [reality], it is inferred through those erroneous [manifestations]. (42) The reality of cognition is partless and not perceptible—that being the position they would adopt if they were to criticize the *sphoṭa*—for if a partless reality that transcends all conceptual construction appears as if it had parts, it is not grasped by perception; this is the same in the other case as well.

That which is without beginning or end appears as if it had a beginning and an end, and that which is without succession appears as if it possessed succession—this could only be so if reality were established by some intrinsic nature; otherwise, there would follow the consequence of universal distrust, since error would be entirely unestablished. There is no identity between the partless essence of cognition and its manifestations in the forms of the apprehended object and so forth, all of which are in every way erroneous; this is the reason for their falsity, for there can be no identity between the non-erroneous and the erroneous due to contradiction.
Likewise, there is no production of that [object] by those [cognitions], because that [object] is inferred from those forms (*ākāra*) on the basis of identity (*tādātmya*).

He states the meaning of the verse with the words "the reality of cognition" (*jñānatattva*), "the measured reality" (*mitatattva*), and so forth. What is the nature of this "reality of cognition"? He says: having accepted and relied upon that partless reality of cognition (*vijñānatattva*), the Buddhists or the proponents of *Śabdabrahman* might criticize the *sphoṭa*; however, since that [reality] is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the term "measured reality" (*mitatattva*) here is redundant.
In this regard, the reading appears to be incomplete:
"The causal relation is established through perception and non-perception" — *Hetubindu*, p. 54.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that reality appears as if possessed of differentiation but is not so grasped—he replies: If the reality that transcends all conceptual constructions such as *sattva* and the rest, which is of the nature of knowledge and partless (*niraṃśa*), were to be known as having parts or appear as if possessing differentiation through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—that is, were it to be determined by conceptualization rather than grasped by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—then what was just mentioned applies equally to other cases, such as words and the like. For it can indeed be said: a word and so forth are perceived without succession (*akrama*) by non-conceptual awareness, but they are determined as if possessing succession by the conceptual cognition that arises subsequent to it.

[Objection: Surely, since all cognition is submerged within its own nature (*svarūpa*), how can it function toward distinct objects such as words? [Reply: Why is it said to be "submerged in its own nature"? [Objection: Otherwise, cognition would not exist there, because no other defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is present. [Reply: For that very reason, let it be granted that it is also submerged in the form of the word. [Objection: No, because it is not observed to be so. [Reply: That is the same in the other case as well.
Likewise, regarding the conceptualization in both cases (p. 656, l.
8): if its own nature were not submerged, then it would not even be cognition.

If it is argued that, precisely because there is no other defining characteristic, let the word, sentence, and so forth be devoid of birth and the like; to this he replies: "beginningless," and so on.

That which has no beginning or end—namely, birth and destruction—is "beginningless and boundless"; it is without sequence, being devoid of the sequence of cause and effect, yet it appears as if having a sequence, as if possessing the sequence of cause and effect. Thus, this would be so only when the nature of reality—which consists of knowledge and so forth—is established and determined through some means of direct perception, inference, or otherwise, by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). Otherwise, if there were no such establishment by way of its own nature, there would follow the consequence of a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) regarding everything, including pleasure and the like.

For instance: "There is no such thing as pleasure and so forth; it is simply that pleasure and so forth do not appear [as they seem to], though one might say they 'appear as if' [they exist]. Indeed, there is no appearance of anything other than pleasure, blue, and so on, because when pleasure, blue, and the like are investigated, they are found to be untenable; and even if they do appear, they are erroneous. To this, he replies: "In every way," etc.—this has already been established.

The proponent of the non-duality of manifestation (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*) says, "Based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*," and regarding this, Prajñākaragupta says: "Since that which is manifesting cannot be an error, let there be non-duality of manifestation"; to that, [the opponent] replies with the words beginning "from sounds" (*dhvanibhyaḥ*), etc.

The wise know that the denotative word is distinct from the sounds [that constitute it], just as the principle of cognition is known to be distinct from its manifestation; otherwise, it would not be so. Thus, the claim "according to how it appears" cannot serve as a basis for investigation, as it lies beyond the scope of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
That is not so...

one should not believe in a denotative entity called *sphoṭa*, which is distinct from and a different thing than the sounds (*dhvani*) that manifest words and the like; for it would not be accessible through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but only accessible through blind faith (*śraddhā*).
Otherwise, the wise would know the reality of cognition (*jñānatattva*) as something to be accepted through faith alone.
Of what nature is it? He says: "The manifestation," and so forth.
Whether it be a manifold manifestation such as pleasure and so on, or blue and so on, [the object] is distinct from that.

Herein this is the intended meaning: would it be non-dual appearance having the nature of a pillar and so forth, or something else? Regarding the first position, he says: "According to how it is perceived" (*yathādarśana*). (Prajñālaṅkāra-vārttika 2)
"Such [statements] as these are not the cause for investigation, for they are not contrary to the principles of the soul (jīva) and so forth.

Thus he states the second fault: "'Beyond the scope of valid means of knowledge' and so forth—that is not tenable—'the illumination of an unknown object' is the ultimate definition of a valid means of knowledge" (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 30).

This establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result is made exactly according to how they appear, even though the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the consciousness [of them] do not [ultimately] exist—
*Pramāṇavārttika*.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore, not... and so forth.
Now, revealing the unstable conduct of the Buddhist, he says: "The external object exists... and so forth;
"the external object exists, and cognition is also formless."
"How can anything more confused than this be possible?

Speaking in such a state of confusion by relying on mutually contradictory conventional doctrines that maintain either absolute affirmation or negation regarding external and internal objects of knowledge—how can one who enters into the system of the critical investigators (parīkṣaka-samaya) be considered a person of sound mind?
For instance, the Sautrāntikas maintain: 'External objects exist, and cognition possesses the form of the object.'"

There is no external object; rather, there are the forms of objects, such as the forms of blue and so forth, because it is precisely in relation to those that the world employs the conventional designation "object. Thus, the Yogācāras maintain that consciousness exists. Since neither an external [object] nor even within consciousness is a gross form of blue possible—given that the form of atoms has been discarded—consciousness is "formless" (*anākṛti*). That which lacks a form, such as the form of blue and so forth, is "formless"; this is another specific qualification of that [consciousness].

Because it does not appear in perception apart from blue and other [colors], like Brahman; because its existence is to be inferred through the impossibility of objects being otherwise than non-delusory, like the cognition of a Mīmāṃsaka; and because, since even that [Mīmāṃsaka’s] cognition lacks simultaneous observation with the object due to occasional error, there can be no inference of it from that—thus, what could be more confused than this state of instability? Indeed, this very confusion is cognition itself.
The statement that "there are forms of objects" refers to a specific Yogācāra-Madhyamika.
Alternatively, demonstrating the Buddhist's habit of denying what he has seen, [the author] says: "The external exists," and so forth.

An insentient external object such as a jar either exists by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or does not; yet, even so, he says "there is no external object. He claims that consciousness exists without form (*anākṛti*), yet even so, he suggests it is possible for it to have the form of an object. This is certain through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), yet even so, he says it is impossible. Apart from pleasure, blue, and so on, it is merely a conceptual determination (*adhyavaseya*). Thus, his speech is confused and incoherent. What could be more than this? This very [position] is called the "proponent of valid cognition" (*pramāṇavādin*).
He states the commentary on the verse beginning with "the external and internal objects of knowledge" (*bahirantarjñeya*), and so forth:

external objects of knowledge are such things as jars (*ghaṭa*) and the like; internal objects of knowledge are such things as cognition (*buddhi*) and pleasure (*sukha*) and the like. Regarding these two, there is first an affirmation (*vidhi*) and then a negation (*pratiṣedha*); these are both absolute positions (*ekānta*) and conventional discourse (*saṃvṛtivāda*).
Of what nature are they? They are mutually distinct, having natures that exist through mutual exclusion (*anyo'nyaparihārasthitasvabhāva*).

What? Having relied upon—that is, having resorted to—a certain collection of aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*), or a collection of suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth, which is agitated and unstable, how can he be called "one whose self is at ease" (*svasthātmā*)? For, by virtue of having a self at ease, this Buddhist enters into the system of the investigators (*parīkṣaka*).

However, in the second interpretation, one should understand that the "assertion" (*vidhi*) regarding external and internal objects of cognition—which consists of the fourfold nature of intrinsic essence (*svarūpa*) and so forth—and the "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) which is its opposite, are both absolute primary properties (*pradhānadharmāu*) consisting of conventional discourse (*saṃvṛtivāda*), specifically distinct verbal expressions fashioned by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
The rest is as before.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is the inclusion of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
by the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of the Noble Truths characterized by origin, cessation, and the path.
If it is argued that since no entity whatsoever can withstand analysis, let there be universal emptiness alone; to this, he says: "This follows from the force of the thing itself," and so forth.

When the World-Honored One declared that this world is empty because it arises through the power of entities (*vastubala*), and since every entity, when investigated, is found to be non-existent— while everything else in the world is unstable—
then indeed the Kali age has entered, and its voice is to be heeded as a great calamity.
Agitated and deceived by the talkative red-robed ones who are devoted to extremist views, [the author says]:
"That which the Sugata, the trustworthy one, has declared—that very thing follows from the power of reality; it has come through the force of the facts.
What is that? He says: "This world is empty."
Why is this? He says: "Because," and so forth.

Because, for whatever reason, when every single object and all other categories are examined, they are found to be "not established"—the word "ca" (and) being used here as an emphatic particle meaning "indeed. Thus, this Dharmakīrti, whose speech is neither to be understood nor accepted in this world, has indeed entered into a great calamity; the Kali age has arrived.

Of what nature was he? To this he says: "Those who are attached through a one-sided grasping, and who are indeed red-robed (Raktapaṭas) and talkative—by them [he] was previously deceived (vipralambha), and afterwards distressed by their words which were deficient in both means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and objects of cognition (prameya). Thus ends the ninth chapter, "The Establishment of Sound," in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by Anantavīrya, the disciple of the venerable Ravibhadra.
The Tenth Chapter.

10. The Establishment of the Nayas: Immediately after the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), wishing to establish the nayas, [the author] first states the verse summarizing their meaning, beginning with "of the knowers" (*jñātṝṇām*):
"The intentions (*abhisandhi*) of the knowers are indeed the nayas; they [arise] from the standpoint of substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*)."
Substance is twofold, consisting of infinite modes; the modes are of the nature of differentiation.
Through the distinction of their purity, the *nayas* are manifold, beginning with seven and based on the objects [of knowledge].
Among these, four begin with the *naigama*, while the remaining three are based on the word (*śabda*). 1.

Those who know their own objects through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, possess intentions (*abhisandhi*) that indeed clearly constitute *nayas*, being conceptual determinations of a single portion of the object established by the *pramāṇas*. This is the general definition of a *naya*;
he states its divisions: "those *nayas* are twofold"—the ellipsis to be supplied is that they are established in two ways.
Why? He says: "In substance," and so forth.

This means that from the perspective of substance (*dravya*), one relies on substance, and from the perspective of modification (*paryāya*), one relies on modifications; this refers to the substantialist (*dravyārthika*) and modificationist (*paryāyārthika*) viewpoints.

He states the nature of substance: "Substance is the locus of infinite modifications. Infinite means endless, without limit; modifications (*paryāya*) mean changes or transformations (*pariṇāma*); it is their locus or station.

This is an elliptical indication; by it, the phrase "the locus of beginningless modifications" (*anādiparyāyapada*) is also to be understood. By this, a substance (*dravya*) that is eternal and of a single uniform nature is rejected.
This has already been established by the statement "the locus of modifications," which negates their independence.
Similarly, what is the locus of substance (*dravya*)? If you say it is another substance, then for that too there would be yet another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If you say that it is independent (*svatantra*), then [we reply]: if it is argued that the modes (*paryāyas*) are likewise [independent] because they possess the cause of specific existence (*sattā-viśeṣa-hetu-bhāva*), it has already been stated in this regard: just as the appearances of blue and so forth within a single variegated cognition appear as dependent (*paratantra*) upon it, so too do those [modes] always appear [as dependent]; therefore, like that cognition itself, it is not logically tenable to necessarily seek another locus for it.
By the phrase "having beginningless modes," he rejects the notion that substances such as the soul (*jīva*) have a beginning;

and by the phrase "having endless modes," he likewise rejects [the notion] regarding lamps and the like. In both cases, [the entity] is a substance (*dravya*), because it is not sublated by the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Of the attributes,
as [in the case] of that which possesses attributes, of the attributes.

The finitude of substances such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth is thereby rejected if they are held to be beginningless, while the finitude of things such as lamps is rejected if they are held to be eternal.

Now, if it is argued: "Even when substances and so forth are distinct and reside therein by way of inherence (*samavāya*), they still possess that status [of being finite or infinite]; why then is this [position] excluded?"—it is precisely for this reason: if there is an absolute distinction between substance, mode, and inherence, there is no basis for certainty as to which belongs to which.

He states the essential nature of synonyms (*paryāya*): "Consisting of difference" means those whose essence or nature is *bheda*, which is mutual exclusion (*parasparavyāvṛtti*); they are thus called synonyms, based on the etymological derivation that they "move through" (*pariyanti*) difference. If it is argued that this [etymology] is contradicted by the rule for the formation of the word "synonyms" (*paryāya*), and therefore its establishment is not proven—[the author replies]: No; for according to the Jaina grammar (Jainendra), the suffix *-vun* is applied after the root *arh* in the sense of "fitting for" (*arha*). (Jainendra 2.3).

In this regard, although the form is established by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the sense of "synonym" (*paryāya*), the *Jainendra-vyākaraṇa* (2.3) states: "The forms *nyāya*, *pariṇāya*, and *paryāya* [are derived as such]."

36. Thus, the formation of this specific grammatical term (*nipātana*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule] is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*), since both cases are established.
Demonstrating once again that duality, he says: "Its purity" (*tacchuddhi*), and so forth.

"Its" refers to those substances (*dravya*) and modes (*paryāya*). "Purity of substance" is the exclusion of modes; "purity of modes" is their mutual dependence. By treating these two as a copulative compound in the singular (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*), the neuter gender and the short vowel substitution are applied.

"That very [nature] or its division by that [duality] makes it twofold"—this formulation depends upon the *sunaya* (correct method). However, this twofoldness depends upon both *sunaya* and *durnaya* (incorrect method); such is the distinction.
Furthermore, showing their internal subdivisions, he says: "they are of many kinds."
"How many are there? he asks; [the answer] is "seven," and here too it should be understood as "in terms of substance and modification.
Showing that there are internal subdivisions even within these seven, he says "from the beginning," and so forth.

Of the seven perspectives (*nayās*), the first four beginning with the figurative (*naigama*) are based on meaning (*arthāśraya*) and prioritize meaning in this world. How many among the remaining ones, such as the verbal (*śabda*), etc., are there? What are those three? To this he says: "Based on words" (*śabdataḥ*), meaning they function by relying upon words; thus the Naiyāyika declares.

The twofold nature of the relationship has been stated: comparison consists of the application of words according to the meaning, while the direct method consists of the sequence of the subject matter.
The abandonment of false speech and the attainment of the goal are what the rest [of the teachers] declare—
Viśeṣāvaśyaka-gāthā 2753;
Laghīyastraya-śloka 72.
*Tattvārthavārttika*, p.
261; *Nayavīthī*, p. 262; *Pramāṇanayatatvāloka*, 7.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 23; Nayapradīpa, p. 104.
Explaining this very same conduct, he says: "Knowledge," and so forth.

They say that knowledge is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the perspective (*naya*) is considered the thought of the knower. The comparison is: "Knowledge becomes the means of valid cognition; the perspective is also the state within the heart of the knower."
"Placement (*nikṣepa*) is also a means (*upāya*) for the comprehension of meaning through reasoning"—
Tattvārthasūtra 1.5. Knowledge is held to be the means for [the comprehension of] the self and other [objects], consisting of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
*Naya* is the intention of the knower; it is the apprehension of an object through reasoning. — *Laghīyastraya*, Śloka 52; *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 127.
This has been extracted from the *Dharmasaṃgrahaṭīkā* (p.
16): "The comprehension of objects characterized by substance and mode [occurs] through those two.
By the restrictive particle *eva* ("only") in the phrase "knowledge alone," there is the exclusion of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and other such factors whose nature is not conscious.
Without the use of the term *syāt* (in some respect), when one seeks to exclude ignorance and the like, knowledge might be excluded even in its unintended form;

for if it were said that "knowledge is indeed a valid means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*), it would follow [absurdly] that it is also [a means of cognition] in its unintended form, because there is no rule of non-contradiction regarding that which is ineffective and so forth, since the definition [of a valid means of cognition] consists in the apprehension of an object not previously apprehended.

If *naya* were identical in nature to *pramāṇa*, its separate mention would be purposeless; otherwise, how could there be "comprehension" (*adhigama*) by means of it, such that "comprehension is established through *pramāṇas* and *nayas*" could be taught? This is not so, because the comprehension of reality is possible through it, since *naya* is characterized by the examination of that [reality]. When there is an investigation into the two—the substantial (*dravyārthika*) and the modal (*paryāyārthika*)—there is no contradiction in the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), as it is stated that "[it] is knowledge. Thus, it should be understood that it is indeed knowledge; the same applies elsewhere. Otherwise, the statement of it [as *naya*] would be purposeless, for [the term] *pramāṇa* refers to each respective...
He states the definition of *naya*: "Because it is rooted in this [pramāṇa], *naya* is considered the opinion or intention of the knower who possesses valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If one asks, "For what purpose is the description of *pramāṇa* and *naya*? he replies here: "From these two, *pramāṇa* and *naya*, comes comprehension (*adhigama*), which is to say, ascertainment (*nirṇaya*)," according to the statement in the *Tattvārthasūtra* (1.6): "Comprehension is by means of *pramāṇa* and *naya*."
Of what things, and of what nature? He says: "of objects" and so forth; this is connected [to the previous statement] because [the treatise] is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In response to the question "Of what kind [of things]? here, the answer must be "those characterized by substance and modes" (*dravyaparyāyaśālinām*).

This is because the commentary on the verse—beginning with "knowledge alone," etc.—establishes that knowledge alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), thereby excluding [the validity of] sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth.

Of what kind [of self]? Of one whose nature is non-cognition (*asaṃvidātman*), such as wrong cognition (*matyajñāna*) and so forth; "exclusion" (*vyudāsa*) means rejection. Now, if you argue: "By the word 'cognition' (*jñāna*), which follows the logical connection here, you indeed exclude wrong cognition and the like; whereas for the Buddhists and others, this is done by the word 'non-erroneous' (*abhrānta*) and so forth. Therefore, what is your distinction from them? To this he says: "In some way," and so on. The connection with the word "entirely" (*kāt*) is as follows: "If there were exclusion of wrong cognition and the like in some way—that is, by any particular mode of delimitation—without the word 'in some way' (*syātkāra*)."

Here is the refutation: Even by the Buddhists and others who hold a particular view of the self, that very nature of the self—such as self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—by which the validity of correct cognition and the like is accepted, would not exclude [the status of] correct cognition and so forth, let alone [invalid cognitions such as] the appearance of two moons;
this has already been examined.
But it is not so. Therefore, the sense is that the term "syāt" (in some respect) must be applied everywhere, for there is a requirement for it.
[The opponent argues: "In that case, the phrase 'because it excludes that' is redundant here.

For while validity (*prāmāṇya*) is shown to be restricted to cognition, cognition itself is not restricted [to validity], as it may also fall into invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). [The author replies: That is not correct, for cognition consists of sensory knowledge (*mati*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), mind-reading (*manaḥparyaya*), and omniscience (*kevala*).

If it is argued that "it is of that same measure" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.9, 10), the response here is as follows: the intention is that there is a double restriction here, namely, "only knowledge is the means of valid cognition.
If it is asked whether this would also apply to those who hold extremist views (ekāntavādin), the response is: "it is not accepted," and so forth.

The phrase "without the term *syāt*" (syātkāram antareṇa) continues [from the previous context], for this is the meaning: if it were said that "knowledge is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even without the term *syāt*," then it would follow—absurdly—that it would also be a means of valid cognition in its aspect as it is not accepted to be a means of valid cognition by the opponent.
Why? To this he says: "because it would be ineffective, etc. (*akiñcitkarādeḥ*).

If it is argued that consciousness at the beginning of sleep is ineffective because it is not a constituent part of purposeful activity, and therefore, in its absence, awakening would lack a material cause—[the answer is:

if it were to have the waking mind as its material cause, why would it not likewise have as its material cause fathers and others who fell asleep at the same time? [If you say] "because they exist at different times," this applies equally to the other case.

Because they belong to different continua (*bhinnasantānatvāt*). [Objection: How can there be a single continuum elsewhere? [Response: Because of the relationship between material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāvāt*). [Reply: This is a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*); for instance, the relationship of material cause and effect is established only when the intended waking consciousness and the awakening [of another] are proven to belong to a single continuum, and conversely, their belonging to a single continuum is established only when that causal relationship exists. If it is argued that, for this very reason, the waking consciousnesses of a father and son should be considered a single continuum because of the absence of that [causal relationship], then from what is that [absence] known? It is known from their belonging to different continua. This is yet another circular argument: their belonging to different continua follows from the absence of that [causal relationship], and from that, the absence of that [causal relationship] follows.

Now, if it is argued that because they reside in different bodies, the waking consciousness of the progenitor is not the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) for the awakening consciousness of the offspring; then, the consciousness of the body at the end of a dream arising from the consciousness of the sleeping body, or the consciousness of the sleeping body arising from the consciousness of the dreaming body, or the consciousness of the awakening from sleep arising from the consciousness of the sleeping body, would all have to be non-conscious as their material cause.
Or how could the consciousness of the body in the next world arise from the consciousness of the body in this life?
[This is] a certainty based on valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*).
If it is argued that this occurs during sleep and so forth, [we reply] no,
because of the absence of the relationship between material cause and its effect.
If it is argued that there is the relationship of material cause and its effect; [we reply] no, because of the absence of the relationship between material cause and its effect.

Furthermore, how could there be identity between the waking, sleeping, and awakened bodies of Devadatta if difference were absolute? [It is possible] because of the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*); therefore, let it be so elsewhere as well.

However, if there were no relationship of material cause and effect between the bodies of a progenitor and his offspring situated in different locations, then there would be no such relationship between the body of one who has fallen asleep and the body in the state of dreaming.

Moreover, if one were to wake up in a place other than where one fell asleep, this would imply that the relationship of material cause and effect exists between two minds located in different places, but not between their respective bodies—this is a point that requires reflection.

It might be thought: "Since the father's body remains in that very same state, how can the body of the offspring, which is to be taken up [as a new entity], arise from it? And how could there be the breathing and so forth of a dream-body while the sleeping body remains in that same state? If you think this is not at all the case; [we reply: it is not so.

Now, it might be thought: since awakening is observed to conform to the specific waking mind intended [at sleep], that [mind] is its material cause. For instance, the awakening of one who was angry, asleep, or in a swoon is seen to be exactly corresponding to that state, as evidenced by the subsequent grasping of weapons and so forth. This is not so, because there is no such rule.
Because consciousness is sometimes observed to be clear and at other times deluded,
it follows that in other cases as well, it may somehow imitate those states;

for instance, when a child is born after some time following the death of the father— occurring after the union of semen and blood in the womb— that offspring is perceived even by the mind to imitate him.

Furthermore, if even a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) that is separated by a long duration [of time] can be such, why should a similar thing not also be the objective support (*ālambana-kāraṇa*) of cognition? If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", [the answer is: there would be no error. If it is argued that this is not the case because, for one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*), things like hair-tufts appear in a different location and so forth, and thus the person engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārī*) does not think so; [we reply: it is the same, for he would likewise not consider the awakening from a consciousness separated [by sleep].
Indeed, the person engaged in worldly transaction does not regard one who is asleep as being dead; rather, through the perception of a specific form, he infers the presence of consciousness.

If it is asked, "How can that [object] exist there when it is not perceived by oneself? [we reply: How does such mental perception exist? Just as it is recited in the scriptures, so too is consciousness during sleep and other states;

yet, one who claims that there is no difference between these two states says that [consciousness] exists unperceived according to his own acceptance, but not according to the acceptance of others—thus he acts according to his own whims.
The practitioner, while asleep, [perceives] that which has been separated by a long period of time.
Mental perception is not itself perceived by itself.

"Surely," says another, "mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), which consists of determinate cognitions such as 'this is blue' or 'this is yellow,' has already been defined. To this it was replied: during the state of sensory activity, if that [determinate cognition] is postulated, it is merely a different name for what is produced by the senses;

there is no other state manifesting color and so forth in which such a conceptualization could occur, as in the case of a "true dream. If you say this, then since visual activity is not perceived either before or after [the cognition], it is produced by sensory knowledge (*indriya-jñāna*). (Nyāyabindu 1)

Thus, that mental consciousness— which is produced by the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) consisting of sensory cognition assisted by its own object and the immediately subsequent object— is contradicted [by the latter]. — *Nyāyabindu* 1.9.

How could such yogic perception not be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Now, if it is maintained that during the stage of practice (*abhyāsa*) this [perception] is mental (*mānasa*), then this must be considered: does it have a future object as its domain, or a present object as its domain? In the first case, that [mental cognition] alone would be the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) there, and not that which is born of the senses; thus, its lack of validity would be like that of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

In the other case, the mental [cognition] lacks validity because it does not prompt action (*apravartakatva*). Furthermore, the operation of the sense organs (*akṣa*) occurs with respect to the present, whereas the mental [cognition] pertains to that; since the operation of the sense organs does not occur with respect to the future, the [cognition] there is born of the senses—this is a great contradiction.
Mental perception is admitted [as occurring] when the activity of the eye has ceased.

It might be thought: "In the state of sensory operation, both types of perception—the mental and the sense-born—function constantly. If that were so, then for this Buddhist, just as for the Naiyāyika, there would always be a dual appearance of forms and other objects.

Now, if you think: "Because it is non-determinative in nature, the mental [perception] remains unobserved due to being overshadowed by the sensory cognition which is free from conceptual construction (avikalpa); likewise, let the experience during sleep and so forth be of such a kind, being overshadowed by torpor (middha)," then it has been well said: "The awareness of sleep and so forth [is established]."

That which has as its beginning [the factors] that cause doubt and error is described as such; because of the transgression of that [reliability], it would follow that even one who considers themselves to possess knowledge [would be so].

If it is argued, "Let there be validity for that too," [the author] says here: "That," etc.—because that non-contradiction, consisting of being "inefficacious" and so forth, is impossible by necessity, that is, by way of its inevitable occurrence.

Alternatively, since the restriction that [a cognition] is non-contradictory with respect to that [object] is impossible, it would follow—absent the use of the term "syāt" (perhaps)—that it would be established as having an unintended nature.

Let it be granted, then, that such a restriction is impossible; nevertheless, if it is argued that its validity arises from the illumination of an unknown object, to this he replies: "In regard to what has not been apprehended," and so forth.
Therefore, he does not explain the statement "knowledge is the means of valid cognition" and "consciousness is held to be the cognizer," because it is easily understood.
Merely to resolve the objection raised there, he says "of the *naya*," and so forth.

[Objection: If the *naya* were of the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its separate mention would be purposeless; one should simply say that "cognition is valid cognition. Furthermore, in that case, there would be identity with the other [type of cognition], and thus it would not have that nature; therefore, its separate mention is justified. To this, he replies: otherwise—that is, in the manner of lacking the nature of valid cognition—how could there be "comprehension" (*adhigama*) by means of that *naya*, i.e., the determination of its own object? For it is because of that comprehension that there is "comprehension through both valid cognitions and *nayas*" (Tattvārthasūtra 1.6).

It might be argued that the meaning of reality should be established by the author of the Sūtras; for there can be no comprehension of anything by means of what is not a valid means of knowledge (apramāṇa), as this would result in the futility of examining the means of knowledge—this is the sense [of the objection].
To this, the reply begins with "No," and so forth.

What was stated by the opponent is not correct. Why? He says: because from that *naya* (perspective), the comprehension of reality (*tattva*)—such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth—is logically established.

Why is this so? He says: because its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the examination of that [reality]; for that *naya* has the very examination—the investigation—of that [reality], such as the soul, as its characteristic or essential nature (*svarūpa*). If one asks, "How then is the comprehension of that [reality] established? he says here: "In substance," and so forth.
