When there is an investigation of either both or each of the two viewpoints (nayas)—namely, the substantialist (dravyārthika) and the modalist (paryāyārthika)—the realization of the ultimate truth occurs; because this realization of the ultimate, or of ultimates, is non-contradictory, reality becomes well-examined and more firmly established. This is the logic of the investigator regarding the viewpoint.
Regarding the phrase "having the nature of a means of valid cognition":
if, indeed, the apprehension of that [object] arises from it, then it follows that it must be a means of valid cognition, because that is the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition.

And if it is argued that the resolution of the final objection does not apply to anything else, [the author] says here: "It might be so even if it were of the nature of a means of valid cognition," and so forth;
by this method, the term *prati* is used here in the sense of "rubbed" (*ghṛṣṭā*).

Even though it consists of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one should understand that *naya* is the source of valid cognition; it is investigation (*vicāra*), the means for reaching a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), and critical examination (*parīkṣā*).

For even when something has been directly perceived by oneself, disputes are observed; therefore, without the intention of reasoning through inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*), there can be no firm adherence to the true nature of reality (*tattva*) therein, since its application is required in all cases.

If it is argued that since there is no distinction between what is examined and what is not for one who perceives directly, and that if the object were established by that alone, no one would possess knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)—for how could there be any other such knowledge?—[we reply: even though direct realization is the same through both sound reasoning (*sunaya*) and fallacious reasoning (*durṇaya*), the adherence to reality or its opposite arises from a difference in intention; for examination (*parīkṣā*) is grounded in that [intention].

It might be that [the term] *pramāṇabhāva* refers to that whose origin or production (*prabhava*) is from valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which consists in the apprehension of the manifold; thus, it means "distinct from that. Since there is some degree of difference between cause and effect, he asks:
"What is it? and replies: "Naya," which is the intention (*abhiprāya*) of determining a single portion grasped by valid cognition.

Even when what is present? He says: "Even though the *naya* has the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), how can it have that [same] nature? He says: "The *naya* is the means for reaching a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*);
how has even that gone? He says: "Because of the absence of dispute (*vivāda*)."

If it is objected: "Does not investigation (vicāra) also occur for those who maintain that perception and other means of knowledge are conceptual (savikalpaka)? What, then, is the distinction of this [naya]? To this he replies: "Investigation (parīkṣā) is the act of examining; let it be understood that *naya* is that investigation which proceeds by way of [determining] whether an entity is eternal or momentary. It might be thought: 'Naya pertains to a single part of an object determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since that [part] is established by the *pramāṇa* itself, wholes are not established without the establishment of their parts.'"

When a tree moves, it moves together with its parts; what, then, is the use of logic (*naya*) in that case? To this he replies: "By oneself," and so forth. This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication), meaning that even when a thing has been directly perceived by oneself, or even when it has been stated or inferred, because disputes are observed regarding that object, there subsequently arises—without the intention of deliberation and exclusion—a persistent attachment to the view of reality (*tattva-abhiprāya*), which is a delight in the truth (*tattva-ruci*). For from that [delight] comes the practice [of the truth] everywhere, both externally and internally.

If it is argued that even without that intention, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding reality—since, just as with what is accepted, there would be the consequence of such insistence (*abhiniveśa*) upon what is not accepted, and thus perception itself prevents this over-extension—the author replies here: because there is no distinction between the examination and its opposite in the case of the perception of a perceptual apprehension, if it were admitted that the object is established merely by that apprehension, then true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) would belong to neither the investigator nor anyone else; consequently, the investigator would not differ from others, and thus investigation would be useless. This is the sense.

The opponent asks: "For what reason, then, does true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) arise, or conversely, false knowledge (*atattvajñāna*)? To this, he replies: "By right method and wrong method" (*sunayadurṇayābhyām*).

[The opponent objects: "If it is argued that, as with the Buddhists and others, true knowledge arises through right method and false knowledge through wrong method"; to this, he says: "Even though the direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is the same for both the Jaina and the proponent of an absolute doctrine (*ekāntavādin*), the distinction between true and false adherence (*abhiniveśa*) is established because of the difference in intention (*abhiprāya*), since intention—being dependent on the knower’s disposition—is characterized by whether it conforms to the object or not."
Why is that so? He says: because examination consists in the nature of a perspective (*naya*) and is grounded therein;
therefore, [the objection] raised here is shattered.

In this context, [the author], showing that [the path] has been broken here and broken there, as well as the distinction between sound reasoning (*sunaya*) and fallacious reasoning (*durṇaya*), says: "Therein," and so forth.
In this regard, the two fundamental standpoints (*naya*) have as their objects substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*).
When these are independent [of one another], they constitute falsity (*mithyātva*); when they are the reverse of that, they constitute rightness (*samyaktva*).
Investigation is established upon difference and non-difference. He states the twofold nature of the standpoints because of the twofold nature of their objects, namely substance and mode.
In that regard, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the apprehension of mutual inseparability (*avinābhāva*);
otherwise, there would be no examination of the means of valid cognition,
because the apprehension of non-existence while [the other] exists is difficult to establish.

Comparison—because valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perspective (*naya*), and fallacious perspective (*durṇaya*) are characterized respectively by the acquisition of other properties, indifference, and abandonment; because no other categories are possible; because through valid cognition there is the comprehension of that [object] as having such a nature or not having it; through perspective there is the comprehension of that [partial aspect]; and through fallacious perspective there is the rejection of what is other than that—as stated in the *Aṣṭaśatī* and *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 279.

"Only that which exists would exist; thus the object is measured in three ways as 'existent' by means of fallacious reasoning, the [pseudo-]standpoint, and valid cognition"—*Anyayogavyavaccheda*, verse 8. *Laghu-īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*, verse 30: "Only that which exists would exist; thus the object is measured in three ways as 'existent' by means of fallacious reasoning, the [pseudo-]standpoint, and valid cognition."—*Anyayogavyavaccheda*, verse 8.

In that regard, concerning the general definition of the *nayas*: the two root *nayas*—the *naigama* and others which serve as their primary forms—are those whose objects (*artha*) or spheres of operation (*gocara*) are substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*). Thus they are described as such: the *dravyārthika*, meaning "having substance as its object," and the *paryāyārthika*, meaning "having modification as its object. *Mithyātva* (falsity) consists in their independence, that is, the absence of mutual dependence; *samyaktva* (correctness) is the opposite of that, meaning dependence upon one another regarding the domain of independence—that is, regarding the domain of dependence.
And so it has been said:
Comparison: "Nayas that are independent are false; those that are dependent on one another are, in reality, effective. — Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 108.
"Therefore, all nayas are false views when they are bound to their own respective sides. — Sanmatitarka-prakaraṇa.
Furthermore, the states of right belief arise as mutually dependent—
Sanmati-tarka 1.21.
Those very same perspectives— such as eternalism, momentariness, and so forth— which, when independent of one another, destroy both themselves and others,
are for you, the stainless Sage, the very truth when they are mutually dependent, as they then benefit both themselves and others. (Bṛhat-sva-vṛtti, Śloka 61)
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "Examination" (*parīkṣā*), and so forth; the meaning is "the nature of the general method of examination.

To the question "Of what [is this]?"—that is, what is its object?—he says: "The establishment of difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedapratiṣṭhā*); that is, that which has as its basis the establishment or existence of difference and non-difference, i.e., particularity and generality. He states the twofold nature of the *naya* because of the twofold nature of its objects, namely substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*).
He explains "rightness" (*samyaktva*) and so forth as follows:

therein, when there exists that nature and differentiation of the *nayas*, that examination in which there is the comprehension of the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the substances and their qualities is "the comprehension of mutual inseparable concomitance.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "It is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), O sages"—this is the sense.

He explains the passage beginning with "If it were otherwise" (*mithyātvaṃ syād*): "Otherwise"—that is, in a manner other than the realization of their mutual inseparability—it would not be an examination by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why? He says: "Only when [it exists]," and so forth.

Only when [the substance] exists—that is, while it is present—does the negation of existence in the mode (*paryāya*) of the modal standpoint (*paryāyārthika*) occur within the substance for the substantial standpoint (*dravyārthika*); therefore, [without that existence], it is not a valid cognition.

For this very reason, showing that the cognition of non-existence occurs only when there is indeed a faulty formulation (*durṇayatā*), he says: "of the substantialist" (*dravyārthikasya*), and so forth.
The repetition here of the phrase "only when there is" (*satyeva*) is redundant.
For the substantialist (dravyārthika), the modes (paryāyas) do indeed exist here, though they are not intended to be expressed;
likewise, for the modalist (paryāyārthika), the substance exists as real from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārthataḥ).

For the substantialist, whose primary intention concerns the object that is substance, the modes—such as the distinctions between a post, a palanquin, and so forth—do indeed exist here; for it has been stated that in their absence, even the substance would be non-existent.

If it is argued that, consequently, there would be no distinction between *nayapramāṇa* (the standpoint as a means of knowledge) and *durṇaya* (a fallacious standpoint), he replies here: "They [the other aspects] exist in it [the *naya*] without being intended for expression (*avivakṣita*) and thus remain subordinate (*guṇībhūta*); however, in the case of *pramāṇa*, both are primary.
What is the point of this? He says: "That which exists" (*sat*) means existing in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

To the question "Of whom?", he says: "Of one for whom the modes (paryāya) are the object," that is, of one whose intention is primarily concerned with the modes; the word "api" is used here to include this intention, and it should be understood that [the mode] is not intended [as the primary object] in this case either.
If that which appears were non-existent, there would be the loss of even its synonym;
since the verse is easy to understand in the absence of a synonym, no commentary has been provided.

If it is asked: "If there are modes (paryāya) for the substantialist (dravyārthika) and substance (dravya) for the modalist (paryāyārthika), how can there be a negation of existence? To this he replies: "Of cognitions," and so forth; [it means] that among the various forms of cognitions which appear as illusory, there exists [a distinction].
Alternatively, there is the perception of contradiction regarding things whose nature is well-known to be non-false.

Without distinction, the determination of the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) through the apprehension of falsity in the qualities and modes (*guṇaparyāya*), whether in some cases or in certain instances, is a "bad method" (*durṇaya*) because it contradicts recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, the determination of the modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*) is a bad method because it contradicts all [recognition], resulting in the perception of contradiction among cognitions—that is, among acts of knowledge—due to the rejection of reality.
Where? He says: "In the various forms," meaning in the specific forms of the perceiving consciousness; this is to be connected with the word "of cognitions" (*saṃvidām*).
Indeed, it is not logical for a single entity to possess multiple forms that are ultimately real, because of contradiction.
This has been stated from the perspective of the proponents of Pure Consciousness (*śuddhavijñānavādin*).
With reference to the perspective of external objects (bāhyārthanaya), he says: "delusion" (vibhrama) and so forth.

"Delusion" (vibhrama) is that which causes one to wander; it refers to appearances characterized by [the perception of] silver and the like. The word "or" (vā) is used in a conjunctive sense to mean "in those [appearances] belonging to things such as fragments of clay perceived by those whose senses are afflicted by mantras and the like."

Of what kind [of things]? It says: "in those whose self is established as unreal" (*prasiddhavitathātmasu*). That is to say, in those whose self (*ātman*) is established—meaning renowned among the world of examiners and others—as unreal (*vitatha*), that is, untrue. What is the apprehension of them? To this he says: "without distinction," and so forth.
Where is there a realization of falsity that is non-distinctive and universal? To this he says: "With respect to qualities and modes (guṇaparyāya);

for instance—the internal distinction of consciousness, pleasure, and so forth, and the external distinction of jars, cloths, and so forth, are false because they are cognized as distinct appearances, like the distinctions between the forms of the grasped object and so on, or like the [illusory] distinction of two moons."

What is achieved by that? He says: by that realization of falsity (*mithyātva-pratipatti*), there is the determination of the substantial object (*dravyārthāvadhāraṇa*). The "substantial object" (*dravyārtha*) means that the substance alone is the object; its determination is the thought, "That alone exists. Just as, even when there is the delusion of forms such as the perceived object (*grāhya*), there is no delusion regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); and just as, even in the error of dreams and the like, there is no error regarding the waking state; so too, even amidst the delusion of all distinctions, there is no delusion regarding pure existence (*sattāmātra*).

Therefore, that which was stated by Prajñākara—"Even if pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth, appear, what confidence can there be in their substantiality (dravya) if they are false?"—is refuted. This is because recognition is non-contradictory in some cases, whether external or internal, regarding certain other objects such as nails that have been cut and grown back again; yet, since that recognition is contradicted in every way, such as by change of location and so forth, he asks: "And what is the determination of modes (paryāya)? The meaning is: the former is a fallacious mode of the substantialist (dravyārthika-naya), and the latter is a fallacious mode of the modalist (paryāyārthika-naya). Thus it is a "bad method" (durṇaya).
Why? He says: because of the rejection—that is, the refutation—of the reality of the soul and so forth.
Demonstrating the determination of the substantial aspect (dravyārtha), he says "pure," etc.:
for the pure substantial standpoint (śuddhadravyārthika), there exists, from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārthataḥ), mere existence (sanmātra).
There is no difference in form, nor color and so forth, nor sequence, nor pleasure and the like.
Indeed, consciousness does not deviate from existence, because it deviates only with respect to particularities,
whereas existence itself is never dissociated from those particularities.

And since there is no cognition that does not deviate from distinction, this is a *durṇaya* (fallacious standpoint) because it propounds pure substance while negating modes, just as [it is said]: "They see the grove, but no one sees it" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.14).

14. Thus, this other perspective based on that [previous view] is the *śuddha-paryāya-naya* (the pure mode-of-aspect standpoint). Furthermore, if it is argued that even when there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*), there is no unity of being (*bhāva-ekatva*) anywhere, and that there is no diversity whatsoever because that would entail the consequence of absolute non-duality (*advaita-prasaṅga*), then this method of defining the mode-of-aspect while completely rejecting substance (*dravya*) is a fallacious standpoint (*durṇaya*). This is because it is another perspective based on the *naigama* [standpoint], which assumes a total lack of identity between these two [substance and mode], whereas the *naigama* is characterized by not intending to exclude their identity.

Comparison (*tulanā*): The *naigama* [standpoint] is defined by the description of the mutual relationship between unity and difference as being subordinate to one another; however, when asserting that they are entirely distinct entities, it is considered a fallacy of *naigama* (*naigamābhāsa*).
— *Laghīyastraya*, Verse 39.

Among these, the *naigama* perspective (*naya*) is that which grasps mere conceptualization; alternatively, it is considered *naigama* by the wise because it does not proceed (*gama*) toward a single [aspect] alone.
It consists of the intentionality regarding two properties, or two substrata, or both property and substratum.
—Tattvasaṃgrahaśloka, p. 269;
Nayaviniścayaśloka, 33–37;
Sanmatitarkaṭīkā, p. 310.
*Nayacakra*, verse 33;
*Tattvārthasāra*, page 107;
*Pramāṇanaya*, verse 7.
7. Syādvādamañjarī, p. 311; Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p. 21.

The *śuddhadravyārthika* (the one who maintains the pure substantial standpoint) is so called because for him the object (*artha*) is the substance (*dravya*) itself—pure, devoid of the stains of conceptual modes (*paryāya*). What does he maintain? He says: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is only pure existence (*sanmātra*), not by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtyā*). There is no differentiation of forms, nor any distinction such as the grasped (*grāhya*) and so forth, nor distinctions such as grossness and so forth, nor form (*rūpa*) and so forth, nor sequence, nor the relation of cause and effect, nor pleasure and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality; rather, these exist only by way of conventional truth.
Thus, the connection is that "they exist" [only conventionally].
Explaining the verse, he says: "Indeed, consciousness does not deviate from the existence (*sadbhāva*) of being (*sattva*).
Why? He says: "In regard to particulars," and so forth.
He states the refutation regarding the deviation from being: "In mere being," and so forth.
If it is argued that consciousness does not deviate even from its specific attributes, to this he replies: "And it is not so," and so forth.

Since pure existence (*sanmātra*) is invariably concomitant with its specific attributes, there is no cognition that does not deviate from those differences, because deviation has been demonstrated therein. Thus, since this is an exposition of the pure substance (*śuddhadravya*), how can there be a fallacious standpoint (*durṇaya*)? This is the logical connection.
Why? To this he says: "In its successive manifestations," and so forth.

He provides an illustration: "Just as people perceive that substance which is mere existence (sattāmātra) through the expansion of traditional scripture (āgamamāṭopa), yet no one perceives its true being (sadbhāva)—that is, another perception based on [the notion of] pure existence (sanmātra) which relies upon that [substance] amidst its various differences."
They see his garden, but no one sees it— Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12.

Showing the intention behind the flawed perspective (*durṇaya*) that seeks the meaning through the mode of modalities (*paryāyārthika*), he says: "Furthermore, the pure modal standpoint (*śuddhaparyāyanaya)... and so forth.

Even if there is a difference in nature—that is, even if there is a plurality of essential forms—if there were no unity of being (*bhāvaikatva*) anywhere, such as in a cloth or other objects, then how could there be plurality in any way, such as through differences in place and so on? Why? He says: because it would result in the absurdity of non-duality (*advaitaprasaṅga*) in every respect, by every manner, such as the case of a jar and so forth.

Showing the result obtained, he says: "In every way," and so forth. To the question, "In what situation does this sequence of defining synonyms constitute a fallacious argument (durṇaya)? he replies: "When there is a rejection of substance (dravya)."
Showing what constitutes a semblance of the *naigama* standpoint, he says "in every way," and so forth.

Because these two—substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*)—are not identical in any respect, such as place and so on, there is the *naigama*; based upon that, how is it that another system of view, namely the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, arises? To this he says: "when not intended to be expressed," and so forth.

Since the Naigama-naya has as its defining characteristic that identity (*tādātmya*) between substance and mode which, though existing, is not intended for expression nor presented, he says "the universal," etc., demonstrating the nature of that other system of views:
[it maintains] the eternality of universals, inherence, and [substances] such as the self.
Therefore, the eternity of that number and so forth [is established], while the remainder is otherwise.

(8) Relying upon the *dravyārthika-naya*, some maintain that substance (*dravya*), its number and so forth, as well as generality (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*), are eternal, whereas the remainder are non-eternal; this is because they accept the non-eternality of produced substances, actions, and specific qualities (*guṇa-viśeṣa*).

However, it is not logical for generality to be a distinct entity (*vastvantara*) [from the individual], just as the conformity to the object (*viṣaya-sārūpya*) is not a distinct entity from cognitions (*saṃvid*).

For entities cannot be said to possess distinctions that are themselves other entities unless there exists a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor; otherwise, the attribution of possession would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Furthermore, it is not even conceivable for that which is unchanging to possess the nature of a real entity.

For such a being, neither occurrence nor non-occurrence anywhere, nor the agency or non-agency in producing cognitions such as "existent" and so forth at any place, at any time, or in any manner, is possible; thus,
[the opposing view] is a fallacious argument.
Just as with existence (*sattā*), if other universals were all-pervading, there would be a confusion of their modes of occurrence and their cognitions;
if they were all-pervading only within their own objects, then since they are inactive and previously non-existent there, they could not reach the location where an object is about to arise.
"Āṭopa" means expansion. Regarding that:

What is the nature of universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*), or of those [categories] beginning with the self (*ātman*)—the word "beginning" (*ādi*) here including the inclusion of all fundamental substances other than the self? To this he says: their eternality (*nityatā*) is due to their being existent and causeless; for that very reason, the eternality of number and so forth as they exist in eternal substances is called the "eternality of number and so forth."
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), transformation and so forth are included;
by this, the ultimate particularities (antyaviśeṣas) residing in eternal and all-pervading substances are explained.
The remainder [of the categories] is "impermanent" in a manner other than what has been stated.
To explain the verse, "Since existence [of the particular] exists, they too are eternal because they lack a cause," he says: "The substantialist perspective (*dravyārthikanaya*)," and so forth.

If entities were eternal, the operation would belong solely to the *dravyārthika* (substantial) standpoint, and not to the *naigama* (holistic) standpoint, because [the latter] involves change; therefore, it is said "relying on the *dravyārthika-naya*. [This means that] the eternity of substance (*dravya*)—such as the self (*ātman*)—and its number, as well as of generality (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*), is established, while the rest are non-eternal. The word "ca" is used for emphasis. Regarding generality and the others, certain [schools] such as the Naiyāyikas maintain or accept this; why? Because [they hold that] the rest are here [in this world] effect-substances (*kārya-dravya*), and so forth.

An effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) is a substance that was previously non-existent and is inherent in its inherent cause of existence (*sattā*). Actions (*karman*), such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth; all specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*) residing in an effect-substance, such as color (*rūpa*) and the rest; and those residing in eternal substances—other than number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth, such as cognition (*buddhi*) and redness (*rakta*) and the rest—are admitted to be impermanent.
Among these, what is the universal (*sāmānya*)? To this he says: "Among them," and so forth.

Among those [categories] beginning with the universal, the universal (*sāmānya*) is the state (*bhāva*) of things that are similar (*samāna*, i.e., resembling); the followers of the Yoga school (*yauga*) maintain that it is indeed distinct from the particulars (*viśeṣa*).

Regarding this, he says: "It is not logical that the universal (*sāmānya*) be a separate entity entirely distinct from the individuals; rather, it is logical that it be somehow non-distinct. He indicates this with the word "only" (*eva*), because there is a lack of evidence for the former case and the opposite for the latter.
[The opponent asks: "How then is that so? [The Buddhist] replies: "Of cognitions," and so forth.

Just as cognitions (*jñāna*) possess a similarity to their objects (*viṣaya-sārūpya*)—that is, just as cognitions have a resemblance to their object—so too is the universal; this has been examined more than once.
If it is asked, "Why is that not simply another entity?"—to this he says: "For indeed," and so forth.

For because [entities] are not distinct from one another by way of being separate entities, the various states (*bhāva*) are mutually different yet identical; otherwise, if they were entirely distinct, just as all the stars are identical to the single moon, there would be no cognition of superimposition (*tāropa*) among them. Thus, it is in every respect due to difference [that they appear as such].

If it should be thought that, despite some degree of difference, the moon does not reside in those [individuals], but rather the universal (*sāmānya*) resides in them all as a residual presence, and therefore this fault does not apply—then he says: "Those possessing it" would mean the particulars (*bheda*) possess the universal, just as a city possesses horses (as in "the horse-city"). To this, he replies: "And how," and so forth.

And in what manner [could this be]? Not by any means other than through the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*), because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). There would be the over-extension that the Vindhya mountain would possess the property of being connected with the probandum (*sādhya*).

Indeed, in your own view, among the clusters of stars, there exists the cognition of form even without the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary; thus, the cognition occurs as possessing the form.

Now, in that case, this very relation of the grasped and the grasper would be their mutual relation; let it be that even for the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), their mutual relation is simply that of the illuminated and the illuminator.

For here, no royal decree prohibits their capacity [to relate], nor does the universal provide any benefit to the individuals—[if you say] "because it generates a qualified cognition" regarding them. To this he replies: For something such as a universal, which is unchanging and eternally of a single form, its status as a real entity—that is, its very existence—is not possible, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For there is no cognition of a universal that is distinct from the sugar-candy and other such things, eternal, partless, and incorporeal, by virtue of which those [individuals] could be its manifestors; rather, it is because those individuals, possessing a similar nature, appear within one's own cognition.

Nor can a universal of such a kind be said to be an "enabler" merely by producing a specific cognition regarding them, since an evolving entity manifests itself directly in cognitions such as those of the eye;
thus, the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary [is established].
If it is argued that individual manifestations are eternal,

Now, if it is thought that because of the relationship of producer and produced (*ropaka-kāryopakāraka-bhāva*), the individuals possess that [universal], whereas the universal possesses it there due to inherence (*samavāya*); to this he says: "of such a kind," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: for something of such a kind—whose existence as a real entity is impossible—there can be no inherence, which is a relation, as its subsistence in some things like a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow), nor can there be its non-subsistence in others like a white horse (*karka*).
For if such a thing were perceived, then one could entertain the conceptualization of whether it subsists in some places or not; otherwise, it is like the son of a barren woman.

By this, the proof for its inherence therein is refuted; for when that [individual] is perceived as existing there, one might think, "The universal exists here" because of that cognition, yet it is not necessarily so. Thus, at the time of the production of the individual, its presence [in the universal] is not possible, nor is its absence at the time of the individual's destruction conceivable.
Indeed, without undergoing transformation, it would be impossible to speak of two distinct forms—relation and its opposite—for a single entity.

For surely it is only the individual aggregate (piṇḍa) that arises or perishes, not the universal (sāmānya) or the inherence (samavāya); nor can one thing possess arising and so forth through the arising of another, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

If it is argued that just as there is no difference [in the entity] despite the presence or absence of agency and non-agency, so too there is none despite the presence or absence of occurrence (*vṛtti*) and non-occurrence (*avṛtti*); this is not correct. For, if its prior nature is not abandoned, the cognitions "this occurs here" and "it does not occur here" would be impossible; or else, such cognitions would arise at all times, since dependence is impossible for that which is eternal.
Therefore, neither partial nor total occurrence or non-occurrence is possible for an entity that is otherwise than what it possesses.

If it is argued that, just as one and the same entity may be both the agent and non-agent of cognitions such as "existence" (sat), so too might it possess both occurrence and non-occurrence [of its own nature], we reply: regarding the phrase "existence and so forth," it is an erroneous position (*durṇaya*) to claim that for any substance, quality, or the like, the agency and non-agency of the cognition of its existence and so forth could possibly occur at some place, at some time, or in any manner whatsoever.

Furthermore, is the universal omnipresent (*sarvagata*), or is it omnipresent only within its own manifestations (*svavyaktisarvagata*)? Regarding the first position, he states the refutation: "Like *sattā*," that is, like the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*). If it is admitted that other universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are omnipresent, there would be a confusion of both occurrence (*vṛtti*) and cognition (*pratyaya*). Just as the occurrence of "cowness" is in a spotted cow (*khaṇḍa*) and so on, so too would the occurrence of "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth be there; thus there is a confusion of occurrence. For that very reason, just as there is the cognition of a "cow" in that instance, there would also be the cognition of "substance" and so forth; thus there is a confusion of cognition. Regarding the second position, [he says] "in its own object" (*svaviṣaye*) and so forth.

The meaning is that, even though [the universal] is omnipresent within its own domain—that is, it pervades all individual instances—it would not [be perceived] by that which is inactive, in the absence of action. "The object" (*artha*) refers to substance and so forth; "in whatever place" means in the location where the object is about to arise (*utpitsu*). The relationship of qualifier and qualified is optional; thus, the word *utpitsu* may function as the qualified term. That place and the attainment of it—prior to its arising, for other classes of things that do not exist in that place—that perception would not occur. As it was stated by the venerable Samantabhadra:
In the case of a sugar-candy and the like, since the universal and the inherence are both obtained in one place,
they could not exist without a substratum; what rule would there be for their destruction and production?

Since it has been stated [in Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 65], "Therefore, it is not logical that this [non-existence] is a separate entity," he says the following to demonstrate this: "When the nature of an existent is perceived... and so forth;
[the question is: when the nature of an existent is perceived, what is the use of existence for those things that possess inherence (*samavāyin*)?
If non-existent things were connected with existence, then there would be no absence of anything anywhere.

If it is argued that for something already existent in itself there is no inherence of existence—just as there is no inherence of universality [in a universal]—then how could one who holds such a view not be a self-contradictor, unless he were mad? Furthermore, what distinction is there between substances and so forth being existent either intrinsically or extrinsically, such that their nature would be specified by a connection with existence?

If, however, because those two are eternal, the report of their non-existence has now been silenced, then this argument of yours is no different from that regarding "existence" (*sattā*); the same analysis applies to other universals (*sāmānya*). Therefore, [the relation] is not mutual...

Those things whose own-nature (*svarūpa*) is existence (*sat*) are "existent by nature" (*satsvabhāva*), such as jars and the like; by this, he rejects the distinction (*vyatireka*) between existence and that which possesses it. When there is their apprehension—that is, their perception—he shows, by this [argument], the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason: "the cognition 'this is a cow' regarding a broken [hornless] ox and so forth is caused by a distinct qualifier, because it is a cognition of one thing as being otherwise, like the cognition 'the man with a staff' regarding a person.
This is because the cognition "jars and the like are existent" occurs even without a distinct qualifier.

If it is argued that even there, a distinct existence (*bhinnasattā*) is manifested, he says in response: "Is it not the case that nothing [is manifested] by means of a connection with a distinct existence?
To whom does this apply? He says: "To the inherent substrates (*samavāyin*), namely substance, quality, and action.

Now, if it is argued that this fault would apply to things that are inherently existent when they enter into that relationship, but not to things that are non-existent; to this he replies: "And if a connection with existence is admitted for non-existent things, then the non-existence of anything—such as a rabbit’s horn—would no longer exist anywhere, such as in a particular place," so the supplement [to the argument].

He states the verse beginning with "of that which exists by itself" (*svataḥ sataḥ*) in order to refute [the opponent's position] regarding the connection with existence (*sattā*) and to provide an explanation.

If it is asked why the mention of "ultimate particulars" (*antyaviśeṣa*) is not included here in the example accepted by others— namely, "like universals and inherence"— it is because these are entirely beyond the senses and thus accepted by [the opponents] themselves,
and because even a fallacious inference cannot apply there, making them unsuitable as examples.

Furthermore, [the claim that] "those ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) are the cause of the cognition of difference among the all-pervading substances for yogins" is not correct; for that cognition arises with respect to them by their very nature. Otherwise, if that cognition regarding them were preceded by yet other [particulars], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding those ultimate particulars asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas.
Because it is not stated by way of illustration,
[the same applies] even to the particulars for yogins.

If it is argued: "Surely universals (*sāmānya*) and the like do not exist through themselves (*svataḥ*), nor through another (*parataḥ*), because within the universal 'Being' (*sattā-sāmānya*) there is no further [universal] of its own kind; how then can they serve as an illustration?"—to this he says: "But if, however," and so forth.
The reply here is easy to understand: how could a Vaiśeṣika or similar proponent, who thus strikes down his own position, not be insane? He is indeed insane.
Since the opponent accepts the non-existence of everything by means of establishing the non-existence of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth—
and because there is no universal without [particulars]—
the author, considering once again the opponent's misconduct, says: "And who," and so on.

If [it is argued that] there is no distinction whatsoever in the case of a cumulative refutation (dūṣaṇasamuccaya), then in what respect? Why [is there no distinction] regarding the existence (sadbhāva) of substances and so forth?

To this he says: [Existence] would have to arise either from itself or from another; for by virtue of some such distinction, an object such as a substance would be differentiated through its connection with existence (sattā).
For instance: for the wise, partiality and its opposite are appropriate only when based on the perception of qualities and defects respectively, and not otherwise.

Now, if it is argued that even when an object exists inherently, there is no perception of even a trace of defect, and thus the very non-perception of it constitutes the perception of it—well then, is there any perception of things that do not exist inherently, such as a rabbit’s horn? No, because of contradiction.

It might be argued that if an object exists by its own nature (*svataḥ-sadbhāva*), there would be an absence of any other universal (*apara-sāmānya*) in it, just as there is none in *sattā* (existence) and so forth. This is not so; for it has been stated here: "Because entities are manifold, some [possess] a further genus while others do not, because we do not observe it to be so in the case of words, just like the connection with qualities (*guṇa*) and the rest."

If it is argued that it is not intended for everything non-existent by its own nature to be perceived, but rather only for that which is related to existence (*sattā*), to this he replies with the words "But if," and so forth. Because those two—existence and inherence (*samavāya*)—are eternal, and because this is an indicative mark [of their nature] due to their omnipresence (*vyāpitva*), the report of non-existence has now perished and been destroyed, since even things such as a donkey’s horn would result in being existent. Therefore, this argument of the opponent is not tenable; such is the conclusion.
Extending this [analysis] to other cases, he says: "Just as with existence," and so forth.
This same immediate and similar investigation applies to other universals (*sāmānya*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like.

For instance, when the nature of substances and so forth is perceived in living beings and the like, what is the use of a separate universal such as substantiality? If things that are themselves not substances were to become substances through a connection with a universal such as substantiality, then nothing would ever remain non-substantial.
The remainder here is the same; as for the conclusion beginning with "that is not so," why is that? He says: "mutually," and so forth.

This too is currently accepted; showing what is merely a semblance of Sāṃkhya and Naigama, he says: "Substance is pure," and so forth—by relying on substance as both pure and impure, there exists another [type of] Naigama.
Just as a fallacious argument (*durṇaya*) might be characterized by a proliferation centered on consciousness (*cit*):

[The Naiyāyika’s position]—relying upon the manifoldness and unity of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which possesses objects not yet manifested, and asserting that *pradhāna*, having entered into the state of cause and effect, undergoes a transformation (*vivarta*) through the sequence of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, and thus offers itself for the sake of the Self (*ātman*)—is a fallacious argument (*durṇaya*). This is because it establishes the nature of the transformation of both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*; furthermore, it is divided into the systems of a single *puruṣa* and multiple *puruṣas* based on the distinction between those who do not accept a Lord (*anīśvara*) and others who do.

The non-theistic distinction [of Sāṃkhya] arises from the possibility of the *pradhāna* acting for the sake of the *puruṣa*; the theistic distinction [of Yoga] arises from the impossibility of such activity [by the *pradhāna* alone]. Furthermore, the reality of consciousness (*caitanya*) as something unchanging has already been refuted by the arguments concerning universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth;
how could it be occasional?

For what discerning person would assert another modification of consciousness belonging to *prakṛti*—which consists of the cognitive functions manifesting in various forms such as joy and sorrow—since it would be useless?
Since the Puruṣa possesses objects shown by Prakṛti, it is difficult to establish its immutability;

for while the Puruṣa’s nature as an enjoyer is eternal, and Prakṛti’s nature as the object of enjoyment is likewise eternal, the occurrence of its activity and cessation remains difficult to reconcile.

Alternatively, if there is transformation (pariṇāma) of Prakṛti, then the power of consciousness (cicchakti) must also undergo a phenomenal modification (vivarta), because it possesses the objects shown by that [Prakṛti].

The genus (*jāti*) designated as *prakṛti*—which consists of the primary matter (*pradhāna*) characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion—is indeed the genus of insentient divisions; it is not, however, the universal (*sāmānya*) that is the genus of the consciousness of all *puruṣas*, for that would be difficult to maintain.
That is not so...

the substance (*dravya*) is of the nature of the *puruṣa*. Of what kind? It is pure (*śuddha*), being devoid of distinctions such as pleasure and the like; and it is impure (*aśuddha*), being the substance characterized as *pradhāna* when surrounded by the modes (*paryāya*) beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*). Relying upon this, there is another *naigama*—distinct from the [logical] *naigama*—who is the conscious *puruṣa*.

How can *pradhāna*, which is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), exist here through their elaboration? The meaning is that just as a fallacious argument (*durṇaya*) might be characterized or determined by a manner in which it is not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too does *prakṛti*— designated as *pradhāna*, the "prolific source" (*bahudhānaka*), and so forth— exist.
Explaining the meaning of the verse regarding the primordial cause, he says: "The power of consciousness," and so forth,
which presents the Pradhāna as the agent.
Of what? He says: of the self, the person (puruṣa).

Of what nature is he? He says: of the power of consciousness (cicchakti). Consciousness (cit) is awareness; he whose power—that is, whose nature—is that, is "of the power of consciousness. For there is the statement in the *Yogabhāṣya* (1.9): "Consciousness is the essential nature of the person."

Having done what? He says: "having resorted to" (samāśritya), that is, having relied upon. What [has he resorted to]? He says: "multiplicity" (nānātva)—namely, the plurality of persons (puruṣa) established by such statements as Sāṃkhyakārikā 18—and "oneness" (ekatva) of the Self according to the doctrine of the Tridaṇḍins; thus it is connected to both.
This is the view of the Ekadaṇḍins:
"For the single Self of all beings resides within each individual being;
though one, it appears as many through speech alone, like the moon reflected in water."
Because of the statement in the *Brahmayāmala* (Bra.vi.), he asks again, "Of what nature is that [state]? and says: "Not shown," and so forth.
The meaning is that [the Self] directly perceives the object not shown by the functioning of the senses, which possess objects shown by those very functions.
What does it offer? To this he says: "Itself," meaning its own essential nature (svarūpa).
Having done what? To this he says: "Having attained," meaning having obtained.
What? The relationship of cause and effect; by this, he states the identity of cause and fruit.
Demonstrating that very point, he asks:
"In what sequence does it evolve? and answers with the words beginning with "the Great One" (*mahān*).

For what purpose [is the statement] "From Prakṛti comes Mahat" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22) and so forth? He says: "For that purpose," meaning for the sake of being enjoyed by the Self; what indeed is such a fallacious argument called? He says: "Naigama."

Why? He says: "Of the primary matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa)," and so forth. Because of the establishment that both the primary matter and the person possess the nature of transformation (*pariṇāma*), he asks again: "What kind of primary matter is it? and answers: "That," and so forth.

The meaning is that *pradhāna* is either "belonging to one person" (*ekapuruṣa*), meaning enjoyable by one person, or "belonging to many persons" (*anekapuruṣa*), meaning enjoyable by many persons; the word *ca* serves as a conjunction.
Furthermore, stating the division of *pradhāna*, he says: "It is divided according to the distinction between non-lords and others"; here, the word *tat* (it) is understood from the previous context.

From what is that *pradhāna* distinguished? It is distinguished from the absence of a Lord (*anīśvara-bheda*). This is because, according to such statements as "that [Pradhāna] is conscious, like milk which flows for the sake of the growth of the calf," there is no Lord who acts as its instigator.

It is distinguished from others due to its lack of differentiation; because it is eternally undifferentiated, [it is said]: "This living being is ignorant and lacks mastery" (Mahābhārata, Vanaparvan 30).
Because of such statements as these, the ignorant and insentient creature is here said to be *prakṛti* itself;
why then is there this distinction? To this he says: "Of the *pradhāna*, etc."

Since the insentient *pradhāna* can act for the sake of the *puruṣa*, the ellipsis "spontaneously" (*svataḥ*) implies the non-theistic dualism; since its activity would otherwise be impossible, the ellipsis "whence [could that be]? implies the theistic dualism—why is that a flawed argument? By the words "of the unchanging," etc., the reality of the *puruṣa*, whose consciousness is devoid of transformation, has been refuted and set aside.
By what [is this refuted]? He says: by the refutation of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, such as genus (*jāti*) and the like.
Not only is this alone answered, but he says that the other [position] is also [refuted]: "Because it is occasional" (*kādācitka*);
for it has been examined that it is not logical for one who is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*) to experience objects at one time and have the opposite of that at another.
What happened then? He says: "From what," and so forth, which is clear.
For there is indeed only one Self of all beings... both as one and as many...—Trika-tantra 5.
From that [Mahat] arises the ego (ahaṅkāra), and from that the group of sixteen;
from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements arise.
This is the remainder [of the verse]:
just as the activity of insentient milk is for the purpose of the growth of the calf,
so too is the activity of the Pradhāna for the purpose of the liberation of the Puruṣa.
— Sāṃkhyakārikā 57:
Impelled by the Lord, the self may go to hell or even to heaven, according to its experiences of pleasure and pain.
This is the remainder [of the argument].
Now, showing that even though consciousness exists, it is fruitless when devoid of the experience of objects, he says: "Joy," and so forth.
What discerning person, acting as an authority, would assert that there is another function of consciousness—characterized by the experience of objects—distinct from Prakṛti?

Of what kind of Prakṛti? To this he says: [it is] that of which there is a transformation (*vivarta*) or modification (*pariṇāma*) consisting of many forms such as joy, sorrow, and so forth; that is what is meant by "of which that is the case. And since that very knowledge is its function—that is, its mode of operation—why would one not assert it? To this he says: because it is useless, since the power of consciousness has no activity anywhere, as its purpose is accomplished by Prakṛti.
With the words "especially" (*viśeṣataḥ*) and so forth, he speaks again, applying a fault to that [position]: "especially" means *viśeṣataḥ*.

By this, he states the superiority [of his own view] over the previous objection: the immutability (*avikāritva*) of the Person (*puruṣa*), who possesses—that is, who experiences—the object that has been manifested by *prakṛti*, brought within the range of vision, is difficult to maintain and lacks proof. He thinks as follows: just as in a lake there is the appearance of various clusters of stars, so too in the Person there is merely the manifestation of various objects manifested by *prakṛti*; this is what constitutes his immutability, provided that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to operate therein. However, its non-establishment follows from mere words.

Furthermore, explaining that [position] as difficult to maintain, he says: "In that case, if there were the eternity of the entire nature (*prakṛti*), the eternity of the form of perception, and the eternity of the state of being an object of perception belonging to *prakṛti*—which is the object of experience for the *puruṣa*—then its activity during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and its cessation in *nirvāṇa* would be difficult to reconcile; the sense is that there would have to be either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception. He states another refutation, beginning with "of *prakṛti*," etc.

Whether it be through the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), involving the abandonment of its nature as an object of experience and the modification into a nature that is not an object of experience, or whether it be a phenomenal appearance (*vivarta*) of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—that is, of the person (*puruṣa*)—involving the abandonment of its nature as an experiencer and the transformation into a nature that is not an experiencer, from what [source] does this arise? To this he says: "Because of that," and so forth.
Because of the existence—that is, the reality—of that which has as its object that which is presented by that primordial nature.

This is what is meant: just as when Prakṛti is conjoined with Puruṣa, she possesses the state of being an object of enjoyment for him only at that time and not otherwise; likewise, when the object is presented to the Puruṣa by Prakṛti, he possesses the state of being an enjoyer only then, because there is no distinction [in their respective capacities]. This applies to both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
Having thus refuted the *puruṣa*, he now speaks while refuting *prakṛti*: "Pleasure," and so forth.
The genus (*jāti*) is *prakṛti* itself; of what nature is it? It is that which has the designation of the *pradhāna* consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Of whom [is this genus]? He says: of the various insentient things (*acetana-bhedānām*), but not of the genus of consciousness (*saṃvedana-jāti*), which is common to all *puruṣas*; for that would be a difficult logical connection (*duranvaya*).
By this, he states the inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) of the reasons for proving the Pradhāna, such as the "limited number of distinct entities" (*bhedānāṃ parimāṇāt*) and so forth;

the conclusion begins with "that is not so" (*tanna*), etc., [stating]: "Because of the limited number of distinct entities, because of homogeneity (*samanvaya*), and because of activity from power (*śaktitaḥ*)."

"From the distinction between cause and effect, and from the non-distinction of the manifold world"—Sāṃkhyakārikā 15. Showing yet another semblance of scriptural authority, he says: "In the same way," and so forth.
Likewise,

for those who maintain that there is only a single universal, existence (sattā) may be designated by the names of universals such as substantiality (dravyatva) and cowness (gotva), depending on its inherent particulars. 11

Since the relationship of universal and particular is established for an entity itself—due to its inherent distinction from that which possesses inherence (samavāyin)—this other [view] is also a flawed non-reasoning (*durṇaya*) by the Naigama school, which asserts an absolute difference between existence (*sattā*) and that which inheres in it.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Existence (*sattā*)," and so forth; [it] would be existence.
Of what nature is it? It is the substratum for universals such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and cowness (*gotva*).
By what [is it so]? To this he says: "by the particular inherent entities" (*samavāyiviśeṣaiḥ*).

Those things, such as substance and the like, or parts such as a fragment, which possess inherence in existence (*sattā*), are the "inherent" (*samavāyin*); their specificities, or those very things themselves, are the "particular inherent entities," and by them [it is so].
As it has been said:
"They declare that [the abstract suffix] to be the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) and the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu);
it is eternal, it is the Great Self (mahān ātmā), and it is what the suffixes -tva, -tal, and so forth, express" (Vākyapadīya 3.34).

[Objection: "Is it not the case that existence (*sattā*) resides only where intermediate universals such as 'cowness' (*gotva*) are inherent? Therefore, because of inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*), existence participates in those designations? [The author] replies here with the words beginning "without" (*vinā*).

[Objection: "But why is the refutation already set forth against the [Vaiśeṣika] doctrine of conjunction (*yoga*) not applied here? [The author] replies here with the words beginning "if there were pervasion" (*vyāpitve*).
The objection raised immediately prior does not apply at all to those who maintain that there is a single universal—namely, the proponents of the genus *sattā*.

Why? He says: because it is possible for existence (*sattā*) itself to function as both a universal and a particular, and thus for the various distinctions among universals such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and "cowness" (*gotva*) to be established.

Why is this? He says: "Because of the distinction of the inherent substratum (*samavāyin*), or because it partakes of designations such as 'red' and so forth, even in the case of the primary [entity]. Thus, under the absolute distinction between existence (*sattā*) and its inherent substratum, this too is a fallacious doctrine (*durṇaya*) according to the previously stated rule. For this very reason, it was said: "In that manner, the other, namely the *naigama* [view], is a fallacious doctrine. Now, refuting the Buddhist's consideration of all *naigama* as fallacious, he says: "Existence," and so forth.

"Since they sustain existence by means of being produced from the word 'knowledge,' therefore let individual manifestations be equal for the cognizers within the form of the object. (12) This objection— that [the cognition] is [identical]— is equally applicable even when cognitions apprehend the form of the object.

Because individual manifestations (*vyakti*) sustain—what?—existence (*sattā*) or another universal (*jāti*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*) by virtue of a specific capacity (*yogyatāviśeṣa*), therefore, due to that specific capacity, they are the causes for the occurrence of inclusive cognition and designation produced by knowledge and words; thus is the objection [answered] equally regarding the grasping of the object-aspect, characterized by color and so forth, by means of cognitions (*vid*).

For instance: since objects such as cloth and the like possess color and other qualities, they will themselves—though not being of the nature of those qualities—serve as the causes for the cognition of color and so forth; what then is the use of postulating [separate] color and the rest? Thus is established the existence of formless objects.
Or, if it is argued that the object is perceived as consisting of color and the rest, then it is equally [the case] that it is perceived as consisting of a universal (sāmānya);
[therefore,] objects devoid of color and the rest [are established].
Teaching the meaning of the verse, he says: "By which," and so forth;
this is easy to understand. Thus, that which is primary [is not common] even when cognitions apprehend the forms of objects; this has been stated repeatedly elsewhere as well.
For instance: since cognitions accept their own nature as self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), for that very reason they may also appear as having a nature other than that [self-awareness];
because they are "self-aware," it appears as if written twice.
Having thus established both the Naigama and Tadābhāsa [standpoints], he speaks while establishing the Saṃgraha standpoint, beginning with "Or from exertion," and so forth.
Or rather, since it is out of necessity that this [consciousness] accepts non-difference despite the existence of differences, why does it alone not carry out the conventional usage of difference?
For it is not as if there were no perception of non-different reality, since such is seen in dreams and the like.

Even for the proponents of difference (*bhedavādin*), that cognition—which is partless and consists of color and so forth—manifests the conventional usage of form and the like as if they were possessed of parts, being non-different from various properties such as grossness; for the perception of reality in its absolute sense is entirely untenable.
Furthermore, since it transcends all conceptual construction, both correspondence and non-correspondence, which serve as the grounds for validity and invalidity, would be indistinguishable therein.
Thus, the *saṃgrahanaya* maintains that the reality is pure existence (*sanmātra*) beyond all conceptualization.
Because it is consciousness itself that appears as if external, that [external appearance] is indeed false, its ultimate reality never being perceived.

In this regard, this conceptual construction regarding the momentary destruction of one's own and others' mental continua would appear to one whose nature is ignorance, just like the appearance of external objects; thus, even though those objects do not exist, it is like another kind of cognitive distortion (*viplava*).

Even through a succession [of moments], the necessity for the arising of another volition (*cetanā*) is a mere grasping at straws (*kuśakāśāvalambana*), because such necessity would follow from the existence of activity and so forth, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of reviving that which has been prohibited; furthermore, there is a distinction between the external and the internal.

As for *saṃgraha* (comprehension): it consists in bringing various categories together into a unity without contradicting their own specific natures, by grasping them collectively without distinction, while their differences remain unassailed by synonyms.
— Sāṃkhyasūtra 1.33;
Tattvavaiśāradī 1.33.
Tattvārthādhi° Bhā° 1.36
The synthesis intends a pure substance because of the non-difference of its manifestations;
for there is not even a single manifestation that is non-existent in nature, due to contradiction.
Dhavalāṭīkā, Satprarūpaṇā-tarka-śloka, page 70;
Nayaviniścaya, verse 67.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 272; Nayacakra, gā. 34;
Tattvārthasāra, p. 107.
Praṇayana, 7.13; Syādvādamañjarī, p. 311.
"The statement of summary (saṃgraha-vacana) expresses the meaning that has been gathered and condensed in brief"—Jainatarkabhāṣā, p.
22; Anuyogadvāra-sūtra 4.
*Āptamīmāṃsā* 756;
*Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya* 2699:

"Or because it begins with effort and ends with [the same]," this indicates another alternative position. Does that non-difference (*abheda*)—which consists of mere existence (*sattāmātra*) and which accepts differences (*bheda*), namely the distinctions between the conscious and the unconscious—not also perform the conventional usage of difference? That non-difference is absolute and devoid of all particularities.

If it is objected: "If there is non-difference, how then can there be the conventional usage of difference? Otherwise, the conventional usage of yellow would arise from blue," [the author] replies here: "Not indeed for that whose reality is non-different," and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because it is seen in dreams and the like.
Here, by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the perception of two moons and so on is included.

The point is that even in a dream, one who is thin appears as fat, a different time and so forth appear as another time and so forth, and Devadatta, though being one, appears as many; likewise, the moon appears as many in a state of sleep. Showing that this [phenomenon] exists for the opponent as well, he says: "Even for the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), not only for the proponent of non-difference (*abheda-vādin*); what is that cognition? It is the cognition of the proponent of difference; of what nature is it? It is partless (*niraṃśa*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It consists of the unmanifested (*avarṇādyātmaka*) and is devoid of form, taste, and so forth. Form and the like are non-distinct from various properties such as grossness and so on, yet that [grossness] is not possible in something partless."
What does it do? He says: it indeed manifests that conventional usage, namely the conventional usage of differentiation.
Of what nature is it? It is as if having parts, as if manifesting as phonemes and so forth; the word "and" (ca) should also be applied here.
At midnight, the vision of a dream occurs at midday.
If it is argued that there is a distinction between these two because difference appears in such a way while non-difference does not, the author replies here with the words "tattva" and so forth:

since the perception of reality— which is partless by nature— is impossible in every respect, whether by all means such as direct perception and the like, or by way of being self-evident or evidenced by another,
its establishment occurs through conceptual construction (kalpanā) in both cases alike.

Regarding difference and non-difference, it might be thought: "That knowledge, being partless and consisting of the unmanifested (avarṇa) and so forth, manifests worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) in that very way. To this, he says: "In reality," and so forth—the explanation is precisely that.

Alternatively, if knowledge—appearing as the manifestation of colors and so forth—propagates a conventional usage that is indeed composed of parts, then that [knowledge] is the reality; such is the connection with the Buddhist view, starting from "because that [view] is in every way untenable" or "even for the proponent of difference," and so on.

Now, if there is non-difference, then how could there be non-discrepancy in the waking state—which is the cause for the establishment of valid cognition—and discrepancy in the dream state—which is the cause for the establishment of non-valid cognition? If you say that these two exist [only] when there is difference, to this he says: "non-discrepancy and discrepancy," and so forth.

Of what nature are they? They are the causes of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its opposite (*itaranimitta*), being respectively the grounds for validity and invalidity. In that regard, how could there be difference or non-difference between those two? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction," meaning due to the difference in the firmness or lack of firmness of the latent impression (*vāsanā*). Since this is so, therefore the reality (*tattva*) transcends all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
What is that? He says: "Pure Being" (*sanmātra*)—thus is the *saṃgrahanaya*.

Here, the refutation stated by the Buddhist—"How can 'pure Being' be the reality when there is a distinction between external and internal appearances? If that [distinction] is an error, what confidence can there be in pure Being?"—is shown to apply equally to him as well. Demonstrating this, he says: "Of consciousness alone," and so forth.

Just as for the proponent of the *saṃgraha* there is "pure Being," for the Buddhist who maintains the doctrine of difference, the reality is "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), which is to say, "consciousness-only" (*buddhimātra*).

If it is argued that "non-contradiction and contradiction exist for the Buddhist as well, since there is indeed a distinction between the external and the internal," he says in response: [This applies] to consciousness alone and nothing else, because it appears *as if* external. Therefore, just as this [consciousness], though not external, shines forth as something external, so too is the non-different considered by another to be different.

The proponent of non-duality might think: "Just as the visible world is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), so too is everything else. To this he replies: "Furthermore, that representation-only is indeed one whose ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) has not been seen;
for it is impossible to establish it as partless, because that consequence would apply elsewhere as well."
What is that? He says: "false," and so forth.
Therefore, the sense is that just as consciousness does not cease even when the conventional usage of difference is false, so it is elsewhere as well; such is the meaning of "falsity."

If it is argued that within mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*), the distinction between one's own and another's mental continuum, as well as the distinction between momentary destruction and so forth, is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*); to this he replies with the words "In that case" (*tatra*) and so on. "In that case," [meaning] in mere cognition, there are the mental continua of self and other, as well as momentary destruction, or rather, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding them, or else the mental cognitions (*mānasa-pratyaya*); from what source would this established order of their appearance arise? He says: "From the nature of ignorance" (*avidyātmanaḥ*), meaning from some latent predisposition for conceptual construction (*vikalpavāsanā*) whose essence is ignorance. This is because, in that regard, there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another [external object].
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "like the appearance of external objects.
He then provides the justification for this illustration with the words "even though that object is non-existent," and so forth;

because the activities of the waking state and the like are subverted, the subversion of those [activities] in dreams and the like is even more evident; therefore, it is said "just as there, so here."

If it is argued that there is no deviation [in the argument] because in the waking state there is a direct manifestation of activity and so forth, whereas in the case of another's mind within another body during a dream, it occurs through a succession; to this he says: "Even by way of succession," and so forth. Regarding the restriction (*niyama*) concerning the possibility of another consciousness—that is, the restriction on the occurrence or production [of cognition] from the consciousnesses of two different mental continua—he asks: "Who has established that restriction? He then says: "Activity," and so forth.

In what manner [is this so]? He says: It is not only in the waking state that there is a direct restriction of that [consciousness] to it; for even in one's own body, which serves as its support, because there is no apprehension of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between the two—the indivisible operation of cognition and [the body]—the universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished due to a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, in sleep and similar states, although consciousness is absent, the operation [of the body] and so forth still exist. Moreover, even though a lotus and the like are seen to arise from a lotus and the like, they are also seen to arise from cow dung and other substances; thus, since deviation is possible, the appearance of an operation is everywhere as erroneous as the appearance of an object. Rather, even indirectly in the waking state, there is a restriction of that [body] to another conscious being directly; whereas in a dream, it is through an indirect succession from the intellect alone that such a cognition arises. That delusion relies upon that [body], because, due to the aforementioned defect, inference does not function, and because everything beginning with the body is illusory.
Why? He says: "Because of the restoration of that object which was prohibited," and so forth.
That object which was prohibited—that is, rejected by the Buddhist, such as an insentient jar and the like—its *pratiprasava* is its revival; [the argument follows] from the contingency of that.
Why is this so? He says: because of the distinction between external and internal, the sense being that the distinction between the external and the internal is thereby established.

For instance— if, in one's own body, a causal relationship between cognition and its activity were perceived in an ultimate sense from some source, then clearly a subject-object relationship would ensue, like the lotus-stalk giving rise to the scorpion;
by this, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) has also been considered.
This same reasoning should also be applied here: that all cognition arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

If it is argued that "the object is established through its appearance, and since that [appearance] occurs even in the absence of the object during a dream, it is inconclusive," we say no; for then the [cognition of] activity and so forth would likewise be [inconclusive], which is a fault. In that case, what causes this distinction—that the nature of another's mind exists there through a causal chain, whereas the appearance of the object does not? It is simply the appearance itself.

Others, however, maintain that even in the absence of an external object, [the cognition] is directly of another's mind itself, because they accept that in that case too, a body existing within a dream is ultimately real. For them, even the appearance of pillars and so forth would be real; consequently, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in the definition of perception—namely, "perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (Nyāyabindu 1.4)—would be purposeless, as there would be nothing to exclude. Furthermore, like that [dream] body, even things such as a double moon would attain the status of reality.

If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), we say no; for by that very [conventional usage], the reality of that body is also admitted, since the next world (*paraloka*) is established through conventional usage. Otherwise, from where would the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) come? Or what is the example (*nidarśana*) in the passage from the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* (p. 361): "All cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), because they are cognitions"? Even if [cognition] has its own nature as its objective basis (*svarūpālambanatva*), there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the re-establishment of the bound soul (*baddha*) who perceives manifold objects. This is because the body and so forth appear as having parts (*sāṃśatva*).
Therefore, this [argument of Prabhākara] is of no consequence, according to Prajñākaragupta and others.

The perception of others is like the body in a dream; there is no continuum (*santāna*) nor another continuum (*santānāntara*), except for conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Thus, the proof of their non-existence is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); the response to that has already been stated and is not repeated here. In the case of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), if blue and other colors do not mutually interpenetrate, then even if they are not perceived by one another, their existence implies the establishment of another continuum; otherwise, there would be universal emptiness (*sakalaśūnyatā*). If, however, they do interpenetrate, then the establishment of manifoldness (*anekānta*) follows.
Therefore, the establishment of a distinction such as the continuity of another’s own nature does not constitute a proof for the non-existence of other continuities;
for in some readings, "due to the distinction between internal and external" means that there is no difference between the external and the internal.

It might be thought: "How can pure existence (*sanmātra*) be the reality, given that there is a cognition of the fourfold non-existence, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)? To this he says: "The object of knowledge," and so forth.

"The fourfold non-existence is an object of knowledge through a cognition of an existing thing; it is not otherwise in any way according to logic. Therefore, cognition has pure existence as its domain. (14)
It is not logical that the cognition of the fourfold non-existence is entirely without an object, because it is admitted to have another thing as its objective support;
at the time of examining the nature of the cognition down to the level of atoms, it would take that very nature as its support and not a distinct external object,
for in the absence of such [a nature], the designation of "cognition" would be untenable.

Therefore, a particularity distinct from existence could not, in any way or anywhere, attain the status of being an object of cognition—that is, it could not be known or determined—as the fourfold non-existence, namely the four types of non-existence beginning with prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).
By what? By the cognition of an existing object, that is, by the knowledge of existence.
In some way—that is, by some mode of fitness for its production, and not otherwise—by the absence of being cognizable by the intellect; this is the connection with "in the fourfold non-existence.
He explains the meaning of the verse: that the intellect has as its object pure existence (*sanmātra*) according to the principle derived from the experience of cognition and so forth.

It is not logical that the cognition of the fourfold negation (*abhāvacatuṣṭaya*) is entirely without an object (*nirviṣaya*), devoid of an objective referent (*viṣayarahita*), and has as its domain only a void non-existence (*tucchābhāva*).

If it is asked: "But if it has non-existence as its object, how can it be said to be without an object?"—it is not so; for this is stated from the perspective of the Buddhist (*saugata*) alone, since he does not accept [the reality of] non-existence.

If it is asked, "Why is it not without an object?"—to this he replies: "Because of the acceptance [by the Buddhist] that it has another thing as its basis," and so forth. This means that because non-existence (abhāva) is, for the Buddhist, of the nature of another entity (bhāvāntara), it is accepted as having as its objective support (*ālambana*) something other than the intended object—that is, another object.

If it is asked, "In this case as well, since one relies on mutually distinct entities, how can cognition have 'pure existence' (*sanmātra*) as its object?"—it is said in response: "That [is not so]," and so forth.

Here, "that" refers merely to the knowledge of the fourfold absence (*tadabhāva-catuṣṭaya*). At the time of examining the nature of the cognition extending down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it would rely upon its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), not upon a difference of objects.
Why? It says: because if that [nature] were absent—that is, if there were no reliance upon the essential nature—the designation of consciousness (*saṃvid-vyapadeśa*) would be untenable.
