If it is argued that cognition is designated as such because it grasps an object (*arthagrahaṇa*) and not by relying on its own nature (*svarūpa*), then how is it known that "the grasping of an object is cognition"? If it is said to be known by that very same cognition, no; for that would entail the consequence of it grasping its own nature, and if that [nature] is not grasped, it is impossible to realize, "I am grasping an object. If it is argued that it is known by a subsequent cognition (*buddhyantareṇa*), then how is that subsequent cognition known to be devoid of self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*)? If it is said to be known from the grasping of the object by the first cognition, then how is that [first cognition] known? Thus the objection remains in the same state, and there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that "cognition is that from which an object is perceived," [the reply is: True, it is perceived; however, it is not perceived by means of a cognition that is not self-cognizing (*asvasaṃvedana*). Otherwise, it would be perceived even by another’s cognition;
by this, the Mīmāṃsaka has also been answered.

Suppose it is granted that cognition has its own nature as its objective support (*ālambana*); yet, if it is argued that that very nature is apprehended as being distinguished [from others], to this he says: "That is not so," and so forth.

Therefore, according to the principle that "one must rely upon its own essential nature," no particularity (*viśeṣa*) or distinction (*bheda*)—which is not separate from the entity and is non-different from the existence of cognition—can in any way whatsoever, whether as one, many, or otherwise, attain the status of an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) within a cognition or elsewhere. For a cognition submerged in its own nature, not taking anything else as its object, cannot apprehend a distinction from that [nature] or anything else; this is because it does not take such an object as its domain.

It might be argued: if cognition itself is non-dual in its own nature (*svarūpa*), then that very non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) has arrived, and that is not undesirable for the Buddhist, since he accepts it.
Or, if [you mean] non-duality of existence (*sattādvaita*) in that way, that is not so; because it is not perceived, and because of the appearance of variety (*citrapratibhāsa*).

If you say that since this [variety] is false, there is no non-duality of existence when there is a difference from that [cognition], to this he replies: "In the case of absolute falsity," and so forth.
The meaning is "because it is not perceived," [namely] because the variegated appearance is not perceived from the variegated cognition.
Since duality would exist in relation to that from which variegated cognition is excluded and that which is excluded,
this absolute difference between the self— which is the reality of the unity of the appearance of various false and manifold manifestations— and momentary consciousness is the same. (15)

Just as the reality of the Supreme Self, whose nature is Being (*sadrūpa*) and which is invisible, would be entirely distinct from everything that is conceptualized—since it is unseen, like the horn of a donkey—so too would the reality of momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-saṃvid*) be likewise distinct from that [conceptualization]. This is because, through its own self-awareness, it transcends the end—that is, the limit—of the false duality of subject and object; and this very distinction or particularity (*viśeṣa*), being described by the opponent as being without end (*niravasāna*), is equal to—that is, identical with—the position of the Proponent of Pure Being (*sanmātra-pakṣa*).
Of what? Of the self, of one's own.
Of what [consciousness]? To this he says: "of momentary cognition," meaning of the intellect belonging to the Buddhists.
Of which two [states] being? To this he says: "false," and so forth.

That which possesses falsity (*mithyātva*) as its absolute nature is so described; and that very thing is manifold (*vividha*), appearing variegated through qualities such as grossness, length, and roundness, as in the manifestation of a jar and so forth. By means of that [manifestation], there exists a perception (*pratibhāsa* = *darśana*) of two principles of unity (*aikyatattva*)—namely, partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) and the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedanasvarūpa*)—which belong to the soul (*ātman*) and momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇikasaṃvid*).

This is what is meant: just as the nature of pure existence (*sattāmātra*)—such as its eternity and so forth—does not manifest because it is obscured by the appearance of other [factors] such as false volition (*mithyācetanā*), so too, because its expansion is obstructed by the variegated appearance of grossness and so on, the manifestation of the two principles of consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the Self (*ātman*) as one does not occur.
With the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse: "the true nature" (*yathātattvaṃ svarūpam*);
of what? Of the substance (*dravyasya*).
Of what nature is he? Of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), consisting of being (*sattātmaka*).
Furthermore, of what nature is he? Of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), whose form (*rūpa*) is the supreme, transcending all.
What, then, would that reality (*tattva*) be? To this he says: "It would be distinct" (*vyatiricyeta*), meaning it would itself be divided.
Why? He says: "From all conceptual construction," that is, from every distinction between sentient and insentient things.
Of what nature is it? He says: "of an invisible essence.
How so? He says: "in every way," that is, by every mode of the collection of attributes inherent in the entity.
Why? He says: "Because that which is unperceived is like a donkey's horn. Likewise, why would the reality of momentary consciousness not be distinguished from that [unperceived]?
He says: "In accordance with reality," and so forth;
because momentary consciousness is itself perceived in accordance with its true nature.
Why is this so? He says: "false," and so forth.

It is because, according to such statements as *Pravāhaṇa-vākya* 2.327, "there is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect other than the grasped and the grasper," she [the intellect] is experienced through a nature of differentiation, that is, through a manifold essence.
By this, he demonstrates the perception of a contradictory [property];
thus, the word "yataḥ" (since) here is indeed redundant.

For it has been established in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅga* that existence (*sattā*) is not accepted as all-pervading, eternal, and unitary, nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a thing.
If it is argued that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that consciousness (*saṃvitti*) is indeed momentary and manifold, he says in response: "No," and so forth.

For conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), which is by nature devoid of [external] color-forms, does not establish the perception of reality as being non-abiding once it has dispelled the defects of falsity. (16)

In dreams and other such delusions, consciousness—which is essentially devoid of phonemes—appears as if consisting of phonemes and the like; it appears as if partless while being as if possessed of parts.

However, this does not mean that its own nature is invisible, for if it were so, it would be entirely distinct from the visible. This is the resolution: the same applies to the Supreme Self even regarding mere substance, as the conceptualization of distinctions between momentary successions is likewise [unreal].
By this, he shows that just as [the opponent] has established eternality and omnipresence, there is no other recourse but conceptual construction (kalpanā) even in other cases.
Of what nature is that [conceptualization]? He says: "false," meaning unreal. Whom indeed does it establish in [the state of] eternality? He says: "the perception of reality," and so forth.
Having asked "What having done [this]? he says: "having cast out those defects from one's own self," the sense being that because they are identical, those defects exist in both cases.

If it is argued: "But consciousness is not perceived as possessing existence, for it appears otherwise, just as in a desert a small thing appears as large"; to this he says: "consisting of no color"—the meaning of this has already been explained.
Even in the case of the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikapakṣa*),
just as even a small object appears large from afar in desert lands,
[the author] explains the *kārikā-sūtra* with the words "in dreams and so forth," and so on.

In dreams and other such delusions, consciousness—which is essentially devoid of phonemes and lacks the form of gross objects—appears through the power of error as if it were composed of phonemes and the like; likewise, though it is partless and undivided, it appears as if it possessed parts. It is not, however, the case that its own nature is invisible—that is, that its essential form (*svarūpa*) is itself unseen—because it is precisely that [consciousness] which appears in such a manner.

For this reason, since it would otherwise be distinct in every way and in every respect from the visible—the delusion consisting of the grasped object and so forth—due to its being of an invisible nature, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) described in this way is "equal" (*sama*).
Where? He says: "Even in mere substance.
Why? He says: "From the Supreme Self," and so forth.
Having refuted the Buddhist position by means of the *saṃgraha-naya*, he now sets aside the semblance of *saṃgraha* by means of the *vyavahāra-naya*, saying: "Difference," and so forth.
Comparison—The *Saṃgraha* intends the unity of all distinctions through their essential nature;
the doctrine of Brahman is its reflection, because it negates the distinction of its own objects.
— *Laghīyastraya*, Verse 38.
*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, verse 270;
*Nayaviniścaya*, verse 68;
*Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, page 85.
Praṇamya-naya-prakaraṇa 7.15–21;
Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p. 24.

Differences regarding the fruits of actions and so forth exist either in this world or in the next; such difference must exist for differentiation to proceed, for it does not proceed in the absence of difference. (17) The duality of worlds...
If there were a distinction, of what things? Of "action, its fruit, and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of the means of action and so on is intended.
What would happen? To this he says: "it would proceed."
Where? To this he says: "The world here" (*ihaloka*); by the word "action" (*karman*), the activity is understood, and by the mention of the "fruit," rice and so forth.
Or, in the next world, or even here, "action" refers to merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and the "fruit" refers to heaven and so forth.
If it is argued that [the agent] proceeds [to act] even when there is no distinction [between self and other], to this he says: "There is no non-distinction," and so on.
With the verse beginning "The duality of worlds," he states the meaning of the *kārikā*;
everything is easy to understand.
The comparison is as follows: there would be for us no duality of karma, no duality of fruit, and no duality of worlds.
"There would be neither the pair of knowledge and ignorance, nor likewise the pair of bondage and liberation"— as stated in Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 25.

Regarding what was said— that "the conventional usage of the appearance of difference for that which is non-different in essence is not contradictory, as seen in dreams and the like"— he refutes this by saying "falsity," and so forth.
Having observed falsity in some cognitions, one who knows that [falsity] should abandon the doctrine of synthesis everywhere; likewise,

since the mere existence [of objects] is established through valid means of knowledge, one should abandon what is merely intended by oneself as the truth, once the distinction between the means of knowledge and mere existence is established.
Since that [distinction] cannot be established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as it would otherwise lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),

let alone the mere substance; for, like the mere mode (*paryāya*), neither of these is established in any way, anywhere, or for anyone without a cognizer of both the right view (*samyaktva*) and the wrong view (*mithyātva*).

Why? Because one who wishes to establish reality either as "this" or otherwise must seek valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the knowledge of reality; for without means and ends, there is no accomplishment.

Having observed the falsity—that is, the unreality—of cognitions that perceive difference, just as it occurs in some cases such as dreams, so too in all cases during the waking state, one should abandon that cognition of difference along with its knower; for the doctrine of synthesis (*saṃgrahavāda*), which is his own preferred view, holds that only pure Being (*sanmātra*) exists.

For just as in some cases, due to the observation of an illusion of difference, there is an illusion of that [difference] everywhere, so too, due to the observation of an illusion of particularity without distinction, there would also be an illusion of pure existence (*sanmātra*).
This is because nothing other than that particularity is perceived, from which this difference might arise; for [everything] is pure existence.

If it is argued: "Surely, duality, 'moon-ness,' and so forth are perceived as distinct; nevertheless, only that [Being] is real and not the duality. The same would apply here as well," that is incorrect. For even if there were such a distinction, it would lead to the untenable consequence of establishing a distinction between reality and unreality. Furthermore, is Being apprehended through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or from some other source? In the first case—[if it is] through a means of valid cognition—the establishment of that [Being] does not occur without a means of valid cognition; rather, because Being is apprehended through a means of valid cognition, one must abandon one's own position, since the distinction between the means of valid cognition and pure Being is thereby established.

This might be so if it were not known from a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, since that very same means of valid cognition [establishes] difference through the cognition of "not this" (*asaṃpratyaya*) with respect to the self, the same must be said for the second position as well: because without a means of valid cognition, there is no establishment of that [difference], and because existence alone would persist, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) that [the object] is nothing but the moon itself.

If it is argued that there would indeed be a distinction in the form of the knower and the known, yet [the object] is merely Being (*sanmātra*), just as the proponent of error (*vibhramavādin*) establishes his own position without relying on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too could it be for me; to this he replies: "Let that be for now," and so forth.
Let it be; let it remain for now—what? Merely substance;
like what? Like merely a modification (paryāya).
This illustration is established for those who maintain that only the existent (*sanmātra*) exists;

however, how could the doctrine of absolute falsity (*mithyaikānta*) itself be established? To this he says: because, without something that cognizes both the true and the false—whether externally or internally, in dreams or elsewhere—neither correctness (*samyaktva*) nor its opposite, error (*viparyaya*), can be established in any way whatsoever, including the manner in which they are asserted. Thus, that [doctrine] is not proven.
Showing the result, he says: "From what," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates that the example is equivalent to the probandum;
or else, by this, emptiness is refuted.
If it is argued that "I do not establish reality through the power of another, but rather through my own power," to this he replies: "Reality," and so forth.

By one who wishes to establish reality—the essential nature of things—either as "this" (as a specific identity), as mere existence, or otherwise, by means of a synthetic doctrine (*saṃgraha*), why must the knowledge of reality and its means (*pramāṇa*) be sought? He says: because there would be no establishment of either the means or the goal (*upeya*).

If it is argued that reality (tattva) cannot be designated as "this" (idantā) or "not-this" (nedantā), to this he replies with the words beginning "from the natural" (prākṛtāt): "The wise man is distinguished from the natural state by his reliance on perfect knowledge; in its absence, even if there were ineffability, the world would clearly be as if asleep. (19)

Right knowledge is the basis for the conventional usage of "existent" and "non-existent. If there were an absolute persistence of either [existence or non-existence], what person of ordinary intellect, or what seeker of truth, would remain, establish themselves, or proceed anywhere by relying on anything at all? A seeker of welfare, in some way, establishes the distinction between truth and falsity; thus, the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekānta*)—and not the false absolutism (*mithyaikānta*)—is that which must be relied upon, and it is precisely therein that one applies oneself.

The ordinary person (*prākṛta*)—one who does not know reality (*atattvajña*) and is attached to the notion that things possess expressibility through attributes such as permanence and so forth—is distinguished from him; that is, he becomes different.
Who is this? It is the learned one (*vidvān*), the knower of reality (*tattvajña*), who realizes the ineffable reality in every respect.

Why is he distinguished from that [ordinary person]? To this he says: "Because of relying upon right knowledge" (*samyagjñānāvalambanāt*). Right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is correct cognition whose range is the ineffable reality and which proceeds unimpeded; because of relying upon—that is, accepting—that [knowledge].
For when that reality is somehow apprehended directly, like seizing a dog by the neck, then all others are seen as different from it; thus, there is no entry into an ineffable reality.

Nevertheless, he states the fault in such an entry: even in its absence—that is, even in the absence of reliance upon correct knowledge—if the ineffability of reality is accepted, then clearly, a person who has "slept" (overcome by sleep) behaves as if asleep.
What is that? He says: the world, namely the people who propound the doctrine of an ineffable reality.
He thinks as follows: "Just as one overcome by sleep, though not perceiving reality, prattles something incoherent, so too does this [person].
Thus, clarifying the verse by way of a specific individual, he says: "The conventional usage of existent and non-existent," and so forth.

The non-duality of being and non-being is inexpressible through attributes such as unity and so forth; the unreal collection of distinctions such as blue and the like is the basis for the regulation of their conventional usage. What is it? It is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). In the case of its absolute persistence, who would possess a common-sense intellect? No one, because they would lack the realization of reality.
By right knowledge, no [erroneous] cognition is sublated...

This is called wisdom (*buddhi*); in its absence, nothing is sublated by anything, nor is there anyone who knows the truth—the knower (*boddhā*). Even he, in the absence of that [wisdom], for this reason, would not remain relying on some scripture or the like, even for a moment; he would not establish himself, nor would he withdraw from any category of duality. The word "from anywhere" (*kutaścit*) is connected here with a change of case ending (from ablative to locative).
Of what nature is he? He is one seeking his own welfare, whose character is to seek the paths to heaven and liberation (*svarga-apavarga*).
In this regard,
demonstrating that when one relies upon right knowledge, the undesirable consequences for the opponent inevitably follow, he says: "In some way," and so forth.
Whatever person establishes the distinction between reality and falsity through any means such as direct perception and so forth, that agent requires a cause;
what is that [cause]? To this he says: "non-absolutism" (anekānta), and so on. Where? To this he says: "in that very [context]," namely, in the establishment of non-absolutism itself.
He states the verse that concludes the present topic, beginning with "What then is false absolutism? and continuing with "The continuum," etc.:
"The continuum, the collection, and so forth, do not exist in either absolute identity or absolute difference."
And therefore, the *vyavahāra* [perspective] does not include [the past and future] as the *ṛjusūtra* does.
Its origin is otherwise... such is the *vyavahāra-naya*.
Comparison: the *vyavahāra* is similar to worldly convention, consists mostly of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), and has an extensive scope of meaning.
And it is said: "One should know the extensive conventional usage as being restricted to worldly practice" (Tattvārthādhigamasūtra-bhāṣya 1.35).
Vyavahāra is the systematic extraction of those meanings implied by the inclusive perspective (saṃgraha-naya) according to the proper method—
Siddhasena Divākara’s *Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa* 1.33.
A *naya* is that which does not contradict worldly convention; otherwise, it is a *durnaya* (a fallacious view).
Such [views] as "external objects exist," "there is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*)," or "[everything is] empty" [are *nayas*].
— *Laghīyastraya*, Verse 42.

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "iva" (like) and is to be understood as displaced [in the sentence], following the term "ṛjusūtra. Therefore, the meaning is this: from that aforementioned property, according to the stated logic, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would not exist in the case of the "saṃgraha" [viewpoint]. Like what? From what? To this he says: "the continuum" (*santāna*), which is a specific causal relationship; "the aggregate" (*samudāya*), which is a collection; and by the word "etc.," other inhabitants of the world are also included. That [conventional usage] does not exist; where? In the cases of absolute non-difference and difference, since this has been demonstrated more than once.

He states the commentary on the verse: "Prabhava" and so forth; "tadanyathā tadanyathā so'nyathā" refers to the means of establishing the difference in effects, and the rest is easy to understand—thus is the *vyavahāra-naya*.
The phrase "tadanyathā" is written twice.
Demonstrating the *ṛjusūtra* [naya] in its practical application (*vyavahāra*), he says: "In that regard," and so forth.
For the *ṛjusūtra*, the mode (*paryāya*) is primary; because the manifold consciousnesses consist of a collection of conscious atoms (*cetanāṇu*), there may be a non-perception of their distinctions.
"The method of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint (*nayavidhi*) should be understood as apprehending the present. — Laghīyastraya, verse 43;
Anuyogadvāra, verse 4.
The Ṛjusūtra [naya] is the thorough knowledge of the designations of things as they exist at the present moment—
Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya 1.35.
"Ṛjusūtra" is so called because it threads (sūtrayati) and extends (tantrayate) that which is straight (ṛju) and correct (praguṇa)— *Sāṃkhyasūtravṛtti* 1.33.
It is called *ṛjusūtra* because it is straight, like the laying down of a measuring line—
Tattvārthavārttika 1.33.
The *Ṛjusūtra*— which is white, characterized by correct discernment, momentary in its destruction, and consisting of real entities—
should delineate the "straight" [present] primarily, because it subordinates the other aspects and does not present the substance as something persisting.
—Tattvasaṃgrahaśloka, p. 271;
Nayaviniścayaśloka 77;
Sanmatitarkaṭīkā, p. 311.
*Nayacakra*, verse 38;
*Tattvārthasāra*, page 107; *Prakaraṇapāda-naya*, 7.
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 312; Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p. 22.

In that regard, just as there is a unity of the continuum among humans despite their difference, so too does the *Ṛjusūtra-naya* [assert this] regarding non-difference; however, because its scope is not universal, it is merely conventional and indeed false, being constructed by the artifice of conceptualization. (21)

Therefore, it is incorrect to establish oneness based on that; for, as in the case of the solar dynasty and so forth, memory, recognition, action, and the connection with results may occur in certain instances due to a specific causal relationship between cause and effect. Here, memory and the like function in a restricted manner not because of identity, but because of contradiction [with the opposite].
Furthermore, when seeing and other such functions belong to a single entity, it is not logical for there to be multiplicity in any respect.

Because conceptual constructions, words, and linguistic conventions exhibit differentiation, there is a comparison: [the present] does not transcend the objects of the three times, but rather takes up the objects of the present time,
since there is no linguistic convention regarding the past and the future due to their being destroyed and unarisen respectively.
— *Siddhasena Divākara*, *Tattvārthavārttika* 1.33.
In this context, the word "objection" (*dūṣaṇam*) is to be supplied [to the sentence], referring to the conventional standpoint (*vyavahāranaya*).

What is it? He says: "the unity of the continuum" (santānaikya), which is the non-difference of the stream; of whom? Of men (nṛṇām)—this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), and by implication, it includes insentient things as well;
when what [is there]? He says: "in difference," that is, in plurality (nānātve).
How so? He says: "In whatever manner"—meaning by that mode superimposed through conceptual construction—there is a synthesis within non-difference;
thus, "leading the object," he becomes the *ṛjusūtra-naya*. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
If it is asked, "Why is there not a unity [of all things] in reality (*bhāvataḥ*)?", he says here: "Not-all," and so forth.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Conceptual construction," and so forth.
Why is worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) merely false? He says: because worldly convention is fashioned by the artisan of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
What happened then? He says: "The establishment of identity based on that age [of the body] due to the force of worldly transaction is improper.

Here he provides an illustration: "If, as in the case of the solar dynasty (*sūryavaṃśa*) and so forth, there were no identity between the preceding and succeeding cognitions in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), then memory and other such functions would not exist, just as they do not exist in another being. To this, he replies: "Memory," and so forth.

Memory (*smṛti*) is the cognition that "it is that"; reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*); action (*karma*) is activity; the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), or the fruit (*phala*) such as heaven and so forth; and the relationship between those two—these are the "beginnings" (*ādi*) of which [the group] beginning with *ūha* consists, and thus they are so described. How could these exist in a single continuum? To this he says: "Because of the specific nature of the relation between cause and effect. Experience is the cause and recollection is the effect; because of the specific nature—that is, the excellence (*atiśaya*)—of that relation, what follows? It is that memory and the others have a restricted occurrence (*niyatavṛtti*) here [in a single continuum].

For instance: an experience occurring within one's own continuum is capable of producing a memory directed toward that same [object] and produces only that, not another, because of the reverse being the case. Otherwise, this same fault would apply even to the proponent of a self (*ātmavādin*): why does the experience of one person not produce the memory of another? [The answer would be] "due to a lack of capacity. [But] this is the same elsewhere; for there is an absence of unity. Why is there no unity between oneself and another? [The answer would be] "because the cause for that has such a capacity. [In that case], the consequence of a pervasive continuity (*anugata*) follows.
Because it is observed to be so; but is remembrance by one person of another's experience ever actually perceived? If you say, "Just as in the case of other living beings";
If this is so; if this is so; if this is so;
These [functions] such as reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) and so forth have not yet been explained.
Now, one might ask: since they are restricted to their specific objects by virtue of those very distinctions, why do they not arise from a state of unity? To this he says: "But not from unity.
*Suḥ* [is used here as a particle of negation].
Why? He says: because of contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*). Is it because of the negation of the remainder, or because of the negation of unity?
Or rather, because of opposition;
for instance, if seeing, remembering, and so forth were not distinct entities, there would be no unity.
If that is so, [you might argue] this fault does not apply to the theory of manifoldness (*anekānta*). To this, he says: "And not," etc.

That is to say, if the nature of perception and so forth is admitted as being manifold—that is, consisting of mutually distinct realities—then multiplicity would not be logical in any single instance such as a foot; rather, everything would become one. This is the meaning.

For this reason as well, that [position] is not tenable; thus he says: "Because of the contradiction"—that is, the opposition—between unity and multiplicity, how can one reality be many, or how can the many be one? Therefore, it is not so; thus he says: "Due to conceptual construction," and so forth. This is what is meant: since we observe a distinction among the various conceptual constructions, verbal expressions, and linguistic usages such as impermanence and other manifold properties within a single locus, a distinction is sought therein; yet, their restriction to the actual nature of the thing (*vastutattva*) is untenable. That is not logical, because of the difference in designation and number, as stated in Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 72, etc.
Furthermore, because it does not follow from the intrinsic nature of the objects, that [unity] is not tenable;
for if there were oneness, then seeing, remembering, and so forth would be separate.
The identity of substance and mode arises from their non-distinction;
yet their plurality exists due to differences in designation and number, and not in every respect— Āptamīmāṃsā.

If it is asked: "But how can there be the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) in the case of absolute difference, such that memory and so forth [arise] from it? To this he says: "In the absence of continuity of intrinsic nature," and so on.

If there were no continuity of intrinsic nature, then just as the relation of cause and effect would exist between two distinct things, so too would that reality be without continuity (*niranvaya*). (22)
Causes do not necessarily possess their effects, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Rather, through a specific similarity, there is sometimes a cognition of a causal relation (*anvaya*) despite the absence of such a relation, as in the case of a magical ball (*māyāgolaka*).
Even though twins lack a cause-and-effect relationship, they possess a similarity from which a cognition of that specific [relation] arises.

Therefore, except in the case of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*) such as sleep, or in the cases of the burning of a creeper and the rotting of leaves in another location—wherein there might be a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) through some manner of fitness (*yogyatāprakāra*) despite the absence of a continuity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānanvaya*), and despite the lack of correspondence between the material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyānanugama*)—such a state of being (*tadbhāva*) would exist between the cause and effect under dispute, namely between the material cause and its effect. Consequently, the reality (*tattva*) is without continuity (*niranvaya*). Teaching this meaning of the verse, he says: "Not necessarily," and so forth.
Why? He says: because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), which would lead to the [absurd] conclusion that the potter and the pot, or sleep and awakening, are identical.

It might be thought: "In the case of two preceding and succeeding moments, which are perceived without interruption and stand in the relation of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*), their continuity (*anvaya*) is also perceived. To this he replies: when there is a distinction between cause and effect within that particularity—wherein the relation of material cause and effect is perceived without interruption in some instances—from what source could there be a cognition of continuity, that is, a perception of identity? He says: from a specific similarity (*sādṛśyaviśeṣāt*), as in the case of a ball of clay (*māyāgolaka*).
As it has been said: "A subsequent similar [moment]," and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that the identity between cause and effect consists precisely in their specific distinction, he replies with "similarity," etc. Why? He says: because even in the case of twins, who are not related as cause and effect, there is the perception of that specific distinction, namely, a specific similarity.
If it is argued that "he is mistaken in that regard," [the author] says here: "That," and so forth.

Thus, the fallacious view (*durṇaya*) of the *Ṛjusūtra* is demonstrated; for one might be deceived by the production of successive similar moments, as in the case of a nail that has been cut and grown back again—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 144.

That substance which it negates, both externally and internally at all times, must be understood as its own manifestation, because the [subjective] cognition cannot be denied— *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 271.
Śloka 78,
Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā, page 88, Prameya-naya 7.
30, 31. *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 24.
If it is asked, "How is this a fallacious argument (*durṇaya*)? the author replies here: "The identity of perception and its opposite," and so forth.
If it is argued that the identity of perception and its opposite contradicts non-absolutism (anekānta), then from where could non-absolutism come, or who would be victorious over the Ṛjusūtra?

If, due to the contradiction with absolutism, consciousness were not established as one with perception and the other means of knowledge, then what would be established by what? Apart from that [non-absolutism], there is no perception of a partless reality constructed by mere whim, because there is no other possible way.

The "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is delimited by perceptual cognition, such as "moon-ness" and so forth; the "other" is that which is not so delimited, such as "oneness" and so forth in the case of an error.

Alternatively, in that very context, the "perceptible" is the nature of cognition itself—free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous—while the "other" is its semblance, such as "duality" and so forth, [appearing] through [the influence of] cataracts and the like.

Alternatively, if the Buddhist has accepted—that is, admitted—the identity between the nature of direct perception, which is conceptual cognition, and that other [nature], which is non-perceptual and inexpressible with respect to the object, then how does this not contradict and undermine the Buddhist view of non-absolutism (anekānta)? It certainly undermines it, because non-absolutism is not avoided in other cases as well.
Now, if that identity has not been admitted, he says: "Who indeed," and so forth; the word "not" (na) carries over from the previous context.

The meaning of this is as follows: who indeed would not be victorious? On the contrary, everyone would be victorious, because it is possible for all to refute one who postulates an unseen, absolute *ṛjusūtra* standpoint, or because it is possible for everyone to postulate such a standpoint themselves—this is the sense [applied] to the cognition of a double moon.

Since the other [part] is easy to understand, he says "ko vā" etc., explaining as follows: "of consciousness," that is, of cognition (*jñāna*), there is identity with perception and so forth; this is the identity of the cognition of consciousness, direct perception, conceptual construction, non-conceptualization, and delusion. If the Buddhist (*saugata*) were not to accept or admit this, he states the reason for this: "because of absolute contradiction."

Regarding this, he states the refutation: "How could [theories] such as momentary destruction not be apprehended by some means of valid cognition, such as perception? To this he replies: "By way of its exclusion," and so forth;
for apart from the very perception of consciousness and the like, there is no apprehension of a partless reality constructed according to one's own whims.

If it is argued that nothing is apprehended from the partless nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*) as accepted by the Jains, but rather from something else; to this he replies: "Because there is no other possibility.

Now, one might object: "Granted that cognition takes the aforementioned form according to the Sautrāntika system, but not according to the system of those who maintain the self-nature of cognition (*jñānavādin*), for in their view, 'the cognition of its own nature occurs through itself' (Pramāṇavārttika 2.374). To this he replies: "Otherwise," and so forth.
According to the Yogācāra school, from the perspective of the wise,
the reality of consciousness is one way, while its manifestation is another.
"...the attainment of the desired state is [achieved through] synthesis (saṃgraha).

|| 24 || If it is imagined that the reality of consciousness is partless and undifferentiated from anything, yet appears as if differentiated, then why should the same not be imagined regarding synthesis as well? For otherwise, one would have to resort to the fruit of mere labor in proving momentary destruction and so forth.

This is the intended meaning: would the nature of consciousness be blue and so on, or would it be something other than blue and so on? In the first case, the reality—the essential nature—of consciousness would appear in one way, while its manifestation would appear in another way, namely through the mode of differentiation such as the distinction between the apprehended object and so forth."

He thinks as follows: "If the reality [of an object] were other than blue and so forth, then the appearance of the distinction between blue and so forth would be merely a delusion regarding that [reality]. To this he replies: "Even so," and so on.
The meaning is: even if this view is held, it results in [the doctrine of] synthesis (*saṃgraha*); it would be overcome by synthesis.
Why? He says: "The arising of happiness," and so forth.

By the words "the reality," and so on, he states the meaning of the verse: "Reality is undivided and partless; yet, due to some internal cause of delusion, it appears as if divided. If such a conceptualization is applied even to the *saṃgraha* (the school of inclusion), why should it not be conceived in the same way for the *ṛjusūtra* (the school of the straight line) alone?
This has been explained in detail.
If one asks, "What kind of proof for momentary destruction and so forth would one rely upon because of non-conceptualization? he says: "Exertion," and so on.

Now, if it is argued that there is a distinction between the two—namely, that in the *Saṃgraha* reality (*tattva*) is eternal, whereas elsewhere it is impermanent and consists of cause and effect, and therefore there is a proof for those [latter qualities]—to this he replies: "Not attained," and so on.

The causality of that which has not reached the time of its effect is uncertain; this [notion], which is never observed in any way at any time, is to be believed in only by those of very extensive intellect. (25) [This concerns] the moment of the effect.

Just as at the moment when the effect arises, the acquisition of its own nature by the cause is ineffective, so too is the immediate succession [of the cause] irrelevant for that which does not depend on any assistance rendered by it; for one would have to describe the arising as being merely a specific kind of contiguity,
rather than [the cause being defined simply by] its priority and posteriority, which constitute the assistance.

What kind of distinction could there be between such things as "material cause" (upādāna) and "other [causes]"? Since causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is impossible both for what is eternal and for what is momentary, how could everything not be neither cause nor effect, provided that the establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta) does not occur?

For that partless entity which has not reached the time of its effect—because it has already perished entirely beforehand—its status as a cause remains uncertain; since even its appearance before the path of experience does not occur, how can there be a certainty regarding its causality? This is the intended meaning.

He says this very thing: in every way—whether in the form of momentary destruction and so forth, or even in the form of existence, consciousness, and so on—it is always "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) and must be accepted by faith, both in the state where conceptualization has been withdrawn, just as in the state of conceptualization, or even in waking life, just as in sleep. This reality of consciousness is extremely manifold; [as stated in] the commentary on the *Kārikā*: "the moment of the effect," and so forth.

"Is it not the case that everything is easily understood? It is not that the cause perishes after having arisen previously, but rather [it perishes] immediately [after arising]. To this, he says: "In the effect," and so forth. At the moment of the production of the effect, the acquisition of its own nature by the cause occurs in such a manner—that is, by that mode of non-causality for its own production—because two things that arise simultaneously cannot have one as the producer of the other. For if both were producers of each other, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus, that which does nothing is likewise simultaneous with what arises immediately after it, and is therefore ineffective.

For instance: if the preceding [moment] is the cause of the subsequent one immediately following it, why does the subsequent [moment] not likewise become the cause of the preceding one? Since the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is equal in respect to both, such being the case, the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) would remain as before.

It might be argued: "Just as there is no assistance of one by the other among two co-existent things, so it is with two immediate [moments]; nevertheless, one is the cause of the other because of its necessary occurrence immediately after that. To this, he says: "of that which is independent of the assistance rendered by it," and so forth.
Otherwise, everything would necessarily follow immediately after everything else;
for, out of faith in that [universal] necessity, the Buddhist would have to assert that the very distinction of immediate succession is the origin of the causal relationship between cause and effect.
Regarding this very point, he states another fault: "And not," and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the refutations;
the point is that assistance does not consist merely in a sequence of before and after, for such assistance would belong to all things, whether they exist in a prior or posterior state.
What kind of distinction between material cause (*upādāna*) and other causes could there be for such things whose nature has just been described?

If it is argued that assistance is indeed nothing at all, because no cause is capable of anything— according to such statements as *Pravacanasāra* 2.4— then [the author] says here: "For that purpose," and so forth.

And that [entity] is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) precisely because of the statement that "whatever possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is ultimately real. Now, if the causal efficiency accepted by the Buddhists is admitted to be impossible both in its permanence and its momentariness, how could everything not become devoid of cause and effect?
And thus, even in the case of the non-eternal position, like that of Brahman, there would be the removal of all conventional discourse regarding causes and so forth; this is the intended meaning.
That which is capable of causal efficiency is what is here [defined as] ultimately real.
Everything else is said to be conventionally real; these two are its particular and universal characteristics. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.3)

If it is argued that for the proponent of the non-duality of appearances (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*), a rain of jewels has fallen from the sky as it were, because he accepts [all things] as eternally like Brahman; to this he replies: "If the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekāntasiddhi*) did not occur, then everything would be without cause and effect"—this is the connection.

For, as has been stated, even for one who asserts that consciousness (*saṃvit*) has the nature of blue and so forth, the establishment of non-absolutism remains consistent with the relationship between cause and effect.

Now, one might ask: "Since there are defects such as contradiction in the case of non-absolutism (anekānta), how can that [non-absolutism] be established? To this, he says: "Because of contradiction," and so forth:
"How is it not contradicted for you—who fear contradiction—that emptiness exists both externally and internally, since the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge have been refuted? (26)

For you, who seek to avoid the suspicion of contradiction regarding non-absolutism (*anekāntatva*)—which is the object of both internal and external experience and falls within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—your recourse to the apprehension of the absolute momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣayaikānta*) and your subsequent rejection of external objects follows the analogy of entering the mouth of a python out of fear of a earthworm. This is an illustrative example; by it, the faults of lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), doubt, infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) are included. O Buddhist, how is it that this [position] of yours does not become contradictory, given that you are terrified of the contradiction inherent in that very non-absolutism?
What is emptiness?
Where is it? And from where do "outer" and "inner" arise? For the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge have been refuted.

He thinks as follows: since no other [position] is found due to the contradiction and other faults of non-absolutism (anekānta), total emptiness—being devoid of any means of protection—is all the more beset by contradiction. Thus, the commentary on the verse beginning with "the object of internal and external experience" refutes the objection of contradiction regarding the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) concerning non-absolutism; yet for that Buddhist who abandons [this position], his recourse to the apprehension of the absolute momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣayaikānta*) and his acceptance of that absolutist view follows the path of entering the mouth of a "silent serpent" (*ajagara*), like one who, out of fear of a small earthworm, enters the mouth of a great python.

It has been stated that if one abandons this non-absolutism (anekānta), reality would become a mere single atom; or else, there would be the non-perception of that [atom]. On what basis, then, could there be the perception of its absolute unity, which follows upon the entry into that [atom]? To this he says: "The refutation of external objects," and so forth; this has been well analyzed.

If it is argued: "Is this investigation of *naya* and *durṇaya* not already established in the scriptures (*āgama*) itself? Therefore, what is the use of this ultimate analysis?"—to this he replies with the verse beginning "dependent" (*sāpekṣā*):

For the proponents of *syādvāda*, *nayas* are established as being dependent [on one another], while even *durṇayas* are established from the worldly perspective according to common usage, like the inhabitants of a village of chickens. (27)

The intention behind the worldly convention "the village-dweller was pecked by a cock" is to include [all relevant factors]. It is not that he was necessarily pecked while actually dwelling in the village; rather, this is seen in worldly usage because [the term] applies to his neighborhood, his house, a tree, a branch, his face, and so forth.
These are *nayās* (standpoints) because they yield a general [truth]; otherwise, they are *durṇayas* (fallacious standpoints).

The particle *api* (even/also) has been displaced; it should be understood as following the word *lokataḥ*. Thus, the meaning is as follows: for the Jains, who maintain the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*), these [principles] are established and reached through certainty not only from scripture (*āgama*), but even from the world (*loka*).
To the question "What are they?", he says: "the standpoints" (*nayāḥ*).

Of what nature are they? He says: "They are dependent (*sāpekṣāḥ*), and *durṇayas* (fallacious reasonings) are established as those which negate the objects of other *nayas*. Furthermore, he says: 'And *durṇayas* are established even from the perspective of common worldly experience (*lokataḥ*). Of what nature are they? They are independent (*nirapekṣāḥ*) and negators of the domain of others."

Because of that faulty reasoning, the secondary factors (*kāraka*) belonging to other systems of logic are indeed [untenable] for those who maintain extremist views (*ekāntavādin*). To the question, "From where are these established in common worldly practice? he says: "In worldly transaction," and so forth.

He states an illustration: "A cock has crowed in the village" (or "in a specific place within a particular house")—this is the intention of the *saṃgraha* [view], because it conveys only the general [locus].

"Not indeed, not at all in the entire village, but rather in its quarter, in one part of the village"—this is the establishment of the *naigama* [view], because it conveys both [the general and the specific] by way of the primary and the secondary.
Demonstrating the *vyavahāra* [view], he says: "In the house," and so forth.
In this case as well, one should apply the principle not merely to a village-quarter (*pāṭaka*), but rather that [the sound] resides in a house, a tree, or a branch;
thus says the *Ṛjusūtra*—beginning with "in pleasure" (*sukhe*) and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the palate and other locations are included, because these are observed in common usage (*vyavahāra*). These are the viewpoints (*naya*s).
How so? He says: "In the universal," and so forth.
He states the fallacious arguments (*durṇaya*) with the words "otherwise," and so forth.
The intention of the *Ṛjusūtra* is that [the object] is merely a fragrance on the mouth, which is called "sound."
To facilitate the recollection of what has already been established, he states at the conclusion of the section on divisions and so forth:
"The *nayas* may be observed even among those objects of cognition that rest upon the nature of both difference and non-difference;
they function through mutual dependence in the world, and in the tradition of the Lord of Jinas, by relying solely upon the object."
And those who are of poor conduct and evil intellect should be recognized as such by the learned among the wise; otherwise, who indeed would bestow honor upon this [view] as being the truth?

(28) Difference and non-difference have their characteristics explained; these two are the very natures of a thing, and they are not absolutely distinct. This [phrase], "even toward those devoted to that [reality]," is to be read immediately after the words "those intent on that."
In what kind of objects? To this he says: "even in those that are objects of the intellect (*mati*) and even in those that are objects of scripture (*śruta*"; the word "even" [api] implies both).
What of them? To this he says: "the *nayas* would be"—that is, they would be the intentions (*abhisandhi*) of the knower. Of what nature are they? He says: "being observed" (*lakṣyamāṇāḥ*).
Where? He says: "In the world, in the tradition of the Lord of Jinas, and in the scripture of the Jinas. How are they observed? He says: "By means of a dependent function.

Of what nature is that [function]? He says: "For the sake of taking hold of the mere object (*arthamātra*). This is an elliptical expression; by it, the grasping of the mere synonym (*paryāya*) is intended. Based upon that, there may be not only *nayas* (standpoints) but also *durṇayas* (fallacious standpoints).
Of what nature are they? To this he says: "It proceeds," and so forth.
By the former [verse], the object is indicated; by this, the cause is pointed out.
The *nayās* and *durṇayas* are to be understood by the learned—that is, by those who are wise among scholars. This is the meaning.
He states its purpose with the words "māna" and so forth. Otherwise—that is, in the manner of the absence of valid cognition—who indeed would [act]? None at all.
How? He says: "as this" (*idantayā*).
What is it? He says: "Pride," and so forth.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the *Arthanayasiddhi*, in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by Anantavīrya, who subsists on the feet of the venerable Raviśena.
The Eleventh Chapter: The Establishment of the Śabdanaya.

It has been stated that "the remaining [nayas] are the Śabdanayas"; therein, in order to explain those remaining ones, the author, defining the word (*śabda*) which serves as their basis, says: "It is declared," and so forth.

In the Grammar previously mentioned on page 662, regarding the syllables and words, therein the syllable consists of atoms of substance; it is corporeal because, despite its motion, it is not devoid of wind.
The origin of those things that undergo infinite transformations through birth is artificial;
for by constantly assuming birth, one would attain the state of being "born" through the non-arising of what is non-existent.

(1) Since it is impossible for that which is eternal and exists in every respect to arise, and since there is no distinction between it and the absolute absence of such arising, why is it that causes exist for the imperishable (*akṣara*) and so forth, but not for anything else? Furthermore, just as the non-existence of a donkey’s horn follows from its non-arising, and its non-arising follows from its non-existence—thus involving the fault of mutual dependence—the same applies here: non-arising follows from the lack of a cause, and the lack of a cause follows from non-arising.

If it is argued that the arising of an entity from itself is contradictory because of the impossibility of an action operating upon itself, then how can there be momentariness if that which was previously non-existent arises and, having reached the time of its effect, produces it? Furthermore, if the illusory son (the Bodhisattva) was previously a transmigrating being, how did he become a Buddha through the practice of reality (*tattvābhyāsa*)? It is logical that one who already exists in some sense attains the state of a Sugata;

nor is it conceivable that the Buddha is anyone other than the illusory son, for [if he were], his birth would have to come from another, which would entail the undesirable consequence that the practice of reality and its fruit would reside in different substrates.

Even though there is unity with respect to the continuum (*santāna*), there is plurality with respect to the substance (*vastu*) even in the case of father and son; we perceive no other cause for why the plurality of the continuum exists in one case and not the other, except for the difference in substance (*dravyabheda*). But how is this so? It has been stated here...

It was said that [this] was "spoken first. In what context? To this he says: "In grammar," which consists of a collection of rules for correct speech. Now, one might object: "Was that not already spoken by someone before? For no one declares, 'This reality of grammar, which was previously entirely non-existent, has now been brought forth by me. To this, he says: "In the past" (*purā*).

It is heard that in the time of the Blessed One, the first Tīrthaṅkara named Purudeva, he indeed composed a grammar called *Svayambhū*, consisting of five hundred chapters, in order to teach Bharata and others; thus it was a grammar.

If it is argued that his sons likewise learned it from another source, just like ourselves and others, then what contradiction is there in [the Vedas] being produced by an agent, as in the case of Bharata and others? If it is argued that this contradicts their status as auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*) of the Veda, we say no; for since the Veda itself has been established as being artificial, its status as an auxiliary to that [Veda] is not proven.

Now, if [the Veda] were produced by someone as a part of that [human activity], then because the Veda would also result in being something created, it would not be undermined merely by the observation of its transmission [from teacher to student]; furthermore, such a consequence would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For Devadatta’s [word] would likewise result in being something created, and it would not be undermined by the observation of its transmission. Thus, there would be an over-extension.

Since all treatises composed by Brahmins, such as those of the nihilists (*nāstika*), would thereby attain the status of being auxiliary to the Veda (*veda-aṅga*), one would consequently have to practice their teachings; yet in that case, such a person would not truly be a Brahmin. Why is this so? Because they propound matters that lack authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). If it is argued: "What is the authority for the correctness of words (*śabda-sādhutva*) such that Pāṇini, by merely repeating them, would become a Brahmin and his work a scripture (*śāstra*)?"—then the same applies elsewhere, since other works as well are established as being auxiliary to the Veda.
If it is argued that he is a Brāhmaṇa because he explains the causes of dharma and its correctness, we say no; for even here there is a lack of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that he is a Brāhmaṇa because he provides instruction on Vedic words, then let anyone else who provides instruction on matters such as Vedic meters and marriage also be a Brāhmaṇa.
If it is argued that this subject matter does not exist in the Veda, we say no; for that treatise is an auxiliary (*vedāṅga*) of the Veda.
If it is asked, "How can that [agency] belong to one created by a person?"— then [the agency] does not belong to Pāṇini either.
If you say, "Because Pāṇini is not remembered as such [an agent]," this is the same in the case of the Blessed One as well.
If it is argued that [the Mahābhārata] is like the Taittirīya Upaniṣad;
For even Devanandin did not attain [the goal] immediately after composing [the work]; thus it is written twice.
Furthermore, why is it not accepted that Jaina-Indra, having worshipped [the deity], learned from the Tīrthaṅkara, and then having forgotten it, remembered it again?—by the teacher Devanandin.

It might be argued: "In that case, the following of other systems is heard of and seen in the *Pāṇinīya*; and there too, the following of yet other systems is heard of and seen. Thus, the following of others is common even to the opponent.

Just as now some compose grammars by following other systems, what contradiction is there in the fact that the twice-born also composed it in the past by following other systems? Therefore, grammar is not an ancillary (*aṅga*) of that [Veda].
If this is the objection:

Now, if it is argued that [grammar] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Veda because it brings about the understanding of the meaning of the Veda, we say no. In that [grammar], words are merely derived; once they have been derived there, they convey other meanings as well through convention, just as they do for their own specific meanings.
Furthermore, just as in some cases Vedic words not included under general definitions (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are derived, so too are others derived elsewhere; thus, the principle is the same.
If you think that [grammar] is an auxiliary to that [Veda] simply because it relies upon words mentioned in the Veda, let that be for now.
Therefore, unlike other treatises, grammar does not possess the status of a Vedic auxiliary (vedāṅga) by virtue of being beginningless.
Having done what was it said? He says: "Aiming at" (uddiśya), that is, relying upon which? "The syllables and words," namely the *Avīkoya-nijainendra* [grammar]. 4.3.156.
In such cases as these, [the rule] "a word ending in a vowel or a case-ending is a *pada*" (Jainendra 1.2.103) applies to the syllables;
however, in the case of a conjunction with a negative particle (*nañ*), [the rule] "in the case of a conjunction with *nañ*" (Jainendra 2... applies to the words.

If it is argued: "Since [the word 'Veda'] refers even to sentences such as those beginning with *ityādi*, how is it that this [word] is not included here? We say: No; because this [word] is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indicator), the inclusion of both [words] would be purposeless, since the indication is accomplished by one alone. If it is further argued: "No; the inclusion of the word [‘Veda’] is for the sake of providing an example for the Mīmāṃsaka."

For instance: just as in the word "gauḥ" there is no word-entity (pada) distinct from the phonemes *g*, *au*, and so on; likewise, regarding the question "What is the word in 'gauḥ'?", the venerable Upavarṣa states: "The phonemes *g*, *au*, and the visarga" (*Śābarabhāṣya* 1.1.5).
Because of this statement, likewise, the *akṣara* (the imperishable) does not exist as something distinct from its parts;
and since he will later state that the *akṣara* is "composed of atoms" (*aṇumaya*), that which consists of those [atoms] must be composite, like a jar or similar objects.
Nevertheless, just as there is the state of being the *akṣara*, so too is there its absence. To the question "What then is the case there?", he says: "In that regard," and so forth.

By this, he denies his own independence regarding the determination of sound—either in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) or, according to some, among those [sounds] themselves. He asks: "Is the singular number used with reference to the universal class (*varṇajāti*) of phonemes (*akṣara*)? To which he replies: "It has the nature of a substance (*dravyātman*)," meaning its essence is that of a substance.
Furthermore, he asks what it is like and says: "consisting of atoms" (aṇumaya), meaning having the nature of a transformation of the subtle atoms of speech;
this refers to that which consists of atoms within both syllables and words.

The commentators [ask]: "But since the transformation of an atom, like that of a jar and so forth, is invariably of the nature of a substance (*dravya*), what is the purpose of the term 'of the nature of a substance'? [The answer is: No; because there is no absolute uniformity. For its transformation may be of one kind as a quality (*guṇa*), such as blackness or redness; another as an action (*karman*), such as going and so forth; and yet another as a substance (*dravya*), such as a jar and so forth. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "of the nature of a substance" is for the purpose of defining this [transformation] by way of excluding the others.

If it is asked, "For what purpose is that [stated]? it is replied: It is for the purpose of demonstrating the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason in the following argument: "Sound is a quality (*guṇa*), because, while being neither a substance nor an action that is being negated, it is related to existence (*sattā*), like color and so forth.

To explain how this is so: although sound lacks the status of an action that is being negated, there is no negation of its being a substance, because that would be contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is asked, "What is that valid cognition? it is stated: "The syllable (*akṣara*) is a substance, because it possesses activity (*kriyāvat*), like a clod of earth."

For even by others, that which possesses action is accepted as being a substance— since it is stated [in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra]: "A substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause" (VS 1.1.15).

Nor is the possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) unestablished in that case; for the syllable possesses action because it reaches another location from one location in succession, like an arrow. This is because even the opponent accepts that [sound] is perceived as having reached the listener’s ear from the location of the speaker’s mouth, based on the statement that "the eye, the ear, and the mind function without reaching their objects" (*aprāptakāritva*), and thus it is a transformation of atoms (*paramāṇuvikāra*).
Regarding inference, the Buddhist says:
"The eye, mind, and ear do not reach [their objects]"— Abhidharmakośa 1.45.

"According to the established tenet [of the Tattvasaṃgraha], the eye, ear, and mind do not reach their objects, whereas sound has as its primary cause both the appropriated and the unappropriated great elements"—
Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 603.
This has been extracted from: *Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 83;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 545;
and *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 333.

Some maintain that [the sound] is perceived at its very place of origin; for them, however, there would be neither perception nor non-perception of it by means of a following or opposing wind, as in the case of a pillar.

Indeed, it is not observed that a pillar, while being perceived in its own location, is perceived when there is a following wind but not when there is an opposing wind. Now, if it is argued that the opposing wind causes an obstruction to the auditory organ; [we reply: surely that which causes the obstruction must reach [the organ], otherwise it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

If it is argued that when the air travels from the location of the sound to the location of the hearer, the perception of the sound would then occur, but that this does not happen because of its resistance [to the air]—we say no; for such a thing is not observed elsewhere. This might be the case: that which is brought to a location contrary to the direction of the wind by a counter-wind is not perceived, like a tuft of cotton and so forth, due to the absence of the necessary capacity (*yogyatā*) for response; thus there is non-perception because of the lack of capacity. Otherwise, if the wind were equal or favorable, there would be no perception at all.
If it is argued that this very collection [of conditions] is the cause, then there would be no perception in a windless place;
if it is further argued that here too this same collection is the cause, it would be so only if the absence of wind were a distinct entity.
If it is argued that it is simply the nature of the sound itself, then it should be perceived even when the wind is unfavorable.

The reply that "its capacity to be perceived has been obstructed" is also no answer; for there is no reason to determine whether its capacity was obstructed while remaining in that very place, or after it had been carried to another location.
We, however, say that it was carried to another location because it is heard by those situated there;
and for one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda), the production of sound in a different location—just as in the case of odors and the like—is not contradictory.
If it is argued that, nevertheless, its production does not occur at the location of the ear; [we reply] that even in the absence of that [production], nothing is contradicted.
If it is argued that the cognition "the sound is far away" is contradicted; [we reply] that this is not so in that case, because that same cognition occurs in the case of odor as well.
Therefore, it is just like the action of a syllable (*akṣara-kriyā*).

He says: "Even by the movement along with the wind" (*anupavanaṃ gatyāpi*). "Along with the wind" (*anupavanaṃ*) refers to the movement of sound together with the wind; by that [movement], the word *api* indicates that the substance itself [is also perceived]. The particle *api* is used for the conjunction of the aforementioned reasons; therefore, "by possessing touch and number," and so forth, should be understood.
The Buddhists [hold] that [sound moves] against the wind.
Or else,
"iti" [is used] by those residing in another country.
The production of sound [is established] because it possesses touch, because it possesses number, because it possesses conjunction, and so forth—this is what should be understood.

Now, one might object: "Even though odor has movement as its subsequent state, it is nonetheless not a substance; therefore, there is a deviation [in the reason]. No; for [odor] is included within the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*).

If it is argued that, just as a substance possessing fragrance does not move in the absence of wind while the fragrance itself does, yet by metaphorical usage that [substance] is also designated as "possessing it," so too is the case with the *akṣara*; [we ask: is there then motion in the substratum of sound, just as there is in the substance which is the substratum of fragrance, such that this [metaphor] could apply? If not, how can there be the postulation of a metaphor? Or, if it is because motion belonging to the air is superimposed upon the *akṣara*, making it appear as if it possesses it; then motion would likewise belong to the fragrance, and thus the fragrance too would appear to be the moving *akṣara*.

It might be argued that [the syllable] would possess action through the superimposition of the movement of the wind; however, there is no cause for such superimposition in the ether (*gagana*). But what, then, exists in the imperishable (*akṣara*)? If it is said to be "concomitance with that" (the wind), we say no; for how can there be concomitance with the wind for that which is devoid of action? Indeed, unlike a king mounted on a horse, there is no reaching of another location for one mounted on the wind; or, if such a thing were to exist, it would imply a relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) within the sound itself.
If one accepts that sound has the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga), its status as a substance (dravyatva) is all the more established.

Now, if it is thought that when the wind reaches a certain location, there is a concomitance (*sāhacarya*) because of the production of successive sounds in that place—arising from the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), space (*ākāśa*), and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), the preceding sound that is perishing—if that were so, what fault would there be in [the sound] itself undergoing a transformation of motion (*gatipariṇāma*), as in the case of dust and the like? If it is argued: "It cannot be a transformation of that [sound], because of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*); how is its momentariness stated? [We reply: "Sound is momentary because, while being perceptible to persons such as ourselves, it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of an all-pervading substance (*vibhudravya*), like pleasure (*sukha*) and the like. [To this we say: No; for its momentariness will be refuted later by the discussion of its qualities.
As he will say, "Because it constantly assumes birth," and this has been discussed by us in the *Dravyasiddhiprakaraṇa*,
it is therefore established that the imperishable (*akṣara*) is the nature of substance (*dravya*), for even though it moves, it is like a clod of earth when devoid of wind.
If this is argued;
if it is argued that it belongs to the word itself;

It might be thought: "Even if it has the nature of a substance, its movement is not impossible because it is all-pervading and formless, like space. To this he says: "Consisting of atoms" (*aṇumayam*).

Atoms are the *bhāṣā-paramāṇus* (speech-atoms); that which is a modification thereof is "consisting of those. Therefore, the reason "because it is all-pervading and formless" is unestablished (*asiddha*), for that which is a modification of those [atoms] cannot possess their [all-pervasive] nature, as that would be a contradiction.
If it is asked, "Why is it composed of that? he says: [It is] "embodied" (*mūrta*), because the former teachers have accepted that which possesses form, taste, smell, and touch as embodied;
for instance: "The syllable (*akṣara*) consists of atoms (*aṇumaya*), because it is embodied, like a cloth and so forth.
And embodiment is established as a modification (*paryāya*) of the *pudgala* (matter), according to the *Siddhivinirṇaya* (7).
This has already been established on that occasion and is not repeated here;
or rather, even the nature of substance as imagined by the Mīmāṃsakas would not exist. To this he says: "How could that [substance] consist of atoms? He replies: "Because it is corporeal."

By what means is this [known]? He says: "Even by movement against the wind"—the word *api* (even/also) implies that it is not known solely through the clear perception of specific parts of the body and so forth. For instance: by its movement against the wind, a specific conjunction with it is inferred, just as in the case of grass and the like; because in the absence of that [conjunction], there is an absence of that [movement].
And from that [conjunction], a specific touch [is inferred]; and from that, color and so forth. Thus, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).

The opponent states the meaning of the word "api" (also/even): "Air-currents are impelled by the wind through the conjunction and disjunction of the palate and other organs, serving as the causes for the manifestation of sounds; by these [currents], the phoneme (*akṣara*) is manifested exactly as it exists. Therefore, its movement without the wind is unestablished. This is not so; for the manifestation of an eternal entity is denied. If it is argued, "Let the phoneme consist of that [air], but let the word (*pada*), which is manifested by it, be eternal and possess form," to this he replies: "A collection of words [is nothing more than] those phonemes, because apart from them, they are not perceived"—this is the sense.

What follows from this? He says: "Accepted" means admitted as artificial—that is, consisting of produced parts—since otherwise there would be no collection of produced things; for that [collection] is momentary, and to avoid the over-extension [of the term], it is not used figuratively. To the Vaiśeṣika and others who hold this view, he replies with the words beginning "eternal," and so forth.

"How can that which is eternal (*nitya*), constant (*dhruva*), and somehow imperishable (*akṣara*) [be so]? To this he says: "Because of the assumption of birth. Now, one might object: "This reason is contradictory; for birth is characterized by the renewed appropriation of a self where there was previously non-existence, and such [birth] is impossible in the case of an eternal entity that persists through the three periods of time. To this he replies: "Because of the non-arising of the non-existent," and so forth.
"How is there the attainment of self-nature for that which exists and is present?

To this he says: "If it is argued that for that which is non-existent—being like the horn of a donkey—the attainment of self-nature from anything whatsoever is a contradiction because of its non-arising," to this he replies: "Birth," and so forth.

The meaning is that at the very moment of birth, there are infinite transformations (vivartas) which are modifications (pariṇāmas) belonging to that [entity]; for that which exists absolutely, no modification is contradictory to its self-acquisition. Establishing its permanence in detail, he says: "eternal," etc.; it is eternally subject to modification and imperishable (akṣara).
Why? If it is argued that [the reason] "because of arising" is a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*), he says here: "He would obtain," etc.
From where does even this [follow]? He says: "Once born," etc.
Easily accessible,
consisting of atoms, and eternal.
However, in order to avoid the contradiction [of the term "arising" being applied to what is non-existent], he states the meaning of the verse beginning with "of that which is eternal," etc.,
[and asks]: "If one objects, 'What fault is there in the arising of that which is absolutely non-existent?'— to this he replies with the words] 'in every way,' etc."

It might be thought: "The ether of the syllables (*akṣarākāśa*) and so forth exist as causes, and from them [the effect] arises, whereas the horn of a donkey and the like do not, because of the opposite case. To this, he says: "In the absence of any distinction in their absolute non-existence," and so on. Since there is no distinction between those two—the ether of the syllables and the horn of a donkey—in terms of their absolute non-existence, what is the basis for saying that the ether of the syllables has a cause while the other, the horn of a donkey, does not? If it is argued: "Indeed, the horn of a donkey is without a cause because it does not arise, whereas the ether of the syllables and the like are not so, because of the opposite case"; to this, he says: "Furthermore," and so on.

The intended meaning is as follows: "The horn of a donkey has no cause" is the thesis (*sādhya*); "because of non-arising" (*anutpatter*) is the reason (*hetu*); and that [reason] must be established. From what, then, is its establishment? If you say, "Because of its non-existence" (*asattvāt*), it is replied: The word "again" (*punar*) is used here in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). Just as the non-existence of a donkey's horn is established from its non-arising, and its non-arising is established from its non-existence—thus there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyo'nyasaṃśraya*)—in the same way, by that method, non-arising follows from its lack of a cause, and lack of a cause follows from non-arising; thus the fault of mutual dependence is identical.

The opponent might say: "It is not because of the non-existence [of the cause] that its non-arising is established—which would lead to this fault—but rather because of the absence of a cause. To this, the following should be said; such is the intended meaning.
Thus, since non-arising is unestablished, the qualification "non-arising" [applied to the letter 'a'] is inconsistent. Now, one might object: "Is this objection not universal?"

To explain: why does the *jīva* not arise from the *pudgala* as its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)? If you say, "Because that [pudgala] is not its cause," then from what [reasoning] is that known?
