If you say, "Because it does not arise from it," then from what is that [non-arising] known? If you say, "Because it is not its cause," then—as before—there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). If you say, "It does not arise because it is non-existent therein," then from what is its non-existence known? If you say, "From its non-arising," then the same logical difficulty (*prasaṅga*) follows. This should be applied in all such cases.

Now, if it is argued that because the soul (*jīva*), though existing as an object of perception, is not perceived as having the person (*pudgala*) as its material cause (*upādāna*), it must therefore be non-existent therein; and since [the effect] cannot arise from that which is non-existent, this [non-existence] cannot be the cause of that [effect], and thus there is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*); and if it is further argued that this same absence of mutual dependence would apply elsewhere as well—[we reply: True, it would be so, but only if one were to follow mere conceptualization (*pratīti*) and not mere logical analysis (*vicāra*). For if that were the case, a jar or the like arises from a lump of clay precisely because it already exists there in the form of the substance of clay, as is perceived; whereas a donkey’s horn does not, for the opposite is true. As he will say: "Both externally and internally" (Siddhiviniścaya 11).

3. Thus, having raised the objection of the opponent's view with the words "from itself" and so forth, [the author asks]: "How is the birth—that is, the production—of an entity (*bhāva*), which is to say an effect-entity, contradicted? Why? To this he says: "If it is argued that [it is impossible] because of the contradiction of action within itself, from its own self, from its own nature; then, refuting this, he says: 'How' and so forth."

If it is argued that there is no fault because its birth occurs when the cause exists, to this he replies: "When [the cause] does not exist," and so forth. The intention here is as follows: if the effect were to arise first and then reach the time of the cause to produce it, would there not be momentariness? Or, if the cause were to arise simultaneously with the effect, there would be the destruction of the continuum (*santāna*). Thus, there is a contradiction.
Therefore, the living being (*jīva*) does not have the person (*pudgala*) as its cause.

Regarding the word "kārya" (to be done), the opponent raises an objection with the words "if again... (*yadi...*) and so forth, deeming it redundant; the refutation of this begins with "how... (*katham...*) and so forth.

Here, "māyāsuta" refers to the Son of Māyā—Māyā being the mother of the Sugata—and her son was formerly a transmigrating being who later, through the practice of reality (*tattva*), became a Buddha whose nature is the state of having shaken off the net of conceptual construction (*kalpanājāla*).

If it is argued that even this is not accepted, he says here: "In some way, as having the nature of existence, consciousness, and so forth, that which is indeed existent attains the state of a Sugata, characterized by the quality of non-return and so on"—this is logical. [Objection:

But surely a son of an illusory woman does not become a Sugata, for there is the statement: "There is no goer toward Śiva, yet there is a going. Rather, the Sugata must be something other than that which is the basis (upādāna) of that [illusory son]. To this, he says: "Nor even... and so forth.

If it is asked: "Since it is not even conceivable that a Buddha could be born from something other than Māyā’s son who serves as the cause— for if birth were to occur from another source entirely, why would it not be conceivable for the Buddha?"— the author anticipates the opponent's view by stating "the continuum" (*santāna*), etc., on the grounds that it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the practice of reality and its fruit would have different loci.

If it is argued that, although the illusory son (*māyāsuta*) and the Sugata are one with respect to their continuum (*santāna*), they are distinct with respect to the entity—that is, with respect to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the illusory son and the Sugata—the author replies: "The father," and so forth. The meaning is that there exists a continuum characterized by the sequence of cause and effect even for the father and the son. It might be thought: "There is no such specific continuum characterized by cause and effect between those two, and thus they belong to different continua. To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

The meaning is that there is a difference in the continuum between those two—the father and the son—but not in the other case; there is no difference in the continuum between Māyā’s son and Sugata, for in that case there is their identity. In this view, we do not perceive any other cause.
Why no other? He says: "In substance," and so forth, where indeed there is a difference in substance.

Where there is a difference in substance, there is a multiplicity of the continuum (*santāna*); where there is no such difference, there is unity. Otherwise, even the specific distinction between cause and effect would be difficult to establish—this has been demonstrated. Furthermore, regarding father and son, he anticipates the opponent's objection with the words "But how... and so forth; the response to that is given with the words "It has been stated here... and so forth.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "If the gross [object] were a single reality," and so forth.

If the external gross object, such as a jar, were to arise as a single reality, then it would have to exist internally in a sequential manner, characterized by the distinction between the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*). (2)
If the external object, such as a jar, belongs to the one [consciousness], what is its nature? To this he says: "gross," and so forth.

Furthermore, the internal characteristic of the known (*vedya*), the knower (*vedaka*), and [the act of] knowing is understood to be the *tattva*. If it were to arise all at once, then a single *tattva* would evolve sequentially;
thus it is stated in the *Kārikā-vivaraṇa*: "Of the one," and so forth.
Since the meaning has been explained in various ways, it is not elaborated upon here.

If it is objected: "Since everything is untenable when subjected to critical inquiry (*vicāra*), for whom and from what source could there be a proof of non-absolutism (*anekānta*)?"—to this he replies: "Externally and internally," and so forth.

Through investigation both externally and internally, there is no stability in absolute positions (*ekānta*); thus, the directly perceived reality of non-absolutism (*anekāntatattva*) establishes itself. 3.

For just as those who maintain extremist views [hold that] atoms do not possess the status of being objects of the eye and other senses because they do not appear [as such], so too [the atom] cannot be designated as "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*), since there is no gross, unitary form within the atoms, nor is there anything else distinct from them, nor is there any "other" at all; for what, then, could have self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? This is because [anything] corresponding to the appearance [of an object] is impossible.

Thus, while attempting to establish his own preferred position by relying on an extreme view, he not only mocks his own conduct through his own words—first by undermining the very nature of inquiry and then by negating existence—but he actually supports the principle of non-absolutism (anekāntatattva).

For where is there room for such extremist doctrines as total emptiness and the like? To this he says: "Externally and internally. And to the question "What [fault] is there in them? he replies: "Instability" (anavasthitiḥ).
The word *tattva*, taken from the preceding verse, is connected here with the locative case ending changed to the genitive;
in what [condition] being present? He says: "in *parīkṣā*," meaning when there is investigation or inquiry. What would that do? He says: "it would establish."
What is it? It is the reality of non-absolutism (anekāntatattva).
Of what nature is it? To this he says: "directly realized" (sākṣātkṛta);
the intended meaning here is that because every form of absolutism (ekānta) lacks stability, no practical discourse of affirmation or negation can occur by relying upon it.
Now, the illumination of the principle of non-absolutism (anekānta) remains;
if that were false, then the system of affirmation and negation would be without a basis.
Therefore, the principle of non-absolutism is the vision of ultimate reality, because the conventional practice of affirmation and negation would otherwise be impossible.
The genitive case signifies the intended meaning,
which is that which has been made the object of the vision of ultimate reality.
He explains the verse with the words "yathaiva hi" and so forth: "yathaiva" [is used] because of the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tad*;
therefore, this is the meaning: "yathaiva hi" means what? It means that for the proponent of an extreme view (*ekāntavādin*), nothing at all possesses the designation of "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
Why? He says: "because atoms are the cause of the objects of the eyes and other senses."
Why? He says: "Because they do not appear," as he will state later: "And it is not contradictory for a single form to represent multiple objects" (*Siddhiviniścaya* 11.21), and so forth.

It might be thought: "There exists some single, gross, auxiliary factor that constitutes the very nature of the atom, and it is that which receives the designation [of 'gross']. To this, he says: because a single gross form is impossible among atoms—among what kind of atoms? Even among those that are accumulated, and not merely those existing separately like jars and so forth, because that would contradict their status as atoms—what is it that receives the designation of being perceived by direct perception?

Now, if it is thought: "The visible form, which possesses the qualities of action and so forth, is distinct from those [atoms] and is what receives that designation"; to this he says: "Since there is no such thing as a composite whole (*avayavin*) or anything else that is separate from and distinct from the atoms, what is it that receives the designation of 'perceptible'? This [issue of the] "other" has already been examined and is not examined here.
If it is argued: "Therefore, the cognition of the essential nature [of things] occurs by itself" (*Pravāṇī-vāda* 1.5); to this he says: "Of something," and so forth.

Since there is nothing else apart from the gross single form existing within atoms, what could possibly have self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? Nothing at all, because the property of self-awareness must reside in a substratum (*dharmin*); otherwise, even a donkey's horn would possess self-awareness and become an object of self-awareness.

If it is argued that blue and so forth are self-cognized exactly as they appear, because of such statements as "whatever appears in a certain way is ultimately real in that very way" and "that which appears is cognition," [the author] replies here: "In accordance with appearance," and so forth. Since reality cannot possibly exist in accordance with appearance, whose is this "self-cognition" that merely partakes of that designation? If it is argued that because such [self-cognition] is impossible due to its resistance to analysis, there would be a total void (sakalaśūnyatā), [the author] replies: "Lacking authoritative means of knowledge," and so forth.

In that very way, while establishing by himself what he considers to be the absolute truth (*ekāntatattva*), if he mocks his own conduct and behavior with his own words, he does not merely mock them but actually establishes the truth of non-absolutism (*anekāntatattva*); for without that [non-absolutism], even such things as the monism of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaita*) would be impossible. What is he doing when he mocks his own conduct with his words? To this he says: "In the case of absolutism," and so forth.

The meaning is that, having first relied upon the extreme view of momentariness and so forth, and then again, being skilled in investigation, relying [on that], and further, by seeing the extreme through investigation, he turns away existence—that is, actual presence—and thus refutes what has been accepted.
If it is argued: "In that case, he establishes the reliance on the view of the extreme as being without the non-extreme (anekānta)," to this he says: "bhāva" and so forth.
An entity is born with that very nature by which it is established in some way; knowledge appears in the form of that nature by which it is established.
A substance must exist in the form of "being" (sat) and so forth, by virtue of which it would differ at each moment of production.

The "mode" (*paryāya*) is that which bears designations such as "syllable" and so forth; because it consists of both being and non-being, even when there is a view of absolute difference, that [common nature] is not excluded.

Just as a single variegated cognition, being undifferentiated everywhere in its form as consciousness, maintains that nature by which it is distinguished with respect to each object, so too is the subject at hand.
Furthermore, this mental aspect (ākāra) is not accepted as ultimately real out of fear of the superimposition of contradictory properties;
for if it were of a manifold nature, there would be no contradiction with transformation (pariṇāma),
since the cognition of what is not real is invariably concomitant with the perception of reality in every respect.

Just as an entity such as a living being (*jīva*), which is established by its own nature—such as existence, consciousness, and so forth—and has always attained its self-nature, is born—that is, comes into being; this is an elliptical expression meaning that by that same nature it perishes and persists. Is this in every way and in its entirety? No; thus he says: "in some respect" (*kathaṃcit*).
This is what is meant: it is only *bhāva* (existence) itself that arises, perishes, and persists; there are no other modes (*paryāya*).
To provide an illustration of this, he says "knowledge," and so forth.

Knowledge is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is established as common to all through its nature as being, consciousness, and so on; or rather, knowledge is that which is accomplished. The connection is: just as that [knowledge] manifests or appears in some way, so does [existence].
To explain: according to the Sautrāntika view, that [cognition] does not appear as momentary destruction, for that would result in the futility of inference regarding it;

nor does it arise from its own cause, because the object would then have to appear with a non-conscious form just as it appears with the form of blue, which would entail the consequence of insentience;
nor does variegated cognition consist solely of the form of pure awareness, for if yellow and other forms were to manifest within the form of blue, its variegated nature would be lost.

The Sugata’s cognition perceives itself as being the material cause (*upādāna*) of its own preceding moment, but not as the material cause of a subsequent moment of that same kind; this is because of the occurrence of error or because of the instability of the causal relationship. Thus, according to the Yogācāra view, it does not perceive itself as being devoid of the form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*), for that would entail the consequence of there being no error at all; yet even in the case of absolute error, there is no delusion [of the self].

Therefore, in the reality that transcends all conceptual constructions, there is that state of transcendence; for when knowledge possesses a form-imparting capacity through the perception of gross objects and so forth, [it is not the ultimate reality].
Upon the attainment of manifestation, one sees by oneself alone.
While explaining the verse himself, he states that [the self] does not perceive its own state of being beyond all conceptual construction: "Of the substance," and so forth.

This means that which has as its beginning the existence of a substance—such as the *jīva*—in terms of its fourfold nature consisting of its own form (*svarūpa*) and so on, and which likewise begins with non-existence in terms of the fourfold nature consisting of other forms (*pararūpa*) and so on; that is what is thus described.

And that [substance] is of such a nature; therefore, it should be understood from the *Devāgama* that "otherwise there would be no establishment of that entity," by which nature the production at each moment might differ or become manifold;
for it is the substance itself—such as the syllable 'a' and so forth—that differs at each production.
As it has been said:
"The non-establishment of substance [is derived] from the *Āptamīmāṃsā* treatise."

If it is argued: "The reality of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahmatattva), which is without beginning or end and imperishable, undergoes transformation (vivartate) into the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds" (Vākyapadīya 1.1); to this he replies: "[That which] possesses designations such as 'syllable' (akṣara) and so forth."

What is it? He says: "Mode" (paryāya) means a transformation of a substance such as *pudgala*, not the fundamental substance itself. Why? He says: because it consists of both the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadātmakatvāt*). A mode that is currently perceived is existent; that which is contrary to it—the preceding and succeeding [modes]—is non-existent. Because that substance possesses these two natures, for that reason it is so. And syllables (*akṣara*) and the like are not of such a nature.
Alternatively, as for what was stated—that a substance must exist in the form of "being" (sat) and so forth—why is this so? To this he says: "Always," etc.

Surely, the past and the future are entirely distinct from the substance [in terms of] arising and so forth; how then could that [substance] differ with each arising? If it is argued that "one thing does not differ because another differs," he says in response: "Even in the view of absolute difference," and so forth.

The absolute distinction between substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) is "the extreme of difference" (*bhedaikānta*). Regarding its view or doctrine, the word "also" (*api*) is used for the purpose of emphasis (*bhāvanā*), because that view has already been refuted previously.
Why [is this said]? He says:

"That," meaning because the nature of the distinction of substance is not rejected at each moment of production; the connection is that by which [substance] would be differentiated at every production. This is because, as understood from the logical reason (*pratyaya*), the arising of distinct [modes] is impossible without a distinction in the nature of the substance.

Therefore, that which was stated—namely, "Sound has a substratum which is a pervasive substance, because, while being a substance, its specific quality is perceptible to us and others, like the self"—is refuted; for the absolute permanence of both the probandum and the example remains unproven, and the pervasiveness of the self has already been denied.
Furthermore, if sound were a quality of either space or something else that is pervasive and imperceptible, it would not be perceptible to us and others, as has already been stated.
This is not at all problematic.
If it is asked, "How can that which is one possess many forms?"—to this he says: "Just as," and so forth.

Consciousness is a single variegated perception; it maintains that nature which is undifferentiated throughout all external objects such as blue and the like, by virtue of which it would otherwise be differentiated for each respective object. Thus, just as in that case, so too is the matter at hand.
This was said with respect to the Sautrāntika; now, regarding the Yogācāra, he says "na ca" and so forth:
"And this coarse aspect (ākāra) of this cognition is not admitted by the Buddhist in an ultimate sense, for fear of the superimposition of contradictory properties upon a single [entity]."

He thinks as follows: "If this erroneous aspect of it [the cognition] were not distinct from its non-erroneous nature—since no distinction between objects is perceived—it would follow that it has both visible and invisible forms. Therefore, that which possesses aspects such as blue and so forth is accepted as a single, variegated entity. To this, he replies with the words beginning "that" (*tad*):

if the non-exclusive nature (*anekāntātmakatva*) of that cognition is admitted, then there is no contradiction with transformation (*pariṇāma*), as the connection is with the substance (*dravya*), and so forth.

If it is argued that the state of being manifold-natured (anekāntātmakatva) is merely an error, to this he says: "From where [does] difference [arise]? and so forth. He explains: "In every way," and so forth, because the cognition of what is not the reality is inseparable from the cognition of the reality itself.
Nevertheless, he states the refutation regarding its logical possibility: "Just as... and so forth;
this is easy to understand because [the reason] is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*).
Having thus explained the phoneme (*akṣara*), he speaks as follows, desiring to explain the word (*pada*): "The phoneme," and so forth.

They declare that a word consists of either one or many phonemes, and nothing else—neither that which is manifested by sound (*dhvani*) nor that which is eternal—because each [of those alternatives] is not observed [to function as a word]. || 5 ||
Even if it were merely indicative, the meaning would still be understood from it because it is a word;

nor can it be maintained that the expressive [word], manifested by sound, attains another nature while abandoning its own unmanifested nature, for that would entail the consequence of its being non-eternal, which contradicts the doctrine of absolute eternality.
Indeed, identity with the manifest is the defining characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

The ancient masters declare that a word (*pada*) consists of either a single phoneme (*varṇa*) without assistance or multiple phonemes; or else, that very word is a single [unit] that conveys meaning. What follows from this? To this he says: "Not," and so forth.

There is no other state than the state already mentioned; of what nature is it? To this he says: "manifested by resonance" (*dhvanivyaṅgya*), meaning that which is revealed by the vowels beginning with *a* and so forth.
Again, of what nature is it? To this he says: "eternal," and so on.

The postulation of that [eternality] is based on the fact that the cognition of objects such as jars would otherwise be inexplicable; however, since that [cognition] employs its power only at the moment of the word's utterance, it cannot be postulated on the basis of that [cognition]. This is the sense.
The postulation of eternality is [itself] the fact that the cognition of objects such as jars would otherwise be inexplicable.

Now, if even a single phoneme (*varṇa*) constitutes a word (*pada*), for what purpose was it stated [in the *Siddhiviniścaya*] that "the collection of those [phonemes] is the word" (Siddhivi. 11.1)? To this, he says: "The phoneme," etc.
Why? To this, he says: "Each individually," etc.

By the phrase "because of non-perception," he demonstrates this: when a listener who has mastered the convention hears the sound *a* and so forth, the cognition of Vāsudeva and others is observed. Does that [cognition] arise from the sound *a* and so forth, or from something else? In the first case, the fact that phonemes (*varṇa*) are expressive is established, and thus the *sphoṭa* is useless.

If it is argued that the *sphoṭa* is simply the sound *a* and so forth; no, for its nature as being composed of atoms has been demonstrated. Furthermore, the *sphoṭa* would have to be formless and eternal, which is contrary to the principle that "each [phoneme] is perceived separately. Therefore, in this context, [the theory of the *sphoṭa*] is meaningless.

Furthermore, according to the lexicon which establishes the convention that the letter *a* is Vāsudeva, is that [Vāsudeva] manifested by it, or is it otherwise the cause for the cognition of him? In the first case, from what does its manifestation arise? If you say "from the auditory organ and so forth," then in the case of the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) as well, since its manifestation would likewise arise from those very [organs], the phonemes *gha*, *ṭa*, and so on would be useless.

If it is argued that [the manifestation occurs] because of the letter *gh* and so forth; [we reply: in the case of the word *iḥ* (Kāmadeva), there is no manifestation because of the absence of a subsequent sound that serves as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Here, the air impelled by the palate and other articulators is the manifestor, whereas elsewhere it is not—what is the basis for this distinction? Alternatively, if it is argued that because a manifestor of the letter *gh* and so forth exists elsewhere, those [air-currents] are not the manifestors of those [letters]; is it that air does not exist there? It does exist, yet they are manifestors of the letters *gh* and so forth, while the letters *gh* and so forth are manifestors of the *sphoṭa*. If this is the case, the same applies elsewhere;
for one could indeed say: "The manifestation of the vowel *a* is from the air, and from that, the *sphoṭa*."

If it is argued that "non-perception in both cases is the cause [of cognition]," and therefore there would always be cognition of that [object] because there is no distinction [between the two states],
and thus the first position is not superior for the opponent,
while the second might be— [we reply: no, because cognition occurs only of the letter 'a' and so forth.
Nevertheless, if that [manifestation] were imagined to come from something else, then even smoke would not be produced by fire.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the letter *a* and so forth are purposeless because they are of no use in some instances, and thus their utility lies in the manifestation [of the word], we say: no; for that would entail the consequence that the meaning is manifested in the same way as those [letters]. Indeed, one does not apply the analysis of individual parts or the whole to a single letter *a*.

Regarding the word "ghaṭaḥ," do the individual [phonemes] manifest [the meaning], or do they manifest it when combined? Now, it is observed that the *visarjanīya* and so forth are not denotative when isolated; and thus is the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*): "A base (*prakṛti*) should not be used alone, nor should an affix (*pratyaya*) be used alone. Consequently, since only the aggregate constitutes a word (*pada*), how can it be said that "a word is an aggregate of phonemes" is merely a general rule (*prāyika*)?

Now, this [rule] might be stated with reference to the elision of case-endings (*vibhakti*) in vocatives and the like; but no, for even when there is elision, the status of being a word (*padatva*) remains functional.
This is comparable to the restriction found in both systems: "A suffix must be employed only after a stem (*prakṛti*), and a stem must be employed only before a suffix" (Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 3).
1 2 Not alone...— Laghuśabdenduśekhara 3

As Akalaṅka stated in the *Siddhiviniścaya*: "The claim that a word is a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) is merely conventional, because each individual phoneme, such as 'a' and so forth, is observed to be occasional."
—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 641.
It might be thought: [according to] the *Jainendra-vyākaraṇa* 1.2.50, [the suffix] *svādau*...
[applies].

106. By this [rule], if the preceding element were considered a *pada*, then a mere vowel such as ‘a’ would be a *pada*. That is not sound, because that which is expressive (*vācaka*) is a *pada*, and that which is expressive must possess an inflection (*savibhaktika*). However, the status of the preceding element as a *pada* is merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*), depending on specific requirements. To this, the following is replied: "A *pada* is that which ends in a nominal suffix (*su*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). (Jainendra Vyākaraṇa 1.2).

103. Regarding the phrase "a technical term" (*pāribhāṣikapada*): here, it is not merely a technical term that is understood by "word" (*pada*), but rather that by which a meaning is reached or understood is a "word. And a meaning is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) even from a word lacking case endings. Otherwise, since the status of being a meaningful unit would be unknown prior to the production of its cognition, the rule for designating a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would not apply, and thus it would be incorrect to say that [the word] is meaningless. This is stated in Pāṇini 1.2.45: *arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam*.
Therefore, since meaning is understood even from a single [word] taken alone, it is written here again that this is a technical term (*pāribhāṣikapada*).

If it is objected: "In that case, prepositions (*upasarga*) would not have the status of being words (*padatva*), for no new meaning is conveyed by them, since they merely indicate the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*)," to this he replies: "Even though they are indicators," and so forth.

Not only in its capacity as a denoter (*vācakatva*), but also in its capacity as an indicator (*dyotakatva*), meaning is understood from it because it is a word (*pada*); otherwise, its employment would be purposeless. By this, words that imitate other sounds are explained. If it is argued that a "word" (*pada*) is that by which a meaning is expressed, and therefore it must be the *sphoṭa* alone—since the meaning is understood through the manifestation of phonemes such as 'a' and so on—the author replies: "And it is not at all logical that [the *sphoṭa*] is the denoter," according to the established reasoning.

What [is the reason]? He says: because it has been stated that the cognition of meaning is seen to arise from the sounds themselves—the sounds such as *a* and so forth—which manifest through other sounds.
He states another refutation: "In the case of absolute eternality," and so on.
Why is that? He says: because it would follow that there is non-eternality if [the sound], abandoning its unmanifest and invisible nature, were to attain another nature that is visible.
From what does this follow? He says: "Because identity with the manifested [form] and its nature as the self are characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*).

If it is argued that its impermanence consists in the fact that nothing unreal is produced or removed by the sounds (*dhvani*s), he replies with the verse beginning "not... arising" (*na hy upajana*), and so forth.
The meaning is that arising and passing away constitute impermanence;
[but] for those things characterized by non-decline and non-arising, there is no modification, because there is no distinction.
(1.2) If such things are necessarily eternal and partless, why should one not likewise postulate the same state for a jar and other objects when they are manifested? For there is no distinction.
Objects [are derived] from sounds... and yet... it is not therefore an existent, immutable entity, because that would entail the impossibility of the movement of the cognition thereof;

for even if [the object] were momentary, the same defect of the non-movement of its cognition would follow, since there is no difference in the absence of that [cognition], as in the case of the immediately subsequent moment, and this would apply at other times as well.
True, this is so.

"Apāya" means destruction, and "upajana" means production or birth; that which has neither destruction nor production is so described. That whose modification (vikāra) is likewise [non-existent] is called "unchanging" (avikāra)—this is the meaning.

Since echoes have no effect upon it, how can they be its manifestors? Furthermore, if it were manifested by them simultaneously, then because it would be manifested in its entirety by a single [sound], the letters such as *ṭ* and so forth would be redundant, due to the fault of illuminating what has already been illuminated.
If it is argued that [this occurs] gradually; to this he replies: "without distinction," and so forth, which is clear.
In the word *ghaṭaḥ*, by means of the first letter *gh*.

Right here, he states another fault, beginning with "tādṛśām" (of such [entities]): if it is admitted that such things—which are absolutely unperceived prior to the operation of sound (*dhvani*) and are perceived when that operation occurs—are necessarily eternal, partless, and without components; and if it is also admitted that such things as the *sphoṭa* are manifested, then why would one not postulate the existence (*sattā*) of a jar or similar object in that same manner—as being eternal, partless, and something to be manifested? Why? He says: "Because there is no distinction," meaning because there is an absence of any excellence (*atiśaya*).

If it is argued that even a jar or similar object might be eternal and partless, being merely manifested by a wheel and other tools rather than being produced—thereby rendering lamps and such useless—the answer is no. This is because there is no contradiction in having two illuminators for a single object, as in the case of color, which is perceived through both the eye and light.

Furthermore, if it were claimed that a lamp and so forth always illuminate an object only when accompanied by a wheel or similar tools, this is not so; for we observe that at times the eye alone acts as an illuminator even in the absence of external light.

Now, if [it is argued that] the wheel and so forth are merely manifestors of the jar and other objects—just as a lamp is for things already existing—how could this be? For that which is incapable of producing any effect cannot be depended upon. If you say they are "producers" (*kāraka*), from what [evidence] is this known? If you say it is because the jar and such, being previously non-existent, obtain their self-nature (*ātmalābha*) from them, then from what is it known that they were previously non-existent? If you say it is because the perceptible is not seen, then is there any perception of the *sphoṭa* prior to the operation of the sounds (*dhvani*)? If there is, then the operation of those sounds would be futile.

If [it is argued]: "How can there be existence? Because of being perceived again; otherwise, it would be impossible, like the horn of a donkey"; [we reply: this is the same in the case of a jar and so forth.
If [the sound] were of that nature [i.e., composed of the letters], then it would not be seen even from the sounds themselves; thus, the assumption that they are manifesters is correct.
It is not that its being of that nature exists previously and ceases later; [this] is the same in the other case as well.
For one who moves at night and whose eyes lack light,
the operation of sound constitutes an invisible nature.

If this is argued— namely, that if sounds are the producers [of the word], what then would be their manifestor? Just as when oil and such are the producers, another manifestor such as a lamp must be sought— enough of this digression regarding the word.

It might be thought: "Since objects such as a jar are perceived as having parts (*sāvayava*), their state of being partless (*niṣkala*) may be postulated as a conceptual construction; likewise, the perception of the *sphoṭa* as having parts when it is manifested sequentially is merely an error that persists. This too is no answer, because the non-perception of a partless form would apply equally to both cases.

Then it is established: because there is no distinction [between the two cases], since a jar or the like is perceived immediately after a wheel or the like, let its manifestation proceed from that [the wheel]; but the *sphoṭa* does not [manifest] from the sounds (*dhvani*), because the reverse is true. Showing this, he says: "From the sounds, the object... (548 ka, kha; 549 ka, kha). These two folios remain unwritten. ...Without the extraction [of the universal], it would be the cause of cognition; that is not so, for the distinct and restricted "cowness" (*gotva*) is not established.
If it is argued that it would be like a "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*); [we reply: no, because in that case there is a relationship of assistance (*upakāra*).
Even if one were to conceive of it otherwise, it was well said: "And not... and so forth;
for there is the state of being manifest and the state of being partless.

Now, as for what has been said by someone—that whatever is being done or is yet to be done must indeed depend upon the assistance rendered by that [cause]—that is incorrect, because it is knowledge itself that is produced therein by that [cause]. This is what is being considered here: Is the universal capable of producing its own cognition, or not? If it is capable, then it would produce it even in the absence of the individual instance (*vyakti*); and the rest has already been considered here.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, that which is existent is not 'immutable' (kūṭastha);

how could it be? To this he replies: "Because of the consequence of the non-transmigration of its cognition. Regarding the term *tadbuddhiḥ*: it is the cognition of that [existent thing], i.e., the cognition of the immutable. *Saṃcaraṇam* means moving to another place or time; this movement is *saṃcāra*. *Asaṃcāraḥ* is the absence of such movement. [The phrase means] because of the consequence (*prasaṅgāt*) of that [absence of movement].

For instance: when its existence occurs in a single moment or at a single location, if its relation to subsequent moments were absolutely non-different from that [initial state], then it would be merely that much; consequently, the second and subsequent moments would be devoid of it, and thus no cognition of it could arise there for fear of being objectless.
Alternatively, if there is difference, then there is momentariness.

Or else, if by whatever nature it produces its own cognition in a certain place and so forth, it produces it by that very same nature elsewhere at another time, then all its effects would be produced simultaneously and in one place; thus, there would be no perception of temporal duration and the like.

[Objection: "In that case, even you, O Prajñākari, must accept momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*); and that [momentariness] cannot be established as distinct from the self, even for a single moment, without relying on perception. To this he says: "Indeed," and so forth.

This fault is common not only to the immutable (*kūṭastha*) [self], but also to momentariness. What is that fault? It is the "non-transference of its cognition"—that is, the non-transference of the cognition of that momentariness.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no difference in the absence of that [transference]."
Because there is no distinction between the non-existence of these two— immutable persistence and momentariness—

it is just as there is an absence of difference between the middle existence and the prior and posterior existences of the immutable; likewise, since the perception of partless, momentary atoms is non-different from the non-perception of persons and so forth,
their existence as both is merely a conceptual construction.

Alternatively, because there is no transition of cognition (*buddhi-saṃcāra*) in either the position of momentariness or its opposite, just as in the case of an immutable and capable [entity], all cognitions arise in a single moment, so too in the case of the momentary, since the cognition exists at that very time, there is no transition through a continuum (*santāna*).
If it is argued that "its effect occurs in the second moment," to this he says: "Like the immediately preceding moment," and so forth.

If it is argued that "the second moment following the causal moment is the immediate moment; just as there [is dependence], so too at other times—that is, at another time—there would be the same consequence because the effect lacks dependence on anything else, and thus the consequence applies elsewhere as well, since we observe waking upon the occurrence of sleep," [we reply]: No; for it has been stated that this would lead to the cessation of conventional usage regarding that [momentary destruction] and so forth, due to the consequence that no certainty regarding it could arise immediately after it, just as in the case of momentary destruction.
To this, he gives the answer: "True," and so on.

As for what was said— that even in the case of momentariness, there is no movement of cognition, just as in the case of the immutable (kūṭastha)— this is true in the manner described; the sense is that this follows from the acceptance of a reality consisting of both natures, because in the second and subsequent moments of the immutable [there is no movement].

If it is argued that even in that case, both faults would follow—since a collection of thieves is not considered non-thieves—the author replies: "If there were identity between cause and effect," and so forth;
"If there were identity between cause and effect, [the result] would be like the principles of the Great, the Gross, and the Subtle."
The faults such as absolute identity or difference do not apply here, as in the case of the cognition of the object and the subject.

Even if there is partial permanence, because of the [partial] identity between the prior and posterior states—just as in the case of atoms, which, despite being permanent or momentary, do not lose their spherical nature (*pārimaṇḍalya*), there is no consequence of their non-perception even when they possess grossness due to their gross form, just like their spherical nature;

or just as in the case of cognition, where the forms of blue and so on do not result in a lack of distinction because of their partial identity with the cognition itself—so it would be for everything, since cause and effect are perceived precisely through their identity.

It might be argued that if there were some kind of identity between cause and effect—that is, between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*)—then neither of the two aforementioned extreme faults would apply; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), contradictions and other such flaws are included.
He provides an example well-known to the Vaiśeṣikas: "like the reality of the great, the gross, and the subtle.

That very same reality is both gross with respect to its composite whole (*avayavin*) and subtle with respect to its parts (*avayava*); it is both great and gross-subtle, and the phrase "like that" refers to being just so.
Just as that fault does not apply when there is a certain degree of identity between a part and the whole, so too has this been considered elsewhere;
he states an example well-known among Buddhists, beginning with the words "the object of cognition" (*vedya*).
He states the example and provides the commentary on the verse: with the words "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*) and so forth,
he explains the two illustrations by means of the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth.

Whether in the case of permanence (*nityatva*) or in the case of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*), atoms possess spherical dimension (*pārimaṇḍalya*), which is a partless roundness that they do not abandon even when [forming a composite]. If that were abandoned, the whole (*avayavin*) would be without parts and would consequently be subject to defects such as total obscuration. Even if there were grossness—that is, the nature of a gross transformation—how could there be the consequence of non-perception? [It would not be so] because of its gross form as well.
By what means? He says: "Just as by sphericity, so too [is it] with those"—meaning that just as with a gross form, there is no perception of sphericity in them.

He states another illustration: "And just as for cognition—that is, for a variegated awareness—the form which is blue and so forth does not entail the consequence of being indistinguishable; of what [does this apply]? He says: "Like the act of perception (saṃvedana)," meaning just as in the case of the act of perception itself.

This is what is meant: just as the self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) of cognition with respect to its own form, such as blue and so forth, is undifferentiated, yet blue and so forth are not [the awareness itself]— lest it follow that there would be no diversity [of objects]— or just as consciousness is not insentient like blue,

or just as the intention (*tātparya*) is not identical to the consciousness because, although it is the same as the blue in its having the form of blue, it is not the same in its being insentient (*jaḍatā*).
Why? To this he says: "Because of some kind of identity" (*kathaṃcittādātmyāt*).
That is to say, because consciousness (*saṃvitti*) has, in some sense, the nature of a stake (*kīla*) through its identity with [the object] in some way;
thus, [the term] "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) appears as if written twice.
[Objection: The word *vā* is used in the sense of *iva*.

If there is indeed some kind of non-difference (*abheda*) in the object taken as an example because it is perceived in such a way, what does that have to do with the prior and subsequent [moments], such that it is said, "even though there is some kind of permanence"? [Response: To this he says: It may be so in some way, because everything is perceived precisely through that identity (*tādātmya*) between cause and effect.

In that case, whether it be the external reality (*bāhyatattva*) or the internal reality (*antastattva*), it shines forth in the non-conceptual state (*avikalpa*) as being partless and momentary (*niraṃśakṣaṇikatayā*).

If it is argued that a false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*) is merely a distorted appearance (*viparītapratibhāsa*), the author replies here: "The reality of permanence and momentariness," and so forth—

referring to the two one-sided conceptualizations (*ekāntavikalpa*) which falsely [assert] the reality of permanence and momentariness as being either exclusively permanent or exclusively momentary, respectively.
There would be no establishment of non-conceptuality, nor would there be the apprehension of the [object's] specific application (niyoga) for these two.

Just as [it was said]: "Because another means of valid cognition operates upon what is already perceived," and because that which is not superimposed is not [a conceptualization], since the nature of determination consists precisely in the exclusion of superimposition; this has essentially been stated before.

Because self-awareness is established by itself through its own determination (*vyavasāya*), otherwise there would be an infinite regress and thus no cognition at all; [this applies] to the case of "from another" (*parataḥ*). Therefore, since the grasping of what is desired and the abandoning of what is undesired cannot logically occur in reality, how could a discerning person ever act?

Regarding the application to some object to be determined—whether that which is enjoined (*niyogin*) be permanent or momentary—there is no such injunction for it; thus it is "without injunction" (*aniyoga*). And that is also a "grasping," meaning a grasping without an object. Of what two things? He says: "of these two"—namely, the principles of permanence and momentariness (*nityakṣaṇikatattvārthayoḥ*); "might be" (*syāt*) means it would occur.
Of which two? He says: "eternal," and so forth.
Regarding the two principles of eternal and momentary existence, these are both false, one-sided conceptual constructions (*mithyaikāntavikalpa*).

If it is argued that "when those two exist, [the agent] exists in the non-conceptual state, and thus there is the apprehension of the injunction (*niyoga*) regarding these two," he replies here: "The non-establishment of the non-conceptual. This means that the non-conceptual is not established by means of the non-conceptual; such is the explanation regarding these two.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "Just as... and so forth, up to "...will be eternal," etc., has been written again;
this is another explanation: the apprehension of the non-connection between the two exclusive conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the reality of permanence and momentariness.

Why? He says: "Because there would be a lack of establishment for these two through non-conceptualization. This has been stated previously here [in the *Siddhitrayī*] in such passages as, "For one who has accepted self-awareness" (Siddhitrayī 1.18), and so forth;
the commentary on this point also states, "otherwise, there would be an infinite regress," and so on.

Likewise, this is another point: there is no fixed rule regarding the apprehension of those two conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), namely, the acceptance of the momentary conceptualization as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) while the other is not. "Non-apprehension" refers to that absence of such a rule or restriction—meaning that both may either be apprehended or not apprehended. If it is argued: "Because the momentary conceptualization is connected to the real entity (*vastu*), and because it is understood through non-conceptual [cognition], it is only that which is apprehended," to this he says: "Because of the establishment of non-conceptuality, reality is not established by non-conceptual [cognition]. If it is further argued that this is indeed the case, he says: "Non-conceptual," and so forth.
Explaining the meaning of the verse by means of its connection, he says: "Just as," and so forth.

He asks why this is so and says: because when [a property] such as momentariness is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in each individual object, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), namely inference (*anumāna*), operates; otherwise, it would not operate.
It might be thought: "In a case where there is no superimposition (*samāropa*), there is establishment even without certainty. To this he says: "not superimposed," etc.
Here he states the reply: "no," etc.
Why is that which was stated by another not [correct]? To this he says: "Superimposition," and so forth.

It has already been largely explained in the first section that the very nature of determinate cognition (*vyavasāyātmaka*) consists in the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of superimposition within that cognition.

By this, the state of practice (*abhyāsadaśā*) is also considered, for even in that state there is only the cognition of that which possesses parts; regarding this, he says: "From self-awareness," and so forth.

Since the self-cognition of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāya*) is established by itself—that is, by its own nature—and since otherwise, in the manner of lacking self-determination, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) leading to non-comprehension because the very ascertainment of the nature of the judgment would require ascertainment by another, he provides an illustration here with the words: "From another," and so forth.
Summing up, he says: "Therefore," and so forth;
this is easy to understand. What follows from that? He says: "In reality," and so forth.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), that [activity] is not desired in those two—namely, grasping and abandoning—because, by necessity, they are themselves untenable. Why would a discerning person proceed on account of the conceptualization of permanence or from anything else? This is [the case] if there is an understanding of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
Then [the opponent] asserts: "The word-sound (akṣara) is eternal and expressive of meaning.
The Mīmāṃsaka might argue that even if it were eternal, it could still be all-pervasive due to its momentary conceptual nature; to this, he replies: "Even though it is eternal," and so forth.
Even if sounds were eternal, there would be simultaneous perception of all of them, because they are pervasive, eternally present, and capable of being grasped by the same sense organ;
for there would be no restriction regarding their occurrence in a specific location, as they would simply appropriate for themselves the assistance provided by that [location].

For that which is immutable (*kūṭastha*), existence in that specific location is impossible by necessity; even if it were all-pervading (*sarvagata*), the intended perception of a single sound would not occur,
for this is not logical for things occupying the same space and being objects of the same sense organ.
If there were a restriction to each individual manifester, the hearing of a cacophony (kalakala) would be impossible;

for how could there be manifestation without the avoidance of attaining a nature that is either manifest or unmanifest? And without the abandonment and adoption of those [respective natures], how could there be concealment? This is comparable to the consequence that all sounds would be perceived simultaneously.

First, the auditory organ does not have as its object those things that are grasped by the same sense organ, occupy the same location, and possess common properties, such that they would be conditioned by a specific conditioner; this is because it is a sense organ, like the visual organ.

Alternatively, sounds do not have as their object that which is conditioned by a specific conditioner, because—while possessing common properties and being grasped by the same sense organ—they are simultaneously connected with the sense organ, like a jar or similar objects.
(Nyāyasāra, p. 30)
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 648;
Nyāyavārttika, p. 288:

Because it is impossible for there to be a rule of manifestation for such [sounds] produced by the same articulatory organs, there would result a confused auditory perception of all [sounds] everywhere and at all times.
—Aṣṭaśa° Aṣṭasa° pṛ 105;
Nyāyakumu° pṛ 708; Prameyaka° pṛ 423.
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 36;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 683; Prameyaratnamālā, 3.

*Śāstravārttāsamuccaya-Ṭīkā*, p. 378: Even if sounds—that is, syllables—were eternal and immutable, not only would their occasional hearing be impossible; rather, since they would have the inherent nature of being heard, their hearing would have to occur at all times. This is the meaning.

Now, when there is cognition, then there is hearing; at other times, the opposite occurs. [If it were otherwise], how could cognition ever arise from them? It might be argued that the dependence on something permanent has already been refuted—namely, that there is no hearing when an obscuration exists, and there is hearing when it is absent. This is plausible: for one whose capacity to produce those [cognitions] is removed by an obscuration, whereas that which is capable produces its own effect even when obstructed, as the eye, though obscured by cataracts, produces the perception of form.
Therefore, not only is occasional hearing impossible, but even the restriction to hearing a single intended sound is impossible; the meaning is that there would be hearing by everyone simultaneously.

Now, if it is argued that even though all [sounds] are present everywhere and at all times, one hears that which has the manifestor (vyañjaka) in its vicinity; to this he replies with "samākṣa" and so forth: this restriction regarding its manifestation—that the manifestation or illumination of the desired *a*-sound or another occurs from the sound produced by the palate and other organs, and not of any other—is not [possible].
Why? He says: because words are perceivable by all the senses (*samākṣagrahayogyatvāt*), being graspable by a single sense-organ (*ekendriyagrāhyatvāt*);
[this is] like the eye of a nocturnal creature.

If it is argued that even jars and other objects, which are distinct in terms of location and so forth, are not manifested by a single lamp despite being equally capable of being grasped by a single sense organ; to this he replies: because those [phonemes] are all-pervading, they exist in a state of co-location—that is, they reside in the same place. Therefore, since there is no such restriction, there would be the simultaneous hearing of all phonemes.

Indeed, no restriction regarding manifestation is observed among things that occupy the same location and are equally capable of being grasped by the same sense organ, such that one could postulate it to be the case elsewhere as well.

Now, it may be argued that a property observed in a jar or similar object cannot be applied elsewhere; otherwise, a property perceived in a man on the street would have to be applied to the very man one intends [as an example]. If you say that there is indeed a distinction among men, then let there likewise be a distinction among manifestors, characterized by their lack of omniscience.

It might be thought: "That [the soul] is postulated because the instruction regarding the pointing out of things, the absence of signs, non-deviation, and the pointing out of lost or grasped objects would otherwise be inexplicable. If that is so, then let it be postulated that there are specific veils for pervasive [senses] capable of being grasped by the senses, because their occasional non-perception would otherwise be inexplicable; or else, let it be postulated that there are specific manifestors, because the perception of such [objects] would otherwise be inexplicable—since there is no distinction [between these cases]. [Reply: No, because the specific veil is denied, and because its essential nature is not undermined.

Now, if it is argued that the capacity of the sense organ to grasp that [object] is obstructed by it, that too is not a sound hypothesis; for when the object is present and capable of producing a perception, perception must necessarily occur. If it is argued that this is not so because the auxiliary factors have their scope obstructed, we say no; for a permanent entity cannot depend on such auxiliaries. Furthermore, the claim that the capacity of the self is obstructed by it is also false, because the self is eternal.

If it is argued that an obstruction to the production of the effect is created [by the veil], we say no; for when a cause is capable, the effect must necessarily arise. Otherwise, the absurdity would follow that the cause produces the effect and simultaneously obstructs it—such a state of affairs regarding entities is impossible.
Therefore, the veil is merely an interposer for all-pervading things.
If you ask, "How can that even be? let this be another fault of his position; we are merely proponents of our own accepted tenets.

And that [obstructing medium], though singular, is common to all things occupying the same location, perceivable by the same sense organ, and situated equally; thus, when it is removed by someone, there is the simultaneous perception of all of them. Just as in the case of jars, so too is the postulation of a "superior person" (puruṣātiśaya) made—this is the comparison—because otherwise it would be impossible to account for the provision of non-erroneous instructions regarding the unseen, the unperceived, and the concomitance or non-concomitance of signs, as well as the teaching of hidden treasures, handfuls of grain, thoughts, gain and loss, pleasure and pain, eclipses of planets, and so forth.
—Bṛhatsarvajña°, p. 130:
the specific capacity for the apprehension of sound.
Capability [is defined] by way of obstruction; both the mat and the cloth serve as obstructions for those two.

Even those who maintain that [the soul] is perceived by the same sense organ located in the same place—namely, that the self is joined with the mind, and that mind is joined with the auditory faculty which is like space, and that this [faculty] is then joined with the object, the sound, such that here there is a relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between the sense organ and the object—they too have their arguments refuted by this [same reasoning]. For them as well, there would be the simultaneous hearing of all sounds, because the ear is entirely pervasive and all sounds inhere therein; thus, the relation of "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) would exist, and since the connection with the mind is no different for one who intends to speak than for another, [all sounds would be heard at once].

If it is argued that a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) acts as the regulator, it has already been stated in this very work on the proof of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) that such a force exceeds the scope of valid cognition (*māna*).
Furthermore, inherence (*samavāya*) likewise cannot be the cause of apprehension;

for by the power of the unseen force, there is no contradiction in the auditory faculty—the ear-cavity—apprehending that which inheres in space, just as the eye apprehends color that inheres in a jar.
Furthermore, the claim that sound is a quality of space has been refuted;

however, that is not correct— the Naiyāyikas maintain that sound is perceived by a sense organ possessing a specific quality of its own kind, because it is perceptible by a single external sense organ, just like color and other such qualities.

The point is that since the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions regarding the mind and sound— which stand in the relation of substance and attribute— could also be explained solely by a specific unseen force (adṛṣṭa), the postulation of a mind (manas) would be redundant.

Inference by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—the weighing [of evidence]: whatever sense organ perceives a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that is perceptible by a single external sense organ must possess that quality as its own. For example, the eye, which perceives color, has color as its substratum; and the ear likewise perceives sound of such a nature, therefore it too has sound as its quality.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 63.

It might be thought: "Because space (*nabhas*) is manifold, this fault does not arise. For instance, the space enclosed by the cavity of Devadatta’s ear is different from that of another; therefore, what inheres in one is not perceived by the other. To this, it is considered: what is its cause? If you say "that very space," then it must be stated whether it is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Nor can there be the status of a quality for another without that [inherent cause]. If you say "the conjunction of the drum and the stick," no; because that is absent there. Or rather, the inherent cause of sound is that which inheres in its own cause.
And once that conjunction has ceased, there would be no further hearing of it because sound is momentary; therefore, the production of sound does not arise from sound. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.34)
31. Thus [the position] is refuted.

Now, if it is argued that the preceding sound is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) and that, being inherent in another space, it is the cause of that [subsequent sound], otherwise the color and other qualities of the potsherds would be the causes of the color and other qualities of the cloth, because of the absence of sound [in the latter case].
From the conjunction of the drum and the stick, from disjunction, and from sound, there is the production of sound
— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra.

If, however, this view is held— that the intermediate space is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) [of the sound], and that it is produced by the preceding sound and spaces, then its inherence in its own causes and its status as a non-inherent cause are not contradictory.

If those [subsequent sounds] were its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), then subsequent sounds would arise only as they ascend into the space already occupied by the first sound; thus, there would be no increase in the extent of space. For when an effect arises while its cause remains present, it is like the non-increase of a continuum (*santāna*). If, on the other hand, they are distinct [from the first], the same fault persists. Consequently, the eternal and all-pervasive nature of space, as asserted by the Vaiśeṣika, would be destroyed.

Now, sound is perceived as being in close proximity to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because it is a specific quality of an all-pervading substance (*vibhudravya*), like pleasure and so forth. Here too, if space were manifold, the same fault [of simultaneous perception] would apply as before; if it were one, then since there is no contact between the partless ether and the mind, the proximity of all sounds to that [mind] would be equal. Thus it is established: there would be the hearing of all [sounds] at once, due to the loss of both the eternity and the omnipresence of space.
The meaning is "refutation.
Explaining the verse, he says: "produced by that" (tatkṛtam), and so forth.

This is the intended sense: does the manifestor produce some excellence (*atiśaya*) in that which is considered the manifested, or not? In the first case, for one who takes as its own that excellence characterized as "perceptibility"—an excellence produced by the manifestor (*vyañjakakṛta*)—there would be no restriction to existing in that same location [as the manifestor], because it would be dependent upon its own nature; [consequently, there would be] the necessity of it existing in the location of the manifestor.

Sound is a category whose nature is to be grasped by the auditory faculty; it exists only where it is heard, and it is heard in the very location of its manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Indeed, a jar seen in one place does not exist elsewhere, for that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being omnipresent (*sarvagata*); this is the intended meaning. To the question "What follows from that restriction? he says: "If there is a restriction for that which is considered eternal and immutable, then [its] existence is only in that specific location. To the question "What follows from that? he says: "Omnipresence is not possible"—this is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied.
By this [statement], the view that sound is pervasive because of its resonance (dhvani) is refuted.
Demonstrating the refutation while accepting [the opponent's position] that [sound] is omnipresent, he says: "Even if there were omnipresence," and so forth.
The word "even" (*api*) is used in the sense of possibility;

the meaning is that even if sounds were omnipresent, one would not hear only the specific sound intended to be expressed, but rather all [sounds] would be heard, because they would all be equally fit for auditory perception.
[Objection: "Is it not the case that restricted audition is produced by a restricted manifestor? To this, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.

For it is not the case that this restriction of manifestors applies to things occupying the same location and being objects of the same sense-organ; nor is it established by any means of valid cognition, because such a thing is never observed, since the presence of an obstructer and its removal are common to all cases. Having accepted the restriction of manifestors, he refutes it with the words: "Each individually," and so forth.

If a restriction regarding the manifestors were accepted for each individual phoneme—such that the manifestor of the sound *a* is not the manifestor of any other—then the perception of a confused din (*kalakala-śruti*) would be impossible; therefore, this [position] is untenable. For indeed, it has been stated that such a restriction is not possible in the case of a manifestor that effects the removal of an obscuration.

Nor is it possible for there to be an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the manifested [phoneme], but rather its impermanence; and it has been stated that [the idea of] producing an excellence in the auditory organ is of no consequence.
Only its manifestor (*vyañjaka*), which generates the cognition of it, remains; and its manifestation (*vyakti*) is also nothing but cognition.

In that case, when a single cognition is produced by someone through some [means], one might argue: "At that time, even though it exists, others should not perceive it, because that single [cognition] is produced in conjunction with the intended manifestors. This is not correct, because it would entail the consequence of there being no restriction regarding manifestors, since the cognitions of one thing could be generated by the manifestors of another.
It is not logical for that [sound] to be produced by a ninth part, because it would entail an absolute loss [of its nature];
likewise, it would follow that phonemes (varṇas) also possess parts, since they are perceived as such;
therefore, there is no hearing of a confused noise (kalakala).

If it is argued that there is only one phoneme [and the appearance of] "kalakala" is an illusion, we say no; for there is a perception of differences among the phonemes, which are objects within the range of the same sense faculty, and there is no obscuration [of their distinctions].
[The opponent argues: "Cognition is that which is manifested by a determinate manifestor;
even though nothing at all is produced in it by the manifestor, it nevertheless becomes manifest through it. To this, he replies: "In the case of 'manifested,' etc."

In the state of the manifestation's operation, there is the manifested [nature], and prior to that operation, the unmanifested nature; since these two natures involve respectively attainment and avoidance, how could there be manifestation without them? Now, refuting the concealment of the manifested, he says "that," etc.
Without the abandonment and the acquisition of those two natures—the manifested and the unmanifested—respectively, how could there be concealment? This has already been largely explained.
If it is argued that there is no omnipresence [of the soul], he says here: "And even if [it exists]," etc.
What [is the reason]? He says: "The manifestor," and so forth;
and when the activity of the manifestor is present, there would not be a restricted cognition of the manifested object.
Therefore, there is no rule of necessity regarding the manifestation [of a word] from the utterance of the audible sound (*śruti*).

Even though words are non-pervasive (*avyāpin*), their manifestation would not be inevitable despite the operation of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), unlike the case with the universal (*jāti*) and its relation [to an individual].
For it is not logical that a relation with a universal could exist prior to the birth of the individual in the place where that individual is produced, since the universal is not yet present there.
If there were activity on the part of the manifestor—such as the palate and so forth—or on the part of the air produced by it, there would not be a restricted perception of the manifested sound;
for when a lamp is active, the perception of a jar does not necessarily follow.

What follows from this? He says: there is no rule of necessary concomitance regarding the hearing of the word [sound] resulting from its utterance, that is, from the activity of the palate and other organs.

Explaining the verse, [the author] says: "Even if it is admitted that words are non-pervasive (avyāpin), manifestation would not necessarily occur even when the operation of the manifestor is present.
He provides an illustration: "like the connection with a universal (jāti)."

The relationship of the universal (*jāti*) with the individual (*vyakti*) belongs to that very [universal] itself; this was stated with reference to the universal residing in the individual. He supports this very point with the words beginning "for not," and so forth.
For [the universal] does not exist prior to the production of the individual;

where, then, would it be? To this he says: "The connection with the place of the individual's birth is logical. Showing that this objection raised by the Mīmāṃsaka against the Buddhist also applies to the latter, he says: "sanniveśa... and so forth.
When there is a connection with a single sense organ due to proximity, there is at one time a complete hearing;
this is not intended to refer to cognitions that are external, internal, partless, or momentary.
Because of the abundance of delusion regarding momentary atoms, when their contrary nature is perceived, there is no perception of reality.

Likewise, having accepted that "the object of knowledge is the same within the internal reality," how could the Buddhist refute the Mīmāṃsaka who asserts that, because a cognizer is incapable of perceiving everything simultaneously according to its proximity, there is somehow the hearing (cognition) of some [object]? This is because the rule of non-discrepancy between the object and the subject entails the necessity of non-absolutism (anekānta), as such a rule would otherwise be impossible; for if there were no discrepancy with one's own intended object, the definition [of valid cognition]—namely, being the cause of a cognition possessing its own form—would not constitute a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For even indirectly, particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are certainly not causes [of cognition] given their momentariness; therefore, in every respect, it is impossible for an object to have the characteristic of non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāda*), and for that very reason, it is impossible for cognition—which possesses that form—to have that as its object, since the Buddhists do not admit such a thing and because it contradicts the appearance [of the object]. How, then, could there be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)? [This applies to] the cognition of the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*).
Cognition...
"At one time," that is, at a single moment, "audition"—meaning hearing—"is possible"; this is the supplementary explanation.

How so? He says: "in its entirety," meaning in its complete form; the sense is that this applies even to [theories such as] momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*), just as it does to [theories such as] eternal existence (*sadātva*). Of what? The term "of sounds" (*śabdānām*) follows from the context.

Why is this so? He says: "Because of proximity, just as [properties] such as being a word [are perceived]. From what kind of proximity? He says: "When there is a connection with a single sense organ (*ekākṣa-sambandhe*). That is, when there is a connection with one sense organ—by whichever sense organ [existence] (*sat*) and so forth are perceived, by that same [organ], momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) and so forth would also be perceived. This is how he thinks: if there were a rule that things occupying the same location and perceivable by the same sense organ are necessarily heard simultaneously, then existence (*sat*), momentary destruction, and so forth would be heard simultaneously, because they share the same substratum and are perceivable by the same sense organ. And thus, the implication is that another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be useless, just like another manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

If it is argued that there is indeed scriptural authority for this in its entirety—based on such statements as *ekasyārthasvabhāvasya* (Pravāhaṇa-vākya, 3.52)—to this he replies: "No," and so forth. The meaning is that not only is there no cognition of a partless, momentary [entity] intended internally, but even externally there is no cognition of a partless, momentary [entity] intended [by scripture]; this has already been discussed.
When [an object] is itself directly perceived, what other part could there be that is not seen and must be examined by means of [other] instruments of knowledge? — *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.419.
In order to explain the verse, he says: "In momentary atoms," and so forth.

[The question is: "When what is present is there no perception of reality—that is, of the partless, momentary nature—within momentary atoms? To this he replies: "In that which is its opposite," and so forth.
When there is the perception of a nature that is the opposite of momentary atoms, from what [does this arise]? It arises from the excess of delusion—that is, from the power of ignorance.
By this, it is explained that [the opponent] intends external, partless, and momentary cognitions.

Likewise, when the internal reality (*antastattva*) is [perceived] as equal, there is no apprehension of that reality; in what respect is this similar? He says: "the object of knowledge" (*vedya*), and so forth.
By this, it is explained that the internal consciousness—which is partless and momentary—is not intended.

Having thus accepted and admitted this, how could the follower of the Sugata (the Buddhist) refute or reject [the opponent]? Against whom? To this he says: "of the cognizer," and so forth. Since it is impossible for a cognizing person to perceive the entire mass of sounds according to their presence—that is, without overstepping their actual presence—how could one possibly hear any particular letter, such as 'a', or any other phonetic entity, in some restricted manner of place and so on? It is against the Mīmāṃsaka who speaks in this way that [the Buddhist] would object.

Just as, even when there is the perception of the mere blueness of external atoms or of internal cognition such as existence and consciousness, there is no perception of [properties] like momentary destruction despite their being present, so too, upon the perception of the letter *a*, there is no hearing or apprehension of other [letters] present [in the same word], because of such incapacity—this is the sense. [Objection: "But surely, neither internally nor externally does reality exist in the form of partless, momentary atoms, by which this fault would arise; rather, it exists according to the rule of non-contradiction. To this, he says: "The object," and so forth.

The object is the jar and so forth, and the subject is cognition; one should understand that "because of the drawing forth of non-contradiction" means because of the drawing forth of that [non-contradiction] which is the rule of non-contradiction between the two.
Why? He says: because that rule cannot be established otherwise—that is, in the absence of such a drawing forth.

Now, as for what was said—"there is no cognition of partless, momentary external objects"—and "because of the drawing forth of non-contradiction from the rule," that is not correct; for there is no cognition of a partless, momentary form apart from atoms.

If it is argued that "that restriction also applies only there," [the author] replies here with the words "due to impossibility" (*asaṃbhavāt*) and so forth: the object desired by our own Buddhist [opponent] is characterized as momentary and partless atoms (*kṣaṇika-niraṃśa-paramāṇu*); when an agreement is being made regarding the non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) of that [object], the definition [of perception] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of the statement: "Its similarity (*sārūpya*) is its means of valid cognition" (*Nyāyabindu* 1.20).
What is it? He says: "The state of being a cause for a cognition having its own form. That is, the state (*tattā*) of a cognition whose cause possesses a form like that of its own object.
Here he states three reasons, beginning with "because of impossibility" (*asaṃbhavāt*), and first demonstrates them with the words "for not," and so forth.
