By this, he has denied that specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [The opponent might argue: "In that case, some effect arising from the specific characteristics serves as a mark (*liṅga*); from that, a cognition bearing their form arises. Thus, indirectly, those specific characteristics are the causes of the cognition having their own form. To this, he says: "Even indirectly, as described, they are not causes at all—not to mention directly.
Why? He says: "Because of momentariness," and so forth.
This has been analyzed repeatedly by him:

therefore, according to this logic, it is in no way possible for there to be a non-erroneous, momentary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is non-discrepant with an object that is a thing imagined by others, whether by way of perception or inference.

If it is argued that while external particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) may lack the characteristic of non-contradiction because they are denied by the Buddhists, this [non-contradiction] might still apply to cognition, the author replies with the words "from that" and so forth.

From that very same direct perception of a gross, unitary continuum—not only of external particular characteristics, but also of cognition—[the latter] being of what nature? It is of the form of that [object], i.e., of the form of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). The syntactical construction of the words is: "in no way is its characteristic possible."

If it is argued that cognition must have as its object only a gross, unitary, and persistent entity—based on such statements as "whatever appears in a certain way, that very thing is introduced into conventional usage as ultimately real"—to this he replies with the words "that" (*tad*) and so forth.

By the word "that," a gross, unitary, and persistent [entity] is referred to; the state of being that (the fact of having that) as its object belongs to a cognition. Since the Buddhists do not accept such a state—due to their fear of the refutation [of their own system] by means of momentary destruction and other arguments—he states another reason: "and because of the contradiction with its appearance."

The appearance of that [object] as a single coarse entity is the cognition’s taking on its form; this is mentioned as an illustration because it is contradictory [to the object], and it also implies the lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the reasons.
The connection is that [the author] refuted in the *Nyāyabindu* that "conformity with the object" (*arthasārūpya*) is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because of the negation of external objects.

In order to explain the second reason, the opponent challenges [the author] regarding the self, asking: "How is there non-pervasion? He provides the answer: "Of the cognition of the material cause and its effect," and so forth—all of which has already been explained.
To explain the non-pervasion, he asks the question: "How is there non-pervasion? Therein, the answer begins with "In consciousness," and so forth, being exactly like that [previous explanation].

Or let the meaning be as follows: even if the apprehension of an entity occurs through a momentary [nature] just as it does for one who asserts permanence, nevertheless, the Mīmāṃsaka remains difficult to defeat for the Buddhist; showing this, he says:
"Of the distinct," and so forth—[the cognition] would determine the distinction of that [entity] from everything else.

Just as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is [restricted] in every respect, so too would there be a restriction of words upon hearing them. (11) If the perception of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct from its own nature, were to produce a direct determination (*vyavasāya*) in some cases—even though there is no difference in the proximity of the specific qualities of that nature—then how could the cognition of words, by negating either itself or another as undivided, be said to grasp all objects present through restriction? Indeed, it has been stated that conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) does not have the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as its object...
[therefore], the excluded [object] of the distinct and the excluded [cognition] are not [identical] for those two... therefore.

From what [is it excluded]? From everything—that is, from all forms, whether homogeneous or heterogeneous. What is that which is related to perception? It is that which determines and ascertains. What does it determine? Difference, or exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Does it not determine that [exclusion] from everything, including the heterogeneous? No; it would not determine it from its own preceding and succeeding moments, because that would result in the futility of the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Just as it is understood from hearing the words "as this, so that," such a restriction would apply. Since this is heard from speech, this ground is merely empty.
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "Intrinsic nature," and so forth;
he provides a qualification for that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) by saying: "Intrinsic nature," and so forth.
What is its [function]? He says: "Perception.

How does it act, and what does it do? He says: "Producing a direct, unmediated determination or ascertainment. In what circumstance, even when something else exists, does this occur? He says: "Having that as its own nature," and so forth. This is because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of [the cognition] being excluded from everything.

That [perception] possesses a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) which produces a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) regarding what has been experienced by itself; otherwise, no determinate cognition would arise with respect to blue and so forth, because that which is incapable cannot be a producer. Alternatively, its distinction [from other things] consists in its being distinct from those that do not produce such a cognition. Such is the perception described.

Even though there is no difference in the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of that [perception], he states the rebuttal beginning with "of words" (*girām*), etc., because the absence of proficiency in perception and so forth is common to both cases.

Now, [the opponent argues that] unlike [the perception of] blue and so forth, there is no such specific feature in the case of momentary destruction and the like that produces a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*); to this, he replies with the words "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*) and so on:

the intellect (*buddhi*), while dividing its own undivided, non-dual self, makes it appear as having parts by way of possessing forms both capable and incapable of producing a determinate cognition regarding its own object.

If it is argued that there is no fault here because the very capacity to produce [a cognition] regarding blue and so forth is itself the incapacity regarding anything else, then even for an eternal entity, there would be capacity at one time and incapacity at another. Consequently, just as an eternal thing would simultaneously and at all times destroy its own nature, so too would cognition; this being established, it further refutes the partless [nature of the object], for instance:

it produces a determination regarding blue, but not regarding momentary destruction; therefore, just as there is a distinction between what is apprehended and what is other, so too there is a distinction between what is determined and what is otherwise.
How is it that, by necessity, [the sense] grasps all objects present?

Just as visual perception, despite the lack of distinction in its own object, produces a determinate cognition by distinguishing between blue and momentariness even when both are equally present, so too does the auditory organ with respect to its own objects such as the letter *ra* and so forth; this is the intended meaning, namely, a specific difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
In the section on momentary destruction and so forth, the word "khaṇḍam" has been written twice.

The phrase "nīlakṣaṇikatvayor api" is written twice. [Objection: This might indeed be so if the conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) had the object as its domain, just like direct perception; however, since it is without an object (*nirviṣayatā*), how can there be a distinction in the object based on a distinction in that [cognition]? To this, he says: "Indeed, the conceptual cognition... and so forth, and therein he recites the refutation beginning with "proktam" and so on.

Even though perception, like [the cognition of] blue, occurs with respect to momentary destruction, it does not produce a determinate ascertainment without distinction due to the futility of auxiliary causes; showing yet another refutation regarding this perception, he says: "Even when the totality," and so forth—meaning that even when the entire mass of sounds is grasped at once by a single cognition...
Only that word is perceived, and no other, for which there exists a cognition when its determination is to be made.

Even when the entire mass of sounds— the collection of phonemes from *a* to *ha*— is grasped all at once through a single act of auditory cognition, only that specific word is perceived, and no other, because there exists a cognition (the auxiliary cause) required for the determination (*vyavasāya*) of that particular word to take place.
Showing the meaning of the verse, he says: "From all [sides]," and so forth;
this is easy to understand.

Having accepted that perception produces conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through its differentiation, this was stated; now, showing that such [differentiation] does not even exist, he says: "Just as," and so forth.
Only that which produces conceptual construction is capable of directly making the experience of the object depend upon itself;
thus, the experience of the object directly effects a determination that is not dependent on another. (13)

Just as it is not logical for the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form, having directly presented itself and produced consciousness, to place before it an aspect that is inseparable from its own nature; likewise, that perception (*darśana*) cannot determine a determination (*vyavasāya*), nor can a distinction (*viśeṣa*) be determined by it. For if there is no determination of the distinction that constitutes the very nature of perception, how could there be recollection of a similar [object], as in the case of momentary destruction and so forth? Just as an object such as form is capable, by a certain mode of fitness, to produce an experience—that is, a perception—directly and without mediation.

Of what nature is it? He says: "Dependent on itself" (*svāpekṣam*). By the word *sva* (self), the object (*artha*) is referred to; that which has its dependence—the desire for the experience of that [object]—is so described. This means it possesses its own form (*svākāra*). Likewise, "the experience of the object in that manner" (*tathā tena prakāreṇa arthānubhavaḥ*) is "not produced by another determination" (*sākṣād-ananya-vyavasāya-kṛt*). That which has no other nature (*ananya*) distinct from its own essence is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); the determination (*vyavasāya*) of that [particular] is what is meant.
This has been discussed [in the following]: "Because of non-difference, in the case of a similar recollection... (*Siddhiviniścaya*, 1).
Showing the meaning of the verse with these words, he says: "The specific characteristic of form," and so forth.

The mention of "form" (*rūpa*) is an illustration for taste and so forth. That very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), having directly presented itself and brought itself forward, generates its own experience in consciousness; in whatever manner this is not improper, even so it is not proper for that perception—the experience of the particular characteristic—to present an aspect that is not inseparable from itself, having directly presented itself and brought it forward as a determination. For that reason, the particular characteristic would be determined as a specific feature.

Now, refuting in another way the claim that perception is the cause of determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), he says: "With the intention of what has been seen"—is perception itself of the nature of determinate cognition, or might it be otherwise? Regarding the first alternative: what need is there for another determinate cognition? Regarding the second: if there is an absence of that specific determinate cognition which constitutes the very nature of perception—i.e., if it were non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*)—how could there be a memory of a similar thing?
He provides an illustration for this: "In a moment," and so forth.
As it was said: "Of perception whose nature is determinate... (*Siddhiviniścaya* 1).
And so forth;
furthermore, there is the recollection of that by another, and because that [recollection] would otherwise be impossible, perception is of the nature of determinate cognition,
since memory would otherwise be inexplicable.

Now, demonstrating that the proponent of *sphoṭa* (sphoṭavādin) is as difficult to defeat as the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), he says "in the case of the established order" (*vyavasthāyām*) and so forth;
[this applies] to the Buddhist just as it does to the Mīmāṃsaka.
In such a systematic arrangement, how could there be reality for both conceptual and non-conceptual [cognitions],

since the established position is that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is neither the word nor the *sphoṭa*? To begin with, non-conceptual cognition whose object is the particular characteristic does not accomplish its own purpose in every respect, because its establishment consists in conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Otherwise, how could there be inference regarding what has been experienced, as [inference] is like that which has already been inferred?

Since it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, it is in reality devoid of an object; because its nature is non-existence (*abhāva*), the conceptual construction (*vikalpaka*) takes that non-existence as its object. Thus, it does not determine [the thing], and being ineffective, how can conceptualization be a means of proof (*sādhana*) through which the establishment of reality (*tattvasiddhi*) occurs, as in the case of another system? Therefore, on what basis of authority (*pramāṇa*) could this person reproach another for [perceiving] a form that is non-verbal (*aśabdarūpa*)?

The meaning is as follows: regarding the established order (*vyavasthā*)—the state of "this is reality" and "this is not"—if that were to exist as a non-differentiating ground, from where could the reality (*tattva*), the true nature of the object, arise? It could not arise from either conceptualization (*vikalpa*) or non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*), because both are equally determinative of that [reality]. Since there is no basis for the existence of one over the other in that regard, the established distinction—that "the word is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)" versus "the word is the *sphoṭa*" or "is not the *sphoṭa*"—is merely an assumption of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa-kalpanā*) common to both, because both serve to determine that [object]. This is the intended sense.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object," and so forth.
The inclusion of the phrase "having the particular characteristic as its object" is for the purpose of excluding [cognition] that has a universal (*jāti*) as its object;
[it refers to] non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) [perception].
What [is this]? Knowledge that accomplishes its own object is not [possible] in every respect, even through the mode of blue and so forth, nor even through the destruction of the eye and so on.
Why? He says: "Because its nature is that of a determinative judgment (adhyavasāya).
If it is argued that, for that reason, establishment would consist merely of a cognition (pratīti); to this he replies: "From establishment," and so forth.

Otherwise, how could inference regarding momentary destruction and the like be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that which has been experienced and grasped by non-conceptual [perception] in a manner that lacks its [the object's] defining characteristic?
He provides an illustration: "as in the case of what is inferred" (*anumite iva*), meaning "like what is inferred";
for it is because it performs the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*) that its status as a valid means of knowledge is also considered.

If it is argued that the establishment of reality does not arise from non-conceptual [cognition] but must arise from conceptual [cognition], the author replies here: the term "conceptual cognition" (*vikalpajñāna*) carries over [from the previous context]. [The opponent asks: "What follows from its having a universal as its object? [The author] says: "In reality, the conceptual [cognition] is without an object."
Why? He says: "Of that," and so forth.

Because that universal (*sāmānya*) consists of non-existence—that is, because it consists of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*)—let the universal be non-existence. What follows from that? He says: "That non-existence," and so forth.

It follows that conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) does not determine [an object] by taking the exclusion of dissimilar things (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*) as its objective domain; therefore, conceptual cognition would be ineffective. Why? Because it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since the establishment of reality (*tattvasiddhi*) results from being a means of proof, [your position] is like other systems where it is said, "it is like that" (*tadvat*), because the establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*) as an objective domain [is required].
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, this... and so forth.
Since this is so, in what manner could this Buddhist (saugata) possibly reproach an opponent (paravādin), by what form? To this he says: "In the form of that which is not sound," and so forth.

Having thus refuted the faults [attributed] to the Buddhist position by the opponent, he now addresses what was stated regarding the Jaina position: that since sound, which is a modification of *pudgala* possessing color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, is perceived by someone, its inseparable qualities such as color-form must also be perceived by that same means—according to the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.44), "Therefore, for an object that is perceived, all its qualities are indeed perceived"—it follows that the other sense organs would be useless elsewhere. Refuting this, he says: "[It is] excluded from non-sound and so forth. (*aśabdādivyavacchinnam*).
According to the Buddhist view, and even in the Jaina system, by means of the auditory faculty.

That single perception, excluded from sound and so forth, would be determined as possessing fragrance in some way, by someone, somewhere. (15) The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is a single, present perception; however many other forms it has, there are that many exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Among these, a certain one is perceived by a certain [means of knowledge]. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to a portion of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśāsiddha*), because [the other exclusions] are simply not perceived.

Therefore, for them, the object [of a word] is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Likewise, regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) consisting of sound and so forth, by means of experience preceded by the causal complex of the auditory organ and so on, only the exclusion of non-sound (*aśabdavyavaccheda*) is cognized.
In that case, even if the specific characteristic of the person (*pudgala-svalakṣaṇa*) were one, what would be the purpose of the remaining sense organs?

[Objection: It is not the same as [the case of the person], because through direct perception there is a cognition of the difference between the specific characteristics of sound and so forth. [Reply: That is not so, because the specific characteristic is not an object of determinate cognition (*avyavaseyatvāt*).

Since it is established that the nature of direct experience (*svārthānubhava*) consists in ascertainment (*vyavasāyātmakatā*) for one whose mind has conquered the superimposition of other [objects], the relationship of sublated and sublator between the minds of certainty and superimposition would not otherwise be possible; for if perception were subject to fragmentation, such as partial clarity and so forth, the consequence of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) would follow. Why, then, would the apprehension of an object not be admitted? For if it were not, there would be no hearing of sound-particles (*śabda-pudgala*) whose essence includes unperceived touch and other qualities.

Therefore, this is not the fault of conceptual constructions alone; rather, the absolutist position (*ekānta*) that "every quality of a perceived object is necessarily perceived" would be the one that appears untenable.

"Soundless" means the absence of sound, and not something other than sound. Otherwise, even for form (*rūpa*) and the rest, one would have to say they are "delimited by the exclusion of sound. If [it is argued that] those things beginning with form—namely form, taste, touch, and smell—which are themselves delimited from those [other categories], would thus not be a single entity like a jar and so forth; [the author] says: "It is indeed one, because the superimposition of contradictory properties results in absolute non-difference"—this is the sense. That [object] should be determined—that is, ascertained—just as it is known through clear perception (*pratyakṣa*).

By this, he states the identity of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and determination (*vyavasāya*): in some way—that is, by means of a mode excluded from non-sound, and not by any mode excluded from non-form and so forth—[this occurs] through the ear, and not through the eye or other [senses].
Here, fragrance-substance (*gandhadravya*) is the illustrative example; [this occurs] in certain places, not everywhere.
By this, someone denies its omnipresence,
because it lacks the quality of being a differentiator.
He demonstrates the meaning of the verse along with its justification by means of the passage beginning with "just as" (*yathā*), etc. He asks:
"Just as what? and answers: "The unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the Buddhist, which is individually perceived.
Of what nature is it? He says: "proximate," and so forth.

There are as many exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) as there are other forms (*pararūpa*) of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Among those exclusions, a certain exclusion from non-sound and so forth is perceived by a certain conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of sound and so forth, through a word that serves as its instrument of expression; however, the exclusion from permanence is not perceived by the conceptualization or the expression "sound. Therefore, for this reason, the logical mark (*hetu*) such as "existence" (*sattva*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*).
Why? He says: "Because it is not perceived," and so forth.
Of what? He says: "namely," and so forth.

Therefore, for this reason, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the object of those other designations and conceptual constructions; thus, in that manner, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the nature of the word. Of what sort is it? He says: "consisting of sound," and so forth. This is the meaning.

In that regard, concerning the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), one might think that based on the experience arising from the auditory complex (sāmagrī) and so forth, only the exclusion of what is non-sound would be cognized through direct perception (pratyakṣa), and not the exclusion of what is non-tangible and so on,
because even experience— just like conceptual construction (vikalpa)— has exclusion as its object.
Since this is so, therefore, there would be no pointlessness or redundancy for the remaining sense organs, because their purpose is to bring about the cognition of what has not yet been perceived.
"Even when what is the case? To this he says: "even though the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the person (*pudgala*) is one.
What is the purpose of *anyāpoha*? "Bhāvaḥ" means existence; "kaimarthakyam" means for what purpose, that is, for what objective. This is the sense.

Now, surely form is perceived by the eye and taste by the tongue; the same may be said for the remaining sense-faculties. Yet, in those cases, nothing else appears, nor is there any other sense-faculty wherein another entity might appear. Therefore, there is no single, distinct *pudgala*-specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that exists apart from form and the rest. Thus he says: "By perception," and so forth.

If it is argued that [the case] is dissimilar—because, according to the stated method, the distinction between the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound and so forth is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as auditory cognition, and thus, just as exclusion from others is perceived by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), so too is it perceived by direct perception—it is not similar; to this he replies: "No," and so forth. Why is that which was stated by the opponent not the case? Because the specific characteristic, characterized by atoms of form and so on, is non-determinable (*avyavaseya*), that is, it cannot be ascertained.

He thinks as follows: "Just as by the eye alone form (*rūpa*) is perceived—not that which is of another nature, nor anything else—and there is no dependence on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the establishment of reality occurs through the very experience of its own object by way of the exclusion of the superimposition of other [attributes]. To this, he replies: "Because the experience of its own object—which is the vision of both self and other—is established as being of a determinative nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*); since that [determinative nature] is not established [without it], there is a dependence upon it. Of what kind [of experience]? He says: "And whose mind has conquered the superimposition of others."
If it is argued that there will be an experience of that [object], yet it will not be of a determinate nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*), to this he replies: "Certainty" (*niścaya*) and so forth.

Certainty (*niścaya*) and the removal of superimposition (*āropamanas*) stand in a relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*), which is accepted by the opponent; otherwise, the experience of that [object] would not be tenable—that is, it would not be possible—in the manner of being non-determinate, because even between non-conceptual [cognition] and the mind of another superimposition, a relationship of sublated and sublator is admitted. And thus, by the mere scent of such experience, the superimposition must perish; otherwise, even the mention of superimposition would not exist, since its occurrence would be impossible. This appears as if written twice.
Because of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator between the mind of certainty and the mind of superimposition— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.48.

If it is argued that the word "not" here is meaningless—since, for instance, regarding blue and so forth, there is no exclusion [of error] based on experience because the mind superimposes something else, but rather [exclusion occurs] because the perception of similarity, which is the cause of that [superimposition], is absent, and thus [the superimposition] does not arise by itself; we say no, because superimpositions such as [the existence of] *pradhāna* and so forth occur even in the absence of a perception of similarity. If it is argued that internal beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the cause in those cases; we say no, because superimposition is seen even from intermediate latent impressions, such as the perception of purity in what is impure, as in the case of a Vedic scholar who has performed sacrifices and is smeared with ashes.

Suppose this were so; what would be the fault? If it is argued that there would be a superimposition (*samāropa*) of "non-blue" and so forth upon the blue and so forth, but that this does not happen because of the ascertainment (*niścaya*) [of the blue], then this must be considered here: does this [ascertainment] arise from direct experience (*anubhava*), or from a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? In the first alternative, you act in a manner favorable to your own position, since the objection beginning with "the experience of its own object" remains unrefuted.
In the second case, if there is an entry into superimposition during the interval, then ascertainment is impossible.

Now, if experience forcibly produces a certainty— that the latent impression of non-blue causes the superimposition of non-blue— then it would follow as a logical absurdity (*kācapacya*) that it would also forcibly produce conceptual constructions of the *pradhāna* and so forth as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas.
Furthermore, if it is argued that he cannot produce even the ascertainment of momentariness because of a lack of capacity, let that same lack of capacity apply to blue and other objects as well;
for the capacity [of perception] exists there [in the case of blue], not elsewhere, since we observe that perception does not absolutely contradict the fact that [objects] possess parts.

Regarding this, he says: Since there is no proficiency—meaning the capacity to produce a certain cognition—in perception regarding blue and so forth with respect to momentary destruction and the like, and since the contingency of inconclusiveness would arise if such [proficiency] were possible through the presence of factors such as habituation (*abhyāsa*), for that reason, why would one not accept—that is, why would one not admit—that the apprehension of an object, which is the seeing of an object, occurs in that manner, namely "part by part" (*khaṇḍaśaḥ*)? Because it is not so accepted, there would be no hearing of the sound-pudgala;
of what kind [would it be]? It is that whose nature as touch and so forth, though present, is unapprehended (*anupātta*). This is the experience.
He states the conclusion of the present topic with the words "Therefore, not...

and so forth. Since this is so, the meaning is that this fault or defect, characterized as a fragmented apprehension, belongs not only to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) but also to perception (*dṛṣṭi*).
For, due to the fault of those [constructions] alone, the absolute certainty (*ekānta*) that "every quality of the perceived object is indeed perceived" would be undermined.
Therefore, even for an object perceived non-conceptually, every quality of that perceived thing is indeed perceived— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.124.

[Objection: But surely, even though sound, form, and so forth do not differ in being attributes of the substance *pudgala*, why is there this distinction that only sound is apprehended and not form and the rest? Likewise, even in the absence of a rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), how can there be identity (*tādātmya*)? If this is asked, he says here: "Of substances," and so forth—namely, the apprehension of substances occurs through their own manifest functions (*udbhūtavṛtti*).
It is not [the case that they are identical] through their qualities, as in the case of light and substance when their functions are unmanifested.

For even though sound and the other [sensory objects], which depend on a single causal complex and possess inseparable functions, lack the necessity of being perceived together, there is no absolute non-distinction between them, just as in the case of the atom and its gross form;
because if either one were absent, the object itself would be untenable.
In the case of absolute difference, there would follow the consequence of separate existence (*pṛthaksiddhi*), and thus no relation could be established;
in the case of absolute non-difference, because of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), the plurality of sense organs would be useless.

Even if there were some form of identity (*tādātmya*), color and so forth, though present, would not be perceived simultaneously even when all other causes for their perception are complete, because their specific qualities have not yet manifested (*udbhūtaguṇatva*).

For example, although the tangible quality (*sparśa*) of a fiery substance (*taijasa-dravya*) is sometimes perceived in some instances, its color (*rūpa*) is not perceived because that [quality] has not manifested; light (*āloka*), however, is perceived for the perception of color, while its tangible quality is not observed;
and in some cases, both are perceived because they have manifested, as in the case of fire.
This same sequence is observed even in the perception of odor and other qualities belonging to earth and the other elements.

Likewise, even though the person (pudgala) consists of taste and other [qualities], it is perceived as having the nature of sound because of the necessity of its manifestation therein; for the operation of transformation is manifold, as is the case with self-awareness itself.
Because they appear as excluded from others, the perception—
that is,
the observation— of substances occurs simultaneously with their qualities, and not in isolation from them.
By what kind [of qualities]? He says: "by their own," meaning by those belonging to the self and not by those residing in other substances;
by this he shows that in the state of liberation, the self is not perceived as being devoid of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa).

Again, by what kind? He says: "by those whose functions have become manifest" (udbhūtavṛttibhiḥ), meaning by those whose transformation (pariṇāma) has become manifest as a function capable of apprehending knowledge for the sake of the Puruṣa alone.
The word "ca" (and) is used in a different syntactical order; it should be understood immediately after this [word "na"].
Therefore, he says: "not by those whose functions are unmanifest.
Here he provides an illustration, beginning with the words "just as," and so forth.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "of fiery substances, etc.," substances possessing odor and so forth are included; [the point is that] there is perception by means of cloth and other things whose qualities are manifested (*udbhūta*), but not by means of those whose qualities are unmanifested (*anudbhūta*). By this, he points out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the principle "because of the rule of simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*), which [otherwise] would imply that [the object] is not an object of perception according to the view of the Vaiśeṣikas.

With the words "not indeed" (*na hi*) and so forth, he demonstrates this very point: regarding those things of which sound is the first—namely, form (*rūpa*) and the rest—of what nature are they? They are dependent on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*), and although they do not possess the rule of non-separable occurrence (*avinirbhāgavṛtti*) or simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there is no absolute identity (*atādātmya*) between them, nor is there an absolute difference (*bhedaikānta*).
Of what are they like? He says: they are like atoms (*paramāṇu*) and gross forms (*sthūlākāra*).

Just as atoms and their gross form [are perceived], so too, even when there is the perception of a gross form, there is no perception of the atoms that compose it; nevertheless, this does not constitute an absolute difference between them. By this, he demonstrates the fallacy of the absence of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) in proving the absolute difference of sound-particles (*śabda-pudgala*) from the qualities of sound, color, and so forth.

Some maintain that the existence [of objects] consists in the perception of atoms (*paramāṇu*), while others hold it consists in the perception of a gross form (*sthūlākāra*). How, then, can there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the logical reason (*hetu*) by them? To this, he says: "Upon the removal of either one of those," and so forth.

Of those two—the atom and the gross form—upon the removal of either one, the object such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) would be untenable. Therefore, like that, there is no absolute identity (*atādātmyaikānta*) between them.

For instance: upon the removal of the gross form, there would be only atoms; since they are not perceived, they would be non-existent. Upon the removal of the atoms, there would be only the gross form, which would be partless; if that were the case, it would follow that there is movement and so forth in only a single part [of the object].

If it is argued that only visible things are subject to destruction and nothing else, then from what does the manifestation of clouds and the like arise when they were previously non-existent? If you say it is causeless, then everything would be so, resulting in the total collapse of the relationship between cause and effect.

If you say this is refuted by the doctrine of non-duality (advaita) and the like, which holds that [manifestation] arises from subtle particles of earth and so forth, then you are acting in a manner contrary [to your own position], since atoms have already been negated.
Or, having yourself accepted the production of visible atoms from invisible atoms, why would you not accept the production of gross objects from them?
The Cārvākas say "non-existence," while the Buddhists say [the same].

If it should be thought that [the atom] is devoid of parts—that is to say, partless—let it be so, being subtle because the cause dissolves at the time of the effect; however, it has already been stated in this regard that this leads to the undesirable consequence of causelessness. Therefore, it is well said: "like the gross form of an atom."

If it is argued: "Surely the gross object is indeed different from the atoms, because the effect is different from its cause; therefore, since they too are included within the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of them," [the author] replies here: "In the case of an absolute distinction—that is, an absolute difference—there follows the consequence of separate establishment (*pṛthaksiddhi*). This means that the parts would be established in one location while the whole (*avayavin*) would be established in another, like a father and his son.
Why does this follow? He says: 'Because the connection is not established,' due to the negation of inherence (*samavāya*);
therefore, the Naiyāyika position is not tenable."

If it is argued that this would be the position of the Sāṃkhya school, [the author] replies here: In the case of absolute non-difference (*abhedaikānta*), there is the necessity of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) between the subtle form of the atom (*paramāṇu*) and its gross form (*sthūlākāra*), because they are one and the same. Since this is the case under the doctrine of absolute unity, the multiplicity of sense organs (*indriyanānātvam*) is rendered useless. Likewise, the perception of the mind (*manas*) and atoms would occur [simultaneously]; so how can there be an absolute non-difference between them? Furthermore, if one were to assume their perception despite this, then upon the perception of color by the eye, there would be the perception of taste and so forth, and thus the multiplicity of sense organs would be useless.

If it is asked, "How is it that this fault does not arise even in the case of 'in some way' (*kathaṃcit*)? he says here: "Even if there is identity in some way (*kathaṃcit-tādātmye*), not only in the case of the opposite [view] regarding form and so forth"—the word "also" (*api*) is to be understood here as well—[meaning] not only in the case of the atom and its shape, but also [the following applies]. Even when what is present is not perceived together [with another], under what condition? He says: "even when there is completeness of other causes for that" (*tatkaraṇāntarasākalye’pi*). That cause is the eye, which is the cause of the cognition of form; "other than that" (*tadantaram*) refers to the tongue and so forth. Even when there is completeness of those, why [is there no perception]? He says: "when the quality has manifested," and so forth.
Then it was stated: "like the form of an atom and a gross object.

Alternatively, if it is argued that because there is no rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) for sound and the other [sensory objects], even though they depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*), there may not be an absolute identity (*tādātmyaikānta*) between them—since color and so forth are not perceived when sound is perceived—but rather an absolute non-existence (*abhāvaikānta*) [of the others] might follow; to this he replies: "like the form of an atom and a gross object.

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Just as in the perception of a gross form, there is no non-existence [of atoms], so too in the perception of sound, even if color and so forth are not perceived, there is no non-existence [of them]."

Why is this? He says: because if either of those two were absent, the other—whether the word, the form and so forth, the deluded [cognizer], the means, the object, the conscious [subject], or the other—would be untenable.

To explain: in the absence of the perceived word, what confidence could there be regarding a jar or similar object? If that [word] were merely inferred there while the form and so forth were absent, there would be no confidence in gross objects, as they would be nothing more than atoms.
As it has been said: "Even by moving through the wind, the corporeal is considered established" (Siddhibindu 11).
Thus, the phrase "of identity and the letter 'e'" is redundantly written here.
If it is argued that even form and other qualities are distinct within the word *bhavantu*, the author replies: "In the case of absolute difference," and so forth.
He states the fault in the extreme of non-difference with the words "In the extreme of non-difference," and so forth;
the remainder is as before.
He demonstrates the example with the words "For instance," and so forth.

In certain cases—such as in a chamber filled with windless darkness, or at the time of a particularly cold night—there is the perception of a substance possessing fire (*tejodravya*) whose tactile quality (*sparśa*) has become manifest; yet, despite this perception of its manifest touch, there is no perception of its form (*rūpa*). Why is this? He says: "Because of the non-manifest operation of that [form]" (*tadanudbhūtavṛtteḥ*). That is to say, because of the non-manifest operation (*anudbhūtavṛtti*) of that form (*rūpa*). Likewise, in the perception of form by means of light—such as the light of a lamp—there is no perception of touch.

In some cases there is the perception of both; from what does the perception of touch and form arise? To this he says: "Only when its activity has become manifest," as in the case of fire, or [the perception of] wind in a void.

Indeed, just as the perception of both [the eye and the object] was demonstrated when the function [of the sense organ] is manifest during the time of a terrifying night, why was the non-perception of both not likewise demonstrated in the opposite case? If it is argued that this is because of the absence of the object, we say no; for there is the existence of an object in the form of the ocular ray.

This is not so, because according to the Sāṃkhya view, the existence of an entity such as a jar—whose specific qualities are unmanifest and whose entire set of qualities is thus unmanifest—is present everywhere.

If it is argued that [the case] regarding the rays of the eye is based on inference, whereas in other cases it is the opposite, and thus they are not equal; we say no, because that [inference] has been refuted—this is the intended meaning.
For one who speaks thus, the existence of unmanifest color and touch is established for that which possesses an unmanifest function.
[Objection: But surely, even though smell exists in some places on earth, it is not perceived, as in the case of a jar; likewise, one must say the same for color and the other qualities.

Similarly, there is smell everywhere in water, smell and taste in fire, and color, taste, and smell in air. What then is the explanation for this? Some say that smell and the others are absent in water and so forth; to that he replies: "That which belongs to earth," and so on.

The word "ādi" (beginning with) is connected to each term, such as "pārthiva" (earthy) and "gandha" (odor), and thus the meaning is as follows: earth itself is the "pārthiva"; those of which water and the other elements are the "ādi" (beginnings), their odors and so forth—even upon their perception, and not only upon their non-perception, this sequence just mentioned is observed.

For instance, for yogins, the odors and other qualities of earth are indeed directly perceived because they are manifest (*udbhūta*); for people like us, however, they exist in both ways, being both manifest and unmanifest (*anudbhūta*).

Nor does the absence of manifestation imply the absence of the thing itself, because that would contradict the existence of the final moment [of a process], and it would lead to the absurd conclusion that there could be no inference of color and so forth from taste.
Furthermore, while odor and other qualities are perceived by yogins even in water and similar substances, for those like us, the opposite is the case due to their non-manifestation.
Thus, the perception of earthy odors and so forth by those like us serves as an example for others.

If it is asked: "Just as there is a non-manifestation of the fragrance of the earth and other qualities even though they exist, what is the proof that water and the other elements also exist therein? We reply: their possession of touch;
yet [that touch] is not perceived.
If there were non-existence at the time of non-manifestation because of the acceptance of a stream of form and so forth,
then, having explained the example in this way, he applies it to the subject of the illustration with the words "In the same way," and so on.
Likewise, why is there no perception of the person (pudgala)—who, though consisting of taste and so forth, also consists of sound—by means of the sense of hearing?
To this he says: "Because of the restriction of its arising," and so forth;
that is, because the arising of that which consists of sound is restricted [to the auditory faculty].

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that, just as with the earth, when smell and other qualities exist in water and so forth, they are manifested in some instance of that same class—just as heat is manifested in fire which is of the same class as gold—and yet this is not so [in the case of the soul]? To this he says: "For manifold indeed... and so on.
For the manifestation (*vṛtti*), that is, the occurrence or transformation (*pariṇāma*) of qualities, is manifold, meaning it takes various forms.
That is to say: in some cases, there is the manifestation of qualities within that very class; for example, the manifestation of knowledge in every soul.

In some cases there is non-manifestation therein, while in others there is manifestation in that which belongs to the same class, as previously stated; or in some cases there is manifestation both therein and in that which belongs to the same class. [Objection: Even according to the opponent's view, just like the omnipresence of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, its non-perception may be due to the non-perception of its substratum.
[Reply: No; for it would follow that sound itself could not be perceived.

And for one for whom earth and the other elements are transformations of the person (*pudgala*), the manifestation of smell and so forth in a transformation of the earthly element—such as water and the like—is quite easily established. Thus, everything is well-ordered.
He states the example well-known to the Buddhist: "Even from self-awareness," and so forth;
this has already been discussed right here.
Why is that impossible? To this he says: because it appears as being excluded from other forms such as the "graspable" (grāhya) and so forth, which belong to that self-consciousness (svasaṃvitti).
Demonstrating the established result, he says "at once" (sakṛt), etc., which is easy to understand.

Just as there is the manifestation of odor and so forth in sound while there is no manifestation of color and so forth, so too is there the manifestation of that [odor] in things such as jars which belong to the class of *pudgala*,
due to the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the self (*ātman*) and other factors.

Since the space that serves as its substratum is imperceptible, it is established for precisely the same reason that transformation is established; thus he says: "Of the universal," and so forth, because the universal's quality of being expressible and so on is the opposite of the particular (svalakṣaṇa).
What was stated has been refuted by the proofs for the nature of manifoldness (*anekānta*).

Furthermore, it is not possible to negate a universal consisting of similar transformation (*sādṛśya-pariṇāma-sāmānya*), because a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that does not possess that [universal] nature would be useless for the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of a cognition having its own form.
For it is not the case that [the universal] in consciousness...

[is mutually...]—this very universal is a non-entity because it is denotable and because it is incapable of causal efficiency; such arguments for its [non-existence] have been refuted by the proof of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
This is because consciousness—which possesses a gross form similar [to its object] and whose unitary nature is otherwise impossible—is in some way directly perceived.

If the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—such as momentariness or circularity—were visible to the eye, then it would follow that [the object] would also be visible as having the nature of taste and so forth;

the capacity of the remaining sense organs, like other means of valid cognition, would not be contradictory for the purpose of excluding superimposition through a mediate process, since the attainment of a specific determination regarding that [object] is possible. "That which has expressibility and so forth" refers to a thing whose first [property] is expressibility, such as being denotable by the appearance of its reality (*tattvābhāsa*); it is described as such because of that. Therefore...

He states another reason: "Because of the reversal of its own characteristic. The "own characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); its "reversal" is the opposite of that. He asks, "By what [is this refuted]? and replies, "By the proofs establishing the nature of non-absolutism (*anekāntātman*). He states the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "For not," and so forth.

If it is argued that the universal (*sāmānya*) is precisely the transformation (*pariṇāma*) similar to yours, and that this too is common to others; to this he says: "That which again... and so forth.
It cannot be refuted, for that would entail the fallacy of perception being erroneous.

If it is argued that only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*); to this he says: "Of that which is not of that nature"—that is, of the particular characteristic devoid of the nature of a similar transformation—the cognition of its own form is the cognition of the form of the particular characteristic. Is that not indeed purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), since it is employed for that very purpose?
Why? He says: "For not in consciousness," and so forth;
this is easy to understand.
Why is that? He says: "Mutually," and so forth.
He sets forth the opponent's position in order to refute it: "This very [entity], namely the universal (*sāmānya*), etc.
Why is this universal, characterized by a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*), not a real entity? To this he replies: "Because it is denotable (*abhidheyatvāt*)," and so forth.
By this, the phrase "of the expressible and so forth" has been explained.

Stating that [the object] is the opposite of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), he says: the statement of the opponent beginning with "because of the incapacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) has been answered by means of the proof of transformation (*pariṇāma*); it has been refuted. If one asks, "Why is that proof refuted?"—to this he replies: "similar," and so forth.
Why is that so? He says: "Of the gross," and so forth.
Establishing its apprehension in some way, he asks: "Of what [is this]?"—even of that whose single, undivided self (akhaṇḍa-ātman), that is, whose nature is conceived as one;
of what? He says: "of consciousness" (saṃvidaḥ), that is, of cognition.

If [it is argued that] it is somehow perceived through its form as volition (*cetanā*) and so forth, but not through its momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) and so forth, then he states the refutation even regarding perception through momentary destruction and so forth—beginning with the words "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*), etc.

That which is momentary, spherical (*parimaṇḍala*), characterized by partlessness (*niraṃśatva*), and—by the force of the word "etc. (*ādi*)—that which possesses [qualities such as] leading to heaven (*svargaprāpaṇa*) and so forth, is thus described; and that is the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic). If that were visible to the eye, this would be an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all sensory perceptions (*adhyakṣasaṃvitti*); it would mean that visibility—even in the form of taste (*rasa*) and so forth—would apply to all sensory perceptions. This is an indicative mark for all sensory perceptions, meaning that there would be visibility even in the nature of taste and the rest.

If it is argued that there is likewise no such cognition [of the object], and that the deficiency of the remaining sense organs would be the same in both cases; to this he replies: "The capacity of the remaining sense organs is like that of another means of valid cognition, namely inference. Just as the capacity of inference is not contradicted when its purpose is the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa*), so too it would not be contradicted even if the eye, while perceiving color-form (*rūpa*), were to perceive taste and other qualities."

Just as, even when momentariness is apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa) as being possessed of blue color, the efficacy of inference (anumāna) for the purpose of excluding the superimposition (samāropa) of that [non-momentariness] is not contradicted; so too, even when taste and other qualities are perceived by the eye along with visible form, the efficacy of the remaining sense-faculties for the purpose of excluding the superimposition of those [qualities] is not contradicted.

How so? He says: "Through a succession (pāramparya), the cognition of taste and so forth arises from the remaining sense-faculties; from that, conceptual construction (vikalpa); from that, the exclusion of superimposition.
For without the remaining sense-faculty, there would be no cognition of that [taste]; and without that, there would be no conceptual construction of it."

Thus he says: "The determination thereof," and so forth; for otherwise, since the specific determination [of the object] would be established either through that [perception] or through the cognition of the remaining sense-faculties, the inference of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) would be rendered useless.
The passage contained within this has been written twice.

Now, demonstrating the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the proofs for [the existence of] denotability and so forth offered by the opponent, he says: "In the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇe*)," and so on;
"denotability and the rest exist in the particular characteristic, therefore that too is not a proof."

One might argue that [the cognition] establishes the absence of that [universal], such as the reality of the universal's non-existence. (18) If the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of visual cognition even though it does not appear as such, why would it not be so for verbal cognition? [The opponent replies: "Because of the difference between the clear and the other... That is not so. And thus, individual particulars are inexpressible as being either identical to or different from the reality [of the universal]. Since they are not the cause of that [verbal cognition], and because the universal is a non-entity due to its commonality, [the same applies to] the gross [object]... By this [same reasoning], [one should understand the refutation of] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), convention (*saṅketa*), and so forth.

Regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), "being denotable" and so forth are mentioned; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of [properties] such as being inexpressible as either identical to or different from the real entity (*vastu*) is intended. It exists—that is, it is found—and therefore, not only by the immediately preceding reasoning, is "being denotable" and so forth a non-prover (*asādhana*) and not a valid logical mark (*aliṅga*).
To the question "Of what [is it not a prover]? he says: "In the universal" (*sāmānye*), etc.
He considers that because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reality of the absence of universals and so forth—of which the absence of the whole (*avayavin*) and so on is the first.

If it is argued that there is no fault because that [particular] is also made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), he says here: the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a shake of the head; the sense is: what indeed could establish the non-existence of that, namely the non-existence of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); for if that were established, all worldly transaction (*sarvavyavahāra*) would collapse.
To explain this verse, he says: "of the visual cognition," and so forth.

Even if there is no appearance of that [external object]—that is, even if there is no appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—if the particular characteristic were the object of words and the like, why would it not be so? It would indeed be the object; however, that is not tenable. This is because, in the case of the particular characteristic, there is no difference in appearance between verbal and sensory cognition for one whose eyes are not engaged by the word, and so forth. Nevertheless, [the author] speaks while provisionally accepting this, saying "clear and otherwise," and so on.

As for that scripture which states: "Because an object whose senses are not engaged by a word does not appear in the intellect, just as it does when [the senses] are engaged"—this is cited on page 6 of the *Apohasiddhi*: "The knower of that which is not designated by a word, just as in the perception of an object whose senses are not engaged..."
Concluding the present topic, he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.
Furthermore, showing a similar argument belonging to another, he says: "And likewise... and so forth.

And likewise, in that very same manner, the individual (*vyakti*)—the particular (*viśeṇa*) whose gross form is made an object of perception—is the "perceptible individual. From that [individual], there is the inexpressibility [of universals] in terms of identity or difference.
Of what things? He says: "of the *svalakṣaṇas*," and so forth, while again refuting another reason by saying: "because the universal is common, if its lack of reality is admitted..."
What [is it]? He says: "of the gross," and so forth.
Making an extension (*atideśa*) of this to other cases, he says: "these," and so forth.
He refutes another logical mark (*liṅga*) with the words beginning "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*).
Again, he refutes another logical mark (liṅga) with the words beginning "convention" (saṅketa).
To the question "Why is this [also not valid]?", he says: "the particular characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa), and so forth;
[for] the particular characteristic is indeterminate, and even that which is determined is non-existent.

[The opponent claims: "Indeed, one attains reality (*tattva*) through the absolute certainty of false objects. [The author asks: How could both of these be established as reality from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), given that they are grasped by cognitions that are indistinguishable from cognitions of non-existent objects? Now, how could this [cognition], occurring with respect to the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of non-existent objects, prove the absence of universals (*sāmānya*)? Or, if it were proving it, why would it not also prove the absence of particular characteristics? Let there be this further fault in both cases; however, the present point cannot be proven merely by the fact that [the cognition] exists with respect to particular characteristics, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is not the nature of the atoms imagined by others—is indeterminate and discernible only through non-conceptual [cognition]; thus, it is certain that it is non-existent and unmanifest. Yet, because of the absolute certainty regarding this false object, the Buddhist, while explaining the verse, says: "He would establish [the view] that the object is the particular characteristic," and so forth, up to the end of the passage, which is easy to understand.

And how so? In no way is this [perception] non-conceptual with respect to its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), nor is conceptual cognition non-existent with respect to its universal-object (*sāmānya*). Thus, both are reality in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). To this he says: "An unreal object," and so forth, providing an illustration. Now, one might argue that this illustration is unestablished (*asiddha*), because even if the universal is non-existent, this reason—"because it is grasped by a cognition not distinct from a cognition of an unreal object"—still applies to the own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) even when it exists; for if it were absent, nothing at all would exist. To this he says: "Lacking continuity" (*ananvaya*), and so forth.

How could this reason just mentioned establish the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to those specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) which are described as having for their nature a cognition of an unreal object—that is, those specific characteristics in which there exists a cognition whose object is non-existent? Or, if it were to establish the absence of a universal, how could it not also establish the absence of those specific characteristics?

"Why?"—to this the Naiyāyika and others reply with the words "in both cases" and so forth. To this, the author gives the following answer: "Let this other fault belong to this Buddhist who maintains the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda), but let it not be said that it exists in the particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇas) themselves; for how could this much establish the Buddhist position under discussion? He says: "Because of non-deviation (avyabhicāra). The meaning is that [the reason] establishes the existence of both [states] for the Jaina; the connection is that this is because [the reason] is common to both.

Furthermore, the universal (*sāmānya*) established by the Jainas cannot be the object of a cognition that is indistinguishable from the cognition of a non-existent thing; thus he says: "How could the establishment of the reality of a single, gross [object] be false through false conceptual constructions (*mithyā-vikalpa*) that rely solely upon their own internal parts? (20)

How can the cognition that discriminates sense objects and faculties—which, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), is a single gross entity based on the contact between sense faculty and object—be called "erroneous"? For, by apprehending external objects, it establishes either its own self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) in the form of the grasped and so forth; how then could it be mistaken? Furthermore, how could the knowledge of a single gross universal, such as the reality of a jar and so forth, constitute a false determination of reality through erroneous conceptual constructions?
By what kind [of means]? To this he says:
"by those who rely on their own portion alone," the sense being that because of the negation of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), [the goal] would not be achieved by other [means].
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "The sense-object," and so forth.

How can conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), which is a cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*), be called an error? What does it do? He says: "Establishing. In what sense, ultimately (*paramārthataḥ*)? He says: "A gross, unitary reality," and so forth.

Why? He says: this was stated with reference to the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, in consideration of external objects. With reference to the internal [factors], he says: how can that which establishes self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), which is the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*), as the object to be proven, be called "erroneous" (*bhrānti*)? Of what nature is it? He says: "the apprehended," and so forth—it is not so in reality; self-awareness is simply manifested as such through error. As it has been said: "Though the nature of cognition is undivided... (Pramāṇavārttika 2).
354. Because of the reason that [cognition] grasps external objects, what [follows]? He says: "By itself," and so forth.
Showing the opposite case in another context, he says: "And of the universal," etc.;
[it refers to] the form of the grasped and the grasper, that is, the form of the grasped and so forth.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: by those whose vision is inverted, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.
Demonstrating that very point, he says: "Perception" and so forth:
"How could perception not be considered to have the universal as its object, since it perceives the form of the object equally in both the cause and its own effect? (21)

If the perception of an object were possible apart from the similarity between the object and the subject—which is characterized by a single experience of their being either existent or non-existent—then, because that [perception] would be separated from it [the object], it would not be the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*), just like the sense-contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth. Furthermore, since that similarity is experienced as the very form of consciousness itself and not as the form of the object, how could there be the apprehension of the object, except through metaphor?

Moreover, this would not even constitute a relationship of cause and effect, because in that case, there would be no perception of something existing at the same time or of something yet to come, since the existence of the latter depends solely upon the former.
Nor would there be a lack of non-contradiction [between the cognition and its object] as in the case of twins;

for why should this knowledge—which possesses a correspondence with an object belonging to the three times—be restricted solely to its cause? Consequently, it would not be a case of having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its domain, like conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).

Furthermore, it is not contradictory for a single form to represent multiple objects, because it is accepted that the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*) have aggregated things as their objective support (*saṃcitālambanatā*).

If it is argued that because of the mention of "the body" (kāya), each [atom] must necessarily have a collection as its object, we say: no, for there is no contradiction in the appearance of a single gross [object]. How could it be that the Buddhist does not accept—indeed, he must accept—that perception has a universal (sāmānya) as its domain, just as in the case of another mental continuum?
What would he be doing [to deny this]? To this he says: "Let him see! What is it that he should see? He says: an object-form (arthākāra) that is equal, that is, similar.
Of which two? Of the two things that have their own respective objects.
Of what nature are they? To this he says: "of cause and effect," explaining the verse according to their respective order, he says: "of the object and the subject," and so forth.
The meaning has been explained repeatedly up to the point characterized by the single experience of similarity between the existent and the non-existent;
he states the refutation [of the opponent] should this not be accepted, beginning with the words "the perception of that," and so forth.

Regarding that direct perception (*pratyakṣabuddhi*) of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), if there were a vision of the object apart from its similarity (*sārūpya*)—that is, if the direct realization of the object occurred through a formless cognition by virtue of a capacity (*yogyatā*)—then, because of that capacity, the cognition would lack the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) due to the intervention [of the capacity], just as in the case of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth. What, then, would be the use of postulating similarity? If it is argued that similarity itself is the most effective instrument, the author replies: Furthermore, that similarity—the resemblance between cognition and the object—is nothing other than the very form or nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness itself, which has been experienced.
He demonstrates the fruit of the particle *eva*: "How is it that the form of the object has not been experienced? To this he says: "From what [source]? and so forth.
From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is there the apprehension of an external object? From none at all, except for figurative usage (*upacāra*).

The apprehension of that [object] arises from that very [perception], just as in the case of Caitra and his friend: upon seeing Caitra, there is a metaphorical application of the term "seeing" to the friend who resembles him.

What is meant is this: the cognition of similarity arises from the perception of both, as in the case of Caitra and his friend; yet, for another person, there is no direct vision of the object. How then can there be a cognition of the similarity residing therein? This was stated by way of concession (*upacārāt*), not in reality (*bhāvataḥ*);
for one who has not seen the friend does not have a vision of him metaphorically applied to Caitra.

If it is argued that "the apprehension of that [object] occurs only through metaphorical designation (upacāra)," to this he replies: This similarity would not exist only in the case of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); rather, the point is that it could also exist even in its absence, as in the case of twins. For, since that [similarity] exists in those very cases, there would be no perception of an object existing at the same time, or of one yet to come into being.

And if that were so, how could the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of Prajñākaragupta be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that it would be directed toward what is yet to come? [This applies] to the Yogācāra.
For a person who does not understand a friend in the ultimate sense, [the relationship] between those born together—

Therefore, [the cognition] which has as its object a thing yet to be realized and which falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), produces conventional understanding through superimposition (*adhyāropa*). — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 5.

If it is objected that there would be no non-discrepancy [between cognition and object] if similarity were without a cause, he says in response: "And thus there would not be non-discrepancy"—this is not so; rather, there *would* indeed be [non-discrepancy], as in the case of twins, with an object that is not the cause [of the cognition].
Concluding the present topic, he says: "That," and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore, how could this cognition possessing the forms of blue and so forth—which has a similarity (*sārūpya*) with objects belonging to the three times (i.e., that similarity whose objects are the three times)—be restricted to a specific cause? For, due to such restriction, like conceptual cognition, it would not have the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. If it is asked, "How is it that for a single [cognition] there is no contradiction in imitating objects belonging to the three times?"—to this he says: "And it is not contradictory for a cognition of a single form—that is, of a single nature—to imitate multiple objects. Why? He says: because of the acceptance that [the cognition] has a collection (*saṃcita*) as its objective support."

The state of being that which has as its objective support atoms (*paramāṇu*) accumulated and distinguished by a particular arrangement—of what things is this? He says: "of the five groups of consciousness" (*pañcavijñānakāyānām*), i.e., of the collections of cognitions such as the visual and so forth; for it is an established tenet (*siddhānta*) that "the five groups of consciousness have accumulated things as their objective supports.

Thus he thinks: just as a single cognition reproduces many objects existing at the same time, so too [it reproduces] those existing at different times. This has been refuted [by the following]: "the operation of the sense organs (*akṣa*) is restricted to the present alone."
It should be observed—page 25, note 10.
For comparison: "The functioning of the senses occurs toward objects situated in a suitable location, not toward those that are past or future;
and the consciousness dependent upon them does not occur toward objects existing at another time."
—*Pra-vārtikālaṅkāra*, p. 246:
Now, it may be argued that the collection of cognitions has an accumulated [object] as its objective support (*saṃcitālambana*), whereas each individual cognition is restricted to a single atom.
To this he says: "Because of the apprehension of the body," and so forth.

If it is argued that because [the cognition] denotes a collection, these cognitions have as their object an aggregate of atoms individually, the author provides the following reply: "No," and so forth.
"No" serves to refute the opposing position.
Why? He says: "Because it contradicts the appearance of a single gross [object]."
He states an illustration: "as in the case of another mental continuum"—this is the remainder [of the argument] considered here.
He states another refutation regarding the apprehension of an object by virtue of similarity: "in the case of a single object," and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no mutual perception between two eyes because they perceive the same object, this is not so; for there is no perception of a single object [by both].

Just as those whose eyes are fixed upon the same object simultaneously imitate the object as it truly is, so too must they necessarily imitate one another. Therefore, just like the apprehension of the object, there is a mutual apprehension of each other, since the very form of the object is the cause of its perception.

If it is argued that an object cannot be an object without a cause, [we reply: in that case, there is no conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*), because even when that conformity exists, there is a deviation from its being a valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*). Furthermore, consciousness does not acquire any distinct quality other than the mere imitation of the form of that which is intended as the objective support (*ālambana*).

Moreover, that [conformity] characterized by being born from and conforming to [the object]—just as in the case of blueness—is all the more subject to deviation regarding insentience (*jaḍātman*), since it occurs in multiple continua where different cognitions perceive the same object.
And as for its being the cause of determination in certain cases...
here is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): therefore, depending upon both the eye and form, visual cognition arises.

If it is asked how that which belongs to a different time can be apprehended, those who know the truth and understand reasoning declare that its very status as an object of cognition consists in its capacity to impart its form to the cognition.
For even though an effect arises by following [its cause] despite having multiple causes,
it is said that its form is grasped therein by that [cause] as well.
"For it connects this [cognition] with the object; for indeed, there is no way to do so except by means of the form of the object.
Therefore, the means of attaining the cognizable is the form of the cognizable itself. — Pramāṇavārttika 3.247–48.
Neither its production, nor its conformity [to the object], nor its ascertainment possesses the status of being a cause for validity here, whether collectively or individually.
— Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra, Verse 58:
If the definition of an object of cognition consists in similarity to it and arising from it,
then a subsequent cognition having the same object would itself be an object of cognition.
— Pramāṇavārttika 3.324,
Pūrvapakṣa: Even perception, though itself free from conceptual construction, possesses the capacity to give rise to conceptual construction.
Therefore, by means of that [perception], it becomes a constituent part of all worldly transactions without exception—
*Tattvasaṃgraha* verse 1306.
The arising of perception does not occur solely through the power of the object, but rather also through the power of the eyes and other sense faculties.

If it is argued that the object appears there in the perception because the perception conforms to the form of the object, and not the instrument [of cognition] because it does not conform to its form, then the instrument ought to appear as the object; yet it does not, because there is no distinction [between them]. Even though there is no distinction in the nature of being produced from that [object], the claim that perception has an external object as its domain based on the restriction of its determination (*adhyavasāya*) is unsubstantial; for then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of determining even the material cause (*upādāna*), just as one determines color and so forth.
— *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 188.
[In the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
108; and the *Sammatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 510:
