Because [the cognition] has that same form (*tādrūpya*) through objects that are similar, because it arises from those [objects] such as the sense organs, and because both of these [factors] arise from objects that are similar and from immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), [this definition] is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the triad [of factors] due to a cognition of a yellow form with respect to a white conch shell.
— Prameyaratnamālā 2.9; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 20.10.158.
Praṇidhānacaryā 4.47;
Ratnākarāvatāra 4.47

Regarding the question: "How can there be mutual observation among those perceptions (*dṛṣṭi*) or visions (*darśana*) whose senses are in close proximity and in contact with a single object characterized as a dancer? [The author] says: Because of the cognition of each other's form—that is, because of their mutual similarity—if there were not such mutual observation, then there would be no observation of a single object, meaning no apprehension of that one object. In that case as well, the cause of apprehension is simply similarity (*sārūpya*), and the point is that this is an invariable factor.
Explaining the verse regarding similarity in meaning (*ekārtha-sārūpya*), he says: "Of those whose views are bound together with a single object," and so forth.

For those persons whose views are fixed upon a single object simultaneously, an imitation of the object as it truly is necessarily entails a mutual imitation of one another; therefore, just like the perception of the object, how could there not be a mutual perception? To this he says: "The very nature of the object," and so forth, raising the objection of the opponent's view: "It is not without a cause," and so forth.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "In that case, [the cognition] would not possess conformity with the object," and so forth.

Why? He says: "Because even when that conformity with the object exists, there is a deviation from its being a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*); if it is argued that [it is still] an object by the aforementioned reasoning..."
It should be observed—page 188, note 7:

Now, if it is argued that there is deviation from that [conclusion] based on mere similarity, and that a specific distinction [of the effect] arises from the cause which is non-deviant; to this he replies: "And from what kind of cause? [The answer is: "From that which is intended as the objective support (*ālambana*)," by which the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and others are excluded. Consciousness does not indeed, nor at all, obtain any other distinction apart from the imitation of its form; the meaning is that it obtains only the distinction of imitating its cause.
If it is argued, "Let it be so," the author replies with the words beginning "But that... and so forth.
By the phrase "even more so" (*svatarām*), he demonstrates that there is a similarity [of the cognition] even with its own self, just as there is with the blueness.
Furthermore, in order to refute [the opponent's argument regarding] birth and so forth, he says "Its birth... and so forth.
Why? He says: "those whose objects are similar," and so forth.

Those philosophical systems (*darśana*) whose objects (*artha*) are similar—that is, identical—are called "those with similar objects. Because these [perceptions] occur within their various and non-various continua (*santāna*), that is, because they occur within the continua of perceptions of similar objects, there is similarity of birth and form.

For instance, just as the body of an offspring born from the body of a father is sometimes of the same shape as that [father's], so too the mind of that offspring is sometimes observed to be of the same shape as the [father's] mind; for it is well known that the mental activities of the produced and the producer, such as renunciation and so forth, are generally identical.

Furthermore, the thought of a child is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the mind of the progenitor; otherwise, there would be the perception of another's mind by an ordinary person, which is a contradiction. Likewise, even though the body is perceived, the intellect (*buddhi*) is not perceived, because there is doubt regarding the conceptualization of the intellect, and so forth.
Similarly, in the case of a single continuum where objects are perceived as identical, those two [the object and its cognition] are distinct, because they arise separately.

For instance, from a blue object arises the cognition of blue, and from that, further successive cognitions of blue arise having that same form; yet these are not valid means of knowledge regarding that [external object], for it would follow that there would be no engagement with it externally.

The specific characteristic of similarity— by the word "etcetera," the cooperative and dominant conditions are to be understood— is contradicted by the definition of similarity as being produced from those [conditions].
Because one observes the engagement in identical acts of giving and so forth among those whose minds are like their fathers, there is similarity of birth and appearance.

Regarding the cognition of blue previously, it might be thought: "From those [atoms] there is only birth, not that [cognition] has their form; even if the object were not [itself] blue, it would appear as blue. If this is argued, then [the response is]: "Because it appears as the nature of consciousness, it is the same even in relation to consciousness itself."
If it is argued that [the subsequent cognition] arises from that much alone and not from the blue-form; no, for this would entail a partial relationship of producer and produced.

Thus, the preceding cognition is the producer of the subsequent one by virtue of its being of the nature of awareness (*bodha*), but not by virtue of its being of the nature of blue. Likewise, the subsequent [cognition] is produced in such a way that its having that form [of blue] follows from awareness; if it were likewise to follow from the blue object, then the object would be redundant. If it is argued that the object is not redundant; even so, the aforementioned fault is not avoided.

Alternatively, it has been stated that it is not contradictory for a single [cognition] to imitate multiple forms; otherwise, how could your omniscient knowledge imitate all the various forms of blue? If you think: "The first cognition of blue arises without a prior cognition of blue, so its blueness is not produced by the blueness of a prior cognition; the same applies elsewhere," that is not sound. Because, as far as possible, there exists a causal relationship [between them], it remains established that [your position] contradicts the definition of [cognition] as having the likeness of what produces it (*tajjanmasārūpya*).

If it is argued that [the subsequent cognition] is not like that because it is accompanied by a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), to this he replies: "Its being the cause of that determinative judgment, and its being the cause of the determinative judgment regarding the object-image, is subject to deviation.
Why? He says: "In some cases," etc.;
for the later cognitions of blue arise merely from the preceding cognitions of blue, yet they do not possess that same form.
Its having that form consists in the arising of a favorable conceptual construction by virtue of its mere nature as consciousness; this is its determination (*adhyavasāya*).
If it is argued that [the cognition] is fallacious because it deviates—
since a cognition produced by the knowledge of yellowness in a white conch shell deviates from the immediately preceding cognition—

and if it is further argued that, since no other alternative is possible, there is thus simply no apprehension of an external object, which would be like a Buddhist's "floating on ghee in milk-porridge," then the author replies: "restricted to each respective object," and so forth.

Cognition is restricted to each respective object; even though it possesses the same origin as that object and a similarity to it, and even though there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it, cognition has the object as its domain.
Thus, even when the grasping of an object is common [to both], there is no contradiction whatsoever in [the cognition] taking the object as its domain without [the object itself] being the cause.
Since even past perception does not appear [in the present],

and since the status of an object is established for a future thing despite its current non-existence, we do not perceive any difference between the senses, words, and cognitions regarding the comprehension of their respective objects, on account of their non-contradiction in worldly practice.

Since a difference in appearance does not necessarily entail a difference in the underlying entity, he asks: "What is the nature of cognition that is restricted to each respective object? and answers with the words beginning "pratyartha" (with respect to each object).
"Even when what [is present]? To this he says: "That birth," etc., showing the meaning of the verse with the words "even though equal," and so forth.

And thus, in that manner, when there is the apprehension of an object, for a cognition that takes an object as its domain even though it is not the cause of that apprehension of the object, there is no contradiction characterized by sublation through perception or other means of valid cognition.
If it is argued that there would be no correspondence (*saṃvāda*); to this he says: "Of correspondence," and so forth—this has already been established.
Even so, if it is argued that non-contradiction resides only in its own cause; to this he says: "Even of perception," and so forth.
The meaning is that [the cognition] does not appear within the nature of knowledge because it has passed away, because its similarity [to the object] is denied, and because a real cause is refuted.

Now, if it is argued: "But a cognition whose object is a future thing is without an object, since at that time the object is impossible and thus does not appear therein; how then can there be non-discrepancy for this [cognition]? To this he says: "Of the future," and so forth.

Even though a future object, such as death and the like, is absent at present—at the time of an ill omen (*ariṣṭa*) and so on—its status as an object is established, because it is established as being within the range of a cognition produced by the sign of an ill omen; thus, there is non-discrepancy.
Why is this so? He says: "In worldly practice," and so forth.

[Objection: Surely, if death and the like are future, how can they be within the scope of a prior manifestation? That which has not yet arisen is called "future"; and what has not arisen, like the horn of a donkey, cannot be its object. Otherwise, it would not be "future," but rather like a present jar or similar thing. Therefore, the cognition of a future object is without an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*). To this, he replies: "The sense organ," and so forth.

Regarding the cognition of an object that is the effect of both the sense-organ (*akṣa*) and the word (*śabda*), the mention of "cognition of the word" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); by this, all cognition—whether its object is future, indistinct, or otherwise—is included.
We perceive no difference or distinction between these two with respect to the comprehension of their respective objects.
He thinks as follows: just as a future object does not exist at the time of its cognition, so too the object of perception does not exist in that [future] place.

For it is not the case that all objects determined by perception are established within the self as their substratum such that they are perceived as being neither in a different location nor at a different time; what, then, is the basis for this distinction? Even future things are not denied existence at their own time; otherwise, they would be present. And even that which is present is "future" in relation to something else.

Now, why is it said—"no difference is stated"—and "we do not perceive any difference"? If it is argued that such a difference exists, being caused by the distinction between clarity and its opposite, the author replies here with the words "difference in appearance," and so forth.
The phrase "no difference is stated" has been written again [to emphasize] the absence of any interval.

Since a difference in appearance does not necessarily entail a difference in the underlying reality, one might think: "It is not because verbal cognition lacks clarity that it is said to be without an object, but rather because the universal (*sāmānya*) grasped by it is not a real entity, and that [non-reality] is due to its being a cognition of an unreal object. To this, he says: "From its own cause," etc.—[meaning] even the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is its own cause exists internally and externally, just like the conceptualized [object].
Neither perception nor inference is non-deceptive with respect to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

Non-deceptiveness regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is consistent with reality; for the intentions of individual perceivers are not fixed, and to conform to them would result in the contradiction of one's own philosophical position.
Dharma [is established] through reality by way of tradition; nor can the establishment of reality be achieved through conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) whose objects are non-beneficial.

Even if for some there were an ascertainment of reality in some manner regarding what is false, that too would be a false conceptual construction—how, then, could there be the realization of reality from such a source? For it is the non-contradiction regarding the determination of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) [that constitutes reality].
That is not so... because of contradiction; nor is it conceptual, since from the perspective of ultimate reality it does not have that as its object;
for that very reason, non-conceptual cognition is not non-contradictory even according to the intention of the commentator.
Just as [external objects],

such as their own causes and their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), should be understood— like conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and like universals (*sāmānya*)— to have unreal things as their objects of cognition,
so he says, beginning with "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha*).

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consists of momentary, partless atoms; however, perception is not non-erroneous with respect to that, according to the reasoning already stated. For this very reason, it is not inferential either. Why? To this he says: "internally and externally," etc. He explains the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "in the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), and so forth.

If it is argued that its non-contradictoriness is "proper" (*yuktam*)—meaning consistent with reality (*yathātattvam*)—insofar as it does not deviate from reality, by virtue of the intention of the cognizer; to this he replies: because the intentions of cognizers are not fixed, it is not tenable that reality is "proper" in that way. For by imitating them—that is, by conforming to the intentions of the cognizers—one contradicts one's own position.
He states this with the words beginning "Dharma... and so forth.

If it is argued that "let it be according to reality (yathātattvam)," he says in response: "In reality," and so forth. [The opponent objects: "Surely, from non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*) arises the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of conceptualization (*vikalpa*); from that, conceptualization; and from that, the establishment of reality (*tattvavyavasthā*). Therefore, this [establishment] proceeds from conceptualization. To this he replies: "Through a succession," and so forth. If it is argued, "Let that be so for those very [conceptualizations]," he replies: "And the establishment of reality is not achieved by conceptualizations whose objects are unreal (*anartha-viṣaya*)."

If it is argued that the determination of that [particular] occurs through a succession of conceptual constructions that are indirectly connected to the real object (*vastu*), to this he replies: "Even if they are false," and so forth. Even if some conceptual constructions are false, how could there be a determination of reality (*tattva*) by some means or through some kind of indirect connection? This being the case, even such [a determination] would be false. From where, then, could there be the realization of reality from a conceptual construction? For if one asks how there could be non-contradiction regarding the determination of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) from that mistaken inference which realizes reality, the answer is: it simply would not exist.

He thinks as follows: There is no connection between some conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the object, whether through a direct sequence or otherwise. It cannot be from a non-conceptual [awareness], because the object is not made an object of that [non-conceptual awareness], and because its establishment would follow from that very [non-conceptual] reality, just like momentary destruction and so forth.
Nor can it be from a conceptual construction that lacks an object; for if one were to establish the connection by means of another conceptual construction, there would be an infinite regress.
If, on the other hand, the connection of one [conceptual construction] with another is established by a single conceptual construction, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

By this, the proof [of self-awareness] based on the cognition of conceptualization as its own nature is refuted; for it is known that [self-awareness] is non-conceptual, because it does not discern an object and because it is free from the defects of conceptualization.
Because of the consequence of the faults introduced into the position of non-conceptual self-awareness by means of another conceptualization.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.
Why? He says: "Because of misconception (*vipratipatteḥ*)," which connects with "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).
Alternatively, it refers to a cognition that is either contrary to or opposed to conceptual construction; [the word *tasyāḥ*] refers to that [cognition].

If it is argued that conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) might be non-erroneous with respect to the reality of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇatattva*), [the author] says here: "Nor even... and so forth. Why? He says: "Because its object is not that," meaning because conceptual cognition does not, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), have the reality of the particular characteristic as its object. If it is argued that, although [conceptual cognition] is merely conceptual, it may nonetheless be non-erroneous with respect to that [particular characteristic] by virtue of the intention of the commentator; to this he replies: "Precisely for that reason"—namely, because its object is not that—or rather, because there is a contradiction regarding conceptual cognition itself, and because there is no comprehension of the non-conceptual, even according to the intention of the commentator, non-conceptual knowledge is not non-erroneous.
"Why? he asks, and says "externally," etc.
"Why even that? he asks, and says "just as," etc.
Establishing this very point, he says "perception," etc.

Perception does not depend upon conceptual determination (*niścaya*) regarding its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); moreover, the appearance of cognitions differs according to the presence or absence [of other factors].
Although perception grasps the object as excluded from everything else, it excludes the superimposition (*samāropa*) of non-blue and so forth; however, this is neither perception nor is it inferable.
Nor is this characteristic [of perception] applicable to mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*), because there would be the consequence that it lacks such a characteristic in dreams and the like;

for even though dreams and so forth exist, how could the mind and mental factors therein be perceptual? And why would they not be so? Because, since reality is partless, there is no clear manifestation, and because there is no determination through the exclusion of other possibilities. (From *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, Chapter 3)

39. Thus, [if one argues that] perception would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather regarding the universal (*sāmānya*), why is this so? He says: because it depends upon ascertainment (*niścaya*) with respect to its own universal; otherwise, the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would be entirely purposeless.

If it is argued that even with respect to that [universal], the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and therefore the logician (*yauga*)—in view of that [dependence]—maintains that the means of valid cognition is independent of it, then the author replies: "The proximity," and so forth. The meaning is that there is no difference in the appearance of the cognition—the perceptual awareness—with respect to the particular characteristic, whether due to its proximity or its otherness (non-proximity). In other words, there is no non-apprehension of its form [in the cognition].
"Yauga" means proximity (*sannikarṣa*); "yauga" is simply *yoga*, or else it refers to the proximity as conceived by the followers of Yoga.

Explaining the verse with the thought that such proximity might be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: even though perception grasps an object as excluded and withdrawn from everything—both of the same class and of different classes—it excludes the superimposition of non-blue and so forth; the meaning is that it does so in whichever aspect it produces a determinate cognition (*niścaya*).
If one asks, "What would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that very case? he says: "In the universal," and so forth.

Since this is so, therefore this [universal] is neither a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor is it inferable, because in the absence of direct perception there is an absence of inference.
If it is argued that "it is the means of valid cognition everywhere regarding what is experienced by oneself," he says here: "And not," and so forth.
Why has this also been explained? He says: "The effect," and so forth;
the effect is cognition (*jñāna*), and the cause is the object (*artha*). Of these two...

Of what nature are these two? They are the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). The object is the thing (*artha*), and the subject is cognition (*jñāna*); [the text says] "of those two which are either destroyed or otherwise," meaning that because there is no difference in their appearance, there is always the appearance of something gross.

If it is argued that since an external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is untenable when not subjected to critical analysis, let there be an internal particular instead; to this he replies: "Nor even... and so forth.

It is representation-only and not an external object; it is "mere representation" (vijñaptimātra), and this applies not only to what is external. This is the definition: the definition—that is, the manifestation—of this self-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) imagined by others is as follows: atoms of cognition do not appear [as external objects], just as a person [does not appear as an atom]; nor is it accepted by others that the reality of pleasure, blue, and so forth, appears as something distinct from consciousness.

If it is argued that even if [the existence of external objects] is accepted, why is the appearance of blue and so forth unreal? What confidence can there be in anything else? And from what source does its unreality derive? If it is said: "Because it appears as something to be grasped, like the hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia," to this he replies with the words "In dreams, etc. A dream is the beginning (*ādi*) of such delusions as those caused by cataracts or jaundice; thus it is so described. In that case, there would follow the consequence of the absence of its defining characteristic, and consequently the absence of the manifestation of cognition (*vijñapti*). Nor is that characteristic present even in the case of mere representation (*tanmātra*).
This is the intended meaning: just as there is an absence of an external object in an illusion, so too is there an absence of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) even in the appearance;
for since even that which does not exist in another continuum appears therein, if it exists there, what aversion can there be toward its existence elsewhere? Thus it has been examined.

If it is argued that, because there is no difference in appearance and because the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is absent, an object exists even in dreams and so forth just as in the waking state; to this he replies: "Even though an external object exists"—that is, even while it is present—how is it that at that time, during the dream and so forth, the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) possess the nature of being perceived, i.e., being graspable by direct perception? And why would they not be so? To him who asks thus, the author gives the answer: "Because of the absence of clear appearance" (*spaṣṭapratibhāsābhāvāt*). He states another reason: "of the partless reality" (*niraṃśatattvasya*), and so forth.

The exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that superimposition of the contrary is its non-existence; and because there is no determination (*anirṇaya*) of that [non-existence], since [it would otherwise follow] from the clear appearance [of the object] and from the determination of it—as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.39 and so forth—therefore, because the partless reality of cognition never appears and the contrary external object does appear, the implication is that for the Buddhist, reality would be reduced to that alone. This is the intended meaning.
The unreality of the appearance of blue and so forth [is established] because all entities, by their own nature,
are established in their respective natures and therefore participate in exclusions from both their own nature and other natures.

—*Pramāṇavārttika*: "In whichever [object] one produces this [cognition], in that alone lies its validity. Showing once again the refutation of this, he says: "Of the six cognitions," and so forth, referring to conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*).

If the six cognitions were to exist simultaneously, because their distinction would not be perceived in the absence of conceptualization, it would follow that even the conceptual mental cognitions must exist simultaneously. (26)

If it is argued that when desired objects such as sound and so forth are simultaneously present, their respective cognitions arise in succession; and that because each is separated by five [moments], a distinct interruption would be perceived for each due to the greater strength of the positive factor (*bhāvapakṣa*), then in the conceptualization "this is that very taste... therefore... and so on, there would follow the consequence of simultaneity in the perception of non-interruption among the conceptual sensory and mental cognitions whose nature consists in the determination of the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyavaccheda*).

For in that very case, the non-perception of a distinction is logical because there is no difference [between the objects]; furthermore, it would follow that even when there is a clear manifestation, there would be a coexistence of cognitions whose nature is the determination of the exclusion of others. This is the intended meaning here: just as the opponent's subsequent admission is that when sound and so forth are simultaneously present, six cognitions arise, so too [it applies] regarding those six.
Of which [cognitions]? Of the cognitions consisting of conceptualizations of form, taste, smell, touch, and sound.

When? At once. From what does their simultaneous existence arise? To this he says: "Because of the non-perception of distinction," that is, because in cases such as eating a *karkaṭī* fruit, there is no ascertainment by the cognition of a temporal interval between them.
Refuting this, he says: "Whose would simultaneous occurrence follow? [It would follow] for those whose mental cognitions (*manodhi*) are conceptual (*savikalpa*).

Because there is a plurality of efficient causes, a plurality of effects cannot be avoided at once; and thus, [the claim that] one sees a cow even while conceptualizing a horse, and so forth, would be contradicted.
Showing the reasoning of the opponent regarding the simultaneous occurrence of the six cognitions, he says: "In respect of sound and so forth," etc.

In respect of what kind of things? In respect of those—sound being the first among them, such as form and so forth—which are intended and present simultaneously; if their respective cognitions, i.e., the cognitions of sound and so forth, were admitted to arise in succession, then a separation would be perceived for each individual one, and there would be no simultaneous perception of sound and the rest.
Why? He says: "Because of the intervention of five [factors] for each.
The Buddhist raises the objection regarding the Naiyāyika position, beginning with "of the category of existence" (*bhāvapakṣasya*), etc.;
therein he states the refutation, beginning with "that very [thing] is the aesthetic flavor" (*sa eva rasaḥ*), etc.
The passage beginning with "tataḥ" is the conclusion.
Now, the Teacher, explaining the *kārikā*, says: "Thus," and so forth;
that is to say, if such a conceptualization were accepted, the consequence of simultaneous existence (*sahabhāva*) would follow.

Of what? He says: "conceptual" and so forth—namely, conceptual cognition (*savikalpamanas*) and sensory cognitions (*akṣajñāna*). Of those again, of what? He says: "exclusion of others" (*tadanyavyavaccheda*) and so forth.

The construction of the words is as follows: "the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of one thing from another" refers to the exclusion of those cognitions from others, which is the "exclusion of the other" (*tad-anyavyavaccheda*); the "ascertainment" (*vyavasāya*), that is, the determination (*nirṇaya*), which is the very nature (*ātmā*) of those cognitions—that is, of those consciousnesses (*saṃvidām*), meaning of the mental conceptualizations (*manovikalpānām*).

Under what condition does this occur? He says: "upon the perception of their non-interruption" (*tad-aviccheda-pratītau*). That is, when there is the perception of the non-interruption of those conceptual cognitions produced by the mind and the senses; for indeed, in the absence of those consciousnesses whose nature is the ascertainment of the exclusion of the other, there can be no perception of their non-interruption.

If it is argued, "What is to be done with those [conceptual cognitions], since the existence of that perception [of difference] occurs through those very cognitions of the object itself?"—to this he says: "For in that very [state]," and so forth.

For it is logical that there is no discernment (*anupalakṣaṇa*) of exclusion—that is, of differentiation from others—only when those very determinate cognitions (*vyavasāyātmaka-saṃvitti*) exist; but not when non-conceptual cognitions (*avikalpa-jñāna*) exist.
Why? To this he says: "That," and so forth.

If it is argued that those conceptual cognitions are not [inherently] non-conceptual because they are not distinguished from sleep and so forth, but rather that other conceptual cognitions possess a clear manifestation precisely because they are followed by conceptual cognitions produced by the mind and the senses— and that for this very reason they are characterized as such— the author replies here: "Even in the case of a clear manifestation," and so forth.

Then, one might think that there would follow the consequence of the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions whose nature consists in the determination of the exclusion of others; [one might argue] that immediately after the six cognitions, a single conceptual mental cognition (*manojñāna*) arises which determines those [six], and therefore this fault does not apply. That is not so, because it would entail the fallacy of non-exclusivity (*anekānta*). Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Of the clear," and so forth.

Since even an illusion such as a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*) is clearly perceived, the perceptions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) do not consist of the observation of a single moment.

If, at every moment, partless, momentary atoms were directly perceived in their mutual non-overlapping, how could there be an illusion of a wheel? And if that [illusion] occurs, how would it not establish the non-one-sided nature (*anekānta*) [of reality], given the contradiction between the perception and non-perception of that [wheel]?

The word "api" (even/also) indicates a shift in the logical sequence. Therefore, the proof of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is established not only because of the observation of the delusion consisting of a single conceptual construction (*antareka-vikalpa-vibhrama*), but also because of the observation of a clear delusion such as that of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*).

If it is argued: "But surely, since cognitions differ with every atom and every moment, there is no single cognition of a variegated fire-brand wheel," the author replies: "Of the perceptions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇopalabdhi*)," etc. The perception of momentary atoms is not a delusion, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
With the words "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse: "At every moment" means at each and every instant.

In what [objects]? In partless, momentary atoms (*paramāṇu*). With respect to each individual atom, in perceptions that are direct (*pratyakṣa*), there is indeed no mutual blending; for if there is no variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), how could there be an illusion of a wheel (*cakrabhrānti*)? The point is that there is no such thing as a visual perception that observes a single [atom]. And when that illusion of a wheel occurs—that is, when it arises—how could it not be the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), [how could it not be] the cognition of non-absolutism? It certainly would be.

Now, [the opponent argues that] for those who approach the different points of the firebrand (*alāta*), even though there is no perception of their mutual distinction, a delusion of a wheel (*cakrabhrānti*) arises because one perceives only a common luminosity (*bhāsuratāmātra*). To this, he replies: "In the perception of that," and so forth.

Because there is a contradiction between the perception of those specific characteristics of the firebrand (*alātasvalakṣaṇa*) as mere luminosity and the non-perception of them in the form of mutual distinction, one of the two must be either visible or invisible; thus, the non-contradictory nature (*anekāntasiddhi*) of each individual spoke of the wheel is established.
Showing that the proof of non-absolutism (anekānta) is established not only by the method just described, but even without it, he says: "From perception," and so forth.
"Other objects than perception, inference, and the like, are within my range"—this knowledge, which is consistent with scripture, is the praise of Syādvāda. (28)
The non-establishment of the reality of objects through the cessation of mental states whose measure has been calculated depends upon non-absolutism (anekānta) therein;
from that direct perception,
there arises the praise of the teaching of Syādvāda— namely, "it may exist," and so forth— from the object as cognized by direct perception.

Immediately following that, because it is conducive to it, there is likewise the praise of *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects) arising from the object of inference—such as the moment-by-moment transformation (*pratikṣaṇapariṇāma*) and so forth—which is to be understood through inference; "and so forth" refers to the domain of the mind and other such objects. Furthermore, there are other objects that fall outside the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumeya*), and the like.

Of what nature are they? They are beyond the range of our perception like those such as ourselves; they are perceived only by yogins. Thus, according to scripture, that non-contradictory knowledge concerning objects such as *dharma* is also a praise of that [scripture].
What is the use of saying more? Even the opening of the eyes does not exist without the principle of manifoldness (*anekānta*).
It is the very opening of the eye [that perceives it].
In order to explain the verse, he says: "Enumerated," and so forth.

Regarding those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) enumerated by the Buddhists and others, their "function" (*vṛtti*) consists of the engagement for the sake of establishing something positive and the withdrawal from something to be negated. The "reality" (*tattva*) of their objects—whether of the nature of sentient beings or otherwise—is their character as consisting of affirmation and negation. The establishment of that [reality] depends upon non-absolutism (*anekānta*). Perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) depends on this because the establishment of the reality of the object occurs through its function;
explaining this dependence, he says: "Perception," and so forth.
Why? He says: "In that regard," and so forth;
"in that regard" means in perception (*pratyakṣa*).
He demonstrates that very point with the words beginning "for instance" (*tathā hi*).

For it has been established as follows: the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is non-conceptual, like an unreal construction, unknowable, inexpressible, and absolutely "not this" (neti). || 29 ||
How could the intrinsic nature of cognitions not be established by themselves? [It cannot be,] because they are non-determinative in nature.

Nor is it logical for that which is eternal to have an occasional manifestation, since such a manifestation is invariably concomitant with transformation. Furthermore, the opponent’s conceptualization—that perception regarding those [cognitions] is itself non-determinative—is contradicted by experience, as it would conflict with the fact that such [non-determinative] cognition is an error.
In all cases... [there is] contradiction... "the reality which is of that nature," "absolute," and "non-conceptual perception" is understood to follow [from the context].

Of what nature is it? To this he says: "it is like a non-existent construction"—that is, devoid of the conceptualization that "it exists"; it is a conceptual cognition that grasps objects as being either absolutely different or non-different in their meaning.

What follows from this? He says: "If it is argued that the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is unknowable and merely inexpressible," he replies to this: "It is more appropriate to say 'it is merely inexpressible' in this way [as a negation], not merely 'inexpressible'. Showing that this has been stated not only here but elsewhere as well, he says: "And thus the particular has been established."
What has been established? To this he says: "Of the nature," and so forth.

Why is there not the self-evident establishment (*svataḥ-siddhi*) of the nature of the self—that is, of cognitions which are partless perceptions? To this he says: because they consist of non-determination (*avyavasāyātmaka*), due to the absence of the nature of determination (*vyavasāya-svabhāva*) in them.
If it is argued that [the object] exists through another [means of knowledge], he says in response: "Nor is it so through another," meaning that there is no manifestation of such partless [entities].
Demonstrating that even the absolute distinction [between objects] has no manifestation, he says "na ca" and so forth:
it is not at all logical for an eternal entity, such as the self (*ātman*), to be perceived only occasionally.
Why? He says: "That," and so forth.
If it is argued that because there is an inseparable connection between that vision and transformation, transformation would belong to it; to this he replies: "Nor even," and so forth.

If it is argued that even for one who investigates, the perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) which has that [object] as its exclusive object does not cease because of the resulting ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), the author replies here with the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth:
"That" refers to that which has that [object] as its exclusive object—what is it? It is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Of what nature is it? He says: "of a non-resolute nature. Thus, the conceptualization of others is contradicted by experience, because the manifold (anekānta) appears in experience.
If it is argued that this is an illusion, he replies with the words beginning "that" (tad), because that appearance of the manifold is incompatible with being an illusion.

If it is argued that the objection is the same for the doctrine of manifoldness (anekānta) as it is for the doctrine of absolute unity (arthaikānta), because manifoldness likewise does not appear [as a distinct entity], he says in response: "In all cases," and so forth.
If it is argued that even if that cognition were to occur, it is nonetheless untenable due to contradiction, he says in response: "Contradiction," and so forth.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That which consists of that"—namely, reality whose nature is manifoldness.
Why? He says: "In the case of absolute [monism]," and so forth.
If it is argued that the realization of non-absolutism (anekānta) is the truth and that it is inexpressible, he replies here: "In some way," and so forth.
The ineffability of reality is accepted in some sense, but not in every respect.
In the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), what is said to whom, and how can there be the establishment of causal efficiency?
Let this matter rest for now.

If it is argued that the reality is intended to be "inexpressible" in the sense of being somehow simultaneously existent and so forth—by way of demonstrating such attributes—but that it is "inexpressible in every respect," [the author] says here: "In every respect," etc.
If it is then argued that the reality must therefore be expressible, [the author] says here: "In mere cognition," etc.
In a mere partless cognition and in selflessness, what statement could there be regarding what object? The sense is that this entire [system], when scrutinized, is untenable.
He states another refutation: "What causal efficiency? and so forth;
in every such extreme view, there is no stability whatsoever for causal efficiency, whether in the form of an agent or a cognizer.
He explains the *kārikā* with the words "Let it be for now," and so forth;
everything is easy to understand.
Having thus defined the nature of sound, he now states the final verse—beginning with "By means of divisions"—in order to demonstrate [the distinctions] based on that [nature].

Leading to a distinction between word and meaning through various divisions such as the nature of the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth, the present view (*pratyutpanna-naya*) intends to further specify the word— Anuogaddārā 4.2.
The word [used] is intended to exclude deviation regarding gender, number, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and so forth; [Āvaśyakaniryukti, Gāthā 757; Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya, Gāthā 2718].
— Sāṃkhyasūtra 1.33:
Due to the differences in time, grammatical case, and gender, a word effects a difference in meaning.
That which is mounted upon [the word] through its various synonyms is thus the locus of action—
*Laghīyastraya*, verse 44.

The *śabdanaya* (linguistic standpoint) is inclined toward grasping the meaning following the word, because it is intent upon the cessation of deviation regarding gender, number, tense, grammatical case, person, and voice.
— *Dhavalāṭīkā*, *Satprarūpaṇā*, verse 84, page 272;
*Nayaviniścaya*, verse 84.
Nyāyakumuda p. 639; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 678; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā p. 312.
*Nayacakragāthā* 40;
*Tattvārthasāra*, p. 107; *Prakaraṇa-naya* 7.
32, 33 *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 313; *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 22.

The *samabhirūḍha* [naya] is that which has as its object the specific application [of a term]; it is the transition from one thing to another based on the distinction between synonyms and their respective meanings.
In the *anuyogadvāra*, it is stated: "In the *samabhirūḍha* [naya], there is a transition from one state to another, even when the substance is not present.
(Anu. 4, Dvā.)

The *samabhirūḍha* [naya] is the non-transference [of a word's meaning] among existing objects; see *Tattvārthādhigamasūtra-bhāṣya* 1.34. *Āvaśyakaniryukti-gāthā* 758; *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya-gāthā* 2727.
The *samabhirūḍha* [etymological] [naya] is so called because it ascends to various distinct meanings— *Samayasāra-saṃgrahaṇī*, 1.35.
Alternatively, one who has ascended to something is "samabhirūḍha" (conventionally designated) because of having ascended to it by meeting with it face-to-face— Tattvārthavārttika 1.5.33.

*Samabhirūḍha*: Thus, when there is a state of facing toward [the object] through the unification of thought, the cognition that "the object is indeed one alone, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth," is *samabhirūḍha*—[Nayacakravṛtti, p.

The *samabhirūḍha* standpoint consists in the ascent to distinct meanings through the differentiation of synonymous words; its determination is as previously described—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 273.
*Nayaviniścaya*, verse 92; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 680;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, page 313.
*Nayacakra*, verse 41;
*Tattvārthasāra*, page 107; *Prakaraṇapāda-naya*, verse 7.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 314; Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, page 22.

The method of "having become thus" (itthambhūtanaya) consists of words expressing an action marked by the suffix -syāt-kāra; it distinguishes the literal meaning (vaṃjaṇa), the intended meaning (attha), and both of them— thus is the "evambhūta" [method].— Anuyogadvāra-sūtra,
Āvaśyaka-niryukti, Gāthā 758.
The *evambhūta* [naya] pertains to both the word and its meaning;
this is stated in the *Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya*, verse 2743.

"Having become [the object] through that very nature, one determines it by means of that same [nature]; thus it is 'thus-become' (*evambhūta*). Alternatively, having become—that is, having transformed—through that very self, which is to say through that very cognition, one determines [the object] by means of that same [cognition].
35 *Dhavalāṭī*, Satpra., p. 90; *Jayadhavalā*, p. 29.
The object is the transformation of that action; because it is determined to be exactly so, one who is averse to other actions would be led by such [an agent]—Tattvasaṃgrahaślokavārttika, p. 274.
*Nayaviniścaya*, verse 94; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 680;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, page 314.
*Nayacakra*, verse 43;
*Tattvārthasāra*, page 107; *Prakaraṇapāda-naya*, 7.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 315; Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, page 23.
Those who perceive reality understand that the portion measured by that [word] is in no way separate from it.

The meaning of a word, which is synonymous with its *vyañjana* (phonetic manifestation), leads to the differentiation—that is, the manifoldness—of that [meaning]; therefore, it is to be understood and expressed through those [differentiations].
By what kind of differentiations? To this he says: "the factor" (*kāraka*), and so forth.
Observing that [the term] "abhirūḍha" has been employed, he says: "The meaning is that the *abhirūḍha-naya* is the object of conventional usage (*abhirūḍhi*).
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "It is a synonym," and so forth;
[it is so called] because it distinguishes word-meanings by means of synonyms (*paryāya*).

Explaining what is meant by "in such a state" (*itthaṃbhūta*), he asks: "What is that which is to be described as being 'in such a state'? He replies: "It is a word expressing an action. The examples for these [categories] should be understood in their respective order from the *Nyāyapraveśaka-prakaraṇa*.
He asks: "Who is 'we' (*vayaḥ*) or who is 'another' (*anya*)? He replies: "The particle *syāt*," and so forth.
It is understood that the other [system] is a fallacious method (*durṇaya*).

That which is measured by that correct method (*samyannaya*)—the aspect of the object so measured—is not in any way separate from its own nature in its entirety; thus do the Tīrthakarās and others, who perceive reality, understand [it] through the natures of the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth.
It is marked with the seal from the *Nayapraveśaka-prakaraṇa*, which is included within the *Laghīyastraya*; this is the remainder [of the title].
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the *Śabdanayasiddhi*, in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by Anantavīrya.
The Twelfth Chapter: The Establishment of the Deposits (Nikṣepasiddhi)
Immediately following the method (*naya*), in order to demonstrate the deposits (*nikṣepa*) which are its fruit, he states the introductory verse beginning with "The deposit is of infinite types.
The deposit is of infinite types, yet it is fourfold according to the minimum; it serves the purpose of explaining the subject at hand.
A deposit (*nyāsa*) is a placement for the sake of comprehension, both in terms of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and its formal arrangement (*vidhāna*).
"Deposition" (nikṣepa) means that which casts [an object] into its definitive determination and ascertainment according to the true meaning of reality. (Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya 1.5)

—*Dhavalā* commentary: For what purpose is this [section] on the "thorough examination of the existent" (*satprarūpaṇā*)? It is for the sake of refuting that which is not the subject under discussion and for the thorough examination of that which is the subject under discussion.
—*Satyaśāsana-siddhānta* 1.
Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti, verse 76:

Now, if it is asked why this method of presentation (nikṣepa) is employed, it is said: there are three types of listeners—the uninitiated, one who has understood all the intended meanings of the subject matter, and one who has understood the intended meanings only partially.

In that regard, the first person, being unlearned, determines the meaning of the intended word; the second person doubts what meaning is applicable to this word, or, taking up a meaning other than the contextual one, he misunderstands it;
and like the second person, the third person also either doubts or misunderstands.

In this regard, if [the person] is unlearned and seeks the meaning through synonyms (*paryāya*), the categories (*nikṣepa*) are taught by way of making the unlearned learned, in order to exclude what is irrelevant.

Alternatively, if [he is one who] seeks the meaning through substance (*dravya*), they are taught by way of that [substance] in order to define the relevant subject. All categories are stated because a definitive determination of the positive injunction (*vidhi*) is impossible without a definitive determination of the distinct properties (*vyatireka-dharma*).
Furthermore, for the destruction of doubt regarding the second and third [categories], all categories are explained.
For those two very [persons] who are acting in reverse, a summary (nikṣepa) is made for the purpose of ascertaining the subject matter at hand;

for it has been said: "It is for the sake of understanding and for warding off [misconceptions], for the purpose of explaining what has been stated, for the destruction of doubt, and for the ascertainment of the true meaning."
—Dhavala-Ṭīkā, Satprarūpaṇā, p. 30:

Since it brings about the differentiation [of objects] according to its capacity, it constitutes the basis for the cognition of the meaning of words—which is the cause of the knowledge of reality, the domain of the two-fold *naya*, and the dispeller of doubt.
Because one perceives conceptual constructions regarding the objects of hearing within the expressive words for those things to be expressed, there arises [the following]:
1. The placement (*nikṣepaṇa*), the application (*yojana*), or the superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*) of attributes that have been understood through reasoning upon a certain subject (*dharmin*).

How many kinds of this placement are there? He says: "Of infinite varieties," meaning it has endless divisions because its objects are infinite. If so, why is placement said elsewhere to be fourfold? He says: "Having at least four varieties," meaning that which possesses at least four internal forms or divisions characterized by name (*nāman*), representation (*sthāpanā*), substance (*dravya*), and mode (*bhāva*).

"What is its purpose? he asks, and replies: "Its purpose is the exposition of the subject at hand. The subject at hand is the matter contained within the introduction (*prastāva*). Its "exposition" (*vyākriyā*) is the thorough (*ā*) and complete (*samantāt*) treatment (*karaṇa*)—that is, the detailed explanation (*vyutpādana*)—characterized by the removal of what is undesirable and so forth; it is for that purpose.

Why? He says: "Because it is the cause of the knowledge of the reality of the categories," since the realities (*tattvārtha*) are the soul (*jīva*) and the rest, and this [work] is the cause (*hetu*) or means for their knowledge.
For there is no comprehension of an object from words and so forth without the application (*nikṣepa*) of words and so forth.

Why is that? He says: "It has the two-fold *naya* as its object; it does not exist elsewhere. This means that [the comprehension] does not arise from anything other than the *naya* characterized by the pair—namely, the *dravyārthika* (substantial) and *paryāyārthika* (modal) aspects—but rather from that alone; thus it is said to have that as its object.
It is not merely the cause for the knowledge of the true nature of reality, but also that which cuts through doubt; this is an indication of the exclusion of error and the like.

The distinction is that by the former [verse], its status as the cause for the knowledge of the reality of things was stated, while by this [verse], its status as the cause for the exclusion of superimposition is stated.

Why is it the cause for that knowledge? He says: "It is the limb of the word, the object, and the cognition. This means it is the cause—the instrumental factor—for that cognition which apprehends an object such as a jar, following upon the imitation of a word.
Why is even this so? He says: "Because it constructs [it]."
What [division]? Which division? In what manner? According to one's ability.
Of what? Of the things to be expressed, that is, the denotable objects.
Where? In the expressive words (vācaka).
Since this is so, therefore, for the sake of the understanding person, there is the application of the "deposit" (nikṣepa) following the arising of conceptualization regarding the objects heard:
"In whatever place and whatever [category] one may know, one should deposit the deposit without remainder."
Even where one might not know [the location], one should deposit the fourfold [set] there—
Tattvārthasūtra, etc., Anuyogadvāra-sūtra 8.
Its placement (nyāsa) is by way of name, representation, substance,
and state— Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.4.
Taking up the subject from its point of non-connection and explaining it, he says: "The *nyāsa*," and so forth.
"Point of connection" means the root aphorism (*mūlasūtra*).
Briefly stated, the *nyāsa* consists of name, representation, substance, and state (*bhāva*).
In detail, there is a classification of the *aṅgapraviṣṭa* (scriptures included within the limbs) and the *aṅgabāhyaśruta* (scriptures external to the limbs).
[The term] "name" (*nāma*) refers to the act of assigning a designation to any object whatsoever— without specifying particular attributes and independent of other causes—
since it is logically applicable to individual or collective objects, whether sentient (*jīva*) or insentient (*ajīva*).
Furthermore, another basis [for classification] is birth (jāti), which is divided into substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and action (kriyā),
according to the distinction between existence and non-existence therein.
"What is this [use] for? says the Buddhist; he is like one who, though mounted on a horse, has forgotten his horse.

Therefore, the "non-existent" mode of designation (*asadbhāva-nikṣepa*) intended here is the "substance-designation" (*dravya-nikṣepa*), which is the persistence of a specific, intended, and present modification (*paryāya-viśeṣa*).
According to the scripture,
the "positional designation" (*bhāvanikṣepa*) is likewise characterized by application and transformation; it is, in detail,
of infinite varieties, [including] its subdivisions such as sentient and non-sentient, and the complete [and incomplete].
"Name" (*nāma*) and "the act of designation" (*saṃjñākarma*) are synonymous— *Tattvārthādhi° Bhāṣya* 1.5.
The act of designation, which is applied by human effort for the sake of conventional usage toward an object that does not possess those qualities, is called "name."
— Sāṃkhyasūtravṛtti 1.5; Tattvavaiśāradī, Tattvasamāsabhāṣya, verse 1.
5 *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya* 65; *Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā*, p. 25.
Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya, Gāthā 11

Comparison: For some names denote a single living being, such as *Ḍittha*; some denote many living beings, such as *yūtha* (a herd); some denote a single non-living thing, such as *ghaṭa* (a jar); some denote many non-living things, such as *prāsāda* (a palace); some denote a single living being and a single non-living thing, such as *pratīhāra* (a doorkeeper); some denote a single living being and many non-living things, such as *kāhāra* (a cook); some denote many living beings and a single non-living thing, such as *mandurā* (a stable); and some denote many living beings and non-living things, such as *nagara* (a city). Thus, for the sake of worldly transaction, a name in the world is divided in many ways due to these internal subdivisions according to each object.
—Tattvasaṅgraha, verse 98. For comparison: "The intention of the speaker is stated to be the common cause of a name;
therefore, other causes such as genus (jāti) and so forth are held to be distinct causes."
—Tattvārtha-sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 99:

That which is established as a "living being" (jīva) in wood, cloth, paintings, dice, and so forth, is a "symbolic living being" (sthāpanājīva), just like an image of a deity, such as Indra, Rudra, Skanda, or Viṣṇu.
In the *Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya* (1.5), it is stated:
"Representation (*sthāpanā*) is that which is established as 'this is that' in relation to objects such as wood, cloth, paintings, or the casting of dice."
But that which is empty of its own object, yet has such a form through the intention directed toward that object— *Sāṃkhyasūtra-bhāṣya* 1.5.2.15.
That [representation] is established either as formless (nirākāra), temporary, or otherwise;
it is a representation (sthāpanā) consisting of an image, a symbol, and so forth, whether based on reality or unreality. (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya, Gāthā 26)
"Temporary and non-temporary is the installation (sthāpanā), while the name (nāman) lasts for the duration of life"—
thus [it is said in] the Bṛhatkalpa-bhāṣya, gāthā 13.
Restraint (niyama) is established through the presence of reality (sadbhāva-sthāpanā), or by way of unreality (asadbhāva) as "not having that form," like the pillar-Indra.
—*Nayacakravṛtti*, Liṅgapṛṣṭha, p.
381; *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 25:
"The establishment of something else, such as a snake, by means of its name, is 'establishment' (*sthāpanā*)."
It is twofold: establishment by existence (*sadbhāva-sthāpanā*) and establishment by non-existence (*asadbhāva-sthāpanā*).

Among these, establishment by existence occurs when the object possesses its essential qualities (*āgāravanta*); the opposite of that is establishment by non-existence—thus it is stated in the *Satprarūpaṇā* of the *Dhavalā*.
A substance that has assumed an orientation toward a specific future transformation, or that which does not yet exist as such— Tattvārthavārttika 1.111.
5th Taṇḍulaśloka, page 111; Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya 14.
*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, Gāthā 28;
*Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā*, p. 25; *Āvaśyaka-niryukti-malaya-vṛtti*, p. 6.
Substance characterized by its present mode is "bhāva" (the state of being) — *Siddhāntasāra*, *Tattvārthavārttika* 1.5.
*Tattvārthādhigamasūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 113;
*Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya*, gāthā 15;
*Āvaśyakaniryukti-malaya-vṛtti*, p. 9.

In brief—that is, in summary—the *nyāsa* (assignment) is the *nikṣepa* (deposition); it occurs by relying on these [fourfold categories] of name, representation, substance, and mode (*nāma-sthāpanā-dravya-bhāva*). In detail—that is, extensively—it consists of the various divisions of the *śruta* (scriptural knowledge) that is either "entered into the limbs" (*aṅgapraviṣṭa*) or "outside the limbs" (*aṅgabahiḥ*). The "limbs" (*aṅga*) refer to the *Ācārāṅga* and so forth; that *śruta* which has entered into them—that is, which is included within them—is the "entered into the limbs.
That *śruta* which is outside the limbs, its various divisions or distinctions, is what is thus described.
He explains the verse with the words beginning "of whom":
for any sentient being or other [entity] whose specific characteristics have not been specified, what is the act of naming? It is a name.

Of what nature is it? He says: "independent of other causes. That for which an action is performed is its cause; anything other than that, such as a kinsman and so forth, is the "other" (antara). That which has no dependence on such an "other" is described as such.
Demonstrating the distinction of that name, he says: "separated," and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) should be supplied, and the connection is with the word "name" (nāma).

Why? He says: because of the logical possibility (*upapatti*) of its being an object of both individual and collective [perception], as well as of being both singular and plural—that is, because it is logically possible for those very souls (*jīva*) to be its objects.
This is like [the expressions] "this lump of flesh is Devadatta" or "this is Devadatta," which illustrate the logical possibility of it being an object of individual souls;
and it is like [the expression] "all these are the Gargas," which illustrates the logical possibility of it being an object of collective souls.
Because it is logically consistent for this [term] to refer to a single soul— just as in cases such as "Nābheya" or "Purudeva"—
and because it is logically consistent for it to refer to multiple souls— as in "This is Ḍittha," "This is Ḍavittha," and "This is Jinadatta," which are four distinct types of souls—
and likewise because it is logically consistent for it to refer to individual non-souls (ajīva), [the term] *sajainendra* [is established].
3.2 Nūtya-jainendra 4.4
4. *kyaca* [is applied] after *jainendra*, etc., according to Pāṇini 3.1.142.
Because it is logically established that the scope [of the rule] encompasses all living beings, just as in the case of the Jaina rule "bhū-ādayo dhātavaḥ" (Jainendra-sūtra 1.2.1) and others.
Because it is possible for [the term] to have a single soul as its object— just as in the case of "space," "time," "dharma," and "adharma"—
and because it is possible for it to have multiple souls as its object, those two [terms, *sat* and *jīva*,] [denote the same thing], according to the Jaina doctrine (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa 2.2.2).
Just as in [verse] 105, what further reason is there for these four alternatives to be called "independent" (*anapekṣa*)? To this he says: "Furthermore, another reason," and so forth.
In expressions such as "cow," the universal (jāti) is the meaning; in expressions such as "staff-bearer," the substance (dravya) is the meaning;
and in expressions such as "white cloth," the quality (guṇa) is the meaning.
In cases such as "cook" (pācaka),
a name is applied elsewhere through the operation [of the word] by means of action, genus, and so forth.
The genus "cowness" is another mark of the non-living.

If a word, while residing in a universal (jāti) and so forth, requires another cause [for its application]— just as the act of cooking requires the substance of fuel— then there would be an infinite regress.

If it is argued that since [the term] occurs there, let it likewise occur elsewhere; what is the use of postulating a different basis for its application? No; for verbal usage is observed in both ways. Even by Prajñākara, who raises this objection, the designation "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is applied to external objects with respect to their being graspable by perceptual cognition, and not otherwise, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For this very reason, the designation "perception" is applied to cognitions with respect to the clarity characterized by dependence on the sense organs (*akṣa*); such is the portion [of the definition], Hetubindu, p. 53.

In this context, the word "part" (*aṃśa*) is not applied with reference to anything whatsoever. And as it has been said: "Words express that which is conventionally agreed upon" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.91). Furthermore, that convention depends upon people engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*); only those practitioners of transaction know [the convention]. What is the use of your exertion in this matter? You should simply conform to them; otherwise, even the consideration of [categories like] the imperceptible would be cast far away from worldly practice. If there were practitioners who followed you, they too would be seen to use words in both ways (as you do and as others do); therefore, this [objection of yours] is trivial.

For that part is indeed its very nature—this would be the reason. One might ask: what would the application of a word to a particular (viśeṣa) by means of a genus (jāti) and so forth be called? It is called "designation" (sthāpanā), because a word for one thing is superimposed upon another, just like the word "Arhat" when applied to that which does not actually exist as such.
For this very reason, the description of *sthāpanā* follows immediately after *nāma*.
He states the divisions of *sthāpanā* immediately after *nāma* with the words beginning "sthāpanā," and asks: "Why? He replies with the words beginning "sadbhāva."
He explains the establishment of existence through the words "In that regard," and so forth.

The Buddhist asks: "What is the purpose of this [establishment], since [the object] exists otherwise? This person, though mounted on a horse, has forgotten his horse, because he himself engages in the conventional usage of that [object] within a cognition that resembles an external object.

He states the establishment of the non-existence [of external objects] with the words "other than this" and so forth: if, while engaging in the practical usage of an object within the form of a conceptual construction that resembles the object, one were to claim that [the object] is useless for me, it should be refuted in exactly that same manner regarding the practical usage of the object.
He states the substance-deposit (*dravyanikṣepa*) by means of the words beginning with "in a substance" (*dravye*).

To the question "What [is it]?", he says: that which is intended (*vivakṣita*), and which is not present (*asāmpratika*)—that is, a future (*anāgata*) specific modification (*paryāyaviśeṣa*)—and wherein its persistence (*sthiti*) resides; such is what is so described.

Who among people is able to cast away the deposition of substance— the very cause of the validity of perception, which consists in the status of being a means of direct perception— while superimposing upon the visible object that which is to be attained?

He states its divisions with the words beginning "āgama" (scripture), and he states the "bhāva-nikṣepa" (the existential designation) with the words beginning "tathopayoga" (functioning in that manner).

That which has as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) its functioning (*upayoga*), its activity (*vyāpāra*), or its transformation (*pariṇāma*) in that very intended manner, is so described; [here] the phrase "the division of scripture and non-scripture" (*āgamanoāgamaprabheda*) is understood to follow, as is the term "existential designation" (*bhāvanikṣepa*).
Are there only four types of *nikṣepa*? No; this *nikṣepa* should be understood as having infinite varieties in detail.
Why? He says: "Because of its divisions," and so forth.
Why is that? He says: "Sentient and non-sentient," and so forth.
Furthermore, why is this so? He says: "The whole," and so forth.
Showing this very point immediately thereafter, he says: "The mode (bhāva)," and so forth.
The mode belongs to the *paryāyārthika* [standpoint], while the remaining three belong to the *dravyārthika*.
"Name, representation, and substance—this is the application of the substantial standpoint (dravyārthika);
while state (bhāva) is the exposition of the modal standpoint (paryāyārthika)—this is the ultimate truth.
This meaning of the exposition currently being presented is set forth by those who perceive reality.
3. It should be understood that for the *dravyārthika* [view], there is merely a synonym; [thus] name... is in every respect the apprehension of substance alone, whether pure or impure.

The mode (*bhāva*) is the "positional deposit" (*bhāvanikṣepa*) for one who holds the perspective of modal reality (*paryāyārthika*); how many remaining deposits are made by one who holds the perspective of substantial reality (*dravyārthika*)? He says: three.
Why are these accepted? He says: "In the present," and so forth.

Explaining the verse, he says: "It is merely a synonym," and so forth; this has been set forth as a royal road in many ways, and in that manner, it is to be understood as the method of categorization (*nikṣepa*) for one who maintains the substantialist standpoint (*dravyārthika*).
Why is this so? He says: "Name," and so forth.
For that [substance] cannot possibly exist as a mere synonym;

indeed, no substance exists, because it is not perceived, like the horn of a donkey. Therefore, how could there be a perspective (*naya*) possessing that [substance], such that there would be the application of categories (*nikṣepa*) like name and so on? To this, he replies: "In every respect," and so forth.
By every mode of perception and inference, and by every internal and external mode, there is the apprehension of substance alone as the cause of both erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions.
Of what kind [of substance]? He says: of the pure, which is without qualification, and of the impure, which is with qualification—the proponent of the substantial reality (*dravyārthika*).
Demonstrating the apprehension of that [Self], he says: "Non-conceptual," and so forth.

Having distinguished his own [nature] from others as pure existence (sattāmātra) apart from insentient matter, one perceives and knows [it]; then, by means of various distinctions of the intellect (mati), one conceptualizes [it] as substance and so on. 4.

For those who, even when there is a distortion of specific qualities in dreams and the like, do not perceive a distortion in pure existence (*sanmātra*), there is the apprehension of the pure substance. Even in a cognition possessing an object, there might once be an error regarding the manifestation of its own nature as the object; however, erroneous cognition is not like that, for one who conceptualizes through the stages of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth must necessarily distinguish between the natures of self and other.
That is not so...
in every respect, what is it that is non-conceptual and uninterrupted? To this he says: "one's own self."
Why? He says: "From what kind of other [cause]?
He says: "Inert," and so forth; and it should be understood that this refers to "in me" and "in non-conceptualization.
Perceiving mere existence—that is, making it an object through vision—the Self is shown to belong to the Pure One.

Likewise, regarding the second [reason]: the apprehension of any particular (*viśeṣa*) is preceded by the apprehension of its universal (*sāmānya*). For example, the apprehension of the two particulars—being a post (*sthāṇu*) and being a person (*puruṣa*)—is preceded by the apprehension of the universal of "uprightness" (*ūrdhvatā*). And the apprehension of a universal-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) is the cognition of *avagraha*; therefore, that too must be preceded by the apprehension of a universal.
Furthermore, there is no universal other than "existence" (*sattā*), from which an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result;
nor is the apprehension of that [existence] an apprehension of a particular, for which reason the [original] logical reason would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).
Seeing this, what does he do? To this he says: "He cognizes"—he knows a substance as qualified by [other] substances and so forth.
By what means? He says: "By the very distinctions of cognition," such as apprehension (*graha*) and the rest.
What is he doing? "Conceptualizing" (*vikalpayan*) and "determining" (*vyavasyan*).
By this, it is stated that [the cognition] of the impure [is not the apprehension of the object].
With the words "from itself" (*svasmāt*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse.

If it is objected: "But if there is no apprehension of the poison, how can there be an apprehension of the substance? For that would entail a difference between the two," he says here: "Even in the case of a distortion (*viplave’pi*)," and so forth.

In the phrase "in dreams and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes states such as that of one suffering from ophthalmia (taimirika). In that context, even regarding the "distortion" (viplava)—that is, the erroneous apprehension (anyathāgraha) of specific particulars (viśeṣa) such as the distinctions of one's own body being small and so on—not to mention when there is no distortion, what is established? He asks: "Of whom is the apprehension of the pure substance (śuddhadravya) established? He replies: "Of those who do not perceive distortion."
He says: "In pure existence" (*sanmātre*).

This is what is meant: just as when there is a distortion in the perception of grossness and so forth, one does not perceive one's own body and the like, yet there is still a perception of mere existence (*sanmātra*); in the same way, even when specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are not perceived, there is a perception of mere existence.
[This concerns] the distinction between the specific and the substance.

If it is argued: "But in dreams and the like, if there is a grasping of an object, how can there be the possibility of error, such that a definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is formulated for the purpose of excluding it? To this he says: "In what kind of cognition? In one that possesses an object (*arthavatī*), [grasping it] all at once, in a single moment."

The intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the two [objects] or of one's own object are emaciation (*kārśya*) and so forth; the manifestation of these would be an error (*bhrānti*), not merely a non-error.

For instance, one who perceives the thickness of an arm during an *ariṣṭa* (omen of death) sees the arm even though he does not see its emaciation. Or, in the absence of seeing that [emaciation], there is no perception of the *ariṣṭa*, because there is no perception of the opposite. Furthermore, [the thought] "this is my arm" would lack correspondence (*avisaṃvāda*).
The remainder has been considered here.
"If it be so, what follows from that? To this he says: "erroneous cognition," and so forth.
Furthermore, the "confused cognition" such as dreams and the like has been explained previously.
Summarizing, he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.

Thus, by that manner of erroneous cognition—whether conceptualizing through the stages of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so on, or ascertaining—it is not necessarily the case that one distinguishes between one's own nature and that of others.
This is the summary of the passage beginning with "therefore, not... and so forth.
Why? He says: "In every way," and so forth.
If it is argued that one who sees [an object] sees only its particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); to this he replies: "And by itself," and so forth.
It is understood that the cognition of objects occurs both by itself and through their effects.
Neither for those things that are impure nor for those that are pure, in their substantial nature, is it otherwise.
For [the self] is not to be perceived either externally or internally; how so?
The cognition or perception of objects is understood to be related to them in three ways: by their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), as an effect (*kāryataḥ*), and as a result (*phalarūpeṇa*).
Of what kind of objects? He says: "of those whose essence is substance" (*dravyātmanām*), that is, those whose intrinsic nature is substantiality.
Furthermore, of what kind? "Whether impure or pure. And it is certainly not the case that cognition is perceived otherwise than in these ways—that is, not through an essence other than these.
By this, he demonstrates the perception of the essential nature and the effect;
with the words beginning "not indeed" (*na hi*) and ending with "to be understood" (*pratyeyam*), he explains the phrase "not otherwise" (*na cānyathā*).
Explaining the remainder, he says: "Externally and internally," and so forth.
To the question "How?", the answer is "Without seeing," and so forth: "without seeing the circularity [of the atoms], because of the perception of gross forms."
Likewise, they would perceive objects as perishing moment by moment in terms of their substantial reality (dravyatattva).

Indeed, while seeing the various distinctions among persons—such as their spherical shape and so forth—they perceive a single, gross commonality as their nature at every moment, because it appears thus in perceptual cognition. If that [gross appearance] were transcended, they would likewise perceive the substantial reality in both cases without even seeing the specific qualities such as momentary destruction, because there is no difference [between the two].
What do they not perceive? They do not perceive sphericity as their form;

from where [does this arise]? He says: because of the perception of gross forms. Or, having not perceived momentary destruction, for that very reason, what would they perceive? He says: they would perceive the object.
By what means? He says: "by way of the reality of substance" (dravyatattvataḥ), that is, by means of the form of substance, simply through the observation of gross forms.
While explaining the verse, he says: "of the *pudgalas*, etc."
Seeing indeed the various distinctions such as sphericity and so forth among persons (pudgala) and atoms (paramāṇu), what do people do? Do they see anything? To this he says: "That," and so forth.
When is there a single, coarse, common nature for those individuals? He says: "at every moment.
Why? He says: "in perceptual cognition," and so forth.
Why is that? He says: "The transgression of that," and so forth;
the meaning is the transgression of that such-like appearance.
"In that manner" means in that way, even without perceiving the specific qualities of those [moments], such as momentary destruction, they perceive the reality of the substance itself.
Where? He says: both externally and internally.
