Why? Because there is no distinction, as they appear in that manner.

It might be thought: "Since a single, gross nature consisting of that generality is untenable—both internally and externally, as in the case of a dense forest and so forth—due to its being an error, therefore the reality of cognition (*jñānatattva*) is something else entirely, namely non-dual"; to this he says: "Cognition," and so forth.

Just as the notion of "a single forest" arises through error regarding distant, widely spaced trees, or just as there is the notion of "a single dense [mass]" or "thick," so too cognition, which is by nature devoid of the appearance of an object to be grasped, [is perceived as such] by itself.

If you somehow claim that consciousness itself is the substance that serves as the means of cognition, then— since it does not experience its own nature as being devoid of the form of the apprehended object, but rather experiences its own nature as having the form of existence and so forth— you must abandon the conceptualization of absolute modality (paryāyaikānta). For, due to the absence of any appearance of momentary destruction and the like,

one who thereby realizes the selflessness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-nairātmya) is merely mocking his own position with his own words, because he has discarded the authoritative scripture (āptāgama).

The claim that "if the non-existence of something can be apprehended without a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), why should its existence not likewise be apprehended? is trivial, as it speaks of something irrelevant to the subject at hand.
To the question, "What does consciousness do when it serves as the proof for a substance?", he says: "by cognizing" (saṃvidat).

What is it? He says: "having as its nature the absence of the manifestation of the object. The manifestation of the object (*grāhya-nirbhāsa*) is the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*); its absence is its non-existence; that itself is the nature (*ātmā*), the essence (*svabhāva*).
Of what? He says: "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*).
Furthermore, doing what? He says: "perceiving its own self in some way," by means of such modes as existence, consciousness, and so forth.

He thinks as follows: if that [external object], which has the nature of a single gross universal, does not exist even for cognition as if it were external, then cognition is in reality distinct from it. And if the self perceives that distinction; then that very [perception] is not an error—for a cognition of blue, when it apprehends itself as distinct from yellow, is not erroneous in that regard. Or, if it perceives its own nature and itself as distinct from that [object], then this is not a fault. [As it is said: "There is no formless perception, nor is there anything else to be experienced by the intellect" (Pramāṇavārttika 2).

327. Furthermore, there is no contradiction [in our position], because, just as in the case of the non-existent, the perception of the existent as distinct is possible, thereby establishing the existence of external objects; and in that regard, the distinction [between the object and its cognition] is established within the context of error.
Now, if it is argued that one does not perceive one's own distinction from that [object], and therefore its own nature is established as non-exclusive (anekānta);
He teaches the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "knowledge" (*jñāna*):

knowledge is the nature of the self; of what kind is it? It is devoid of the form of the apprehended object (*grāhya*), and while not experiencing that [form], it experiences the self’s own forms such as reality (*satyatā*) and so forth.
What should one do? He says: "In the case of absolute [succession] (paryāyaikānte)," and so forth.
Furthermore, he states "momentary destruction" (kṣaṇakṣaya), and so forth, to show that one should understand that such a conceptualization leads to this [consequence].

"In that case, the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādī*) [argues] that the self does not experience even the aspect of existence (*sattā*) and so forth, just as it does not experience an essence devoid of the form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*). To this, he replies with the words "for that very reason" (*tata eva*), and so on:

"For that very reason—namely, by the immediately preceding logic—the Buddhist, while establishing the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanairātmya*), which is the emptiness of all things, mocks and contradicts his own position and his own conduct, characterized as the acceptance of emptiness and so forth, by means of his own speech; for if one accepts the words that establish that [position], such [selflessness] is impossible because there would be no appearance [of those words]."
Because [the opponent] does not accept the emptiness of parts and accepts the existence of the statement, he asks another question in order to understand the underlying reasoning:
"How is this so? To him, the author provides the answer, beginning with "The authoritative scripture," and so forth.

If it is argued that "its destruction is accepted in reality (tattvataḥ), because it is admitted [only] conventionally (saṃvṛtyā)," to this he replies: If the cognition of their non-existence—that is, the awareness of the non-existence of those [authorities] such as the *āpta*s—is accepted without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then why would there not be the very same cognition of existence for things such as the self (*ātman*)? It would certainly be so; therefore, this [opponent's position] is trivial—it is nothing at all. Why is this the case? He says: "Therefore, of what is under discussion," and so forth, meaning the destruction of the *āpta* and the scripture (*āgama*).

Regarding the phrase "because of the statement," he says the following [extending this principle elsewhere]: "In the case of sound and the determination of sound, etc., there is a total reliance on the exclusion of others (anyāpoha)."
The follower of the Sugata has countered this by the following direction:

"For indeed... again... even this [word or determination] is exactly like that, because it does not convey the reality; what is it doing that it performs the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? Even when following the intention of the cognizer, just as the meaning is the exclusion of others, so too is the conveying of its own object, since there is no difference."
Otherwise— asking "What is the relationship between word and determination?"— he says: "It rests solely upon the exclusion of others (anyāpoha)."
Of what nature is he? He is one who has "accepted" (pratipanna), that is, been acknowledged by the Buddhist.
What is that [which was accepted]? To this he says: "refuted" (prativyūḍha), meaning cast out.
By whom? To this he says: "by this direction," namely by the path beginning with "one's own commentary through one's own words" (svāmeva vṛttiṃ svavācā).
On page 744,
he clarifies the meaning of the verse with the words "nahi" and so forth; this has already been explained.
If it is argued that conceptual thought (savikalpa) accomplishes that [objective], he says here: "In the city," and so forth. Even that is just like the previous case.

Now, if it is argued that although conceptual thought is without an object, it is nonetheless useful for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) because it performs the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); to this he says: "Doing what? and so forth.
Doing nothing at all—neither sound nor determination performs the exclusion of others; it is merely said to do so.

He thinks as follows: if that [word] makes the reality its object, then, by understanding that "this is such-and-such" as being excluded from others—such as the horse and so forth—it is said to perform *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others); otherwise, it would be a mere verbal expression.
Thus he says: "Because of the non-comprehension of the reality," whether it be the word or the determination (*nirṇaya*).

If it is argued that, in ultimate reality, this [word] does not even effect the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), but is merely said to do so by virtue of the intention of the cognizer, to this he replies: "The intention of the cognizer," and so forth.

Even when following the intention of cognizers—namely, that from a thing such as sound, only the exclusion of [the opposite], such as permanence, is effected through the determinations (*nirṇaya*) of words such as "impermanent," and the thing itself is not made an object by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*)—just as the exclusion of others is the referent (*artha*) of both the word and the determination, so too is the communication of its own meaning (*svārthapratyāyana*), because there is no difference in that regard in the intention of those [cognizers].

In both cases there is sublation by reasoning; thus, in the statement "sound is impermanent," [the author] has declared that words have the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) as their object and the universal (sāmānya) as their domain.
And because words and cognitions cannot possibly pertain to these [universals as real entities],
the Teacher has declared that they have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as their object,
stating that "exclusion is conveyed by means of words and logical marks."
— *Prajñāpradīpa*, *Manorathanandinī* 3.133.
He states the refutation of not accepting that [position] with the words "Otherwise," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: Is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) of the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), or is it of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajya*)? In the first case, those two would have real entities as their object, whereas [according to the opponent] they do not; otherwise, there would be the aforementioned refutation. Thus [it is argued] in the *Śabdanirṇaya*.

Regarding the position of the *prasajya* negation, he says: "From the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), how could there be establishment? If there were establishment, it would consist of a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*).

How can there be establishment [of reality] through conceptual construction? For if reality is not within its range, then the Buddhist, while attributing the nature of the modes (*paryāya-tattva*) to either the soul (*jīva*) or the non-soul (*ajīva*), ought not to attribute it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); because that [perception] is non-determinative in nature and lacks the capacity to exclude superimposition (*samāropa-vyavacchedaka*), otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor [can it be established] through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); because that has as its object the existence of that [reality], and because it is no different from the counter-position (*vipakṣa*).

Since even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the perception of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is in every respect false, how could there possibly be a "deposition" (*nikṣepa*) through meditative cultivation? For those who disregard the true nature of reality, if they were to effect a deposition according to the appearance of conceptual construction, why would even the "substantial deposition" (*dravya-nikṣepa*) not occur? Why is it that realization—the comprehension of reality—is not established from non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*)? If it is argued that realization is established [only] if it consists of a definitive determination (*niścaya*), then how could it be established from conceptual cognition? If reality were the object-domain of that conceptual cognition, it would follow as a consequence that there is no distinction between that state and deep sleep.
Explaining the verse, he says: "The reality of the modes (*paryāya-tattva*)," and so forth.

Whether regarding the soul (*jīva*) or the non-soul (*ajīva*), the Buddhist (*saugata*), while attempting to project or apply the reality of the modes, is not able to project or apply it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Why? He says: "That," and so forth.
By the word "that" (tat), he refers back to non-conceptual perception.
To the question "Why is that so? he says: "superimposition," and so forth.
He states the refutation should that [superimposition] not be admitted: "otherwise," and so forth.

If it is argued that [the universal] can be set aside by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the author replies: "Nor even... and so forth. Why? He says: "Because it does not have its existence as its object," meaning because conceptual construction does not have the existence of the particular (*paryāya*) as its domain.
He states another reason: "In the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)," and so forth.
The counter-position is that [conceptualization] is a real entity (*dravyatattva*), because there is no distinction therein.

Now, if it is argued that conceptual inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to its connection with the real object (*vastu*), and thus it ought not to be rejected, the author replies: "In the perception of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)," and so forth.

Regarding the view held that the reality is merely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇamātra-tattva*): if this vision of the particular characteristic is accepted, then since even the determination of cause and effect—and not only the determination of identity—is in every respect false, how could there possibly be the application of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanikṣepa*)? One considers that even the state of cause and effect is to be accomplished by conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and not by non-conceptualization, because it lacks the nature of a definitive determination and lacks the quality of exclusion (*vyavacchedaka*).
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument] through conceptualization by way of a succession.

It might be thought: "Let it be that the conceptual construction of origination is entirely false; nevertheless, out of fear of the collapse of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the Buddhists establish the relation of cause and effect and thereby engage in the transaction of inference and the object of inference (*anumāna-anumeya*). Thus, the application of that [cause] follows from that inferential construction. To this, he says: "That which is disregarded," and so forth.

For those Buddhists who disregard and despise the reality of the ultimate truth—which is momentary and partless—why would there not also be a "rejection of substance" (*dravyanikṣepa*) when they formulate [their views] according to the appearance of conceptual construction, without transcending that appearance? The sense is that even in the case of a rejection of substance, the relationship of cause and effect, which serves as the basis for conventional practices such as inference, exists through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Thus, even in the rejection of substance, [the same fault applies].

[Objection: "Is it not the case that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the non-dual reality of manifestation (*pratibhāsādvaitatattva*) is partless, while everything else is false, being merely a delusion of conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*); and by virtue of that [falsehood], there is the application of the categories of reality (*tattvanikṣepa*)? To this, he says: "False," and so forth.
Since one accepts the non-dual reality, when false conceptual constructions are set aside, the "Compendium" (*saṃgraha*) is better relied upon.

Setting aside other [theories of] mental continua, which are subject to momentary destruction and lack continuity, [it is held that] every reality is of a single nature; it is solely ignorance (*avidyā*) that, through the appearance of distinctions within the self, displays the birth of non-existent things. By this much, everything is well-established, for there is no characteristic of difference.

It cannot [arise] by itself, nor is it impossible for something else; for a cognition appearing as activity, speech, and so forth cannot arise from the nature of its own material cause—so what is the point of postulating another cause? When the application of synonyms and principles is undertaken through the deposition of false conceptualization, it is better to remain within the scope of the synthetic perspective (*saṃgraha*).
Having done what? He says: having abandoned—that is, having cast aside—momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Of what nature is it? It is "without continuity" (*ananvaya*), meaning devoid of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); or alternatively, having abandoned that which perishes as a substance (*dravya*) and other successions (*santānāntara*).
He explains the *kārikā* with the words "all," and so forth.

If it is asked: "How can all things—such as blue and so on, or pleasure and so on—which are of a single nature (*ekātmaka*), that is, a single essence (*ekasvabhāva*) as reality in its ultimate form (*paramārtharūpa*), appear as variegated? To this he says: "Only," and so forth.
What does ignorance show? He says: "birth," and so forth.
Of what kind [of beings]? Of those that are non-existent.
Where? He says: "In the Self.
Why? He says: "Because of the difference in manifestation; by relying on that difference. Thus, everything is well-established up to this point.

If it is argued: "Since there is a difference in appearance and a superimposition of contradictory properties, multiplicity alone is logical; how then can everything be of a single nature? To this he replies: "Not indeed," and so forth, up to the definition of difference, which is easy to understand.
Why? He says: "By itself," and so forth.
If it is argued that there is another characteristic of difference [from that]; to this he replies: "And not another," and so forth.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says: "That is impossible," and so forth.
Beginning with "Not so" (*na hi*), [the author] addresses the objection:

"Granted that there may be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*), nevertheless, existence and the like establish momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) through the principle of 'otherwise-unaccountability' (*anyathānupapatti*). To this, he says: "Not so," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
If it is asked, "How does the misfortune regarding another continuum contradict the speaker's status as a prudent investigator? To this he says: "Activity," and so forth.

Knowledge appearing as activity, speech, and the like must arise from its own material cause, which is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*). Why, then, postulate another cause characterized by another continuum? Why? He says: "Because of the absolute falsity [of such a thing]," and so forth; for that being established, another continuum is established.
The cause is as follows: for one who performs [the rites] consisting of the means of integration (*saṃgraha*), he states their deposition with the words beginning with "knowledge" (*vidyā*),
because of the manifestation of knowledge and ignorance, and because of the possibility of permanence and impermanence.
The Naigama [view] holds that the establishment of both one's own object and its essential nature consists of two forms.

(11) Therein, the determination regarding the absolute permanence or momentariness of all things, as well as the appearance of the grasped and the grasper, or of the outward-turned and inward-turned, is established;
for among these, self-awareness alone is permanent, since it is without distinction everywhere.
The remainder is occasional;
and this has been stated:
"The object, which is non-different from the nature of consciousness, nevertheless appears as if it were differentiated."

"In the differences of appearances and so forth, such as sleep and waking, [consciousness] does not differ. Thus, there is no distinction anywhere in terms of the form of consciousness (*bodhākāra*), because there is no disagreement [on this point]; for in its absence, states such as torpor (*middha*) would be impossible, and the non-existence of the four stages [of life] would remain exactly as it is.

Likewise, when the intellect (*vidyā*), which is knowledge of reality, experiences a function that appears as if divided by adventitious manifestations such as pleasure or the color blue—whereas ignorance (*avidyā*) is a cognition corrupted by delusion—the perception of these two distinct appearances gives rise to the possibility of both permanence and impermanence in a single locus. Consequently, the establishment, accomplishment, or determination of both its own nature and the nature of the object is twofold, consisting of the essential natures of permanence and impermanence; such is the view of the Naigama [Naya].

He explains the verse beginning with *sākalyena* as follows: "In its entirety" (*sākalyena*) means without parts (*anavayavena*). Regarding the two extremes of permanence and momentariness—that is, in the extreme of eternal permanence and the extreme of momentary flux—how is there an established order or stability (*vyavasthā*) such that "this is the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*), such as the blue or gross forms; this is the form of the subject (*grāhakākāra*"; "this is an outward-directed manifestation; this is an inward-directed manifestation"? To answer this, he says: "In that case," and so forth. "In that case" (*tatra*) means when that aforementioned principle holds; [there would be] "nothing but self-consciousness" (*svasaṃvinmātram*). By the word "self" (*sva*), he excludes the consciousness of another. It is "eternal," meaning it persists through time.
Why? Because here, first of all, one's own consciousness alone is without distinction everywhere, including within one's own continuum of pleasure and so forth;
what, then, is the remaining pleasure and so forth like? It is occasional and indeed impermanent.
Showing that this has been stated elsewhere as well, he says: "And this has been said," and so forth.

If one asks, "How was it said? it is replied: "What is the undivided, partless [reality]? He says: "The self of consciousness (saṃvidātman); that alone is the object; the meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) has the nature of consciousness."
Is it absolutely non-different? No; thus he says: "It appears as if divided," meaning it appears as having some slight differentiation.
Why? He says: "By means of the difference in manifestation and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the difference in purpose and other factors is included.
Why is it not non-different? He says: "That," and so on.

That object which is the nature of consciousness does not differ—meaning it does not become manifold as another continuum—in states such as sleep and waking; by the word "etcetera," birth, death, and so forth are included.

He explains this very point: why is there no distinction—that is, non-difference—of cognition everywhere, including in one's own pleasure and so forth? He says: "Because there is no disagreement," and so on.
Why is that so? He says: "In sleep," and so forth.

If it is argued that "in sleep there is no cognition at all," he replies here: "In its absence," and so forth; for if that [cognition] were absent, the occurrence of *middha* (torpor) and the like would be impossible.

If it is argued that there is no occurrence of the four states—because states such as fainting, which have sleep and so forth as their beginning, do not arise [in that state], and because death does occur; and that these very states [of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death] reappear in that very same place due to the arising of cognition, and thus this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) does not apply—[we reply: No, for an arising without a cause is impossible.

The dependence on the waking cognition as a cause has already been refuted, since that which has long since perished cannot be a cause; otherwise, the final moment of consciousness would again be the cause of consciousness in that very body, and thus there would be no such thing as death.

If it is argued that, by the power of the act of impregnation (*āvedha-karma*), that [karma] which initiates the next body is desired [to exist at the time of death]; we say no, because there is no karma apart from that [moment]. If it is argued that "it is that very same karma, but as something qualified"; we say no—what indeed is this so-called "qualification" of that which is like the horn of a donkey? If it is argued that "everything exists at its own time, and thus the vision of dreams and the like would not be without a causal basis, since such usage [of objects] would otherwise be absent"; [we reply] that this is the same in the other case as well.
Therefore, it does not negate the absence of cognition in dreams and the like;
rather, there exists a vacant space measuring four syllables within the *prati*.
In the manuscript, a space measuring eight syllables remains blank,
representing the four states of the self characterized by waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death.
The impetus (*āvedha*) of awakened knowledge—
that is, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of waking knowledge.
Now, what is this so-called *middha* (torpor) and so forth? If it is the absence of cognition, then there is an absence of sleep;
if it is the absence of that [sleep], then the reason is contradictory. To this, it has been established that it is the existence of cognition that is not perceived.
Its existence is easily stated by the subsequent arising of the conceptual construction: "I slept soundly," for one who is again conceptualizing [the experience] says, "I slept well" (*pra.vā. 2*).
125. Showing its impermanence in this manner, he says "tathā" and so forth;
that is, by way of the lack of any distinction in consciousness during states such as sleep and waking.
The reading "tad" and so forth occurs in some versions;
its meaning is "that consciousness.

Through adventitious, occasional manifestations of pleasure and so forth, and manifestations of blue and so forth—by means of these [manifestations] such as pleasure and the manifestations of blue—the cognition experiences a mode of being that appears, as it were, differentiated during the experience of those [objects].
"During sleep and so forth, there was some state of consciousness in me"—such is the conceptual construction [one has].
Just as a person, after the state of conceptualization, while conceptualizing again, knows: "Such was the conceptual construction that occurred in me."
"—'The desire of Prajñāpāramitā is accomplished.
To the question 'What is accomplished by that?', he says: 'Just as,' and so forth."
Just as this diversity of consciousness would be adventitious, so too would the diversity of genus; therefore, reality would be distinct and eternal in nature.
For if a manifold cognition—which is presumed to have an impartite essence—is not perceived in any way, it would result in its being indefinable, due to the consequence of infinite regress.

Nor is there any realization of that [connection], because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By this, the examination of connection (*sambandhaparīkṣā*) has been refuted. For how could a restriction regarding the manifestation of internal and external aspects and so forth be perceived anywhere in the absence of a connection? Indeed, [there is no such thing], for why would there be a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) of the forms of the apprehended object and so on? Because that would entail the loss of their unity. Thus, the method of classification (*nikṣepa*) therein is based on the distinctions of name, representation, substance, and so forth.

He asks: "By what means would this diversity, this manifoldness of consciousness, come to be? He replies: "By the adventitious [factors] just mentioned. Likewise, there is the distinction of genus and the multiplicity of the continuum; from that, if it is argued that the reality would be of a permanent nature and thus there would be a confusion [of categories], he says here: "[It is] separate and mutually distinct. By this, everything possesses both forms (*pramāṇavārttika* 3).
Such [objections] as these are refuted,
because that specific [quality] has been rejected; for when one is commanded, "Eat curd," why would one run toward a camel?
Thus, completing the sense, he says while explaining the verse: "Manifold," and so forth.
Now, is it not the case that even for a single consciousness, manifoldness is not admitted? What would that manifoldness be in a single [consciousness]? (Pravā. 2)

If it is argued that, according to such statements, although consciousness is partless (*niraṃśa*), it appears as if it were possessed of parts (*sāṃśa*); to this he replies with the words beginning "saṃbhāvya" (conceivable).

Since that partless intrinsic nature of consciousness cannot be apprehended in any way—neither through direct perception nor through inference—and since there is no possibility of conceiving a differentiated nature whose essence is unapprehended by means of contradiction, it would follow that it is merely a non-entity (*nirupākhyatā*), that is, a state of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Why? He says: because it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅgāt*).

If it is argued that this [non-existence] is indeed accepted—because there is no consequence of its non-abiding in any reality, and because, like illusions, mirages, and so forth, there is no fault even if it is non-existent, according to the statement in the *Prakaraṇavārtikālaṃkāra* (3.211)—to this he replies: "And not," and so forth;
for there is simply no apprehension of that indefinable [non-existence].
Why? He says: "Because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Some maintain that self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) is the direct perception (adhyakṣa) that serves as the means of valid cognition there;
others maintain that it is one [of the two].
And what follows from this? He says: "By this," and so forth.
By this demonstration of the manifoldness (*citrata*) of a single consciousness, the examination of relations—that is, the refutation of relations pertaining to Dharmakīrti—is countered.

Why? He says: For how (*katham hi*), in the absence of a relation, could there be observed a restriction of the appearances of the external and internal aspects, a restriction of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender, or their dependence on a specific cognition? If it is argued that the restriction arises from identity (*tādātmya*); to this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
How could there be a difference in intrinsic nature among the forms of the apprehended object and so forth?
Nevertheless, he states the refutation regarding the extreme of identity: "In that case, due to oneness," and so forth; the construction is: "for that reason, because of the loss of oneness."

Why? He says: "In that very context, even within the doctrine of the fourfold nikṣepas—namely name, representation, substance, and mode—it would not exist [as a distinct entity] if this [doctrine] itself were pleasing to people regarding its objects; in that case, what can we do?"
The remainder [of the text] is as follows:
this section bearing that name was composed by Dharmakīrti;
it is quoted in its entirety on page 509 of the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*.
Showing the application of the method of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-naya*), he says: "Worldly transaction proceeds"—this is the connection.
For if there were no worldly transactions, the world would cease to exist even with the application of [categories] such as consciousness (*cetanā*).
In every respect, causal efficiency is impossible both in the case of permanence and in the case of momentary destruction.
Conventional discourse proceeds through the mutual dependence of the momentary and the non-momentary;
without such conventional discourse, the world would not exist.
In what [context]? He says: "when the attribution of consciousness and so forth is being made to both permanence and momentary destruction.

Why? He says: "in every way"—meaning by way of succession or simultaneity—there is an impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in both permanence and momentary destruction; this is the connection.
Demonstrating the meaning of the verse, he says: "momentary," and so forth.
In what [context]? He says: "mutually," and so forth.
When there is mutual dependence between the momentary and the non-momentary, how then does the application of conventional discourse proceed? He says: "living beings," and so forth.

For it is well known that the falsity of conventional discourse (vyavahāra) is based upon the distinction [of categories] such as the living being (jīva) and so forth, as one projects their various modes (paryāya).
Even while relying on the absolute difference between substance (dravya) and mode, the fact that substance possesses the nature of its modes must be admitted.

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction between non-existence, what would be the point of separately postulating synonyms? Since the establishment of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is achieved by that much alone, the conventional standpoint (*vyavahāranaya*) would dispose [of things] in exactly that way. That which belongs to a soul (*jīva*) and so forth, such as matter (*pudgala*), is described as "that [belonging to] a soul and so forth. Relying upon its differentiation—that is, its manifoldness—and relying upon its synonyms—that is, the synonyms of the soul and so forth—the conventional standpoint proceeds by applying the synonyms of the soul and so forth to the soul and so forth within their respective contexts; this is the supplementary explanation (*upaskāra*).
Why is this so? He says: "For it is well known that the falsity of conventional discourse (vyavahāra) rests upon duality—that is, it relies on the manifoldness of substance and modification.

He explains the meaning of the verse: even by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, who rely on the absolute difference between substance and modification, it must be admitted that the self and other substances possess the nature of modification, which consists in the transformation of their internal capacity to produce successive effects.
Why? He says: "Otherwise," and so forth.

Otherwise—that is, by way of not accepting that [substance]—since there would be no distinction from non-existence, and since it would be indistinguishable from a rabbit's horn and the like, that [substance] must be accepted as existing.

If it is argued, "Let that acceptance stand"; to this he replies: "And thus, by that mode of acceptance, what is the use of a separate postulation of modes (paryāya)? Why? He says: "Because the establishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) occurs through that alone, namely, through the mere transformation of its capacity. Such is the *vyavahāra-naya*.
In that very same manner, with the ellipsis "the substances and their modes" (*dravyaparyāyān*) to be supplied,
he says "time," etc., while demonstrating the *nikṣepa* (categorical placement) of the *śabda* and other *nayās*;
the meaning of this has already been explained.

Comparison—due to differences in tense, grammatical case, and gender, a word effects a difference in meaning; however, that which is established by synonyms is "thus-qualified" (itthambhūta) and serves as the basis for the action.

First, due to the difference in time [there are distinctions such as] "it was," "it is," and "it will be"; due to the difference in the agent [there are distinctions such as] "he does" and "it is done," and so forth; due to the difference in gender [there are distinctions such as] "Devadatta" and "Devadattā"; likewise, due to the difference in synonyms [there are distinctions such as] "Indra," "Śakra," and "Purandara. Similarly, these two—*śabdasamabhirūḍha* and *evambhūta*—are based on action (*kriyā*). For the *evambhūta*, agency belongs only to that which is currently acting—*Laghīyastraya-svavṛtti*, verse 44.
"Time...
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "not only," and so forth.
He provides an example regarding the difference in the nature of things due to a difference in gender, beginning with the words "dhiṣaṇā" and so forth;
he demonstrates the *samabhirūḍha* [naya] with the words "not only gender," and so forth.
Just as in the example beginning with "Indra," he concludes the meaning of the treatise on this very point with the words "of such a nature" and so forth, saying: "Thus, therefore," and so on.
As an illustration, he states the auspicious benediction at the end of the treatise: "May [he] be victorious," and so forth.
May [he] be victorious... [etc.]
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the *Nikṣepasiddhi*, in the *Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā* composed by Anantavīrya. May there be peace. This work is completed.
